units.la: DISPVTATIONVM De argumentis, quibus efficitur Dominum nostrum esse Deum essentia diuina praeditum. PRIMA
units.tr: DISPUTATIONS On the arguments by which it is shown that our Lord is God, possessed of the divine essence. FIRST

units.la: De Arg. I. Ex visione Esaiae cap. VI. In anno quo mortuus est Rex Ozias vidi Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum, &c. collata cum Ioh. XII. 41. Haec dixit Esaias cùm vidit gloriam eius, &c.
units.tr: Argument I, from the vision of Isaiah, ch. VI: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne, etc. Compared with John 12:41: These things said Isaiah, when he saw his glory, etc.

units.la: IN nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spiritus Sancti probare institutimus hoc secundo libro, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum esse Deum diuina essentia praeditum. Ita enim potius concipimus statum controuersiae quàm vt solent Aduersarij, quibus placuit vt quæreretur, sitne Christus Deus summus necne?
units.tr: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, we have undertaken to prove in this second book that our Lord Jesus Christ is God, possessed of the divine essence. For we frame the state of the controversy in this way, rather than as our opponents, who have chosen to ask, Is Christ the supreme God or not? usually do.

units.la: II. Haec enim locutio, Deus summus, primùm à forma sermonum, quam nobis imitandam Apostoli proposuerunt, discedit. Nomen enim עליון ὕψιστος summus, altissimus, etsi nominibus Dei אל, אלהים, יהוה additur nonnunquam in Veteri Testamento, tamen in Novo perpetuò vsurpatur tanquam nomen Dei, neque nomini Dei subjungitur vt epitheton, nisi quater tantùm: Semel ab Apostolo Heb. 7.1. ἱερεὺς τῷ Θεῷ τῷ ὑψίστῳ[?], sed vt reddat verba Gen. 14.18. כהן לאל עליון : ter à Diabolo Marc. 5.7. Luc 8.28. Act. 16.17. etiam cùm veritatem confitetur maligno. cuius discriminis haec ratio esse videtur, quod in Veteri Testamento Dei nomen tribuitur aliquoties Angelis, immò Iudicibus, atque ita erant quodammodo dij inferiores Deo summo [illegible, ~10 letters]. In
units.tr: II. For this expression, supreme God, departs first from the form of speech which the Apostles have set before us to imitate. For the name עליון [elyon], ὕψιστος [hypsistos], supreme, most high, although it is sometimes added to the names of God, אל, אלהים, יהוה, in the Old Testament, is nevertheless used constantly in the New Testament as a name of God, and is not joined to the name of God as an epithet, except only four times: once by the Apostle at Heb. 7.1, ἱερεὺς τῷ Θεῷ τῷ ὑψίστῳ [priest of God Most High], but to render the words of Gen. 14.18, כהן לאל עליון; three times by the Devil at Marc. 5.7, Luc. 8.28, Act. 16.17, even when he confesses the truth while being evil. The reason for this distinction seems to be that in the Old Testament the name of God is sometimes given to angels, indeed to judges, and so they were in a way lesser gods beneath the supreme God, [illegible]. In

units.la: Nouo vero Dei nomen ei soli vendicatur, qui coelorum & terrae dominus est, ab ipsis etiam Angelis adorandus, iuxta vaticinium Esaiae 2.27. Exaltabitur Dominus solus in die illa. Exorto enim & revelato sole iustitiae tantum discrimē inter Deum & Angelos apparuit, vt dij appellari desierint in ordinem seruorum redacti.
units.tr: In the New Testament, however, the name of God is claimed for him alone who is Lord of heaven and earth, to be adored even by the angels themselves, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, Esai. 2.27: The Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. For when the sun of righteousness had risen and been revealed, so great a distinction between God and the angels appeared that they ceased to be called gods, being reduced to the order of servants.

units.la: III. Deinde periculosa est: innuit enim plures Deos, vnum summum, reliquos inferiores, qui Gentium error erat praedicatione Euangelij abolendus in aeternum. Denique laborat ambiguitate disputantibus incommoda. Dicitur enim Deus ὕψιστος summus ratione, vel loci, quia sedet ἐν ὑψίστοις in locis altissimis: vel naturae, quia praeditus est natura altissima: vel personae, quia personam sustinet in Scriptura omnium summam: vel denique exaltationis, quia super omnes, qui putantur aut dicuntur dij, exaltatus est, כי אתה יהוה עליון על כל הארץ מאד נעלית על כל אלהים quoniam tu Domine altissimus es super omnem terram: valde exaltatus es super omnes Deos.
units.tr: III. Next, the expression is dangerous, for it hints at several gods, one supreme and the others inferior, which was the error of the Gentiles, to be abolished for ever by the preaching of the gospel. Finally, it labours under an ambiguity that troubles the disputants. For God is called ὕψιστος, supreme, either by reason of place, because he sits ἐν ὑψίστοις, in the highest places; or of nature, because he is endowed with the highest nature; or of person, because in Scripture he bears the highest of all persons; or finally of exaltation, because he is exalted above all who are thought or called gods: כי אתה יהוה עליון על כל הארץ מאד נעלית על כל אלהים [for you, O Lord, are Most High over all the earth; you are greatly exalted above all gods].

units.la: IV. Certum est autem Dominum nostrum, seu locum spectes, seu exaltationem dici posse Altissimum. Nam, & sedet ad dextram Majestatis in excelsis, supra omnes coelos, excelsior coelis factus, & habet nomen quod est supra omne nomen, jubenturque cum כל אלהים omnes Angeli adorare. Certum etiam est eundem Dominum nostrum, si personā eius cum persona Patris conferas, ita altissimum esse respectu angelorum & hominum, vt in comparatione cum Patre non tam ipse quam Pater sit altissimus. Est enim à Patre, cum Pater à nullo sit; & partes suscepit mediatoris inter Patrem & homines, cum Pater nullas partes sustineat nisi Dei & Patris: quam praerogatiuam Patris personalem nos vltrò conficemur.
units.tr: IV. It is certain, however, that our Lord may be called Most High, whether you look at place or at exaltation. For he sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, above all the heavens, made higher than the heavens, and has a name which is above every name, and all angels are commanded to adore him [כל אלהים]. It is also certain that the same Lord, if you compare his person with the person of the Father, is so Most High with respect to angels and men that, in comparison with the Father, it is not so much he himself as the Father who is Most High. For he is from the Father, since the Father is from no one; and he has taken up the part of mediator between the Father and men, whereas the Father sustains no part except that of God and Father. This personal prerogative of the Father we ourselves freely confess.

units.la: V. De Natura igitur seu essentia omnis inter nos est quaestio, Situne Christus praeditus natura altissima, hoc est, divina, necne? Nos affirmamus, Negant Aduersarij, Conuenit de Iudice Scriptura sacra. Cum enim in genere omnis de veritate controuersiae iudex seu norma sit veritas ab utraque parte contendente agnita & confessa, partibus quaestionis ita applicabilis, vt quae cum illa congruat, quae non congruat liquidò constare possit, vt patet inductione, manifestum est talem veritatem esse, non traditionem non scriptam, nec ingentia Patrum volumina, nec ecclesiae iudicium vel testimonium, sed Scripturam vtriusque Testamenti diuinitus inspiratam, quam omnes Christiani, ut ut in partes diuisi, pro canonica habent unanimi consensu. Eam igitur, ut libro praecedente fecimus, scrutemur diligenter, non viribus nostris, sed Dei Patris & Domini nostri Iesu Christi promissionibus, & misericordia quam implo-ramus, freti.
units.tr: V. Concerning nature or essence, then, the question between us is this: Is Christ endowed with the highest nature, that is, the divine nature, or not? We affirm; our opponents deny. We agree on the judge: holy Scripture. For since in general the judge or rule of every controversy about truth is a truth acknowledged and confessed by both contending parties, and so applicable to the parts of the question that what agrees with it and what does not can be clearly ascertained, as is plain from induction, it is evident that such a truth is not unwritten tradition, nor the vast volumes of the Fathers, nor the judgment or testimony of the Church, but the Scripture of both Testaments, divinely inspired, which all Christians, however divided into parties, hold as canonical with unanimous consent. Let us therefore examine it diligently, as we did in the preceding book, relying not on our own strength but on the promises of God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, and on the mercy which we implore.

units.la: VI. Testimonia Scripturæ quibus divina Filij Dei essentia probari potest, quoniam multa sunt, distribuemus in tres classes seu sectiones. Quædam enim ex utroque Testamento promemus, Quædam ex solo Vetere, Quædam ex solo Novo.
units.tr: VI. The testimonies of Scripture by which the divine essence of the Son of God can be proved are many, so we shall distribute them into three classes or sections. For some we shall draw from both Testaments, some from the Old alone, and some from the New alone.

units.la: VII. Primi generis sunt testimonia Veteris Testamenti laudata in Novo, quorum agmen ducet illustris illa visio gloriæ Domini, quæ describitur Esaiæ cap. vi. 1. Anno quo mortuus esse rex Oziæ[?], vidi Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum & devatum[?], &c. cuius is fuit exitus, ut mitteretur propheta, qui diceret populo Iudaico, Excæca cor populi huius, & aures eius aggrava, & oculos eius claude: ne forte videat oculis, & auribus suis audiat, & corde suo intelligat, & convertatur, & sanem eum.. Quæ verba citantur ab Apostolo Ioh. xii. 39. ut probet, Iudæos non potuisse credere in Iesum, addito hoc breve commentario, Hæc dixit Esaias cum vidit gloriam eius, & locutus est de eo, quo docet verba illa Esaiæ de Iudæis illis esse intelligenda, qui positam ob oculos Christi gloriam neque oculis viderunt, neque corde intellexerunt, neque ut sanarentur ad eum conversi sunt. Hinc ducitur.
units.tr: VII. Of the first kind are the testimonies of the Old Testament cited in the New, of which the leader will be that famous vision of the glory of the Lord described in Isaiah, ch. 6.1: In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lifted-up throne, &c. The outcome of this was that a prophet was sent to say to the Jewish people: Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them. These words are cited by the Apostle, John 12.39, to prove that the Jews could not believe in Jesus, with this brief comment added: These things said Isaiah, when he saw his glory, and spoke of him, by which he teaches that those words of Isaiah are to be understood of those Jews who, though Christ's glory was set before their eyes, neither saw it with their eyes, nor understood it with their heart, nor turned to him so as to be healed. From this the following argument is drawn.

units.la: VIII. Arg. 1. Ille cuius gloriam Esaias vidisse dicitur cap. vi. libri sui est Deus Israelis essentia divina præditus. Dominus Iesus est ille cuius gloriam Esaias vidisse dicitur illo[?] capite. Ergo Dominus Iesus est Deus Israelis divina essentia præditus. Major legenti illud caput ita manifesta est, ut probatione non egeat, unica enim toto illo capite visio continetur magnificæ gloriæ Dei Israelis, qui nomine maximè proprio יהוה צבאות Dominus exercituum bis appellatur. Minor duplici genere argumentorum nititur, quorum alterum à testimonio Apostoli & Euangelistæ Iohannis petitur, alterum ab ipso textu Esaiæ. Testimonium Apostoli disertum est, Hæc, inquit, dixit Esaias cum vidit gloriam eius: & locutus est de eo, eum sine dubio pronominibus eius & eo significans, de quo uno loquebatur, nempe, Dominum Ie-sum.
units.tr: VIII. Argument 1. He whose glory Isaiah is said to have seen in chapter 6 of his book is the God of Israel, possessed of the divine essence. The Lord Jesus is he whose glory Isaiah is said to have seen in that chapter. Therefore the Lord Jesus is the God of Israel, possessed of the divine essence. The major premise is so manifest to anyone who reads that chapter that it needs no proof, for the whole chapter contains a single vision of the magnificent glory of the God of Israel, who is twice called by his most proper name, יהוה צבאות [Lord of hosts]. The minor premise rests on a twofold kind of argument, of which one is taken from the testimony of the Apostle and Evangelist John, the other from the text of Isaiah itself. The testimony of the Apostle is explicit: These things, he says, Isaiah said when he saw his glory, and spoke of him, clearly signifying by the pronouns his and him the one of whom he was speaking, namely the Lord Jesus.

units.la: IX. Ad hoc testimonium nihil potest responderi, nisi, aut pronomina illa eius, eo, non referri ad Iesum, aut si referantur; gloriam illam Iesu non eam esse cuius visio descripta est Esai. v 1[?] 1. 2. 3. &c, aut, si sit illa gloria quae ibi descripta est, tamen Iesum non esse illum Dominum quem Esaias eo loco describit & vidisse se profitetur. Quae tria, quoniam ab Aduersarijs reponuntur, ordine refellenda sunt.
units.tr: IX. To this testimony nothing can be replied, unless either those pronouns his, him are not referred to Jesus, or, if they are, that glory of Jesus is not the one whose vision is described in Isaiah ch. 6, vv. 1, 2, 3, etc., or, if it is the glory described there, still Jesus is not the Lord whom Isaiah describes in that place and professes to have seen. Since our opponents put forward these three points, they must be refuted in order.

units.la: X. Primum igitur negant pronomina illa eius, eo, referri debere ad Iesum: posse enim ad Deum commode referri: cui rei ut colorem aliquem conciliet Socinus ait à v. 37. quatuor consequentes versiculos per parenthesim legi aut debere, aut saltem posse. Apertissimum enim est, inquit, versiculum demum 42. cum isto v. 37. & sensu & verbis coniungi, cum alij quatuor intermedij videri possint aliquantum à proposito digredi. Idem ijsdem fere verbis dicit Vvolkelius. Sed notam parenthesis neque fontes graeci, neque versiones ullae habent, neque verba Euangelistae innuunt aut poscunt (cohaeret enim sensu & verbis vers. 42. non modo cum v. 37. sed etiam cum v. 39. & 40.) imo respuunt. Quid enim est parenthesis nisi ut loquitur Quintilianus, medio sermone aliquis infertus sensus, vel, ut plenius Valla, interiectio orationis in sermone, quae remota sermo manet integer? Itaque pars sermonis non est, sed aliquid interiectum inter partes sermonis. Quis autem non videt initium v. 38. ut sermo Esaiae prophetae impleretur, non esse aliquid interpositum, sed cohaerere cum fine v. 37. non credebant in eum, tanquam cum altera parte sermonis? Est enim sermo integer, non credebant in eum, ut sermo Esaiae propheta impleretur, &c. à quo, quin mutiletur, rescindi non potest membrum, ut sermo Esaiae impleretur. Hoc vel caeco visibile est.
units.tr: X. First, then, they deny that the pronouns his, him must be referred to Jesus, for they can fitly be referred to God. To lend some colour to this, Socinus says that from v. 37 the four following verses may, or at least ought, to be read in parentheses: For it is most evident, he says, that verse 42 is joined both in sense and in words with this v. 37, whereas the other four intervening verses may seem somewhat to digress from the purpose. Volkelius says the same thing in nearly the same words. But neither the Greek sources nor any versions have a mark of parenthesis, nor do the words of the Evangelist imply or require one (for verse 42 coheres in sense and in words not only with v. 37 but also with vv. 39 and 40); indeed they reject it. For what is a parenthesis, if not, as Quintilian says, a sense inserted into the middle of a discourse, or, as Valla puts it more fully, an interjection in the speech which, when removed, leaves the discourse intact? Thus it is not part of the discourse, but something interposed between its parts. Who, however, does not see that the beginning of v. 38, that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, is not something interposed, but coheres with the end of v. 37, they did not believe in him, as with the other part of the discourse? For the sentence is whole: they did not believe in him, that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, etc. The clause that the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled cannot be cut off from it without mutilating the sentence. This is visible even to a blind man.

units.la: XI. Si quis tamen aliquam confirmationem desiderat, Id primum firmat Euangelistae mens, qui verba, non credebant in eum, non tam propter ipsa quam propter sequentia posuit. Non enim incredulitatis Iudaeorum meminit, nisi ut scandalum, quod ex ea nasci videbatur, remoueret prolatis oraculis ex quibus liquet, eam à Deo non solum praevisam & praedictam, sed etiam aliquomodo praeordinatam fuisse. Deinde id confirmat similis sermo frequens in Novo Testamento. Ut Math. 1. 22. Hoc autem totum factum est, ut impleretur quod dictum est à Domino per prophetam: Et Math. 2. 15. Et erat ibi usque ad obitum Herodis vt adimpleretur quod dictum est à Domino: & ψ[?] f. 23. & veniens habitauit in ciuitate quæ vocatur Nazareth. vt adimpleretur quod dictum est, &c. Et Math. 4. 13. habitauit in Capernaum maritima in finibus Zabulon & Nephtalim, vt adimpleretur quod dictum est per Esaiam prophetam. Insaniret qui in his locis & similibus verba, vt adimpleretur, ab antecedentibus inserta parenthesis nota diuideret: sunt tamen isti nostro tam similia quàm ouum ouo.
units.tr: XI. If anyone still wants some confirmation of this, first the mind of the Evangelist confirms it. He placed the words they did not believe in him not so much for their own sake as for what follows. He mentions the unbelief of the Jews only to remove the scandal that seemed to arise from it, by bringing forward prophecies from which it is clear that this unbelief was not only foreseen and foretold by God but also in some sense foreordained. Second, a similar expression, found frequently in the New Testament, confirms this. Matt. 1:22: Now all this took place that what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled. Matt. 2:15: And he was there until the death of Herod, that what was spoken by the Lord might be fulfilled, and Matt. 2:23: and coming he dwelt in a city called Nazareth, that what was spoken might be fulfilled, etc. Matt. 4:13: he dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled. Anyone who in these and similar places cut the words that it might be fulfilled off from what precedes by marking them as an inserted parenthesis would be mad; yet those passages are as like our case as one egg is like another.

units.la: XII. Adde quod Euangelista non contentus dixisse Iudæos non credidisse ψ[?] f. 37. vlterius progreditur v. 39. affirmatque eos non potuisse credere, quæ sermonis progressio & quasi gradatio, si quid video, parenthesis esse non potest. Denique versus 42. iungi gestit non tantùm cum 37. sed etiam, & quidem maximè, cum 39. & 40. vt sit sensus, quamuis dixerim Iudæos non credidisse in eum, quamuis addiderim eos non potuisse credere, quamuis vtrumque distinctis verbis Esaias prædixerit, tamen id non est ita accipiendum, quasi nulli prorsus crediderint: nam præter plebeios non paucos, quales nos sumus, etiam ex primoribus multi crediderunt in eum, &c. Esto igitur conclusum non esse parenthesim: vnde sic possum argumentari. Si pronomina eius & eo non essent referenda ad Iesum, versus quatuor inter 37. & 42. interpositi parenthesi includi deberent, vel saltem possent. Hoc autem falsum est, vt iam probaui. Ergo & illud.
units.tr: XII. Add that the Evangelist, not content to have said that the Jews did not believe (v. 37), goes further (v. 39) and asserts that they could not believe. That progression of thought, and this kind of gradation, if I see anything, cannot be a parenthesis. Finally, verse 42 is eager to be joined not only with verse 37 but also, and most of all, with verses 39 and 40, so that the sense is this: although I have said that the Jews did not believe in him, and although I have added that they could not believe, and although Isaiah foretold both in distinct words, yet this must not be taken as if absolutely no one believed. For besides the not few common people, such as we are, many even of the leading men believed in him, etc. Let it then be granted that there is no parenthesis. From this I can argue as follows. If the pronouns him and to him were not to be referred to Jesus, the four verses interposed between verses 37 and 42 ought to be enclosed in a parenthesis, or at least could be. But this is false, as I have already shown. Therefore that too is false.

units.la: XIII.[?] Deinde negari non potest, quin illa pronomina, nisi quid impediat, ad Iesum referenda sint. Id enim series narrationis flagitare videtur. Quod autem impediat in verbis Euangelistæ nihil prorsus occurrit. Id quod argumento est, non cauisse Spiritum Sanctum, ne referrentur ad Christum. Cur autem non cauerit causa dici non potest, nisi quia in ea relatione nihil erat periculi. Si quod enim fuisset, id, & qua erat perspicientia sine dubio vidisset, & qua pro Ecclesia vigilabat charitate, suffulisset[?], vel mutato pronomine in nomen Dei, vel aliqua alia ratione prospiciendo veritati. Tanta enim tamque admirabili sapientia diuinus liber corusçat, nulla vt possit eius verbis falsa interpretatio affingi, quam, si est alicuius momenti, ipse textus non redarguat: cuius rei specimen vel hæ nostræ disputationes non dubium exhibent. Si quis impedimentum arcessat à præiudicata opinione Aduersariorum essentiam Christo diuinam detrahentium, is cogitet hoc quicquid est impedimenti non esse in textu, sed extra textum in corde ipsorum, instar velaminis illius, quod ad hunc usque diem, cum legitur Moses cordi Iudæorum impositum esse Paulus testatur. Quando autem de persona agitur, quam ipso Christo teste Math. 11. 27. nemo novit nisi Pater, non est præiudicium ullum ad lectionem Scripturæ qua revelatur afferen-dum.
units.tr: XIII. Next, it cannot be denied that those pronouns, unless something prevents it, are to be referred to Jesus. For the sequence of the narrative seems to demand this. But nothing at all presents itself in the Evangelist's words that prevents it. This is an argument that the Holy Spirit did not take care to prevent them from being referred to Christ. And the reason why he did not take care can only be that in that reference there was no danger. For if there had been any, he would undoubtedly have seen it with his foresight, and with the love by which he watches over the Church he would have provided for the truth, either by changing the pronoun into the name of God or by some other means. For the divine book shines with such great and admirable wisdom that no false interpretation can be fastened upon its words, which the text itself does not refute if it has any importance; and these very disputations of ours furnish no doubtful example of this. If anyone seeks an obstacle in the prejudged opinion of the opponents who deprive Christ of the divine essence, let him consider that whatever obstacle there is lies not in the text but outside the text, in their own heart, like that veil which, as Paul testifies, was placed upon the heart of the Jews when Moses is read, even to this day. But when it is a question of the person whom, by the testimony of Christ himself (Matt. 11:27), no one knows except the Father, there is no prejudice to be brought to the reading of Scripture by which he is revealed.

units.la: XIV. Tertiò, cum pronomina illa Eius, eo, sint in verbis non Prophetæ Esaiæ, sed Euangelistæ, ad eum referri debent de quo loquebatur Euangelista. Loquebatur autem de uno Christo. Ad eum igitur unum referri debent. Quis enim credat sacrum historicum eum illis pronominibus designasse de quo non agebat, cum verò de quo agebat, de quo narrationem institutam continnuabat non designasse? Potestne exemplum afferri pronominis eiusmodi, quod sacer autor ad eum referendum voluerit, quem ipse non nominauit? Huc accedit quod Apostolus septem istis versibus inter 36. & 44. in quibus Iesum nominat, insertis, Iesum non aliter quàm istiusmodi pronominibus significauit: bis enim cum sic designauit vers. 37. semel v. 41. illo lectorem ad Christum eo pronomine intelligendum veluti præparans & assuefaciens, hoc, si aberraret, revocans.
units.tr: XIV. Third, since those pronouns him, to him stand in the words not of the prophet Isaiah but of the Evangelist, they ought to be referred to the one of whom the Evangelist was speaking. But he was speaking of Christ alone. They ought therefore to be referred to him alone. For who would believe that the sacred historian designated by those pronouns one of whom he was not speaking, but of whom he was speaking, and whom he was continuing the narrative he had begun, he did not designate? Can an example be cited of a pronoun of this kind which the sacred author wished to be referred to someone whom he did not name? Add to this that the Apostle, in the seven verses inserted between verses 36 and 44 in which he names Jesus, designated Jesus in no other way than by pronouns of this kind: for he did so twice in verse 37 and once in verse 41, thereby preparing and accustoming the reader to understand Christ by that pronoun, and recalling him if he should go astray.

units.la: XV. Quartò, pronomina illa, aut ad Iesum, aut ad alium referenda sunt. Non ad alium. Ad quem enim? Ad Deum, inquit Socinus, Atqui Deus non est ab Euangelista nominatus. Imò, inquit, Proximè ante in verbo Sanem, licet tacitè, nominatus est: Et prius eodem modo in verbis excæcauit, & induravit (quamvis hac tertiæ personæ sint, illud vero primæ) nominatus fuit. Demus nominari eum cuius nomen tacetur, hoc est, qui non nominatur, illud urgeamus; nequidem sic tacitè nominatum esse Deum ab Euangelista: non enim verba illa recitat ut sua, sed ut verba Esaiæ: nec ut aliquid doceat de Deo, sed ut probet duntaxat non potuisse Iudæos credere in Iesum.
units.tr: XV. Fourth, those pronouns must be referred either to Jesus or to someone else. Not to someone else. For to whom? To God, says Socinus. But God was not named by the Evangelist. Indeed, he says, in the word "heal" just before he was named, though tacitly; and earlier, in the words "blinded and hardened," he was named in the same way (although these are in the third person, while that one is in the first). Let us grant that he is named whose name is passed over in silence, that is, who is not named; yet let us press this point: not even so is God tacitly named by the Evangelist. For he does not recite those words as his own, but as the words of Isaiah; nor to teach something about God, but merely to prove that the Jews could not believe in Jesus.

units.la: XVI. Unde etiam habet Socinus Iesum non fuisse sic tacitè in verbo illo Sanem nominatum? Nam si de illa excæcatione & induratione verba excæcauit & induravit intelligenda sunt teste Apostolo, quibus factum est, ut Iudæi non potuerint credere in Iesum. Annon manifestum est de illa sanatione verbum Sanem accipien-dum esse, cuius autor est Iesus illis omnibus qui in ipsum credunt? Et quis est medicus, quis seruator populi sui à peccatis, quis me detur confractis corde, quis peccati seruos in libertatem vindicat, quis à maledictione legis redemit, quis ius filiorum Dei confert, quis peccata delet & remittit, quis vitam æternam largitur, quis ab hostibus liberat, quis denique mortuos suscitabit in die nouissimo nisi Dominus Iesus in quo solo est salus? Quid est igitur cur nolit Socinus istam, quæ in verbo Sanem includitur, sanationem Domino Iesu tribuere?
units.tr: XVI. Whence does Socinus also have that Jesus was not tacitly named in that word "heal"? For if the words "blinded" and "hardened" are to be understood, as the Apostle testifies, of that blinding and hardening by which it came about that the Jews could not believe in Jesus, is it not plain that the word "heal" must be taken of that healing whose author is Jesus to all who believe in him? And who is the physician, who is the saviour of his people from their sins, who restores the broken in heart, who frees the slaves of sin into liberty, who redeemed us from the curse of the law, who confers the right of the sons of God, who blots out and forgives sins, who bestows eternal life, who delivers from enemies, who finally will raise the dead on the last day, if not the Lord Jesus, in whom alone is salvation? Why, then, is Socinus unwilling to ascribe to the Lord Jesus that healing which is included in the word "heal"?

units.la: XVII. Hinc pulsus Socinus confugit ad verf. 38. in quo Dominus est nominatus. Domine quis credidit auditui nostro? Et cui brachium Domini est revelatum? Si quis obijciat versiculi illius distantiam ab hoc nostro 41. reponit, pronomina relativa non semper ad proxima referri, maximè ubi, vt hoc loco fit, de Deo & Christo agitur. Et profert exemplum ex 1. Ioh. 2. 28. Et nunc filioli manete in eo, vt cum apparuerit, habeamus fiduciam, & non confundamur ab eo in aduentu eius, quæ verba nemo dubitare poterit quin de Christo sint dicta. At quæ illico adduntur verf. 29. Si scitis quoniam iustus est, scitote, quoniam & omnis qui facit iniustitiam ex ipso natus est, de Deo, non de Christo, dicta esse affirmat, sed perperam mea sententia: flagitat enim series sermonis vt tam de Christo, quàm quæ antecedunt, accipiantur: ex quo qui nati non sunt, ij profectò nati non sunt ex Deo. Est enim etiam, Christus nostrûm omnium, hoc est, fidelium parens, teste ipso Christo, Heb. 2. 13. Ecce ego & pueri mei quos dedit mihi Deus. Et Propheta Esai 53. 10. videbit semen. Is enim est sponsus Ecclesiæ castæ matris omnium nostrum, & secundus Adamus in quo omnes viuificamur. Addit Socinus Paulo ante in eodem cap. 2. 1. Ioh. miram videri esse confusionem pronominum relatiuorum, nec satis dignosci posse ad Christumne an vero ad Deum, siue ad Filiumne an vero ad Patrem hæc aut illa verba referenda sint. Nempe, quia ad vtrumcunque referantur nihil interest: sunt enim Pater & Filius ita vnum, vt ambobus idem verbum singularis numeri, idem pronomen relatiuum accommodetur Apoc. xi. 15. & 20. 6. & 22. 3. &c.
units.tr: XVII. Driven from here, Socinus takes refuge in verse 38, in which the Lord is named: Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? If anyone objects the distance of that verse from this verse 41 of ours, he answers that relative pronouns are not always referred to the nearest word, especially where, as happens in this place, the discussion concerns God and Christ. And he cites an example from 1 John 2:28: And now, little children, abide in him, that when he appears we may have confidence and not be ashamed before him at his coming. No one can doubt that these words are spoken of Christ. But what is immediately added in verse 29: If you know that he is righteous, know that everyone who does righteousness is born of him, he asserts is said of God, not of Christ, but in my judgment wrongly: for the sequence of the discourse requires that both the things said of Christ and those that precede be understood in the same way; for from him those who are not born, certainly are not born of God. For Christ is also the parent of all of us, that is, of the faithful, as Christ himself testifies (Heb. 2:13): Behold, I and the children whom God has given me. And the prophet Isaiah (53:10): he shall see his seed. For he is the bridegroom of the chaste Church, the mother of us all, and the second Adam in whom we are all made alive. Socinus adds that a little before, in the same chapter 2 of 1 John, there seems to be a strange confusion of relative pronouns, and it cannot be sufficiently discerned whether these or those words are to be referred to Christ or to God, or to the Son or to the Father. Of course, because it makes no difference to which of them they are referred: for the Father and the Son are so one that the same verb of the singular number and the same relative pronoun are applied to both (Rev. 11:15, 20:6, 22:3, etc.).

units.la: XVIII. Subjungit idem Socinus, nullum exemplum accommodatius inueniri posse, quàm illud in hoc ipso Euangelio cap. 9. 22. vbi pronomen αὐτὸν[?] siue eum, Iesum referrt nec aperte nec tacite, nisi multò ante nominatum; cùm proximè ter eodem pronomine cæcus ille natus significatus fuisset. Certè nullum accommodatius inueniri potuit ad refellendum ipsum Socinum. Nam utrumque Euangelista diserte nominauerat, Iesum & cæcum illum: de utroque agebatur, de hoc quidem ut de miraculi subjecto, de illo vero ut de miraculi autore, de Iesu per se, de cæco propter Iesum. Deinde Euangelista ad pronomen αὐτὸν adjungit χειστὸν, ἐὰν τις αὐτὸν ὁμολογήσῃ χριστὸν Si quis eum confiteretur Christum, atque ita omnem ambiguitatem, omnem dubitandi ad Christumne an ad cæcum referendum sit occasionem tollit. Hic vero neque ab ipso Euangelista nominatus fuit Deus, neque Euangelista de Deo agebat aut loquebatur, sed de Christo tantum, neque ad pronomen adiungitur nomen Dei, aut aliud quiddam quo, Christo exclu so, referri doceatur ad Deum: multa autem suadent imo persuadent referendum esse ad Christum, ut mox liquebit. Adde quod uocatiuo Domine non Filium Dei compellari nihil est quo possit euinci.
units.tr: XVIII. Socinus adds: no example can be found more suitable than that in this same Gospel, chapter 9, verse 22, where the pronoun αὐτὸν [autón], that is, him, refers neither openly nor tacitly to Jesus unless he has been named long before, since the blind man born had been referred to three times just before by the same pronoun. Certainly no more suitable example could have been found for refuting Socinus himself. For the Evangelist had named both, Jesus and the blind man: both were the subject of discussion, the one as the subject of the miracle, the other as its author, Jesus in himself, the blind man on account of Jesus. Further, the Evangelist adds to the pronoun αὐτὸν [autón] the word χριστὸν [christón]: If anyone confesses him Christ [ἐὰν τις αὐτὸν ὁμολογήσῃ χριστὸν], and so removes all ambiguity and every occasion for doubt whether it should be referred to Christ or to the blind man. Here, however, God was not named by the Evangelist himself, nor does the Evangelist speak or write about God, but only about Christ; nor is the name of God attached to the pronoun, or anything else that would show, with Christ set aside, that it refers to God. Many considerations, indeed, persuade (rather, compel us to believe) that it must be referred to Christ, as will soon be clear. Add that the vocative Lord does not show that the Son of God is being addressed, and nothing can be shown from it to prove this.

units.la: X IX. At, inquit Socinus, In graeca Roberti Stephani editione in folio (ut vocant) annotatum est in margine nota quadam id significante codicem quendam vetustissimum in Italia ab amicis Typographi collatum pro τῷ δόξαν αὐτῷ, id est, gloriam eius, habuisse τῷ δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ, id est, gloriam Dei. Eadem lectio adnotata est in margine codicis graeci editi a Christoph. Froschouero Tiguri anno 1559. Et ego habui quondam in Italia graecum codicem manu scriptum antiquissimum & elegantissimum, quem mihi eripuit quidam, in quo, nisi me memoria fallit, eadem lectio in ipso contextu consignata erat. Quorsum haec? vultne Socinus unius codicis graeci ab uno aut altero visi authoritate præponderari consensum omnium aliorum codicum graecorum, omniumque versionum, etiam antiquissimarum, quæ habent constanter τῷ δόξαν αὐτῷ gloriam eius? Id nimis iniquum foret. Nonne potuit codex ille manuscriptus alicuius Arriani vel photiniani fuisse, qui cum pronomen αὐτῷ putaret ad Deum referendum esse, ut errandi scilicet ansam præscinderet, scripserat τῷ Θεῷ? Nam non esse illam lectionem de mente Apostoli sequentia argumenta planum, ut spero, facient.
units.tr: XIX. But, says Socinus, in Robert Stephanus's Greek edition in folio (as they call it) a note in the margin records, by a certain mark, that a very old manuscript in Italy, collated by friends of the printer, had τῷ δόξαν αὐτῷ, that is, his glory [tō doxan autō], but had τῷ δόξαν τῷ Θεῷ, that is, the glory of God [tō doxan tō Theō]. The same reading is noted in the margin of the Greek codex published by Christoph Froschauer at Zurich in 1559. And I once had in Italy a most ancient and most elegant Greek manuscript, which someone snatched from me, in which, unless my memory fails me, the same reading was written in the text itself. To what end are these things? Does Socinus wish the authority of one Greek manuscript, seen by one or two people, to outweigh the agreement of all the other Greek manuscripts and of all the versions, even the most ancient, which constantly have τῷ δόξαν αὐτῷ [tō doxan autō], his glory? That would be far too unfair. Could that manuscript not have belonged to some Arian or Photinian who, thinking the pronoun αὐτῷ [autō] ought to be referred to God, wrote τῷ Θεῷ [tō Theō], evidently to cut off the occasion of error? For the following arguments will, I hope, make it plain that this reading does not reflect the mind of the Apostle.

units.la: X X. Ut igitur pergamus, Hoc esto quintum argumentum. Ad utrumque Esaiae testimonium, inquit ipse Socinus, verba ista Iohannis sine dubio referri debent, præsertim cum dicat, Haec dixit, non autem Hoc dixit. Iam autem negari non potest, quin Esaias, cum dixit prius testimonium, loqueretur de Christo. Legatur cap. 52. pros
units.tr: XX. Let us therefore go on. Let this be the fifth argument. To both testimonies of Isaiah, says Socinus himself, these words of John should undoubtedly be referred, especially since he says, He said these things, and not, He said this. Now it cannot be denied that Isaiah, when he spoke the first testimony, was speaking of Christ. Let chapter 52 be read

units.la: 52. pros 52. proximè antecedens versiculum primum capitis 53. quem Apostolus laudauit: legantur versus sequentes toto cap. 53. de Christo ubique loquitur, Christum ubique describit, Deum quatenus à Christo differt, non item. At Deum compellat versu illo primo. Esto, nempe aliud est Deum alloqui, aliud de Deo loqui. Eum sæpe alloquimur de quo tamen non loquimur. Si igitur Esaias prius testimonium dixit cum de Christo, non de Deo loqueretur, annon manifestum est in verbis Euangelistæ, Hæc dixit Esaias cum vidit gloriam eius, & loquutus est de eo, pronomen eo ad Christum, non ad Deum esse referendum?
units.tr: 52. pros— 52. the verse immediately preceding, the first verse of chapter 53, which the Apostle quoted. Let the following verses be read throughout chapter 53: it speaks of Christ everywhere, describes Christ everywhere, and describes God only insofar as he differs from Christ, but not otherwise. Yet in that first verse it addresses God. Granted: it is one thing to address God, another to speak about God; we often address one of whom we are not speaking. If, then, Isaiah when he spoke the first testimony was speaking of Christ and not of God, is it not clear from the words of the Evangelist, These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory, and spoke of him, that the pronoun him must be referred to Christ and not to God?

units.la: XXI. Idem dicendum esse de posteriore testimonio, nemo, opinor, inficiabitur, præsertim cum in confesso sit, verba illa Euangelistæ ad utrumque testimonium referri: Nec possit negari in eo sermonem esse de ea Judæorum incredulitate, qua factum est, ut Christum videndo & audiendo non viderent oculis, nec intelligerent corde, nec in eum crederent, aut credere possent, ad quem tamen ut sanarentur respicere & converti eos necesse erat. Quod si in verbis, locutus est de eo, pronomen Eo ad Christum referetur, quis non videt, etiam in verbis, vidit gloriam eius pronomen eius ad eundem Christum referendum esse?
units.tr: XXI. I suppose no one will deny that the same must be said of the second testimony, especially since it is agreed that those words of the Evangelist refer to both testimonies. Nor can it be denied that the discourse there concerns that unbelief of the Jews by which it came about that, seeing and hearing Christ, they did not see with their eyes or understand with their heart, nor believed in him, or were able to believe in him, though it was necessary for them to look to him in order to be healed and converted. But if, in the words he spoke of him, the pronoun him is referred to Christ, who does not see that in the words he saw his glory the pronoun his must likewise be referred to the same Christ?

units.la: XXII. Sexto, aut pronomina ista referri debent ad Christum, aut intelligi non potest quorsum post recitata duo Esaiæ testimonia prudentissimus Euangelista verba illa addiderit. Hæc dixit Esaias cum vidit gloriam eius, & locutus est de eo: de Deo enim, non de Christo, intellecta quid faciunt ad propositum? quem usum habent? Non modò inutilia sunt, sed, quod deterius est, lectorem vel incautum fallunt, vel attentum implicant pronominum ambiguitate fallaci.
units.tr: XXII. Sixth, either these pronouns must be referred to Christ, or it cannot be understood why the most wise Evangelist added, after the two quoted testimonies of Isaiah, those words: These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory, and spoke of him. For if they are understood of God and not of Christ, what do they contribute to the purpose? What use do they have? They are not only useless, but, what is worse, they either deceive the careless reader or entangle the attentive one with the deceptive ambiguity of the pronouns.

units.la: XXIII. Socinus dicit, Johanni causam addendi, quod Esaias illa dixisset, cum vidit gloriam Dei, hanc fuisse, ut indicaret locum in Esaiæ libro, ubi hæc scripta erant. Visio enim illa magnifica & gloriosa admodum celebrem locum faciebat; gloriaque Dei nominata, quam Esaias vidisset, statim visio ista intelligebatur. Nihil enim simile nec ante, nec post, ei conspectum fuisse legitur. Visionem intelligit descriptam Esai. cap. vi. Hæc vero causa quatuor rationibus refellitur. Nam primo recurrit quæstio, quorsum Apostolus locum in Esaiæ libro indicasset, ubi hæc scripta erant? Id enim aliis locis ubi laudatur idem testimonium factum non est; nec cum alia citantur testimonia factum est unquam à scriptoribus sacris, nisi cum illa loci notatio juvavit eorum scopum. Deinde sic Evangelista locum indicasset posterioris testimonij duntaxat, non autem prioris, cum tamen ipse Socinus affirmauerit ad utrumque verba, Haec dixit Esaias cum vidit gloriam eius, &c. sine dubio debere referri. Deinde, Sic sapientissimus autor lectorem lusisset innuendo duo illa testimonia eodem tempore dicta, eodemque loco scripta fuisse, quæ tamen quadraginta nouem capitum interuallo à se invicem distant. Postremò id non inutiliter tantùm Apostolus obseruasset, sed periculosè etiam, multis inde occasionem accipientibus existimandi, eum, cuius gloriam Esaias vidit eo capite, Iesum fuisse. Non autem tanti esse apud Apostolum non necessaria, nec utilis loci notatio debuit, ut propterea vel minimam errandi occasionem fidelibus præberet.
units.tr: XXIII. Socinus says: The reason why John added that Isaiah said those things when he saw the glory of God was this, to indicate the place in Isaiah's book where these things were written. For that vision, magnificent and very glorious, made a famous passage; and when the glory of God, which Isaiah had seen, was named, that vision was at once understood. For we read that nothing similar was seen by him either before or after. He means the vision described in Isaiah chapter 6. But this reason is refuted on four grounds. First, the question arises why the Apostle should have indicated the place in Isaiah's book where these things were written. For this was not done in other places where the same testimony is cited, nor has it ever been done by the sacred writers when other testimonies are cited, unless such a notice of the place served their purpose. Next, the Evangelist would then have indicated the place of the second testimony only, and not of the first, although Socinus himself has affirmed that the words These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory, etc., undoubtedly must refer to both. Further, the most wise author would thus have misled the reader by implying that the two testimonies were spoken at the same time and written in the same place, although they are forty-nine chapters apart from each other. Lastly, the Apostle would have observed this not merely uselessly but dangerously, since many would thereby have been given occasion to think that he whose glory Isaiah saw in that chapter was Jesus. Yet the indication of a place, which was neither necessary nor useful, ought not to be so important to the Apostle that for its sake he should offer even the smallest occasion of error to the faithful.

units.la: XXIV. Pergit Socinus, Quod autem adiungit, & locutus est de eo, ideò pertinet, ut sciamus, verba, quæ ex eo loco recitauerat, ad id confirmandum, quod dixerat, Iudæos credere non potuisse, ad ipsum Deum referenda esse: verba, inquam, illa, Excæcauit oculos eorum, & induravit cor eorum; quatenus scilicet Dei consilio excæcatio ista, & induratio eventura prædicitur, quod alioqui non facilè animadversum[?] fuisset, Ita rursus verba illa ad posterius testimonium restringit contradicens sibi affirmanti, ut est à nobis observatum § xx. verba illa Iohannis ad utrumque testimonium sine dubio referri debere, idemque paulò post inculcanti his verbis, Cum ad utrumque locum Iohannis verba respiciant, & illa duo, vidisse gloriam eius, & locutum fuisse de eo coniunctim ponantur; verisimile planè est, vel potius necessarium, ut istorum duorum utrumque similiter ad utrumque locum spectet. Hoc primum. Deinde, verba, induravit & excæcavit, ad ipsum Deum referenda esse, neque verbis illis dicit Iohannes diserte, neque per consequentiam. Nam dicit quidem Esaiam, testimonium illud dixisse cum vidit gloriam eius & locutus est de eo, sed non dicit Esaiam, aut vidisse gloriam eius, aut locutum esse de eo in illis ipsis verbis quæ citauit.
units.tr: XXIV. Socinus goes on: But what he adds, and spoke of him, is there so that we may know that the words he had quoted from that place, to confirm what he had said, that the Jews could not believe, are to be referred to God himself: those words, I mean, He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart; namely, insofar as this blinding and hardening is foretold as coming about by the counsel of God, which otherwise would hardly have been noticed. Thus again Socinus restricts those words to the second testimony, contradicting himself when he affirms, as we have observed in § xx, that the words of John should undoubtedly be referred to both testimonies, and when he insists on this again a little later in these words: Since John's words refer to both passages, and those two phrases, to have seen his glory and to have spoken of him, are placed together, it is quite plausible, or rather necessary, that each of these two should apply similarly to both passages. This is the first point. Next, that the words he has hardened and blinded are to be referred to God himself is not stated by John in express words, nor is it implied by consequence. For he does say that Isaiah spoke that testimony when he saw his glory and spoke of him, but he does not say that Isaiah saw his glory, or spoke of him, in those very words which he quoted.

units.la: XXV: Adde quod istiusmodi observatio, verba, induravit & excæcavit, ad Deum esse referenda, nihil facit ad scopum Evangelistæ. Is enim probare instituit Iudæos non potuisse credere in Jesum. In eum finem profert Esaiæ testimonium, Excæca-uit oculos eorum, & induravit cor eorum : ut non videant oculis, & non intelligant corde, & convertantur & sanem eos. Egregium argumentum. Qui non possunt videre oculis, intelligere corde, converti, illi non possunt credere. Quorum oculi sunt excæcati & cor induratum, illi non possunt videre oculis, intelligere corde, converti. Ergo quorum oculi sunt excæcati & cor induratum, illi non possunt credere, tales autem erant Judæi quibus Christus prædicauit Evangelium Esaia teste: quare non poterant credere. Quis eos excæcauit, ipse Deus; an natiua prauitas ( sumus enim omnes natura filij, ut irae, sic rebellionis, ) an Deus huius seculi, quem Apostolus Paulus testatur excæcasse mentes incredulorum, ne irradiet eos illuminatio Evangelij gloriæ Christi, ad vim argumenti nihil interest. Oculi excæcati à quocunque sint excæcati videre non possunt. Cor induratum à quocunque sit induratum, cum sit durum rigidum & lapideum, nec intelligere potest, nec flecti, nec converti ad Deum.
units.tr: XXV: Add that this observation, that the words he has blinded and hardened are to be referred to God, does nothing for the purpose of the Evangelist. For he undertook to prove that the Jews could not believe in Jesus. To that end he brings forward the testimony of Isaiah: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes, nor understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them. An excellent argument. Those who cannot see with their eyes, understand with their heart, or be converted, cannot believe. Those whose eyes are blinded and whose heart is hardened cannot see with their eyes, understand with their heart, or be converted. Therefore those whose eyes are blinded and whose heart is hardened cannot believe. Such were the Jews to whom Christ preached the Gospel, as Isaiah bears witness; therefore they could not believe. Who blinded them, God himself, or their innate depravity (for we are all by nature children of wrath, and likewise of rebellion), or the god of this world, whom the Apostle Paul testifies to have blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of Christ should shine on them: for the force of the argument this makes no difference. Eyes that are blinded cannot see, by whomever they have been blinded. A heart that is hardened, by whomever it has been hardened, since it is hard, stiff and stony, can neither understand nor be bent, nor turned to God.

units.la: XXVI. Denique non solum inutilis fuisset illa Evangelistæ observatio, sed noxia etiam & periculosa, quippe quæ neque facilè sic accipi posset, & sic accepta lectorem perturbaret. Nam seu locum ut est in libro prophetæ inspicias, seu eum quemadmodum extat in editione græca quæ 70. interpretibus tribuitur, & citatus est ab Apostolo Act. 28. spectes, non videtur illa excæcatio & induratio Deo tanquam autori ascribi: Neque isto loco, quo graviter, uti par est, Judæorum cæcitas, durities, incredulitas reprehenditur, conveniebat eam cæcitatem & duritiem ad Deum tanquam ad autorem referre, idque ne præteriret inobservatum, lectorem monere. Ad hæc posset quis, ipso teste, nec refellente, Socino, apud Johannem verba excæcauit, & indurauit, hebraica phrasi ita interpretari, acsi scriptum fuisset excæcati sunt & induratum est.
units.tr: XXVI. Finally, that observation of the Evangelist would not only have been useless but also harmful and dangerous, since it could not easily be taken in that sense, and taken so would disturb the reader. For whether you look at the passage as it stands in the book of the prophet, or as it is found in the Greek edition attributed to the Seventy, and cited by the Apostle in Acts 28, that blinding and hardening do not seem to be ascribed to God as author. Nor, in a place where the blindness, hardness and unbelief of the Jews are rebuked severely, as is proper, was it fitting to refer that blindness and hardness to God as author, and that so that it would not pass unnoticed, to warn the reader. Besides, one could say, on the testimony of Socinus himself, and he does not refute it, that in John the words "he has blinded and hardened" are to be interpreted in the Hebrew manner, as if it had been written "they have been blinded and it is hardened".

units.la: XXVII. Ut sit finis, vel verba Excæcauit & induravit non referuntur ad Deum, vel sunt plures personæ diuinæ. Non enim possunt ad eandem personam referri, ad quam refertur verbum Sanem: sunt enim tertiæ personæ, cum hoc sit primæ. Excæcauit oculos eorum & induravit cor eorum, &c. ne sanem eos. Non potuerunt apertius personæ distingui. Affirmat quidem Socinus personarum tertiæ & primæ distinctionem non obstare, quominus idem sit omnium illorum verborum nominatiuus: sed affirmat tan-tùm, non probat, imò ne conatur quidem probare. Atqui nominatiuus verbi Sanem est ego: verborum verò excæcauit & induravit est ille. Num fit verisimile pronomina, Ille, & Ego, ad eãdem personam loquentem in eadem sententia referri debere? An est quisquam qui de se uno sic loquatur, ille hoc fecit ne illud Ego faciam, semetipsum duobus pronominibus altero tertiae personæ, altero primæ designans?
units.tr: XXVII. So the end is that either the words "he has blinded and hardened" are not referred to God, or there are several divine persons. For they cannot be referred to the same person to whom the word "I should heal" is referred, since the former are third persons and this is first person. He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, etc., lest I should heal them. The persons could not have been distinguished more plainly. Socinus indeed affirms that the distinction of third and first persons does not prevent the subject of all those words from being the same; but he merely affirms, he does not prove, and indeed does not even try to prove. Yet the subject of "I should heal" is I, while the subject of "he has blinded and hardened" is he. Is it likely that the pronouns "he" and "I" must be referred to the same speaking person in the same sentence? Is there anyone who speaks of himself alone in this way: "he did this, lest I should do that", designating himself by two pronouns, one of the third person and the other of the first?

units.la: XXVIII. Ad superiora argumenta illud septimo loco accedit, quod hoc idem testimonium Esaiæ ad incredulitatem Iudæorum accommodatur ab ipso Christo Math. xiii. 14. necnon ab Apostolo Paulo Act. 28. 25. quibus tamen in locis additum non est, hæc dixisse Esaiam cum vidit gloriam eius, & de eo locutus est, aut aliud simile quidpiam. Quod cum non temerè acciderit vt sit additum isto loco, quod duobus illis additum non fuit, huius discriminis subesse aliquam rationem oportet: mirabili enim sapientia vbique Scriptura collucet. Ea verò ratio, si ad Iesum pronomina, Eius & eo non referuntur, nulla prorsus apparet, si referuntur, obuia est: Ad eam enim accommodationem huius testimonij, quæ Math. 13. & Act. 28. facta est, satis fuit cum vaticinio congruere euentum. Hic verò aliquid amplius desidera-batur: instituit enim probare sapiens Euangelista, non simpliciter quod Iudæi non crediderunt id consentaneum esse cum hoc Esaiæ vaticinio, sed Iudæos non potuisse credere in Christum. Ad id autem probandum accommodatione vaticinij opus fuit, quæ euentum antecederet, atque nominatim ad illos ipsos Iudæos pertineret, quibus suam Christus gloriam contemplandam & credendam ob oculos posuit. Quominus autem sic accommoda-retur obstare videbatur, quod eo loco nulla fit Christi mentio, tantum gloria Dei quæ Prophetæ apparuit magnificentissimè describitur. Monet igitur Apostolus non esse cur lector propterea conturbetur: Iesum enim esse illum Dominum cuius gloriam Esaias vidit, & de quo tam magnificè locutus est eo loco. Quod moniti fideles facilè credunt: quippe quos Filij Dei Seruatoris sui amor, admiratio, imò adoratio totos occupat. Hanc eandem fidem iuuant multa alia prophetarum & Apostolorum testimonia: Nec desunt in ipso textu prophetæ quibus fulcire possit, in ex-tremo huius disputationis protrahenda in lucem.
units.tr: XXVIII. To the arguments above is added, seventh, that this same testimony of Isaiah is applied to the unbelief of the Jews by Christ himself, Matt. 13:14, and also by the Apostle Paul, Acts 28:25; yet in those places it is not added that Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him, or anything similar. Since it has not happened by chance that in this place something is added which was not added in those two, some reason for this difference must lie beneath it, for Scripture shines everywhere with wonderful wisdom. Now this reason, if the pronouns "his" and "him" are not referred to Jesus, appears not at all; if they are referred, it is obvious. For for the application of this testimony made in Matthew 13 and Acts 28 it was enough that the event agreed with the prophecy. Here, however, something more was required: the wise Evangelist undertook to prove not simply that the unbelief of the Jews was consistent with this prophecy of Isaiah, but that the Jews could not believe in Christ. To prove this, an application of the prophecy was needed which would precede the event, and would pertain by name to those very Jews to whom Christ set his glory before their eyes to be contemplated and believed. That such an application was not possible seemed to be hindered by the fact that in that place there is no mention of Christ at all, only the glory of God which appeared to the prophet is described most magnificently. The Apostle therefore warns that there is no reason for the reader to be disturbed on that account: Jesus is that Lord whose glory Isaiah saw, and about whom he spoke so magnificently in that place. Faithful people, being warned, readily believe this, since the love, admiration and indeed adoration of the Son of God their Saviour occupies them wholly. Many other testimonies of the prophets and Apostles support this same faith, and there are in the text of the prophet itself things by which it can be upheld, to be brought out into the light at the end of this disputation.

units.la: XXIX. Addamus & octauum argumentum. Hoc Esaiæ vaticinium, vel relationem habet ad magnificam illam visionem, quæ eo capite vi. describitur: vel non habet. Si non habet, intelligi non potest, quare visio illa nec antè nec post prophetæ exhibita nullum alium exitum habuit, nisi quod missus est ad promulgandum hoc vaticinium. Si habet, necesse est, ut visio fuerit gloriæ Christi, quam Iudæi neque oculis visuri erant, neque corde intellecturi. Cum enim vaticinium teste Euangelista de Iudæorum incredulitate intelligi debeat, qui Christum videndo non viderunt oculis, & audiendo non audierunt auribus, nec corde intellexerunt, nec ad eum conuersi sunt ut sanarentur, manifestum est nullam esse inter vaticinium & visionem χίαν[?], si Dominus, cuius gloriam Esaias vidit, Christus non fuit.
units.tr: XXIX. Let us add an eighth argument. This prophecy of Isaiah either has a relation to that magnificent vision which is described in the sixth chapter, or it does not. If it does not, it cannot be understood why that vision, shown to the prophet neither before nor after, had no other outcome than that he was sent to proclaim this prophecy. If it does, it must be that the vision was of the glory of Christ, which the Jews were neither going to see with their eyes nor understand with their heart. For since, on the Evangelist's testimony, the prophecy must be understood of the unbelief of the Jews, who by seeing Christ did not see with their eyes, and by hearing did not hear with their ears, nor understood with their heart, nor were converted to him that they might be healed, it is plain that there is no difference between the prophecy and the vision, if the Lord whose glory Isaiah saw was not Christ.

units.la: XXX. Sed ne longior sim in re clara probanda, sic argumentor. Iis quæ Iudæi videndo non erant visuri, & audiendo non erant audituri, & ad quem non erant convertendi ut sanarentur, est ille Dominus qui sese videndum & audiendum ostendebat paratus ad sanandum eos qui ad ipsum converterentur. Atqui Iesus est ille quem Iudæi videndo non erant visuri, & audiendo non erant audituri, & ad quæ ut sanarentur non erant convertendi. Ergo Iesus est ille Dominus qui sese videndum & audiendum ostendebat paratus ad sanandum eos qui ad ipsum converterentur. Minor conceditur à Socino: fatetur enim, sic descriptam fuisse ab Esaia cæcitatem & indurationem Iudæorum in Christo non agnoscendo & amplectendo: nec potest negari quin contradicatur Apostolo Iohanni. Major autem vix eget probatione. Primum enim negari nequit, quin is Dominus qui sese videndum & audiendum ostendebat debuerit cordis oculis & auribus videri, audiri, intelligi, cum tamen à Iudæis rebellibus visus, auditus, intellectus non sit. Negari non potest quin ad eum conuerti debuerint, cum tamen ad eum conuersi non sint. Negari igitur non potest major propositio argumenti nostri. Deinde cur Dominus gloriam suam reuelauit, seseque ostendit videndum & audiendum, ut mandaret dici populo Iudaico videndo videte & ne intelligatis, audiendo audite & ne cognoscatis, &c. nisi ut significaret fore ut quum sese populo illi videndum & audiendum præbiturus esset, populus tamen ille eum videndo non esset agnoscturus nec audiendo intellecturus. Denique perspicuum est eundem esse autorem sanationis qui est objectum conversionis, visionis, auditus. Sanationis autem sese autorem esse ille ipse Dominus profitebatur, qui Esaiam conspicuus alloquebatur.
units.tr: XXX. But lest I be too long in proving a matter that is clear, I argue thus. Concerning those whom the Jews were not going to see by seeing, nor hear by hearing, and to whom they were not to be converted that they might be healed, it is that Lord who showed himself to be seen and heard, ready to heal those who should be converted to him. But Jesus is the one whom the Jews were not going to see by seeing, nor hear by hearing, and to whom they were not to be converted that they might be healed. Therefore Jesus is that Lord who showed himself to be seen and heard, ready to heal those who should be converted to him. The minor premise is conceded by Socinus: for he confesses that Isaiah described thus the blindness and hardening of the Jews in not acknowledging and embracing Christ; nor can it be denied that this contradicts the Apostle John. The major premise hardly needs proof. For first, it cannot be denied that the Lord who showed himself to be seen and heard ought to have been seen, heard and understood by the eyes and ears of the heart, though he was not seen, heard or understood by the rebellious Jews. It cannot be denied that they ought to have been converted to him, though they were not converted to him. Therefore the major premise of our argument cannot be denied. Next, why did the Lord reveal his glory and show himself to be seen and heard, so that he commanded the Jewish people to be told "by seeing see, and do not understand; by hearing hear, and do not know", etc., unless to signify that when he was about to present himself to that people to be seen and heard, that people would nevertheless not acknowledge him by seeing nor understand him by hearing. Finally, it is evident that the same one is the author of healing who is the object of conversion, sight and hearing. Moreover, that same Lord who spoke to Isaiah face to face professed himself the author of healing.

units.la: XXXI. Denique hoc Esaiæ testimonium laudat Euangelista, ut probet Iudæos, quibus sese Iesus videndum & audiendum multis editis miraculis exhibuit, credere in eum præ cæcitate & duritie cordis non potuisse, vel igitur de eiusmodi Iudæorum tali incredulitate testimonium illud dictum esse colligi potest ex textu Esaiæ, vel non potest. Si non potest, haud satis prudens fuit Apostolus, qui testimonium ctkauit cuius nulla vis esset ad id probandum, quod eo probare instituit. Id quod de tanto Apostolo vel cogitare nefas duco. Si potest, igitur aliquid est vel in illo ipso testimonio, vel in antecedentibus aut consequentibus versibus, unde id colligi possit. Atqui nihil est prorsus præter magnisicam illam visionem: quæ si non est visio gloriæ Christi, contendo nihil prorsus esse in toto capite unde possit concludi, quod concludi voluit Apostolus, Iudæos non potuisse credere in Iesum.
units.tr: XXXI. Finally, the Evangelist cites this testimony of Isaiah to prove that the Jews, to whom Jesus showed himself to be seen and heard through many miracles, could not believe in him because of blindness and hardness of heart. Either this testimony can be shown from the text of Isaiah to refer to such unbelief of the Jews, or it cannot. If it cannot, the Apostle was not very wise, since he cited a testimony that had no force to prove what he set out to prove. I consider even to think this a sin against so great an Apostle. If it can, then something in that very testimony, or in the verses before or after it, must allow this to be inferred. But there is nothing at all except that magnificent vision. If that is not a vision of the glory of Christ, I maintain that there is nothing whatever in the whole chapter from which one could conclude what the Apostle wished to conclude, namely that the Jews could not believe in Jesus.

units.la: XXXII. Refutata prima responsione confugit Socinus ad secundam, Demus, inquit, Aduersarijs, omnino pronomina eius & eo Christum referre. Num continuo sequetur, Christum esse illum Dominum ab Esaia in visione illa conspectum? Nullo modo. Immo id continuo sequitur: nullius enim gloriam vidit Esaias eo capite nisi Domini illius & Seraphim. Vidit autem gloriam Christi. Christus igitur erat ille Dominus. Nam eum fuisse Seraphim illos, aut unum ex illis non dicent, opinor, Aduersarij. Subijcit rationis loco, Vtrumque testimonium ad rem futuram respiceret & si ad rem futurum non respicerent, minimè potuisse à Iohanne proferri ad confirmandum id quod voluit. Esto. Addit ex eo etiam sequi gloriam istam ab Esaia visam, futuram gloriam fuisse illi repræsentatam, &c. nempe specimen fuit gloriæ Christi reuelandæ, quid id facit ad infirmationem argumenti nostri?
units.tr: XXXII. After the first answer was refuted, Socinus fled to a second: "Let us grant to our opponents that the pronouns and the 'eo' refer to Christ. Does it follow at once that Christ is that Lord whom Isaiah saw in that vision? By no means." But in fact it does follow at once. For Isaiah saw the glory of no one in that chapter except that Lord and the Seraphim. He did see the glory of Christ. Therefore Christ was that Lord. For I suppose our opponents will not say that Christ was one of the Seraphim. As a reason, he adds: "Both testimonies would have to look to a future thing, and if they did not look to a future thing, they could hardly have been brought forward by John to confirm what he wished." Granted. He adds that "from this it also follows that the glory which Isaiah saw was represented to him as a future glory," and so on. Certainly it was a specimen of the glory of Christ to be revealed. But what does this have to do with weakening our argument?

units.la: XXXIII. Sed Nihil cogit, inquit, gloriam istam quam vidisse Esaiam Iohannes affirmat, ad illam gloriam referre, cuius visio describitur apud eundem Esaiam cap. vi. Immo cogunt rationes multæ partim iam propositæ, partim mox proponendæ. Sed fac nihil cogere, Num ita durum est cor aduersariorum cum de redemptore suo agitur, ut eum, cum se reuelat, agnoscere nolint, nisi cogantur? Nonne sufficit probabilis ratio, cum in contrarium vel nulla est, vel minus probabilis? Ego vero putabam admonitos ab Apostolo, Esaiam illa dixisse cum vidit gloriam Christi, dubitare amplius nos non debere, quin gloriam Domini intelligamus, quam Esaias vidisse se profitetur, neque ut id credamus coactione opus esse, sed potius ne id credamus, siquidem credendum non esset. Cui enim legenti, deque Christo, ut par est, accipienti verba Euangelistae, haec dixit Esaias cum vidit glo-riam eius, non veniat in mentem Domini gloria, quam eo loco vidisse Esaias perhibetur, quo illa dixit? Si igitur illa gloria intelligenda non est, obstare rationes graues &c, ut loquuntur Aduersarii, cogentes. Nihil tamen afferri potest praeter haec duo: unum, Christum tunc nondum fuisse: alterum, eum divina essentia praeditum non esse: quorum illud libro praecedente multis argumentis refutavimus; istud toto isto, Domino fauente, refutabimus. Argumenta autem quibus utrumque probare conantur, facile & solide diluere libro tertio, dabit, ut spero idem misericors Dominus.
units.tr: XXXIII. But Socinus says: "Nothing compels us to refer that glory which John affirms Isaiah saw to that glory whose vision is described in the same Isaiah, chapter 6." On the contrary, many arguments compel it, some already set out and some to be set out shortly. But grant that nothing compels it. Is the heart of our opponents so hard, when their Redeemer is in question, that they refuse to recognise him when he reveals himself, unless they are forced to? Is a probable reason not sufficient, when there is either no reason on the other side or a less probable one? I, for my part, thought that we had been instructed by the Apostle that when Isaiah said these things, he saw the glory of Christ, and that we ought no longer to doubt that we understand the glory of the Lord which Isaiah professes to have seen. Nor is there any need for compulsion to make us believe it, but rather we would need something to stop us believing it, if it were not to be believed. For who, reading the words of the Evangelist about Christ, as is proper, "These things said Isaiah, when he saw his glory," would not think of the glory of the Lord which Isaiah is said to have seen in the place where he spoke those words? If that glory is not to be understood as such, then there are, as our opponents say, "weighty reasons compelling otherwise, etc." Yet nothing can be offered except these two things: first, that Christ had not yet existed; second, that he is not endowed with the divine essence. We have refuted the first with many arguments in the preceding book; the second we will refute throughout this whole book, the Lord being favourable. The arguments by which they try to prove each of these, the same merciful Lord will, as I hope, enable me to dissolve easily and solidly in the third book.

units.la: XXXIV. Nunc si nolunt Aduersarii verba Enangelistae de gloria illa Domini intelligere, quam eo loco vidisse Esaias dicitur, ostendant nobis in eodem illo capite gloriam Christi, quam tunc Esaias viderit. Nulla enim totum caput attente perlegenti mihi alia apparet. Eo capite, inquit Socinus, Christi gloria praedicitur, eaque non vulgaris, sed maxima & praeclarissima. Quandoquidem post mentionem factam futurae caecitatis & indurationis Iudaeorum in Christo non agnoscendo & amplectendo, praedicitur desolatio, & vastatio illius populi, eiusque reiectio: & v. 12. qui per parenthesim legi debet, Gentium post Iudaeorum reiectionem istam vocatio, & ad Christum conversio, idque ingente numero, ac statim postea subiungitur eiusdem populi Iudaici in pristinum, atque adeo meliorem statum restitutio; quae nimirum per Christi agnitionem illis est obventura. En gloriam Christi quam Esaias scilicet vidit, Judaeorum desolationem vers. xi. Gentium vocationem vers. xii. Judaeorum restitutionem vers. xiii. Egetne refutatione tam aperta Scripturae contortio, quae, praeterquam quod rationes modo expositas § 28. 29. 30. 31. non declinat, tota absurda est?
units.tr: XXXIV. Now, if our opponents are unwilling to understand the words of the Evangelist as referring to that glory of the Lord which Isaiah is said to have seen in that place, let them show us the glory of Christ which Isaiah then saw in that same chapter. For to me, reading the whole chapter attentively, none other appears. In that chapter, says Socinus, "the glory of Christ is foretold, and not an ordinary glory but a very great and most splendid one. For after mention has been made of the future blindness and hardening of the Jews in not recognising and embracing Christ, there is foretold the desolation and devastation of that people and their rejection; and in verse 12, which must be read in parentheses, the calling of the Gentiles after the rejection of the Jews, and their conversion to Christ, and that in great numbers; and immediately afterwards it is added that the Jewish people is restored to its former and indeed better state, which will certainly come to them through the recognition of Christ." Behold the glory of Christ which Isaiah, of course, saw: the desolation of the Jews in verse 11, the calling of the Gentiles in verse 12, the restoration of the Jews in verse 13. Does such a plain refutation of Scripture need any further refutation, since this twisting not only does not avoid the arguments just set out in §§ 28, 29, 30, 31, but is wholly absurd?

units.la: XXXV. Primum ista Esaias vidisse non dicitur, sed audivisse, & dixi, inquit, usquequo Domine? & dixit, Donec desolentur ci-uitates absque habitatore, & domus sine homine, & terra relinquatur deserta. Hoccine est videre? igitur audire est videre, audi-tus est visus. At dicuntur prophetae videre quae praedicunt & futura norunt. Non certè omnia, sed quaecunque illis in visione vel per somnium videnda objecta sunt. Tota quidem prophetia visio saepè dicitur à majori vel potiori parte; sed in visione alia prophetis ostenduntur, alia tantummodò dicuntur: Haec cum ab ostensis & visis seorsum sumuntur, audita ab illis, dicta, praedicta dici possunt, visa nequaquam. Haud enim audita & visa magis in visione quàm extra visionem confundi debent. Non hoc igitur duntaxat affirmare Socinum decebat, sed exemplo aliquo firmare, quo, id quod in visione tantummodò auditum est, nullo modo visum, praecisè sumptum dicatur visum fuisse. Resistit igitur huic Aduersariorum interpretationi videndi verbum quantum potest, quo non est Euangelista visus temerè & praeter suam, & omnium sacrorum autorum, atque hominum loquendi consuetudi-nem.
units.tr: XXXV. First, these things are not said to have been seen by Isaiah, but heard: "And I said, 'How long, Lord?' And he said, 'Until the cities are laid waste without inhabitant, and the houses without man, and the land is left desolate.'" Is this seeing? So hearing is seeing, and hearing is sight! But "the prophets are said to see what they foretell, and to know future things." Certainly not all things, but whatever objects were to be seen by them in vision or through a dream. Indeed, prophecy as a whole is often called vision, from the greater or more important part; but in a vision some things are shown to the prophets, and other things are only said. When these are taken separately from what was shown and seen, things heard, spoken and foretold by them can be called such, but in no way seen. For things heard and seen ought not to be confused in a vision any more than outside a vision. It therefore was not enough for Socinus merely to assert this; he ought to confirm it by some example in which what was only heard in a vision is, in no way seen, yet is said, taken strictly, to have been seen. So the word "to see" resists this interpretation of our opponents as far as it can. By it the Evangelist would not have been using the word "seen" rashly, and contrary to his own usage and that of all the sacred writers and of human speech.

units.la: XXXVI. Deinde, amabo te, desolatio, vastatio, rejectio populi Iudaici est ne gloria Christi? Videre desolationem & vastationem gentis Iudaicae, est ne videre gloriam Christi? Quid est magis oppositum gloriae, quam desolatio, vastatio, rejectio? At ista desolatio est gloriosa punitio inimicorum Christi. Primùm non commemoratur tanquam punitio, sed tanquam temporis, quo duratura erat Iudaeorum induratio & incredulitas, circunstantia & declaratio. Nihil enim aliud petit prophetae interrogatio, usquequo Domine? Nihil aliud exprimit Domini responsio, donec desolentur civitates, &c. Deinde si spectatur ut punitio, quis autor illius punitionis ex textu Esaiae colligi potest, nisi ille Dominus qui eam revelabat? quod peccatum, nisi illius non agnitio, illi non habita fides? Si igitur punitio ista gloria est, utique gloria est illius Domini qui sese ostendebat prophetae, non autem alterius, quantum quidem ex verbis Esaiae intelligi potest. Aut igitur non est gloria Christi, aut Christus est ille Dominus quem Esaias vidit.
units.tr: XXXVI. Next, I ask you, is the desolation, devastation and rejection of the Jewish people really the glory of Christ? Is seeing the desolation and devastation of the Jewish nation the same as seeing the glory of Christ? What is more opposed to glory than desolation, devastation and rejection? Yet this desolation is "a glorious punishment of the enemies of Christ." First, it is not mentioned as a punishment, but as a circumstance and declaration of the time during which the hardening and unbelief of the Jews was to last. For the prophet's question, "How long, Lord?", seeks nothing else, and the Lord's answer, "until the cities are laid waste," etc., expresses nothing else. Second, if it is viewed as a punishment, what author of that punishment can be inferred from the text of Isaiah, except that Lord who revealed it? And what sin, except their not recognising him and not giving him faith? If therefore that punishment is a glory, it is certainly the glory of that Lord who showed himself to the prophet, and not of another, at least as far as can be understood from the words of Isaiah. Either therefore it is not the glory of Christ, or Christ is that Lord whom Isaiah saw.

units.la: XXXVII. Quod si desolatio ista & vastatio, punitio est contemptus Christi, ex quibus prophetae verbis id colligitur? Annon ex eo quod, ut dicit Socinus, post mentionem factam futura caecitatis & indurationis Iudaorum in Christionen agnoscendo & amplectendo praedicitur ista desolatio? unde verò colligitur in versibus antecedentibus factam esse mentionem cæcitatis Iudæorum in Christo non agnoscendo, si Christus non est ille Dominus, qui se tanquam fidei & conuersionis obiectum videndum & agnoscendum præbebat? Quis verborum audiendi, videndi, intelligendi accusatiuus subaudiri debet in verbis Domini sese magnificè reuelantis, audiendo audite, & ne intelligatis: & videndo videte, neque cognoscatis? Profectò nullus ex Prophetæ verbis subintelligi potest, præter illum ipsum Dominum, qui sese audiendum & videndum exhibebat: neque negari potest quin is accusatiuus subintelligi debeat, & puniti sint Iudæi propterea quod non habuerunt fidem illi Domino qui Esaiæ apparuit. Si in versibus antecedentibus de Christo agitur tanquam de fidei & conuersionis obiecto, cur in illis potius non agnoscunt Christi gloriam, quàm in hac Iudæorum vastatione? non potest enim sic considerari, quin spectetur vt Dominus templi & populi Iudaici, qui non agnosci pertinaciter à subditis sine grandi & inexpiabili scelere non potest, alioqui peccati Iudæorum gravitas non ex Chris-ti, sed ex Dei, cuius seruus erat, dignitate æstimanda esset.
units.tr: XXXVII. But if this desolation and devastation is a punishment for contempt of Christ, from what words of the prophet is that inferred? Is it not from the fact that, as Socinus says, "after mention has been made of the future blindness and hardening of the Jews in not recognising and embracing Christ, this desolation is foretold"? But from where is it inferred that in the preceding verses mention was made of the blindness of the Jews in not recognising Christ, if Christ is not that Lord who presented himself as the object of faith and conversion, to be seen and recognised? What accusative of the verbs "to hear", "to see" and "to understand" must be understood in the words of the Lord who reveals himself so majestically: "Hearing, hear, and do not understand; and seeing, see, and do not know"?
