Surely no accusative can be understood from the prophet's words except that very Lord who showed himself to be heard and seen; nor can it be denied that this accusative must be understood, and that the Jews were punished precisely because they did not have faith in that Lord who appeared to Isaiah. If in the preceding verses Christ is spoken of as the object of faith and conversion, why are they not rather to recognise the glory of Christ in those verses than in this devastation of the Jews? For it cannot be viewed in such a way that it is not seen as the Lord of the temple and of the Jewish people, who cannot be stubbornly refused recognition by his subjects without a great and unatoning crime. Otherwise the gravity of the Jews' sin would have to be judged not from the dignity of Christ, but from the dignity of God, whose servant he was.

units.la: XXXVIII. Sit ergo ista vastatio & desolatio punitio Iudæorum ob fidem non habitam Christo, Num propterea dici potest Christi gloria? Num possunt Aduersarij locum proferre in quo per gloriam Dei aut Christi nihil significatum sit, nisi vastatio & desolatio hostium? Quis ferat dicentem in inferis conspectum iri gloriam Christi, & quidem maximè? illic enim maximè punientur increduli & contumaces. Quousque abutentur pro libitu Aduersarij verbis & phrasibus Scripturæ sacræ?
units.tr: XXXVIII. Grant then that this devastation and desolation is the punishment of the Jews for not having faith in Christ. Can it on that account be called the glory of Christ? Can the opponents produce a passage in which the glory of God or of Christ means nothing but the devastation and desolation of enemies? Who could bear someone saying that the glory of Christ will be seen in hell, and above all there? For it is there that unbelievers and the obstinate will be most severely punished. How far will our opponents go in twisting the words and phrases of Holy Scripture to suit their whim?

units.la: XXXIX. Quid quod ista Iudæorum vastatio conjuncta est cum horribili contemptu Christi, & blasphemijs execrandis, quibus eum, quantum in ipsis est, contumeliosè dilacerant, & summa ignominia afficiunt? videre gloriam Christi, est ne talem vastationem videre? Num prudentissimus Euangelista præter suum & aliorum sacrorum autorum morem sic visus fuisset phrasi videre gloriam Christi, quasi ænigmata potius quàm historiam scriberet, & decipere potius lectores suos quam docere studeret? Nonne enim & verba Euangelistæ, Hæc dixit Esaias cum vidit gloriam Iesu, & Esaiæ cum dicit, se eo loco vidisse Dominum sedentem super solio excelso, lectoris animum præiudicijs vacuum statim occupant, nec sinunt ab illa visione gloriæ Domini divertere ad vastationem Judæorum non visam ab Esaia, sed auditam, ac con-tumeliis iactis in Christum & contemptu eius gloriæ ubique aspe-ctu horrendam & detestandam, ut eam pro gloria Christi, eiusque auditionem pro visione gloriæ Christi, non sine stupenda quadam cæcitate, accipiat.
units.tr: XXXIX. What of the fact that this devastation of the Jews is bound up with a dreadful contempt for Christ and with execrable blasphemies, by which, as far as they can, they tear him apart with insults and load him with the utmost disgrace? Is that to see the glory of Christ, to see such a devastation? Would the most careful evangelist, against his own custom and that of the other sacred writers, have used the phrase to see the glory of Christ as if he were writing riddles rather than history, and were more eager to deceive his readers than to teach them? For the words of the evangelist, Isaiah said these things when he saw the glory of Jesus, and Isaiah's statement that in that place he saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne, immediately fill the mind of a reader free of prejudice, and do not allow him to turn from that vision of the glory of the Lord to the devastation of the Jews. That devastation was not seen by Isaiah but heard of, and it is, with its insults hurled at Christ and its contempt for his glory, everywhere terrible and detestable to behold. Yet our opponents, with a certain astonishing blindness, take it as the glory of Christ, and the hearing of it as the seeing of the glory of Christ.

units.la: XL. Ad verba Euangelistæ & Prophetæ accedit natura gloriæ Christi per ipsummet Judæis revelatæ, quæ posita non fuit in vastatione, desolatione, reiectione, punitione, sed in rebus contrariis, lenitate, mansuetudine, patientia, charitate, misericordia, clementia, liberatione à peccatis & pœnis peccatorum, potentia in fugandis Diabolis, ægris sanandis, mortuis ad vitam revocandis, &c. quam gloriam & Judæi non agnoverunt, & qui agnoscunt in desolatione hominum non collocant. Certè, præ-ter Adversarios, nemo est qui, cùm nominari audit gloriam Christi, vastationem & desolationem Judæorum cogitet. Christus enim non venit ut judicaret mundum, sed ut mundus servaretur per eum, non ut perderet Judæos, sed ut servaret quod perierat. Itaque Jacobum & Johannem petentes Samaritanorum, qui eum non receperant, punitionem obiurgavit dicens, nescitis qualis spiritus vos estis. Filius enim hominis non venit ut perderet animas hominum, sed ut servaret: Idemque Christus super Hierusalem fleuit futuram eius vastationem cogitans.
units.tr: XL. To the words of the evangelist and the prophet is added the nature of the glory of Christ, revealed to the Jews themselves. That glory did not lie in devastation, desolation, rejection or punishment, but in the opposite things: gentleness, meekness, patience, love, mercy, clemency, deliverance from sins and from the punishments of sins, power in putting demons to flight, healing the sick, raising the dead to life, and so on. The Jews did not recognise this glory, and those who do recognise it do not locate it in the desolation of men. Certainly, apart from our opponents, no one hearing the glory of Christ named thinks of the devastation and desolation of the Jews. For Christ did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him; not to destroy the Jews, but to save what had perished. So when James and John asked for punishment on the Samaritans who had not received him, he rebuked them, saying: You do not know what manner of spirit you are of. For the Son of man came not to destroy men's lives, but to save them. And Christ likewise wept over Jerusalem, thinking of its coming devastation.

units.la: XLI. Adhæc, vastatio ista & desolatio Judæorum non dicitur gloria Christi ab Adversarijs, nisi quatenus est punitio gloriosa Christo. Non potest autem dici gloriosa Christo, nisi quia, aut à Christo inflicta est, aut propter Christum. Priore respectu considerari hoc loco nihil est quod juvat. Fac tamen sic considerari, gloriosa est punitio infligenti quatenus eius, aut potentiæ, aut iustitiæ effectum illustre est. Potentiæ Christi, (præsertim divina essentia non prædixi, qualem sibi fingunt Adversa-rij) documentum illustre non est vastatio & desolatio Judææ, à Romanis profecta, numero viribus peritia militari potentioribus, quique Judæos, iam antequam veniret Christus, sibi subjecerant armis. Iustitia quoque Christi in ea reiectione & vastatione, neque celebratur uspiam ab Apostolis, quod sciam, neque ita aperta est, quin cùm reiectionem Judæorum & vocationem gen-tium Apostolus attentè consideraret, exclamet, O profunditatem divitiarum sapientiæ & cognitionis Dei! quam inscrutabilia sunt eius iudicia, & imperuestigabiles viae eius! Non sunt autem iudicia inscrutabilia in quibus iustitia gloriosè conspicua elucet. Posteriore respectu ut gloriosa Christo vastatio illa nobis appareat, primum spectanda est ut punitio, deinde inquirendum est in causam meritoriam illius punitionis, sive non agnitio Christi, quo comperto rursus considerandum est, an Christi non agnitio merita sit tantam poenam, quia est peccatum aduersus Deum, an quia est peccatum aduersus Christum: si hoc posterius agnoscitur, inde tandem deuenitur in cognitionem gloriæ Christi, ex magnitudine peccati aliquomodo æstimandæ. Sed quis unquam, quia vidit unum ex quo per multas ambages & consequentias alterum quoddam deduci potest, hoc alterum vidisse dictus est, præsertim cum hoc in illo non continetur? potest videri desolatio nec tamen videri ut punitio, potest videri punitio, nec tamen videri crimen ob quod punitio irrogatur, potest crimen videri, nec tamen videri gloria eius in quod crimen commissum est. Sed vereor ne ineptus videar, qui tamdiu immoror in refutanda tam inepta responsione. Vnum tantùm addam videre gloriam Christi singulare Dei beneficium esse: optare ut gloria Christi sit diuturna, immò æterna, officium esse hominis Christiani. Absit tamen ut indurationem & desolationem Iudæorum, vel videre lætemur, vel esse perpetuam optemus.
units.tr: XLI. Moreover, this devastation and desolation of the Jews is called by our opponents the glory of Christ only in so far as it is a punishment glorious to Christ. But it cannot be called glorious to Christ unless it was either inflicted by Christ or inflicted on account of Christ. In the first respect, nothing that helps our case can be considered here. But suppose it is considered in this way: a punishment is glorious to the one who inflicts it insofar as it is a distinguished effect of his power or of his justice. The devastation and desolation of Judea, brought about by the Romans, who were superior to the Jews in numbers, strength and military skill, and who had already subjected the Jews by arms before Christ came, is not a distinguished proof of the power of Christ (least of all of the divine essence, which our opponents imagine for him, which I have not described). Nor, so far as I know, is the justice of Christ celebrated anywhere by the apostles in that rejection and devastation, nor is it so manifest that when the Apostle carefully considers the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, he does not cry out: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! But judgments in which justice shines forth gloriously are not unsearchable. In the second respect, for that devastation to appear to us as glorious to Christ, it must first be regarded as a punishment; then one must inquire into the meritorious cause of that punishment, namely the non-recognition of Christ. Once that is found, it must again be considered whether the non-recognition of Christ deserved so great a punishment because it is a sin against God, or because it is a sin against Christ. If the latter is acknowledged, then at last we arrive at knowledge of the glory of Christ, to be estimated in some measure from the magnitude of the sin. But who has ever been said to have seen a second thing merely because he saw one thing from which, through many detours and consequences, the other can be deduced, especially when the second is not contained in the first? A desolation may be seen without being seen as a punishment; a punishment may be seen without the crime for which it is inflicted being seen; a crime may be seen without its glory, against which the crime was committed, being seen. But I fear I may seem foolish for lingering so long in refuting so foolish a reply. I will add only this: to see the glory of Christ is a singular benefit of God, and it is the duty of a Christian man to wish that the glory of Christ be lasting, indeed eternal. Far be it from us, however, either to rejoice in seeing the hardening and desolation of the Jews, or to wish them perpetual.

units.la: XLII. Propior est Christi gloriæ vocatio gentium, Sed eam prædici in verf. 12. eumque versum per parenthesin legi debere, unde habet Socinus? parenthesi certè conjunctio & repugnat, necnon series orationis.
units.tr: XLII. Closer to the glory of Christ is the calling of the Gentiles. But Socinus says that this is foretold in verse 12, and that this verse should be read in parentheses. Where does he get that? The conjunction certainly does not allow a parenthesis, and neither does the sequence of the discourse.

units.la: In verbis autem prophetæ gentium aut vocationis gentium, neque vola neque vestigium vllum apparet, aut ab interpretibus obseruatur. Nam, neque multiplicari est vocari ad communionem Christi, & [?]עזובה derelicta est gens Iudaica à Deo deserta, de qua sola in verbis præcedentibus & sequentibus agi manifestum est. Quanquam multi vertere malunt vastitatem, desolationem, derelictionem, &c. alius multiplicatio, vel secundum durationem, vel secundum numerum, vel secundum magnitudinem prædicitur. Munsterus, Et Dominus elongabit homines, eritque multo (tempore) derelictio in medio terra. Vatablus, longissimè autem ablegabit Dominus homines, eritque desolatio multa in terra. Tremell. & Iun. & procul amovente Iehova hominem quemque, maxima sit ipsa derelictio in ista terra. Alij iudem satis multi, quos breuitatis causa omitto.
units.tr: In the words of the prophet, however, there appears no trace or vestige of the Gentiles or of their calling, nor do the interpreters observe any. For to be multiplied does not mean to be called into communion with Christ, and [עזובה] desolate is the Jewish nation forsaken by God, and it is clear that it is this alone that is spoken of in the preceding and following words. Yet many prefer to render it waste, desolation, forsaking, etc., and another multiplication is foretold either with respect to duration, or number, or magnitude. Münster: And the Lord will remove men far away, and there will be a long (time) forsaking in the midst of the land. Vatablus: But the Lord will banish men far away, and there will be great desolation in the land. Tremellius and Junius: And with Jehovah removing every man far off, that very forsaking will be greatest in this land. Many others too, whom I omit for the sake of brevity.

units.la: XLIII. Restitutio populi Iudaici in pristinum, atque adeo meliorem statum, an praedicatur versu 13. dubitari potest; varie enim ab interpretibus redditur & exponitur. Si praedicitur, id sic ita obscure, ut qualis futura, & quam [illegible, ~4 letters] habitura sit ad Christum ex verbis prophetae colligi nequeat. At per agnitionem Christi Iudais obuentura est. Id in eo versu non dicitur, neque excludi potest ex verbis prophetae, si Dominus qui ei apparuit Christus non est. Deinde, num praedicere restitutionem Iudaorum per Christi agnitionem illis obuenturam, est videre gloriam Christi? Vno verbo cum locutio ista, gloria Christi, cum phrasis, videre gloriam Christi, in Scriptura occurrit, nunquam accipi debet de vastatione aut restitutione populi Iudaici. Itaque nouam & inusitatam isti phrasi in Scriptura satis frequenti, significationem pro libitu affingunt Aduersarij: quod fideles & religiosos interpretes minime decet.
units.tr: XLIII. Whether the restoration of the Jewish people to their former and indeed better state is foretold in verse 13 may be doubted, for the interpreters render and explain it in various ways. If it is foretold, it is so obscurely that what it will be like, and what [illegible, about four letters] it will have with respect to Christ, cannot be gathered from the words of the prophet. But it will come to the Jews through the recognition of Christ. That is not said in that verse, nor can it be drawn from the words of the prophet, unless the Lord who appeared to him is Christ. Next, is to foretell the restoration of the Jews, which is to come to them through the recognition of Christ, the same as seeing the glory of Christ? In a word, since the expression the glory of Christ, and the phrase to see the glory of Christ, occur in Scripture, they must never be taken to refer to the devastation or restoration of the Jewish people. Therefore our opponents, at their pleasure, attach a new and unusual meaning to this phrase, which occurs quite often in Scripture; something that faithful and religious interpreters ought by no means to do.

units.la: XLIV. Adde quod nullo modo intelligi posset, quorsum testimonijs Esaiae subjunxisset Euangelista, Hac Esaiam dixisse cum vidit gloriam Christi, aut quid ista obseruatio faceret ad propositum. Nam neque valet ad locum designandum unde petitum est testimonium, neque ad firmandum argumentum Apostoli. In istis enim versibus aliquid praedici quod ad gloriam Christi pertinet, non aliunde colligunt Aduersarij, quam ex versibus antecedentibus, in quibus praedici caecitatem & duritiem cordis Iudaeorum in fide Christo adhibenda constat ex Apostolo. Denique desolati sunt Iudaei propter non agnitam gloriam Christi, & restituentur per agnitionem gloriae Christi. Itaque aliud est Christi gloria, aliud illa vel desolatio vel restitutio. Itaque veniamus ad tertiam Responsionem.
units.tr: XLIV. Add that it could in no way be understood why the evangelist would have appended to the testimony from Isaiah, Isaiah said these things when he saw the glory of Christ, or what that remark would contribute to his purpose. For it serves neither to designate the place from which the testimony was taken, nor to confirm the Apostle's argument. Our opponents do not gather from those verses that anything is foretold which pertains to the glory of Christ, except from the preceding verses, in which, according to the Apostle, it is plain that the blindness and hardness of heart of the Jews in regard to faith in Christ is foretold. Finally, the Jews have been desolated because the glory of Christ was not recognised, and they will be restored through the recognition of the glory of Christ. Therefore the glory of Christ is one thing, and that desolation or restoration is another. So let us come to the third reply.

units.la: XLV. Dominus[?] praeterea Aduersarius, inquit Socinus, Iohan-nem locutum fuisse de gloria in visione illa Esaiae conspecta. Non tamen ex hoc concludere poterunt, Christum esse illum Dominum seu Iehovam, quem Esaias tunc se vidisse ait. Quam igitur propositionem argumenti nostri negat? Num majorem, ille cuius gloriam Esaias vidit initio cap. vi. est ille Dominus seu Iehova quem vidit? alium igitur nobis in visione illa magnifica ostendat, cuius gloriam Esaias viderit. Nullum certe alium animaduerto. Num minorem, Atqui Christus est ille cuius gloriam Esaias vidit initio cap. vi. Eam hac responsione aperte concedit. Quid igitur superest, nisi ut admittat conclusionem?
units.tr: XLV. Moreover, the Adversary, says Socinus, has John speaking of the glory seen in that vision of Isaiah. Yet they will not be able to conclude from this that Christ is that Lord or Jehovah whom Isaiah says he then saw. Which premise of our argument, then, does he deny? Is it the major: that he whose glory Isaiah saw at the beginning of chapter 6 is the Lord or Jehovah whom he saw? Then let him show us some other in that magnificent vision whose glory Isaiah saw. I certainly notice no other. Is it the minor: But Christ is he whose glory Isaiah saw at the beginning of chapter 6? He plainly concedes this in his reply. What then remains, except that he admit the conclusion?

units.la: XLVI. Subjicit tamen aliquid quod ad infirmationem majoris spectare videtur, praesertim, addit, tum aliud sit videre gloriam alicuius, aliud vero aliquem videre, & Iohannes dicat Esaiam non quidem ipsum Christum vidisse, sed gloriam eius. Id vero non fuit sine aliquo exemplo affirmandum. Nullus enim occurrit locus in quo dicatur videri gloria eius qui non videtur. Est enim gloria vel res, vel rei opinio, vel prædicatio. Opinio & prædicatio hoc loco intelligi non possunt. Res autem quid est, nisi pondus, magnitudo, splendor pulchritudinis aut virtutis alicuius, qui si nullomodo est aut videtur, qui videtur eius magnitudo aut splendor? Erit gloria absque glorioso, hoc est, accidens absque subjecto.
units.tr: XLVI. He adds, however, something that seems to bear on weakening the major premise, especially since, he adds, it is one thing to see someone's glory and another to see someone, and John says that Isaiah saw not Christ himself but his glory. But this could not be asserted without some precedent. For no passage occurs in which someone is said to see the glory of one who is not seen. Glory is either a thing, or an opinion of a thing, or a proclamation. Opinion and proclamation cannot be understood here. But what is a thing, if not the weight, greatness, or splendour of someone's beauty or virtue? If that someone is in no way present or visible, whose greatness or splendour is seen? It would be glory without a glorious one, that is, an accident without a subject.

units.la: XLVII. Addit rursus, Iam in illa Dei unius gloria, quam Esaias vidit, Christi quoque gloria continetur, propter quam causam tunc Christi gloriam vidisse à Iohanne dicitur: non autem propterea quod Christus sit ille Deus. Atqui primum ea causa nulla est. Quis enim credat Apostolum inductum esse ut hoc diceret mero sophismate vel paralogismo, Esaias vidit gloriam Dei. Christi gloria continetur in gloria Dei. Ergo Esaias vidit gloriam Christi. Vel, Qui videt continens videt id quod continetur. Gloria Dei continet gloriam Christi. Ergo qui videt gloriam Dei videt gloriam Christi. Prior syllogismus constat ex quatuor terminis, posterioris major falsa est. Num fit verisimile sic ratiocinatum fuisse Apostolum, ac quia Esaias vidit gloriam Dei, & in gloria Dei continetur gloria Christi, collegisse Esaiam vidisse gloriam Christi?
units.tr: XLVII. He adds again, Now in that glory of the one God which Isaiah saw, the glory of Christ is also contained, and for this reason it is said by John that he then saw the glory of Christ, but not because Christ is that God. But first, there is no such reason. For who would believe that the Apostle was led to say this by a mere sophism or paralogism: Isaiah saw the glory of God; the glory of Christ is contained in the glory of God; therefore Isaiah saw the glory of Christ? Or: He who sees what contains, sees what is contained; the glory of God contains the glory of Christ; therefore he who sees the glory of God sees the glory of Christ? The first syllogism has four terms, and the major of the second is false. Is it likely that the Apostle reasoned in this way, that because Isaiah saw the glory of God, and the glory of Christ is contained in the glory of God, he therefore concluded that Isaiah saw the glory of Christ?

units.la: XLVIII. Deinde ut se habet gloria Christi ad gloriam illius Domini, sic se habet Christus ad illum Dominum. Si igitur gloria Christi continebatur in gloria illius Domini, Christus continebatur in illo Domino, cur igitur non vult Socinus Christum quia continebatur in Domino illo quem vidit Esaias, pariter visum ab Esaia fuisse?
units.tr: XLVIII. Again, as the glory of Christ stands to the glory of that Lord, so Christ stands to that Lord. If therefore the glory of Christ was contained in the glory of that Lord, then Christ was contained in that Lord. Why then does Socinus not want Christ, because he was contained in the Lord whom Isaiah saw, to have been equally seen by Isaiah?

units.la: XLIX. Tum in Domini illius gloria ita continebatur Christi gloria, ut, aut Domini illius gloria sola Esaiæ appareret, lateret gloria Christi; aut lateret Domini illius gloria, sola Christi conspicua esset; aut appareret simul utraque. Si primum, solam Domini illius gloriam Esaias vidit, non vidit gloriam Christi: quod contra Apostolum dicitur. Si secundum, non vidit Domini il-lius gloriam, sed solam Christi: quod cum visione non congruit. Si tertium, utraque illa gloria in visione apparet distincte, id quod experientiae repugnat. Non potest enim in magnifica illa visione distingui gloria Christi à gloria illius Domini quem Esaias videbat; ac quàm vanus est qui ap-paret, tam gloria quae apparet, unius videtur esse. Certè nihil vidisse Esaias memoratur praeter Dominum sedentem, solium super quo Dominus sedebat, fimbrias Domini, Seraphim, templum, altare, fumum, prunas, forcipes. Ostendant nobis in harum rerum una vel pluribus contentam illam gloriam Christi, quam ab Esaia conspectam fuisse testis est Iohannes.
units.tr: XLIX. Further, the glory of Christ was contained in the glory of that Lord in one of three ways: either the glory of that Lord alone appeared to Isaiah and the glory of Christ lay hidden; or the glory of that Lord lay hidden and the glory of Christ alone was visible; or both appeared at once. If the first, Isaiah saw only the glory of that Lord and did not see the glory of Christ, which is contrary to what the Apostle says. If the second, he did not see the glory of that Lord but only that of Christ, which does not agree with the vision. If the third, both glories appear distinctly in the vision, which is contrary to experience. For in that magnificent vision the glory of Christ cannot be distinguished from the glory of that Lord whom Isaiah was seeing; and as empty as the one who appears, so the glory that appears seems to belong to one only. Certainly Isaiah is recorded as having seen nothing but the Lord sitting, the throne on which the Lord sat, the hem of the Lord's robe, the Seraphim, the temple, the altar, the smoke, the coals, the tongs. Let them show us that glory of Christ, which John witnesses was seen by Isaiah, contained in one or several of these things.

units.la: L. Audiuit etiam (at non vidit: nam vox non videtur) clamantes Seraphim, Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus exercituum, plena est omnis terra gloria eius. Num in hoc clamore contineri volunt gloriam Christi, quam vidisse prophetam confitentur? Certè in extrema illius parte eam collocare videtur Socinus, cum eam dicit, in verbis in visione ipsa ab Esaia auditis aperte commemorari. Dicitur enim, inquit, in illis, plenam esse omnem terram Iehovae seu unius illius Dei gloriâ. Hoc enim tunc venerat fe-stum est, quando Christus primum Israelis populo apparuit, & deinde praedicatus est gentibus per universum orbem. At non profitetur Esaias se vidisse omnem terram plenam gloria Domini, sed id Seraphim clamasse, quae duo quantum differant nemo non videt. Deinde Deus Pater non apparuit Israelis populo, neque praedicatus est gentibus, nisi quia Filius apparuit, Filius praedicatus est, nec gloria eius repleuit omnem terram, nisi quia gloria Filij in omnem terram pervenit. Itaque potius continetur gloria Patris in gloria Filij, quàm contrà, & potius videtur gloria Patris quia videtur gloria Filij, quàm contrà.
units.tr: L. He also heard (but did not see, for a voice is not seen) the Seraphim crying out, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. Do they want the glory of Christ, which they confess the prophet saw, to be contained in this cry? Certainly Socinus seems to place it in the last part of that cry, when he says that it is plainly recorded in the words heard by Isaiah in the vision itself. For it is said in them, he says, that the whole earth is full of the glory of Jehovah, or of that one God. For this was fulfilled when Christ first appeared to the people of Israel, and then was preached to the Gentiles throughout the whole world. But Isaiah does not profess that he saw the whole earth full of the glory of the Lord, but that the Seraphim cried this out; and how much these two differ, no one fails to see. Furthermore, God the Father did not appear to the people of Israel, nor was he preached to the Gentiles, except that the Son appeared and the Son was preached; nor did his glory fill the whole earth, except that the glory of the Son reached the whole earth. Thus the glory of the Father is rather contained in the glory of the Son than the reverse, and the glory of the Father is seen rather because the glory of the Son is seen than the reverse.

units.la: L I. Porrò hinc sequitur, Esaiam vidisse gloriam Dei revelandam per Christum. Id quod etiam Socinus diserte affirmat. Intelligendum enim est, inquit, Esaiae, in visione illa, non praesentem quidem Dei gloriam, sed futuram representatam fuisse. Inde sequitur, Deum non apparuisse Esaiae, nisi, quia apparuit ei Christus, Esaiam non conspexisse gloriam Dei, nisi quia conspexit gloriam Christi. Non enim futurum erat, ut Deus aliter; videretur quàm videndo Christo, aut gloria eius aliter videretur quàm videndo gloriam Christi. Philippe, inquit ipse Christus, qui vidit me vidit Patrem, & quomodo tu dicis ostende nobis Patrem? Itaque fatetur Socinus, non modò, cognito Christo, cognosci Patrem, sed non nisi per Christi cognitionem ad Patris cognitionem perueniri.
units.tr: LI. Further, it follows from this that Isaiah saw the glory of God to be revealed through Christ. Socinus himself affirms this expressly. For it must be understood, he says, that in that vision of Isaiah it was not the present glory of God but the future glory that was represented. It follows that God did not appear to Isaiah except because Christ appeared to him; and that Isaiah did not behold the glory of God except because he beheld the glory of Christ. For it was not going to happen that God would be seen otherwise than by seeing Christ, or that his glory would be seen otherwise than by seeing the glory of Christ. Philip, says Christ himself, he who has seen me has seen the Father; and how do you say, show us the Father? Thus Socinus confesses that not only, once Christ is known, is the Father known, but one does not come to the knowledge of the Father except through the knowledge of Christ.

units.la: Resp. ad Arg. 5. classf. 3: Vvjeki.
units.tr: Answer to Argument 5, class 3: Vvjeki.

units.la: LII. Adde quod aliud est nosse omnem terram plenam esse gloria Dei, aliud gloriam illam Dei qua plena est omnis terra videre. Aliud est praedicere omnem terram fore plenam gloria Christi, aliud praedicere quae & qualis gloria futura sit. Prius in Prophetam cadit, non posterius. Quid quod non fit mentio illius gloriae, nisi quatenus est gloria Domini, hoc est, Iehouae. Si igitur Christus non est Dominus Iehoua, non fit mentio gloriae Christi. Si contingit gloriam illam, aut eandem Christi gloriam esse, aut eam continere, id, si Christus non est Dominus quem Esaias vidit, non est de visione Esaiae: Non enim eam gloriam Esaias vidit sub eo respectu. Vidit eam vt est gloria Dei, non autem vt est gloria Christi. Id autem non est gloriam Christi videre, & de eo loqui.
units.tr: LII. Add to this that it is one thing to know that the whole earth is full of the glory of God, and another to see that glory of God with which the whole earth is full. It is one thing to foretell that the whole earth will be full of the glory of Christ, and another to foretell what and of what kind that glory will be. The former falls to the Prophet, the latter does not. Moreover, there is no mention of that glory except insofar as it is the glory of the Lord, that is, of Jehovah. If therefore Christ is not the Lord Jehovah, there is no mention of the glory of Christ. If it happens that that glory is either the same as the glory of Christ or contains it, this, if Christ is not the Lord whom Isaiah saw, is not about Isaiah's vision: for Isaiah did not see that glory under that aspect. He saw it as the glory of God, not as the glory of Christ. But to see the glory of Christ and to speak about him is not that.

units.la: LIII. Hic libenter quaererem, quae sit Christi gloria, quam contineri in Domini gloria revelata & posita ob oculos Esaiae volunt Adversarij? Estne potentia, authoritas, maiestas, pulchritudo, dignitas, etiam religiosè, atque in templo, colenda? Ad talem gloriam revelandam nihil potuit esse visione illa Domini super solio excelso in ipso templo sedentis accommodatius. Sed neque illa videri potuit non viso Christo, neque repraesentari non repraesentato Christo. Itaque Christus aut fuit ille Dominus qui Esaiae se videndum praebuit, aut, quod maius est, per eum fuit repraesentatus. Estne mirabilis illa sanctitas, qua Christus & in se sanctus est & nos sanctificat? Ea non est Esaiae representata, nisi clamore Seraphim, Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus exercituum, in quo de nullius, nisi Domini seu Iehouae exercituum, sanctitate agitur. Ostendant nobis Adversarii, quomodo in Iehouae gloria ita contineretur gloria Christi, vt illa visa haec visa fuerit, viso vero Iehoua non sit visus Christus, quàm enim nullus visus est praeter illum Dominum & Seraphim, tam nullius gloria, praeter gloriam Domini illius & Seraphim visa nobis videtur.
units.tr: LIII. Here I would gladly ask what the glory of Christ is, which our adversaries want to be contained in the glory of the Lord revealed and set before the eyes of Isaiah. Is it power, authority, majesty, beauty, dignity, to be worshipped even religiously and in the temple? Nothing could have been more suited to revealing such glory than that vision of the Lord sitting on a high throne in the temple itself. But that glory could be seen neither without seeing Christ, nor represented without Christ being represented. Therefore Christ was either that Lord who presented himself to Isaiah to be seen, or, what is greater, was represented by him. Is it that wonderful holiness by which Christ is both holy in himself and sanctifies us? That was represented to Isaiah only by the cry of the Seraphim, Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts, in which the holiness of no one is at issue except the Lord or Jehovah of hosts. Let our adversaries show us how the glory of Christ could be so contained in the glory of Jehovah that, when that was seen, this was seen, yet when Jehovah was seen Christ was not seen. For just as no one was seen except that Lord and the Seraphim, so the glory of no one seems to us to have been seen except the glory of that Lord and of the Seraphim.

units.la: LIV. Quaero etiam quomodo gloria Christi in gloria Iehouae contineretur? Non continebatur, opinor, tanquam in loco vel vase, aut tempore, aut subiecto inhaesionis, aut genere, aut specie vel individuo, aut parte, aut toto, aut materia; aut effecto, continebaturne igitur tanquam in causa efficiente, aut finali? Eo modo tam ipse Christus continebatur in Deo, quam eius gloria in Dei gloria, cur igitur pariter visus non creditur ad Aduersarios, ac ipsius gloria? Deinde, quid est quod priusquam fieret, non sic fuerit in Deo, Deinue gloria? Et, an vila causa dici potest id videri, quod ex ea libere post annos multos proficiscetur? Forte contineri dicitur ob similitudinem, quia gloria Dei ostensa Esaiae simillima erat gloriae Christi, sed ita etiam Deus visus ab Esaia simillimus fuisset Christo. Non minus igitur ipse Christus visus fuisset quam ipsius gloria, quod tamen Socinus & Volkelius negant. Deinde, ut propter similitudinem simile dicatur in simili contineri, alienum est ab vsu loquendi. Tum si gloria Domini illius ita similis fuit gloriae Christi, ut illa vita haec conspecta dicatur, necesse fuit ut illa hanc representaret. Nam alioqui absolute & citra comparationem non potuisset Esaias dici gloriam Christi vidisse, propterea quod similem gloriam vidit. Iam si constituta ob oculos prophetae species gloriae Domini representauit gloriam Christi, quid est cur obiecta Domini species non representauerit similiter Christum? Certe si nulla species, nulla imago gloriae Christi posita fuit ob oculos Prophetae, intelligi non potest, quomodo dicatur ab Apostolo vidisse gloriam Christi. Nulla autem illi ob oculos constituta species legitur, nisi Domini gloriosi. Ea igitur aut representauit Christum, aut quomodo vere & absolute dictus sit ab Apostolo vidisse gloriam Christi intelligi non potest. Itaque posita opinione Aduersariorum magis ad decipiendos lectores, quam ad propositum Apostoli confirmandum valeret obseruatio, Haec dixit Esaias enim vidit gloriam eius. Quis enim existimans, & pronomen eius ad Christum, & verbum vidit ad illustrem illam visionem Esaiae referri, nihilque in ea visione animaduertens praeter gloriosum representamen Domini exercituum, non inducatur vt putet, eundem esse Dominum illum & Christum, praesertim si sit, & praeiudicio vacuus, & Christi, vt decet, adorator?
units.tr: LIV. I ask further how the glory of Christ could be contained in the glory of Jehovah. It was not contained, I suppose, as in a place or vessel, or in a time, or as in a subject of inherence, or as a genus, species or individual, or as a part or whole, or as matter. Was it then contained as an effect, as in an efficient or final cause? In that way Christ himself was contained in God as much as his glory was in God's glory. Why then is it not believed that Christ was seen by Isaiah, just as his glory was? Further, what is the reason that he was not in God, or his glory either, before it came to be? Can a cause be said to be seen in that which proceeds freely from it many years later? Perhaps it is said to be contained by reason of likeness, because the glory of God shown to Isaiah was most like the glory of Christ. But in that case God, too, would have been seen by Isaiah as most like Christ. Therefore Christ himself would have been seen no less than his glory, which Socinus and Volkelius nevertheless deny. Further, that a thing is said to be contained in something like it by reason of likeness is foreign to the usage of language. Moreover, if the glory of that Lord was so like the glory of Christ that the one is said to be beheld in the other, then the one must have represented the other. For otherwise Isaiah could not have been said, absolutely and without comparison, to have seen the glory of Christ, merely because he saw a similar glory. Now if the form of the glory of the Lord, set before the prophet's eyes, represented the glory of Christ, why should the appearance of the Lord set before him not likewise have represented Christ? Certainly, if no form or image of Christ's glory was placed before the prophet's eyes, it cannot be understood how it is said by the Apostle that he saw the glory of Christ. But no form is read as set before his eyes except that of the glorious Lord. Either that form represented Christ, or it cannot be understood how he was truly and absolutely said by the Apostle to have seen the glory of Christ. Therefore, on the opinion of our opponents, the observation that He said these things, for Isaiah saw his glory would serve rather to deceive readers than to confirm the Apostle's point. For who, supposing that the pronoun his refers to Christ and the verb saw to that famous vision of Isaiah, and noticing nothing in that vision but the glorious representation of the Lord of hosts, would not be led to think that this Lord and Christ are the same? Especially if he is free of prejudice and is, as is fitting, a worshipper of Christ.

units.la: LV Hactenus autoritate pugnauimus Apostolici testimonij. Nunc, ea seposita, quid ex visione illa Esaiae colligi possit videamus.
units.tr: LV Hitherto we have argued from the authority of the Apostle's testimony. Now, setting that aside, let us see what can be gathered from that vision of Isaiah.

units.la: deamus. Principiò notanda est temporis circunstantia. In Anno, inquit, quo mortuus est rex Ozias vidi Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum & elevatum, &c. Extincto rege Iudæ umbratili verus Rex apparuit, innuens se tum demum prodituram majestatem suam regiam, cum fuerint de medio reges Iudæ sublati. Itaque & Ozias, & is qui eo sublato sese ostendit Rex appellatur. Sed cur non potius anno quo mortuus est Iotham hæc tam magnifica visio objecta est prophetæ, quam anno quo mortuus est Ozias? Aut cur non est potius alicui prophetæ indulta anno quo vel Ezechias, vel Iosias mortem obiit? Equidem cur selectus fit Ozias nulla mihi ratio succurrit præter istam quam lectori diiudicandam propono. Fuerunt Reges Iudæ typi Christi veri regis Iudæorum, præsertim illi, qui aliquid non commune nec vulgare habuerunt. In eo numero censendus videtur Rex Ozias pius, bellicosus, turrium & propugnaculorum extructor, puteorum effossor, pecora multa habens in deserto, in montibus, in locis planis, necnon agricolas & vinitores, & exercitum numerosissimum, cui vniuerso arma omnis generis paravit clypeos, hastas, galeas, loricas, arcus, fundas, etiam tormenta & machinas bellicas ad eiaculandum sagittas & lapides magnos, quibus rebus nomen sibi maximum comparavit, etiam apud alias gentes: quorum omnium qui non videt spiritualem veritatem in rege Christo reperiri nemo est, opinor, verè Christianus.
units.tr: Let us see. First, the circumstance of time must be noted. "In the year," he says, "that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up," etc. With the king of Judah, who was a mere shadow, dead, the true King appeared, signifying that his royal majesty would be revealed only when the kings of Judah had been taken out of the way. So both Uzziah and the one who showed himself after Uzziah's removal are called King. But why was this so magnificent a vision presented to the prophet in the year that Uzziah died rather than in the year that Jotham died? Or why was it not granted to some prophet in the year that either Hezekiah or Josiah died? Indeed, I can think of no reason why Uzziah was chosen, except that which I put before the reader for judgment. The kings of Judah were types of Christ, the true King of the Jews, especially those who had something not common or ordinary. Among these, King Uzziah seems to deserve a place: pious, warlike, a builder of towers and bulwarks, a digger of wells, having many cattle in the desert, in the hills and on the plains, and also farmers and vinedressers, and a very numerous army, for which he provided all kinds of arms: shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, slings, and also engines and war machines for shooting arrows and great stones. By these things he won for himself the greatest name, even among other nations. Whoever does not see the spiritual truth in these things, as found in the King Christ, is, I suppose, no true Christian.

units.la: LVI.
units.tr: LVI.

units.la: Sed nisi longiùs progrediamur, nondum videmur assecuti mentem Spiritus Sancti. Solus rex Ozias coniungere sacerdotium voluit cum regio munere, ausus adolere incensum super altare thymiamaris. Quod fecit Ozias malè, id Christus fecit optimè: utrumq; enim munus regium & sacerdotale in se suscepit vocatione legitima, sed Iudæis ignota. Restitit Oziæ summus Sacerdos cū reliquis Sacerdotibus, benè: restitit Christo summus sacerdos cum reliquis sacerdotibus, pessimè. Non potuit à malo illo proposito dimoueri Ozias, Nec à bono illo proposito Christus. Percussus est Ozias lepra, plaga immunditiem legalem secum trahente, Percussus est Christus ea plaga, quam ut immundam horrebant Iudæi cruci suffixus, ac, si vulgatam versionem audis, nos putavimus eum quasi leprosum, & percussum à Deo. Ozias pro immundo à Sacerdotibus & populo habitus excommunicatus est, & eiectus è Templo, & domo regia, & aliorum Iudæorum consortio. Christus itidem pro immundo à Sacerdotibus & populo habitus ex communicatus est, ac extra vrbē eiectus à reliquorū Iudaeorum commercio separatus. Ita Rex Ozias desiit dominari Iudaeis, ac cum eis vllum amplius habere commercium: Similiter Rex Iudaeorum Christus in Iudaeos regnare desiit nullum amplius cum eis habens commercium. Interim tamē retinuit Ozias ius regni, quauis illud non exerceret. Christus quoq; retinet ius regni, quauis eo in Iudaeos non vtatur.
units.tr: But unless we advance further, we do not yet seem to have grasped the mind of the Holy Spirit. Only King Uzziah wished to join the priesthood to the royal office, presuming to burn incense upon the altar of incense. What Uzziah did wickedly, Christ did most rightly. For he took upon himself both the royal and the priestly office by lawful calling, though this was unknown to the Jews. The high priest opposed Uzziah with the other priests, rightly; the high priest opposed Christ with the other priests, most wickedly. Uzziah could not be turned from that wicked purpose, nor Christ from that good purpose. Uzziah was struck with leprosy, a plague that brings legal uncleanness with it. Christ was struck with that plague which the Jews dreaded as unclean, being fastened to the cross; and if you hear the Vulgate version, we thought him as a leper, and struck by God. Uzziah, regarded as unclean by the priests and people, was excommunicated and cast out of the Temple, out of the royal house, and out of the company of the other Jews. Christ likewise, regarded as unclean by the priests and people, was excommunicated and cast outside the city, separated from the dealings of the other Jews. So King Uzziah ceased to rule the Jews and to have any further dealings with them. Similarly, Christ, the King of the Jews, ceased to reign over the Jews, having no further dealings with them. Yet in the meantime Uzziah retained the right of kingship, though he did not exercise it. Christ too retains the right of kingship, although he does not use it over the Jews.

units.la: Haec omnia manifestum est competere in Christum seruata proportione inter vmbram & corpus, ac dempto peccato, quod vmbrae est proprium. Sublata igitur vmbra viva imago veritatis sese ostendit Esaiae. Apparuit enim illi vt Rex super solio excelso, necnon vt summus Sacerdos intra templum, quod suffitus fumo impleuit: sed augustiore quam caperet templum maiestate, ita enim fimbriae vestis eius amplae erant, vt eas continere templum vix posset. Addidit congruens typo vaticinium, fore vt suam illam regiam & Sacerdotalem dignitatem ad contemplandum & credendum expositam Iudaei prae nimia caecitate & duritie, neque oculis videant, neque corde intelligant, neque ad ipsum conuertantur vt fiant participes sanationis, quam vt rex & Sacerdos ex altari suo emittit, ac ministerio Seraphim applicat: quo fiet vt reiectus ab illis ipse eos reiiciat à se ac deserat, & procul submoueat, & in manus hostium tradat, nihilque cum illis commercij per multa secula habeat. Sic omnia congruunt inter se, visio, vaticinium, notata typi circunstantia, quae posita interpretatione Aduersariorum quam χίαν[?] inter se habeant non intelligo.
units.tr: It is clear that all these things apply to Christ, with the proportion between shadow and body preserved, and with sin removed, which is proper to the shadow. Therefore, the shadow being taken away, the living image of the truth showed itself to Isaiah. For it appeared to him as a King upon a high throne, and also as the high priest within the temple, which the smoke of incense filled. But its majesty was more august than the temple could hold; for the hem of his garment was so wide that the temple could scarcely contain it. He added a prophecy agreeing with the type: that the Jews, through excessive blindness and hardness, would neither see with their eyes nor understand with their heart, nor turn to him so as to become partakers of the healing which the King and Priest sends forth from his altar and applies by the ministry of the Seraphim. The result would be that he, rejected by them, would in turn reject them, cast them off, and deliver them into the hands of enemies, having no dealings with them for many ages. Thus all things agree among themselves: the vision, the prophecy, and the noted circumstance of the type. I do not understand how these things can have any agreement among themselves on the interpretation of our opponents.

units.la: Vidi, inquit Esaias, Dominum sedentem, &c. Is qui apparuit Esaiae, vel fuit persona Patris separatim à Filio, vel Filius, vel Angelus creatus. Hoc vltimum dici non potest. Nam nec nomina Domini, Regis, יהוה צבאות cadunt in Angelum, nec tanta maiestas, praesertim in Dei templo. Soli Patri & Filio erectus est in templo Dei thronus excelsus, & quidem non alius Patri, alius Filio, sed idem vtrique. Necesse est igitur vt qui Esaiae apparuit, Pater aut Filius fuerit. Non fuit autem Pater, intellige immediatè, & Filio excluso. Id quod probo, 1. Qui hoc loco Esaiae apparuit est ille idem, qui olim patriarchis & Israelitis apparuit, vocaturque יהוה, אלהים, אל[?]. Deus Abrahami, Isaaci & Iacobi.
units.tr: I saw, says Isaiah, the Lord sitting, etc. The one who appeared to Isaiah was either the person of the Father, separate from the Son, or the Son, or a created angel. The last cannot be said. For the names Lord, King, and Jehovah Sabaoth do not fit an angel, nor does such majesty, especially in the house of God. A high throne was set up in the temple of God for the Father and the Son alone, and not one throne for the Father and another for the Son, but the same for both. It is necessary, therefore, that the one who appeared to Isaiah was either the Father or the Son. But it was not the Father, understood immediately and with the Son excluded. This I prove: (1) The one who appeared to Isaiah in this place is the same who formerly appeared to the patriarchs and Israelites, and who is called Jehovah, Elohim, El: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

units.la: Hic autem non fuit Pater separatus à Filio. vocatur enim etiam Angelus, quod nomen tribuitur quidem Filio aliquando, Patri vetò numquam. Hic enim nullo modo, neque naturæ, neque muneris respectu angelus dici potest. ii. Si Pater immediatè sese reuelauit & videndum exhibuit Patriarchis & Prophetis, quomodo verum est, quod dicitur Ioh. 1. 18. Deum nemo vidit vnquam: vnigenitus Filius qui est in sinu Patris ipse enarrauit? Quominus enim hoc ad præsens vel futurum restringatur, obstat aduerbium vnquam. Et Math. 11. 27. Nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius, & cui voluerit filius revelare. & Ioh. 14. 16. Ego sum via veritas & vita nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me? iii. Cur etiam Philippi petentis Patrem sibi immediatè ostendi, petitionem Dominus vt absurdam reiecit Ioh. 14. 9. si Pater separatim à Filio & ostendi potuit, & ostensus est olim prophetis? Cur enim Apostolis, quifuerunt prophetis maiores, vtrumque illud concedi non potuit, vt, & Patrem viderent immediatè in Filio tunc temporis multiplici infirmitate & ignominia circundato, & eunde etiam viderent extra Filium immediatè summa maiestate adorandum, siquidem hoc posterius Esaiæ indultum est? iv. Cur etiam Dominus eam rationem subiecit, quamobrem absurda videri debeat petitio Philippi, quæ pariter, nec videri posse filium quin videatur Pater innuit, nec Patrem quin videatur Filius? Non credis, inquit, me in Patre & Patrem in me esse? Itaque alterum seorsum ab altero videri non posse. v. Euangelium anteponitur legi Heb. 2. 1. quòd hæc per Angelos, illud per Filium angelis præstantiorem promulgari cœpit. Ratio sine dubio optima, sed quæ ad vocationem Esaiæ & Apostolorum accómodata illum his præstare doceret, siquidem Ille patrem immediatè vidisset; Hi Patrem non vidissent nisi mediatè: Ille à Patre missus esset immediatè, Hi tantùm mediatè: Ille Patrem audiuisset loquentem immediatè, Hi tantum loquentè mediatè. Quis tamen nescit Apostolos singulos non Esaia solùm, sed etiam ipso Mose præstantiores fuisse? Nam, si inter natos mulierum nemo surrexerat maior Ioh. Baptista, & tamen minor in regno cœlorum maior illo erat, quis propheta non concedat Apostolis sedentibus super duodecim thronis & iudicantibus duodecim tribus Israelis?
units.tr: Nor was this the Father, separate from the Son. For he is also called the Angel, a name given sometimes to the Son but never to the Father. In no way can he be called an angel, either with respect to his nature or to his office. ii. If the Father immediately revealed himself and let himself be seen by the patriarchs and prophets, how is what is said in John 1:18 true, No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him? The adverb ever rules out restricting this to the present or the future. Likewise Matthew 11:27, No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him, and John 14:6, I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me. iii. Again, when Philip asked that the Father be shown to him immediately, the Lord rejected the request as absurd (John 14:9). Why would he do so, if the Father could be shown separately from the Son, and had in fact been shown to the prophets of old? For why could the Apostles, who were greater than the prophets, not be granted both things: to see the Father immediately in the Son, who at that time was surrounded by manifold weakness and disgrace, and also to see him immediately outside the Son, to be adored in supreme majesty, since this latter privilege was granted to Isaiah? iv. Again, why did the Lord add the reason why Philip's request should seem absurd, a reason which likewise implies that the Son cannot be seen without the Father being seen, nor the Father without the Son being seen? Do you not believe, he said, that I am in the Father and the Father in me? Therefore the one cannot be seen apart from the other. v. The Gospel is placed above the Law (Heb. 2:1), because the latter was announced through angels, the former through the Son, who is superior to the angels. This is certainly an excellent reason, but it would teach, as applied to the calling of Isaiah and the Apostles, that the one was superior to the others only if Isaiah had seen the Father immediately, and they had seen him only mediately; if he had been sent by the Father immediately, and they only mediately; if he had heard the Father speaking immediately, and they only speaking mediately. Yet who does not know that each of the Apostles was superior not only to Isaiah but even to Moses himself? For if, among those born of women, no one had risen greater than John the Baptist, and yet the least in the kingdom of heaven was greater than he (Matt. 11:11), what prophet would not grant that the Apostles, sitting on twelve thrones and judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19:28), were greater?

units.la: LVIII. Huc accedit quod, cum Pater in Scriptura partes Dei perpetuò agat, censetur omni tempore sedere in cœlis in throno maiestatis gloriosus, indeq; omnia gubernare. Itaque mittit semper, nunquam mittitur; Et si quid facit id emisso verbo & spiritu facere credicur. Quare qui in terra apparet, is ab eo missus, eiusque legatus dici potest: eo magis quod constat ipsam Patris personam immediatè non venire cum agitur de negotijs summi momenti. Certè non venit immediatè cum redimendum fuit genus humanum à peccato, à Diabolo, à morte, à lege, nec venient immediatè cùm erunt suscitanda corpora, & universus mundus iudicandus ultimò. Si igitur cum de rebus tantis, de negotijs tam divinis agitur, Pater tamen non venit, non apparet immediatè, quanto minus existimandum est, eum immediatè venisse & apparuisse Esaiæ isto loco, ut id faceret per se, quod neque tanti momenti erat; & per legatum fieri optimè potuit?
units.tr: LVIII. Moreover, since in Scripture the Father always performs the part of God, he is thought to sit in heaven at all times, glorious on the throne of majesty, and from there to govern all things. Thus he always sends and is never sent; and whatever he does, he is believed to do by emitting his Word and Spirit. Therefore the one who appears on earth can be called sent by him and his legate, all the more because it is clear that the person of the Father himself does not come immediately when matters of the highest importance are in hand. Certainly he did not come immediately when the human race had to be redeemed from sin, from the Devil, from death, from the law; nor will he come immediately when bodies are to be raised and the whole world is at last to be judged. If, then, when such great matters, such divine affairs, are in hand, the Father nevertheless does not come or appear immediately, how much less should we think that he came and appeared immediately to Isaiah in that passage, to do by himself what was of no such great moment, when it could very well be done through a legate?

units.la: LIX. Adde quod, ut vaticinium in quod hæc visio desinit, ad tempus prædicationis Christi & Apostolorum pertinet, testibus hoc nostro Euangelista, & ipso eventu; sic ista revelatio gloriæ Dei ad idem tempus referenda est. Id quod & Socinus agnoscit, & ipsa visio clamat: quæ cum talis, tam clara, tam gloriosa semel tantùm, certo tempore, nec ante, nec post, vel ipsi Esaiæ, vel alij prophetæ indulta sit, cum revelatione maximæ & longissimæ populi Iudaici indurationis & vastationis, sine dubio specimen est revelationis illius divinæ omnium illustrissimæ ac clarissimæ, quam sequuta est Iudæorum maxima maximeque diuturna & contumacia, & desolatio. Talis autem est ea, quæ in consummatione seculorum facta est, Dei in carne patefactio quo tempore, ut jam observaui, Pater non apparuit, nisi quia Filius apparuit, non est conspectus, nisi quia Filius est conspectus, non est reiectus à Iudæis, nisi quia Filius est reiectus. Non igitur in hac visione sese Pater immediatè conspiciendum dedit, sed in Filio, quo videndo, & non aliter, videri debuit & potuit Pater.
units.tr: LIX. Add that, just as the prophecy in which this vision ends pertains to the time of the preaching of Christ and the Apostles, as our Evangelist and the event itself bear witness, so this revelation of the glory of God must be referred to the same time. Socinus also acknowledges this, and the vision itself cries it out. Since such a vision, so clear, so glorious, was granted only once, at a fixed time, neither before nor after, either to Isaiah himself or to another prophet, it is without doubt a sign, coinciding with the revelation of the greatest and longest hardening and desolation of the Jewish people, of that most illustrious and clearest divine revelation of all, which was followed by the greatest and most lasting obstinacy and desolation of the Jews. Such is that manifestation of God in the flesh that took place at the consummation of the ages. At that time, as I have already observed, the Father did not appear except because the Son appeared; he was not seen except because the Son was seen; he was not rejected by the Jews except because the Son was rejected. Therefore in this vision the Father did not give himself to be seen immediately, but in the Son; by seeing the Son, and in no other way, the Father ought to be seen and could be seen.

units.la: LX. Sed ipsam visionem expendamus. In ea consideranda sunt eius qui apparuit Nomina, Munera, Beneficia, ministri. Vocatur primò אדני [?] Dominus: quod nomen Christi proprium esse docet Apostolus 1. Cor. 8. 6. & 12. 5. & Eph. 4. 5. Deinde Rex: quod etiam nomen Christo convenire κατ' ἐξοχὴν ac tanquam proprium, & quidem tum cum Dei gloria omnium magnificentissimè revelatur, & Scriptura docet multis locis, & ipse Christus testatur Math. 25. 34. Tandem Iehova Sabaoth, Dominus exercituum: quod nomen ei quoque Regi convenire, qui est גבור מלחמה [?] & [illegible, ~12 letters] & [illegible, ~10 letters]. [?]aes Dei & nostros hostes vicit, alio loco opportuniore Deo dan- te probabimus. Nunc satis sit monuisse, qui id neget, huic refutanda esse argumenta illa omnia, quibus eum Esaiæ apparuisse probamus.
units.tr: LX. But let us weigh the vision itself. In considering it we must note the names, offices, benefits, and ministers of the one who appeared. First he is called Adonai [אדני], Lord, a name which the Apostle teaches is proper to Christ (1 Cor. 8:6; 12:5; Eph. 4:5). Next, King: a name which also belongs to Christ by pre-eminence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], and indeed as though it were his own, especially at the time when the glory of God is most magnificently revealed; Scripture teaches this in many places, and Christ himself bears witness to it (Matt. 25:34). Finally, Jehovah Sabaoth, the Lord of hosts: a name which also belongs to that King who is gibbor milchamah [גבור מלחמה], a mighty man of war, and [illegible], and [illegible]. He conquered the enemies of God and of ourselves; we will prove this in another, more suitable place, with God's help. For now it is enough to have warned that whoever denies this must refute all those arguments by which we prove that he appeared to Isaiah.

units.la: LXI. Nominibus subiungo Munera. Apparet enim Esaiæ hic Dominus, vt Rex & summus Sacerdos simul. De regio munere res clara est: nam & Rex appellatur & sedet in throno sublimi. Sacerdotium colligitur 1. ex eo quod intra templum apparet. Est enim, non regis populi Dei qua rex est, sed Sacerdotis ingredi in templum, hoc est, in loca sancta & sanctissima. 2. ex fimbriis eius, quæ dicuntur replevisse templum. Est enim allusio, non tam ad fimbrias vestis regiæ, de quibus in Scriptura nulla mentio, quam ad fimbrias vestis summi Sacerdotis, quæ describuntur accurate Exod. 28. 33. & 39. 23. & erant admodum amplæ: habebant enim in ambitu multa aurea tintinabula malis punicis pretiosissimis ordine dispositis interjecta, cuius umbræ corpus est in Christo, quem certum est, vt regem & summum Sacerdotem, sedere in domo Dei, hoc est, in sua sublimem, eamque totam implere aureis tintinabulis & malis punicis, id est, pretiosissimis Sacerdotii sui nuntijs & fructibus. Idem enim ipse qui descenderat, ascendit supra omnes cœlos vt impleret omnia, & est omnia in omnibus. Si igitur negari nequit, quin Rex Christus ita sedeat in throno excelso valdè, vt fimbriæ eius impleant templum, nonne id argumento esse debet, Christum esse illum ipsum regem, quem Esaias sic sedentem vidit?
units.tr: LXI. To the names I add the offices. For this Lord appears to Isaiah as King and at the same time as High Priest. The royal office is clear enough: he is called King and sits on a lofty throne. The priesthood is gathered, first, from the fact that he appears within the temple. For it belongs not to a king as king of the people of God, but to a priest, to enter the temple, that is, the holy and most holy places. Second, from his skirts, which are said to have filled the temple. The allusion is not so much to the skirts of a royal garment, of which Scripture makes no mention, as to the skirts of the high priest's garment, which are described accurately in Exodus 28:33 and 39:23, and were quite wide: for around their hem were many golden bells, interspersed with most precious pomegranates arranged in order. The reality of which this is the shadow is in Christ, who is certainly to sit, as King and High Priest, in the house of God, that is, sublime in his own house, and to fill it entirely with golden bells and pomegranates, that is, with the most precious messages and fruits of his priesthood. For the same one who had descended ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things, and is all in all (Eph. 4:10). If, then, it cannot be denied that Christ the King sits so high on the lofty throne that his skirts fill the temple, should this not be an argument that Christ is that very King whom Isaiah saw sitting thus?

units.la: LXII. Tertiò id etiam colligitur ex altari super quo erant prunæ, & fumo quo templum replebatur: fumo, inquam, sacrificij, & suffimenti, huius præcipuè. Nam victimæ, quæ in Atrio sub dio offerebatur, fumus in columnæ morem sursum ferebatur: suffimenti verò fumus, cum exitum non haberet, per loca sancta & loca sanctissima peruagabatur, eaque odore complebat: Hæc enim præsentiam arguebat Sacerdotis in templo sacra peragentis: Non Sacerdotis Leuitici: (nullus enim in illa visione comparet: neque ei locus fuisset in templo, fumo & fimbrijs Domini pleno: & contactus prunæ ex altari sumptæ tollens à Propheta præputium labiorum & iniquitatem, diversum à Leuitico altare arguit: nihil enim tale de prunis altaris legitur in lege.) Ergo Sacerdotis Christi, qui cum sit Rex, etiam in templo, religiosè adorandus, post peractum sacrificium sedens in excelsissimo solio thymiama intercessionis offert, & coelesti sanctuario ministrat teste Apostolo Heb. 8. 1. 2. & Rom. 8. 33. Sic enim post oblatum sacrificium decuit eum Sacerdotem ministrare qui Rex est, iuxta illud Zach. 6. 13. sedebit, & dominabitur super solio suo, & erit Sacerdos super solio suo. Itaque respondentes viginti quatuor Sacerdotum leviticorum ordinibus seniores viginti quatuor, quos ex omni tribu, & lingua, & populo, & natione agnus fecit reges & sacerdotes, coram Dei throno coronati & sedentes in solijs inducuntur Apoc. 4. ac tenentes phialas aureas plenas suffitum Ap. 5. 8.
units.tr: LXII. Thirdly, this is also gathered from the altar upon which there were coals, and from the smoke with which the temple was filled: the smoke, I say, of sacrifice and incense, and especially of incense. For the smoke of the victim, which was offered in the court under the open sky, rose upward in the manner of a column; but the smoke of incense, since it had no outlet, spread through the holy and most holy places and filled them with its odor. For this indicated the presence of the priest performing sacred rites in the temple: not a Levitical priest (for none appears in that vision; nor would there have been room for him in a temple full of smoke and of the skirts of the Lord). And the touching of the prophet's lips with a coal taken from the altar, taking away his uncleanness and iniquity, shows that it was not the Levitical altar, for nothing of the kind is read in the law about the coals of the altar. Therefore it is the priesthood of Christ, who, since he is King, is also to be adored reverently in the temple; after the sacrifice has been completed, sitting on the most lofty throne, he offers the incense of intercession and ministers in the heavenly sanctuary, as the Apostle witnesses (Heb. 8:1-2; Rom. 8:33-34). For thus it was fitting that after the sacrifice was offered, he should minister as priest who is King, according to that saying of Zechariah 6:13, He shall sit and rule upon his throne, and he shall be a priest upon his throne. Accordingly, the twenty-four elders, answering to the twenty-four orders of the Levitical priests, whom the Lamb made kings and priests out of every tribe, and tongue, and people, and nation, are introduced crowned and seated on thrones before the throne of God (Rev. 4), and holding golden vials full of incense (Rev. 5:8).

units.la: LXIII. Muneribus addo Beneficia, & sic argumentor. Is ad quem qui aspicit & conuertitur sanatur, est ille quem Esaias vidit. Christus est is ad quem qui aspicit & conuertitur sanatur. Ergo Christus est ille quem Esaias vidit. Maior probatur 2. argumentis. Primum ducitur à verbis eius quem vidit Esaias, Ne videant oculis, & intelligant corde, & convertantur, & sanè eos: significat enim se paratum sanare quotquot videntes oculis, & corde intelligentes, ad ipsum convertentur. Alterum à specimine illius sanationis edito in Esaia, qui simul ac vidit Dominum, & confessus est immunditiem suam sanatus est vi oblati sacrificij, adhibito instrumento idoneo, per vnum è Seraphim applicata.
units.tr: LXIII. I add miracles to the gifts, and argue thus. He to whom whoever looks and turns is healed is the one whom Isaiah saw. Christ is the one to whom whoever looks and turns is healed. Therefore Christ is the one whom Isaiah saw. The major premise is proved by two arguments. The first is drawn from the words of him whom Isaiah saw: Lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I should heal them. For he signifies that he is ready to heal as many as, seeing with their eyes and understanding with their heart, turn to him. The second is drawn from the example of that healing given in Isaiah, who, as soon as he saw the Lord and confessed his uncleanness, was healed by the power of the sacrifice offered, the suitable instrument being applied by one of the Seraphim.

units.la: LXIV. Beneficijs addo ministros, quorum opera deferuntur, annuntiantur, & applicantur. Quandoquidem enim Dominus sese ostendit paratum ad sanandum eos, qui ad ipsum aspiciunt & conuertuntur, isque ad vim illam inexhaustam sanandi, quae ab eo eiusq; sacrificio & intercessione copiosa manat, hominibus monstrandam, ferendam, applicandam, ministris suis est quos secum, & populo Iudaico videndos & audiendos exhibuit, & populus ille prae excitate [?] & duritia cordis reiecit, consentaneum rationi fuit, ut una cum ipso Domino illi eius ministri Esaiae apparerent. Unde sic argumentor. Si Seraphim supernè Domino astantes comparati sunt ad repraesentandum Christi ministros, beneficium sanationis à peccato & morte, quod ab eius regio Sacerdotio proficiscitur, deferentes, revelantes, applicantes, Dominus ille est Christus. Prius autem verum est. Ergo & posterius. Negabitur antecedens. Id autem multis argumentis ex hac ipsa visione petitis probari potest, nullo refelli.
units.tr: LXIV. To the benefits I add the ministers, by whose work they are brought, announced and applied. For since the Lord showed himself ready to heal those who look to him and turn, and since that inexhaustible power of healing, which flows abundantly from him, his sacrifice and his intercession, was to be shown, carried and applied to men, and he presented it through his ministers, whom he had with him and who were to be seen and heard by the Jewish people, but that people rejected them through their stubbornness and hardness of heart, it was reasonable that those ministers of his should appear to Isaiah together with the Lord himself. Hence I argue thus. If the Seraphim, standing above the Lord, were arranged to represent Christ's ministers, bringing, revealing and applying the benefit of healing from sin and death, which proceeds from his royal priesthood, then that Lord is Christ. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also true. The antecedent will be denied. This, however, can be proved by many arguments drawn from this very vision, and refuted by none.

units.la: LXV. Primum ducitur à nomine Seraphim, quod, si originem spectes, comburentes: si usum Scripturæ, præsteres, seu serpentes urentes significat: quales illi fuerunt, quos Deus misit in populum ob viæ tædium & mannæ fastidium murmurantem, morsu, velut admoto igne, homines comburentes & destruentes. Horum morsibus ut mederetur Moses iussu Dei fecit Saraph, præsterem, eumque perticæ impositit, ut quicunque à præstere morsus suis-set in illum aspiciens sanaretur. Hic Saraph salutaris Seraphim illis perniciosis & lethiferis figura similis, natura diversus, effectu contrarius, typus fuit Christi: quem, ut Moses serpentem extulit in deserto, ita extolli oportuit, ut quisquis credit in eum non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam.
units.tr: LXV. The first is drawn from the name Seraphim, which, if you consider its origin, means "burning ones", but if you consider the usage of Scripture, means "fiery serpents" [saraph], such as those God sent among the people when they murmured at the tedium of the journey and the loathing of manna, burning and destroying men with their bites as if fire had been applied. To heal their bites, Moses, at God's command, made a Saraph, a fiery one, and fixed it to a pole, so that whoever had been bitten by a fiery serpent and looked at it would be healed. This Saraph, the saving Seraph, similar in figure to those deadly and lethal ones, different in nature, contrary in effect, was a type of Christ, whom, as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must he be lifted up, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.

units.la: Constat autem hos Seraphim, qui superne Domino adstabant, perniciosos non fuisse, sed potius salutiferos. Constat etiam eos ipsum Christum non fuisse, Nam & plures erant, & faciem suam ac pedes tegebant, & Dominum non seipsos prædicabant, & prophetam non virtute insita, sed rebus à se diversis sanabant, &c. Necesse est igitur, ut Domini illius, qui apparebat sedens in excelso throno, διάκονοι & οἰκονόμοι fuerint, gratiam sanationis & salutis, quæ penes ipsum est, deferentes, offerentes, conferentes ministerio, volatu, voce, mediis convenientibus.
units.tr: It is established that these Seraphim, who stood above the Lord, were not destructive but rather saving. It is established also that they were not Christ himself. For they were many, they covered their face and feet, they proclaimed not themselves but the Lord, and they healed not by any power inherent in themselves but by means other than themselves, and so on. It is necessary, therefore, that they were ministers and stewards [διάκονοι καὶ οἰκονόμοι] of that Lord who appeared sitting on the high throne, carrying, offering and conferring the grace of healing and salvation, which rests in him, by their ministry, their flight, their voice and fitting means.

units.la: Quoniam igitur comparati sunt ad medendum morsibus præsterum seu serpentium urentium spiritualiter intellectorum, idcirco videntur appellati Seraphim, hoc est, præsteres, allusione ad Saraph illum quem Moses in deserto erexit. Ut enim Christus in crucem primum, deinde in cœlum sublatus omnibus locis & temporibus videri posset fidei oculis, minis-tris volantibus opus fuit, qui ad eius imaginem transformati, Salutem eius deportarent, ostenderent, & applicarent.
units.tr: Since therefore they were arranged to heal the bites of fiery serpents, or of serpents burning in the spiritual sense, they seem to have been called Seraphim, that is, fiery ones, with an allusion to that Saraph which Moses raised up in the desert. For just as Christ, first lifted up on the cross and then taken up into heaven, could be seen with the eyes of faith in all places and at all times, there was need of flying ministers, who, transformed into his image, should carry, show and apply his salvation.

units.la: Alioqui cur sic appellarentur causam non video: nam, qui huius appellationis rationem ab ignis vel motu, vel calore, vel luce petunt, illi, nec Scripturæ niituntur, quæ ea voce constanter præsteres aut noxios, aut his oppositos intelligit: Nec vi vocis, quæ nihil potest significare nisi ἐμπρηστής [?], hoc est, incendentes vel comburentes, à verbo שׂרף [?] quod urere, comburere, incedere significat, nihil præterea, & dicitur raro de igne, frequenter de homine adhibito igne aliquid comburente ac destruente: nec ab eo vox ulla nascitur, quæ splendorem vel illuminationem vel igneum colorem significet. Itaque animalia quæ vidit Ezechiel, quorum aspectus erat quasi carbonum ignis ardentium, & quasi aspectus lampadum non vocantur Seraphim, sed Cherubim.
units.tr: Otherwise I do not see why they were so called. For those who seek the reason for this name in fire, or its motion, or its heat, or its light, rely neither on Scripture, which constantly uses that word for fiery or harmful serpents, or for things opposed to these, nor on the force of the word itself, which can signify nothing but an incendiary [ἐμπρηστής], that is, one who burns or consumes, from the verb [שׂרף], which means to burn, to consume, to set on fire, and nothing more. It is said rarely of fire, but frequently of a man who applies a burning fire that consumes and destroys something. Nor does any word arise from it that signifies splendour, illumination or a fiery colour. Thus the living creatures which Ezekiel saw, whose appearance was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps, are not called Seraphim but Cherubim.

units.la: LXVI. Alterum ducitur à clamore horum Seraphim : clamabat enim זה אל זה iste ad istum, hoc est, vnusquisque ad proximum & quidem in templo. Cur clamabat, nisi vt longe lateque audiretur? cur in templo, nisi vt à tota Ecclesia exaudiretur? Quid autem clamat? duo. Primum praedicat ac reuelat summam illam Domini potentissimi sanctitatem, qua in se sanctus est, & qua autor est sanctificationis nostrae, Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus Dominus exercituum, vt intelligamus non ipsos, sed Dominum esse eum qui nos sanctificat, nostram sanationem, quae in sanctificatione sita est, in Domino solo quaerendam, ab eo solo petendam sperandamque. Deinde addit, plena est omnis terra gloria eius, innuens locorum in terra & gentium sublatum discrimen, atque adeo abrogatum foedus legale. Quinam autem ista duo, & in Ecclesia, & ad obuium quemque clamauerint, est ne obscurum?
units.tr: LXVI. The second is drawn from the cry of these Seraphim. For they cried זה אל זה [zeh el zeh], this one to that one, that is, each to his neighbour, and indeed in the temple. Why did they cry out, unless so that they might be heard far and wide? Why in the temple, unless so that they might be heard by the whole Church? But what did they cry? Two things. First, they proclaimed and revealed that supreme holiness of the most powerful Lord, by which he is holy in himself and is the author of our sanctification: Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of hosts. Thus we understand that it is not they but the Lord who sanctifies us, and that our healing, which lies in sanctification, is to be sought in the Lord alone, asked of him alone, and hoped for from him alone. Then they add: the whole earth is full of his glory, implying that the distinction of places on earth and of nations has been removed, and thus that the legal covenant has been abrogated. Now, is it obscure who it was that cried out these two things, both in the Church and to everyone they met?

units.la: LXVII. Huius clamoris duo commemorantur effecta. Vnum, quod superliminaria & postes templi, tot seculis vno in loco immobiliter fixi, moti sunt loco, atque ita ingressus in loca sancta & sanctissima apertus. Alterum, quod domus repleta est fumo, nempe commotione illa postium ac liminum, atque adeo totius aeris, & fumus victimae, qui in Atrio ex altari ascendebat, & fumus sufsitus, qui in interiore domo offerebatur, ad latera quoquoversum sparsi sunt, omniaque templi loca suo odore compleuerunt. Quinam rursus praedicatione sua duo illa praestiterint satis notum est.
units.tr: LXVII. Two effects of this cry are recorded. One is that the lintels and doorposts of the temple, fixed immovably in one place for so many ages, were moved from their place, and so the entrance into the holy and most holy places was opened. The other is that the house was filled with smoke: namely, by that shaking of the doorposts and thresholds, and thus of all the air, and the smoke of the victim which ascended from the altar in the court, and the incense which was offered in the inner house, were scattered on every side and filled every part of the temple with their odour. It is well known what these two things accomplished by their proclamation.

units.la: LXVIII. Tertium ex eo petitur quod simul ac Esaias Dominum agnouit, & suam immunditiem confessus est, volauit ad eum vnus ex Seraphim habens in manu prunam, quam ab altari forcipibus sumpserat, admonitque ori eius dicens, attingit hoc labia tua, iam amouetur iniquitas tua, & peccatum tuum expiatur. Cuius autem quaeso munus est, agnoscenti Dominum, & peccata sua confitenti sacrificii Christi vim applicare mediis ad eam rem aptis & destinatis, ac remissionem peccatorum verbis annunciare? Reliqua arg. ab apparitione, loco, vsu alarum, collatione cum animalibus Ap. 4. &5. studio breuitatis praetereo: nec addo, nisi Dominum cum suis ministris visum & auditum oculis & auribus corporis, nec tamen agnitum & intellectum corde à populo Iudaico eam ob causam reiecto ac dissipato, praeter Christum, nullum me nosse.
units.tr: LXVIII. A third argument is taken from this: as soon as Isaiah recognised the Lord and confessed his uncleanness, one of the Seraphim flew to him, holding in his hand a live coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and touched his mouth, saying: Behold, this has touched your lips; your iniquity is taken away and your sin is expiated. But whose office, I ask, is it to apply the power of Christ's sacrifice to one who recognises the Lord and confesses his sins, by means fitted and appointed for that purpose, and to announce the remission of sins in words? For the sake of brevity I pass over the remaining arguments, from the appearance, the place, the use of the wings, and the comparison with the living creatures of Ap. 4. & 5. Nor do I add that I know of no one, except Christ, who, the Lord having been seen and heard with his ministers by the eyes and ears of the body, yet not recognised and understood by the heart, was rejected and scattered by the Jewish people for this very reason.

units.la: DISPUTATIO SECUNDA
units.tr: SECOND DISPUTATION
