units.la: De Arg. II. Ex Esaiæ Cap. VII. v. 14. Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabitur nomen eius Emmanuel, laudato Matth. 1. 23.
units.tr: On the Second Argument, from Isaiah chapter 7 verse 14, Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, cited at Matthew 1.23.

units.la: I. APUD eundem Esaiam cap. VII. vers. 14. habetur vaticinium, Ecce virgo concipiet, & pariet filium, & vocabis nomen eius Emmanuel, quod Matthæus laudat his verbis, Hoc autem totum factum est, ut impleretur quod dictum est à domino per prophetam dicentem, Ecce virgo in utero habebit, & pariet filium, & vocabis nomen eius Emmanuel, quod est, si quis interpretetur, μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς nobiscum Deus: Hinc sic argumentor.
units.tr: I. In the same Isaiah, chapter 7 verse 14, there is the prophecy Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel, which Matthew cites in these words: Now all this was done that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall have a child in her womb, and shall bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which means, if one interprets it, μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς [God with us]. From this I argue as follows.

units.la: Emmanuel est Deus præditus essentia divina. Christus est Emmanuel. Ergo Christus est Deus præditus essentia divina. Minor, cùm habeat autorem Apostolum, negari nequit, Major sic probatur, Deus nobiscum, ὁ θεὸς μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν, est præditus essentia divina. Emmanuel est Deus nobiscum, ὁ θεὸς μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν. Ergo Emmanuel est præditus essentia divina. Minor est Apostoli. Major est certa: adjectio enim עמנו μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν nobiscum, non mutat significationem huius nominis אל ὁ θεός, Deus. Id autem nomen ipsi Aduersarij fatentur Deum significare præditum essentia divina.
units.tr: Emmanuel is God endowed with the divine essence. Christ is Emmanuel. Therefore Christ is God endowed with the divine essence. The minor premise cannot be denied, since its author is the Apostle. The major is proved thus: God with us [ὁ θεὸς μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν] is endowed with the divine essence. Emmanuel is God with us, [ὁ θεὸς μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν]. Therefore Emmanuel is endowed with the divine essence. The minor premise is the Apostle's. The major is certain: for the addition of עמנו [with us] or μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν [with us] does not change the meaning of the name אל [God], ὁ θεός [God], Deus. And the opponents themselves admit that this name signifies God, that is, one endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: II. Ad hoc argumentum nihil legi à Socino responsum. At Crellius duo obicit, unum respondet. Obicit 1. sic damnari eos omnes, qui id nomen olim hodieque, vel aliis imposuerunt, vel usurpa-runt ipsi. Non desunt è nostris qui eos damnent. Ego, quia in im-positione & usurpatione illius nominis gratum sonum seu pronunciationem cogitasse tantum arbitror, non significationem, excusatos cupio, alioqui graviter culpandos.
units.tr: II. No reply by Socinus to this argument has been read. But Crellius raises two objections and answers one. He objects first that in this way all are condemned who either have imposed that name on others, or have assumed it themselves, both in the past and today. Among our own people there are not lacking those who condemn them. I, however, since I think that in imposing and assuming that name they had in mind only a pleasing sound or pronunciation, not its meaning, wish them excused; otherwise they would be gravely to be blamed.

units.la: III. Obijcit ii. Christum, cui id nomen Deus per Esaiam destinavit, eius Prophetae ætate suam habuisse imaginem, cui eadem appellatio, istius temporis ratione habita competeret, imperfecta quidem significatione, sed tamen vera. Resp. i. ullum ætate Prophetæ natum fuisse hoc insignitum nomine nullo sacrarum literarum testimonio doceri posse. ii. Ut fuerit aliquis, in eum tamen nullo modo significationem illius nominis, ne imperfectam quidem, competivisse: nullus enim post editum à Propheta istud vaticinium vivente natus est, aut qui Deus fuerit, aut per quem Deus cum populo Iudaico fuerit, illiue opem tulerit. iii. Fac tamen aliquem eiusmodi fuisse, cui, & nomen illud, & eius significatio conveniret aliquomodo, id de argumenti nostri robore nihil detrahit. Fuit enim ille Emmanuel typicè tantùm: Christus est verè. Typus autem non est præditus illius rei essentia cuius est typus. Itaq; potuit mera creatura typicè Deus dici, verè non item.
units.tr: III. He objects secondly that Christ, to whom God through Isaiah assigned that name, had in the age of that prophet his own image, to whom the same appellation, taking account of the circumstances of that time, would apply, imperfect indeed in meaning, but nonetheless true. I reply: first, that some person born in the prophet's age and marked with this name cannot be shown by any testimony of the sacred letters. Second, even if there was such a person, the meaning of that name, not even imperfectly, could in no way have applied to him, for no one born after this prophecy was uttered, while he lived, was either God, or one through whom God was with the Jewish people, or one who brought them help. Third, grant that there was someone of this kind, to whom the name and its meaning agreed in some measure; this takes nothing from the strength of our argument. For that Emmanuel was so only typically; Christ is so truly. But a type does not possess the essence of the thing of which it is a type. And so a mere creature could be called God typically, but not truly.

units.la: IV. Respondet hoc unum, verbis nobiscum Deus, addendum esse est; integram enim enunciationem in unum nomen coaluisse. Itaque sic appellari Christum, non quod sic ille Deus qui nobiscum est, sed quod per eum & in eo Deus ille summus revera nobiscum sit, hoc est, nobis insigniter faveat, nobis opituletur, nobis ingentia beneficia præstet. Verùm unde habet addendum esse verbum ἐστι [?] est, potius quàm participium ὢν [?] existens, quo addito roboraretur potius quàm infirmaretur argumentum nostrum? Immò unde habet aliquid esse addendum? Num sibi tale quid addi flagitat nomen Emmanuel? non certè qua nomen, sunt enim innumera nomina quibus verbum est, addi non debet; Nec qua nomen compositum, sunt enim etiam multa nomina composita absque tali additamento completa; Nec denique qua nomen sic compositum: Id quod intelliges, si articulum nomini ὁ θεὸς ab Euangelista præfixum, primo loco ponas, ὁ μεθ' ἡμῶν [?] θεός. Hinc enim liquet non magis id nomen enunciationem esse quàm est hæc oratio, Deus pacis, Deus omnis consolationis, & similes. Nec reponendum est esse in Scriptura nomina quædam quæ sint enunciationes, id enim non nego, tantùm nego inde sequi nomen Emmanuel esse enunciationem.
units.tr: IV. He answers only this, that the words God with us must have is added, for the whole statement has coalesced into one name. Thus Christ is so called not because the God who is with us is such, but because through him and in him that highest God really is with us, that is, favours us remarkably, helps us, and bestows great benefits upon us. But from where does he get the notion that the verb ἐστι [is] must be added, rather than the participle ὢν [being], by which our argument would be strengthened rather than weakened? Indeed, from where does he get the notion that anything must be added at all? Does the name Emmanuel demand any such addition? Certainly not as a name, for there are countless names to which a verb need not be added; nor as a compound name, for there are many compound names complete without any such addition; nor finally as a name compounded in this particular way. You will understand this if you place first the article ὁ θεὸς, which the Evangelist prefixed to the name: [ὁ μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν θεός]. For it is clear from this that the name is no more a statement than this phrase, God of peace, God of all consolation, and similar ones. Nor is it to be answered that there are in Scripture certain names which are statements; for I do not deny that, I only deny that it follows that the name Emmanuel is a statement.

units.la: V. Iam autem ut vox Emmanuel de sermone Hebræo [?] in græcum aut latinum vertatur, addendum non esse vocibus, Nobiscum Deus, verbum substantivum his argumentis probari poterit. Primò, Nemo melius id nomen interpretari potest quàm Euangelista & Apostolus Matthæus id interpretatus est, atqui is verbum est non adjecit ; adjecturus sine dubio si opus fuisset. Cur enim id omisisset, si pars censeri debet illius nominis ? An quia sponte subauditur ? Non, potest enim, vt dixi, subaudiri participium, potest nihil subaudiri, vt in hac propositione, Deus nobiscum est Deus noster, Deus nobiscum est subjectum, seu nomen completum. An quia nihil interest vtrum sine an cum, est, intelligatur ? Ne id quidem respondere possunt Aduersarij adjunctionem verbi illius vrgentes, qua sublata quod huic nostro argumento respondeant non habent. Si igitur prudentissimus Apostolus verbum, est, de nominis illius, vt ita loquar, essentia putauit esse, si vidit plurimi interesse Ecclesiæ vt adjiciatur ad euitandum errorem momentosum, qui sibi ab eo addendo temperauit, autor nobis exemplo suo ne illud addamus? Quod siid is non putauit addendum, sunt ne tanto Apostolo sapientiores Aduersarij? quanquam quid Apostolum nomino, & non potius Christum qui in eo loquebatur ?
units.tr: V. Now, that the word Emmanuel, from the Hebrew speech, is to be turned into Greek or Latin without adding the substantive verb to the words God with us, can be proved by these arguments. First, no one can interpret that name better than the Evangelist and Apostle Matthew, who did interpret it; yet he did not add the verb is, and he would undoubtedly have added it had it been necessary. For why would he have omitted it, if it ought to be counted a part of that name? Is it because it is understood of its own accord? No, for, as I have said, a participle may be understood, or nothing may be understood, as in this proposition, God with us is our God, where God with us is the subject, or complete name. Or is it because it makes no difference whether is is understood or not? Not even this can our opponents claim, since they urge the addition of that verb, and without it they have no answer to this argument of ours. If therefore the most prudent Apostle thought that the verb is belonged to the essence of that name, so to speak, if he saw that it mattered greatly to the Church that it be added in order to avoid a weighty error, yet he refrained from adding it, does he not, by his own example, advise us not to add it? But if he did not think it should be added, are our opponents wiser than so great an Apostle? Yet why do I name the Apostle, rather than Christ who was speaking in him?

units.la: V I. Deinde, cum neminem fugiat nomen de persona cuius est nomen prædicari in casu recto, quis credat ita stupidum & cæcum fuisse Apostolum, vt non intellexerit, se Christi nomen Emmanuel interpretando μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς[?] Christum appellare ὁ θεὸς[?], indeque sequi eum esse prædicatum natura seu essentia diuina? Hoc igitur si putauit & falsum & Deo patri injuriosum, posse autem ei malo occurri necessaria verbi ἐστὶ[?] adjectione, cur id non adjecit, vt sic veritati, gloriæ Dei, ædificationi Ecclesiæ consuleret.
units.tr: VI. Next, since it escapes no one that the name of a person can be predicated of that person in the nominative case, who would believe that the Apostle was so dull and blind as not to have understood that, by interpreting the name Emmanuel as μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός, he was calling Christ ὁ θεός, and that it follows from this that he is predicated as divine by nature or essence? If, therefore, he thought this both false and injurious to God the Father, but that this evil could be met by the necessary addition of the verb ἐστὶ, why did he not add it, so as to consult thus for the truth, the glory of God, and the edification of the Church?

units.la: V I I. Tertiò, hæc propositio, Christus est Emmanuel, quomodo latinè reddi debet? Num sic, Christus est nobiscum Deus? non concedent Aduersarij: sic enim valeret argumentum nostrum. Num igitur sic, Christus est nobiscum Deus est ? ita oportet eos interpretari si sibi constare volunt. Sed quis talem ferat interpretationem? Similiter hæc propositio, Emmanuel est Seruator noster, non erit sic reddenda Nobiscum Deus est seruator noster, sed sic, Nobiscum Deus est est seruator noster. Similiter cum sic loquitur Esaias cap. viii. verf. 8. Et extensio alarum eius implebit latitudinem terræ tuæ O Emmanuel, quomodo reddendum erit græcè vel latinè illud O Emmanuel? certè autore Matthæo ὦ μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ θεός, O nobiscum Deus. Sic ne puer quidem dubitabit quin nomen ὁ Θεὸς (Deus) sit vocatiui casus. Crellio vero autore sic erit vertendum ὦ μεθ' ἡμῶν ὁ Θεὸς ἐστι [?] O nobiscum Deus est, vtrum autorem sequi tibi magis placet, lector pie, Apostolum an Crellium? Sic si dixero, Christum esse Emmanuelem, quomodo retento verbo infinitiui modi, esse, reddent Emmanuelem? Num, Christum esse Deum nobiscum? minimè, sic enim nomen Deus, ὁ Θεὸς, praedicaretur de Christo, quod illi nolunt; sed sic, Christum esse Deus est nobiscum.
units.tr: VII. Thirdly, how ought this proposition, Christ is Emmanuel, to be rendered in Latin? Surely thus: Christ is God with us? Our opponents will not concede this, for thus our argument would hold. Is it then to be rendered Christ is God with us is? They must interpret it so if they wish to be consistent. But who could endure such a translation? Similarly, this proposition, Emmanuel is our Saviour, is not to be rendered God with us is our Saviour, but God with us is is our Saviour. Likewise, when Isaiah speaks thus in chapter 8 verse 8, And the extension of his wings shall fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel, how is that O Emmanuel to be rendered in Greek or Latin? Certainly, on Matthew's authority, O God with us [ὦ μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός]. Thus not even a boy would doubt that the name ὁ Θεὸς (God) is in the vocative case. But on Crellius's authority it must be rendered thus: O God with us is [ὦ μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν ὁ Θεὸς ἐστι]. Which author, pious reader, do you prefer to follow, the Apostle or Crellius? If I say that Christ is Emmanuel, how, retaining the infinitive verb to be, will they render Emmanuel? Surely Christ to be God with us? By no means, for thus the name God, ὁ Θεὸς, would be predicated of Christ, which they are unwilling to allow; but thus: Christ to be, God is with us.

units.la: VIII. Quartò, Apoc. 21. verf. 3. Audiuit Iohannes vo-cem magnam de Throno dicentem, Ecce tabernaculum Dei cum ho-minibus, (loquitur de noua Hierusalem) & habitabit cum eis, & ipsi populus eius erunt, & ipse Deus erit cum ipsis Deus ipsorum ὁ αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἐσται μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς αὐτῶν [?]. His verbis sine dubio vim nominis Emmanuel expressit, nisi quod pronomen primae personae mutauit in pronomen tertiae, quia ipse qui loquebatur hominibus non aggregabatur; referrur enim pronomen primae personae nobis ad homines vocantes filium virginis Emmanuelem, itaque non dicitur Deus sic vocaturus eum, sed virgo, vel Ecclesia. Quàm igitur dixit vox illa, Ipse Deus erit cum ipsis Deus, tam dicere possumus nos fideles, Ipse Deus erit nobiscum Deus, id quod est dicere, erit Emmanuel. Hinc multa colligo 1. sic argumentor, qui tunc erit Emmanuel idem nunc est Emmanuel. Sed tunc ipse Deus erit Emmanuel. Ergo nunc ipse Deus est Emmanuel. Minor nititur illo loco. Major est certa: idem enim tunc erit nobiscum Deus qui nunc est nobiscum Deus, tantùm erit nobiscum ratione perfectiore atque illustriore. Adde quod Filius est haeres Patris, non contrà. Itaque non fit verisimile Patrem haeredem futurum nominis Emmanuel, quod proprium esse Filij ipsi Aduersarij confitentur. II. vt se habet μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς cum illis Deus, sic se habet μεθ' ἡμῶν Θεὸς nobiscum Deus. Sed μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς est elogium completum sine additione verbi est, vt patet ex illa propositione ipse Deus erit cum ipsis Deus, ineptus enim esset qui post Deus adderet, est, ergo etiam nobiscum Deus est elogium completum sine illa additione. III. Quomodo intelligendum est μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς, eodem modo intelligédum est μεθ' ἡμῶν Θεὸς: sed μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς non significat eum per quem Deus est cum illis. Ergo etiam μεθ' ἡμῶν Θεὸς non significat eum per quem Deus est nobiscum.
units.tr: VIII. Fourthly, Revelation 21:3. John heard "a great voice from the throne saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men" (he is speaking of the New Jerusalem), "and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself will be with them, their God" [ὁ αὐτὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἐσται μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς αὐτῶν]. Undoubtedly these words express the force of the name Emmanuel, except that he changed the first-person pronoun into the third, because the one who was speaking was not joined to men. The first-person pronoun "us" refers to the men who call the son of the virgin Emmanuel, so it is not God who is said to call him this, but the virgin, or the Church. Therefore, as that voice said, "God himself will be with them God," so we believers can say, "God himself will be with us God," which is the same as saying, "he will be Emmanuel." From this I draw several conclusions. 1. I argue thus: whoever will then be Emmanuel is now Emmanuel. But then God himself will be Emmanuel. Therefore now God himself is Emmanuel. The minor rests on that passage. The major is certain: the one who will then be God with us is the one who now is God with us; only he will be with us in a more perfect and more illustrious way. Add that the Son is the heir of the Father, not the reverse. Therefore it is not likely that the Father will be heir to the name Emmanuel, which our opponents themselves confess is proper to the Son. II. As μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς [God with them] stands, so μεθ' ἡμῶν Θεὸς [God with us] stands. But μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς is a complete predicate without the addition of the verb "is," as is clear from the proposition "God himself will be with them God"; for it would be foolish to add "is" after "God." Therefore "God with us" is also a complete predicate without that addition. III. As μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς must be understood, so μεθ' ἡμῶν Θεὸς must be understood in the same way. But μετ' αὐτῶν Θεὸς does not signify the one through whom God is with them. Therefore μεθ' ἡμῶν Θεὸς does not signify the one through whom God is with us either.

units.la: IX. Quintò, si addatur verbum, est, enunciatio seu nomen fiet ambiguum: vel enim totum hoc, nobiscum Deus est, erit attributum, persona subiectum, & subaudietur pronomen iste, vel ille, vel hic, vt fit in nomine Iisiachar significante est merces: vel erit integra enunciatio, cuius subiectum erit Deus, attributum est nobiscum. Si prius eligitur, accessio verbi, Est, nihil obest argumento nostro. Si posterius: oportet Christum esse comparatum ad significandum quod Deus nobiscum sit. Nunquam enim integra enunciatio imponitur vt nomen alicui vel rei vel personæ, nisi vt res illa vel persona sit veritatis eiusmodi enunciationis monumentum vel signum. Itaque quod dicunt Dominum nostrum vocari Emmanuelem, hoc est ipsis interpretibus, Deus nobiscum est, quoniam per eum Deus nobiscum est, seu nobis opem fert, in eo destituuntur omni exemplo. Non enim est vocatus filius Esaiæ accelera, detrahe spolium, festina prædari, quoniam per eum detrahendum esset spolium; Nec mons in quo Abraham filium suum immolare voluit, Dominus videbit, quod per eum montem Dominus esset visurus; nec altare Deus fortis est Deus Israëlis, quod per illud Deus esset Deus Israëlis; nec, vt mea memoria est, quisquam aut quidquam eo sensu enunciationem vice nominis obtinet in Scriptura. Conuenire autem Christo nomen Emmanuel tantum vt signo quod Deus sit nobiscum, non puto Christianum vllum dicturum: potuit enim illius rei signum instituì, si Deus voluisset, quæuis alia persona, immò res visibilis.
units.tr: IX. Fifthly, if the word "is" is added, the statement or the name becomes ambiguous. For either this whole "God is with us" will be the predicate, with a person as subject, and this or that pronoun will be understood, as happens in the name Issachar, which means "there is a reward"; or it will be a complete statement, whose subject is "God" and whose predicate is "is with us." If the former is chosen, the addition of the verb "is" does no harm to our argument. If the latter, it is necessary that Christ be taken as a sign that God is with us. For a complete statement is never imposed as a name on any person or thing unless that person or thing is a monument or sign of the truth of such a statement. Therefore, when they say that our Lord is called Emmanuel, which by their own interpreters means "God is with us, because through him God is with us, or brings help to us," they are without any example in this. For the son of Isaiah was not called "Hasten to take spoil, hurry to plunder" because through him spoil would be taken; nor was the mountain on which Abraham wished to sacrifice his son called "The Lord will see" because through that mountain the Lord would see; nor was the altar "God is the mighty God of Israel" because through it God would be the God of Israel. As far as I remember, nobody and nothing in Scripture takes a statement in place of a name in that sense. Moreover, I do not think any Christian will say that the name Emmanuel belongs to Christ merely as a sign that God is with us. Any other person, or even a visible thing, could have been appointed as a sign of that matter, if God had willed it.

units.la: X. Sextò, Huc accedit quod negari non potest quin Christus vocetur אל Deus, & quidem ab hoc ipso propheta Esaia cap. 9. 6. vocabitur nomen eius Admirabilis, consiliarius, Deus fortis אל גבור, Pater seculi, Princeps pacis, nec id diffitetur Crellius. Si igitur vocandus erat אל Deus, cur non cum ista addițione, עמנו nobiscum? Rursus negari non potest quin sit reuera nobiscum, Ecce, inquit, vobiscum sum omnibus diebus vsque ad consummationem seculi. Si igitur nominis עמנואל pars ista עמנו nobiscum prædicatur de Christo vere & proprie, cur non similiter pars altera nimirum אל Deus de eodem Christo vere & proprie prædicabitur, præsertim cum certum sit eum nobiscum esse modo plane diuino? Certè non dicitur nobiscum esse quia per eum alius est nobiscum; nec dicitur Deus quia per eum alius est Deus: sed nobiscum est vere & proprie, Deus est vere & proprie, non figurate, non metaphorice.
units.tr: X. Sixthly, to this it must be added that it cannot be denied that Christ is called אל [God], and indeed by this very prophet Isaiah in chapter 9:6: "his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God [אל גבור], Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace." Crellius does not deny this. If, then, he was to be called אל [God], why not with that addition, עמנו [with us]? Again, it cannot be denied that he really is with us: "Behold," he says, "I am with you all days, even to the end of the age." If, therefore, that part of the name עמנואל, namely עמנו [with us], is predicated of Christ truly and properly, why should the other part, namely אל [God], not likewise be predicated of the same Christ truly and properly, especially since it is certain that he is with us in a manner that is plainly divine? Certainly he is not said to be with us because through him another is with us, nor is he called God because through him another is God. But he is with us truly and properly, and he is God truly and properly, not figuratively, not metaphorically.

units.la: Math. 28. 20
units.tr: Math. 28. 20

units.la: XI. Septimò, nomina Emmanuel & Iesus idem valent testibus Matthæo & re ipsa: Matthæo quidem, Is enim quod dixerat de virgine Maria, pariet filium, & vocabis nomen eius Iesum: ipse enim saluum faciet populum suum à peccatis eorum, confert vt euentum cum hoc Esaiæ vaticinio, ecce virgo in vtero habebit, & pariet filium, & vocabitur nomen eius Emmanuel, quod est interpre-tatum, Nobiscum Deus. Itaque vt virgo virgini, partus partui, vocatio nominis vocationi nominis in illa collatione respondet, sic consentaneum est vt nomen nomini respondeat, non quidem li-terarum & soni ratione, sed rei. Re verò ipsa: Nam quid est nobiscum Deus nisi Iesus, hoc est, Seruator, qui nos à peccatis nostris, atque adeò ab omni malo seruat? Certè Deus nobiscum est Deus nos seruans, id est, Seruator, Et rursus Seruator est Deus nobiscum, Ego sum, Ego sum Dominus, inquit ipse Deus Esaiæ cap. 43. vers.11. Et non est absque me (Heb. [?]בלעדי praeter me, me excepto, vt patet ex Esaiæ 44.6. & Psal. 18. 32.) Seruator. Si non est præter Deum seruator, quomodo Iesus est seruator si non est Deus? Itaque ipse sibi Deus hoc tanquam proprium tribuit vt seruet populum suum à peccatis ipsorum, Esai. 43. 25. Ego sum, inquit, Ego sum ipse, qui deleo iniquitates tuas propter me. Si igitur Christus is est qui delet iniquitates nostras, & nos seruat ab omnibus malis vi sua, quid est cur non credatur esse Emmanuel, hoc est, Deus nobiscum, nobis fauens, nobis opem ferens.
units.tr: XI. Seventhly, the names Emmanuel and Jesus have the same value, as Matthew testifies and as the thing itself shows. Matthew indeed: for when he had said of the Virgin Mary, "she shall bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins," he compares this outcome with that prophecy of Isaiah, "Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." Therefore, just as virgin corresponds to virgin, birth to birth, and the giving of a name to the giving of a name in that comparison, so it is fitting that name should correspond to name, not indeed in respect of letters and sound, but of the thing. And in fact: for what is "God with us" except Jesus, that is, Saviour, who saves us from our sins and so from every evil? Certainly God with us is God saving us, that is, Saviour. And again the Saviour is God with us. "I am, I am the Lord," says God himself in Isaiah 43:11, "and there is none beside me" (Heb. בלעדי, [besides me, apart from me], as is clear from Isaiah 44:6 and Psalm 18:32), "a Saviour." If there is no Saviour besides God, how is Jesus the Saviour if he is not God? Thus he himself claims this as his own, that he saves his people from their sins: Isaiah 43:25, "I am," he says, "I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake." If, therefore, Christ is he who blots out our iniquities and saves us from all evils by his own power, why is there no reason to believe that he is Emmanuel, that is, God with us, favouring us and bringing us help?

units.la: XII. Præterea Si Dominus noster vocatur Emmanuel hanc vnam ob causam, quoniam per eum Deus nobis opitulatur, cum Deus sit hominibus opitulatus per multos iudices, reges, prophetas, Sacerdotes, multi etiam alij potuerunt eo nomine insigniri, qui ergo factum est, vt nemini alij tributum legatur in Scriptura, non Mosi, non Iosue, non iudicum aut regum vllì, &c. Posita expositione Aduersariorum nulla ratio reddi potest, cur hoc nomen soli Christo reseruatum fuerit, nec fit vlli alij communicatum: posita vero nostra, ratio aperta est, nemo alius Deus fuit: itaque nemo alius Deus nobiscum fuit.
units.tr: XII. Moreover, if our Lord is called Emmanuel for this one reason, that through him God helps us, then, since God has helped men through many judges, kings, prophets and priests, many others might also have been marked with that name. How is it, then, that it is nowhere read in Scripture as given to anyone else: not to Moses, not to Joshua, not to any of the judges or kings, and so on? On the explanation of our opponents no reason can be given why this name was reserved for Christ alone and was communicated to no one else. On our explanation, however, the reason is plain: no one else was God. Therefore no one else was God with us.

units.la: XIII. Deniquè nullus melior vaticinii interpres quàm ipse euentus. Constat autem ab omnibus Christianis Christum vo-catum esse & vocari Emmanuelem non tam habita ratione syllabarum & soni quàm rei: nempe creditur Deus esse nobiscum, nobis coniunctissimus, cum igitur prædictioni respondeat congruens nostræ interpretationi eventus apertissimè, non est cur de veritate prædictionis sic acceptæ dubitemus.
units.tr: XIII. Finally, there is no better interpreter of a prophecy than the event itself. It is agreed by all Christians that Christ was called, and is called, Emmanuel, not so much with regard to the arrangement of syllables and sound as with regard to the thing itself: namely, it is believed that God is with us, most closely joined to us. Since, therefore, the event corresponds most clearly both to the prediction and to our interpretation, there is no reason for us to doubt the truth of the prediction as so understood.

units.la: XIV. Nunc Apostoli authoritate sepositā ex ipso textu Esaiæ hoc argumentum ducimus. Caput regni Iudaici Achazo superius unde pendebat illius conseruatio erat Deus. Emmanuel erat caput regni Iudaici Achazo superius, ex quo pendebat illius conseruatio. Ergo Emmanuel erat Deus. propositio, opinor, non negabitur. Quis enim nescit populi illius caput & regem Achazo superiorem ipsum Deum fuisse? Non te (inquit ipse Deus ad Samuelem quod Israelitæ regem sibi imponi flagitassent graviter ferentem,) reiecerunt, sed me ne regnem super eos. Tu ipse, clamabat psaltes, Rex meus es o Deus. Minor incumbit mihi probanda: ac illud quidem nequit negari Emmanuelem esse Regem Iudæorum seu regni Iudaici caput, negabitur tantùm eum fuisse caput illius regni tempore Prophetæ. At si tunc fuit, certè tunc fuit caput illius regni. Tunc autem fuit. Id enim & probatum est toto libro superiori, & deducitur ex ipsis verbis Esaiæ.
units.tr: XIV. Now, setting aside the authority of the Apostle, I draw this argument from the text of Isaiah itself. The head over the kingdom of Judah, on whom Ahaz depended for his preservation as his superior, was God. Emmanuel was the head over the kingdom of Judah, on whom Ahaz depended for his preservation as his superior. Therefore Emmanuel was God. I think the major premise will not be denied. For who does not know that the head and king of that people, Ahaz's superior, was God himself? "They have not rejected you," God said to Samuel, being grieved that the Israelites had demanded a king to be set over them, "but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." "You yourself," the psalmist cried, "are my King, O God." The minor premise remains to be proved. It cannot be denied that Emmanuel is the King of the Jews, or the head of the kingdom of Judah; it will only be denied that he was the head of that kingdom at the time of the prophet. But if he was then, he was certainly then the head of that kingdom. And he was then. This has been both proved throughout the preceding book and follows from the very words of Isaiah.

units.la: XV. Primùm enim cum hoc signum fuerit ab ipso Deo prudentissimè electum ac per Prophetam propositum, negari non potest, quin ad id confirmandum accommodatissimum fuerit, quod eo confirmari Deus voluit, voluit autem confirmari id quod Esaias ipsius nomine credendum proposuerat Achazo. Proposuerat autem credendam assertionem & assertionis rationem. Assertio erat, consilium Retsin regis Syriæ & filii Romeliæ regis Samariæ de Iudæa capienda, inter se diuidenda, Regeque in ea constituendo filio Tabeæ irritum fore. Ratio erat, quia caput Syriæ Damascus, & caput Damasci Retsin & caput Ephraim Samaria & caput Samariæ filius Romeliæ, hoc est, quia regnorum Syriæ & Ephraim nullum erat caput Retsin & filio Romeliæ superius unde penderet illorum conseruatio & consiliorum eventus, cum esset Regni Iudaici caput superius Achaso, videlicet Deus, qui duorum illorum regum tam scelerato consilio non minus quàm Achazus petebatur. Quæ ratio, quoniam, & propter eam assentiendum erat assertioni, & eius probè perceptæ ac persuasæ vi omnis alia similis tentatio superari poterat, proposito signo confirmari debuit, Magis enim confirmare voluit Deus quod magiscredi voluit. Confirmata autem fuit illa ratio, quantum quidem ad seculum illud attinuit, non ipso euentu seu exhibitione reali illius signi, neque etiam sola repetitione promissionis de venturo Messia: ita enim neque ad rationem illam accommodatum fuisset signum, & virginis mentio obfuisset: potuisset enim videri vel vnam virginem è Dauidica stirpe conseruatam ad promissionis de Messia nascituro veritatem tuendam satis esse posse. Sed declaratione solenni, ac veritatis suae notas quasdam prae se ferente, fore vt tandem aliquando caput regni Iudaici (quod tunc temporis, quoniam sola natura diuina praeditum erat, non videbatur) fieret virgineo conceptu & partu visibile, Deusque cum Iudaeis esse visibiliter appareret, & à piis agnosceretur: id quod Apostolus Iohannes expressit his verbis, verbum erat Deus, & caro factum est, & habitauit inter nos plenum gratia & veritate, & spectauimus gloriam eius, &c. caro enim factum est in vtero virginis.
units.tr: XV. First, since this sign was chosen most wisely by God himself and set forth through the prophet, it cannot be denied that it was most suitable for confirming that which God wished to be confirmed. He wished confirmed what Isaiah, in God's name, had proposed to Ahaz to be believed. Now he had proposed for belief both an assertion and the reason for the assertion. The assertion was that the plan of Rezin, king of Syria, and of the son of Remaliah, king of Samaria, to seize Judah, divide it between themselves, and set up the son of Tabeel as king in it, would come to nothing. The reason was: "for the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin, and the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah." That is, the kingdoms of Syria and Ephraim had no head above Rezin and the son of Remaliah on whom their preservation and the outcome of their plans depended, whereas the head of the kingdom of Judah, above Ahaz, was God, who was no less sought by those two kings' wicked plan than Ahaz himself was. Since this reason was such that, on account of it, assent had to be given to the assertion, and since by the force of this reason, rightly perceived and believed, every other similar temptation could be overcome, it had to be confirmed by the sign that was set forth. For God wished to confirm more strongly what he wished to be more firmly believed. Now that reason was confirmed, so far as concerned that age, not by the actual outcome or real exhibition of that sign, nor even by the mere repetition of the promise about the coming Messiah. For in that case the sign would not have fitted the reason, and the mention of a virgin would have been out of place; for it might have seemed that a single virgin preserved from the Davidic line would be sufficient to guard the truth of the promise about the Messiah who was to be born. Rather, by a solemn declaration, and bearing certain marks of its own truth, it set forth that the head of the kingdom of Judah, which at that time did not appear, since it possessed only the divine nature, would at last become visible through a virginal conception and birth; that God would visibly appear to be with the Jews, and would be recognised by the godly. This the Apostle John expressed in these words: "the Word was God, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth, and we beheld his glory," etc. For he became flesh in the womb of the virgin.

units.la: XVI. Hinc perspici facile potest, cur Virginis mentio fiat hoc loco, cur nominis Emmanuel, cur educationis eius. Nimirum, neque Deum decebat carnem fieri ex viri concubitu cum muliere; & pertinebat ad scopum Prophetae vt Deus esse cum Iudaeis, caput eorum & rex, agnosceretur; & obuiam eundum erat cogitationi obrepturae lectori, Emmanuelem futurum fuisse quàm diuinitate & conceptu, & nomine tam naturae humanae conditione à reliquis hominibus diuersum, cui vt occurrat subjicit Propheta eum nasciturum infantem, nondum internoscentem obiecta, & cibis consuetis vtentem, hoc est, aliis hominibus peccato excepto per omnia similem, quarum rerum cur hoc vno loco mentio facta sit, quae alibi non fit in Veteri Testamento admissa opinione Aduersariorum nulla prorsus reddi potest ratio, vti nec cur potissimum nitatur Esaias Emmanuelis nomine, quod bis repetit cap. viii.
units.tr: XVI. From this it can easily be seen why the mention of the virgin is made in this place, why the name Emmanuel, and why his upbringing. Clearly, it was not fitting that God should become flesh from the intercourse of a man with a woman; and it pertained to the prophet's purpose that God should be recognised as being with the Jews, as their head and king; and the reader's thought, which was about to creep in, had to be met: that Emmanuel would be different from other men in his divinity and in his conception and name, no less than in the condition of human nature. To meet this, the prophet adds that he will be born as an infant, not yet knowing how to distinguish objects, and feeding on ordinary food; that is, that apart from sin he would be like other men in all things. Why mention of these things is made in this one place, and is not made elsewhere in the Old Testament, no reason at all can be given if the opinion of our opponents is admitted; nor why Isaiah rests especially on the name Emmanuel, which he repeats twice in chapter 8.

units.la: XVII. His accedit pronomen vobis, non enim dicit Propheta simpliciter, dabit Dominus ipse signum, sed addit vobis, innuens etiam ad eos quos alloquebatur Emmanuelem aliquo modo pertinere, quomodo? si tunc temporis nullus omnino erat, si nulla ab eo protectio, liberatio, salus, vtilitas proficisci poterat? cur etiam eius futura conceptio & natiuitas & reuelatio credenda & speranda ipsis proponebatur, si ab eo nihil erat ipsis sperandum boni?
units.tr: XVII. To this is added the pronoun you. For the prophet does not simply say, "the Lord himself will give a sign," but adds "to you," indicating that Emmanuel in some way concerns those whom he was addressing. How could he, if at that time there was absolutely no such person, if no protection, deliverance, salvation or benefit could come from him? Why also was his future conception and birth and revelation proposed to them to be believed and hoped for, if nothing good was to be hoped for from him?

units.la: XVIII. Id ipsum confirmat pronomen nobis expressum in voce Emmanuelis: hoc enim etiam ad ipsum Esaiam aliosque illius seculi fideles referri ex eo patet, quod Esaias innuere vult eo nomine Deum esse secum, ac cum populo Judaico, & domo Davidis, ut eam conseruet. Id quod perspicuum est ex Prophetæ verbis cap. 8. vers. 8. in quibus ipsis, magnum est pondus, ibit (nempe Rex Assyriorum) per Judam, inundans & transiens usque ad collum veniet, & erit extensio alarum eius implens latitudinem terræ tuæ O Emmanuel. His enim verbis primùm Emmanuelem compellat tanquam iam reuera existentem. Deinde Judæam vocat eius terram, significans Emmanuelem esse illius terræ dominum. Tum ad eum in summa illa calamitate confugit, eique quanta esset illa miseria futura misericordiæ excitandæ causa exponit. Denique ab Emmanuele sic compellato tantam spem tantamque fiduciam concipit, ut non dubitet hostibus veluti insultare, congregamini, inquit vers. 9. populi & vincimini, & audite universa procul terra: confortamini & vincimini, accingite vos & vincimini, inite consilium & dissipabitur, loquimini verbum & non fiet, quia (Emmanuel) Nobiscum Deus, potuitne clarius innuere ita Emmanuelem τὸ χ̄ σὺν πνεῦμα[?] nascituram fuisse, ut tamen iam reuera esset τὸ χ̄ πνεῦμα[?], Judeae curam gerens tanquam rex & Dominus, ac tutissimum aduersus ingruentes calamitates perfugium.
units.tr: XVIII. The pronoun us, expressed in the word Emmanuel, confirms the same thing. For that this too refers to Isaiah himself and the other faithful of that age is clear from the fact that Isaiah wishes to signify by that name that God is with him, and with the Jewish people and the house of David, to preserve it. This is plain from the prophet's words in chapter 8, verse 8, where the weighty point lies: "He (namely the king of the Assyrians) will pass through Judah, overflowing and passing through, he will come up to the neck, and the extension of his wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel." For in these words he first addresses Emmanuel as one who already truly exists. Then he calls Judah his land, signifying that Emmanuel is the lord of that land. Then he flees to him in that great calamity, and sets out how great the misery to come would be, in order to stir up his mercy. Finally, having addressed Emmanuel thus, he conceives such great hope and such great confidence that he does not hesitate almost to mock the enemies: "Gather yourselves, O peoples, and be broken; and give ear, all you far countries of the earth; gird yourselves and be broken; take counsel and it will come to nothing; speak the word and it will not stand, for (Emmanuel) God is with us." Could he have indicated more clearly that Emmanuel, although he was to be born as God-with-us [ὁ θεὸς μεθ' ἡμῶν], was nevertheless already truly God-with-us, caring for Judah as king and lord, and the safest refuge against the calamities that threatened?

units.la: XIX. Reponit Crellius, in hoc loco, ut in aliis multis, duplicem esse sensum, literalem nimirum seu historicum, & mysticum, hunc de Christo, illum de filio prophetissæ qui tunc conceptus & natus fuit esse accipiendum. Sed ipse sese statim refellit: subjicit enim verba huius loci ita esse comparata, ut nonnisi duriter, ac sensu valde tenui ad puerum Esaia tempore natum accommodari queant. Certè tum demum locus est distinctioni isti sensus literalis & mystici, cum literalis Christo non conuenit, sed Christi typo. Hic verò contra res habet: literalis enim Christo conuenit, & quidem proprie, immò magis proprie quam vlli alij, immò nulli alij nisi duriter acsensu valde tenui ipso confitente Aduersario. Ad literam enim Maria maximè proprie & virgo fuit, & concepit, & peperit filium, & vocauit nomen eius Emmanuel, & is puer mel & butyrum comedit donec sciret reprobare malum & eligere bonum: abundabat enim regio in qua natus & educatus est lacte & melle non solum domestico, sed etiam syluestri, ut patet ex
units.tr: XIX. Crellius replies that "in this place, as in many others, there is a twofold sense, namely the literal or historical, and the mystical; the one is to be understood of Christ, the other of the son of the prophetess who was then conceived and born." But he immediately refutes himself, for he adds that "the words of this place are so constructed that they can be applied to the boy born in Isaiah's time only harshly, and in a very thin sense." Certainly the distinction between literal and mystical sense has its place only when the literal sense does not fit Christ but Christ's type. Here, however, the case is the reverse: the literal sense fits Christ, and indeed properly, even more properly than it fits anyone else; indeed it fits no one else except harshly and in a very thin sense, as the opponent himself admits. For according to the letter, Mary was most properly both a virgin, and conceived and bore a son, and called his name Emmanuel, and that child ate butter and honey until he knew how to refuse the evil and choose the good. For the region in which he was born and brought up abounded in milk and honey, not only domestic but also wild, as appears from

units.la: XX. Nulla alia virgo concepit vnquam aut peperit. Virginem autem literali sensu חלמה significare notius est quàm vt probatione egeat. Nullus alius Emmanuelis nomine insignitus comparet in Scriptura. Aut igitur non fuit vllus, aut is silentio Scripturæ contectus pro nullo habendus est. Taceo nomen Emmanuelis augustius quiddam sonare quam vt convenire potuerit puero tempore Achazi nato. Taceo cap. 8. Iudæam appellari terram istius Emmanuelis non vulgari, vt ipse Crellius fatetur, ratione, sed aliqua peculiari, quæque cadere non potuit in filium prophetissæ.
units.tr: XX. No other virgin ever conceived or bore a child. That the word virgin in the literal sense is almah [חלמה] is too well known to need proof. No other person bearing the name Immanuel appears in Scripture. Either there was no such person, or, if there was, he must be regarded as nobody, since Scripture passes him over in silence. I say nothing of the fact that the name Immanuel has a loftier ring than could suit a boy born in the time of Ahaz. I say nothing of chapter 8, where the land of Judah is called the land of this Immanuel, not, as Crellius himself admits, for any ordinary reason, but for some special one, which could not apply to the son of the prophetess.

units.la: XXI. Virgeo miraculum, Quis hic, inquit ipse Crellius, non videt miraculum valde insigne diuinitus promissti? Quis enim credat, cum data fuisset Achazo facultas petendi signum aliquod maximè illustre atque admirabile, Deum, postea signum, quod Achazus petere noluisset, eligentem & proferentem signum valde vulgare & tale in quo vix quicquam miraculosi extitisset, tantummodo præbere voluisse? Atqui nihil fuit miraculosi si fœmina iuuenis concepit ex viro & peperit filium. Dices in eo consistere miraculum quod Esaias iam antea præscierit ac prædixerit eam & omnino concepturam & pariturum non filiam, sed filium. Primum aliud est præscientia aut prædictio miraculi, aliud ipsum miraculum. Esaias miraculum in conceptione & partu, & Emmanuele posuit, non in sua ipsius præscientia & prædictione, Dabit, inquit, vobis ipse Deus signum, quodnam? vtique quod verbis sequentibus exprimitur, Ecce virgo concipiet & pariet filium, &c. Deinde miraculum intelligitur singulare, non autem eiusmodi quod in omni vero vaticinio continereturr: omnis enim futuri contingentis certa prædictio tale quid miraculi continet. Tum parum illustre fuisset hoc miraculum: Id enim euenturum Propheta prædixisset quo I secundum ordinem naturæ sæpenumero euenit, vt quod euentus prædictioni respondisset posset ab Achazo fortunæ vel casui adscribi, & ta nen in præsentissi no discrimine suspensos populi Dei animos expectatione sui tenuisset forè per annum, ad sufficiendum fidem nutantem n parum potens & præsens adminiculum.
units.tr: XXI. I press the miracle. Who here, says Crellius himself, does not see a miracle of great distinction promised by God? For who would believe that, when Ahaz had been given the opportunity to ask for some very striking and wonderful sign, God then chose and offered a sign that was very commonplace, one in which hardly anything miraculous would have occurred? Yet there is nothing miraculous if a young woman conceives by a man and bears a son. You will say that the miracle consists in this, that Isaiah had foreseen and foretold that she would conceive and bear, not a daughter, but a son. But first, the foreknowledge or prediction of a miracle is one thing, the miracle itself another. Isaiah placed the miracle in the conception, the birth and Immanuel himself, not in his own foreknowledge and prediction. The Lord himself, he says, will give you a sign; what sign? Surely the one expressed in the words that follow: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, etc. Next, the miracle must be understood as a singular one, not of the kind that is contained in every true prophecy: for the sure prediction of any future contingent event contains something of that kind of miracle. Then this miracle would have been of little distinction. For the prophet would have foretold an event that, by the order of nature, happens very often, so that, when it came to pass, Ahaz could ascribe the outcome to fortune or chance; and yet it would scarcely have held in suspense for a year the minds of the people of God, who were in the most pressing danger, nor provided a powerful and present support to sustain their wavering faith.

units.la: XXII. Virgeo etiam prædictionem. Cuius enim prædicta fuisset diuinitus solenni ratione conceptio, natiuitas, no minus impositio, & educatio, hunc oportuisse virum admodum insignem. ac plane extraordinarium esse, vt patet inductione eorum quorum natiuitas praedicitur in Scriptura, talis tamen aliquis Achazi vel Esaiae tempore natus fuisse non legitur, haud tacendus in Scriptura si vllus extitisset.
units.tr: XXII. I press the prediction too. For if the conception, the birth, and no less the naming and upbringing of the child had been solemnly foretold by God, this boy must have been a very remarkable and altogether extraordinary man, as is clear from a survey of those whose birth is predicted in Scripture. Yet no such person is read of as born in the time of Ahaz or Isaiah, and he would certainly not have been passed over in silence in Scripture had there been any such person.

units.la: XXIII. Vrgeo denique differentiam & analogiam inter vmbram & corpus, typum & τὸ πνευματικὸν[?], quae hic nullae apparent. Nam quae est proportionum similitudo inter signum positum in certitudine praescientiae, & signum positum in conceptione virginea? Aut sensu literali virginem עלמה[?] significat, aut mystico: si literali, non igitur mystico: differt enim literalis à mystico. Si mystico, ostende in Prophetissa virginitatis Mariae typum, & quomodo non virgo virginem, concipiens ex viro concipientem absque viri opera, conceptio vacans miraculo conceptionem miraculosam qua talem, hoc est, quomodo affirmatio negationem sibi oppositam, vel contrà negatio affirmationem adumbrauerit. Num per filium Prophetissae Deus Iudaeis opem tulit, eosque liberauit ab hostibus quibusdam, vt typus esset Emmanuelis per quem liberamur à peccato morte & Diabolo? Quid etiam in sequentibus Esaiae verbis butyrum & mel comedet vt sciat reprobare malum & eligere bonum, butyrum mysticè significat? quid mel? quid reprobatio mali? quid electio boni? Quid quae sequuntur, quia antequam sciat puer reprobare malum & eligere bonum derelinquetur terra quam tu detestaris a facie duorum regum eorum, &c. quem habent mysticum sensum? Nullum equidem rationi consentaneum excogitare valeo: itaque contentus sum literali apprimè congruente.
units.tr: XXIII. Finally I press the difference and the analogy between shadow and body, type and to pneumatikon [τὸ πνευματικὸν], which do not appear here at all. For what similarity of proportion is there between a sign set in the certainty of foreknowledge and a sign set in a virginal conception? Either almah means a virgin in the literal sense, or in the mystical sense. If literal, then not mystical, for the literal differs from the mystical. If mystical, show me in the prophetess a type of Mary's virginity, and show how a non-virgin, conceiving a virgin, conceiving without the work of a man, a conception empty of miracle, adumbrates a miraculous conception as such; that is, how an affirmation may foreshadow the negation opposed to it, or, conversely, a negation the affirmation. Did God bring help to the Jews through the son of the prophetess, and deliver them from certain enemies, so that he might be a type of Immanuel, through whom we are freed from sin, death and the Devil? What too does the butter and honey of the following words of Isaiah, he shall eat butter and honey so that he may know to refuse evil and choose good, mystically signify? What does honey signify? What the refusing of evil? What the choosing of good? And what of the words that follow, for before the child knows to refuse evil and choose good, the land whose two kings you dread shall be forsaken, etc.? What mystical sense do they have? Indeed I cannot think of any interpretation consistent with reason, and so I am content with the literal sense, which fits very well.

units.la: XXIV. Objicit Crellius, talis ibi pueri natiuitatem promitti, in cuius adhuc infantia debeant relinquere terram, nempe Iudaeam, duo illi reges. Id nego, vnde enim id habet? ex versu 16. proximè à me commemorato, quia antequam sciat puer reprobare malum, &c? Minimè. Intelligitur enim hic versus 16. vel de eodem puero de quo duo proximè antecedentes, vel de alio. Si de alio, nihil ex eo colligi potest quod pertineat ad vaticinium de nascituro ex puella seu virgine filio. Si de eodem, occurrit Propheta cogitationi cuius proximo versu occasionem dederat, fore virginis filium insignem bellatorem, qui postquam adoleuisset, vel insito robore vt Samson, vel contracto exercitu vt Gedeon Iudaeam ab illis regibus alisque hostibus liberaret, cui falsae opinationi vt aditum præcludat subjicit fore vt ante id tempus & duo illi reges abducantur in captiuitatem aut etiam interficiantur, & Deus Iudæos per Regem Assyriorum, cuius opem implorare cogitabant, seuerè admodum castiget: id quod partim Achazi tempore, partim anno filij eius Ezechiæ decimo quarto factum est.
units.tr: XXIV. Crellius objects that a birth is promised there of a child in whose infancy those two kings are to abandon the land, namely Judah. I deny it. For where does he get this? From verse 16, which I cited just above: for before the child knows to refuse evil, etc.? Not at all. For this verse 16 is to be understood either as referring to the same child as the two verses immediately preceding, or to another. If to another, nothing can be drawn from it that pertains to the prophecy of a son to be born of a girl or virgin. If to the same child, the prophet meets a thought that he had given occasion for in the immediately preceding verse, namely that the son of the virgin would be a distinguished warrior who, once grown, would free Judah from those kings and other enemies, either by his innate strength like Samson or by an army he had raised like Gideon. To block this false opinion from gaining entry, he adds that before that time both those kings would be carried off into captivity or even killed, and that God would sharply punish the Jews through the king of the Assyrians, whose help they were planning to seek. This was partly fulfilled in the time of Ahaz, and partly in the fourteenth year of his son Hezekiah.

units.la: XXV. Instat Crellius, ex capite, inquit, 8 si cum 7. conferatur, facile apparet, intelligi nomine huius pueri filium Prophetissæ, per quam Esaiæ ipsius uxor intelligitur: quandoquidem ita ibi scribit Propheta, & accessi ad prophetissam (id quod verecunde vsum, coniugalem significare docentes omnes intelligunt) Et concepit & peperit filium. & dixit Dominus ad me: voca nomen eius, accelera spolia detrahere, festina prædari. Quia antequam sciat puer vocare patrem suum & matrem suam, auferetur fortitudo Damasci (quæ nimirum erat sedes regis Syriæ) & spolia Samariæ coram rege Assyriorum, vbi verba, quia antequam sciat, & correspondere illis cap. 7. verf. 16. quia antequam sciat reprobare malum, &c. facile est videre. Falla quadam specie similitudinis delusus Crellius veras dissimilitudines non animaduertit. Nam cap. 7. virgo nominatur, cap. 8. prophetissa iam amissa virginitate mater. Illic conceptio miraculosa prædicitur, hic miraculo vacans narratur. Illic puer vocatur Emmanuel nobiscum Deus, hic vocatur Maher S. halal Has Bas, quod vetus interpres reddidit, Accelera spolia detrahere, festina prædari: quæ nomina quantum inter se distent nemo non videt. Illic dicitur Antequam puer sciat reprobare malum & eligere bonum, &c. Hic Antequam sciat vocare patrem suum & matrem suam, quæ duo differunt, potest enim puer sonare Abi & Imi, hoc est, Tatam & Mammam satis diu antequam sciat reprobare malum & eligere bonum.
units.tr: XXV. Crellius presses further: if chapter 8 is compared with chapter 7, it readily appears that by the name of this child is meant the son of the prophetess, through whom is understood Isaiah's own wife, since the prophet writes there thus: and I went in to the prophetess (which everyone who understands the discreet usage recognises as signifying marital intercourse), and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: call his name, hasten to carry off spoils, make haste to plunder. For before the child knows to call his father and his mother, the strength of Damascus (which was of course the seat of the king of Syria) and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians. The words for before he knows and their correspondence to chapter 7, verse 16, for before he knows to refuse evil, etc., are easy to see. Crellius, deceived by a certain appearance of resemblance, has not noticed the real dissimilarities. For in chapter 7 the woman is called a virgin; in chapter 8 she is a prophetess, a mother who has already lost her virginity. There a miraculous conception is foretold; here it is narrated as lacking any miracle. There the child is called Immanuel, God with us; here he is called Maher-shalal-hash-baz, which the old translator rendered Hasten to carry off spoils, make haste to plunder. Nobody fails to see how far apart these names are. There it is said before the child knows to refuse evil and choose good, etc.; here before he knows to call his father and his mother. These two differ, for the word child can mean Abi and Imi, that is, Daddy and Mummy, well before he knows to refuse evil and choose good.

units.la: XXVI. Opponent etiam huic secundo nostro argumento Aduersarij similia nomina composita, vrbis Hierosolymæ voluntas mea in ea Esaiæ 62. 4. Dominus illic Ezechielis verf. vlt. Dominus iustitia nostra Ierem. 33. 16. Altaris Dominus exaltatio mea, vel Dominus vexillum meum Exod. 17. 15. Dominus pax Iud. 6. 24. quorundam virorum, Elnathan Deus dedit, Eliana Deus Zelotes, Elimelec Deus meus rex, &c. Ex quibus concludi non potest Hierosolymam, Altare, viros illos ipsum Deum fuisse. Respondeo illorum nominum & Emmanuelis rationem esse valde disparem: est enim Emmanuelis nomen personæ adorabili diuininitus impositum, cum illa nomina memorata, vel non personæ, vel non diuinitus impositá sint. Adde quod in nominibus voluntas mea in ea, & Dominus illic, ea, & illic, ipsam Hierusalem cuius sunt nomina designant, impedíuntque quominus voluntas Dei, vel Dominus dici putetur. Nomen autem Dominus institia nostra, vel non tribuitur Hierosolymæ eo loco, vel si tribuitur, ei tribuitur quatenus Hierosolyma, id est, Ecclesia Christus dici potest teste Apostolo. 1. Cor. 12. 12. Sed de eo nomine disputandum erit copiosius alio loco. Ad altare quod spectat, id typus fuit veri altaris, verum autem altare est ipse Christus: Idem enim sacerdos victima, altare, & quodam respectu tabernaculum fuit. Itaque nomina illa Altaribus tributa typicè, Christo conueniunt verè. Ad viros quod attinet, humanitus sic appellati sunt, ac proinde eorum nominum nulla ratio haberi debet, aut si qua haberi debet, ea ad Christum tanquam ad veritatem, ad viros autem illos tanquam ad vmbras & typos Christi referenda est, causæque quam agimus fauet.
units.tr: XXVI. The adversaries will also oppose this second argument of ours with similar compound names: my delight is in her (the name of Jerusalem), Isaiah 62. 4; the Lord is there (the last verse of Ezekiel); the Lord our righteousness, Jeremiah 33. 16; the name of an altar, the Lord my exaltation or the Lord my banner, Exodus 17. 15; the Lord is peace, Judges 6. 24; and the names of certain men, Elnathan, God has given; Eliana, God is zealous; Elimelech, my God is king, etc. From these it cannot be concluded that Jerusalem, the altar, or those men were God himself. I answer that the reason for those names and for Immanuel is very different. For the name Immanuel was divinely given to a person worthy of worship, whereas those names mentioned are either not of persons, or not divinely given. Add that in the names my delight is in her and the Lord is there, the words her and there refer to Jerusalem itself, whose names they are, and prevent it from being thought that the will of God or the Lord is meant. As for the name the Lord our righteousness, either it is not applied to Jerusalem in that passage, or, if it is, it is applied to her inasmuch as Jerusalem, that is, the Church, can be called Christ, as the Apostle witnesses (1 Cor. 12. 12). But this name will have to be discussed more fully in another place. As for the altar, it was a type of the true altar, and the true altar is Christ himself: for the same is priest, victim, altar and, in a certain respect, tabernacle. Thus those names given to altars belong to Christ truly, though typically. As for the men, they were so named in a human way, and therefore no account should be taken of those names; or, if any account is to be taken, it should be referred to Christ as the truth, and to those men as shadows and types of Christ, which favours the cause we are arguing.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TERTIA.
units.tr: Disputation III.

units.la: De Arg. III. Ex Esaiæ Cap viii. v. 13. Dominum exercituum ipsum sanctificate. ipse pauor vester & ipse terror vester: & erit vobis in sanctificationem, in lapidem autem offensionis & in petram scandali duabus domibus Israël, &c. Collato cum Rom. 9. 30. & 1. petr. 2. 3.
units.tr: On Argument III, from Isaiah ch. 8 v. 13: "Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, &c." Compared with Rom. 9. 30 and 1. Petr. 2. 3.

units.la: 1. PERGAT, vt coepit, Esaias, iudice Hieronymo non solùm Propheta sed Euangelista & Apostolus, testimonium de diuina Christi essentia dicere. Apud eum cap. viii. verf. 13. Dominus sic loquitur, Dominum exercitum [?]את יהוה צבאות ipsum sanctificate: ipse pauor vester, & ipse terror vester: & erit vobis in sanctificationem, in lapidem autem offensionis, & in petram scandali duabus domibus Israel, in laqueum & in ruinam habitantibus Ierusalem, &c. Ex illis verbis sic argumentor
units.tr: 1. Let Isaiah continue as he has begun. Jerome judged him not only a prophet but an evangelist and an apostle, and so Isaiah bears witness to the divine essence of Christ. In him, ch. 8 v. 13, the Lord speaks thus: "Sanctify the LORD of hosts [את יהוה צבאות] himself: let him be your fear, and let him be your dread: and he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling, and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem", &c. From these words I argue thus.

units.la: Ille qui Esai. viii. verf. 13. dicitur futurus in lapidem offensionis & petram scandali est Deus praeditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: He who, in Isaiah 8 v. 13, is said to be going to be a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence is God, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est ille qui Esai. viii. 13. dicitur futurus in lapidem offensionis & in petram scandali.
units.tr: Christ is he who, in Isaiah 8. 13, is said to be going to be a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence.

units.la: Ergo Christus est Deus praeditus essentia diuina
units.tr: Therefore Christ is God, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Major nec negatur ab Aduersarijs nec potest negari. Minor probatur testimonio Apostoli Rom. ix. 30. Offenderunt enim in lapidem offensionis, sicut scriptum est, Ecce pono in Sion lapidem offensionis & petram scandali. Quem enim lapidem offensionis intelligit nisi Christum? Quem dicendo lapidem offensionis & petram scandali locum Veteris Testamenti citat, nisi istum Esaiae viii. 13. Docet igitur Christum esse illum lapidem offensionis & petram scandali, cuius mentio fit Esai. viii. 13.
units.tr: The major premise is neither denied by our opponents nor can it be denied. The minor is proved by the testimony of the Apostle, Rom. 9. 30: "For they stumbled at that stumbling-stone; as it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence." For whom else does he understand by the stone of stumbling than Christ? And when, by naming the stone of stumbling and the rock of offence, he cites a passage of the Old Testament, which passage can it be but Isaiah 8. 13? He therefore teaches that Christ is that stone of stumbling and rock of offence which is mentioned in Isaiah 8. 13.

units.la: II. Quid respondet Socinus? Negat locum Esai. 8. 13. citari ab Apostolo, Ipsa prima verba, inquit, recitati ab ipso loci aperte docent, Paulum non istum (Esai. 8. 13.) sed illum alterum cap. 28. reuera citare. Docent quidem certe prima verba Paulum citare locum Esai. 28. 16. At eum simul non citare locum Esai. 8. 13. quomodo docent? diuersis verbis? An per consequentiam? nullo modo. Quid enim prohibuit duo loca Esaiae citari ab Apostolo conjunctim? Annon idem Apostolus ad Rom. 3. verf. 10. & seqq. deprompta ex variis Psalmis aliquot loca in vnum quasi testimonij corpus compegit? Non citari igitur illum locum nihil docet, citari multa euincunt.
units.tr: II. What does Socinus reply? He denies that the passage Isaiah 8. 13 is cited by the Apostle: "The very first words he quotes, he says, plainly show that Paul is really citing not that passage (Isaiah 8. 13) but the other one in ch. 28." The first words certainly show that Paul is citing Isaiah 28. 16. But how do they show that he is at the same time not citing Isaiah 8. 13? In different words? By inference? In no way. For what prevents the Apostle from citing two passages of Isaiah together? Did not the same Apostle, at Rom. 3. 10 and following, gather several passages drawn from various Psalms into one body, as it were, of testimony? That it is not cited shows nothing; that many things are cited proves it.

units.la: III. Ac primò quidem verba, lapidem offensionis & petram scandali. Nam si prima verba, Ecce pono in Sion, docent Paulum citare locum Esai. 28. 16. nonne similiter verba sequentia lapidem offensionis & petram scandali docent Paulum citare locum Esai. 8. 13? par enim est ratio, Quàm enim prima illa non leguntur Esai. 8. sed Esai. 8. 28. tam sequentia ista non leguntur Esai. 28. sed Esai. 8.
units.tr: III. And first, the words "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence." For if the first words, "Behold, I lay in Sion", show that Paul is citing Isaiah 28. 16, do not the following words, "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence", similarly show that Paul is citing Isaiah 8. 13? The reasoning is the same. For just as those first words are not read in Isaiah 8 but in Isaiah 28, so these following words are not read in Isaiah 28 but in Isaiah 8.

units.la: IV. Id quoque euincunt verba, Sicut scriptum est: notant enim conuenientiam citati vaticinij cum euentu memorato verbis immediatè praecedentibus, Offenderunt in lapidem offensionis. Cum illo autem euentu congruit vaticinium Esai. 8. 13. non vero vaticinium Esai. 28. 16. ut cuiuis patet. Citatur igitur vaticinium Esai. 8. 13. vel solum, vel saltem praecipuè.
units.tr: IV. The words "as it is written" also prove this: they mark the agreement of the cited prophecy with the event recorded in the words immediately preceding, "They stumbled at the stone of stumbling." Now the prophecy of Isaiah 8. 13 agrees with that event, not the prophecy of Isaiah 28. 16, as is plain to anyone. The prophecy of Isaiah 8. 13 is therefore cited either alone or at least chiefly.

units.la: V. Idem etiam docet scopus Apostoli, qui sine dubio fuit scandalum, quod ex Iudaeorum[?] incredulitate & reiectione nasci poterat, tollere: poterat enim offendi lector cogitans illum populum, cui promissus fuerat Christus & soli, & toties, tot subinde repetitis oraculis, Christum non agnouisse. Tollit autem hoc scandalum prolato Esaiae vaticinio. Quis enim pius offendi possit eo euentu, quem tot ante seculis praedictum legit in Scriptura? Ad hunc scopum conducit per se locus Esai. 8. 13. non autem locus Esai. 28. Is igitur locus vel solus vel praecipuè citatus fuisse putandus est. Hoc etiam innuunt verba proximè antecedentia, offenderunt enim in lapide offensionis, quis enim non videt per lapidem offensionis sic antonomasticè seu ἐξοχὴν appellatum eum potius intelligi debere, qui sic in Veteri Testamento appellatur, quàm eum qui sic nunquam vocatur? Nunquam autem sic Christus vocatur, si de eo locus Esaiae cap. 8. intelligi non debet.
units.tr: V. The aim of the Apostle also shows the same, which was without doubt to remove the offence that might arise from the unbelief and rejection of the Jews. For a reader might be offended, thinking that that people, to whom Christ had been promised, and who had received so many oracles, repeated again and again, had not recognised Christ. But the citation of the prophecy of Isaiah removes this offence. For what pious person could be offended by an event which he reads was foretold in Scripture so many centuries before? To this aim the passage Isaiah 8. 13 contributes of itself, not Isaiah 28. That passage, therefore, must be thought to have been cited alone or chiefly. The words immediately preceding also hint at this: "for they stumbled at the stone of stumbling." For who does not see that by "the stone of stumbling," named thus by eminence [ἐξοχὴν], one ought rather to understand him who is so called in the Old Testament, than him who is never so called? But Christ is never so called, if the passage of Isaiah ch. 8 is not to be understood of him.

units.la: VI. Adde quod prima illa verba petita ex Esai. 28. Ecce ego pono in Sion, per se citari non potuerunt cum per se sola sensum perfectum non habeant. Cum igitur negari non posset quin citetur enuntiatio, non autem duntaxat enuntiationis pars lectoris animum suspensum tenens alterius partis expectatione, fatendum est non minus citari verba, lapidem offensionis & petram scandali, quaedam antecedentia, Ecce pono in Sion, eandem enim componunt enuntiationem citatam, cuius neutra pars citari per se seu separatim potuit.
units.tr: VI. Add that those first words taken from Isaiah 28, "Behold, I lay in Sion," could not be cited by themselves, since by themselves they do not have a complete sense. Since, therefore, it cannot be denied that a whole statement is cited, and not merely a part of a statement which keeps the reader's mind in suspense awaiting the other part, it must be admitted that the words "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence" are cited no less than the preceding words, "Behold, I lay in Sion". For together they make up the one statement that is cited, neither part of which could be cited by itself or separately.

units.la: VII. Praetermittenda non videtur hoc loco Apostoli prudentia. Non enim potuit apertius innuere eandem petram intelligi Esai. 8. & Esai. 28. quae duo illa loca in unum testimonium, immo in unam enuntiationem coniungendo, ac verba quae desumpsit ex Esai. 8. media interiecta inter illa quae ex cap. 28. transcripsit, ut nihil dubitemus de quo lapide agitur in uno loco, de eodem agi in altero. Certum est autem in cap. 28. 16. agi de Christo ipso teste Socino. Agitur ergo etiam in cap. 8. de Christo.
units.tr: VII. The prudence of the Apostle does not seem to be passed over here. For he could not more plainly have hinted that the same rock is meant in Isaiah 8 and in Isaiah 28, by joining these two passages into one testimony, indeed into one statement, and by placing the words he drew from Isaiah 8 in the middle, between those he copied from ch. 28, so that we need not doubt which stone is meant in one passage is the same that is meant in the other. "But it is certain that in Isaiah 28. 16 the subject is Christ himself, according to Socinus." Therefore the subject in ch. 8 is also Christ.

units.la: VIII. Denique quid facit Apostolus cum verba cap. 8. transcribit, ac cum antecedentibus connectit per illud, [?]sicut scriptum est, si ea non citat? Ostendit tantùm, inquit Socinus, verba, qua Esaia cap. 8. de illo vno Deo dicuntur, ad Christum accommodari posse, dum ea tanquam si de Christo dicta fuissent, adiungit verbis eiusdem prophetae cap. 28. quem locum revera citat, & merito de Christo exponit. At quomodo ad Christum accommodari possunt, si de Christo nec dicta sunt, nec intelligi debent? Aut, cur ea tanquam si de Christo dicta fuissent, adjungit verbis eiusdem prophetae de Christo intelligendis, si non vult ea à nobis accipi tanquam si de Christo dicta fuissent? Certè talis accommodatio menti prophetae magis repugnans quàm congruens nihil probaret, nihil faceret ad tollendum vel minuendum scandalum, nihil ad firmandam lectoris fidem, aut scopum Apostoli iuuandum: pertineret tantùm cum ad praebendam Iudæis occasionem querendi de Apostolo ad meram creaturam transferente praeter mentem Veteris Testamenti, ea quae de creatore, vno illo vero Deo, dicta sunt à Propheta, tum ad fallendos Christianos, qui videntes ea quae dicta sunt ab Esaia de Domino exercituum ad Christum, tanquam si de eo à Propheta dicta fuissent, aptari, inducuntur auctoritate Apostoli & Christi admiratione, vt credant Christum esse Dominum exercituum.
units.tr: VIII. Finally, what is the Apostle doing when he copies the words of ch. 8 and connects them with what precedes by that "as it is written," if he is not citing them? "He shows only," says Socinus, "that the words which in Isaiah ch. 8 are said of that one God can be applied to Christ, since he adds them, as if they had been said of Christ, to the words of the same prophet in ch. 28, which he really cites, and rightly expounds of Christ." But how can they be applied to Christ if they were not said of Christ and ought not to be understood of him? Or why does he add them as if they had been said of Christ to the words of the same prophet, which are to be understood of Christ, if he does not want us to take them as if they had been said of Christ? Certainly such an application, more repugnant than congruent to the mind of the prophet, would prove nothing, would do nothing to remove or lessen the offence, nothing to strengthen the reader's faith or to help the Apostle's aim. It would only serve, on the one hand, to give the Jews an occasion of complaint against the Apostle for transferring to a mere creature what the Prophet said of the Creator, that one true God, contrary to the mind of the Old Testament; and on the other hand, to deceive Christians, who, seeing that the things said by Isaiah of the LORD of hosts are fitted to Christ, as if the Prophet had said them of him, are led by the authority of the Apostle and the wonder at Christ to believe that Christ is the LORD of hosts.

units.la: I X. Paulo suffragatur Petrus, qui prioris Epist. suae cap. 2. verf. 6. 7. 8. tres Scripturae locos si nul iunxit, primum ex Esaiae cap. 28. alterum ex Psal. 118. tertium ex hoc Esaiae 8. 13. Propter quod, inquit, continet Scriptura, Ecce pono in Sion lapidem summum angularem, probatum, electum, pretiosum, & qui credit in eum non confundetur. vobis igitur honor credentibus: non credentibus autem lapis quem reprobauerunt aedificantes, hic factus est in caput anguli, & lapis offensionis & petra scandali, his qui offendunt verbo. Horum trium locorum constat primum & secundum cum citari ab Apostolo tum de Christo debere intelligi, cur non igitur idem sentiamus de tertio, eoque magis quod Apostolus tertium diuisit, ac inter eius partes secundum locauit, & cum illis ita copulauit, vt videri possint in vnum testimonium coaluisse? Nam verba, vobis igitur honor credentibus, respondent verbis Esaiae cap. 8. & erit vobis in sanctificationem, seu potius in sanctuarium: מקדש[?] enim proprie sanctuarium, non autem sanctificationem significat, posuit autem Apostolus honorem pro sanctuario, hoc est, consequens pro antecedente: erat enim sanctuarium honor & gloria Israelis: & quibus hic lapis est honori illis est in sanctuario, & vice versa. Mirum certè est Apostolos verba Esaiae cap. 8. 13. si de Patre non de Christo dicta fuerunt, de Patre nunquam, de Christo perpetuò exponere, ac verba Esaiae cap. 8. aliis locis, in quibus de Christo agi certum est, constanter admisce re & implicare, & cum eis in eandem enunciationem compingere.
units.tr: IX. Peter supports Paul, who, in ch. 2 vv. 6, 7, 8 of his first Epistle, if I may say so, joined three passages of Scripture: the first from Isaiah ch. 28, the second from Psalm 118, the third from this passage of Isaiah 8. 13. "Wherefore," he says, "it is contained in Scripture: Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner-stone, elect, precious; and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded. To you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word." Of these three passages it is agreed that the first and second are cited by the Apostle and must be understood of Christ. Why then should we not think the same of the third, especially since the Apostle divided the third and placed the second among its parts, and so joined them together that they can seem to have grown into one testimony? For the words "to you therefore which believe he is precious" correspond to the words of Isaiah 8, "and he shall be for a sanctuary", or rather "for a sanctuary" [מקדש]: for מקדש properly means sanctuary, not sanctification; and the Apostle put "honour" for "sanctuary", that is, the consequent for the antecedent, since the sanctuary was the honour and glory of Israel; and for those to whom this stone is precious, it is a sanctuary, and vice versa. It is certainly remarkable that the Apostles, if the words of Isaiah 8. 13 were spoken of the Father and not of Christ, should never expound them of the Father but constantly of Christ, and constantly mix and entwine the words of Isaiah 8 with other passages, in which it is certain that Christ is the subject, and join them into one statement.

units.la: X. Praeterea confitentur Aduersarij in locis Esaiae c. 28. & Ps. 118. certum esse agi de Christo. Peto unde id eis constet? Num ex eo quod Apostoli locos illos ad Christum accommodarunt? At illi etiam locum Esaiae cap. 8. ad eundem Christum accommodarunt: nec est in eorum verbis quicquam unde possis colligere locum illum Esai. 8. 13. duobus aliis esse disparem. Cur igitur pari ratione pariter non assentiuntur? Num ex locorum illorum circumstantiis? An igitur deprehenderunt aliquid in locis Esaiae cap. 28. 16. & Ps. 118. 21. quod dici nequeat de eo de quo agitur Esaiae 8. vel contrà in Esaiae 8. quod non conveniat ei de quo agitur Esaiae 28. & Ps. 118? Nihil prorsus. Quicquid enim de lapide seu petra dicitur Esaiae 28. 16. & Ps. 118. 21. id etiam de petra memorata Esaiae 8. 13. dici posse manifestum est. Nam qui potuit Lapis descriptus Esaiae 8. esse lapis offensionis & petra scandali duabus domibus Israelis, si positus in Sion (poni autem nisi à Deo non potuit) & à duabus illis domibus, hoc est, ab aedificantibus reiectus non fuit? Quis lapis eo magis probatus, pretiosus, angularis, solidus „caput anguli? Quis magis cavet ne confundatur quisquis credit in eum? Conveniunt igitur illi quaecunque de lapide dicta leguntur Esaiae 28. 16. & Psal. 118. 21.
units.tr: X. Besides, the opponents admit that the passages in Isaiah 28 and Psalm 118 are certainly about Christ. I ask: how does that become clear to them? Is it because the Apostles applied those passages to Christ? But they also applied the passage in Isaiah 8:13 to the same Christ, and nothing in their words allows you to infer that Isaiah 8:13 differs from the other two. Why, then, do they not agree to it by the same reasoning? Is it from the circumstances of those passages? Have they found something in Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:21 that cannot be said of the one Isaiah 8 is about, or conversely something in Isaiah 8 that does not suit the one Isaiah 28 and Psalm 118 are about? Nothing at all. For whatever is said of the stone or rock in Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:21 can clearly be said also of the rock mentioned in Isaiah 8:13.
