For how could the stone described in Isaiah 8 be a stone of offence and a rock of scandal to the two houses of Israel, if it was laid in Zion (which it could not be unless by God) and was not rejected by those two houses, that is, by the builders? What stone is more tested, precious, a cornerstone, solid, the head of the corner? Who guards more against being confounded than whoever believes in him? Therefore all that is read of the stone in Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:21 fits it.

units.la: XI. Rursus quid dicitur de lapide Esaiae 8. quod negari possit de lapide descripto aliis illis duobus locis? Hoc unum, inquies quod vocatur Dominus exercituum. Unde vero habes id nomen non convenire lapidi descripto Esaiae 28. & psal. 118? Lapis ille est Christus. Christus autem non est Dominus exercituum. Praeter hanc τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ[?] petitionem causari nihil possunt Aduersarii. Nihil enim est in locis Esaiae 28. & Psal. 118. quod lapidem quem describunt vocari Dominum exercituum prohibeat, est potius quod iubeat: cum enim constet lapidem de quo agitur in duobus illis locis esse lapidem offensionis & petram scandali, lapidem autem offensionis & petram scandali esse dominum exercituum, patet lapidem de quo agitur in duobus illis locis esse Dominum exercituum. Id quod etiam non obscure innuunt verba illa Esaiae 28. Qui credit in eum non confundetur. sic enim commendari solet in Veteri Testamento fides in Deum, non vero fides in meram creaturam.
units.tr: XI. Again, what is said of the stone in Isaiah 8 that could be denied of the stone described in those other two passages? Only this, you will say: that it is called the Lord of hosts. But where do you get the idea that this name does not belong to the stone described in Isaiah 28 and Psalm 118? That stone is Christ. But Christ is not the Lord of hosts. Beyond this begging of the question [τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ], the opponents have nothing to allege. For there is nothing in Isaiah 28 and Psalm 118 that forbids the stone they describe being called the Lord of hosts; there is rather something that enjoins it. Since it is agreed that the stone spoken of in those two passages is a stone of offence and a rock of scandal, and that a stone of offence and a rock of scandal is the Lord of hosts, it is plain that the stone spoken of in those two passages is the Lord of hosts. The words of Isaiah 28 also hint at this not obscurely: Whoever believes in him will not be confounded. For faith in God is commended in this way in the Old Testament, not faith in a mere creature.

units.la: XII. Responsionem suam Socinus tot telis confossam recreare conatur vnica ratione, certum est, inquit, ista quae de illo vno Deo apud Esaiam praedicantur, multo ante Christi aduentum & eius tempora impleta fuisse. Hoc qua facilitate ab ipso affirmatur, eadem à me negatur. At subiicit rationem, Est enim, inquit, ibi praedictio de vtriusque domus Israelis captiuitate, quarum altera, id est, decem tribuum, iam instabat, & propterea pluribus verbis paulo ante eodem cap. aperte praedicta fuerat, altera vero, id est, tribus Iudae & Beniamin captiuitas, vt pote, quae plurimis annis post sutura erat breuius & obscurius (vrbe ipsa tamen Hierusalem nominata) in istis ipsis verbis quae de illo vno Deo dicuntur, pronunciata fuit. Hoc quoque nego: captiuitatis enim Babylonicae nullum animaduerto vestigium in toto hoc cap. 8. vti nec nominatam vrbem Hierusalem. Addit, Nec quisquam affirmare potest, istam praedictionem figurate ad Christi quoque tempora pertinere. Ego vero affirmo istam praedictionem non iam figurate, sed proprie ad Christi tempora pertinere. Cum enim vaticinium istud tria contineat, Mandatum, Timorem eius populi ne timeatis, neque paueatis. Dominum exercituum ipsum sanctificate, &c. Promissionem, & erit vobis in sanctuarium: comminationem, in lapidem autem offensionis & in petram scandali duabus domibus Israel, Mandatum ad Christi tempora pertinere testis est omni exceptione maior Petrus 1. Ep. 3. 14. Timorem, inquit, eorum ne timete, neque turbamini. Dominum Deum sanctificate in cordibus vestris. Si Mandatum ad Christi tempora pertinet, quis non videt ad eadem Christi tempora etiam promissionem & comminationem pertinere? Potest ne etiam quisquam negare Deum temporibus Christi fuisse tum in sanctuarium fidelibus ipsum sanctificantibus, tum in lapidem offensionis & petram scandali duabus domibus Israëlis? Hoc vtrumque profecto aut ante impletum non fuit, aut saltem tunc quoque, & quidem maxime, impletum fuit. Quod si antecedentia spectes, praecesserat cap. 7. praedictio de nascituro ex virgine Emmanuele, & hoc ipso cap. bis iniecta Emmanuelis mentio. Emmanuel autem est Christus. Si sequentia, sequùntur verba illa, Ecce ego & pueri quos dedit mihi Dominus de Christo exposita Heb. 2. 13.
units.tr: XII. Socinus tries to revive his answer, riddled with so many weapons, by a single reason. "It is certain," he says, "that the things foretold of that one God in Isaiah were fulfilled long before Christ's coming and his times." Whatever he asserts with such ease, I deny with equal ease. But he adds a reason: "For there is," he says, "in that place a prediction of the captivity of both houses of Israel. Of these, the one, that is the ten tribes, was already imminent, and so had been openly foretold in more words a little before in the same chapter; the other, that is the captivity of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, since it was to come many years later, was announced more briefly and obscurely (though the city of Jerusalem is named) in those very words which are spoken of that one God." This too I deny. For I can see no trace of the Babylonian captivity in the whole of this chapter 8, nor is the city of Jerusalem named in it. He adds: "Nor can anyone affirm that this prediction pertains figuratively to the times of Christ as well." But I affirm that this prediction pertains not figuratively but properly to the times of Christ. For since that prophecy contains three things, a command, "Fear not the fear of that people, neither be afraid. Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself," etc.; a promise, "and he will be for you a sanctuary"; and a threat, "but for a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to the two houses of Israel": the command pertains to the times of Christ, as witness 1 Peter 3:14, which is beyond all exception: "Fear not their fear, neither be troubled. Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts." If the command pertains to the times of Christ, who does not see that the promise and the threat pertain to the same times of Christ? Can anyone deny that in the times of Christ God was a sanctuary to the faithful who sanctified him, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to the two houses of Israel? Certainly both of these either were not fulfilled before, or else were fulfilled then as well, and indeed most of all. But if you look at what goes before, chapter 7 had foretold the one to be born of a virgin, Immanuel, and in this very chapter the mention of Immanuel is introduced twice. Immanuel is Christ. If you look at what follows, the words "Behold I and the children whom the Lord has given me" are expounded of Christ at Heb. 2. 13.

units.la: XIII. Sed ut clarius perspici possit nec agi de captivitate Iudæorum in hoc Esaiæ loco, & Spiritum Sanctum potissimum respexisse ad tempora Christi, eius mens pro mensura indultæ nobis gratiæ aperienda est. Habemus in hoc cap. 8. & superiore specimen ex una parte hostium Christi & Ecclesiæ in Filio Romeliæ rege Samariæ atque Ephraim, & Retsin rege Damasci & Syriæ, Ex altera vero parte Ecclesiæ quatenus in ea sunt [illegible, ~8 letters] & hypocritæ in Achazo rege Iudæ populoque eius. Pekah enim & Retsin, Ephraimitæ & Syri, hostes inter se acerrimi, religione & animis discordes, alteri Iudæorum fratres, alteri à Dei fœdere alieni positis inimicitiis, communi consilio contra domum Davidis & Iudæam conjurantes, ut illa destructa hanc partiantur inter se, & filio Tabeel subjiciant, specimen sunt illustre talium Christi eiusque Ecclesiæ hostium, quales fuerunt Herodes & Pontius Pilatus, populi Israëlis & gentes, ut cuiusvis conferenti illos inter se manifestum est. Achazus vero & populus eius, audita illa coniuratione, agnita sua imbecillitate & hostium potentia, metu vehementissimo perturbati, opem regis Assyriorum contempto Dei verbo implorantes, eorum nobis in se specimen exhibent, qui ingruente persecutione Deo diffidentes metu velut vento agitantur, & ad fallacia perfugia verbo Dei neglecto confugiunt. Propheta quoque Esaias partibus ministri Christi apud eum strenuè fungitur. Hortatur metum deponat: pollicetur irritum fore hostium conatum: rationem addit, disparem esse rationem regni Iudæ & regnorum Samariæ & Syriæ, illius caput esse Deum horum non item: necessitatem hoc credendi aperit: offert media ad fidem firmandam apta: ea respuentes increpat: Ac illud nihilominus proponit quod est fidei objectu & pabulum, capitis Iudæ incarnatione, Dei nobiscum pactefactione in vera carne humana, signum salutis credentibus exitij incredulis, cuius intuitu tunc promissi nunc exhibiti fides roboratur, omnisque tentationis victrix evadit. Denique vanitatem ostendit carnalis prudentiæ & perfugij. In rege Assyriorum cernitur specimen primo carnalis præsidij, quod perpetuò fallit & nocet, Deo per illud ipsum Ecclesiam castigante, ad quod ipso spreto confugit: Deinde hostis impudentis & blasphemi, qualem se prodidit tempore Ezechiæ, speciminis eorum qui Deo reuera fiduut : quo respectu re-gem Assyriorum Prophcta describens cap. viii. ad Emmanuelem confugit, eiusque ope implorata hostium destructionem, quantacunque eorum multitudo & potentia sit, exultabundus prædicit, quàm præstet carnali spirituale perfugium non obscure significans.
units.tr: XIII. But so that it may be seen more clearly that this passage of Isaiah is not about the captivity of the Jews, and that the Holy Spirit chiefly had in view the times of Christ, his meaning must be unfolded according to the measure of grace granted to us. In this chapter 8 and the one before it we have, on the one side, an example of the enemies of Christ and of the Church in the son of Remaliah, king of Samaria and Ephraim, and Rezin, king of Damascus and Syria; and on the other side, the Church, insofar as there are in it [illegible] and hypocrites, in Ahaz, king of Judah, and his people. For Pekah and Rezin, Ephraimites and Syrians, most bitter enemies of each other, discordant in religion and temperament, the one brother-nations to the Jews, the other alien from God's covenant, their enmities laid aside, conspiring by common counsel against the house of David and Judah, so that they might destroy the one, divide the other between themselves, and subject it to the son of Tabeel, are an illustrious specimen of such enemies of Christ and his Church, such as Herod and Pontius Pilate, the people of Israel and the Gentiles were, as is plain to anyone who compares them. Ahaz and his people, however, when they heard of that conspiracy, recognising their own weakness and the power of their enemies, were struck with the most violent fear, and, despising God's word, implored the help of the king of the Assyrians. They present us in themselves with a picture of those who, when persecution rises, distrust God, are tossed about by fear like the wind, and flee to deceitful refuges, neglecting God's word. The prophet Isaiah also acts vigorously among them, playing the part of Christ's minister. He urges them to lay aside their fear; he promises that the enemies' attempt will come to nothing; he adds the reason that the position of the kingdom of Judah differs from that of the kingdoms of Samaria and Syria, for its head is God, whereas theirs is not; he sets out the necessity of believing this; he offers means suited to strengthening faith; he rebukes those who reject them. And he nonetheless sets before them what is the object and food of faith: the incarnation of the head of Judah, God's covenant with us in true human flesh, a sign of salvation to believers and of ruin to unbelievers. By regard to this, the faith in the promise, then given and now shown, is strengthened and comes out victorious over every temptation. Finally, he shows the vanity of carnal prudence and of refuge. In the king of the Assyrians is seen, first, a specimen of carnal protection, which always deceives and harms, God through that very thing chastising the Church, which, having spurned him, flees to it. Then there is the impudent and blasphemous enemy, such as he showed himself to be in the time of Hezekiah, a specimen of those who truly trust in God. In regard to this the Prophet, describing the king of the Assyrians in chapter 8, flees to Immanuel, and, his help having been implored, exultantly foretells the destruction of the enemies, however great their number and power, not obscurely signifying how much spiritual refuge excels carnal.

units.la: XIV. Quoniam autem præter hostes externos latent in Ecclesia [illegible, ~9 letters] & hypocritæ veris fidelibus permixti, eosque nonnunquam auctoritate & numero superantes, qui ingruente persecutione cum trepidant ipsi, tum exemplo & sermonibus fideles ad similem trepidationem vitandæque persecutionis carnalem rationem impellunt: quod genus tentationis eo nocentius est quo occultius: horum specimen Propheta nobis exhibet in populo Iudaico, cui ex adverso fidelium specimen opponit in se ipso &c. filijs suis conteplandum, edoctis à Domino manu forti non eadem via cum populo illo incedere, non iisdem sermonibus uti, non iisdem rebus terreri: quæ ab illo populo diuinitus & forti manu præcepta secessio Christi & Apostolorum tempore demum perfecta est. Sic antecedentia citatum ab Apostolis testimonium percurrentibus nobis neque captiuitas Babylonica occurrit, neque quicquam quod ad Christi tempora, saltem vt vmbra aut typus non pertineat.
units.tr: XIV. Since, besides external enemies, hidden hypocrites are mixed in the Church [...] with true believers, and sometimes surpass them in authority and number, they tremble when persecution comes, and by their example and words they push the faithful towards the same trembling and towards a carnal way of avoiding persecution. This kind of temptation is the more harmful the more hidden it is. The Prophet shows us an example of it in the Jewish people, and sets over against it an example of the faithful in himself and his sons, to be contemplated, taught by the Lord with a strong hand not to walk the same road as that people, not to use the same words, and not to be terrified by the same things. This withdrawal, commanded by God and by a strong hand from that people, was finally completed in the time of Christ and the Apostles. So, as we run through the testimony cited by the Apostles, we meet neither the Babylonian captivity nor anything that does not pertain to the time of Christ, at least as a shadow or type.

units.la: XV. Ad citatum testimonium quod attinet, teneri nos Christianos mandato illo, Sanctificate Dominum exercituum ipse pauor vester, & ipse terror vester jam probaui §12. Addo, Emmanuelem esse huius sanctificationis & pauoris obiectum: quippe, habet omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra, iudex est supremus totius mundi, potest animam & corpus mittere in gehennam ignis, Ne timete ab iis qui occiduntcorpus, animam autem non possunt occidere: sed potius timete eum, qui potest & animam & corpus perdere in gehenna, Math. 10. 20.
units.tr: XV. As regards the cited testimony, I have already proved in §12 that we Christians are bound by the command, "Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; let him be your fear, and let him be your dread." I add that Immanuel is the object of this sanctification and fear. Indeed, he has all power in heaven and on earth, he is the supreme judge of the whole world, and he can cast body and soul into the fire of hell: "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell," Math. 10. 20.

units.la: XVI. Promissio, Et erit vobis in sanctuarium, nobis argumentum suppeditat. Est enim credentibus ac timentibus Deum Christus in Sanctuarium proprie, non Pater præcise, &c seorsim. Quod ut manifestum fiat ratio observanda est, cur sic promissionem Dominus conceperit. Iusserat suos fideles à populi Iudaici viis, sermonibus, &c. secedere: quod fieri vix poterat quin synagoga mouerentur, iisque templo interdiceretur cui Deus præntiam suam salutarem & cultum affixerat. Id quoniam vnum oderat[?] eos admodum perturbare, pollicetur, vt vt destituantur sanctuario terreno, non tamen defuturum illis sanctuarium, imò abitufos Sanctuarium infinitiès perfectius: ipsum enim Dominum illis fore ipSanctuarium. patiantur igitur æquo animo se vmira[?] priuari, ab incredulis Iudæis retenta, gaudentes corpore & veritate. Itaque tacita fit oppositio inter Sanctuarium typicum & verum, carnale & spirituale, terrenum & cœleste, legale & euangelicum, illudque cum adhærente illi populo deferendum [?]andem fuit fidelibus vt hoc fruerentur.
units.tr: XVI. The promise, "And it shall be to you a sanctuary," supplies us with an argument. For to those who believe and fear God, Christ is properly the Sanctuary, not the Father precisely and apart. To make this clear, we must observe the reason why the Lord framed the promise in this way. He had commanded his faithful to withdraw from the ways, speeches, and so on of the Jewish people. This could hardly be done without the synagogue being stirred up and the temple, to which God had attached his saving presence and worship, being forbidden to them. Since this greatly troubled them, he promises that although they are deprived of the earthly sanctuary, a sanctuary will not be lacking to them; indeed, they will have a sanctuary infinitely more perfect, for the Lord himself will be their sanctuary. Let them therefore bear with equanimity being deprived of what the unbelieving Jews hold, and rejoice in the body and the truth. Thus there is an implicit opposition between the typical and the true sanctuary, the carnal and the spiritual, the earthly and the heavenly, the legal and the evangelical; and that sanctuary, along with the people who clung to it, had to be abandoned, so that the faithful might enjoy this one.

units.la: XVII. Ostendimus autem alibi Sanctuarium terrenum prodiuerso respectu tria adumbrasse, cœlum, Ecclesiam, Christum. De Cœlo & Ecclesia nunc quidem dicere nihil opus est. Christum fuisse Sanctuario seu tabernaculo vel templo adumbratum, & ipse innuit, cum corpus suum vocat templum, & Apostolus, cum carnem eius velum appellat (non enim seruabuntur proportiones inter velum & sanctuarium, si caro Christi dicatur velum esse tabernaculi, quod locum seu cœlum significat) & ipsa res id clamat: videmus enim in Christo tabernaculi terreni foris vilis intus magnifici cœlestem veritatem. In eo enim, non iam vmbratiliter, vt in sanctuario typico, sed σωματικῶς corporaliter habitat omnis plenitudo deitatis. In eo est vera arca fœderis, verum propitiatorium, verum altare, verum sacrificium, verus intercessionis suffitus, verus panis propositionis, vera lux aurei candelabri, omnia denique quæcunque sunt nobis ad salutem & cultum diuinum necessaria. Ab eo vno manat omnis peccati expiatio, omnis sanctificatio & perfectio, omnis benedictio spiritualis, orationes nostræ, gratiarum actiones, sacrificia spiritualia in eo & per eum offerri debent. In eo præsentissimum numen habemus, ac tutissimum perfugium omni tempore, &c. In Patre si separetur à Christo illa non habemus, nec vllus nobis patet ad eum aditus teste ipso Christo, Ego sum via, veritas, & vita, nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me.
units.tr: XVII. I have shown elsewhere that the earthly sanctuary, viewed in different respects, foreshadowed three things: heaven, the Church, and Christ. There is no need to say anything now about heaven and the Church. That Christ was foreshadowed by the sanctuary, tabernacle or temple, he himself hints when he calls his body a temple, and the Apostle when he calls his flesh the veil. (For the proportions between veil and sanctuary would not be preserved if Christ's flesh were said to be the veil of the tabernacle, which signifies the place or heaven.) The thing itself cries this out: for in Christ we see the heavenly truth of the earthly tabernacle, humble outside and magnificent within. For in him, not now shadowily as in the typical sanctuary, but bodily [σωματικῶς, corporaliter], dwells all the fullness of the Godhead. In him is the true ark of the covenant, the true mercy seat, the true altar, the true sacrifice, the true incense of intercession, the true bread of the presence, the true light of the golden lampstand, and in short all things necessary for us for salvation and divine worship. From him alone flows all expiation of sin, all sanctification and perfection, every spiritual blessing; our prayers, thanksgivings and spiritual sacrifices ought to be offered in him and through him. In him we have the most present divinity and the safest refuge at all times, and so on. Apart from Christ, in the Father we do not have these things, nor is any access to him open to us, as Christ himself testifies: "I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me."

units.la: XVIII. Comminatio, & in lapidem offensionis & petram scandali duabus domibus Israelis, ipsa per se aliquot argumenta nobis suppeditat. Primum ducitur à Petra; & sic habet. Petra est Deus. Christus est Petra. E. Christus est Deus. Deum intelligo Israëlis prædictum essentia diuina. Major non videtur negari posse, est enim petra vnû ex nominibus Dei non infrequens in Scriptura.Id quod ita clarum est, vt non dubitauerint 70. Interpretes viginti fere locis pro πέτρα θεὸν[?] vsurpare, vnum exempli causa citasse sufficiet ad firmandam maiorem nostram aptissimum Ps. 18.34. Quis est Deus praeter Dominum? & quis est צור petra praeter Deum nostrum? Ierfio graeca & vulgata latina habent, Et quis est Deus praeter Deum nostrum? Haec interrogatio negandi vim habet, idemque valet ac propositio negatiua, nullus est petra nisi Deus Israelis. Respondent etiam sibi inuicem duae illae interrogationes, ac vocibus mutatis idem sonant: vt igitur Dominus Iehouah, & Deus noster, sic Deus & Petra æquiualent. Christum autem esse petram, quae minor est argumenti, quis possit inficiari?
units.tr: XVIII. The threat, "and for a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to the two houses of Israel," supplies several arguments by itself. The first is drawn from the Rock, and runs thus: the Rock is God; Christ is the Rock; therefore Christ is God. By God I understand the God of Israel, the divine essence as predicated. The major premise seems impossible to deny, for "rock" is one of the names of God, not infrequently found in Scripture. This is so clear that the Seventy translators did not hesitate to render πέτρα [petra] by θεός [theos] in about twenty places. It will suffice to cite one example, very apt for confirming our major premise, Ps. 18.34: "Who is God except the Lord? And who is a rock [צור, tsur] except our God?" The Greek and the Vulgate Latin have: "And who is God except our God?" This question has the force of a denial, and it amounts to the negative proposition, "there is no rock except the God of Israel." The two questions also answer each other, and with the words changed they sound the same: thus, as Lord Jehovah and our God, so God and Rock are equivalent. That Christ is the Rock, which is the lesser point of the argument, who could deny?

units.la: XIX. Nobis sine dubio Petrum Apostolum Aduersarij opponent petram appellatum ab ipso Christo super qua ædificetur Ecclesia: ita enim sentit V Volkelius. Sed quominus existimemus per petram eo loco Petrum esse intelligendum obstant, vt cæteras nunc omittam, tres hæ rationes. Prima ducitur ab auctoritate Euangelistæ mentis Christi optimi interpretis, qui non temerè sed prudenter inter Petram & Petrum distinxit, quæ autem ille distinxit actus à Spiritu Sancto nostrum non est confundere. Cur enim πέτραν dixit non πέτρον, si Petrum intelligi voluit? Christus, inquies, non distinxit, non mutauit genus, eadem vocis forma Petrum & Petram designauit. Unde id habetur, nisi quia creditur Syriacè locutus, quæ lingua distinctionem illam non admittit? Cur ergo id linguæ illius inopiæ non adscribis potius quàm menti Christi per interpretem suum, cum id lingua tulit, Petram à Petro distinguentis? Dices, Matthæum non dixisse ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ πέτρῳ quoniam vox πέτρος, nisi apud autores Attica dialecto vtentes, est insolens. At quid erat causæ cur ab illa voce attica Apostolus magis abhorreret quàm autor libri 2. Maccab. qui ea voce bis vsus est, semel cap. 1. 16. & iterum cap. 4. 41.? Sic tamen ita. Cur igitur vt dialectum atticum vitaret & seruaret genus vocis non dixit οὐ εἶ πέτρα, ἡ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ, vel οὐ εἶ λίθος, ἡ ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ λίθῳ? Non patiebantur leges græcæ linguæ, vt rei nomen abiq;[?] aliqua inflexione personæ imponeretur. At id aliæ linguæ, Hebrææ, Syriaca, &c. patiebantur quarum idiotismos non refugiunt Apostoli græcè scribentes. Itaque neglectis illis linguæ græcæ legibus occurrunt in Nouo Testamento græcis nominibus appellatiuis finę. ulla mutatione insigniti Viri quidam, ut στέφανω [?] corona Act. 6. 8. σάχυς spica Rom. 16. 9. ῥάφανος [?] narcissus flos Rom. 16. 11. καρπὸς fructus 2. Tim. 4. 13. βλάστ[?] germen Act. 12. 20. Nec non mulieres, ut δορκὰς [?] capraffylueftris Act. 9. 39. ῥόδη rosa Act. 12. 13. χλόη herba virens, 1. Cor. 1. 11. εὐωδία [?] bonus odor Phil. 4. 2. εὐκτὴν [?] bona victoria 2. Tim. 1. 5. &c. Sed tamen ut valeat illa ratio, cur igitur saltem non dixit Apostolus ἐπὶ σοὶ τῇ πέτρᾳ? cur pronomen secundæ personæ mutauit in pronomen demonstratiuum tertiæ? imò cur non dixit simpliciter ἐπὶ σοί? quid opus fuit addere τῇ πέτρᾳ? stat igitur firma hæc prima ratio.
units.tr: XIX. The adversaries will undoubtedly oppose to us Peter the Apostle, whom Christ himself called a rock, upon which the Church is to be built; for so Volkelius thinks. But three reasons, leaving the others aside for now, stand in the way of our thinking that Peter is to be understood by "rock" in that place. The first is drawn from the authority of the Evangelist, the best interpreter of Christ's mind, who did not distinguish between Rock and Peter carelessly but prudently; and it is not for us to confuse what the Holy Spirit distinguished. For why did he write πέτραν [petran] and not πέτρον [petron], if he wanted Peter to be understood? Christ, you will say, did not distinguish, did not change the gender; the same word form designated both Peter and Rock. But whence is this known, unless because it is believed that he spoke in Syriac, a language which does not admit that distinction? Why then do you not ascribe this to the poverty of that language rather than to the mind of Christ, through his interpreter, since the Greek allowed it, distinguishing the Rock from Peter? You will say that Matthew did not write ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ πέτρῳ [epi touto tō petrō] because the word πέτρος [petros], except among authors using the Attic dialect, is unusual. But what reason was there for the Apostle to shrink from that Attic word more than the author of the second book of Maccabees, who used it twice, once at 1 Macc. 1.16 and again at 4.41? Nevertheless, so it is. Why then, to avoid the Attic dialect and keep the gender of the word, did he not say εἰ σὺ πέτρα, ἡ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ, or εἶ λίθος, ἡ ἐπὶ τούτῳ τῷ λίθῳ? The laws of the Greek language did not permit the name of a thing to be imposed without some inflection of the person. But other languages, Hebrew, Syriac and so on, did permit it, and the Apostles writing in Greek do not shun their idioms. Thus, disregarding those laws of the Greek language, there occur in the New Testament some men and women whose Greek appellative nouns carry no change at all: Stephen, meaning crown [στέφανος], Acts 6.8; Stachys, meaning ear of corn [στάχυς], Rom. 16.9; Narcissus, meaning a flower, Rom. 16.11; Carpus, meaning fruit [καρπός], 2 Tim. 4.13; Blastus, meaning a sprout [βλάστος], Acts 12.20; and among the women, Dorcas, meaning a wild goat [δορκάς], Acts 9.39; Rhoda, meaning a rose [ῥόδη], Acts 12.13; Chloe, meaning green herb [χλόη], 1 Cor. 1.11; Euodia, meaning good odour [εὐωδία], Phil. 4.2; Eunice, meaning good victory [εὐνίκη], 2 Tim. 1.5; and so on. But even granting that this reason holds, why at least did the Apostle not say ἐπὶ σοὶ τῇ πέτρᾳ [epi soi tē petra]? Why did he change the pronoun of the second person into the demonstrative of the third? Indeed, why did he not simply say ἐπὶ σοί [epi soi]? What need was there to add τῇ πέτρᾳ? So this first reason stands firm.

units.la: XX. Secunda ratio petitur ab ipsa veritate sententiæ Christi, quæ non patitur Petrum per Petram intelligi. Non enim super Petrum Christus ædificauit Ecclesiam suam, ædificatus fuit ipse Petrus, ædificati sunt alij Apostoli & discipuli à Christo, nec tamen super Petrum: Ipse Petrus tanquam minister Christi ædificauit, non tamen super semetipsum, ædificauit Paulus, ædificauerunt alij Apostoli, ædificant hodie pastores fideles sed super Christum, non super Petrum. Christus quatenus ædificat petra non dicitur, sed quatenus super eo ædificatur, quis enim unquam architectum aut structorem lapidem vel petram vel domus alicuius fundamentum appellauit, propterea quod is fundamentum illius domus jecit, aut lapides posuit ut eam ædificaret? separanda est relatio Architecti vel ædificantis quatenus est talis à relatione petræ, fundamenti, lapidis. Lapis non ædificat sed ædificatur. Petra super quam ædificatur qua talis non ædificat, sed lapides qui ædificantur suscipit, sustinet, eorumque ædificationem passiuam & unionem terminat. Cum igitur Petrus spectari possit duobus modis, ut ædificans & ut ædificatus, lapidis autem sit ædificari non vero ædificare, satius est existimare lapidis seu petri nomen illi quatenus ædificatus est potius tributum fuisse à Christo, quàm quatenus ædificauit: ædificatus est autem ut electus aut fidelis, ædificauit vero ut pastor & Apostolus; Itaque fideles quatenus ædificantur omnes lapidum elogio ornantur & quidem ab ipso Petro. Pastores vero aut Apostoli qua tales nunquam. Et sunt multi architecti multi ædificantes partim coordinati partim subordinati inter se, sed unica est Petra, unicum fundamentum totius ædificii, quod, si Paulum audis, Petrus non est sed Christus. Fundamentum, inquit, aliud nemo potest ponere, præter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Id de primario aedificiy istius fundamento intelligendum est, inquit VVolkelius [?]. Sed fi duo ponuntur fundamenta unum primarium alterum secundarium, cur non addetur & tertium & quartum & sic deinceps. Id enim mihi demum fundamentum appellandum videtur, quod in aedificio imum ac primum est, cuique aedificium quamdiu stat innititur. At dicuntur fideles aedificati super fundamento prophetarum & Apostolorum Eph. 2. 19. Fundamentum intelligitur, non quod ipsi Prophetæ & Apostoli fuerunt, sed quod illi posuerunt, & super quo semetipsos & alios fideles aedificauerunt. At Apoc. 21. 14. Murus vrbis dicitur, habere fundamenta duodecim, isque inscripta nomina duodecim Apostolorum Agni. Certé, & duodecim etiam portas, eisque inscripta nomina duodecim tribuum Israelis. Ut igitur duodecim tribus Israelis non sunt duodecim illæ portæ, sic nec duodecim Apostoli sunt duodecim illa fundamenta, unica est porta Christus Ioh. 10. 7.9. & 14. 6. sed per quam undiquaque patet commodissimus ad vitam & ad Patrem accessus. Unicum etiam est fundamentum idem Christus, sed à duodecim Apostolis separatim diuersis in locis aedificantibus positum ita, ut cuiusque Apostoli opus proprium & laus operi consentanea in eo jaciendo dilucear. Enimuero fundamento nomen fundamenti non solet inferibi, sed eius potius qui fundamentum iacit: hic autem qua talis ut fundamentum dicatur, nisi me animus fallit, alienum est à consuetudine Scripturæ, & omnium hominum. Ipse Christus dicendo super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam ædificantem, ædificium, & petram per oppositas relationes distinguit, ac proinde ædificans qua talis nec est ædificium quod ædificat, nec petra super quam ædificat.
units.tr: XX. The second reason is drawn from the very truth of Christ's saying, which does not allow Peter to be understood by "Petra." For Christ did not build his Church upon Peter. Peter himself was built up, and the other apostles and disciples were built up by Christ, yet not upon Peter. Peter himself, as Christ's minister, built, but not upon himself. Paul built, the other apostles built, and faithful ministers build today, but they build upon Christ, not upon Peter. Christ is not called a rock insofar as he builds, but insofar as the building is raised upon him. For who has ever called an architect or builder a stone, or a rock, or the foundation of some house, merely because he laid the foundation of that house or set the stones to build it? The relation of the architect or builder, as such, must be separated from the relation of the rock, the foundation, the stone. A stone does not build but is built. A rock upon which a building is raised, as such, does not build, but it bears and supports the stones that are built into it, and it marks the end of their passive building and their union. Since Peter can therefore be considered in two ways, as builder and as built, and since it belongs to a stone to be built and not to build, it is better to judge that the name stone or Peter was given to him by Christ insofar as he was built, rather than insofar as he built. He was built up as one chosen or as a believer, but he built as a minister and an apostle. Thus believers, insofar as they are being built up, are all adorned with the title of stones, and indeed by Peter himself; but ministers or apostles, as such, never are. There are many architects and many builders, some coordinated and some subordinated to one another, but there is one rock and one foundation of the whole building, and, if you listen to Paul, this is not Peter but Christ. "Another foundation, he says, no one can lay, besides that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ." "That must be understood of the primary foundation of this building," says Volkelius [?]. But if two foundations are posited, one primary and the other secondary, why should not a third and a fourth be added, and so on? For that alone seems to me properly to be called the foundation which is lowest and first in the building, and on which the building rests for as long as it stands. But believers are said to be built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles (Eph. 2:19). The foundation is understood not as the prophets and apostles themselves were, but as what they laid down, and upon which they built themselves and other believers. And in Rev. 21:14 the wall of the city is said to have twelve foundations, and on them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb written. Certainly it also has twelve gates, and on them the names of the twelve tribes of Israel written. Just as the twelve tribes of Israel are not those twelve gates, so the twelve apostles are not those twelve foundations. There is one gate, Christ (John 10:7, 9; 14:6), through which there is a most convenient access to life and to the Father from every side. The same Christ is also the one foundation, but he was laid by the twelve apostles, building separately in diverse places, so that the particular work of each apostle and the praise corresponding to his work shine forth in the laying of it. Now the name of foundation is not usually ascribed to the foundation itself, but rather to him who lays it. Here, however, to call Peter a foundation as such is, unless my mind deceives me, foreign to the usage of Scripture and of all men. Christ himself, by saying upon this rock I will build my Church, distinguishes by opposed relations the one who builds, the building, and the rock; and therefore the builder, as such, is neither the building that he builds nor the rock upon which he builds.

units.la: XXI. Tertia ratio inde oritur, quod totius Ecclesiæ & singularum eius partium firmitas & soliditas pendet à Petra, cui inædificata est. Non pendet autem à Petro sed à Christo. Non igitur Petrus sed Christus est petra cui inædificata est. Pendere firmitatem & constantiam ædificij ex petra, super qua extructum est, ipse Christus docet Math. 7. 25. Decidit, inquit, nimbus, & venerunt flumina, & flauerunt venti, & irruerunt in domum illam, & non cecidit: fundata enim erat super petram: nec-non hoc loco cum addit, Et porta inferorum non prævalebunt aduersus eam. Unde enim ista firmitas, nisi à fundamento, quia non super arenam, sed super Petram ædificata est ; quale enim est fundamentum ta-le est ædificium prudenter ædificatum. Hæc autem firmitas, & toti Ecclesiæ, & singulis eius membris conuenit, id est, omnibus verè fidelibus, propterea quod omnes super Petram ædificati per fidem viuam ei immutabili, mundi, Satanæ, mortis, sepulchri victrici immediatè adhærent.
units.tr: XXI. The third reason arises from the fact that the firmness and solidity of the whole Church and of each of its parts depends upon the rock on which it has been built. But it does not depend upon Peter, but upon Christ. Therefore it is not Peter but Christ who is the rock upon which the Church is built. That the firmness and constancy of a building depend upon the rock on which it is erected Christ himself teaches in Matt. 7:25: the rain came down, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house, and it did not fall, for it was founded upon a rock. And in this place also he adds: and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Whence does that firmness come, if not from the foundation, because it is built not upon sand but upon the Rock? For as the foundation is, so is the building that has been wisely built. This firmness belongs both to the whole Church and to each of its members, that is, to all who are truly believers, because all who are built upon the Rock, by living faith, immediately cling to him who is immutable and who is victorious over the world, Satan, death, and the grave.

units.la: Vt igitur promissa hæc firmitas ad omnes verè fideles pertinet, ne Petro quidem excepto, & Ecclesia, quam erat Christus ædificaturus, omnes fideles complectitur, etiam Petrum ipsum, qui ipse quoque à Petra super quam ædificatus fuit suam soliditatem & à morte resurrectionem accepit. Iam verò firmitatem illam fidelium, quos neque mors, neque sepulchrum, neque Diabolus vincere potest, non à Petro, sed à Christo, cui innituntur, proficisci, non puto opus esse vt probem.
units.tr: Therefore, just as this promised firmness pertains to all true believers, Peter not excepted, and the Church that Christ was about to build embraces all believers, Peter himself included, who also received his own solidity from the Rock upon which he was built, and resurrection from death, I do not think I need to prove that the firmness of those believers, whom neither death, nor the grave, nor the devil can overcome, proceeds not from Peter but from Christ, upon whom they rest.

units.la: XXII. Quid igitur, inquies, Christus reponit Petro hoc loco? & cur Petram dicendo ad Petri nomen alludit? Petrus ex interrogatis discipulis dignitatem personæ & muneris Christi, quam omnes fideles confiteri tenentur, primus erat confessus: Christus vicissim dignitatem personæ & muneris, aliis etiam Apostolis prædestinatis communem, Petro primo pollicetur, & veluti applicat: Et dignitatem quidem personæ prius vers. 18. Deinde muneris vers. 19. Tu dixisti mihi me esse Filium Dei, Et ego dico tibi quod tu es beneficio meo Petrus, lapis vivus, & quod super me, qui sum Petra solidissima, ædificabo Ecclesiam meam usque adeo firmiter, vt ne portæ quidem inferorum ei prævalere possint, quo non obscurè innuit Petrum unum fore ex lapidibus, ex quibus indissolubile illud & magnificentissimum templum erat ædificandum. Quod beneficium omnium maximum auditoribus Euangelij promittitur quidem, sed promissione generali & sub conditione fidei & perseverantiæ, Petro verò primo & soli singulariter à Christo promittitur absolutè hoc loco: qua prærogatiua nulla potuit esse optabilior. Eius autem veluti tessera Petri nomen fuit illi à Christo impositum, aduersus ipsius naturalem inconstantiam, ob quam paulo post audiit à Christo Satan, & qua factum est, vt ter Christum, & quidem se devouendo & iurando, abnegauerit, magnum solamen. In se igitur Christus dicendo hanc Petram, vti dicendo hoc templum Ioh. 2. 19. digitum intendebat: Erat enim tam visibilis quam Petrus, quamuis non qua Petra, aut templum, ut nec iste qua Petrus, hoc est, lapis.
units.tr: XXII. What then, you will say, does Christ reply to Peter in this place? And why, by saying "Rock," does he allude to Peter's name? Peter, when the disciples were questioned, was the first to confess the dignity of Christ's person and office, which all believers are bound to confess. Christ, in turn, promises to Peter first, and as it were applies to him, the dignity of his person and office, which was common to the other apostles also who were predestined. He gives the dignity of his person first, in verse 18, and then that of his office, in verse 19. You said to me that I am the Son of God, and I say to you that by my favour you are Peter, a living stone; and that upon me, who am the most solid Rock, I will build my Church so firmly that not even the gates of hell shall prevail against it. In this he clearly hints that Peter will be one of the stones from which that indissoluble and most magnificent temple was to be built. This greatest of benefits is indeed promised to the hearers of the Gospel, but by a general promise and under the condition of faith and perseverance; but to Peter first and alone, in this place, Christ promises it singly and absolutely. No privilege could be more desirable than this. Moreover, the name Peter given to him by Christ was, as it were, a token of this, and a great consolation against his natural inconstancy, on account of which he soon heard from Christ, "Satan," and by which it came about that he denied Christ three times, cursing himself and swearing. Therefore in saying this rock, Christ was pointing at himself, just as in saying this temple (John 2:19) he was pointing at himself. For he was as visible as Peter, though not as Rock or temple, just as the other was not visible as Peter, that is, as a stone.

units.la: XXIII. Hanc expositionem ipse Petrus tradidisse videtur prioris Ep. suæ cap. 2. verf. 3. Si tamen gustastis quam dulcis est Dominus, ad quem accedentes lapidem vivum, ab hominibus quidem reprobatum, à Deo autem electum & honorificatum: & ipsi tanquam lapides vivi superædificamini, domus spiritualis, &c. docet enim fideles esse lapides vivos: docet eos, non super se Petrum, sed super Christum lapidem vivum ædificari. Qui locus ad rem quam agimus non parum facit: verba enim, Si tamen gustastis quoniam suavis est Dominus, transcripsit Apostolus è Ps. 34. verf. 8. ubi Dominus hebraicè est Iehovah. Docet igitur Petrus Christum esse Iehouah. Merito autem locum illum de Christo exponit: Is[?] enim semetipsum gustandum & videndum quàm sit suavis præbet immediatè. Edimus eius carnem, bibimus eius sanguinem. Eoque cibo & potu nihil est suavius. Si Patrem gustamus, non extra Christum separatim, sed gustando Christum eum gustamus, videndo Christum eum videmus.
units.tr: XXIII. Peter himself seems to have handed down this explanation in the second chapter, verse 3, of his first Epistle: If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet, to whom coming, a living stone, rejected indeed by men but chosen and honoured by God, you yourselves also, as living stones, are built up a spiritual house, and so on. For he teaches that believers are living stones, and he teaches that they are built upon Christ, the living stone, not upon Peter over themselves. This passage contributes no little to the matter we are treating. For the words if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet the Apostle transcribed from Ps. 34:8, where "Lord" in Hebrew is Iehovah. Peter therefore teaches that Christ is Jehovah. And he rightly explains that passage of Christ, for he immediately offers himself to be tasted and seen, how sweet he is. We eat his flesh and drink his blood, and there is nothing sweeter than this food and drink. If we taste the Father, we do not taste him apart from Christ, but in tasting Christ we taste him; in seeing Christ we see him.

units.la: XXIV. Adde quod si Pater est una Petra & Christus altera, duæ sunt Petræ fundamentales, duo fundamenta Ecclesiæ, quomodo igitur Paulus clamat, pone non posse aliud fundamentum præter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus? Non potest V Volkelius confugere ad distinctionem fundamenti primarij & secundarij. Fassus enim est Paulum loqui de fundamento primario. Et, si potest aliud poni, sive dicatur esse secundarium, sive primarium, verum non est quod dicit Apostolus, aliud non posse poni. Quid quod Christus, non modò spectatur ut Ecclesiæ fundamentum unicum, sed etiam ut tenens in fundamento locum imum & primum? dicitur enim lapis ἀκρογωνιαῖος[?], & caput anguli. Quis locus relinquitur Deo Patri, si is quoque Petra est à Christo diversa? Aut igitur is Petra non est, aut saltem Petra non est à Christo diversa.
units.tr: XXIV. Add that if the Father is one Rock and Christ another, there are two foundational rocks and two foundations of the Church. How then does Paul cry out, no one can lay another foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ? Volkelius cannot take refuge in the distinction between a primary and a secondary foundation. For he admits that Paul is speaking of the primary foundation. And if another foundation can be laid, whether it is called secondary or primary, then what the Apostle says, that no other can be laid, is not true. Moreover, Christ is regarded not only as the one foundation of the Church but also as occupying the lowest and first place in the foundation, for he is called the cornerstone [ἀκρογωνιαῖος] and the head of the corner. What place is left for God the Father, if he too is a Rock different from Christ? Either, then, he is not a Rock, or at least he is not a Rock different from Christ.

units.la: XXV. Hic notandum est petram super quam ædificatur Ecclesia duobus modis accipi posse, uno proprie, pro rupe immobili: altero minus proprie, pro lapide illo qui primus ab ædificante ponitur, quique est pars prima & ima totius ædificij. Utroque modo Christus dicitur Petra: posteriore quidem Matth. 21. 42. & Eph. 2. 20. priore verò, ne longè abeam, loco citato Matth. 16. 18. & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. In eo enim petra consideratur non vt pars ædificij, sed vt distinguitur a toto ædificio, non tanquam ab ædificante ponenda, atque aliquo modo ædificanda, sed tanquam toti ædificationi substrata, non tanquam firmitatem aliunde accipiens, sed tanquam eam toti ædificio impertiens. Pendet autem ædificij firmitas, non tam a primo & imo eius lapide quàm a rupe seu petra, cui primus ille lapis adhæret. Vt vt enim solidus sit in se primus lapis, tamen si super arenam ædificatur, non est stabile ædificium. Itaque tacita fit hoc loco oppositio inter petram & arenam: opponitur autem petra arenæ, quatenus rupem proprie significat, non autem quatenus improprie pro lapide vsurpatur: quemadmodum rursus hæc petra alij omni petræ vel rupi tacitè opponitur, tanquam quæ sola possit tribuere ædificio eiusmodi firmitatem, cui ne portæ quidem inferorum possint prævalere. Id vidit Cardinalis Perronius. Itaque petram vertit gallicè Roc, Rocher, quod nomen spiritualiter intellectum, et Scriptura, vt dixi, soli Deo vendicat, & quomodo Petro tribui possit ab ipso Christo ædificato equidem non intelligo. Petra enim eo sensu accepta super quam extruitur ædificium, etiam ipsum lapidem ἀκρογωνιαῖον sustinet. Itaque Christus non esset lapis ille qui est prima pars Ecclesiæ, si homo non esset; nec rupes seu petra super quam ædificatur Ecclesia, si Deus non esset. Ea in re, vt in aliis omnibus, verum esse deprehenditur quod ait Apostolus, Christum omnia esse in omnibus.
units.tr: XXV. Here it must be noted that the rock upon which the Church is built can be understood in two ways: in one way properly, as an immovable crag; in the other less properly, as that stone which is first laid by the builder and which is the first and lowest part of the whole building. In both senses Christ is called the Rock: in the latter sense indeed at Matt. 21:42 and Eph. 2:20, but in the former, not to go far afield, in the passage cited, Matt. 16:18, and upon this rock I will build my Church. For there the rock is considered not as a part of the building, but as distinguished from the whole building; not as something to be laid by the builder and in some way built, but as something underlying the whole construction, not receiving its firmness from elsewhere, but imparting it to the whole building. The firmness of a building depends not so much on its first and lowest stone as on the crag or rock to which that first stone adheres. For however solid the first stone may be in itself, if the building is erected upon sand, it is not a stable building. Thus at this point a tacit contrast is made between the rock and the sand. The rock is contrasted with the sand insofar as it signifies a crag properly, not insofar as it is used improperly for a stone. Likewise, this rock is tacitly set over against every other rock or crag, as the only one able to give a building such firmness that the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. Cardinal Perron saw this, and so he translated the word "rock" into French as Roc, Rocher. Yet how this name, understood spiritually, and which Scripture, as I have said, claims for God alone, can be ascribed to Peter by Christ himself who builds, I do not in fact understand. For a rock, taken in that sense, upon which a building is erected, also supports the cornerstone [ἀκρογωνιαῖον] itself. Thus Christ would not be that stone which is the first part of the Church, if he were not a man; nor the crag or rock upon which the Church is built, if he were not God. In this matter, as in all others, what the Apostle says is found to be true, that Christ is all things in all.

units.la: XXVI. Aliud argumentum nobis dant voces offensionis & scandali duabus domibus Israelis. Significant enim corporis populi illius, vt loquitur Apostolus Rom. 11. παράπτωμα & ἥττημα, atque adeò ἀποβολὴ & πρόσλημψις, quæ tum accidit cum, (vt idem Apostolus testatur loco laudato Rom. 9. 32.) offenderunt in lapidem offensionis, hoc est, in Christum. Id negabunt Aduersarij: probandum est igitur, non auctoritate Apostoli, (Hoc enim jam præstitimus octo primis thesibus huius disputationis) sed argumentis ductis ab ipso textu Esaiæ. Primum non significatur illis verbis ruina temporalis seu abductio tribus Iudæ & Benjamin in captivitatem Babylonicam, vti velle videtur Socinus. Nam, & nihil est in antecedentibus & sequentibus versibus quod eò spectet: Et in ea captivitate domus Iudæ perseuerauit populus Dei esse, ac stetit in duino[?] foedere. Hic autem intelligitur lapsus & ruina spiritualis. Opponuntur enim duæ domus Israëlis illis qui sanctificant Dominum, hoc est, fidelibus: sanctificatur enim per fidem, vt patet ex Num. 20. 12. Innuitur igitur populi Israëlitici incredulitas & rebellio. Deinde opponitur prædictio, erit in lapidem offensionis & Petram scandali, promissioni, erit in Sanctuarium. Quàm igitur ista de bono spirituali, tam illa de malo spirituali intelligenda videtur. Præterea captiuitas temporalis communis fuit pijs & impijs, sanctificantibus Dominum & eis qui Dominum non sanctificabant, cum tamen Dominus non fuerit in lapidem offensionis & Petram scandali nisi illis qui ipsum non sanctificarunt. Captiuitas etiam illa temporalis Iudæos omnes nullo excepto complexa est: si qui relicti sunt in Iudæa, illi in Ægiptum descenderunt, inque captiuitatem deteriorem inciderunt[?]: lapsione verò & ruina quæ hoc loco describitur, ita populus Iudaicus & nominatum incola Hierusalem implicandi erant, vt ea ad discipulos Domini non pertineret, vt patet ex versibus sequentibus.
units.tr: XXVI. Another argument is given us by the words of offence and stumbling to the two houses of Israel. For they signify, as the Apostle speaks in Rom. 11, the fall [παράπτωμα] and the diminution [ἥττημα] of that body of people, and thus the rejection [ἀποβολή] and the acceptance [πρόσλημψις], which happened when, as the same Apostle testifies in the passage cited, Rom. 9:32, they stumbled at the stone of stumbling, that is, at Christ. The adversaries will deny this. It must therefore be proved, not by the authority of the Apostle (for we have already done that in the first eight theses of this disputation), but by arguments drawn from the text of Isaiah itself. First, these words do not signify the temporal ruin or the carrying away of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin into the Babylonian captivity, as Socinus seems to wish. For nothing in the preceding or following verses points to this; and in that captivity the house of Judah continued to be the people of God and stood in the covenant of God. Here, rather, a spiritual fall and ruin is meant. For the two houses of Israel are opposed to those who sanctify the Lord, that is, the faithful; for he is sanctified through faith, as is clear from Num. 20:12. Thus the unbelief and rebellion of the Israelite people is implied. Next, the prediction, he will be for a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling, is opposed to the promise, he will be for a sanctuary. So just as the latter is to be understood of a spiritual good, the former seems to be understood of a spiritual evil. Moreover, the temporal captivity was common to the godly and the ungodly, to those who sanctified the Lord and to those who did not sanctify him; yet the Lord was not for a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling except to those who did not sanctify him. That temporal captivity also embraced all the Jews without exception: those who were left in Judea went down into Egypt and fell into a worse captivity. But the stumbling and ruin described in this passage were such that the Jewish people and the inhabitants of Jerusalem by name were to be ensnared by them, and it did not pertain to the disciples of the Lord, as is clear from the following verses.

units.la: XXVII. Denique infidelitas & rebellio populi Iudaici intelligitur quàm sequuta est reiectio a fœdere separatioque Ecclesiæ ab illius populi corpore: sequitur enim hæc verba V. 16. liga testimonium & signa legem in discipulis meis, quibus innuitur testimonium seu legem atque adeo fœdus diuinum non amplius ad populum illum pertinere, sed proprium esse eorum, qui a populo illo secessionem fecerunt, Domini discipulorum, hoc est, Christianorum. Itaque continuò Christus sub alia relatione cum filijs ac discipulis suis Ecclesiam a Synagoga diuersam constituentibus inducitur fidem suam profitès his verbis, Et expectabo Dominum qui abscondit faciem suam à Domo Iacob, (quibus verbis rursus populi excæcatio & reiectio innuitur) sefeq; cum filijs & discipulis suis, seorsum ab illo populo in vnam societatem religiosam coactis, cognoscendū ostendens ac dicens, Ecce ego & pueri quos dedit mihi Dominus &c. Dixi sub alia relatione. Fuit enim lapis offensionis, & petra scandali, & in laqueum et tendiculam incolis Hierusalem potissimum ratione diuinitatis suæ, quam cum ptofiteretur, pro blasphemo habitus est, & condemnatus in illa vrbe. Rursus ratione humanitatis docuit verbo & exemplo, fuitque instar doctoris ac patris familias discipulos suos ac filios ad se in vnum congregantis. Id quod certo, eoque breui, temporis spatio ab eo ita factum est in diebus carnis eius, ut tamen pertineat ad fideles omnes usque ad consummationem seculi. Utrumque illud, quoniam eodem tempore factum est, consentaneum fuit ut eadem contextus serie prædiceretur, atque ea ratione Emmanuel describeretur. Ne tamen qui dicit Expectabo Dominum &c. alius videretur a Domino qui dicebat liga testimonium &c, duas illas sententias Propheta copulavit interposita coniunctione, &, continuatum ab eodem loquente sermonem, non autem ab alio inchoatum, non obscurè significante, quem ipsum sermonem Christi hominis versibus 17. & 18. comprehensum copulat etiam per eandem coniunctionem cum verbis sequentis versiculi, Et cum dixerint vobis &c, quæ sunt manifesta continuatio inchoatæ V. 11. concionis Domini suos discipulos docentis. Ex quo intelligitur eundem esse Deum & hominem, et modo ut Deum, modo ut hominem decet, loqui.
units.tr: XXVII. Finally, the unbelief and rebellion of the Jewish people is understood as the rejection from the covenant and the separation of the Church from the body of that people, which followed. For there follow the words of verse 16: bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples, by which it is implied that the testimony or law, and therefore the divine covenant, no longer pertains to that people, but belongs to those who have seceded from that people, the disciples of the Lord, that is, Christians. Hence immediately Christ is introduced under another aspect, with his sons and disciples who constitute a Church distinct from the Synagogue, professing his faith in these words: and I will wait for the Lord who hides his face from the house of Jacob (by which words again the blindness and rejection of the people is implied), and showing himself together with his sons and disciples, gathered apart from that people into one religious society, saying: Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me, etc. I said under another aspect. For he was a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling, and a snare and a trap to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, chiefly on account of his divinity, which, when he professed it, was held to be blasphemy, and he was condemned in that city. Again, in respect of his humanity he taught by word and example, and was like a teacher and a father of a family gathering his disciples and sons to himself into one. This indeed was certainly done by him in such a short span of time in the days of his flesh, yet it pertains to all the faithful until the consummation of the age. Since both of these took place at the same time, it was fitting that they be foretold in the same sequence of the context, and so Immanuel be described in this way. Yet, lest he who says I will wait for the Lord, etc., should seem to be other than the Lord who said bind up the testimony, etc., the Prophet joined those two sentences with an interposed conjunction, and, not obscurely signalling a discourse continued by the same speaker rather than one begun by another, he also joins that discourse of Christ the man, contained in verses 17 and 18, by the same conjunction to the words of the following verse, And when they say to you, etc., which is the manifest continuation of the sermon of the Lord, begun in verse 11, teaching his disciples. From this it is understood that the same one is God and man, and speaks now as God, now as man, as is fitting.

units.la: XXVIII. Ex his omnibus perspicuum est Lapidem offensionis & Petram scandali esse non proprie Patrem, sed eius Filium Dominum nostrum. Offendit enim in lapidem seu petram, non qui petram videt & agnoscit, sed qui eam non videt, aut si aliquomodo videt, pro petra non habet. Cum igitur Christus profiteretur se esse Petram, id est, Deum, Dei filium, Iudæi præ cæcitate & duritie cordis eum non agnoscentes, ac temerario quodam zelo Dei, qui pater est Christi, abrepti totis viribus in eum irruerunt & confracti corruerunt. Incurrerunt etiam ijdem in Christi Apostolos & discipulos, qui tamen propterea lapides offensionis vel petræ scandali nunquam dicuntur. Causa enim per accidens offensionis non erat in personis Apostolorum & discipulorum Christi, sed in solo Christo, quem per Apostolos prædicatum & oblatum nolebant agnoscere. Deum etiam ante adventum Christi peccatis suis ad iram provocarunt frequenter, Is tamen propterea petra scandali & lapis offensionis dici non potuit. Non enim in persona dei Patris hæsit causa per accidens scandali. Etenim de se nihil dixit, quod populo illi absurdum videretur usque adeo, ut cum non haberet pro Deo: tantum eius servos & prophetas, pro veris Dei prophetis, cum ingrata docuerunt, habere noluit. In ipsam personam Dei Patris nunquam ausu nefando incurrit. In solam Filij personam fecit impetum, eamque agnoscere noluit, & persecutus est aperte, atque ita ad eum solum tanquam ad lapidem seu petram scandali offendit.
units.tr: XXVIII. From all of this it is clear that the Stone of offence and the Rock of scandal is properly not the Father but his Son, our Lord. For a man stumbles over a stone or rock not when he sees and recognises the rock, but when he does not see it, or, if he sees it in some way, does not take it for a rock. Therefore, when Christ professed that he was the Rock, that is, God, the Son of God, the Jews, not recognising him through blindness and hardness of heart, and carried away by a certain reckless zeal for God, who is the Father of Christ, rushed upon him with all their strength and, broken, fell. The same men also ran against Christ's apostles and disciples, yet these are never for that reason called a stone of offence or a rock of scandal. For the cause of offence was not, by accident, in the persons of the apostles and disciples of Christ, but in Christ alone, whom they refused to recognise when he was preached and offered through the apostles. Before the coming of Christ they also frequently provoked God to anger by their sins, yet he could not for that reason be called a rock of scandal or a stone of offence. For the accidental cause of scandal did not lodge in the person of God the Father. He said nothing about himself that seemed so absurd to that people that they did not take him for God; he refused only that they should regard his servants and prophets as true prophets of God when they taught ungratefully. Against the very person of God the Father they never made an impious attack. They made their assault only on the person of the Son, and refused to recognise him, and openly persecuted him; and so they stumbled against him alone, as against a stone or rock of scandal.

units.la: XXIX. His omnibus addi potest typus illustris. Constat Petram ex qua percussa aquae manarunt ad restinguendam sitim populi siticntis in deserto typum Christi fuisse. Id enim & Paulus disertis verbis docet 1. Cor. 10. 4. & ipse Christus innuit Ioh. 7. 37. & res ipsa abunde testatur. Peto igitur quorsum Dominus non dixit simpliciter Exod. 17. 6. percuties Petram, & exibit ex ea aqua, ut bibat populus, sed praemisit haec verba, Ecce ego sto ante te, ibi, super Petra, in Horeb, & percuties Petram, &c. Id enim non est nullo consilio dictum & factum: potuit enim hoc totum omitti, potuit dixisse tantum, Ego ibi ero, sed his non contentus verba accumulat singula per se digna attentione, Ecce, ego sto-bo, vel potius, sto, coram te, ibi, super Petra, in Horeb. Ut videri posset Moses percutiendo Petram, ipsum Dominum quodammodo percussisse stantem coram ipso percutiente, ibi super Petra quam percutiebat, an esset in medio ipsorum Dominus populo ignorante. Sic quoad eius fieri potuit adumbratum est veram Petram, ex qua in consummatione seculorum percussa aquae manarunt salientes in vitam aeternam, ipsum Dominum seu Iehouah esse, quamuis nihil nisi vilis quidam lapis Iudaeis percutientibus visus fuerit.
units.tr: XXIX. To all these things may be added an illustrious type. It is established that the rock from which, when struck, waters flowed to quench the thirst of the thirsty people in the desert, was a type of Christ. Paul teaches this in express words, 1 Cor. 10. 4, and Christ himself hints at it, John 7. 37, and the thing itself bears ample witness. I ask, then, why the Lord did not say simply, Exod. 17. 6, you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, that the people may drink, but prefaced these words: Behold, I will stand before you there upon the rock in Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, etc. For this was not said and done without purpose. It could all have been omitted; he could have said only, "I will be there"; but not content with this he piles up individual words each worthy of attention: "Behold, I will stand," or rather "I stand before you there upon the rock in Horeb." So that it might appear that by striking the rock Moses had in some way struck the Lord himself, who stood before the one striking, there upon the rock he was striking, while the people did not know whether the Lord was in their midst. In this way it was foreshadowed, as far as it could be, that the true Rock, from which waters flowed out springing up to eternal life when struck at the consummation of the ages, is the Lord himself, Jehovah, although to the Jews who struck him he seemed nothing but a worthless stone.

units.la: XXXI. Unum adhuc addam, maledicet inquit Propheta hoc capite Ꝟ. 21. Regi suo & Deo suo. Cui Deo suo? Idolo? dixisset igitur potius idolo suo: nunquam enim Deus populi Iudaici eum dicitur, idolum intelligitur. Adde quod sic describitur summa populi illius impietas, non autem resipiscentia (qua nemo inducitur ut maledicat regi suo: hoc enim lege prohibitum est) nam ante & post quae commemorantur mala sunt. Si non intelligitur idolum, intelligitur Iehouah. Hoc enim nomen est Dei Israelis. Atqui intelligitur Christus. Is igitur est Deus Israelis, est Iehouah. Probo Christum intelligi. Intelligitur aut Pater aut Filius. Non Pater praecisè, nunquam enim legitur populus ille ei maledixisse. Etiam prolapsis in Idololatriam, etiam vicinis gentibus, etiam reiecto usque a tot seculis populo illi nomen Iehouah fuit estque sacrosanctum. Sed maledixit horribiliter, atque etiamnum maledicit Deo suo Dei sui Filio. Id etiam colligitur ex regis nomine: nam cui regi suo populus ille post editum istud vaticinium maledixisse legitur? Praeter unum Christum nullus comparet in Scriptura, Nullus etiam præter eum idem simul proprie rex est & Deus Iudæorum. Nisi autem idem utroque illo Regis & Dei nomine intelligeretur, post positum fuisset pro more Scripturæ Regis nomen nomini Dei.
units.tr: XXXI. I will add one thing more. The prophet in this chapter says, he shall curse, v. 21, his king and his God. To which God of his? An idol? For then he would rather have said "his idol": the God of the Jewish people is never understood to be an idol. Add that this describes the utmost impiety of that people, not repentance (no one is introduced as cursing his king, for this is forbidden by law); for what is recorded before and after are evils. If an idol is not meant, Jehovah is meant, for this is the name of the God of Israel. But Christ is meant. Therefore he is the God of Israel, he is Jehovah. I prove that Christ is meant. Either the Father or the Son is meant. Not the Father strictly, for it is never read that that people cursed him, even when they had fallen into idolatry, even among the neighbouring nations, even after being rejected by that people for so many centuries; the name Jehovah was and is holy to them. But they cursed horribly, and still curse, their God, the Son of God. This is also gathered from the name of the king: for to what king of theirs is it read that that people cursed after this prophecy was uttered? Apart from Christ alone no one appears in Scripture, and no one else is at once properly both king and God of the Jews. Unless the same person were understood by both names, king and God, the name of king would, according to the manner of Scripture, have been placed after the name of God.

units.la: XXXII. Accedit quod describitur illis verbis vel Rex Assyriorum, cuius mentio facta est V.[?] 7. & 8. vel populus Iudaicus de quo agebatur in versibus proximis, suadet proximitas ut hic potius intelligatur: suadet hoc ipsum connexio huius descriptionis cum versibus immediatè præcedentibus & sequentibus: necnon hæc ipsa verba, Regi suo, Deo suo: Nam maledixit quidem Deo Israelis Rex Assyriorum: sed abhorret a stilo Scripturæ Veteris Testamenti, ut Deus Israelis dicatur Rex & Deus gentis aut regis a republica Israelis origine & religione prorsus alieni. Describitur ergo populus Iudaicus incredulus, qualis fuit tempore aduentus Christi. Describitur enim populus cui non fuit matutina lux V.[?]20. Intelligitur autem sine dubio lux Christi, solis iustitiæ, lucis mundi: quis enim alius oriens diem mundo intulit? Sic autem lux venit in mundum, seseque omnibus promiscuè ostendit, ut tamen Iudæis diligentibus magis tenebras quàm lucem non fuerit aurora: lucem enim orientem non receperunt. Transfibit, inquit Propheta, per eam, Si terram intelligit, notat irrequietum animum mare terramque circumeuntium, ut faciant unum proselytum, & ut lucem, quominus ad alios perueniat, impediant. Si legem in proximo antecedente versu nominatam, significat populum illum legem vel transgressurum, vel lecturum & auditurum transeundo per eam, non immorando &, ut ita dicam, habitando in ea, quemadmodum is facit, qui reiectis humanis traditionibus eam habet pro fundo suo hæreditario, ac in ea cum maximo gaudio meditatur die & nocte. Addit induratus, id quod Euangelium passim testatur, & famelicus, non fame iustitiæ quæ est ex fide, sed, iustitiæ ex operibus, Et cum Esurierit irascetur, & maledicet regi suo & Deo suo, quo fuerit vehementior ista fames, eo magis intumescet atque efferuescet ira aduersus Euangelium, usque adeo ut regem suum & deum suum, sese ei tam familiariter ostendentem, ae vitam æternam offerentem maledictis & conuiciis prosequatur: & tamen sursum aspiciet, quasi culturus deum, ab eoque salutem expectaturus, sed terram intuebitur, terrena quæret, terrena sapiet. Ubicunque autem erit, quocunque se vertet, quacunque spe se lactabit, Ecce afflictio, tenebrae, obscuritas, angustia, caligo, inquietudo. Non potuit conuenientius describi interna constitutio animi Iudaorum rebellium, præsertim scribarum, pharisaeorum, & ut loquitur Apostolus, τῶν ἀρχόντων τῶ αἰῶνος τύτυ [?], qui crucifixerunt Dominum gloriæ. Sed, addit, non erit obscuritas ei cui fuit afflictio: orietur enim Euangelium pauperibus, contemptis, paruulis, confractis corde peccatoribus, Quemadmodum primo tempore contemptibilis fuit terra Zabulon, & terra Nephtali, sic vltimo tempore eam glorificabit. via maris, trans Iordanem, Galilæa gentium, populus qui ambulabat in tenebris vidit lucem magnam: habitantibus in regione vmbræ mortis lux orta est eis. Sic enim Prophetæ verba reddi posse nemo, opinor, inficiabitur, debere autem cum Matthæus innuere, tum oppositio inter tempus primum & vltimum & verba הקל [?] & הכביד [?] suadere videtur, eventu aperte consentiente. Ex quibus omnibus apparet Prophetam loqui de tempore aduentus Christi, & inchoatæ prædicationis Euange-lij.
units.tr: XXXII. Add that it is described by these words. Either the king of the Assyrians, whose mention was made in v. 7 and 8, or the Jewish people, of whom the preceding verses speak; the proximity suggests that the latter is rather to be understood here, and the connection of this description with the verses immediately before and after suggests the same, as do the very words, his king, his God. For the king of the Assyrians indeed cursed the God of Israel, but it is quite foreign to the style of the Old Testament Scripture that the God of Israel should be called the king and God of a nation or of a king wholly alien in origin and religion to the commonwealth of Israel. Therefore the unbelieving Jewish people is described, such as it was at the time of Christ's coming. For the people described is one for whom there was no morning light, v. 20. Without doubt the light of Christ is meant, the sun of righteousness, the light of the world: for what other rising sun brought the day to the world? Thus the light came into the world and showed itself to all indiscriminately, yet to the Jews, who loved darkness more than light, it was not a dawn, for they did not receive the rising light. It shall pass through it, says the prophet. If he means the land, it denotes a restless spirit going round sea and land to make one proselyte and to hinder the light from reaching others. If he means the law, named in the immediately preceding verse, it signifies that that people will either transgress the law or read and hear it while passing through it, not dwelling in it or, so to speak, living in it, as does the one who, rejecting human traditions, holds it as his hereditary ground and meditates on it with the greatest joy day and night. He adds hardened, which the Gospel attests everywhere, and hungry, not hungry for the righteousness which is of faith, but for the righteousness of works: And when he is hungry, he shall be angry and curse his king and his God. The fiercer this hunger, the more the anger against the Gospel swells and boils up, to the point that they pursue with curses and reproaches their king and their God, who shows himself to them so familiarly and offers eternal life. And yet he shall look upward, as if about to worship God and expecting salvation from him, but he shall look on the land: he seeks earthly things and savours earthly things. Wherever he will be, whichever way he turns, in whatever hope he rejoices, behold affliction, darkness, obscurity, distress, gloom, unrest. The inner condition of the rebellious Jews could not be described more fittingly, especially of the scribes and Pharisees, and, as the Apostle puts it, of the rulers of this age [τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου], who crucified the Lord of glory. But, he adds, there shall be no gloom for her who had affliction: for the Gospel will arise for the poor, the despised, the little ones, the sinners broken in heart. As in the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, so in the latter time he will make glorious the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; upon those who dwell in the land of the shadow of death a light has risen. For no one, I think, will deny that the prophet's words ought to be rendered thus; that Matthew hints at this, and that the opposition between the former and the latter time and the words hikel and hikbid [הקל ... הכביד] seem to suggest it, the outcome clearly agreeing. From all these things it appears that the prophet speaks of the time of the coming of Christ and of the beginning of the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: De Arg. IV. Ex Esaiae Cap. xxxxv. v. 23. Per memetipsum iuraui, &c. quod mihi curuabitur omne genu, citato Rom. 14.10.
units.tr: Concerning Argument IV: from Isaiah 45:23, "By myself have I sworn," etc., that to me every knee shall bow, cited at Romans 14:10.

units.la: I. IDEM Esaias Dominum inducit sic loquentem & iurantem cap. 45. vers. 22. Respicite ad me, & salui eritis omnes fines terrae: quia ego Deus, & non est alius. Per memetipsum iuraui, Egressum est ex ore meo iustitia verbum, & non reuertetur, quod mihi curuabitur omne genu, & iurabit omnis lingua. Eum, qui sic loquitur & iurat, Deum Israelis esse diuina essentia praeditum ambigit nemo. Eundem autem esse Christum non obscure significat Apostolus Rom. 14.10. his verbis, Omnes enim sistemur tribunali Christi, Scriptum est enim, viuo ego, dicit Dominus, quod mihi sese flectet omne genu, & omnis lingua confitebitur Deo. Itaque unusquisque nostrum de se rationem reddet Deo.
units.tr: I. Isaiah likewise introduces the Lord speaking and swearing in this way, Isaiah 45:22: Look to me, and be saved, all you ends of the earth, for I am God, and there is no other. By myself have I sworn; the word has gone out of my mouth in righteousness, and shall not return: that to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall swear. No one doubts that he who thus speaks and swears is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence. That this same one is Christ the Apostle clearly indicates at Romans 14:10, in these words: For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ. For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God. Therefore each one of us shall give account of himself to God.

units.la: II. Respondet Socinus, Hoc argumentum constare ex quatuor terminis. Nam inquit, in propositione medius terminus reuera est, Omne genu alicui curuari, in assumptione vero, Omnes stare ante tribunal alicuius. Atqui aliud est curuare genua alicui, aliud vero, ante tribunal eius stare, & potest quis uno & eodem tempore vni curuare genua, & ante tribunal alterius stare, veluti si Rex aliquis, cui praesenti genua omnes flectere semper debeant, praesens esse velit, cum coram tribunali Iudicis à se delegati causa indicantur; annon qui venient, ut ab isto delegato iudice causa sua indicentur uno & eodem tempore & ante iudicis istius tribunal stabunt, id est, apparebunt, sesequé[?] tribunali illius subiicient, & Regi praesenti genua curuabunt? Nonne ex eo, quod stant ante tribunal iudicis istius, consequitur necessario, quia Rex perpetuò sit praesens, ut Regi genua flectant? Nec tamen ulla prorsus ratione inde sequetur, iudicem istum esse unum & eundem cum ipso Rege.
units.tr: II. Socinus replies that this argument consists of four terms. For, he says, the middle term is truly present in the major premise, every knee bows to someone, but in the minor, all stand before someone's tribunal. Yet it is one thing to bow the knee to someone, and another to stand before his tribunal, and a person can at one and the same time bow the knee to one and stand before the tribunal of another. For example, if some king, to whom all ought always to bow the knee when he is present, should wish to be present while causes are judged before the tribunal of a judge he has appointed: will not those who come to have their causes judged by that appointed judge, at one and the same time, stand before that judge's tribunal (that is, appear there and submit themselves to his tribunal), and bow the knee to the king who is present? Does it not follow necessarily from their standing before the tribunal of that judge that they bow the knee to the king, since the king is always present? Yet by no reasoning at all does it follow from this that that judge is one and the same as the king himself.

units.la: III. Primùm hac responsione Socinus per latus nostrum ipsum Apostolum ferit. Is enim ex propositione Domini, vivo ego, quod mihi curvabitur omne genu, infert hanc conclusionem, Ergo Stabimus (vel potius, Sistemur) omnes ante tribunal Christi. Itaque in enthymemate Apostoli, Socini iudicio, sunt quatuor termini: curvare genua Domino in propositione, sisti tribunali Christi in conclusione, nullusque terminus est in conclusione, qui fuerit in praemissa expressa. Sed recidit hic ictus in Socinum illæsis Apostolo & nobis. Quamvis enim in genere curvare genua alicui, & sisti ad tribunal alicuius admodum differant, tamen cum de supremo totius mundi iudice & Domino agitur, omne genu illi curvari, & omnem personam creatam illius tribunali sisti, phrases sunt reciprocæ, atque æquipollentes. Christum autem esse totius mundi iudicem & Dominum omnis Christianus confitetur, alioqui non dignus Christiani nomine. Supremum autem esse iudicem & Dominum credit quisquis apud se perpendit, nullam ab eo provocationem dari, eum habere omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra, (qui autem dicit omnem, nullam excludit) Eum esse hæredem omnium. Tantum autem est ius Hæredis quantum fuit illius cuius est hæres. Nos quidem etiam hæredes sumus, sed Christi beneficio, cuius membra suo modo participant id quod est capitis.
units.tr: III. First, by this reply Socinus strikes at the Apostle himself, and at our side.
