For from the Lord's proposition, As I live, every knee shall bow to me, the Apostle infers this conclusion: therefore we shall all stand (or rather, be brought) before the tribunal of Christ. So in the Apostle's enthymeme, by Socinus' judgment, there are four terms: bowing the knee to the Lord in the premise, being brought before the tribunal of Christ in the conclusion; and there is no term in the conclusion that was not expressed in the premise. But this blow recoils on Socinus, leaving the Apostle and ourselves unharmed. For although, in general, bowing the knee to someone and being brought before someone's tribunal differ greatly, yet when the supreme judge and Lord of the whole world is in question, to have every knee bow to him and every created person be brought before his tribunal are reciprocal and equivalent phrases. Now every Christian confesses that Christ is the judge and Lord of the whole world, or else is not worthy of the name of Christian. And whoever weighs in his own mind that no appeal can be made from him, that he has all power in heaven and on earth (and he who says "all" excludes nothing), and that he is heir of all things, believes that he is the supreme judge and Lord. Now the right of an heir is as great as the right of him whose heir he is. We too are indeed heirs, but by the benefit of Christ, whose members in their own way share in what belongs to the head.

units.la: IV. Deinde Socinus sua ista responsione Christo facit iniuriam. Perinde enim loquitur, ac si ipsi Christo curvandum non esset omne genu, cum tamen Apostolus clamet, in nomine Iesu flectendum esse omne genu cœlestium, & terrestrium & infernorum. Itaque claudicat omni ex parte Regis & delegati à Rege iudicis quam subijcit, similitudo. Primò iudex à Rege delegatus non est Rex, non est Regi æqualis, datur ab eo provocatio ad Regem, non debetur ei adoratio. Contrà hic res habet. Christus enim Rex est, Deus est, Deo æqualis, Iudex supremus, cui tanquam suo Domino, Regi, Deo, debent genua flectere omnes Angeli & homines, atque data opera Pater noluit per suam ipsius personam iudicem agere: sed dedit omne iudicium Filio, ut omnes honorent Filium, sicut honorant Patrem, qui non honorat Filium, non honorat Patrem. Secundò Iudici delegato non flectit genua quisquis se illius tribunali sistit, in quo valdè distat à Christo, cui, si vnquâ omne genu flectetur, (flectetur autem certè tandem aliquando) flectetur profectò ei sedēti Iudici in throno gloriæ suæ. Tertiò, Rex non est in iudice delegato, nec iudex in Rege: sed Rex est persona separata à Iudice, & iudex à Rege: præsens est Rex in propria persona, neque idem est Regis throno & Iudicis, eadem gloria, ijdem ministri, idem regnum, iidem subditi, &c. vt hîc cernitur. Nam Pater est in Filio & Filius in Patre: Pater non ostenditur, non videtur, nisi quatenus ostenditur & videtur Filius: Idemque vtriusque est throno, idem regnum, iidem subditi, iidem ministri, eadem gloria, idem honor, vno verbo omnia quæcunque sunt Patris sunt etiam Filij, & vice versa. Itaque non apparebit in Iudicio Pater in propria, vt loquuntur, persona nec videbitur nisi quia videbitur Filius.
units.tr: IV. Next, by this reply Socinus does wrong to Christ. For he speaks as if every knee ought not to be bowed to Christ himself, whereas the Apostle cries out that in the name of Jesus every knee of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth should bow. Therefore the comparison he subjoins, of a king and a judge appointed by the king, limps in every respect. First, a judge appointed by a king is not the king, is not equal to the king, an appeal is made to the king from him, and adoration is not due to him. Here the case is otherwise. For Christ is King, is God, equal to God, the supreme Judge, to whom, as to his Lord, King and God, all angels and men ought to bow the knee; and the Father deliberately did not wish to exercise judgment through his own person, but gave all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father; he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father. Second, a man who presents himself before an appointed judge's tribunal does not bow the knee to the judge, and in this he differs greatly from Christ, to whom, if ever every knee is bowed (and certainly at some time it will be bowed), it will surely be bowed to him sitting as Judge on the throne of his glory. Third, the king is not in the appointed judge, nor the judge in the king: rather the king is a person separate from the judge, and the judge from the king. The king is present in his own person, and the throne of the king and of the judge is not the same, nor the glory, nor the same ministers, nor the same kingdom, nor the same subjects, and so on, as is seen here. For the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father; the Father is not shown or seen except insofar as the Son is shown and seen. And the throne of both is the same, the kingdom the same, the subjects the same, the ministers the same, the glory the same, the honour the same; in a word, whatever belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son, and vice versa. Therefore the Father will not appear in judgment in his own person, as they say, nor will he be seen except inasmuch as the Son is seen.

units.la: V. Applicat hoc exemplum Socinus ad rem nostram. Certum est, inquit, Christum in munere mundi iudicandi esse iudicem à Deo delegatum: per quem videlicet, Deus mundum iudicare constituerit. Id enim expressè affirmat Paulus Act. 17. 31. Quantum intersit inter iudicem delegatum & Christum iam ostendimus. Nec nobis obest locus Act. 17.31. Decreuit enim Deus omnia quæcunque facit, & quomodo ea facit. Cum igitur tres sint, secundum Scripturam & fidem nostram, personæ diuinæ, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus, quæ potuerunt mundum iudicare, quod ex partes potius personæ Filij quàm personæ Patris aut Spiritus Sancti sint attributæ à diuino consilio & beneplacito proficisci oportuit. Pergit Socinus. Hinc sequitur, quod cum Christus in tribunali suo sedebit, mundum iudicaturus, ibi Dei maiestas vehementissimè & clarissimè, immò magis quàm vnquam antea, elucebit: & consequenter ab ijs, qui ante istud tribunal stabunt, agnoscetur & approbabitur. Itaque istis Deus, vt mortalibus esse potest, planè erit præsens. Sunt quidem ista vera, sed nihil obsunt argumento nostro. Illa enim Dei maiestas quæ tunc elucebit, erit eadem maiestas Christi, & elucebit non extra Christum in persona Patris, sed in persona Christi; & videbitur agnoscetur q; non extra Christum, sed in Christo; & Deus erit præsens, non diuersus aut separatus à Christo, sed quia Christus erit præsens. Eadem erit Dei & Christi præsentia. Videre Deum & videre Christum idem erunt. Itaque venturū & apparituru Filium Scriptura Novi Testamenti sæpè docet & inculcat: venturum & apparituru Patrem, nunquam. Et, si Philippo dicenti Domine, ostende nobis Patrem, Christus respondit tanto tempore vobiscum sum, & non cognovisti me? Philippe, qui vidit me, vidit & Patrem. Et quomodo tu dicis ostende nobis Patrem? Et tamen Christus tunc apparebat in carne mortali nostræ per omnia, si peccatum excipias, simili, quid ei diceret, qui cum ipsum gloria & Majestate coronatum vidisset, sibi tamen Patrem ostendi postularet? Nihil profectò est, quo se Pater hominibus ostendat excellentius, clarius, magnificentius, quàm Filius, qui est ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, [?]καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ.
units.tr: V. Socinus applies this example to our matter. It is certain, he says, that Christ in the office of judging the world is the judge delegated by God, through whom, namely, God has determined to judge the world. For Paul expressly affirms this, Acts 17:31. How great the difference is between a delegated judge and Christ we have already shown. Nor does the passage Acts 17:31 harm us. For God has decreed all that he does, and how he does it. Since, then, according to Scripture and our faith, there are three divine persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who could judge the world, it was necessary that by the divine counsel and good pleasure this function should be attributed rather to the person of the Son than to the person of the Father or of the Holy Spirit. Socinus goes on: Hence it follows that when Christ sits on his tribunal to judge the world, the majesty of God will shine most vehemently and most clearly, indeed more than ever before; and consequently it will be recognised and approved by those who stand before that tribunal. Thus God, so far as it is possible for mortals, will be plainly present to them. These things are indeed true, but they do nothing to harm our argument. For that majesty of God which will then shine forth will be the same majesty of Christ, and it will shine forth not outside Christ, in the person of the Father, but in the person of Christ; and it will be seen and recognised not outside Christ but in Christ; and God will be present, not different or separate from Christ, but because Christ will be present. The presence of God and of Christ will be one and the same. To see God and to see Christ will be the same thing. Hence the Scripture of the New Testament often teaches and impresses that the Son will come and appear, but never that the Father will come and appear. And when Philip said, Lord, show us the Father, Christ replied, Have I been with you so long, and yet you have not known me? Philip, he who has seen me has seen the Father also. And how do you say, Show us the Father? And yet Christ at that time appeared to them in our mortal flesh, like us in all things except sin; what would he say to one who, having seen him crowned with glory and majesty, still asked that the Father be shown to him? Surely there is nothing by which the Father shows himself to men more excellently, more clearly, more magnificently, than the Son, who is [ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ] the radiance of his glory and the very stamp of his substance.

units.la: VI. Addit Socinus, Præsente autem Deo, genua ipsi flectenda esse, nemo est qui neget. Ergo qui ante Christi tribunal stabunt, genua Deo flectent. Stabunt autem omnes. Omne igitur genu se Deo flectet tunc[?], cum ante Christi tribunal stabitur. Atque hoc pacto verba illa ipsius Dei apud Esaiam, de curvando sibi omne genu, ad effectum perducentur. Vides, conclusum esse id ipsum quod Paulus concludere voluit, idque ea ratione, quæ in verbis ipsius expressa est: nec tamen necesse fuisse statuere, quod Christus sit ipse Deus. Ludit hoc loco lectorem suum Socinus. Sic enim ratiocinando neque concludit id ipsum quod Paulus concludere volut, neque ea ratione quæ in verbis ipsius expressa est, sed oppositâ planè. Invertit enim argumentationem Apostoli, atque utitur conclusione Apostoli tanquam medio ad id concludendum, quod in argumento Apostoli tenet medii locum. Quod Apostolus vult concludere habetur verf. 10. his verbis, Omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Christi. Medium cuius vi id vult concludere habetur verf. 11. Scriptum est enim, vivo ego, dicit Dominus, quod mihi curvabitur omne genu. Concludit nos omnes sistendos esse tribunali Christi, quia omne genu Domino curvabitur. Contrà Socinus concludit omne genu Deo curvandum esse, quia omnes sistemur tribunali Christi. Hoc non est exponere argumentationem Apostoli, sed convertere faciendo ex præmissa conclusionem & ex conclusione præmissam. Ita Socinus inducit Apostolum sumentem, aut, ut vulgò loquuntur, præsupponentem id quod probare instituit, & contra probantem id quod sumit, tanquam argumentum seu medium, ex Propheta Esaia: quæ stupenda est Socini ἀβλεψίᾳ[?] , ad quam tamen altera accessit. Inducit enim Apostolum praemissa angustiore utentem ad probandam conclusionem multò latius patentem. Id quod fieri vetant Logici. Nam in illa propositione Apostoli, Omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Christi, nota quantitatis, omnes, de Christianorum universitate intelligitur, ut patet ex antecedentibus & scopo Apostoli, & vers. 12. In propositione vero Domini, mihi curvabitur omne genu, vox, omne, de omni persona creata angelica & humana, nulla excepta, intelligitur. Itaque ex nostra omnium coram tribunali Christi apparitione non probat Apostolus, omne genu curvatum iri Deo, (vitiosa enim esset argumentatio) sed ex eo quod curvabitur omne genu Domino probat omnes nos, hoc est, Christianos staturos ante tribunal Christi, quae optima est argumentatio, quod dictum est de genere ad speciem applicans.
units.tr: VI. Socinus adds: Yet when God is present, no one can deny that knees must be bent to him. So those who stand before the tribunal of Christ will bend their knees to God. All will stand. Therefore every knee will bow to God at the time when people are made to stand before the tribunal of Christ. In this way those words of God himself in Isaiah, that every knee shall bow to him, are fulfilled. You see that this is the very conclusion Paul wanted to draw, and by the reasoning expressed in his words, yet it was not necessary to maintain that Christ is God himself. Socinus here mocks his own reader. For by reasoning in this way he does not draw the conclusion Paul wanted to draw, nor by the reasoning expressed in Paul's words, but by a plainly opposite method. He inverts the Apostle's argument, and uses the Apostle's conclusion as the means of proving what, in the Apostle's argument, holds the place of the middle term. What the Apostle wants to conclude is found in verse 10, in these words: For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. The middle term by whose force he wants to conclude this is found in verse 11: For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me. Paul concludes that we all must appear before the tribunal of Christ, because every knee shall bow to the Lord. Socinus, on the contrary, concludes that every knee must bow to God, because we all shall appear before the tribunal of Christ. This is not to expound the Apostle's argument, but to turn the conclusion into the premise and the premise into the conclusion. So Socinus makes the Apostle assume, or, as people commonly say, presuppose, what he sets out to prove, and makes him prove, using as argument or middle term, from the prophet Isaiah, what he has assumed. This is a remarkable piece of Socinian blindness [ἀβλεψία], yet he adds another fault to it. For he makes the Apostle use a narrower premise to prove a conclusion of much wider scope, which the logicians forbid. For in the Apostle's proposition, For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, the quantifier all is understood of the whole body of Christians, as is clear from the context, from the Apostle's purpose, and from verse 12. But in the Lord's proposition, every knee shall bow to me, the word every is understood of every created person, angelic and human, none excepted. So the Apostle does not prove from our all appearing before the tribunal of Christ that every knee will be bowed to God (for the argument would be faulty), but from the fact that every knee will bow to the Lord he proves that we all, that is, Christians, shall stand before the tribunal of Christ. This is an excellent argument, applying what is said of the genus to the species.

units.la: VII. His igitur duobus foedis vitiis laborat expositio Sociniana argumenti Apostolici, & tamen vix aliud concludere potest, quàm quod conclusum volumus. Sic enim habet, cum Christus in tribunali suo sedebit mundum Iudicaturus, Deus illis qui ante eius tribunal stabunt plane erit praesens. Praesente autem Deo genua ipsi flectenda esse, nemo est qui neget. Ergo qui ante Christi tribunal stabunt genua Deo flectent, stabunt autem omnes. Omne igitur genu se Deo flectet. Propositio, praesente Deo genua ipsi flectenda esse, eget distinctione. Est enim Deus praesens invisibiliter cum non apparet, & est praesens visibiliter cum apparet creaturae. Verba etiam, genua Deo flectenda esse, ambigua sunt: nam, vel officium creaturae, sive ab ea omitti possit, sive non possit, significant, vel necessarium atque inevitabilem eventum. Priore significatu Deo, seu visibiliter seu invisibiliter praesens sit, genua flectenda esse nemo negat, sed ea significatio non est huius loci. Verbis enim illis, Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, quod mihi curvabitur omne genu, non tam officium creaturae significatur, quàm eventus prorsus necessarius & inevitabilis. Intelligitur enim omne genu, etiam impiorum, etiam diabolorum, nullo excepto, ut manifestum est. Posteriore significatione Deo praesente curvandum est ipsi omne genu, non quoquo modo praesente, sed quemadmodum decet summum mundi Iudicem, cum eius tribunali omnis creatura sistitur. Quis autem tum praesens erit eo modo[?]? quis visibiliter aderit? quis sedebit pro tribunali? Quis? nisi is qui cum venerit in majestate sua, & omnes sancti Angeli cum eo, sedebit in solio majestatis suæ, & congregabuntur ante eum omnes gentes? Hic enim est ille Dominus à cuius facie, & à gloria virtutis eius luent pœnas æterni supplicij omnes increduli & rebelles, cum venerit vt glorificetur in sanctis suis, & admirandus fiat in omnibus credentibus. Ex eo igitur quod omnes cogentur se sistere coram tribunali supremo magni illius Dei, qui est Rex regum & Dominus dominantium, sequitur necessariò omnes illi genua flexuros. Si Iosepho, insigni Christi typo, in secundo curru Pharaonis sedente, præco clamabat, vt omnes genua coram eo flecterent, (sic enim habet vetus versio) quanto verisimilius est, Christo sedente in throno majestatis suæ ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos, proclamatum iri, Incurvate[?] vos ei omnes θεοί[?], hoc est, Angeli, omnesque homines?
units.tr: VII. Socinus's exposition of the Apostle's argument therefore labours under these two serious faults, and yet it can hardly conclude anything other than what we want concluded. For he puts it thus: when Christ sits on his tribunal to judge the world, God will plainly be present to those who stand before his tribunal. But with God present, no one denies that knees must be bent to him. Therefore those who stand before the tribunal of Christ will bend their knees to God, and all will stand. Therefore every knee will bow to God. The proposition, with God present knees must be bent to him, needs a distinction. For God is present invisibly when he does not appear, and he is present visibly when he appears to a creature. The words, knees must be bent to God, are also ambiguous, for they signify either the duty of the creature, whether or not it can omit it, or a necessary and inevitable event. In the former sense, whether God is present visibly or invisibly, no one denies that knees must be bent to him, but that sense does not belong to this place. For in those words, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, what is signified is not so much the duty of the creature as an event utterly necessary and inevitable. For it is understood that every knee, even of the impious, even of devils, without exception, bows, as is plain. In the latter sense, with God present, every knee must be bowed to him, not merely in any manner of presence, but as befits the supreme Judge of the world, when every creature is made to stand before his tribunal. But who will then be present in that manner? Who will be visibly present? Who will sit upon the judgement seat? Who, except he who, when he comes in his majesty, with all the holy angels with him, shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, and before him shall be gathered all nations? For this is that Lord from whose face and from the glory of his power all unbelievers and rebels shall suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be admired in all believers. From the fact, then, that all will be compelled to present themselves before the supreme tribunal of that great God, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, it necessarily follows that all will bow their knees to him. If, when Joseph, the notable type of Christ, sat in the second chariot of Pharaoh, a herald cried out that all should bend their knees before him (for so the old version has it), how much more likely is it that, when Christ sits on the throne of his majesty to judge the living and the dead, it will be proclaimed: Bow down to him, all you gods, that is, angels, and all men?

units.la: VIII. Socinus deprauata argumentatione Apostoli eo modo, quem commemoraui, concludit, Ex hoc loco Pauli nullo modo posse colligi, Christum esse illam unum Deum Israelis: quippe, quod ibi non dicatur id, quod assumendum in argumentatione ista fuisset, videlicet, Christo curvatum iri omne genu: sed tantum omnes staturos ante tribunal Christi. Atqui istæ phrases Apostolo æquipollent, sese enim mutuò ponunt & tollunt. Nam si curuabitur omne genu Domino, sistentur omnes tribunali Domini, alioqui falsa esset argumentatio Apostoli; & , si omnes sistentur tribunali Domini, omne genu curuabitur Domino. Cogentur enim sine dubio omnes, cum sistentur tribunali Domini, eius auctoritatem & majestatem summam agnoscere, ei se subjicere, cum ea reverentia & demissione, quæ tanto Iudici, Regi, immò Deo debetur: debetur autem illi adoratio seu genu flexio. Flectent igitur illi genua. Et quando quæso in nomine Iesu flectetur omne genu, si non flectetur tunc cum ad eius tribunal omnes sistentur?
units.tr: VIII. Socinus, having distorted the Apostle's argument in the way I have mentioned, concludes: From this passage of Paul it cannot in any way be inferred that Christ is that one God of Israel; for it is not said there what would have had to be assumed in that argument, namely that every knee will be bowed to Christ, but only that all will stand before the tribunal of Christ. Yet these phrases are equivalent for the Apostle, for they mutually posit and remove each other. For if every knee will be bowed to the Lord, all will be made to stand before the tribunal of the Lord; otherwise the Apostle's argument would be false. And if all will be made to stand before the tribunal of the Lord, every knee will be bowed to the Lord. For without doubt all, when they are made to stand before the tribunal of the Lord, will be compelled to acknowledge his authority and supreme majesty, and to submit themselves to him with that reverence and humility which is owed to so great a Judge, King, and indeed God; and adoration, or the bending of the knee, is owed to him. Therefore they will bend their knees to him. And when, I ask, will every knee bow in the name of Jesus, if it does not bow when all are made to stand before his tribunal?

units.la: I X. Progreditur longius Socinus, Finge inquit, Paulum dixisse, Christo omne genu curvatum iri. Nunquid hinc necessariò sequetur, Christum esse illum ipsum Dominum, qui apud Esaiam dixit, Mihi curvabitur omne genu, quia videlicet Paulus ex hoc Esaia loco, istud de Christo concludat? Nullo pacto. Non videtur Socinus percepisse vim argumenti quod ex hoc loco ducimus. Id quale sit, Deo dante, statim proferemus. Interim dico, non esse fingendum id quod reuera est. Non dixit quidem Paulus totidem verbis, Christo omne genu curuatum iri, sed dixit quod idem valet. Nam, & necesse erit omnes flectere genua Christo, quotquot stabunt ante eius tribunal iudicandi, (stabunt autem omnes:) is enim honor Christo debetur, etiam ab ipsis Angelis, teste Apostolo Heb. 1. 6. & tacitè sumit Apostolus, Dominum qui iurat apud Esaiam, sibi curuatum iri omne genu, eundem esse Christum. Id enim cum ad eius argumentationem est necessarium, tum ex verbis ipsis Domini colligi poterit. Quod vtrumque ipso Domino dante faciam, vt spero, manifestum.
units.tr: IX. Socinus goes further: Suppose, he says, that Paul had said that every knee would be bowed to Christ. Would it necessarily follow that Christ is that very Lord who said in Isaiah, To me every knee shall bow, because, of course, Paul would be drawing that conclusion about Christ from this passage of Isaiah? By no means. Socinus does not seem to have grasped the force of the argument we draw from this passage. What kind of argument it is, God willing, we shall set out immediately. Meanwhile I say that one must not suppose what is not actually the case. Paul did not indeed say in so many words that every knee would be bowed to Christ, but he said something of the same force. For it will be necessary that all who stand before his tribunal for judgement bend their knees to Christ (and all will stand): for this honour is owed to Christ even by the angels themselves, as the Apostle testifies in Heb. 1. 6; and the Apostle tacitly assumes that the Lord who swears in Isaiah, that every knee shall bow to him, is the same as Christ. For this is necessary to his argument, and it can also be gathered from the very words of the Lord. I shall, as I hope, make both of these plain, the Lord himself granting it.

units.la: X. Dico etiam id necessario sequi, quod sequi negat Socinus. Nam quo pacto ex verbis Domini, mihi curuabitur omne genu, concluderet Apostolus curuatum iri omne genu alij, quam Domino, qui hoc dixit? Qui dicit mihi curuabitur, per pronomen mihi seipsum significat, non alium, praesertim à se tota essentia, immò toto genere diuersum, ac nondum existentem.
units.tr: X. I also say that the conclusion necessarily follows, which Socinus denies. For how could the Apostle conclude from the Lord's words, to me every knee shall bow, that every knee will bow to anyone other than the one who spoke them? One who says to me it shall bow signifies himself by the pronoun me, not someone else, especially someone who is wholly different from him in essence, and indeed of a different kind altogether, and not yet existing.

units.la: XI. Conatur tamen Socinus quomodo id non sequatur docere. Nam, inquit, cum ex eiusdem Pauli clarissimis verbis, quae alibi id est Philip. 2. scripsit, apertissimè constet, hoc, quod Christo omne genu curuari aliquando debeat, ex illius vnius Dei dono profectum esse: & sic, Christum, hac in re, vt in aliis omnibus, totum ab illo vno Deo pendere & huius ipsius rei ratione, ab vno illo Deo distingui; necesse est, Christum, etiam quatenus omne genu illi curuari debet, illi vni Deo subordinatum esse; ita vt quicunque Christo genua flectit, illi vni Deo genua flectat. Ex quo consequitur, iure potuisse Paulum affirmare, impletum iri vaticinationem illam apud Esaiam de curuando vni illi Deo omni genu, hac ratione, quod Christo omne genu curuabitur, etiamsi Christus non sit ille vnus Deus. His verbis tria peccat Socinus. Primò, ait Christum, etiam quatenus illi omne genu curuari debet, illi vni Deo subordinatum esse: Idque effici putat ex Phil. 2. 10. Ex quo tamen contrarium sequitur. Subordinatio enim inæqualitatem significat, cum tamen ex loco illo summa æqualitas concludi possit. Nam eo loco Christus dicitur cum sese exinaniuit fuisse in forma Dei: Non autem forma Dei falsa intelligitur, sed vera. Vera autem non est forma Dei, cum abest essentia diuina. Deinde additur, cum non duxisse rapinam esse se aequalem Deo. Erat igitur aequalis Deo, & quidem iure. Id quod veram Dei formam arguit. Plurimum enim interest inter similitudinem aliquam & æqualitatem. Tum subiungitur, Deum habita ratione tantæ eius cum dignitatis naturalis, tum voluntariæ humiliationis, cum superexaltasse, hoc est, vt Vatablus, & Beza vertunt, in summam extulisse sublimitatem, summa autem sublimitas diuinæ æqualis est: alioqui non esset summa, sic respondet dignitati personæ, (nulla enim dignior forma concipi potest quàm Dei, nulla maior dignitas quàm ea quæ diuinæ est æqualis.) & voluntariæ humiliationi, qua, spectatis terminis à quo & ad quem, nulla maior esse potuit. Denique subiungitur, Deum illi nomen dedisse, quod est supra omne nomen, hoc est, nomen supremum. Quod est autem nomen supremum nisi nomen proprium Dei? Illud enim nomen non est supra omne nomen, quo est nomen aliquod superius. Atque hæc forte causa est cur Apostolus subiiciens, vt in nomine Iesu flectat se omne genu cœlestium & terrestrium & subterraneorum, & omnis lingua confiteatur, quod Dominus est Iesus Christus ad gloriam Dei Patris, non dixit cum articulo ὅτι[?] ὁ Κύριος, sed absque articulo ὅτι Κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός: constat enim, nomen Κύριος absque articulo præfixo id esse, quo 70. interpretes, omnesque Noui Testamenti autores nomen Dei Israëlis proprium, quod est supra omne nomen, exprimunt. Itaque non potuit clarius innuere supremum illud nomen Christo conuenire. Taceo nullam dari prouocationem à Christo, quæ tamen dari solet à subordinato iudice ad eum cui subordinatus est. Taceo Christum habere omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra: non autem habere omnem potestatem cum, qui summam non habet. Taceo omnia quæcunque sunt Patris esse etiam Filii: id quod æqualitatem summam arguit, cui cum subordinatione non bene conuenire palam est. Hæc enim iam attigi thes. 3. & 4.
units.tr: XI. Socinus nevertheless tries to teach how this does not follow. For, he says, since it is perfectly clear from the very clear words of the same Paul, which he wrote elsewhere, namely in Philippians 2, that the fact that every knee must at some time bow to Christ comes from the gift of that one God, and so Christ, in this matter as in all others, depends wholly on that one God and is distinguished from that one God by reason of this very matter, it is necessary that Christ, even insofar as every knee must bow to him, is subordinate to that one God, so that whoever bends the knee to Christ bends the knee to that one God. From this it follows that Paul could rightly affirm that the prophecy in Isaiah about every knee bowing to that one God would be fulfilled in this way, that every knee will bow to Christ, even if Christ is not that one God. Socinus errs in three ways in these words. First, he says that Christ, even insofar as every knee must bow to him, is subordinate to that one God, and he thinks this follows from Philippians 2:10. Yet the opposite follows from it. For subordination signifies inequality, whereas from that passage the greatest equality can be concluded. For in that place Christ is said, when he emptied himself, to have been in the form of God. But the form of God is not understood as false but as true. And the form of God is not true where the divine essence is absent. Then it is added that he did not consider it robbery to be equal to God. He was therefore equal to God, and rightly so, which proves a true form of God. For there is a great difference between some likeness and equality. Next it is added that God, taking into account both the greatness of his natural dignity and his voluntary humiliation, super-exalted him, that is, as Vatablus and Beza translate, raised him to the highest sublimity; but the highest sublimity is equal to the divine, for otherwise it would not be the highest. Thus it corresponds to the dignity of the person (for no more worthy form can be conceived than that of God, and no greater dignity than that which is equal to the divine), and to the voluntary humiliation, which, considering the terms from which and to which, could be no greater. Finally it is added that God gave him the name which is above every name, that is, the supreme name. But what is the supreme name, unless it is the proper name of God? For that name is not above every name, if there is some name higher than it. And perhaps this is the reason why the Apostle, adding, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father, did not write with the article ὅτι ὁ Κύριος, but without the article, that Jesus Christ is Lord [ὅτι Κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός]. For it is established that the word Κύριος without a prefixed article is the form by which the Seventy and all the authors of the New Testament express the proper name of the God of Israel, which is above every name. Thus he could not more clearly hint that this supreme name belongs to Christ. I say nothing of the fact that no appeal is made to Christ, although such an appeal is usually made by a subordinate judge to the one to whom he is subordinate. I say nothing of Christ having all power in heaven and on earth, whereas one who does not have the highest power does not have all power. I say nothing of all things whatsoever that are the Father's being also the Son's, which proves the highest equality, and it is plain that this does not agree well with subordination. For I have already touched on these matters in theses 3 and 4.

units.la: X I. Addo verba Apostoli, 1. Cor. 15. 28. Cum vero subiecta fuerint illi omnia, tunc & ipse Filius subiicietur ei, qui subiece-rit ei omnia, vt Deus sit omnia in omnibus. Innuunt enim Christum, quandiu regnat & iudicat, Patri subiectum non esse. Regnat enim cum Patre vt æqualis cum æquali, summa cum autoritate & Maiestate. Iudicabit eos qui flexis genibus ante ipsius tribunal erunt, non tanquam alienos seruos aut subditos, sed tanquam suos, ac prout sui vnius Domini ipsorum rationem habuerint, vel non habuerint in hac vita, absoluet, vel damnabit. Quibus omnibus peractis, tum demum, quatenus homo est, quiescet ab imperando & iudicando. Non quiescet tamen Pater atque diuinitas à Sanctis suis omni gaudio & fœlicitate perpetuò beandis. Ita Patri regnum tradet & subjicietur Filius. Ad regendos enim atque in beatitudine & gloria conseruandos glorificatos sola diuinitatis efficacitas abundè sufficiet, nec erit opus ut Filius, quatenus à Patre distinguitur, aut quatenus homo est munere aliquo fungatur.
units.tr: XI. I add the words of the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 15:28: When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all. For these words imply that Christ, as long as he reigns and judges, is not subject to the Father. For he reigns with the Father as an equal with an equal, with the highest authority and majesty. He will judge those who stand before his tribunal with bent knees, not as strangers' servants or subjects, but as his own, and according as they have or have not acknowledged him as their one Lord in this life, he will acquit or condemn them. When all these things have been completed, then at last, insofar as he is man, he will cease from ruling and judging. Yet the Father and the divinity will not cease from endlessly blessing his saints with all joy and happiness. So the Son will hand over the kingdom to the Father and be subjected. For the power of the divinity alone will be more than enough to govern the glorified and to preserve them in blessedness and glory; nor will there be any need for the Son, insofar as he is distinguished from the Father, or insofar as he is man, to perform any office.

units.la: XII. Alterum Socini peccatum in illis verbis est illa ipsa argumentationis Apostolicæ inuersio, quam in eo iam reprehendi. Conatur enim explicare, qnomodo quicunque genua flectet Christo, ea flectet etiam Deo, id quod ad exponendam argumentationem Apostoli nihil prorsus facit. Non enim Apostolus ex eo quod omne genu flectetur Christo concludit omne genu flexum iri Deo, sed contrà ex eo quod flectetur Deo concludit flexum iri Christo. Itaque frustrà laborat Socinus in deducenda consequentia à Christo ad Deum: aberrat enim ab Apostoli scopo & verbis.
units.tr: XII. The second error of Socinus in those words is that very inversion of the Apostle's argument which I have already criticised. For he tries to explain how whoever bends the knee to Christ also bends it to God, which contributes absolutely nothing to explaining the Apostle's argument. For the Apostle does not conclude from the fact that every knee will bow to Christ that every knee will bow to God; on the contrary, he concludes from the fact that every knee will bow to God that it will bow to Christ. Therefore Socinus labours in vain in drawing the inference from Christ to God; for he strays from the purpose and the words of the Apostle.

units.la: XIII. Tertium Socini peccatum est in istis verbis, Ex quo consequitur, iure potuisse Paulum affirmare impletum iri vaticinationem illam apud Esaiam de curuando illi uni Deo omni genu, hac ratione, quod Christo omne genu curuabitur. Perinde enim accipit verba Apostoli, ac si dixisset, Omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Christi, ut impleatur quod scriptum est, viuo ego, dicit Dominus, quod mihi flectet se omne genu; Cum tamen Apostolus longè aliter sit locutus, Omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Christi: Scriptum est enim, ego viuo, dicit Dominus, quod mihi curuabitur omne genu. Illud, enim, clamat Apostolum argumentari? Nonne manifestum est, Apostolum necessitatem apparitionis omnium coram tribunali Christi probare, ducto ab illo Domini iureiurando argumento? Nonne Apostolus, prolato illo iureiurando, rursus ex eo eandem diuersis verbis necessitatem deducit atque repetit? Itaque, inquit, unusquisque nostrum de seipso rationem reddet Deo ? Certè nullum locum dubitandi relinquit, quin ex verbis illis Domini apud Esaiam necessitatem illam certissimè concludat. Et tamen Socinus, quasi putaret se posse lectorem ludificare ac fallere nuda affirmatione, paulò post subjicit hæc verba, Est praterea animadvertendum, Paulum non dixisse, scriptum esse, id tribuendum esse Christo, quod ipse commemorat: sed tantummodo, se propterea id commemorare quia scriptum sit, viuo ego, &c. Ad hoc refellendum sola lectione verborum Apostoli opus est. Quod enim iste negat Paulum dixisse, Paulus dixit; & quod affirmat Paulum dixisse, Paulus non dixit. Negat Paulum dixisse, scriptum esse, omnes staturos ante tribunal Christi. Non dicit quidem Paulus id scriptum esse in eo Esaiæ loco totidem verbis, at dicit quod idem valet, cum id ex eo quod ibi scriptum est, colligit, & deducit necessaria consequentia. Quomodo enim ex verbis Domini scriptis ab Esaia id elicuisset atque expressisset, si in illis non continebatur? Affirmat Paulum dixisse Tantummodo, se propterea id commemorare, quia scriptum sit, viuo ego, &c. Id nullo modo Paulus dixit, nec ex ipsius verbis colligi potest, sed contrarium potius. Non enim quia scriptum sit viuo ego, &c. idcirco commemorat nos staturos omnes ante tribunal Christi: sed contrà illud propter istud commemorat & citat. Absterret enim nos à iudicandis & spernendis fratribus nostris argumento ducto à necessitate nos omnes sistendi ad tribunal Christi. Hanc vero necessitatem probat iureiurando isto Domini apud Esaiam, viuo ego, &c.
units.tr: XIII. The third error of Socinus is in these words: From this it follows that Paul could rightly affirm that the prophecy in Isaiah about every knee bowing to that one God would be fulfilled, in this way, that every knee will bow to Christ. For he understands the Apostle's words as if he had said: For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that what is written may be fulfilled: As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me. Yet the Apostle spoke quite differently: For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. For it is written: As I live, saith the Lord, to me every knee shall bow. Who would not cry out that the Apostle is reasoning in that way? Is it not plain that the Apostle proves the necessity of all appearing before the tribunal of Christ by the argument drawn from that oath of the Lord? Does not the Apostle, having brought forward that oath, then draw out and repeat the same necessity from it in different words? Therefore, he says, each of us will give an account of himself to God. Certainly he leaves no room for doubt that he concludes that necessity most certainly from those words of the Lord in Isaiah. And yet Socinus, as if he thought he could mock and deceive the reader with a bare assertion, adds a little later these words: Furthermore, it is to be noted that Paul did not say that it is written that what he mentions should be ascribed to Christ, but only that he mentions it because it is written, as I live, etc. To refute this, the mere reading of the Apostle's words is needed. For what this man denies that Paul said, Paul said; and what he asserts that Paul said, Paul did not say. He denies that Paul said that it is written that all shall stand before the tribunal of Christ. Paul does not indeed say that this is written in that passage of Isaiah in exactly these words, but he says something that amounts to the same thing, since he draws it from what is written there by necessary consequence. For how would he have drawn out and expressed it from the words of the Lord written by Isaiah, if it were not contained in them? He asserts that Paul said only that he mentions it because it is written, as I live, etc. Paul did not say this in any way, nor can it be gathered from his words; rather the opposite. For it is not because it is written, as I live, etc., that he mentions that we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ; rather, on the contrary, he mentions and cites the one because of the other. For he deters us from judging and despising our brothers by the argument drawn from the necessity of all of us appearing before the tribunal of Christ. Moreover, he proves this necessity by that oath of the Lord in Isaiah, as I live, etc.

units.la: XIV: Sic refutatis responsionibus Socini, qui argumenti nostri neruum non tetigit, (suane an eorum quibus respondebat culpa, alij viderint) id nunc, quale esse debet, paucis exponamus. Id ita concipi potest.
units.tr: XIV: Having thus refuted the replies of Socinus, who did not touch the sinew of our argument (whether the fault lies with him or with those he was answering, let others judge), let us now set out briefly what the argument should be. It can be framed as follows.

units.la: Ille qui Esaiæ 45. 23. iurat, Viuo ego, &c. quod mihi curuabitur omne genu, est Deus Israelis præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: He who swears in Isaiah 45:23, As I live, &c., to me every knee shall bow, is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est ille qui Esaiæ 45. 23. iurat, viuo ego, &c. quod mi-hi curuabitur omne genu.
units.tr: Christ is he who swears in Isaiah 45:23, As I live, &c., to me every knee shall bow.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israelis præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: De maiore nulla potest esse controuersia. Immediatè enim præcedunt apud Esaiam hæc verba, Ego sum Deus, & non est alius. Minor probatur primùm autoritate Apostoli, Deinde argumentis ex illo ipso loco Esaiæ petitis. Apostolus probat omnes sta-turos ante tribunal Christi, quia omne genu se flectet Domino, argumentatur autem sine dubio bene & prudenter, sequitur ergo id quod concludit necessaria consequentia ex eo unde id concludit. Ostendant igitur nobis, si possunt, Aduersarij, quomodo posita ipsorum sententia ex hoc antecedente, Omne genu se fleEt[?] Domino sequatur hoc consequens, Ergo omnes stabimus ante tribunal Christi. Nam aliud Socino est flecti omne genu alicui, aliud stare ante tribunal alicuius, alius etiam est Dominus alius Christus. Doceant igitur quomodo ex flexione omnis genu Domino, sequatur apparitio omnium coram tribunali Christi. Certè si Dominus idem non est Christus, quomodo id doceri possit non video. Nam à Christi cultu ad cultum Dei valet secundum eorum doctrinam argumentatio, à cultu verò Dei ad cultum Christi non item. Nam & olim colebatur Deus & hodie coli potest ac colitur nonnunquam non culto Christo. Itaque, si illis creditur, possumus genua curuare Domino iuranti apud Esaiam sibi omne genu curuatum iri, nec tamen ea curuare Christo. Si dixerint non curuatum iri omne genu Deo in hoc seculo, nec post latam sententiam ab iis qui erunt in inferno, quare id impletum iri in die iudicii. Non repugnabimus. verum id nondum satis erit ad eliciendam hanc conclusionem, ergo stabimus omnes ante tribunal Christi. Relinquitur enim ostendendum, quomodo ex eo, quod in die iudicii curuabitur omne genu Domino, deduci possit bona consequentia, ergo stabimus omnes ante tribunal Christi, siquidem Dominus non est Christus. Si addiderint, omnes esse per Christum iudicandos: quippe cui omne iudicium sit à Patre datum, ex eo quidem sequetur, omnes staturos ante tribunal Christi. Sed sequetur via assumptæ propositionis, non vi citati loci. Aut igitur non bene argumentatus est Apostolus, aut falluntur Aduersarii. Absit ut prius dicamus: id enim non Apostolo modò, sed Domino etiam, qui in Apostolo loquebatur, iniuriosum foret. Posterius igitur verum est.
units.tr: No controversy can arise over the major premise, for the words I am God, and there is none else immediately precede in Isaiah. The minor premise is proved first by the authority of the Apostle, and secondly by arguments drawn from that same passage of Isaiah. The Apostle proves that all will stand before the tribunal of Christ because every knee shall bow to the Lord, and he argues, without doubt, well and wisely. What he concludes therefore follows by a necessary consequence from that from which he concludes it. Let our opponents show us, if they can, how, on their own position, the consequent Therefore we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ follows from the antecedent Every knee shall bow to the Lord. For, according to Socinus, it is one thing for every knee to bow to someone, another for us to stand before someone's tribunal, and the Lord is one person and Christ another. Let them therefore teach how the appearance of all before the tribunal of Christ follows from every knee bowing to the Lord. Certainly, if the Lord is not the same as Christ, I do not see how this can be taught. For by their doctrine the argument holds from the worship of Christ to the worship of God, but not conversely from the worship of God to the worship of Christ. For God was worshipped of old, and can be worshipped today, and is sometimes worshipped without Christ being worshipped. So, if we believe them, we may bend our knees to the Lord who swears through Isaiah that every knee shall bow to him, and yet not bend them to Christ. If they say that every knee will not bow to God in this age, nor after the sentence is pronounced by those who will be in hell, why should it be fulfilled on the day of judgment? We will not object. But this will not yet be enough to draw the conclusion, therefore we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. For it remains to be shown how from the fact that on the day of judgment every knee will bow to the Lord, a sound consequence can be drawn: therefore we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, since the Lord is not Christ. If they add that all are to be judged through Christ, to whom all judgment has been given by the Father, then indeed it will follow that all shall stand before the tribunal of Christ. But it will follow by means of the assumed proposition, not by the force of the cited passage. Either the Apostle has not argued well, or our opponents are mistaken. Far be it that we should say the former, for that would be an insult not only to the Apostle but also to the Lord who spoke in the Apostle. The latter, then, is true.

units.la: XV. Adde quod hæ duæ locutiones, curuari omne genu Domino, & sisti tribunali Domini, idem Apostolo valent, vel non. Si non idem valent, fieri poterit ut Domino qui sic iurauit curuetur omne genu, nec tamen omnes sistantur eius tribunali, & rursus ut omnes sistantur tribunali Christi, nec tamen illi curuetur omne genu: Attamen constat quàm omnes sistentur tribunali Christi, tam omne genu illi curuatum iri. Et quàm omne genu curuabitur Domino apud Esaiam iuranti, tam omnes eius tribunali sistendos esse. Hoc si negant Aduersarij, dicant igitur nobis, quomodo ex eo quod Domino flectetur omne genu sequitur, omnes staturos ante tribunal Christi; & tamen non sequitur omnes staturos ante tribunal Domini. Si igitur phrases illæ reipsa idem valent, seseque mutuò ponunt & tollunt, idem etiam dicendum est de duobus istis nominibus, Dominus & Christus, ut quemadmodum se habent omnes ad omne genu, &, sisti omnes tribunali, ad, curuari omne genu; sic se habeat etiam Christus ad Dominum, atque adeò tota conclusio ad totam præmissam unde deducitur. Idem igitur valent Apostolo Dominus & Christus, quod ut facilius insinuaret in mentem lectoris, quinque proximis versibus antecedentibus Domini nomen septics usurpauit pro Christi nomine: ac ne nos à Christo intelligendo absentia articuli in verbis, dicit Dominus, absterreret, quater eo nomine absque præfixo articulo Christum designauit. Ac ut res esset testatior, subjunxit alteram æquipollentem conclusionem vers. 12.
units.tr: XV. Add to this that these two expressions, every knee bows to the Lord and to be brought before the tribunal of the Lord, either mean the same thing to the Apostle or they do not. If they do not mean the same, it may happen that every knee bows to the Lord who so swore, and yet not all are brought before his tribunal; and conversely that all are brought before the tribunal of Christ, and yet every knee does not bow to him. But it is certain that as all are brought before the tribunal of Christ, so every knee will bow to him. And as every knee will bow to the Lord who swears in Isaiah, so all are to be brought before his tribunal. If our opponents deny this, let them tell us how it follows from the fact that every knee bows to the Lord that all shall stand before the tribunal of Christ, and yet it does not follow that all shall stand before the tribunal of the Lord. If, then, those phrases really mean the same and set one another up and take one another down, the same must be said of the two names, Lord and Christ: just as all stand in relation to every knee, and all are brought before the tribunal, in relation to bowing every knee, so Christ stands in relation to the Lord, and thus the whole conclusion stands in relation to the whole premise from which it is drawn. The Lord and Christ therefore mean the same to the Apostle. And so that this might more easily be impressed on the reader's mind, he used the name of the Lord seven times in the five preceding verses in place of the name of Christ. And lest the absence of the article in the words the Lord says should deter us from understanding Christ, he designated Christ four times by that name without a prefixed article. And to make the matter clearer still, he added in verse 12 another conclusion equivalent to the first:

units.la: Itaque unusquisque nostrum rationem de se reddet Deo. Cui Deo, nisi ei cuius ante tribunal omnes stabimus, hoc est, Christo[?] ut enim in hac conclusione consequente, unusquisque nostrum idem valet quod nos omnes in conclusione antecedente, & rationem reddere de se quod sisti tribunali; sic Deus idem valet quod Christus quem igitur Christum appellauerat in antecedente conclusione, eundem appellat in consequente, Deum, ὁ Θεὸν[?]. Id quod etiam hoc argumento potest firmari. Ille cui unusquisque nostrum rationem de seipso reddet, est Deus, Apostolo teste. Christus est ille cui unusquisque nostrum de seipso rationem reddet. Ergo Christus est Deus. Quam propositionem possint Aduersarij negare non video, reddemus enim rationem unusquisque nostrum pro se ei, qui nos iudicaturus est. Hic autem est Christus, non Pater quatenus à Filio distinguitur, teste ipso Filio, Ioh. 5.22. Cui enim serui potius reddant rationem de seipsis quàm Domino suo, cui viuunt, cui morinntur, cuius, siue viuunt siue moriuntur, sunt, cui faciunt quicquid faciunt, & cui non faciunt quicquid non faciunt? Talem autem omnium nostrum Dominum esse Christum, ipse Paulus totis ferè septem proximis versibus inculcauit.
units.tr: So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God. To what God, if not to him before whose tribunal we all shall stand, that is, to Christ? For just as in this consequent conclusion every one of us means the same as we all in the antecedent conclusion, and to give account of oneself the same as to stand before a tribunal, so God means the same as Christ; so he calls by the name God the one whom he had called Christ in the antecedent conclusion [ho Theos]. This can also be confirmed by the following argument. He to whom each one of us shall give account of himself is God, by the Apostle's testimony. Christ is he to whom each one of us shall give account of himself. Therefore Christ is God. I do not see how our opponents could deny this proposition, for each of us will give account for himself to him who is to judge us. Now this is Christ, not the Father as distinguished from the Son, as the Son himself testifies in John 5:22. For to whom should servants rather give account of themselves than to their Lord, for whom they live, for whom they die, whose they are whether they live or die, for whom they do whatever they do, and to whom they do not do whatever they do not do? That Christ is such a Lord of us all, the Apostle himself has pressed home almost throughout the seven verses that follow.

units.la: XVI. Sed age, misso Apostolo, videamus quid ex ipsis Domini verbis colligi possit. Si Domino se flectet omne genu, & omnis lingua iurabit, vel, confitebitur, Dominus sese tam clarè tamque potenter reuelabit atque ostendet, ut non possit non agnosci ab omnibus, etiam ab illis qui omnium maximè incredduli[?], rebelles, contumaces fuerint: nec id modò, sed hi etiam non poterunt sese occultare, aut ab eo fugere, aut majestatem eius effugere, sed cogentur coram eo apparere, ac genua flectere, ei iurare vel confiteri. Nam contumacissimi vel homines vel diaboli, si Dominum possent non agnoscere, ei nunquam se honoris causa incuruarent, aut si possent eius praesentiam vitare, atque aliquo fugere aut latere, id sine dubio eligerent potius, quàm ei sese maxima cum demissione subijcere. Itaque cogentur, velint nolint, Dominum agnoscere, atque ei praesenti cum debita tantae majestati reuerentia sese sistere, alioqui nunquam sua illi genua flecterent. Quis autem ita clarè, ita apertè, cum tanta gloria maiestate potentia omnibus apparebit, vt ab omnibus nullo excepto agnoscatur? quis mittet Angelos suos vt omnes è latibulis ipsorum pertrahat atque congreget, & sistat ante se, cogatque sibi debitam exhibere reuerentiam, atque, quod solet exigi à reis, sibi iurare & confiteri? Quis? nisi iudex viuorum & mortuorum, Dominus Iesus, qui veniet cum nubibus, quem omnis videbit oculus, etiam illi qui eum compunxerunt? Nullius aduentus, nullius reuelatio, nullius praesentia promittitur, praedicitur, creditur, expectatur in Ecclesia, Nisi gloriae magni Dei, & Seruatoris Iesu Christi. Ipsius Patris, quatenus à Christo distinguitur, aduentus futurus neque promissus est, neque speratur.
units.tr: XVI. But come, leaving the Apostle aside, let us see what can be gathered from the Lord's own words. If every knee shall bow to him, and every tongue shall swear, or confess, the Lord will reveal and show himself so clearly and so powerfully that he cannot fail to be recognised by all, even by those who have been most unbelieving, rebellious and stubborn. And not only this, but they also will not be able to hide themselves, or flee from him, or escape his majesty, but they will be compelled to appear before him, to bend their knees, and to swear or confess to him. For the most stubborn, whether men or devils, if they could fail to recognise the Lord, would never bow to him out of respect; or if they could avoid his presence, and flee or hide somewhere, they would without doubt prefer that to submitting themselves to him with the utmost humility. Therefore, whether they will or not, they will be compelled to recognise the Lord, and to present themselves to him in the presence of such majesty with due reverence; otherwise they would never bend their knees to him. But who will appear so clearly, so openly, with such glory, majesty and power to all, that he is recognised by all without exception? Who will send out his angels to drag and gather all from their hiding places, and set them before himself, and compel them to show him the reverence due to him, and to swear and confess to him, as is usually required of accused persons? Who? None but the judge of the living and the dead, the Lord Jesus, who will come with the clouds, whom every eye shall see, even those who pierced him? No coming, no revelation, no presence of anyone is promised, foretold, believed, or expected in the Church, except the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ. The coming of the Father himself, as distinguished from Christ, is neither promised nor hoped for.

units.la: XVII. Hoc ipsum confirmant versus qui apud Esaiam antecedunt & sequuntur. Qui proximè antecedit sic habet, Respicite ad me & salui eritis omnes fines terrae, quia ego sum Deus, & non est alius. Primùm compellat non gentem Iudaicam, sed omnes fines terrae, id est, omnes gentes, etiam procul à Iudaea dissitas. Itaque non proponit legem sed Euangelium, & pertinet haec Domini concio, non ad tempus legis, sed ad tempus Euangelij. Deinde pollicetur, non simpliciter vitam vt fit in lege, sed salutem vt in Euangelio. Denique conditionem ab iis exigit, non obedientiam vt in foedere legali, sed fidem vt in foedere Euangelico, Aspicite, inquit, ad me & salui eritis. Atque sub ea conditione salutem omnibus gentibus absque discrimine offert. Est igitur concio Euangelica, non ad tempus Esaiae, sed ad tempus Christi reuelati spectans. Si igitur quaeritur cuius sit concio, si Esaiam audis, Deus est, si Euangelium, est Christus. Dic eundem esse Deum & Christum; & utrumque conciliasti. Non enim Deus qua Pater sub Euangelio concionatur, non promulgat Euangelium, non compellat & vocat ad se gentes vt seruentur. Hæ sunt partes Filij.
units.tr: XVII. The verses of Isaiah that come before and after confirm this very point. The one immediately preceding reads: Look to me and be saved, all you ends of the earth, for I am God, and there is no other. First, he addresses not the Jewish nation but all the ends of the earth, that is, all nations, even those far removed from Judea. So he does not propose the law but the gospel, and this address of the Lord belongs not to the time of the law but to the time of the gospel. Next, he promises not simply life, as is the case under the law, but salvation, as in the gospel. Finally, he requires of them a condition, not obedience as in the legal covenant, but faith as in the evangelical covenant: Look, he says, to me and you will be saved. On that condition he offers salvation to all nations without distinction. This is therefore a gospel address, looking not to the time of Isaiah but to the time of Christ revealed. If, then, you ask whose address it is: if you listen to Isaiah, it is God's; if to the gospel, it is Christ's. Say that God and Christ are the same, and you have reconciled both. For God as Father does not preach under the gospel, does not publish the gospel, does not summon and call the nations to himself that they may be saved. These are the offices of the Son.

units.la: XVIII. Sed expendamus verba, Respicite, inquit', ad me, פני־אל[?] omnes fines terræ. Primùm qui sic loquitur sese ostendit & revelat & offert conspiciendum omnibus finibus terræ, omnibus gentibus. Id proprium est Dei patefacti in carne. Pater enim non præbet se videndum, nisi quatenus, cum sit in Filio & Filius in ipso, qui videt Filium videt Patrem, qui contemplatur Filium contemplatur Patrem. Itaque toto Euangelio describitur, prædicatur, aspiciendus proponitur omnibus Christus. Deinde qui sic loquitur, iubet ad se aspici, atque ad se respiciendum omnes obligat. Et Christus etiam omnes gentes, quibus sese Euangelii sui prædicatione contemplandum offert, iubet ad ad se vnum oculos fidei conuertere.
units.tr: XVIII. But let us weigh the words: "Look," he says, "to me" [פנו אלי], "all the ends of the earth." First, he who speaks thus shows and reveals himself, and offers himself to be looked upon by all the ends of the earth, all nations. This is proper to God made manifest in the flesh. For the Father does not present himself to be seen, except insofar as, since he is in the Son and the Son in him, he who sees the Son sees the Father, and he who contemplates the Son contemplates the Father. Thus throughout the whole gospel Christ is described, preached, and set forth to be looked upon by all. Next, he who speaks thus bids them look to him and binds all to look to him. And Christ, offering himself to be contemplated by all nations through the preaching of his gospel, bids them turn the eyes of faith to him alone.

units.la: XIX. Huic mandato subnectit promissionem, & salui eritis, id quod de salute spirituali accipiendum esse nemo, opinor, ambigit. Promittit igitur salutem omnibus illis qui ipsum aspexerint, quæ promissio facta est ab ipso Christo iis qui ipsum aspexerint Ioh. vi. 40. Hæc est autem voluntas eius qui misit me, vt omnis qui conspicit Filium, & credit in eum habeat vitam æternam, & suscitabo eum ego in vltimo die. Certè Pater qua distinguitur à Filio, neque se ostendit nobis, neque ad se videndum nos obligat, neque potest videri à nobis, neque vlla occurrit promissio in Euangelio, qua Patrem aspicienti salus promittatur.
units.tr: XIX. To this command he attaches a promise: "and you will be saved," which, I think, no one doubts is to be understood of spiritual salvation. He therefore promises salvation to all who look upon him, a promise made by Christ himself to those who look upon him, John 6:40: For this is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who beholds the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. Certainly the Father, insofar as he is distinguished from the Son, neither shows himself to us, nor obliges us to look to him, nor can be seen by us, nor does any promise occur in the gospel by which salvation is promised to one who looks upon the Father.

units.la: XX. Rationem addit, quia, inquit, Ego sum Deus & non est alius, innuens frustrà eos ad alium respecturos, frustrà in alio quæsituros salutem. Hoc Euangelium inculcat, credentem in Christum seruari, non credentem damnari. Non est, inquit Petrus Act, 4. 12. in alio quoquam salus. Nec enim aliud nomen est sub cælo datum hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri. Cum igitur qui sic loquitur significet in se vno salutem esse, & non in alio, & constet in vno Christo salutem esse, & non in alio, fatendum est qui sic loquitur Christum esse.
units.tr: XX. He adds a reason: "for," he says, "I am God and there is no other," implying that they will look to another in vain and seek salvation in another in vain. The gospel inculcates this: he who believes in Christ is saved, he who does not believe is condemned. There is salvation in no one else, says Peter, Acts 4:12, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. Since therefore he who speaks thus signifies that salvation is in him alone and not in another, and it is established that salvation is in Christ alone and not in another, it must be admitted that he who speaks thus is Christ.

units.la: XXI. Aliud argumentum nobis hæc verba suppeditant. Negat enim qui sic loquitur alium Deum esse præter se: idque proximo versu inculcauerat, Nunquid non ego Dominus, inquit, & non est vltra Deus absque me? Deus iustus & seruans non est præ[?]ter me. Quod quomodo congruat cum opinione Aduersariorum duos Deos esse existimantium, verè inquam & proprie dictos Deos, non metaphoricè aut figuratè, totis essentijs diuersos ac separatos, equidem non intelligo. Non enim possunt eò confugere vt dicant, Deum sic loqui habita ratione temporis Veteris Testamenti, cum nondum esset alter ille Deus, videlicet, Christus. Inducitur enim hoc loco omnibus finibus terræ salutem euangelisans, ac propterea hæc eius concio ad tempora Euangelij pertinet. Quod etiam iurat versu sequente referetur ad tempus iudicij vltimi docente Apostolo, & agnoscente Socino. Et quorsum gentes alloquens clamaret & inculcaret se Deum esse, & præter se non esse amplius Deum, nisi quia vult hoc credi ab omnibus gentibus? vultne igitur ab omnibus gentibus credi Christum non esse Deum, non esse adorandum, non esse ad eum, vt in eo vno salus quæratur, aspiciendum? Hoc esset Euangelium non prædicare sed abolere. Non possunt etiam confugere ad solennem illam suam distinctionem Dei summi, & Dei subordinati. Nam dicendo, Ego sum Deus, & non est עוד amplius, Ego sum Iehouah, & non est amplius Deus, אלהים[?] præter me, si non prorsus tollit omnem alium Deum proprie dictum, sine ponatur summus siue non summus, quomodo prorsus tolli possit non intelligo. Certè negari non potest quin illis verbis vniuersæ multitudini deorum, quos gentes colebant, diuinitatem omnem detrahat: colebant tamen illæ vnum duntaxat summum Deum.
units.tr: XXI. These words supply us with another argument. For he who speaks thus denies that there is any God besides himself, and he had inculcated this in the next verse: Is it not I the Lord, and there is no God beyond me? A righteous God and a Saviour; there is none besides me. How this agrees with the opinion of our opponents, who think there are two Gods, truly and properly so called, not metaphorically or figuratively, totally diverse and separate in essence, I truly do not understand. For they cannot take refuge in saying that God speaks thus with regard to the time of the Old Testament, when that other God, namely Christ, did not yet exist. For in this place he is introduced proclaiming salvation to all the ends of the earth, and therefore this address pertains to the times of the gospel. And that he swears in the following verse is referred to the time of the final judgment, as the Apostle teaches and Socinus acknowledges. And why, addressing the nations, would he cry out and insist that he is God, and that there is no further God besides himself, unless he wishes this to be believed by all nations? Does he then wish it to be believed by all nations that Christ is not God, not to be worshipped, not to be looked to, that salvation is not sought in him alone? This would be not to preach the gospel but to abolish it. Nor can they take refuge in their well-known distinction between the supreme God and the subordinate God. For in saying, "I am God, and there is no more" [עוד], "I am Jehovah, and there is no God besides me," if it does not wholly remove every other God properly so called, whether that God is posited as supreme or not supreme, I do not see how it could be wholly removed. Certainly it cannot be denied that by those words he strips of all divinity the whole multitude of gods whom the nations worshipped; yet those nations worshipped only one supreme God.

units.la: XXIII.[?] Certè vel Tantùm (אך enim vtrumque significat) in Domino mihi, dicet, iustitia & robur, &c. nempe ad salutem nostram duabus rebus opus est, iustitia nos iustificante vt de iure; & robore vt de facto à peccatis nostris & hostibus liberemur. Ambæ sunt in vno Christo, vt patet ex toto Euangelio. Quid ergo cunctamur affirmare Christum esse vnum illum Dominum, præter quem nullus est Deus?
units.tr: XXIII. Surely or only (for אך means both): In the Lord, he will say, are righteousness and strength, and so on. For our salvation two things are needed: righteousness, justifying us as to right, and strength, freeing us from our sins and enemies as to fact. Both are in Christ alone, as is clear from the whole gospel. Why then do we hesitate to affirm that Christ is that one Lord, besides whom there is no God?

units.la: XXIIII.[?] Hunc versum excipit vltimus capitis, In Domino iustificabuntur, & gloriabuntur omne semen Israëlis. Atqui iustificabuntur in Christo, in quo vno habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum, propitiationem pro peccatis, iustificationem, atque omnia: est enim omnia in omnibus. In eo solo habitat corporaliter plenitudo diuinitatis. Qui eum habet habet vitam, qui eum non habet non habet vitam. In eo est Pater, in eo est Spiritus Sanctus: Qui eum habet habet etiam Patrem, qui non habet non habet Patrem. Qui eum honorat honorat Patrem, qui eum non honorat non honorat Pa-trem, Concludimus igitur eum esse eundem cum Patre, necnon cum Spiritu Sancto, Deum, Deum, inquam, illum unum præter quem nullus est alius Deus, ei sit gloria in secula seculorum, Amen.
units.tr: XXIIII. This verse is followed by the last of the chapter: In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified and glory. Yet they will be justified in Christ, in whom alone we have redemption through his blood, remission of sins, propitiation for sins, justification, and all things, for Christ is all in all. In him alone dwells bodily the fullness of the Godhead. He who has him has life, he who does not have him does not have life. In him is the Father, in him is the Holy Spirit: he who has him has the Father too, and he who does not have him does not have the Father. He who honours him honours the Father; he who does not honour him does not honour the Father. We conclude therefore that he is the same as the Father, and likewise the same as the Holy Spirit, God, God, I say, that one God besides whom there is no other God. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: DISPUTATIO QUINTA De Arg. V. Ex verbis Domini apud Esaiam Cap. 41. 4. & Cap. 44. ν. 6. & Cap. 48. ν. 12. Ego primus, & ego nouissimus, collatis cum verbis Christi apud Iohannem in Apocalypsi Cap. 1. ν. 11. 17. & Cap. 2. ν. 8. & Cap. 22. ν. 13. Ego sum primus & nouissimus.
units.tr: FIFTH DISPUTATION, on the fifth argument, from the words of the Lord in Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12, "I, the first, and I, the last," compared with the words of Christ in John's Apocalypse 1:11, 17; 2:8; 22:13, "I am the first and the last."

units.la: I. IDEM Dominus apud eundem Esaiam clamat ter se esse primum & ultimum. Christus similiter apud Iohannem in Apocalypsi clamat ter se esse primum & ultimum, quo aperte innuit se illum ipsum Dominum esse, qui sese sic descripsit apud Esaiam. Hinc oritur Arg. V.
units.tr: I. The same Lord, in the same Isaiah, three times declares that he is the first and the last. Likewise Christ, in John's Apocalypse, three times declares that he is the first and the last, by which he plainly intimates that he is that very Lord who described himself in this way in Isaiah. From this arises the fifth argument.

units.la: Ille qui est primus & ultimus est Deus Israëlis præditus essentia divina.
units.tr: He who is the first and the last is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est ille qui est primus & ultimus.
units.tr: Christ is he who is the first and the last.

units.la: E. Christus est Deus Israëlis præditus essentia divina.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Maior nititur locis Esaiæ 41. 4: 44. 6: 48. 12. Minor locis Apoc. 1. 11. 17: 2. 8: 22. 13. conclusio igitur vera est.
units.tr: The major premise rests on the passages of Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12. The minor rests on Revelation 1:11, 17; 2:8 and 22:13. The conclusion, therefore, is true.

units.la: II. Respondeo, inquit Socinus, Aut istud, quod Christus in Apocalypsi de seipso dicit, habet per seipsum hanc vim, vt ostendat, cum esse vnum illum verum Deum, aut non habet. Si habet, nihil attinuit, aut certè nihil necesse fuit ad argumentum formandum, afferre loca illa Esaia, vbi hoc idem de Deo Israëlis dicitur. Quod si non habet, iam non satis est, ad argumentum concludendum, do-cere, hoc idem de Israëlis Deo dici. Huius dilemmatis neutrum cornu ferit argumentum nostrum. Non prius. Habet enim id quod Christus de se dicit illam vim, & perseipsum, & quatenus de se ipso idem Dominus dixit apud Esaiam. Nec posterius. Non enim sic argumentamur, Deus est primus & vltimus. Christus est primus & vltimus. Ergo Christus est Deus. Argumenti enim forma nihil valeret. Nec item sic, Christus aliquid de se dicit in Novo Testamento, quod Deus Israëlis de se dixit in Veteri T. Ergo Christus est Deus Israëlis. Argumentum aliter formauimus, nec id tangit responsio.
units.tr: II. "I answer," says Socinus, either that which Christ says of himself in the Apocalypse has this force by itself, to show that he is that one true God, or it does not have it. If it has it, it was pointless, or at least there was no need, to bring in those passages of Isaiah, where the same thing is said of the God of Israel, in order to form the argument. But if it does not have it, it is not enough, in order to conclude the argument, to teach that the same thing is said of the God of Israel. Neither horn of this dilemma strikes our argument. Not the first: for what Christ says of himself does have that force, both by itself and insofar as the same Lord said the same thing of himself in Isaiah. Nor the second: for we do not argue thus, "God is the first and the last; Christ is the first and the last; therefore Christ is God." The form of such an argument would be worthless. Nor do we argue thus: "Christ says something of himself in the New Testament which the God of Israel said of himself in the Old; therefore Christ is the God of Israel." We have formed the argument in another way, and the reply does not touch it.

units.la: III. Si respondere volunt Aduersarii, necesse est, vt, aut alteram præmissarum negent, aut medium terminum distinguat. Negare minorem non possunt. Contradicerent enim dissertis verbis Christi. Maiorem si negauerint, reuincentur ipsius Dei testimonio, qui de se id dicit, cum se describit per propria, & ostendit quantum ab omnibus falsis numinibus, & creaturis distet. Esai 41. 4. Quis operatus est & fecit? Ille qui vocat generationes ab exordio. Ego Dominus, primus & cum vltimis, ego ipse. An est alius quàm Deus, qui vocet generationes ab exordio? qui sit Dominus, Iehouah? qui sit הוא ipse? Nonne illa elogia reciprocantur cum Deo? Cur idem non censetur de elogio primi & vltimi?
units.tr: III. If the adversaries wish to reply, they must either deny one of the premises or distinguish the middle term. They cannot deny the minor, for they would be contradicting the plain words of Christ. If they deny the major, they will be refuted by the testimony of God himself, who says this of himself when he describes himself by his own attributes and shows how far he is from all false gods and creatures. Isaiah 41:4: "Who has worked and made it? He who calls the generations from the beginning. I, the Lord, the first, and with the last, I myself." Is there anyone other than God who calls the generations from the beginning? Who is the Lord, Iehouah? Who is הוא [hu], he himself? Are not those titles interchangeable with God? Why should the same not be held of the title "first and last"?

units.la: IV. Clarior est locus Esai. 44. 6. Hac dicit Dominus, Rex Israëlis, & redemptor eius, Dominus exercituum, ego primus; & ego vltimus, & præter me non est Deus, & quis similis mei? Nonne enim his verbis, quàm negat vllum esse similem sui, vllum esse Deum præter se, tam negat vllum alium esse primum, vllum alium esse vltimum? Cum audio Dominum dicentem Ego primus, concludo, ergo ante ipsum nullus alius Deus fuit. Cum audio dicentem, Ego vltimus, concludo, ergo post eum nullus alius Deus erit. Si bona est illatio, conuertuntur illa elogia cum Deo. Sume enim quemcunque alium, non est primus: Nam ante ipsum Deus fuit. Si bona non est, dicant quid in ea desiderent Aduersarii, & quorsum Deus hoc de se dicat tam solenni ratione, praemissis mandato Audi Israel, & descriptione sui ad conciliandam attentionem quandam non vulgarem aptissima? Ipse mihi in ea deducenda consequentia Dominus aliquomodo praeiuit, Esai. 43. 10. cum ait, Ego ipse sum. Ante me non est formatus Deus, & post me non erit. Id quod si negetur proprium esse Dei, nihil ei relinquetur proprium, quo possit describi, & ab aliis omnibus rebus distingui.
units.tr: IV. The passage in Isaiah 44:6 is clearer: "Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the Lord of hosts: I am the first, and I am the last, and besides me there is no God; and who is like me?" For by these words, in which he denies that anyone is like him, and that there is any God besides himself, he equally denies that anyone else is the first and equally denies that anyone else is the last. When I hear the Lord saying I am the first, I conclude: therefore no other God existed before him. When I hear him saying I am the last, I conclude: therefore no other God will exist after him. If this inference is sound, those titles are interchangeable with God. For take any other being you like: it is not the first, since God existed before it. If the inference is not sound, let the adversaries say what they find lacking in it, and why God would say this of himself in such a solemn manner, preceded by the command Hear, O Israel, and by a description of himself most apt for winning an unusual degree of attention. In drawing out this consequence the Lord himself, in some measure, went before me, Isaiah 43:10, when he said: "I myself am. Before me no God was formed, and after me there will be none." If this is denied to be a property of God, nothing will be left that is proper to him by which he can be described and distinguished from all other things.

units.la: V. His duobus locis tertius accedit Esai. 48. 12. Audi me Iacob, & Israel quem ego voco, ego ipse, ego primus, etiam ego ultimus, manus quoque mea fundauit terram, &c. vides Dominum in hoc loco, vt in praecedente, sibi populi sui attentionem conciliare antequam pronunciet verba illa, Ego primus, ego ultimus, quorsum, si sunt elogia communia, quae tribui possint alicui creaturae, quaeque non conuertantur cum Deo? vides eum attributa illa non connectere cum aliis ac compingere in vnam descriptionem, sed diuidere, interjecto ac repetito pronomine primae personae, tanquam totidem descriptiones sui. Descriptionis autem vitium est, cum latius patet descripto. Vides denique nulla attributa adiungi, quae non sint vnius Dei propria. Cur ergo non vis elogia illa primi & vltimi vnius Dei esse propria? Nosti ne aliquem vno illo Deo Israelis priorem aut posteriorem, aut ei coaeuum seu coaeternum? Nullum profecto noui, nullum in Scriptura, nullum in Mundo deprehendi, mihique implicari contradictio videretur, si praeter vnum illum Deum aliquis alius eodem sensu primus & vltimus esse affirmaretur. Manet igitur fixum, Elogium primi & vltimi, vnius illius Dei praeter quem non est Deus, proprium esse; ac proinde veram esse propositionem argumenti nostri, Quicunque est primus & vltimus, ille est praeditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: V. To these two passages a third is added, Isaiah 48:12: "Hear me, Jacob, and Israel whom I call: I myself, I am the first, and I am also the last; my hand also founded the earth," etc. You see that in this passage, as in the previous one, the Lord secures the attention of his people before he utters the words "I am the first, I am the last." Why would he do so, if these were common titles which could be applied to some creature and which are not interchangeable with God? You see that he does not join those attributes to others and fit them into one description, but separates them, interposing and repeating the pronoun of the first person, as though they were so many separate descriptions of himself. Now a description is faulty when it applies more widely than the thing described. Finally, you see that no attributes are added which are not proper to the one God alone. Why then will you not allow that those titles, first and last, are proper to the one God? Do you know of anyone who is before or after that one God of Israel, or co-eval or co-eternal with him? I certainly know of no one; I have found no one in Scripture, no one in the world. And it would seem to me a contradiction if anyone were said, in the same sense, to be the first and the last besides that one God.
