It therefore remains fixed that the title of first and last is proper to that one God, besides whom there is no God; and consequently the proposition of our argument is true: Whoever is the first and the last is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: VI. Restat altera solutio per distinctionem medii termini, qua etiam Socinus vtitur. Istius argumenti, inquit, propterea nulla vis esse potest, quia nihil impedit, quominus alio sensu dictum fuerit de Deo, quod sit primus & nouissimus, & alio, de Christo. Sed alius ille sensus, vel est de mente Christi, vel non. Si non est de mente Christi, nullus est, Si est de mente Christi, aliquid esse in verbis Christi oportet, unde colligi possit. Alioqui nihil erit certi, si cum verba sunt omnino eadem, licet pro libitu sensus illis affingere diversos. Cum eadem sunt verba, putandi sunt iidem esse conceptus: quippe qui nobis, nisi per verba, non innotescunt. Sed isti homines Christi mentem & sensum forte aliunde quàm ex eius verbis tenent. Docent igitur, quo sensu Deus dicitur apud Esaiam primus & novissimus, & quo sensu Christus in Apocalypsi dicitur primus & novissimus, & unde istam sensus diversitatem deprehenderint. Non enim à nobis peti debet ratio, cur iisdem verbis eundem sensum aptemus: ipsa enim, ut ita loquar, identitas verborum impedit nos quominus sensum putemus esse diversum, sed eorum potius est docere, quare, cum verba sint eadem, nolint tamen sensum esse eundem. Rationem petant à suo dogmate vel potius errore necesse est: Nam à verbis Dei vel Christi peti non potest. Clamat Deus apud Esaiam, Ego primus ego novissimus, & quidem ter, audiente universa Ecclesia: Clamat Similiter Christus apud Iohannem, Ego sum primus & novissimus, & quidem sine controversia quater, audiente itidem universa Ecclesia, nulla addita limitatione, nulla restrictione, immò aucta emphasi per articulum praefixum, ὁ πρῶτος[?], ὁ ἔσχατος[?], qui articulus illis vocibus apud Esaiam in graeca versione praefixus non est. Augent etiam emphasim additae voces, τὸ Α[?] ȳ τὸ Ω[?], ἀρχὴ ȳ τέλος[?]. Itaque si verba Dei apud Esaiam & verba Christi apud Iohannem inter se conferas, illustriora ista, quàm illa magisque absolutè & emphaticè dicta videri possint.
units.tr: VI. There remains the other solution, by distinguishing the middle term, which Socinus also uses. There can be no force in this argument, he says, because nothing prevents the statement that God is first and last from having one sense, and the statement about Christ having another. But that other sense either is in the mind of Christ or it is not. If it is not in the mind of Christ, there is no such sense. If it is in the mind of Christ, there must be something in the words of Christ from which it can be inferred. Otherwise nothing will be certain, if we may attach different senses at will to words which are entirely the same. When the words are the same, the concepts must be thought to be the same, since these do not become known to us except through words. But these men perhaps hold the mind and sense of Christ from some source other than his words. Let them therefore teach in what sense God is called first and last in Isaiah, and in what sense Christ is called first and last in the Apocalypse, and where they have discovered this difference of sense. For the reason why we should apply the same sense to the same words must not be demanded of us: the very identity of the words, so to speak, prevents us from thinking the sense is different; rather it is for them to show why, though the words are the same, they are unwilling to have the sense be the same. They must necessarily seek their reason from their own dogma, or rather their error, for it cannot be drawn from the words of God or of Christ. God cries out in Isaiah, I am the first, I am the last, and that three times, with the whole Church hearing. Likewise Christ cries out in John, I am the first and the last, and without question four times, with the whole Church hearing in the same way, with no limitation or restriction added, indeed with the emphasis increased by the article prefixed, ὁ πρῶτος [ho prōtos] and ὁ ἔσχατος [ho eschatos]; an article which in the Greek version of Isaiah is not prefixed to those words. The added words also increase the emphasis: τὸ Α [to alpha] and τὸ Ω [to ōmega], ἀρχὴ and τέλος [archē and telos]. Therefore, if you compare the words of God in Isaiah with the words of Christ in John, the latter may seem clearer, and expressed more absolutely and emphatically than the former.

units.la: VII. Quis igitur credat Christum, si nihil nisi creatura suisset, toties, tam solenni ratione, tam ἐμφατικῶς, sibi met ipsi hunc titulum assumpturum, eoque se ipsum descripturum, quem sibi Deus tam disertè tribuerat in Veteri Testamento, quo se descripserat, quem Scriptura ipsi reseruauerat, quemque proprium esse Dei res ipsa clamabat? Non possem id conciliare cum Christi, si nihil nisi creatura esset, perfecta erga Deum reverentia, pietate, gratitudine. Sed neque id possem conciliare cum eius erga Ecclesiam perfecta charitate. Quotus enim quisque est, qui sese sic describentem Christum audiens, non intelligat ipsum sibi æternitatem ac divinam essentiam attribuere? ut nihil isto sibi tribuendo elogio voluisse videri posset, nisi Ecclesiam suam in errorem conjicere. Id quod vel cogitare pia mens horret.
units.tr: VII. Who, then, could believe that Christ, if he were nothing but a creature, would so often, in such a solemn manner, and so emphatically [ἐμφατικῶς], claim for himself this title and describe himself by it, the very title that God had so plainly given himself in the Old Testament, by which he had described himself, which Scripture had reserved for him, and which the nature of the thing itself declared to be proper to God? I could not reconcile that with a perfect reverence, piety and gratitude toward God in Christ, if he were nothing but a creature. Nor could I reconcile it with his perfect love toward the Church. For how many are there who, hearing Christ describe himself in this way, do not understand that he thereby attributes eternity and the divine essence to himself? So that by ascribing this description to himself he could seem to have intended nothing but to lead his Church into error. A pious mind shudders even to think this.

units.la: VIII. Huc accedit, quod intelligi non potest, quo sensu Christus, si Deus non est, dicatur, ὁ πρῶτος [?] καὶ [?] ὁ ἔσχατος [?], primus & vltimus. Cum enim primus dici quis possit, teste Aristotele, quinque modis. Non potest aliquis esse simul primus & vltimus dignitate, nec existendi consequentia, nec natura seu, vt loquuntur, causalitate: (implicaretur enim contradictio) sed tantum ordine, cum quidam sit quasi circulus; & tempore, cum qui ante alios fuit, esse perseverat post alios. Ordine, quomodo primus idemque vltimus dici possit Christus, assequi nequeo, nisi forte hoc sensu, quia abeo Euangelij praedicatio, fides nostra, gratiarum actio, &c. incipit atque in eo desinit. Sed si nihil nisi creatura esset, is honos Deo, non ipsi, conueniret. Tempore, quomodo primus esset is, ante quem, non solum Deus, sed Angeli omnes, sed homines innumeri tamdiu fuissent?
units.tr: VIII. In addition, it cannot be understood in what sense Christ, if he is not God, is called ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος, the first and the last. For, as Aristotle teaches, one can be called first in five ways. No one can be at once first and last in dignity, nor in the consequence of existing, nor in nature, or, as they say, in causality, for a contradiction would be involved. He can be so only in order, since a thing may be like a circle, or in time, when one who was before others also continues after them. How Christ could be first and last in order, I cannot see, unless perhaps in this sense: that the preaching of the Gospel, our faith, thanksgiving and so on begin with him and end in him. But if he were nothing but a creature, that honour would belong to God, not to him. And in time, how could he be first, when God and all the angels, and countless men, had existed for so long before him?

units.la: IX. Si dixeris, primum dici, non absolute, sed respectu nouarum creaturarum, quia primus fuit noua creatura, quaeram ex quibus Christi verbis ista limitatio petatur, & cur Abraham pater credentium, Dauid vir secundum cor Dei, Prophetae, Martyres Veteris testamenti, necnon Iob, Daniel, Noe, Zacharias, Simeon, Iohannes Baptista Spiritu Sancto repletus iam inde ab vtero matris suae, ipsa denique beata virgo e numero nouarum creaturarum ab istis hominibus remoueantur? Quaeram etiam quo sensu dici possit Christus nouarum creaturarum vltimus? Nam, si primus dicitur quia primus factus est noua creatura, vltimus dicetur quia vltimus fiet noua creatura: quod falsum esse nemo non videt.
units.tr: IX. If you say that he is called first not absolutely but with respect to new creatures, because he was the first new creature, I would ask from which words of Christ this limitation is drawn, and why Abraham, the father of believers, David, the man after God's own heart, the prophets and martyrs of the Old Testament, and also Job, Daniel, Noah, Zechariah, Simeon, and John the Baptist, who was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb, and finally the blessed Virgin herself, are removed from the number of new creatures. I would also ask in what sense Christ can be called the last of new creatures. For if he is called first because he was made the first new creature, he will be called last because he will be made the last new creature. That this is false, everyone can see.

units.la: X. Si dixerint, eum dici primum & vltimum, quia ante eum nullus fuit seruator, & post eum nullus erit, imprudentes dixerint, id quod res est, Christum esse vnum illum Deum. Sic enim Christus, dicendo se esse primum & vltimum, dixerit, praeter se non esse seruatorem. Ex quo fluit haec argumentatio. Ille praeter quem non est seruator est Deus Israelis, ipsomet Deo te-ste Esaiae 43. 11. Ego Ego Dominus, & praeter me non est seruator. Christus est ille praeterquem non est seruator. Christus igitur est Deus Israelis. Et quomodo quaeso Christus, si nihil nisi creatura esset, dici posset primus Seruator? Nonne Deus ipse quoque Seruator est & dicitur, tam in nouo, quam in antiquo testamen-to? Nonne is prior est Christo tantum homine? Reliquisset igitur Deo Seruatori primas partes Christus, si tantùm homo fuisset, contentus sibi sumpsisse secundas. Quid quod multi, antequam nascerentur τὸ χ̄ σάρκα[?], sunt à peccatis suis seruati? tot certè quod sunt per fidem iustificati, ac sanctificati. In quo enim sita est salus seu liberatio à peccatis, si non consistit in remissione peccatorum, & sanctificatione, & Spiritu Sancto perfundente corda gaudio? Quæ omnia fideles ante Christi aduentum in carne fuisse assecutos, vel soli Dauidis psalmi, testes sunt luculenti.
units.tr: X. If they say that he is called the first and the last because before him there was no Saviour and after him there will be none, they speak without thinking, and say what is in fact the case: that Christ is that one God. For by saying that he is the first and the last, Christ would be saying that there is no Saviour besides himself. From this the following argument arises. He besides whom there is no Saviour is the God of Israel, as God himself testifies in Isaiah 43:11: I, I am the Lord, and besides me there is no saviour. Christ is he besides whom there is no Saviour. Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. And how, I ask, could Christ, if he were nothing but a creature, be called the first Saviour? Is not God himself also called Saviour, and is he not so in the New Testament as well as the Old? Is he not earlier than Christ, who was only a man? Christ would therefore have yielded the primary role to God the Saviour, and would have been content with taking the secondary one, if he had been only a man. Moreover, many were saved from their sins even before Christ was born in the flesh, and certainly all who have been justified and sanctified through faith. For where does salvation, or liberation from sins, lie, if not in the remission of sins, in sanctification, and in the Holy Spirit filling hearts with joy? That the faithful obtained all these things before Christ's coming in the flesh, the Psalms of David alone are clear witnesses.

units.la: XI. Peto etiam quorsum sese Dominus sic describit, Ego sum primus & vltimus? Annon vt ex hac descriptione quis quantusque sit intelligatur? Certè. Hic enim est finis descriptionis, vt per eam quod describitur cognoscatur. Itaque clarior esse debet descriptio quàm descripti nomen. Contrà tamen hic res habebit, si Socinum audiamus, Describet enim sese Christus per obscuriora, atque multa ratiocinatione opus erit, vt sensus huius descriptionis eruatur descripto conueniens, si tamen vllus eiusmodi poterit reperiri: Ac quod minus rationi consentaneum est, per descriptum cognoscenda erit descriptio: contrà quàm fieri oportuit. Metiuntur enim Aduersarij descriptionis istius sensum, non ex ipsis verbis quibus concepta est, nec ex collatione locorum Scripturæ inter se, in quibus habetur eadem descriptio, sed ex præconcepta & præiudicata opinione de persona & dignitate Christi: quam quia perspectam habent & accuratè cognitam, frustrà Christus, vt quis quantusue sit se prodat, descriptionem Dei Israëlis sibi aptabit, vt vt verba sint eadem, nunquam tamen, dabunt eundem esse sensum: Decretum enim illis est thesim Διαχω[?]-λύειν:
units.tr: XI. I ask further, to what end does the Lord describe himself in this way, I am the first and the last? Is it not so that from this description one may understand who and how great he is? Certainly. For the purpose of a description is that what is described may be known through it. Therefore the description ought to be clearer than the name of the thing described. Here, however, the matter would stand otherwise if we listened to Socinus. For Christ would describe himself through things more obscure, and much reasoning would be needed to draw out a sense of this description that fits the one described, if indeed any such sense can be found. And, what is less reasonable, the description would have to be known through the thing described, when it ought to be the other way round. For the opponents measure the sense of this description not from the words in which it is framed, nor from comparing the passages of Scripture with one another, in which the same description occurs, but from a preconceived and prejudiced opinion about the person and dignity of Christ. Because they have this opinion firmly fixed and accurately known, Christ in vain would fit to himself the description of the God of Israel, so that he might reveal who and how great he is. Although the words are the same, they will never grant that the sense is the same. For they have resolved to dissolve the thesis [διαχωλύειν].

units.la: XII. Sed pergamus. Aut fortuitò & συγχωρείᾳ[?] quadam accidit, vt iisdem verbis sese Deus apud Esaiam, Christus apud Iohannem describeret, aut data opera certoque consilio. Prius dici non potest. Nam & Deus cum sese sic describeret, sciebat Christum sese olim sic descripturum, & Christus itidem non ignorabat sic se Deum descripsisse, & suppetebant ipsi aliæ voces, qui[?]bus mentem suam æquè bene exprimeret. Si igitur id factum est destinato consilio, factum est in gratiam fidelium, quorsum, nisi vt intelligeremus descriptionem Dei apud Esaiam pertinere ad Christum? quo sic monente & oculos mentis aperiente, rem ita se habere deprehendimus.
units.tr: XII. But let us go on. Either it happened by chance and by a certain concession [συγχωρείᾳ] that God in Isaiah and Christ in John described themselves in the same words, or it was done deliberately and by settled design. The former cannot be said. For when God described himself in this way, he knew that Christ would one day describe himself in the same way, and Christ likewise was not ignorant that he had described God thus, and other words were available to him by which he could express his mind equally well. If then it was done by a deliberate design, it was done for the sake of the faithful: for what purpose, unless that we might understand the description of God in Isaiah to pertain to Christ? And when he so admonishes us and opens the eyes of our mind, we perceive that the matter stands thus.

units.la: XIII. Primùm enim in loco tertio Esai. 48. 12. verba citata proximè antecedit Dei protestatio alibi repetita, Gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Ex qua sic argumentor. Deus non erat daturus gloriam suam alteri. Atqui eam erat daturus Christo. Christus igitur non est alter, sed idem cum Deo.
units.tr: XIII. First, in the third passage, Isaiah 48:12, the words cited are immediately preceded by a declaration of God, repeated elsewhere: My glory I will not give to another. From this I argue as follows. God was not going to give his glory to another. But he was going to give it to Christ. Therefore Christ is not another, but the same as God.

units.la: XIV. In secundo loco citato Esai. 44. 6. sequuntur proximè verba, Et absque me Heb. ומלבדי [?] prater me non est Deus. Ex quibus sic colligo. Aut Christus non est Deus, aut Christus non est Deus praeter eum qui se sic describit apud Esaiam. Illud salsum est. Non enim possunt Aduersarii negare Christum esse Deum, nisi contradicendo sibi & diuersis locis Scripturae. Hoc igitur est verum. Non est autem verum, si Christus est Deus tota essentia diuer-sus, ac separatus ab eo qui verba illa pronunciauit apud Esaiam. Non est igitur Christus Deus tota essentia diuersus ac separatus ab eo, sed vnus idemque cum eo Deus, ac proinde eiusdem cum eo essentiae seu deitatis.
units.tr: XIV. In the second passage cited, Isaiah 44:6, the words immediately following are, and apart from me [ומלבדי] there is no God. From these I conclude as follows. Either Christ is not God, or Christ is not God apart from him who describes himself thus in Isaiah. The first is false. For the opponents cannot deny that Christ is God without contradicting themselves and various passages of Scripture. Therefore the second is true. But it is not true if Christ is a God wholly different in essence from, and separate from, him who uttered those words in Isaiah. Therefore Christ is not a God wholly different in essence from and separate from him, but one and the same God with him, and consequently of the same essence or deity.

units.la: XV. In vtroque loco Deus antequam verba illa proferat, Ego sum primus, Ego sum vltimus, conciliat sibi attentionem populi sui non vulgari ratione, his verbis Esai. 44. 6. Haec dicit Dominus Rex Israël, & redemptor eius, Dominus exercituum. Iis verò Esai. 48. 12. Audi me Iacob, & Israel quem ego voco. Non autem id facit sine graui ratione. Cum enim ipse idem verbis proximè antecedentibus loqueretur, poterat sermonem suum continuare, ac praecedente populi sui attentione contentus esse. Quod igitur verba ista pronunciare noluit duobus illis locis, nisi praefatione aliqua praemissa, atque noua conciliata populi sui attentione, in eo latet aliquid mysterij. Subesse enim oportet rationem aliquam memorabilem, quamobrem Deus id duobus illis locis fecerit. Sic enim loca illa duo insigniuit, ac singularem in modum commendauit populo suo, & curauit ne pius lector ea praeteriret festinanter, sed gradum paulisper sisteret, suamque ar[?]tionem excitaret & acueret ad sequentia verba, Ego primus, & vltimus, expendenda, quod fieri non potuit, quin ea loca ita memoriae eius infigerentur, vt auditis verbis illis Christi ter quaterque repetitis, Ego sum primus & vltimus, non possent non statim ei in mentem venire, vt ex descriptionis, vt ita loquar, identitate descripti identitatem intelligeret. Quò enim aliò id pertinere pos-sit ?
units.tr: XV. In both passages, before God utters those words, I am the first, I am the last, he secures the attention of his people in no ordinary way, with these words in Isaiah 44:6: Thus says the Lord, the King of Israel and his redeemer, the Lord of hosts. And in Isaiah 48:12: Hear me, Jacob, and Israel whom I call. Nor does he do this without a weighty reason. For since he himself had been speaking in the immediately preceding words, he could have continued his discourse and been content with the attention his people had already given. Therefore, since he was unwilling to utter those words in these two passages without some preface first, and without securing fresh attention from his people, something of a mystery lies hidden here. For there must be some memorable reason why God did this in those two passages. In this way he marked out those two passages and commended them in a singular manner to his people, and took care that the pious reader should not pass them over in haste, but pause a little and stir and sharpen his attention for the following words, I am the first and the last, to be weighed. This could not fail to fix those passages so firmly in his memory that, when he heard the words of Christ repeated again and again, I am the first and the last, they would at once come to his mind, so that he would understand, from the identity of the description, as I may put it, the identity of the one described. For to what else could this point?

units.la: XVI. Hinc mihi alia ratio surgit. Cum enim Deus nihil nisi sapientissimè prudentissimèque faciat, subesse causam oportuit grauem, cur sese ita describeret apud Israelem, populum suum[?], conciliata prius atque excitata eius attentione. Cur autem sese ita describeret Deus Pater praecisè ac seorsim à Filio, causa nulla apparet. Quae enim afferri posset? Dubitabat-ne Israël de aeternitate Iehouah Dei Israëlis? Ne nunc quidem eam Israël excaecatus atque induratus vocat in dubium. Estne aeternitas Dei Israëlis dogma tam paradoxum, tam mirabile, tam difficile creditu, vt proponi non debuerit, nisi prius non vulgarem in modum conciliata fidelium benevolentia, attentione, fide? tantum abest vt sit paradoxum, nullum vnquam fuit dogma in Israële, in Ecclesia, notius, certius, testatius. Nihil enim vnquam in Patris persona apparuit, quod vel leuissimam dubitationem, num esset Deus aeternus necne, afferret. Cur verò sese sic describeret Filius causa est obuia. Quoniam enim is sese vltrò exinaniuit sumpta serui forma, nihil difficilius fuit, quàm persuadere hominibus, praesertim Israelitis, cum esse reuera Deum principio & fine durationis carentem. Itaque in diebus carnis suae, quoties suam aeternitatem aut deitatem verbis reuelare aliquomodo voluit, toties Iudaei cum blasphemiae accusarunt & lapidibus obruere voluerunt. Notum etiam est, quantae olim, ac postremis hisce seculis, excitatae sint in Ecclesia de eius diuinitate controuersiae.
units.tr: XVI. From this another argument arises for me. Since God does nothing except most wisely and prudently, there must have been a weighty cause why he described himself in this way before Israel, his people, after first winning and rousing their attention. But no cause appears why God the Father should describe himself in this way precisely and apart from the Son. For what could be offered? Did Israel doubt the eternity of Jehovah, the God of Israel? Not even now does Israel, blinded and hardened, call this into doubt. Is the eternity of the God of Israel a dogma so paradoxical, so wonderful, so hard to believe, that it ought not to have been proposed unless the good will, attention and faith of the faithful had first been won in no ordinary manner? So far is it from being paradoxical, there has never been a dogma in Israel or in the Church more familiar, more certain, more attested. For nothing ever appeared in the person of the Father that would raise even the slightest doubt whether he was eternal God or not. But why the Son should describe himself in this way is an obvious matter. For since he emptied himself of his own accord, taking the form of a servant, nothing was more difficult than to persuade men, especially Israelites, that he was really God, without beginning or end of duration. Accordingly, in the days of his flesh, whenever he wished in some way to reveal his eternity or deity in words, the Jews accused him of blasphemy and wished to stone him. It is also well known how great controversies about his divinity were stirred up in the Church in former times and in these latter centuries.

units.la: XVII. Praeterea notandum est in loco Esai. 48. 12. praeter mandatum audiendi cum blanda Israelis appellatione, verbis, Ego sum primus, Ego sum vltimus, praemitti ista אני הוא: In loco vero Esaiae 41. 4. postponi: quae verba 70. Interp. reddere solent ἐγὼ εἰμι, Ego sum. Quae Dei descriptio ipsa quoque est descriptio Christi, ei magis proprie conueniens quàm Patri, Ioh. 8. 24. Si enim non crediderit quod ego sum, moriemini in peccatis vestris, Ioh. 8. 28. Cum exaltaueritis Filium hominis, tunc cognoscetis quod ego sum, Ioh. 13. 19. Nunc dico vobis priusquam fiat: vt cum factum fuerit, credatis, quod ego sum. ἵνα &c. πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐγὼ εἰμι, quae sunt ipsissima Dei verba Esaiae 43. 10. Nomen autem istud הוא magis proprium esse Filij quàm Patris suadet eius significatio. Est enim pronomen demonstratiuum, Ille, ipse; Itaque melius ei conuenit qui potest demonstrari, quàm ei qui nullo modo demonstrari potest. Adde quod aduentus Patris, quatenus à Christo distinguitur, non est promissus, nec expectatus in Ecclesia. Christus vero ab initio Mundi toties promissus, praedictus, praefiguratus est, vt docuerit omnes Angelos & homines in illius vnius ex pectationem intentos esse, Itaque is vnus fuit qui maximè digito monstrari & dicier, Hic est, Ille est, Ipse est, debuit: Quae causa videtur esse, cur hoc pronomen in duobus locis citatis; & in alijs nonnullis, junctum pronomini primae personae, descriptionem Dei perfectam efficiat. Hic fortasse non erit abs re obseruare Iudaeos in id imprudentes incidere, quod vitare volunt. Negantes enim Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum esse Seruatorem, non vocant eum ישוע, sed י dempto ישוע. Quid autem esse posset ישוע, nisi contractum ישוע est ipse? Nam & א abest nonnunquam ab illo pronomine, & aspiratio facilè inter pronunciandum excidit. ישוע autem significat eum esse Messiam tamdiu expectatum & exoptatum, Seruatorem mundi promissum, nihilque differt à nomine tetragrammato, nisi inserta pronunciandi causâ litera ו & mutato א in ה, quod fit interdum.
units.tr: XVII. Moreover, it should be noted that in the passage of Isaiah 48:12, apart from the command to listen, with the flattering address to Israel, the words "I am the first, I am the last" are preceded by the words אני הוא; but in the passage of Isaiah 41:4 they are placed after; and the Seventy usually render these words ἐγὼ εἰμι, "I am." This description of God is itself also a description of Christ, belonging to him more properly than to the Father: John 8:24, "For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins"; John 8:28, "When you have lifted up the Son of man, then you will know that I am"; John 13:19, "I tell you now before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe that I am," ἵνα ... πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐγὼ εἰμι, which are the very words of God in Isaiah 43:10. But that the word הוא belongs more properly to the Son than to the Father is suggested by its meaning. For it is a demonstrative pronoun, "he," "that one," "himself." Therefore it fits better him who can be pointed out than him who cannot in any way be pointed out. Add that the coming of the Father, as distinguished from Christ, was neither promised nor expected in the Church. Christ, however, from the beginning of the world was so often promised, foretold and foreshadowed that he taught all angels and men to be intent upon the expectation of that one alone. Therefore he alone had to be the one who is most of all pointed to with the finger and called "This is he," "That one is," "He himself is." This seems to be the reason why this pronoun, joined to the pronoun of the first person, makes the description of God complete in the two passages cited and in some others. Here it will perhaps not be out of place to observe that the Jews, in trying to avoid it, fall into the very thing they wish to avoid. For while denying that our Lord Jesus Christ is the Saviour, they do not call him ישוע, but י with ישוע removed. What then could ישוע be, except ישוע contracted to "he himself"? For the א is sometimes dropped from that pronoun, and the breathing easily falls away in pronunciation. ישוע, however, signifies that he is the Messiah so long expected and desired, the Saviour of the world promised, and it differs from the tetragrammaton only by the insertion, for ease of pronunciation, of the letter ו and the change of א into ה, which is sometimes done.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Possem addere elogia Regis Israëlis & redemptoris Israelis, quibus sese Dominus insignit Esaiae 44. 6. convenire Christo, & quidem peculiari ratione: Itaque χριστος Christus appellatur, hoc est, Rex, & nos redemit soluto pretio, non auro aut argento, caducis rebus, sed pretioso sanguine suo. Possem quaerere ab Aduersariis quo sensu Pater vltimus dicatur, qui convenire Christo non posset? Cum enim primus oponatur relatiuè vltimo, si Filius eodem, quo Pater, sensu vltimus dicitur, consentaneum rationi videtur, vt eodem etiam sensu primus esse dicatur. Sed nolo hanc disputationem facere longiorem. Nam, & alia satis multa Dei beneficio argumenta suppetunt, & de locis Apocalypsis, in quibus sese ipse Dominus Alpha & Omega, primum & vltimum vocat, actum est vltima libri superioris disputatione.
units.tr: I might add the titles of the King of Israel and the Redeemer of Israel, by which the Lord distinguishes himself in Isaiah 44:6, as fitting Christ, and indeed in a special way. So he is called Christ [χριστος], that is, King, and he has redeemed us, not with gold or silver, perishable things, but with his precious blood, the price paid. I might ask the adversaries in what sense the Father is called the last, which could not apply to Christ. For since the first is opposed relatively to the last, if the Son is called last in the same sense as the Father, it seems reasonable that he should also be called first in the same sense. But I do not wish to make this disputation longer. For by God's favour there are many other arguments enough at hand, and the passages of the Apocalypse, in which the Lord himself calls himself Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, were dealt with in the last disputation of the previous book.

units.la: DISPUTATIO SEXTA
units.tr: Sixth Disputation

units.la: De Arg. VI. Ex loco Zachar. xi. 13. Et dixit Do- minus ad me, proice illud ad figulum, magnificum pretium quo appretiatus sum ab eis, &c, collato cum Matth. xxvii. 9.
units.tr: On Argument VI, from Zechariah 11:13, "And the Lord said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: that goodly price that I was prised at of them," etc., compared with Matthew 27:9.

units.la: I. EXPENDIMUS loca Esaiæ citata in Novo Testamento, Nunc pergamus in aliis prophetis. Apud Zachariam cap. xi. V. 12. & 13. leguntur hæc verba. Appenderunt mercedem meam triginta argenteos. Et dixit Dominus ad me, proice illam ad figulum, magnificum pretium quo appretiatus sum ab eis. Et tulisti triginta argenteos, & proieci illos in domum Domini ad figulum. Hunc locum Matthæus citat his verbis, Tunt impletum est quod dictum est per Jeremiam prophetam dicentem,. & acceperunt triginta argenteos pretium appretiati, quem appretiauerunt à filiis Israel, & dederunt eos in agrum figuli, sicut constituit mihi Dominus. Ex duobus illis locis sic argumentor.
units.tr: I. We have examined the passages of Isaiah cited in the New Testament. Now let us go on to the other prophets. In Zechariah 11:12-13 these words are read: They weighed for my hire thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: that goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the Lord. Matthew cites this passage in these words: Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value; and gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord appointed me. From these two passages I argue as follows.

units.la: Ille qui apud Zachariam æstimatus dicitur à filiis Israel triginta argenteis est Dominus (Iehovah) Deus Israelis.
units.tr: The one who is said in Zechariah to have been valued by the children of Israel at thirty pieces of silver is the Lord (Jehovah), the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est ille qui apud Zachariam æstimatus dicitur à filiis Israel triginta argenteis.
units.tr: Christ is the one who is said in Zechariah to have been valued by the children of Israel at thirty pieces of silver.

units.la: Christus igitur est Dominus Deus Israel.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the Lord God of Israel.

units.la: Major nititur testimonio ipsius Dei loco Zachariæ citato. Minor testimonio Apostoli Matthæi.
units.tr: The major premise rests on the testimony of God himself in the passage of Zechariah cited. The minor rests on the testimony of the apostle Matthew.

units.la: I I. Responsum apud Aduersarios nullum legi, forte, quia hi loci non sunt eis objecti. Quid autem possint respondere, nisi Aut non citari locum Zachariæ à Matthæo; Aut si citatur, alio modo posse exponi, quàm à nobis fit?
units.tr: II. I have not read any answer from our opponents, perhaps because these passages have not been put to them. But what could they reply, except either that Matthew does not cite the passage of Zechariah, or, if he does cite it, that it can be explained in some other way than we explain it?

units.la: III. Non citari locum Zachariæ duo suadent, nomen Ieremiæ, & verborum aliqua discrepantia, sed non persuadent. Nihil enim exstat eiusmodi in libro Ieremiæ. Fit quidem mentio cap. 9. figuli, & cap. 32. agri empti, sed reliqua sunt omnino diuersa. Legisse quidem se eadem verba, quæ Matthæus citauit, dicit Hieronymus in libro quodam apocrypho Nazoreorum, sed ex eo citatum esse hoc testimonium non credit, & recte sane. Quis enim credat Matthæum commendare voluisse, tanquam scriptum à Ieremia propheta, librum eiusmodi apocryphum? Nonne eo significasset, cum autorem illius libri esse Ieremiam prophetam, tum oportere impleri quæ in eo libro scripta fuissent? Non dicent Aduersarij, citatum esse testimonium ex traditione non scripta. Agnoscunt enim nobiscum perfectionem Scripturæ sacræ. Nunquam sacri autores probant Iesum esse Christum per traditiones non scriptas, aut libros apocryphos. Nunquam aliunde petunt testimonia, quibus fidem nostram de Christo fulciant, quàm è Scripturis canonicis. Parum etiam ad eam rem valeret eiusmodi traditio, cuius fides penes suum laudatorem esset. Hinc ita argumentor. Citatum est hoc testimonium, aut ex Ieremia, aut ex Zacharia: Non ex Ieremia, ut ex dictis patet. Ergo ex Zacharia. Tertius enim autor, qui id sibi vindicet, nullus est.
units.tr: III. That Matthew does not cite Zechariah is suggested by two things, the name of Jeremiah and some discrepancy in the words, but these do not persuade. For nothing of the kind exists in the book of Jeremiah. There is indeed mention of the potter in chapter 18 and of the purchased field in chapter 32, but the rest is wholly different. Jerome says that he had read these very words which Matthew cites in a certain apocryphal book of the Nazarenes, but he does not believe that this testimony was cited from it, and rightly so. For who would believe that Matthew wished to commend, as written by the prophet Jeremiah, an apocryphal book of that sort? Would he not by this have signified both that Jeremiah was the author of that book and that the things written in it must be fulfilled? The opponents will not say that the testimony was cited from unwritten tradition. For they acknowledge with us the perfection of holy Scripture. The sacred authors never prove that Jesus is the Christ by unwritten traditions or apocryphal books. Never do they seek from elsewhere the testimonies by which they strengthen our faith concerning Christ, except from the canonical Scriptures. Nor would such a tradition, whose credibility rested with its own commender, be of much use for that purpose. Hence I argue thus. This testimony has been cited either from Jeremiah or from Zechariah. Not from Jeremiah, as is clear from what has been said. Therefore from Zechariah. For there is no third author who could lay claim to it.

units.la: IV. Ad hoc argumentum accedit alterum ex collatione laudati à Matthæo testimonij cum loco Zachariæ memorato. Congruunt enim omnia, pretium, triginta argentei: æstimatores, filij Israël: æstimatus, Christus: is cui aliquid emendi causa data sunt illi triginta argentei, figulus: Denique prouidentia Dei cuius ex decreto id factum est. Verba etiam erunt fermè eadem, si apud Matthæum XV.[?] 9. ἔλαβον sit primæ personæ, & XV.[?] 10. legatur ἔδωκα detracto ν.[?] Sed nos mouere non debet verborum aliqua dissimilitudo, cum sensus quadrat. Retinent enim perpetuò sensum locorum quæ laudant Apostoli, verba non raro paululum immutant, atque ita citando exponunt.
units.tr: IV. To this argument is added another, from the comparison of the testimony cited by Matthew with the passage of Zechariah mentioned. For everything agrees: the price, thirty pieces of silver; the appraisers, the children of Israel; the one appraised, Christ; the one to whom the thirty pieces of silver were given to buy something, the potter; and finally the providence of God, by whose decree this was done. The words will also be nearly the same, if in Matthew 27:9 the verb elabon [ἔλαβον] is in the first person, and in 27:10 edōka [ἔδωκα] is read with the final ν removed. But some dissimilarity of words ought not to move us, when the sense agrees. For the apostles always retain the sense of the passages they cite, and often change the words slightly, explaining them as they cite.

units.la: V. At Matthæus hoc vaticinium Ieremiæ tribuit; Ergo non est Zachariæ, non sequitur. Sic potius colligendum est. Hoc dixit Ieremias teste Matthæo. Hoc dixit Zacharias teste ipsa re. Ergo Zacharias idem est Ieremias. Cur enim binominis esse non potuit, ut alii pene innumeri, siue id pluribus impositionibus factum sit, siue vna duntaxat? Cum enim in imponendo nomine habetur tantùm significationis ratio, quodcunque nomen eandem habet significationem, id quodammodo impositum censetur. Sic Ionathan, Elnathan & Nathanael, Huzija & Hazaria, Iudas & Thadeus, Cephas, & Petrus, &c. pro eodem nomine habentur. Eandem autem uim habent Zacharias & Ieremias: illud exponitur, qui recordatur Dei, qui commemorat Deum; hoc, qui exaltat Deum. Exaltat autem Deum quicunque eius recordatur vel eum commemorat, & vice versa, recordatur Dei qui cum exaltat. Maluit autem Matthaeus scribere Ieremiam quàm Zachariam, vt studium lectoris excitaret & acueret ad libros Prophetarum diligenter euoluendos, vt memorabilem istam circunstantiam passionis Domini altius animis nostris infigeret, ob eius insignes vtilitates; vt doceret nominum quibus Prophetæ appellantur vim atque significationem non esse negligendam; vt innueret Zachariam illis verbis, quæ ex eo laudauit, alienam sustinere personam & quidem illius, cuius nomen quidem significatione affine esset nomini Ieremiæ, persona verò nomini non responderet. Non timuit autem ne propterea Euangelij sui autoritas in dubium vocaretur, conscientia diuinitatis eius fretus.
units.tr: V. But it does not follow that because Matthew attributes this prophecy to Jeremiah, it is not Zechariah's. It is better to conclude thus. Jeremiah said this, according to the testimony of Matthew. Zechariah said this, according to the testimony of the thing itself. Therefore Zechariah is the same as Jeremiah. For why could he not have had two names, as many others almost countless did, whether this came about by several impositions or by only one? For when only the meaning is considered in the giving of a name, any name having the same meaning is in a sense regarded as having been given. Thus Jonathan, Elnathan and Nathanael, Huzijah and Hazariah, Judas and Thaddaeus, Cephas and Peter, etc., are regarded as the same name. Now Zechariah and Jeremiah have the same force: the one means one who remembers God, who recalls God; the other, one who exalts God. But whoever remembers God or recalls him exalts him, and conversely, whoever exalts God remembers him. Matthew, however, preferred to write Jeremiah rather than Zechariah, so as to rouse and sharpen the reader's zeal for diligently unrolling the books of the prophets, so as to fix more deeply in our minds this memorable circumstance of the Lord's passion, on account of its remarkable usefulness; so as to teach that the force and meaning of the names by which the prophets are called is not to be neglected; so as to hint that Zechariah, in those words which he cited from him, was sustaining a character not his own, namely the character of one whose name was indeed related in meaning to the name Jeremiah, but whose person did not correspond to that name. Nor did he fear that for this reason the authority of his Gospel would be called into doubt, relying on the consciousness of its divinity.

units.la: VI. Sed finge Matthaeum non citasse uaticinium Zachariæ. Id tamen impleri debuit. Non potuit autem accuratius adimpleri quàm factum legimus in illa Matthaei historia. Euentus prophetiæ omni ex parte respondet. Etiamsi igitur id tacuisset Matthæus, tamen fateri necesse esset, hanc Zachariæ prophetiam tunc fuisse impletam. Siue igitur laudetur hæc prophetia à Matthæo, vti reuera laudatur, siue non laudetur, stat firmum, pretium illud triginta argenteorum esse accipendum de pretio, quo Dominus noster à filijs Israël æstimatus fuit & emptus à Iuda proditore.
units.tr: VI. But suppose Matthew had not cited the prophecy of Zechariah. It must nevertheless have been fulfilled. Yet it could not have been fulfilled more exactly than we read it was in that history of Matthew. The outcome of the prophecy corresponds in every part. Therefore, even if Matthew had said nothing about it, it would still have had to be admitted that this prophecy of Zechariah was then fulfilled. So whether this prophecy is cited by Matthew, as indeed it is, or not cited, it stands firm that the price of thirty pieces of silver must be understood of the price by which our Lord was valued by the children of Israel and bought by Judas the traitor.

units.la: VII. Restat altera responsio, ad quam quomodo confugere possint Aduersarij non video, verba enim Prophetæ aliter exponi non possunt, quàm quemadmodum à nobis exponuntur. Et ait, inquit Propheta, Dominus ad me, negare nequeunt, quin hoc loco Dominus (Iehouah) sit Deus Israëlis præditus essentia diuina. Quid ergo ait? proijce, inquit, eam (mercedem tuam) ad figu[?]lum, quo mandato significatur efficacitas diuinæ prouidentiæ, qua factum est, vt Iudas tactus pœnitentia tringenta argenteos proiecerit in templum, iique[?] à Sacerdotibus figulo dati sint. Addit Dominus, Magnificum pretium quo appretiatus sum ab eis. Potuit ne disertius dicere se fuisse à filiis Israël æstimatum triginta illis argenteis? æstimatus autem siue appretiatus non est Deus Pater, sed Christus. Christus igitur est Dominus (Iehouah) qui sic loquitur.
units.tr: VII. There remains another answer, to which I do not see how our opponents can take refuge, for the words of the prophet cannot be explained otherwise than as we explain them. And he said, says the prophet, the Lord unto me, they cannot deny that in this place the Lord (Jehovah) is the God of Israel endowed with the divine essence. What then does he say? Cast, he says, it (your hire) unto the potter, by which command is signified the efficacy of divine providence, by which it came about that Judas, touched by repentance, cast the thirty pieces of silver into the temple, and they were given by the priests to the potter. The Lord adds, That goodly price that I was prised at of them. Could he have said more plainly that he was valued by the children of Israel at those thirty pieces of silver? But it was not God the Father who was valued or appraised, but Christ. Christ, therefore, is the Lord (Jehovah) who speaks thus.

units.la: VIII. Reponent sine dubio, ipsum Deum dici eo pretio æstimatum, quia eo pretio æstimatus est eius seruus & filius Iesus Christus: ignominiam enim qua Christus affectus est, in ipsum Deum redundare. Quominus vero sic respondere possint obstat primo verbum appretiatus sum. Alia enim est appretiatio seu æstimatio serui, alia domini, alia filii, alia patris, terminatur enim æstimatio in persona æstimata. Dici quidem potest unus ignominia affici quia alter afficitur, sed non dicetur appretiari quia alter appretiatur, & quidem illo ipso pretio eodem numero quo alter appretiatur, est enim sua cuiusque personæ, vt propria vita, sic propria æstimatio, proprium pretium quo æstimatur.
units.tr: VIII. Without doubt they will reply that God himself is said to have been valued at that price, because his servant and Son Jesus Christ was valued at that price; for the ignominy with which Christ was affected, they say, redounds upon God himself. But what prevents them from answering thus is first the verb appretiatus sum. For the appraisal or valuation of a servant is one thing, that of a lord another, that of a son another, that of a father another, for the valuation terminates in the person valued. One may indeed say that one is affected with ignominy because another is affected, but one will not be said to be appraised because another is appraised, and especially not at that very same price, numerically the same, by which the other is appraised. For just as each person has his own life, so each has his own valuation and his own price by which he is valued.

units.la: IX. Alioqui nihil erit proprium Christi quod Deo Patri eodem modo tribui non possit. Nam, si triginta argenteis æstimatus fuit à Iudæis Deus Pater, certè etiam proditus est à Iuda, atque adeo vinctus deductus est ad pontificem primum, deinde ad Pilatum, damnatus est, cruci affixus est, mortuus est, sepultus est, resurrexit, &c. Hoc si non placet Aduersariis, reddant rationem, cur Deus Pater appretiatus dici possit à Iudæis triginta argenteis, proditus vero, vinctus, damnatus, &c. dici non possit. Nulla enim mihi apparet.
units.tr: IX. Otherwise nothing that is proper to Christ could fail to be attributed in the same way to God the Father. For if God the Father was valued at thirty pieces of silver by the Jews, he was certainly also betrayed by Judas, and so was bound, led to the chief priest, then to Pilate, condemned, nailed to the cross, dead, buried, raised, and so on. If the Adversaries do not like this, let them give a reason why God the Father can be said to have been valued by the Jews at thirty pieces of silver, but cannot be said to have been betrayed, bound, condemned, and so on. For I can see no reason.

units.la: X. Hoc idem confirmat oppositio quam Dominus instituit inter vilitatem pretii æstimationis & dignitatem personæ æstimatæ. Magnificum, inquit, pretium quo appretiatus sum à filijs Israel. Quibus verbis ironicè, & non sine aliqua significatione indignationis, exiguitatem & vilitatem illius pretii exaggerat ducto à sua ipsius appretiati summa dignitate argumento. Triginta argenteis erant pretium quo æstimabatur seruus, vel ancilla, à boue cornupeta occisus, persona omnium vilissima; Exod. 21. 32. Qui hoc pretio æstimatus est à filiis Israel est Dominus, Iehouah, persona omnium dignissima. Hinc æstimationis illius summa iniquitas atque indignitas. Perinde enimDeus loquitur ac si diceret, si me voluerunt appretiare, (liceat enim nobis eo verbo uti cum antiquo interprete latino,) debuit saltem pretium esse magnificum, & valore atque magnificentia meæ dignitati aliquo modo respondere. Contrà verò illi me non pluris æstimauerunt quàm vilem aliquem seruulum, aut ancillulam. Hanc tantam oppositionem & exaggerationem quis non videt perire, si contra diserta ipsius Dei verba appretiatus dicitur non ipse Dominus, sed alius ab eo separatus, toto genere diuersus, ac longè inferior dignitate: quippe qui, docentibus Aduersariis, nihil nisi creatura, nihil nisi homo sanctus erat, deposita aduentitia quadam Dei forma, tunc existens tantum in forma serui? Adde quod ex duabus istis rebus inter se oppositis, vilitate pretii, & dignitate personæ eo pretio æstimatæ, alteram constat qualis hic dicitur, talem, immò eandem, reuera fuisse, absque vlla mutatione additione aut detractione: triginta enim argenteis, vt est apud Zachariam, non pluris nec minoris, æstimatus est Dominus noster; cur igitur non credamus similiter alteram, nempe dignitatem personæ æstimatæ, eandemque quoque fuisse, non autem multò minorem? Si pretium est idem, si æstimatores sunt iidem nempe εἰ ἀπὸ τῆς ψυχῆς Ἰσραὴλ, annon consentaneum est, vt etiam æstimatus sit idem?
units.tr: X. The same point is confirmed by the contrast that the Lord draws between the meanness of the price of valuation and the dignity of the person valued. Magnificent, he says, is the price at which I was valued by the sons of Israel (Zech. 11. 13). With these words he speaks ironically, and not without some sign of indignation, and heaps up the smallness and worthlessness of that price, drawing the argument from the very great dignity of the one who was valued. Thirty pieces of silver was the price at which a male or female slave gored by an ox was valued, the most worthless of persons (Exod. 21. 32). The one who was valued at this price by the sons of Israel is the Lord, Jehovah, the most worthy of all persons. Hence the great injustice and indignity of that valuation. For God speaks as if he were saying: "If they wanted to value me (for we may use that word with the ancient Latin translator), the price should at least have been magnificent, and somehow matched my worth in value and magnificence. Instead they have valued me no more than some worthless slave or little maidservant." Who does not see this great contrast and exaggeration collapse, if the one who was valued is said not to be the Lord himself, but another separated from him, wholly different in kind and far inferior in dignity? For, according to the Adversaries, he was nothing but a creature, nothing but a holy man, who, having laid aside a certain adventitious form of God, then existed only in the form of a servant. Add that of these two things set against each other, the smallness of the price and the dignity of the person valued at that price, we know that the first is as it is described here, and indeed that the second was the same, without any change, addition or subtraction: for our Lord was valued at thirty pieces of silver, neither more nor less, as it is in Zechariah. Why then should we not believe that the other thing, namely the dignity of the person valued, was likewise the same, and not much less? If the price is the same, and the valuers are the same, namely [εἰ ἀπὸ τῆς ψυχῆς Ἰσραὴλ] (that is, the sons of Israel), is it not fitting that the one valued is also the same?

units.la: XI. Si quis nobis obijciat, eundem esse non posse. Qui enim apud Zachariam eo pretio æstimatum se dicit, Deum Patrem esse. Respondebimus primò, hoc nihil obesse sententiæ nostræ. Credimus enim Patrem & Filium unum esse essentia, atque adeò dignitate essentiali & naturali: ex quo sequitur, catenus eandem esse vtriusque æstimationem, idem pretium. Respondebimus secundò, eum qui se triginta argenteis æstimatum ab Israelitis dicit, ipsum Dei Filium esse. At alloquitur Filium, itaque Filius non est, sed Pater. Alloquitur Prophetam per μεταφορὰν, referentem modò Filium Dei pascentem oues suas, modò Iudam pascentem cum Iudæis de proditionis mercede, ac deinde acceptam mercedem proiicientem in Templum dandam figulo, non vasa testacea, quorum nullus erat vsus in templo, sed agrum emendi causa. Id enim cum ipsa res loquitur, tum Dominus innuit, cum V. 15. iubet Prophetam adhuc sumere sibi vasa pastoris stulti: significat enim eum iam antea sibi stulti pastoris vasa sumpsisse, cuius stulti pastoris? vtique proditoris Iudæ.
units.tr: XI. If someone objects to us that it cannot be the same, since the one who in Zechariah says that he was valued at that price is God the Father. We reply first that this does nothing against our position. For we believe that the Father and the Son are one in essence, and thus in essential and natural dignity; from which it follows that, so far, the valuation of each is the same, and the price is the same. We reply secondly that the one who says he was valued at thirty pieces of silver by the Israelites is the Son of God himself. But he is addressing the Son, and so the Son is not the one speaking, but the Father. He is addressing the prophet [μεταφορὰν], by metaphor: at one moment referring to the Son of God feeding his sheep, at another to Judas feeding with the Jews on the wages of betrayal, and then casting the received wages into the Temple to be given to the potter, not as earthenware vessels, which had no use in the Temple, but as the price for buying a field. For the thing itself speaks thus, and the Lord indicates it when, in verse 15, he orders the prophet to take up again the instruments of a foolish shepherd. For this signifies that he had earlier taken up for himself the instruments of a foolish shepherd. Whose foolish shepherd? Surely that of Judas the traitor.

units.la: DISPUTATIO SEPTIMA
units.tr: DISPUTATION SEVEN

units.la: De Arg. VII. Ex loco Zach. Cap. XII. V. 10. Aspicient ad me quem transfixerunt, laudato Ioh. xix. 37. & Apoc. i. 7.
units.tr: On Argument VII. From Zechariah 12:10, They shall look on me whom they have pierced, with John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 cited.

units.la: I. ALIUS apud eundem Zachariam Cap. 12. V. 10. extat admodum illustris locus, in quo Dominus (Iehouah) sic loquitur, Effundam super Domum Dauid & super habitatores Hierusalem spiritum gratiæ & miserationum, & aspicient ad me quem transfixerunt, &c. quem locum laudat, & de Christo exponit Apostolus & Euangelista Iohannes Euang. cap. 19. V. 37. Et rursus alia Scriptura dicit, videbunt quem transfixerunt. Et Apoc. 1. 7. Ecce venit cum nubibus, & videbit eum omnis oculus, etiam qui eum compunxerunt. Ex quibus locis sic argumentor.
units.tr: I. Another very famous passage in the same Zechariah, chapter 12, verse 10, has the Lord (Jehovah) speaking thus: I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of compassions, and they shall look on me whom they have pierced, and so on. The Apostle and Evangelist John cites this passage and applies it to Christ, John 19:37: And again another Scripture says, They shall see him whom they pierced. And Revelation 1:7: Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him. From these passages I argue as follows.

units.la: Ille, quem domus Dauid & habitatores Hierusalem dicuntur aspecturi & transfixisse Zach. 12. 10. est præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: He whom the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem are said to look upon and to have pierced (Zech. 12:10) is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est ille, quem domus Dauid & habitatores Hierusalem dicuntur aspecturi & transfixisse Zach. 12. 10.
units.tr: Christ is he whom the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem are said to look upon and to have pierced (Zech. 12:10).

units.la: Ergo, Christus est præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Maior nititur disertis apud Zachariam ipsius Domini (Iehouah) spiritum gratiæ & miserationum, vel, ut habet vetus versio, precum in domum Dauidis & incolas Hierusalem effusuri, verbis. Minor nititur diserto Apostoli Iohannis testimonio. Neutra igitur negari potest.
units.tr: The major premise rests on the explicit words of the Lord (Jehovah) in Zechariah, who will pour out the spirit of grace and of supplications upon the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem (or, as the old version has it, of prayers). The minor premise rests on the explicit testimony of the Apostle John. Neither, therefore, can be denied.

units.la: II. Quid potuit responderi, nisi, aut textum Hebraicum Zachariæ corruptum esse, aut, si non est corruptus, male versum esse, aut si bene sit versus, tamen non eam esse sententiam quàm verba præ se ferunt? Hæc igitur tria responderunt Aduersarij, sed tertium primò excogitasse videntur, deinde primùm, tandem secundum illis subministrauit Marcus Marinus Brixianus Can. reg. D. Saluatoris. Quem eorum ordinem, ne ab eorum vestigiis recedamus, sequemur in tribus illis refellendis.
units.tr: II. What could be answered, except that the Hebrew text of Zechariah is corrupt, or, if it is not corrupt, that it has been badly translated, or, if it has been well translated, that nonetheless the meaning is not what the words themselves express? So the opponents gave these three answers. But they seem to have devised the third first, then the first, and finally the second was supplied to them by Marcus Marinus of Brescia, canon regular of the Holy Saviour. In refuting these three we shall follow their order, so as not to depart from their footsteps.

units.la: III. Primùm ait Socinus illa Zachariæ & Iohannis testimonia, non probare, Christum esse illum unum Deum Israelis, non magis, quàm apud eundem Zachariam probent, Dei oculi pupillam esse populum Iudaicum, illa Dei verba, Qui tangit vos (id est, populum Iudaicum) tangit pupillam oculi eius; aut quàm apud Lucam in Actis Apostolorum probent, Iesu Nazareni cultores, esse ipsum Iesum Nazarenum, verba illa ipsius Iesu ad Paulum adhuc Saulum, Saule Saule quid me persequeris? & rursus Ego sum Iesus Nazarenus quem tu persequeris; aut denique non magis quàm similiter probent, Christi minimos, esse ipsum Christum, verba illa, quae se in die iudicij dicturum, ipse Christus testatur, iis quos in possessionem coelestis regni est introducturus, Esuriui & dedistis mihi manducare; sitiui & dedistis mihi bibere, &c. Quis tam stupidus est, quin videat, his loquendi modis, non quidem eandem essentiam sed summam coniunctionem & amorem significari? Iam quis Deo coniunctior quàm Christus homo, quis carior, aut fuit unquam, aut esse potest, quamvis utriusque essentia sit admodum diuersa?
units.tr: III. First, Socinus says that those testimonies of Zechariah and John do not prove that Christ is that one God of Israel, any more than in the same Zechariah they prove that the Jewish people is the pupil of God's eye, those words of God, "He who touches you (that is, the Jewish people) touches the pupil of his eye"; or than in Luke in the Acts of the Apostles they prove that the worshippers of Jesus of Nazareth are Jesus of Nazareth himself, those words of Jesus himself to Paul, still Saul, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" and again "I am Jesus of Nazareth whom you persecute"; or finally no more than they similarly prove that the least of Christ's people are Christ himself, those words which Christ himself declares he will speak on the day of judgment to those whom he is about to lead into possession of the heavenly kingdom, "I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me to drink," and so on. Who is so stupid as not to see that by these ways of speaking is signified not the same essence but the closest union and love? Now who is closer to God than Christ as man, who is or ever was or can be dearer, although the essence of each is quite different?

units.la: IV. Vocemus ad examen hanc Socini responsionem. Exemplum è Zach. 2. 8. petitum, quod tanquam omnium maximè idoneum Socinus paulò post repetit & valdè exaggerat, ad rem non est, Instituitur enim comparatio inter tangentem populum Dei & tangentem pupillam oculi Dei. Itaque pupilla oculi Dei aperte distinguitur à populo Dei, neque vlla arte potest inde legitimo syllogismo concludi, populum Dei esse pupillam oculi Dei, non magis quàm ex his Christi verbis, Qui vos audit me audit, &, quodcunque ligaueritis in terra ligatum erit in coelo, concludi potest Apostolos esse ipsum Christum, terram esse coelum. Hic verò nulla instituitur comparatio inter Deum & alium, inter confixionem alius, & confixionem Dei, sed simpliciter absque vlla eiusmodi comparatione Deus dicit, adspicient ad me quem confixerunt. Itaque nullus alius intelligi potest aspiciendus & confixus quàm Deus, itaque firma argumenti nostri propositio. Ille qui dicitur Zach. 12. 10. ab incolis Hierusalem aspiciendus & confixus est Deus, cui similis ex verbis, qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi eius, confici non potest. Adde quod nũquam creditum est, populum Iudaicum esse pupillam oculi Dei, nec est quicquam in sacris literis quo id probari possit: quocirca absque vllo periculo talis locutio vsurpari potuit. At Christum esse Deum diuina essentia prædituin, & plerique omnes Christiani crediderunt, ac credunt summo consensu, & scaturiunt è sacris literis quæ id probent argumenta plurima, vt, si id error est, non potuerit non periculosa esse sic concepta Dei prædictio, aspicient ad me quem transfixerunt.
units.tr: IV. Let us bring this answer of Socinus to the test. The example taken from Zech. 2:8, which Socinus, as the most suitable of all, repeats a little later and greatly exaggerates, is beside the point. For a comparison is set up between one who touches the people of God and one who touches the pupil of God's eye. Thus the pupil of God's eye is plainly distinguished from the people of God, and no skill can validly conclude by syllogism from this that the people of God is the pupil of God's eye. No more can one conclude from these words of Christ, "He who hears you hears me," and "whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven," that the apostles are Christ himself, or that earth is heaven. Here, however, no comparison is set up between God and another, between the piercing of another and the piercing of God; rather, simply and without any such comparison, God says, they shall look on me whom they have pierced. Therefore no one other than God can be understood as the one to be looked upon and pierced. Hence the firm premise of our argument: he who is said in Zech. 12:10 to be looked upon and pierced by the inhabitants of Jerusalem is God, and no parallel to the words he who touches you touches the pupil of his eye can be made out of them. Add that it was never believed that the Jewish people is the pupil of God's eye, nor is there anything in the sacred letters by which this could be proved; wherefore such a manner of speaking could be used without any danger. But that Christ is God, endowed with the divine essence, most Christians have believed and do believe with near-universal agreement, and the sacred letters overflow with many arguments proving it. So if this were an error, the prediction of God as it is phrased, they shall look on me whom they have pierced, could not have failed to be dangerous.

units.la: V. Quare inepta est Socini interrogatio, Cur, inquit, si per suum Angelum Deus olim monuit, quod qui tangeret populum Iudaicum, is tangeret pupillam oculi sui; non potuit etiam dicere se configi ab illis qui Christum configebant, quamuis Christus non sit vnus & idem essentia cum ipso? Nam si Deus dixisset, qui Christum configit me configit, distinxisset se aperte à Christo, & significasset duntaxat affectum suum & amorem erga Christum. At Deus apud Zachariam eo loco non nominat Christum, non distinguit se à Christo, non comparat transfixionem Christi cum sua, non significat qua mente, quo animo sit erga Christum. Tantum dicit incolas Hierusalem ad se quem confixerunt aspecturos. Potuit ne disertius dici aspiciendus & transfigendus? cum dicit aspicient ad me, significatne quàm sibi charus esset futurus Christus, quanto Christum amore esset prosecuturus? tamen quàm dicit adspicient ad me, tam dicit me confixerunt. Idem aspectus & confixionis est in Dei verbis objectum.
units.tr: V. Hence Socinus' question is clumsy: "Why, he says, if God once warned through his Angel that whoever touched the Jewish people would touch the pupil of his own eye, could he not also have said that he was pierced by those who pierced Christ, although Christ is not one and the same in essence with him?" For if God had said, "He who pierces Christ pierces me," he would have distinguished himself plainly from Christ and signified merely his feeling and love towards Christ. But God, in Zechariah in that place, does not name Christ, does not distinguish himself from Christ, does not compare the piercing of Christ with his own, and does not signify with what mind or disposition he stands towards Christ. He says only that the inhabitants of Jerusalem will look to him whom they pierced. Could he have said "to be looked upon and pierced" more plainly? When he says "they will look to me," does it not signify how dear Christ would be to him, with what love he would pursue Christ? Yet just as he says "they will look to me," so he says "they have pierced me." The same object stands in God's words for both looking and piercing.

units.la: VI. Haud melius quadrat secundum exemplum: Primùm, quia quos persequebatur Paulus Lucas disertè nominauerat V. 1. & 2. discipulos nimirum Domini. Apud Zachariam verò quem transfixerint Iudæi, præter vnum Deum, nemo occurrit. Deinde quia Paulus, tunc Saulus, reuera persequebatur Christum, hoc est, Christi nomen, famam, doctrinam, religionem, discipulos, membra: scopus enim eius erat doctrinam religionem famam Ecclesiam, regnum denique Christi funditus abolere. Hoc si ipsum Christum persequi non est, quid sit persequi non intelligo.
units.tr: VI. The second answer fits no better. First, because Luke had expressly named those whom Paul persecuted, in verses 1 and 2: the disciples of the Lord, namely. In Zechariah, however, apart from the one God, no one appears whom the Jews pierced. Second, because Paul, then Saul, was in reality persecuting Christ, that is, Christ's name, fame, doctrine, religion, disciples and members. For his aim was to root out utterly the doctrine, the religion, the fame, the Church, and finally the kingdom of Christ. If this is not to persecute Christ himself, I do not understand what persecuting is.

units.la: VII. Tertium exemplum, Esurivi & dedistis mihi manducare, &c, quominus obstit argumento nostro impediunt quædam, primò explicatio quam ipse dominus statim subjicit, Amen dico vobis, quatenus fecistis vni de his fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis, sised tertium primò excogitasse videntur, deinde primum, tandem secundum illis subministrauit Marcus Marinus Brixianus Can. reg. D. Saluatoris. Quem eorum ordinem, ne ab eorum vestigijs recedamus, sequemur in tribus illis refellendis.
units.tr: VII. The third example, I was hungry and you gave me to eat, and so on, is prevented from obstructing our argument by certain things. First, the explanation which the Lord himself immediately adds: Amen I say to you, inasmuch as you did it to one of these my least brothers, you did it to me, if but they seem to have devised the third first, then the first, and finally the second was supplied to them by Marcus Marinus of Brescia, canon regular of the Holy Saviour. In refuting these three we shall follow their order, so as not to depart from their footsteps.

units.la: III. Primùm ait Socinus illa Zachariæ & Iohannis testimonia, non probare, Christum esse illum vnum Deum Israëlis, non magis, quàm apud eundem Zachariam probent, Dei oculi pupillam esse populum Iudaicum, illa Dei verba, Qui tangit vos (id est, populum Iudaicum) tangit pupillam oculi eius; aut quàm apud Lucam in Actis Apostolorum probent, Iesu Nazareni cultores, esse ipsum Iesum Nazarenum, verba illa ipsius Iesu ad Paulum adhuc Saulum, Saule Saule quid me persequeris? & rursus Ego sum Iesus Nazarenus quem tu persequeris; aut denique non magis quam similiter probent, Christi minimos, esse ipsum Christum, verba illa, quae se in die iudicij dicturum, ipse Christus testatur, iis quos in possessionem coelestis regni est introducturus, Esuriui & dedistis mihi manducare; sitiui & dedistis mihi bibere, &c. Quis tam stupidus est, quin videat, his loquendi modis, non quidem eandem essentiam sed summam coniunctionem & amorem significari? Iam quis Deo coniunctior quàm Christus homo, quis carior, aut fuit vnquam, aut esse potest, quamuis vtriusque essentia sit admodum diuersa?
units.tr: III. First, Socinus says that those testimonies of Zechariah and John do not prove that Christ is that one God of Israel, any more than in the same Zechariah they prove that the Jewish people is the pupil of God's eye, those words of God, "He who touches you (that is, the Jewish people) touches the pupil of his eye"; or than in Luke in the Acts of the Apostles they prove that the worshippers of Jesus of Nazareth are Jesus of Nazareth himself, those words of Jesus himself to Paul, still Saul, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" and again "I am Jesus of Nazareth whom you persecute"; or finally no more than they similarly prove that the least of Christ's people are Christ himself, those words which Christ himself declares he will speak on the day of judgment to those whom he is about to lead into possession of the heavenly kingdom, "I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me to drink," and so on. Who is so stupid as not to see that by these ways of speaking is signified not the same essence but the closest union and love? Now who is closer to God than Christ as man, who is or ever was or can be dearer, although the essence of each is quite different?

units.la: IV. Vocemus ad examen hanc Socini responsionem. Exemplum è Zach. 2. 8. petitum, quod, tanquam omnium maximè idoneum, Socinus paulò post repetit & valdè exaggerat, ad rem non est. Instituitur enim comparatio inter tangentem populum Dei & tangentem pupillam oculi Dei. Itaque pupilla oculi Dei apertè distinguitur à populo Dei, neque vlla arte potest inde legitimo syllogismo concludi, populum Dei esse pupillam oculi Dei, non magis quàm ex his Christi verbis, Qui vos audit me audit, &, quodcunque ligaueritis in terra ligatum erit in cœlo, concludi potest Apostolos esse ipsum Christum, terram esse cœlum. Hic verò nulla instituitur comparatio inter Deum & alium, inter confixionem alius, & confixionem Dei, sed simpliciter absque vlla eiusmodi comparatione Deus dicit, adspicient ad me quem confixerunt. Itaque nullus alius intelligi potest aspiciendus & confixus quàm Deus, statque firma argumenti nostri propositio, Ille qui dicitur Zach. 12. 10. ab incolis Hierusalem aspiciendus & confixus est Deus, cui similis ex verbis, qui vos tangit tangit pupiljam oculi eius, confici non potest. Adde quod nunquam creditum est, populum Iudaicum esse pupillam oculi Dei, nec est quicquam in sacris literis quo id probari possit: quocirca absque vllo periculo talis locutio usurpari potuit. At Christum esse Deum divina essentia praeditum, & plerique omnes Christiani crediderunt, ac credunt summo consensu, & scaturiunt è sacris literis quae id probent argumenta plurima, ut, si id error est, non potuerit non periculosa esse sic concepta Dei praedictio, aspicient ad me quem transfixerunt.
units.tr: IV. Let us now examine Socinus's reply. The example he takes from Zechariah 2:8, which he repeats shortly afterwards and sets out at great length as the most suitable of all, has nothing to do with the matter. The comparison there is between one who touches the people of God and one who touches the pupil of God's eye. The pupil of God's eye is plainly distinguished from the people of God, and by no skill can a valid syllogism conclude from this that the people of God is the pupil of God's eye. No more can it be concluded from Christ's words, He who hears you hears me, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, that the apostles are Christ himself or that earth is heaven. In the passage of Zechariah, however, no comparison is drawn between God and another, or between the piercing of another and the piercing of God. God simply says, without any such comparison, they shall look upon me whom they have pierced. Therefore no one other than God can be understood as the one to be looked upon and pierced, and the proposition of our argument stands firm: He who is spoken of in Zechariah 12:10 is God, to be looked upon and pierced by the inhabitants of Jerusalem. A parallel to this cannot be drawn from the words he who touches you touches the pupil of his eye. Add that it has never been believed that the Jewish people is the pupil of God's eye, and there is nothing in the sacred letters by which this could be proved. So such an expression could be used without any danger. But that Christ is God, endowed with the divine essence, has been believed by almost all Christians with the greatest agreement, and many arguments proving it flow from the sacred letters. So if this is an error, the prediction of God, they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, could not fail to be a dangerous way of putting it.

units.la: V. Quis etiam est tam stupidus, (ut sua Socino verba reponam) quin videat, hoc loquendi modo; Qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi Dei, summam conjunctionem & amorem, quo Deus populum suum prosequebatur, significari? sensus enim est apertus, qui vos tangit, gravissimè Deum offendit, Deo non minus vos chari estis, nec minus grave est vos laedi quàm vobis metipsis chara est pupilla oculorum vestrorum, quàmque grauiter fertis, si quis eam tangat. At quis est, praeter Aduersarios, tam oculatus, tamque perspicax, ut in hac propositione, Aspicient ad me quem confixerunt, talem conjunctionem & amorem erga populum, vel personam à Deo diversam, significari perspiciat? Agnoscant igitur Aduersarij discrimen inter compositam illam enunciationem, qui vos tangit tangit pupillam oculi eius, & simplicem istam, me confixerunt. At configi Deus non potest. Distinguo: ratione naturae divinae, concedo: ratione carnis in qua apparuit hominibus, nego. Quid enim prohibuit, quominus Deus patefieret, seu, appareret in carne, ut ita loquar, configibili, qua ab hominibus per summum scelus confixa Deus diceretur confixus? Certè verbum, quod erat Deus & caro factum est, confixum est, non qua Deus, sed qua caro.
units.tr: V. And who is so dull (to borrow Socinus's own words) as not to see that this manner of speaking, he who touches you touches the pupil of God's eye, signifies the closest union and the love with which God cherished his people? The meaning is plain: he who touches you gravely offends God; you are no less dear to God, and it is no less grievous for you to be harmed than it is for you to lose the pupil of your own eyes, which you bear badly if anyone touches. But who, apart from our adversaries, is so sharp-sighted and perspicacious that he can discern in this proposition, they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, such a union and love towards the people, or a person distinct from God? Let our adversaries therefore recognise the difference between that compound statement, he who touches you touches the pupil of his eye, and this simple one, they have pierced me. But God cannot be pierced. I distinguish: with respect to the divine nature, I grant it; with respect to the flesh in which he appeared to men, I deny it. For what prevented God from being made manifest, or appearing, in a flesh that could be pierced, so that by the wicked deed of men he could be called pierced? Surely the Word, which was God, was made flesh, was pierced, not as God, but as flesh.

units.la: V I. Quare inepta est Socini interrogatio, Cur, inquit, siper suum Angelum Deus olim monuit, quod qui tangeret populum Iudaicum, is tangeret pupillam oculi sui; non potuit etiam dicere se configi ab illis qui Christum configebant, quamvis Christus non sit unus & idem essentia cum ipso? Nam si Deus dixisset, qui Christum configit me configit, distinxisset se aperte à Christo, & significasset duntaxat affectum suum & amorem erga Christum. At Deus apud Zachariam eo loco non nominat Christum, non distinguit se à Christo, non comparat transfixionem Christi cum sua, non significat qua mente, quo animo sit erga Christum. Tantum dicit incolas Hierusalem ad se quem confixerunt aspecturos. potuit ne distertius dici aspiciendus & transfigendus? cum dicit aspicient ad me, significatne quàm sibi charus esset futurus Christus, quanto Christum amore esset prosecuturus? tamen quàm dicit adspicient ad me, tam dicit me confixerunt. Idem aspectus & confixionis est in Dei verbis objectum. Quid? An, quia scriptum est, qui tangit populum Iudaicum tangit pupillam oculi Dei, potuit Deus dici occidi ab illis qui occidebant Iudæos, abduci in captiuitatem ab illis qui abducebant in captiuitatem Iudæos? Iudæi quidam Deo admodum chari & conjuncti, lapida-ti fuerunt, dissecti, gladio cæsi, interfecti. Num igitur propte-rea dici potuit Deus absolutè lapidatus, dissectus, gladio cæsus, interfectus? Non arbitror. Non sic loquitur Scriptura, Non sic loquuntur Theologi, Nec sic loquentem facilè ferrent aures Christianæ.
units.tr: VI. Therefore Socinus's question is pointless: Why, he says, when God once warned through his angel that whoever touched the Jewish people touched the pupil of his eye, could he not also say that he was pierced by those who pierced Christ, although Christ is not one and the same in essence with him? For if God had said, "whoever pierces Christ pierces me," he would have plainly distinguished himself from Christ, and would have signified only his affection and love towards Christ. But in that passage of Zechariah God does not name Christ, does not distinguish himself from Christ, does not compare the piercing of Christ with his own, and does not indicate with what mind or disposition he stands towards Christ. He says only that the inhabitants of Jerusalem will look to him whom they pierced. Could he have said more plainly that he is to be looked upon and pierced? When he says they shall look upon me, does he signify how dear Christ would be to him, with what great love he would cherish Christ? Yet as he says they shall look upon me, so he says they have pierced me. The same object is in view in God's words, both of looking and of piercing. What then? Because it is written, he who touches the Jewish people touches the pupil of God's eye, could God be said to be slain by those who slew the Jews, or carried into captivity by those who carried the Jews into captivity? Certain Jews, very dear and close to God, were stoned, cut in pieces, struck by the sword, and killed. Could it therefore be said absolutely that God was stoned, cut in pieces, struck by the sword, and killed? I think not. Scripture does not speak so, theologians do not speak so, and Christian ears would hardly bear anyone who spoke so.

units.la: VII. Haud melius quadrat secundum exemplum: Primum quia quos persequebatur Paulus Lucas diserte nominauerat V. 1. & 2. discipulos nimirum Domini. Apud Zachariam verò quem transfixerint Iudæi, præter unum Deum, nemo occurrit. Deinde quia Paulus, tunc Saulus, reuera persequebatur Christum, hoc est, Christi nomen, famam, doctrinam, religionem, discipulos, membra: scopus enim eius erat doctrinam religionem famam Ecclesiam, regnum denique Christi funditus abolere. Hoc si ipsum Christum persequi non est, quid sit persequi non intelligo. Denique apud Zachariam non dicit Deus, aspicient ad me quem persecuti sunt, sed, quem confixerunt: quod verbum non simplipiciter persecutionem, sed certam quandam speciem persecutionis, immò certam quandam passionem à Iudæis illatam & à Deo receptam significat. Qui discipulos Christi securi percusserunt, igni combusserunt, vel eorum ossa confregerunt, illi sine dubio persecuti sunt Christum.
