Nemo tamen propterea absolutè dixerit, Christum fuisse decollatum, combustum, eiusque ossa confracta.
units.tr: VII. The second example fits no better. First, because Luke had expressly named those whom Paul was persecuting, namely the disciples of the Lord (Acts 9:1–2). In Zechariah, however, apart from God alone, no one appears as the one whom the Jews pierced. Next, because Paul, then Saul, was in truth persecuting Christ, that is, the name, the fame, the teaching, the religion, the disciples, and the members of Christ. For his aim was to overthrow utterly the teaching, the religion, the reputation, the Church, and finally the kingdom of Christ. If this is not to persecute Christ himself, I do not understand what persecuting is. Lastly, in Zechariah God does not say, they shall look upon me whom they have persecuted, but whom they have pierced. This verb signifies not simply persecution, but a certain definite kind of persecution, indeed a certain suffering inflicted by the Jews and received by God. Those who put the disciples of Christ to the sword, burned them with fire, or broke their bones, undoubtedly persecuted Christ. Yet no one would therefore say absolutely that Christ was beheaded, burned, or had his bones broken.

units.la: VIII. Tertium exemplum, Esurini & dedistis mihi manducare, & c, quominus obsit argumento nostro impediunt quædam. Primò explicatio quam ipse Dominus statim subjicit, Amen dico vobis, quatenus fecistis vni de his fratribus meis minimis, mihi fecistis, eâ enim, & quis proprie esurierit declarat, & omnem errandi ansam à verbis suis remouet. Hic verò apud Zachariam nulla vel praemittitur vel subiicitur explicatio. Nullus memoratur confixus praeter Deum. Nihil est quod doceat, non ipsum Deum, in forma quae configi posset apparentem, confixum fuisse, sed alium quendam Deo valde charum. Deinde, actio in qua Christus versatur cum sic loquitur. Id enim agit, ut hominum opera aestimet, & quo loco & numero habeat, exponat. Quare mirum videri non debet, si phrasibus ad eam rem efficacissimis, ac officia charitatis nobis, quàm maximè fieri potuit, commendantibus utatur. Apud Zachariam verò aliud agit. Docet enim quantam mutationem effectura sit in incolis Hierusalem effuso Spiritus gratiae & precum. Nempe, inquit, aspicient ad me quem confixerunt. Cum antea me contumeliosissimè ac crudelissimè, tanquam blasphemum, impostorem, sceleratum, reiecissent, assixissent cruci, confixissent, ac confixum auersati essent, tunc aspicient ad me, conuertentur ad me, me Deum suum & Seruatorem suum agnoscent, quodque me ita tractarint ac confixerint cum plangore multo acerrimè dolebunt.
units.tr: VIII. As for the third example, I was hungry and you gave me food, and so on, certain features prevent it from harming our argument. First, the explanation which the Lord himself immediately adds: Truly I say to you, inasmuch as you did it to one of these my least brothers, you did it to me. By this he both declares who is properly hungry and removes every occasion of error from his words. Here in Zechariah, however, no explanation is either placed before or added after. No one is named as pierced except God. Nothing teaches that it was not God himself, appearing in a form that could be pierced, who was pierced, but some other person very dear to God. Next, consider the action in which Christ is engaged when he speaks thus. For he is concerned to assess the works of men and to set forth what place and number they hold. It ought not therefore to seem strange if he uses phrases most effective for that purpose, and commends the duties of charity to us as strongly as possible. In Zechariah, however, he is doing something else. For he teaches what great change will be wrought among the inhabitants of Jerusalem when the Spirit of grace and of prayer is poured out. Namely, he says, they shall look upon me whom they have pierced. Whereas before they had rejected me most insultingly and most cruelly as a blasphemer, an impostor, and a criminal, had fastened me to the cross, had pierced me, and had turned away from me when I was pierced, then they will look to me, turn to me, and acknowledge me as their God and their Saviour; and they will grieve most bitterly, with great lamentation, that they treated me so and pierced me.

units.la: I X. Denique natura coniunctionis fidelium cum Christo. Sunt enim fratres & membra Christi, ac proinde eiusdem cum eo homine naturae humanae, nec non eiusdem Spiritus sanctitatis & vitae participes. Est autem mutua quaedam inter membra eiusdem corporis συμπάθεια, & quicquid unum membrum patitur, id ei cuius est membrum tribui solet. Dei vero & Christi, si tantum homo fuit, dispar est ratio. Nam, si Scripturam consulis, nunquam Christus membrum Dei dicitur: aliena est haec locutio à Scripturae & theologorum stilo. Si rem ipsam. Christus tantum homo plusquam specie, immò genere à Deo distat. Itaque non si membrorum Christi passiones praedicantur de Christo, consequitur, passiones Christi (si tantum homo fuit, vt volunt Aduersarij) praedicari posse de Deo. Quanquam ne illa quidem Christi cum fidelibus conjunctio facit, vt Christus dici possit absolutè & sine explicatione, lapidatus, crematus, viuus sepultus, securi percussus, saepius occisus, in puluerem aut cineres redactus, &c, quemadmodum Deus hoc loco dicitur à Iudaeis confixus.
units.tr: IX. Finally, consider the nature of the union of believers with Christ. For they are the brothers and members of Christ, and therefore partakers of the same human nature as he, and likewise of the same Spirit, holiness, and life. Now among the members of one body there is a mutual sympatheia [συμπάθεια], and whatever one member suffers is commonly attributed to the one whose member it is. But the case is different for God and Christ, if Christ was only a man. For if you consult Scripture, Christ is never called a member of God; this manner of speaking is foreign to the style of Scripture and of theologians. And if we consider the matter itself: Christ, being merely a man, however exalted in species, differs from God even in kind. Therefore it does not follow, because the sufferings of Christ's members are predicated of Christ, that the sufferings of Christ (if he was merely a man, as our adversaries hold) can be predicated of God. Indeed, even that union of Christ with the faithful does not make it possible to say absolutely and without explanation that Christ was stoned, burned, buried alive, struck with the axe, killed many times, reduced to dust or ashes, and so on, just as God in this passage is said to have been pierced by the Jews.

units.la: X. Ad tria illa exempla Smalcius alia duo adjecit. Vnum ex Apoc. 1. 7. Alterum ex Malach. 3. 8. In priore loco affirmatur, inquit, Quod Christum sit visurus omnis oculus, & quicunque (sic enim est in graeco) eum pupugerunt. Ibi de solo Christo absolutè, absque vlla comparatione sermo est: & tamen certum est, id non de Christo, sed de eius populo intelligendum esse. De Christo enim solo dici non potest, quicunque eum transfixerunt, cùm tantùm vnus id fecerit, vel saltem semel tantùm id factum sit. Vox autem, quicunque, & multos fuisse, qui illum transfixerunt, & sapius id ac-cidisse, indicat.
units.tr: X. To those three examples Smalcius added two others. The first is from Apoc. 1. 7, the second from Malach. 3. 8. In the first passage, he says, it is affirmed that every eye will see Christ, and those who (for so it is in Greek) pierced him. There the discourse is about Christ alone, absolutely and without any comparison: and yet it is certain that this must be understood not of Christ but of his people. For it cannot be said of Christ alone that those who pierced him, since only one did so, or at least that it was done only once. The word "those who" indicates that there were many who pierced him, and that this happened often.

units.la: Miseret me Smalcij tam malè ratiocinantis. Primùm nititur voce, quicunque, quae non est in textu. Nam in versionibus est simplex qui, in graeco ὅστις. ὅστις[?] autem proprie significat qui, ac interdum quisquis, quicunque, sed rarò in plura-li, vt patet ex Eph. 3. 13. Heb. 10. 11. Col. 3. 23. &c. Sed fac vocem illam extare in ipso textu, quid inde sequitur? Tantùm vnus, inquit, transfixit Christum. Non dicam eum non fuisse vnioculum, non dicam esse enallagen numeri, dicam, tantùm vnum manu sua, sed multos iussu, consensu, approbatione Christum transfixisse, hos autem etiam ipsos transfixionis illius reos esse. Sic soli milites romani manibus propriis Christum crucifixerunt, & tamen Iudaei Act. 2. 36. primores populi & Seniores Israëlis Act. 4. 10. Principes seculi huius 1. Cor. 2. 8. dicuntur eum crucifixisse: quia nimirum eorum vel auctoritate, vel suasione, vel consensione, vel approbatione crucifixus fuit. Quod autem ait, vocem, quicunque, indicare saepius id accidisse, refutatione non eget. Est enim homine rationis compote indigna assertio.
units.tr: I pity Smalcius, who reasons so badly. First he relies on the word those who, which is not in the text. In the versions it is simply who, and in the Greek it is whoever [ὅστις]. ὅστις properly means who, and sometimes whoever, but rarely in the plural, as is clear from Eph. 3. 13, Heb. 10. 11, Col. 3. 23, and so on. But suppose that word really stands in the text itself: what follows from it? Only one, he says, pierced Christ. I will not say that he was not one-eyed, nor that this is an enallage of number. I will say that only one pierced Christ with his own hand, but that many pierced him by command, by consent, or by approval, and that these too are guilty of that piercing. So the Roman soldiers alone crucified Christ with their own hands, and yet the Jews (Acts 2. 36), the chief men and elders of Israel (Acts 4. 10), and the rulers of this age (1 Cor. 2. 8) are said to have crucified him, because he was crucified by their authority, persuasion, consent, or approval. As for his claim that the word those who indicates that this happened often, it needs no refutation. It is an assertion unworthy of a man in possession of his reason.

units.la: X I. Ad locum Malach. 3. 8. quod attinet, ibi, inquit Smalcius, diserte bis dicitur, absolutè absque vlla comparatione, Deum fuisse confixum vel affixum vel spoliatum à populo suo, quia scilicet decimas non reddebat seruis Dei. Eligat, quaeso Smalcius, ex tribus illis vocibus, confixum vel affixum vel spoliatum, quam volet. Si victimam, spoliatum, nihil nobis nocet hic locus. Debebantur enim decimæ & primitiæ Deo: sed eas sibi oblatas Deus Sacerdotibus & Leuitis concedebat, vt in ipsius domo ipsi ministrarent. Itaque cum decimæ & primitiæ non soluebantur, iure suo spoliabatur Deus, nec-non debito à Leuitis ministerio. Si superiores, confixum vel affixum, primùm nititur non textu hebraeo, sed vulgata versione latina, quam esse corruptissimam ipse Smalcius hoc ipso loco contendit, (cap.scil. 23.de Verbi incarnati natura aduersus Smiglecium ) Nam, & in Heb. est verbum דקרו[?] quod in sacris literis rapere, spoliare, omnium interpretum consessione, non autem configere vel affigere, significat; & intelligi non potest, cur Deus se confixum vel affixum in decimis & primitijs dixisset. Adde quod explicationem statim subjicit, cum addit, in decimis & primitijs, vt, sive affixus sive spoliatus dicatur, ambiguum esse non possit, quin id sit intelligendum habita ratione decimarum & primitiarum.
units.tr: XI. As for the passage Malach. 3. 8, Smalcius says, there it is plainly said twice, absolutely and without any comparison, that God was pierced, or fixed, or despoiled by his own people, because they did not render tithes to the servants of God. Let Smalcius choose, I beg him, whichever of those three words he likes: pierced, or fixed, or despoiled. If he chooses despoiled, this passage does us no harm. For tithes and firstfruits were owed to God, but God granted them, once offered to him, to the priests and Levites, so that they might minister in his house. Therefore when tithes and firstfruits were not paid, God was despoiled of his right, and of the ministry owed to him by the Levites. If he chooses the earlier words, pierced or fixed, this rests not on the Hebrew text but on the Latin Vulgate version, which Smalcius himself, in this very place (namely chapter 23 of his work on the nature of the incarnate Word, against Smiglecius), contends is most corrupt. For in the Hebrew the verb is דקרו [daqaru], which by the agreement of all interpreters means to seize or despoil in sacred writings, and not to fix or fasten. Nor can it be understood why God would say that he was fixed or fastened in the matter of tithes and firstfruits. Add that he immediately gives the explanation when he adds in tithes and firstfruits, so that whether he is said to be fixed or despoiled, there can be no doubt that it must be understood with regard to tithes and firstfruits.

units.la: XII. Vt igitur iam inoffenso pede progrediamur, Quandoquidem Deus hoc Zachariæ loco transfixus vel confixus dicitur absolutè, sine comparatione vlla, sine explicatione, sine mentione vllius alius confixi, non potest id accipi de transfixione alterius à Deo tota natura diuersi, sed duntaxat de transfixione Dei apparentis in carne transfixionis capaci. Alioqui quid erit in Sacra Scriptura certi? quid tam diserte & absolutè de aliquo dici poterit, quod non transferatur ad alium ab eo qui volet vti hac arte & responsione Aduersariorum? Quis etiam non videt eos, vim huius testimonij ab Apostolo Iohanne laudati, quantum in ipsis est, debilitare & frangere? Potuit enim, si illis creditur, Deus transfixus, dici, quia quidam è populo Iudaico ipsi charissimo transfixi fuerunt ante ortum Christi? Quid quod causæ nihil erit, cur Deus Pater, dici non possit absolutè crucifixus, mortuus, sepultus, à mortuis suscitatus, &c? Is enim certè non magis transfixus fuit, quàm occisus aut mortuus.
units.tr: XII. So that we may now proceed with an unstumbling foot: since God is said in this passage of Zechariah to be pierced or fixed absolutely, without any comparison, without explanation, without mention of any other who was pierced, this cannot be taken of the piercing of another being wholly different in nature from God, but only of the piercing of God who appeared in the flesh, a being capable of being pierced. Otherwise, what will be certain in Holy Scripture? What could be said so plainly and absolutely of anyone that could not be transferred to another by anyone who wishes to use this trick and answer of our opponents? Who also does not see that they, as far as in them lies, weaken and break the force of this testimony, which the Apostle John cited? For if we believe them, could God be called pierced because some of the Jewish people, most dear to him, were pierced before Christ's birth? What then will be the reason why God the Father could not be called absolutely crucified, dead, buried, raised from the dead, and so on? For he was surely no more pierced than killed or dead.

units.la: XIII. Adde loci huius circumstantias esse eiusmodi, vt conueniant Christo. Effundam, inquit, super domum Dauid & super habitatores Hierusalem spiritum gratiæ & precum. Quis Spiritum illum effudit? Christus. Noli mihi credere, crede Apostolo Petro. Ergo, inquit, dextra Dei sublatus, & promissum Spiritum Sanctum adeptus à Patre, effudit hoc, quod nunc videtis, & auditis. Et quis alius baptisat Spiritu Sancto & igne? quis alius mittit ad fideles Spiritum Sanctum? Addit, & aspicient ad me, Num ad Patrem recta, immediatè, sine Filij interuentu? Non fit verisimile. Nam, si ad Patrem accedere & aspicere possumus immediatè, quid opus fuit Mediatoris interuentu? & cur clamat Christus, Ego sum via, veritas, & vita: nemo potest venire ad Patrem, nisi per me? cur etiam Christus fatigatos & oneratos ad se vocat, & non potius amandat ad Patrem immediatè? Cur ad se contemplandum peccatores inuitat promissione vitæ æternæ & beatæ resurrectionis. Et non potius iubet eos rectâ contemplari Patrem? Immò cur aliquoties illud inculcat, qui me videt videt Patrem meum, qui me contemplatur contemplatur eum qui me misit, nisi vt intelligamus, tum demum nos, vti par est, Deum aspicere & contemplari, cum oculos conuertimus ad Christum, in quo vno nobis est salus repositá? cum igitur salutaris aspectus intelligatur hoc loco, is immediatè fertur in Christum, eoque mediante in Patrem, quem aspicimus aspiciendo Christum. Subjungit, quem transfixerunt, quod cum Filij proprium sit, nec conueniat Patri, dubitari non sinit, quin qui loquitur sit Filius. Iunge simul ista tria, & quàm appositè fuerit hic locus de Christi transfixione ab Apostolo Iohanne expositus, statim deprehendes. Iuncta enim soli Dei Filio conueniunt, præterea nemini. Is enim solus & transfixus est à Iudæis, & in eos Spiritum gratiæ effudit & effundet, & is est ad quem transfixum aspicere omnes resipiscentes necesse est. Id quod subsecutus luctus maximus, nec tam externus quàm internus, nec tam ob alia peccata, quàm ob istam transfixionem, quæ synecdochicè totam Christi crucifixionem complectitur, confirmat. Docet enim agi de conuersione Iudæorum ad Christum aspiciendum & agnoscendum, qui quo dignior videbitur, eo crucifixio & transfixio eius grauius & atrocius peccatum fuisse cognoscetur. Ex quo sequitur, huius aspectus obiectum esse Dominum gloriæ à Iudæis crucifixum: ac proinde eos ad eum aspecturos, quem proprie, non autem in aliena persona, transfixerunt.
units.tr: XIII. Add that the circumstances of this passage are of such a kind that they fit Christ. I will pour out, it says, upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and of prayers. Who poured out that Spirit? Christ. Do not believe me; believe the Apostle Peter. Therefore, he says, exalted at the right hand of God, and having received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father, he has poured out this which you now see and hear. And who else baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire? Who else sends the Holy Spirit to believers? He adds, and they will look to me. Is this to the Father directly, immediately, without the intervention of the Son? That is not likely. For if we could approach and look upon the Father immediately, what need was there of the intervention of the Mediator? And why does Christ cry out, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no one comes to the Father except through me? Why also does Christ call the weary and burdened to himself, and not rather send them directly to the Father? Why does he invite sinners to contemplate him with the promise of eternal life and blessed resurrection, and not rather bid them contemplate the Father directly? Indeed, why does he so often press this upon us: he who sees me sees my Father, he who contemplates me contemplates him who sent me? Unless it is that we understand that we then truly, as is fitting, look upon and contemplate God, when we turn our eyes to Christ, in whom alone salvation is laid up for us. Since therefore a saving look is understood in this place, it is directed immediately to Christ, and through him to the Father, whom we behold by beholding Christ. He adds, whom they pierced, which, since it belongs to the Son and does not fit the Father, does not allow it to be doubted that the one who speaks is the Son. Join these three things together, and you will at once perceive how aptly this passage was expounded by the Apostle John as referring to Christ's piercing. For joined together they belong to the Son of God alone, and to no one else. For he alone was pierced by the Jews, and he has poured out and will pour out the Spirit of grace upon them, and he is the one to whom all who repent must look upon as pierced. This is confirmed by the great mourning that followed, which was not so much external as internal, and not so much for other sins as for this piercing, which by synecdoche embraces the whole crucifixion of Christ. For it teaches that the passage is about the conversion of the Jews to looking upon and acknowledging Christ, and the more worthy he appears, the more grievous and atrocious will his crucifixion and piercing be known to have been as a sin. From this it follows that the object of this look is the Lord of glory crucified by the Jews; and therefore they will look to him whom they pierced, properly and not in another's person.

units.la: XIV. Sic refutata est prima Socini responsio. Altera est, quamuis apud Zachariam vulgò legantur vocula illa, ad me, in illis verbis, & aspicient ad me quem confixerunt, seu compunxerunt; tamen ex verbis Iohannis satis constare ipsius tempore, voculas istas in eo loco non fuisse lectas, aut certe à Iohanne locum istum ad Christum accommodatum fuisse, secundum eam lectionem, quæ illas non haberet (cur enim alioquin eas plane omisisset?) adeò vt hic de vno illo Deo verba non fierent[?]. Quid non audet hæreticus erroris tenax? Si minus potest sensum Scripturæ detorquere ad libitum, ipsam Scripturam adoritur, corruptionis insimulat, & verba, quibus reuincitur, inserta illi fuisse à Iudæis clamat. Dubitat tamen vtrum vocula illæ abfuerint ab omnibus codicibus, an à quibusdam tantùm, & duæ fuerint lectiones, vna, quæ haberet, altera quæ non haberet illas voculas. Ad hoc refutandum nonne omnium codicum hæbraorum constans fidęs consensus autoritas sufficit abunde? Si contra fidem omnium codicum licet disputanti dicere, textus est corruptus, verba quæ contra me citantur olim aberant ab omnibus, vel saltem à multis codicibus, & ab hostibus religionis Christianæ addita sunt, quid erit certi? aut quæ erit controuersiarum norma? Demonstrent igitur, si possunt, Aduersarij Iohannis tempore voculas illas, aut non fuisse lectas, aut duas fuisse lectiones, alte-ram quæ illas haberet, alte-ram quæ omitteret.
units.tr: XIV. In this way the first response of Socinus has been refuted. The second is that, although in Zechariah the little words to me, in the phrase they will look to me whom they have pierced, are commonly read, nevertheless it is clear enough from the words of John that in his time these little words were not read in that place, or at least that John applied the passage to Christ according to a reading which did not have them (for why else would he have omitted them altogether?), so that the words were not spoken here about that one God. What will a heretic clinging to error not dare? If he cannot twist the sense of Scripture at will, he attacks Scripture itself, accuses it of corruption, and cries out that the words by which he is refuted were inserted by the Jews. Yet he is uncertain whether those little words were absent from all manuscripts, or only from some, and whether there were two readings, one which had them and another which lacked them. Is not the constant and faithful consensus of all the Hebrew manuscripts, to refute this, more than sufficient? If it is allowed to a disputant, against the agreement of all manuscripts, to say that the text is corrupt, that the words quoted against me were once absent from all, or at least from many manuscripts, and were added by enemies of the Christian religion, then what will be certain? or what will be the rule of controversies? Let my opponents therefore demonstrate, if they can, that in John's time those little words were either not read, or that there were two readings, one which had them and another which omitted them.

units.la: XV. Id quidem Socinus duabus rationibus probare conatur, sed admodum infirmis, vna est, omissas esse illas voculas à Iohanne locum Zachariæ ad Christum accommodantę. Quid tum postea? Quis nescit Scripturas ab Euangelistis non ipsdem prorsus verbis semper citari, sed interdum aliquid omissi, vel in aliud commutari? Non valet igitur consequentia, Hæc vocula omissa est ab Euangelista. Ergo non extabat tunc temporis in textu hebræo. Hoc agnoscit Smalcius, Sed, addit, huiusmodi omissiones vel mutationes sine causa nunquam fieri solere. Fateor, verum ea causa potest interdum nobis esse ignota. Utinam omnium eiusmodi vel omissionum, vel mutationum rationes Aduersarij nobis exposuissent! Cur ergo Iohannes eas voculas omisisset? ratio nobis succurrit duplex. Id unum agebat, ut locum illum Zachariæ de Christo exponendum esse doceret. Erant autem in illo loco aliæ quidem voces ad id docendum & probandum accommodatæ; aliæ non item. Illas expressit, has omisit; nec necessarias ad suum illum scopum, & quæ prioribus nondum consideratis aliò mentem lectoris abducere possent. Huic rationi aliam subjungo. Duo ex loco illo Zachariæ probari poterant. Transfixio & diuinitas Christi. Agebat autem Iohannes hoc loco de transfixione, non de diuinitate Christi. Itaque locum illum citat, quatenus accommodatus erat ad confirmandam transfixionem, omissis voculis ad solam diuinitatem probandam comparatis. Voculam autem duntaxat unam omisit (pronomen scilicet ἐμέ) facilè supplendam. Aspicient in quem transfixerunt, subintelligendum est pronomen, vel me, vel eum: quid facilius fuit, quàm ex textu Zachariæ subintelligere potius pronomen primæ personæ me, quàm tertiæ, eum?
units.tr: XV. Socinus tries to prove this on two grounds, but both are very weak. The first is that John omitted those little words when he applied the passage of Zechariah to Christ. So what? Who does not know that Scripture is not always quoted by the Evangelists in exactly the same words, but sometimes something is omitted, or changed into something else? The inference therefore does not hold: "This little word was omitted by the Evangelist; therefore it was not then in the Hebrew text." Smalcius admits this, but adds that omissions or changes of this kind never happen without a cause. I grant that, but the cause may sometimes be unknown to us. I wish our Adversaries had explained to us the reasons for all such omissions or changes! Why, then, would John have omitted those little words? Two reasons occur to me. He had one aim: to teach that the passage of Zechariah must be explained of Christ. In that passage, some words were suited to teaching and proving this, and others were not. He expressed the former and omitted the latter, which were not necessary for his purpose and which, if the earlier words had not yet been considered, could draw the reader's mind elsewhere. To this reason I add another. Two things could be proved from that passage of Zechariah: the piercing and the divinity of Christ. But John was speaking in this place of the piercing, not of the divinity of Christ. Therefore he cites the passage insofar as it was suited to confirming the piercing, omitting the words that were fitted only to proving the divinity. He omitted only one little word, the pronoun ἐμέ [emé], which is easily supplied. They will look on him whom they pierced: one must understand a pronoun, either me or him. What could be easier than to understand from Zechariah's text the first-person pronoun me rather than the third-person him?

units.la: XVI. Altera Socini ratio petitur à verbis, quæ sequuntur apud Zachariam, Et planget super eum, vt in planctu super vnigenitum; & mœrere (continget) super ipsum sicut mœrere (contingit) super primogenitum. Ex quibus verbis, inquit Socinus, apparet, non de eo ipso, qui loquitur, sed de alio supra verba fieri, & sic redundare illud ad me, quod ibi legitur. Non dicam pro super eum, legi posse super hoc, vt verterunt Tremellius & Iunius, & referri non ad personam transfixam, sed ad ipsum transfixionis factum, seu peccatum, causam tam acerbi luctus. Quid enim opus est, vt laborem in conquirenda responsione, cum ipse sibi pro me Socinus alibi respondeat. Haud raro (inquit resp. ad 7.c. VujeKi clasf.2.Arg.7.) apud prophetas Iehova de seipso in tertia persona loquitur. Quid igitur prohibuit quominus hoc loco, vt alibi non raro, de seipso in tertia persona loqueretur? Hoc ipsum Smalcius confirmat de hoc ipso loco Zachariæ aduersus Smiglecium disputans cap. 23. Non negari potest, inquit, Deum interdum persona mutatâ de seipso loqui in tertia persona. Potuitne difertius hæc secunda Socini ratio dilui? tamen aliquid reponit Smalcius, Sed hoc, inquit, non est pro regula aliqua communi habendum.
units.tr: XVI. Socinus's second reason is drawn from the words that follow in Zechariah: And they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for an only son; and they shall grieve over him, as one grieves over a firstborn. From these words, says Socinus, it appears that the speech is not about the one who speaks, but about another, and so the "me" read there refers elsewhere. I will not say that instead of "super eum" one may read "super hoc", as Tremellius and Junius rendered it, and refer it not to the person pierced but to the act of piercing itself, or the sin, which was the cause of so bitter a mourning. For why should I labour to find an answer, when Socinus himself answers for me elsewhere? Quite often, he says (in reply to 7.c. VujeKi clasf.2.Arg.7.), among the prophets Jehovah speaks of himself in the third person. Why then should anything have prevented him from speaking of himself in the third person in this place, as he does not rarely elsewhere? Smalcius himself confirms this about this very passage of Zechariah, arguing against Smiglecius in chapter 23: It cannot be denied, he says, that God sometimes, changing the person, speaks of himself in the third person. Could this second reason of Socinus have been refuted more plainly? Yet Smalcius replies with something: But this, he says, is not to be held as some common rule.

units.la: Neque etiam hoc volumus pro regula haberi: satis enim est ad infirmandam eorum rationem id fieri interdum, imò haud raro. Addit, & nonnisi tunc adhibendum, cum nullus alius modus datur intelligendi sacras literas, & cum ipsa res ita prorsus exigit. Quasi verò vocem aliquam de textu sacrarum literarum tollere & auferre sit modus intelligendi sacras literas.
units.tr: Nor do we wish it to be held as a rule either. It is enough, to weaken their argument, that it happens sometimes, indeed quite often. He adds: and it is to be employed only when no other way of understanding the sacred letters is available, and when the thing itself absolutely demands it. As if removing and taking away a word from the text of the sacred letters were a way of understanding the sacred letters!

units.la: XVII. Sed redeamus ad Socinum, is suam istam intolerabilem in sacris literis mutilandis audaciam calumnia cumulat. Erat nimirum, inquit, hic locus, insignis de Iesu Nazareno clavis confixo, & lancea perfosso prædictio, & propterea Iudæos illum, ab ipso Euangelij initio corrupisse est admodum verisimile. Sicut similem locum corruperunt ps. 22. 17. Summa Iudæorum in conseruanda Scriptura Veteris Testamenti diligentia, fides, religio, à multis Theologis antiquis & recentibus celebrata, gratiam potius & laudem merebatur, quàm hanc atrocem calumniam. Si autoritate certandum est, major est Hieronymi, Augustini, aliorumque grauissimorum Theologorum Iudæos ab hac accusatione defendentium quàm Socini accusantis auctoritas. Si consulitur experientia, plenum est Vetus Testamentum locis ad reuincendam incredulitatem Iudæorum idoneis, quos illi non corruperunt. Ipse ille locus Ps. 22.17. quem citat Socinus ad eos purgandos valet: veram enim lectionem, quæ in sequitorem[?], non malitia Iudæorum sed similitudine figuræ literarum Vau & Iod degenerauit, non dissimularunt, sed ingenuè fassi sunt, & annota-runt.
units.tr: XVII. But let us return to Socinus, who piles calumny upon his intolerable audacity in mutilating the sacred letters. Clearly, he says, this passage was a notable prediction of Jesus of Nazareth, fastened to the cross with nails and pierced with a spear; and therefore it is very probable that the Jews corrupted it from the very beginning of the Gospel, just as they corrupted a similar passage in Ps. 22.17. The Jews' diligence, faithfulness and piety in preserving the Scripture of the Old Testament, which many ancient and recent theologians have celebrated, deserved praise and thanks rather than this atrocious calumny. If the matter must be settled by authority, the authority of Jerome, Augustine and other most weighty theologians who defend the Jews against this accusation is greater than the authority of Socinus, who accuses them. If experience is consulted, the Old Testament is full of passages suited to refuting the unbelief of the Jews, and they did not corrupt those. That very passage, Ps. 22.17, which Socinus cites to convict them, serves to clear them: for the true reading, which in the copies has been corrupted, was not corrupted by the malice of the Jews but by the similarity of the letters Vau and Yod. They did not conceal this but frankly confessed it and noted it.

units.la: XVIII. Fac tamen (quòd verum non est) eos quosdam Scripturæ locos corrupisse; At profectò hunc non corruperunt. Primùm enim codice usus est Euangelista noster non corrupto, teste Socino. Scripsit autem post alios Euangelistas. Erant igitur eo tempore codices aliqui non corrupti, & quidem penes Christianos. Quis igitur credat, Iudæos corrupisse codices Christianorum, quos in sua potestate non habebant, Christianis non reclamantibus, sed conniuentibus aut consentientibus potius. Nemo enim quod sciam, ante Socinum eos depravati huius loci accusauerat. Deinde, Si hunc locum corruperunt Iudæi inserta voce אֶת[?] ad me, vtique eum corruperunt in gratiam Christi & fidei Christianæ. Quod quis credas? Nam non obstant vocula illa, quominus locus Zachariæ intelligi possit & debeat de Christo clauis confixo & hasta transfixo: inseruiunt autem multùm ad probandam Christi diuinitatem, quam Iudæi præfractè negant. Quid dico, non obstant? Immò cauent ne hic locus ad alium transferri possit. Etenim præter vnum Iesum Christum nullus alius fuit, estue[?], qui idem credatur & prædicetur simul, & Deus esse ac Spiritum gratiæ in homines effundere, & confixus à Iudæis fuisse. Impediunt ergo hæ voculæ ne vaticinij huius implettionem in alio, quàm in Iesu Christo, quæramus, causamq; Christianorum, non minus aduersus Iudæos, quàm aduersus Socinum, iuuant.
units.tr: XVIII. Suppose, however (which is not true), that they corrupted certain passages of Scripture; surely they did not corrupt this one. For first, our Evangelist used an uncorrupted copy, as Socinus himself testifies. Moreover, he wrote after the other Evangelists. So at that time there were some uncorrupted copies, and indeed they were in the hands of Christians. Who then would believe that the Jews corrupted the copies of the Christians, which were not in their power, without the Christians objecting, or rather while conniving at or even consenting to it? For no one, so far as I know, had accused them of corrupting this passage before Socinus. Next, if the Jews corrupted this passage by inserting the particle אֶת [ʼet] before "me", they certainly corrupted it for the sake of Christ and the Christian faith. Who could believe that? For that little word does not prevent the passage of Zechariah from being understood, and rightly understood, of Christ fastened with nails and pierced with a spear. Rather, it greatly serves to prove the divinity of Christ, which the Jews stubbornly deny. What am I saying, "does not prevent"? Indeed it guards against this passage being transferred to someone else. For apart from the one Jesus Christ there was no other who is believed and proclaimed at once to be God, to pour out the Spirit of grace on men, and to have been pierced by the Jews. These little words therefore keep us from seeking the fulfilment of this prophecy in anyone other than Jesus Christ, and they support the Christian cause no less against the Jews than against Socinus.

units.la: XIX. Venio nunc ad tertiam Socini Responsionem, quam Monachus ei subministrauit. Addendum est, inquit, locum Zachar. cap. 12. Etiamsi hebraica lectio, quam hodie habemus, omninò incorrupta esse statuatur, posse tamen ex hebræo ita verti, vt nulla in eo, quemadmodum nec in loco apud Ioh. 19. Dei Israelis confixi mentio fiat. Hoc nimirum pacto, Et aspicient ad me cum illo quem confixerunt. Monuit huius rei nos Marcus Marinus D. Salvatoris canonicus regularis. Si huius Monachi autoritate pu-gnas[?] (quæ apud nos nulla est) ei omnium aliorum interpretum antiquorum & recentium, (ex quibus sine dubio non pauci fuerunt æque pij atque linguæ hebrææ periti ac fuit pontificius ille monachus) autoritatem opponimus. Respondet Smalcius pro more suo satis inconsiderate, Plus uni interpreti, dum nulla est suspicio hanc[?] esse tribui debere, quam multis aliis, qui interpretes non sunt. Nempe iudicio Smalcij iste unus Monachus, qui dictionarium seu Thesaurum linguæ hebrææ scripsit, solus est interpres Scripturæ, reliqui omnes, quicunque olim & his postremis seculis diligenter & accurate Scripturam interpretati sunt, interpretes non sunt. Egerne tam impudens & temeraria affirmatio ulla refutatione? Addit, cum nihil excogitari possit, quod illum unum ad istam interpretationem sequendam movere potuerit, præter solam veritatem, quam ex diligenti verborum Prophetæ consideratione assecutus est. Reliquos vero dormitasse hîc dici potest, qui alienas interpretationes secuti potius sunt, quàm vel cogitarunt, ut suas sequerentur. Cur tam præclarè sentit de isto monacho, & tam malè de omnibus interpretibus antiquis & recentibus? Non potuit canonicus ille studio novitatis, aut aucupandæ ex ista subtilitate gloriolæ, inducci, ut novam illam huius loci versionem excogitaret, & proferret in lucem? Ac ut veritatis speciem secutus fuerit, non potuit falli? videbatne Smalcius eius animum? intererat ne eius cogitationibus? An vero sic iudicat de eo tantum ex charitate? Egregia profectò charitas unum complexa Monachum, ut plurimos Patres & Theologos admodum pios & doctos, indicta causa, damnet! unus ille vigilavit, quia excogitavit aliquid quod placeret Smalcio, Reliqui omnes dormitarunt, quia tale quid non excogitarunt. Piget me ista refutare, quæ hoc ipso quod proponuntur, satis ipsa per se refelluntur.
units.tr: XIX. I come now to Socinus's third answer, which the Monk supplied to him. It must be added, he says, that the passage of Zechariah ch. 12, even if the Hebrew reading we have today is held to be entirely uncorrupted, can nevertheless be translated from the Hebrew in such a way that no mention is made in it of the God of Israel being pierced, as in the passage in John 19. In this way: "And they shall look on me with him whom they pierced." Marcus Marinus, a regular canon of our Saviour, reminded us of this. If you rely on the authority of this monk (which among us is nothing), we set against it the authority of all the other interpreters, ancient and recent, among whom without doubt there were not a few as pious and as skilled in the Hebrew language as that Papist monk was. Smalcius replies, rather carelessly, as is his way: More weight must be given to one interpreter, when there is no suspicion, than to many others who are not interpreters. Clearly, in Smalcius's judgement, this one monk, who wrote a dictionary or thesaurus of the Hebrew language, is alone the interpreter of Scripture; all the rest, whoever in ancient times or in these latest centuries have interpreted Scripture diligently and accurately, are not interpreters. Has such a shameless and rash assertion been refuted by anyone? He adds: since nothing can be devised which could have moved him alone to follow that interpretation, except the truth alone, which he attained from a careful consideration of the words of the Prophet. But the rest may be said to have slept here, who followed others' interpretations rather than even thought of following their own. Why does he think so highly of that monk, and so badly of all interpreters, ancient and recent? Could that canon not have been led, by eagerness for novelty or by hunting a little glory from this subtlety, to devise and bring to light that new version of the passage? And even if he followed the appearance of truth, could he not have been mistaken? Did Smalcius see into his mind? Was he present at his thoughts? Or does he judge him thus out of charity alone? An excellent charity indeed, which embraces one monk and condemns, without a hearing, very many Fathers and theologians who were most pious and learned! That one man kept watch because he devised something that pleased Smalcius; all the rest slept because they devised nothing of the kind. I am vexed to refute these things, which by the very fact that they are put forward are sufficiently refuted by themselves.

units.la: XX. Si, sepositâ autoritate hominum, rationem consulamus, Is, fatente Socino, nullam suæ interpretationis rationem attulit. Nullam etiam afferre potuit Socinus, præter illas duas, quas iam hac ipsa disputatione diluimus §. xv. & xvi. Sed age hoc commentum reuocemus ad examen. Primum non congruit cum interpretatione Apostoli, qui non vertit, aspicient cum eo quem transfixerunt, sed, aspicient in (me) quem transfixerunt. Vera quæso melior interpretatio, illa monachi pontificij, an hæc Apostoli Iohannis? Num etiam Apostolus cum reliquis omnibus interpretibus dormitauit? Cur igitur maluit vertere in quem, quàm, cum quo, vel cum eo quem, si hæc vera est & genuina illius loci versio? Cur etiam non addidit voculas, ad me, posita ista interpretatione prorsus necessarias? Nihil enim Euangelistæ loca Veteris Testamenti citantes omittunt aut mutant sine causa. Reddant igitur nobis Aduersarij huiusmodi omissionis & mutationis, posita Marci Marini interpretatione, rationes: quas enim omissi pronominis primæ personæ reddidimus §. xv. ad nostram interpretationem, minimè verò ad nouitium istud inuentum, accommodatæ fuerunt.
units.tr: XX. If, setting aside the authority of men, we consult reason, he (as Socinus admits) gave no reason for his interpretation. Nor could Socinus bring any reason except those two which we have already refuted in this very disputation, §§ xv and xvi. But come, let us bring this invention to examination. First, it does not agree with the interpretation of the Apostle, who did not render "they will look with him whom they pierced," but "they will look on (me) whom they pierced." Pray, which is the better interpretation: that of the Papist monk, or that of the Apostle John? Did the Apostle too slumber with all the other translators? Why then did he prefer to render "on whom" rather than "with whom" or "with him whom", if this is the true and genuine version of that passage? Why also did he not add the little words "to me", which are absolutely necessary on that interpretation? For the evangelists, when they cite passages of the Old Testament, omit or change nothing without cause. Let our opponents, then, give us reasons for such omission and change, given Marcus Marinus' interpretation. For the reasons we gave in § xv for the omitted first-person pronoun fitted our interpretation, and by no means this novel invention.

units.la: XXI. Deinde non bene conuenit isti versioni cum textu hebræo, qui sic habet, והביאו אלי את אשר דקרו. Nam את hoc loco non potest accipi pro præpositione עם cum, vt fit interdum, sed, qui proprius eius maximèque frequens est vsus, nota est accusatiui casus. Id hoc argumento concludo. Vbicunque vocula את iungitur cum accusatiuo verbi actiui, ibi non est præpositio cum, sed nota accusatiui casus. Hic autem iungitur cum accusatiuo verbi actiui. Hic igitur non est præpositio cum, sed nota accusatini casus. Maior probatur inductione omnium locorum, in quibus vocula illa iuncta cum accusatiuo verbi alicuius actiui occurrit; nec potest contraria instantia refelli. Minor manifesta est. את enim iungitur hoc loco cum אשר, qui est accusatiuus verbi actiui דקרו. Nihil enim aliud est cum quo iungatur. Non autem, opinor, dicent Aduersarij, præpositionem copulatiuam poni hoc loco per se & solitariè, nec habere quocum iungatur aut construatur: adeo id cum per se absurdum est, tum grammaticæ, & omnium autorum, nedum Scripturæ, consuetudini repugnans.
units.tr: XXI. Next, that version does not agree well with the Hebrew text, which reads "vehevi'u elai et asher diqqaru" [והביאו אלי את אשר דקרו]. For את cannot here be taken as the preposition עם, "with", as sometimes happens; its proper and most frequent use is as the sign of the accusative case. I conclude this by the following argument. Wherever the particle את is joined with the accusative of an active verb, there it is not the preposition "with" but the sign of the accusative case. Here, however, it is joined with the accusative of an active verb. Here, therefore, it is not the preposition "with" but the sign of the accusative. The major premise is proved by induction over all the passages in which that particle occurs with the accusative of some active verb, and it cannot be refuted by any contrary instance. The minor is plain: את here is joined with אשר, which is the accusative of the active verb דקרו, for there is nothing else for it to be joined with. Nor, I suppose, will our opponents say that the copulative preposition stands here by itself and alone, with nothing to join or govern it. That is absurd in itself, and contrary both to grammar and to the usage of all authors, not to mention Scripture.

units.la: XXII. Sed, vt ineptæ huius versionis absurditas magis pateat, quid ea posita את אשר significent videamus. את significabit cum, אשר quid? quo? sententia igitur erit, Aspicient ad me cum quo confixerunt. Versio aperte absurda, & cum Grammaticæ legibus pugnans. Num ergo significabit quem? sententia igitur erit, Aspicient ad me cum quem confixerunt, constructio æquè aut magis quàm præcedens inepta. Dicent esse ellipsin pronominis eo. Facilis responsio, Sed an vnquam talem Ellipsin obseruarunt in Scriptura, aut in probato aliquo autore? Quisquamne vnquam dixit cum quem, pro, cum eo quem? Quisquamne vnquam præpositionem, cum, vsurpauit non expresso vllo modo vel nomine, vel pronomine, quocum illa construi deberet?
units.tr: XXII. But, so that the absurdity of this inept version may be more plain, let us see what את אשר would signify. את will mean "with", and אשר "what"? or "to which"? The sense will then be, "They will look to me with what they pierced." That version is plainly absurd and at odds with the laws of grammar. Will it then mean "whom"? The sense will be, "They will look to me with whom they pierced", a construction equally inept, or even more so, than the previous one. They will say there is an ellipsis of the pronoun "him". The reply is easy: but did they ever observe such an ellipsis in Scripture, or in any approved author? Has anyone ever said "with whom" for "with him whom"? Has anyone ever used the preposition "with" without any noun or pronoun, expressed in some way, with which it ought to be construed?

units.la: XXIII. Non modo pugnat illa versio cum interpretatione Apostoli, & verborum legitima constructione, sed etiam cum ipsa re, quam significatam Deus voluit. Quis enim potest esse sensus istius propositionis, Aspicient ad me cum eo quem transfi-xerunt, nisi hic, Illi & is quem transfixerunt, vel, illi una cum eo quem transfixerunt ad me aspicient? Qui sensus aperte pugnat cum Dei loquentis mente, & Apostoli interpretatione, aspicient in quem transfixerunt. Proponitur enim is quem transfi-xerunt, tanquam aspiciendus, non tanquam aspecturus. Dicet forte aliquis verba, cum eo quem, &c. iungi debere, non cum nominativo verbi aspicient, sed cum accusatiuo me. Primum quomodo id probabunt Aduersarij? Autoritate Apostoli? Iam ostendimus versionem Apostoli cum ista versione Aduersariorum nostrorum non congruere. Addo ea admissa destitui Apostolum ratione, qua probet, quod ex Zacharia transcripsit contineri in textu Zachariæ. Deinde nescio an eiusmodi conjunctionis seu constructionis exemplum ullum proferri possit.
units.tr: XXIII. That version conflicts not only with the Apostle's interpretation and the lawful construction of the words, but also with the very thing which God willed to signify. For what can be the sense of this proposition, "They will look to me with him whom they pierced", except this: they, together with him whom they pierced, will look to me? That sense plainly conflicts with the mind of the God who speaks, and with the Apostle's interpretation, "they will look on him whom they pierced." For he whom they pierced is put forward as one to be looked upon, not as one who is going to look. Perhaps someone will say that the words "with him whom", etc., must be joined not with the nominative of "they will look" but with the accusative "me". First, how will our opponents prove this? By the authority of the Apostle? We have already shown that the Apostle's version does not agree with this version of our opponents. I add that if this is admitted, the Apostle is deprived of the reason by which he shows that what he transcribed from Zechariah is contained in Zechariah's text. Next, I do not know whether any example of such a conjunction or construction can be produced.

units.la: XXIV. Sed fac (quod non credo) aliquod exemplum proferri posse, rursus erit Ellipsis in textu Zachariæ: supplendum enim erit aliquid, Aspicient ad me existentem, vel sedentem, vel apparentem cum eo quem transfixerunt. Nam quid sit præcisè quod sit supplendum ambiguum erit, ac proinde incertum, an is quem transfixerunt proponatur ut aspectus objectum. Quod si voluisset Deus sese ab eo, quem transfixerunt Judæi, distinguere, seque & illum ab illis aspiciendum dicere, quis credat eum non fuisse dicturum potius, aspicient אֵלַי וְאֶל ad me & ad eum, quem transfixerunt, quàm, aspicient ad me cum eo quem transfixerunt? Sic enim mentem suam & clarius & certius & congruenter stilo Scripturæ significasset. Judicet jam lector, an verum sit quod affirmauit Smalcius, unum Marcum Marinum vigilasse, reliquos omnes interpretes dormitasse hoc loco.
units.tr: XXIV. But grant (which I do not believe) that some example can be produced. Again there will be an ellipsis in Zechariah's text: something will have to be supplied, such as "they will look to me" being present, or sitting, or appearing "with him whom they pierced." For what exactly is to be supplied will be ambiguous, and therefore uncertain: whether he whom they pierced is put forward as the object of the looking. But if God had wished to distinguish himself from him whom the Jews pierced, and to say that both he and that one were to be looked upon by them, who would believe he would not rather have said "they will look to me [elai ve-el: אֵלַי וְאֶל] and to him whom they pierced" than "they will look to me with him whom they pierced"? For thus he would have signified his mind more clearly, more certainly and more consistently in the style of Scripture. Let the reader now judge whether it is true, as Smalcius asserted, that Marcus Marinus alone kept watch and all the other interpreters slept at this point.

units.la: XXV. Cæterum, ut omnis eximatur scrupulus, observo, notam accusatiui casus adhibitam fuisse hoc loco prudenter, ut alibi passim, vitandæ ambiguitatis causa. Relatiuum enim אשר ea absente verti potuisset qui, & referri ad incolas Hierusalem, Aspicient ad me qui transfixerunt: Eâ verò præfixa reddi non potest nisi per accusatiuum quem, nec referri nisi ad pronomen me, Aspicient ad me quem transfixerunt.
units.tr: XXV. Moreover, so that every scruple may be removed, I observe that the sign of the accusative was used here prudently, as it is everywhere, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. For the relative אשר, without it, could have been rendered "who" and referred to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: "They will look to me who pierced." But with it prefixed it can be rendered only by the accusative "whom", and it can refer only to the pronoun "me": "They will look to me whom they pierced."

units.la: DISPVTATIO OCTAVA.
units.tr: DISPUTATIO OCTAVA.

units.la: De Arg. VIII. Ex Malach. Cap. iii. v.[?] 1. Ecce Ego mitto angelum (seu nuncium) meum, & præparabit viam ante faciem meam. Col-lato cum Matth. ii. 10. Marc. 1. 2. Luc. 1. 76. &c.
units.tr: On the eighth argument, from Malachi chap. 3, verse 1: Behold, I send my angel (or messenger), and he shall prepare the way before my face. Collated with Matt. ii. 10, Mark 1. 2, Luke 1. 76, etc.

units.la: I. ARGVMENTVM sic habet. Ille ante cuius faciem vt viam præpararet, mittendus dicitur Angelus, hoc est, Johannes Baptista, Malach. 3. 1. est Deus Is-raëlis.
units.tr: I. The argument runs thus. He before whose face an angel is said to be sent to prepare the way, that is, John the Baptist (Malachi 3. 1), is the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est ille ante cuius faciem, vt viam præ-pararet, mittendus dicitur Angelus, hoc est, Johannes Baptista, Malach. 3. 1.
units.tr: Christ is he before whose face an angel, that is, John the Baptist, is said to be sent to prepare the way (Malachi 3. 1).

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis. Major nititur loco Malach. 3.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The major premise rests on the passage in Malachi 3.

units.la: 1. Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum, & præparabit viam ante faciem meam. Qui enim loquitur est Deus Israëlis. Id quod, & connexio illorum verborum cum antecedentibus & consequentibus; Et Domini exercituum. quo insignitur, elogium; & nomen κύριος[?] sine articulo, quo eum Zacharias Luc. 1. 76. appellat, satis docent, & Socinus vltrò fatetur. Minor nititur testimonio ipsius Domini Matth. xi. 10. Hic enim est de quo scriptum est, Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum ante faciem tuam, qui præparabit viam ante te. Constat enim eum, & per Angelum illum seu nuncium Johannem Baptistam intelligere, & per pronomen te, Christum, hoc est, seipsum. Id autem alibi scriptum non est quàm in isto Malachiæ loco. Hoc ergo in loco Malachiæ dicitur Johannes Baptista mittendus, vt præpararet viam ante faciem Christi. Vera igitur est conclusio.
units.tr: (1) Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face. The one who speaks is the God of Israel. The connection of these words with what precedes and follows, the title the Lord of hosts by which he is marked out, and the name Kyrios [κύριος] without the article, by which Zacharias calls him in Luke 1. 76, sufficiently show this, and Socinus freely admits it. The minor premise rests on the testimony of the Lord himself, Matt. xi. 10: For this is he of whom it is written, Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you. It is clear that by that angel or messenger he means John the Baptist, and by the pronoun you he means Christ, that is, himself. Now this is written nowhere else than in this passage of Malachi. Therefore in this passage of Malachi it is said that John the Baptist is to be sent to prepare the way before the face of Christ. The conclusion is therefore true.

units.la: II. Ad hoc argumentum ita formatum quid respondeant Adversarij conabor ex Socini verbis promere. Ad Majorem nihil dici posse videtur, nisi, aut qui loquitur apud Malachiam Deum Israëlis non esse, aut textum esse corruptum, & loco pronominis primæ personæ me, debere esse pronomen secundæ te. Prius nec dicunt, nec dicere possunt, adeò manifestum est, ipsum Deum esse, qui inducitur dicens, Ecce mitto nuncium meum, &c. Posterius Socinus propè asserit his verbis, Non plane constat, inquit, Malachiæ prophetiam, ut nunc quidem legitur, in Christo impletam fuisse, nec Christus id sanè dicit; immò ipse aliter eam citat, & non ante faciem meam, sed, ante te, & ante faciem tuam, legit. Id quod non tantùm apud Matthæum facit, sed apud Lucam quoque cap. 7. 27. Nec est dicendum, Christum ita legere, ut ostenderet, quomodo ipse interpretaretur illud, ante faciem meam, sed necesse est confiteri, ita tunc temporis in vulgatis codicibus scriptum extitisse. Si tunc temporis ita scriptum erat in vulgatis codicibus, qui factum est, ut hodie in nullis prorsus codicibus ita scriptum extet? vel omnes codices tunc habebant ante faciem tuam, vel aliqui tantùm. Si prius, corrupti sunt omnes codices. Si posteri-us, lectio à Christo & Euangelistis probata periit; quam verò illi non probarunt, ea omnes codices invasit. A quo id factum est? à Iudæis? qui potuerunt codices Christianorum pro libitu mutare? qui ab eis corrumpi suos codices passi sunt Christiani? A Christianis? qui potuerunt Christiani ita amentes esse, ut loca Veteris Testamenti laudata ab Euan-gelistis ac transcripta, qualia tunc temporis in vulgatis codicibus extabant, mutarent ac corrumperent? Si quoties in locis Veteris Testamenti, quæ Euangelistæ & Apostoli laudarunt, verba aliqua omissa, aut addita, aut mutata videntur, toties necesse esset fateri, ita tunc temporis in vulgatis codicibus scriptum extitisse, multum differrent nostri codices hodierni ab antiquis illis, quos Christus & Apostoli Ecclesiæ commendarunt. Nam si loca citata in Novo Testamento postea corrupta fuerunt, quid erit de non citatis existimandum? Quorsum igitur spectant temerariæ istæ Socini assertiones, nisi, ut omnium codicum hodiernorum integritas & autoritas in dubium vocetur? Id quod fieri non potest, nisi calumniosè criminando Iudæos, & Christianos, immò ipsam Dei providentiam,
units.tr: II. I will try to bring out from the words of Socinus what our opponents reply to this argument so framed. To the major premise nothing seems able to be said, except either that the one who speaks in Malachi is not the God of Israel, or that the text is corrupt and that in place of the first person pronoun me there ought to be the second person pronoun you. They neither say nor can say the former, so plain is it that God himself is the one introduced as saying, Behold, I send my messenger, and so on. As to the latter, Socinus nearly asserts it in these words: "It is not plainly established," he says, "that the prophecy of Malachi, as it is now read, was fulfilled in Christ, nor does Christ himself say so. Rather, he cites it differently, and reads not before my face but before you and before your face. This he does not only in Matthew but also in Luke, chap. 7. 27. Nor may it be said that Christ read it in that way in order to show how he himself interpreted the words before my face; rather, we must admit that it stood thus in the common manuscripts of that time." If it stood thus in the common manuscripts of that time, how has it come about that today it is found in no manuscripts at all? Either all manuscripts at that time had before your face, or only some did. If the former, then all manuscripts are corrupt. If the latter, then the reading approved by Christ and the Evangelists has perished; but whatever they did not approve, that has taken over all the manuscripts. By whom was this done? By the Jews? How could they change the manuscripts of the Christians at will? Or did the Christians allow their own manuscripts to be corrupted by the Jews? By the Christians? How could the Christians be so mad as to change and corrupt the passages of the Old Testament cited and transcribed by the Evangelists, such as they then stood in the common manuscripts? If, whenever in passages of the Old Testament which the Evangelists and Apostles cited some word seems to have been omitted, added or changed, we had to admit that it so stood in the common manuscripts of that time, our present manuscripts would differ greatly from those ancient ones which Christ and the Apostles commended to the Church. For if the passages cited in the New Testament were corrupted afterwards, what is to be thought of those that are not cited? To what end, then, do these rash assertions of Socinus tend, except that the integrity and authority of all present manuscripts should be called into doubt? This cannot be done without slanderously accusing the Jews and the Christians, indeed God's very providence itself,"

units.la: III. Quid igitur, inquiet aliquis, causæ fuit, cur Euangelistæ & Apostoli Scripturas citantes vocem aliquam interdum omiserint, addiderint, aut mutauerint? primò ne viderentur dum scriberent, loca Scripturæ, ut nos humano consilio scribentes facimus, consuluisse ac inspexisse, sed, prout decebat majore, quàm fuerunt olim Moses & Prophetæ, autoritate præditos, ac Dei mentem perfectè tenentes, memoriter & liberius recitasse. Deinde, ut Scripturas citando interpretarentur, sensumque earum genuinum insinuarent. Denique, ut mentes nostras acuerent & excitarent ad loca Prophetarum diligentius expendenda, necnon ad eiusmodi mutationum rationes inquirendas, id quod quàm sit nobis vel necessarium uel utile, ipsi quotidie experimur.
units.tr: III. "What, then," someone will say, "was the reason why the Evangelists and Apostles, when citing Scripture, sometimes omitted, added or changed some word?" First, so that they should not seem, while writing, to have consulted and examined the passages of Scripture, as we do when we write by human counsel, but rather, as was fitting for men endowed with greater authority than Moses and the Prophets once had, and who held the mind of God perfectly, to have recited them from memory and more freely. Next, so that by citing the Scriptures they might interpret them and make their genuine sense known. Finally, so that they might sharpen and rouse our minds to weigh the passages of the Prophets more diligently, and also to inquire into the reasons for such changes. How necessary or useful this is to us we ourselves experience every day.

units.la: IV. Sed cur Dominus mutare voluisset hoc loco me in te? ut suam ipsius, qui apud Malachiam loquitur, mentem aperiret, & clarius exprimeret. Id enim operam dabat, ut probaret Johannem Baptistam esse non modò prophetam, sed plusquam prophetam. Affert autem pro argumento hoc testimonium. Hic est enim, inquit, de quo scriptum est, Ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam, qui praeparabit viam tuam ante te. Ex quo liquet Johannem prophetis fuisse praestantiorem, primò, quia communi cum Sanctis Angelis elogio ornatur Angeli Dei. Deinde, quia munus eius describitur tanquam praestantius munere prophetarum. Hos enim inter & Christum aliquot seculorum interpositum est interuallum, Johannes vero Baptista ante eum immediatè processit, tam parua distantia, ut eum post se venientem digito monstraret, eiqueque festinanter viam pararet. Id quod apud Malachiam insinuatur obscurius verbis, ut præparet viam ante faciem meam, non distincta persona Christi à persona Dei Patris quo fit ut nihil verbis illis significari primo aspectu videatur, quod non conueniat aliquomodo reliquis prophetis. Itaque Dominus, ut Johannis munus clarius exprimeret, lucemque illi loco aspergeret, personam suam cum Patris persona eo loco, ut fit alibi saepe, ob essentiæ unitatem confusam, ab ea distinxit, mutato pronomine primæ personæ, quod æquè ad Patrem atque ad Filium referri posse videbatur, in pronomen secundæ personæ, additis etiam uberioris lucis causa vocibus [illegible, ~12 letters] ut ante faciem tuam. Atque ita personam suam, quæ confusè significabatur communi pronomine me, recitando locum illum distinctè expressit verbis ego mitto angelum meum, quae communiter de Patre & Filio intelligi poterant, Patri attributis. Hinc sicut conferentes locum Malachiae cum eius expositione quam Dominus tradidit, ex illo vnitatem essentiae, ex hac distinctionem personarum Patris & Filij; ex illo Dominum esse eundem Deum cum Patre, ex hac Dominum esse distinctam à Patre personam colligamus, qui vsus vix percipi potuisset ex eo loco, si Christus pronomen primae personae retinuisset. Nihil est igitur, quamobrem corruptum velint Aduersarij hunc locum in omnibus codicibus hebraeis hodiernis, nec non in omnibus versionibus, praeter hoc vnum, quoniam dogmati eorum vel potius errori repugnat, quae causa si recipitur, quis error non poterit defendi? ad eum enim tanquam adnormam ipsa Scriptura exigetur, non ipse ad Scripturam.
units.tr: IV. But why would the Lord have wished to change me into you in this passage? In order to reveal and express more clearly the mind of him who speaks in Malachi. For he was taking pains to prove that John the Baptist was not only a prophet but more than a prophet. He brings forward for this argument the testimony: For this is he, he says, of whom it is written, Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you. From this it is clear that John was more excellent than the prophets, first, because he is adorned with the title common to the holy angels of God, the angel of God. Then, because his office is described as more excellent than the office of the prophets. For between them and Christ there lay a considerable interval of several centuries, whereas John the Baptist came immediately before him, at so short a distance that he could point him out with a finger as he came after him, and prepare the way for him in haste. This is hinted at more obscurely in Malachi by the words that he may prepare the way before my face, since the person of Christ is not distinguished from the person of God the Father; so that at first sight nothing seems to be signified by those words that does not in some way apply to the other prophets. Therefore the Lord, in order to express the office of John more clearly and to shed light on that place, distinguished his own person from the person of the Father in that place, as often happens elsewhere on account of the confused unity of essence. He did this by changing the first person pronoun, which seemed to refer equally to the Father and to the Son, into the second person pronoun, adding also, for the sake of fuller light, the words [illegible, about twelve letters] before your face. And so, by reciting that passage, he expressed distinctly his own person, which had been signified confusedly by the common pronoun me, in the words I send my angel, which could be understood commonly of the Father and the Son, ascribing them to the Father. Hence, just as by comparing the passage of Malachi with the exposition which the Lord gave of it, we gather from the one the unity of essence and from the other the distinction of persons of the Father and the Son; from the one that the Lord is the same God as the Father, and from the other that the Lord is a person distinct from the Father, a use which could scarcely have been perceived from that passage if Christ had kept the first person pronoun. There is therefore no reason why our opponents should want this passage to be corrupt in all the present Hebrew manuscripts, and in all the versions, except this one alone, since it runs counter to their dogma, or rather their error. For if this reason is accepted, what error could not be defended? For Scripture itself will then be brought into conformity with that error, as a rule, and not the error brought into conformity with Scripture.

units.la: • V. Repudiata igitur illa responsione videamus quid possit ad hunc ab Aduersarijs responderi. Aut pronomine primae personae apud Malachiam & pronomine secundae personae apud Matthaeum eadem persona significatur, aut non eadem. Si prius, ea persona, vel Patris persona est, vel Filij. Si Patris, Pater suam ipsius personam in vna simplici enunciatione duobus pronominibus, vno primae, altero secundae personae designat, Ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam, quod quis credere possit? meum scilicet & tuam ad eandem personam referri? Si Filij, habemus quod volumus, personam Filij significatam esse pronomine meam in his Dei verbis apud Malachiam, Ego mitto angelum meum, qui praeparet viam ante faciem meam. Constat enim pronomen illud meam eo loco Deum Israelis significare. Si non eadem persona significatur, necesse est, vt apud Malachiam persona Patris, apud Matthaeum persona Filij significetur, quo posito sequitur absurdum, Dominum, etiamsi id diserte verbis profiteatur apud Matthaeum & Lucam, tamen id non recitare quod scriptum est apud Malachiam. Duae enim istae enunciationes, praeparabit viam ante faciem Dei Patris, & praeparabit viam ante faciem Christi, inter se valde differunt. Deus enim Pater & Christus, si fides habetur Aduersarijs, totis naturis differunt. Praeparauit autem Iohannes viam ante faciem Christi, quatenus ante eum proximè sequentem processit, eum iam iam aduentare, immò adesse praedicauit, de eo testimonium dixit, eum digito ostendit, discipulosque suos ad eum post se venientem, vt par est, recipiendum præparavit: quo certè modo viam ante faciem Dei Patris non præparavit. Sunt igitur illæ enunciationes, quarum altera esset apud Malachiam, altera apud Matthæum, seu personas seu rem ipsam spectes, admodum diversæ. Id quod ipse Socinus confiteri videtur, cum ait, Citra Christi personam merito dici posse, Johannem Deo ipsi, sive ante Deum ipsum viam parasse, qui populum venit moniturus, ut pœnitentiam agerent, & ad Deum converterentur, iam enim Dei judicium instare. Si quod scriptum est apud Malachiam, non modo de alia persona quàm de Christo, scriptum est, sed etiam verum est, & dici potuit citra personam Christi, consequens est, quod de sua persona Christus dicit, id nullo modo scriptum esse apud Malachiam; quandoquidem, neque totidem verbis ibi scriptum est, neque ex eo quod ibi scriptum est, potest deduci necessaria consequentia. Quid est ipsi Christo contradicere, si hoc non est ?
units.tr: V. Setting aside that answer, let us see what the Adversaries can reply to this. Either the first person pronoun in Malachi and the second person pronoun in Matthew signify the same person, or they do not. If the former, that person is either the person of the Father or the person of the Son. If of the Father, then the Father designates his own person in one simple statement by two pronouns, one of the first person and one of the second: I send my angel before your face. Who could believe that? That my and your refer to the same person? If of the Son, then we have what we want: the person of the Son is signified by the pronoun my in these words of God in Malachi, Behold, I send my angel, who shall prepare the way before my face. For it is established that the pronoun my in that place signifies the God of Israel. If the same person is not signified, then it must be that the person of the Father is signified in Malachi and the person of the Son in Matthew. Given this, there follows the absurdity that the Lord, even though he plainly states in Matthew and Luke that it is written this way, did not in fact quote what is written in Malachi. For these two statements, he shall prepare the way before the face of God the Father and he shall prepare the way before the face of Christ, differ greatly from each other. God the Father and Christ, if the Adversaries are to be believed, differ in their whole natures. John did prepare the way before the face of Christ, inasmuch as he went before him who was coming next, proclaimed that he was already at hand, indeed already present, bore witness concerning him, pointed to him with his finger, and prepared his own disciples to receive him, as is fitting, when he came after. In that manner, certainly, he did not prepare the way before the face of God the Father. Those statements, therefore, one of which would be in Malachi and the other in Matthew, are very different, whether you look at the persons or at the thing itself. Socinus himself seems to admit this when he says: Apart from the person of Christ it can rightly be said that John prepared the way for God himself, or before God himself, since he came to warn the people that they should repent and turn to God, for the judgment of God was already at hand. If what is written in Malachi was written not only of a different person than Christ but is also true and could be said apart from the person of Christ, it follows that what Christ says of his own person was written in no way in Malachi. For it is not written there in so many words, nor can a necessary consequence be drawn from what is written there. What is this, if it is not to contradict Christ himself?

units.la: VI. Quid possit responderi non occurrit: Nam quæ duo respondit Socinus, ea ab argumento nostro sic concepto aberrant. Dixit enim primò, Johannem ante faciem non modo Christi, sed alterius etiam, hoc est, Dei ipsius viam paravisse. Facta esse. Hoc nihil facit ad infirmandum argumentum nostrum, quod non sumit pro concesso Johannem non præparasse viam ante faciem illius, præterquam Christi, sed nititur diserto Christi testimonio affirmantis scriptum esse in eo loco Malachiæ, Ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam, qui præparabit viam tuam, ante te. Id quod tamen scriptum in eo loco non est, si alia persona significatur apud Malachiam verbis ante faciem meam, alia apud Matthæum verbis ante faciem tuam. Unde concludo, nisi velimus contradicere Christo, hoc est, ipsi veritati, confitendum esse eandem personam utroque illo pronomine significari. Constat autem in verbis ante faciem tuam, per tuam Christum intelligi, & in verbis ante faciem meam, per meam Deum Israëlis. Confitendum igitur est personam Christi eandem esse Deum Israëlis.
units.tr: VI. I cannot see what could be answered. The two answers that Socinus gives are wide of our argument as it is framed. For he first says: John prepared the way before the face not only of Christ but also of another, that is, of God himself. Let it be so. This does nothing to weaken our argument, which does not take for granted that John did not prepare the way before the face of anyone except Christ, but rests on the explicit testimony of Christ, who affirms that this passage of Malachi reads: Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you. Yet this is not written in that place if one person is signified in Malachi by the words before my face and another in Matthew by the words before your face. From this I conclude that, unless we wish to contradict Christ, that is, truth itself, we must confess that the same person is signified by both pronouns. It is established that in the words before your face the word your means Christ, and that in the words before my face the word my means the God of Israel. It must therefore be confessed that the person of Christ is the same as the God of Israel.

units.la: VII. Adde quod si apud Malachiam verbis, ante faciem meam, persona Patris significatur, & præparatio viæ ante eius faciem, quæ citra personam Christi merito dici potuerit, in eo sita, quod Johannes populum venit moniturus, ut pœnitentiam agerent, & ad Deum converterentur, ut dicebat Socinus, non fuerunt verba illla accommodata ad probandum, Iohannem fuisse plusquam prophetam; id quod tamen vt probaret, Dominus verba illa citauit. Quis enim prophetarum missus non fuit vt populum moneret, vt poenitentiam agerent, & converterentur ad Deum? Cum igitur negari non posset, quin Dominus ratiocinatus sit optimè, fatendum est ea praeparatione significari, non id solum, quod Socinus dixit commune omnium prophetarum, sed peculiare quiddam, quod aliis prophetis tributum non est, quorum munus nunquam sic exprimitur (quantum quidem meminisse possum) in sacris literis,
units.tr: VII. Add that if in Malachi the person of the Father is signified by the words before my face, and the preparation of the way before his face, which could rightly be said apart from the person of Christ, consists in this, that John came to warn the people that they should repent and turn to God, as Socinus said, then those words were not suited to prove that John was more than a prophet. Yet the Lord quoted those words precisely to prove this. For which of the prophets was sent without also being sent to warn the people that they should repent and turn to God? Since it cannot be denied that the Lord reasoned very well, it must be admitted that this preparation signifies not only what Socinus called common to all the prophets, but something peculiar which was not granted to the other prophets, whose office, as far as I can remember, is never expressed in this way in the sacred letters.

units.la: VIII. Expositionem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, sententiamque nostram confirmat Angelus Gabriel Luc. i. v. 17. munus Iohannis Baptistae praedicens. Etipse, inquit, praecedet ante illum in spiritu & virtute Elia. Intelligit autem per illum, vt patet ex verbis immediatè antecedentibus, ᾧετον ᾗ ἀυτὸν ἀυτῶν Dominum Deum Israelis. Illud praecedet, seu praebit προεπλευσεται aperte innuit, eum ante quem praeiturus erat sequuturum, ac post eum statim venturum. Quis ergo post Iohannem Baptistam venit? Pater? non certè qua distinguitur à Filio, sed Filius duntaxat. Non praecessit igitur Iohannes ante Patrem, sed ante Filium. Praecessit tamen ante Dominum Deum Israelis. Ergo Filius est Dominus Deus Israelis. IX. Hinc quoque expositionem confirmat Zacharias Luc. i. v. 76. praibis, inquit, ante faciem Domini ut pares vias eius. Dominus intelligitur, Socino confitente immò probante, Deus Israelis. Intelligitur autem non Pater sed Filius. Id patet ex verbo quo utitur. Nam, vt Angelus non dixerat ἱκεύσεται, sed προσλεύσεται, sic non dicit Zacharias πρεύση ibit, sed προπρεύση ... προσώπῳ ... praebit ante faciem Domini. Haec praegressio, seu antecessio sine dubio relationem dicit ad personam post venientem. Quaenam autem persona post Iohannem venit? certè persona Christi, non autem Patris. Nullibi enim scriptum est Patrem venisse post Iohannem. Hoc de vno Filio Dei dicitur constanter, nunquam de Patre. Non venit in mundum Pater, sed missus à Patre vnigenitus eius Filius. Filius igitur est ille Dominus, cuius ante faciem praeiuit Iohannes, ac proinde est Deus Israelis. X. Idipsum locus Malachiae non obscurè innuit. Nam post verba, Ecce ego mitto Angelum meum & praeparabit viam ante faciem meam, sequūntur ista, & statim veniet ad templum suum Dominator quem vos quaeritis. Ex quibus patet hunc angelum seu nuncium viam fuisse praeparaturum ante faciem venientis post ipsum dominatoris. Quis autem est ille dominator? Pater qua distinguitur à Filio? Nullo modo, vocatur enim verbis sequen-tibus Angelus foederis, quod nomen Patri non convenit. Est igitur sine vlla dubitatione Filius, id quod etiam Socinus confitetur. Idem etiam ille Dominator est Deus: Alioquin alius esset is cuius ante faciem viam praepararet iste nuncius, alius is Dominator qui post eum viam praeparantem veniret, quod non fit vllo modo verissimile.
units.tr: VIII. The angel Gabriel confirms our exposition and the view of our Lord Jesus Christ, Luke 1:17, when he foretells the office of John the Baptist: And he himself, he says, shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah. That him, as is clear from the immediately preceding words, is the Lord their God [κύριον τὸν θεὸν αὐτῶν], the Lord God of Israel. The word shall go before [προελεύσεται], which he uses, plainly implies that the one before whom he was to go was to follow, and was to come immediately after him. Who, then, came after John the Baptist? The Father? Certainly not as he is distinguished from the Son, but the Son alone. John therefore went before not the Father but the Son. Yet he went before the Lord God of Israel. Therefore the Son is the Lord God of Israel. IX. Zacharias too confirms this exposition, Luke 1:76: You shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways. The Lord is understood, Socinus himself admitting and even affirming, to be the God of Israel. And he is understood to be not the Father but the Son. This is clear from the verb he uses. For just as the angel had not said will come [ἥξει] but will go before [προελεύσεται], so Zacharias does not say you will go [πορεύση] but you will go before [προπορεύση] ... before the face [προσώπου] ... of the Lord. This going before, or preceding, undoubtedly refers to a person who comes after. Now what person came after John? Certainly the person of Christ, not that of the Father. For nowhere is it written that the Father came after John. This is said constantly of the one Son of God, never of the Father. The Father did not come into the world, but his only begotten Son, sent by the Father. Therefore the Son is that Lord before whose face John went, and consequently he is the God of Israel. X.
