The passage of Malachi hints at the same thing not obscurely. For after the words, Behold, I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face, there follow these: and presently the Lord whom you seek will come to his temple. From these it is evident that this messenger or angel was to prepare the way before the face of the Lord who was to come after him. Who, then, is that Lord? The Father, as distinguished from the Son? By no means, for in the following words he is called the Angel of the covenant, a name that does not belong to the Father. Therefore it is without any doubt the Son, as Socinus also confesses. This same Lord is also God. Otherwise the one before whose face this messenger was to prepare the way would be different from the Lord who was to come after him to prepare the way, which is in no way probable.

units.la: XI. Adde quod iste Dominator primùm vocatur absolutè & sine limitatione אדון, quod nomen absolutè positum vnum est ex nominibus Dei Israëlis. Deinde Additur, Quem vos quaeritis. Quem autem Dominatorem seu Dominum quaerebant? Constat eos quaesiuisse Deum Israëlis. Alium quaesiuisse non constat, quaeritur porrò magis proprie is qui est, quàm is qui prorsus non est. Denique tribuitur ei templum, id quod est proprium numinis, veniet, inquit, in templum suum. Respondet Socinus, vocem hebraam Hechal, quae apud Malachiam in loco isto reddita est Templum, proprie significare Regiam & per translationem ad templum quoque significandum, quippe quod diuini numinis Regia esse censeatur, vsurpatam fuisse. Et citat duos locos 3. Reg. 21.4. & Dan. 1.4. in quibus vox Hechal de Regia Achabi & Nebucadnezaris, regum idololatrarum, ac forte diuinitatis aliquam famam aucupantium, vsurpatur. In quo miror hominis iudicium propriam illius vocis significationem potius ex quinque aut sex locis in quibus regiam significat, quàm ex septuaginta locis in quibus significat templum, metientis. Fac tamen hanc vocem proprie significare Regiam. Annon vt Patris, sic Filij regia templum est? Si vtriusque idem est populus, eadem Ecclesia, idem regnum, idem Thronus, annon etiam eadem est regia, idem templum? Dicant igitur nobis Aduersarij quae fuerit Christi regia in quam venit. Templum Hierosolymitanum? Id solius Dei Israëlis, templum seu regia fuit. Ecclesia, templum viuum ex viuis lapidibus extructum? Haec vero longè praestat templo Herosolymitano. Coelum? Hoc quoque corpus est cuius templum Hierosolymitanum vmbra fuit. Si igitur Filius Dei dominus est corporis, quanto magis umbrae? Et, si nemo fuit umbrae dominus praeter Deum Israëlis, certè Christus est Deus Israelis, quippe qui non solùm umbrae, sed corporis etiam & veritatis Dominus fuit, estque hodie, eritque in æternum.
units.tr: XI. Add that this Lord is first called absolutely and without qualification adon [אדון], a name which, when used absolutely, is one of the names of the God of Israel. Then it is added: whom you seek. Now whom were they seeking as Lord or Master? It is established that they were seeking the God of Israel. It is not established that they were seeking another, and what is sought is more properly that which exists than that which does not exist at all. Finally, a temple is attributed to him, which is proper to the divine majesty: he will come, it says, to his temple. Socinus replies that the Hebrew word hechal, which in this place of Malachi is rendered temple, properly signifies a royal palace, and was used by transference to signify also the temple, since it is thought to be the palace of the divine majesty. He cites two passages, 3 Kings 21:4 and Dan. 1:4, in which the word hechal is used of the palace of Ahab and of Nebuchadnezzar, idolatrous kings who perhaps sought some reputation for divinity. In this I marvel at the man's judgment, measuring the proper meaning of that word by five or six passages in which it signifies a palace rather than by seventy passages in which it signifies a temple. Yet grant that this word properly signifies a palace. Is not the palace of the Son a temple just as the palace of the Father is? If they have the same people, the same Church, the same kingdom, the same throne, is it not also the same palace, the same temple? Let the Adversaries therefore tell us what was the palace of Christ into which he came. The temple at Jerusalem? That was the temple or palace of the God of Israel alone. The Church, the living temple built of living stones? But this far surpasses the temple at Jerusalem. Heaven? This also is the body of which the temple at Jerusalem was a shadow. If, then, the Son of God is lord of the body, how much more of the shadow? And if no one was lord of the shadow except the God of Israel, then surely Christ is the God of Israel, since he was Lord not only of the shadow but also of the body and of the truth, and is so today, and will be for ever.

units.la: XII. Altera Socini responsio sic se habet. Quamuis, inquit, alius sit ipse Deus, alius vero Christus; nihil impedit, quominus eo ipso, quod Iohannes viam ante Christi faciem parauit, ante ipsius Dei faciem quoque parauerit. Primùm fac itâ esse, nondum intelligo quid id faciat ad soluendum argumentum nostrum, quemadmodum à nobis conceptum est, aut infirmandas eas rationes quibus illud confirmauimus. Non enim efficit hæc responsio, ut apud Prophetam pronomen meam, simul Deum & Christum significet, si Christus non est Deus; nec impedit quominus verba Dei apud Prophetam citra Christi personam merito, ut modò affirmabat Socinus, dici potuerint. Neruum igitur argumenti non tangit. Deinde, Si Deus & Christus totis naturis seu substantijs differunt, non capio, quomodo Iohannes eo[?] ipso, quod viam ante Christi faciem parauit, ante ipsius Dei faciem quoque parauerit: viam enim ante faciem Christi parauit, tanquam eius praecursor, seu anteambulo, quomodo viam ante faciem ipsius Dei non parauit. Cur enim, aut qua ratione, viam parasset ante faciem illius, qui post eum non veniebat? præparatio enim viæ ante faciem alicuius, eum venire arguit. Aut igitur post Iohannem Baptistam venit ipse Deus, aut non venit. Si non venit, viam ante faciem eius Iohannes non parauit. Si venit, Christus est ipse Deus. Pater enim certè quidem non venit.
units.tr: XII. Socinus's second answer runs as follows. Although, he says, God himself is one person and Christ another, nothing prevents John, by the very fact that he prepared the way before the face of Christ, from having also prepared it before the face of God himself. First, suppose it is so. I still do not see what this contributes to answering our argument as we have framed it, or to weakening the reasons by which we confirmed it. This answer does not make the pronoun my in the Prophet signify God and Christ together if Christ is not God, nor does it prevent the words of God in the Prophet from being said, as Socinus just now asserted, with reason, without reference to the person of Christ. So it does not touch the core of the argument. Next, if God and Christ differ in their whole natures or substances, I cannot grasp how John, by the very fact that he prepared the way before the face of Christ, also prepared it before the face of God himself. For he prepared the way before the face of Christ as his forerunner or herald; why would he not prepare it before the face of God? For what reason, or on what ground, would he have prepared the way before the face of one who was not coming after him? For the preparation of a way before someone's face implies that that person is coming. Either God himself came after John the Baptist, or he did not. If he did not come, John did not prepare the way before his face. If he came, Christ is God himself. The Father, certainly, did not come.

units.la: XIII. Suam tamen istam affirmationem Socinus ratione confi-mat. Nempe quia, inquit, Christus ipsius Dei personam, idque omnium excellentissima ratione, in suo munere in terris obeundo, sustinuit. Hoc quale sit non explicat, Ego verò non satis intelligo. Sustinet personam regis, iudicis, Philosophi, Rex, Iudex, Philosophus, sed tanquam suam. Num sic ipsius Dei per-sonam Christus sustinuit? fuit igitur ipse Deus. Sustinet alienam Regis personam histrio in scena. Non putant, opinor, Aduersarij sic Christum Dei ipsius personam sustinuisse, qui si eam sic sustinuisset, tam dici potuisset ipse Deus, Deus summus, Deus Pater, quàm histrio dicitur rex, cum regis partes agit in fabula. Quid igitur tandem sibi hac phrasi volunt Aduersarij? Christum non suo sed ipsius Dei nomine venisse, tanquam eius legatum & ministrum, qui nihil diceret faceretue[?],nisi ab eo mandatum? Hoc verò est, non ipsius Dei, sed legati, ministri, prophetæ, doctoris, Mediatoris denique inter Deum & homines personam sustinere.
units.tr: XIII. Socinus nevertheless confirms this assertion by an argument: Namely because, he says, Christ sustained the very person of God, and that in the most excellent manner, in discharging his office on earth. He does not explain what this means, and I do not fully understand it. A man sustains the person of a king, a judge or a philosopher, but as his own. Did Christ sustain God's person in this way? Then he was God himself. An actor on the stage sustains the person of a king who is not his own. I suppose our opponents do not think Christ sustained the very person of God in this sense; for if he had sustained it in this sense, he could have been called God himself, the highest God, God the Father, just as an actor is called a king when he plays a king's part in a play. What, then, do our opponents finally mean by this phrase? That Christ came not in his own name but in the name of God himself, as his envoy and minister, who would say or do nothing unless commanded by him? But this is to sustain not the person of God himself, but the person of an envoy, minister, prophet, teacher, and finally Mediator between God and men.

units.la: XIV. Sed missa phrasi rem ipsam spectemus. Esto aliquis legatus missus in prouinciam à Rege. Eum præcedat anteambulo, qui viam ei paret. Num hic dicetur præire Regi, aut parare viam ante faciem Regis? Num Rex ad prouinciæ illius incolas his aut similibus verbis scribet, Ecce mitto ante me nuncium meum vt præparet viam ante faciem meam, si nolit ipse venire, sed suum duntaxat legatum? quàm enim legatus regis non est ipse Rex, tam ipse rex non venit hoc ipso quod venit eius legatus; quàm autem ipse Rex non venit, tam ei non præit, nec parat viam anteambulo legati.
units.tr: XIV. But setting the phrase aside, let us look at the matter itself. Suppose some envoy is sent into a province by a king. Let a forerunner go before him to prepare his way. Will it be said that this man goes before the king, or prepares the way before the king's face? Will the king write to the inhabitants of that province in these or similar words: "Behold, I send my messenger before me to prepare the way before my face," if he himself does not wish to come, but only his envoy? For just as an envoy of the king is not the king himself, so the king himself does not come by the very fact that his envoy comes; and just as the king himself does not come, so no one goes before him, nor does the forerunner of the envoy prepare a way for the king.

units.la: XV. At Deus in Christo fuisse dicitur tunc, cum Christus in terris munus summum obibat 2. Cor. 5. 19. Quid tum? Nonne etiam Christus fuit in Apostolis & fidelibus? Num igitur hoc ipso quod quis præiuit Apostolo vel fideli præiuit Christo? Erat Deus pater in Christo, & tamen Christus non erat Deus Pater. Venit in carne Christus, non venit in carne Deus Pater. Ambulauit Christus iuxta mare, circumiuit totam galileam, professus est se esse Filium Dei missum à Patre, accusatus est, damnatus, cruci affixus, &c. Idem de Patre dici non potest. Esto igitur, sustinuerit personam ipsius Dei Christus, ipse Deus in Christo fuerit, id non satis est (si Christus non fuit ipse Deus) ut putetur Iohannes Baptista eo ipso quod præcessit ante faciem Christi, præcessisse ante faciem ipsius Dei, eo ipso quod parauit viam Christo parasse viam ipsi Deo.
units.tr: XV. But God is said to have been in Christ at the time when Christ was discharging his supreme office on earth, 2 Cor. 5:19. What of it? Was not Christ also in the Apostles and the faithful? Does it follow that whoever went before an Apostle or a believer went before Christ? God the Father was in Christ, and yet Christ was not God the Father. Christ came in the flesh; God the Father did not come in the flesh. Christ walked by the sea, travelled through all Galilee, professed that he was the Son of God sent by the Father, was accused, condemned, nailed to the cross, and so on. None of this can be said of the Father. Grant, then, that Christ sustained the person of God himself, and that God himself was in Christ; this is not enough (if Christ was not God himself) to make it thought that John the Baptist, by the very fact that he went before the face of Christ, went before the face of God himself, or that by preparing the way for Christ he prepared the way for God himself.

units.la: XVI. Sed fac valere à Christo ad ipsum Deum consequentiam. Id ad locum Malachiæ nihil conducit, nisi eam esse reciprocam docueris, pariterque ab ipso Deo valere ad Christum. Id quod cum opinione Aduersariorum non congruit, Deum à Christo naturâ, loco, & tempore separantium. Agitur enim in loco Malachiæ de paranda via ipsi Deo, non autem de paranda via Christo, siquidem Christus per pronomen meam in verbis parabit viam ante faciem meam, non intelligitur. Non autem intelligitur, si, neque is est qui verba illa loquitur, neque eiusdem cum eo essentiæ. Esto igitur, non potuerit parari via Christo, quin pararetur ipsi Deo. At contendunt Aduersarij potuisse ipsi Deo parari viam, & paratam aliquando fuisse absque Christo, immò antequam Christus esse inciperet: ex quo sequitur nulla necessaria consequentia, ex eo quod paranda via ipsi Deo dicatur apud Malachiam, concludi posse, eam fuisse parandam Christo.
units.tr: XVI. But grant that the inference from Christ to God himself holds. This contributes nothing to the passage in Malachi, unless you show that it is reciprocal, and that it likewise holds from God himself to Christ. That does not agree with the opinion of our opponents, who separate God from Christ in nature, place and time. For in the passage of Malachi the subject is the preparing of a way for God himself, not the preparing of a way for Christ, since Christ is not understood through the pronoun my in the words he shall prepare the way before my face. Nor is he understood, if the one who speaks those words is neither he himself nor of the same essence as he. Grant, then, that a way could not be prepared for Christ without its being prepared for God himself. Our opponents contend that a way could be prepared for God himself, and was at some time prepared, without Christ, indeed before Christ began to exist. From this it follows that, from the fact that a way is said in Malachi to be prepared for God himself, nothing can be concluded by any necessary consequence about its having been prepared for Christ.

units.la: XVII. Non faciam hanc disputationem longiorem. Tantùm obseruabo, quod negari non potest, Deum optimum & sapientissimum perscienter ac prudenter sic mentem suam expressisse vt dixerit ante faciem meam, potius quàm, ante faciem Dominatoris quem queritis. tamen posita sententia Aduersariorum nulla capi animo potest ratio, nullus vsus, cur phrasim illam huic adeò obuiæ antetulerit: nihil enim sic significauit, quod altera ista phrasi non æquè benè significari, potuisse videatur, immò multò melius: pronomen enim illud primæ personæ in verbis ante fa-ciem meam, & facessit negotium Aduersarijs, & nostræ de Christi diuinitate ac, vt ita loquar, identitate cum Deo Israelis sententiæ apertè fauet. Quis igitur credat Deum;cum sine vlla obscuritate & periculo dicere posset. & parabit viam ante faciem Dominatoris quem vos queritis, maluisse dicere obscurè & periculosè & parabit viam ante faciem meam, quasi de industria nos vellet difficultate, aut etiam errore graui implicare? Sic igitur proculdubiò mentem suam significauit, vt insinuaret, Dominatorem illum non diuersum à Deo Israelis Deum putandum esse, sed vnum eundemque cum eo benedictum in secula seculorum,
units.tr: XVII. I will not make this discussion longer. I will only observe what cannot be denied: God, the best and wisest, expressed his mind so knowingly and prudently that he said before my face, rather than before the face of the Lord whom you seek. Yet on the opponents' view of the matter, no reason or use can be conceived for why he preferred that phrase to this obvious one. For by it he signified nothing which the other phrase could not seem to signify equally well, indeed much better. For that first-person pronoun in the words before my face both removes the difficulty for our opponents and openly favours our view of Christ's divinity and, if I may so speak, his identity with the God of Israel. Who, then, would believe that God, when he could say without any obscurity or danger, and he shall prepare the way before the face of the Lord whom you seek, preferred to say obscurely and dangerously and he shall prepare the way before my face, as if he deliberately wished to entangle us in difficulty or even in grave error? He therefore surely signified his mind in this way in order to suggest that the Lord in question is not to be thought different from the God of Israel, but one and the same with him, blessed for ever and ever,

units.la: AMEN,
units.tr: AMEN,

units.la: DISPUTATIO NONA. De Arg. IX. Ex verbis Psalmi xcvii. ṽ. 8. Adorate eum omnes Angeli, laudatis Heb. i. ṽ. 6.
units.tr: Disputation Nine. On Argument IX. From the words of Psalm 97:8, Worship him, all you angels, compared with Hebrews 1:6.

units.la: VATICINIIS prophetarum illud subjungimus quod extat Ps. 97. ṽ. 8. Adorate eum omnes Dij[?], citatum ab Apostolo Heb. 1. 6. his verbis, Adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei. Unde sic argumen-tor.
units.tr: To the prophetic testimonies we add the passage in Psalm 97:8, which the Apostle cites in Hebrews 1:6 in these words, Let all the angels of God worship him. From this I argue as follows.

units.la: Ille quem Ps. 97. ṽ. 8. iubentur adorare omnes Angeli, est Deus Israëlis.
units.tr: The one whom all the angels are commanded to worship in Psalm 97:8 is the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est ille, quem Ps. 97. ṽ. 8. iubeatur adorare omnes Angeli.
units.tr: Christ is the one whom all the angels are commanded to worship in Psalm 97:8.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis. Major nititur testimonio Prophetæ, Minor Apostoli.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The major premise rests on the testimony of the Prophet, the minor on the testimony of the Apostle.

units.la: II. Respondet Socinus dupliciter. Primùm negat majorem, Non, inquit, necesse est verba illa psalmi referre ad unum illum Deum Israelis. Immò id necesse est. Verba enim illa Psalmi sine dubio referuntur, ipso teste Socino, ad illum, qui paulò ante postremo nominatus est; nempe ad Dominum vniuersæ terræ. Atqui Dominus vniuersæ terræ est Iehovah, Deus Israëlis. Id probahis argumentis. Primò autoritate Scripturæ, apud quam elogium Domini vniuersæ terræ proprium est Dei Israëlis nomen, Ios. 3. 11. Ecce, Arca fœderis Domini vniuersa terra antecedet vos per Iordanem. Zach. 4. 14. Isti sunt duo[?] filij olei, qui assistunt Dominatori vniuersæ terræ. Zach. 6. Isti sunt quatuor venti cœli, qui egrediuntur, ut stent coram dominatore omnis terræ. Mich. 4. 13. Denunebis[?] Domino opes eorum, & substantiam eorum Domino vniuersæ universæ terræ. Nonne ex his & similibus locis patet Dominum universæ terræ esse Deum Israelis? Quàm ergo constat verba illa psalmi, Adorate eum omnes Angeli, referri ad Dominum universæ terræ, tam constat ea referri ad Deum Israelis.
units.tr: II. Socinus replies in two ways. First he denies the major premise: It is not necessary, he says, to refer those words of the psalm to that one God of Israel. On the contrary, it is necessary. For those words of the Psalm, as Socinus himself testifies, undoubtedly refer to the one who was named a little before, last of all, namely to the Lord of the whole earth. But the Lord of the whole earth is Jehovah, the God of Israel. I prove this by the following arguments. First, by the authority of Scripture, in which the title "Lord of the whole earth" is applied to the name of the God of Israel: Josh. 3:11, Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of the whole earth will go before you over the Jordan. Zech. 4:14, These are the two sons of oil who stand before the Lord of the whole earth. Zech. 6, These are the four winds of heaven, which go out to stand before the Ruler of all the earth. Mic. 4:13, I will consecrate to the Lord their wealth and their substance to the Lord of the whole earth. Does it not appear from these and similar passages that the Lord of the whole earth is the God of Israel? Therefore, just as it is established that the words of the psalm, Let all the angels worship him, refer to the Lord of the whole earth, so it is established that they refer to the God of Israel.

units.la: III. Ad hoc argumentum planè inuictum videtur Socinus aliquid primò obijcere, deinde respondere. Obijcit, vulgatam editionem latinam, & græcam unde illa fluxit, habere ad Dominum simpliciter. Quod nomen (Hebraicè enim legitur Adon) ita simpliciter & absolutè positum, nimis, inquit, absurdum esset, vt post Iehoua nomen sequeretur, si ad eundem Iehouam referendum esset; cum ipsum nomen per se multò inferius sit nomine Iehoua, & rebus creatis quacunque vel minima dominatione praeditis passim accommodetur. Sed editio græca cum veritate hebræa consentire mihi videtur, Latinæ autem (quam hoc loco, vt alijs innumeris, mendosam esse ipsi Aduersarij non negabunt, (facilè reuincendi si negarent) autoritate non mouemur. Quanquam si ea moueremur, nullum nobis negotium exhiberet Socini obiectio. Nomen enim Adon, etsi per se inferius est nomine Iehouæ, tamen cum absolutè & sine affixo aut adiectione vsurpatur, inferius non est, sed Dei nomen est ea ratione proprium, vt patet ex psal. 114. 7. A facie Domini (heb. Adon) mota est terra. Itaque ei apponi solet nomen Iehouæ, vt Exod. 23. 17. & 34. 23. Esai. 1. 24. & 3. 1. & 10. 16. 33. & 19. 4. Et, vt absolutè positum illud nomen proprium non esset Dei Israëlis, tamen hoc loco idem valeret, ac si scriptum esset Domini omnis terræ. Quis enim non videt eum Dominum, à cuius facie vel fluunt sicut cera montes omnis terræ, vel fluit omnis terra, Dominum esse omnis terræ? Sed fac nomen Adon quomodo vsurpatur hoc loco inferius esse quàm nomen Iehouæ, causam non video cur post Iehouam sequi non potuerit, æquè saltem ac nomen Elohim, quod quamuis Angelis & iudicibus tribuatur nonnunquam, tamen passim nomini Iehouæ subjicitur.
units.tr: III. Against this argument, which seems entirely unanswerable, Socinus first raises an objection and then replies to it. He objects that the Latin Vulgate, and the Greek text from which it flowed, have simply "to the Lord." This name (for in Hebrew it is read Adon), placed so simply and absolutely, would be quite absurd, he says, if it were to be referred to the same Jehovah, since the name itself in its own right is far inferior to the name Jehovah, and is applied everywhere to created things endowed with any, even the smallest, dominion. But the Greek text seems to me to agree with the Hebrew truth, whereas we are not moved by the authority of the Latin edition, which in this place, as in countless others, even our opponents will not deny is faulty (and they could be easily refuted if they did deny it). Yet even if we were moved by it, Socinus's objection would give us no trouble. For the name Adon, although in itself it is inferior to the name Jehovah, nevertheless, when it is used absolutely and without a suffix or addition, is not inferior, but is for that reason a proper name of God, as is clear from Psalm 114:7, At the presence of the Lord (Hebrew Adon) the earth trembled. Accordingly, the name Jehovah is usually added to it, as in Exodus 23:17 and 34:23, Isaiah 1:24, 3:1, 10:16, 33, and 19:4. And even if that absolutely used proper name were not a name of the God of Israel, it would still in this place have the same force as if it had been written Lord of all the earth. For who does not see that the Lord at whose face the mountains melt like wax, or the whole earth melts, is the Lord of all the earth? But suppose the name Adon, as it is used in this place, is inferior to the name Jehovah; I see no reason why it could not follow after Jehovah, at least as well as the name Elohim, which, although sometimes attributed to angels and judges, is nevertheless everywhere placed beside the name Jehovah.

units.la: IV. Sic se habuit obiectio. Respondet autem his verbis, Annon, inquit, cum inter omnes constet, in psalmo isto esse vaticinationem de regno Christi, potuit Christus homo. cui data est omnis potestas in coelo & in terra, tanquam in possessionem regni sui intrans, propheticè descriptus & pronunciatus, merito vocari Dominus universæ terræ? At non quæritur nunc quidem quid dici po[?] tuerit, sed quid scriptum sit in illo psalmo. Aio hoc nomen, Dominus universæ terræ, nomen esse Dei Israelis in Scriptura. Id iam probaui, nec possant negare aduersarij. Aio id nomen in V. T. nisi Deo Israëlis tributum esse nemini. Reuincant me si possunt aliqua instantiâ. Afferre hunc ipsum locum de quo agimus non possunt, quin, aut petitionem, ut loquuntur, principij committant, aut necessaria aliqua re addicant, per Dominum universæ terræ intelligi hoc loco Deum Israëlis, vel non posse, vel non debere, quod nunquam efficient. Unde enim argumentum ducerent? Ab hoc ipso nomine? Id, ut dixi, proprium est Dei Israëlis. Ab antecedentibus & consequentibus? In eis palam est agi de Deo Israëlis. Ab illis rebus quæ de Domino universæ terræ dicuntur in eo psalmo? Nihil de eo dicitur quod non possit dici, quodque adeò non dicatur de Deo Israëlis. Adde quod Dominus universæ terræ nomen est Iehouæ nomine vel in-serius vel non. Si inserius, qui post Iehouæ nomen sequitur Ios. 3. 13? Si non est inferius, qui convenit Christo tantùm homini? Annon etiam convenientius est eo psalmo per Dominum universæ terræ, eum intelligere qui sæpè vocatur Dominus universæ terræ in Scriptura Veteris Testamenti, quique reuera erat, & futurus erat in per-petuum Dominus universæ terræ, quàm eum qui nunquam sic alibi appellatur, quique non erat Dominus universæ terræ, neque suturus erat nisi demum post aliquot secula, siquidem fides habetur Adversarijs? Manet igitur firmum hoc primum argumentum.
units.tr: IV. Such was the objection. He replies with these words: Since it is agreed by all that this psalm contains a prophecy about the kingdom of Christ, could not Christ, the man to whom all authority in heaven and on earth was given, being prophetically described and proclaimed as entering into the possession of his kingdom, rightly be called Lord of the whole earth? But the question now is not what could have been said, but what is written in that psalm. I affirm that this title, Lord of the whole earth, is the name of the God of Israel in Scripture. I have already proved this, and our opponents cannot deny it. I affirm that in the Old Testament this name is ascribed to no one but the God of Israel. Let them refute me, if they can, by some instance. They cannot bring forward this very passage that we are discussing without either begging the question, as they say, or committing themselves to some necessary point: that by "the Lord of the whole earth" in this place the God of Israel is either not able or not obliged to be meant, which they will never establish. For where would they derive their argument? From this very name? As I said, it is proper to the God of Israel. From what precedes and follows? In these the matter is plainly about the God of Israel. From the things said of the Lord of the whole earth in that psalm? Nothing is said of him that could not be said of the God of Israel, and that is not said of the God of Israel. Add that the title Lord of the whole earth is either inferior to the name Jehovah or not. If it is inferior, how does it follow after the name Jehovah, as in Joshua 3:13? If it is not inferior, how does it fit Christ as a mere man? Is it not also more fitting to understand by "the Lord of the whole earth" in that psalm him who is often called the Lord of the whole earth in the Scripture of the Old Testament, and who truly was, and was to be forever, the Lord of the whole earth, than him who is never so called elsewhere, and who was not the Lord of the whole earth, nor was to be so except after some centuries, if the Adversaries are to be believed? Therefore this first argument stands firm.

units.la: V. Alterum ducitur ab omissione conjunctionis copulatiuæ & emphasi repetitionis vocum à facie. Montes sicut cera fluxerunt à facie Domini, à facie Domini universa terra. Quis enim legens hæc verba vacuus præiudicio non videt per Dominum (Iehouam) & Dominum universæ terræ eundem significari? planè ut ps. 114. 7. A facie Domini mota est terra, à facie Dei Iacob, certum est Dominum (Adon) & Deum Iacobi eundem esse.
units.tr: V. The second argument is drawn from the omission of the copulative conjunction and from the emphatic repetition of the words from the face of. The mountains melted like wax from the face of the Lord, from the face of the Lord of the whole earth. For who, reading these words without prejudice, does not see that "the Lord" (Jehovah) and "the Lord of the whole earth" signify the same one? Just as in Psalm 114:7, At the presence of the Lord the earth trembled, at the presence of the God of Jacob, it is certain that "the Lord" (Adon) and the God of Jacob are the same.

units.la: Respondet Socinus, Non esse perpetuum in ipsis sacris literis, ut cum sub eadem structura verborum diversi comprehenduntur, copula, Et, inter eos ponatur, præsertim si alius ab alio pendeat, eique sit subordinatus; ut sine dubio à Iehoua pendet, illique subordinatus est homo Christus Iesus. Sed argumentum nostrum non ducitur à sola omissione copulæ &, sed à tali eius omissione conjuncta cum emphatica repetitione faciei eius à quo terra tremefacta sit, A fa[?]ie Domini, à facie, inquam, Domini totius terrâ: prorsus vt laudato à me loco ps. 114. à facie Domini, à facie, inquam, Dei Iacob. Itaque frustrà responsionem suam conatur firmare exemplo.
units.tr: Socinus replies that it is not a constant rule in the sacred writings itself that when diverse things are included under the same grammatical construction, the conjunction "and" is placed between them, especially if one depends on the other and is subordinate to it; as undoubtedly the man Christ Jesus depends on Jehovah and is subordinate to him. But our argument is not drawn from the omission of the conjunction "and" alone, but from such an omission joined with the emphatic repetition of the face of him from whom the earth was made to tremble, from the face of the Lord, from the face, I say, of the Lord of all the earth: just as in the passage I cited from Psalm 114, from the face of the Lord, from the face, I say, of the God of Jacob. Therefore he vainly tries to confirm his answer by an example.

units.la: VI. Exemplum, inquit, huius rei, quam dico, idque similiter vbi de diuinitate est sermo suppeditare nobis possunt verba Iacobi Patriarchæ Iosepho filio suo benedicentis Gen. 48. 15. & 16. Deus in cuius conspectu ambulauerunt Patres mei Abraham & Isaac, Deus qui pascit me ab adolescentia mea vsque in præsentem diem, Angelus qui eruit me de cunctis malis benedicat &c. vbi nemo negauerit, Angelum postremò nominatum, licet nulla precedente copula, illi Deo, qui ante nominatus est, adiunctum, diuersum tamen ab eo esse. Hoc enim exemplum simile non est, vt cuiuis patet; & tamen causæ nostræ fauet potius quàm obest. Quid enim prohibet dicere tres esse eiusdem Dei descriptiones? Certè constat duabus primis eundem describi, Deus in cuius conspectu ambulauerunt patres mei Abraham & Isaac, Deus qui pascit me ab adolescentia mea vsque in præsentem diem, cur non idem dicamus de tertia, Angelus qui eruit me de cunctis malis? Dubitas? Illum ipsum Angelum audi. Gen. 31. 12. 13. dixit, inquit Iacob, Angelus Dei ad me, &c, vidi omnia quæ fecit tibi Laban. Ego sum Deus Beth-el, vbi vnxisti lapidem, & votum vouisti mihi. Quid clarius? Hoc ipsum confirmat verbum singularis numeri benedicat, nec-non pietas Prophetæ ab omni Idololatria abhorrentis. Quid enim? Inuocassetne vir sanctus ac Dei fœderatus angelum creatum, nec apparentem? Eumne Deo tanquam socium & æqualem adiunxisset? Petiuissetne ab eo, non minus quàm à Deo, benedictionem omnimodam? [?]Eine tam solenne laudis sacrificium, ac spiritualem precum sufficum, non minus quàm ipsi Deo, obtulisset? Hoc mihi non [?]& vllo modo verisimile. Quis etiam, quæso, de cunctis malis temporalibus & æternis (nam qui cuncta dicit nullum excipit) Patriarcham eruit? Quis illius seruator fuit? Hæc confessio, hæc laus, hæc gratiarum actio ei vni debetur, qui Esai. 43. 11. testatur præter se seruatorem esse neminem. Esto igitur conclusum ex absentia copulæ, ex repetitione faciei, ex subintellecto eodem subiecto & verbo sententiæ, ex ipsa re denique quæ clamat Iehouam esse Dominum omnis terræ, per Iehouam & per Dominum omnis terrę eundem esse intelligendum.
units.tr: VI. For an example, he says, of this thing which I speak of, and of the same kind, where the discussion is about divinity, the words of the Patriarch Jacob blessing his son Joseph in Genesis 48:15–16 can supply us: "God, before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has fed me from my youth until this day, the Angel who has redeemed me from all evils, bless..." where no one will deny that the Angel named last, although with no preceding conjunction, is joined to that God who was named before, and yet is different from him. For this example is not similar, as is plain to anyone; and yet it favours our cause rather than harms it. For what prevents us from saying that these are three descriptions of the same God? It is certain that the first two describe the same one: "God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, God who has fed me from my youth until this day." Why should we not say the same of the third, "the Angel who has redeemed me from all evils"? Do you doubt it? Hear that same Angel. In Genesis 31:11–13 Jacob says, the Angel of God spoke to me, etc., I have seen all that Laban has done to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed the stone and vowed a vow to me. What could be clearer? The singular verb bless confirms this, and so does the piety of the Prophet, who abhors all idolatry. For what? Would a holy man, a covenanted servant of God, have invoked a created angel, one who was not even appearing to him? Would he have joined him to God as a partner and an equal? Would he have asked of him, no less than of God, a blessing in every respect? Would he have offered to him, no less than to God himself, so solemn a sacrifice of praise and a spiritual sweet offering of prayers? This to me is not credible in any way. And who, I ask, redeemed the Patriarch from all evils, temporal and eternal (for he who says "all" excepts none)? Who was his saviour? This confession, this praise, this thanksgiving, is due to him alone who testifies in Isaiah 43:11 that there is no saviour besides himself. Let it therefore be concluded, from the absence of the conjunction, from the repetition of "face," from the same subject and verb being understood in the clause, and finally from the very matter, which cries out that Jehovah is the Lord of all the earth, that Jehovah and the Lord of all the earth are to be understood as the same.

units.la: VII. Hoc ipsum arguit numerus singularis pronominum in verbis sequentibus. Propheta enim postquam dixit, Montes sicut cera fluxerunt à facie Domini, à facie Domini omnis terra, subiecit, Annunciauerunt cœli iustitiam eius, & viderunt populi gloriam eius, tanquam de vno loquens, non de duobus. Nam si duos intelligi voluit totis essentiis diuersos, cur non dixit in plurali numero iustitiam eorum, gloriam eorum? Miluitne [?] peccare in grammaticam, quàm distinguere eos, quos à suis lectoribus distingui voluit? Forte pronomina illa ad eorum duorum alterum tantum retulit. Ad quem? Ad Dominum Iehouam? causam igitur vicimus. Nam ad eundem sine dubio referri debent eadem pronomina in verbis sequentibus, Adorate eum omnes Angeli eius, ut cuiuis manifestum est. Ad Dominum (Adon.) omnis terræ? Ergo non referuntur ad Iehouam, ad Deum Israelis toto psalmo descriptum, siquidem, ut volunt Aduersarij, Iehoua non est dominus vniuersæ terræ. Quis hoc credat?
units.tr: VII. The singular number of the pronouns in the following words proves this very point. After saying, "The mountains melted like wax before the face of the LORD, before the face of the Lord of all the earth," the prophet adds, "The heavens declared his righteousness, and all the peoples have seen his glory," speaking as of one, not of two. For if he meant two, wholly different in essence, why did he not say in the plural "their righteousness, their glory"? Would he rather offend against grammar than distinguish those whom he wanted to be distinguished from his readers? Perhaps he referred those pronouns to only one of the two. To which one? To the Lord Jehovah? Then we have won the case. For the same pronouns in the following words, "Worship him, all his angels," must undoubtedly be referred to the same one, as is plain to anyone. To the Lord (Adon) of all the earth? Then they are not referred to Jehovah, the God of Israel described throughout the psalm, since, as our opponents maintain, Jehovah is not Lord of the whole earth. Who could believe this?

units.la: VIII. Quartum argumentum nobis hæc ipsa verba suppeditant, Confundantur omnes qui adorant sculptilia, qui gloriantur in simulachris, (Heb. Elilim, falsis dijs, idolis,) Adorate eum omnes Angeli, heb. Elohim dij. Quis enim religiosè adorandus est, nisi Iehoua? Quis adorandus est ab omnibus dijs, nisi is qui est Deus Deorum, hoc est, κατ' ἐξοχὴν [?] Deus? Quis omnibus sculptilibus, simulachris, idolis, fallis dijs opponitur, nisi is qui natura Deus est?
units.tr: VIII. The fourth argument is supplied by these very words: "Let all be confounded who worship graven images, who glory in idols" (Heb. elilim, false gods, idols), "worship him, all gods" (Heb. Elohim, gods). For who is to be worshipped religiously except Jehovah? Who is to be worshipped by all gods except the one who is God of gods, that is, God par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν]? Who is set against all graven images, idols and false gods, except the one who is God by nature?

units.la: IX. Quintum argumentum nobis dant verba prima vers. 10. Quoniam tu Dominus (Heb. Iehoua) altissimus super omnem terram. Continent enim rationem cur vocatus sit Dominus omnis terræ, & quidem Dominus tantus, ut ab eius conspectu montes colliquescant. Quorsum enim illud Quoniam, si ratio non redditur alicuius rei iam dictæ? Quid autem dictu fuit in illo psalmo rationi illi congruentius, quàm Elogium Domini vniuersæ terræ? De eodem igitur subiecto Elogium illud intelligi debet, de quo eius expositio & ratio dicitur. (Alioquin in ratiocinio Prophetæ quatuor essent termini) Hæc autem de Iehoua dicitur. Ergo & illud.
units.tr: IX. The fifth argument is given by the first words of verse 10: "For you, Lord (Heb. Jehovah), are most high over all the earth." For these words contain the reason why he is called Lord of all the earth, and indeed so great a Lord that the mountains melt away at his presence. For why the "For," if no reason is being given for something already said? What could be said in that psalm more fitting to such a reason than the title Lord of all the earth? That title, therefore, must be understood of the same subject of whom the explanation and the reason are spoken. (Otherwise there would be four terms in the prophet's reasoning.) But this is said of Jehovah. Therefore that title is too.

units.la: X. Hinc etiam licet ita argumentari. Altissimus super omnem terram est Iehoua, Deus Israelis. Dominus vniuersæ terræ, à cuius facie montes sicut cera funduntur, est altissimus superom-nem terram. Dominus igitur omnis terræ, &c, est Iehoua, Deus. Israëlis. Præmissarum neutra potest negari. Non major. Eam enim esse universaliter veram patet ex veri. ultimo ps. 83. Et cognoscant quod tu, cuius nomen est Iehoua, solus es altissimus super omnem terram. Si Iehoua solus est altissimus super omnem terram, nullus est altissimus super omnem terram nisi Iehoua: ac proinde quicunque est altissimus super omnem terram is est Iehoua. Nec minor. Est enim ipsa per se satis manifesta. Nam quid est esse altissimum, seu, ut multi vertunt, excelsum (est enim Heb. עליון, quæ vox usurpatur de Christo psal. 89. 27. de populo Israëlitico Deut. 26. 19. & 28. 1. de Templo 1. Reg. 9. 8. &2. Chron. 7. 21. de porta quadam templi 2. Reg. 15. 35. & 2. Chr. 23. 20. de canistro Gen. 40. 17. deque aliis rebus. Quod noto ne quam latebram in ea voce quærant Aduersarij.) Quid, inquam, est esse altissimum super omnem terram? Annon esse Dominum omnis terræ, & quidem dominum tanta auctoritate & potentia præditum, ut ab eius facie montes sicut cera liquescant & fluant, & cum omnes non modo reges, sed etiam dij seu Angeli adorare teneantur?
units.tr: X. From this one may also argue as follows. Jehovah, the God of Israel, is most high over all the earth. The Lord of the whole earth, at whose face the mountains flow like wax, is most high over all the earth. Therefore the Lord of all the earth, etc., is Jehovah, the God of Israel. Neither premise can be denied. Not the major: that it is universally true is plain from Psalm 83, "that they may know that you, whose name is Jehovah, alone are most high over all the earth." If Jehovah alone is most high over all the earth, then no one is most high over all the earth except Jehovah, and so whoever is most high over all the earth is Jehovah. Nor the minor: it is plain enough in itself. For what is it to be most high, or, as many render it, exalted (the Hebrew is 'elyon [עליון], a word used of Christ in Ps. 89:27, of the Israelite people in Deut. 26:19 and 28:1, of the Temple in 1 Kings 9:8 and 2 Chron. 7:21, of a certain gate of the temple in 2 Kings 15:35 and 2 Chron. 23:20, of a basket in Gen. 40:17, and of other things). I note this so that our opponents may not look for some hiding place in that word. What, I say, is it to be most high over all the earth? Is it not to be Lord of all the earth, and indeed a lord endowed with such authority and power that the mountains melt and flow like wax at his face, and when not only kings but even gods or angels are bound to worship him?

units.la: XI. Possumus etiam argumentum ducere à reliquis eiusdem vers. 10. verbis, valde exaltatus es super omnes Deos. Illa enim rationem, cur eum omnes dij seu Angeli adorare debeant, continere, neminem tam cæcum esse arbitror qui non videat. Cur adorandus est ab omnibus Dijs? quia super omnes Deos valdè exaltatus est. Optima ratio: ex qua intelligitur, quem tenentur adorare omnes dij, illum ipsum esse qui est valdè super omnes deos exaltatus. Hic autem est Iehoua, ut patet ex verbis proximè antecedentibus, Quoniam tu Dominus (Iehoua) altissimus super omnem terram, valdè exaltatus es super omnes Deos.
units.tr: XI. We can also draw an argument from the remaining words of the same verse 10: "you are exalted far above all gods." I think no one is so blind as not to see that these words contain the reason why all gods or angels ought to worship him. Why is he to be worshipped by all gods? Because he is exalted far above all gods. An excellent reason, from which it is understood that the one whom all gods are bound to worship is the very one who is exalted far above all gods. Now this is Jehovah, as is clear from the words immediately preceding: "For you, Lord (Jehovah), are most high over all the earth, you are exalted far above all gods."

units.la: XII. Denique hunc omnes Angeli adorare jubentur, cuius regnum majestas adventus potentia, &c, eo psalmo describuntur. Hic autem est Deus Israëlis: Iehoua enim sexies appellatur, nec aliud occurrit aut describitur in eo psalmo nomen, nisi quod semel Dominus universæ terræ vocatur, quod esse Dei Israëlis Elogium, & cum no mine Iehoua tanquam synonymum interdum jungi, nemo est tam hospes in Scriptura ut nesciat. Certum est neminem versibus primis quatuor, neminem versibus ultimis quinque describi præter Iehouam. Quatuor autem versibus intermediis, & Iehoua semel nominatur [?], & manifesta est inchoatæ. descriptionis continuatio, & nihil prorsus est unde vel probabiliter colligi possit interruptionem esse descriptionis versibus antecedentibus inceptae & sequentibus absolvendae, atque adeo defcriptionem esse alterius cuiusdam, qui non sit Iehoua.
units.tr: XII. Finally, the one whom all angels are commanded to worship is the one whose kingdom, majesty, coming, power, and so on, are described in that psalm. Now this is the God of Israel. Jehovah is named six times, and no other name occurs or is described in that psalm, except that once he is called Lord of all the earth, which is an epithet of the God of Israel; and that the name Jehovah is sometimes joined with it as a synonym, no one is so much a stranger to Scripture as not to know. It is certain that no one except Jehovah is described in the first four verses, or in the last five. But in the four intermediate verses Jehovah is named once [?], and the continuation of the description begun is plain, and there is absolutely nothing from which it could be probably inferred that the description begun in the preceding verses is interrupted and to be completed in the following, and that the description is therefore of some other person who is not Jehovah.

units.la: XIII. Sic satis confirmata videtur major argumenti nostri. Minor, quia diserto testimonio Apostoli nititur, ab Aduersariis negari nequit. Stat igitur firma conclusio. Et tamen Socinus alteram responsionem attulit & exposuit pluribus verbis, quæ quomodo ad majorem vel minorem syllogismi nostri accommodari possit, non satis intelligo. Eam tamen, nequid prætermissum à nobis videatur, expendam non illibenter.
units.tr: XIII. Thus the major premise of our argument seems sufficiently confirmed. The minor, since it rests on the express testimony of the Apostle, cannot be denied by our opponents. The firm conclusion therefore stands. Yet Socinus brought forward a second answer and set it out at some length, though I do not understand well enough how it could be applied to either the major or the minor of our syllogism. Nevertheless, lest anything be thought to have been passed over by us, I will examine it not unwillingly.

units.la: XIV. Is primum hoc veluti fundamentum jacit, Certum est, inquit, Christo homini, & quidem ut homini, id est sine ulla consideratione, quod in se habeat essentialiter aliquam naturam divinam, adorationem ab ipsis angelis deberi. Contrarium pro certo habeo, habentque omnes propemodum Christiani. Sed pergat, postquam, addit, à Deo, propter sui ipsius demissionem & obedientiam usque ad mortem crucis, nomen supra omne nomen est adeptus. Quæ verba cum præcedentibus pugnant: nam & magnitudo demissionis atque obedientiæ ex obedientis divinitate æstimata est, nec fuisset nomen supra omne nomen adeptus qui sic obediit, si nihil nisi homo fuisset. Audiamus tamen quomodo hoc probet Adversarius. Id enim, inquit, apertissime constat ex verbis Pauli ad Philip. c. 2. ubi hac de re agit. Diserte enim ibi dicit: Deum propter prædictas causas, Iesum Christum supra modum evexisse, & dedisse illi nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, ut in nomine Iesu omne genu flectatur cælestium, terrestrium, & subterraneorum. Iam quemadmodum obedientia sine dubio ad humanam tantum naturam pertinet, sic exaltationem propter obedientiam, ad humanam tantum naturam pertinere necesse est. Præterquam quod certum alioqui est, divinam naturam exaltari vere ac proprie non posse, & consequenter necesse est, ut adoratio, quæ Christo ab omnibus cælestibus, & sic ab ipsis angelis, propter istam exaltationem, debetur, ei, ut homini debeatur. Hæc ne nobis iterum reponantur discutia-mus.
units.tr: XIV. He first lays down this as a kind of foundation: "It is certain," he says, "that adoration is due from the angels themselves to Christ as man, and indeed as man, that is, without any consideration of whether he has in himself essentially some divine nature." I hold the contrary as certain, and almost all Christians hold it. "But let him proceed," he adds, "after he obtained from God the name above every name, on account of his own self-abasement and obedience even to the death of the cross." These words clash with what precedes: for the greatness of the humbling and obedience is measured by the divinity of the one who obeys, nor would one who obeyed in this way have obtained the name above every name if he had been nothing but man. Let us hear, nevertheless, how the adversary proves this. "For this," he says, "is most clearly established from the words of Paul in Philippians chapter 2, where he treats of this matter. For there he plainly says that God, for the reasons mentioned, exalted Jesus Christ beyond measure and gave him the name which is above every name, so that in the name of Jesus every knee of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth should bow. Now just as obedience undoubtedly pertains to human nature alone, so exaltation on account of obedience must pertain to human nature alone. Besides, it is otherwise certain that the divine nature cannot truly and properly be exalted, and consequently the adoration which is owed to Christ by all in heaven, and so by the angels themselves, on account of that exaltation, must be owed to him as man." Let us discuss these points, lest they be thrown back at us again.

units.la: XV. Obedientia, inquit, sine dubio ad humanam tantum naturam pertinet. Rationem requiro. Nullam affert. Ego obedientiam distinguo. Alia est debita & necessaria, ac proinde inferioris siue naturæ siue personæ erga superiorem. Alia est indebita & merè voluntaria, ac proinde potest ab æquali, immò à superiori proficisci. Hæc cur ad diuinam etiam naturam aliquomodo pertinere non possit causam non video, qui lego in vulgata editione latina Jos. 10. 14. Deum obedinisse [?] voci hominis, versione non prorsus repudianda, congruit enim non modo cum verbis hebræis quæ exprimit, sed etiam cum verbis Josuæ tanquam præceptum, non tanquam votum conceptis, Sol siste [?] gradum in Gibeon, & Luna in valle Aialon. Sed missa editione illa Latina, Nonne Deus in historia creationis inducitur imperans? unde psalmes ps. 33. 9. Ipse dixit & facta sunt: Ipse mandauit & creata sunt. Nonne in eadem historia Deus inducitur imperata faciens, atque adeo obediens? Id non potest negari. pertinuit sine dubio talis obedientia ad naturam diuinam, tam certè quàm ipsa effectio seu creatio mundi. Jam autem huius generis esse obedientiam illam Filii Dei, ob quam supra modum exaltatus dicitur, ipse Apostolus autor est. Qui, inquit, cum in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est esse se æqualem Deo, sed exinaniuit seipsum formam serui accipiens, &c. Quorsum obseruat eum in forma Dei fuisse, non duxisse rapinam esse se æqualem Deo, semetipsum exinaniuisse, nisi ut significet indebitam mereque voluntariam illam obedientiam fuisse? Quid enim? teneturne æqualis obedire ac seruire æquali? Nonne etiam ista exinanitio suiipsius & formæ serui acceptio obedientia memorabilis fuit? Atqui illa antecessit formam serui, quam ὁ λόγος [?] verbum simul cum natura humana sumpsisse in virginis utero probauimus lib. 1. Disp. v. Ex quo sequitur eam obedientiam ad Dei formam seu diuinam verbi naturam pertinuisse.
units.tr: XV. "Obedience," he says, "without doubt pertains only to human nature." I ask for the reason, and he gives none. I distinguish obedience. One kind is owed and necessary, and so belongs to a lesser being, whether nature or person, toward a superior. Another kind is not owed and is purely voluntary, and so can come from an equal, or even from a superior. I do not see why this second kind could not in some way pertain also to the divine nature. I read in the Latin Vulgate, Joshua 10:14, that God "obeyed the voice of a man." That rendering is not to be wholly rejected, since it agrees not only with the Hebrew words it translates but also with the words of Joshua, which are framed as a command and not as a wish: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and Moon in the valley of Aijalon." But setting that Latin version aside, is God not portrayed as commanding in the account of creation? Hence Psalm 33:9: "He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created." In the same account, is God not portrayed as doing what is commanded, and so as obeying? That cannot be denied. Such obedience certainly pertained to the divine nature, just as surely as the making or creating of the world itself. Now the Apostle himself vouches that the obedience of the Son of God, on account of which he is said to be exalted above measure, is of this kind. "Who," he says, "being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant," and so on (Phil. 2:6-7). Why does he note that he was in the form of God, and did not think equality with God a robbery, and emptied himself, unless to show that this obedience was undue and purely voluntary? For is an equal bound to obey or serve an equal? Was not this self-emptying and taking of the form of a servant also a notable act of obedience? But that act preceded the form of a servant, which we proved in book 1, disputation 5, the Word [ὁ λόγος] took on together with human nature in the Virgin's womb. From this it follows that this obedience pertained to the form of God, that is, to the divine nature of the Word.

units.la: XVI. Porrò nescio cur Socinus dicere naturam maluit quàm personam, cum sit in confesso personam proprie, non autem naturam, obedire. Principium, ut loquuntur, quod obedit est persona, quo obedit est natura, vel aliquod organum. Idem de passionis ac de obedientiæ subiecto vel principio dicendum. Æstimatur autem obedientia ex dignitate personæ obedientis, seu illa ex natura seu aliunde pendeat. Fac ergo ad naturam tantùm humanam pertinere Christi obedientiam, pertinebit ad eam ut ad principium quo, ad personam verò Christi ut ad principium quod, ex cuius dignitate debet æstimari. Huius autem personæ dignitatem Apostolus non in natura humana sed in forma Dei, & æqualitate cum Deo collocat, ex quibus exinanitionis humiliationis atque obedientiæ magnitudo metienda fuit. Itaque seponere considerationem formæ Dei & æqualitatis cum Deo ab obedientia Christi & exaltatione quæ illius magnitudini proportione respondet, Apostolo repugnat, illique ipsi obedientiæ est iniuriosum. Hoc autem fecit Socinus, cum ab ea seponit considerationem naturæ diuinæ, sine qua nec forma Dei vera esse potest, nec æqualitas cum Deo intelligi. Idem de exaltatione dicendum, quæ passim Deo tribuitur in Scriptura, & Filio Dei [ira?] propter obedientiam conuenit secundum naturam humanam, vt si ab eo formam Dei & æqualitatem cum Deo, hoc est, diuinam naturam detraxeris, eadem opera, & pondus eius obedientiæ ademeris, & magnitudinem exaltationis. Itaque ei quidem homini adoratio debetur, vbicunque suam naturam humanam visendam præbet, non tamen vt homini, sed potius vt Deo, immensa autoritate & potentia prædito, quæ tam diuinam arguunt naturam, quâ non olim eius infirmitas carnem arguebat nostræ similem. Vno verbo, adorari debet ab omnibus Angelis, quia, vt habetur hoc ipso psalm., valde super omnes angelos est exaltatus. Videsis Disp. iv. §. xi. necnon lib. i. Disp. v.
units.tr: XVI. Moreover, I do not know why Socinus preferred to say "nature" rather than "person," when it is agreed that it is the person, and not the nature, who obeys. The principle, as they put it, is that the person is that which obeys, and the nature, or some organ, is that by which it obeys. The same must be said of the subject or principle of suffering and of obedience. Obedience, however, is valued by the dignity of the obeying person, whether that dignity depends on nature or on something else. Suppose, then, that Christ's obedience pertained only to his human nature. It would pertain to that nature as the principle by which, but to the person of Christ as the principle which obeys, and from whose dignity the obedience must be measured. The Apostle, however, places the dignity of this person not in his human nature but in the form of God and in equality with God, and by these the greatness of his self-emptying, humiliation and obedience was to be measured. Therefore to set aside the consideration of the form of God and of equality with God from Christ's obedience and exaltation, which correspond in proportion to its greatness, is to contradict the Apostle and to do wrong to that very obedience. Socinus did this when he separated from it the consideration of the divine nature, without which the form of God cannot be true, nor equality with God be understood. The same must be said of the exaltation, which is attributed to God throughout Scripture, and which belongs to the Son of God on account of his obedience according to his human nature. If you take from him the form of God and equality with God, that is, the divine nature, you will at the same stroke remove the weight of that obedience and the magnitude of the exaltation. Therefore, indeed, adoration is owed to that man wherever he shows his human nature to be seen, yet not as to a man, but rather as to God, endowed with immense authority and power, which argue a divine nature, whereas once his weakness argued a flesh like ours. In a word, he is to be adored by all the angels, because, as is said in this very psalm, he is exalted far above all the angels. See disputation 4, §11, and also book 1, disputation 5.

units.la: XVII. Sed pergamus in verbis Socini expendendis. Ex quo, inquit, sequitur, adorationem illam in ipso Christo non terminari: sed in Deum, qui illum exaltauit, ab ipso Christo transfire, ut in ultimum suum scopum. Quid? vultne Socinus non adorari Christum, nisi adoratione relatiua, propter alienam dignitatem, seu personam quam repræsentet? Nam si quâ talis persona ob insitam & propriam & perpetuam dignitatem adoratur, vt alibi confitetur Socinus, adoratio illa in ipsius persona terminatur. At Deus illum exaltauit. Certè. Ergo cum adoratur, adoratio non terminatur in eius persona. Non sequitur. Exaltauit etiam Deus Reges terræ, tamen ciuilis adoratio, quæ Regi exhibetur homini quidem, non tamen vt homini, sed vt Regi, (quod enim alicui homini vt homini conuenit, omni homini conuenire necesse est) terminatur in regis persona. Concilat enim personæ, cui inest, adorationem summa ὑπεροχὴ[?] & dignitas, non qua refertur ad dantem, sed qua subditos immenso quodam interuallo supereminet vndecunque sit.
units.tr: XVII. "But let us go on to weigh Socinus's words. From this," he says, "it follows that that adoration does not terminate in Christ himself, but passes from Christ, as to its ultimate goal, to God who exalted him." What? Does Socinus wish that Christ should be adored only with a relative adoration, on account of another's dignity, or the person whom he represents? For if such a person is adored on account of an inborn, proper and perpetual dignity, as Socinus elsewhere confesses, that adoration terminates in the person himself. But God exalted him. Certainly. Therefore, when he is adored, the adoration does not terminate in his person. That does not follow. God also exalted kings of the earth, yet civil honour, which is paid to a king as a man, but not as a man, rather as a king (for what belongs to a man as a man must belong to every man), terminates in the king's person. For it gives to the person in whom it dwells the highest pre-eminence and dignity, not in relation to the one who gives it, but in that by which he rises above his subjects by an immense interval, wherever he may be.

units.la: XVIII. Addit, Et sic verissimum esse, in Christo & per Christum, & quidem vt hominem, ipsum Deum adorari, id est, eo ipso, quod Christus homo adoretur, adorari ipsum Deum. Est id quidem verissimum nostræque fidei maximè consentaneum, eo ipso quod Christus adoratur, adorari Deum, quia Christus idem est Deus; immò Patrem, quia Pater est in ipso, & ipse in Patre, quo fit vt alter absque altero neque videri neque adorari possit. Sed si ponas Christum & Deum personas esse totis essen-tijs diuersas, non video cur alter ab altero separatim adorari non possit.
units.tr: XVIII. He adds: "And so it is most true that in Christ and through Christ, and indeed as man, God himself is adored; that is, by the very fact that Christ as man is adored, God himself is adored." This is indeed most true and most consonant with our faith: by the very fact that Christ is adored, God is adored, because Christ is the same God; indeed the Father too, because the Father is in him and he in the Father, so that the one cannot be seen or adored without the other. But if you hold that Christ and God are persons wholly different in essence, I do not see why the one cannot be adored separately from the other.

units.la: XIX. Sed quonam tandem ista spectant, & quid ad dissol-uendum argumentum nostrum faciunt? Id sequentibus verbis conatur explicare, Et consequenter, quamuis Christus non sit ille vnus Deus, rectissimè tamen nouam illam quandam adorationem, quam ab omnibus Angelis, in Christi regno, illi vni Deo tribuendam Propheta praedixerat, de ipsius Christi adoratione ab auctore epistola ad Hebraeos expositam, siue ad ipsum Christum accommodatam fuisse. Certè enim nouus prorsus vnum illum Deum adorandi modus angelis fuit, eum in Christo homine adorare. Si de Christi regno agitur in eo psalmo, Christus est Iehoua, de huius enim vnius regno agitur, vt legenti patet. Nouitatis adorationis, vel modi adorandi nullum indicium in Prophetæ verbis deprehendere potui: Nec intelligo, quomodo adoratio, quam ab angelis illi vni Deo tribuendam Propheta praedixerat, rectissimè de ipsius Christi adoratione exponi possit, si Christus nullo modo est ille vnus Deus. Vt igitur pressius agamus, In verbis huius psalmi ab auctore Epistolæ ad Hebraeos laudatis, adorate eum omnes Angeli, vel, adorent eum omnes Angeli, quem significat pronomen, Eum? quem jubentur adorare Angeli? Idemne apud Prophetam & Apostolum intelligi debet, an vero alius apud Prophetam, alius apud Apostolum? Si idem, Christus est vnus ille Deus: Hunc enim apud Prophetam intelligi hæc Socini responsio concedit. Si alius, estne bona expositio, cum quod de vno dictum est, de alio exponitur?
units.tr: XIX. But to what, pray, do these things pertain, and what do they contribute to dissolving our argument? He tries to explain this in the words that follow: "And consequently, although Christ is not that one God, nevertheless that new kind of adoration, which the Prophet had foretold would be paid by all the angels in Christ's kingdom to that one God, was most rightly expounded by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews as concerning the adoration of Christ himself, or was applied to Christ himself." Certainly it was a wholly new mode of adoring that one God for the angels, namely, to adore him in Christ as man. If the psalm speaks of Christ's kingdom, Christ is Jehovah, for it is of this one kingdom that it speaks, as is plain to any reader. I could find no sign of a novelty of adoration, or of a new mode of adoring, in the Prophet's words. Nor do I understand how the adoration which the Prophet foretold the angels would pay to that one God could be most rightly expounded of Christ's own adoration, if Christ is in no way that one God. So that we may press the point more closely: in the words of this psalm, which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews cites, "adore him, all you angels," or "let all the angels adore him," what does the pronoun "him" signify? Whom are the angels commanded to adore? Must the same be understood in the Prophet and in the Apostle, or is one thing meant in the Prophet and another in the Apostle? If the same, then Christ is that one God, for this Socinian answer grants that it is he who is meant in the Prophet. If another, is it a good exposition when what was said of one is expounded of another?

units.la: X X. Quid quod Apostolus citat hoc testimonium, vt probet Christum ab omnibus angelis esse adorandum, ad quod probandum nihil prorsus valet, si in eo de Christo non agitur, sed de Deo Israelis tota essentia diuerso à Christo? Debere omnes Angelos Iehouam seu Deum Israelis adorare nemo eorum ad quos diuinùs auctor scribebat, in dubium vocabat. Quærebatur tantùm de Filio, tenerenturne etiam eum adorare omnes Angeli? teneri docet hoc vno testimonio, Adorent eum omnes Angeli, quod nemo non videt ad id probandum ineptum esse, si in eo vt habetur in psalmo, pronomen eum illum vnum Deum significat; isque est tota essentia diuersus à Filio.
units.tr: X X. Moreover, the Apostle cites this testimony to prove that Christ must be adored by all the angels. Yet it proves nothing for that purpose if the passage is not about Christ at all but about the God of Israel, whose whole essence is different from Christ's. None of those to whom the divinely inspired author was writing doubted that all angels ought to adore Jehovah, that is, the God of Israel. The only question was about the Son: were all angels bound to adore him as well? The Apostle teaches that they are, by this one testimony, "Let all the angels adore him." Anyone can see that this would be an unsuitable proof if, in the psalm as it stands, the pronoun "him" meant that one God, whose essence is different from the Son's.

units.la: XXI. Respondet Socinus, Apostolum non tam hoc loco probare, quàm docere velle; id est, occultum psalmi verborum sensum quendam patefacere. Non tam, inquit, probare vult, Respondeant quæsò rotundè Aduersarij, vultne Apostolus, probare, necne? Si probare vult, faciunt eum inepte argumentantem, qui scilicet vt probet, Iesum tantum hominem præstantiorem esse omnibus angelis, affert pro argumento mandatum quo iubentur omnes Angeli adorare Deum Israelis. Agitur, inquiet aliquis, de Christo qui non est Deus Israelis, & tu Apostole testimonium affers, in quo agitur de Deo Israelis. Quæritur, an debeant omnes Angeli adorare quendam hominem, & tu affers testimonium, in quo iubentur adorare Deum illum vnum creatorem mundi. Hoccine est argumentari? Si non vult probare, errat igitur ipse Socinus cum sic loquitur, Resp. ad Classis. 1. Arg. 1. V[?]jcki. Patet hoc ex ipso initio disputationis, vbi diserte Thesis ipsa exponitur: qua talis est: Dei filius tanto præstantior angelis est tactus [?], quanto excellentius, præ illis, nomen hæreditauit. Hæc, inquam est Thesis, quam Apostolus sibi probandam proponit. Errant etiam omnes interpretes, qui summo consensu Apostolum probare velle asserunt: & quorsum tot testimonia laudaret, si nihil probare vellet?
units.tr: XXI. Socinus replies that "the Apostle wants not so much to prove this point as to teach it; that is, to disclose a certain hidden sense of the words of the psalm." "Not so much to prove," he says. I ask our opponents to answer plainly: does the Apostle want to prove the point or not? If he wants to prove it, they make him an inept arguer. To prove that Jesus, a mere man, is superior to all the angels, he offers as his argument the command by which all the angels are bidden to adore the God of Israel. Someone will say: "The passage is about Christ, who is not the God of Israel, and yet you, Apostle, cite a testimony in which the God of Israel is the subject. The question is whether all the angels ought to adore a certain man, and you cite a testimony in which they are commanded to adore that one God, the creator of the world." Is that how one argues? If he does not want to prove the point, then Socinus himself is wrong when he speaks thus (Resp. ad Classis 1, Arg. 1, V[?]jcki): "This is clear from the very beginning of the disputation, where the thesis itself is expressly set out, and it is this: the Son of God has been made as much superior to the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than they. This, I say, is the thesis which the Apostle sets out to prove." All the interpreters who with almost unanimous agreement assert that the Apostle wants to prove something are also wrong. And why would he cite so many testimonies if he wanted to prove nothing?

units.la: XXII. Docet, inquit, id est occultum psalmi verborum sensum patefacit. Sensus Scripturæ distingui solet in Literalem & Mysticum: Illum verba proximè significant, Hunc res per verba significatæ. Verum igitur literalis est iste scilicet occultus quidam sensus, an mysticus? Si literalis, vel proprius est, vel figuratus. Non figuratus: quænam enim figura, quis tropus esse posset in pronomine eum, in verbis, adorent eum omnes angeli Dei? (De huius enim vnius pronominis significatione instituta est hæc nostra disputatio.) Et cur sensum comminiscerentur figuratum, cum obuius est: proprius verus & appositus? Nec etiam proprius. Quis enim credat illius pronominis in verbis illis minimè ambiguis[?] duos esse sensus literales & proprios? Sola enim ambiguitas, quæ hinc omnis abest, gignere potest plures sensus proprios. Certè pronomen illud Eum referri non potest, nisi ad eum qui est in versibus antecedentibus nominatus. Nullus autem nominatus fuit præter Iehouam. Non potest igitur referri nisi ad Iehouam. Mysticum quominus dicant eum sensum esse vel ipsorum dogma prohibet. Facerent enim adorationem Dei typum adorationis Christi, atque adeo ipsum Deum typum Christi, quod esset Christum supra ipsum Deum extollere. Pluris enim fieri debet res adumbrata quam eius typus vel umbra. Vno verbo: vel colligi potest, occultus iste sensus ex psalmi verbis, vel non potest. Si non potest, pro vero sensu haberi non debet. Si potest, ostendant qua ratione ex verbis Prophetæ deduci possit.
units.tr: XXII. "He teaches," he says, "that is, he discloses a hidden sense of the words of the psalm." The sense of Scripture is customarily divided into literal and mystical. The former is what the words signify directly; the latter is what is signified by the things expressed in the words. Is this hidden sense, then, literal or mystical? If literal, it is either proper or figurative. Not figurative: what figure or trope could there be in the pronoun "him" in the words "let all the angels of God adore him"? (For our whole dispute concerns the meaning of this one pronoun.) And why should they invent a figurative sense when the plain, true, and fitting proper sense lies ready to hand? Nor is it a proper sense either. For who would believe that this pronoun, in those words which are by no means ambiguous, has two literal and proper senses? Only ambiguity, and there is none of that here, can produce several proper senses. Certainly the pronoun "him" cannot refer to anyone except the one named in the preceding verses. But the only one named was Jehovah. It can therefore refer only to Jehovah. As for the claim that it is a mystical sense, their own doctrine forbids them to say so. For they would then make the adoration of God a type of the adoration of Christ, and so make God himself a type of Christ, which would be to exalt Christ above God himself. For the thing foreshadowed must be valued more highly than its type or shadow. In a word: either this hidden sense can be gathered from the words of the psalm, or it cannot. If it cannot, it ought not to be held as the true sense. If it can, let them show by what reasoning it can be deduced from the words of the prophet.

units.la: XXIII. Socinus Ait, si modo velimus, verba quæ ex psalmo citat, de uno illo Deo dicta esse, divini huius scriptoris hanc mentem fuisse, ut, quia iam inter peritiores Hebræos constaret, de futuro Christo, eoque in sui regni possessionem mittendo, in eo psalmo, sub illius unius Dei nomine, agi, non quia Christus futurus esset ille unus Deus, sed quia unius illius Dei personam singulari quadam ratione sustinere debebat, ex eiusdem psalmi verbis, sua interpretatione adhibita, persuaderet, Christum ab ipsis angelis adorandum esse; nempe quia non modo multa alia, quæ in eo psalmo de illo uno Deo dicuntur, ut facile{y} concedebant, ad quos scribebat (scribebat enim ut ex epistola patet ad Iudæos quidem, sed iam Christianos factos) ad Christum accommodanda essent: sed etiam illud ipsum, quod ibi habetur de omnibus angelis illum unum Deum adoraturis. Id quod non facile cuiquam persuaderi potest, nisi, præter id, quod verisimile est, si multa alia, quæ de illo uno Deo ibi dicuntur, idcirco ad Christum accommodanda sunt, quia de ipsius Christi regno sub unius illius Dei nomine ibi agitur, hoc etiam ad Christum accommodandum esse, quod nimirum ad ipsius regnum pertinet, accedat quoque ipsius scriptoris auctoritas & prophetiæ spiritus, quo patefacit, quale & quantum [?]vera sit Christi regnum, & quam divina prorsus & perfectissima ratione Christus illius unius Dei personam sustineat. In quibus verbis quædam sunt reprehensione digna. Illud primò, quod affirmat, Iam inter peritiores Hebræos constitisse, de futuro Christo, eoque in sui regni possessionem mittendo, in eo psalmo, sub illius unius Dei nomine agi. Unde enim id rescire potuit? Num id scripsit Aposto-
units.tr: XXIII. Socinus says: "If we are willing to take the words he cites from the psalm as having been spoken of that one God, the mind of this divine writer was that, since it was already established among the more learned Hebrews that in that psalm, under the name of that one God, there is talk of the future Christ, and of his being sent to take possession of his kingdom, he might persuade them, by applying his own interpretation to the words of the same psalm, that Christ is to be adored by the angels themselves. The reason is that they readily granted that not only many other things said in that psalm of that one God, to whom he was writing (for he was writing, as the letter makes plain, to Jews who had by then become Christians), had to be applied to Christ, but also that very thing which is there said about all the angels adoring that one God. This cannot easily be persuaded to anyone, unless, besides the probability that if many other things said there of that one God are therefore to be applied to Christ, because the psalm there speaks under the name of that one God of the very kingdom of Christ, this too, which pertains to his kingdom, must likewise be applied to Christ; and besides the authority of the writer himself and the spirit of prophecy, by which he discloses how true and how great Christ's kingdom is, and how divinely and most perfectly Christ sustains the person of that one God." In these words there are certain things worthy of blame. First, what he affirms: that it was already established among the more learned Hebrews that in that psalm, under the name of that one God, there is talk of the future Christ and of his being sent to take possession of his kingdom. But from where could he have known this? Did the Apostle, or any other author of that age, write it?

units.la: {y} lus, aut aliquis alius author illius seculi? Num id potest probabili aliqua ratione conjici? Nullo modo. Temeraria igitur est assertio, & homine veritatis studioso & modesto prorsus indigna. At, inquit alibi, nisi ijs, ad quos hic author epistolam eam scribebat, vel iam constitissent, vel facile constare potuissent, Scriptura locos ab ipso allatos ad Messiam pertinere, frustra & prorsus ridiculè eos attulisset. Bene, vel jam constitisset, vel facilè constare potuisset. Vitat enim illa disjunctione, eius, quod scire non poterat, affirmandi temeritatem. Sed unde constare? Ex attenta locorum illorum, ut habentur in Veteri Testamento, & citantur ab Apostolo, inspectione? Nihil verius. Ita enim Berœenses scrutabantur Scripturas, an hæc ita se haberent. Si ita sentit, concedit locos illos vim per se id probandi habuisse, ad quod probandum adducti sunt. Sin verò (quæ videtur eius mens hoc loco) vult eos locos vim illam ex sese non habuisse, sed ex hypothesi opinionis jam ab Hebræis præconceptæ, atque adeo argumenta esse, ut loquuntur, ad hominem, graviter errat, & quantum in ipso est, Dei & Apostoli sapientiam vehementer obscurat. Atque hoc est illud alterum, quod in verbis Socini reprehendendum putavi. Nam si huius, de quo agimus, testimonij vis in opinione præjudicata Hebræorum, ad quos Apostolus scribebat, sita erat, ea per se, & apud alios nulla erat. Si autoritate Apostoli nitebatur, consultius fecisset Apostolus, si testimonium non laudasset. Nam qui laudat testimonium præ se fert, se testimonij illius vi niti velle, non sua unius autoritate. Itaque deludi lector videtur, cum citatur testimonium, cuius vis pendet ab autoritate citantis.
units.tr: {y} Could it be conjectured by any probable reasoning? In no way. The assertion is therefore rash, and wholly unworthy of a man who studies the truth and is modest. But he says elsewhere: "Unless those to whom this author was writing had already been persuaded, or could easily be persuaded, that the Scripture passages he cited pertain to the Messiah, he would have cited them in vain and quite ridiculously." Good: "had already been persuaded or could easily be persuaded." By that disjunction he avoids the rashness of affirming what he could not know. But persuaded from where? From a careful examination of those passages as they stand in the Old Testament and as the Apostle cites them? Nothing could be truer. For the Bereans searched the Scriptures, to see whether these things were so. If that is his view, he concedes that the passages had in themselves the force to prove what they were brought forward to prove. But if (which seems to be his mind at this point) he means that those passages did not have that force of themselves, but only from the hypothesis of an opinion already conceived among the Hebrews, and so are, as they say, arguments ad hominem, then he gravely errs, and as far as in him lies, he greatly obscures the wisdom of God and of the Apostle. And this is the second thing I thought worth criticizing in Socinus's words. For if the force of this testimony, the one we are discussing, lay in a prejudiced opinion of the Hebrews to whom the Apostle was writing, then in itself and among others it had no force at all. If it rested on the authority of the Apostle, the Apostle would have done better not to cite the testimony at all. For whoever cites a testimony gives the impression that he wishes to rest on the force of that testimony, not on his own authority alone. Thus the reader seems to be deceived when a testimony is cited whose force depends on the authority of the one citing it.

units.la: XXIV.[?] Quod bis dicit, de Christi regno sub unius illius Dei nomine agi in eo psalmo, argumentum nostrum confirmat. Sic enim colligo. Ille cuius de regno agitur in eo psalmo est Iehova, ut patet ex toto psalmo. Christus est ille de cuius regno agitur in eo psalmo, confitente Socino. Ergo Christus est Iehova. Hoc primum. Deinde, quid significant illa verba, sub unius illius Dei nomine, vel ut alibi loquitur, sub ipsius Dei persona? significant ne unius illius Dei nomine Christum significari, per ipsius Dei personam Christum intelligi? Hoc ipsum est quod dicimus, nimirum per Iehovam in eo psalmo intelligendum esse Filium Dei. Cum igitur Propheta sic loquitur, Iehova Regnat, &c. quàm verbum, regnat, regnum Christi significat, tam nomen, Iehova, personam Christi significat.
