Si aliud volunt illis verbis aduersarij, id quale sit nobis quæso exponant. Nam si sub vnius illius Dei nomine agitur de Christi regno, vt se habet regnum quod ibi describitur ad regnum Christi, sic se habet vnus ille Deus ad Christum. Sed regnum illud est regnum Christi. Ergo vnus ille Deus est Christus. Nempe vt regnum illud se habet ad regnum Christi, sic se habet rex illius regni ad Christum. Si regnum Christi eo psalmo describitur, certè Rex qui eo psalmo describitur est Christus. Is autem Rex est Iehoua. Iehoua igitur est Christus.
units.tr: XXIV. That he says twice that the reign of Christ is spoken of in that psalm under the name of that one God supports our argument. My inference runs like this. He whose reign is spoken of in that psalm is Jehovah, as is plain from the whole psalm. Christ is he whose reign is spoken of in that psalm, as Socinus admits. Therefore Christ is Jehovah. This is the first point. Next, what do the words under the name of that one God, or as he says elsewhere, under the person of God himself, mean? Do they mean that Christ is signified by the name of that one God, and that Christ is understood through the person of God himself? That is exactly what we say: that in that psalm Jehovah must be understood as the Son of God. So when the prophet speaks thus, Jehovah reigns, etc., just as the word reigns signifies the kingdom of Christ, so the name Jehovah signifies the person of Christ. If our opponents mean something else by those words, I ask them to explain what it is. For if the reign of Christ is described under the name of that one God, then the one God stands to Christ as the kingdom described there stands to the kingdom of Christ. But that kingdom is the kingdom of Christ. Therefore that one God is Christ. Indeed, just as that kingdom stands to the kingdom of Christ, so the king of that kingdom stands to Christ. If the kingdom of Christ is described in that psalm, certainly the King who is described in that psalm is Christ. But that King is Jehovah. Therefore Jehovah is Christ.

units.la: XXV. Fortasse lucem aliquam isti locutioni ratio, quam subjicit, aspergat. Quia, inquit, Christus vnius illius Dei perso-nam singulari quadam ratione sustinere debebat. Sed contrà est. Implicat enim potius quàm explicat, euertit potius quàm con-firmat. Nam si sub vnius illius Dei nomine, si sub ipsius Dei persona regnum Christi describitur, non iam Christus sustinet aut repræsentat personam vnius Dei in eo psalmo, sed contrà potius, vnus ille Deus sustinet & repræsentat personam Christi. Adde quod, quoties in Veteri Testamento sub vnius nomine aut persona, alter describitur, toties ille huius typus est. Porrò typus est vmbra eius cuius est typus. Est ne igitur vnus ille Deus typus Christi tantùm hominis? Dicant etiam nobis Aduersarij, si Christus non est vnus ille Deus, cur Spiritus Sanctus eum voluisset sub vnius illius Dei nomine & persona toto psalmo, toties, tam constanter, tamque periculosè describere? Nam si sub ipsius Christi vel Filij nomine regnum Christi descripsisset, æquè profuisset ædificationi Ecclesiæ, nec nobis ansam præbuisset credendi Christum eundem esse Iehouam, hoc est, vt putant Aduersarij, grauiter errandi. Haud enim decet prudentiam & charitatem Dei, innocenti atque æquè vtili locutioni, aliam admodum impropriam obscuram & periculosam anteponere. Quis enim legens hæc verba, Iehoua regnat, &c, si regnum Christi describi putat, non statim inducatur vt credat, per Iehouam Christum significari?
units.tr: XXV. Perhaps the explanation he offers will throw some light on that phrase. Because, he says, Christ had to sustain the person of that one God in a singular way. But the opposite is true. The reasoning entangles rather than explains, and overturns rather than confirms. For if the reign of Christ is described under the name of that one God, under the very person of God, then Christ no longer sustains or represents the person of the one God in that psalm; rather, the one God sustains and represents the person of Christ. Add that whenever in the Old Testament one is described under the name or person of another, the former is a type of the latter. But a type is a shadow of that of which it is a type. Is that one God, then, a type of Christ, who is merely a man? Let our opponents also tell us this: if Christ is not that one God, why would the Holy Spirit have wished to describe him so constantly, so often, and so hazardously under the name and person of that one God throughout the psalm? For if he had described the reign of Christ under the name of Christ or of the Son himself, it would have been equally useful for the edification of the Church, and would not have given us occasion to believe that Christ is the same as Jehovah, which, as our opponents think, is a serious error. For it is not fitting for the wisdom and charity of God to prefer, to an innocent and equally useful form of speech, another that is wholly improper, obscure and dangerous. Indeed, who reading these words, Jehovah reigns, etc., if he thinks the reign of Christ is being described, would not at once be led to believe that Christ is signified by Jehovah?

units.la: XXVI. Ad hæc, Si de Christi regno in eo psalmo agitur sub vnius illius Dei nomine, necesse est, vt vnius illius Dei nomen aliquo modo significet Christum regnantem seu regem. Vel igitur eum significat proximè, & proprié, vel figuratè, vel me[?]diante[?] uno illo Deo, proximo scilicet suo significato, vel per consequentiam quandam. Si primum, Christus est unus ille Deus. Secundum autem dici non potest: Nunquam enim auditum est in Ecclesia nomen unius illius Dei proprium nempe Jehouam, usurpari aliquando figuratè, aut Christum dici in Scriptura Jehouam figuratè. Tertium quoque nemo dixerit: ita enim nomen esset signum ipsius Dei, ipse Deus Christi. Id quod absurdum esse perspicuum est. Pluris enim fieri debet res significata quàm eius signum. Quartum ne dicant error ipsorum vetat. Eo enim admisso ab ipso Deo ad Christum non valet consequentia. Is enim, si credimus Aduersarijs, & regnauit olim, & ab Angelis adoratus est antequam Christus esset, & potest hodieque adorari Christo non adorato.
units.tr: XXVI. Besides, if the reign of Christ is spoken of in that psalm under the name of that one God, the name of that one God must in some way signify Christ as reigning or as king. Either it signifies him directly and properly, or figuratively, or through that one God as its immediate meaning, or by some consequence. If the first, Christ is that one God. But the second cannot be said: for it has never been heard in the Church that the proper name of that one God, namely Jehovah, is used figuratively, or that Christ is called Jehovah figuratively in Scripture. Nor would anyone say the third: for then the name would be a sign of God himself, and God himself would be the sign of Christ. That this is absurd is plain. For the thing signified ought to be of greater account than its sign. As for the fourth, their own error forbids them to claim it. For if that is granted, the inference from God himself to Christ does not hold. For, if we believe our opponents, that God both reigned in former times and was adored by the angels before Christ existed, and can even today be adored without Christ being adored.

units.la: XXVII. Praeterea, constat inter nos de Christi regno in eo psalmo agi. Certum est autem in eo non agi de regno, nisi quatenus agitur de regnante, cuius persona, praesentia, majestas, potentia, honor, judicia describuntur. Si igitur agitur de regno Christi, agitur utique de Christo regnante. Quo igitur nomine insignitur? Ipso nomine tetragrammato Dei Israelis proprio, idque sexies in illo psalmo. Potuitne distinctius doceri, Christum eundem esse Deum Israelis? Quid Aduersarij? Negantne ista? verbo eludunt, sub nomine, inquiunt, unius illius Dei agitur de Christi regno. Sub ipsius Dei persona vaticinatio est de Christi regno. Quid erit tam clarum tamque disertum, ad quod tale effugium accommodari non possit? Fac describi in aliqua historia Regis Galliae praesentiam & Majestatem, verbis, ut par est, magnificentissimis, eius etiam nomine proprio aliquoties expresso. Nonne deridendum se praeberet, qui contenderet sub ipsius Regis nomine & persona descriptum esse munus praecipui eius ministri? Idem tamen hic faciunt Aduersarij. Mirum si suae istius subtilitatis eos non suppudet. Ita enim magnificè describitur regnantis Dei majestas in hoc psalmo, ut nunquam alibi describatur magnificentius.
units.tr: XXVII. Moreover, it is agreed between us that the reign of Christ is spoken of in that psalm. But it is certain that the psalm does not speak of a reign except insofar as it speaks of the one who reigns, whose person, presence, majesty, power, honour and judgements are described. If, then, the reign of Christ is spoken of, surely Christ reigning is spoken of. By what name, then, is he designated? By the very tetragrammaton, the proper name of the God of Israel, and that six times in that psalm. Could it have been taught more distinctly that Christ is the same God as the God of Israel? What do our opponents say? Do they deny these things? They evade the point with words: they say that the reign of Christ is spoken of under the name of that one God, and that the prophecy about the reign of Christ is under the person of God himself. What is so clear and so plainly stated that such an escape cannot be applied to it? Suppose that in some history the presence and majesty of the King of France were described in suitably magnificent words, with his proper name also mentioned several times. Would not someone deserve to be laughed at if he contended that under the name and person of the king the office of his chief minister was described? Yet our opponents do the same here. It would be strange if they were not ashamed of such subtlety. For the majesty of God reigning is so magnificently described in this psalm that it is nowhere described more magnificently.

units.la: XXVIII. Age verò etiam expendamus, quam subjunxit Socinus, rationem. Quia, inquit, unius illius Dei personam singulari quadam ratione sustinere debebat. Hoc multis locis Socinus inculcat, nec tamen explicat. Itaque quo sensu ab eo dicatur, non satis intelligo. Nam per illum unum Deum solum Patrem intelligit. Quæro igitur, quomodo vnius illius Dei, hoc est, Dei Patris, personam Christus sustineat? An vt Histrio personam Regis in scena? Non hoc, opinor, dixerint, Christo nimis injuriosum. Quanquam sic tam dici posset, non modo Iehoua, sed etiam Deus Pater, quàn histrio rex appellatur dum regis personam agit. Quid ergo sibi volunt, cum dicunt, Christum diuina & perfectissima ratione sustinere personam ipsius Dei? Christum profiteri se esse ipsum Deum, eique professioni congruenter loqui & agere? (persimili enim sensu dicere solemus, consulem consulis, iudicem iudicis, oratorem oratoris personam sustinere.) Quare igitur eum negant ipsum Deum esse? Christum non suas, sed alienas partes agere, ac perinde, vel ipsum loqui & agere, vel de ipso Scripturam, ac si ipse Deus esset, cum tamen non esset ipse Deus? At si, vel Christus de se, vel Scriptura de ipso perinde loquitur ac si esset ipse Deus, vnde habent eum non esse ipsum Deum? Aut cur suos & conceptus & sermones, non exigunt ad normam sacrarum literarum, præsertim cum de eo sit quæstio, quem nemo novit nisi Pater? Tres personas pro triplici munere vnus Christus sustinet, Prophetæ, Sacerdotis, Regis. Quando ergo alienam ipsius Dei personam sustinet? cum partes agit Prophetæ? aut Sacerdotis? Non arbitror. Hæ enim nullo modo sunt partes Patris. An igitur eam sustinet cum regio munere fungitur? Certè etiam tunc suas ipsius, non alienas Patris, partes sustinet. Verissimè enim ac propriissimè loquendo Rex est, suumque regnum, non alienum, administrat.
units.tr: XXVIII. Come now, let us also weigh the argument Socinus added. Because, he says, Christ had to sustain the person of that one God in a singular way. Socinus insists on this at many points, yet he does not explain it. So I do not sufficiently understand in what sense he says it. For by that one God he means the Father alone. I ask, then, how Christ sustains the person of that one God, that is, of God the Father. As an actor sustains the role of a king on the stage? I do not think they would say this, as it would be too injurious to Christ. Although in that sense not only Jehovah but also God the Father could be called an actor, as an actor is called a king while he plays the part of a king. What, then, do they mean when they say that Christ sustains the person of God himself in a divine and most perfect way? That Christ professes that he is God himself, and speaks and acts in accordance with that profession? (For we commonly say in a similar sense that a consul sustains the person of a consul, a judge that of a judge, an orator that of an orator.) Why, then, do they deny that he is God himself? That Christ does not play his own part but another's, and that he either speaks and acts as if he were God himself, or Scripture speaks of him as if he were God himself, although he is not God himself? But if either Christ speaks of himself, or Scripture speaks of him, as though he were God himself, whence do they have that he is not God himself? Or why do they not require their own conceptions and words to be measured by the rule of the holy writings, especially since the question concerns one whom no one knows except the Father? Christ alone sustains three persons in his threefold office: of prophet, priest and king. When, then, does he sustain the alien person of God himself? When he plays the part of prophet? Or of priest? I think not. For these are in no way the parts of the Father. Does he then sustain it when he exercises the kingly office? Certainly even then he sustains his own part, not the Father's alien one. For, speaking most truly and most properly, he is King, and administers his own kingdom, not another's.

units.la: XXIX. Fortè volunt Christum sustinere ipsius Dei, hoc est, Patris personam, quomodo magistratus vulgò dicitur sustinere personam principis, seu Regis. Sed omnia ferè dissimilia sunt. Primùm Regis est ius dicere subditis, quod cum ipse per semetipsum facere non possit, creat magistratus, per quos id faciat, quique istis regij muneris partibus tanquam eius ministri, &, vt ita dicam, vicarii defungantur. Itaque quæcunque ad regem pertinent, ea non suo nomine sed regio, non sua auctoritate sed regia, non tanquam sua ipsius, sed tanquam aliena, vt fideles ministros decet, administrant. Ministri enim sunt regis, non reges, eorum non est regnum, non thronus, non potestas regia, non Majestas, non ministri & serui regis. Christi dispar ratio est. Regnat enim cum Patre similiter, immò pariter. Eius sunt descriptionis continuatio, & nihil prorsus est unde vel probabiliter colligi possit interruptionem esse descriptionis versibus antecedentibus inceptæ & sequentibus absoluendæ, atque adeo descriptionem esse alterius cuiusdam, qui non sit Jehoua.
units.tr: XXIX. Perhaps they want Christ to sustain the person of God, that is, of the Father, just as a magistrate is commonly said to sustain the person of the prince or king. But almost everything here is unlike. First, it is the king's right to declare the law to his subjects. Since he cannot do this in person, he creates magistrates through whom he may do it, and these discharge the parts of royal office as his ministers and, so to speak, his vicars. Therefore whatever belongs to the king, they administer not in their own name but in the royal name, not by their own authority but by the royal authority, not as their own but as belonging to another, as faithful ministers should. For they are the king's ministers, not kings. The kingdom, the throne, the royal power and majesty are not theirs, and they are the king's ministers and servants. Christ's case is different. For he reigns with the Father in like manner, indeed equally. The passage is a continuation of the description, and there is nothing at all from which it could even probably be inferred that there is an interruption of the description begun in the preceding verses and to be completed in the following, and that the description is therefore of some other person who is not Jehovah.

units.la: XIII. Sic satis confirmata videtur major argumenti nostri. Minor, quia dicto testimonio Apostoli nititur, ab Aduersariis negari nequit. Stat igitur firma conclusio. Et tamen Socinus alteram responsionem attulit & expositionem pluribus verbis, quæ quo-modo ad majorem vel minorem syllogismi nostri accommodari possit, non satis intelligo. Eam tamen, nequid prætermissum à nobis videatur, expendam non illibenter.
units.tr: XIII. In this way the major premise of our argument seems sufficiently confirmed. The minor premise rests on the testimony of the Apostle just cited, and so cannot be denied by our opponents. The conclusion therefore stands firm. Yet Socinus offered a second response and exposition, in many words, and I do not clearly see how it can be applied to either the major or the minor premise of our syllogism. Nevertheless, lest anything seem to have been passed over by us, I shall examine it willingly enough.

units.la: XIV. Is primùm hoc veluti fundamentum jacit, Certum est, inquit, Christo homini, & quidem ut homini, id est sine ulla consideratione, quod in se habeat essentialiter aliquam naturam divinam, adorationem ab ipsis angelis deberi. Contrarium pro certo habeo, habentque omnes propemodum Christiani. Sed pergat, postquam, addit, à Deo, propter sui ipsius demissionem & obedientiam usque ad mortem crucis, nomen supra omne nomen est adeptus. Quæ verba cum præcedentibus pugnant: nam & magnitudo demissionis atque obedientiæ ex obedientis dignitate æstimata est, nec fuisset nomen supra omne nomen adeptus qui sic obediit, si nihil nisi homo fuisset. Audiamus tamen quomodo hoc probet Aduersarius. Id enim, inquit, apertissimè constat ex verbis Pauli ad Philip. c. 2. vbi hac de re agit. Diserte enim ibi dicit: Deum propter prædictas causas, Jesum Christum supra modum euexisse, & dedisse illi nomen, quod est supra omne nomen, vt in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, cœlestium, terrestrium, & subterraneorum. Iam quemadmodum obedientia sine dubio ad humanam tantùm naturam pertinet, sic exaltationem propter obedientiam, ad humanam tantùm naturam pertinere necesse est. Præterquam quòd certum alioqui est, divinam naturam exaltari vere ac proprie non posse, & consequenter necesse est, vt adoratio, quæ Christo ab omnibus cœlestibus, & sic ab ipsis angelis, propter istam exaltationem, debetur, ei, vt homini debeatur. Hæc ne nobis iterum reponantur discutiamus.
units.tr: XIV. He first lays this down as a foundation: "It is certain," he says, "that adoration is owed by the angels themselves to Christ as man, and indeed as man, that is, without any consideration of whether he has in himself essentially some divine nature." I hold the contrary as certain, and almost all Christians hold it too. But let him go on: "after he was exalted by God, on account of his own humbling and obedience unto the death of the cross, he obtained the name which is above every name." These words clash with what precedes. For the greatness of his humbling and obedience is estimated from the dignity of the one who obeys, and one who had obeyed in this way would not have obtained the name above every name if he had been nothing but a man. Let us hear, however, how the adversary proves his point: "For this is most plainly established," he says, "by the words of Paul to the Philippians, chapter 2, where he treats of this matter. For there he clearly says that God, on account of the aforesaid causes, exalted Jesus Christ beyond measure and gave him the name which is above every name, so that in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth and under the earth. Now just as obedience without doubt pertains only to the human nature, so the exaltation on account of obedience must pertain only to the human nature. Besides, it is otherwise certain that the divine nature cannot truly and properly be exalted; and consequently it is necessary that the adoration which is owed to Christ by all heavenly beings, and so by the angels themselves, on account of that exaltation, is owed to him as man. Let us discuss these points, lest they be thrown at us again."

units.la: XV. Obedientia, inquit, sine dubio ad humanam tantùm naturam pertinet. Rationem requiro. Nullam affert. Ego obedientiam distinguo. Alia est debita & necessaria, ac proinde inferioris siue naturæ siue personæ erga superiorem. Alia est indebita & merè voluntaria, ac proinde potest ab æquali, immò à superiori proficisci. Hæc cur ad diuinam etiam naturam aliquomodo pertinere non possit causam non video, qui lego in vulgata editione latina Jos. 10. 14. Deum obedivisse voci hominis, versione non prorsus repudianda, congruit enim non modo cum verbis hebraeis quæ exprimit, sed etiam cum verbis Josuæ tanquam præceptum, non tanquam votum conceptis, Sol siste[?] gradum in Gibeon, & Luna in valle Aialon. Sed missa editione illa Latina, Nonne Deus in historia creationis inducitur imperans? unde psaltes ps. 33. 9. Ipse dixit & facta sunt: Ipse mandavit & creata sunt. Nonne in eadem historia Deus inducitur imperata faciens, atque adeo obediens? Id non potest negari. pertinuit sine dubio talis obedientia ad naturam divinam, tam certè quàm ipsa effectio seu creatio mundi. Jam autem huius generis esse obedientiam illam Filij Dei, ob quam supra modum exaltatus dicitur, ipse Apostolus autor est. Qui, inquit, cum in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est esse se æqualem Deo, sed exinaniuit seipsum formam servi accipiens, &c. Quorsum observat eum in forma Dei fuisse, non duxisse rapinam esse se æqualem Deo, semetipsum exinaniuisse, nisi ut significet indebitam merèque voluntariam illam obedientiam fuisse? Quid enim? teneturne æqualis obedire ac servire æquali? Nonne etiam ista exinanitio suiipsius & formæ servi acceptio obedientia memorabilis fuit? Atqui illa antecessit formam servi, quam ὁ λόγος[?] verbum simul cum natura humana sumpsisse in virginis utero probavimus lib. 1. Disp. v. Ex quo sequitur eamobedientiam ad Dei formam seu divinam verbi naturam pertinuisse.
units.tr: XV. "Obedience," he says, "without doubt pertains only to the human nature." I ask for the reason; he gives none. I distinguish obedience. One kind is owed and necessary, and so belongs to an inferior, whether by nature or by person, toward a superior. Another kind is not owed but purely voluntary, and so can proceed from an equal, or even from a superior. I do not see why this kind could not pertain in some way also to the divine nature. I read in the Latin Vulgate, Josh. 10. 14, that God obeyed the voice of a man. That version is not to be wholly rejected, for it agrees not only with the Hebrew words it renders but also with Joshua's words, which were framed as a command, not as a wish: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the valley of Aijalon." But setting aside that Latin edition: is not God in the account of creation introduced as commanding? Hence the psalmist, Ps. 33. 9: "He spoke and they were made; he commanded and they were created." In the same account is God not introduced as doing what was commanded, and so as obeying? This cannot be denied. Such obedience pertained without doubt to the divine nature, as surely as the very effecting or creation of the world did. Now the Apostle himself vouches that the obedience of the Son of God, on account of which he is said to have been exalted beyond measure, is of this kind. "Who," he says, "though he was in the form of God, did not consider being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant," and so on. Why does he note that he was in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal to God, and emptied himself, unless to signify that this obedience was not owed but purely voluntary? For what? Is an equal bound to obey and serve an equal? Was not this self-emptying and taking of the form of a servant also a notable obedience? But surely it preceded the form of a servant, which the Word [ὁ λόγος] took together with human nature in the Virgin's womb, as we proved in book 1, disputation 5. From this it follows that that obedience pertained to the form of God, that is, to the divine nature of the Word.

units.la: XVI. Porrò nescio cur Socinus dicere naturam maluit quàm personam, cum sit in confesso personam proprie, non autem naturam, obedire. Principium, ut loquuntur, quod obedit est persona, quo obedit est natura, vel aliquod organum. Idem de passionis ac de obedientiæ subiecto vel principio dicendum. Æstimatur autem obedientia ex dignitate personæ obedientis, seu illa ex natura seu aliunde pendeat. Fac ergo ad naturam tantùm humanam pertinere Christi obedientiam, pertinebit ad eam ut ad principium quo, ad personam verò Christi ut ad principium quod, ex cuius dignitate debet æstimari. Huius autem personæ dignitatem Apostolus non in natura humana sed in forma Dei, & æqualitate cum Deo collocat, ex quibus exinanitionis humiliationis atque obedientiæ magnitudo metienda fuit. Itaque seponere considerationem formæ Dei & æqualitatis cum Deo ab obedientia Christi & exaltatione quæ illius magnitudini proportione respondet, Apostolo repugnat, illique ipsi obedientiæ est injuriosum. Hoc autem fecit Socinus, cum ab ea seponit consideratione naturæ divinæ, sine qua nec forma Dei vera esse potest, nec æqualitas cum Deo intelligi. Idem de exaltatione dicendum, quæ passim Deo tribuitur in Scriptura, & Filio Dei ira[?] propter obedientiam conuenit secundum naturam humanam, vt si ab eo formam Dei & æqualitatem cum Deo, hoc est, divinam naturam detraxeris, eadem opera, & pondus eius obedientiæ ademeris, & magnitudinem exaltationis. Itaque ei quidem homini adoratio debetur, vbicunque suam naturam humanam visendam præbet, non tamen vt homini, sed potius vt Deo, immensa auctoritate & potentia prædito, quæ tam divinam arguunt naturam, quàm olim eius infirmitas carnem arguebat nostræ similem. Vno verbo, adorari debet ab omnibus Angelis, quia, vt habetur hoc ipso psalm[?], valde super omnes angelos est exaltatus. Videsis Disp. iv. §. xi. necnon lib. i. Disp. v.
units.tr: XVI. Further, I do not know why Socinus preferred to say "nature" rather than "person", since it is agreed that the person, not the nature, properly obeys. The principle, as they say, which obeys is the person; the means by which it obeys is the nature, or some organ. The same must be said of the subject or principle of suffering and of obedience. Obedience is estimated from the dignity of the obeying person, whether that dignity depends on nature or on something else. Grant, then, that Christ's obedience pertains only to the human nature; it will pertain to that nature as the principle by which, but to the person of Christ as the principle who obeys, and from whose dignity it must be estimated. The Apostle locates the dignity of this person not in the human nature but in the form of God and equality with God, from which the magnitude of the emptying, humbling and obedience was to be measured. Therefore to set aside consideration of the form of God and equality with God from the obedience of Christ and from the exaltation which corresponds in proportion to its magnitude is to contradict the Apostle and to do injury to that very obedience. Socinus did this when he set aside from it the consideration of the divine nature, without which the form of God cannot be real, nor equality with God be understood. The same must be said of the exaltation, which is attributed to God throughout Scripture and which befits the Son of God on account of obedience according to the human nature. So if you take from him the form of God and equality with God, that is, the divine nature, you at the same time remove the weight of that obedience and the magnitude of the exaltation. Thus, indeed, adoration is owed to that man wherever he presents his human nature to be seen; yet it is owed not to him as a man but rather as to God, endowed with immense authority and power, which argue a divine nature just as his former weakness argued flesh like ours. In a word, he must be adored by all the angels, because, as is said in this very psalm, he has been exalted far above all the angels. See disp. 4, §11, and also book 1, disp. 5.

units.la: XVII. Sed pergamus in verbis Socini expendendis. Ex quo, inquit, sequitur, adorationem illam in ipso Christo non terminari: sed in Deum, qui illum exaltauit, ab ipso Christo transfire, vt in vltimum suum scopum. Quid? vultne Socinus non adorari Christum, nisi adoratione relatiua, propter alienam dignitatem, seu personam quam repræsentet? Nam si quâ talis persona ob infinitam[?] & propriam & perpetuam dignitatem adoratur, vt alibi confitetur Socinus, adoratio illa in ipsius persona terminatur. At Deus illum exaltauit. Certè. Ergo cum adoratur, adoratio non terminatur in eius persona. Non sequitur. Exaltauit etiam Deus Reges terræ, tamen ciuilis adoratio, quæ Regi exhibetur homini quidem, non tamen vt homini, sed vt Regi, (quod enim alicui homini vt homini conuenit, omni homini conuenire necesse est) terminatur in regis persona. Concilat enim personæ, cui inest, adorationem summa ὑπεροχὴ[?] & dignitas, non qua refertur ad dantem, sed qua subditos immenso quodam interuallo super-eminet vndecunque sit.
units.tr: XVII. But let us go on to weigh Socinus's words. "From this," he says, "it follows that this adoration does not terminate in Christ himself, but passes from Christ, as its ultimate goal, to God, who exalted him." What? Does Socinus want Christ to be adored only with a relative adoration, on account of another's dignity, or of the person he represents? For if such a person is adored on account of an infinite, proper and perpetual dignity, as Socinus elsewhere confesses, that adoration terminates in the person himself. But God exalted him. Certainly. Therefore, when he is adored, the adoration does not terminate in his person. That does not follow. God also exalted the kings of the earth, yet the civil honour shown to a king, a man indeed but shown not as to a man but as to a king (for what belongs to someone as a man must belong to every man), terminates in the king's person. For it confers on the person in whom it resides the highest preeminence [ὑπεροχή] and dignity, not in the sense that it is referred to the one who gives it, but in the sense that he stands far above his subjects by an immense interval, from whatever source that comes.

units.la: XVIII. Addit, Et sic verissimum esse, in Christo & per Christum, & quidem vt hominem, ipsum Deum adorari, id est, eo ipso, quod Christus homo adoretur, adorari ipsum Deum. Est id quidem verissimum nostraeque fidei maximè consentaneum, eo ipso quod Christus adoratur, adorari Deum, quia Christus idem est Deus; immò Patrem, quia Pater est in ipso, & ipse in Patre, quo fit vt alter absque altero neque videri neque adorari possit. Sed si ponas Christum & Deum personas esse totis essentijs diuersas, non video cur alter ab altero separatim adorari non possit.
units.tr: XVIII. He adds: "And so it is most true that God himself is adored in Christ and through Christ, and indeed as man: that is, by the very fact that Christ as man is adored, God himself is adored." This is indeed most true and wholly consistent with our faith, that by the very fact that Christ is adored, God is adored, because Christ is the same God; indeed the Father is adored, because the Father is in him and he in the Father, so that the one can neither be seen nor adored without the other. But if you hold that Christ and God are persons wholly different in essence, I do not see why one cannot be adored separately from the other.

units.la: XIX. Sed quonam tandem ista spectant, & quid ad dissoluendum argumentum nostrum faciunt? Id sequentibus verbis conatur explicare, Et consequenter, quamvis Christus non sit ille vnus Deus, rectissimè tamen nouam illam quandam adorationem, quam ab omnibus Angelis, in Christi regno, illi vni Deo tribuendam Propheta praedixerat, de ipsius Christi adoratione ab auctore epistola ad Hebraeos expositam, siue ad ipsum Christum accommodatam fuisse. Certè enim nouus prorsus vnum illum Deum adorandi modus angelis fuit, eum in Christo homine adorare. Si de Christi regno agitur in eo psalmo, Christus est Iehoua, de huius enim vnius regno agitur, vt legenti patet. Nouitatis adorationis, vel modi adorandi nullum indicium in Prophetae verbis deprehendere potui: Nec intelligo, quomodo adoratio, quam ab angelis illi vni Deo tribuendam Propheta praedixerat, rectissimè de ipsius Christi adoratione exponi posset, si Christus nullo modo est ille vnus Deus. Vt igitur pressius agamus, In verbis huius psalmi ab auctore Epistolae ad Hebraeos laudatis, adorate eum omnes Angeli, vel, adorent eum omnes Angeli, quem significat pronomen, Eum? quem iubentur adorare Angeli? Idemne apud Prophetam & Apostolum intelligi debet, an vero alius apud Prophetam, alius apud Apostolum? Si idem, Christus est vnus ille Deus: Hunc enim apud Prophetam intelligi haec Socini responsio concedit. Si alius, estne bona expositio, cum quod de vno dictum est, de alio exponitur?
units.tr: XIX. But to what end does all this bear, and how does it help to dissolve our argument? He tries to explain this in the following words: "And consequently, although Christ is not that one God, nevertheless that new kind of adoration, which the Prophet had foretold would be paid by all the angels in the kingdom of Christ to that one God, was most rightly expounded by the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews as referring to the adoration of Christ himself, or was fitted to Christ himself. For it was certainly a wholly new mode of adoring that one God for the angels, to adore him in Christ the man." If the psalm is speaking of the kingdom of Christ, then Christ is Jehovah, for it is of the kingdom of this one God that it speaks, as anyone who reads it can see. I could find no sign of any novelty of adoration, or of a new mode of adoring, in the Prophet's words. Nor do I understand how the adoration which the Prophet foretold the angels would pay to that one God could be rightly expounded as the adoration of Christ himself, if Christ is in no way that one God. So, to press the matter more closely: in the words of this psalm, which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews cites, "Let all the angels adore him" (or "let all the angels adore him"), whom does the pronoun "him" signify? Whom are the angels commanded to adore? Must it be understood in the same sense by the Prophet and by the Apostle, or is it one sense in the Prophet and another in the Apostle? If the same, then Christ is that one God, for the response of Socinus concedes that this is what is meant in the Prophet. If different, is it a good exposition to explain of another what has been said of one?

units.la: XX. Quid quod Apostolus citat hoc testimonium, vt probet Christum ab omnibus angelis esse adorandum, ad quod probandum nihil prorsus valet, si in eo de Christo non agitur, sed de Deo Israelis tota essentia diuerso à Christo? Debere omnes Angelos Iehouam seu Deum Israelis adorare nemo eorum ad quos diuinus auctor scribebat, in dubium vocabat. Quærebatur tantùm de Filio, tenerenturne etiam eum adorare omnes Angeli? teneri docet hoc uno testimonio, Adorent eum omnes Angeli, quod nemo non videt ad id probandum ineptum esse, si in eo vt habetur in psalmo, pronomen eum illum vnum Deum significat; isque est tota essentia diuersus à Filio.
units.tr: XX. Moreover, the Apostle cites this testimony to prove that Christ is to be adored by all the angels; yet it proves nothing at all for this purpose if the passage is not speaking of Christ but of the God of Israel, whose whole essence is different from Christ's. No one among those to whom the divine author was writing called in doubt that all the angels ought to adore Jehovah, that is, the God of Israel. The question was only about the Son: whether all the angels were also bound to adore him? That they are bound, he teaches from this single testimony, "Let all the angels adore him," which everyone sees to be unsuitable for proving the point if the pronoun "him", as it stands in the psalm, signifies that one God, whose essence is wholly different from the Son's.

units.la: XXI. Respondet Socinus, Apostolum non tam hoc loco probare, quàm docere velle; id est, occultum psalmi verborum sensum quendam patefacere. Non tam, inquit, probare vult, Respondeant quæso rotundè Aduersarij, vultne Apostolus probare, necne? Si probare vult, faciunt eum ineptè argumentantem, qui scilicet vt probet, Iesum tantùm hominem præstantiorem esse omnibus angelis, affert pro argumento mandatum quo iubentur omnes Angeli adorare Deum Israelis. Agitur, inquiet aliquis, de Christo qui non est Deus Israelis, & tu Apostole testimonium affers, in quo agitur de Deo Israelis. Quæritur, an debeant omnes Angeli adorare quendam hominem, & tu affers testimonium, in quo iubentur adorare Deum illum vnum creatorem mundi. Hoccine est argumentari? Si non vult probare, errat igitur ipse Socinus cum sic loquitur, Resp. ad Classis. 1. Arg. 1. Vijcki[?]. Patet hoc ex ipso initio disputationis, vbi diserte Thesis ipsa exponitur: qua talis est: Dei filius tanto præstantior angelis est tactus, quanto excellentius, præ illis, nomen hæreditauit. Hæc, inquam est Thesis, quam Apostolus sibi probandam proposuit. Errant etiam omnes interpretes, qui summo consensu Apostolum probare velle asserunt: & quorsum tot testimonia laudaret, si nihil probare vellet?
units.tr: XXI. Socinus replies that "the Apostle does not wish so much to prove this in the passage as to teach, that is, to bring out a certain hidden sense of the words of the psalm." "Not so much to prove," he says. Let our opponents please answer plainly: does the Apostle wish to prove or not? If he wishes to prove, then they make him an inept arguer, who, in order to prove that Jesus is merely a man more excellent than all the angels, brings forward as his argument the command by which all the angels are bidden to adore the God of Israel. "The passage," someone will say, "is about Christ, who is not the God of Israel, and you, Apostle, cite a testimony in which the God of Israel is spoken of. The question is whether all the angels ought to adore a certain man, and you bring a testimony in which they are bidden to adore that one God, the creator of the world." Is that what arguing is? If he does not wish to prove, then Socinus himself is wrong when he says, in his Reply to Classis, Argument 1, Vijcki[?]: "This is plain from the very beginning of the discussion, where the thesis itself is clearly set out, which is as follows: the Son of God has been made as much superior to the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than they. This, I say, is the thesis which the Apostle set himself to prove." All the interpreters are also wrong who with one voice assert that the Apostle wished to prove; and to what end would he have cited so many testimonies if he wished to prove nothing?

units.la: XXII. Docet, inquit, id est occultum psalmi verborum sensum patefacit. Sensus Scripturæ distingui solet in Literalem & Mysticum: Illum verba proximè significant, Hunc res per verba significatæ. Verum igitur literalis est iste scilicet occultus quidam sensus, an mysticus? Si literalis, vel proprius est, vel figuratus. Non figuratus: quænam enim figura, quis tropus esse posset in pronomine eum, in verbis, adorent eum omnes angeli Dei? (De huius enim vnius pronominis significatione instituta est hæc nostra disputatio.) Et cur sensum comminiscerentur figuratum, cum obuius est: proprius verus & apposicus? Nec etiam proprius. Quis enim credat illius pronominis in verbis illis minimè ambiguis duos esse sensus literales & proprios? Sola enim ambiguitas, quae hinc omnis abest, gignere potest plures sensus proprios. Certè pronomen illud Eum referri non potest, nisi ad eum qui est in versibus antecedentibus nominatus. Nullus autem nominatus fuit praeter Iehouam. Non potest igitur referri nisi ad Iehouam. Mysticum quominus dicant eum sensum esse vel ipsorum dogma prohibet. Facerent enim adorationem Dei typum adorationis Christi, atque adeo ipsum Deum typum Christi, quod esset Christum supra ipsum Deum extollere. Pluris enim fieri debet res adumbrata quam eius typus vel umbra. Vno verbo: vel colligi potest, occultus iste sensus ex psalmi verbis, vel non potest. Si non potest, pro vero sensu haberi non debet. Si potest, ostendant qua ratione ex verbis Prophetae deduci possit.
units.tr: XXII. "He teaches," he says, "that is, he brings out the hidden sense of the words of the psalm." The sense of Scripture is customarily divided into literal and mystical: the former is what the words signify directly, the latter what is signified by the things through the words. Is this hidden sense, then, literal, or mystical? If literal, it is either proper or figurative. Not figurative: for what figure or trope could there be in the pronoun "him", in the words "let all the angels of God adore him"? (For it is the meaning of this one pronoun that our present disputation is about.) And why should they devise a figurative sense, when the proper, true and obvious sense lies to hand? Nor is it even proper. For who would believe that there are two literal and proper senses of that pronoun in those words, which are by no means ambiguous? Only ambiguity, which is wholly absent here, can give rise to several proper senses. Certainly that pronoun "him" cannot refer to anyone except the one named in the preceding verses. But no one was named except Jehovah. It can therefore refer only to Jehovah. As for calling it a mystical sense, their own doctrine forbids it. For they would make the adoration of God a type of the adoration of Christ, and so God himself a type of Christ; and that would be to exalt Christ above God himself. For the thing foreshadowed ought to be valued more than its type or shadow. In a word: either this hidden sense can be gathered from the words of the psalm, or it cannot. If it cannot, it ought not to be held as the true sense. If it can, let them show by what reasoning it can be deduced from the words of the Prophet.

units.la: XXIII. Socinus Ait, si modo velimus, verba quae ex psalmo citat, de uno illo Deo dicta esse, divini huius scriptoris hanc mentem fuisse, ut, quia iam inter peritiores Hebraeos constaret, de futuro Christo, eoque in sui regni possessionem mittendo, in eo psalmo, sub illius unius Dei nomine, agi, non quia Christus futurus esset ille unus Deus, sed quia unius illius Dei personam singulari quadam ratione sustinere debebat, ex eiusdem psalmi verbis, sua interpretatione adhibita, persuaderet, Christum ab ipsis angelis adorandum esse; nempe quia non modo multa alia, quae in eo psalmo de illo uno Deo dicuntur, ut facile ij concedebant, ad quos scribebat (scribebat enim ut ex epistola patet ad Iudaeos quidem, sed iam Christianos factos) ad Christum accommodanda essent: sed etiam illud ipsum, quod ibi habetur de omnibus angelis illum unum Deum adoraturis. Id quod non facile cuiquam persuaderi potest, nisi, praeterid[?], quod verissimile est, si multa alia, quae de illo uno Deo ibi dicuntur, idcirco ad Christum accommodanda sunt, quia de ipsius Christi regno sub unius illius Dei nomine ibi agitur, hoc etiam ad Christum accommodandum esse, quod nimirum ad ipsius regnum pertinet, accedat quoque ipsius scriptoris auctoritas & prophetiae spiritus, quo patefacit, quale & quantum revera sit Christi regnum, & quam divina prorsus & perfectissima ratione Christus illius unius Dei personam sustineat. In quibus verbis quaedam sunt reprehensione digna. Illud primò, quod affirmat, Iam inter peritiores Hebraeos constitisse, de futuro Christo, eoque in sui regni possessionem mittendo, in eo psalmo, sub illius unius Dei nomine agi. Unde enim id rescire potuit? Num id scripsit Apostolus, aut aliquis alius author illius seculi? Num id poterit probabili aliqua ratione conjici? Nullo modo. Temeraria igitur est affertio, & homine veritatis studioso & modesto prorsus indigna. At, inquit alibi, nisi iis, ad quos hic auctor epistolae eam scribebat, vel iam constitisset, vel facile constare potuisset, Scripturae locos ab ipso allatos ad Messiam pertinere, frustra & prorsus ridiculè eos at-tulisset. Benè, vel jam constitisset, vel facilè constare potuisset. Vitat enim illa disjunctione, eius, quod scire non poterat, affirmandi temeritatem. Sed unde constare? Ex attenta locorum illorum, ut habentur in Veteri Testamento, & citantur ab Apostolo, inspectione? Nihil verius. Ita enim Berœnses scrutabantur Scripturas, an hæc ita se haberent. Si ita sentiebat, concedit locos illos vim per se id probandi habuisse, ad quod probandum adducti sunt. Sin verò (quae videtur ejus mens hoc loco) vult eos locos vim illam ex sese non habuisse, sed ex hypothesi opinionis jam ab Hebraeis praeconceptae, atque adeò argumenta esse, ut loquuntur, ad hominem, graviter errat, & quantum in ipso est, Dei & Apostoli sapientiam vehementer obscurat. Atque hoc est illud alterum, quod in verbis Socini reprehendendum putavi. Nam si huius, de quo agimus, testimonii vis in opinione praejudicata Hebraeorum, ad quos Apostolus scribebat, sita erat, ea per se, & apud alios nulla erat. Si autoritate Apostoli nitebatur, consultius fecisset Apostolus, si testimonium non laudasset. Nam qui laudat testimonium præ se fert, se testimonii illius vi niti velle, non sua unius auctoritate. Itaque deludi lector videtur, cum citatur testimonium, cuius vis pendet ab auctoritate citantis.
units.tr: XXIII. "Socinus says that if we are willing, the words he cites from the psalm may be said to refer to that one God; that it was the mind of this divine writer, since it was already established among the more learned Hebrews that the future Christ, sent into the possession of his kingdom, is spoken of in that psalm under the name of that one God, and not because Christ would be that one God, but because he was to sustain the person of that one God in a singular way; and that from the words of the same psalm, with his own interpretation applied, he would persuade them that Christ is to be adored by the angels themselves. For not only many other things said in that psalm of that one God, as those to whom he wrote readily conceded (for he was writing, as the Epistle shows, to the Jews, but now made Christians), are to be applied to Christ; but also this very thing which is there said of all the angels who are to adore that one God. This cannot easily be persuaded to anyone, unless, besides the fact that it is very likely that if many other things said there of that one God are therefore to be applied to Christ, because the kingdom of Christ itself is spoken of there under the name of that one God, this too is to be applied to Christ, namely that which pertains to his kingdom, and there is added also the authority of the writer himself and the spirit of prophecy, by which he reveals what and how great the kingdom of Christ truly is, and in how wholly divine and most perfect a manner Christ sustains the person of that one God." In these words there are certain things worthy of reproof. First, that he affirms that "it was already established among the more learned Hebrews that in that psalm, under the name of that one God, the future Christ, sent into the possession of his kingdom, is spoken of." For from where could he have learned this? Did the Apostle write it, or any other author of that age? Could it be conjectured with any probable reason? In no way. The assertion is therefore rash, and wholly unworthy of a man who is a lover of truth and modest. But he says elsewhere: "Unless it were already established, or could easily have been established, for those to whom this author was writing, that the passages of Scripture which he cited refer to the Messiah, he would have cited them in vain and quite ridiculously." Well said: "already established, or could easily have been established." By that disjunction he avoids the rashness of affirming what he could not know. But established from where? From a careful inspection of those passages as they stand in the Old Testament and as the Apostle cites them? Nothing could be truer; for so the Bereans "searched the Scriptures, whether these things were so." If he thought so, he concedes that those passages had in themselves the force to prove what they were brought forward to prove. But if (which seems to be his meaning here) he wishes to say that those passages did not have that force of themselves, but derived it from a hypothesis of an opinion already preconceived by the Hebrews, and so are arguments, as they say, "to the man", he is gravely mistaken, and as far as in him lies he greatly obscures the wisdom of God and of the Apostle. And this is the second thing I thought ought to be censured in the words of Socinus. For if the force of this testimony, which we are discussing, rested on a prejudged opinion of the Hebrews to whom the Apostle was writing, then in itself, and among others, it had no force at all. If it rested on the authority of the Apostle, the Apostle would have done more wisely not to cite the testimony. For he who cites a testimony gives to understand that he wishes to rest on the force of that testimony, not on his own authority alone. And so the reader seems to be deceived when a testimony is cited whose force depends on the authority of the one citing it.

units.la: XXIV. Quod bis dicit, de Christi regno sub unius illius Dei nomine agi in eo psalmo, argumentum nostrum confirmat. Sic enim colligo. Ille cuius de regno agitur in eo psalmo est Iehova, ut patet ex toto psalmo. Christus est ille de cuius regno agitur in eo psalmo, confitente Socino. Ergo Christus est Iehova. Hoc primum. Deinde, quid significant illa verba, sub unius illius Dei nomine, vel ut alibi loquitur, sub ipsius Dei persona? significant ne unius illius Dei nomine Christum significari, per ipsius Dei personam Christum intelligi? Hoc ipsum est quod dicimus, nimirum per Iehovam in eo psalmo intelligendum esse Filium Dei. Cum igitur Propheta sic loquitur, Iehova Regnat, &c. quàm verbum, regnat, regnum Christi significat, tam nomen, Iehova; personam Christi significat. Si aliud volunt illis verbis aduersarij, id quale sit nobis quæso exponant. Nam si sub unius illius Dei nomine agitur de Christi regno, ut se habet regnum quod ibi describitur ad regnum Christi, sic se habet unus ille Deus ad Christum. Sed regnum illud est regnum Christi. Ergo unus ille Deus est Christus. Nempe ut regnum illud se habet ad regnum Christi, sic se habet rex illius regni ad Christum. Si regnum Christi eo psalmo describitur, certè Rex qui eo psalmo describitur est Christus. Is autem Rex est Iehoua. Iehoua igitur est Christus.
units.tr: XXIV. That he says twice that the reign of Christ is treated in that psalm "under the name of that one God" confirms our argument. For I reason thus. He of whose reign that psalm treats is Jehovah, as is plain from the whole psalm. Christ is he of whose reign that psalm treats, as Socinus confesses. Therefore Christ is Jehovah. This is the first point. Next, what do those words "under the name of that one God", or as he says elsewhere, "under the very person of God", signify? Do they signify that Christ is meant by the name of that one God, and that Christ is understood through the person of God itself? This is precisely what we say, namely that by Jehovah in that psalm the Son of God is to be understood. So when the Prophet speaks thus, "Jehovah reigns", etc., just as the word "reigns" signifies the kingdom of Christ, so the name Jehovah signifies the person of Christ. If our opponents mean something else by those words, I beg them to explain to us what it is. For if the reign of Christ is described under the name of that one God, then just as the kingdom described there stands to the kingdom of Christ, so that one God stands to Christ. But that kingdom is the kingdom of Christ. Therefore that one God is Christ. Indeed, just as that kingdom stands to the kingdom of Christ, so the king of that kingdom stands to Christ. If the reign of Christ is described in that psalm, certainly the King who is described in that psalm is Christ. But that King is Jehovah. Therefore Jehovah is Christ.

units.la: XXV. Fortasse lucem aliquam isti locutioni ratio, quam subjicit, aspergit. Quia, inquit, Christus unius illius Dei personam singulari quadam ratione sustinere debebat. Sed contrà est. Implicat enim potius quàm explicat, euertit potius quàm confirmat. Nam si sub unius illius Dei nomine, si sub ipsius Dei persona regnum Christi describitur, non iam Christus sustinet aut repræsentat personam unius Dei in eo psalmo, sed contrà potius, unus ille Deus sustinet & repræsentat personam Christi. Adde quod, quoties in Veteri Testamento sub unius nomine aut persona, alter describitur, toties ille huius typus est. Porrò typus est umbra eius cuius est typus. Est ne igitur unus ille Deus typus Christi tantùm hominis? Dicant etiam nobis Aduersarij, si Christus non est unus ille Deus, cur Spiritus Sanctus eum voluisset sub unius illius Dei nomine & persona toto psalmo, toties, tam constanter, tamque periculosè describere? Nam si sub ipsius Christi vel Filij nomine regnum Christi descripsisset, æquè profuisset ædificationi Ecclesiæ, nec nobis ansam præbuisset credendi Christum eundem esse Iehouam, hoc est, ut putant Aduersarij, graviter errandi. Haud enim decet prudentiam & charitatem Dei, innocenti atque æquè utili locutioni, aliam admodum impropriam obscuram & periculosam anteponere. Quis enim legens hæc verba, Iehoua regnat, &c, si regnum Christi describi putat, non statim inducatur ut credat, per Iehouam Christum significari?
units.tr: XXV. Perhaps the reason he adds throws some light on that expression. "Because," he says, "Christ had to sustain the person of that one God in a singular way." But the opposite is true. For it entangles rather than explains, and overturns rather than confirms. For if the kingdom of Christ is described under the name of that one God, if under the very person of God, then Christ no longer sustains or represents the person of the one God in that psalm, but on the contrary the one God sustains and represents the person of Christ. Add to this that, whenever in the Old Testament one is described under the name or person of another, the former is a type of the latter. Now a type is a shadow of that of which it is a type. Is that one God then a type of Christ merely as a man? Let our opponents also tell us: if Christ is not that one God, why would the Holy Spirit have wished to describe him so often, so constantly, and so perilously under the name and person of that one God throughout the psalm? For if he had described the reign of Christ under the name of Christ or the Son himself, it would have served the edification of the Church equally well, and would not have given us occasion to believe that Christ is the same as Jehovah, that is, as our opponents think, to err grievously. For it does not befit the wisdom and charity of God to prefer another, quite improper, obscure and dangerous expression to one that is innocent and equally useful. For who, reading these words, "Jehovah reigns, etc.", if he thinks that the reign of Christ is described, is not at once led to believe that Christ is signified by Jehovah?

units.la: XXVI. Ad hæc, Si de Christi regno in eo psalmo agitur sub unius illius Dei nomine, necesse est, ut unius illius Dei nomen aliquo modo significet Christum regnantem seu regem. Vel igitur eum significat proximè, & proprie; vel figuratè; vel mergit. Quæro igitur, quomodo unius illius Dei, hoc est, Dei Patris, personam Christus sustineat? An ut histrio personam Regis in scena? Non hoc, opinor, dixerint, Christo nimis injuriosum. Quanquam sic tam dici posset, non modo Iehova, sed etiam Deus Pater, quàm histrio rex appellatur dum regis personam agit. Quid ergo sibi volunt, cum dicunt, Christum divina & perfectissima ratione sustinere personam ipsius Dei? Christum profiteri se esse ipsum Deum, eique professioni congruenter loqui & agere? (persimili enim sensu dicere solemus, consulem consulis, Iudicem iudicis, oratorem oratoris personam sustinere.) Quare igitur eum negant ipsum Deum esse? Christum non suas, sed alienas partes agere, ac perinde, vel ipsum loqui & agere, vel de ipso Scripturam, ac si ipse Deus esset, cum tamen non esset ipse Deus? At si, vel Christus de se, vel Scriptura de ipso perinde loquitur ac si esset ipse Deus, unde habent eum non esse ipsum Deum? Aut cur suos & conceptus & sermones, non exigunt ad normam sacrarum literarum, præsertim cum de eo sit quæ-stio, quem nemo novit nisi Pater? Tres personas pro triplici munere unus Christus sustinet, Prophetæ, Sacerdotis, Regis. Quando ergo alienam ipsius Dei personam sustinet? cum partes agit Prophetæ? aut Sacerdotis? Non arbitror. Hæ enim nullo modo sunt partes Patris. An igitur eam sustinet cum regio munere fungitur? Certè etiam tunc suas ipsius, non alienas Patris, partes sustinet. Verissimè enim ac propriissimè loquendo Rex est, suumque regnum, non alienum, administrat.
units.tr: XXVI. Besides, if the reign of Christ is treated in that psalm under the name of that one God, it is necessary that the name of that one God signify in some way Christ reigning, or the King. Either it signifies him directly and properly, or figuratively, or... Then I ask how Christ sustains the person of that one God, that is, of God the Father. As an actor sustains the person of a king on the stage? I suppose they would not say this, as it would be too injurious to Christ. Although in that sense one could say not only Jehovah but also God the Father, just as an actor is called a king while he plays the king's part. What then do they mean when they say that Christ sustains the person of God himself in a divine and most perfect manner? That Christ professes himself to be God himself, and speaks and acts in accordance with that profession? (For we commonly speak in a very similar sense of a consul sustaining the consulship of a consul, a judge the office of a judge, an orator the role of an orator.) Why then do they deny that he is God himself? That Christ does not play his own part but another's, and that he speaks and acts, or Scripture speaks of him, as though he were God himself, when yet he is not God himself? But if either Christ speaks of himself, or Scripture speaks of him, as though he were God himself, whence do they have that he is not God himself? Or why do they not require their concepts and sayings to be measured by the rule of the holy Scriptures, especially since the question concerns one whom no one knows except the Father? One Christ sustains three persons for the threefold office: of Prophet, of Priest, of King. When then does he sustain the alien person of God himself? When he performs the part of Prophet? Or of Priest? I think not. For these are in no way the parts of the Father. Does he then sustain it when he exercises the kingly office? Certainly even then he sustains his own part, not the Father's. For, speaking most truly and most properly, he is King, and administers his own kingdom, not another's.

units.la: XXIX. Forte volunt Christum sustinere ipsius Dei, hoc est, Patris personam, quomodo magistratus vulgò dicitur sustinere personam principis, seu Regis. Sed omnia ferè dissimilia sunt. Primùm Regis est ius dicere subditis, quod cum ipse per semetipsum facere non possit, creat magistratus, per quos id faciat, quique istis regij muneris partibus tanquam eius minis-tri, &, ut ita dicam, vicarii defungantur. Itaque quæcunque ad regem pertinent, ea non suo nomine sed regio, non sua autoritate sed regia, non tanquam sua ipsius, sed tanquam aliena, ut fideles ministros decet, administrant. Ministri enim sunt regis, non reges, eorum non est regnum, non thronus, non potestas regia, non Majestas, non ministri & serui regis. Christi dispar ratio est. Regnat enim cum Patre similiter, immò pariter. Eius suæ[?] quæcunque Patris sunt, regnum, thronus, sceptrum, potentia, majestas, ministri, subditi. Si regnum accepit à Patre, accepit vt Filius vnigenitus, vt hæres ex asse, vt suum, non vt alienum. Itaque non regnat vt seruus, vt minister Patris, dicam aliquid amplius, non regnat, accuratè loquendo, vt vicarius Patris. Id quod ipse Smalcius agnoscit. Enumerans enim Smiglecij, vt loquitur, calumnias in aliquot capita distributas. Octauum, inquit, caput est, nos Christum Dei vicarium facere. Et hic canillus[?] est, quo remoto, ipsa Christi diuinitas relucebit. Nos enim cum scriptura dicimus, Christum Deum esse vnà cum illo vno Deo. Quemadmodum filius regis, si à Patre ad regnum admittatur, non proprie vicarius eius, sed vnà cum Patre sub Rex esse dicitur. Non igitur cum regnat alienam Patris personam sustinet, sed suam.
units.tr: XXIX. Perhaps they mean that Christ sustains the person of God himself, that is, of the Father, in the way that the magistrate is commonly said to sustain the person of the prince or king. But almost everything is dissimilar. First, it belongs to the king to declare law to his subjects; since he cannot do this in person, he appoints magistrates through whom he may do it, and who discharge these parts of the royal office as his ministers and, so to speak, his vicars. Therefore whatever pertains to the king, they administer not in their own name but in the royal name, not on their own authority but on the royal authority, not as their own but as another's, as faithful ministers ought. For they are the king's ministers, not kings; the kingdom is not theirs, nor the throne, nor the royal power, nor the majesty; they are the king's ministers and servants. Christ's case is different. For he reigns with the Father in like manner, indeed in equal manner. Whatever belongs to the Father is his: kingdom, throne, sceptre, power, majesty, ministers, subjects. If he received the kingdom from the Father, he received it as the only-begotten Son, as heir of the whole estate, as his own and not another's. Therefore he does not reign as a servant, as a minister of the Father; I may say more: strictly speaking he does not reign as the Father's vicar. This Smalcius himself acknowledges. For, listing the calumnies of Smiglecius, as he calls them, distributed under several heads: "The eighth head," he says, "is that we make Christ the vicar of God. And this is a mere trifle, which removed, the very divinity of Christ will shine forth. For we, with Scripture, say that Christ is God together with that one God. Just as the son of a king, if he is admitted by his father to the kingdom, is not properly called his vicar, but is said to be king together with the Father." Therefore when he reigns, he sustains not the alien person of the Father, but his own.

units.la: XXIX. Fac tamen eum se habere ad Patrem, quemadmodum inferior magistratus ad Regem. Quis vnquam sub nomine Regis Magistratum descripsit Regi subordinatum? Quis mandatum legens, quo omnes regni proceres jubentur ciuiliter adorare regem, id exponat de Regio aliquo ministro, aut magistratu constituto à Rege, vt hunc ministrum, aut magistratum probet omnibus regni proceribus dignitate longè antecellere.
units.tr: XXIX. Suppose, however, that he stands towards the Father as an inferior magistrate stands towards the King. Who has ever described, under the name of a King, a magistrate subordinated to the King? Who, reading a command by which all the nobles of the realm are bidden to adore the king with civil reverence, would explain it of some royal minister or magistrate appointed by the King, so as to prove that this minister or magistrate far surpasses all the nobles of the realm in dignity?

units.la: XXX. Denique, consilium Apostoli est, probare hanc thesin, Christum esse angelis præstantiorem. Id omnes interpretes agnoscunt, id causalis, enim, docet, id citatio tot è Veteri Testamento testimoniorum clamat, id huius ipsius testimonij collatio cum thesi probanda confirmat, id ipse Socinus vi veritatis victus confitetur. Istud ipsum, inquit, vrget Apostolus, Christo videlicet adorationem ab ipsis angelis deberi ex quo apertissimè omnes possint intelligere, Christum angelis præstantiorem esse, quod illud ipsum est, quod ab initio probandum sibi proposuit. Probat igitur Christum angelis præstantiorem esse, quia debetur ei ab angelis adoratio. Hoc autem probat testimonio petito è ps. 97. 8. quo iubentur eum adorare omnes angeli. Quod tamen testimonium nullam prorsus ad id probandum vim habet, si in eo de adorando vno illo Deo agitur, isque vnus Deus nullo modo est Christus.
units.tr: XXX. Finally, the Apostle's purpose is to prove this thesis: that Christ is superior to the angels. All the interpreters acknowledge this. The causal word for shows it, the citation of so many testimonies from the Old Testament proclaims it, the comparison of this very testimony with the thesis to be proved confirms it, and Socinus himself confesses it, overcome by the force of truth. "This very thing, he says, the Apostle presses, namely that adoration is owed to Christ by the angels themselves, from which everyone can most clearly understand that Christ is superior to the angels, which is exactly what he proposed at the outset to prove." Therefore he proves that Christ is superior to the angels because the angels owe him adoration. He proves this by a testimony taken from Ps. 97:8, where all the angels are bidden to adore him. Yet this testimony has no force at all for that purpose if the passage is speaking of adoring that one God, and that one God is in no way Christ.

units.la: XXXI. Regerit Socinus, Si simpliciter probare vult, quomodo, quaeso, probat, id quod de vno illo Deo in psalmo dictum est, de Christo dictum fuisse, vt inde concludat, Christum ab angelis adorandum esse? Necesse est, vt dicas, eum istud propterea probare, quia pro concesso sumat, Christum esse illum unum Deum. Hoc non est necesse. Quomodo autem id probet, statim, Deo dante, explicabo. Addit, Ad argumentationem, ex loco isto sacri illius scriptoris ductam, omnino ac penitus dissoluendam, hoc dilemmate utor: aut colligitur ex ipsius verbis, quod Christus sit ille unus Deus Israëlis, quia id ipse probet, Aut quia, etiamsi id non probat, tamen ita eum sensisse, ex iis, quae dicit, intelligi potest. Quorsum istae nugae? Id colligitur ex verbis huius scriptoris collatis cum verbis Prophetae, eo syllogismo, quem initio huius disputationis proposui, & refutatis separatim duabus Socini responsionibus firmaui. Supersunt tamen adhuc aliquot argumenta, quibus eundem confirmem, easdemque illas duas responsiones conjunctè confutem.
units.tr: XXXI. Socinus replies: "If he simply wants to prove it, how, I ask, does he prove that what is said in the psalm of that one God was said of Christ, so that he may conclude that Christ is to be adored by the angels? You must say that he proves this because he takes it as granted that Christ is that one God." This is not necessary. How he proves it I will explain shortly, God willing. He adds: "To overturn wholly and utterly the argument drawn from this passage of that sacred writer, I use this dilemma: either it is gathered from his words that Christ is that one God of Israel, because he himself proves it; or, even if he does not prove it, it can be understood from what he says that he thought so." Why these trifles? It is gathered from the words of this writer, compared with the words of the Prophet, by the syllogism which I set out at the beginning of this disputation, and which I confirmed after separately refuting Socinus's two replies. Still, there remain some further arguments by which I may confirm the same point and at the same time refute those two replies together.

units.la: XXXII. Primum à verbis Apostoli ducitur, Et, cum iterum introducit primogenitum in orbem terræ, dicit, &c. Docent enim aperte, cum describi eo psalmo secundam introductionem, seu secundum aduentum, Filij Dei in orbem terræ, tum eum, quem eo loco jubentur adorare Angeli, non ipsum Deum Patrem esse, sed primogenitum eius Filium. Quæ duo cum Socini responsionibus non obscurè pugnant. Quàm enim alius est Filius primogenitus à Patre, tam alius est ab eodem Patre is, qui teste Apostolo introducitur in orbem terræ, quemque Angeli adorare jubentur eo psalmo. Et tamen is eo psalmo sexies Iehoua nominatur, itaque magnificè describitur, vt non possit magnificentius ipse Pater describi. Adde quod Apostolus distinguere videtur eum qui introducit ab eo qui introducitur, illumque esse Patrem innuere. Ex quo intelligitur, qui jubet Angelos adorare, Patrem, qui jubetur adorari, Filium esse, huncque, non illum, eo psalmo describi.
units.tr: XXXII. The first is drawn from the words of the Apostle: "And when he again brings the firstborn into the world, he says, etc." For they clearly teach that, when that psalm describes the second introduction, or second coming, of the Son of God into the world, the one whom the angels are bidden to adore in that place is not God the Father himself but his firstborn Son. These two points clash plainly with Socinus's replies. For the firstborn Son is as distinct from the Father as the one who, as the Apostle witnesses, is introduced into the world, and whom the angels are bidden to adore in that psalm, is distinct from the same Father. Yet in that psalm he is named Jehovah six times, and is described so magnificently that the Father himself could not be described more magnificently. Add that the Apostle seems to distinguish the one who introduces from the one who is introduced, and to indicate that the former is the Father. From this it is understood that the one who bids the angels adore is the Father, and the one who is bidden to be adored is the Son, and that it is he, not the Father, who is described in that psalm.

units.la: XXXIII. Alterum argumentum petitur ab illis ipsis verbis, Adorate eum omnes dij, vel, adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei, vtrovis enim modo reddantur ad sensum nihil interest. Considerandum enim est cuius sint verba. Scripta quidem sunt à propheta: sed Prophetae non est ad homines missi, omnibus angelis imperare & præscribere, quem adorare debeant. Hoc ad eum solum pertinet, qui supremam habet in omnes angelos potestatem. Is autem vel Pater est, vel Filius. Non sunt autem Filij verba, sed eius à quo introducitur in orbem terræ teste Apostolo, necnon ipsa re: est enim magis consentaneum rationi, vt ab omnibus angelis adorari Pater Filium jubeat, quàm Filius Patrem. Si igitur is qui adorationem istam imperat est pater, necesse est vt Filius is sit, quem adorari imperat: non enim dicit, adorate me, sed adorate eum, non suam ipsius personam adorari jubet, sed aliam, nempe eam, quæ psalmo illo Iehoua appellatur, & describitur. Cæterum latet emphasis in voce primogeniti. Cum enim Christus primogenitus dicatur πρωτότοκος [?] &, vt loquitur Apostolus, πάσης κτίσεως [?], quoniam per ipsum creata sunt omnia quæ in cœlis sunt & in terra, visibilia & invisibilia; sive throni, sive dominationes, sive principatus, sive potestates, omnia per ipsam & in ipso creata sunt, & ipse est ante omnia, & omnia in ipso consistunt, merito ab omnibus angelis adoratur, creaturis nimirum suis.
units.tr: XXXIII. The second argument is taken from those very words, "Adore him, all gods" or "let all the angels of God adore him", for it makes no difference to the sense in which of these ways they are rendered. For we must consider whose words they are. They were indeed written by the prophet, but it does not belong to a prophet, sent to men, to command all the angels and prescribe whom they ought to adore. This belongs only to the one who has supreme power over all the angels. And that one is either the Father or the Son. But these are not the words of the Son, but of him by whom he is introduced into the world, as the Apostle witnesses, and as the thing itself shows. For it is more in keeping with reason that the Father should command all the angels to adore the Son, than that the Son should command them to adore the Father. If then the one who commands this adoration is the Father, it must be that the Son is the one whom he commands to be adored. For he does not say "adore me" but "adore him". He does not bid his own person be adored, but another, namely the one who is called and described as Jehovah in that psalm. Moreover, the emphasis lies in the word firstborn. For since Christ is called firstborn [πρωτότοκος] of every creature [πάσης κτίσεως], as the Apostle says, "for by him were all things created that are in heaven and in earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created by him and in him, and he is before all things, and in him all things consist" (Col. 1:16–17), he is rightly adored by all the angels, namely by his own creatures.

units.la: XXXIV. Tertium argumentum sumitur à connexione huius psalmi 97. cum antecedente & sequente. Non observabo psalmorum esse, vt ita dicam, tres Iubilæos (sunt enim ter quinquaginta.) Extremos autem cuiusque Iubilæi sive quinquagenarij pertinere ad Domini nostri aduentum, præcipuè ad secundum, ex quo victoria nostra, & triumphus, & plena liberatio ab omnibus malis, atque adeo lætitia & jubilum pendent. Tantùm dicam, hunc psalmum 97. inter duos medium interjectum esse, quorum verba extrema sensu prorsus, syllabis propè eadem sunt. Excitant enim omnes creaturas, etiam inanimas, ad jubilandum & exultandum, subjecta hac ratione, quia venit, quoniam venit iudicare terram: iudicabit orbem terræ in æquitate, & populos in veritate sua. Quæ verba qui non videt de Christo dicta esse veniente ad iudicandum orbem terræ, claudere oculos sponte videtur: tamen qui venire dicitur utroque illo psalmo Iehoua appellatur. Cum autem veniet Christus, tunc sedebit in solio maiestatis suæ, Tunc magnificentissima ratione regnabit, suosque regnando lætitia implebit, Tunc reliqua præstabit quæ hoc psal. 97. describuntur. Ex quo intelligitur illius regnum lætificum, aduentum magnificum, iudicia celebranda in hoc psalmo exponi, qui in antecedentis & sequentis extremo venire nunciatur. Is autem testibus illis psalmis est Iehoua, testibus Apostolis est Christus, quid ergo confiteri cunctamur, eundem esse Iehouam & Christum ?
units.tr: XXXIV. The third argument is taken from the connection of this psalm, 97, with what precedes and what follows. I will not point out that the psalms are, so to speak, three jubilees (for they are three times fifty). But the final parts of each jubilee, or fifty, pertain to the coming of our Lord, especially the second, on which our victory, our triumph, and full deliverance from all evils depend, and therefore our joy and jubilation. I will only say that this psalm, 97, is placed between two others, whose final verses are almost identical in sense and nearly in syllables. For they rouse all creatures, even inanimate ones, to jubilate and exult, adding this reason: "because he comes, because he comes to judge the earth: he will judge the world with righteousness and the peoples with his truth." Whoever does not see that these words are spoken of Christ coming to judge the world seems to close his eyes wilfully. Yet he who is said to come is called Jehovah in both of those psalms. Now when Christ comes, "then he will sit on the throne of his majesty." Then he will reign in the most magnificent manner, and fill his people with joy by reigning; then he will perform the other things described in this Ps. 97. From this it is understood that the joyful kingdom, the glorious coming, and the judgments to be celebrated are set out in this psalm, which is announced as coming at the end of the one before and the one after it. He is Jehovah by the witness of those psalms, and Christ by the witness of the Apostles. Why then do we hesitate to confess that Jehovah and Christ are the same?

units.la: XXXV. Vt taceam Regnum, quod certo tempore incepit, & cuius nũntium lætificare debet insulas multas, regnum esse Christi, non Patris præcisè, verborum illorum, ꝟ. 3. Ignis ante ipsum precedet, & inflammabit in circuitu inimicos eius, nonne egregius est commentarius id quod dicit Apostolus 2. Thess. 7. In revelatione Domini Iesu de coelo cum angelis virtutis eius in flamma ignis, dantis vindictam iis, qui non noverunt Deum? Verba etiam illa ꝟ. 4. vidit & commota est terra, & ꝟ. 5. Montes sicut cera fluxerunt a facie Domini, a facie Domini omnis terra. Et ꝟ. 6. viderunt omnes populi gloriam eius, eum sine dubio significant, qui venit vel venturus est, qui se videndum omnibus populis exhibuit vel exhibiturus est. Quis autem ille est? Pater, an Filius? certè Filius potius quàm Pater. Addit ꝟ. 7. Confundantur omnes qui adorant sculptilia, &c. Quis suo aduentu, & ut loquitur Apostolus, τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ [?] omnes idololatras confundet, nisi Christus? ꝟ. 10. Valde exaltatus es super omnes Deos, hoc est, angelos, de utro convenientius id dicitur, de Patre, an de Filio? exaltatio super angelos de Filio prædicari solet ab Apostolis, de Patre non item. Denique inde propheta ansam arripit hortandi pios ad odium mali; quoniam, quamvis in hoc seculo floreant impij, affligantur autem pij, tamen in aduentu illo Domini bene erit pijs, liberabuntur ab impijs, & sempiterni gaudij messem amplam referent, hoc quidem tempore jam sati, sed adhuc, vel latentis in terra, vel saltem fructum suum nondum edentis id quod nullius alius aduentu fiet, quam unius Domini nostri Iesu Christi, cui sit gloria in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: XXXV. To say nothing of the kingdom, which began at a certain time and whose announcement should gladden many islands: that it is the kingdom of Christ, not of the Father strictly speaking, is shown by those words of v. 3, "A fire goes before him and burns up his enemies round about," is not this an excellent commentary on what the Apostle says in 2 Thess. 1:7, "At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, rendering vengeance on those who do not know God"? So too the words of v. 4, "the earth saw and trembled," and of v. 5, "the mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord all the earth," and of v. 6, "all peoples have seen his glory," undoubtedly signify him who has come or will come, who has shown himself or will show himself to be seen by all peoples. But who is that? The Father, or the Son? Certainly the Son rather than the Father. He adds in v. 7, "Let all who worship graven images be confounded, etc." Who, by his coming, and in the Apostle's words, "by the appearing of his presence" [τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ], will confound all idolaters, if not Christ? In v. 10, "You are greatly exalted above all gods," that is, above the angels. Of which of the two is this more fittingly said, of the Father or of the Son? Exaltation above the angels is commonly predicated of the Son by the Apostles, not of the Father. Finally, the prophet seizes on this as an occasion to exhort the godly to hatred of evil: although in this age the wicked flourish and the godly are afflicted, yet at that coming of the Lord it will go well for the godly, they will be delivered from the wicked, and they will reap an ample harvest of everlasting joy. The seed is already sown in this time, but still lies hidden in the earth, or at least has not yet borne its fruit. This will be done at the coming of no one but our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever, Amen.

units.la: DISPVTATIO DECIMA De Arg. X. Ex verbis Psal. xxiv. v. 1. & L. 13. Domini est terra & plenitudo eius, Laudatis 1. Cor. x. 26.
