units.tr: TENTH DISPUTATION. On Argument X, from the words of Psalm 24:1 and 50:13, "The Lord's is the earth and its fullness," compared with 1 Cor. 10:26.

units.la: I. ARGVMENTVM tale est. Ille cuius terra & plenitudo eius esse dicitur ps. xxiv. 1. & L. 13. est praeditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: I. The argument is this. He of whom it is said that the earth and its fullness are his (Ps. 24:1 and 50:13) is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est ille cuius terra & plenitudo eius esse dicitur ps. xxiv. 1. & 50. 13.
units.tr: Christ is he of whom it is said that the earth and its fullness are his (Ps. 24:1 and 50:13).

units.la: Christus igitur est praeditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: Christ, therefore, is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Major extra omnem controuersiam, posita est. Nam ps. 24. 1. quo loco verba illa extant totidem syllabis, Domini est terra & plenitudo eius, Dominus Heb. est Iehoua. Psalmo vero 50. v. 13. qui sic loquitur Meus enim est orbis terra, & plenitudo eius, is primo versu eiusdem psalmi Deus deorum, & Iehoua vocatur.
units.tr: The major premise is posited beyond all controversy. For in Ps. 24:1, where those words stand in the same number of syllables, The Lord's is the earth and its fullness, the Hebrew word for "Lord" is Jehovah. In Psalm 50:13, which speaks thus, For mine is the world, and its fullness, the speaker is called, in the first verse of the same psalm, "God of gods" and Jehovah.

units.la: II. Minor partim Apostoli partim Prophetae auctoritate nititur. Apostoli quidem. Is enim 1. Cor. 10. cum dixisset v. 25. Omne quod in macello venit manducate, nihil interrogantes propter conscientiam, rationem subjunxit petitam ab illis verbis ps. 24. Domini enim, inquit, est terra & plenitudo eius. Eum autem per Dominum ὁ κύριος intelligere Christum, vix eget probatione. Id enim nomen, ipso eodem Apostolo teste, & quidem in hac ipsa Epistola ad Cor. cap. 8. 6. & cap. 12. 5. necnon Eph. 4. 5. singulari quadam ratione proprium est Christi. Itaque passim eo nomine, praesertim articulo, ut fit hoc loco, praefixo significatur. Accedit quod ratio à jure Christi in terram & plenitudinem eius ducta propinquior est ei, quod Apostolus probare instituebat, quàm si petita fuisset à jure Dei Patris.
units.tr: II. The minor premise rests partly on the authority of the Apostle and partly on that of the prophet. First the Apostle. In 1 Cor. 10, having said at v. 25, Eat whatever is sold in the meat market, asking no questions for conscience' sake, he added a reason taken from those words of Ps. 24: For the Lord's, he says, is the earth and its fullness. That by "the Lord" (ὁ κύριος [ὁ κύριος]) he means Christ hardly needs proof. For that name, by the Apostle's own witness, and indeed in this very Epistle to the Corinthians (ch. 8:6 and ch. 12:5), and also in Eph. 4:5, belongs to Christ in a singular way. So it is everywhere signified by that name, especially with the article prefixed, as it is here. Moreover, the reasoning drawn from Christ's right over the earth and its fullness is closer to what the Apostle was setting out to prove than it would have been had it been drawn from the right of God the Father.

units.la: III. Prophetæ verò. Nam quod attinet ad psal. 24. Idem ille Dominus cuius terra esse dicitur ℣. 1. ipse est, qui versib. 7. 8. 9. & 10. Rex gloriæ appellatur: id quod in dubium neque vocatur, neque vocari potest. Hic autem est Christus. Id probo duobus argumentis, quibus illud ipsum concludo, quod mihi toto hoc libro probandum suscepi. Primum est eiusmodi. Rex gloriæ est Iehoua, Deus Israëlis. Christus est Rex gloriæ. E. Christus est Iehoua, seu Deus Israëlis. Majorem probo ex ℣. 7. & 9. introibit Rex gloriæ; ibi enim elogium Regis gloriæ ponitur pro nomine proprio & reciproco Dei Israëlis. Idem liquet ex versus 8. & 10. quibus Rex gloriæ describitur. Cum enim bona sit descriptio, reciprocari debet cum descripto. Est autem illa descriptio vers. 8. Iehoua fortis & potens, Iehoua potens in prælio, & vers. 10. Iehoua exercituum. Reciprocatur igitur Iehoua fortis & potens, Iehoua exercituum cum Rege gloriæ: Minorem probo testimonio Apostoli, qui similiter 1. Cor. 2. 8. pro Christi nomine elogium Domini gloriæ usurpavit, Nunquam, inquit, Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. Dominus autem gloriæ & Rex gloriæ, quin idem valeant, nemo, opinor, negabit. Nam & Christus Rex est, immò Rex Regum Apoc. 17.14. & 19.16. & nomen ὁ κύριος, etiam præfixo articulo, in Bibliis græcis pro Iehoua usurpatur, ut, vel ex vers. 1. huius psal. 24. manifestum est, & Christus vocatur ὁ κύριος Dominus κατ' ἐξοχήν.
units.tr: III. Now the prophets. As for Ps. 24, the same Lord of whom the earth is said to be his (v. 1) is himself the one who, in vv. 7–10, is called the King of glory. This is neither called into doubt nor can be. Now this is Christ. I prove it by two arguments, by which I conclude the very thing I have undertaken to prove in this whole book. The first is of this kind. The King of glory is Jehovah, the God of Israel. Christ is the King of glory. Therefore Christ is Jehovah, or the God of Israel. I prove the major from vv. 7 and 9, the King of glory shall enter; for there the title "King of glory" is put in place of the proper name, and is reciprocal with "the God of Israel." The same is clear from vv. 8 and 10, where the King of glory is described. For since the description is a good one, it must be reciprocal with what is described. The description in v. 8 is Jehovah strong and mighty, Jehovah mighty in battle, and in v. 10 Jehovah of hosts. Therefore "Jehovah strong and mighty" and "Jehovah of hosts" are reciprocal with "King of glory." I prove the minor by the testimony of the Apostle, who likewise in 1 Cor. 2:8 used the title "Lord of glory" for Christ's name: They would never have crucified the Lord of glory, he says. That the Lord of glory and the King of glory mean the same thing, I think no one will deny. For Christ is also King, indeed King of kings (Rev. 17:14 and 19:16), and the name ὁ κύριος [ὁ κύριος], even with the article prefixed, is used in the Greek Bibles for Jehovah, as is clear even from v. 1 of this Ps. 24; and Christ is called ὁ κύριος [ὁ κύριος], the Lord par excellence.

units.la: IV. Alterum argumentum sic habet. Rex gloriæ, qui hoc psal. 24. describitur, est aut Pater, aut Filius. Non est Pater quatenus à Filio distinguitur. Est igitur Filius. Non esse Patrem, quatenus à Filio distinguitur, ut probem, primum psalmi mentem aperiam, deinde argumento rem concludam. Duobus primis versibus Propheta clamat, Domini esse terram, & plenitudinem eius, orbem terræ & omnes qui in eo habitant, subjecta hac ratione, quia ipse eam fundavit super maria, & super flumina præparavit eam. Ex quo sequebatur, omnes terræ regiones, omnes nationes absque discrimine ex æquo Dei esse. Hinc nascitur quæstio ℣. 3. Quis ascendet in montem Domini, & quis consistet in loco sanctitatis eius? Hoc est, quis accedet ad Deum, quis consistet in eius conspectu, An omnes homines cuiuscunque nationis & regionis sint, quandoquidem omnes ad eum pari iure pertinent, an vero duntaxat gens aliqua, aut tribus, aut familia? Respondet, Qui innocens est manibus, & purus corde, qui ad vanitatem animam suam non effert, neque iurat in dolo, Significans, vt verbis vtar Apostoli Petri, Deum non esse personarum acceptorem, sed in omni gente, qui timet eum, & operatur iustitiam, acceptum esse illi: qui vero iustitiam non operatur, non esse illi acceptum. Ex quo apparet, per montem Domini, & locum sanctitatis eius, non tam montem illum terrenum & locum intelligi in quo templum erat a Salomone aedificandum, quam illud, cuius mons ille & locus vmbra seu typus fuit.
units.tr: IV. The second argument runs thus. The King of glory described in this Ps. 24 is either the Father or the Son. He is not the Father insofar as the Father is distinguished from the Son. Therefore he is the Son. That the Father, insofar as he is distinguished from the Son, is not this King, I shall prove by first explaining the psalm's meaning and then concluding the matter by argument. In the first two verses the prophet cries out, The Lord's is the earth and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it, with this reason added: for he founded it upon the seas, and prepared it upon the rivers. From this it followed that all regions of the earth and all nations, without distinction, belong equally to God. Hence arises the question in v. 3: Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place? That is, who shall draw near to God, who shall stand in his sight? Do all men, of whatever nation and region they are, since all belong to him by equal right, or only some nation, or tribe, or family? He answers: He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart, who does not lift up his soul to vanity, nor swears deceitfully, signifying, to use the words of the Apostle Peter, that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him; but he who does not work righteousness is not acceptable to him. From this it appears that by the mountain of the Lord and the place of his holiness is understood not so much that earthly mountain and place in which the temple was to be built by Solomon, as that of which that mountain and place were a shadow or type.

units.la: V. Subijcit Propheta declarationem beatitatis eiusmodi hominis Ψ. 5. Accipiet, inquit, benedictionem a Domino, & iustitiam a Deo salutis suae. Quamuis enim operetur iustitiam, tamen non iustificabitur operibus suis, sed dono Dei seruatoris sui. Deinde, vt carnalibus Israëlitis omnem de suo genere gloriandi ansam praescindat, addit, Ψ. 6. Hanc esse generationem quaerentium eum, quaerentium faciem tuam Iacob. Hoc est, qui tales sunt, hos demum esse verum Dei populum, veram posteritatem Iacobi: qui Patris sui faciem quaerunt, festinant ad eum accedere, nullumque periculum recusant, vt benedictionem accipiant, qua ratione supplantant fratres suos primogenitos, id est, seculi huius principes, sapientes, nobiles: qui coelestis benedictionis minimè sitientes non quaerunt Seruatorem suum, non procedunt ei obuiam, immò venienti portas non apperiunt, sed claudunt potius, nec sese ab ista sua contumacia dimoueri patiuntur. Horum enim talem generationem verè fidelium generationi oppositam, quae sese in principibus huius seculi, qui Dominum gloriae noluerunt agnoscere, Propheta in spiritu describere videtur versibus sequentibus.
units.tr: V. The prophet adds a declaration of the blessedness of such a man (v. 5): He shall receive, he says, a blessing from the Lord, and righteousness from God his saviour. For although he works righteousness, yet he is not justified by his works, but by the gift of God his Saviour. Then, so that he cuts off from the carnal Israelites every occasion of boasting in their descent, he adds (v. 6): This is the generation of those who seek him, who seek your face, O Jacob. That is, those who are such are at last the true people of God, the true posterity of Jacob: those who seek their Father's face, hasten to approach him, and refuse no danger in order to receive the blessing, by which they supplant their elder brothers, that is, the princes, wise men and nobles of this age. Not thirsting at all for heavenly blessing, these do not seek their Saviour, do not go out to meet him, and when he comes do not open the gates but rather shut them, nor do they allow themselves to be moved from their obstinacy. For in the verses that follow, the prophet seems, in the Spirit, to describe the generation of these men, opposed to the generation of the truly faithful: the princes of this age who were unwilling to acknowledge the Lord of glory.

units.la: VI. Attollite, inquit, porta capita vestra (Graeca & vulg. attollite portas principes vestras,) & elevamini fores seculi, & introibit Rex gloriae. Quaeris interpretem? ipsum Christum audi. Ecce sto ad ostium, & pulso: si quis audierit vocem meam, & aperuerit ianuam, intrabo ad illum. Portas plurali numero compellat, hoc est, eos, quorum est portas aperire, & iubet eas attolli; aperimus enim Christo, cum sursum ad coelestia feriamur, non, cum conuersi ad terrena, quiescimus. Mandato adjungit promis-sionem, & ingredietur Rex gloriae. Rex antonomasticè, & Christus, seu Messias reciprocantur. Christus igitur gloria & honore coronatus Rex est gloriae. Compellat autem eos qui Regi gloriae venienti obuiam ire noluerunt, sed sese intrà clausas domos continuerunt. Itaque pulsandum fuit, & iubendum vt aperirent. Adesse enim Regem illum gloriosissimum toties promissum, & tandiu expectatum, qui ingredi cupiat. Quid principes huius seculi? paruerunt ne celeriter illi mandato? Num tanto Regi consestim, vt par erat, aperuerunt? Num eum summa cum alacritate exceperunt? Nihil minus. Quis est, inquiunt, iste Rex gloriae? Non dicunt quis est Rex gloriae, quemadmodum dicendum erat congruenter mandato, sed quis est iste Rex gloriae? Profitentur se istum regem gloriae non cognoscere, ac, nisi prius quis scit doceantur, se aperire nolle. Respondetur, esse Dominum (Iehouam) fortem & potentem, Dominum potentem in praelio. Ita Christus passim inculcat se esse Dei Filium, vnum cum Patre, Patri aequalem, vsque adeo potentem, vt verbo diabolos fugaret, caecis visum restitueret, mortuos suscitaret, omnis generis morbos curaret, ac in ipsum credentibus vitam aeternam & gloriosam resurrectionem polliceretur. Potuitne cogitari animo rex potentior fortiorue in praelio eo, qui hostes omnes nostros, etiam ipsam mortem deuicit, & tandem abolebit, quique, verus Iacob, strenuè se gessit cum Deo, & cum hominibus, & praevaluit? Num huiusmodi concioni, & Regis gloriae revelationi principes huius seculi fidem habuerunt? Nequaquam. Non parent enim: Itaque iteratur idem illud mandatum, Attollite portas capita vestra, eleuamini fores seculi, & introibit Rex gloriae, non iterandum si parumfsent. Parent ne saltem iterum pulsanti & aperire iubenti? Haud magis quàm antea. Perinde ac si surdis praedicatum fuisset, prae se ferunt se aeque ac antea nescire quis sit ille Rex gloriae. Quis est, inquiunt, iste Rex gloriae? accumulant pronomina, מי הוא זה innuentes se quidem regem gloriae agnoscere, sed istum tam humilem & abiectum pro rege gloriae non habere.
units.tr: VI. Lift up, he says, your heads, O gates (the Greek and the Vulgate read lift up, princes, your gates), and be lifted up, doors of the age, and the King of glory will enter. Do you seek an interpreter? Hear Christ himself: Behold, I stand at the door and knock: if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him. He addresses the gates in the plural, that is, those whose task it is to open the gates, and bids them be lifted up; for we open to Christ when we are lifted up towards heavenly things, not when we turn to earthly things and rest. To the command he adds a promise: and the King of glory will enter. "King" is used as the King par excellence, and Christ and Messiah are reciprocal. Christ, therefore, crowned with glory and honour, is the King of glory. He addresses those who were unwilling to go out to meet the King of glory as he came, but kept themselves shut up within their houses. So it was necessary to knock, and to bid them open; for that most glorious King, promised so often and awaited so long, is present and desires to enter. What of the princes of this age? Did they obey that command quickly? Did they immediately open to so great a King, as was fitting? Did they receive him with the greatest eagerness? Nothing of the kind. Who is, they say, this King of glory? They do not say "who is the King of glory," as the command required, but who is this King of glory? They profess that they do not know this King of glory, and that unless they are first taught who he is, they are unwilling to open. The answer is given: he is the Lord (Jehovah), strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle. Thus Christ everywhere insists that he is the Son of God, one with the Father and equal to the Father, so mighty that by a word he drove out demons, restored sight to the blind, raised the dead, cured every kind of disease, and promised eternal life and a glorious resurrection to those who believe in him. Could any king be thought more powerful, or stronger in battle, than he who has conquered all our enemies, even death itself, and will finally destroy it, and who, as the true Jacob, strove with God and with men, and prevailed? Did the princes of this age give faith to such a preaching and revelation of the King of glory? By no means. For they do not obey. Therefore the same command is repeated: Lift up your heads, O gates, be lifted up, doors of the age, and the King of glory will enter, a repetition that would not have been needed had they obeyed. Do they at least obey when he knocks again and bids them open? No more than before. As if it had been preached to the deaf, they show that, just as before, they do not know who that King of glory is. Who is, they say, this King of glory? They pile up pronouns, [mi hu zeh], hinting that they indeed recognise a King of glory, but do not regard this one, so humble and abject, as the King of glory.

units.la: VII. His ita explicatis sic argumentor. Rex iste gloriae venit ad suos, & sui ipsum non receperunt, venit ad Ecclesiam Iudaicam, & portas sibi clausas inuenit, pulsauit, iussit aperiri, quis esset expositum, nec tamen agnitus est: quóque magis instituit, & seipsum per se & ministros suos descripsit, suamque diuinitatem, potentiam, virtutem declarauit, eó magis Sacerdotes, primores populi, Judæi obduruerunt, nolueruntque eum pro rege gloriæ habere. Hoc autem non conuenit Patri præcisè & quatenus à Filio distinguitur, sed Filio: Est igitur Rex ille gloriæ non Pater præcisè, sed Filius. Propositio patet ex dictis. Illam enim interrogationem, Quis est iste Rex gloriæ? Non esse interrogationem fidelium Regem gloriæ noscere cupientium, sed incredulorum potius & rebellium, jam, opinor, satis ostendi. Si quis tamen dubitat, is cogitet, istos quorum in potestate portæ illæ erant, non processisse obuiam Regi gloriæ, non curasse ut ei ad-ventanti portæ paterent, iubenti sibi portas aperiri & attolli non statim paruisse, profitentis se Regem esse gloriæ vocem non agnovisse, nec ei fidem habuisse, sed intempestiuis interrogationibus prolatando tantam Majestatem contempsisse. Nulla enim causa erat sic quærendi; Nam & mandatum satis erat perspicuum, & nullus erat locus dubitandi quin Regi, Regi gloriæ sic absolutè nominato portæ aperiri deberent celeriter: præsertim à subditis, à seruis eius. Adde quod, ut iam observavi, non quærunt quis est Rex gloriæ, sed quis est iste Rex gloriæ, cum tamen in mandato non iste Rex gloriæ, sed absolutè & sine limitatione Rex gloriæ dictus fuisset. Deinde accepta responsione, qua Rex gloriæ abundè descriptus est, non parent tamen, nop credunt, rursus opus est mandato, rursus interrogant: tam sunt quàm prius ignari, tam rebelles. Denique responsis describitur, non à clementia, sed à potentia & robore, & præliandi virtute, quæ terrori esse debent incredulis & rebellibus.
units.tr: VII. With these points explained, I argue as follows. That King of glory came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. He came to the Jewish Church, found its gates shut against him, knocked, and commanded that they be opened. Who he was was made known, yet he was not recognised. The more he taught, and described himself through himself and his ministers, and declared his divinity, power and virtue, the more stubbornly the priests, the leading men of the people and the Jews refused to regard him as the King of glory. Now this does not apply to the Father precisely and as distinguished from the Son, but to the Son. That King of glory is therefore not the Father precisely, but the Son. The proposition is evident from what has been said. I think I have already shown sufficiently that the question, Who is this King of glory?, was not the question of believers eager to know the King of glory, but rather of unbelievers and rebels. If anyone still doubts it, let him consider that those in whose power those gates were did not go out to meet the King of glory, did not take care that the gates should stand open to him as he came, and did not promptly obey when he ordered the gates to be opened and lifted up. They professed that they did not recognise the voice of the King of glory, did not believe him, and by their untimely questions they despised so great a Majesty. For there was no reason to ask in this way. The command was plain enough, and there was no room for doubt that the gates should quickly be opened to the King, to the King of glory so named without qualification, least of all by his subjects and servants. Add that, as I have already observed, they do not ask who is the King of glory, but who is this King of glory, whereas in the command he was named not as this King of glory but absolutely and without limitation, the King of glory. Then, when the answer was given, by which the King of glory was fully described, they still do not obey or believe; the command must be repeated, and they ask again. They are as ignorant as before, and as rebellious. Finally, he is described in the answers not by clemency but by power, strength and military prowess, which ought to be a terror to unbelievers and rebels.

units.la: VIII. Propositione majore sic probata, Minor versantibus nobis in luce Euangelij Regis gloriæ obscura esse non potest. Deum enim Patrem præcisè, quatenus à Filio differt, Judæi, etiam hodie, pro Rege gloriæ habent. Immò eius Zelo, sed non secundum scientiam, abrepti Filium eius, cum maximè se Filium Dei esse, atque adeò Deum & Regem gloriæ professus est, tum maximè contempserunt. Caucant Adversarij ne simili aliquo Zelo impediantur, quominus eum esse Regem gloriæ, seu Jehouam credant.
units.tr: VIII. With the major premise so proved, the minor is this: while we live in the light of the Gospel, the King of glory cannot be obscure. For the Jews, even today, regard God the Father precisely, as he differs from the Son, as the King of glory. Indeed, carried away by zeal, but not according to knowledge, they most of all despised his Son when he professed himself to be most of all the Son of God, and thus God and the King of glory. Let our opponents beware lest some similar zeal prevent them from believing that he is the King of glory, that is, Jehovah.

units.la: X. Hinc liquidum esse potest, falsam esse Socini responsionem. Respondemus, inquit, locum istum psalmi vel ad Christum referri non posse, vel certe non tanquam ad eum, qui sit ille ipse Jehona, de quo ibi nominatim agitur; sed tanquam ad eum, in cuius persona, persona, licet diuersa essentia ab ipso Iehoua, id impletum fuerit, quod de Iehoua ibi prædictum fuit. Iam enim, opinor, ex dictis patet, locum istum psalmi ad Christum referri non modo posse, sed etiam debere. Intelligi autem non potest, quomodo id quod habetur in isto psalmo impleri potuerit in persona Christi, si Christus non est Rex gloriæ, nec quomodo sit Rex gloriæ, si descriptio Regis gloriæ, quæ ibidem bis facta est, ei non conue-nit.
units.tr: X. From this it can be clear that the response of Socinus is false. "We reply," he says, "that this psalm passage cannot be referred to Christ, or at least not as to him who is that very Jehovah of whom it speaks by name there; but as to him in whose person, though of a different essence from Jehovah himself, that which was foretold there of Jehovah was fulfilled." For I think it is now plain from what has been said that this passage of the psalm can be referred to Christ, and not only can be but must be. Nor can it be understood how what is found in this psalm could have been fulfilled in the person of Christ, if Christ is not the King of glory; nor how he is the King of glory if the description of the King of glory, which is given twice in the same place, does not apply to him.

units.la: X. Ad psalmum 50. quod spectat, dubitari non potest, quin is, qui dicit Ps.[?] 13. meus est orbis, & plenitudo eius, sit Deus Israëlis præditus essentia diuina: vocatur enim, vt iam obseruaui, Deus Deorum & Iehoua Ps. 1. dubitari etiam non debet, quin idem sit Christus. Dicitur enim de eo Ps. 3. & 4. Deus illucescet, Deus noster veniet, (Græca & vulgata editio habent, Deus manifestè veniet, Deus noster) & non silebit. Ignis ante eum deuorabit, & in circuitu eius tempestas valida. Aduocabit cælum desursum & terram vt iudicet populum suum, Quis autem veniet ad Iudicandum, & quidem manifestò ac cum igne præcedente? Pater? Non: Neque enim Pater iudicat quenquam. Filius? Certè; id enim Euangelium constanter testatur, & inculcat.
units.tr: X. As regards Psalm 50, there can be no doubt that he who says, "the world is mine, and the fullness thereof" (Ps. 13), is God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence; for, as I have already observed, he is called God of gods and Jehovah (Ps. 1). Nor should it be doubted that this is Christ. For of him it is said (Ps. 3 and 4): God shall shine forth, our God shall come (the Greek and the Vulgate edition have, God shall manifestly come, our God), and he shall not keep silence. A fire shall devour before him, and about him a mighty tempest. He shall call the heaven from above and the earth, that he may judge his people. But who is to come to judge, and indeed manifestly and with a fire going before him? The Father? No: for the Father judges no one. The Son? Certainly; for the Gospel bears constant witness to this and insists upon it.

units.la: DISPUTATIO UNDECIMA De Arg. XI. Ex Psal. LXVIII. v. 19. Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captiuitatem, accepisti dona in hominibus, collato cum Eph. 4. 8.
units.tr: DISPUTATION ELEVEN On Argument XI, from Psalm 68:19: Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive, thou hast received gifts among men, compared with Eph. 4:8.

units.la: I. EGREGIUM etiam argumentum nobis suppeditant verba illa psalmi 68. 19. Ascendisti in altum, cepisti captiuitatem, accepisti dona in hominibus, laudata ab Apostolo Eph. 4. 8. quod sic concipi potest. Ille qui dicitur psal. 68. 19. ascendisse in al-tum, &c, est Deus Israelis.
units.tr: I. The words of Psalm 68:19, Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive, thou hast received gifts among men, which the Apostle praises at Eph. 4:8, also furnish us with an excellent argument. It can be framed as follows: he who is said in Psalm 68:19 to have ascended on high, and so on, is the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est ille qui dicitur psal. 68. 19. ascendisse in altum, &c.
units.tr: Christ is he who is said in Psalm 68:19 to have ascended on high, and so on.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israelis. Major legenti sine prejudicio psalmum, Minor legenti Apostolum non vera nequit videri. Tamen aduersarij minore, ut videtur, concessa, negant Majorem. Aiunt enim, illa verba, Ascendisti in altum, &c, esse prophetiam de Christo futuro, & non dici ista de ipso uno Deo Israelis. Quomodo enim, addit Socinus, cum Paulus ista ad Christum accommodet supra omnes cœlos exaltatum, negare primùm quis audebit, hanc esse de Christo futuro prophetiam? Deinde quid erit, quod suadere possit, ista nihilominus de uno illo Deo Israelis fuisse dicta? Suadent multa,
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The major premise cannot seem false to someone who reads the psalm without prejudice, and the minor premise cannot seem false to someone who reads the Apostle. Yet our opponents, who seem to grant the minor premise, deny the major. For they say that those words, "Thou hast ascended on high," and so on, are a prophecy about the future Christ, and that these words are not said of the one God of Israel himself. For how, Socinus adds, since Paul applies them to Christ, exalted above all the heavens, will anyone dare first to deny that this is a prophecy about the future Christ? And then, what is there that could persuade us that these words were nevertheless spoken of that one God of Israel? Many things persuade us.

units.la: II. Primùm verborum totius psalmi series & contextus. Nam seu antecedentes versus, seu sequentes spectes, ubique de Deo Israelis modò in tertia, modò in secunda persona agitur. Fitne verisimile, sermonis, qui de Deo Israelis toto psalmo habetur, & quo Deus Israelis aliquoties compellatur, filum continuum interposito isto versiculo decimo nono medium secari & interrūmpi, conuersa ad alium oratione, cuius, neque in antecedentibus facta esset mentio, neque in sequentibus fieri deberet? Ita versus iste 19. quem vulgata versio diuidit in duos, lacinia quædam esset neque cum ijs quæ antecedunt, neque cum ijs quæ sequuntur cohærens, sed aliorsum pertinens. Quod nullo modo probabile est. Huc accedit, quod non obscura est connexio huius versus cum proximè antecedente. In illo enim describitur exercitus, in isto parta victoriâ reditus in cœlum, & de spolijs hostium largitio, vt dubium esse non possit, quin de eodem sit sermo.
units.tr: II. First, the sequence and context of the whole psalm. For whether you look at the verses before or after, everywhere the God of Israel is spoken of, now in the third person, now in the second. Is it likely that the continuous thread of the discourse, which concerns the God of Israel throughout the psalm and in which the God of Israel is addressed several times, should be cut and broken in the middle by the interposition of this nineteenth verse, the speech being turned to someone else, of whom no mention had been made in what precedes and none ought to be made in what follows? So this verse 19, which the Vulgate divides into two, would be a scrap of cloth, cohering neither with what comes before nor with what comes after, but belonging elsewhere. This is in no way probable. Moreover, the connection of this verse with the one immediately before it is obvious. For in the earlier verse the army is described, and in this one, after victory has been won, the return to heaven and the distribution of the enemy's spoils are described, so that there can be no doubt that the same subject is being discussed.

units.la: III. Id vidit Socinus, addit enim, Sed concedamus (vt quidem mihi maximè probatur) liquidò constare, ea referri debere ad illum Deum proximè ante nominatum, quamuis ille in tertia persona nominetur, is verò, de quo hæc dicuntur, in secunda, non tamen euincetur, hunc esse illum vnum Deum Israelis. In Hebræo enim nomen Deus est Elohim, quod alijs præter vnum illum Deum Israelis, præsertim Christo homini, tribui rectè posse nemo est qui neget. Præterea hunc non esse illum vnum Deum Israelis, suadere omnino videtur, quod eo cum suis curribus, &c, nominato, statim subiungitur, Dominus in eis. Verisimile enim est prorsus, hunc Dominum alium esse ab illo Deo; quippe de quo dicatur quod in curribus &c, illius Dei sit, id est, illis virtute sua ac fauore adsit. Est autem hic Dominus ille vnus Deus Israelis. Primum istæ duæ rationes nihil valent. Prior quidem: Nam si ducitur à Christo homine, qui, cum Deus Israelis non sit, dicitur tamen Elohim, petitio est quæsiti: si ducitur ab angelis & magistratibus, quibus in plurali numero nomen Elohim tribuitur nonnunquam, aberratio est à textu Prophetæ. Certum enim est in versu 18. huius psalmi per Deum, Elohim, intelligendos non esse angelos, nec summos inter homines Magistratus. Posterior verò: Quid est enim cur in eo versu non sit idem Deus, & Dominus, cum constet hæc nomina passim eundem significare? Nempe, currus dicuntur esse Dei, Dominus dicitur esse in curribus: Currus Dei sunt viginti millia, millia multiplicia, Dominus in illis, &c. Ergo Deus & Dominus non sunt idem. Egregia argumentatio! quasi Deus dici non possit esse in suo ipsius exercitu, in suis curribus, hoc est, interprete Socino, illis virtute sua ac fauore adesse? Canit Propheta exercitum Dei esse numero & virtute fortissimum, quippe in quo sunt viginti millia curruum, & quidem iterata, & præterea Deum in eo esse, eius ducem esse. Id quod erat addendum, pendet enim victoria non tam à numero & robore militum, quam à ducis peritia, prudentia, vigilantia, fortitudine, &c.
units.tr: III. Socinus saw this, for he adds: But let us grant (as I myself especially approve) that it is clear that these things must be referred to that God named just before, although he is named in the third person, while he of whom these things are said is addressed in the second person; yet it will not be proved that this is that one God of Israel. For in the Hebrew the name is God, Elohim, and no one denies that it can rightly be attributed to others besides that one God of Israel, especially to Christ as man. Moreover, that this is not that one God of Israel seems entirely to be suggested by the fact that, once "with his chariots," and so on, has been named, it is immediately added, "the Lord is among them." For it is quite likely that this Lord is other than that God, since it is said of the chariots that they belong to that God, that is, that they are present to help them by his power and favor. But this Lord is that one God of Israel. First, these two arguments have no force. The first: if the name is taken from Christ as man, who, although he is not the God of Israel, is nevertheless called Elohim, this is begging the question; if it is taken from angels and magistrates, to whom the name Elohim is sometimes given in the plural, this is a departure from the Prophet's text. For it is certain that in verse 18 of this psalm, by God, Elohim, angels are not to be understood, nor the highest magistrates among men. The second argument: for what reason is there that in that verse God and Lord should not be the same, when it is agreed that these names everywhere signify the same? Namely, the chariots are said to be God's, and the Lord is said to be among the chariots: The chariots of God are twenty thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them, and so on. Therefore God and the Lord are not the same. An excellent argument! As if God could not be said to be present in his own army, in his own chariots, that is, in Socinus's interpretation, to be present to them by his power and favor! The Prophet sings that the army of God is most strong in number and power, since in it there are twenty thousand chariots, and indeed repeated many times, and moreover that God is in it, as its leader. This is what had to be added, for victory depends not so much on the number and strength of the soldiers as on the skill, prudence, watchfulness, courage, and so on of the commander.

units.la: IV. Deinde, quis credat nomen Dei (heb. Elohim) in ver-bis, currus Dei sunt viginti millia, &c, non eundem significare, quem in præcedentibus & sequentibus huius psalmi versibus significat, in quibus plusquam vicies usurpatum est [?]? Quis credat Prophetam, cum exercitum Dei describit, non eum Deum intelligere, quem iam toties nominauit, cuique toto psalmo canit epinicia? Quid? erantne duo dij, quorum alterius essent victo-riæ, alterius currus seu exercitus? Nonne tunc, cum hæc scri-bebat Dauid, currus Dei erant viginti millia, &c? quis ergo credat, Deum intelligendum esse in illis verbis, qui nunquam antea fuerat, nondum erat, nec futurus erat nisi post mille annos, ac proinde cuius tunc temporis nulli erant currus? talem enim Deum cogitant aduersarij.
units.tr: IV. Next, who would believe that the name of God (Hebrew Elohim) in the words the chariots of God are twenty thousand, and so on, does not signify the same God whom it signifies in the preceding and following verses of this psalm, where it is used more than twenty times? Who would believe that the Prophet, when he describes the army of God, does not mean the God whom he has already named so often, and to whom he sings triumphal songs throughout the psalm? What? Were there two gods, one of whom owned the victory and the other the chariots or army? Were not the chariots of God twenty thousand, and so on, when David was writing these things? Who then would believe that God is to be understood in those words as one who had never existed before, who did not yet exist, and who was not to exist until a thousand years later, and who therefore at that time had no chariots at all? For that is the kind of God our opponents imagine.

units.la: V. Præterea, sic argumentor. Deus ℵ[?]. 16. Mons Dei, mons Bascan, mons Gibbosus, mons Bascan, & ℵ. 17. Mons in quo be-neplacitum est Deo habitare in eo, est Deus Israelis. Atqui Deus cuius currus ℵ. 18. dicuntur bis decem millia, est idem Deus. Id enim non modo nominis, ut ita loquar, identitas, & versuum propinquitas, & Dei unitas arguit, sed etiam sensus & argumenti seu materiæ conjunctio. Cum enim Propheta, qui toto fere hoc psalmo alludit ad historiam populi Dei in deserto, montem Dei dixisset esse montem Bascan, qui giganti Og bello ereptus, populo adhuc agente in deserto, & Mose viuente, dimidiæ tribui Manasse in hæreditatem cessit, subjunxit statim apostrophen ad alios montes, hoc est, regna & societates, quæ erant montem Dei, hoc est, Ecclesiam oppugnaturæ, Quare, inquit, exilitis montes gibbosi? Deinde monet eorum conatus omnes fore irritos. Deum enim montem illum concupivisse ut habitaret in eo, & revera in eo habitaturum perpetuò. Neque vero esse cur confidant in militum suorum numero & robore, in curribus & equitibus: Deo enim etiam currus esse, & quidem longè plures, & potentiores, & præterea suo exercitui præsentem ipsum adesse; Itaque Sinai esse sanctitate inuiolabili reuerendum, qui impune tangi aut violari non possit. Quis non videt eiusdem Dei & montem esse, & exercitum ad montem illum tuendum?
units.tr: V. Moreover, I argue as follows. God (v. 16): The mountain of God, the mountain of Bashan, the high mountain, the mountain of Bashan, and (v. 17): the mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell, is the God of Israel. But the God whose chariots are said in v. 18 to be twice ten thousand is the same God. For this is shown not only by the identity of the name, as it were, and the nearness of the verses and the unity of God, but also by the connection of sense and subject matter. For when the Prophet, who in almost the whole of this psalm alludes to the history of the people of God in the wilderness, had said that the mountain of God was the mountain of Bashan, which, taken in war from the giant Og, while the people were still wandering in the wilderness and Moses was alive, was given to the half-tribe of Manasseh as an inheritance, he immediately added an apostrophe to other mountains, that is, to kingdoms and societies, which were going to attack the mountain of God, that is, the Church. Why, he says, do you leap, you high mountains? Then he warns that all their attempts will be in vain. For God has desired that mountain for his dwelling, and indeed he will dwell in it forever. Nor is there any reason for them to trust in the number and strength of their soldiers, in chariots and horsemen: for God too has chariots, and indeed far more numerous and more powerful ones, and moreover God himself is present with his army. And so Sinai is to be revered with an inviolable holiness, which cannot be touched or violated with impunity. Who does not see that the mountain and the army defending that mountain both belong to the same God?

units.la: VI. Quæro etiam, cui Deo cantat Propheta, cui psallit, cuius laudes, victoriam, triumphum, beneficentiam concelebrat hoc versu 19. certè ei, ad quem laudandum alios hortatus ℣. 4. Cantate Deo, psallite nomini eius, &c, ipse vt aliis præeat exemplo, canit & psallit reliquis versibus? Quem Deum potius (si tamen fas est plures cogitare Deos) describit, victis & dissipatis inimicis, ascendentem, atque adeo redeuntem in cœlum, captiuam ducentem captiuitatem, dona bello parta distribuentem homini-bus, quàm eum, de quo cecinit ℣. 1. Exurgat Deus & dissipentur inimici eius, &c. Ille autem quin sit Deus Israëlis, nec negatur ab aduersariis, nec negari potest.
units.tr: VI. I ask also to which God the Prophet sings, to which he psalms, whose praises, victory, triumph, and beneficence he celebrates in this verse 19? Surely to him to whom, in verse 4, he exhorts others to sing praise: Sing to God, sing praises to his name, and so on, while he himself goes before the others as an example, singing and psalming in the remaining verses. Which God, if indeed it is right to imagine several gods, does he describe rather as ascending, and indeed returning to heaven, after his enemies have been defeated and scattered, leading captivity captive, distributing among men the gifts won in war, than the one of whom he sang in verse 1: Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and so on? That this is the God of Israel is neither denied by our opponents nor can it be denied.

units.la: VII. Cæterum verba illa, Exurgat Deus & dissipentur inimici eius, &c. sunt Mosis verba, quæ, cum Arca proficisceretur, solebat pronunciare. Erat autem arca, saltem ratione operculi seu propitiatorij, typus Christi, sed typus imperfectus: propitiato-rium enim non erat persona, non loquebatur, non erat vllo mo-do Deus. Consideremus igitur quo Deo surgente inimici dissipantur. Vel hostes intelliguntur carnales, vel spirituales. Si spirituales, Nonne Christus is est, quo surgente primo suo aduentu hostes nostri spirituales dissipati sunt, & quo iterum surgente secundo suo aduentu, peribunt in æternum. Si carnales, nonne vt se habent hostes carnales ad spirituales, sic se habet victor hostium carnalium ad victorem hostium spiritualium? vel igitur idem est, vel ille huius est typus.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, those words, "Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered," etc., are the words of Moses, which he used to utter when the Ark set out. The Ark, at least in respect of its cover or mercy-seat, was a type of Christ, but an imperfect type: for the mercy-seat was not a person, did not speak, and was in no way God. Let us consider, then, by which God rising the enemies are scattered. Either the enemies meant are carnal or spiritual. If spiritual, is it not Christ who, rising at his first coming, scattered our spiritual enemies, and who, rising again at his second coming, will destroy them forever? If carnal, is not the conqueror of carnal enemies related to the conqueror of spiritual enemies just as carnal enemies are related to spiritual ones? Either then they are the same, or the one is a type of the other.

units.la: VIII. Potest etiam argumentum duci à ℣. 20. Benedictus Dominus quotidie onerans nos, &c. Cui enim gratiæ illis verbis aguntur? nonne apparet ex versu antecedente eum esse, qui deiectis hostibus reuersus in cœlum dona dedit hominibus? itaque pro illa beneficentia & largitione summa maximèque commemorabili gratiæ ei continuò, vt par erat, aguntur.
units.tr: VIII. An argument can also be drawn from verse 20, "Blessed be the Lord, who daily loads us with benefits," etc. For to whom are thanks given in those words? Does it not appear from the preceding verse that it is he who, having put the enemies to flight, returned to heaven and gave gifts to men? Therefore, for that kindness and generous bounty, and for this most memorable and supreme grace, thanks are rightly and continually offered to him.

units.la: IX. Finem imponerem huic argumento, nisi Socinus addidisset, minus verum esse ad, quod Vvjekus Bellarmini verbis de suo addidit, videlicet Paulum affirmare, Danidem verba illa de Christo dixisse. Aliud enim est; inquit, in Christo illa impleta esse, siue impleri dekuisse (quod est quicquid necessario ex Pauli verbis elicipotest) aliud verò, de Christo dicta fuisse. In quo primùm con-tradictio implicari videtur. Deo enim certè illa dicta sunt in quo impleta sunt vel impleri debuerunt, potius quàm de eo in quo non sunt impleta. Nullus enim melior est vaticinii commentarius, quàm ipse eventus. Hoc volo, Is dicitur à Propheta ascendisse in altum, captiuam duxisse captiuitatem, &c, qui revera ascendit in altum, &c, non autem is qui non ascendit. Deinde dicta illa esse de Christo tam disertè Paulus affirmat, ut disertius vix potuerit. Unicuique, inquit, nostrum data est gratia secundum mensuram donationis Christi. Propter quod dicit, (sic λέγει, expendat lector illud propter quod, &, dicit) Ascendens in altum captiuam duxit captiuitatem, & dedit dona hominibus. Quod autem ascendit, quid est, nisi quia & descendit primùm in inferiores partes terrae? Qui descendit ipse est qui etiam ascendit supra omnes coelos ut impleret omnia. Si verba illa, ascendit in altum, &c, non sunt in psalmo dicta de Christo, sed de alio aliquo, qui non descendit prius in partes inferiores terrae, & deinde ascendit supra omnes coelos, quomodo sic ratiocinatur & colligit Apostolus? quomodo dicit, quod ascendit quid est nisi quod descendit, &c? sic enim aperte significat, id aliter accipi non posse.
units.tr: IX. I would end this argument here, were it not that Socinus has added that Bellarmine's words, which Vvjekus took over and added to on his own account, are less true, namely that Paul affirms David to have spoken those words of Christ. "For it is one thing," he says, "that they were fulfilled in Christ, or ought to have been fulfilled (which is whatever can necessarily be drawn from Paul's words), and another that they were said of Christ." In this, first of all, a contradiction seems to be involved. For those words were certainly spoken of him in whom they were fulfilled, or ought to have been fulfilled, rather than of him in whom they were not fulfilled. For there is no better commentary on a prophecy than the event itself. This I maintain: he is the one of whom the Prophet says that he ascended on high, led captivity captive, and so on, who really ascended on high, and not the one who did not ascend. Next, Paul affirms so plainly that those words were said of Christ that he could hardly have said it more plainly. "To each one of us," he says, "grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. Therefore it says" (so the Greek reads; let the reader weigh that "therefore" and "it says") "When he ascended on high he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men. Now that he ascended, what does it mean but that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things." If those words, "he ascended on high," etc., were not spoken in the psalm of Christ, but of some other who did not first descend into the lower parts of the earth and then ascend above all the heavens, how does the Apostle reason and infer in this way? How does he say, "that he ascended, what does it mean but that he descended," etc.? For in this way he plainly signifies that it cannot be understood otherwise.

units.la: X. Id quod etiam res clamat, de quo enim alio dicta illa suissent à Propheta? de Mose? repugnat scopus Prophetae, qui est laudes & victorias Dei canere, non Mosis: repugnant verba: Dei enim tot psalmo meminit, Mosis nunquam: repugnat res ipsa: nam ascendit quidem Moses in montem, verum non dicitur hoc loco, ascendisti in montem, sed ascendisti למרום [?] εἰς ὕψος [?], quae vox sic absolutè posita montem Sinai nunquam, coelum verò persæpè significat. Deinde reliqua non congruunt: non enim Moses ascendendo in montem captiuos abduxit, non accepit dona distribuenda inter homines, multò minus rebelles ut in iis habitaret Dominus Deus. Denique si de Mose verba illa accipiantur, non cohærebunt cum antecedentibus neque cum sequentibus, sed erunt veluti scopae dissolutae, quod non congruit cum Spiritus Dei, qui in Davide loquebatur, sapientia. De Davide illa multò minus dicuntur: Nam ut taceam Davidem nec sui meminisse hoc psalmo, nec suas laudes cecinisse, nec sic in altum ascendisse, nec causam fuisse cur tale quid de seipso diceret eo versu, manifestum est, eum verbis illis, ascendisti in altum, non semetipsum, sed alium alloquutum fuisse.
units.tr: X. The matter itself also cries out for this. For of whom else could those words have been spoken by the Prophet? Of Moses? The purpose of the Prophet repels this, which is to sing the praises and victories of God, not of Moses. The words repel it: for the psalm mentions God throughout, never Moses. The thing itself repels it: for Moses did indeed ascend a mountain, but it is not said in this place "you ascended the mountain," but "you ascended to the height" [למרום; εἰς ὕψος], a phrase which, used absolutely in this way, never means Mount Sinai but very often means heaven. Further, the rest does not fit: Moses, by ascending a mountain, did not lead captives away, did not receive gifts to distribute among men, much less among rebels, that the Lord God might dwell among them. Finally, if those words are taken of Moses, they will not cohere either with what precedes or with what follows, but will be like loose broom-twigs, which does not agree with the wisdom of the Spirit of God, who spoke in David. Those words are said of David even less: for, to pass over the fact that David neither remembers himself in this psalm, nor sings his own praises, nor ascended thus on high, nor had any cause to say such a thing of himself in that verse, it is evident that in the words "you ascended on high" he addressed not himself but another.

units.la: XI. De quo igitur alio ista dicerentur? de Deo Patre, alius non succurrit. Quando ergo Deus Pater ascendisset in altum? Cum ascendit in montem Sinai? At in eum montem descendisse Deus dicitur in Scriptura, non autem ascendisse: Et vox מרום cum de Deo agitur coelum significat, non autem terrenum montem: & Deus ascendendo in montem Sinai non abduxit captivitatem, nec parta bello antecedente dona accepit quae ad homines mitteret, inter quae etiam quidam rebelles essent, ut in ijs habitaret, sed contra potius iussit sibi munera ab Israelitis offerri, ex quibus tabernaculum fieret, in quo habitaret. Tantum igitur abest, ut afcensus iste in altum sit idem cum descensu Dei in montem Sinai, ut ei oppositus videri possit.
units.tr: XI. Of whom else, then, could these things be said? Of God the Father, no other comes to mind. When, then, did God the Father ascend on high? When he ascended Mount Sinai? But in Scripture God is said to have descended upon that mountain, not to have ascended; and the word מרום, when said of God, signifies heaven, not an earthly mountain; and God, by ascending Mount Sinai, did not lead captivity away nor receive gifts, won by a prior war, to send to men, among whom there were even some rebels, that he might dwell among them; on the contrary, he commanded that offerings be brought to him by the Israelites, from which a tabernacle might be made in which he would dwell. So far is that ascent on high from being the same as God's descent upon Mount Sinai, that it could seem to be its opposite.

units.la: XII. Necesse ergo est ut dicant Adversarij, Deum Patrem dici ascendisse in altum, cum eius Filius Iesus Christus ascendit in cœlum: id quod tamen dici non potest. Nam si habita ratione afcensus Christi Deus pater dici potest ascendisse in cœlum, idem etiam dici poterit descendisse in partes inferiores terræ. Nam qui dicit, ascendisti in altum, is eum significat, de quo hoc dicit, antequam ascenderet, in loco inferiore fuisse. Hoc autem concesso, cur non posset Deus Pater crucifixus & mortuus pari iure dici, equidem non intelligo. Si hoc absurdum est, etiam illud absurdum videri debet. Concludo igitur de eo dicta esse verba illa, ascendisti in altum, &c, qui ascendit in altum, &c, non autem de eo qui non ascendit in altum, &c. Ascendisse autem in altum, &c. Filium, non vero Patrem, testibus omnibus Evangelistis & Apostolis: De Filio igitur non de Patre verba illa dicta fuisse.
units.tr: XII. It is necessary, therefore, for the opponents to say that God the Father is said to have ascended on high when his Son Jesus Christ ascended into heaven: which, however, cannot be said. For if, with regard to Christ's ascent, God the Father can be said to have ascended into heaven, the same could also be said of his having descended into the lower parts of the earth. For he who says "you ascended on high" signifies that the one of whom he says this was previously in a lower place before he ascended. Granting this, I do not see why God the Father could not with equal right be said to have been crucified and to have died. If this is absurd, that too ought to seem absurd. I conclude, therefore, that those words, "you ascended on high," etc., were spoken of him who ascended on high, etc., and not of him who did not ascend on high, etc. Now it was the Son, not the Father, who ascended on high, as all the Evangelists and Apostles testify. Those words were therefore spoken of the Son, not of the Father.

units.la: DISPUTATIO DUODECIMA
units.tr: Disputation Twelve

units.la: De Arg. XII. Ex his verbis Psal. cii. v. 26. Tu initio terram fundasti, & opera manuum tua- rum sunt cœli. Ipsi peribunt, tu autem perma- nes, &c. laudatis Heb. 1. 10.
units.tr: On Argument XII, from these words of Psalm 102:26, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of thy hands. They shall perish, but thou remainest, etc. cited at Hebrews 1:10.

units.la: I. ACCEDIT ad superiora testimonium disertissimum, quod Apostolus Heb. 1. 10. laudauit è ps. 102. v. 26. Tu initio terram fundasti, &c. Qui enim sic compellatur, quin sit Deus Israëlis cœli & terræ creator, nec negant, nec negare possunt Adversarij, adeò manifestum est. Quod autem is sit Filius Dei, tam clarè docet & testatur Apostolus Heb. 1. 10. ut clarius vix possit, nec puto præter Adversarios, quibus decretum est quoquomodo tueri thesim, ullum esse Christianum, vel Iudæum, vel Mahometanum, vel Ethnicum, qui si primum caput Epistolæ ad Hebræos legat, id ab eius autore doceri non animadvertat.
units.tr: I. A most express testimony comes next. The Apostle in Hebrews 1:10 cites from Psalm 102:26 the words Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast founded the earth, etc. That the one so addressed is the God of Israel, the Creator of heaven and earth, neither our opponents deny nor can they deny, so plain is it. That he is the Son of God, the Apostle teaches and attests in Hebrews 1:10 so clearly that nothing could be clearer. I think there is no Christian, Jew, Muslim or heathen, except the opponents who have resolved to defend their thesis at all costs, who, if he reads the first chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, does not notice that its author teaches this.

units.la: II. Excogitarunt tamen Adversarij, quo sunt acumine, duas loci illius ab Apostolo citati distortiones. Primùm euim aiunt verba illa ps. 102. 26. ab autore illius Epistolæ commemorata fuisse, non ut testimonium de Christo proferret, sed ut illis uteretur ad apostrophen ad Deum Patrem faciendam. Deinde (quod sibi plus probari dicit Socinus) confitentur in his verbis (nempe Heb. 1. 10.) testimonium quidem de Dei Filio esse, inter alia antecedentia numerandum, quæ ibi Apostolus attulit. Quid ergo posita illa confessione respondere possunt? Nam versus ille decimus nihil habet præter ista verba, Et, Tu Domine terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli, quæ si testimonium sunt de Filio, Filius est cœli & terræ creator. Quid ergo respondent? Audi lector & mirare subtilitatem, negant testimonij partem illam quæ recitatur Ψ. 10. ad Filium dirigi, aut ad eum vllo modo pertinere. Quorsum ergo citatur? non propter se, sed propter sequentia, quæ recitantur Ψ. 12. Ac velut amictum circumvolues eos, & mutabuntur. Quid igitur? dirigunturne ista verba ad Filium? Minimè. Aut est ne in illis verbis mentio aliqua Filij? Nulla prorsus. Quomodo igitur sunt testimonium de Filio? Quia in eis mentio fit abolitionis seu mutationis cœlorum. Quid hoc ad rem? Hæc mutatio, inquiunt, fiet per Christum in eius postremo adventu. Istudne dicitur à Propheta? nullo modo. Sic confessio, Testimonium esse de Filio Dei, evanescit tandem in auras, nihilque esse nisi illusio deprehenditur.
units.tr: II. Nevertheless, our opponents, with all their sharpness, have devised two distortions of that passage cited by the Apostle. First, they say that the author of that Epistle recalled those words of Psalm 102:26 not to produce a testimony about Christ, but to use them for an apostrophe addressed to God the Father. Second, (which Socinus says is more probable for him) they confess that in these words (namely Hebrews 1:10) there is indeed a testimony concerning the Son of God, to be counted among the other preceding things which the Apostle brought forward there. What, then, can they answer, given that confession? For that tenth verse contains nothing but these words, And, Thou, Lord, hast founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of thy hands; and if these are a testimony about the Son, then the Son is the Creator of heaven and earth. What, then, do they answer? Listen, reader, and marvel at their subtlety: they deny that the part of the testimony recited in v. 10 is directed to the Son, or pertains to him in any way. Why, then, is it cited? Not for its own sake, but for what follows, recited in v. 12: And as a garment thou wilt roll them up, and they shall be changed. What then? Are these words directed to the Son? By no means. Is there any mention of the Son in those words? None at all. How, then, are they a testimony concerning the Son? Because in them mention is made of the abolition or change of the heavens. What has this to do with the matter? This change, they say, will be brought about through Christ at his last coming. Is that said by the Prophet? In no way. Thus the confession that it is a testimony concerning the Son of God vanishes into thin air, and is found to be nothing but illusion.

units.la: III. Sed quoniam duæ istæ citationis huius testimonij depravationes satis refutatæ nobis videntur lib. 1. Disp. de Arg. xxxi. nihil addemus hoc loco, nisi quod, ut hæc quoque disputatio momenti nonnihil ad superiora adjungat, confirmabimus, Filium Dei mundum creasse, duobus argumentis, si non prorsus necessarijs, saltem valdè probabilibus. Prius ducetur à Typo. Constat enim Christi quidem propitiatorium, Angelorum verò cherubim illos typos fuisse, qui faciebus [?] in propitiatorium conversis, illud alis tegebant, quò alludere videtur Petrus 1. Pet. 1. 12. Hoc posito (nam, quia non videtur ab adversarijs negatum iri, confirmatione supersedeo) quæro, cur duos illos cherubim ex ipso propitiatorio fieri oportuit? Id enim, & Deus diserris [?] verbis præcepit Exod. 25. 18. & factum fuisse congruenter præcepto narratur Exod. 37. 8. Cum enim id neque fortuitò, neque temerè acciderit, neque frustrà ab autore Scripturæ observatum fuerit, & quidem tam accuratè, causam aliquam grauem eius rei oportet subesse, quæ aliundè quàm ab ipsa re adumbrata peti non potest. Talem enim umbram seu figuram esse oportuit, ut, quoad eius fieri potuit, corpori suo seu veritati responderet. Credendum est igitur idcirco cherubim illos originem ab ipso propitiatorio ducere debuisse, ut illud nobis adumbrarent, quod Apostolus diserte affirmavit Col. 1. 16. & nos lib. 1. disp. seu Arg. 20. 25. 27. 28. 29. 30. 31. probavimus, Angelos ab eo, qui est verum propitiatorium, originem ducere, hoc est, creatos fuisse. Quid enim aliud potuit ea re adumbrari?
units.tr: III. But since these two corruptions of the citation of this testimony seem to us sufficiently refuted in book 1, Disputation on Argument 31, we shall add nothing here, except that, so that this disputation may also add something of weight to what precedes, we shall confirm that the Son of God created the world by two arguments, if not wholly necessary, at least very probable. The first will be drawn from a type. It is established that the mercy seat was indeed a type of Christ, and the cherubim of the angels, who, with faces turned toward the mercy seat, covered it with their wings, to which 1 Peter 1:12 seems to allude. This being granted (since our opponents will not, it seems, deny it, I dispense with confirming it), I ask why those two cherubim had to be made out of the mercy seat itself? For God expressly commanded this in Exodus 25:18, and the making of it is narrated in agreement with the command in Exodus 37:8. Since this did not happen by chance, nor rashly, nor was it observed without purpose by the author of Scripture, and indeed so carefully, some weighty cause for this thing must lie underneath, which cannot be sought from anywhere other than the thing itself which is foreshadowed. For the shadow or figure had to be such that, as far as possible, it corresponded to its body or truth. It is to be believed, therefore, that those cherubim had to derive their origin from the mercy seat itself, so that they might foreshadow for us what the Apostle affirmed expressly in Colossians 1:16, and what we proved in book 1, Disputation or Argument 20, 25, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31: that the angels derive their origin from him who is the true mercy seat, that is, that they were created. For what else could this have foreshadowed?

units.la: IV. Alterum argumentum petetur ex Apoc. v. 13. quo loco testatur Apostolus, se, cum primum sigillum Agnus aperuisset, omnem creaturam, quae in coelo est, & quae in terra, & sub terra, & in mari, & quae in iis sunt omnia, audiuisse dicentes, Sedenti in throno & Agno benedictio, & honor, & gloria, & robur in secula seculorum. Quomodo omnis creatura nulla excepta (ne qua enim excipi posset cauisse dal[?] genter[?] Apostolus videtur)hoc dicit? Proprie enim id dicere neque creaturae mentis expertes possunt, neque rebelles volunt. Nempe id creatura dicere intelligitur, quod aliquomodo significat: dicere enim est aliquid significare. Signa porro vel naturā suā, vel ex instituto significant. Dicitur proprie quod significatur vocibus ex instituto significantibus; improprie vero, quod significatur signis naturalibus. Quod igitur sunt voces loquenti, id sunt facultates & operationes rebus: Haec enim sese, non minus quam voces, ingerunt sensibus, & praeter se aliquid aliud menti. Itaque non raro Scriptura per metaphoram, aut etiā prosopopoeiam, rebus inanimatis tribuit sermonem. Hoc ergo dicit omnis creatura, quod eam dicentem Iohannes audiuit, quatenus id significat. Quomodo autem id significat, si non est creatura, seu opus Agni?
units.tr: IV. The second argument will be drawn from Revelation 5:13, where the Apostle testifies that when the Lamb had opened the first seal, he heard every creature which is in heaven, and which is on the earth, and under the earth, and in the sea, and all that are in them, saying: Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth on the throne, and unto the Lamb, for ever and ever. How can every creature, none excepted (for the Apostle seems to have taken care that none be excluded), say this? For creatures devoid of mind cannot properly say it, and rebellious ones will not. Indeed, a creature is understood to say that which in some way signifies it: for to say is to signify something. Now signs signify either by their own nature or by institution. That is properly said which is signified by words that signify by institution; but improperly, that which is signified by natural signs. Therefore, as words are to a speaker, so are the faculties and operations to things: for these, no less than words, press themselves upon the senses and signify something other than themselves to the mind. Hence Scripture often ascribes speech to inanimate things by metaphor, or even by prosopopoeia. Therefore every creature says what John heard it saying, insofar as it signifies that. But how does it signify that, if it is not a creature, or a work of the Lamb?

units.la: V. Id enim dicit sine dubio, aut quatenus eius creatura, aut quatenus ab eo reformata, aut quatenus, quamuis nec eius creatura sit, nec ab eo reformata, tamen eius imperio subjecta est. Quartū enim excogitari non potest. Primum si conceditur causam vicimus, verbum seu Dei Filius creauit omnia. Secundū dici non potest. Nam, neq; nomen creaturae positum absolutè pro noua creatura vsurpatur vnquam; neque omnis creatura quae est in coelo, & in terra, & sub terra, & in mari, &c, dici potest reformata per Christum. Quis enim diabolos aut homines incredulos & impios, aut cadauera hominum putrescentia in terra, aut pisces, aut metalla per Christum reformata fuisse dicat? Legatur disp. de Arg. 29. lib. 1. à §. 12. ad finem vsque. Sed pone, quod falsum est, omnes creaturas esse aliquomodo reformatas per Christum, tamen huius reformationis nullum prorsus apparet in plurimis creaturis indicium, nullum signum: quomodo ergo ratione huiusmodi reformationis significant benedictionem, honorem, gloriam, robur pertinere ad eum qui sedet in throno & ad Christum? Tertium quoque dici non potest. Primum quia nondum videmus omnia Christo esse subiecta. Deinde quia ad eiusmodi δοξολογίαν[?] sola subjectio non sufficit. Non enim quicquid subjicitur alicui, id continuò laudes eius celebrat cui subjicitur. Multae sunt regiones, multi mortales, ut de iis quae sunt sub terra & in mari nihil dicam, in quibus subjectionis Christo quatenus est homo, aut propter istam subjectionem confessionis illius nullum prorsus vestigium apparet. Quomodo igitur tot creaturae id dicentes audiri possunt, quod nullo modo significant? Fatendum est igitur omnes creaturas id dicere quatenus sunt creaturae. Opus enim benefactum non potest non laudare opificem suum.
units.tr: V. For it undoubtedly says this either insofar as it is his creature, or insofar as it has been reformed by him, or insofar as, although it is neither his creature nor reformed by him, it is nevertheless subject to his command. For a fourth cannot be devised. The first: if it is granted, we have won the cause; the Word, that is the Son of God, created all things. The second cannot be said. For the noun creature, used absolutely, is never employed for a new creature; nor can every creature which is in heaven, and in the earth, and under the earth, and in the sea, etc., be said to have been reformed through Christ. For who would say that the devils, or unbelieving and impious men, or the corpses of men rotting in the earth, or fish, or metals, have been reformed through Christ? Let the disputation on Argument 29 of book 1 be read, from §12 to the end. But suppose, what is false, that all creatures are in some way reformed through Christ; still, there appears in most creatures no trace or sign at all of this reformation; how, then, by reason of such reformation, do they signify that blessing, honour, glory and power belong to him who sits on the throne and to Christ? The third also cannot be said. First, because we do not yet see all things subjected to Christ. Second, because subjection alone is not sufficient for such a doxology [δοξολογίαν]. For whatever is subjected to someone does not at once celebrate the praises of the one to whom it is subjected. There are many regions and many mortals (not to mention those under the earth and in the sea) in which no trace of subjection to Christ, insofar as he is man, or of that confession on account of that subjection, appears at all. How, then, can so many creatures be heard saying what in no way signifies it? It must be admitted, therefore, that all creatures say this insofar as they are creatures. For a work well made cannot but praise its maker.

units.la: VI. Id quod etiam nonnulla suadent. Primò nomen creaturae isti significationi congruens. Deinde similis confessio quatuor animalium & viginti quatuor seniorum cap. iv. 9. 11. Dignus es Domine Deus noster accipere gloriam, & honorem, & robur; versu 9. etiam benedictio exprimitur: quae quatuor hoc loco & omnia & sola memorantur. Subjicitur autem ratio ducta à creatione, quia tu creasti omnia, & per voluntatem tuam sunt, & creata sunt. Ex quo intelligitur, eiusmodi δοξολογίαν[?] deberi & reddi Deo ob creationem. Tum, adoratio seu confessio Angelorum proximè antecedens v. 12. ijsdem enim etiam verbis concepta est, quibus illa cap. iv. 11. Nisi quod ad majorem emphasim plura nomina congesta sunt. Ut appareat quaecunque sunt Patris, eadem etiam Filij esse, ne gloria quidem illa excepta quae ei propter creationem mundi debetur. Denique, conjunctio Sedentis in throno cum Agno. Non enim potuit apertius innui inter utriusque adorationem & gloriam nihil interesse. Quomodo dicit omnis creatura, Sedenti in throno benedictio, & honor, & gloria, & robur in secula seculorum, eodem modo id ipsum dicit Agno: nullum est discrimen: est enim una eademque δοξολογία[?]. Constat autem omnem creaturam id dicere Sedenti in throno, quia est eius creatura, eo modo quo praeclarum opus causae suae virtutes declarat. Eodem igitur etiam modo id dicit Agno.
units.tr: VI. Several considerations also support this. First, the name "creature" fits this meaning. Second, there is the similar confession of the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, Rev. 4:9, 11: "Thou art worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory, and honour, and power" (4:11). In verse 9, "blessing" is also expressed. These four, and no others, are mentioned here, and they are mentioned in full. The reason given is drawn from creation: "for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created." From this it is understood that such a doxology [δοξολογίαν] is owed to God and rendered to him for creation. Third, there is the adoration or confession of the angels immediately before, in verse 12. It is framed in the same words as that of 4:11, except that several names are heaped together for greater emphasis, so that it appears that whatever belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son, not even excepting that glory which is due to him for the creation of the world. Fourth, there is the conjunction of him who sits on the throne with the Lamb. It could not have been suggested more plainly that there is no difference between the adoration and glory given to the one and to the other. As every creature says, "Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, for ever and ever," to him who sits on the throne, so it says the same thing to the Lamb. There is no distinction, for it is one and the same doxology. Now, it is agreed that every creature says this to him who sits on the throne because it is his creature, in the way that a noble work declares the virtues of its maker. Therefore it says the same thing to the Lamb in the same way.

units.la: DISPVTATIO DECIMA TERTIA
units.tr: DISPUTATIO DECIMA TERTIA

units.la: De Arg. XIII. Ex verbis Apostoli 1. Cor. x. 9. Neque tentemus Christum, sicut & quidam illo- rum tentaverunt, & perierunt à serpentibus, collatis cum Num. 21. 5. 6.
units.tr: On Argument XIII, from the words of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 10:9, Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed by serpents, compared with Num. 21:5, 6.

units.la: I. ARGVMENTVM sic potest concipi. Ob quem tentatum in deserto quidam Israelitarum perierunt à serpentibus, ille est Deus Israëlis. Ob Christum tentatum in deserto quidam Israelitarum perierunt à serpentibus.
units.tr: I. The argument may be framed thus. He whom some of the Israelites tempted in the wilderness, and who for that reason they perished by serpents, is the God of Israel. Christ was tempted in the wilderness by some of the Israelites, and for that reason they perished by serpents.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis. Vel sic, ille quem quidam Israëlitæ tentarunt in deserto & perierunt à serpentibus,est Deus Israëlis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. Or thus: he whom some Israelites tempted in the wilderness and who destroyed them by serpents is the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est ille quem quidam Israëlitæ tentarunt in deserto & perierunt à serpentibus.
units.tr: Christ is he whom some Israelites tempted in the wilderness and who destroyed them by serpents.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus. Major nititur historia, quæ narratur Num. 21. 5. necnon constanti testimonio Scripturæ Veteris testamenti, quæ Deum Israëlis tentatum fuisse ab Israëlitis dicit aliquoties, alium vero ab illis tentatum fuisse nunquam dicit. Minor nititur diserte Apostoli testimonio 1. Cor. 10. 9.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is God. The major premise rests on the history narrated at Num. 21:5, and also on the constant testimony of the Scripture of the Old Testament, which repeatedly says that the God of Israel was tempted by the Israelites, and never says that anyone else was tempted by them. The minor premise rests plainly on the testimony of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 10:9.

units.la: I I. Socinus primùm negat majorem. Nam præter Deum Israëlis tentatum fuisse Mosem, necnon Angelum illum, cuius ductu populus ex Ægypto liberatus fuerat, & qui fuit in deserto perpetuò cum populo. Quod ut confirmet ait, Num. 21. 5. Mosem diserte nominari, Illum autem unum Deum Israelis non diserte nominari: Nomine enim Dei, Elohim non significari unum illum Deum Israelis, sed Angelum cuius ministerio Israelita educti fuerant ex Ægypto, quem Angelum ait, cum in sua propria persona consideratur, Elohim aperte vocari: cum vero sustinet alienam personam unius illius Dei Israelis, Jehouam appellari. De hoc Angelo alias. Nunc satis est monuisse frustra laborasse Socinum in excogitanda, & multis verbis explicanda responsione, quam parua quadam declinatione possumus effugere. Sic enim argumentum reformo. Quicunque tentatus fuit ab Israelitis Num. 21. is fuit aut Deus Israelis, aut Angelus creatus, aut Moses. Christus tentatus fuit ab Israelitis Num. 21. Christus igitur fuit aut Deus Israelis, aut Angelus creatus, aut Moses. Atqui non fuit Moses, nec Angelus creatus. Ergo fuit Deus Israelis. Non fuit Moses, ut patet. Nec Angelus, ut liquet ex Heb. 1. 5. & 2. 2. 5. Itaque nunquam in Novo Testamento Angelus appellatur nisi forte in Apocalypsi, in qua etiam pastores seu Episcopi angeli vocantur.
units.tr: II. Socinus first denies the major premise. For, he says, besides the God of Israel, Moses was tempted, and also that Angel by whose guidance the people had been freed from Egypt, and who was in the wilderness with the people continually. To confirm this he says that at Num. 21:5 Moses is named expressly, but that the one God of Israel is not named expressly; for the name God, Elohim, does not signify that one God of Israel but the Angel by whose ministry the Israelites had been led out of Egypt, whom he says is openly called Elohim when considered in his own person, but when he sustains the foreign person of that one God of Israel, is called Jehovah. I will speak of this Angel elsewhere. For now it is enough to have pointed out that Socinus has laboured in vain in devising a reply, and in explaining it at length, which we can escape with a slight change of position. For I reframe the argument thus: whoever was tempted by the Israelites at Num. 21 was either the God of Israel, or a created angel, or Moses. Christ was tempted by the Israelites at Num. 21. Therefore Christ was either the God of Israel, or a created angel, or Moses. But he was neither Moses nor a created angel. Therefore he was the God of Israel. That he was not Moses is plain. Nor was he an angel, as is clear from Heb. 1:5 and 2:2, 5. Indeed, in the New Testament an angel is never so called, except perhaps in the Apocalypse, where pastors or bishops are also called angels.

units.la: III. Interim moneo duo: unum, Israelitas loquutos quidem fuisse contra Deum & contra Mosem, tamen Mosem non tentasse, sed Deum. Nunquam enim Moses tentatus dicitur in Scriptura. Quanti autem fieri debeat perpetuum Scripturae silentium ignorare non potest, qui eo nitentem contemplatus fuerit Apostolum Gal. 3. 16. Heb. 1. 5.: & 7. 3. Sed neque Lex vetabat tentare hominem, neque quisquam, quod sciam, reprehenditur in Scriptura quod tentarit hominem. Alterum, Si per Deum, Elohim, eo loco non intelligitur unus ille Deus Israelis, jam tum duos Deos fuisse, qui populum Israeliticum eduxerunt e captivitate Ægyptiaca, qui eum duxerunt per desertum, quos populus ille tentavit, contra quos peccavit, quosque adeo colere debuit. Quis hoc credat? Quomodo etiam Apostolus Christum Angelis praestare docet argumento ducto ab Elogio Filij Dei Heb. 1. 5. si uni cuidam Angelo in propria persona consiederato Dei nomen tributum est in Scriptura, si etiam is nonnunquam appellatus est Jehoua? Sed ea de re disputandum nobis erit, Deo fauente, alio loco diligentius, nunc dico, uno verbo, illum Angelum aut Christum fuisse, aut Christi typum. Si prius, jam tum Christus fuit, & quidem Deus, populi ex Ægypto liberator, & qui se Jehouam esse aliquoties dixit. Si posterius, cur ille Angelus Deus appellatus est, & Jehoua etiam, nisi ut id eo adumbraretur quod homine adumbrari non potuit, Christum esse revera Deum & Jehouam?
units.tr: III. Meanwhile I note two things. First, the Israelites did indeed speak against God and against Moses, yet they did not tempt Moses but God. For Moses is never said in Scripture to have been tempted. And how much weight this perpetual silence of Scripture ought to carry, no one can fail to know who has considered the Apostle leaning on it at Gal. 3:16, Heb. 1:5, and 7:3. Yet neither did the Law forbid tempting a man, nor, so far as I know, is anyone in Scripture reproved for tempting a man. Second, if by God, Elohim, in that place is not understood that one God of Israel, then already there were two Gods who led the Israelite people out of Egyptian captivity, who led them through the wilderness, whom that people tempted, against whom they sinned, and whom they therefore ought to have worshipped. Who would believe this? Likewise, how does the Apostle teach that Christ is superior to the Angels, by an argument drawn from the title of the Son of God at Heb. 1:5, if a certain single Angel, considered in his own person, is given the name of God in Scripture, and if he was sometimes also called Jehovah? But we shall have to discuss this matter more carefully elsewhere, God willing; for now I say, in a word, that this Angel was either Christ, or a type of Christ. If the former, then Christ was already there, and indeed God, the deliverer of the people from Egypt, who several times said that he was Jehovah. If the latter, why was that Angel called God, and also Jehovah, unless it was so that by this there might be shadowed forth what could not be shadowed forth by a man, namely that Christ is truly God and Jehovah?

units.la: Reliquas Aduersariorum responsiones habes, lector, refutatas lib. I. Disp. de Arg. XII.
units.tr: The remaining replies of the adversaries you will find, reader, refuted in Book I, Disputation on Argument XII.

units.la: DISPUTATIO DECIMA QUARTA
units.tr: DISPUTATION FOURTEEN

units.la: De Arg. XIV. Ex Esai. xxxv. 4. Deus ipse veniet, & seruabit vos. Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, & aures surdorum reserabuntur, &c, collato cum Matth. xi. 5.
units.tr: On Argument XIV, from Isaiah xxxv. 4: God himself will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped, etc. Compared with Matthew xi. 5.

units.la: REDEAMVS ad Esaiam Prophetam, & loca quædam expendamus in extremo huius primæ Sectionis, quæ aliquomodo ambiguum est, utrum ad hanc, an ad sequentem sectionem potius referri debeant. Occurrit mihi primus ille locus, qui extat Esai 35. 4. Ecce Deus vester cum ultione & retributione veniet. Deus ipse veniet & seruabit vos. Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum & aures surdorum reserabuntur. Tunc saliet sicut ceruus claudus & cantabit lingua muti. Hoc intelligendum esse de aduentu Christi ipse Christus docet Matth. 11. 4. Quærenti enim per discipulos Iohannis Baptistæ. Tu ne is es qui venturus est, an alium expectamus? Respondit, ite & renunciate Iohanni quæ auditis, & cernitis.
