Cæci visum recipiunt, & claudi ambulant, leprosi mundantur, surdi audiunt, mortui suscitantur, & pauperibus evangelizatur. Quibus verbis manifestum est eum ad vaticinium illud Esaiæ alludere. Argumentum sic potest confici.
units.tr: Let us return to the Prophet Isaiah and weigh certain passages at the end of this first section, which may be referred either to this section or more properly to the next. The first passage that comes to mind is Isaiah 35. 4: Behold your God will come with vengeance and recompense. God himself will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then the lame man will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the dumb will sing. Christ himself teaches that this is to be understood of his coming, Matthew 11. 4. For when the disciples of John the Baptist asked him, Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another? he replied, Go and report to John what you hear and see. The blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the gospel is preached to the poor. In these words it is plain that he is alluding to that prophecy of Isaiah. The argument can be framed thus:

units.la: Deus, cuius aduentus prædicitur Esai. 35. 4. est Deus Israëlis, seu est prædicitus [?] essentia diuina.
units.tr: The God whose coming is foretold at Isaiah 35. 4 is the God of Israel, or is predicated of the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est Deus cuius aduentus prædicitur Esai. 35. 4.
units.tr: Christ is the God whose coming is foretold at Isaiah 35. 4.

units.la: Ergo Christus est Deus Israëlis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel.

units.la: II. Quid respondet Socinus? Primo, inquit, loco nego, necesse esse ut locus Esaiæ de uno illo Deo Israelis accipiatur. Possunt enim verba eius ita intelligi, ut, quando de re futura manifeste loquitur, quidquid in illis dicitur: in futurum respiciat. Et sic, quamvis Deus, qui ibi nominatur, hac appellatione Deus vester, vocetur, non tamen continuo sequitur, ibi sermonem esse de uno illo Deo Israelis, qui iam tum erat. Potuit enim Christus homo, qui nasciturus erat, illorumque Deus futurus ista appellatione insigniri. Laudo confessionem, Christum Dei nomine hoc loco insigniri. Probo id nomen non posse hoc loco nisi de uno illo Deo Israelis intelligi. Primùm enim negari non potest nomen Elohim Dei Israelis nomen esse, & quidem omnium & primum & maximè usitatum: Itaque quoties occurrit in Scriptura, toties Deum illum unum Israelis cogitandum esse, nisi gravis ratio obstet, quæ hîc nulla est. Si idolis gentium tribuitur aliquando, id fit cum adjectione quæ idolum significari innuit: Si Iudicibus aut Angelis, id fit cum metaphoricè seu figuratè, tum in plurali numero, ita ut propterea eorum nemo singulariter Elohim seu Deus appellari potuerit. Si singulari numero de aliquo Angelo dicitur, aut is Angelus non est natura angelus, sed officio tantùm, atque adeò idem cum Christo; aut si est angelus creatus, is quis sit ignoratur prorsus, nec potest ab aliis Angelis ullo modo internosci, & sine dubio Deus dictus est typicè tantùm. Hoc autem loco nomen Dei, Elohim, usurpatur absolutè, singulariter, subjectiuè, non metaphoricè sed propriè, non typicè sed verè, quomodo contendo, nisi Deo Israelis, tribui in Scriptura nemini. Adde quod construitur cum verbo singularis numeri, ut solet cum de uno illo Deo Israelis agitur.
units.tr: II. What does Socinus reply? First, he says, I deny that it is necessary for the passage of Isaiah to be taken of that one God of Israel. For his words can be understood in such a way that, since he speaks clearly of a future event, whatever is said in them looks to the future. And so, although the God who is named there is called by this title, "your God," it does not follow at once that the discourse there is about that one God of Israel, who already existed at that time. For Christ, who was to be born as a man and who was to be their God, could have been designated by that title. I praise the admission that Christ is named by the name of God in this place. I prove that the name cannot in this place be understood of anyone but that one God of Israel. For first, it cannot be denied that the name Elohim is the name of the God of Israel, and indeed of all names the first and most commonly used. Therefore whenever it occurs in Scripture, we must think of that one God of Israel, unless a serious reason stands in the way, and here there is none. If it is sometimes given to the idols of the nations, this happens with an addition that signals that an idol is meant. If it is given to judges or angels, this happens metaphorically or figuratively, and then in the plural number, so that none of them could for that reason be called Elohim or God in the singular. If it is said in the singular of some angel, either that angel is not an angel by nature but only by office, and so the same as Christ; or, if he is a created angel, who he is remains utterly unknown and he cannot be distinguished in any way from other angels, and without doubt he is called God only typically. But in this place the name of God, Elohim, is used absolutely, in the singular, as subject, not metaphorically but properly, not typically but truly; and I contend that in Scripture it is attributed to no one except the God of Israel. Add that it is construed with a verb in the singular, as usually happens when the discourse concerns that one God of Israel.

units.la: III. Deinde dicitur Deus vester. Quos autem alloquitur? Quandoquidem confitetur Socinus Christum sic appellari, alloquitur eos quibus promissus est adventus Christi. Hoc negari non potest. Promissus est autem Israelitis. Vocatur ergo Deus Israelitarum. Clamat autem Scriptura Deum Israelitarum esse unum. Unus igitur Deus Israelis intelligitur. Certè cum de Israelitis agitur de idololatria non reprehendendis, aut de fidelibus, nunquam Deus noster, Deus vester quisquam dicitur, qui non sit Deus Israelis.
units.tr: III. Then it says your God. But whom is he addressing? Since Socinus admits that Christ is so called, he is addressing those to whom the coming of Christ was promised. This cannot be denied. But it was promised to the Israelites. Therefore he is called the God of the Israelites. But Scripture proclaims that the God of the Israelites is one. Therefore the one God of Israel is meant. Certainly when the discourse concerns Israelites who are not to be rebuked for idolatry, or the faithful, no one is ever called "our God" or "your God" who is not the God of Israel.

units.la: IV. Tum, non modo dicitur hoc loco Deus, & Deus vester, sed Deus ipse. Potuitne Propheta clarius significare, se Deum intelligere, qui tunc[?] vera[?] Deus erat, & præter quem nullus est Deus?
units.tr: IV. Furthermore, in this place he is called not only God and your God, but God himself. Could the Prophet have indicated more clearly that he means the God who was then the true God, and besides whom there is no God?

units.la: ℣. Præterea, quis non videt, qui vocatur hoc ℣. 4. Deus vester, Deus ipse, eundem cum eo esse qui ℣. 2. Deus noster appellatur, videbunt gloriam Domini, & decorem ( seu, vt alij vertunt magnificentiam, maiestatem) Dei nostri. Nam, quàm dicitur verè Deus vester Israelitas vel fideles alloquendo, tam dici potest ab Israelitis vel à fidelibus Deus noster. Quis etiam legens verba illa videbunt decorem Dei nostri, & continuò post, Deus ipse veniet, eundem Deum non intelligat, præsertim si credat ( qua fide & persuasione imbutos esse omnes Israelitas decuit ) nullum esse Deum nisi vnum ? Adde quod videbunt sine dubio decorem Dei qui veniet, atque adeo veniens sese ostendet, gloriamque suam revelabit aperiendo oculos cæcorum, & aures surdorum, &c. Iam autem eo ℣. 2. Deus noster idem Dominus, heb. Iehoua, appellatur: vt enim gloria & decor seu magnificentia idem sunt, sic idem est Dominus cuius gloriam videbunt cum Deo nostro, cuius magnificentiam seu decorem videbunt. Videbitur qui apparebit, apparebit qui veniet, veniet autem Deus ipse. Est igitur Deus ipse ille Deus noster ille Iehoua, cuius gloria & decor videbitur.
units.tr: V. Moreover, who does not see that he who is called in v. 4 your God, God himself is the same as he who in v. 2 is called our God, they shall see the glory of the Lord and the splendour (or, as others translate it, the majesty and magnificence) of our God. For just as he is truly called your God when addressing Israelites or the faithful, so Israelites or the faithful may call him our God. Who too, reading the words they shall see the splendour of our God, and immediately after, God himself will come, would not understand the same God, especially if he believes (a faith and conviction with which all Israelites ought to have been imbued) that there is no God but one? Add that without doubt they shall see the splendour of the God who will come, and thus, coming, he will show himself and reveal his glory by opening the eyes of the blind and the ears of the deaf, etc. Now in v. 2 our God is also called by the same name Lord, in Hebrew Jehovah: for as glory and splendour or magnificence are the same, so the Lord whose glory they shall see is the same as our God whose magnificence or splendour they shall see. He will be seen who appears; he will appear who comes; and God himself will come. Therefore God himself is that our God, that Jehovah, whose glory and splendour will be seen.

units.la: VI. Hoc ipsum docet collatio huius loci cum similibus, in quibus Deus prædicitur venturus. Esai. 25. 9. Ecce Deus noster iste. Expectauimus eum & seruabit nos: iste est Dominus quem expectauimus: exultabimus & latabimur in salute eius. Hunc enim Deum esse Deum Israelis liquet ex verbis, Iste est Dominus Heb. Iehoua quem expectauimus. Eundem autem esse cum eo qui venire dicitur hoc loco Esai. 35. 1. ex nomine Deus noster: quibus enim dicitur Deus vester veniet, hi inducuntur dicentes postquam venit, Ecce Deus noster iste. 2. ex verbo repetito expectauimus. Non enim expectatur nisi qui venturus creditur. 3. ex verbis seruabit nos, notant enim finem aduentus eundem: dicunt seruabit nos, vt hic seruabit vos, Esai. 40. 10. Ecce Deus vester, Ecce Dominus Deus in fortitudine veniet, &c. Hic similiter Deus vester appellatur, & venturus promittitur; & tamen dicitur Dominus Deus, heb. Adonai Iehoua, quæ duo nomina maximè propria sunt Dei Israelis. Sic psal. 50. 3. Deus manifestè veniet, Deus noster, & non silebit. Deus est, Elohim, additur pronomen noster, eius aduentus prædicitur, & tamen negari nequit, quin intelligendus sit Deus Israelis, vt patet ex ℣. 1. & 8. Sic psal 96. 12. & 98. 9: 98. 9. promittitur aduentus Domini, Iehouæ, ad Iudicandum orbem. Concludimus igitur per Deum ipsum, Deum vestrum, cuius aduentum Esaias prædicit ad vlciscendum & ad feruandum, Deum Israelis intelligendum esse. Clamat Deus Israelis apud Esai.& inculcat,se Deum esse,& præter se nullum Deum esse, Et tu putabis apud Esaiam per Deum,Deum ipsum, non esse intelligendum Deum Israelis! Clamat Deus Israelis & inculcat apud Esaiam, Seruatorem esse se & præter se neminem,&tu putabis apud Esaiam cum dicitur, Deus ipse veniet & nos seruabit,Deum seruatorem intelligendum esse tota substantia, totoque genere à Deo Israelis diuersum! Appello, lector, fidem & conscientiam tuam, num id tibi videatur vllo modo verisimile? Manet igitur firma Major argumenti nostri. Minorem quoque Socinus tentat, sed frustra.
units.tr: VI. The comparison of this passage with similar ones, in which God is foretold as coming, teaches this very thing. Isaiah 25. 9: Behold this is our God. We have waited for him, and he will save us: this is the Lord whom we have waited for: we will exult and rejoice in his salvation. That this God is the God of Israel is clear from the words This is the Lord [Jehovah] whom we have waited for. That he is the same as the one said to come in this place, Isaiah 35. 1, is shown: first, from the name our God: for those to whom it is said your God will come are introduced as saying, after he has come, Behold this is our God. Second, from the repeated word we have waited for: for no one is waited for except one believed to be coming. Third, from the words he will save us, which mark the same purpose of the coming: they say he will save us, as here he will save you, Isaiah 40. 10: Behold your God, behold the Lord God will come in strength, etc. Here likewise he is called your God, and is promised as coming; and yet he is called the Lord God [Adonai Jehovah], which two names are most especially proper to the God of Israel. So Psalm 50. 3: God will come openly, our God, and will not be silent. God is [Elohim]; the pronoun our is added, his coming is foretold, and yet it cannot be denied that he must be understood as the God of Israel, as is clear from v. 1 and v. 8. So too Psalms 96. 12 and 98. 9: the coming of the Lord, Jehovah, to judge the world is promised. We conclude, therefore, through God himself, your God, whose coming Isaiah foretells for avenging and for saving, that the God of Israel is to be understood. The God of Israel cries out in Isaiah and insists that he is God and that there is no God besides him. And will you think that in Isaiah, through God himself, the God of Israel is not to be understood! The God of Israel cries out and insists in Isaiah that he is the Saviour and that there is no other besides him; and will you think that in Isaiah, when it is said God himself will come and save us, a Saviour God is to be understood who is wholly different in substance and in kind from the God of Israel! I appeal, reader, to your faith and conscience: does this seem to you in any way probable? The major premise of our argument therefore stands firm. Socinus also attempts the minor premise, but in vain.

units.la: VII. Secundò, inquit, respondeo, Etiamsi concedatur, Esaiam de illo uno Deo Israelis verba facere, non tamen sequi, Christum esse illum Deum. Quamuis enim facile concedam, prædictionem istam pertinere ad Christi tempora; non tamen hinc sequitur, Christum esse illum vnum Deum, de quo Esaias loquitur. Immo sequitur. Nam si ille cuius aduentus promittitur & prædicitur ab Esaia est ille vnus Deus Israelis, & prædictio pertinet ad Christi tempora, venit Christi temporibus ille vnus Deus Israelis. Vel igitur alius aduentus eius fuit, alius aduentus Christi, vel idem. Alium nemo dixerit. Non enim venit ille vnus Deus, nisi quia Christus venit. Si est idem, etiam Christus & vnus ille Deus idem sunt. Nam, vt se habet aduentus ad aduentum, sic se habet venturus ad venturum. Si igitur aduentus illius vnius Dei & Christi vnus idemque aduentus sunt, etiam ille vnus Deus venturus & Christus venturus vnus idemque qui erat venturus sunt. Deinde respondet ad amussim euentus prædictioni. Quem igitur Esaias venturus prædixit, is venit. Considera igitur quis venerit: venit enim certè is quem venturum prædixerat. Quis ergo venit? venit vnus Christus, alius nemo. Venit quidem Iohannes Baptista, sed vt Christi anteambulo & minister: venerunt Apostoli, sed missi à Christo ipsorum domino. Vnum igitur Dominum venisse video. Id clamat vniuersum Euangelium, hoc est optatissimus de eius aduentu nuncius. Christus igitur est ille, quem Esaias venturum prædixerat. Congruunt omnia; Nomen, nam & in Veteri & in Nouo Testamento Deus appellatur: Miracula aduentus effecta & signa, aduentu enim & virtute Christi oculi cæcorum aperti sunt, & aures surdorum reseratæ &c: Finis, venit enim ad seruandum, vt esset autor salutis cum ab omni malo, cum æternæ, nec in alio est salus.
units.tr: VII. Secondly, he says, I reply that even if it be granted that Isaiah is speaking of that one God of Israel, it does not follow that Christ is that one God. For although I will readily grant that this prediction belongs to the time of Christ, it does not follow from this that Christ is the one God of whom Isaiah speaks. On the contrary, it does follow. For if he whose coming is promised and foretold by Isaiah is that one God of Israel, and the prediction belongs to the time of Christ, then that one God of Israel came in the time of Christ. Either his coming was one thing and Christ's coming another, or they were the same. No one would say they were different, for that one God came only because Christ came. If they are the same, then Christ and that one God are also the same. For as the coming stands related to the coming, so the one who is to come stands related to the one who is to come. Therefore, if the coming of that one God and the coming of Christ are one and the same coming, then the one God who is to come and Christ who is to come are one and the same who was to come. Next, the event corresponds exactly to the prediction. Whoever Isaiah foretold would come, that one has come. Consider, then, who has come, for certainly he has come whom he had foretold would come. Who, then, has come? Only the one Christ; no one else. John the Baptist indeed came, but as the forerunner and minister of Christ; the Apostles came, but sent by Christ their Lord. I see, therefore, that one Lord has come. The whole Gospel proclaims this, that is, the most welcome news of his coming. Christ, therefore, is he whom Isaiah foretold would come. Everything agrees: the name, for God is called by this name both in the Old and in the New Testament; the miracles and signs wrought by his coming, for by the coming and power of Christ the eyes of the blind were opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped, and so on; the purpose, for he came to save, to be the author of salvation from every evil and to eternal life, and there is no salvation in any other.

units.la: VIII. Præterea quorsum pertinet quod subjungit Esaias, Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum, & aures surdorum reserabuntur &c? Nonne eo pertinet, vt intelligamus, quicunque venerit, nisi miracula illa edantur, Deum non venisse, cum autem miracula illa patrabuntur, tunc esse colligendum, Deum venisse? certè negari non potest, quin proponantur miracula illa tanquam efsecta & signa aduentus ipsius Dei: cur ergo cum ea videamus à Christo & quidem virtute ipsi insita, cum per se, tum per Apostolos suos patrata, non concludimus ipsum Deum venisse?
units.tr: VIII. Furthermore, what is the force of what Isaiah adds, Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will be unstopped, etc.? Does it not serve to make us understand that, whoever comes, unless those miracles are performed, God has not come; but when those miracles are wrought, then we must conclude that God has come? Certainly it cannot be denied that those miracles are set forth as the effects and signs of the coming of God himself. Why, then, when we see them performed by Christ, and indeed by his own inherent power, both by himself and through his Apostles, do we not conclude that God himself has come?

units.la: IX. Atque hoc est quod sua responsione Christus innuit. Tune, dixerant discipuli Iohannis, is es qui venturus erat, an alium expectabimus? Venturum sine dubio intelligunt præstantissimum, in quo sit acquiescendum, nec expectandus præstantior. Respondet Christus, se illum ipsum esse, non quidem totidem verbis, sed aduocata in testimonium ipsa experientia, ite & renunciate Iohanni quæ auditis & videtis, cæci visum recipiunt, &c. Quasi diceret, quærit Iohannes num sim ὁ ἐρχόμενος, ille καὶ ἐξ-ὡ venturus ad seruandum, in quo debeant omnes acquiescere. At quid opus est id à me sciscitari, quod ipsa res tam clarè loquitur. reputet cum animo suo quis sit omnium, quos Prophetæ venturos prædixerunt, dignissimus, nullum comperiet præstantiorem ipso Deo. Cogitet quæ Prophetæ prædixerunt tunc euentura cum Deus ipse venerit, eaque conferat cum illis quæ videtis & auditis à me patrari miracula, & statim quis sim cognoscet, nec alia ei opus erit responsione. Facilis ratiocinatio. Prædictum fuerat à Prophetis ipsum Deum venturum esse vt seruaret populum suum, & cum venisset, tunc futurum, vt cæci visum recuperarent, surdi auditum &c. Venit Christus, & cæci visum receperunt, surdi auditum &c. Ergo Christus est ipse Deus qui erat venturus. Nemo enim ante Christum ea miracula edidit, nedum tanta copia. Si opera, inquiebat, non fecissem inter eos quæ nemo alius fecit, peccatum non haberent &c. A seculo, dicebat visu recepto cæcus, non est auditum quenquam aperuisse eius oculos, qui cæcus natus fuisset: quæ causa fortasse est, cur id vnum miraculum selectum sit; cuius tam enucleatè historia exponeretur. Nemo post Christum venit qui non fuerit servus Christi, quique, si miracula eiusmodi edidit, ea, nomini Christi accepta non retulerit. Itaque aut in Christo impletum est istud Esaiae de ipso Deo venturo vaticinium, aut nondum impletum est. Si prius, testantur illa signa Christum esse illum ipsum Deum, cuius adventus salutaris promissus Ecclesiae fuerat hoc in loco. Itaque ipse Christus in Evangelio profitetur, se Dei Filium, atque adeo Deum esse, unum cum Patre, testesque suae divinitatis profert opera & miracula, quae propria virtute & autoritate patrabat. Si posterius, non erat acquiescendum in Christo, sed expectandus alius Chri-sto praestantior, scilicet ipse Deus, id quod & cum responsione Christi, & cum universo eius Evangelio pugnare manifestum est.
units.tr: IX. And this is what Christ implies in his reply. Are you the one who was to come, the disciples of John had said, or shall we look for another? They understand the one who was to come to be the most excellent, in whom one may rest, and that no more excellent one is to be awaited. Christ replies that he himself is that one, not indeed in so many words, but by calling experience itself as witness: Go and report to John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, etc. As if he were saying: John asks whether I am the one who is to come [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], the one who is to come to save, in whom all should rest. But why need he ask me this, when the thing itself speaks so clearly? Let him consider in his own mind who is the most worthy of all those whom the Prophets foretold would come, and he will find no one more excellent than God himself. Let him think of what the Prophets foretold would happen when God himself came, and let him compare it with what you see and hear that I am doing in the way of miracles, and at once he will know who I am, and he will need no other answer. It is an easy argument. It had been foretold by the Prophets that God himself would come to save his people, and that when he came, the blind would recover sight, the deaf hearing, and so on. Christ has come, and the blind have received sight, the deaf hearing, and so on. Therefore Christ is the very God who was to come. For no one before Christ performed such miracles, let alone in such abundance. If I had not done among them works that no one else has done, they would not have sin, etc. From the beginning of the world, said the man who had received sight and had been blind, it has not been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one who was born blind. Perhaps this is the reason why this one miracle was chosen, whose history is set out so clearly. No one has come after Christ who was not a servant of Christ, and who, if he performed miracles of this kind, did not refer them to the name of Christ. Therefore either the Isaianic prophecy about God himself coming has been fulfilled in Christ, or it has not yet been fulfilled. If the former, those signs bear witness that Christ is that very God whose saving coming had been promised to the Church in this place. Accordingly Christ himself in the Gospel professes that he is the Son of God, and therefore God, one with the Father, and he brings forward as witnesses of his divinity the works and miracles which he performed by his own power and authority. If the latter, we were not to rest in Christ, but were to await another more excellent than Christ, namely God himself; and this is clearly at odds both with Christ's reply and with his whole Gospel.

units.la: X. Si ipse Deus, qui venturus praedicebatur à Propheta, non est Christus, sed alius ab eo tota essentia, immò genere diversus, certè Christus tantùm homo non fuit κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν[?] ὁ ἐρχόμενος, sed alius multò praestantior nempe ipse Deus. Qui fit igitur, ut Christus venisse ad nos servandos toto Evangelio nunciétur, venisse alium Christo praestantiorem, aut venturum, nunquam dicatur? Patrem quatenus differt à Filio venisse in mundum, ut peccatores servaret, nusquam lego. Dicit quidem Filius Patrem secum esse, se esse in Patre, Patrem in se: cum enim ipse & Pater unum sint, aliter se res habere non potuit: sed nunquam dicit, Patrem venisse in mundum, immò mundum opponit Patri. Exini[?], inquit, Patre, & veni in mundum; iterum relinquo mundum, & abeo Patrem. Adde quod si ipse Pater venisset, non potuisset maiore quàm Filius, vel autoritate peccata condonare, spiritibus immundis, mari & ventis imperare, vel virtute miracula omnis generis facere, atque discipulis suis in suo ipsius nomine faciendi potestatem indulgere, ut non potuerit ipsa experientia clariori voce testari, praesentissimum maximeque salutiferum numen ad esse.
units.tr: X. If God himself, who was foretold by the Prophet as coming, is not Christ, but another wholly different from him in essence, and indeed different in kind, then certainly Christ was not merely a man who came par excellence [κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν], but another far more excellent, namely God himself. How does it come about, then, that the whole Gospel announces that Christ came to save us, while it is never said that another more excellent than Christ came or will come? I nowhere read that the Father, as distinct from the Son, came into the world to save sinners. The Son indeed says that the Father is with him, that he is in the Father and the Father in him: for since he and the Father are one, things could not be otherwise. But he never says that the Father came into the world; rather he sets the world over against the Father. I came forth from the Father, he says, and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father. Add that if the Father himself had come, he could not have forgiven sins by any greater authority than the Son's, nor commanded unclean spirits, the sea and the winds, nor performed miracles of every kind by his own power, nor granted to his disciples the power of doing these things in his own name; so that experience itself could not have testified in a clearer voice that a most present and most saving divine power was there.

units.la: XI. At, inquit Socinus, in Christi verbis, non tantùm ista commemorantur, quae in loco Esaiae leguntur: sed praeterea, mortuos resurgere, pauperes evangelizari, & beatum esse, qui in Christo scandalisatus non fuerit. Quid inde colligi potest, nisi, ad ea, quae in loco Esaiae leguntur, maximum accessisse cumulum: Christum non modò ea omnia præstitisse, sed etiam plura atque majora: itaque vaticinium illud in Christo cumulatissimè impletum esse? Adde quod superadditis illis verbis alludere videtur ad alios locos quibus eius diuinitas à nobis confirmatur. Esai. 25. 8. Ose. 13. 14. Esai. 61. 1. Esai. 8. 14.
units.tr: XI. But, says Socinus, in the words of Christ, not only those things are recalled which are read in the place of Isaiah, but in addition, that the dead rise, the poor are evangelised, and blessed is he who is not offended in Christ. What can be inferred from this except that a very great addition has been made to the things read in the place of Isaiah: that Christ not only performed all those things but also more and greater ones, and so that prophecy was fulfilled in Christ most abundantly? Add that by these additional words he seems to allude to other passages by which we confirm his divinity: Isa. 25. 8; Hos. 13. 14; Isa. 61. 1; Isa. 8. 14.

units.la: XII. Pergit Socinus, Affirmo, inquit, eam Esaiæ prædictionem commodè posse, vel potius, vt multa alia similes, debere ad tempora etiam liberationis ex captiuitate Babylonica referri, tanquam redemptionis nobis per Christum partatypum. Temeraria affirmatio. Nihil enim eo loco occurrit, quod agi de liberatione ex captiuitate Babylonica suadeat, multa dissuadent. Immò inquit, indicant hoc satis aperte vltimus & penultimus cap. versiculus, vbi prædictio ista demum terminatur, in quibus diserte redemptorum, id est, ex captiuitate liberatorum, & eorum in Sion reditus fit mentio. Quid? nullane est redemptio, nullus reditus in Sion nisi ex captiuitate Babylonica, vt quoties mentio fit redemptorum à Domino, toties cogitanda sit captiuitas Babylonica? Atqui nescio an vspiam in Scriptura verbum redimendi de liberatione ex captiuitate Babylonica legatur vsurpatum. In causa fortasse est, quod nulla commemoratur Dei apud Cyrum per Prophetas aut legatos suos externa actio, qua populi sui dimissionem ab eo impetrauerit. Sed præterea adduntur hoc loco, quæ ab eiusmodi carnali & temporali liberatione mentes nostras auocent. Sic enim versiculus habet, Et redempti à Domino conuertentur & venient in Sion cum laude: & latitia sempiterna super caput eorum. Gaudium & lætitiam obtinebunt, & fugiet dolor & gemitus. Nam lætantes quidem Iudæi reuersi sunt in Iudeam é Babylone, sed nec perpetua fuit ea lætitia, nec dolor & gemitus fugerunt; fuit enim illis statim multis cum molestijs doloribus & angustijs confligendum, vt patet ex Neh. 1. 3. &c. Adde quod versus immediate præcedentes carnali eiusmodi liberationi nullo modo conueniunt, & erit ibi semita & via, & vocabitur via sancta: non transibit per eam pollutus, & hæc erit vobis directa via, ita vt stulti non errent per eam. Sic vulg. At Heb. Et ipsa illorum: viator & stulti non errabunt. Quid si sic vertas, & ipse, (heb. יהוה[?], quod Dei nomen est non infrequens apud Esaiam) cum eis ambulans, via, & stulti non errabunt? Deus enim, hoc est, Christus, qui nobiscum ambulauit & ad gloriosam immortalitatem nobis præiuit, ipse via est, nec possunt errare stulti cum in eo incedunt, & per eum eunt ad Patrem. Ut ut fit, clarum est id de via, qua reuersi sunt è Babylone Iudæi, intelligi hoc magis posse, quàm quod sequitur, Non erit ibi leo, & mala bestia non ascendet per eam, &c.
units.tr: XII. Socinus goes on: I affirm, he says, that this prediction of Isaiah can fittingly, or rather, as it resembles many other passages, ought to be referred also to the time of the liberation from the Babylonian captivity, as a type of the redemption we have through Christ. This is a rash assertion. For nothing in that place suggests that it is about liberation from the Babylonian captivity; many things argue against it. Indeed, he says, the last and penultimate verses of the chapter indicate this quite clearly, where this prediction finally ends, and where mention is expressly made of the redeemed, that is, those freed from captivity, and of their return to Zion. What then? Is there no redemption, no return to Zion, except from the Babylonian captivity, so that whenever mention is made of those redeemed by the Lord, we must think of the Babylonian captivity? Yet I do not know whether the word "redeem" is anywhere in Scripture used of liberation from the Babylonian captivity. The reason is perhaps that no external action of God is recorded through his Prophets or messengers before Cyrus, by which he obtained the release of his people from him. But in addition, things are added in this place which turn our minds away from liberation of this carnal and temporal kind. For the verse reads thus: And the redeemed of the Lord shall return and come to Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads. They shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and mourning shall flee away. For the Jews who returned from Babylon into Judea did indeed rejoice, but that joy was not lasting, and sorrow and mourning did not flee; for they had at once to contend with many troubles, sorrows and distresses, as is clear from Neh. 1. 3, etc. Add that the verses immediately preceding do not in any way fit such carnal liberation: And there shall be a path and a way, and it shall be called the holy way: the unclean shall not pass over it, and this shall be a straight way for you, so that fools shall not go astray in it. So the Vulgate. But the Hebrew reads: And he himself of theirs: the wayfarer, and fools shall not go astray. What if you translate it thus: And he himself (Hebrew [יהוה], which is a name of God not infrequent in Isaiah) walking with them, the way, and fools shall not go astray? For God, that is Christ, who walked with us and went before us to glorious immortality, is himself the way, and fools cannot go astray when they walk in him and go through him to the Father. However that may be, it is clear that this can be understood of the way by which the Jews returned from Babylon more easily than what follows: There shall be no lion there, and no evil beast shall go up by it, etc.

units.la: XIII. Sed quid clarius verbis, Deus ipse veniet, & seruabit vos. Tunc aperientur oculi caecorum, & aures surdorum reserabuntur, &c. Lege historiam reditus è captiuitate Babylonica, nihil in eareiusmodi commemoratur. Non dicitur venisse Deus ut populum suum seruaret. Caecorum, surdorum, claudorum, mutorum nec mentio quidem est. Nullum prorsus narratur miraculum tunc patratum. Respondet Socinus, hoc nihil impedire. Allegoricè enim, inquit, sunt miracula ista saltem pro eo tempore accipienda. At cur sunt accipienda allegoricè, quæ videmus à Christo edita historicè, sensu proprio, & literali? Tunc enim demum ad allegoriam confugiendum est, cum sensus literalis non quadrat. Nam si sine necessitate confingere licet sensus allegoricos pro arbitratu, quid non poterit conuerti in allegoriam? quid tam diserte & proprie dictum fuerit de Christo, quod non aliorsum allegoricè detorqueatur? Hoc est primum Socini peccatum in illis verbis. Accedit alterum. Ult liberationem è captiuitate Babylonica typum fuisse redemptionis nobis per Christum partæ. Id, quo sensu ab eo intelligitur, falsum esse puto. Sit tamen ita. Quid absurdius, quàm Prophetæ verba de typo quidem allegoricè, de re verò adumbrata proprie exponere? Contrà enim fieri debet. Quoties enim cunque de Typo agitur, toties sensus literalis ad typum pertinet, allegoricus verò ad rem per typum significatam. Verba enim typum significant immediatè, rem verò adumbratam non nisi mediante typo.
units.tr: XIII. But what could be clearer than the words, God himself will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf unsealed, etc.? Read the history of the return from the Babylonian captivity: nothing of this kind is recorded there. It is not said that God came to save his people. There is not even a mention of the blind, deaf, lame or dumb. No miracle at all is related as having been performed then. Socinus replies that this makes no difference, since these miracles must at least be taken allegorically for that time. But why should miracles that we see Christ performing be taken allegorically, when they are reported historically, in the proper and literal sense? An allegorical sense must be resorted to only when the literal sense does not fit. For if one may invent allegorical senses at will, without any necessity, what could not be turned into allegory? What so plainly and properly said of Christ could not be twisted into some other allegorical meaning? This is Socinus's first error in these words. There is a second. He says that the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity was a type of the redemption won for us through Christ. I think that is false in the sense he intends it, but let it be so. What could be more absurd than to explain the prophet's words allegorically when they concern the type, but literally when they concern the thing foreshadowed? It ought to be the other way round. Whenever a type is in question, the literal sense belongs to the type, and the allegorical sense to the thing signified through the type. For words signify the type directly, but the thing foreshadowed only through the type.

units.la: XIV. Video etiam in illis verbis tertium peccatum, falsam nimirum assertionem. Nihil enim deprehendo in historia liberationis Iudæorum è captiuitate Babylonica, ad quod verba illa, tunc caecorum oculi aperientur, &c, allegoricè possint accommodari: Nec ullam possum excogitare allegoricam expositionem, quæ quadret. Sed fac tale quid in ea historia deprehendi posse, necesse erit, ut sit typus miraculorum illorum, quæ Christus in cæcis, surdis, mutis & claudis edidit. Alioqui periret typi analogia, & verba Prophetæ, ad Christi tempora, aut citra typi interuentum, aut nullo modo pertinerent. Ostendant igitur nocommemorare hoc loco necesse non est. Dicam tantùm, quando tam diserte, tam emphaticè, tam sæpe venturus Deus prædicitur & promittitur, eum veniendi modum esse intelligendum, qui sit omnium maximè & proprius, & perfectus, & exoptandus, qualis profectò est hic unus, cum Deus hominibus apparet, seque contemplandum exhibet in specie visibili, non terribili aut diuersæ ab hominibus speciei, sed humana, non euanida sed perpetua, non apparente tantùm, sed vera, per quam homines blandè alloquatur & doceat, eorum tecta subeat, cum ijs conuiuat, &c. Atque hoc modo ut ad nos seruandos ipse Deus veniret, necessarium fuisse, alijs argumentis hoc loco confirmaremus, nisi nobis visa essent digna, quæ seorsim proprijs disputationibus exponerentur.
units.tr: XIV. I see also a third error in those words, namely a false assertion. For I find nothing in the history of the Jews' deliverance from the Babylonian captivity to which those words, then the eyes of the blind will be opened, etc., could be allegorically applied; nor can I devise any allegorical interpretation that fits. But suppose something of the kind could be found in that history; it would necessarily have to be a type of those miracles which Christ performed on the blind, deaf, dumb and lame. Otherwise the analogy of the type would perish, and the prophet's words would apply either to Christ's time without the intervention of a type, or in no way at all. Let them therefore show such a type; but it is not necessary to recount it here. I will say only this: when God is foretold and promised to come so plainly, so emphatically, so often, we must understand that manner of coming which is the greatest, most proper, most perfect and most to be desired. Such indeed is this one, when God appears to men and shows himself to be contemplated in a visible form, not a terrible one or one of a species unlike men's, but a human form; not one that only seems to appear, but a real one, through which he speaks to men kindly and teaches them, enters their dwellings, and lives among them, and so on. That God himself had to come in this way to save us we would confirm by other arguments here, were it not that these seemed worthy of being set out separately in their own disputations.

units.la: XVII. Itaque venio ad tertiam Socini responsionem, quæ est, Deum tunc venire dici, cum aliquis eius loco venit, & propterea singulari quadam ratione Deum venturum dictum fuisse, cum Christus venturus esset, quippe quod Christus singulari quadam ratione eius loco venturus erat. Primùm ubi legit Socinus Christum venisse, aut venire debuisse loco Dei, hoc est, Patris? Idne Euangelium dicit alicubi? Deinde, Si Patris loco venit, debebat Pater venire: cur ergo Pater non venit? mutauit fortasse consilium. Nam homines isti ita præclarè de Deo sentiunt, ut eum putent essentia & loco finitum, duratione successiua præditum, futurorum contingentium ignarum, decreta sua pro re nata mutare & refigere, quæ mihi contradictionem implicare videntur, adeò sunt salsa & absurda. Tum, si Christus venit loco Dei, hoc est, Patris, utique venit ut partes Patris ageret, non suas ipsius. Dicant igitur nobis aduersarij quid fuit aut fecit Patris loco. Fuitne mediator Propheta Sacerdos Rex seu Christus Patris loco? Num ministrauit, num actus est in crucem, num resurrexit, num ascendit in coelum Patris loco? fecit quidem opera Patris, sed, ut Filium decuit, suo, non Patris loco. suo fungi desijt conjectus in carcerem, ac tandem de medio sublatus. Postquam enim Dominus venit, præcursore, seu anteambulone opus non fuit amplius, qui clamaret, parate viam Domino. Concludimus igitur Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, esse illum Dominum Deumque nostrum, cui via paranda fuit. Hunc autem Dominum & Deum nostrum esse Deum Israelis quominus negent Aduersarij obstat nomen Domini, quod hebraicè est Iehoua.
units.tr: XVII. So I come to Socinus's third reply, which is this: God is said to come when someone comes in his place; and therefore God was said to be going to come in a special way when Christ was going to come, since Christ was going to come in a special way in God's place. First, where does Socinus read that Christ came, or ought to have come, in the place of God, that is, of the Father? Does the Gospel say so anywhere? Next, if he came in the Father's place, the Father ought to have come. Why then did the Father not come? Perhaps he changed his mind. For these men think so nobly of God that they hold him to be finite in essence and in place, endowed with successive duration, ignorant of future contingents, and to change and revise his decrees as circumstances require. These seem to me to involve a contradiction, so false and absurd are they. Then, if Christ came in the place of God, that is of the Father, he surely came to act the part of the Father, not his own. Let our opponents therefore tell us what Christ did or was in the Father's place. Was he the Mediator, Prophet, Priest or King in the Father's place? Did he minister, was he put to death on the cross, did he rise, did he ascend into heaven in the Father's place? He did indeed do the works of the Father, but as became the Son, in his own place and not in the Father's. He ceased to fill his own role when he was cast into prison and at last taken out of the way. For once the Lord had come, there was no more need of a forerunner or herald, one who would cry, Prepare the way of the Lord. We conclude, therefore, that our Lord Jesus Christ is that Lord and God of ours for whom the way was to be prepared. That he is the Lord and God of Israel the opponents cannot deny without running into the name of Lord, which in Hebrew is Iehoua.

units.la: II. Alterum Arg. peti potest ex V. 5. Nam post auditam illam vocem, & complanatam viam sequitur, & reuelabitur gloria Domini, & videbit omnis caro pariter, quoniam os Domini loquutum est. Cuius, quæso, Domini post Iohannis prædicationem reuelata est gloria? Nonne illius, qui post Iohannem venit, se ostendit, gloriam suam reuelauit, & contemplandam omni carni præbuit? Atqui is fuit Christus. Ioh. 1. 14. verbum caro factum est, & habitauit in nobis (& vidimus gloriam eius, gloriam sicut unigeniti a Patre) plenum gratia & veritate. Ioh. 2. 11. Manifestam fecit gloriam suam, & crediderunt in eum discipuli eius. Itaque Euangelium vocatur ab Apostolo 2. Cor. 4. 4. Euangelium gloriæ Christi. Descendit enim Filius de cœlo, & se mundo ostendit, vt quicunque contemplatur Filium, & credit in eum habeat vitam aeternam, & ab eo suscitetur ultimo die: ac propterea oportuit gloriam Filij reuelari, & contemplandam omni carni proponi. Manifestam quidem etiam Patris gloriam fecit, sed manifestando suam. Ita enim Pater in ipso est & ipse in Patre, vt quicunque eum contemplatur, Patrem contempletur.
units.tr: II. A second argument may be drawn from verse 5. For after that voice is heard and the way made level, it follows: And the glory of the Lord will be revealed, and all flesh will see it together, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken. Whose glory, I ask, was revealed after John's preaching? Was it not the glory of him who came after John, showed himself, revealed his glory, and offered it to all flesh to behold? And that was Christ. John 1:14: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (and we saw his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father), full of grace and truth. John 2:11: He manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him. So the Gospel is called by the Apostle the gospel of the glory of Christ (2 Cor. 4:4). For the Son came down from heaven and showed himself to the world, so that whoever beholds the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, and be raised by him on the last day. It was therefore fitting that the glory of the Son should be revealed and set before all flesh to behold. He also indeed made the glory of the Father manifest, but by manifesting his own. For the Father is in him and he in the Father, so that whoever beholds him beholds the Father.

units.la: III. Hoc confirmari potest V. 8. huius cap. XL. Esai. Exaruit fœnum & cecidit flos: verbum autem Dei nostri manet in aeternum. Hic Deus noster est Christus. Est enim verbum Dei nostri hoc loco Euangelium Christi, teste Apostolo Petro 1. Pet. 1. 25. cui consonat illud Christi, cœlum & terra prætereibunt, verba autem mea non prætereibunt.
units.tr: III. This can be confirmed from verse 8 of this chapter, Isaiah 40: The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of our God stands for ever. Here our God is Christ. For the word of our God in this place is the Gospel of Christ, as the Apostle Peter testifies (1 Pet. 1:25), and Christ's saying agrees with it: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

units.la: IV. Vltimum argumentum petam ex versu sequente, Super montem excelsum ascende euangelisatrix Sion: attolle vocem tuam fortiter Euangelisatrix Hierusalem: attolle, noli timere, dic ciuitatibus Iuda, ecce Deus vester, &c. Potestne dubitari, quin ista Sion siue Ierusalem Euangelisatrix sint Apostoli Christi, iuxta illud Matth. 5. 14. vos estis lux mundi. Non potest ciuitas abscondi supra montem posita; Et Rom 10. 15. Quàm speciosi sunt pedes Evangelizantium pacem, evangelizantium bona? quae verba desumpta sunt ex Esai. 52. 7. Quàm speciosi sunt super montes pedes evangelisantis pacem, &c. Dicitur enim Sion & Ierusalem, ut significetur societas & multitudo hominum penes quos est cultus Dei. Additur Evangelisatrix, ut distinguatur à Sione & Hierosolyma, quae aut Evangelium respuit, aut non est ad Evangelisandum vocata. Iubetur ascendere in montem excelsum & vocem attollere, ut longè latèque Evangelium audiri possit. Timere prohibetur, ne pudore vel metu persecutionis ab evangelisando absterreatur. Summa evangelij, quod debet proclamare, his verbis continetur, Dic civitatibus[?] Iudæ, ecce Deus vester: Ecce Dominus cum robore veniet, & brachium eius dominabitur ei: Ecce merces eius cum eo, & opus eius coram eo. Partes enim duas habet Evangelium: altera Christus venisse nunciatur & ostenditur, & describitur tanquam Deus noster Dei nostri Filius, fidei obiectum & salutis auctor: altera venturus promittitur & praedicitur cum summa potentia & gloria, ut gratuita mercede beet[?] omnes[?] qui in ipsum crediderint, ipsique obediverint.
units.tr: IV. I will take my last argument from the following verse: Get you up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good tidings; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good tidings; lift it up, do not fear; say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God, etc. Can it be doubted that this Zion or Jerusalem, the herald of good tidings, is the Apostles of Christ, in accordance with Matthew 5:14, You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden; and Romans 10:15, How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace and bring good tidings? These words are taken from Isaiah 52:7, How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news of peace, etc. Zion and Jerusalem are named so that the fellowship and multitude of men among whom the worship of God is found may be signified. The term herald of good tidings is added to distinguish them from Zion and Jerusalem, which either reject the Gospel or have not been called to proclaim it. They are bidden to go up to a high mountain and lift up their voice, so that the Gospel may be heard far and wide. They are forbidden to fear, lest through shame or fear of persecution they be deterred from proclaiming the Gospel. The sum of the Gospel that they must proclaim is contained in these words: Say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God. Behold, the Lord will come with might, and his arm will rule for him. Behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him. For the Gospel has two parts. The first announces and shows that Christ has come, and describes him as our God, the Son of our God, the object of faith and the author of salvation. The second promises and foretells that he will come again with great power and glory, so that he may bless with a free reward all who have believed in him and obeyed him.

units.la: V. Hanc esse mentem illius loci res ipsa loquitur. Primùm enim manifestum est agi de Evangelio summo consensu à pluribus in publicum proponendum ante illud tempus non promulgato. Attamen illum unum Deum Israëlis esse Deum civitatum Iudæ propositum semper fuit publicè, ac creditum in illo populo, ex quo populus fuit, hodieque etiam à rebellibus Iudæis creditur. Deinde cum dicitur Ecce Deus vester, ostenditur & demonstratur aliquis, quemadmodum cum dicebat Baptista, Ecce agnus Dei, & Dominus, Ecce verè Israelita, in quo dolus non est, ostendebat ille Iesum, hic Nathanaelem. Quem igitur ostenderunt, demonstrarunt, contemplandum proposuerunt, praedicarunt Apostoli? Patrem? An Filium? Lege Evangelium, & considera quis eo toto describatur, & annuncietur. Audi etiam Paulum, Non enim statui, inquit, quicquam scire inter vos nisi Iesum Christum, eumque crucifixum. Et alio loco, Non enim nosmetipsos praedicamus, sed Christum Iesum Dominum, nos autem ipsos servos vestros propter Iesum. Idem docet materiam Evangelij, seu, ut vulgò loquuntur, subiectum, esse Filium Dei Rom. 1. 3. Et alibi passim. Deinde de eo, quem ostendunt, aliquid, alioqui occulcûm, manifestant prædicant testantur, eum nempe Deum nostrum esse. Ita Apostoli de Iesu, quem annunciant, prædicant & testantur eum esse Filium Dei, Deum nostrum, Dominum nostrum, in quem credere, cui parere, quem invocare, colere, adorare omnes tenentur. Tum ista Sion sive Ierusalem vetatur timere, attolle, inquit, vocem tuam, ne time, dic civitatibus Iuda, Ecce Deus vester. Suberat igitur aliqua causa timendi, vel quod hæc veritas videretur absurda carni, vel quod odium pareret, & persecutionem accenderet, quod utrumque verissimum est. Quid enim magis vel absurdum iudicio carnis, vel inflammans animos incredulorum ira atque odio, quàm hæc veritas, Iesum, quem Iudæi & Pilatus ignominiosissimè condemnarunt & in crucem egerunt, esse Filium Dei, Deum nostrum, seruatorem mundi? Præterea hoc alta voce proclamare iubetur: quoniam alioqui ignoratum fuisset nec creditum à ciuitatibus Iudæ. Quod si verbis, Ecce Deus noster, Pater ostenditur, nunquam ignoratum est, aut negatum à Iudæis, Patrem esse Deum ipsorum: negant tantum eius filium atque adeò Deum suum esse Iesum Christum. Denique alterum huius Euangelij membrum, Ecce Dominus cum virtute veniet, &c, de eo qui venturus est intelligi debet. Quis autem venturus est, nisi Dei Filius? Certè idem intelligitur hoc loco, qui Esai. 62. 11. Dicite filiæ Sion, Ecce Seruator tuus venit. Ecce merces eius cum eo, & opus eius coram eo, Et Apoc. 22. 12. Ecce venio citò, & merces mea mecum est, ut reddam unicuique prout opus ipsius erit. Hic autem quin sit Filius nemo, opinor, ambigit. Postremò subjungitur V. 11. Sicut pastor gregem suum pascet, & brachio suo congregabit agnos, inque sinu suo feret, & fœtas suauiter ducet. Utrum de Patre, an de Filio hoc sit accipiendum quæris? consule Euangelium. Luce enim sua Vetus Testamentum illustrat. Id Filio Pastoris nomen & partes vendicat, additis etiam boni & magni epithetis. Ipse Petrus eum vocat ἀρχιποίμενα [?] princi- pem pastorum. Patri verò id nomen Euangelium nunquam tribuit. Ex quo intelligitur, cum Deus, cum Iehoua pastor dicitur in Veteri Testamento, Deum significari, non qua Pater est, sed qua Filius.
units.tr: V. The matter itself shows that this is the meaning of that passage. First, it is plain that the subject is the Gospel, which by common consent had not been published before that time for proclamation to the public. Yet that this one God is the God of Israel, the God of the cities of Judah, has always been openly set forth and believed among that people from whom the people came, and it is still believed today even by the rebellious Jews. Next, when it says Behold your God, someone is pointed out and shown, just as when the Baptist said Behold the Lamb of God and and Behold the Lord, and Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile, the one pointed to Jesus, the other to Nathanael. Whom then did the Apostles point out, show, set forth to be contemplated, and preach? The Father? Or the Son? Read the Gospel, and consider who is described and announced throughout it. Hear Paul too: For I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified. And elsewhere: For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus' sake. The same teaches that the matter of the Gospel, or as they commonly say, its subject, is the Son of God (Rom. 1. 3.), and so it is everywhere else. Next, concerning the one they point out, they make manifest, preach and testify something otherwise hidden, namely that he is our God. So the Apostles, concerning Jesus whom they announce, preach and testify that he is the Son of God, our God, our Lord, whom all are bound to believe in, obey, invoke, worship and adore. Then Zion or Jerusalem is forbidden to fear: lift up your voice, do not fear, say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God. There was therefore some cause for fear, either because this truth seemed absurd to the flesh, or because it would stir hatred and kindle persecution; both are most true. For what is more absurd to the judgment of the flesh, or more likely to inflame the minds of unbelievers with anger and hatred, than this truth: that Jesus, whom the Jews and Pilate condemned most ignominiously and brought to the cross, is the Son of God, our God, the Saviour of the world? Moreover, this is ordered to be proclaimed with a loud voice, since otherwise it would have been unknown and not believed by the cities of Judah. But if by the words Behold our God the Father is pointed out, that the Father is their God was never unknown or denied by the Jews; they deny only that his Son, Jesus Christ, is their God. Finally, the other member of this Gospel, Behold the Lord will come with power, etc., must be understood of him who is to come. Who is to come, however, but the Son of God? Surely the same is meant here as in Isaiah 62. 11: Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold your Saviour comes; behold his reward is with him, and his work before him; and Rev. 22. 12: Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each according as his work shall be. That this one is the Son, I think no one doubts. Lastly, it is added (v. 11): As a shepherd will feed his flock, and with his arm he will gather the lambs, and carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that give suck. Do you ask whether this is to be understood of the Father or of the Son? Consult the Gospel. For the Gospel sheds its own light on the Old Testament. It claims for the Son the name and the offices of the Shepherd, adding also the epithets good and great. Peter himself calls him the chief shepherd [ἀρχιποίμενα], the prince of shepherds. The Gospel never gives that name to the Father. From this it is understood that when God, when Jehovah, is called shepherd in the Old Testament, God is meant not as Father but as Son.

units.la: DISPUTATIO DECIMA SEXTA
units.tr: Disputation Sixteen

units.la: De Arg. XVI. Ex Esai. LII. ỹ. 6. 7. Propterea cognoscet populus meus nomen meum, propterea co-gnoscet in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquor, ecce adsum. Quàm speciosi super montes pedes euangelisantis, prædicantis pacem, euangelisantis bonum, &c, collat. cum Rom. 10. 15.
units.tr: On Argument 16, from Isaiah 52:6-7: Therefore my people shall know my name; therefore they shall know in that day that I myself who speak am here, behold, I am present. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings the good news, who proclaims peace, who brings good tidings, etc. Compare Rom. 10:15.

units.la: I. SUPERIORIBUS locis non absimilis est iste Esaiæ LII. 6. Propterea cognoscet populus meus nomen meum, propterea cognoscet in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquor, ecce adsum, &c. Ex eo sic argumentor. Ille, qui Esai. 52. 6. dicit Ecce adsum, est Deus Israëlis.
units.tr: I. THE passage in Isaiah 52:6, which is not unlike the places above, reads: Therefore my people shall know my name; therefore they shall know in that day that I myself who speak am here, etc. From this I argue as follows. He who says in Isaiah 52:6, Behold, I am here, is the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est ille, qui Esai. 52. 6. dicit Ecce adsum.
units.tr: Christ is he who says in Isaiah 52:6, Behold, I am here.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis. Major in confesso est: Nam is qui hoc dicit eo loco aliquoties Dominus, Iehova, appellatur, & Israëlem, qui descendit in Ægyptum, quemque Assur oppressit, populum suum vocat. Minor à nobis probanda est. Primò autem obseruo, verba Ecce adsum, referri debere ad certum quoddam tempus futurum designatum verbis in die illa. Id autem est tempus aduentus Christi.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The major premise is conceded, for he who speaks here is several times called the Lord, Jehovah, and calls Israel, who went down into Egypt and whom Assur oppressed, his people. The minor premise must be proved by us. First, I observe that the words Behold, I am here must be referred to a certain future time marked by the words in that day. That time is the time of the coming of Christ.

units.la: II. Respondeo, inquit Socinus, me non negare, Esaie locum mysticè ad Christi tempora pertinere. Sed affirmo aperte constare, eum secundum literam (ut vocant) ad liberationem ex captivitate Babylonica referendum esse. Cur? Quia, inquit, in precedentibus versiculis huius capitis, qui plane cum istis sunt coniungendi, expressa fit mentio, inter alia, quæ huc pertinent, soluenda captiuitatis filia[?] Sion, & Assyrij, qui oppressurus erat Dei populum, ex cuius manu redimendi erant. Atqui alij tunc erant Assyrij, alij Babylonij, alius rex Assyriorum, alius rex Babyloniorum; alia oppressio populi Israelitici ab Assyrijs, alia à Babylonijs, vt patet ex illa ipsa historia regis Ezechiae, quam, quia necessaria erat ad antecedentia & sequentia melius intelligenda, propheta inter cap. 34. & cap. 40. Prophetiae suae, tanquam parenthesin, inseruit. Anno sexto Ezechiae Salmanasar Rex Assyriorum abduxit in captiuitatem perpetuam decem tribus annis 130. aut circiter, ante captiuitatem Babylonicam. Anno decimoquarto Ezechiae Sennacherib rex Assyriorum ascendit contra omnes vrbes munitas Iudaeae & cepit eas. Ab eo liberata est Iudaea opera Angeli, qui vna nocte centum octogintaquinque millia percussit in castris Assyriorum. Inde natus est typus valdè diuersus à typo Babylonicae captiuitatis & liberationis. Tamen, quoniam tandem Rex Babylonis Assyriam in suam ditionem redegit, & quasi consiliorum regis Assur haeres, id perfecit, quod ille designauerat atque aggressus fuerat, confunduntur eum Babylonijs Assyrij, & sic vtriusque typi cinnus quidam, ad quem hoc loco Deus obiter alludit instituta inter Ægyptum & Assur oppositione ad vtriusque illius typi cognitionem apprimè necessaria.
units.tr: II. Socinus replies, "I do not deny that the passage of Isaiah refers mystically to the times of Christ. But I affirm that it is plainly established that, according to the letter (as they say), it must be referred to the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity. Why? Because, he says, in the preceding verses of this chapter, which must be joined plainly with these, mention is made expressly, among other things that pertain to this, of the daughter of Sion who is to be loosed, and of the Assyrian who was about to oppress God's people and from whose hand they were to be redeemed. But the Assyrians of that time were one people and the Babylonians another; the king of the Assyrians was one and the king of the Babylonians another; the oppression of the Israelite people by the Assyrians was one thing and by the Babylonians another, as is clear from that very history of King Hezekiah, which the prophet, because it was necessary for a better understanding of what precedes and follows, inserted as a parenthesis in his prophecy between chapter 34 and chapter 40. In the sixth year of Hezekiah, Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians led the ten tribes into perpetual captivity, about 130 years before the Babylonian captivity. In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went up against all the fortified cities of Judea and took them. Judea was delivered from him by the work of an angel, who in one night struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. From this arose a type very different from the type of the Babylonian captivity and deliverance. Yet, since at last the king of Babylon brought Assyria under his power, and, as heir of the designs of the king of Assur, accomplished what that king had planned and attempted, the Assyrians are confounded with the Babylonians, and so there is a certain blend of both types, to which God here alludes in passing, the opposition between Egypt and Assur having been established, which is very necessary for a knowledge of each of those types."

units.la: III. Caeterum quae antecedunt quaeque sequuntur ad Euangelij tempora ita pertinent, vt eorum vel nihil prorsus, vel vix vmbra aliqua ad tempora Assyriae aut Babyloniae captiuitatis referri possit. Primus capitis versus sic habet, Consurge, consurge, induere fortitudine tua Sion, induere vestimentis gloriae tua Ierusa-lem ciuitas sancta: quia non adijciet vltra, vt pertranseat per te in-circuncisus & immundus. Quis nos videt hoc minimè conuenire terrenae Sion & Ierusalem habita ratione temporalis liberationis: tam enim per eam, postquam ab Assyrijs & Babylonijs liberata est, incircuncisus & immundus pertransijt, quàm antea, immò multò magis. Versus vltimi capitis de alio quàm de Christo intelligi nequeunt. In versibus quoque intermedijs, qui cum extremis cohaerent & consentiunt, de eadem liberatione agitur, quae verae Sioni per Christum obtigit, sed iniecta aliqua mentione Ægyptiorum & Assyriorum sub quibus etiam Babylonij comprehenduntur, propterea quod isti typi ad eam liberationem enu-cleatius intelligendam conducunt.
units.tr: III. Moreover, the things that precede and the things that follow pertain to the times of the Gospel in such a way that nothing at all, or scarcely any shadow, of them can be referred to the times of the Assyrian or Babylonian captivity. The first verse of the chapter reads: Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Sion; put on your garments of glory, O Jerusalem, holy city; for there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean. Who does not see that this agrees very ill with earthly Sion and Jerusalem, considering a temporal deliverance? For the uncircumcised and unclean passed through her after she had been freed from the Assyrians and Babylonians just as much as before, indeed much more. The last verses of the chapter cannot be understood of anyone other than Christ. In the intervening verses also, which cohere with and agree with the final ones, there is a discussion of the same deliverance that came to true Sion through Christ, but with some mention made of the Egyptians and Assyrians, under whom the Babylonians too are included, because those types serve to make that deliverance understood more clearly.

units.la: IV. Sed in versibus laudatis consistamus. Propter hoc sciet populus meus nomen meum, propter hoc illud sciet in die illa, quoniam ego ipse qui loquor, ecce adsum. Num populus Israëliticus, quo tempore liberatus est ab Assyrijs vel Babylonijs, eo cognouit nomen Domini ante ignoratum? Num tunc noua aliqua reuelatio, multò quàm antè clarior, nominis Dei populo illi indulta est?
units.tr: IV. But let us stay with the verses cited. Therefore my people shall know my name; therefore they shall know it in that day, because I myself who speak am here. Did the Israelite people, at the time when they were freed from the Assyrians or the Babylonians, then come to know the name of the Lord, which had previously been unknown? Was some new revelation of God's name, far clearer than before, then granted to that people?

units.la: Quà u[?] hoc melius quadrat in tempus Christi, qui suum & Patris nomen discipulis suis notum fecit. Et quis alius id notum facere potuisset? Nemo enim Patrem nouit nisi Filius, & cui voluerit Filius reuelare. At, reponit Socinus, verba, sciet populus meus nomen meum, significant, cognoscet populus meus, quis sim reuera; id est, quàm fidelis in promissis meis seruandis. Esto. Nonne id demum cognitum est aduentu Christi, in quo omnes Dei promissiones sunt etiam atque amen? Tenuis quidem aliqua hujus fidelitatis umbra cernitur in liberatione à captiuitate Babylonica, sed dubia & obscura, quamdiu promissioni illius liberationis intextæ promissiones spirituales & magnificæ nondum fuerunt impletæ. Adde quod patefactio nominis Dei posita non est in vnius fidei, sed in omnium virtutum diuinarum reuelatione, quæ sese, non in liberatione è captiuitate Babylonica, sed in Christo mirabiliter ostenderunt.
units.tr: How much better this fits the time of Christ, who made known his own and the Father's name to his disciples. And who else could have made it known? For no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. But, Socinus replies, the words my people shall know my name mean my people shall know what I really am, that is, how faithful I am in keeping my promises. Granted. But was this not finally known at the coming of Christ, in whom all the promises of God are yea and amen? Some slight shadow of this faithfulness is seen in the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity, but it was doubtful and obscure, as long as the spiritual and great promises interwoven with the promise of that deliverance had not yet been fulfilled. Add that the manifestation of God's name is set not in the revelation of one attribute but of all the divine virtues, which showed themselves wonderfully not in the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity but in Christ.

units.la: V. Cur verò populus Dei cognoscet nomen Dei in die illa? quia, inquit Deus, Ego ipse qui loquor, ecce adsum, hoc est, quia ego ipse qui loquor veniam, meque ipsum ostendam & videndum cognoscendumque præbebo. Nihil enim nominis significationem æquè declarat, ac rei significatæ exhibitio & ostensio. Loquitur ergo Deus de reuelatione nominis sui, non de ea, quæ fit per nuncios, aut per typos, sed de ea quæ fit per ipsius Dei præ-sentiam, atque adeò præsentis intuitum.
units.tr: V. But why will the people of God know the name of God in that day? Because, says God, I myself who speak am here, that is, because I myself who speak will come, and I will show myself and offer myself to be seen and known. For nothing so clearly declares the meaning of a name as the exhibition and manifestation of the thing signified. God therefore speaks of the revelation of his name, not of that which is made through messengers or types, but of that which is made through the very presence of God himself, and indeed through the sight of his presence.

units.la: V I. Sed quid opus est argumentis, quando videmus verba sequentia, O quam speciosi sunt super montes pedes euangelisantis & proclamantis pacem &c, de Christi ministris ipsum annunciantibus ab Apostolo expositå Rom. 10. 15. Quam Apostoli expositionem res ipsa confirmat. Num enim in eiusmodi exclamationem erupisset, siue Deus siue Propheta, si de pace, de bono temporali ageretur? Quis non videt Euangelium, pacem, bonum, quod sic κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν appellatur, intelligi? Bona enim temporalia neque Deus, neque Prophetæ magni faciunt, aut admirantur. apud Esaiam bis clamat non esse pacem impijs, quibus tamen maxi- mè pax est temporalis, & putaremus eum apud eundem Esaiam exclamare, O quàm speciosi sunt pedes euangelizantis pacem temporalem! Absit.
units.tr: VI. But why need we arguments, when we see the following words, O how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who proclaims and heralds peace, etc., explained by the Apostle in Rom. 10:15 as referring to the ministers of Christ announcing him? The thing itself confirms this apostolic exposition. For would God or a prophet have burst into such an exclamation if the subject were temporal peace, temporal good? Who does not see that the Gospel, peace, and good are meant, which is so called by eminence [κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν]? For neither God nor the prophets esteem or admire temporal goods. In Isaiah he twice cries out that there is no peace for the wicked, to whom nevertheless temporal peace is most of all available; and should we think that he cries out in the same Isaiah, O how beautiful are the feet of him who brings temporal peace! Far be it.

units.la: VII. Non modo autem quod annunciatur pax & bonum dicitur, sed vocatur etiam salus, quæ trium vocum accumulatio non caret emphasi. Additur etiam, tanquam prædicationis seu Euangelij summa, dicentis Sioni, regnat Deus tuus. Ex quo apparet Euangelium regni Dei intelligi; atque bonum illud, pacem, & salutem regno Dei contineri. Quid ergo annunciarunt Apostoli? Regnum Dei, teste ipso Apostolo Act. 19. 7. & 20. 25. & 28. 23. 31. Quid autem est regnum Dei? Justitia, & pax, & gaudium per Spiritum Sanctum, teste eodem Apostolo Rom. 14. 17. Regnavitne Deus liberatis è Babylone Judæis? minus quàm antea. Jacuit enim prorsus dissipatum regnum decem tribuum. Judæa autem graui jugo incircuncisorum pressa, aut æquè, aut magis etiam quàm antea ingemuit.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, not only is what is announced called peace and good, but it is also called salvation, and the accumulation of these three words is not without emphasis. There is also added, as the sum of the preaching or the Gospel, saying to Sion, your God reigns. From this it appears that the Gospel of the kingdom of God is meant, and that that good, peace, and salvation are contained in the kingdom of God. What then did the Apostles announce? The kingdom of God, as the Apostle himself testifies in Acts 19:8, 20:25, and 28:23, 31. And what is the kingdom of God? Righteousness, and peace, and joy through the Holy Spirit, as the same Apostle testifies in Rom. 14:17. Did God reign over the Jews freed from Babylon? Less than before. For the kingdom of the ten tribes lay wholly scattered. And Judea, pressed under the heavy yoke of the uncircumcised, groaned either just as much as before, or even more.

units.la: VIII. Omitto brevitatis studio id quod dicitur Ψ. 10.[?] Nudauit Dominus brachium suum sanctum in oculis omnium gentium, & viderunt omnes fines terra salutem Dei nostri, quod magnificentius est, quàm ut referri possit ad liberationem è captivitate Babylonica. Taceo etiam quod subjungitur Ψ. 12. Dominus enim ante vos incedet, & congregabit vos Deus Israel, quemadmodum, ut verbis utar ipsius Socini, idem Dominus, idest Jehova, dicitur præcessisse eundem populum ex Ægypto liberatum, in nube & in columna ignis, Exod. 13. 21. Id quod tempore solutionis captivitatis Babylonicæ nullo modo est impletum, neque typicè, id enim jam satis adumbratum fuerat, cum soluta est captivitas Ægyptiaca, (non multiplicat autem Scriptura typos sine aliqua necessitate) Neque reipsa: Non enim liberationi-ex Ægypto respondet liberatio è Babylone ut veritas typo, sed typi sunt diversi diversas vel res, vel etiam eiusdem rei perfectiones & circumstantias adumbrantes.
units.tr: VIII. For the sake of brevity I omit what is said in Psalm 98 (Ψ. 10.[?]): "The Lord has made bare his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God," which is too magnificent to be referred to the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity. I also pass over what follows in Psalm 12 (Ψ. 12.): "For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel will gather you," as Socinus himself puts it, "the same Lord, that is Jehovah, is said to have gone before the same people when they were freed from Egypt, in a cloud and in a pillar of fire," Exod. 13. 21. This was in no way fulfilled at the time the Babylonian captivity was loosed, neither typically (for this had already been sufficiently foreshadowed when the Egyptian captivity was loosed, and Scripture does not multiply types without some necessity), nor in reality. For the deliverance from Babylon does not correspond to the deliverance from Egypt as truth to type; rather, the types are different and foreshadow either different things or different perfections and circumstances of the same thing.

units.la: IX. Sed fac verba illa, propter hoc cognoscet populus meus nomen meum in illa die: quia ego ipse qui loquor, ecce adsum, ad tempus etiam liberationis ex captivitate Babylonica referri posse. Cum illa liberatio, affirmante Socino, typus sit redemptionis partæ per Christum, Præsentia Dei intelligenda erit illi liberationi consentanea, hoc est, typica. Fuit igitur præsens Deus tempore reditus è captiuitate Babylonica typicè, tempore verò Christi verè & reipsa. Præsentia illa umbra fuit, hæc corpus. Illa figura fuit, hæc veritas. Non igitur si illa nihil fuit nisi Dei præsens fauor & gratia, vt vult Socinus, consequens est hinc quoque nihil aliud esse. Contrarium consequitur potius. Perit enim ratio typi, si typus & id cuius typus esse dicitur, ponantur esse eiusdem rationis. Itaque fauor Dei præsens inuisibiliter, quatenus talis, adumbrari nec potuit nec debuit, cum sit communis omnium liberationum, quæ Deus populo suo indulsit. Adde quod qui sic loquitur, Ego ipse qui loquor ecce adsum, præsentiam personæ suæ non præcisè fauoris sui, significat; alioqui quomodo personæ significari præsentia possit, me fugit. Nihil enim ad eam exprimendam significantius succurrit.
units.tr: IX. But grant that those words, "therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I myself who speak, behold, I am present," can also be referred to the time of the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity. Since, as Socinus affirms, that deliverance is a type of the redemption obtained through Christ, the presence of God must be understood as corresponding to that deliverance, that is, as typical. God was therefore present at the time of the return from the Babylonian captivity in a typical way, but at the time of Christ truly and in reality. That presence was a shadow, this one the body; that was a figure, this the truth. Therefore, if that presence "was nothing but God's present favour and grace," as Socinus holds, it does not follow that this too is nothing else. The opposite follows rather. For the nature of a type is lost if the type and that of which it is said to be the type are placed as being of the same kind. Accordingly, the present favour of God invisibly, as such, could neither be nor needed to be foreshadowed, since it is common to all the deliverances which God granted to his people. Add that he who speaks thus, "I myself who speak, behold, I am present," signifies the presence of his own person, not precisely of his favour; otherwise I do not see how a presence of a person could be signified. For nothing more expressive comes to mind for expressing it.

units.la: X. Hoc confirmat causalis quia. Docet enim verbis, Ego ipse qui loquor, ecce adsum, causam contineri eius quod antecessit, cognoscet populus meus nomen meum in illa die. Significat igitur se tunc temporis per suam ipsius præsentiam à populo suo cognitum iri. In quo tacita quædam oppositio potest obseruari inter modum sui reuelandi, quem hactenus Deus sequutus erat, & eum quem hoc loco pollicetur. Quasi diceret, Populus meus nondum nomen meum cognoscit, quoniam eum non sum per meipsum alloquutus, sed per alios, ministros meos: at in illa die nomen meum cognoscet, quia ego ipse, qui hoc promitto, meipsum illi præsentem & contemplandum exhibebo, atque adeò ego ipse eum præsens alloquar. Quemadmodum hæc personæ ipsius Dei præsentia nullo typo adumbrata est, qui quidem deprehendi possit in historia liberationis è captiuitate Babylonica, sic ea adumbrata est in historia redemptionis ex seruitute Ægyptiaca typis admodum illustribus, præsentia Dei in monte Sinai, è quo populum suum immediatè, id est non mediante Mose, alloquutus est; præsentia Dei populum suum in columna nubis & ignis ducentis, tegentis, & illuminantis in deserto: & præsentia Dei in propitiatorio, quod erat operculum arcæ testimonii. quibus typis negari non potest, quin significata sit potius ipsius Dei fauentis præsentia, quàm præcisè fauoris. Sed de illis typis alius erit disputandi locus.
units.tr: X. The causal particle "because" confirms this. For by the words "I myself who speak, behold, I am present," he teaches that the cause of what went before, "my people shall know my name in that day," is contained in them. He signifies, therefore, that at that time he will be known by his people through his own presence. In this there can be observed a certain tacit opposition between the manner of his self-revelation which God had followed hitherto and the one he promises in this place. As if he said: My people do not yet know my name, since I have not addressed them in my own person, but through others, my ministers; but in that day they will know my name, because I myself, who make this promise, will show myself present to them and open to their gaze, and so I myself will speak to them present. Just as this presence of God's own person was not foreshadowed by any type which could be detected in the history of the deliverance from the Babylonian captivity, so it was foreshadowed in the history of the redemption from Egyptian servitude by types most illustrious indeed: the presence of God on Mount Sinai, from which he addressed his people immediately, that is, not through Moses; the presence of God leading, covering and lighting his people in the desert by a pillar of cloud and fire; and the presence of God over the mercy seat, which was the lid of the ark of the testimony. By these types it cannot be denied that what was signified was rather the presence of God himself showing favour, than favour precisely. But of those types there will be another place for discussion.

units.la: DISPVTATIO DECIMA SEPTIMA
units.tr: DISPUTATION SEVENTEEN

units.la: De Arg. XVII. Ex Esaiæ Lx. ℣. 1. Surge, illuminare, &c, citato Eph. 5. 14.
units.tr: On Argument XVII. From Isaiah 60:1, Arise, shine, &c., quoted at Ephesians 5:14.

units.la: I. VENIT etiam nobis in mentem locus Esaiæ r. x. 1. Surge, illuminare, quoniam venit lux tua & gloria Domini super te orta est. Quia ecce tenebræ operient terram, & caligo populos: super te autem orietur Dominus & gloria eius super te videbitur, quem Apostolus laudauit Eph. 5. 14. insertis explicationis gratia nonnullis vocibus, Propterea dicit, Expergiscere qui dormis, & surge à mortuis, & illucescet tibi Christus. Vnde sic argumentor.
units.tr: I. There also comes to mind for us the passage of Isaiah 60:1: Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the Lord shall arise upon you, and his glory shall be seen over you, which the Apostle praised at Ephesians 5:14, adding a few words by way of explanation: Therefore it says, Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall shine upon you. From this I argue as follows.
