units.la: Ille qui Esai. Lx. 1. dicitur illuminaturus Ecclesiam, & super eam oriturus est Deus Israëlis, seu, est præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: He who, according to Isaiah 60:1, is to illuminate the Church, and over whom the God of Israel is to rise, or who is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est ille qui Esai. Lx. 1. dicitur illuminaturus Ecclesiam, & super eam oriturus.
units.tr: Christ is he who, according to Isaiah 60:1, is to illuminate the Church and rise over it.

units.la: E. Christus est Deus Israëlis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel.

units.la: II. Major ex verbis Prophetæ clara est. Is enim, qui, tanquam sol, super Ecclesiam oriturus erat, eamque illuminaturus, Iehoua bis appellatur, nec alio nomine ab omnibus aliis eo loco distinguitur. Minor autem a Apostoli testimonio probatur. Is enim laudat Scripturæ locum, vt patet ex verbis, Propterea dicit. Nullibi autem id dicit Scriptura, nisi in hoc Esaiæ loco. Citat igitur hunc Esaiæ locum, sed, vt ita loquar, paraphrasticè; Nam & illius, qui jubetur surgere, statum, & illius, qui surgenti illucescet nomen exprimit, quo solet in Novo Testamento, non modo ab hominibus & Angelis, sed etiam à Deo Patre, & à Spiritu Sancto distingui. Cum igitur Apostolus locum illum citaret, non dixit, & illuminabere, tacito illuminantis nomine, nec dixit, & illucescet tibi Dominus (hoc enim nomen accipi potuisset de Patre) nee dixit illucescet tibi Dominus per Christum, potuisset enim videri non ipsa lux, non ipse sol Christus esse; sed simpliciter commutato Domini nomine in nomen Christi, illucescet tibi Chri-stus. Quo significauit per Dominum apud Esaiam Christum esse intelligendum. Alioqui causa nulla apparet, cur Christum dicere maluerit, quàm Dominum, quo uno nomine Propheta usus est. Huc accedit, quod non tantùm alludit ad Prophetæ verba, aut verba mutuatur à Propheta, sed aperte significat se locum citare, adeoque id quod sequitur dici eo loco, quod non dicitur, si Dominus non est idem cum Christo.
units.tr: II. The major premise is clear from the words of the Prophet. For he who was to rise over the Church like the sun, and to illuminate it, is called Jehovah twice, and is distinguished in that place by no other name from all others. The minor premise is proved from the testimony of the Apostle. For he cites a passage of Scripture, as is plain from the words Therefore it says. Yet Scripture says this nowhere except in this passage of Isaiah. He therefore cites this passage of Isaiah, but, so to speak, in paraphrase; for he expresses both the condition of the one who is bidden to arise and the name of him who shall shine upon the one who rises, a name which in the New Testament is customarily distinguished not only from men and angels but also from God the Father and the Holy Spirit. When the Apostle therefore cited that passage, he did not say and you shall be illuminated, leaving unspoken the name of the one who illuminates; nor did he say and the Lord shall shine upon you (for this name could have been taken of the Father); nor did he say the Lord shall shine upon you through Christ, for it might then have seemed that Christ was not the light itself, not the sun itself. Rather, by simply changing the name of the Lord into the name of Christ, he said Christ shall shine upon you. By this he signified that the Lord in Isaiah is to be understood as Christ. Otherwise no reason appears why he should have preferred to say Christ rather than Lord, the one name the Prophet used. Moreover, he does not merely allude to the words of the Prophet or borrow words from the Prophet, but plainly indicates that he is citing the passage; and so what follows is said in that place, which would not be said if the Lord were not the same as Christ.

units.la: III. Apostolo res ipsa succlamat. A quo enim alio illuminaretur Ecclesia, quàm à Luce? Quis alius super eam oriretur, quàm sol Iustitiæ? Est autem ipsa lux Christus. Ioh. 12. 46. Ego lux in mundum veni. Ioh. 8. 12. 9. 5. Ego sum lux mundi, Ioh. 3. 19. lux venit in mundum. Ioh. 1. 9. Erat lux illa vera quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum. Matth. 4. 16. positis in regione & umbra mortis lux orta est. Idem vocatur oriens ex alto, Luc 1. 78. & sol iustitia, exoriturus illis qui nomen Domini timent, Malach. 4. 2. Reuera exortus est Christus primo suo aduentu, & exorietur aduentu suo secundo Ecclesiæ suæ: alius solis spiritualis ortus vel aduentus non commemoratur in Scrip-tura.
units.tr: III. The thing itself cries out in support of the Apostle. For by what other light would the Church be illuminated than by Light? Who else would rise over it than the Sun of Righteousness? Now Christ himself is the light. John 12:46: I have come into the world as a light. John 8:12, 9:5: I am the light of the world. John 3:19: The light has come into the world. John 1:9: That was the true light which enlightens every man coming into the world. Matthew 4:16: To those sitting in the region and shadow of death, a light has risen. He is called the dayspring from on high, Luke 1:78, and the Sun of Righteousness, who shall rise for those who fear the name of the Lord, Malachi 4:2. Indeed Christ has risen at his first coming, and he will rise at his second coming upon his Church; no other rising or coming of a spiritual sun is recorded in Scripture.

units.la: DISPUTATIO DECIMA OCTAVA De Arg. XVIII. Ex Esai. LXI. ℣. 1. Spiritus Domini Dei est super me, eo quod unxit me, &c, laudato Luc. 4. 18.
units.tr: EIGHTEENTH DISPUTATION: On the Argument XVIII, from Isaiah 61:1, "The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because he has anointed me," etc., compared with Luke 4:18.

units.la: I. DABIT etiam hic locus nobis argumentum. Cum res ipsa, tum autoritas Domini nostri Iesu Christi locum illum Esaiæ, Spiritus Domini est super me, &c, de seipso exponentis Luc. 4. 18. prohibet, quominus in dubium vocari possit, quin is, qui sic apud Esaiam loquens inducitur, sit Christus. Itaque unus nobis restat labor, ut probemus, qui sic apud Esaiam loquitur, eum revera Deum esse, hoc est, præditum essentia divina. Id autem concludo hoc syllogismo. Dominus (Iehoua) est præditus essentia divina. Ille qui dicit apud Esaiam Spiritus Domini super me, &c, est Dominus (Iehoua) Ergo ille qui dicit apud Esaiam, Spiritus Domini super me, &c, est præditus essentia di-vina. Majorem non negabunt Adversarij.
units.tr: I. This place will also furnish us with an argument. Both the thing itself and the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in Luke 4:18 expounds that passage of Isaiah, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," etc., as referring to himself, prevent anyone from calling in doubt that he who is introduced speaking thus in Isaiah is Christ. Our only remaining task, then, is to prove that he who speaks thus in Isaiah is truly God, that is, endowed with the divine essence. I conclude this by the following syllogism. The Lord (Jehovah) is endowed with the divine essence. He who says in Isaiah, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," etc., is the Lord (Jehovah). Therefore he who says in Isaiah, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," etc., is endowed with the divine essence. The adversaries will not deny the major premise.

units.la: II. Minor probatur ex ℣. 8. Quia ego Dominus diligens iudicium, & odio habens rapinam in holocausto, &c. Qui hoc dicit est Dominus (Iehoua) Deus Israelis, præditus essentia divina. Id vocari in dubium non potest. Hic tamen idem est cum eo, qui dixit vers. 1. Spiritus Domini super me, &c, ut legenti manifestum est: Nam versus iste octavus cohæret cum septimo, ut patet ex conjunctione quia, septimus autem cohæret cum antecedentibus, ut à primo versu ad octavum usque manifesta sit eiusdem sermonis continuatio ab eodem loquente, qui primis capitis versiculis loquitur ut Propheta, versibus 8. & 9. ut Deus, ℣. 10. & 11. ut unum corpus mysticum cum Ecclesia sua componens, sic tamen vt ipse Sponsi, illa sponsæ personam sustineat.
units.tr: II. The minor premise is proved from verse 8: "For I the Lord love judgment, and hate robbery in the burnt offering," etc. He who says this is the Lord (Jehovah), the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence. This cannot be called in question. Yet this same speaker is the one who said in verse 1, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," etc., as is plain to the reader. For verse 8 coheres with verse 7, as is evident from the conjunction "for" (quia), and verse 7 coheres with what precedes, so that from the first verse to the eighth the discourse is clearly one continuous speech by the same speaker. He speaks in the first verses of the chapter as the Prophet; in verses 8 and 9 as God; in verses 10 and 11 as one mystical body, constituting one with his Church, yet in such a way that he himself bears the person of the Bridegroom and she the person of the Bride.

units.la: III. Frustrà nobis obijcient Aduersarij, Christūm versu primo semetipsum à Domino distinguere, cum ait, Spiritus Domini est super me &c, Agnoscimus enim distinctionem personæ Filij à persona Patris, etsi communi vt essentia diuina, sic nomine Dei & Iehouæ gaudere credamus vtrumque, quæ distinctio personarum, vnitatem communis essentiæ non dissoluit, vt lib. 3. Deo fauente, fusius explicabitur.
units.tr: III. The adversaries will vainly object to us that Christ, in the first verse, distinguishes himself from the Lord when he says, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me," etc. For we acknowledge the distinction of the person of the Son from the person of the Father, and yet we believe that both share in the common divine essence and in the name God and Jehovah. This distinction of persons does not dissolve the unity of the common essence, as will be explained more fully, God willing, in book 3.

units.la: DISPVTATIO DECIMA NONA
units.tr: Disputation Nineteen

units.la: De Arg. XIX. Ex Esai. LIV. 5. Quoniam maritus tuus factor tuus, Dominus exercituum nomen eius, & redemptor tuus, sanctus Israëlis, Deus vniuersæ terræ vocabitur, necnon ex aliis locis, in quibus Deus Israëlis Ecclesiæ maritus seu sponsus appellatur, collatis cum Matth. 9. 15. & 25. 1. Ioh. 3. 29. 2. Cor. 11. 12. Eph. 5. &c.
units.tr: Concerning Argument XIX, from Isaiah 54:5: "For thy Maker is thy husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; the God of the whole earth shall he be called," and likewise from other passages in which the God of Israel is called the husband or bridegroom of the Church, compared with Matthew 9:15 and 25:1, John 3:29, 2 Corinthians 11:2, Ephesians 5, etc.

units.la: PENE præter miseram locum Esai. LIV. 5. Quoniam maritus tuus factor tuus, Dominus exercituum nomen eius, &c: Ex quo tamen argumentum peti potest multum[?], quod sic concipio.
units.tr: Almost beyond the wretched place, Isaiah 54:5, "For thy Maker is thy husband, the LORD of hosts is his name," etc. From this an argument can be drawn, which I conceive as follows.

units.la: Maritus Ecclesiæ est Deus Israëlis, præditus essentia divina.
units.tr: The husband of the Church is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est maritus Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: Christ is the husband of the Church.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis, præditus essentia divina.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Major propositio niticur[?] loco laudato Esaiæ LIV. 5. ex quo luce meridiana clarius est, legitimum sponsum seu maritum Ecclesiae Deum esse, cuius nomen est Dominus (Iehoua) exercituum. id quod passim toto Veteri Testamento inculcatur. Minor nititur testimonijs ipsius Christi Matth. 9. 15. & 25 1. Iohannis Baptistae Ioh. 3. 29. Apostoli Pauli 2. Cor. 11. 12. Eph. 5. nec non Apostoli Iohannis Apoc. 21. 9. &c.
units.tr: The major premise rests on the cited passage of Isaiah 54:5, from which it is clearer than noonday light that the lawful bridegroom or husband of the Church is God, whose name is the LORD (Jehovah) of hosts; this is pressed everywhere throughout the Old Testament. The minor rests on the testimonies of Christ himself, Matthew 9:15 and 25:1; of John the Baptist, John 3:29; of the Apostle Paul, 2 Corinthians 11:2 and Ephesians 5; and likewise of the Apostle John, Revelation 21:9, etc.

units.la: II. Non video quid possit ab Aduersarijs responderi. Nam si Ecclesiam Veteris Testamenti distinxerint ab Ecclesia noui, quasi illius maritus Pater fuerit, huius Filius, distinctionem loca laudata respuent, resque ipsa refutabit. Eius enim Ecclesiae se Deus maritum esse profitetur hoc loco, quam compellat versibus proximè antecedentibus, Latare sterilis quae non paris, erumpe, canta, clama quae non parturis, quoniam plures sunt filij deserta, quam eius quae habet virum, &c. Compellat autem illis verbis eam quae sursum est Hierusalem, quae libera est, quae est mater omnium nostrum teste Apostolo Gal. 4. 27. quo eodem teste sibi mutuò respondent Agar, foedus legale, & Ierusalem terrena, quibus opponuntur Sara, foedus gratiae, Ierusalem quae sursum est. Idem autem fuit Agaris & Sarae maritus Abrahamus, sed Sarae prius ac magis legitimè, Agaris ad tempus propter Sarae sterilitatem. Qui typus sublata deitate seu diuina Domini nostri essentia explicari non potest, eadem vero posita mirabiliter cum sua veritate congruit.
units.tr: II. I do not see what the opponents can answer. For if they distinguish the Church of the Old Testament from the Church of the New, as though the Father were its husband and the Son the husband of the other, they will reject the cited passages, and the matter itself will refute them. For in this passage God professes himself the husband of that Church which he addresses in the verses immediately preceding: "Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail; for the desolate hath more children than she which hath an husband," etc. He addresses her with those words as "that Jerusalem which is above, which is free, which is the mother of us all," as the Apostle witnesses in Galatians 4:27; and by the same witness Hagar, the legal covenant, and earthly Jerusalem answer one another, and are set over against Sarah, the covenant of grace, and Jerusalem which is above. Now Abraham was the husband of both Hagar and Sarah, but of Sarah first and more lawfully, of Hagar only for a time, on account of Sarah's barrenness. This type cannot be explained if the deity, that is the divine essence of our Lord, is removed; but with that essence posited, it agrees wonderfully with its truth.

units.la: III. Hoc etiam ipse Deus confirmat Ose. 2. 16. Et erit in die illa dicit Dominus, vocabis me vir meus, & non vocabis me ultrà Baal meus, diem autem intelligit, quo veritatem typo ascensionis ex Ægypto adumbratam erat exhibiturus reque ipsa daturus effectam. Id autem est tempus Noui Testamenti. Ne quis verò putaret tandem aliquando hoc Dei & Ecclesiae matrimonium dissolutum iri, subjicit V. 19: Et desponsabo te mihi in sempiternum, desponsabo te mihi in iustitia, & in iudicio, & in gratia, & in miserationibus: desponsabo te mihi in fide, & cognosces Dominum.
units.tr: III. God himself confirms this in Hosea 2:16: "And it shall be in that day, saith the LORD, that thou shalt call me Ishi, and shalt call me no more Baali," and by "that day" he means the day on which he was about to exhibit the truth foreshadowed by the type of the ascent out of Egypt, and to give the thing itself accomplished. That is the time of the New Testament. Lest anyone should think that this marriage of God and the Church would at some time be dissolved, he adds in verse 19: "And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies. I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness; and thou shalt know the LORD."

units.la: IV. His testimonijs ipsa res consentit. Nam si ponitur Ecclesia Veteris Testamenti sponsa ipsius Dei fuisse, Ecclesia verò Noui Testamenti sponsa Christi tantùm hominis, consequitur Ecclesiam Veteris Testamenti praestantiorem ac digniorem Ecclesia Noui Testamenti fuisse, quippe dignioris sponsam. Id quod tamen falsum esse perspicuum est. Illa enim umbras & typos habebat, Hæc corpus & veritatem: Illa tractabatur ut infans, & sub elementis mundi in servitutem redacta erat, Hæc asserta in libertatem adoptionem accepit, tractaturque ut filius adultus: Illa promissiones eminus aspexit & salutavit, Hæc illis fruitur: Illa cupiebat id quod ista assequuta est, &c.
units.tr: IV. The thing itself agrees with these testimonies. For if the Church of the Old Testament is posited to have been the bride of God himself, and the Church of the New Testament the bride of Christ only as man, it follows that the Church of the Old Testament was more excellent and worthier than the Church of the New Testament, being the bride of the worthier husband. Yet this is plainly false. For that Church had shadows and types, this one the body and the truth; that one was treated as an infant and was reduced to servitude under the elements of the world, this one, claimed back into liberty, has received adoption and is treated as a grown son; that one saw the promises from afar and greeted them, this one enjoys them; that one longed for what this one has obtained, etc.

units.la: V. Quid ergo respondebunt Aduersarij? Dicentne eiusdem Ecclesiæ duos esse sponsos, Patrem & Filium? Non arbitror hoc eos esse dicturos, Nam præterquam quod manifestam præ se fert absurditatis speciem, elogium sponsi Ecclesiæ totum novum Testamentum vendicat Filio constanter, nec unquam tribuit Patri. Sunt etiam in Veteri Testamento typi multi matrimonij spiritualis Christi & Ecclesiæ, sed nulli duos sponsos Patrem & Filium adumbrant, cum tamen vix quicquam in eo conjugio possit observari, cuius non extet aliquis typus. Adde quod Deus se multis locis Zelotypum esse testatur, si igitur Pater est maritus Ecclesiæ, quomodo patitur alium se eiusdem Ecclesiæ maritum profiteri tam sæpe, tamque constanter? Sed quid opus est argumentis, cum habeamus disertum Apostoli testimonium 2. Cor. 11. 2. vos, inquit, aptaui uni viro virginem castam exhibendam Christo. Non sunt igitur duo viri Ecclesiæ, sed unus. Nec possunt respondere Aduersarij, Filium esse subordinatum Patri, subordinationem enim maritorum matrimonium non recipit. Nihil igitur nobis occurrit quod possit responderi.
units.tr: V. What then will the opponents answer? Will they say that this same Church has two husbands, the Father and the Son? I do not think they will say this, for besides bearing on its face a clear appearance of absurdity, the whole New Testament constantly ascribes the title of bridegroom of the Church to the Son and never once attributes it to the Father. There are also in the Old Testament many types of the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church, but none of them represents two bridegrooms, Father and Son, although scarcely anything can be observed in that marriage of which some type does not exist. Add that God testifies in many places that he is jealous; if then the Father is the husband of the Church, how does he suffer another to profess himself the husband of the same Church so often and so constantly? But why need arguments, when we have the explicit testimony of the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 11:2: "For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ." There are therefore not two husbands of the Church, but one. Nor can the opponents reply that the Son is subordinate to the Father, for a marriage does not admit subordination of husbands. Therefore nothing occurs to us that could be answered.

units.la: DISPUTATIO VIGESIMA De Arg. XX. ex Deut. vi. 13. citato Matth. 4. 10. & Luc 4. 8. Dominum Deum tuum adorabis, & ei soli seruies.
units.tr: DISPUTATION TWENTY: On argument XX, from Deut. 6:13, cited at Matt. 4:10 and Luke 4:8: "You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve him only."

units.la: I. CLAVDAT hanc sectionem locus Deut. vi. 13. ab ipso Domino nostro laudatus Matth. 4. 10. & Luc. 4. 8. Deminum Deum tuum adorabis & ei soli seruies. Quod ex eo ducitur argumentum tale est.
units.tr: I. This section is supported by the passage of Deut. 6:13, which our Lord himself cited at Matt. 4:10 and Luke 4:8: "You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." The argument drawn from it runs as follows.

units.la: Qui est religiosè adorandus & colendus, ille est Deus Israelis.
units.tr: Whoever is to be worshipped and served religiously is the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est religiosè adorandus & colendus.
units.tr: Christ is to be worshipped and served religiously.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israelis. Major nititur loco laudato: Nam si solus Deus Israelis est adorandus, si soli Deo Israelis est seruiendum, negari non potest, quin, quicunque adorandus & colendus est religiosè sit Deus Israelis. Minor conceditur ab Aduersarijs. Est igitur argumentum omni ex parte inuictum.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The major premise rests on the cited passage. For if the God of Israel alone is to be worshipped, and the God of Israel alone is to be served, it cannot be denied that whoever is to be worshipped and served religiously is the God of Israel. The minor premise is conceded by our opponents. The argument is therefore unassailable on every side.

units.la: II. Respondet tamen V Volkelius, illud Dei praeceptum sententia sua triplici de causa nihil quicquam officere. Primo enim, inquit, ut sacra litera solum Deum immortalem, aut sapientem nominando, Christum aliosque immortalitate ac sapientia minimè spoliant, sed tantum Deum solum à semetipso talem esse significant: sic de solo quoque Deo, ut pote primario omnium rerum autore adorando indicandum est. Particulis enim istis exclusiuis, inquit Schlichtingius, qualis est solus & similes, cum de Deo usurpantur, nunquam ij simpliciter excluduntur, qui à Deo ea in re, de qua agitur, dependent. Principiò hinc colligo, falsum esse quod ait & urget Crellius, Eam esse vim vocis solius, ut omnes alios excludat à communione praedicati, praeter[?] eum cui apponitur. Deinde propositiones, solus Deus est immortalis, solus Deus est sapiens interpretari, solus Deus est immortalis à semetipso, solus Deus est sapiens à semetipso, non est proprie loquendo eas exponere, sed tantùm aliquid eis addere & apponere. Est enim propositio solus Deus est immortalis, ut loquuntur scholastici, exponibilis, & debet per duas istas exponi, Deus est immortalis, & alius nullus est immortalis, quae respondent quaestioni an sit, non verò cur sit, aut unde sit. Dicitur igitur Deus solus immortalis quia solus absolutè loquendo mori non potest, implicat contradictionem eum mori cum creaturae omnes, ut aliquando non fuerunt, sic possint non esse. Dicitur solus sapiens, quia sapientia creaturarum ad diuinam collata vix eam proportionem habet quàm gutta ad oceanum, ac pro nulla habetur. Sic Esai. 40. 15, 17. gentes comparatione Dei dicuntur esse tanquam gutta situlae, puluisculus trutinae, nihil, immò minus nihilo & inanitate.
units.tr: II. Volkelius nevertheless replies that in his view this divine precept does not hinder the argument, for three reasons. "First, when Scripture calls God alone immortal, or alone wise, it does not thereby strip Christ or others of immortality and wisdom, but only signifies that God alone is such from himself. So also what is said of God alone must be understood of him alone as the primary author of all things, who is to be worshipped." For Schlichting says: "When such exclusive particles as alone and similar words are applied to God, they never simply exclude those who depend on God in the matter under discussion." First, from this I conclude that what Crellius says and presses is false: that the force of the word alone is to exclude all others from sharing the predicate except the one to whom it is attached. Next, the propositions "God alone is immortal," "God alone is wise," "God alone is immortal from himself," and "God alone is wise from himself" cannot properly be explained by merely adding something to them. The proposition "God alone is immortal," as the Scholastics put it, is exponible, and must be expounded by these two: "God is immortal" and "no other is immortal." These answer the question whether something is, not why it is or whence it is. God is therefore called alone immortal because, speaking absolutely, he alone cannot die; it implies a contradiction for him to die, whereas all creatures, since they once did not exist, are able not to exist. He is called alone wise because the wisdom of creatures, compared with the divine wisdom, bears the same proportion as a drop to the ocean, and is reckoned as nothing. So in Isaiah 40:15, 17 the nations, in comparison with God, are said to be as a drop from a bucket, as dust on the scales, as nothing, indeed less than nothing and emptiness.

units.la: III. Tertiò, Quis est VVolkelio judice sensus huius propositionis, solus Deus est adorandus, vel mandati, adorabis Dominum Deum tuum & illi soli seruies, Num hic, solus Deus est adorandus à seipso, Adorabis Dominum Deum tuum, & illi soli seruies à seipso? Nimis[?] esset absurdus. Num ille, solus Deus est adorandus tanquam primarius omnium rerum autor? Estne igitur aliquis secundarius omnium rerum autor? suntne plures creatores, vnus primarius, alius secundarius? Deinde si sic accipi deberet mandatum, non illud violaret, qui alium religiosè adoraret & coleret, modò non tanquam primarium omnium rerum autorem. Atque ita omnis fere excusari posset idololatria. Perquam multos enim idololatrae gentiles & Israelitae religiosè adorarunt, quos non putarunt esse primarios rerum omnium autores. Quid quod ne ipse quidem diabolus adorari voluit à Christo tanquam primarius omnium rerum autor? quam enim et potestatem & gloriam regnorum offerebat, eam sibi datam fuisse prositebitur Luc. 4. 6. & tamen ad eius tentationem repellendam nihil visum est Christo aptius, quàm istud praeceptum, adorabis Dominum Deum tuum, & illi soli seruies. Petrus Apostolus, quamuis, diuina muneris auctoritate, admirandisque donis instructus esset, tamen à Cornelio adorari noluit propterea quod non minus quàm Cornelius homo esset. Nec tamen Cornelius tanto stupore mentis oppressus fuit, ut Petrum non hominem, sed ipsummet Deum esse, seu primarium rerum omnium autorem, sibi persuaderet. Num Iohannes Angelum, qui se pro Dei ac Christi ministro apertissime gerebat, pro ipso Deo, vel pro rerum omnium autore, adorare voluit? Hic tamen adorationem magno zelo respuit, adhibita ratione, & insinuato hoc ipso mandato, vide ne: conseruus enim tuus sum, & fratrum tuorum qui habent testimonium Iesu, Deum adora. Quibus verbis non obscurè significat, solum Deum esse adorandum. Nam, & hoc mandatum, de quo agimus, Iohanni reuocat in mentem, & quis sit adorandus ei ostendit, & eum ab adoratione eorum qui non sunt Deus[?] reuocat ad adorationem ipsius Dei. Ex quo intelligitur, Dei nomine Christum comprehendi una cum Patre.
units.tr: III. Third, what, in Volkelius's judgment, is the sense of this proposition, "God alone is to be worshipped," or of the command, "Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve"? Does it mean that God alone is to be worshipped by himself: "Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve," by himself? That would be absurd. Does it mean that God alone is to be worshipped as the primary author of all things? Is there then some secondary author of all things? Are there several creators, one primary and another secondary? Further, if the command were to be understood in that way, it would not be violated by one who worshipped and served another religiously, provided he did not regard him as the primary author of all things. And so almost every idolatry could be excused. For the idolatrous Gentiles and Israelites worshipped many religiously, whom they did not think to be the primary authors of all things. What is more, the devil himself did not wish to be worshipped by Christ as the primary author of all things. For he offered the power and glory of the kingdoms, and he confessed that these had been given to him (Luke 4:6). Yet to repel that temptation Christ found nothing more fitting than this precept: "Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve." The Apostle Peter, although he was endowed with divine authority and remarkable gifts, nevertheless refused to be worshipped by Cornelius, because he was no less a man than Cornelius was. Nor was Cornelius so overwhelmed with astonishment that he persuaded himself that Peter was not a man, but God himself, or the primary author of all things. Did John wish to worship the angel, who plainly presented himself as a minister of God and of Christ, as God himself, or as the author of all things? Yet John rejected the worship with great zeal, offering a reason and bringing to mind this very command: "See that you do not do it; for I am your fellow servant, and of your brethren who have the testimony of Jesus; worship God." By these words it is clearly signified that God alone is to be worshipped. For he both recalls to John this command under discussion, and shows him whom he is to worship, and recalls him from the worship of those who are not God to the worship of God himself. From this it is understood that Christ is included together with the Father under the name of God.

units.la: IV. Secundò respondet VVolkelius, cum Christum Patri subordinatum esse constet, sequi, noi[?] Christum adorando, ipsum Patrem, à quo tanta potestate ac gloria donatus est, adorare. Sic ita, adorando Christum adoretur Pater, quid hoc ad rem? Num propterea solus Pater adoratur? Non adoratur homo diuersus tota natura à Patre? Si sunt Pater & Filius duo dij totis substantijs diuersi: Ille Deus naturâ, hic gratia: Ille ab æterno, hic factus in consummatione seculorum: Ille creator, hic tantùm creatura: Ille summus, hic summo subordinatus &c. vterque adorandus, certè non solus Pater, sed eius etiam Filius, ab eo magis, quàm quiuis alius à suo patre, differens, est adorandus.
units.tr: IV. Secondly, Volkelius replies that, since it is agreed that Christ is subordinate to the Father, it follows that in worshipping Christ one worships the Father himself, from whom he has received such power and glory. Even if the Father is worshipped in worshipping Christ, what does this have to do with the matter? Is the Father alone therefore worshipped? Is not a man, whose whole nature differs from the Father's, worshipped? If the Father and the Son are two gods, wholly different in substance, the one God by nature, the other by grace; the one from eternity, the other made at the consummation of the ages; the one Creator, the other only a creature; the one supreme, the other subordinate to the supreme, and so on, then both are to be worshipped. Surely it is not the Father alone who is to be worshipped, but also his Son, who differs from him more than any other man differs from his father.

units.la: V. Tertiò denique respondet, Mandatum de solo Deo adorando ad Veteris Testamenti tempora proprie spectare. Hoc idem respondet Socinus, sed minus rotundè, Respondeo, inquit, quod ad Dei præceptum attinet, Deut. 6. nihil contra illud à Deo fieri, licet inbeat, Christum hominem, seu Christum, quamuis prorsus, res creata sit, cultu diuino affici. Neque enim, cum istud præceptum datum est, Christus extabat, nedum diuina potestate atque imperio esset præditus. Quod imperium ac potestas omnino per se, etiam Deo tacente, cultu diuino affici debet. Atqui jam extabat Christus, jam Dei Filius erat, jam de eo Pater clamauerat è cœlo, Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo acquiesco, jam in eum visibiliter descenderat Spiritus sanctus, jam Deus erat dignus cultu diuino, cum mandatum illud laudauit, & tanquam homines etiam tunc temporis obligans vrsit, inserta etiam particula exclusiua; ac mirum est huius mandati, quatenus à Christo vsurpatum est, Socinum & VVolkelium non meminisse. Consentit Christo Angelus ille, quem Iohannes vidit volantem per medium cæli, habentem Euangelium æternum, vt euangelisaret incolis terra, & omnigenti, & tribui, & lingua, & populo, dicentem magna voce, Timete Deum, & ei tribuite gloriam: nam venit hora iudicij eius, & adorate eum qui fecit cœlum & terram & mare & fontes aquarum. Vrget enim verbis illis & inculcat hoc ipsum mandatum Deut 6. 13. Idem fecit ille Angelus, qui cum nollet adorari à Iohanne dixit, adora Deum. Non adhibent, inquies, particulam exclusiuam. Facilè subintelligitur: auocant enim eos quos alloquuntur ab adoratione creaturarum.
units.tr: V. Thirdly and finally, he replies that "the command concerning worshipping God alone properly looks to the times of the Old Testament." Socinus gives the same reply, though less smoothly: "As to God's precept in Deut. 6, I reply that God does nothing against it, even if he commands that Christ, a man, or Christ, although he is wholly a created thing, be honoured with divine worship. For when that precept was given, Christ did not yet exist, much less was he endowed with divine power and authority. Power and authority of that kind must in themselves, even if God is silent, be honoured with divine worship." But Christ already existed; he was already the Son of God; the Father had already cried from heaven, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"; the Holy Spirit had already descended visibly upon him; he was already God, worthy of divine worship, when that command was uttered in praise, binding men at that time as well. The exclusive particle was also inserted. It is remarkable that Socinus and Volkelius do not mention that this command has been used by Christ. The angel whom John saw flying through the midst of heaven, having the eternal gospel, to preach to those who dwell on the earth, to every nation, tribe, tongue and people, saying with a loud voice, "Fear God and give him glory, for the hour of his judgment has come, and worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and the fountains of waters" agrees with Christ. For in those words he urges and inculcates this very command of Deut. 6:13. That angel did the same, when, refusing to be worshipped by John, he said, "Worship God." You will say they do not use the exclusive particle. It is easily understood by implication: they call those whom they address away from the worship of creatures.

units.la: VI. Profectò si qua sunt in Vetere Testamento præcepta moralia, perpetua, ad tempora Euangelij pertinentia, in eo numero est præceptum de solo Deo adorando. Cum enim resolui possit in duo: vnum affirmans quo iubemur adorare Deum, alterum negans quo prohibemur alios adorare, Vtrumque Christianos obligat. Nos enim hodie æquè ac olim Iudæi, aut magis etiam, & Deum adorare tenemur, & ab idololatria fugere: quàmque illud in natura Dei fundatur quæ perpetuò dignissima est adoratione, tam istud eius vnitate nititur, quæ & Deut. 6. præmittitur isti mandato, & in Noua Testamento, non minus quàm in veteri, docetur & confirmatur: ac quum Christus ita præceptum illud Deut. 6. vsurpauerit, vt exclusiuam particulam, quæ abest à textu hebræo, addiderit, major exclusiuæ illius, apud nos Christianos debet esse auctoritas quàm apud Iudæos. Satius igitur multò est, Filium confiteri, vnum cum Patre Israëlis Deum, quàm tantum præceptum soluere & homines ita docere. Quid quod ne ad veteris quidem testamenti tempora proprië spectare hoc mandatum dicere coguntur, si consentanea loqui volunt? Contendunt enim Angelum propriedictum fuisse illum, qui Patriarchis & Mosi apparuit, & legem promulgauit, & nomen Dei ac Ichouæ sibi tribuit, & adorati se passus est, quo posito sequitur necessariò, ne veteris quidem testamenti temporibus solum illum vnum Deum, qui essentia diuina præditus est, adorandum fuisse.
units.tr: VI. Surely, if there are any moral precepts in the Old Testament that are perpetual and pertain to the times of the Gospel, the precept about worshipping God alone is among them. For it can be resolved into two parts: one affirming that we are commanded to worship God, the other denying that we are forbidden to worship others. Both bind Christians. For we today, just as the Jews of old, or even more so, are bound both to worship God and to flee from idolatry. And just as this rests on the nature of God, who is always most worthy of worship, so it rests on his unity, which is set before this commandment in Deut. 6 and is taught and confirmed in the New Testament no less than in the Old. Since Christ quoted that precept from Deut. 6 in such a way as to add the exclusive particle, which is absent from the Hebrew text, the authority of that exclusive should be greater among us Christians than among the Jews. It is far better, therefore, to confess the Son, together with the Father, as the one God of Israel, than to dissolve so great a precept and teach men accordingly. And what of the fact that they are not even compelled to say that this commandment properly pertains to the times of the Old Testament, if they wish to speak consistently? For they contend that the one who appeared to the Patriarchs and to Moses, and promulgated the law, and claimed for himself the name of God and Jehovah, and allowed himself to be worshipped, was properly called the Angel. Granted this, it necessarily follows that not even in the times of the Old Testament was that one God alone, who is endowed with the divine essence, to be worshipped.

units.la: DISPVTATIO VIGESIMA PRIMA
units.tr: Disputation Twenty-One

units.la: De Arg. XXI. Ex 1. Reg. 8. 39. 2. Chron. 6. 30. Tu solus nosti corda filiorum hominum collat. cum Apoc. 2. 23.
units.tr: On Argument XXI. From 1 Kings 8:39; 2 Chronicles 6:30: "You alone know the hearts of the sons of men," compared with Revelation 2:23.

units.la: I. ACCEDENT etiam, velut cumulus quidam, ad hanc Sectionem verba Salomonis 1. Reg. 8. 39. 2. Chr. 6. 30. Tu solus nosti corda filiorum hominum: collata enim cum ipsius Christi verbis Apoc. 2. 23. Et scient omnes Ecclesiæ quod ego sum scrutator renum & cordium, & dabo unicuique secundum opera sua, suggesunt nobis hoc argumentum.
units.tr: I. To this section are added, as a kind of heap of further proofs, the words of Solomon in 1 Kings 8:39 and 2 Chronicles 6:30, "You alone know the hearts of the sons of men," which, when compared with the words of Christ himself in Revelation 2:23, "And all the churches shall know that I am he who searches the reins and hearts, and I will give to each one according to his works," suggest the following argument to us.

units.la: Solus Deus Israëlis novit corda hominum.
units.tr: Only the God of Israel knows the hearts of men.

units.la: Christus novit corda hominum.
units.tr: Christ knows the hearts of men.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis. Major probatur testimonio Salomonis 2. Chr. 6. 30. 1. Reg. 8. 39. Minor ipsius Christi Apoc. 2. 23. Quid ergo poterunt respondere Adversarij? Si quid coniicio, Respondebunt duo: primùm enim verba illa, Tu solus nosti corda hominum, dicent accipienda esse cum limitatione à temetipso. Deinde ea restringenda esse ad tempora Veteris Testamenti. quæ duo paucis refellenda sunt.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The major premise is proved by the testimony of Solomon, 2 Chronicles 6:30 and 1 Kings 8:39; the minor by Christ's own words, Revelation 2:23. What, then, will our opponents be able to reply? If I may guess, they will give two answers. First, they will say that the words "You alone know the hearts of men" must be understood with the limitation "from yourself." Second, that they must be restricted to the times of the Old Testament. These two points must be refuted briefly.

units.la: II. Primùm igitur si propositio, solus Deus novit corda hominum, intelligenda est cum tacita illa limitatione à semetipso, cadet vis exclusiuæ solus, non super id quod exprimitur, sed super illam limitationem quæ non exprimitur, sed ab Adversarijs additur, excludetque omnes alios, non à communione prædicati quod exprimitur, sed à communione [illegible, ~5 letters] prædicati quæ non exprimitur. Id quod num sit verisimile, lectori judicandum relinquo. Certè propositio affirmatiua, Deus novit corda hominum, non eget illa limitatione, à semetipso, sed absolutè vera est. Inserta autem exclusiua, solus, affirmatiuam illam nullo modo limitat, tantùm alios excludit à communione prædicati, impeditque ne latius attributum quàm subjectum pateat.
units.tr: II. First, then, if the proposition "the God alone knows the hearts of men" is to be understood with that tacit limitation "from himself," the force of the exclusive "alone" will fall not on what is expressed but on that limitation which is not expressed but is added by our opponents. It will exclude all others not from sharing in the predicate that is expressed, but from sharing in the predicate that is not expressed. I leave it to the reader to judge whether this is plausible. Certainly the affirmative proposition, "God knows the hearts of men," does not need that limitation "from himself" but is absolutely true. The exclusive "alone," when inserted, in no way limits the affirmative proposition; it only excludes others from sharing in the predicate, and prevents the attribute from extending more widely than its subject.

units.la: III. Hoc confirmatur inductione similium propositionum. Nehem. 9. 6. Tu ipse, solus es Dominus (Iehoua) Tu fecisti cœlum & cœlos cœlorum &c. Ps. 86. 9. Tu solus es Deus. Esai. 37. 16. Tu solus es Deus regnorum omnium terrae, tu fecisti cœlum & terram: & XY[?]. 20. Tu es Dominus solus. Ps. 83. 17. Tu solus es altissimus super omnem terram. Esai. 2. 11. 17. exaltabitur Dominus solus in die illa. Num in his & similibus propositionibus subintelligenda est limitatio à temetipso, vel à semetipso? Non hoc dicent Adversarij: nolunt enim duos esse altissimos, duos Dominos. Cum de creaturis agitur, non puto ullum exemplum proferri posse, ubi talis limitatio adhiberi debeat: quæ si possit subintelligi, nihil tam commune est, quod Deo tribui non possit soli. Solus Deus est, agit, loquitur, solus Deus novit Christum venisse in carne, solus Deus credit veram esse hanc propositionem, Qui credit in Filium habet vitam æternam, solus Deus cognoscit Christum resurrexisse, &c. Veræ erunt propositiones si addas à semetipso. Quis tamen sine expressa illa limitatione, aut sic unquam loquitur ; aut ferre possit ita loquentem? Fac aliquem suo, ut loquuntur, marte veritatem aliquam invenisse in Physica aut Mathematica aut Medicina, eamque cum aliis multis communicasse, dicetur nihilominus solus eam nosse, & poterunt reliqui negare se veritatem illam, vt vt eam ab alio reuelatam animo comprehenderint, cognitam habere subintellecta nimirum ista limitatione, & poterit tadjuratus [?] testis negare se scire quod reuera scit, aut quivis alius negare se fecisse quod reuera fecit, subintelligendo à semetipso. Atque ita lata porta mendacijs aperietur. Quid quod admissa ista limitatione & opinione Aduersariorum, quàm vera erit ista propositio Tu solus nosti corda hominum, tam verae erunt istae, Christus non novit corda hominum, Christus non venit in mundum, Christus non iudicabit viuos & mortuos, &c. Mirum est si suae istius limitationis iam aduersarios non pudet. Itaque missis ijs quae possent adjici, progrediar ad responsionem alteram.
units.tr: III. This is confirmed by an induction of similar propositions. Nehemiah 9:6: "You yourself, you alone are the Lord (Jehovah); you made heaven and the heaven of heavens," etc. Psalm 86:9: "You alone are God." Isaiah 37:16: "You alone are the God of all the kingdoms of the earth; you made heaven and earth." And "XY[?]. 20": "You are the Lord alone." Psalm 83:17: "You alone are the Most High over all the earth." Isaiah 2:11, 17: "The Lord alone shall be exalted in that day." Do our opponents say that in these and similar propositions the limitation "from yourself" or "from himself" is to be understood? They will not say so, for they do not want there to be two Most Highs, two Lords. When the subject is creatures, I do not think any example can be produced where such a limitation ought to be applied. And if it could be understood there, nothing so common could be said which could not be attributed to God alone. God alone is, acts, speaks; God alone knows that Christ has come in the flesh; God alone believes that this proposition is true, "He who believes in the Son has eternal life"; God alone knows that Christ has risen, and so on. These propositions would be true if you added "from himself." Yet who, without that express limitation, ever speaks like this, or could bear someone speaking like this? Suppose someone, as they say, by his own effort has discovered some truth in physics, mathematics or medicine, and has communicated it to many others; he will nevertheless be said to be the only one who knows it, and the rest will be able to deny that they have that truth, even though they have grasped it from another who revealed it, by understanding, of course, that limitation. A sworn witness will be able to deny that he knows what he really knows, or anyone at all will be able to deny that he has done what he really has done, by understanding "from himself." And so a wide door will be opened to lies. What is more, if this limitation and the opinion of our adversaries were admitted, then just as true as this proposition, "You alone know the hearts of men," would be these: "Christ does not know the hearts of men," "Christ has not come into the world," "Christ will not judge the living and the dead," and so on. It is remarkable if our adversaries are not ashamed of this limitation of theirs. So, setting aside what could be added, I shall go on to the second answer.

units.la: IV. Non esse propositionem, tu solus nosti corda hominum, restringendam ad tempus quo loquebatur Salomon, aut V.T. ex eo intelligitur, quod ea dogma est; dogmata autem sunt perpetuae veritatis: continet enim diuini attributi diuinae proprietatis revelationem. Quoniam [?] autem Deus perpetuo idem est, nec potest vllo modo [?] mutari, eius attributa & proprietates nunquam mutantur. Itaque in illa propositione verbum nosti non adsignificat praesentis aut praeteriti temporis certam differentiam, vt solet in propositione contingente; sed, vt fit in necessaria, ab ea adsignificatione solutum est. Vera enim illa enunciatio, & ab omni aeternitate ad illud vsque tempus quo loquebatur Salomon, fuerat, & futura erat vsque ad tempora revelati Messiae; & quominus ad omnem vsque aeternitatem vera fore credatur ab Aduersarijs nihil impedit, praeter hunc ipsorum errorem, quem confutamus: Ac cum propositio, Tu solus nosti corda hominum resolui debeat in has duas, Tu nosti corda hominum, &, alius nullus novit corda hominum, quarum illa in Dei natura, haec in eius vnitate fundatur, cumq; illam constet necessariam esse ac perpetuae veritatis, idem etiam de hac judicandum est: alioquin erit eadem propositio, tu solus nosti corda hominum, necessaria & contingens, perpetuae & non perpetuae veritatis, cum tamen tota nitatur principijs seu fundamentis aeternis, essentia Dei & eius vnitate.
units.tr: IV. That the proposition "you alone know the hearts of men" is not to be restricted to the time when Solomon was speaking, or to the Old Testament, is shown by the fact that it is a dogma; and dogmas concern perpetual truth, for they contain the revelation of a divine attribute and divine property. Since God is always the same and cannot in any way be changed, his attributes and properties never change. Accordingly, in that proposition the verb "know" does not signify a definite difference of present or past time, as it usually does in a contingent proposition; rather, as in a necessary one, it is freed from that signification. For that true statement was true from all eternity up to the time when Solomon spoke, and was to remain true until the times of the revealed Messiah; and nothing prevents our adversaries from believing that it will be true to all eternity, except their own error, which we are refuting. And since the proposition "You alone know the hearts of men" must be resolved into these two: "You know the hearts of men," and "no other knows the hearts of men," of which the first is founded in the nature of God and the second in his unity, and since it is agreed that the first is necessary and of perpetual truth, the same must be judged of the second as well. Otherwise the same proposition, "you alone know the hearts of men," would be both necessary and contingent, of perpetual and non-perpetual truth, although it altogether rests on principles or foundations that are eternal: the essence of God and his unity.

units.la: V. Adde quod cur Deus perspecta habeat corda hominum duas solet Scriptura rationes afferre, unam ab eorum creatione, alteram à Dei immensitate, quia fecit cordahominum, & quia replet cœlum & terram, quæ duæ rationes omnium confessione propriæ sunt solius Dei. Ecquis verò legens ista Dei verba Ierem. 17. 9. Prauum est cor hominis & inscrutabile. Quis cognoscet illud? Ego Dominus scrutans cor, & probans renes &c, non intelligat, Deum sibi tribuere scrutationem cordium, tanquam attributum proprium, quo ab omnibus creaturis distinguitur? Cum ergo videamus hoc idem sibi Christum tribuere, & quidem ita emphaticè, ut magis non potuerit: (non enim dicit scient omnes Ecclesiæ ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐρευνῶ quod ego scrutor, sed, ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἐρευνῶν quod ego sum ille qui scrutor, ille scrutator) cur non inde concludimus, eum esse Deum, hoc est, præditum essentia divina, præsertim cum fateri necesse sit, eum habere perspecta atque explorata corda omnium, etiam illorum, qui adventum eius antecesserunt, ubicunque & quandocunque vixerint? Est enim omnium, quot quot unquam fuerunt, hominum Iudex, & quidem supremus.
units.tr: V. Add that Scripture usually gives two reasons why God has perfect knowledge of the hearts of men: one from their creation, the other from the immensity of God, "because he made the heart of man," and "because he fills heaven and earth." Both reasons are, by universal agreement, proper to God alone. Who, then, reading these words of God in Jeremiah 17:9, "The heart of man is deceitful and inscrutable. Who shall know it? I the Lord search the heart and prove the reins," etc., would not understand that God ascribes to himself the searching of hearts as a proper attribute by which he is distinguished from all creatures? Since, then, we see that Christ ascribes this same thing to himself, and indeed so emphatically that he could not have done so more, (for he does not say "all the churches shall know that I search" [ὅτι ἐγὼ ἐρευνῶ], but "that I am he who searches" [ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἐρευνῶν], that is, "I am that one, the searcher, the scrutiniser"), why should we not conclude from this that he is God, that is, endowed with the divine essence? This is especially so since one must confess that he has perfect and thoroughly examined knowledge of the hearts of all, including those who went before his coming, wherever and whenever they lived. For he is the judge of all men who have ever existed, and indeed the supreme judge.

units.la: VI. Afferrem hoc loco argumentum ab ipsa rei natura petitum; Mihi enim contradictio implicari videtur, si dicatur intellectus humanus vi sibi insita & propria omnium hominum corda scrutari, & cogitationes noscere, multòque difficilius id capio, quàm Deum patefactum fuisse in carne nostra, sibique in perpetuum naturam nostram univisse, in qua sese nobis præsentem exhiberet. Hoc enim nihil habet quod rationi repugnet, quodque non sit maximè & generi humano honorificum atque utile, & Scripturæ consentaneum. Illud verò est virtutem infinitam finitæ menti, hoc est, accidens infinitum subjecto finito attribuere, Sed eam rationem in alium locum differo. Nunc enim id unum ago, ut quæ sit Scripturæ de natura divina Domini nostri sententia exquiram & proferam in lucem. Quod cum à me fuerit Deo benefício perfectum, tunc eiusdem opera ostendam, cum in sententia Scripturæ & fide nostra nihil esse quod pugnet cum recta ratione, tum in errore Adversariorum quædam esse, quæ cum recta ratione conciliari non posse videantur.
units.tr: VI. I would bring forward at this point an argument drawn from the very nature of the thing. For it seems to me a contradiction to say that the human intellect, by a power implanted and proper to itself, can search the hearts of all men and know their thoughts; and I grasp this far less easily than that God was made manifest in our flesh, and united our nature to himself forever, in which he presented himself to us as present. For this contains nothing that is repugnant to reason, and it is most honourable and useful for the human race, and agreeable to Scripture. But to attribute infinite power to a finite mind, that is, to ascribe an infinite accident to a finite subject, is indeed a different matter, but I defer that reasoning to another place. For now I am doing only this one thing: to seek out and bring to light what Scripture's view of the divine nature of our Lord is. When, by God's blessing, I have completed this, I shall then show by his work that in the teaching of Scripture and in our faith there is nothing that conflicts with sound reason, whereas in the error of our adversaries there are some things which seem unable to be reconciled with sound reason.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA
units.tr: SECTION TWO

units.la: Locos Veteris Testamenti continens non lau- datos in Novo.
units.tr: Containing passages of the Old Testament that are not praised in the New.

units.la: DISPUTATIO VIGESIMA SECUNDA
units.tr: Disputation Twenty-Two

units.la: De Arg. XXII. Ex apparitione Dei quæ describitur Gen. cap. 18.
units.tr: On Argument XXII. From the appearance of God described in Genesis chapter 18.

units.la: I. QUONIAM Dominus noster universam Veteris Testamenti Scripturam partitus est in legem Mosis, Prophetas, & Psalmos, eundem ordinem sequemur in hac Sectione, exordiemurque à Mose, qui Gen. cap. 18. insignem quandam Dei apparitionem describit: Ex qua tribus modis argumentari possumus.
units.tr: I. Since our Lord divided the whole of the Scripture of the Old Testament into the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms, we shall follow the same order in this section, and begin with Moses, who in Genesis chapter 18 describes a remarkable appearance of God. From it we can argue in three ways.

units.la: II. Primò sic, Is qui eo loco dicitur apparuisse Abrahamo duobus angelis viris comitatus vocatur vir & Jehoua, seque gerit ut homo & ut Deus, habeturque ab Abrahamo pro homine & pro Deo. Ergo non est impossibile, nec repugnat Scripturæ, aut rectæ rationi, ut Deus appareat hominibus in natura humana, idemque dicatur Deus & homo, se gerat ut Deum & hominem, & à fidelibus habeatur pro vero Deo prædito essentia divina, & vero homine prædito essentia humana. Negari enim non potest, quin is, qui apparuit Abrahamo, verus homo fuerit. Nam & vir appellatur, & præ se ferebat figuram humanam, & ambulabat, pedes lavabat, edebat, loquebatur ut homo: & rursus negari nequit, quin verus Deus fuerit: sexies enim vel septies vocatur Jehoua, quinquies Adonai, loquiturque ut Judex mundi penes quem est suprema puniendi & parcendi potestas. Quid possunt Adversarii adversus unionem divinæ & humanæ naturæ in persona Christi afferre, quod non possit exemplo huius apparitionis Dei in humana forma refelli? Si Deus voluisset eiusmodi divinae & humanae naturae conjunctionem haberi pro absurda & impossibili, num illius tam illustre exemplum & specimen ostendisset in Scriptura ad instructionem & ædificationem Ecclesiæ usque ad finem seculorum?
units.tr: II. First, as follows. He who in that place is said to have appeared to Abraham, accompanied by two angels in the form of men, is called a man and Jehovah, and he conducts himself both as a man and as God, and Abraham regarded him both as a man and as God. It is therefore not impossible, nor contrary to Scripture or to sound reason, that God should appear to men in human nature, and that the same person should be called God and man, should conduct himself as God and as man, and should be held by the faithful to be the true God endowed with the divine essence and a true man endowed with the human essence. For it cannot be denied that he who appeared to Abraham was a true man. He is called a man, he presented the figure of a man, he walked, washed his feet, ate, and spoke as a man. And again, it cannot be denied that he was the true God: he is called Jehovah six or seven times, Adonai five times, and he speaks as the Judge of the world, in whose power lies the supreme authority to punish and to spare. What can the adversaries bring against the union of the divine and human natures in the person of Christ that cannot be refuted by the example of this appearance of God in human form? If God had wished such a union of the divine and human natures to be regarded as absurd and impossible, would he have shown so illustrious an example and pattern of it in Scripture, for the instruction and edification of the Church until the end of the ages?

units.la: III. Frustrà reponent verisimile non esse, Deum eo tempore sibi naturam humanam personaliter uniuisse, modò enim simpliciter, &, ut sapientiam quæ supernè est decet, ἀδιαιρέτως [?] confiteantur Christum Deum & hominem, divina & humana natura prædictum esse, id nobis nunc quidem sufficit. Certè divinæ & humanæ naturæ personalis unio clarius & melius repræsentari non potuit. Idem enim & Deus & vir appellatur, & præsefert cum proprietates & infirmitates humanas, mouetur enim loco, ambulat, edit, bibit, pedes abluit, loquitur, videtur, tum proprietates divinas, cogitationum cordis & rerum futurarum cognitionem infallibilem, iudicandi atque adeo puniendi & parcendi autoritatem summam, &c. Erat igitur quâ Deus seu Iehoua ab æterno, quâ homo in tempore, quâ Deus etiam in cœlo, qua homo in terra tantùm, qua Deus infinitus, qua homo finitus, qua Deus creator, qua homo creatura. Si sic Deus naturam humanam assumpsit ad tempus, cur non potuit eam assumere in perpetuum? Si in gratiam Abrahæ & Saræ, cur non in gratiam totius Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: III. They will vainly reply that it is not probable that God at that time personally united human nature to himself. For now it is enough for us that they simply confess, and as the wisdom which is from above requires, indivisibly [ἀδιαιρέτως], that Christ is God and man, endowed with the divine and the human nature. Certainly the personal union of the divine and human natures could not have been represented more clearly and better. For he is called both God and man, and he presents both human properties and infirmities (he moves from place to place, walks, eats, drinks, washes his feet, speaks, is seen) and divine properties (knowledge of the thoughts of the heart and an infallible knowledge of future things, and the supreme authority to judge and therefore to punish and to spare, etc.). He was therefore God, or Jehovah, from eternity in one respect, and man in time in another; God in heaven in one respect, man only on earth in another; infinite as God, finite as man; creator as God, creature as man. If God assumed human nature for a time, why could he not have assumed it forever? If for the sake of Abraham and Sarah, why not for the sake of the whole Church?

units.la: IV. Secundò sic argumentor. Si apparitio illa Iehouæ in carne humana specimen fuit adventus & convictus Christi cum hominibus, certè qualem sese ille qui tunc apparuit ostendit, talem Christum esse oportuit. Ille autem sese ostendit tanquam Deum Iehouam & hominem. Christum igitur esse Deum seu Iehouam & hominem oportuit. Quale enim est specimen, tale debet esse id cuius est specimen. Fuisse autem illam apparitionem specimen adventus & convictus Christi cum hominibus, probatur, primò testimonio ipsius Christi Ioh. 8. 56. Abraham Pater vester exultavit ut videret diem meum, & vidit & gavisus est. Quomodo vidit diem Christi, si ei non est eius aliquod specimen ostensum? nulla autem visio seu apparitio ei est indulta diei Christi similior quam ista. Est igitur hæc apparitio specimen & ut ita dicam, prælusio revelationis seu adventus Christi in carne. Hoc ipsum eodem illo cap. jam Christus insinuauerat V. 39. & 40. Si filij Abrahæ essetis, opera Abrahæ faceretis. Nunc autem queritis me interficere hominem, qui veritatem vobis loquutus sum, quam audiui à Deo. Hoc Abraham non fecit. Hominem enim illum, quem cum alijs duobus hospitio exceperat, se pro Deo gerentem non voluit interficere ut blasphemum, sed reuerenter allocutus est ut Deum.
units.tr: IV. Secondly, I argue as follows. If that appearance of Jehovah in human flesh was a pattern of the coming and the converse of Christ with men, then certainly Christ had to be such as he who then appeared showed himself to be. But he showed himself as Jehovah God and as man. Christ therefore had to be God, or Jehovah, and man. For such as a pattern is, such must be that of which it is the pattern. That this appearance was a pattern of the coming and converse of Christ with men is proved, first, by the testimony of Christ himself, John 8. 56: Abraham your father rejoiced to see my day, and he saw it and was glad. How did he see Christ's day, unless some image of it had been shown to him? Now no vision or appearance granted to him was more like the day of Christ than this one. This appearance is therefore a pattern and, as I may say, a prelude of the revelation or coming of Christ in the flesh. Christ had already hinted at this in the same chapter, verses 39 and 40: If you were the children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth, which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this. For the man whom Abraham received into his hospitality, along with two others, and who called himself God, Abraham did not wish to kill as a blasphemer, but addressed him reverently as God.

units.la: V. Ad Christi testimonium accedit, quod sine dubio destructio Sodomeorum specimen fuit destructionis impiorum per ignem judicij extremi. Id Christus innuit Luc. 17. 28. Similiter etiam ut accidit in diebus Lot. edebant, bibebant, emebant, vendebant, plantabant, edificabant. Quo autem die Lot exiit Sodomis pluit ignem & sulphur, & omnes perdidit. Secundum hac erit dies, qua Filius hominis revelabitur. Et Judas V[?]. 7. Sicut Sodoma & Gomorrha & his finitimae civitates simili modo atque illae scortatae, & carnem alteram sectatae, propositae sunt exemplo, ignis aeterni poenam sustinentes. Hinc Dauid psal. xi. 6. pluet super impios laqueos, ignem & sulphur, &c. Quod si destructio Sodomae & Gomorrhae specimen fuit destructionis mundi, fatendum est Abrahamo ostensum fuisse specimen quoddam utriusque adventus Christi. Primo venit Christus ad semen Abrahae, cum eo ad breve tempus conuixit, ei promissionem jamjamque impletum iri annunciauit, clementiam admirabilem ostendit, Judicium futurum praedixit, ad quod exercendum professus est se descensurum; tum se subduxit ex oculis hominum, misitque nuntios suos atque legatos in mundum praecipuè in magnam illam civitatem, quae vocatur spiritualiter Sodoma & Ægyptus, qui dicerent Seruamini ex generatione ista prava, in promptu habentes quo vindicent omnem inobedientiam, postquam impleta fuerit electorum obedientia. Tandemque ipse nocte elapsa die illo magno mane veniet, mundumque impiorum igne destruet. Haec tanta similitudo non obscurè testatur, specimen quoddam seu exemplum utriusque adventus Christi memorabili illa apparitione contineri: ac proinde talem oportuisse Christum reuera esse, qualem ille, qui apparuit, se exhibuit. Id quod ipsa experientia confirmat. Ut enim ille vir appellatur, seque hominem fuisse figura externa & actionibus probauit; sic Christus homo dicitur, & se hominem verè fuisse multis rebus docuit: ut ille se mundi judicem esse professus est, sic itidem Christus. Ut ille Deus vocatur, sic Christus dicitur Deus. Quid est igitur, quamobrem non existimemus, quàm ille Jehoua nominatur, tam Christum eodem nomine insigniri?
units.tr: V. To the testimony of Christ is added that the destruction of the Sodomites was without doubt a pattern of the destruction of the wicked by the fire of the last judgment. Christ hints at this in Luke 17. 28: Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot, they ate, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they built. But on the day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all. Even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man is revealed. And Jude 7: Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them, in like manner giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire. Hence David, Psalm 11. 6: Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone, etc. If the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah was a pattern of the destruction of the world, we must confess that a certain pattern of both comings of Christ was shown to Abraham. At first Christ came to the seed of Abraham; he lived with them for a short time; he announced to them that the promise was about to be fulfilled at once; he showed admirable mercy; he foretold the future judgment, for the carrying out of which he professed that he would come down. Then he withdrew from the eyes of men, and sent his messengers and legates into the world, especially into that great city which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, to say Save yourselves from this untoward generation, having ready at hand the means to punish every disobedience once the obedience of the elect has been completed. And at last, when the night has passed, he will come on that great morning and destroy the world of the wicked with fire. This great likeness clearly witnesses that a certain pattern or example of both comings of Christ was contained in that memorable appearance; and accordingly Christ had to be in truth such as he who appeared showed himself to be. This is confirmed by experience itself. For just as that man is called a man, and proved himself to be a man by his outward form and actions, so Christ is called man, and by many things showed that he was truly man. As that one professed himself to be the judge of the world, so too Christ. As that one is called God, so Christ is called God. Why, then, should we not think that he who is named Jehovah is marked with the same name as Christ?

units.la: VI. Tertiò denique sic possum argumentari. Qui apparuit Abrahamo Gen. 18. is fuit prædītus essentia diuina. Christus est ille qui apparuit Abrahamo Gen. 18. Christus igitur est prædītus essentia diuina. Major sic probatur. Iehoua est prædītus essentia diuina. Ille qui apparuit Abrahamo Gen. 18. fuit Iehoua. Ille igitur qui apparuit Abrahamo fuit prædītus essentia diuina. Vocatur enim, vt dixi, septies Iehoua, nomen omnium confessione Dei Israelis maximè proprium: vocatur aliquoties Adonai, quod etiam nomen est vnius illius Dei: dicitur judex totius terræ, quod elogium nisi vniilli Deo conueniebat nemini.
units.tr: VI. Thirdly and finally, I can argue as follows. He who appeared to Abraham in Genesis 18 was endowed with the divine essence. Christ is he who appeared to Abraham in Genesis 18. Christ therefore is endowed with the divine essence. The major premise is proved thus: Jehovah is endowed with the divine essence; he who appeared to Abraham in Genesis 18 was Jehovah. He who appeared to Abraham was therefore endowed with the divine essence. For, as I have said, he is called Jehovah seven times, a name which by the confession of all is most proper to the God of Israel; he is called Adonai several times, which is also the name of that one God; and he is called the judge of all the earth, an attribute which belongs to no one but that one God.

units.la: VII. Minor ex eo probatur quod 1. hic qui apparuit Abrahæ dicitur Iudex vniuersæ terræ V.[?] 25. Solus autem Christus est Iudex vniuersæ terræ. 2. dicitur etiam homo. Nullus autem homo iudicat vniuersam terram præter vnum Christum. 3. Is fuit aut Deus Pater, aut Angelus creatus, aut Filius Dei. Non enim Aduersarij dicent fuisse Spiritum Sanctum, quemadmodum[?] personam quidem fuisse autumant. Atqui non fuit Deus Pater. Primùm enim Deus Pater nunquam venit aut apparuit immediatè seu, vt loquuntur, in propria persona, ne tum quidem cum, aut annuncianda fuit beatæ Virgini conceptio & natiuitas Christi, aut seruandum genus humanum. Quis ergo credat eum venisse in propria persona vt annunciaret instantem Isaaci conceptionem, deque Sodomæ exitio cum Abrahamo colloqueretur? Deinde quorsum Deus Pater pransus fuisset apud Abrahamum, ijsque rebus se verum fuisse hominem docuisset, quibus Christus post resurrectionem suam se verum esse hominem confirmauit. Huius enim rei tam inusitatæ & memorabilis nullus vsus apparet. Sed nihil opus est pluribus id refellere, quod aduersarij neque dicunt, neque seruatis hypothesibus suis de Dei natura loco & motu dicere possunt.
units.tr: VII. The minor premise is proved from the fact that (1) he who appeared to Abraham is called the judge of the whole earth, Gen. 18. v. 25. But Christ alone is the judge of the whole earth. (2) He is also called a man. But no man judges the whole earth except the one Christ. (3) He was either God the Father, or a created angel, or the Son of God. For the adversaries will not say that it was the Holy Spirit, though they assert that it was a person. But he was not God the Father. For God the Father never came or appeared immediately, or, as they say, in his own person, not even when the conception and birth of Christ were to be announced to the blessed Virgin, or when the human race was to be saved. Who then could believe that he came in his own person to announce the imminent conception of Isaac, and to speak with Abraham about the destruction of Sodom? Further, why would God the Father have dined with Abraham, and shown by these things that he was a true man, as Christ after his resurrection confirmed that he was a true man? For no use of so unusual and memorable a thing appears. But there is no need to refute this at greater length, since the adversaries neither say it, nor, keeping to their own hypotheses about the nature of God, can say it, with regard to place and motion.

units.la: VIII. Num ergo fuit Angelus? affirmant quidem Socinus Crellius & VVolkelius. Quo autore, aut teste? Nullo prorsus. Id enim Scriptura nusquam dicit. Vtris igitur potius credendum, nobis qui Deum fuisse dicimus, & probamus testimonio Scripturæ eum plusquam septies Iehouam appellantis, an verò Aduersarijs qui Angelum fuisse volunt, neque locum vllum proferre possunt vbi angelus appelletur? At duo eius comites vocantur angeli Gen. 19. 1. 15. funto igitur illi angeli, quia angeli dicuntur: Hic vero qui nunquam angelus, sed tam sæpe Iehoua nominatur, habeatur pro Deo, non pro angelo.
units.tr: VIII. Was he then an angel? Socinus, Crellius and Volkelius do affirm this. On whose authority or testimony? On none at all, for Scripture nowhere says so. Which side, then, should we rather believe: we, who say that he was God and prove it from the testimony of Scripture, which calls him Jehovah more than seven times; or our opponents, who want him to be an angel but cannot produce a single passage where he is called an angel? Two of his companions are called angels (Gen. 19. 1, 15). Let those be angels, since they are called angels. But this one, who is never called an angel and is so often named Jehovah, should be held to be God, not an angel.

units.la: IX. At, inquit Crellius, aliud D. Auctor Epistolæ ad Hebr. docet. Is hospitalitatem commendaturus, quosdam, ait, insciós eius virtutis beneficio excepisse hospitio Angelos. Ad hanc autem de Abrahamo, & qua de Lotho subjicitur, historiam eum respicere, prater tem ipsam, arguunt Scriptura loca, quæ in ora sacri codicis vulgò solent adjci. Quod si Deus ipsemet tunc adfuisset; ad laudem hospitalitatis tanto maiorem dicturus potius fuisset scriptor divinus, quosdam per eam Deum ipsum hospitio excepisse. Fallacia est à non causa pro causa. Quisquis enim ille fuerit quem Abrahamus hospitio excepit, nihil prohibuit Apostolum congruenter loqui Scripturæ, quæ eum non Angelum, sed Deum, immò Iehouam sæpius appellauit. Cur igitur id non fecit, si faciebat magis ad scopum? Cur etiam ille toties Iehoua appellatur, cur non secus ac Deu[?]ipse loquitur, cur Iudex totius terræ dicitur cur eum tanquam Deum Abrahamus alloquitur, si nec Deus fuit, nec pro Deo haberi aut potuit, aut debuit? Non igitur illa causa fuit quam reddit Crellius, cur Deum ipsum sacer autor non dixerit hospitio fuisse exceptum, sed ista potius, quia nimirum voluit prudenter ratiocinari. Non videtur autem ratiocinari prudenter, qui aliquos ad certum officium hortatur argumento inde ducto, quòd id officij facientibus ingens quoddam bonum olim euenerit, si tale bonum palam est eis quos hortatur, ut ut hortanti pareant, neque euenturum esse vnquam, neque euenire posse. Iam autem, certum est contingere amplius non posse, ut Deus ipse hospitio excipiatur: Pater enim extra Christum hominibus ostendi aut non potest, aut non debet, teste ipso Christo Ioh. 14. 9. Filius vero vetat admodum accuratè Matth. 24. 5. 23. 26. dicenti, ego sum Christus, aut dicentibus, Ecce hic est Christus, aut illic, credere, addita hac ratione, quod non sit venturus, nisi adeò splendidus & illustris, ut nemo eum non videat. Ad Spiritum autem sanctum quod attinet, is non venit nisi inuisibiliter in corda fidelium. Quapropter noluit Apostolus vllam ipsius Dei hospitio excipiendi spem Christianis ostendere. Angelorum ratio est dispar: Apparuerunt enim in figura humana mulieribus Marc 16. 5. Luc. 24. 4. Apostolis Act. 1. 10. Cornelio Act. 10. 3. Petro Act. 12. 7. aliisque nonnullis, si fides habenda est historijs non sacris, constat atque, tum omnes esse administratorios spiritus, qui in ministerium emittuntur propter eos qui futuri sunt haeredes salutis, tum eos mittendos esse à Christo, ut colligant de regno eius scandala, & eos qui faciunt iniquitatem, necnon congregent electos.
units.tr: IX. But, says Crellius, the holy author of the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches. He, wishing to commend hospitality, says that some, unaware of its virtue, received angels as guests by the benefit of that hospitality. That this refers to the story of Abraham, and to the story of Lot that follows it, is shown by the passages of Scripture which are commonly added in the margins of the sacred codex, apart from the story itself. But if God himself had been present on that occasion, the divine writer would rather have said, to the far greater praise of hospitality, that some had received God himself as their guest. This is a fallacy of non causa pro causa. Whoever he was whom Abraham received as a guest, nothing prevented the Apostle from speaking in keeping with Scripture, which calls him not an angel but God, indeed Jehovah, very often. Why then did he not do so, if it would have served his purpose better? Why is he so often called Jehovah, why does he speak just as God does, why is he called the Judge of all the earth, why does Abraham address him as God, if he was not God and could not or ought not to be regarded as God? So the reason Crellius gives, why the sacred author did not say that God himself had been received as a guest, is not the true one; rather, the author wished to reason prudently. But he does not reason prudently who urges some people to a certain duty by an argument drawn from the fact that a great good once came to those who performed that duty, when it is plain to those whom he urges that such a good will never happen again and cannot happen, even though they obey the one urging them. Now it is certain that God himself cannot be received as a guest again: the Father cannot, or ought not, be shown to men apart from Christ, as Christ himself testifies (John 14. 9). The Son, indeed, most carefully forbids believing those who say, "I am Christ," or who say, "Behold, here is Christ, or there" (Matt. 24. 5, 23, 26), adding the reason that he will not come unless so splendid and illustrious that no one can fail to see him. As for the Holy Spirit, he comes only invisibly into the hearts of believers. Therefore the Apostle did not wish to hold out to Christians any hope of receiving God himself as a guest. The case of the angels is different. They appeared in human form to women (Mark 16. 5; Luke 24. 4), to the Apostles (Acts 1. 10), to Cornelius (Acts 10. 3), to Peter (Acts 12. 7), and to some others, if non-sacred histories are to be believed. It is also clear that all of them are ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who are to be heirs of salvation, and that they are to be sent by Christ to gather out of his kingdom all the stumbling-blocks and those who do iniquity, and to gather the elect.

units.la: X. Objiciet forte aliquis, Si quia is qui apparuit Deus & homo vocatur, Christum oportuit simul Deum & hominem esse, consequens esse, ut quia illius ministri Angeli & homines appellantur, etiam Christi ministri esse debuerint simul Angeli & homines, ac proinde si Deus incarnari debuit, etiam Angelos incarnari debuisse. Respondeo, Angelum nomen esse officij, quod de hominibus in utroque testamento usurpatur non infrequenter, itaque posse eundem esse natura hominem & munere Angelum, ut patet exemplo Iohannis Baptistae, qui Angelus Dei appellatur Malach. 3. 1. & Matth. 11. 10. Iehovam vero non esse nomen officij seu muneris: itaque non posse eundem Iehovam & hominem esse, nisi qui sit divina & humana natura praeditus. Adde quod non venit Filius, deinde Pater, sed venerunt ministri Christi homines, deinde venturi sunt tandem ultimo die, aut circa ultimum diem Angeli; cuius rei confusum quoddam specimen in historia Gen. 18. & 19. offensum Ecclesiæ est.
units.tr: X. Someone may perhaps object: if he who appeared is called God and man, Christ had to be at once God and man; it follows that, since his ministers are called angels and men, the ministers of Christ too ought at once to be angels and men; and accordingly, if God had to be made flesh, the angels too ought to have been made flesh. I answer that "angel" is the name of an office, which is applied not infrequently to men in both Testaments. So the same person may be an angel by office and a man by nature, as is clear from the example of John the Baptist, who is called the angel of God (Mal. 3. 1; Matt. 11. 10). But Jehovah is not the name of an office or function; so the same person cannot be Jehovah and man unless he is endowed with both divine and human nature. Add that the Son did not come, then the Father; rather, the ministers of Christ, who were men, came, and afterwards angels are to come at the last day, or about the last day. Some confused image of this was perceived by the Church in the story of Genesis 18 and 19.

units.la: XI. At, inquit Crellius, is ipse, qui nomen Iehova, cum Mose colloquens sibi imposuit, eoque tam frequenter in ea sermocinatione insignitur, Angelus fuit. De hoc videbimus disputatione sequente. Interim dico duo: unum, Hunc qui Abrahamo apparuit non vocari Angelum: Alterum, etiam Christum Angelum dici Malach. 3. 1. Apoc. 8. 3. &c. nec mirum, Est enim Angelus proprie nuncius.
units.tr: XI. But, says Crellius, he who gave himself the name Jehovah when speaking with Moses, and is so frequently designated by it in that discourse, was an angel. We shall look into this in the following disputation. Meanwhile I say two things: first, that the one who appeared to Abraham is not called an angel; second, that Christ too is called an angel (Mal. 3. 1; Rev. 8. 3, etc.), and this is no wonder, for an angel is properly a messenger.
