units.la: DISPVTATIO VIGESIMA TERTIA
units.tr: DISPUTATION TWENTY-THREE

units.la: De Arg. XXIII. Ex Gen. 31. 11. 13. Exod. 3. 2. 6. aliisque locis similibus, in quibus An- gelus se Deum esse profitetur, aut Deus appellatur.
units.tr: On Argument XXIII: from Genesis 31:11, 13, Exodus 3:2, 6 and other similar places, in which the Angel professes himself to be God, or is called God.

units.la: I. NUNC de illo Angelo consideremus, qui dicit Iacobo Gen. 31. 11. Ego sum Deus Bethel, ubi vouisti votum mihi: & Mosi Exod. 3. 6. Ego sum Deus Patris tui, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, & Deus Iacob, & alijs multis locis, vel profitetur se Deum esse, vel Dominus seu Iehouah appellatur. Aut enim officio, aut natura Angelus fuit. Si officio tantùm, sine dubio Deus fuit praeditus essentia diuina. Tamen Deus Pater non fuit. Deus enim Pater dici non potest Angelus Dei. Fuit igitur Filius Dei. Nam Spiritus Sanctus non fuit: Hunc enim contendunt Aduersarij nec personam esse, nec Deum dici in sacris literis: quod vtrumque quidem falsum est, Sed tamen Spiritus Sanctus non apparet extrinsecus corpori, sed illabitur intrinsecus cordi, seque potius habet vt facultas interna, quàm vt objectum externum.
units.tr: I. Now let us consider that Angel who says to Jacob, Gen. 31:11, I am the God of Bethel, where you vowed a vow to me, and to Moses, Exod. 3:6, I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, and in many other places either professes himself to be God or is called the Lord, or Jehovah. For the Angel was either such by office or by nature. If by office only, then without doubt he was God endowed with the divine essence. Yet he was not God the Father, for God the Father cannot be called the Angel of God. Therefore he was the Son of God. For he was not the Holy Spirit: our opponents contend that the Holy Spirit is neither a person nor called God in the sacred writings. Both claims are certainly false. Yet the Holy Spirit does not appear outwardly to the body, but glides inwardly into the heart, and stands rather as an inner faculty than as an external object.

units.la: II. Si natura sua Angelus fuit, vt affirmant Aduersarij quomodo tam clare, tam diserte, tam saepe clamauit se Deum esse, Iehouam, Deum Abrahami Isaaci & Iacobi, hoc est, illum Deum praeter quem alius nullus est Deus? Quomodo e monte Sinai tanta cum Majestate legem ferens pronunciauit, Ego sum Iehoua Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de Terra Ægypti, &c? Quomodo se vnum pro Deo haberi & coli jussit, alium verò neminem? Quomodo dicit Auctor Ep. ad Heb. Christo praestantiora quàm cuiquam Angelorum tributa esse in Scriptura nomina, si vnus aliquis Angelus appellatus est Iehoua tam saepè tamque diserte? Quid quod Christus ipse testis est, Deum fuisse qui dixit Mosi, Ego sum Deus Abraham, &c.
units.tr: II. If he was an Angel by nature, as our opponents affirm, how is it that he so clearly, so expressly and so often cried out that he was God, Jehovah, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, that is, that God besides whom there is no other God? How, bringing the law down from Mount Sinai with such majesty, did he pronounce, I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, and so on? How did he command that he alone be held and worshipped as God, and no one else? How does the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews say that the names given in Scripture to Christ are more excellent than those given to any of the Angels, if some one Angel was so often and so expressly called Jehovah? What of the fact that Christ himself bears witness that it was God who said to Moses, I am the God of Abraham, and so on?

units.la: III. Respondet Crellius, illum Angelum alienam personam ac nomen assumpsisse, Deo ita volente, ut tanto plus auctoritatis habe-ret res & oratio, & in auditorum animos altius ascenderet, ad-ditque in dramatibus similia quodammodo cerni. In iis enim, inquit, alter alterius personam ita sustinet, ut res non referri, sed geri vi-deatur, quanquam illic, ad delectationem spectantium, & in rebus saepe minime seriis: illic ad utilitatem audientium, ac in rebus ma-xime seriis: &, quod discrimen hic maximè attendendum est, Angeli Dei personam ita sustinent, ut eius auctoritatem simul habeant: longe secus quàm in dramatibus contingit. Prudenter hoc discrimen, ne sibi objiceretur, observavit. Sed sunt alia. Primùm enim in dramate omnes actores sunt per-sonati, omnes alienas personas agunt. Hic secus res habet. Solus enim iste Angelus fuisset per-sonatus, reliqui quibuscum loquebatur & agebat suas ipsi proprias personas sustinebant, id quod non videtur ullo modo Dei sapientiae fuisse consentaneum: Fateor equidem omnia, aut fere omnia, typica fuisse: nam & Iacobus, & Moses, & populus Israëliticus, & mons Sinai, & legis è monte Sinai promulgatio, & tabulis lapideis inscriptio, & desertum, & tabernaculum, & reliqua fere omnia typi fuere. Sed typi suas agebant proprias partes, non autem alienas earum scilicet rerum, quarum erant typi. Deinde in dramate qui Regis nomen & personam assumit non dicitur Regis legatus aut nuncius: sunt enim oppositae personae Regis & legati Regis. Si igitur similiter pugnant Angeli Dei, & Dei personae, qui fit ut dicatur Angelus Dei sic loquutus, Ego sum Deus &c, Ego sum Iehova &c? Sic enim quaedam quasi contradictio lectori objicitur. Non enim (ut bene observavit Crellius) solent eandem rationem principum personas assumendi, ac loquendi formam servare legati. Praeterea in dramate res ipsa non geritur, sed iam gestę imago effingitur: itaque veritas non est, sed fabula veritatis aemula. Scriptura vero ipsius veritatis seu rei gestae simplex est historia, quae nihil habet cum fabula commune. Quod si Angelus Dei nomen & personam assumit, ut tanto plus auctoritatis habeat res & oratio, qui factum est ut eodem loco, quo se Deum esse clamat, dicatur Angelus Dei? Sic enim non modo minuitur auctoritas, sed speciem quandam mendacij prae se fert oratio, siquidem non potest idem simul & officio Angelus, & natura Deus esse. Hinc apparet, Angelum, cum dicit, Ego sum Deus Abrahami &c, aut, Ego sum Dominus, Iehova, non loqui vt decet merum Dei angelum, hoc est, nuncium seu legatum (nunquam enim nuncius se illum ipsum dicit esse cuius est nuncius) nec tanquam si drama aut fabula ageretur: caetera enim fabulae non conuenient, sed repugnant potius.
units.tr: III. Crellius replies that that Angel assumed a foreign person and name, God so willing, so that the matter and the speech might have so much more authority and rise higher into the minds of the hearers; and he adds that in dramas something similar is in some way seen. For in them, he says, one actor so sustains the person of another that the matter seems not to be related but to be done, although there it is for the delight of the spectators and often in matters far from serious, but here it is for the benefit of the hearers and in the most serious matters; and, which distinction must be especially attended to here, the Angels of God so sustain the person of God that they at the same time have his authority: far otherwise than happens in dramas. He has wisely observed this distinction, so that it might not be objected to him. But there are other points. For first, in a drama all the actors are masked; all play foreign persons. Here it is otherwise. For only that Angel would have been masked, while the rest with whom he spoke and acted sustained their own proper persons, which does not seem in any way to have agreed with the wisdom of God. I grant indeed that all, or nearly all, things were typical: for both Jacob, and Moses, and the people of Israel, and Mount Sinai, and the promulgation of the law from Mount Sinai, and its inscription on stone tablets, and the desert, and the tabernacle, and almost all the rest were types. But types performed their own proper parts, not foreign ones, namely of those things of which they were types. Next, in a drama, one who assumes the name and person of a King is not called the King's envoy or messenger: for the persons of the King and of the King's envoy are set in opposition. If, then, the Angels of God and the person of God are similarly opposed, how does it come about that the Angel of God is said to have spoken thus, I am God, etc., I am Jehovah, etc.? For thus a kind of contradiction is put before the reader. For (as Crellius rightly observed) envoys do not usually keep the same manner of assuming the persons of princes and of speaking. Moreover, in a drama the thing itself is not done, but an image of what has been done is fashioned; and so it is not the truth but a fable rivalling the truth. But Scripture is the plain history of the truth itself, or of the deed done, and has nothing in common with fable. And if the Angel of God assumed the name and person so that the matter and the speech might have more authority, how does it happen that in the very place where he cries out that he is God, he is called the Angel of God? For thus not only is authority diminished, but the speech presents a certain appearance of falsehood, since the same being cannot at once be an Angel by office and God by nature. Hence it is clear that the Angel, when he says, I am the God of Abraham, etc., or I am the Lord, Jehovah, does not speak as befits a mere angel of God, that is, a messenger or envoy (for a messenger never says that he is that very one whose messenger he is), nor as if a drama or a fable were being performed: for the rest of the fable would not agree, but rather would conflict.

units.la: IV. At, inquit Crellius, eum, qui Mosi apparuit in rubo & dixit Ego sum Deus patris tui &c eum, qui e monte Sinai tanta cum maiestate legem ferens pronunciauit, Ego sum Iehova Deus tuus, qui eduxi te de terra Ægypti, & quae sequuntur, qui in tota illa historia passim Iehova appellatur à Mose, angelum fuisse, testis est Stephanus Act. 7. 53. testis Paulus Gal. 3. 19. testis diuinus ad Hebræos scriptor Heb. 2. 2. Hi namque omnes uno affirmant ore, per angelos dispositam, seu latam pronunciatamque Legem. Et Auctor quidem diuinus Epistolæ ad Hebræos eo argumento Euangelium præfert Legi, quod hac per Angelos, illud per Dominum nempe Christum, quem angelis longè præstantiorem esse factum prolixè docuerat, primò fuerit promulgatum. Quò respicit etiam Paulus, Colossenses monens, ne à Christo ad mundi rudimenta relabantur quæ in Lege Mosaica continentur: & estis, inquit, in ipso (Christo) impleti, qui est caput omnis principatus & potestatis, quasi dicat, si quis forte cogitet, Legem per angelos, & quidem principes, esse latam, gloriosum esse, ab illis diuina voluntatis notitia imbutum censeri; Longè gloriosius est, vos per eum, qui omnium illorum principum ac potestatum caput est ac dominus, diuina voluntatis notitiam fuisse consecutos, eamque plenam & perfectam, non, vt sub lege, imperfectam. Hæc transcripsi, non quo refutem, sunt enim si bene accipiantur vera, sed vt conciliem cum mea sententia. Fateor enim angeli alicuius operam adhibitam fuisse, cum ad visibiles illas formas efficiendas, quæ sunt oculis Mosis & populi Israelitici obversatæ, tum ad sonum illum edendum & articulandum, quo verba illa prolata sunt, Ego sum Iehova, &c. Sed quæritur quo modo Angelus creatus sic loqui potuit, Ego sum Iehova &c. Ego sum Deus Abrahæ &c. Aduersarij aiunt eum sic loqui quia sustinet Dei personam vt fit in drama te, & quia est Dei nuncius vel legatus. Hoc jam refutaui. Addoque in Nouo testamento missos à Deo angelos non assumere nomen & personam Dei ; Itemque Christum præstantissimum legatum Patris, nunquam sibi Patris nomen sumere. Immò negant Aduersarij eum vocatum fuisse vllo in loco Scripturæ Iehouam, cum tamen affirment, eum, & Dei personam perfectissima ratione sustinuisse, & qui passim Iehoua appellatur à Mose, angelum fuisse.Reddant igitur, quæso, rationem, cur passim Angelus se Deum esse profiteatur, & vocetur Iehoua, Christus verò, quem aiunt perfectiore ratione Dei Patris personam sustinuisse, nunquam se profiteatur esse Deum Patrem ?
units.tr: IV. But, says Crellius, that he who appeared to Moses in the bush and said I am the God of your father, etc., that he who from Mount Sinai, bringing the law with such majesty, pronounced, I am Jehovah your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and what follows, who throughout that whole history is everywhere called Jehovah by Moses, was an angel, is witnessed by Stephen, Acts 7:53; witnessed by Paul, Gal. 3:19; witnessed by the divine writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews, Heb. 2:2. For all of them with one voice affirm that the Law was arranged, or rather proclaimed, through angels. And indeed the divine author of the Epistle to the Hebrews prefers the Gospel to the Law on this ground, that the Law was first promulgated through Angels, the Gospel through the Lord, namely Christ, whom he had at length taught to have been made far more excellent than the Angels. To this also Paul looks when he warns the Colossians not to fall back from Christ to the rudiments of the world, which are contained in the Mosaic Law; and, he says, you are filled in him (Christ), who is the head of every principality and power, as if to say: if anyone perhaps thinks that the Law was given through angels, and indeed princely angels, and that it is glorious to be imbued with knowledge of the divine will by them, it is far more glorious that you have obtained knowledge of the divine will through him who is the head and lord of all those princes and powers, and that knowledge full and perfect, not imperfect as under the law. I have transcribed these things, not because I refute them (for they are true if rightly understood), but in order to reconcile them with my own opinion. For I grant that the work of some angel was employed, both in producing those visible forms which presented themselves to the eyes of Moses and of the people of Israel, and in producing and articulating that sound by which those words were uttered, I am Jehovah, etc. But the question is how a created Angel could speak thus, I am Jehovah, etc. I am the God of Abraham, etc. Our opponents say that he speaks thus because he sustains the person of God as happens in a drama, and because he is God's messenger or envoy. This I have already refuted. I add that in the New Testament the Angels sent by God do not assume the name and person of God; and likewise that Christ, the most excellent envoy of the Father, never assumes the Father's name for himself. Indeed our opponents deny that he was called Jehovah in any place of Scripture, although they affirm both that he sustained the person of God in the most perfect manner, and that he who is everywhere called Jehovah by Moses was an angel. Let them therefore give, I ask, the reason why the Angel everywhere professes himself to be God and is called Jehovah, while Christ, who they say sustained the person of God the Father in a more perfect manner, never professes himself to be God the Father?

units.la: V. Vt igitur eadem opera simul & respondeamus & argumentemur, Angelus creatus (vnus an plures fuerint, nihil refert.) cuius opera Lex è monte Sinai promulgata est, vel Iehoua dicitur seque esse Iehouam profitetur, vel non. Si prius: Necesse est vt à se & ab alijs Iehoua, Deus Abrahami Isaaci & Iacobi &c dicatur non proprie, sed figurate: Proprie enim Deus non fuit, sed Dei creatura & minister. Nemo enim, opinor, dicet Deum sibi personaliter angelicam vniuisse naturam. Figurate autem Deus & Iehoua dici non potuit, nisi ea figura, qua nomen rei significatæ eius signo tribuitur, vt reliquas figuras seu tropos percurrenti manifestum esse potest. Quæ figura in Scriptura, & in quotidiano omnium hominum sermone frequentissima est. Porrò ea figura non potuit Angelus dici Deus seu Iehoua, nisi, aut quemadmodum histrio in fabula rex dicitur, & imago eius nomine appellatur, cuius est imago, aut quemadmodum Typus nonnunquam id esse dicitur cuius est typus. Priorem modum jam rejecimus: nam nec fabula agitur, sed res verè gesta, nec vllus alius in ea historia alienam agit personam, nec vllus angelus dicitur in Scriptura imago Dei, aut Deo similis, nec si diceretur imago Dei,propterea sic loqui posset, Ego sum Iehoua &c, vt viri exemplo patet, qui Dei imago & gloria dicitur 1. Cor. xi. 7. nec Angelus ille quis, qualisue fuerit, reuelatur in Scriptura, aut à nobis cognosci potest.
units.tr: V. So, in order to answer and argue at the same time, consider this: the created angel (whether there was one or several does not matter), by whose agency the Law was promulgated from Mount Sinai, is either called Jehovah and professes himself to be Jehovah, or not. If the former, then it must be that he, and others, call him Jehovah, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, etc., not properly but figuratively. For he was not God properly, but a creature and minister of God; for nobody, I think, will say that God personally took upon himself an angelic nature. Yet he could not be called God or Jehovah figuratively except by that figure in which the name of a thing is given to its sign, as anyone who runs through the other figures or tropes can see. This figure is very frequent in Scripture and in the everyday speech of all people. Moreover, the angel could be called God or Jehovah by this figure only in one of two ways: either as an actor on the stage is called a king and is named by the name of the one whose image he is, or as a type is sometimes said to be that of which it is a type. We have already rejected the first way: for this is no fable being acted out but a real event, nor does any other actor in that history play an alien part; no angel is called in Scripture an image of God or like God; and even if he were called an image of God, he could not on that account speak in the words, "I am Jehovah," etc., as the example of man makes clear, who is called the image and glory of God (1 Cor. 11:7). Nor is that angel, whoever or whatever he was, revealed in Scripture or can be known by us.

units.la: VI. De posteriori duo certa sunt: vnum, posse typo tribui rei quam adumbrat nomen & quædam attributa. Sic Petra dicitur fuisse Christus 1. Cor. 10. 4. Sic de Dauide Ps. 16. 10. & 22. 18. 19. &c, & de Salomone Ps. 45. 8. & 2. Sam. 13. 14. &c. quædam dicuntur, quæ Christi sunt propria. Alterum, Angelum illum qui Legem è monte Sinai promulgauit typum fuisse Cum enim reliqua omnia, vt jam dixi, typi fuerint, mons Synai, Moses, Aaron, tabulæ lapideæ, Lex, Legis promulgatio, liberatio à seruitute Ægyptiaca, desertum &c, consentaneum fuit, vt is etiam qui legem promulgauit typus fuerit. Cuius autem typus fuit? Christi. Id ipsa res testatur: cuius enim typus fuisset is qui Legem promulgauit, nisi eius qui promulgauit Euangelium? Atque vt ille Angelus (siue vnus fuerit siue plures) coepit Legem per seipsum immediatè pronunciare, Deinde vius est ad eam rem Mosis ministerio; sic Christus per seipsum Euangelium prædicare coepit, Deinde id perfecit per Apostolos, sicut est obseruatum ab Apostolo Heb. 2. 3. 4. Id etiam colligitur ex Heb. 2. 2. & 12. 18. 25. Coloss. 2. 1c. 2. Cor. 3. 13. 16 18. qui postremus locus est maximè notandus. Si igitur iste Angelus (vnus, vt dixi, an plures fuerint, nihil ad hoc quod agimus interest) typicè Deus & Iehoua dicitur, necesse est vt Christus sit Deus & Iehoua reuera. Itaque in ipso, teste Apostolo, inhabitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis corporaliter, quæ non habitauit in Angelo, in propitiatorio & templo Hierosolymitano nisi vmbratiliter.
units.tr: VI. Of the latter, two things are certain. The first: a name and certain attributes of the thing which a type foreshadows can be given to the type. Thus the rock is said to have been Christ (1 Cor. 10:4). Thus of David (Ps. 16:10; 22:18, 19, etc.) and of Solomon (Ps. 45:8; 2 Sam. 13:14, etc.) certain things are said which are proper to Christ. The second: that the angel who promulgated the Law from Mount Sinai was a type. For since all the other things, as I have already said, were types (the mount Sinai, Moses, Aaron, the stone tablets, the Law, the promulgation of the Law, the liberation from Egyptian bondage, the desert, etc.), it was fitting that he also who promulgated the Law should be a type. But of whom was he a type? Of Christ. The thing itself bears witness to this: for whose type would he be who promulgated the Law, if not of him who promulgated the Gospel? And just as that angel (whether one or several) began to proclaim the Law immediately through himself, and afterwards used Moses' ministry for that purpose, so Christ began to preach the Gospel through himself, and afterwards accomplished it through the Apostles, as was observed by the Apostle (Heb. 2:3, 4). This is also gathered from Heb. 2:2; 12:18, 25; Col. 2:1, 2; 2 Cor. 3:13, 16, 18, the last of which passages is to be noted most of all. If therefore that angel (one or several, as I have said, it makes no difference to what we are doing) is called God and Jehovah typically, it must be that Christ is truly God and Jehovah. Accordingly, in him, as the Apostle testifies, "all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily," which did not dwell in the angel, nor in the propitiatory and the Jerusalem temple, except in shadow.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Si quis obiiciat, typos non adumbrasse nisi res futuras, reuincetur exemplo tabernaculi quod cœlum, & immunditiei legalis quæ peccati immunditiem significabat. Si obiiciat, non tam frequenter typis tribui quod proprium est rerum adumbratarum, is recordetur nihil occurrere frequentius in lege, quàm sacrificijs legalibus peccata expiari, id quod tamen proprium esse sacrificij Christi Auctor Ep. ad Heb. testatur & probat capp. 9. & 10. Si objiciat, non solere typo tribui nomen rei adumbratæ, is cogitet nonnullos esse typos, qui communi cum rebus significatis nomine gaudeant. Sic exempli causa, Christi Sacerdotis typus fuit sacerdos, Regis rex, Mediatoris mediator, Sacerdotij sacerdotium, Sacrificij sacrificium, Tabernaculi tabernaculum &c. Si denique adjiciat, typicos Reges, Sacerdotes &c vere & proprie reges & sacerdotes fuisse, ac propterea hunc Angelum, si typicus Deus fuit, vere & proprie Deum fuisse. Concedam vere, id est, non falsò, & proprie Deum fuisse, sed deitate typica & vmbratili, quæ cum reliquis vmbris exoriente Christo, sole iustitiæ, euanuit.
units.tr: If someone objects that types foreshadow only future things, he is refuted by the example of the tabernacle, which foreshadowed heaven, and of legal uncleanness, which signified the uncleanness of sin. If he objects that what is proper to the things foreshadowed is not so often attributed to types, let him recall that nothing occurs more often in the Law than that sins are expiated by legal sacrifices, which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews nonetheless testifies and proves to be proper to the sacrifice of Christ, in chapters 9 and 10. If he objects that the name of the thing foreshadowed is not usually given to the type, let him consider that there are some types which share a common name with the things signified. Thus, for example, the type of Christ the Priest was a priest, of the King a king, of the Mediator a mediator, of the priesthood a priesthood, of the sacrifice a sacrifice, of the tabernacle a tabernacle, and so on. Finally, if he adds that the typical kings, priests, and so on were truly and properly kings and priests, and that therefore this angel, if he was a typical God, was truly and properly God: I will grant that he was truly, that is, not falsely, and properly God, but with a typical and shadowy deity, which vanished with the other shadows when Christ, the sun of righteousness, arose.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Si Angelus creatus non tribuit sibi nomen Dei, necesse est vt verba illa, Ego sum Iehova &c. proferat non tanquam sua, sed tanquam aliena. Vel igitur ea pronunciat tanquam nuncius recitans eius à quo est missus, verba; vel tanquam seruus, cuius opera alius utitur ad exprimendos suos conceptus. Prius mihi non fit verisimile. Nunquam enim sic loquuntur, vel Angeli in Nouo Testamento, vel Prophetae in veteri, vel hominum nuntij, nisi praemissa aliqua praefatione, qua doceant se eius à quo sunt missi verba referre. Deinde qui pronunciat illa verba Ego sum Iehova, ab ipso sacro historico Iehova appellatur, & cum eo tanquam cum Ichova agitur. Posterius intelligi potest duobus modis. Vno, vt Deo loquenti operam suam angelus accommodauerit ad sonum producendum & articulandum, quomodo Tertius scripsit Epistolam ad Romanos Paulo dictante; altero, vt Angelus ipsa quidem verba conceperit pro sua prudentia, sed ad significandos Dei conceptus, quomodo solent notarij, siue scribae regij regis edicta & epistolas ita concipere, vt Rex perpetuo loquatur, ipsi nunquam. Hoc quidem satis fuisse videtur, vt Lex dici potuerit accepta per dispositionem Angelorum Act. 7. 53. ordinata per Angelos Gal. 3. 22. per Angelos dictus sermo Heb. 2. 2. Non uero vt dicatur Angelus in singulari numero dixisse, Nunc cognoui quod timeas Deum, cum non peperceris filio tuo unigenito propter me Gen. 22. 12. Ego sum Deus Bethel, vbi unxisti lapidem, & votum vouisti mihi Gen. 31. 13. Ego sum Deus Patris tui, Deus Abraham, Deus Isaac, & Deus Iacob. Exod. 3. 6. Eduxi vos de Aegypto, & introduxi in terram pro qua iurani patribus vestris, & dixeram, non faciam irritum pactum meum vobiscum in sempiternum, &c Iudic. 2. 1. Non etiam id satis fuit, vt posset ille Angelus appellari Iehova, vt factum est persaepe. Ac propterea confitendum est, Angelum illum, qui sic loquitur & appellatur, causam principalem illius apparitionis, & sermonis fuisse: quo posito necesse est eum non fuisse, aut Angelum officio, & Deum natura; aut, si natura Angelus fuit, Deum deitate, vt ita loquar, umbratili & typica. Vtrumuis eligant Aduersarij, oportet Christum esse Iehovam. Nam, si prius placet, Angelus ille est Filius Dei, quis enim alius dici possit simul Legatus Patris & Deus? Si posterius, Christus est id verè, quod ille Angelus fuit typicè.
units.tr: If the created angel did not claim for himself the name of God, he must have uttered those words, I am Jehovah, etc., not as his own but as another's. Either he pronounces them as a messenger reciting the words of the one who sent him, or as a servant whose work another uses to express his own thoughts. The former does not seem probable to me. Neither the angels of the New Testament, nor the prophets of the Old, nor human messengers ever speak in this way unless some preface comes first, by which they show that they are reporting the words of the one who sent them. Next, the one who utters the words I am Jehovah is called Jehovah by the sacred historian himself, and is treated as Jehovah. The latter can be understood in two ways. In one, the angel lent his service to the God who was speaking, to produce and articulate the sound, as Tertius wrote the Epistle to the Romans at Paul's dictation. In the other, the angel himself framed the words by his own judgement, but to signify God's thoughts, as royal secretaries are accustomed to compose the edicts and letters of a king so that the king always speaks and they never do. This seems to have been enough for the law to be called received by the disposition of angels (Acts 7:53), ordained by angels (Gal. 3:22), and the word spoken by angels (Heb. 2:2). But it was not enough for the angel, speaking in the singular, to say, Now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from me (Gen. 22:12); I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst the pillar, and vowedst a vow unto me (Gen. 31:13); I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Exod. 3:6); I brought you up out of Egypt, and into the land which I swore to your fathers; and I said, I will never break my covenant with you for ever, etc. (Judg. 2:1). Nor was it even enough that the angel could be called Jehovah, as happened very often. Therefore it must be confessed that the angel who thus speaks and is so called was the principal cause of that appearance and speech. Given this, he must either not have been an angel by office and God by nature, or, if he was an angel by nature, God only by a deity, so to speak, shadowy and typical. Whichever the adversaries choose, Christ must be Jehovah. For if the first is preferred, that angel is the Son of God; for who else could be called at once the Father's messenger and God? If the second, Christ is truly what that angel was in type.

units.la: 1 X. Sic quidem confectum est argumentum nostrum. Verum vt veritas clarior fiat, loca quaedam Scripturae breviter percurrenda sunt. Exod. 24. 9. oblato sacrificio confirmatoque fœdere Legali Moses, Aaron, Nadab, & Abihu, & septuaginta ex senioribus Israel ascenderunt in montem, & viderunt Deum Israel. eratque sub eius pedibus quasi opus lapidis saphirini, & quasi cœlum cum est serenum. Dubitari non potest, quin, ut typica fuerunt, fœdus legale, sacrificium quo illud confirmatum est, selecti illi septuaginta è filijs Israël, & Mons in quem ascenderunt, sic typica etiam fuerit admissio eorum ad præsentiam & aspectum Dei serenum. Ut igitur sancito & confirmato vetere testamento per mortem victimæ atque oblatum sacrificium, cuius sanguine liber legis & omnis populus aspersus fuit, Moses Aaron Nadab & Abihu & septuaginta è filijs Israël admissi sunt in conspectum Dei Israëlis, qui illos benignè accepit, atque etiam, (ut colligi posse videtur ex V. 11. & tanti principis erga eos, quibuscum fœdus percutiebat, liberalitate) convivio excepit, Sic sancito & confirmato testamento nouo per mortem Christi & oblatum sacrificium cuius sanguine fideles omnes aspergunt, & à peccatis purgantur, Apostoli & septuaginta discipuli admissi sunt ad Dei aspectum, atque adeo conuiuium. Quem igitur viderunt? Christum. Quis eis quod spiritualiter ederent & biberent apposuit? Christus. Patrem certè non viderunt, nisi quatenus Filium viderunt.
units.tr: 1 X. Thus our argument is established. But to make the truth clearer, certain passages of Scripture must be briefly run through. In Exod. 24:9, after the sacrifice was offered and the legal covenant confirmed, Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the God of Israel: and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness. No one can doubt that, as the legal covenant and the sacrifice by which it was confirmed were typical, so also that selected seventy from the sons of Israel and the mount on which they ascended, and likewise their admission to the presence and sight of God in his clear brightness, were typical. Therefore, just as the old covenant was ratified and confirmed through the death of the victim and the sacrifice offered, with whose blood the book of the law and the whole people were sprinkled, so Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy of the sons of Israel were admitted into the sight of the God of Israel, who received them kindly and even (as may be gathered from v. 11, and from the generosity of so great a prince toward those with whom he was making the covenant) entertained them at a feast. So, now that the new covenant has been ratified and confirmed through the death of Christ and the sacrifice offered, with whose blood all the faithful are sprinkled and cleansed from sins, the apostles and the seventy disciples are admitted to the sight of God, and so to a feast. Whom, then, did they see? Christ. Who set before them what they should eat and drink spiritually? Christ. Certainly they did not see the Father, except insofar as they saw the Son.

units.la: X. Exodi cap. 34. V. 29. Legimus cutem faciei Mosis, cum manu teneret duas tabulas fœderis, descenderetque è monte, splenduisse contracto ex Dei aspectu splendore, ac propterea Mosem velamen posuisse super faciem suam, quod auferebat, cum ingrederetur in conspectum Domini: Ad quam historiam alludit Apostolus 2. Cor. 3.13. seque ita cum Mose confert, ut perspicuum sit, Domino, qui cum Mose loquebatur in monte, respondere Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, ad quem cum fuerint Judæi conversi tolletur velamen, cuiusque gloriam, detecta facie, tanquam in speculo, intuentes Apostoli transformati sunt in eandem imaginem ex gloria in gloriam. Christum enim ab Apostolo per Dominum intelligi patet ex V. 14. & V. 17. & nomine Domini, quod Christi proprium esse testatur Apostolus 1. Cor. 8. 6. (quod loco non dicitur cum articulo εἷς ὁ κύριος[?], sed fine articulo εἷς κύριος[?]) necnon ex ipsa experientia, quæ docuit Apostolos gloriam Filij vidisse, Patris, nisi in Filio, non vidisse. Aut igitur ille Dominus (Iehoua) quem Moses vidit, ipse Dei Filius fuit, aut eius typus. Utrumlibet eligatur, Filius Dei est Deus Israëlis, est Iehoua.
units.tr: X. Exodus chapter 34, verse 29. We read that the skin of Moses' face shone, when he came down from the mountain holding the two tables of the covenant in his hand, because of the brightness received from the sight of God. For this reason Moses put a veil over his face, which he removed when he went in before the presence of the Lord. The Apostle alludes to this story in 2 Cor. 3:13, and compares himself with Moses in such a way that it is plain that our Lord Jesus Christ answers to the Lord who spoke with Moses on the mount. When the Jews are converted to him, the veil will be taken away; and the apostles, beholding his glory with unveiled face as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory. That the Apostle means Christ by "the Lord" is clear from verses 14 and 17, and from the name "Lord", which the Apostle affirms to be proper to Christ in 1 Cor. 8:6 (which in that place is said not with the article, as "one Lord" [εἷς ὁ κύριος], but without it, as "one Lord" [εἷς κύριος]); and also from experience itself, which taught the apostles that they had seen the glory of the Son, and that they had not seen the Father except in the Son. Either, then, that Lord (Jehovah) whom Moses saw was himself the Son of God, or his type. Whichever is chosen, the Son of God is the God of Israel, is Jehovah.

units.la: XI. Exod. cap. 33. V. 1. Dominus idololatria populi offensus dicit Mosi, mittam ante te Angelum, & eiciam Chananaum, & Amorrhaum &c, Non enim ascendam in medio tui, quia populus dura cervicis tu es, ne forte consumem te in via. Audiens autem populus verbum istud malum, luxerunt, nec posuit ullus ornamentum suum super se. Itaque eodem capite V. 12. & seqq. Moses Deum obnixè rogat, ut velit ipse cum eis ire. Nisi, inquit, facies tua ierit, ne nos hinc educas. Id quod etiam impetrat. Quid? Populus Israëlicus non fuit contentus Angelo ductore per typicum desertum ad Canaam typicam, & nos Christiani contenti erimus homine tantum homine, ad verâ & coelestem Canaam duce? Pugnabimusque obnixè, ne ipse Deus dicatur ad nos seruandos venisse, nobisque in coelum deducendis praeiuisse: adeò differunt Aduersarij ab illo populo, à Mose! Num ad eiusmodi liberationem carnalem & typicam opus fuit ipsius Dei facie & praesentia, nec satis fuit praesentia Angeli; ad liberationem verò spiritualem & aeternam non opus fuit ipso Deo, sed homo tantum homo satis fuit? Quis hoc credat? Fuit-ne hac in parte ministerij mortis quàm ministerij Spiritus major gloria? Absit. Agnoscamus igitur ducem nostrum, eumque, reuera Deum seu Iehouam esse credamus.
units.tr: XI. Exodus chapter 33, verse 1. The Lord, offended by the idolatry of the people, says to Moses, I will send an angel before thee, and I will drive out the Canaanite, and the Amorite, etc. For I will not go up in the midst of thee, for thou art a stiffnecked people; lest I consume thee in the way. And when the people heard this evil word, they mourned, and no man did put on him his ornaments. Accordingly, in the same chapter, v. 12 and following, Moses earnestly asks God that he himself would go with them. If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence. And this he obtains. What then? Was the people of Israel not content with an angel as guide through the typical wilderness to the typical Canaan, and shall we Christians be content with a mere man as guide to the true and heavenly Canaan? Shall we strive earnestly that God himself is not said to have come to save us and to have gone before us in leading us to heaven? So greatly do our adversaries differ from that people, from Moses! Was the presence and face of God needed for such carnal and typical deliverance, and was the presence of an angel not enough; but for spiritual and eternal deliverance, was God himself not needed, and a mere man sufficed? Who could believe this? Is there greater glory in the ministry of death than in the ministry of the Spirit in this respect? Far from it. Let us acknowledge, then, our leader, and let us believe that he is truly God, or Jehovah.

units.la: XII. His accedat memorabilis illa historia, quae extat Ios. 5.13. Contigit autem cum esset Iehosua prope Iericho, ut attolleret oculos, & videret, & ecce vir stabat contra eum habens in manu sua districtum gladium. Et abijt Iehosua ad eum, & dixit ei, noster es, an hostium nostrorum? Qui dixit, Non: sed ego princeps exercitus Domini nunc veni. Procidens autem Iehosua super faciem suam in terram, adoraurt [?] &c. Negari non potest, quin princeps ille exercitus Domini, aut Filius Dei fuerit, aut typus eius. Vocatur autem cap. sequenti V. 2. Dominus seu Iehoua. Mirum est Iudæos tot Dei in forma humana apparitionibus, tot Patriarcharum exemplis, qui hominem, cum se professus est Deum esse, pro Deo habere & adorare non dubitarunt, praeparatos non fuisse ad Christum reuerenter accipiendum, cum se Dei Filium, Deum, unum cum Patre profiteretur, multisque & maximis miraculis confirmaret. Reliquas Angeli Domini siue Dei in humana specie seu figura apparitiones breuitatis studio praetermitto. Illud dūntaxat unum addam hoc loco, concurrisse eodem tempore ad Christum adumbrandum duos typos naturæ admodum diuersæ, Angelos & Mosem, quorum illi diuinitatem, iste humanitatem præcipuè repræsentarunt.
units.tr: XII. To these may be added that memorable story which is found in Josh. 5:13. And it came to pass, when Joshua was by Jericho, that he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand. And Joshua went unto him, and said unto him, Art thou for us, or for our adversaries? And he said, Nay; but as captain of the host of the Lord am I now come. And Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and did worship, etc. It cannot be denied that that prince of the host of the Lord was either the Son of God or his type. In the following chapter, v. 2, he is called the Lord, or Jehovah. It is strange that the Jews, with so many appearances of God in human form and so many examples of the patriarchs, who did not hesitate to hold and worship a man as God when he professed himself to be God, were not prepared to receive Christ reverently when he professed himself to be the Son of God, God, one with the Father, and confirmed this by many great miracles. I pass over the remaining appearances of the angel of the Lord, or God, in human form or shape, for the sake of brevity. I will add only this one thing here: at the same time, two types of very different nature concurred to foreshadow Christ, the angels and Moses, of whom the former chiefly represented his divinity, the latter his humanity.

units.la: DISPVTATIO VIGESIMA QVARTA
units.tr: DISPUTATION TWENTY-FOUR

units.la: De Arg. XXIV. Ex Esai. 2. 11. 17. Exaltabitur Dominus solus in die illa.
units.tr: On Argument XXIV. From Isaiah 2. 11. 17. The Lord alone shall be exalted in that day.

units.la: I. ARGVMENTVM est eiusmodi. Solus Dominus (Iehoua) exaltabitur in die illa.
units.tr: I. The argument runs as follows. The Lord alone (Jehovah, Iehoua) shall be exalted in that day.

units.la: Christus exaltabitur, & quidem maximè, in die illa.
units.tr: Christ shall be exalted, and most of all, in that day.

units.la: Christus igitur est Dominus, Iehoua. Maior est Prophetæ. Minor in dubium vocari nequit. Nihil potest responderi, nisi per diem illam tempus denotari, quod Christi natiuitatem antecessit. Hoc verò falsum esse ex eo manifestum est, quod huius cap. 2. visionem Propheta orditur à designatione temporis, Et erit, inquit, in nouissimis diebus &c. Quinam autem sunt nouissimi dies, nisi tempora Messiæ? Deinde continuò prædicit vocationem gentium ℣. 2. & 3. Deinde pacem illam, quam nobis Christus dedit, iis verbis describit, quibus solet à Prophetis describi ℣. 4. Tum prædicit Iudæorum reiectionem ℣. 6. Ac tandem iudicium Dei, quo omnem hominum sublimitatem ℣. 10. omnemque idololatriam ℣. 18. prorsus abolebit, iisdem ferè verbis prædicit, quibus illud cum ipse Christus Luc. 23. 30. tum eius Apostolus Iohannes Apoc. 6. 15. 16. prædixerunt.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the Lord, Jehovah. The major premise is the prophet's, and the minor cannot be called into doubt. The only possible reply is that "that day" denotes a time which preceded the birth of Christ. That this is false is clear from the fact that the prophet opens his vision in this second chapter with a designation of time: "And it shall come to pass," he says, "in the last days," and so on. But who are the last days, if not the times of the Messiah? Then, straight away, he foretells the calling of the Gentiles (vers. 2 and 3). Next he describes the peace that Christ gave us, in the words with which the prophets usually describe it (v. 4). Then he foretells the rejection of the Jews (v. 6). Finally, God's judgment, by which he will utterly abolish all human loftiness (v. 10) and all idolatry (v. 18), he foretells in almost the same words that Christ himself used in Luke 23. 30, and that his apostle John used in Revelation 6. 15, 16.

units.la: II. Ad Prophetæ testimonium accedit ipsa experientia, quæ clamat nondum impletum esse hoc Esaiæ vaticinium. Nondum enim abolita est omnis idololatria. Nondum depressa est omnis hominum altitudo. Nondum exaltatus est Dominus solus. Nunquam autem Deus exaltabitur nisi cum exaltabitur Christus. Itaque, aut Dominus nunquam exaltabitur solus, aut Christus idem est Dominus, hoc est, Iehoua.
units.tr: II. To the testimony of the prophet is added experience itself, which cries out that this prophecy of Isaiah has not yet been fulfilled. For idolatry has not yet been wholly abolished. The loftiness of men has not yet been brought low. The Lord has not yet been exalted alone. Yet God will never be exalted except when Christ is exalted. Therefore either the Lord will never be exalted alone, or Christ is the same Lord, that is, Jehovah.

units.la: III. Similis locus extat ps. 148. 12. Iuvenes & virgines, senes cum pueris, Laudent nomen Domini, quia exaltatum est nomen eius solius. Pertinent autem psalmi ultimi praecipuè ad ultima tempora, aut etiam ad ultimum diem, quo demum Regis & iudicis omnium Christi nomen ita exaltabitur, ut ei se flectat omne genu caelestium, terrestrium & infernorum, adoreturque ab Angelis, & quidem omnibus. Quomodo igitur tunc solum, vel solius Domini nomen exaltabitur, si Christus non est Dominus? Porrò Dominus heb. est Iehoua.
units.tr: III. A similar passage is found in Psalm 148. 12: Young men and maidens, old men with children, let them praise the name of the Lord, for his name alone is exalted. The final psalms, however, pertain especially to the last times, or even to the last day, on which at length the name of Christ, King and Judge of all, will be so exalted that every knee of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth bows to him, and he is worshipped by the angels, all of them. How, then, will the name of the Lord alone, or of the Lord only, be exalted at that time, if Christ is not the Lord? Moreover, "Lord" in Hebrew is Iehoua (Jehovah).

units.la: DISPUTATIO VIGESIMA QUINTA. De Arg. XXV. Ex Esai. ix. 6. Puer enim natus est nobis, Filius datus est nobis &c.
units.tr: TWENTY-FIFTH DISPUTATION. On Argument XXV, from Isaiah ix. 6. For a child is born to us, a son is given to us, etc.

units.la: I. SUPERIORI loco subjungo celeberrimum illum, qui habetur Esai. ix. 6. Puer enim natus est nobis. Filius datus est nobis, & factus est principatus super humerum eius, & vocabitur nomen eius, Ad-mirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis, Pater aeter-nitatis, Princeps pacis. Ex quo hic argumentor. Deus fortis est praeditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: I. Above, I add the very famous text in Isaiah ix. 6: For a child is born to us, a son is given to us, and the government will be upon his shoulder, and his name will be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. From this I argue as follows. The Mighty God is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est Deus fortis.
units.tr: Christ is the Mighty God.

units.la: Christus igitur est praeditus essentia diuina. Maior nulla in-stanua potest infirmari. Minor est ipsius Prophetae. Conclusio igitur non potest negari.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is endowed with the divine essence. No instance can weaken the major premise. The minor premise is the Prophet's own words. So the conclusion cannot be denied.

units.la: II. Respondet Socinus nihil, nisi, non absolute nomen Deus esse ibi positum, sed cum adiecto fortis. Primum autem hoc nihil facit ad argumentum nostrum soluendum, cuius medius terminus non est nomen Deus absolute, sed cum ista adiectione fortis. Hoc enim elogium Deus fortis Deo Israëlis tribuitur aliquoties in Scriptura, ut Esai. 10. 21. Reliquiae convertentur, reliquiae Iacob ad Deum fortem, quo loco Deus fortis idem valet quod Deus Israëlis; Angelo vero non tribuitur, nisi ei, qui Iehoua appellatur; nec homini, nisi ei, qui Dei Filius est ab hominibus & Angelis adorandus. Deinde colorem aliquem haberet haec responsio, si epitheton fortis aliquomodo frangeret, aut debilitaret, aut minueret, aut mutaret vim & significationem nominis Deus. Nunc autem eam non minuit nec mutat, non magis certè quàm similia adjecta, magnus, viuens, iustus, seruator &c. Immò contrà eam auget: solet enim tunc nomini Dei adjici, cum Deus describitur magnificentissimè, ut Deut. 10. 17. & Nehem. 9. 32. Deus magnus, fortis, & terribilis. Ierem. 32. 18. Deus magnus & fortis, Dominus exercituum nomen eius. Hoc usque adeò verum est, ut etiam nomini Iehoua adjungatur ad majorem emphasim. Ut ps. 24. 8. Quis est iste Rex gloriae? Dominus fortis & potens, Dominus potens in prælio. Sic enim distinguitur verus Deus ab idolis, quibus nomen Dei tribui solet, virtus & potentia non potest. Nihil enim boni maliue facere possunt cultoribus suis.
units.tr: II. Socinus replies only that the name God is not placed there absolutely, but with the added word "mighty." But first, this reply does nothing to undo our argument, whose middle term is not the name God absolutely, but the name with that addition, "mighty." For the title Mighty God is given several times in Scripture to the God of Israel, as in Isaiah x. 21: The remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the Mighty God, where "Mighty God" means the same as "God of Israel." But it is not given to an angel, except to the one who is called Jehovah; nor to a man, except to the one who is the Son of God and is to be adored by men and angels. Next, this reply would have some plausibility if the epithet "mighty" in some way broke, weakened, diminished or changed the force and meaning of the name God. But it does not diminish or change it, certainly no more than similar additions such as great, living, just, saviour, and so on. On the contrary, it increases it. For it is added to the name of God when God is described most magnificently, as in Deuteronomy x. 17 and Nehemiah ix. 32: God great, mighty and terrible. Jeremiah xxxii. 18: God great and mighty, the Lord of hosts is his name. This is so true that it is even added to the name Jehovah for greater emphasis, as in Psalm xxiv. 8: Who is this King of glory? The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle. For in this way the true God is distinguished from idols, to which the name of God is customarily given, but not power and might. For they can do nothing good or evil to their worshippers.

units.la: III. Socinus suæ isti tam breui & futili responsioni, Duas alienas subjungit, unam Iudæorum, alteram aliorum. Ut interim, inquit, taceam, quod Rabbini appellationem istam unà cum cæteris, quæ ibi recensentur, non ad Messiam referunt, de quo ibi alioqui vaticinationem esse concedunt: sed ad illum, qui eius nomen vocabit; nempe ad unum illum Deum. In hebraeo enim vocabit legitur, non vocabitur, ut habet vulgata editio. Probatne igitur Socinus hanc Rabbino-rum interpretationem? Non. Haec autem dico, inquit, non quòd interpretationem Rabbinorum probem in loco isto ab aduer-sarijs allato. Cur igitur eam attulit? ut, inquit, eò magis appa-reat, non esse certam probationem, quam inde illi sumunt. At, si falsa est, cur incertam facit nostram ex hoc loco probationem? si vera est, cur eam Socinus non probat? Est igitur haec Rabbinorum interpretatio, ne ad eam confugere possint Aduersarij, paucis refellenda.
units.tr: III. To this so brief and frivolous reply, Socinus adds two foreign interpretations, one of the Jews and the other of others. "Meanwhile," he says, "to say nothing of the fact that the rabbis refer this appellation, together with the others listed there, not to the Messiah, about whom they otherwise concede there is a prophecy, but to him who will call his name, that is, to that one God. For in the Hebrew it is read he will call, not will be called, as the Vulgate has." Does Socinus therefore approve this interpretation of the rabbis? No. "But I say these things," he says, "not because I approve of the rabbis' interpretation of the passage alleged by our opponents." Why then did he bring it up? "So that," he says, "it may more clearly appear that it is not a certain proof, which they draw from it." But if it is false, why does he make our proof from this passage uncertain? And if it is true, why does Socinus not prove it? This interpretation of the rabbis, lest our opponents take refuge in it, must therefore be refuted briefly.

units.la: IV. Non dicam hanc interpretationem esse quorundam Rabbinorum recentium inventum. Non dicam eam ab odio eorum in Messiam profectam esse. Non dicam verbum ויקרא, si consonas spectes, æque legi posse V éykare & vocabitur, ac Vaijkra & vocabit: Non esse autem puncta subiecta paris antiquitatis & auctoritatis cum consonis: Sed dicam in Scriptura, cum de nomine imponendo agitur, perpetuò post שם nomen poni nomen vocati, nunquam vocantis: hoc enim, si exprimitur, semper præcedit, nunquam sequitur. Id quod inductione omnium locorum in quibus verbum קרא iungitur cum שם vel את שם perspicuum esse potest. Huic regulæ generali opponunt instantiam ex Esai. 45. 3. quo loco post הקורא בשמך sequitur אלהי ישראל nomen vocantis, sed perperam: dissimilis enim est cum constructio, tum sensus. Constructio quidem: Nam Esai. 9. שם regitur a verbo יקרא: Esai. vero 45. non regitur a verbo הקורא nisi mediante præpositione ב. Sensus vero: Nam קרא שם vel את שם est nomen imponere, & קרא בשם est vocare nominatim, sive expresso nomine. Non solet autem expresso nomine vocari Deus ab homine nisi ut invocetur, nec homo a Deo, nisi ut ad munus aut rem aliquam faciendam vocetur. Potest etiam observari alia constructionis dissimilitudo. Nam Esai. 45. 3. nomen Deus Israel construi debet non cum verbo voco, sed cum antecedente sciat, ut patet ex particulis, ut, quod: Sensus enim est, ut sciasquod ego Dominus, qui te nomine tuo voco, sum Deus Israelis. Hic vero Esai. 9. 6. nomina Admirabilis, consiliarius &c necessariò construenda sunt cum verbo vocabitur: aliud enim verbum a quo regantur, nullum est.
units.tr: IV. I will not say that this interpretation is the invention of some recent rabbis. I will not say that it sprang from their hatred of the Messiah. I will not say that the word ויקרא, if you look only at the consonants, can equally be read Véykare, "and it will be called," or Vaijkra, "and he will call"; nor that the vowel points added to it have the same antiquity and authority as the consonants. But I will say this: in Scripture, when the giving of a name is in question, the name of the one called always follows the word שם, "name," and never the name of the one calling. For the name of the one calling, when it is expressed, always comes before, never after. This can be seen clearly from a review of all the passages in which the verb קרא is joined with שם or את שם. Against this general rule they oppose an instance from Isaiah xlv. 3, where after הקורא בשמך there follows אלהי ישראל, the name of the one calling. But this is wrong, for the construction and the sense are both different. The construction is different: in Isaiah ix. 6 the word שם is governed by the verb יקרא, but in Isaiah xlv. 3 it is not governed by the word הקורא except through the preposition ב. The sense is different: קרא שם or את שם means to impose a name, while קרא בשם means to call by name, that is, by an expressed name. But God is not usually called by man by an expressed name except in order to be invoked, nor is man called by God by name except in order to be summoned to some office or task. Another difference of construction can also be observed. For in Isaiah xlv. 3 the name God of Israel ought to be construed not with the verb I call, but with the preceding that you may know, as is clear from the particles that, because. For the sense is: that you may know that I, the Lord, who call you by your name, am the God of Israel. But here, in Isaiah ix. 6, the names Wonderful, Counsellor, and so on, must necessarily be construed with the verb will be called, for there is no other verb by which they could be governed.

units.la: V. Ad hoc primum argumentum accedit secundum. Nam immediatè post verba, vocabitur nomen eius, oportuit nomen illud exprimi. Id enim & perpetua Scripturæ consuetudo flagitabat, & ipsa ratio, alioquin enim maneret & suspensa sententia, & frustratus auditoris, vel lectoris, animus; qui cum audit aut legit, & vocabitur nomen eius, expectat ut nomen illud quale sit futurum exprimatur.
units.tr: V. To this first argument a second is added. For immediately after the words his name will be called, that name ought to have been expressed. Both the constant custom of Scripture required this and reason itself did too. Otherwise the sentence would remain suspended, and the mind of the hearer or reader would be left frustrated: when he hears or reads and his name will be called, he expects that name to be given, to show what sort of name it will be.

units.la: VI. Sequatur & tertium argumentum. Causa enim nulla erat cur imponentis nomen seu vocantis subjicerentur nomina & elogia, cum de eo non ageretur proprie. Contrà causa erat cur vocati seu vocandi nomina subjungerentur, cum in eo describendo versaretur Propheta, ut ex antecedentibus & sequentibus verbis manifestum est.
units.tr: VI. Let a third argument follow. There was no reason for the names and praises of the one imposing the name, or calling, to be added, since the matter did not properly concern him. On the contrary, there was reason for the names and praises of the one called, or to be called, to be added, since the Prophet was engaged in describing him, as is clear from the words before and after.

units.la: VII. Præterea, vel Propheta nomen exprimit quo erat appellandus Filius, vel non exprimit. Hoc dici non potest. Nam, & se nomen illud dicere velle præ se fert, cum ait, & vocabit, sive vocabitur nomen eius, & alioqui digna non effet Prophetæ sententia. Quis enim nesciebat futurum esse, ut aliquo nomine appellaretur? Si igitur nomen eius exprimit, vel illud est totum quod sequitur, Admirabilis, Consiliarius, Deus fortis, Pater aeternitatis, Princeps pacis, vel ex his elogiis unum aliquod. Si prius, falsa est Rabbinorum interpretatio. Si posterius, vel est primum nomen, vel medium, vel ultimum. Non dicent medium; Nam, & illud est Deus fortis, & qui elogio medio describitur, is sine dubio describitur etiam extremis: Nec primum, aut ultimum: Quis enim non videt illis omnibus elogijs eundem describi, ad quem unum refertur, ad eundem reliqua referri? Estne aliquid, quo doceas, duas esse descriptiones, unam vocantis, alteram vocandi, & quot, quibusque elogijs utrque describitur, in-ternoscas? Exempli causa, si refertur ultimum ad Filium, cur non etiam penultimum? Si penultimum cur non antepenultimum? Hoc enim decet nos in Scripturis interpretandis versari temerè, ac cæcorum instar sine luce, sine ratione. At, inquiet forte aliquis, debuit etiam eius, à quo sic erat appellandus, nomen exprimi. Cur? Annon enim sic debuit appellari à Deo Patre, ab Angelis, & ab hominibus? Deinde si de impositione nominis agitur, nonne facilè patens subintelligitur? Huius enim certè est Filio nomen imponere. Denique quis non videt, neque sic unquam Deum Patrem describi in Scriptura, & prima illa elogia Admirabilis, Consiliarus, maximè proprie conuenireFilio Dei?
units.tr: VII. Moreover, either the Prophet expresses the name by which the Son was to be called, or he does not. The second cannot be said. For he shows that he wishes to state that name when he says and he will call, or his name will be called; otherwise the Prophet's sentence would not be worthy of him. For who did not know that he would be called by some name? If therefore he does express his name, it is either the whole that follows, Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, or one of these praises. If the former, the rabbis' interpretation is false. If the latter, it is either the first, or the middle, or the last. They will not say the middle, for that is Mighty God, and whoever is described by the middle praise is undoubtedly described also by the extremes. Nor the first or the last: for who does not see that all these praises describe the same one, and that the rest refer to the same one to whom the one refers? Is there anything by which you could teach, and distinguish, that there are two descriptions, one of the one calling and the other of the one to be called, and by how many and which praises each is described? For example, if the last is referred to the Son, why not also the penultimate? If the penultimate, why not the antepenultimate? For it would not become us to handle Scripture rashly in interpreting it, like the blind, without light, without reason. But someone may perhaps say: the name of the one by whom he was to be called thus ought also to have been expressed. Why? Was he not to be called thus by God the Father, by angels, and by men? Next, if the imposition of the name is in question, is it not easily understood by implication? For it is certainly the business of the Father to impose the name on the Son. Finally, who does not see that God the Father is never described in Scripture in these terms, and that those first praises, Wonderful, Counsellor, belong most properly of all to the Son of God?

units.la: VIII. Addit Socinus tertiam interpretationem. Multi, inquit, verba ista, Deus fortis, ex hebraeo aliter legunt, videlicet, Fortis heros, vel, conuerso ordine, Heros fortis. Probetne an improbet, non significat. At quid illi est Heros? Num, ut loquitur Lucianus, ὅ μήτε ἀνθρωπος ἦν, μήτε θεὸς, ἀ̔ συναμφότερον ἦν? Solus Christus est eiusmodi, ut è simul & Deus & homo; Alioqui nomen est alienum à Scriptura, & quod potius respondeat hebraeo גבור quàm אל. Est enim nomen אל in singulari numero proprium Dei, quodque nunquam de creatura vsurpatur, nisi forte.
units.tr: VIII. Socinus adds a third interpretation: "Many read these words, 'mighty God,' differently from the Hebrew, namely as mighty hero, or, with the order reversed, hero mighty." Whether he approves or disapproves is not clear. But what is this "hero" to him? Is he, as Lucian puts it, one who was neither man nor god but both together [ὃ μήτε ἄνθρωπος ἦν, μήτε θεὸς, ἃ συναμφότερον ἦν]? Only Christ is of such a kind, being both God and man at once. Otherwise the name is foreign to Scripture, and it corresponds rather to the Hebrew gibbor [גבור] than to el [אל]. For the name el in the singular is proper to God, and is never applied to a creature, unless perhaps once.

units.la: Ref 3. Resp. fortè Ezech. 31. 11. quo tamen loco & in multis exemplaribus plenius scribitur inserto , , & non ponitur absolutè , sed cum adjecto גוים gentium, quæ limitatio vim eius aliquo modo minuit. Aut igitur aliquo exemplo doceant Aduersarij nomen אל singulariter & absolutè, aut cum adjecto אל גבור de eo vsurpari qui non sit vnus ille Deus, Aut fateantur Christum, cum sit אל גבור Deus fortis, cumque illud elogium sit illius nomen, esse cum Patre illum vnum Deum.
units.tr: Objection 3. Answer: perhaps Ezek. 31. 11, though in that place, in many copies, the word is written more fully with an insertion, and it is not used absolutely but with gentium [גוים, "of the nations"] added, a qualification that in some way weakens its force. Therefore either let the opponents show by some example the name el used singly and absolutely, or used of one who is not that one God when el gibbor [אל גבור] is added. Or let them confess that Christ, since he is el gibbor, "mighty God," and since that title is his name, is together with the Father that one God.

units.la: IX. Potest etiam ex sequenti elogio duci argumentum, Quomodo enim potuit Filius appellari Pater æternitatis , si nihil nisi homo fuit recens natus ? Nam seu Pater æternitatis sit Pater æternus, quomodo puer dici potest Pater æternus , si nihil est nisi puer ? Seu Pater æternitatis sit fons & autor æternitatis, quomodo id tribui potest puero, in quo nulla natura præter humanam recens productam ac mortalem agnoscitur? Respondent per æternitatem significari futurum seculum. Unde id colligunt? ex vocabulo quo Propheta vsus est? Non. Illud enim est עד : quod æquè æternitatem à priori ac à posteriori, vt loquuntur, significat. Itaque apud hunc ipsum Prophetam Deus dicitur habitare עד æternitatem, & apud Habacuc montes quidam dicuntur montes עד æternitatis seu æterni. Nec vllus occurrit locus, vbi per se seu absolutè positum, vt hoc loco, futurum seculum præcisè significet. Num igitur id colligunt ex eo, quod Filius non potuit Pater æternitatis dici habita ratione temporis, quod eius durationem antecessit ? At cur non potius ex istis attributis Deus fortis, Pater æternitatis, colligunt, Filium non merum hominem esse, sed Deum in vera carne humana apparentem ad homines seruandos ? Nam quî potest is, qui natura sua nihil nisi homo est, reuera Deus fortis Paterque æternitatis esse? At nihil prohibet, quominus is, qui est naturâ sua Deus fortis & Pater æternitatis, patefaciat sese in carne seu natura humana, vt variis apparitionibus sub Vetere Testamento Deus olim testatum fecit. Reuera Pater æternitatis elogium est ipso Deo dignum, & quo nullum videtur cogitari posse augustius ac diuinius.
units.tr: IX. An argument can also be drawn from the following title. For how could the Son be called Father of eternity, if he was nothing but a man newly born? For if Father of eternity means eternal Father, how can a child be called eternal Father, if he is nothing but a child? And if Father of eternity means the source and author of eternity, how can that be ascribed to a child, in whom no nature is recognised except a human nature, newly produced and mortal? They answer that by eternity is meant the age to come. From what do they gather this? From the word the Prophet used? No. For the word is ad [עד], which signifies eternity equally from the past and from the future, as they say. Accordingly, in this same Prophet, God is said to dwell ad [עד], for eternity, and in Habakkuk certain mountains are called mountains of ad, that is, of the eternal. Nor does any passage occur where ad, used by itself or absolutely as it is here, means precisely the age to come. Do they then gather it from the fact that the Son could not be called Father of eternity with regard to time, since he preceded its duration? But why do they not rather gather from these attributes, Mighty God, Father of eternity, that the Son is not a mere man, but God appearing in true human flesh to save men? For how can one who by his nature is nothing but a man really be mighty God and Father of eternity? Yet nothing prevents one who is by nature mighty God and Father of eternity from manifesting himself in flesh or human nature, as God in the past showed himself in various appearances under the Old Testament. Indeed, Father of eternity is a title worthy of God himself, and no title seems conceivable that is more majestic or more divine.

units.la: X. Sed esto, sit æternitas hoc loco futurum seculum. Nonne futurum seculum multis partibus præstantius est seculo præsente vel præterito ? Plus igitur est esse Patrem futuri seculi quàm præsentis aut præteriti. Ita Relinquetur soli Deo quod minus est, quod vero multò plus est id tribuetur homini tantùm homini. Sed quid tandem, Christum esse Patrem futuri seculi, significat? Respondet Socinus, significare, Christum esse, ut alibi vocatur, principem & auctorem vitae, nempe aeternae, quae futura est: non autem esse Patrem omnium nostrum. Primùm igitur per aeternitatem intelligunt futurum seculum. Deinde per futurum seculum vitam aeternam. Verum vitam aeternam, ut loquuntur, in abstracto, an in concreto? opinor, in abstracto; alioqui Pater diceretur omnium nostrum, siquidem omnes vitae aeternae compotes sumus.
units.tr: X. But grant that eternity here means the age to come. Is not the age to come in many respects more excellent than the present or past age? It is therefore a greater thing to be Father of the age to come than of the present or the past. So what is less is left to God alone, and what is far greater is given to man, and to mere man. But what, after all, does it mean that Christ is Father of the age to come? Socinus answers that it means that Christ is, as he is elsewhere called, the prince and author of life, namely of eternal life, which is to come; but not that he is Father of all of us. First, then, they understand eternity to mean the age to come. Then they understand the age to come to mean eternal life. But is eternal life, as they say, taken in the abstract or in the concrete? I suppose in the abstract; otherwise he would be called Father of all of us, since all of us share in eternal life.

units.la: Quod mirum est, dici Patrem vitae aeternae, & tamen non dici Patrem eorum, qui habent vitam aeternam ab ipso communicatam? Dici Ecclesiam matrem omnium nostrum, & tamen non dici maritum seu sponsum Ecclesiae Patrem omnium nostrum! Addit Socinus, Et, si esset, non satis esset. Aliud est enim, esse Patrem omnium nostrum, aliud verò, esse Patrem omnium. Qui enim est pater omnium, non nostrum modò omnium, sed omnium etiam Angelorum, & ipsius Christi est pater. Hic autem solus Deus pater est; nec vllus alius esse potest. Quid? potest ne dubitari quin sit Pater omnium Angelorum, cum per eum, teste Apostolo Col. 1. 16. creata sint omnia, quae in coelis sunt & quae in terra, visibilia & invisibilia, sive throni, sive dominationes, sive principatus, sive potestates, omnia per eum & in eum creata sint; & ipse sit ante omnia, & omnia per ipsum consistant? Decet ne Christi sanguine redemptos gloriam & elogia Christi, quantum possunt, minuere & angustis limitibus circumscribere? Caeterum non posse Christum dici Patrem omnium, nisi sit suimetipsius Pater, miror excidisse Socino. Cur enim aequè[?] dici non possit pater omnium, ac dicitur Dominus omnium Act. 10. 36. omne genu illi curvatum iri Phil. 2. 10. per eum omnia facta fuisse Ioh. 1. 3?
units.tr: Is it not remarkable that he should be called Father of eternal life, and yet not be called Father of those who have eternal life communicated by him? The Church is called mother of us all, and yet the husband or bridegroom of the Church is not called Father of us all! Socinus adds: And even if he were, it would not be enough. For it is one thing to be Father of us all, and another to be Father of all. For he who is Father of all, not only of all of us but also of all the angels, is also the Father of Christ himself. But God alone is Father in this sense, and no other can be. Can it be doubted that he is the Father of all the angels, since, as the Apostle witnesses in Col. 1. 16, through him were created all things that are in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and in him all things consist? Is it fitting for those redeemed by the blood of Christ to diminish the glory and titles of Christ as far as they can, and to confine them within narrow limits? Moreover, I wonder that Socinus overlooked the point that Christ cannot be called Father of all unless he is his own Father. For why could he not be called Father of all just as he is called Lord of all (Acts 10. 36), that every knee shall bow to him (Phil. 2. 10), that all things were made through him (John 1. 3)?

units.la: XI. Denique nullus est vaticinij commentarius ipso euentu melior. Atqui vocatur Filius, Deus fortis & Pater aeternitatis, non modò eo sensu parco & restricto quem excogitarunt Aduersarij, sed isto etiam ampliore & augustiore, qui diuinam arguit essentiam, & nominum illorum majestati respondet. Vocatur, inquam, non à paucis quibusdam, & quodam seculo, sed ab omnibus fere, quotquot vbique terrarum profitentur religionem Christianam, magno consensu, omnibus seculis. Ex quo veritas ac diuinitas huius prophetiae elucescit. Quippe cui euentus jam per tot secula ad amussim respondet, & vt spero, respondebit in æternum.
units.tr: XI. Finally, there is no commentary on a prophecy better than the event itself. And yet the Son is called Mighty God and Father of eternity, not only in that sparing and restricted sense which the opponents have devised, but also in that wider and more exalted sense which points to the divine essence and answers to the majesty of those names. He is so called, I say, not by a few people in a certain age, but by almost all who profess the Christian religion wherever on earth, with great agreement, in all ages. From this the truth and divinity of this prophecy shine forth. For the event has agreed with it exactly through so many ages, and, as I hope, will agree with it for ever.

units.la: DISPUTATIO VIGESIMA SEXTA. De Arg. XXVI. Ex Esai. 42. 8. & 48. 11. Gloriam meam alteri non dabo.
units.tr: DISPUTATION TWENTY-SIX. On Argument XXVI. From Isaiah 42:8 and 48:11. I will not give my glory to another.

units.la: I. PROTESTATVR Deus apud Esaiam cap. 42. V. 8. & cap. 48. V. 11. se gloriam suam alteri non daturum. Quid procliuius, quàm inde concludere, aut Deum qui sic loquitur esse Christum, aut certè Christum non esse alterum, sed eundem cum eo Deum? Syllogismus sic poterit concipi, Deus non dedit gloriam suam alteri. Atqui dedit gloriam suam Christo. Christus igitur non est alter, sed idem cum ipso Deus.
units.tr: I. God declares in Isaiah 42:8 and 48:11 that he will not give his glory to another. What is more natural than to conclude from this either that the God who speaks thus is Christ, or at least that Christ is not another but the same God as he? The syllogism may be framed thus: God has not given his glory to another. But he has given his glory to Christ. Therefore Christ is not another, but the same God as he.

units.la: II. Tres affert Socinus responsiones. Prima sic habet. Respondemus, inquit, satis ex eodem loco constare, quid alterius nomine Deus intelligat. Illico enim addit, nec laudem meam sculptilibus. Loquitur igitur Deus, sub nomine isto, de ijs, qui cum ipso nihil commune habent: & quibus si gloria & laus aliqua tribuatur, ea ad ipsum Deum non referetur, sed contrà tantumdem gloria & laudis ipsi auferetur: cuiusmodi sunt sculptilia, non autem dicit Deus, se suam gloriam cum nemine à se omnino dependente sibiq; subordinato communicaturum. Sic enim nihil ipsius gloria decedit; cum ad ipsum quidquid gloriæ talis ei subordinatus habet prorsus referatur. Immo eius gloria augetur, cum consideratur, illum & potuisse & voluisse cum aliqua re creata, ex summa potestate ac benignitate sua, communicare suam gloriam. Primùm ista responsio Alterum sive Aliam ita interpretatur, vt non sit alter sive alius quicunque dependet à Deo, eique est subordinatus. Quæ noua est vocabuli illius acceptio, probanda aliquo exemplo. Ita nulla creatura, quatenus creatura, erit alia à Deo: dependet enim omnis creatura à Deo, eique subordinatur: Nullus etiam subditus fidelis erit alius à Rege, cui subest, & à quo dependet: Nec effectum erit aliud à causa; pendet enim omne effectum à sua causa: nec quicquam erit in hoc mundo inferiori, quod sit aliud à coelo vel sole; Quæcunque enim in hoc mundo inferiori extant, ea dependent à cœlo & sole, eique subordinantur. At Deus Esai. 42. 8. addit, Nec laudem meam sculptilibus. Primum id non addidit Esai. 48. 11. Deinde nihil est prorsus unde concludi possit, nihil esse significatum voce Alteri, quod non sit significatum voce sculptilibus. Sic loquitur Christus apud hunc eundem Prophetam cap. 50 6. Dedi corpus meum percutientibus, & genas meas vellicantibus, ineptiret qui inde colligeret, nihil significare in illis verbis, aut corpus nisi genas, aut percutientes nisi vellicantes. Quid? Ex hac tam solenni Dei protestatione, Ego non dabo gloriam meam alteri, non poterit colligi, Ergo Deus non dabit gloriam suam Angelis, non dabit gloriam suam hominibus, non dabit gloriam suam antichristo &c. Sed sola excludentur Sculptilia? Agnoscant igitur Adversarij alterius significationem latius patere quam sculptilium.
units.tr: II. Socinus offers three replies. The first runs as follows: We reply that it is sufficiently clear from the same passage what God means by the name "another". For he immediately adds, nor my praise to graven images. God therefore speaks under this name of those who have nothing in common with him, and to whom, if any glory and praise is given, it is not referred to God himself but, on the contrary, the same amount of glory and praise is taken away from him. Such are graven images. But God does not say that he will share his glory with anyone who is wholly dependent on him and subordinate to him. For nothing is taken from his glory in this way, since whatever glory such a subordinate has is referred entirely to him. Indeed his glory is increased, when it is considered that he both could and would, from his great power and goodness, share his glory with some created thing. First, this reply interprets another or otherwise so that it means no one who depends on God and is subordinate to him. This is a new sense of the word, and it needs to be proved by some example. On this reading no creature, as a creature, will be other than God, for every creature depends on God and is subordinate to him. Likewise no faithful subject will be other than the king under whom he lives and on whom he depends. Nor will an effect be other than its cause, for every effect depends on its cause. Nor will anything in this lower world be other than heaven or the sun, for whatever exists in this lower world depends on heaven and the sun and is subordinate to them. But in Isaiah 42:8 God adds, nor my praise to graven images. He did not add this in Isaiah 48:11. Further, there is nothing at all from which it could be concluded that the word another signifies nothing other than what the word graven images signifies. Christ speaks in the same prophet, Isaiah 50:6, I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them. Someone would be foolish to infer from this that the words mean nothing other than that the body means only the cheeks, or the strikers only the pluckers. Moreover, from this so solemn declaration of God, I will not give my glory to another, it cannot be inferred that therefore God will not give his glory to angels, will not give his glory to men, will not give his glory to the Antichrist, and so on. Yet are graven images alone to be excluded? Let our opponents therefore acknowledge that the meaning of another extends more widely than that of graven images.

units.la: III. Adde quod fieri non posset, ut Deus daret gloriam suam sculptilibus, quin eo ipso Sculptilia penderent à Deo eique subordinarentur. Esto enim sculptile comparatum ad repræsentandum Deum, aut Christum, aut Angelum, aut Apostolum Christi, & huic det Deus gloriam suam, nonne omnibus modis pendebit à Deo, eique subordinabitur, seu materiam eius spe&cies, seu formam, seu consilium hominum, seu Dei voluntatem? Ita profectò est, faciunt Aduersarij ista sua responsione hanc Dei protestationem tam solennem, prorsus inanem & nullam. Implicat enim contradictionem, Deum dare gloriam suam alteri ab ipsò non dependenti aut ipsi non subordinato. Quicunque enim alij rei ponatur Deus dedisse gloriam suam, ea res erit creatura Dei. Omnis autem creatura dependet à suo creatore, & suo creatori subordinatur naturâ suâ. Deinde eadem subordinabitur Deo ratione illius gloriæ sibi à Deo communicatæ, & hoc ipso quod ob gloriam illi à Deo datam coletur, coletur etiam illius gloriæ dator Deus. Immò Dei gloria augebitur, cum considerabitur illum & potuisse & voluisse cum aliqua re creata, quæcunque tandem illa fit, ex summa potestate ac benignitate sua, communicare suam gloriam. Ponamus igitur Deum dedisse gloriam suam Beatæ Virgini, aut Petro Apostolo, aut Angelo Gabrieli, aut alicui homini nunc in terris agenti, aut alicui imagini, aut alicui alii rei, nihil fecerit huic suæ protestationi repugnans, ac nihilominus verè dicetur non dedisse gloriam suam alteri. Dicam aliquid amplius, nullus est usque adeò impius, aut hostis Dei, cui si Deus ponatur dedisse (id quod nobis videtur impossibile) gloriam suam, hoc est, nomen suum & virtutes, Spiritum Sanctum absque mensura, omnes thesauros sapientiæ, iustitiam quæ sit idonea ad iudicandum mundum, vitam quæ possit mortuos vivificare, omnem plenitudinem deitatis &c, is eo ipso non mutetur, & fiat amicus Dei, Deo subordinatus. Est igitur hæc responsio insulsa [?].
units.tr: III. Add that God could not give his glory to graven images without by that very fact making the graven images dependent on God and subordinate to him. Suppose the graven image is made to represent God, or Christ, or an angel, or an apostle of Christ, and God gives his glory to it. Will it not in every way depend on God and be subordinate to him, whether in its material, its form, or the design of men, or the will of God? That is certainly so. By this reply our opponents make this so solemn declaration of God wholly empty and void. For it involves a contradiction to say that God has given his glory to another who is not dependent on him or subordinate to him. For whatever thing God is said to have given his glory to, that thing will be a creature of God. But every creature depends on its creator and is by its nature subordinate to its creator. Further, it will be subordinate to God by reason of that glory communicated to it by God, and by the very fact that it is honoured for the glory given to it by God, God, the giver, will also be honoured. Indeed the glory of God will be increased when it is considered that he both could and would, from his great power and goodness, share his glory with some created thing, whatever that thing may be. Let us suppose, then, that God gave his glory to the Blessed Virgin, or to Peter the apostle, or to the angel Gabriel, or to some man now living on earth, or to some image, or to some other thing. He would have done nothing inconsistent with this declaration of his, and yet it would still rightly be said that he had not given his glory to another.
