I will say more: there is no one so impious, or so much an enemy of God, that if God were supposed to have given him his glory (which seems to us impossible), that is, his name and virtues, the Holy Spirit without measure, all the treasures of wisdom, the righteousness fit to judge the world, the life able to raise the dead, all the fullness of the Godhead, and so on, he would not thereby be changed and become a friend of God, subordinate to God. This reply is therefore insipid [?].

units.la: IV. Itaque ad alteram confugit Socinus, Adde, inquit, quod ex ipsdem verbis, nec laudem meam sculptilibus, aperte colligitur, verbum Dandi, hoc loco, non verae dationis, sed permissionis tantum significationem habere, ut etiam aliis in locis, nominatim verò psal. 15 in illis verbis, nec dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Cui enim dubium esse potuisset unquam, ne Deus proprie loquendo, suam laudem sculptilibus esset daturus, id est, eam cum ipsis sua sponte communicaturus? Non negat igitur Deus, se sua sponte cum alio suam gloriam communicaturum sed ait, se non permissurum, ut cuiquam a se alieno sua gloria tribuatur. Sed Primum exemplum desidero, quo verbum Dandi, cum non sequitur infinitivum, aut aliud verbum eius significationem limitans, doceatur, non verae dationis, sed permissionis tantum significationem habere. Nullum enim mihi succurrit. Quis enim cum audit has phrases, dare panem, dare aquam, dare pecuniam, dare gloriam, nihil nisi permissionem cogitat? Deinde, Ratio quam affert tam permissionis significationem, quam dationis oppugnat. Nam, si nemini dubium esse potuit unquam, ne Deus suam laudem sculptilibus esset sua sponte daturus, certè nemini etiam dubium esse potuit unquam, ne sculptilia Dei laudem ipso inuito & renitente sibi vendicarent. Quàm enim illud pugnat cum Dei sapientia, tam illud pugnat cum eius potentia. Sed revera illa ratio nulla est: omnes enim sculptilium cultores sibi persuadent, Deum cum illis sculptilibus, quos colunt, gloriam suam aliquomodo communicasse; alioqui ea non putarent cultu relig-ioso digna.
units.tr: IV. So Socinus takes refuge in a second reply: Add, he says, that from the very words, nor my praise to graven images, it is plainly gathered that the verb "to give" in this place has not the sense of true giving but only of permitting, as also in other places, and especially in Psalm 16 in those words, "you will not give your holy one to see corruption". For who could ever have doubted that God, properly speaking, would give his praise to graven images, that is, would of his own accord share it with them? God therefore does not deny that he would of his own accord share his glory with another, but he says that he will not permit his glory to be given to anyone alien to him. But first I want an example in which the verb "to give", when it is not followed by an infinitive or by another verb limiting its meaning, is shown to have the sense of permitting only, not of true giving. I can recall none. For who, on hearing such phrases as to give bread, to give water, to give money, to give glory, thinks of nothing but permission? Next, the reason he gives attacks the sense of permission as much as the sense of giving. For if no one could ever have doubted that God would of his own accord give his praise to graven images, then certainly no one could ever have doubted that graven images might claim God's praise for themselves against his will and resistance. For that is as inconsistent with the wisdom of God as the other is with his power. But in truth that reason is worthless. For all worshippers of graven images persuade themselves that God has in some way shared his glory with the very images they worship; otherwise they would not think them worthy of religious worship.

units.la: V. Præterea quoties negatio præfigitur verbo Dandi, toties, si negatur permissio, negatur etiam, immò fortius, datio ; ut patet ex loco laudato ps. 16. Nam si eo loco Deus negat, se permissurum ut sanctus suus corrumpatur, multò magis negat, se eum corrupturum. Si igitur negat hoc loco se permissurum ut alter habeat gloriam suam, multò magis negat se alteri gloriam suam daturum. Alioqui huiusmodi propositiones magis falsæ essent quàm veræ: proprie enim loquendo falsæ essent, improprie tantùm veræ: Atque horum verborum, Non dabo gloriam meam alteri, sensus esset, Ego dabo gloriam meam alteri, sed non permittam ut alter gloriam meam habeat, qui-sensus non modò verbis esset contrarius, sed ipse secum pugnaret.
units.tr: V. Moreover, whenever a negation is placed before the verb "to give", then if permission is denied, giving is denied as well, and indeed more strongly, as is clear from the passage cited, Psalm 16. For if in that place God denies that he will permit his holy one to be corrupted, he much more denies that he will corrupt him. So if in this place he denies that he will permit another to have his glory, he much more denies that he will give his glory to another. Otherwise such propositions would be more false than true: properly speaking they would be false, and only improperly true. And the sense of these words, I will not give my glory to another, would be: I will give my glory to another, but I will not permit another to have my glory. This sense would not only contradict the words but would contradict itself.

units.la: VI. Huc accedit quod sumendo verbum Dandi sensu positiuo, ut significat dationem, verissima est propositio Dei, Non dabo gloriam meam alteri. Nullus enim unquam extitit aut extabit, cui Deus dederit aut daturus sit gloriam suam, vel ad momentum, præter unum Christum, quem contendimus alterum non esse, &, nisi vehementer fallor, certis argumentis probamus. Sensu verò permissiuo si verbum Dandi accipitur, propositio haud æquè vera videtur, passus enim est Deus jam inde à mundi initio, usque ad hoc tempus, ut diabolus divinos sibi arrogaret honores, & idola ac sculptilia religiosè colerentur à plurimis gentibus.
units.tr: VI. In addition, if the verb "to give" is taken in its positive sense, as meaning a giving, the statement of God, "I will not give my glory to another," is entirely true. For no one has ever existed, or ever will exist, to whom God has given or will give his glory, even for a moment, except Christ alone. We contend that Christ is not "another," and, unless I am greatly mistaken, we prove this by certain arguments. But if the verb "to give" is taken in a permissive sense, the proposition does not seem equally true. From the beginning of the world until now, God has allowed the devil to claim divine honours for himself, and has allowed idols and graven images to be religiously worshipped by very many nations.

units.la: VII. Tandem confugit Socinus ad tertiam Responsionem. Præterea, inquit, quidquid gloriæ Deum Christo dedisse, & ad quamcunque sui æqualitatem eum euexisse dicamus; agnoscimus tamen, gloriam, quæ ipsius Dei propria est, Christo ab ipso nec datam nec permissam fuisse. Ut scilicet, Christus omnis salutis omniumque bonorum primus auctor & fons habeatur. Sibi enim hanc gloriam Deum integram penitus reseruasse affirmamus. Egregia responsio! Quasi vero Deus negaret his duobus Esaiæ locis se daturum alteri istam suam gloriam, quòd sit primus auctor & fons salutis & omnium bonorum, quam gloriam sole meridiano clarius est, adeò alteri communicari non posse, ut sese ipsa eius datio apertis-sima contradictione implicet! Quis unquam talem gloriam tribuit sculptili? Aut putavit alteri dari posse à Deo? Aut non videt implicari contradictionem si dicatur dari? Quomodo enim maximorum bonorum ab alio sibi benignè datorum acceptor, posset esse primus auctor & fons seu dator omnium bonorum? Facit igitur hæc responsio Deum frustrà, sine occasione, sine fructu, bis id clamantem & sanctè affirmantem, quod à nemine in dubium aut vocatum est, aut vocari potuit vnquam. Deinde vocis gloriæ significationem ita restringit, vt non putem vllum extare Scripturæ locum, in quo ita restrictè & circunciscè accipi debeat.
units.tr: VII. Finally, Socinus takes refuge in a third reply. "Moreover," he says, "whatever glory we say God gave to Christ, and however far we say he raised him to equality with himself, we nonetheless acknowledge that the glory which is proper to God himself was neither given nor permitted to Christ by him. Namely, that Christ may be regarded as the first author and fount of all salvation and of all good things. For we affirm that God has kept this glory entirely whole for himself." An excellent reply! As if God, in these two passages of Isaiah, were denying that he would give to another that glory of his, because he is the first author and fount of salvation and of all good things, a glory clearer than the noonday sun, and so incapable of being shared with another that its giving would involve itself in the most obvious contradiction! Who has ever ascribed such glory to a graven image? Or thought that it could be given to another by God? Or does he not see that a contradiction is involved if it is said to be given? For how could one who receives the greatest goods graciously given by another be the first author and fount, or giver, of all good things? So this reply makes God speak in vain, without occasion and without purpose, crying out and solemnly affirming twice what no one has ever called, or could ever call, into doubt. Further, it restricts the meaning of the word "glory" so narrowly that I do not think there is any passage of Scripture in which it ought to be understood in such a restricted and confined way.

units.la: VIII. Sed missa ista responsione, quæ vix digna videtur vlla refutatione, consideremus quo consilio id Deus pronunciare voluerit. Esai. 42. 8. Hoc dixit Deus, cum de Christo loqueretur, vt patet ex versibus antecedentibus & consequentibus, quorsum? Nisi, ne putaretur Christus à Deo ibi loquente tota essentia diuersus, sed potius vnus idemque cum eo Deus? Id quod potest colligi ex V. [?] sequente, Priora ecce venerunt, & nona ego annuncio &c. Cuius enim fuit noua annunciare, nisi Christi, qui est ὁ λόγος [?]? Nec non ex V. 13. Dominus sicut fortis egredietur, & sicut vir bellicosus excitabit zelum, vociferabitur, & clamabit, super inimicos suos roborabitur. Quis enim sicut vir fortis & bellicosus egressus est, vt aduersus omnes Dei & Ecclesiæ hostes pugnaret? Quis eos omnes vicit? Quis rursus egredietur, vt eos aboleat, & perdat in æternum? Is profectò est Christus, teste toto Euangelio. Nec obstat nomen Domini seu Iehouæ, quo apud Esaiam appellatur. Id enim nomen conuenire Christo, & jam aliquoties probauimus, & ex professo probaturi sumus hac sectione, Deo dante, ad locum Ierem. 23. 6.
units.tr: VIII. But setting aside that reply, which hardly seems worth any refutation, let us consider with what purpose God wished to pronounce this. Isaiah 42:8. God said this while speaking of Christ, as is clear from the verses before and after. With what purpose? Surely so that Christ should not be thought, while God is speaking there, to be wholly different in essence from God, but rather that God and Christ are one and the same? This can be gathered from the following verse, "Behold, the former things have come, and new things I declare," etc. For whose was it to announce new things, if not Christ's, who is the Word [ὁ λόγος]? Likewise from v. 13: "The Lord shall go forth like a mighty man, and like a man of war he shall stir up zeal; he shall cry out and shout; he shall prevail against his enemies." For who has gone forth like a mighty and warlike man to fight against all the enemies of God and the Church? Who has conquered them all? Who will go forth again to destroy them and bring them to nothing for ever? That is certainly Christ, as the whole Gospel bears witness. Nor does the name of the Lord, or Jehovah, by which he is called in Isaiah, stand in the way. For we have already proved on several occasions that this name belongs to Christ, and by God's help we shall prove it expressly in this section, at Jeremiah 23:6.

units.la: IX. Cur etiam illud addit, & laudem meam sculptilibus, nisi vt idololatris, & sculptilium cultoribus omnem excusationem adimat? solent enim idololatræ, præsertim Noui Testamenti temporibus, facto suo obtendere Dei voluntatem, qui scilicet rebus illis, quas colunt, gloriam suam aliqua ex parte dederit, easque ea ratione fecerit adoratione vel veneratione dignas. Quem colorem Deus, de tempore Noui Testamenti verba faciens, vt illis detrahat, clamat & inculcat, se non esse gloriam suam alteri daturum: Ac proinde non esse audiendos eos, qui beatam Virginem, vel Sanctos mortuos, vel Angelos, vel sculptilia, vel aliam vllam rem, quæ non sit Deus, hoc obtentu colunt, quasi Deus illi gloriam suam dedisset. Hoc si non admittunt, Aduersarij, dicant igitur nobis, quo consilio Deus id clamauit, & inculc[?]auit, & quem vsum id habere possit, aut debeat?
units.tr: IX. Why does he also add, "and my praise to graven images," except to strip idolaters and worshippers of graven images of every excuse? For idolaters, especially in the times of the New Testament, are wont to pretend, by their deed, that this is the will of God, who, they suppose, has given some part of his glory to the things they worship, and so made them worthy of adoration or veneration. Speaking of the time of the New Testament, God cries out and presses upon them this pretext in order to take it away from them: he will not give his glory to another. Therefore those who worship the Blessed Virgin, or dead saints, or angels, or graven images, or any other thing which is not God, under this pretence, as though God had given his glory to them, are not to be listened to. If our opponents do not admit this, let them tell us what purpose God had in crying out and pressing this point, and what use it can or ought to have.

units.la: X. Esaiæ autem 48. 11. locus sic habet, Propter me, propter me faciam, ne prophanetur nomen meum, & gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Loquitur de liberatione è carnali & spirituali Babylone. Vel igitur significat, se id facturum propter se duntaxat, non autem propter populi sui, (cuius incredulitatem & cordis duritiem eo loco exaggerat) aut alterius alicuius, iustitiam vel merita; Hanc enim gloriam ad se unum pertinere, ac sibi soli reservari oportere, ut sit simul, & is qui servat, & is propter quem servat: quæ gloria ad Christum maximè proprie pertinet. Vel, si id non significat, dicant nobis, quæso, Adversarij, quæ sit Dei sententia eo loco. Quamcunque enim aliam excogitaverint, ea, nisi vehementer fallor, aut non congruet cum verbis Dei, aut pugnabit cum illis tribus Socini responsionibus, quas jam refutavimus.
units.tr: X. Now the passage of Isaiah 48:11 reads: "For my own sake, for my own sake will I do it, lest my name be profaned; and my glory I will not give to another." It speaks of the deliverance from carnal and spiritual Babylon. Either it signifies that God will do this for his own sake alone, and not for the sake of his people (whose unbelief and hardness of heart he magnifies in that place), or for the righteousness or merits of some other person. For this glory belongs to him alone and ought to be reserved for himself alone, so that he may be at once both the one who saves and the one for whose sake he saves. This glory belongs most properly to Christ. Or, if it does not signify this, let our opponents tell us, I beg, what the opinion of God is in that place. For whatever other meaning they devise, unless I am greatly mistaken, either it will not agree with the words of God, or it will clash with those three replies of Socinus which we have already refuted.

units.la: XI. Cæterum cum Deus testatur, se gloriam suam alteri non daturum, nemo est, opinor, qui non intellegat gloriam sicam[?] tum in laude, honore, cultu, adoratione, Deo debitis, tum in virtutibus gloriosissimis, ob quas cultus eiusmodi Deo debetur. Quod observo, ne quis nobis objiciat quosdam Scripturæ locos, in quibus Deus dicitur credentibus in Christum gloriam suam daturus, hoc est, salutem seu vitam æternam, quæ gloria Dei vocatur, quoniam, & præstantissima est, & Deus est illius autor, & dator.
units.tr: XI. Moreover, since God testifies that he will not give his glory to another, there is, I think, no one who does not understand that glory to consist both in the praise, honour, worship and adoration owed to God, and in the most glorious virtues on account of which such worship is owed to God. I note this so that no one may object to us certain passages of Scripture in which God is said to give his glory to those who believe in Christ, that is, salvation or eternal life, which is called the glory of God, since it is most excellent and God is its author and giver.

units.la: DISPUTATIO VIGESIMA SEPTIMA
units.tr: DISPUTATIO VIGESIMA SEPTIMA

units.la: De Arg. XXVII. Ex locis Exod. 20. 3. Esai. 43. 2. & 44. 6. & 45. 5. 14. 21. 22. & 46. 9. &c. in quibus Deus Israëlis, aut vetat alium haberi pro Deo, aut negat esse alium Deum.
units.tr: Argument 27, from Exodus 20:3, Isaiah 43:2, 44:6, 45:5, 14, 21, 22, 46:9, etc., in which the God of Israel either forbids anyone to be regarded as God, or denies that there is another God.

units.la: I. OMNIA ista loca, & similia, si qua sunt, visum est in hanc unam disputationem conferre, quòd eandem ferè vim probandi habeant. Ex primo decalogi præcepto, Non halebis Deos alienos coram me, hoc duco Argumentum.
units.tr: I. It has seemed best to bring all these passages, and any similar ones, into this one disputation, since they have almost the same force in proving the point. From the first precept of the Decalogue, You shall have no other gods before me, I draw this argument.

units.la: Nullus Deus habendus est pro Deo praeter Deum Israëlis, au-torem legis.
units.tr: No one is to be held as God except the God of Israel, the author of the law.

units.la: Atqui Christus habendus est pro Deo. Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis. Minor est in confesso. Major nititur illo praecepto, quod Aduersarij in sua Catechesi his verbis exponunt, Quid vero hoc praeceptum continet? Haec duo: Primum, quod Deus pro nostro Deo habendus sit, & is diuino cultu & honore à nobis sit afficiendus. Deinde, quod nullus alius praeter eum sit pro nostro Deo habendus, nec diuino cultu & honore afficiendus. Similiter Crellius, Non erit tibi Elohim (id est Dy) aliy, hoc est, Non erit tibi Deus alius Optimè: In textu enim hebraeo, non est זרים aut נכרים alienos, sed אחרים alios.
units.tr: But Christ is to be held as God. Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The minor premise is admitted. The major rests on that precept, which our opponents in their Catechism explain in these words: What, then, does this precept contain? These two things: first, that God is to be held as our God and is to be honoured and worshipped by us with divine worship. Then, that no one else besides him is to be held as our God, nor honoured with divine worship. Likewise Crellius: There shall not be to you Elohim (that is, God) other, that is, there shall not be to you another God. Rightly so: for in the Hebrew text the word is not זרים or נכרים [strangers], foreign, but אחרים [others], other.

units.la: II. Argumentum videtur insolubile. Conantur tamen aliquid respondere. Catechesis ipsorum hanc quaestionem proponit, Ea vero additione quod Christum pro Deo agnoscere, & eum cultu prosequi diuino teneamur, nonne hoc praeceptum prorsus immutatur? Respondet, Nequaquam ipsum praeceptum immutatur: omnis enim qui Christo exhibetur cultus in Dei Patris gloriam redundat. Verum ipsius ratio & modus nonnihil immutatus est. Etenim ante Christum immediatè tantum, at sub Christo etiam mediatè Deus colitur. Sed haec responsio ipso praecepto refellitur. Nam cum Deus vetat alium haberi pro Deo diuinoque cultu affici, vetat eo ipso se coli mediante cultu alterius Dei.
units.tr: II. The argument seems insoluble, yet they try to offer some answer. Their Catechism puts this question: But by the addition that we are bound to acknowledge Christ as God and to honour him with divine worship, is not this precept altogether changed? It replies: The precept itself is in no way changed: for every worship offered to Christ redounds to the glory of God the Father. Yet its manner and mode have been somewhat changed. For before Christ God was worshipped immediately only, but under Christ he is worshipped also mediately. But this answer is refuted by the precept itself. For when God forbids anyone to be held as God and to be honoured with divine worship, he thereby forbids himself to be worshipped through the worship of another god.

units.la: III. Addit, Praterea cum ea lex vetet, ne deos alienos habeamus coram Deo. Christus vero Deus alienus non sit; sed in eo ipso cultu, qui ipsi exhibetur, Deo sit subordinatus, apparet legem nullo modo mutari, cum subordinata non pugnent. Si nititur voce alieni, pugnat ipsa secum, & cum textu hebraeo, vt jam ostendi, & cum officio hominis pij, cuius est legem Dei summa cum fide & reuerentia tractare, neque eius verba aut mutare, aut parte significationis mutilare. Dat etiam latebram idololatris, in quam se conjiciant si hoc praecepto vrgeantur, colere enim se alios quidem Deos fatebuntur, at non alienos. Nescio etiam an Deus non modo numero, sed specie, immo toto genere, immo plusquam genere differens à Deo Israelis, non debeat aut possit pro alieno haberi?
units.tr: III. They add: Moreover, since that law forbids us to have other gods before God. But Christ is not another god; and since he is subordinate to God in that very worship which is offered to him, it appears that the law is not changed in any way, since subordination does not conflict with it. If they rely on the word other, it contradicts itself, and the Hebrew text, as I have already shown, and the duty of a godly man, whose task is to handle God's law with the utmost faith and reverence, and neither to change its words nor to mutilate their meaning in part. It also gives a hiding place to idolaters, into which they may retreat if pressed by this precept: for they will admit that they worship other gods, but not other gods in the sense of strange ones. I also wonder whether God, differing not merely in number but in kind, indeed in whole genus, indeed more than in genus, from the God of Israel, ought not, or cannot, be held as other?

units.la: IV. Responsio igitur est, Deum Israelis prohibere hoc praecepto, ne habeamus alios Deos ipsi non subordinatos, non verò ne habeamus alios Deos, modò sint ipsi subordinati, & cultus eorum in ipsius gloriam redundet. Quæ interpretatio primùm in[?] vocis alius significationem ita decurtat, ut non sit alius quicunque est subordinatus. Si Rex ita subditos suos alloqueretur, Ego sum Rex vester. Non habebitis alium regem quoad vixero, eamque legem curaret æri incidi. Aut si maritus diceret uxori, non habebis alium virum me viuente. Num id accipiendum esset duntaxat de alio non subordinato? Eo etiam illa interpretatio refellitur, quod durante fœdere legali nullus fuit eiusmodi subordinationi deorum locus; sed debuit lex illa ab Israëlitis, quibus lata fuit, absque eiusmodi distinctione simpliciter accipi: consilium enim Legislatoris fuit, ne quem alium sive subordinatum, sive non subordinatum, pro Deo haberent toto illo tempore. Sensus autem legis qualis sit, ex eo maximè tempore intelligi debet, cum fertur, & cum viget maximè.
units.tr: IV. The answer, therefore, is that the God of Israel forbids by this precept that we have other gods who are not subordinate to him, but not that we have other gods, provided they are subordinate to him and their worship redounds to his glory. This interpretation, first, cuts down the meaning of the word other so that it does not mean any being at all that is subordinate. If a king addressed his subjects thus: I am your king. You shall have no other king as long as I live, and had this law engraved on bronze, would it have to be understood only of another king who is not subordinate? This interpretation is also refuted by the fact that, while the legal covenant endured, there was no place for such a subordination of gods; that law had to be taken by the Israelites, to whom it was given, simply, without any such distinction. For the purpose of the Lawgiver was that they should hold no other god, subordinate or not, as God during that whole period. Moreover, the sense of a law ought to be understood above all from the time when it is given and when it is most in force.

units.la: V. Præterea, Si primum præceptum recipit eiusmodi glossema, causam non video, cur secundum præceptum non possit eodem modo accipi, Non facies tibi sculptile &c, Nisi quod sit mihi subordinatum, & cuius cultus in meam gloriam redundet, id quod erit latam portam aperire idololatriæ. Deinde eodem præcepto Deus se Zelotypum esse profitetur, quo elogio se marito comparat, populum suum uxori, cultum suum legitimæ viri & uxoris conjunctioni, cultum aliorum Deorum & simulachrorum adulterio: quæ similitudo ab ipso Deo per Prophetas exponitur multis locis: ac quàm maritorum tam deorum subordinationem excludit.
units.tr: V. Besides, if the first precept admits such a gloss, I do not see why the second precept cannot be taken in the same way: You shall not make for yourself a graven image, etc., except that it be subordinate to me and its worship redound to my glory. This would open a wide door to idolatry. Further, in the same precept God declares himself a jealous God, a title by which he compares himself to a husband, his people to a wife, his worship to the lawful union of husband and wife, and the worship of other gods to adultery. This likeness God himself explains in many places through the prophets, and it excludes the subordination of gods just as much as that of husbands.

units.la: VI. His accedit, quod hoc primum præceptum morale est, ac legis naturæ, fundatum in unitate naturæ Dei. Cum enim plures dij nec sint, nec esse possint, sive subordinati, sive coordinati, perpetua est lex naturæ, plures Deos, sive subordinati sive coordinati dicantur esse, coli non debere. Jam autem plures naturas seu essentias divinas non esse, nec esse posse, cum omnes conficeantur, etiam ipsi Adversarij, nihil est opus ut probemus. Certè si plures esse possent, possent esse plures, immò innumerabiles dij, & cum in æternis idem sit esse & posse, revera essent. Cum igitur implicet contradictionem esse eum vere & proprie Deum qui præditus non est natura divina, (tam certè quàm esse verè & proprie hominem qui prædi[?]tus non est natura humana) Nec possint esse plures naturæ diuinæ proprie sic dictæ siue coordinatæ, vt dixi, siue subordinatæ, perspicuum est, falsam esse distinctionem & limitationem, quàm Aduersarij maximo isti mandato pro ingenio aptare frustrà conantur, Non esse habendos alios deos, qui quidem scilicet non sint Deo Israëlis subordinati.
units.tr: VI. To this is added that this first precept is moral and belongs to the law of nature, grounded in the unity of the nature of God. For since there are not, and cannot be, several gods, whether subordinate or coordinate, it is a perpetual law of nature that several gods, whether they are said to be subordinate or coordinate, ought not to be worshipped. Now that there are not, and cannot be, several divine natures or essences, since all, even our opponents themselves, concede this, there is no need for us to prove. Certainly, if several could exist, they could be several, indeed innumerable gods, and since in eternal things being and being able are the same, they would really be such. Therefore, since it implies a contradiction that one should be truly and properly God who is not endowed with the divine nature (just as surely as it is a contradiction to be truly and properly a man who is not endowed with human nature), and since there cannot be several divine natures properly so called, whether coordinate, as I have said, or subordinate, it is plain that the distinction and limitation which our opponents vainly try to fit to that great command, namely that we should not have other gods who are not subordinate to the God of Israel, is false.

units.la: VII. Hic mirari subit acumen Aduersariorum, qui, cum negent duas esse naturas diuinas, contendunt tamen duos esse Deos verè & proprie sic dictos. Atque ita multiplicant Deos non multiplicata deitate. Deitas enim, opinor, est essentia Dei. Multiplicant etiam attributa diuina, vitam, sapientiam, potentiam seu robur, autoritatem, cultum &c, & tamen non multiplicant naturam seu essentiam diuinam cuius sunt propria. Hæc tantùm obiter attingo hoc loco, id enim vnum toto hoc libro quærimus, vtri melius cum oraculis Scripturæ conueniat, nostræ an Aduersariorum sententiæ? Quæ autem cum Scriptura congruere reperietur, eadem sine dubio deprehendetur etiam rectæ rationi consentanea.
units.tr: VII. Here one is moved to wonder at the subtlety of our opponents, who, while denying that there are two divine natures, nevertheless contend that there are two gods truly and properly so called. Thus they multiply gods without multiplying the deity. For deity, I suppose, is the essence of God. They also multiply the divine attributes, life, wisdom, power or strength, authority, worship, and so on, and yet they do not multiply the divine nature or essence of which these are the properties. I touch on these matters only in passing here, for in this whole book we seek only one thing: which view agrees better with the oracles of Scripture, ours or that of our opponents? And whatever is found to agree with Scripture will undoubtedly also be found to be consonant with sound reason.

units.la: VIII. Instat VVolkelius, Neque enim, inquit, Deus hoc præcepto potestatem sibi ipsi eripuit, eum, quem velit, nobis præficiendi & honorem cum eo suum communicandi: cum hac ipsa imperij ac potestatis suprema, quam hoc præcepto sibi uni asserit, pars sit maxima: sed populum tantùm obligauit, ne is pro suo arbitrio diuinum cultum cuiquam exhiberet: huic, inquam, nem sibi[?], legem istam tulit. Atqui omnis potestatis in cœlo & in terra, summiqué in res omnes, se uno excepto, imperij, & virtutum diuinarum ad illud imperium exercendum necessariarum communicatio, absque communicatione essentiæ diuinæ, nobis videtur, Primùm contradictionem implicare: Deinde pugnare cum declaratione voluntatis Dei se gloriam suam daturum alteri pernegantis: Tum etiam huic ipsi præcepto repugnare: ferendo enim hanc perpetuam legem, ne quem alium habeamus pro Deo, non obscurè significauit, se alium Deum nobis neque præfecisse, neque præfecturum vnquam. Cum enim sic loquitur, vt eum hoc præcepto loquentem facit Volkelius, Ita me colas, vt omnes alios Deos valere iubeas. Is enim sum, qui riualem, pati ferreque minimè possum; ideoque fieri nullo pacto potest, vt vna mecum alios Deos colas ac reuerearis[?], latus profecto significat, se nolle populum suum ad alium Deum colendum vllo tempore obligare. Denique ; non habebis alium Deum coram me , & , habebis alium Deum coram me , si sunt opposita præcepta , si alterum euertit alterum, fatendum est, aut Christum non esse alium à Deo Israëlis Deum, aut eius Euangelio primum & maximum & perpetuum legis naturæ & moralis præceptum fuisse abrogatum. Hoc cum sit absurdum , illud ve-rum esse necesse est. Deus quidem certè legem populo suo, non sibi, tulit ; sed si voluit ea lege populum suum perpetuò obligare, voluit etiam nihil vnquam facere, quod legi illi derogaret: &, si populus Dei tenetur omni tempore præceptum istud obseruare, tenetur etiam omni tempore alium nullum pro Deo habere, vel colere.
units.tr: VIII. Wolzogen presses the point: For God, he says, has not by this precept taken away from himself the power of setting over us whom he wills and of sharing his honour with him, since this very supreme command and power, which by this precept he claims for himself alone, is the greatest part of it; but he has bound only the people, that they should not on their own judgement give divine worship to anyone. To this, I say, he gave that law. But the communication of all power in heaven and on earth, and of supreme command over all things, except himself alone, and of the divine virtues necessary for exercising that command, without communication of the divine essence, seems to us, first, to imply a contradiction. Second, it conflicts with the declaration of God's will that he will not give his glory to another. Third, it also opposes this very precept: for in giving this perpetual law, that we should have no other as God, he has clearly signified that he has neither set over us, nor will ever set over us, another god. For when he speaks thus, as Volkelius makes him speak in this precept: Worship me in such a way that you bid all other gods farewell. For I am the one who cannot bear or endure a rival; therefore it cannot in any way happen that you worship and revere other gods along with me, he certainly signifies that he is unwilling to bind his people at any time to worship another God. Finally, you shall not have another God before me and you shall have another God before me: if these are opposed precepts, if one overturns the other, we must confess either that Christ is not another God than the God of Israel, or that the first and greatest and perpetual precept of the law of nature and of morality has been abrogated by his Gospel. Since the latter is absurd, the former must be true. God indeed gave the law to his people, not to himself; but if he willed to bind his people perpetually by that law, he also willed never to do anything that would derogate from that law; and if the people of God is bound at all times to observe that precept, it is bound at all times to hold and worship no other as God.

units.la: IX. Nunc alia loca percurramus , in quibus Deus Israëlis negat vllum alium esse, præter se, Deum. Esai. 43. 10. Ante me non est formatus Deus, & post me non erit. Quomodo hoc verum est, si Christus alius est ab eo, qui sic loquitur, & post eum formatus Deus? V. 11. Ego sum, Ego sum Dominus, & non est præterme seruator. Si nullus est Seruator, præter Deum Israëlis, & Christus est maximè proprie loquendo Seruator, Certè Christus est Deus Israëlis. Alioqui sepositio discrimine originis, sine quo Patris & Filij distinctio nequit consistere, ita diuideretur Seruatoris nomen & gloria inter Deum Israëlis & alium Deum, vt hic fi-bi Seruatoris nomen & laudem, tanquam magis propria, vendicaret. De nomine res clara est. Iesus enim Seruatorem significat. Ad rem quod attinet, hic vnus proprie venit vt seruaret peccatores. Quam ad rem si Sacerdote, sacerdotio, victima, & sacrificio opus fuit, is solus Sacerdos & victima fuit, & sacrificium, quo peccata nostra purgauit, obtulit. Si prædicatione Euangelij, is per semetipsum primò, deinde per Apostolos & legatos suos Euangelium annunciauit. Si victoria opus fuit, is solus & pug-nauit & vicit. Si satisfactione, (quam necessariam prorsus suisse, quicquid Socinus & Crellius reclamant, mihi est certissimum) solus pro nobis satisfecit, & pretioso sanguine suo nos redemit. Si sapientia , si virtute seu potentia, si authoritate, si Charitate &c seruari nos oportuit, eas tantas Christus exeruit & exeret, vt maiores concipi animo nequeant. Si mortui e sepulchris excitandi sunt, & cum viuentibus judicandi, suscitabit eos omnes & judicabit Christus. Si Denique laus & honor & cultus, qui ipsi debetur, spectetur, tantus est, ut major esse non possit. Qui potest[?] igitur verum est; nullum esse Servatorem praeter Deum Israelis, si alius plusquam toto genere ab ipso diversus Servator est proprie immo maxime proprie, & quidem eius salutis respectu, quæ omnium maxime salus dici meretur? Quis credat Deum Israelis, qui toties clamavit se Zelotypum esse, nec daturum gloriam suam alteri, & ut vera[?] loquar, gloriatus est, præter se unum, Servatorem esse neminem, voluisse gloriam & nomen Servatoris alteri tradere, & quidem in æternum.
units.tr: IX. Let us now run through the other passages in which God of Israel denies that there is any other God besides himself. Isaiah 43:10: "Before me there was no God formed, and after me there shall be none." How can this be true if Christ is other than the one who speaks thus, and a God formed after him? V. 11: "I am, I am the Lord, and there is no saviour beside me." If there is no Saviour besides the God of Israel, and Christ is most properly speaking the Saviour, then surely Christ is the God of Israel. Otherwise, setting aside the distinction of origin, without which the distinction between Father and Son cannot stand, the name and glory of Saviour would be so divided between the God of Israel and another God that this other would claim the name and praise of Saviour for himself as being more properly his. As for the name, the matter is clear: Jesus means Saviour. As for the thing itself, this one alone came properly to save sinners. If a priest, priesthood, victim and sacrifice were needed for this purpose, he alone was both priest and victim, and he offered the sacrifice by which he cleansed our sins. If the preaching of the Gospel was needed, he himself first announced it in person, and then through his apostles and legates. If victory was needed, he alone both fought and conquered. If satisfaction was needed (which was altogether necessary, whatever Socinus and Crellius protest; this is most certain to me), he alone satisfied for us and redeemed us with his precious blood. If wisdom, virtue or power, authority, charity, etc., were needed for our salvation, Christ has displayed and will display them so greatly that they cannot be conceived greater. If the dead are to be raised from their graves and judged along with the living, Christ will raise them all and judge them. Finally, if the praise, honour and worship due to God be considered, it is so great that it cannot be greater. How, then, can it be true that there is no Saviour besides the God of Israel, if another Saviour, wholly different from him in nature, is truly, indeed most properly, a Saviour, and that with respect to that salvation which most deserves to be called salvation above all? Who would believe that the God of Israel, who so often declared himself jealous and that he would not give his glory to another, and who, to speak truly, boasted that there is no Saviour beside him alone, wished to hand over the glory and name of Saviour to another, and that for ever?

units.la: X. Quid quod attentius introspicienti hunc locum, qui in eo loquitur, Christus esse videtur? Nam, si antecedentia verba spectes, scopus eius fuit, ut sciatis, inquit, & credatis mihi, & intelligatis quod ego sum. Idem fuit scopus Christi, Nunc, inquit Ioh. 13. 19. dico vobis priusquam fiat, ut postquam factum fuerit credatis quod ego sum. Et Ioh. 8. 24. Si enim non credideritis quod ego sum, morsemini in peccatis vestris & V. 28.[?] Tunc cognoscetis quod ego sum. In eum autem finem testes instituit auditores seu discipulos suos, vos testes mei, dicit Dominus, & servus meus quem elegi. Christus similiter testes sibi comparavit Iohannem Baptistam, Apostolos, & discipulos suos quos elegit Ioh. 15. 26. 27. Act. 1. 22. & 10. 41. Quod si quis nobis objiciat verbis illis, & servus meus quem elegi, Christum significari, non valde repugnabo. Nihil enim prohibet, eundem diverso respectu dominum suiipsius & servum dici; Dominum quatenus est Deus, servum quatenus est homo. Sic enim merus homo, quia constat ex animo & corpore, dicitur animi imperio, corporis servitio uti, ac ne recedam à Scriptura, corpus eius cuius est pars, vocatur tabernaculum 2. Cor. 5. 4. & 2. Petr. 1. 13. 14. & vas 1. Thess. 4. 4. & in unoquoque homine duo distinguntur homines, unus internus alter externus, ille renovatur dum hic corrumpitur 2. Cor. 4. 16. & denique qui facit peccatum servus peccati dicitur Ioh. 8. 34. Rom. 6. 16. minus certè proprie quàm si dicatur Christus, quatenus est homo, servus ipsius quatenus est Deus.
units.tr: X. Moreover, if one looks more carefully into this passage, does it not seem to be about Christ, who is speaking in it? For if you look at the preceding words, its purpose is "that you may know," he says, "and believe me, and understand that I am." This was also the purpose of Christ: "Now," he says, John 13:19, "I tell you before it comes to pass, that when it has come to pass you may believe that I am." And John 8:24: "For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins;" and v. 28: "Then you will know that I am." To this end he appointed as witnesses his hearers or disciples: "You are my witnesses," says the Lord, "and my servant whom I have chosen." Christ likewise gathered as witnesses John the Baptist, the apostles and his disciples whom he chose: John 15:26-27; Acts 1:22; 10:41. But if anyone objects to us that by the words "and my servant whom I have chosen" Christ is meant, I will not strongly resist. For nothing prevents the same person from being called lord and servant of himself in different respects: lord inasmuch as he is God, servant inasmuch as he is man. Thus a mere man, because he consists of soul and body, is said to use the rule of the soul and the service of the body; and, not to depart from Scripture, the body of the one of whom it is a part is called a "tabernacle" (2 Cor. 5:4; 2 Pet. 1:13-14) and a "vessel" (1 Thess. 4:4); and in every man two men are distinguished, one inward and the other outward, the one renewed while the other decays (2 Cor. 4:16); and finally, he who commits sin is called a slave of sin (John 8:34; Rom. 6:16). This is certainly said less properly than if one should say that Christ, inasmuch as he is man, is the servant of himself inasmuch as he is God.

units.la: XI. Sequentia verba idem innuunt, Ego annunciavi, & salvavi, atque audire feci. Conveniunt enim magis proprie Filio quam Patri. Hic enim nec nuntius fuit, nec annunciavit & servavit, nisi quatenus id fecisse dici potest, quod Filius fecit. Sic porrò annunciavit & servavit, ut tamen à multis agnitus non fuerit. Idquod ex antecedentibus liquet, vt sciatis, & credatis mihi, & intelligatis quod ego sum: & sequentibus, vos testes mei, dicit Dominus, quod ego sum Deus. Hoc egregiè conuenire Filio, cum ipsius Euangelium, tum experientia docet. Subnectit autem rationes duas, vnam ab antiquitate sua, alteram à potentia: etiam, inquit, antequam dies esset, (vel, ex quo dies fuit) Ego sum, & non est qui de manu mea eruere possit. Operabor, & quis auertet? posterior conuenit Christo: habet enim omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra: necnon prior, vt probatum est superiore libro. Si igitur duae istae rationes bonae sunt (Sunt autem sine dubio optimae) necesse est Christum esse Deum, hoc est, praeditum essentia diuina.
units.tr: XI. "The following words point to the same thing: I have announced, and I have saved, and I have caused to be heard." For they belong more properly to the Son than to the Father. For he was not a messenger, nor did he announce and save, except insofar as that can be said to be done which the Son did. He announced and saved in such a way, however, that he was not acknowledged by many. This is clear from what precedes: "that you may know, and believe me, and understand that I am;" and from what follows: "you are my witnesses, says the Lord, that I am God." That this agrees splendidly with the Son is taught both by his Gospel and by experience. He adds, moreover, two reasons, one from his antiquity and the other from his power: "Even," he says, "before the day was (or, from the time the day was), I am; and there is none who can snatch out of my hand. I will work, and who will turn it back?" The latter agrees with Christ, for he has all power in heaven and on earth; and the former, as has been proved in the previous book. If therefore these two reasons are good (and they are without doubt most excellent), it is necessary that Christ is God, that is, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Adde quod vix vnquam in Ecclesia vocata est in dubium Dei Patris aut diuinitas, aut antiquitas, aut potentia, vt ad eam probandam opus fuerit[?] testibus & argumentis. Denique Hæc ipsa verba; praeter me non est Seruator, cui melius conueniunt, quàm ei, qui cit[?] ita Seruator, vt in alio nullo fit Salus? Argumentum est huiusmodi. Ille in quo est salus, cum in alio nullo fit salus, est Seruator praeter quem nullus est seruator. Christus est ille in quo est salus, cum in alio nullo fit salus, testi-bus Petro & reliquis Apostolis Act. 4. 12, Ergo Christus est ille Seruator, praeter quem non est seruator.
units.tr: Add that the divinity, or the antiquity, or the power of God the Father has scarcely ever been called into doubt in the Church, so that witnesses and arguments would be needed to prove it. Finally, do these very words, "there is no Saviour besides me," fit anyone better than him who is a Saviour in such a way that salvation is in no other? The argument is of this kind: he in whom is salvation, since salvation is in no other, is the Saviour beside whom there is no saviour. Christ is he in whom is salvation, since salvation is in no other, as witnessed by Peter and the remaining apostles (Acts 4:12). Therefore Christ is that Saviour beside whom there is no saviour.

units.la: XII. Similia loca sunt multa apud hunc Propheram Esai. 44. 6. Ego sum primus, & ego sum nouissimus, & praeter me non est Deus, & V. 8. vos estis testes mei. Nunquid est Deus praeter me? Et Esai. 45. V. 5. Ego Dominus & non est amplius: praeter me non est Deus. Et V. 7. Ego Dominus, & non est alter & V. 14. tantùm in te est Deus, praeter quem nullus est Deus. & V. 18. Ego Dominus, & non est amplius Deus praeter me, Deus iustus & saluans non est praeter me? & V. 22. Respicite ad me, & salui eritis omnes fines terrae, quia ego sum Deus. & non est amplius. Et Esai. 46. 9. Ego sum Deus, & non est vltra Deus, & nihil est mihi simile, Quorsum toties affirmat, clamat, inculcat se Deum esse, & praeter se nullum Deum esse, & quidem cum loquitur de tempore N. Testamenti, si tempore Noui Testamenti firmiter credendum est praeter ipsum alium esse Deum tota natura ab ipso diuersum, nempe Christum, natura seu essentia nihil nisi hominem?
units.tr: XII. There are many similar passages in this prophet. Isaiah 44:6: "I am the first, and I am the last, and besides me there is no God;" and v. 8: "You are my witnesses. Is there any God besides me?" And Isaiah 45: v. 5: "I am the Lord, and there is none else; besides me there is no God;" v. 7: "I am the Lord, and there is none other;" v. 14: "Surely God is in you, and there is no God besides him;" v. 18: "I am the Lord, and there is none else, no God besides me, a just God and a saviour; there is none besides me;" and v. 22: "Look to me, and be saved, all you ends of the earth, for I am God, and there is none else." And Isaiah 46:9: "I am God, and there is no other God, and there is nothing like me." Why does he so often affirm, cry out and inculcate that he is God and that there is no God besides himself, and that too when he speaks of the time of the New Testament? If in the time of the New Testament we must firmly believe that there is another God besides him, wholly different from him in nature, namely Christ, who is by nature and essence nothing but a man?

units.la: DISPVTATIO VIGESIMA OCTAVA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION TWENTY-EIGHT.

units.la: De Arg. XXVIII. Ex Esaiae 43. 24. Seruire me fecisti in peccatis tuis &c.
units.tr: On Argument XXVIII, from Isaiah 43:24: You have made me to serve with your sins, etc.

units.la: I. PERPENDAT etiam apud se pius lector, quis hoc eodem c. 43. 24. sic loquatur, Non emisti mihi argento calamum, & adipe victimarum tuarum non inebriasti me: verumtamen seruire me fecisti in peccatis tuis, (heb. בחטאותיך quod verti potest propter peccata tua, vt Gen. 29. 18. Seruiam tibi septem annis ברחל propter Kachel) & laborare me fecisti in iniquitatibus tuis. Is enim, si Prophetam audis, est Dominus, Iehoua, vt patet ex ℣. 16. si rem spectes, quam sibi ipse tribuit, ea proprie & χρ̄ τὸ ῥητὸν[?] Christo conuenit, Patri non item. Non enim formam serui sumpsit, non seruiuit Pater, sed Filius, eoque suo seruitio seu obedientia peccata nostra deleuit. Hinc possumus ita argu-mentari.
units.tr: I. Let the pious reader also consider for himself who speaks thus in the same chapter 43:24: You have not bought me calamus with silver, nor have you filled me with the fat of your sacrifices; but you have made me to serve with your sins (Hebrew [בחטאותיך], which may be rendered on account of your sins, as in Gen. 29:18, I will serve you seven years for [ברחל] Rachel), and you have made me to labour with your iniquities. For if you listen to the Prophet, it is the Lord, Jehovah, as is clear from verse 16. If you look at the matter, which he ascribes to himself, it properly and according to the letter [κυρίως καὶ κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν] belongs to Christ, not to the Father. For it was not the Father who took the form of a servant, nor did the Father serve, but the Son, and by that service or obedience of his he blotted out our sins. From this we may argue as follows.

units.la: - Ille qui propter peccata fidelium seruiisse & laborasse dicitur Esai. 43. 24. est Dominus (Iehoua) Deus Israëlis. Christus est ille qui propter peccata fidelium seruiisse & laborasse dicitur Esai. 43.24.
units.tr: – He who is said to have served and laboured on account of the sins of the faithful, Isa. 43:24, is the Lord (Jehovah) God of Israel. Christ is he who is said to have served and laboured on account of the sins of the faithful, Isa. 43:24.

units.la: Christus igitur est Iehoua seu Deus Israëlis. Major patet ex textu Propheta. Minor ex toto Euangelio: Docet enim, vt jam dixi, Non Patrem, sed Filium, in peccatis nostris, vel propter peccata nostra, reuera seruiisse, eaque ratione nos redemisse.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is Jehovah, or the God of Israel. The major premise is plain from the text of the Prophet. The minor premise is plain from the whole Gospel: for it teaches, as I have already said, that not the Father but the Son truly served in our sins, or on account of our sins, and by that means redeemed us.

units.la: II. Respondere potest, seruiendi verbum apud Prophetam accipi non proprie, sed figurate. Ita fit, sepositis praejudi-cijs, inquiramus. Primum autem mihi explicari velim verbis proprijs, quid igitur eo verbo, seu potius ea phrasi, seruire me fecisti in peccatis, vel, propter peccata tua, fuerit significatum? Num hoc, molestiam mihi exhibuisti, molestus mihi fuisti peccatis tuis? Ita rursus locutio erit, aut figurata, aut de Christo exponenda. Num illud, valde mihi displicuisti peccatis tuis? Certè quocunque modo exponatur de Deo Patre, locutio erit eo sensu sacris autoribus inusitata. Cum igitur phrasis sit frequens in sacris literis, non est, nisi cogente necessaria ratione, sensu inusitato accipienda. Nulla autem impedit ratio quominus Deus, quàm dicitur redemisse Ecclesiam suam sanguine proprio, tam dicatur servisse pro peccatis Ecclesiæ suæ. Quàm enim ille sanguis fuit sanguis Christi, tam ista servitus fuit servitus Christi.
units.tr: II. It may be answered that the word "to serve" in the Prophet is taken not properly but figuratively. Let us inquire in this way, setting aside prejudices. But first I would like to have it explained in proper words what was signified by that word, or rather that phrase, you have made me to serve in your sins, or on account of your sins. Does it mean this: you have caused me trouble, you have been a burden to me by your sins? Then again the expression will have to be taken either figuratively or expounded of Christ. Does it mean that: you have greatly displeased me by your sins? Certainly, however it is explained of God the Father, the expression will be in a sense unusual to the sacred writers. Since, then, the phrase is frequent in the Holy Letters, it is not to be taken in an unusual sense unless compelled by necessary reason. Nor is there any reason why God, who is said to have redeemed his Church with his own blood, should not also be said to have served for the sins of his Church. For as that blood was the blood of Christ, so that service was the service of Christ.

units.la: III. Hoc eo confirmari potest, quod eo loco de fœdere gratiæ, deque redemptione spirituali, quam nobis obedientia Christi peperit, agi palam est. Meminit enim Deus redemptionis Ægyptiacæ V.[?] 16. & 17. Deinde novam pollicetur adeò illustrem, ut splendore suo superiorem illam obscurare debeat V. 18. 19. &c. Eam autem redemptionem tribus in rebus potissimum sitam esse docet, Productione viæ & aquarum per desertum V. 19. & 20. Formatione populi electi ad laudem suam V. 21. & remissione peccatorum V. 25. Ex quibus intelligitur non agi de liberatione è captiuitate Babylonica: Hæc enim, & minus fuit quàm Ægyptiaca illustris, nec in ijs rebus posita fuit, quas memoraui. Cum igitur sermo sit de redemptione spirituali, quæ per Christi servitutem seu obedientiam parta est, consentaneum est, ut per servitutem Dei servitus Christi hoc loco intelligatur.
units.tr: III. This can be confirmed by the fact that in that place it is plainly a matter of the covenant of grace and of the spiritual redemption which the obedience of Christ has procured for us. For God recalls the redemption from Egypt, vv. 16 and 17. Then he promises a new one, so illustrious that it ought to overshadow the former by its brightness, vv. 18, 19, etc. He teaches that this redemption consists chiefly in three things: the bringing forth of a way and waters through the wilderness, vv. 19 and 20; the forming of a chosen people to his praise, v. 21; and the forgiveness of sins, v. 25. From these things it is understood that the matter is not about deliverance from Babylonian captivity. For that was less illustrious than the Egyptian deliverance, and it did not consist in those things which I have mentioned. Since, then, the discourse concerns spiritual redemption, which was obtained through the servitude, or obedience, of Christ, it follows that by the service of God the service of Christ is to be understood in this place.

units.la: IV. Præterea considerandum est, quo consilio Deus neget hoc loco, cum sibi a populo suo oblata fuisse sacrificia, tum ea se illi præscripsisse. Nam vel id facit reprehendendi animo, vel alia mente. Si prius, reprehendit Iudæos, aut quod non obtulerint sacrificia, aut quod male. Neutrum dici posse videtur. Non prius illud: Nam quod in captiuitate Babylonica non dederint operam sacrificijs reprehendendi non fuerunt: id enim eis per legem Dei non licebat. Tantùm autem abest, ut arguendi fuerint ob neglecta sacrificia, ut contrà potius quòd ea pluris, quàm par erat, facerent & digni reprehensione, & procul à regno Dei fuerint. Non videntur etiam reprehendi hoc loco quòd male obtulissent. Nam si vituperarentur quod, aut alijs, aut vero quidem Deo, sed sine interna fide & pietate sacrificassent, id exprimeretur aliquo modo, & dixisset Deus, non mihi sacrificastis, sed Idolis, vt factum est ab eo Amos 5. 25. aut certè addidisset, Sed provocastis me ad Zelotypiam, aut tale quid dixisset, ex quo mens eius elucesceret. Certè non potuit magis absolutè res ipsa, hoc est, oblatio sacrificiorum negari, quam negatur hoc loco. Quid quod negat Deus disertis verbis, se jugum illud populo suo imposuisse? Non te, inquit, seruire feci in oblatione, nec te laborare feci in thure.
units.tr: IV. Besides, we must consider with what purpose God here denies that sacrifices were offered to him by his people, and also that he had prescribed them to them. For he does this either with a mind to rebuke, or with another intention. If the former, he rebukes the Jews either because they did not offer sacrifices or because they offered them badly. Neither seems possible to say. Not the former: for that they did not give attention to sacrifices during the Babylonian captivity is not a matter for rebuke, since that was not permitted them by the law of God. So far is it from being the case that they were to be accused for neglecting sacrifices, that on the contrary they were rather worthy of reproof, and far from the kingdom of God, because they made more of them than was fitting. Nor does God seem here to rebuke them for offering badly. For if he were finding fault that they had sacrificed either to others, or indeed to the true God but without inward faith and piety, this would be expressed in some way, and God would have said, you have not sacrificed to me, but to idols, as he did through Amos 5:25; or certainly he would have added, but you have provoked me to jealousy, or would have said something of that sort by which his mind would shine forth. Certainly the thing itself, that is, the offering of sacrifices, could not have been denied more absolutely than it is denied in this place. What of the fact that God denies in express words that he had imposed that yoke on his people? I did not make you serve, he says, in offering, nor make you labour in incense.

units.la: V. Quid autem sibi Deus voluerit, id facilè ex antecedentibus & sequentibus colligi potest. Si enim antecedentia spectes, Deus, vt dixi, mentione injecta liberationis ex Ægypto, liberationem similem quidem, sed multò præstantiorem promittebat. Quid autè erat conuenientius, quàm vt exposita inter vtramque illam liberationem maximè memorabili similitudine, ex qua reliquæ facilè colligi possent, discrimen quoddam insigne commemoraret, vnde reliqua deprehendi possent. Similitudinem insinuant hæc verba, Ecce ego facio noua &c, ponam viam in deserto, & flumina in solitudine. Hinc enim reliqua intelliguntur, Ægyptus vnde, Canaam quo iter fiat, Mare, sitis, fames, columna ignis & nubis, &, ne cætera percurram, fœdus. Ne igitur putarentur omnia prorsus similia futura, vtque præstantia fœderis & populi noui innuerctur[?], addit Deus, nec sibi populum illum nouum oblaturum sacrificia, oblationes, thus, &c. nec amplius in huiusmodi oblationibus cultum suum positum iri, nec se tale aliquod jugum populi sui ceruicibus impositurum. Sic enim olim populum suum è seruitute Ægyptiorum asseruerat, vt tamen eum in deserto sub Legis jugo & pædagogia in aliam seruitutem redigeret admodum operosam & molestam magna ex parte in oblationibus & sacrificijs & suffitu, aliisque id genus ceremonijs positam. Submotis igitur omnibus eiusmodi sacrificijs typicis, in eorum locum Deus id sacrificium suffecit, quod illorum corpus est, sine quo nulla est peccati expiatio. Hoc enim cum lectoris ædificatio flagitabat, cui alioqui necessitatem sacrificiorum ad peccata purganda toties in vtroque testamento inculcatam reputanti grauis scrupulus injectus fuisset, tum oppositio innuit, quam Deus inter suam & populi sui seruitutem instituit. Ego, inquit, non feci te seruire in oblatione, neque feci te laborare in thure &c, sed tu fecisti me seruire in peccatis tuis, & fecisti me laborare in iniquitatibus tuis. Palam est cum de oblationibus & sacrificijs agere, & quicquid in ea seruitij vel laboris insumendum fuisset in se unum deriuare, populo suo ad eam rem nihil præter peccata sua expianda contribuente.
units.tr: V. What God meant by this can easily be gathered from what goes before and what follows. For if you look at what precedes, God, as I said, by mentioning the deliverance from Egypt, was promising a deliverance similar indeed, but far more excellent. What was more fitting than that, between the two deliverances, he should set out a most memorable likeness from which the rest could easily be inferred, and then mention a certain notable difference by which the remaining points might be perceived? The likeness is hinted at by these words: Behold, I do a new thing, etc., I will make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert. For from this the rest are understood: Egypt whence, Canaan whither the journey is made, the Sea, thirst, hunger, the pillar of fire and cloud, and, not to run through the rest, the covenant. So that it should not be thought that all things would be altogether similar, and that the excellence of the new covenant and the new people might be indicated, God adds that that new people would not offer him sacrifices, oblations, incense, etc., nor would his worship be placed any longer in such offerings, nor would he lay any such yoke on the necks of his people. For thus he had once asserted his people from the servitude of the Egyptians, yet in the wilderness, under the yoke of the Law and its pedagogy, he had reduced them to another servitude, very laborious and burdensome, for the most part placed in offerings and sacrifices and incense and other ceremonies of that kind. Therefore, with all such typical sacrifices removed, God substituted in their place that sacrifice which is the body of them, without which there is no expiation of sin. For this the edification of the reader required, to whom, otherwise, considering the necessity of sacrifices for purging sins, which is so often inculcated in both Testaments, a heavy scruple would have been cast. Then the opposition indicates the contrast which God sets up between his own servitude and the servitude of his people. I, he says, did not make you serve in offering, nor did I make you labour in incense, etc., but you have made me serve in your sins, and you have made me labour in your iniquities. It is plain that when he speaks of offerings and sacrifices, and of whatever service or labour was to be spent on them, he takes it all upon himself alone, the people contributing nothing to that matter except their sins to be expiated.

units.la: VI. Si spe[?]tes id quod sequitur, Ego Ego ipse sum qui deleo iniquitates tuas propter me, & peccatorum tuorum non recordabor, apparet Deum oppositionem inter se & populum suum tacitè instituere hoc aut simili modo. Neque tu, neque alius quispiam, deles peccata tua, sed ego, ego, inquam, ipse sum qui ea deleo. Neque tu, neque alius quispiam, is es propter quem ea deleo, sed ego ipse is sum propter quem ea deleo: qua ratione significat se peccata ipsorum delere non propter eorum oblationes sacrificia suffitum obedientiam, sed quicquid eiusmodi ad delenda peccata necessarium est, id in se uno reperiri.
units.tr: VI. If you look at what follows, I, I myself am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins, it appears that God tacitly sets up an opposition between himself and his people in this or a similar manner. Neither you nor anyone else blots out your sins, but I, I, I say, am he who blots them out. Neither you nor anyone else is the one for whose sake I blot them out, but I myself am the one for whose sake I blot them out. By this reasoning he signifies that he does not blot out their sins on account of their offerings, sacrifices, incense, or obedience, but that whatever is necessary for blotting out sins of this kind is found in him alone.

units.la: VII. Hinc succrescit hoc argumentum. Ille qui delet peccata populi sui est Iehoua seu Deus Israëlis, non autem alius, ut patet ex verbis illis Dei, Ego Ego ipse sum qui deleo peccata tua propter me. Atqui Christus delet peccata populi sui, teste totoEuangelio. Christus igitur est Iehoua, seu Deus Israëlis. Item, Ille propter quem Deus delet peccata, est Iehoua. Christus est ille propter quem Deus delet peccata. Christus igitur est Iehoua. Major patet ex verbis ipsius Dei sibi uni utramque illam gloriam, & quod sit causa quæ delet peccata, & quod sit causa propter quam peccata delet, pariter vendicantis. Minor omnibus Christianis ita manifesta esse debet, ut confirmatione non egeat.
units.tr: VII. From this the following argument arises. He who blots out the sins of his people is Jehovah, or the God of Israel, and no other, as is clear from those words of God, I, I myself am he who blots out your sins for my own sake. But Christ blots out the sins of his people, as the whole Gospel bears witness. Christ, therefore, is Jehovah, or the God of Israel. Likewise, he for whose sake God blots out sins is Jehovah. Christ is he for whose sake God blots out sins. Christ, therefore, is Jehovah. The major premise is plain from the words of God himself, who claims both of these glories for himself alone: that he is the cause that blots out sins, and that he is the cause for whose sake he blots them out. The minor premise ought to be so evident to all Christians that it needs no confirmation.

units.la: VIII. Hanc eandem disputationem communiam alio Dei testimonio. Esa. 50. 2. Deus hanc rationem affert, cur repudium Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ renunciarit, quoniam, inquit, veni & non fuit vir, vocaui, & non fuit qui responderet. Quis autem, quæso, venit, quis vocauit, & quia eum non receperunt Iudæi rejecti sunt? Hunc Filium esse, non Patrem, totum Euangelium testatur; Ipseque etiam docet ℣. 4. Idem enim Dominus, Iehoua, qui dixit ℣. 2. veni, & non erat vir: vocaui, & nemo respondit, sic loquitur ℣ 4. Dominus Deus dedit mihi linguam eruditam, &c. Eundem esse ex eo perspicuum est, quod continuatio est descriptionis inchoatæ duobus versibus antecedentibus, eo pertinentis, ut Iudæorum[?] incredulitatem & contumaciam arguat, qui sibi, Deo & homini, omnibus rebus ad eos seruandos necessariis cumulatissime instructo auscultare noluerunt. Certé idem Chris[?] stus[?] & diuinam suam ad liberandum ac redimendum potentiam miraculis, & sapientiam suam admirabilem sermonibus, & patientiam insuperabilem perpessionibus suis abunde declarauit: quæ tria hoc loco semetipsum describens commemorat.
units.tr: VIII. This same argument is confirmed by another testimony of God, Isaiah 50:2. God gives this reason why he put away the divorce of the Jewish Church: I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was none who answered. Who, I ask, came, and who called, and because the Jews did not receive him, were rejected? The whole Gospel testifies that this is the Son, not the Father. He himself also teaches this in verse 4. For the same Lord, Jehovah, who said in verse 2 I came, and there was no man: I called, and none answered, speaks thus in verse 4: The Lord God has given me a learned tongue, etc. That it is the same speaker is clear from the fact that this is the continuation of the description begun in the two preceding verses, and it serves to rebuke the unbelief and obstinacy of the Jews, who were unwilling to listen to God and to a man who was most abundantly furnished with everything necessary for their salvation. Certainly this same Christ, by his miracles, by his admirable teaching, and by his unconquerable patience in suffering, has amply declared both his divine power to deliver and redeem, and his wisdom; and these three things, describing himself in this place, he recalls.

units.la: DISPVTATIO VIGESIMA NONA
units.tr: Disputation Twenty-Nine

units.la: De Arg. XXIX. Ex Esai. LXIII. 1. Ego qui loquor in iustitia, &c.
units.tr: On Argument XXIX, from Isaiah 63.1: "I who speak in righteousness, etc."

units.la: I. ECVM etiam, quæso, pie lector, quis sit ille reputa, qui Esaiæ cap. 63. primis sex versiculis describitur. Certè videtur esse Deus Israelis. Quærenti enim quis sit, respondet se esse eum, qui loquitur in iustitia, & est ad seruandum copiosus. Quæ elogia itâ antonomasticè seu κατ' ἐξοχῶ[?] accepta, vt sint instar nominis vel descriptionis, vnius Dei Israelis propria sunt. Adde quod non fit vllo modo verisimile, quenquam alium se profiteri Seruatorem potentissimum apud eum Prophetam, apud quem Deus Israelis se seruatorem esse profitetur, & præter se neminem. Idem loquitur, vt Deum decet, V. 4. Dies vltionis est in corde meo, & annus quo meos redimam venit, nec non V. 6. conculcaui populos in ira mea, & inebriaui eos in indignatione mea. Itaque non dicit V. 5. Brachium Dei, sed Brachium meum, inquit, me seruauit, & excandescentia mea ipsa me fulsit. Sibi ipsi hanc laudem ascribit, id quod meram creaturam piam & religiosam haudquaquam decere videtur.
units.tr: I. Please, kind reader, consider also who it is that is described in the first six verses of Isaiah 63. It seems certainly to be the God of Israel. For when asked who he is, he answers that he is the one who speaks in righteousness, and is mighty to save. These attributes, taken antonomastically [κατ' ἐξοχήν], so that they serve as a name or a description, belong peculiarly to the one God of Israel. Add that it is in no way likely that anyone else would profess himself the mighty Saviour in the sight of that prophet, in whose sight the God of Israel professes himself to be the Saviour and no one besides him. The same speaker says, as befits God, at verse 4: The day of vengeance is in my heart, and the year of my redeemed has come, and also at verse 6: I have trodden down the peoples in my anger, and made them drunk in my indignation. So at verse 5 he does not say the arm of God, but my arm, he says, has saved me, and my own fury has upheld me. He ascribes this praise to himself, which does not seem at all fitting for a mere pious and religious creature.

units.la: II. Rursus qui sic describitur est Christus. Hoc ex tribus colligi potest, vno, quod procedit cum veste sanguine respersa V. 2.3. Altero, quod dicitur Torcular calcasse solus V. 3. quod vtrumque ad Christum describendum adhibetur: Apoc. 19. V. 13. & 15. Tertio, quòd describitur, tanquam qui per sese immediatè cum hostibus certamen iniisset, seseque ipse in summo discrimine constitutum virtute sua expediuisset, hostesque calcauisset Ψ. 5. Id quod de Filio Dei verè & proprie dicitur, de Deo Patre non item.
units.tr: II. Again, the one who is so described is Christ. This can be gathered from three things. First, that he comes forward with a garment sprinkled with blood (verses 2–3). Second, that he is said to have trodden the winepress alone (verse 3), which both are applied to the description of Christ in Revelation 19.13 and 15. Third, that he is described as one who entered the struggle directly by himself, and who, placed in the greatest peril, extricated himself by his own strength and trampled his enemies (Ψ. 5). This is said truly and properly of the Son of God, but not in the same way of God the Father.

units.la: III. Ad hunc Esaiæ locum alium adjungam non absimilem ex Esai. 59. 16. Et vidit (Iehoua) quod non esset vir, & obstupuit quod nemo occurreret, & seruauit eum brachium eius, & iustitia eius ipsa fulsit eum. Quod quomodo dici potuerit de Deo Patre equidem haud intelligo.
units.tr: III. To this passage of Isaiah I shall add another, not unlike it, from Isaiah 59.16: And he saw (Jehovah) that there was no man, and he was astonished that no one intervened, and his arm saved him, and his righteousness itself upheld him. How this could have been said of God the Father I certainly do not understand.

units.la: IV. Fortasse ad duo illa loca lux aliqua accedet ex tertio simili, qui extat ps. 98. 1. Cantate Domino (Iehouæ) canticum nouum: quia mirabilia fecit. Seruauit eum dextera eius, & brachium sanctum eius. Negari non potest, quin agatur de salute parta per Christum. Id enim totus psalmus apertissimè innuit. Iam autem non descendit in arenam cum omnibus nostris hostibus pugnaturus Pater, sed Filius. Non Patrem, sed Filium perdere conati sunt hostes Ecclesiæ. Non expauit, non obstupuit, non defertus fuit ab omnibus Pater, sed Filius. Opus salute fuit non Patri, qui nullum subjit discrimen, sed Filio. Non seruauit se Pater, sed Filius, eaque salus opus fuit, quo nullum vnquam mirabilius factum est. Inde totius Ecclesiæ salus pependit. Hoc profectò non frustrà ter inculcatum fuit. Non est autem quod figuras Aduersarij comminiscantur, vt quod experientia, optimus vaticinij commentarius, Christi proprium fecit, id à Christo auffe-rant atque alio detorqueant, Iudæos imitati rebelles.
units.tr: IV. Perhaps some light will fall on those two passages from a third, similar one, which is found in Psalm 98.1: Sing to the Lord (Jehovah) a new song, for he has done wonderful things. His right hand and his holy arm have saved him. It cannot be denied that this concerns salvation obtained through Christ. For the whole psalm clearly points to this. Now, the Father did not descend into the arena to fight with all our enemies, but the Son did. It was not the Father but the Son whom the enemies of the Church tried to destroy. The Father was not terrified, was not astonished, was not forsaken by all; the Son was. The work of salvation was needed not by the Father, who underwent no peril, but by the Son. It was not the Father who saved himself, but the Son, and that salvation was a work than which none more wonderful was ever done. On it the whole salvation of the Church depended. This was certainly not repeated three times for nothing. Nor is there any reason for the adversaries to devise figures, so that they may take away from Christ, and twist to something else, what experience, the best commentator on prophecy, has made Christ's own, imitating the rebellious Jews.

units.la: DISPVTATIO TRIGESIMÁ
units.tr: DISPUTATION XXX

units.la: De Arg. XXX. Ex Ier. 10. ii. Dii qui non fecerunt cœlum & terram tollantur de terra, & de sub cœlis ipsis.
units.tr: On the Argument XXX, from Jer. 10:11: "The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, let them perish from the earth, and from under these heavens."

units.la: I. AB Esaia progrediamur ad Ieremiam. Is cap. 10. primùm idolorum vanitatem describit. Deinde quantoperè Deus Israëlis illis præstet ostendit adhibita eius descriptione Ψ. 6. Non est, inquit, similis tui Domine: Magnus es tu, & magnum est nomen tuum in fortitudine. Quis non timebit te o Rex gentium? tuum enim est decus: inter cunctos sapientes gentium, & in universis regnis eorum non est similis tui, & rursus Ψ. 10. Dominus (Iehoua) autem Deus verus est: ipse Deus vivens est Rex sempiternus, ab indignatione eius commouebitur terra: & non sustinebunt gentes comminationem eius. Quas descriptiones posse ad Christum accommodari, eique verè conuenire nemo Christianus non videt. Cui autem descriptio proprie conuenit, eidem etiam conuenit descripti nomen. Est autem descripti nomen hoc loco Dominus Iehoua. Est igitur Christus Dominus seu Iehoua.
units.tr: I. Let us move from Isaiah to Jeremiah. In chapter 10 he first describes the vanity of idols. Then, by way of contrast with that description, he shows how far the God of Israel surpasses them. In v. 6 he says: "There is none like unto thee, O Lord; thou art great, and thy name is great in might. Who would not fear thee, O King of the nations? For this belongs to thee; among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, there is none like unto thee." And again, v. 10: "But the Lord (Jehovah) is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth shall tremble, and the nations shall not be able to abide his indignation." No Christian fails to see that these descriptions can be applied to Christ and truly belong to him. But whoever properly fits the description is also the one to whom the name of the one described belongs. In this place the name of the one described is the Lord Jehovah. Therefore Christ is the Lord or Jehovah.

units.la: II. Tandem Iudæos aduersus omnem idololatriam hoc veluti gladio spirituali armat, Sic ergo, inquit, dicetis eis, Dii qui cœlos & terram non fecerunt, tollentur de terra, & de sub cœlis ipsis. Ex quo sic argumentor.
units.tr: II. At last he arms the Jews against all idolatry with this, as it were, spiritual sword: "Thus shall you say to them, The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth, they shall perish from the earth, and from under these heavens." From this I argue as follows.

units.la: Deus qui fecit cœlum & terram est Deus Israëlis.
units.tr: The God who made heaven and earth is the God of Israel.

units.la: Christus est Deus qui fecit cœlum & terram.
units.tr: Christ is the God who made heaven and earth.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel.

units.la: Minor probatur sic, Dii qui non fecerunt cœlum & terram tollentur de terra &c. Christus non tolletur de terra &c. Christusigitur est Deus qui fecit cœlum & terram. Hoc argumentum jam non semel attigi. Id hoc loco ab Aduersariorum exceptionibus vindicandum est.
units.tr: The minor premise is proved thus: the gods that have not made heaven and earth shall perish from the earth, etc. Christ shall not perish from the earth, etc. Therefore Christ is the God who made heaven and earth. I have already touched on this argument more than once. Here it must be defended against the objections of our opponents.

units.la: III. Respondet Socinus, Primùm, Ieremiam non loqui de om-nibus dijs. Alioqui, inquit, multi, qui & vocantur & sunt dij, exterminandi essent; quos tamen Deus caros habet. Sed de iis, qui, ut primi bonorum fontes & auctores, colantur, quique ipsi Iehouae Deo opponuntur, atque eo cultu & honore afficiuntur, quo ipse Iehouae Deus, nec praeterea alius, eo loco manifestè agitur. Atqui nos, etiamsi Christum, Deum nostrum agnoscimus, eumque adoramus; non tamen primum bonorum auctorem & fontem facimus, eumue Iehouae Deo opponimus: nec porro eodem prorsus cultu & honore illum afficimus, quo Iehouae Deus pater ipsius afficiendus est. Indigna est viro docto haec responsio. Primùm enim si qui vocantur, vel sunt dij, chari Deo minimeque exterminandi, qui non fecerunt coelum & terram, illi non dicuntur dij, nisi improprie, figuratè, aut etiam typicè, ac propterea non coluntur religiosè. Itaque non vocantur dij eo sensu, quo palam est deorum nomen hoc loco usurpari, nimirum pro illis dijs, qui putantur dij proprie dicti religiosèque colendi. Alioqui, si scientes & volentes religiosè colantur, non sunt chari Deo, sed tandem aoblendi; sin inscij aut inuiti coluntur religiosè, non peribunt quidem ipsi, sed eorum tamen eiusmodi diuinitas tandem de medio tolletur. Itaque nihil impedit, quominus propositio illa Prophetae, aut potius ipsius Dei, de omnibus dijs, quotquot religiosè colantur, hoc est, diuino cultu afficiuntur, intelligi debeat. Sunt autem multa, quae, ut accipiatur tanquam universaliter vera, non modò suadent, sed persuadent etiam.
units.tr: III. Socinus replies: "First, Jeremiah is not speaking of all gods. Otherwise, he says, many who are called and are gods would have to be destroyed, yet God holds them dear. But the passage clearly refers to those who are worshipped as the first fountains and authors of good things, who are set over against Jehovah God himself, and who receive that cult and honour which belongs to Jehovah God and to no other. We, however, although we acknowledge Christ as our God and adore him, do not make him the first author and fountain of good things, nor set him over against Jehovah God; nor do we pay him exactly the same cult and honour that is due to Jehovah God the Father." This answer is unworthy of a learned man. For first, if those who are called gods, or are gods, are dear to God and by no means to be destroyed, then those who did not make heaven and earth are not called gods except improperly, figuratively, or even typically, and therefore they are not worshipped religiously. So they are not called gods in the sense in which it is plain that the name of gods is used in this place, namely for those gods who are thought to be gods properly so called and to be worshipped religiously. Otherwise, if they are worshipped religiously with knowledge and consent, they are not dear to God but are in the end to be destroyed; and if they are worshipped religiously in ignorance or against their will, they will not indeed perish themselves, but their divinity of this kind will at last be removed from the midst. Therefore nothing prevents that proposition of the prophet, or rather of God himself, from being understood of all gods whatsoever who are worshipped religiously, that is, who receive divine worship. There are, moreover, many considerations which not only suggest but even persuade that it should be taken as universally true.
