units.la: IV. Hoc quidem primum, quod Deus illam propositionem populo suo suggessit, ut eâ Babylonios idololatras refelleret. Id autem fieri oportuit hoc modo. Dij qui coelum & terram non fecerunt, perdentur de terra, & de sub coelis ipsis. Uestri dij, sunt dij qui coelum & terram non fecerunt. Uestri igitur dij perdentur de terra & de sub coelis ipsis. Quae argumentatio, cum sit in prima figura, vitiosa erit, nec vim ullam concludendi habebit, si propositio sit particularis, de quibusdam dijs, non de omnibus, qui coelum & terram non fecerunt, accipienda. Quis autem credat, Deum voluisse eos docere male argumentari, paralogismoque uti ad refellendos idololatras? Deinde illa propositio, vel necessariò , vel contingenter vera est. Si necessariò, habenda est pro vniuersali. Omnis enim enunciatio indefinita necessariò vera vniuersaliter accipi debet. Si contingenter, mirum est Deum populum suum, vt refutaret idololatras, maluisse docere propositionem contingentem ex qua nulla posset conclusio nisi contingens elici, quàm propositionem necessariam.
units.tr: IV. First, this is the case: God suggested that proposition to his people so that by it they might refute the idolatrous Babylonians. This had to be done in the following way. The gods that did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from under these heavens. Your gods are gods that did not make heaven and earth. Therefore your gods shall perish from the earth and from under these heavens. This argument, being in the first figure, will be faulty, and will have no force in concluding, if the proposition is to be taken as particular, concerning certain gods and not all who did not make heaven and earth. But who would believe that God wished to teach his people to argue badly and to use a paralogism in refuting idolaters? Next, that proposition is either necessarily or contingently true. If necessarily, it must be held as universal, for every indefinite enunciation that is necessarily true must be understood universally. If contingently, it is strange that God, in order to refute idolaters, should have preferred to teach his people a contingent proposition from which no conclusion could be drawn except a contingent one, rather than a necessary proposition.

units.la: V. Huc accedit, quod veritas illius propositionis, aut solo Dei decreto occulto nititur, aut etiam euidenti ratione. Si prius, non fuit admodum accommodata ad reuincendos idololatras. Potuit enim ab ijs occulta Dei decreta ignorantibus æquè facilè negari ac à Iudæis affirmabatur: quippe cuius veritas neutris cuidens esset. Si posterius, necessariam atque adeò vniuersalem eam esse necesse est. Adde quod, verba illa, qui cœlum & terram non fecerunt, limitatio quædam sunt, qua insertæ propositioni veram esse vniuersaliter oportet, alioqui frustrà limitatio est adhibita: adhibetur enim vt propositio, quæ alioqui particulariter tantùm vera esset, sic restricta vniuersalis & necessaria euadat. Mirum est igitur, Deum limitationibus, quæ propositionem efficerent necessariam, antepositisse istam, qua adhibita nihilominus propositio permanet particularis & contingens.
units.tr: V. Moreover, the truth of that proposition rests either on the secret decree of God alone or also on evident reason. If the former, it was not very well suited to confuting idolaters. For it could be denied by those who were ignorant of God's secret decrees just as easily as it was affirmed by the Jews, since its truth was evident to neither side. If the latter, it must necessarily be universal. Add that the words "which did not make heaven and earth" are a certain limitation, which, inserted into the proposition, must make it true universally; otherwise the limitation has been added to no purpose. It is added so that a proposition which otherwise would be true only in particular becomes, thus restricted, universal and necessary. It is strange, then, that God should have placed before this limitation, which would make the proposition necessary, one by which the proposition nevertheless remains particular and contingent.

units.la: VI. Sed tres limitationes, quas Socinus pro ingenio excogitauit, videamus quàm sint ineptæ. Prima est, Prophetam loqui de ijs, qui, vt primi bonorum fontes & auctores, coluntur. Quid autem est esse primum bonorum fontem & auctorem? Num fecisse cœlum & terram? igitur per Deos qui cœlum & terram non fecerunt intelliguntur dij, qui primi bonorum fontes & auctores non sunt, quo posito sic colligo: Aut Babylonij crediderunt suos deos fuisse primos bonorû fontes & auctores, aut non crediderunt. Si crediderunt, quomodo illa propositione refelli potuerunt: siquidem suos Deos existimarunt fecisse cœlum & terram? Si non crediderunt, quomodo Deos suos coluerunt vt primos bonorum fontes & auctores, quos non crediderunt esse primos bonorum fontes & auctores? Sed fortasse esse primum bonorum fontem & auctorem non est Aduersarijs fecisse cœlum & terram. Quid ergo est? bona aliqua insita authoritate & virtute hominibus conferre? Christus igitur, etiam ab ipsis Aduersarijs, colitur vt primus bonorum fons & auctor, ac proinde ad rem nihil facit hæc eorum exceptio seu limitatio. Fortasse illis est ab alio non esse, alij non subordinari. Ac sic nihil valuisset hæc limitatio aduersus Ethnicorum Deos, quos vt genitos ab alijs, ac vni summo Deo tanquam Regi & parenti subordinatos coluerunt.
units.tr: VI. But let us see how unfitting are the three limitations which Socinus has devised as he pleased. The first is that the prophet speaks "of those who are worshipped as the first fountains and authors of good things." But what is it to be the first fountain and author of good things? Is it to have made heaven and earth? Then by "gods that did not make heaven and earth" are meant gods who are not the first fountains and authors of good things. Given this, I argue as follows: either the Babylonians believed that their gods were the first fountains and authors of good things, or they did not. If they believed it, how could they be refuted by that proposition, since they held that their gods had made heaven and earth? If they did not believe it, how did they worship their gods as the first fountains and authors of good things, when they did not believe them to be such? But perhaps to be the first fountain and author of good things is, for our opponents, not to have made heaven and earth. What then is it? To confer some good things on human beings by an authority and power inherent in oneself? Then Christ is worshipped, even by our opponents themselves, as the first fountain and author of good things, and so this exception or limitation of theirs has nothing to do with the matter. Or perhaps it means not to be from another, and not to be subordinate to another. And in that case this limitation would have been of no value against the gods of the Gentiles, whom they worshipped as begotten by others and subordinate to the one supreme God as King and Father.

units.la: VII. Præterea Deos suos Ethnici, vt primos fontes & auctores bonorum, vel nullos, vel omnes, vel aliquos tantum coluerunt. Nullos Aduersarij non dicent, ita enim Propheta de nullis Ethnicorum dijs loqueretur. Omnes si dixerint, reuincentur ipsorum Ethnicorum testimonijs innumeris aperte confitentium deos suos vel omnes, vel plerosque omnes, ortos genitos, educatos, cibo & potu vsos, immo homines fuisse post mortem in deorum numerum relatos; ne dicam eos etiam bruta animantia, etiam plantas, etiam perturbationes animi, etiam malos genios, ne nocerent, coluisse. Aliquos si dixerint vt primos rerum auctores cultos fuisse, reliquos vero non item, non quæram quinam illi fuerint (omnes enim, etiam illi, qui maiorum gentium dij appellabantur, putabantur geniti) tantum reponam, igitur sententiam istam, qua Deus maximè refelli voluit omnes idololatras ad quasdam duntaxat idola, ad quosdam tantum Ethnicorum deos applicari posse. Erit igitur rursus quod mirentur, Deum eam propositionem ex omnibus vnam selegisse, quam populum suum doceret, & qua vellet idololatras maximè reuinci, quæ tamen aut de nullis, aut de paucis tantum quibusdam Ethnicorum dijs intelligi deberet, quamque etiam facilè declinare possent idololatræ dicendo se deos quidem suos colere vt bonorum auctores, at non vt primos.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, the Gentiles worshipped their gods as first fountains and authors of good things either none of them, or all of them, or only some. The opponents will not say none, for then the prophet would be speaking of none of the gods of the Gentiles. If they say all, they are refuted by the countless testimonies of the Gentiles themselves, who openly confess that their gods, all or nearly all, were born, begotten, and brought up, ate and drank, and indeed that men were after death counted among the gods; not to mention that they worshipped even brute animals, even plants, even the passions of the mind, even evil spirits, lest these should harm them. If they say that only some were worshipped as first authors of things, while the rest were not, I will not inquire who those were (for all of them, even those who were called gods of the greater nations, were thought to have been begotten). I will only reply that this opinion, by which God chiefly wished all idolaters to be refuted, can be applied only to certain idols and to certain gods of the Gentiles. There will therefore again be cause for wonder that God chose from all propositions that one which he would teach his people, and by which he wished idolaters to be most of all refuted, yet which ought to be understood either of none or of only a few of the gods of the Gentiles, and which the idolaters could also easily evade by saying that they worshipped their gods indeed as authors of good things, but not as the first.

units.la: VIII. Quid quod aplerisque omnibus Christianis Dominus noster Iesus Christus colitur vt Alpha & Omega, primus & ultimus, principium & finis, creator cœli & terræ, ac cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto unus ille Deus, bonorum omnium fons inexhaustus? Ac propterea [?] ista, quam commentus est socinus, limitatio nihil officit [?] argumento nostro.
units.tr: VIII. What of the fact that by nearly all Christians our Lord Jesus Christ is worshipped as the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end, the creator of heaven and earth, and, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, that one God, the inexhaustible fountain of all good things? And therefore that limitation which Socinus has devised does nothing to harm our argument.

units.la: IX. Veniamus igitur ad secundam. Loquitur, inquit, Propheta de iis, qui Iehoua Deo opponuntur. Cur ergo id non dixit? cur non sic potius concepit propositionem, dicetis eis, Dij, qui Deo Israelis opponuntur, perdentur &c? Sic enim & vniuersalis, & perspicua, & sine eiusmodi additamentis vera fuisset. Quis enim credat, cum id expressisse, quod per se vim nullam habebat, id vero tacuisse, in quo vno vis propositionis hærebat? Quid etiam opus fuit, ut alias limitationes Aduersarij excogitarent? Hac enim una adhibita, etiam detracta ea, qua Propheta usus est, propositio fit universaliter vera. Sed si licet tales limitationes pro ingenio comminisci, & Dei verbo addere, nulla erit propositio adeo diserta & perspicua, ut eam hæreticus non possit, adiecta aliqua eiusmodi limitatione, ad mentem suam detorquere.
units.tr: IX. Let us come, then, to the second. The prophet speaks, he says, "of those who are opposed to Jehovah God." Why then did he not say so? Why did he not rather frame the proposition thus: "Say to them, the gods who are opposed to the God of Israel shall perish," and so on? For in that form it would have been universal, plain, and true without additions of this kind. For who would believe that he expressed what in itself had no force, but kept silent about the one thing in which the force of the proposition lay? Why, too, was it necessary for the adversaries to devise other limitations? For with this one applied, even without the words the prophet used, the proposition becomes universally true. But if it is permitted to invent such limitations according to one's own wit and add them to the word of God, there will be no proposition so clear and plain that a heretic cannot, by adding some limitation of this sort, twist it to his own meaning.

units.la: X. Cæteroquin nihil juvat Adversarios sua ista limitatio. Nam, si rem ipsam spectes ut in se est, omnis alius Deus, hoc ipso quod alius est, opponitur Deo Israëlis. Cum enim hic alium, præter se, Deum, & esse neget; & haberi pro Deo colive vetet, non potest alius Deus, vel esse affirmari, vel pro Deo haberi aut coli, quin eo ipso cum Dei Israëlis veritate & voluntate pugnetur. Sin mentem idololatrarum consideres, illi nonnunquam Deos suos non opponunt Deo Israëlis, sed ei vel ut amicos adjungunt, vel etiam ut inferiores subjiciunt. Quid quod, cum Chri-stus à nobis ut Deus summus, ut præditus essentia divina, ut creator mundi colitur, putant Adversarij Deo summo injuriam fieri? Quod si ita est, etiam Christus, quod absit, Deo Israëlis opponitur.
units.tr: X. Moreover, that limitation of theirs does the adversaries no good at all. For if you look at the thing as it is in itself, every other god, by the very fact that he is other, is opposed to the God of Israel. For since the God of Israel denies that there is any other God besides himself, and forbids him to be held as God or worshipped, no other god can be affirmed to exist, or be held or worshipped as God, without by that very fact contending with the truth and will of the God of Israel. But if you consider the mind of the idolaters, they sometimes do not oppose their gods to the God of Israel, but either join them to him as friends or even set them under him as inferiors. What of the fact that, when Christ is worshipped by us as the highest God, as endowed with the divine essence, as the creator of the world, the adversaries think an injury is done to the highest God? And if so, then Christ too, God forbid, is opposed to the God of Israel.

units.la: XI. Ad tertiam limitationem quod attinet, Agitur, inquit Socinus, eo loco de diis, qui eo cultu & honore afficiuntur, quo ipse Iehova Deus, nec preterea alius. Quorsum addidit, nec preterea alius, nisi ut se gladio suo jugularet ipse?
units.tr: XI. As for the third limitation, Socinus says: "The passage is concerned with gods who are honoured with that worship and honour with which Jehovah God himself is honoured, and with no other." Why did he add "and with no other," unless to fall upon his own sword?

units.la: Nam si nullus alius quàm ipse Iehova Deus, eo cultu & honore afficitur quo ipse Iehova Deus, facit ista limitatio divinam propositionem ad revincendos idololatras prorsus inutilem & ineptam, immò ridiculam: ita enim ageret Propheta de diis, quales nullos Babyloniii, aliique idololatræ coluerunt unquam. Hocque ipsum, etiamsi verba illa Socinus non addidisset, res clamat. Ipse enim sese Iehova coli vetuerat eo modo quo colebantur gentium dii: Neque ulla gens unquam extitit, quæ idola sua eodem prorsus modo coleret, quo se Deus coli voluit. Nihil igitur excogitari potuit hac limitatione ineptius: & tamen ad eam absurditatem accedit veluti cumulus, quod si quisquam Deus eodem cultu affectus est unquam, quo ipse Iehova Deus, is profectò est Christus, quem tenentur omnes colere quemadmodum colunt Patrem, quique unum est cum Patre, eodem throno & imperio, iisdem ministris, eadem gloria, ac δοξολογίᾳ[?], necnon omni potestate in cœlo & in terra gaudens.
units.tr: For if no one other than Jehovah God himself is honoured with the worship and honour with which Jehovah God himself is honoured, this limitation makes the divine proposition wholly useless and unfit for refuting idolaters, indeed ridiculous: for the prophet would then be speaking of gods such as the Babylonians and other idolaters never worshipped at all. And even if Socinus had not added those words, the thing itself cries out. For Jehovah had forbidden himself to be worshipped in the way in which the gods of the nations were worshipped; and no nation has ever existed that worshipped its idols in exactly the same way in which God wished to be worshipped. Nothing more absurd could therefore have been devised than this limitation. Yet to this absurdity there is added, as it were a crowning, the fact that if any God has ever been honoured with the same worship as Jehovah God himself, that God is surely Christ, whom all are bound to worship just as they worship the Father, who is one with the Father, on the same throne and in the same dominion, with the same ministers, the same glory and doxology, and rejoicing also in all power in heaven and on earth.

units.la: XII. Venio igitur ad alteram Socini responsionem: Altera causa, inquit, cur iste Hieremiæ locus nihil ad rem faciat, est, quod ista dicta sunt, antequam Christus existeret, non modo antequam adorandus constitueretur. Tunc certè verum erat, idque absolutè, nullum Deum adorandum esse qui cœlum & terram non fecisset: Nec ullo modo, inquit resp. ad VVickium, apparet, dictum istud ad omnia consequentia tempora pertinere. Non dicam, propositionem, quæ uno tempore vera est, alio falsa, contingentem esse. Omnem autem propositionem indefinitam, qualis hæc est, & contingentem particularem esse; Ex propositione autem majore particulari nihil concludi in prima figura, in qua tamen figura necesse est argumentationem esse, quæ vi divinæ illius propositionis idololatras refellit. Non dicam, propositionem illam, si vera fuit antequam Christus existeret, falsa vero postquam extitit, abrogatam fuisse à Christo, qui tamen dogmata (est autem illa propositio dogma) non abrogavit, sed tantùm fœdus seu jugum legale.
units.tr: XII. I come, then, to Socinus's other answer: "Another reason," he says, "why that passage of Jeremiah has nothing to do with the matter is that these words were spoken before Christ existed, not merely before he was to be constituted as one to be worshipped. At that time it was certainly true, and absolutely so, that no God ought to be worshipped who had not made heaven and earth. Nor in any way, he says in his reply to Wickius, does it appear that the saying pertains to all subsequent times." I will not say that a proposition which is true at one time and false at another is contingent. But every indefinite proposition of this kind is a contingent particular; and nothing follows from a particular major premise in the first figure, though in that figure the argument must be one which, by the force of that divine proposition, refutes the idolaters. I will not say that this proposition, if it was true before Christ existed and false after he appeared, was abrogated by Christ, who did not abrogate doctrines (and that proposition is a doctrine), but only the legal covenant or yoke.

units.la: XIII. Illud dicam, omnem enunciationem quæ certo tantùm tempore vera est, verbum habere quod tempus illud ad significet. Id quod hic locum non habet. Sunt enim in hac enunciatione, Dii qui cœlum & terram non fecerunt &c, duo tantùm verba, alterum præteriti temporis, alterum futuri, quorum illud præteritum, istud futurum absque certa limitatione significat, neutrum ad illud tempus restringi debet, quod Christi nativitatem vel glorificationem antecessit, ut cuiuis patet. Tertium autem verbum in illa propositione nec exprimitur, nec subintelligi potest.
units.tr: XIII. This I will say: every statement which is true only for a certain time has a word that signifies that time. This does not hold here. For in this statement, "gods who have not made heaven and earth, etc.," there are only two verbs, one of past time and one of future, and these signify without any definite limitation. Neither ought to be restricted to the time that preceded the birth or glorification of Christ, as is plain to anyone. The third verb, moreover, is neither expressed in that proposition nor can it be understood.

units.la: XIV. At, inquit Socinus, Ex loco ipso constat, hanc fuisse admonitionem Hieremiæ ad Judæos, qui tunc temporis in Babylonia degebant, ut scirent, quid sibi respondendum esset Chaldaïs illis, si ab ipsis ad idola colenda sollicitati fuissent. Quid tum? Num propterea non potuit aut debuit dictum illud ab aliis usurpari quàm à Judæis illis, aut aliis responderi quàm Chaldæis illis, aut alio tempore, quàm quo Judæi degebant in Babylonia? Non puto tam ineptum fuisse Socinum, ut hoc concludere voluerit. Quorsum ergo id observavit? aut quid inde colligere voluit vel potuit, quod argumento nostro obesset? quacunque occasione & fine propositionem illam Hieremias docuerit, estne in ea quicquam quod non æquè ad aliarum gentium atque ad Chaldæorum deos accommodari possit? aut quod, non possit & debeat Ethnicis ad idololatriam inuitantibus, æquè hodie ac olim, responderi? Nonne enim eadem erat ratio deorum quos Babylonij colebant & deorum quos colebant aliæ gentes, & eorum quos etiamnum hodie colunt Ethnici? Cur ergo non possimus & debeamus, etiam hodie, idololatriam repellere illis armis, quæ Deus, ut ad eam rem aptissima, olim populo suo, nobisque adeò, quorum in doctrinam scripta sunt quaecunque scripta sunt, suppeditauit? Attamen admisso errore Aduersariorum possent arma illa aduersus Deum nostrum Iesum Christum retorqueri, illudque oraculum illustri exemplo, seu, ut loquuntur, instantia infirmari. Sed pergamus.
units.tr: XIV. "But," says Socinus, "from the passage itself it is clear that this was an admonition of Jeremiah to the Jews who at that time were living in Babylon, so that they might know what to answer those Chaldeans if they were solicited by them to worship idols." What then? Was it therefore not possible, or not right, for that saying to be used by others than those Jews, or to be answered to others than those Chaldeans, or at a time other than when the Jews were living in Babylon? I do not think Socinus was so foolish as to wish to conclude this. Why then did he observe it? Or what did he want, or what could he gather from it, that might harm our argument? On whatever occasion and for whatever purpose Jeremiah taught that proposition, is there anything in it that cannot equally be applied to the gods of other nations as to those of the Chaldeans? Or anything that cannot and should not be answered to the heathen who invite us to idolatry, today just as formerly? For was not the reasoning about the gods worshipped by the Babylonians the same as about those worshipped by other nations, and those which the heathen still worship today? Why then can we not, and ought we not, even today, to repel idolatry with those weapons which God, as most fitted for that purpose, long ago supplied to his people, and indeed to us, "for whose instruction all things have been written"? Yet, granting the error of the adversaries, those weapons could be turned against our God Jesus Christ, and that oracle weakened by a striking example, or, as they say, by an instance. But let us proceed.

units.la: XV. Nonne veritas illius dicti ad ea tempora extendi debet ex quibus illa pendebat[?]. & quibus innitebatur? Atqui illa pendebat ex futuro tempore, non quod antecessit aduentum Christi, sed quod illum, præsertim secundum sequi oportebat. Nonne tunc maximè verum esse dictum illud necesse est, cum fit maximè id quod eo prædictum est? Atqui id demum & fieri cœpit per primum Christi aduentum, & perficietur per aduentum eius secundum. Nonne hoc oraculum Iudæos impedire debuit ne quem pro Deo haberent & colerent, qui non fecisset cœlum & terram? Impedire igitur eos debuit ne Christum reciperent & colerent si non fecit cœlum & terram. Ita Iudæis Aduersarij excusationem suppeditant incredulitatis. Cur enim, si vera esset opinio Aduersariorum, non possent Iudæi respondere Deo, Tu Domine nos docuisti Deos qui cœlum & terram non fecerunt destructum iri, idque oraculum voluisti à Propheta Chaldaicè scribi, à nobis memoriter edisci[?], haberique in promptu ad repellendam idololatriam, atque adeò altissimè cordibus nostris infigi, ne quem Deum qui non fecisset cœlum & terram reciperemus aut coleremus. Noli igitur, quæso, nobis succensere si tuo isto tanto oraculo admoniti Deum qui non fecit cœlum & terram recipere & colere renuimus. Tu Domine prohibuisti ne præter te vnum quenquam alium haberemus pro Deo, quod omnium tuorum mandatorum primum & maximum est. Non potuimus isti tuo tanto mandato parere, & pro Deo eum habere qui si Deus est, Deus est à te valdè diuersus. Tu Domine nobis sæpius inculcasti, neminem esse Deum aut seruatorem præter te, idque cūm loquebaris de temporibus Messiæ, quomodo igitur alium Deum, alium seruatorem præter te agnouissemus, aut diuinis honoribus affecissemus? Quomodo possint Aduersarij Iudæis os occludere equidem non video. Nam si ad miracula confugiant, quibus moueri Iudæos decuerit, reponent illi continuò id quod scriptum est Deuter. 13. V.[?] 1. & seqq. Aut igitur excusandi videntur Iudæi, aut fatendum est, id quod res est, Dominum nostrum fecisse cœlum & terram, eundemque esse cum Patre Deum, qui & populum Israëliticum è seruitute Ægyptiaca eduxit, & per prophetas locutus est. Itaque cum Vetus Testamentum comparatum fuerit ad homines præparandos & deducendos ad Christum, ei scopo obesset, vt quod maximè, hoc oraculum, siquidem vera esset responsio Socini.
units.tr: XV. Ought not the truth of that saying to be extended to the times on which it depended, and on which it rested? Yet it depended on a future time, not one that preceded the coming of Christ, but one that had to follow him, especially his second coming. Must not that saying be most true at the time when most of what was foretold in it comes to pass? Yet this began to happen through the first coming of Christ, and will be fulfilled through his second coming. Ought not this oracle to have prevented the Jews from taking as God and worshipping anyone who had not made heaven and earth? It ought therefore to have prevented them from receiving and worshipping Christ, if he did not make heaven and earth. Thus the adversaries supply the Jews with an excuse for unbelief. For if the opinion of the adversaries were true, why could the Jews not answer God: "You, Lord, taught us that gods who did not make heaven and earth would be destroyed, and you wished that oracle to be written by the prophet in Chaldee, to be learned by heart by us, and kept ready to repel idolatry, and so deeply fixed in our hearts that we should receive and worship no God who had not made heaven and earth. Therefore, we beg you, do not be angry with us if, admonished by that great oracle of yours, we refuse to receive and worship a God who did not make heaven and earth. You, Lord, forbade us to have any other God besides you alone, which is the first and greatest of all your commandments. We could not obey that great command of yours and yet hold as God one who, if he is God, is very different from you. You, Lord, have often impressed upon us that there is no God or saviour besides you, and you said this when you spoke of the times of the Messiah. How then could we have acknowledged another God, another saviour besides you, or honoured him with divine honours?" How the adversaries can shut the mouths of the Jews I do not indeed see. For if they flee to miracles, by which the Jews ought to have been moved, the Jews will at once reply with what is written in Deuter. 13. V. 1. and following. Either therefore the Jews seem excusable, or it must be admitted what is the truth: that our Lord made heaven and earth, and is one God with the Father, who both led the people of Israel out of Egyptian bondage and spoke through the prophets. And so, since the Old Testament was framed to prepare men and lead them to Christ, that answer of Socinus, if it were true, would harm that purpose most of all, and this oracle especially.

units.la: XVI. Quid quod, admisso errore Aduersariorum, ne Veteris quidem Testamenti temporibus verum fuisset hoc oraculum, potuissentque Babylonij, nisi per ipsorum ignorantiam stetisset, illud in Iudæos retorquere, & quidem duobus modis. Primò sic, Obiicitis nobis, Deos qui cœlum & terram non fecerunt sublatum iri de terra & de sub cœlis ipsis, non cogitantes vobis in lege & prophetis vestris promissum esse Messiam, qui, quamuis non fecerit cœlum & terram, futurus tamen sit veré & proprie Deus, ab omnibus angelis, non modo ab hominibus, adorandus, beatumque prædicari qui in eum crediderit. Hoc igitur telum, quod in deos nostros iacitis, in eum quem expectatis Deum recidit, atque ita pugnantes vestram spem euertitis. Deinde sic, Nullus Angelus fecit cœlum & terram. Aliquis Angelus vocatur in lege vestra Deus, immò Ichoua, atque vt talis adoratur. Aliquis igitur qui in lege vestra vocatur Deus, Ichoua, legitimèque adoratur, non fecit cœlum & terram. Num ergo ille etiam exterminabitur? Quid possit ab Aduersariis nostris reponi non video. Concedit enim maiorem Crellius:quippe,negat Deum vlliusopera ad tanta rei molitionem vsum fuisse. Minorem aliquot locis Socinus & Crellius inculcant, vt partim iam vidimus, partim videbimus disp. 32.
units.tr: XVI. Moreover, granting the error of our opponents, this oracle would not have been true even in the times of the Old Testament, and the Babylonians could have turned it back against the Jews, had their own ignorance not stood in the way. They could have done so in two ways. First, thus: "You object to us that gods who did not make heaven and earth will be removed from the earth and from under the very heavens. You do not consider that your law and prophets promised you a Messiah who, although he did not make heaven and earth, will nonetheless truly and properly be God, to be adored by all angels, not only by men, and who will be declared blessed, those who believe in him. Therefore this weapon which you hurl at our gods recoils upon the God you expect, and so, in fighting, you overthrow your own hope." Second, thus: "No angel made heaven and earth. Some angel is called God in your law, indeed Jehovah, and is adored as such. Therefore some one who is called God, Jehovah, in your law and is lawfully adored, did not make heaven and earth. Will he too then be destroyed?" I do not see what our opponents can reply to this. Crellius indeed grants the major premise, for he denies that God used the work of any creature for so great a construction. Socinus and Crellius press the minor premise in several places, as we have partly seen already and shall see in Disputation 32.

units.la: XVII. Vltimò hoc ipso Dei oraculo Aduersarios hoc loco oppugnabimus. Docuit enim sine dubio Deus populum suum rectissimè argumentari. Tale autem, vt dixi, est argumentum. Dii qui cœlum & terram non fecerunt tollentur de terra & de sub cœ-lis ipsis. Dii quos adoratis non fecerunt cœlum & terram. Dii igitur quos adoratis tollentur de terra & de sub cœlis ipsis. De minore non potuit esse controuersia: non enim tantum diis suis tribuebant Ethnici, vt eos dicerent fecisse cœlum & terram. Maior autem per se ipsa lucet. Nam qui specie aut genere aut etiam plusquam genere à Deo differunt, illi dii appellari non possunt nisi æquiuocè, aut figuratè, aut falsò. Id quod inductione probari potest. Nam qui differt specie aut genere, exempli causa, à Leone, vel vulpe, vel lapide, is non potest Leo, vel vulpes, vel lapis appellari, nisi æquiuocè, aut figuratè, aut falsò. Atqui dii qui non fecerunt cœlum & terram differunt à Deo specie, aut genere, aut potius plusquam genere. Dii igitur qui non fecerunt cœlum & terram dii appellari non possunt nisi æquiuocè aut figuratè aut falsò. Minor probatur: Differunt enim plusquam genere ab eo qui fecit cœlum & terram. Hic enim est ens absolutè necessarium, æternum, immutabile, fons omnis entitatis, illi verò aut nihil sunt, aut sunt entia contingentia, certo tempore creata, mutationi obnoxia, ac guttæ quædam ab immenso illo fonte productæ. Dicent fortasse Aduersarii, differre quidem plusquam genere àDeo, qui fecit cœlum & terram, eum qui non fecit cœlum & terram si naturam seu essentiam spectes, non vero si deitatem. Atqui deitas est essentia Dei, & ille qui fecit cœlum & terram est natura sua seu essentia Deus, notatque nomen Dei id quo differt à creaturis. Tum Deitas aut est substantia, aut est accidens. Si substantia, differunt igitur plusquam genere ratione deitatis, si accidens, substantia non est præstantior accidente, sed contrà potius: nihil enim cogitari potest præstantius deitate. Item Deus qui fecit cœlum & terram, & Deus qui non fecit cœlum & terram, dicuntur dii, vel ob diuersam vel ob eandem rationem. Si ob diuersam, dicuntur dij æquiuocè vel figuratè? Si ob eandem, Illa Identitas (liceat enim mihi illa voce vti) erit vel analogica, vel generica, vel specifica, vel numerica. Si analogica tantum, ea non erit tanti, vt propterea diuinis honoribus affici debeant. Si generica aut specifica, non implicabit contradictionem, & nullum Deum esse, & plures Deos esse, & poterit qui non fecit cœlum & terram æquè Deus esse atque is qui fecit cœlum & terram. Sed Hæc eadem erunt tum accuratius disputanda, cum seposita [?] Scriptura sacra recta ratio à nobis consuletur. Nunc satis sit addidisse, qui religiosè coluntur eos non appellari deos æquiuocè aut figuratè, sed propriè; ac proindè, si non fecerunt cœlum & terram, falsò. Qui autem falsò dij dicuntur diuinisque honoribus afficiuntur, illi tandem aliquando destruentur. Nam, nec mendacium potest esse perpetuum, neque is qui fecit cœlum & terram pati in æternum, vt qui Deus non est nomen & cultum Dei sibi vendicet, & constat iudicium tandem aliquando futurum esse, quo, quid bene quidue malè factum fuerit, tandem inno-tescet.
units.tr: XVII. Finally, we shall attack the Adversaries at this point by this very oracle of God. For God, without doubt, taught his people to reason most rightly. Such an argument, as I have said, is this: Gods who did not make heaven and earth will be removed from the earth and from under the very heavens. The gods whom you worship did not make heaven and earth. Therefore the gods whom you worship will be removed from the earth and from under the very heavens. There could be no controversy about the minor premise, for the Gentiles did not attribute so much to their gods as to say that they made heaven and earth. The major premise shines by itself. For those who differ from God in species, or in genus, or even in more than genus, cannot be called gods except equivocally, or figuratively, or falsely. This can be proved by induction. For one who differs in species or genus from, for example, a lion, or a fox, or a stone, cannot be called a lion, or a fox, or a stone, except equivocally, or figuratively, or falsely. But gods who did not make heaven and earth differ from God in species, or in genus, or rather in more than genus. Therefore gods who did not make heaven and earth cannot be called gods except equivocally, figuratively, or falsely. The minor premise is proved thus: they differ in more than genus from him who made heaven and earth. For he is a being absolutely necessary, eternal, immutable, the fount of all being; but they are either nothing, or are contingent beings, created at a certain time, subject to change, and drops produced from that immense fount. The Adversaries will perhaps say that those who did not make heaven and earth do indeed differ in more than genus from him who made heaven and earth, if you regard nature or essence, but not if you regard deity. But deity is the essence of God, and he who made heaven and earth is God by his nature or essence, and the name of God marks that by which he differs from creatures. Then, deity is either a substance or an accident. If a substance, then they differ in more than genus by reason of deity; if an accident, a substance is not more excellent than an accident, but rather the contrary, for nothing can be conceived more excellent than deity. Likewise, God who made heaven and earth and God who did not make heaven and earth are called gods either for a different reason or for the same reason. If for a different reason, are they called gods equivocally or figuratively? If for the same reason, that identity (for I may be allowed to use that word) will be either analogical, or generic, or specific, or numerical. If merely analogical, it will not be of such worth that they ought therefore to be honoured with divine honours. If generic or specific, it will involve no contradiction, and it will be possible for there to be no God and for there to be several gods, and he who did not make heaven and earth could be as much God as he who made heaven and earth. But these same matters will be discussed more accurately when, setting aside holy Scripture, we consult sound reason. For now it is enough to have added that those who are religiously worshipped are called gods not equivocally or figuratively, but properly; and therefore, if they did not make heaven and earth, falsely. Those who are falsely called gods and honoured with divine honours will at length at some time be destroyed. For neither can a lie be perpetual, nor can he who made heaven and earth suffer for ever that one who is not God should claim the name and worship of God for himself; and it is certain that a judgment will at some time come, in which what has been done well or badly will at last be made known.

units.la: DISPUTATIO TRIGESIMA PRIMA
units.tr: Disputation Thirty-One

units.la: De Arg. XXXI. Ex Ierem. CAP. XXIII. V. 6.
units.tr: On Argument XXXI, from Jeremiah 23:6

units.la: Et hoc est nomen quo vocabit eum, Jehoua Iustitia nostra.
units.tr: And this is the name by which he shall be called: Jehovah our righteousness.

units.la: ALIUD argumentum desumi solet ex eodem Ieremia cap. 23. V. 5. & 6. Et suscitabo Davidi Germen iustum; & regnabit Rex, & sapiens erit, & faciet iudicium & iustitiam in terra. In diebus illius salvabitur Iuda, & Israël habitabit confidenter, & hoc est nomen quo vocabunt (heb. vocabit) eum, Iehoua iustitia nostra. Ex quo sic argumentor.
units.tr: ANOTHER argument is commonly drawn from the same passage of Jeremiah, chapter 23, verses 5 and 6: Behold, I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely; and this is the name whereby he shall be called (Heb. vocabit), Jehovah our righteousness. I argue from this as follows.

units.la: Cuius nomen est Iehoua iustitia nostra, is est Deus Israëlis prædictus essentia diuina: Est enim Iehoua nomen maximè proprium Dei Israëlis.
units.tr: He whose name is Jehovah our righteousness is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence, for Jehovah is the most proper name of the God of Israel.

units.la: Christi nomen est Iehoua iustitia nostra, vt patet ex laudato loco.
units.tr: The name of Christ is Jehovah our righteousness, as is evident from the passage cited.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis prædictus essentia diuina.
units.tr: Christ, therefore, is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: II. Negant Aduersarij vtramque præmissam, & primò qui-dem minorem; dicit enim Socinus, hæc postrema verba, & hoc est nomen quo vocabunt eum &c, potius ad Israelem, quàm ad regem illum, id est, Christum referri debere. Argumentum nullum affert, nisi quod id firmare conatur loco plane simili Hierem. 33. 15. Is locus, inquit, ex hebraeo ad verbum sic habet: In diebus illis & in tempore illo germinare faciam Dauid germen iustum: & faciet iudicium & iustitiam in terra. In diebus illis seruabitur Iuda, & Hierusalem habitabit confidenter; & hoc (subaudi nomen eius, ut habes in superiore loco) quo vocabit eam, Iehoua iustitia nostra, eam enim expresse habet hebraicus codex; quod pronomen necesse est, ut referat Hierusalem: quae hic manifeste eundem locum tenet, quem in superiore testimonio Israel. Itaque ibi pronomen eum similiter Israelem referre, prorsus est verissimile. Quod si regem etiam illum, id est, Christum ibi referret; iam ex hoc altero testimonio constaret, vel non propterea absolute affirmari posse, Christum Iehouam fuisse appellatum, vel certè ex tali appellatione non consequi, eum revera esse ipsum Iehouam; nisi similiter concludere velimus, Hierusalem revera esse ipsum Iehouam.
units.tr: II. Our opponents deny both premises, and first of all the minor. Socinus says that these last words, "and this is the name whereby he shall call him," etc., ought to be referred to Israel rather than to that king, that is, to Christ. He offers no argument except that he tries to confirm this from a wholly similar passage, Jeremiah 33:15. That passage, he says, reads word for word in the Hebrew as follows: "In those days, and at that time, I will make the Branch of David to spring forth, a righteous Branch, and he shall execute judgment and justice in the land. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Jerusalem shall dwell safely; and this is the name (understand, his name, as you have it in the earlier passage) by which she shall be called, Jehovah our righteousness." For the Hebrew text expressly has "her," and that pronoun must refer to Jerusalem, which here plainly holds the same place that Israel held in the earlier testimony. So it is quite probable that the pronoun "him" there refers likewise to Israel. But if it referred to that king as well, that is, to Christ, then this second testimony would show either that it cannot be affirmed absolutely that Christ was called Jehovah, or at least that from such a name it does not follow that he is really Jehovah himself, unless we are willing to conclude in the same way that Jerusalem is really Jehovah himself.

units.la: III. Sed similis iste locus, ut inde ordiar, non fauet causae Socini. Potest enim aliter verti, nimirum sic, Ille qui vocabit eam est Iehoua iustitia nostra. Quid enim impedit? non certè verba; verbum enim è verbo sic exprimitur. Nec res; dicitur enim Deus multis locis vocare Ecclesiam Esai. 48. 12. Audi me Iacob & Israel quem ego voco, ego ipse, ego primus & ego novissimus. Rom. 8. 30. quos autem praedestinavit, eosdem etiam vocavit, & quos vocavit, eosdem etiam iustificavit. 1. Thess. 5. 24. Fidelis est qui vocavit vos, qui etiam faciet, &c.
units.tr: III. But this similar passage, to begin from it, does not favour Socinus's cause. For it can be translated otherwise, namely thus: He who shall call her is Jehovah our righteousness. For what prevents it? Certainly not the words, for the word is rendered word for word in this way. Nor the matter itself, for God is said in many places to call the Church: Isaiah 48:12, Hearken unto me, O Jacob and Israel, whom I have called: I am he, I am the first, I also am the last. Romans 8:30, Whom he did predestinate, them he also called; and whom he called, them he also justified. 1 Thessalonians 5:24, Faithful is he that calleth you, who also will do it, etc.

units.la: IV. Dicam amplius, debet aliter verti mea quidem sententia, eo videlicet modo quem dixi. Primùm enim ut eo modo vertatur verba flagitant. Iis enim ita redditis nulla est ellipsis, nisi verbi substantivi frequentissima in Scriptura, nec euitabilis hoc loco. Sin verò vertantur ut vult Socinus, Et hoc est nomen quo vocabit eam, Iehoua iustitia nostra, erit insuper ellipsis huius vocis nomen, necnon nominatiui verbi vocabit. Versio autem sine ellipsi congruens verbis melior est ea quae supplemento indiget. Idem quoque res ipsa poscit. Quis enim esset nominatiuus verbi vocabit? Deus? non. Obstat enim pronomen nostra. Ipsa Ierusalem? non itidem: sese enim ipsa, opinor, non vocat Iehouam iustitiam nostram. Quilibet homo? ne hoc quidem: non enim infideles cam[?] sic vocant : fideles autem quid aliud sunt quàm Ecclesia quàm Hierusalem? quid plura? prouoco ad experientiam, optimum vaticinij commentarium. Num vocatur à quoquam Ecclesia Iehoua iustitia nostra? profectò à nullo. Est igitur hoc nomen non Ecclesiæ seu Hierusalem, sed eius qui eam vocat, qui eam iustificat.
units.tr: IV. I will say more: in my own view it ought to be translated otherwise, namely in the way I have indicated. For first, the words themselves demand this rendering. With them so rendered there is no ellipsis, apart from the substantive verb, which is very frequent in Scripture and cannot be avoided in this place. But if they are rendered as Socinus wishes, And this is the name by which he shall call her, Jehovah our righteousness, there will be an ellipsis of the word name as well as of the nominative of the verb shall call. A translation that fits the words without ellipsis is better than one that needs a supplement. The matter itself also requires this. For who would be the nominative of shall call? God? No, for the pronoun our stands in the way. Jerusalem herself? No, for she does not, I think, call herself Jehovah our righteousness. Any man? Not even this, for unbelievers do not call her so; but what are believers other than the Church, than Jerusalem? What more is there to say? I appeal to experience, the best commentary on prophecy. Does anyone call the Church Jehovah our righteousness? Certainly no one does. This name therefore belongs not to the Church or to Jerusalem, but to him who calls her and justifies her.

units.la: V. Ponamus tamen sic vocari Ecclesiam, certè ita appellabitur quemadmodum appellatur Christus 1. Cor. 12. 12. nempe tribuetur toti nomen primæ & præcipuæ eius partis, hoc est, Christi. Ita elogium istud per se Christi nomen erit, Ecclesiæ verò non conueniet, nisi ratione Christi capitis sui. Alioqui quid absurdius quàm Ecclesiam dici Iehouam, ac iustitiam fidelium, id est, sui metipsius?
units.tr: V. Yet let us suppose that the Church is so called. Then she will be called so in the way that Christ is called Christ in 1 Corinthians 12:12, namely, the name of the first and chief part will be given to the whole, that is, the name of Christ. Thus that title will be Christ's name in its own right, and will belong to the Church only by reason of Christ her head. Otherwise, what could be more absurd than to say that the Church is Jehovah, and the righteousness of believers, that is, of herself?

units.la: VI. Sed redeamus ad locum nostrum. Aio in verbis, Et hoc est nomen quo vocabit eam Iehoua iustitia nostra, pronomen Eum ad Regem illum seu Christum potius quàm ad Israëlem referri debere. Primùm enim ad eum potius referri debet qui per se & primariò & præcipuè eo loco describitur, quàm ad eū cuius mentio non injicitur, nisi quia confert aliquid ad alterius illius descriptionem. Atqui Rex ille per se & primariò & præcipuè describitur eo loco, Israëlis verò mentio non injicitur, nisi quia confert aliquid ad Regis illius descriptionem. Ad illum igitur Regem potius quàm ad Israëlem referri debet: Et quidem eo magis quod, & eodem versiculo pronomen eius ad eum refertur, & causa erat quærendi quale Regis illius nomen futurum esset, id enim Propheta nondum expresserat, cum audito Israelis nomine nemini veniat in mentem, vt quærat, quo nomine appellandus sit Israel.
units.tr: VI. But let us return to our passage. I maintain that in the words, And this is the name by which he shall call her, Jehovah our righteousness, the pronoun him ought to be referred to that king, or Christ, rather than to Israel. For, first, a pronoun ought to refer rather to the one who is described in that place in his own right, primarily and chiefly, than to one whose mention is introduced only because it contributes something to the description of the other. But that king is described in that place in his own right, primarily and chiefly, whereas Israel's mention is introduced only because it contributes something to the description of that king. Therefore the pronoun ought to refer to that king rather than to Israel. And all the more so because, in the same little verse, the pronoun his refers to him, and the reason for inquiring what the name of that king would be was that the prophet had not yet expressed it. When the name Israel is heard, no one thinks to ask by what name Israel is to be called.

units.la: VII. Deinde quæro quis sit nominatiuus verbi vocabit? Est enim in hebræo, agnoscente Socino, vocabit, non vocabunt. Annon idem est qui verbi proximè antecedentis habitabit? Annon ille est, qui immediatè ante nominatus est, Israel? Certè is est aut Deus, aut Rex Messias, aut Israel vel Iuda, aut non extat in textu, sed subintelligi debet quilibet, vel vnusquisque, aut aliquid eiusmodi. Non est autem Deus: Is enim dixisset vocabo, non autem vocabit; & iustitia vestra, non autem nostra. Nec Rex Messias: nam, neque is sic vocasse legitur Israelem, neque dixisset Iustitiam nostram; is enim sua ipsius propria iustitia iustus ac iustificatus est, non autem aliena. Sed neque subintelligi debet quilibet aut vnusquisque: cur enim nominatiuus subintelligeretur, cum sit in proximo, nempe Israel? Addequod non quilibet absolute sic eum vocaturus erat, sed quilibet eum vere agnoscens, hoc est, fidelis. Alij enim aut nolunt, aut non possunt vere dicere iustitiam nostram. Atqui Israel hoc loco Ecclesiam seu fideles significat. Quare necesse est, vt ille qui vocabit sit Israel, ac proinde vt pronomen eum non referatur ad Israelem, sed ad Messiam.
units.tr: VII. Next I ask: who is the nominative of the verb shall call? For in the Hebrew, as Socinus acknowledges, it is shall call, not shall call in the plural. Is it not the same subject as that of the verb immediately preceding, shall dwell? Is it not the one named immediately before, Israel? Surely it is either God, or the Messiah King, or Israel or Judah, or else it is not in the text but must be understood as anyone, or each one, or something of that kind. But it is not God, for he would have said I shall call, not shall call, and your righteousness, not our righteousness. Nor is it the Messiah King, for it is not read that he called Israel in this way, nor would he have said our righteousness, for he is righteous and justified by his own righteousness, not by another's. But nor ought anyone or each one to be understood. For why should a nominative be understood when there is one close at hand, namely Israel? Moreover, it is not anyone at all who would call her so, but anyone who truly acknowledges him, that is, a believer. For others either are unwilling or are unable truly to say our righteousness. But Israel in this place signifies the Church, or believers. Therefore it must be that the one who shall call is Israel, and consequently that the pronoun him does not refer to Israel but to the Messiah.

units.la: VIII. Tum sine dubio hoc nomen, Iehova iustitia nostra, rationem seu causam continuit salutis Iudae, & securitatis Israelis in diebus Regis Messiae. Quoniam autem rex est spiritualis, salus & securitas etiam spiritualis intelligitur, quae sine remissione peccatorum seu iustificatione nulla esse potest. Est autem iustificationis & salutis Iudae & Israelis, hoc est, Ecclesiae, causa, non ipse Israel seu Ecclesia, sed Christus, in quo vnoe[?] est salus, & qui nobis factus est à Deo Patre iustitia, & in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem eius, remissionem peccatorum. Christus igitur, non Israel, vocari debuit Iehova iustitia nostra.
units.tr: VIII. Then without doubt this name, Jehovah our righteousness, contained the reason or cause of the salvation of Judah and of the security of Israel in the days of the Messiah King. But since the king is spiritual, the salvation and security understood are also spiritual, which cannot exist without the remission of sins, or justification. Now the cause of the justification and salvation of Judah and Israel, that is, of the Church, is not Israel or the Church itself but Christ, in whom alone is salvation, and who is made unto us of God the Father wisdom, righteousness, and in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. Christ, therefore, and not Israel, ought to have been called Jehovah our righteousness.

units.la: IX. Hoc ipsum docet euentus. Nunquam enim Israel eo nomine appellatus est. Nunquam res, quae eo nomine significatur, Israeli, hoc est, Ecclesiae tributa est. Sed & nomen illud, & res eo nomine significata tributa est Christo, tribuiturque hodie ab omnibus, aut saltem à plerisque omnibus, Christianis. Habentibus igitur in ipso euentu tam clarum huius vaticinij commentarium dubitabile non est, vter eo nomine potius appellandus fuerit, Israel an Rex ille, hoc est, Ecclesia an Christus? vt iam taceam, nec posse nomen illud conuenire Ecclesiae nisi ratione Christi, nec intelligi, quo sensu Ecclesia sic appellari queat.
units.tr: IX. The outcome itself teaches this. Israel was never called by that name, and the thing signified by that name was never assigned to Israel, that is, to the Church. But both the name and the thing it signifies were assigned to Christ, and today they are attributed to him by all Christians, or at least by nearly all of them. Since the outcome itself offers such a clear commentary on this prophecy, there can be no doubt which of the two was rather to be called by that name: Israel, or that King, that is, the Church or Christ? To say nothing of the fact that the name could not belong to the Church except by reason of Christ, nor can it be understood in what sense the Church could be so called.

units.la: X. Sed venio ad alteram responsionem Socini. Iam, inquit, sive de Christo, sive de Israele vltima verba Hieremiae testimonij dicantur; sensus est, tunc futurum, vt Iehova ille vnus Deus noster nos iustificet. Hoc enim tempore illo, per Christum, in Israele populo suo Iehova facturus erat. Docent nos hunc sensum alij locisimiles non pauci: ex quibus duos aduersum se ex Rabbinis Bellarminus citat: videlicet, Exod. 17. 15. Aedificauit Moses altare, & vocauit nomen eius, Iehova exaltatio mea: & Ezechielis prophetia vltima verba, Et erit ex eo die nomen vrbis Iehova illic. In quibus & alijs eiusmodi locis non tribuitur ipsum nomen Iehoua rebus istis; sed aliquid de Iehoua per illas, aut circa illas significatur. Volunt igitur Aduersarij, quod etiam affirmat Schlichtingius, hoc nomen esse integram hanc sententiam; Iehoua iustitia nostra, (intellige est.) De qua verbi est adjectione, deque duobus illis exemplis, & similibus potest sibi Lector in memoriam ea reuocare quae sunt à nobis disputata ad Arg. huius libri secundum. Nunc enim eos alia via aggrediar.
units.tr: X. But I come to Socinus's second answer. Now, he says, whether the last words of the testimony of Jeremiah are spoken of Christ or of Israel, the sense is that then Jehovah, that one God of ours, would justify us. For at that time he was going to act through Christ in Israel, his people. Not a few other passages of similar meaning teach us this sense; from among them Bellarmine cites two from the rabbis against us, namely Exod. 17:15: "Moses built an altar and called its name Jehovah is my exaltation", and the last words of Ezekiel's prophecy: "And from that day the name of the city shall be Jehovah is there." In these and other passages of this kind the name Jehovah is not ascribed to those things, but something about Jehovah is signified through them, or in connection with them. The opponents therefore want this name to be a complete sentence, is being understood, namely "Jehovah is our righteousness"; which Schlichting also affirms, Jehovah [is] our righteousness, is understood. The reader can recall to mind what we have argued concerning the addition of the word "is" and concerning those two examples and similar ones, in our discussion of the second argument of this book. For now I shall approach them by another route.

units.la: XI. Principio de duobus inter nos conuenit. Vnum est, vocari Iehouam, in nomine Iehoua iustitia nostra, cum qui appellatur iustitia nostra. Alterum, agi de nomine vsurpando tempore Noui Testamenti. Videamus igitur vter in Nouo Testamento vocetur iustitia nostra, Pater an Filius? Certè Filius eo elogio insignitur in Nouo Testamento, Pater verò nunquam. Cur non igitur concludamus per Iehouam, in eo nomine, Filium esse intelligendum, non verò Patrem praecisè? Quod si rem spectes eo elogio significatam, ea Filio conuenit, Patri quatenus à Filio distinguitur, non item: Itaque potest Filius dici iustitia nostra, Pater verò non potest ita appellari, saltem prudenter. Hìc exclamat Socinus, Quid audio? Deus pater non est iustitia nostra, id est, non ipse nos iustificat? Potuitne quidquam minus theologicè, vel potius magis impiè dici? Bona verba quaeso, abest vt negemus Deum patrem nos iustificare: tantùm negamus, quicunque nos iustificat, eum appellari posse prudenter iustitiam nostram: verbi gratia Iudex iustificat, nec tamen aut vocatur, aut vocari potest illius iustitia quem iustificat, non magis certè quàm vocari potest illius crimen, quem condemnat. Non igitur quicunque nos iustificat quocunq; modo, dici potest iustitia nostra, sed is demum, qui nos iustificat per modum iustitiae, seu qui tenet in iustificatione nostra eum locum, quem teneret operum nostrorum iustitia, si ea iusti essemus. Longè enim aliter quàm iudex, & crimen reum condemnat, & iustitia iustificat. Illud condemnat quia mouet iudicem ad condemnandum, haec iustificat quia mouet iudicem ad iustificandum. Illud est id ob quod reus damnatur, haec est id ob quod absoluitur siue iustificatur. Iam autem in iustificatione nostra Deus pater partes agit vel Iudicis, vel Regis, vel etiam Patris, non verò iustitiae nostrae, hae enim sunt propriae partes Filij, qui est finis Legis in iustitiam omni credenti, qui nobis factus est à Deo iustitia, qui nos redemit à maledictione Legis cum factus est pro nobis maledictio, qui semetipsum dedit pretium redemptionis pro omnibus, qui peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, eaque per semetipsum purgauit, per suimetipsius sacrificium sustulit, qui denique ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Itaque merito iustitia nostra dicitur: est enim dono Patris & suo nostraque consensione & acceptatione, quæ fides vocari solet, verè noster. Ac propterea Euangelium, vt iustificemur, non exigit à nobis legis implendæ conditionem, sed, vt loquitur Crellius, fidem tantùm in Christum postulat, fide in Iesum Christum contenta est: soletque in Nouo Testamento iustificatio passim tribui, non fidei in Deum præcisè, sed fidei in Iesum Christum, & sanguini ipsius, qui fide fit noster, nobisque, per prædicationem Euangelij aspersus, adhæret intimè. Cum igitur Deus pater, quatenus à Filio distinguitur, iustitia nostra nec vocetur vnquam in Euangelio, nec vocari prudenter possit; sed hoc sit elogium Filij proprium, fatendum est per Iehouam, in nomine Iehoua iustitia nostra, Filium Dei esse intelligendum.
units.tr: XI. First, we agree on two points. One is that Jehovah is called, in the name "Jehovah is our righteousness", the one who is called our righteousness. The other is that the question concerns the use of the name in the time of the New Testament. Let us see, then, which of the two is called our righteousness in the New Testament, the Father or the Son? Certainly the Son is honoured with that title in the New Testament, but the Father never is. Why, then, should we not conclude that by Jehovah, in that name, the Son is to be understood, and not the Father strictly speaking? If you look at the thing signified by that title, it belongs to the Son, and to the Father only insofar as he is distinguished from the Son; and so the Son can be called our righteousness, but the Father cannot be so called, at least not with propriety. Here Socinus cries out: "What do I hear? God the Father is not our righteousness, that is, does not himself justify us? Could anything be said less theologically, or rather more impiously? Good words, I beg you! Far be it from us to deny that God the Father justifies us; we only deny that whoever justifies us can properly be called our righteousness. For example, a judge justifies, and yet he is not, nor can he be, called the righteousness of the one whom he justifies, no more certainly than his crime can be called the crime of the one he condemns." Therefore it is not whoever justifies us in any way that can be called our righteousness, but only the one who justifies us by way of righteousness, or who holds in our justification the place which the righteousness of our works would hold if we were righteous by them. For a judge condemns the guilty in a quite different way from that in which righteousness justifies. The one condemns because it moves the judge to condemn; the other justifies because it moves the judge to justify. The one is that on account of which the accused is condemned; the other is that on account of which he is acquitted or justified. Now in our justification God the Father plays the part of the Judge, or of the King, or even of the Father, not of our righteousness; for these are the proper parts of the Son, who is the end of the Law unto righteousness for everyone who believes, who is made unto us by God righteousness; who redeemed us from the curse of the Law when he was made a curse for us; who gave himself as the ransom price for all; who bore our sins himself in his body upon the tree, and by himself cleansed them, and took them away by his own sacrifice; who, finally, is himself the propitiation for our sins. Therefore he is rightly called our righteousness: for by the gift of the Father and by his own, and by our consent and acceptance, which is usually called faith, he is truly ours. And for this reason the Gospel does not require of us the condition of fulfilling the law in order that we be justified, but, as Crellius puts it, it demands only faith in Christ; it is content with faith in Jesus Christ. And in the New Testament justification is commonly ascribed not to faith in God strictly speaking, but to faith in Jesus Christ, and to his blood, which becomes ours through faith, and which, sprinkled upon us through the preaching of the Gospel, cleaves to us intimately. Since, then, God the Father, insofar as he is distinguished from the Son, is never called our righteousness in the Gospel, nor can he properly be so called, but this title is proper to the Son, it must be admitted that by Jehovah, in the name Jehovah is our righteousness, the Son of God is to be understood.

units.la: XII. Etiamsi autem præter omnem rationem daremus Aduersarijs iustitiam hoc loco significare iustificatorem, tamen eos oportéret causa cadere. Quorsum enim pertineret illud nomen, nisi vt significaret, eum qui nos iustificat esse Iehouam? Atqui Christus nos iustificat, non modo quia est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, id quod eius est proprium, sed etiam quia nobis peccata nostra condonat, & debita remittit, haud secus quàm si esset ipse creditor cui ea debentur. Immò cum Pater non iudicet quemquam, sed dederit omne iudicium Filio, necesse est vt partes Filij sint iudicare, hoc est, iustificare & condemnare. Cum igitur omni ratione & modo, quo possumus iustificari, nos Christus iustificet, si is qui nos iustificat est Iehoua, necesse est Christum esse Iehouam. Itaque non posset illud nomen, Iehoua iustitia nostra, vt jam ei addatur est, & Israeli tribuatur, aliò pertinere, quàm, vel ad confirmandum Christum esse Iehouam, vel ad negandum eum esse iustitiam nostram: quod posterius esset vniuersum eius euangelium conuellere. Annon enim eo nomine tacita quædam continetur oppositio inter iustitiam nostram, quæ est Iehoua, & aliam quamlibet iustitiam, quam homines putant se posse iustificari? Nonne eo elogio significatur, nos non nostra iustitia quæ est ex lege, non à nobis, non ab aliis hominibus, non ab angelis iustificari? Certè publica est confessio causam adæquatam iustificationis nostræ esse Iehovam: non enim, opinor, in eo nomine iustitia particularis aut imperfecta intelligitur, sed plena & perfecta.
units.tr: XII. Even if, however, we were to grant the opponents, contrary to all reason, that righteousness here signifies the one who justifies, they would still have to fall in their cause. For to what purpose would that name serve, unless to signify that the one who justifies us is Jehovah? But Christ justifies us, not only because he is the propitiation for our sins, which is his proper office, but also because he forgives us our sins and remits our debts, just as if he were the creditor to whom they are owed. Indeed, since the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, it is necessary that it be the Son's part to judge, that is, to justify and to condemn. Therefore, since Christ justifies us by every reason and in every way by which we can be justified, if the one who justifies us is Jehovah, it is necessary that Christ be Jehovah. And so that name, Jehovah is our righteousness, as it is now added to him and ascribed to Israel, could not refer to anything else than either to confirming that Christ is Jehovah, or to denying that he is our righteousness; and the latter would be to overturn his whole Gospel. For does not a certain tacit opposition lie in that name between our righteousness, which is Jehovah, and any other righteousness which men think they can be justified by? Is it not signified by that title that we are justified neither by our own righteousness, which is from the law, nor by ourselves, nor by other men, nor by angels? Certainly it is the public confession that the adequate cause of our justification is Jehovah; for in that name, I think, righteousness is understood not as partial or imperfect, but as full and perfect.

units.la: XIII. Huc accedit, quod nomen istud, Iehova iustitia nostra, nomen est Domini nostri Iesu Christi, vt iam probaui, non autem Israëlis. Quare si per Iehovam alius ab ipso tota specie, vel genere, diuersus intelligitur, suo isto nomine significabit Christus, se non esse iustitiam nostram, nosque ad illum alterum, vt ab eo iustificemur amandabit: id quod non est eius Evangelio consentaneum: eo enim toto nos ad se vocat, tanquam is sit, in quo vno iustitia nostra & vita & salus reposita sit. Ipse Deus pater nos trahit ad Filium, nos dat Filio, nos docet venire ad Filium, vt iustitiam vitamque æternam per eum & in eo obtineamus. Præterea, fit ne tibi, lector pie, verisimile, Dominum nostrum non vocari Iehovam, id est, ipso Christo, eiusque Apostolis interpretibus, Dominum iustitiam nostram, nisi quia sit si-gnum, typus, monumentum vel memoriale quoddam, alium toto genere ab ipso diuersum esse iustitiam nostram? Potestne in mentem venire Christianis ex gentibus linguæ hebreæ ignaris, græcæ tantùm aut latinæ peritis, cum Christum nominari audiunt Dominum iustitiam nostram, Christum non esse illum Dominum, sed illius duntaxat signum & memoriale? Profectò non potest ea cogitatio cadere, nisi in eum, qui sit hoc præjudicio occupatus, aut Christum non posse appellari Dominum, aut non posse dici iustitiam nostram. Non potest enim ea cogitatio enasci ex impositione illius nominis, quasi alicubi scriptum fuisset, id Christo nomen eo consilio inditum fuisse; (hoc enim nusquam legitur:) neque ex intuitu personæ Christi, quasi ea instituta & destinata fuisset ad tale quid significandum: Hoc enim nullo Evangelij loco docetur. Sed neque videtur consentaneum maiestati Christi, vt putetur ad hoc fuisse destinatus, vt esset typus, vel monumentum quoddam, seu signum, non ipsum, sed alium quendam ab eo tota natura diver-sum nostram esse iustitiam. Ve-rum consulamus tandem experientiam. Sibi enim mutuo respondere debent vaticinium[?] & euentum, alterumque ex altero cognosci. Nonne passim in toto orbe[?] Filius vocatur, & creditur, a Christianis Dominus, id est, Iehova? Nonne appellatur, &c.[?] creditur esse, iustitia nostra? Congruit certè cum nostra sententia & fide, inde à prædicato euangelio ad hunc usque diem, euentus, egregius, uti jam aliquoties monui, prophetiæ commentarius.
units.tr: XIII. Moreover, this name, Jehovah is our righteousness, is the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, as I have already proved, and not of Israel. Therefore, if by Jehovah is understood someone else wholly different from him in kind or genus, Christ would by that name signify that he is not our righteousness, and would send us away to that other one to be justified by him; which is not consistent with his Gospel. For through the whole of it he calls us to himself, as if he were the one in whom alone our righteousness, life and salvation are laid up. God the Father himself draws us to the Son, gives us to the Son, teaches us to come to the Son, so that we may obtain righteousness and eternal life through him and in him. Moreover, dear reader, does it seem likely to you that our Lord is not called Jehovah, that is, by Christ himself and his apostolic interpreters the Lord our righteousness, unless because he is a sign, a type, or some kind of memorial of another who is wholly different in kind from him, and who is our righteousness? Could it come into the minds of Christians from the Gentiles, ignorant of the Hebrew tongue and skilled only in Greek or Latin, when they hear Christ named the Lord our righteousness, that Christ is not that Lord but merely his sign and memorial? Certainly such a thought cannot arise, except in one who is occupied with this prejudice, either that Christ cannot be called the Lord, or that he cannot be said to be our righteousness. For that thought cannot spring from the imposition of that name, as if it had been written somewhere that this name was given to Christ with that purpose (for this is nowhere read), nor from a consideration of the person of Christ, as if he had been appointed and destined for the signifying of any such thing; for this is taught in no passage of the Gospel. Nor does it seem consistent with the majesty of Christ that he should be thought to have been destined to be a type, or some memorial or sign, not himself, but another wholly different in nature, to be our righteousness. But let us at last consult experience. For prophecy and event ought to answer each other, and each be known from the other. Is not the Son everywhere in the world called, and believed by Christians, Lord, that is, Jehovah? Is he not called, and believed to be, our righteousness? Certainly this agrees with our opinion and our faith; from the preaching of the Gospel down to this day, the outcome, as I have already several times pointed out, is an excellent commentary on the prophecy.

units.la: XIV. Ad exempla quod attinet, quæ laudant Aduersarij, ea nobis nihil obsunt. Id satis fuerit ostendisse in primo, omnium in speciem maximè apposito[?]. Exod.17. 15. Ædificauit Moses altare, & vocauit nomen eius, Iehoua exaltatio mea, vel vt alij vertunt, vexillum meum. Longè enim diuersa fuit ratio illius altaris & Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Nam primò illud altare fuit omni vita destitutum, nihilque habuit seu materiam, seu formam, seu usum spectes, quod vel minimam ansam præberet suspicandi, illud esse Iehouam, contrà quominus putaretur Iehoua esse pugnabant in eo omnia; ac propterea in ea appellatione nihil fuit periculi. Dispar est ratio Christi, cuius ea est sapientia, auctoritas, dignitas, virtus, majestas, atque in nos clementia munificentia charitas, vt nihil à nobis cogitari possit maius aut diuinius.
units.tr: XIV. As for the examples which our opponents praise, they do us no harm. It will be enough to have shown this in the first, which seems most similar to all of them. Exod. 17. 15. "Moses built an altar, and called its name Jehovah my exaltation," or, as others translate it, my banner. The reason for that altar and for our Lord Jesus Christ is far from the same. For first, that altar was wholly lacking in life, and whether you look at its matter, its form or its use, it had nothing that might give even the slightest occasion to suspect that it was Jehovah; on the contrary, everything about it argued against its being thought to be Jehovah. For that reason there was no danger in that name. Christ's case is different: his wisdom, authority, dignity, power, majesty, and his clemency, bounty and love toward us are such that nothing greater or more divine can be conceived.

units.la: Deinde nulla sunt loca Scripturæ, nulla argumenta, quæ probent illud altare fuisse Iehouam; sunt verò multa, quæ nobis persuadent, Christum esse Iehouam. Tum constat illud altare non fuisse Mosis vel populi Israëlitici exaltationem, siue vexillum, cum certum sit, Christum esse reuera iustitiam nostram. Præterea in confesso est, altare illud typum vel monimentum seu memoriale fuisse: id quod de Christo, qui est ipsa veritas, & in quo habitat corporaliter omnis plenitudo diuinitatis, nefas videtur dicere. Denique Altare illud typus fuit Christi. Non enim temerè Moses illud monumentum altare esse voluit, sed propter analogiam aliquam cum re significata.
units.tr: Next, there are no passages of Scripture and no arguments which prove that the altar was Jehovah; but there are many which persuade us that Christ is Jehovah. Again, it is clear that the altar was not the exaltation, or banner, of Moses or of the Israelite people, since it is certain that Christ is truly our righteousness. Moreover, it is agreed that the altar was a type, or monument, or memorial; and this seems wrong to say of Christ, who is the very truth, and in whom dwells bodily all the fullness of the Godhead. Finally, that altar was a type of Christ. For Moses did not rashly wish that monument to be an altar, but on account of some analogy with the thing signified.

units.la: Iam autem si vmbra est altare typicum, quid erit corpus nisi altare verum? Porrò non Pater, sed Christus eius filius est verum altare. Iuuat igitur causam nostram hoc exemplum. Nam si nomen, Iehoua exaltatio mea, tributum est altari vt vmbræ Christi, certè id nomen conuenit Christo vt corpori, vt veritati, non autem vt signo alterius.
units.tr: Now, if the typical altar is a shadow, what will the body be but the true altar? Furthermore, it is not the Father but Christ his Son who is the true altar. This example therefore helps our cause. For if the name, "Jehovah my exaltation," was given to the altar as to the shadow of Christ, then certainly that name belongs to Christ as to the body, as to the truth, and not as to the sign of something else.

units.la: DISPUTATIO TRIGESIMA SECUNDA
units.tr: Disputation Thirty-Second

units.la: De Arg. XXXII. Ex nomine Tetragramma-to, vulgò Iehoua.
units.tr: On Argument XXXII. From the name Tetragrammaton, commonly Jehovah.

units.la: I. Hic tenere me non possum, quin adhuc unum aut alterum argumentum adjiciam, quo probem Dominum nostrum esse Iehouam. Quod ut fiat cum majore fructu, esto Arg. xxxii. eiusmodi.
units.tr: I. Here I cannot restrain myself from adding one or two more arguments by which I may prove that our Lord is Jehovah. So that this may be done with greater profit, let Argument XXXII be of this kind:

units.la: Iehoua est Deus Israëlis præditus essentia di-vina.
units.tr: Jehovah is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christus est Iehoua.
units.tr: Christ is Jehovah.

units.la: Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis, præditus essentia divina.
units.tr: Therefore Christ is the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Utramque præmissam negat Socinus. Et majorem quidem his verbis, Nihil autem dico, quòd, si angeli ipsi multò Christo inseriores, cum Iehoua personam aliquam in re sustinent, Iehoua nomine appellati inveniantur, ut non uno in loco sup. à nobis demonstratum est; multò magis fieri potest, ut Christus, qui perpetuò in toto salutis nostra negotio Iehoua Dei personam sustinet, ipsiusque perpetuus in Ecclesia vicarius est, Iehoua nomine appelletur: nec tamen ipse sit revera Iehoua, sine eiusdem cum ipso essentia. Nam certè nullus angelorum est revera Iehoua, eandemue cum ipso Iehoua essentiam ha-bet. Hæc responsio multas continet assertiones. Una est, Nullum angelorum esse revera Iehouam. Hæc vera est, nec egeret probatione. Altera est, Angelos Iehouæ nomine appellari in Scriptura. Hæc præcedenti repugnat. Quomodo enim eo nomine appellantur, si id nomen eis non convenit? quomodo id esse dicuntur, quod revera non sunt?
units.tr: Socinus denies both premises. The major he denies in these words: "I say nothing of the fact that, if the angels themselves, far inferior to Christ, when they sustain some person in the matter of Jehovah, are found to be called by the name Jehovah, as has been demonstrated by us in more than one place above, it is much more possible that Christ, who in the whole business of our salvation perpetually sustains the person of Jehovah God, and is His perpetual vicar in the Church, should be called by the name Jehovah; yet he himself is not really Jehovah, without the same essence as He. For certainly none of the angels is really Jehovah, nor has the same essence as Jehovah has." This answer contains many assertions. One is that none of the angels is really Jehovah. This is true, and would need no proof. Another is that angels are called by the name Jehovah in Scripture. This contradicts the preceding claim. For how are they called by that name if the name does not belong to them? How are they said to be what they really are not?

units.la: II. Deinde falsum est, Angelos in plurali numero eo nomine appellari: appellatur quidem Angelus in singulari numero, sed quo sensu is dicatur angelus, natura an officio tantùm, quæri potest. Ego verò sic argumentor. Is fuit, aut utrumque natura sua, nimirum Iehoua & Angelus: aut utrumque officio tantùm: aut alterum natura, alterum officio. Primum nemo dixerit: id enim sine unione hypostatica diuinæ & angelicæ naturæ intelligi non potest. Nec secundum; fuisset enim ille tertia quadam natu-ra à Diuina & Angelica diuersa præditus, quæ cuiusmodi fuisset, aut esse potuisset, intelligi nequaquam potest. Tertium igitur admit-tendum est. Utrum ergo natura Iehoua fuit, officioq; Angelus; an contrà, natura Angelus, & officio Iehoua? Certè prius longè probabilius est. Angelus enim nomen est muneris seu officij, Iehoua non item. Angelus nomen est appellatiuum, quod de alijs, qui non sunt natura angeli, frequenter usurpatur in utroque testamento; Iehoua verò nomen est proprium Dei Israëlis. Adde quod non fit probabile, Deum, qui est gloriæ suæ studiosissimum, quique passim Iehouam esse se inculcat & præter se neminem, voluisse nomen istud suum, omnium maximè & proprium & sacrosanctum, transferre ad angelos meras creaturas ac seruos suos? Quod autem ait Socinus se hoc demonstrasse, si quod argumentum ad id probandum, vel ipse, vel Crellius, attulit, id à nobis refutatum est Disp. de Arg. xxii. §. ix. & Disp. de Arg. xxiii.
units.tr: II. Next, it is false that angels are called by that name in the plural; the Angel is indeed called so in the singular, but it may be asked in what sense he is called an angel, by nature or only by office. My own argument is this. Either he was both by his own nature, namely Jehovah and Angel; or both only by office; or one by nature and the other by office. Nobody would say the first, for this cannot be understood without a hypostatic union of the divine and the angelic nature. Nor the second; for he would then have been endowed with some third nature, different from the divine and the angelic, and what sort of nature that would be, or could be, cannot be understood at all. The third must therefore be admitted. Was he then Jehovah by nature and Angel by office, or on the contrary Angel by nature and Jehovah by office? Certainly the former is far more probable. For "angel" is the name of a function or office, but "Jehovah" is not. "Angel" is an appellative noun, which is frequently applied in both Testaments to others who are not angels by nature; but "Jehovah" is the proper name of the God of Israel.
