Add that it is not probable that God, who is most zealous for His own glory, who everywhere insists that He is Jehovah and that there is none besides Him, would have wished to transfer that name of His, the most proper and most sacred of all, to angels, mere creatures and His servants. As for Socinus saying that he has demonstrated this, if he or Crellius has brought forward any argument for proving it, that has been refuted by us in Disputation on Argument XXII, §9, and in Disputation on Argument XXIII.

units.la: III Præterea sic Aduersarium aggredior. Tu vis, istum Angelum, qui Iehouæ nomine appellatur, esse naturâ angelum, hoc est, præditum natura angelica. Ego contendo eum esse natura Deum seu Iehouam. Vter nostrum rectius sentiat consideremus. Quo argumento efficies, cum esse naturâ angelum? Istone; Appellatur Angelus: Ergo est naturâ angelus? Nego consequentiam. Multi enim homines, quod tu ignorare non potes, in utroque testamento angeli appellantur. Nec mirum: est enim angelus proprie, vt jam aliquoties monui, nuncius. Num hoc potius, appellatur Angelus Iehouæ: Ergo est naturâ angelus? Hanc quoque consequentiam nego, quoniam, & Sacerdos & Iohannes Baptista appellantur angeli Iehouæ, Ille Malach. 2. 7. [?] hic Malach. 3. 1. & Matth. 11. 10. quos tamen certum est meros homines fuisse.
units.tr: III. Furthermore, I address my opponent thus. You wish that angel who is called by the name Jehovah to be an angel by nature, that is, endowed with an angelic nature. I contend that he is God, or Jehovah, by nature. Let us consider which of us holds the more correct view. By what argument will you prove that he is an angel by nature? Is it this: He is called an Angel, therefore he is an angel by nature? I deny the inference. For many men, as you cannot fail to know, are called angels in both Testaments. This is no wonder, since an angel is properly, as I have already said several times, a messenger. Or is it this: He is called the Angel of Jehovah, therefore he is an angel by nature? I deny this inference too, since both the priest and John the Baptist are called angels of Jehovah: the former in Malachi 2:7 [?], the latter in Malachi 3:1 and Matthew 11:10, and yet it is certain that both were mere men.

units.la: IV. Fortasse vteris hoc argumento. Is, aut homo fuit, aut Deus, aut angelus. Non fuit homo, saltem illo tempore, vt patet. Nec fuit Deus seu Iehoua. Ergo fuit angelus naturâ. Immo, inquā, Deus seu Iehova fuit; testibus, sacro historico, qui cum non raro Iehovam appellat, ipsoque illo angelo, qui se Deum esse seu Iehovam testatur aliquot locis. Atqui, inquies, appella-tur angelus Iehovae. Non potest autem angelus Iehovae esse Iehova. Contrarium docet Scriptura, cum eundem aliquoties simul & angelum Iehovae & Iehovam appellat, utri potius habenda fides, tibine pro ingenio affirmanti, Angelum Iehovae non esse Iehovam, An Scripturae asserenti, Angelum Iehovae esse Iehovam? Clamat hic Angelus, se esse Iehovam. Idem testatur sacer historicus. Quis tu es, qui audes contrarium docere, mendaciisque eos insimulare?
units.tr: IV. Perhaps you use this argument: He was either a man, or God, or an angel. He was not a man, at least at that time, as is plain. Nor was he God or Jehovah. Therefore he was an angel by nature. No, I reply, he was God or Jehovah; the witness is the sacred historian, who often calls him Jehovah, and that angel himself, who in several places testifies that he is God or Jehovah. But, you will say, he is called the angel of Jehovah, and the angel of Jehovah cannot be Jehovah. Scripture teaches the contrary, since it sometimes calls the same person at once both the angel of Jehovah and Jehovah. Which should we rather believe: you, who affirm by your own wit that the angel of Jehovah is not Jehovah, or Scripture, which asserts that the angel of Jehovah is Jehovah? Here the Angel cries out that he is Jehovah. The sacred historian bears the same witness. Who are you, that you dare to teach the contrary and to accuse them of lies?

units.la: V. Adjicies, Non posse vnum eundemque suimetipsius angelum dici. Quid inde cōcludis? Angelum Iehovae non esse Iehovam? Hoc, vt dixi, contradicere est illi ipsi Angelo, sacrisque historicis. Cur non potius inde concludis, plures esse personas diuinas. At, instabis, Iehova est vnus Deut. 6. 4. &, nullus est Deus alius nisi vnus 1. Cor. 8. 4. Credimus vtrumque, & plures esse personas diuinas, & nonnisi vnum Deum, vnum Iehovam esse: quia vtrumque Scriptura docet, quam multis inuictis argumentis certissimè scimus diuinitus inspiratam esse. At quomodo est vnus Iehova, si duo sunt, quorum alter simpliciter Iehova, alter simul Iehova & Angelus Iehovae appellatur? Nempè duo illi vnum sunt. Conuenit autem illis Iehovae nomen quatenus sunt vnum, non verò quatenus inter se distinguuntur.
units.tr: V. You will add that one and the same being cannot be called his own angel. What do you conclude from this? That the angel of Jehovah is not Jehovah? As I have said, this is to contradict that very Angel and the sacred historians. Why do you not rather conclude from this that there are several divine persons? But, you will press, "Jehovah is one" (Deut. 6:4) "and there is no other God but one" (1 Cor. 8:4). We believe both: that there are several divine persons, and that there is only one God, one Jehovah; because Scripture teaches both, and we know with most certainty, from many unconquerable arguments, that it is divinely inspired. But how is there one Jehovah if there are two, one of whom is simply Jehovah and the other is called at once Jehovah and the Angel of Jehovah? Surely those two are one. The name Jehovah belongs to them insofar as they are one, not insofar as they are distinguished from one another.

units.la: VI. Objicies, non posse duas personas eandem numero habere naturam. Quo argumento id probabis? Testimonio Scripturæ? nullum extat. Ratione aliqua Metaphysica? vtra igitur est regula fidei nostræ, Scriptura, an Philosophia? Certè fides est ex auditu verbi Dei, non autem Philosophiæ; & quis melius novit quomodo se habeat Deus, cui nihil est in rerum natura simile, quàm ipse Deus? Refellit autem ipse Deus omnes subtilitates Metaphysicas, quibus personarum diuinarum distinctio, & naturæ diuinæ vnitas oppugnatur, quoties vtramque verbo suo inculcat. Innuit enim se vnitatem intelligere, quæ non repugnet eiusmodi distinctioni, &distinctionem, quæ non repugnet eiusmodi vnitati. Repones, non pugnare Theologiam cum Philosophia. Agnosco, modò Philosophiam intelligas veram & rectam[?]. Hæc verò objectum suum transgredi non debet, nec se mysteriis omnem modum reuelationis naturalis exsuperantibus immiscere, nec Deum, quatenus à creaturis differt, creaturarum pede & modulo metiri. Alioquin si falcem immittit[?] in propriam Theologiae supernaturalis messem, verbo Dei corrigi debet, non contrà verbum Dei Philosophiâ. Caeterum omnes illas subtilitates, quas è Philosophia depromunt Aduersarij, Deo dante, di-luemus alio loco. Nunc enim de Scripturae verbis duntaxat disputamus, vt quae huius controuersiae pars cum illis consentiat, quae dissentiat, agnoscamus.
units.tr: VI. You will object that two persons cannot have the same nature in number. By what argument will you prove this? By the testimony of Scripture? There is none. By some metaphysical reasoning? Which, then, is the rule of our faith, Scripture or Philosophy? Certainly faith comes from hearing the Word of God, not from Philosophy; and who knows better how God is, when nothing in the nature of things is like Him, than God Himself? Moreover God Himself refutes all the metaphysical subtleties by which the distinction of the divine persons and the unity of the divine nature are assailed, whenever He impresses both upon us in His Word. For He indicates that He understands a unity which does not conflict with such a distinction, and a distinction which does not conflict with such a unity. You will reply that theology does not clash with philosophy. I grant it, provided you understand philosophy to be true and right. But philosophy ought not to overstep its object, nor mix itself with mysteries that surpass every mode of natural revelation, nor measure God, insofar as He differs from creatures, by the foot and measure of creatures. Otherwise, if it puts its sickle into the proper harvest of supernatural theology, it must be corrected by the Word of God, and not the Word of God by philosophy. Meanwhile, all those subtleties which our opponents draw from philosophy we shall, God willing, answer in another place. For now we are disputing only the words of Scripture, so that we may recognize which part of this controversy agrees with them and which dissents.

units.la: VII. Non potuisti probare, illum, qui simul Angelus Iehouae appellatur & Iehoua, praeditum esse natura angelica. Ego vero probo eum esse praeditum natura diuina. Et primò quidem sic. Appellatur Iehoua: Ergo est reuera Iehoua. Probo consequentiam. Cui nomen diuinitus tribuitur, ei conuenit nominis illius significatio. Illi autem, qui simul Angelus & Iehoua appellatur, tribuitur diuinitus nomen Iehouae, & quidem saepe. Ergo illi conuenit nominis Iehouae significatio. Est autem nomen Iehoua, nomen Dei Israelis creatoris coeli & terrae, & quidem nomen proprium, saltem pro tempore Veteris Testamenti, non autem nomen commune sicut Angelus. Id enim, & Deus ipse sibi vni imposuit, suumque nomen esse testatus est plurimis locis, & se habet perpetuò vt nomen proprium. Cui igitur id nomen diuinitus tributum est, eum oportet Deum Israelis esse. Haec enim est vnica nominis illius significatio.
units.tr: VII. You have not been able to prove that he who is at once called the Angel of Jehovah and Jehovah is endowed with an angelic nature. But I prove that he is endowed with the divine nature. And first, indeed, thus: He is called Jehovah; therefore he really is Jehovah. I prove the inference. To whom the name is divinely given, to him the meaning of that name belongs. Now to him who is at once called Angel and Jehovah the name Jehovah is divinely given, and indeed often. Therefore the meaning of the name Jehovah belongs to him. The name Jehovah, however, is the name of the God of Israel, the creator of heaven and earth, and it is a proper name, at least for the period of the Old Testament, not a common name like "Angel". For God Himself imposed it on Himself alone, and testified in very many places that it is His name, and it always stands as a proper name. Therefore he to whom that name has been divinely given must be the God of Israel. For this is the sole meaning of that name.

units.la: VIII. Deinde sic, Qui profitetur in Veteri Testamento se esse Deum, Iehouam, Deum Abrahami, Isaaci, &c, is haberi debet pro Deo Israelis praedito essentia diuina. Quis enim illi dicere ausit, Tu is reuera non es, quem te esse profiteris? Tu te dicis esse Iehouam, & Deum Abrahami, Isaaci, & Iacobi, cum tamen reuera nihil sis nisi Iehouae seruus. Nisi fallor, hoc esset cum mendacij, immò sacrilegij accusare. Atqui iste Angelus profitetur se esse Iehouam, Deum Abrahami, Isaaci, & Iacobi Gen. 31. 11. 13. Exod. 3. 2. 6. Iudic. 2. 1. &c. Ergo iste Angelus haberi debet pro Deo Israelis praedito essentia diuina. Sed pergamus. Quid enim opus est pluribus argumentis?
units.tr: VIII. Next, thus: whoever professes in the Old Testament that he is God, Jehovah, the God of Abraham, Isaac, etc., must be held to be the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence. For who would dare to say to him, "You are not really the one you profess to be? You call yourself Jehovah and the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, when in truth you are nothing but a servant of Jehovah." Unless I am mistaken, this would be to accuse him of lying, or rather of sacrilege. But that Angel professes that he is Jehovah, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Gen. 31. 11, 13; Exod. 3. 2, 6; Judg. 2. 1, etc.). Therefore that Angel must be held to be the God of Israel, endowed with the divine essence. But let us go on. For why do we need more arguments?

units.la: IX. Tertia Socini assertio est, Angelos, Iehouae personam quibusdam in rebus sustinuisse. Id mihi probari velim. Rationem nullam affert: nec video quomodo probari possit. Haud satis etiam assequor ; quo sensu id ab eo dicatur. Phrasis enim illa Iehovae personam sustinere, quàm est à Scriptura aliena, tam mihi ambigua & obscura videtur. Quid est enim, quaeso, Angelos Iehovae personam sustinere? Eam veluti ferre & gestare? dicitur enim Iehova super cherub æquitare ps. 18.2. & sedere Ezech. 10. 4. Id ad rem quam agimus nihil facere prorsus. Eius causam tueri? Id quoque [illegible, ~8 letters] Iehovae nomine appellari, & se profiteri Iehovam esse? Nugantur igitur Aduersarij, cum dicunt angelos Iehovae nomine appellari & se profiteri Iehovam esse, quia Iehovae personam sustinent. Iehovae legatum esse, eique legationi consentanea dicere & facere? sustinent igitur perpetuò & omnibus in rebus Iehovae personam Angeli : id quod tamen negat Socinus. In nomine Iehovae loqui & agere? Id etiam perpetuò & omnibus in rebus conuenit angelis. Nos etiam Christiani tenemur omnia facere in Christi nomine, num igitur eius personam omnibus in rebus tenemur sustinere? Quid ergo tandem est Iehovae personam sustinere? Typum esse Iehovae? Certè Angeli typi fuerunt Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Cum enim fœdus legale contraheretur & promulgaretur, inter Deum & Israelitas interponebantur , illinc quidem Angeli, hinc verò Moses, cui successit Iosue, adjunctus autem fuit Aaron : Itaque Dominum nostrum, qui his omnibus respondet, Auctor Ep. ad Heb. confert primò cum Angelis, deinde cum Mose, tum cum Iosuè, & tandem cum Aarone. Verùm typi in historijs Veteris Testamenti suas ipsi personas sustinent, non autem alienas, earum scilicet rerum, quarum sunt typi. Fortè volunt Angelos Iehovae personam in historijs sacris, tanquam in dramate, repræsentasse. Hoc verò esset verissimas ac diuinissimas Scriptura historias in dramata seu fabulas conuertere : quo nihil fingi potest magis blasphemum. Ita Angelus ille, qui Iehova vocatus est & se Iehovam esse professus est sæpius, fuisset Iehova personatus &, ut Plautino verbo utar, histricus. Isque, ut iam monui, solus personatus fuisset, præter eum alius nemo : Et tamen habuisset veram Iehovae auctoritatem eique fides habenda fuisset in omnibus, vocareturque simul Iehova & Angelus Iehovae. Quae omnia, quàm sint à dramate aliena nemo non videt.
units.tr: IX. The third assertion of Socinus is: Angels, in certain matters, have sustained the person of Jehovah. I would like this to be proved. He gives no reason, nor do I see how it could be proved. Nor do I sufficiently grasp in what sense he means it. For the phrase "to sustain the person of Jehovah" seems to me as foreign to Scripture as it is ambiguous and obscure. What, I ask, does it mean for Angels to sustain the person of Jehovah? To bear and carry it, as it were? For Jehovah is said to ride upon a cherub (Ps. 18:2) and to sit (Ezek. 10:4). That has nothing whatever to do with the matter we are discussing. To defend his cause? [illegible] To be called by the name of Jehovah and to profess that they are Jehovah? The opponents, then, talk nonsense when they say that the angels are called by the name of Jehovah and profess themselves to be Jehovah because they sustain the person of Jehovah. To be Jehovah's envoy, and to say and do what suits the embassy? Then the angels sustain the person of Jehovah always and in all things; yet Socinus denies this. To speak and act in the name of Jehovah? That too applies to angels always and in all things. We Christians too are bound to do all things in the name of Christ; are we therefore bound to sustain his person in all things? What, then, finally, is it to sustain the person of Jehovah? To be a type of Jehovah? Certainly angels were types of our Lord Jesus Christ. For when the legal covenant was made and promulgated, angels stood between God and the Israelites on the one side, and Moses, whom Joshua succeeded, with Aaron joined to him, on the other. Accordingly the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews compares our Lord, who answers to all of these, first with the angels, then with Moses, then with Joshua, and finally with Aaron. But types in the histories of the Old Testament sustain their own persons, not those of others, namely of the things of which they are types. Perhaps they wish to say that the angels represented the person of Jehovah in the sacred histories, as in a drama. But this would be to turn the most true and most divine histories of Scripture into dramas or fables, than which nothing more blasphemous can be imagined. Thus that Angel who was called Jehovah and very often professed himself to be Jehovah would have been a Jehovah in costume and, to use Plautus' word, a stage-player. And, as I have already noted, he alone would have worn the mask, and no one else besides him. Yet he would have possessed the true authority of Jehovah, and faith would have to be placed in him in all things, and he would be called at once Jehovah and the Angel of Jehovah. That all these things are foreign to a drama, no one can fail to see.

units.la: X. Quarta Socinii assertio est, Angelos, cum Iehova personam aliqua in re sustinent, Iehova nomine appellari. Hoc falsum esse contendo. Quo enim sensu Angeli dici possint Iehova equidem non intelligo. Nemo profecto, nisi cum fabula seu drama agitur, ita alterius personam sustinet, ut eius nomine proprio appelletur, & se illum ipsum profiteatur esse, cuius personam sustinere dicitur. Nam, si id extra drama fiat, pro mendacio habebitur. Mentietur Legatus, si se illum ipsum profiteatur esse à quo sit missus. Mentietur typus, si se dicat illum esse cuius est typus, Moses verbi gratia, si se dicat esse Iesum Christum. Mentietur inferior Magistratus si se regem esse profiteatur. Quid? Nonne Iesu Christi personam Apostoli æquè, aut etiam magis, sustinuerunt, quàm Iehovæ Angeli? tamen Apostoli nunquam Iesu Christi nomine appellantur. Nunquam quisquam eorum ita fideles alloquutus perhibetur, Ego sum Iesus Christus qui vos sanguine meo redemi. Nec intelligi potest quomodo sic Petrus, aut Paulus, aut aliorum Apostolorum aliquis Ecclesiam sine mendacio affari potuisset. Cum igitur idem simul & Angelus Iehovæ & Iehova appelletur sæpe, seseque ipsum profiteatur esse Iehovam, idque citra mendacium, verissimè, omninò tenemur id credere. Docet igitur Scriptura & restatur & inculcat, esse quandam personam, quæ ita sic Iehovæ angelus, ut tamen sit Iehova. Docet igitur & testatur, & inculcat, esse duas personas quæ sint Iehova.
units.tr: X. The fourth assertion of Socinus is: Angels, when they sustain the person of Jehovah in some matter, are called by the name of Jehovah. I maintain that this is false. In what sense angels could be called Jehovah I certainly do not understand. Surely no one, except when a fable or drama is being staged, sustains another's person so as to be called by that person's proper name and to profess himself to be the very one whose person he is said to sustain. For if this were done outside a drama, it would be held to be a lie. An envoy would lie if he professed himself to be the very one by whom he was sent. A type would lie if he said that he was the one of whom he is a type: Moses, for example, if he said he was Jesus Christ. A lesser magistrate would lie if he professed himself to be king. What? Did not the Apostles sustain the person of Jesus Christ equally, or even more, than the Angels of Jehovah did? Yet the Apostles are never called by the name of Jesus Christ. Nowhere is it recorded that any one of them addressed the faithful thus: "I am Jesus Christ, who redeemed you with my blood." Nor can it be understood how Peter, or Paul, or any other of the Apostles could have addressed the Church in this way without lying. Since, then, the same being is often called both the Angel of Jehovah and Jehovah at once, and professes himself to be Jehovah, and this without falsehood and most truly, we are altogether bound to believe it. Scripture therefore teaches, repeats and impresses that there is a certain person who is so the Angel of Jehovah, and yet is Jehovah. Scripture therefore teaches, attests and impresses that there are two persons who are Jehovah.

units.la: XI. Quinta Socini assertio est, Christum perpetuò in toto salutis nostræ negotio Iehovæ Dei personam sustinere.
units.tr: XI. The fifth assertion of Socinus is that Christ, throughout the whole business of our salvation, perpetually bears the person of Jehovah God.

units.la: Eamne sustinet tanquam suam, an tanquam alienam? Si prius, igitur est Iehova Deus. Si posterius, quomodo id conuenit cum Euangelio, quod nihil prorsus tribuit Christo, & in quo Christus nihil prorsus sibi tribuit, quod ipsi reuera non conueniant in propria sua persona? Deinde, An Christus cum baptisabatur à Iohanne, tentabatur à diabolo, docebat turbas è navicula, orabat Patrem in horto, damnabatur à Synedrio, verberabatur à satellitibus, interrogabatur à Pilato, agebatur in crucem, pendebat in cruce inter duos latrones, spiritum suum commendabat Patri, moriebatur, sepeliebatur, resurgebat &c, alienam Iehovæ Dei sustinebat personam? Vtinam quæ asseuerant Aduersarij vel considerarent attentius, vel explicarent distinctius! Quod addit Socinus, Christum Iehovæ Dei perpetuum in Ecclesia vicarium esse, id negatum est à Smalcio, vti à nobis est obseruatum. Arg. IX. §. xxx x.[?] quàm thesim & præcedentem, tu, quæso, lector re-lege.
units.tr: Does he bear that person as his own, or as another's? If as his own, then he is Jehovah God. If as another's, how does this agree with the Gospel, which attributes nothing at all to Christ, and in which Christ claims for himself nothing that does not really belong to him in his own person? Again, when Christ was baptized by John, tempted by the devil, taught the crowds from a boat, prayed to the Father in the garden, was condemned by the Sanhedrin, struck by the guards, questioned by Pilate, led away to the cross, hung on the cross between two thieves, commended his spirit to the Father, died, was buried, rose again, and so on, did he bear the person of Jehovah God as another's? I wish our opponents would either consider what they assert more attentively or explain it more distinctly! As for what Socinus adds, that Christ is the perpetual vicar of Jehovah God in the Church, this was denied by Smalcius, as we have also pointed out. Arg. IX, §. xxx [?]. Let the reader, I beg, reread that thesis and the preceding one.

units.la: XII. Ex suis illis assertionibus deducit hanc conclusionem Socinus, fieri potuisse ut Christus Iehova nomine appelletur, nec tamen ipse sit revera Iehova. Nempe ex præmissis falsis mirum non est si sequatur falsa conclusio. Sed quæro jam, non an potuerit Iehovæ nomine Christus appellari, sed an reipsa appellatus fuerit in Scriptura, necne? Negat Socinus: Atque ita quod minus probabile est id affirmat, quod magis probabile est id negat. Minus enim probabile est Angelos nomine Iehovæ appellari, quàm Christum. Nam si utrisque commune fuit sustinere personam Iehovæ, Illi eam sustinuerunt ad tempus, Hic perpetuò: Illi quibusdam duntaxat in rebus, Hic in toto salutis nostræ negotio: Illi minus perfectè, Hic perfectissimè. Si igitur angeli, quia sustinuerunt personam Iehovæ aliquando, & quibusdam in rebus, & imperfectè, nomine Iehovæ appellati sunt frequenter; nonne Christus, qui personam Iehovæ perpetuò & omnibus in rebus & perfectissimè sustinuit, potiori jure nomine Iehovæ appellari debuit? Quis ergo credat tantum honorem tributum fuisse angelis sæpe; quibus tamen minus conveniebat: Christo verò, cui magis debebatur, denegatum fuisse constanter?
units.tr: XII. From these assertions Socinus draws the conclusion that it could happen that Christ is called by the name Jehovah and yet is not really Jehovah himself. Certainly it is no wonder that a false conclusion follows from false premises. But I now ask not whether Christ could have been called by the name Jehovah, but whether he really was so called in Scripture or not. Socinus denies it. And so he affirms the less probable thing and denies the more probable. For it is less probable that the angels were called by the name Jehovah than that Christ was. If both were alike in bearing the person of Jehovah, the angels bore it for a time, Christ perpetually; the angels in certain matters only, Christ in the whole business of our salvation; the angels less perfectly, Christ most perfectly. If then the angels, because they sometimes bore the person of Jehovah, and in certain matters, and imperfectly, were often called by the name Jehovah, should not Christ, who bore the person of Jehovah perpetually, in all things, and most perfectly, have been called by the name Jehovah with even greater right? Who then would believe that such great honour was often given to the angels, to whom it was less fitting, while it was constantly denied to Christ, to whom it was more due?

units.la: XIII. Aiunt Angelos Iehovæ personam & nomen assumpsisse, ut tanto plus auctoritatis haberet res & oratio, & in auditorum animos altius descenderet. Atqui multò plus auctoritatis habere Euangelium oportuit quàm legem, multòque altius in auditorum animos descendere. Cur igitur similiter Christus Iehovæ personam & nomen non assumpsit? cauendumne fuit ne nimium tribuere-tur Filio, neue honoraretur sicut honoratur Pater, cum cauen-dum non fuerit ne nimium tribueretur angelis, neue illi divino honore afficerentur?
units.tr: XIII. They say that the angels assumed the person and name of Jehovah so that the matter and the speech might have so much more authority, and might descend more deeply into the minds of the hearers. Yet the Gospel ought to have far more authority than the Law, and to descend far more deeply into the minds of hearers. Why then did Christ not likewise assume the person and name of Jehovah? Was there a need to guard against attributing too much to the Son, and against his being honoured as the Father is honoured, when there was no need to guard against attributing too much to the angels, or against their being honoured with divine honour?

units.la: XIV. Aut igitur Deus voluit ut angelus ille crederetur Iehova esse, aut non voluit. Si voluit, parendum est eius voluntati. Si noluit, cur eum voluit Iehovam toties & appellari, & esse se profiteri? Nam si Iehova esse creditur, plus habet auctoritatis res & oratio, altiusque in animos auditorum descendit: si non creditur: tacitè falsitatis accusatur minuiturque rei & orationis pondus.
units.tr: XIV. Either God willed that this angel should be believed to be Jehovah, or he did not will it. If he willed it, we must obey his will. If he did not will it, why did he will that the angel should so often both be called Jehovah and profess himself to be Jehovah? For if he is believed to be Jehovah, the matter and the speech have more authority and descend more deeply into the minds of hearers; if he is not believed to be Jehovah, he is tacitly accused of falsehood, and the weight of the matter and the speech is diminished.

units.la: XV. Sed quid immoror in refutanda responsione, quam argumentum nostrum parua declinatione potest effugere? si nempe sic concipiatur.
units.tr: XV. But why do I linger in refuting this answer, which our argument can evade with a slight dodge? Namely, if it is put in this form:

units.la: Cui verè, & non quatenus alienam personam sustinet, convenit nomen Iehouæ, ille reuera est Iehoua, præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: He to whom the name Jehovah truly belongs, and not insofar as he bears another's person, is really Jehovah, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Christo verè, & non quatenus alienam personam sustinet, convenit nomen Iehouæ.
units.tr: The name Jehovah truly belongs to Christ, and not insofar as he bears another's person.

units.la: Christus igitur est reuera Iehoua, præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: Christ, therefore, is really Jehovah, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: Erit etiam nobis iterum hac eadem de re disputandum ad Arg. sequens, cui suum aliquod proprium momentum conseruari oportet. Hoc igitur tantùm dicam hoc loco. Si fieri potuit, vt Christus Iehouæ nomine appelletur, nec tamen ipse sit reuera Iehoua, fieri potuit vt Scriptura mentiatur & nos fallat. Negabunt sine dubio consequentiam. Dicant igitur nobis quid sit mentiri, si hoc non est. Si veritas est orationis cum ipsa re consensio, quid est orationis ab ipsa re dissensio, nisi falsitas? Si, vt Crellij verbis vtar, veritatis est curare, vt verba cum re ipsa consentiant, nec aliter loquaris quàm rem sese habere sentis, nonne is à veritate discedit, cuius verba cum re ipsa non consentiunt, quicunque aliter loquitur, quàm rem sese habere sentit? Frustrà reponent, Christum Iehouæ nomine appellari, quia Iehouæ personam sustineat. Nam aliud est esse Iehouam, id quod Iehouæ nomine appellari significat, aliud Iehouæ personam sustinere, hoc est vt ego interpretor, eius seruum & legatum esse. Si profanus aliquis historicus Christianissimi regis legatum, regem Galliæ vel Ludouicum XIV. appellaret, aut esse affirmaret, quis id ferret? quis frigidam illam & ineptam excusationem admittendam censeret, potuisse legatum sic appellari, quod legatus seu vicarius Regis cum esset, eius personam sustineret? Magnam igitur sacris autoribus injuriam faciunt Aduersarij, cum eos existimant, Iehouæ nomine Angelum vel Christum appellasse, ac esse Iehouam sanctè affirmasse, cum tamen reuera Iehoua, nec angelus ille, nec Christus esset.
units.tr: We shall also have to dispute again on this same matter at the following argument, which must preserve some proper weight of its own. So I will say only this here. If it could happen that Christ is called by the name Jehovah and yet is not really Jehovah, it could happen that Scripture lies and deceives us. They will doubtless deny the consequence. Let them then tell us what it is to lie, if this is not it. If truth is the agreement of speech with the thing itself, what is the disagreement of speech from the thing itself, if not falsehood? If, to use the words of Crellius, it is the business of truth that words agree with the thing itself, and that you do not speak otherwise than you feel the thing to be, does not he depart from the truth whose words do not agree with the thing itself, whoever speaks otherwise than he feels the thing to be? They vainly reply that Christ is called by the name Jehovah because he bears the person of Jehovah. For to be Jehovah, which is what being called by the name Jehovah signifies, is one thing; to bear the person of Jehovah, that is, as I interpret it, to be his servant and envoy, is another. If some secular historian were to call the envoy of the most Christian king the king of France, or Louis XIV, or were to affirm that he is, who would put up with it? Who would think that the cold and foolish excuse should be admitted, that the envoy could be so called because, being the king's envoy or vicar, he bears his person? The opponents therefore do great injury to the sacred writers when they think that the angel or Christ was called by the name Jehovah, and solemnly affirmed that he was Jehovah, when in truth he was neither Jehovah, nor that angel, nor Christ.

units.la: XVI. Venio igitur ad alteram Socini responsionem. Ea negat minorem argumenti nostri, hoc est, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum esse aut appellari Iehouam, id quod & probatum est à nobis superioribus argumentis, & probatum imus hoc loco his paucis. Primum sic habet. Cui passim in sacris literis græcis tribuitur absolutè, seu κατ' ἐξοχὴν, & tanquam aliquo modo proprium, illud nomen graecum, quod omnium nominum graecorum maximè accommodatum ad hebraicum Jehova exprimendum non modo 70. interpretibus, sed ipsis etiam Jesu Christi Apostolis, ipsíque adeo Spiritui sancto visum est, ei tributum censeri debet nomen Jehova, cuius graecum illud est versio seu interpretatio. Christo passim in sacris literis graecis tribuitur absolutè seu κατ' ἐξοχὴν, & tanquam aliquomodo proprium id nomen, quod omnium nominum graecorum maximè accommodatum ad heb. Jehova exprimendum, non solum 70 interpretibus, sed ipsis etiam Jesu Christi Apostolis, ipsique adeo Spiritui sancto visum est. Christo igitur tributum censeri debet nomen Jehova. Non video quomodo major negari possit, nam & per se clara est, & potest inductione probari. Cui enim nomen graecum convenit, huic convenit etiam hebraeum, quod per graecum illud constanter exponi solet, ut patet inductione omnium eiusmodi nominum. Minor etiam ita manifesta est, ut vocari in dubium non possit. Nam & 70 interpretes in Veteri Testamento, & Apostoli in novo hebraeum Jehovam vertunt κύριον passim & constanter, quod nomen absolutè seu κατ' ἐξοχὴν, & tanquam eius aliquomodo proprium Servatori nostro Jesu Christo convenire Christianus non est qui neget.
units.tr: XVI. I come therefore to Socinus's second answer. It denies the minor premise of our argument, that is, that our Lord Jesus Christ is, or is called, Jehovah. This has been proved by us in the earlier arguments, and we shall prove it here in a few words. The first argument runs thus. To whom, throughout the Greek sacred books, the Greek name is attributed absolutely, or kat' exochēn [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], and as though in some way its own, that Greek name [kyrios, κύριον], which was judged most suitable of all Greek names for expressing the Hebrew Jehovah, not only by the Seventy interpreters but also by the very apostles of Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit himself, ought to be considered as bearing the name Jehovah, of which that Greek word is the version or translation. Throughout the Greek sacred books the name [kyrios, κύριον] is attributed to Christ absolutely, or kat' exochēn [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], and as though in some way its own, a name which was judged most suitable of all Greek names for expressing the Hebrew Jehovah, not only by the Seventy interpreters but also by the apostles of Jesus Christ and by the Holy Spirit himself. Therefore the name Jehovah ought to be considered as attributed to Christ. I do not see how the major premise can be denied, for it is clear in itself and can be proved by induction. For whoever has the Greek name also has the Hebrew, which is constantly rendered by that Greek word, as is evident from induction over all such names. The minor premise is also so plain that it cannot be called into doubt. For both the Seventy interpreters in the Old Testament and the apostles in the New translate the Hebrew Jehovah as kyrios [κύριον] throughout and constantly; and no Christian denies that this name belongs absolutely, or kat' exochēn [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], and as in some way its own, to our Saviour Jesus Christ.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: XVII. Hoc argumentum Socinus primum dilemmate oppugnat, deinde solvere conatur, sed frustrà. Dilemma est eiusmodi. Aut istud, inquit, quod de Christo dicitur, significatum à nomine Jehova, eiusmodi est, ut soli illi uni Deo conveniat: aut non est. Si est; quid ineptius, quàm ex re ipsa, quæ de Christo dicitur, non statim argumentari, illum esse illum unum Deum: sed ex ea prius colligere, nomen quod eam significat, Christo convenire, ut inde postmodum concludatur, Christum esse illum unum Deum? Si non est; Frustrà ex nomine, quod propter rem, quam significat, Christo convenire Bellarminus ratiocinatur, id concludit, quod ex ipsa re concludere nequit. Sophistam agit Socinus. Quid enim refert unde argumentemur? Nam, vel praemissae syllogismi nostri, nullo formae vitio laborantis, ambae verae sunt; vel ambae falsae, aut saltem earum altera. Si prius; cur totum non concedit, & dat manus? si posterius; cur rectà falsitatem non retegit solvendo argumentum? cur tempus terit inutili vitilitigatione? Respondeo tamen ad dilemma; significationem nominis Iehouæ eiusmodi esse, vt soli illi vni Deo conueniat: nec tamen nos inepte facere, qui ex ea, hoc quidem in loco, recta seu immediate non concludimus, Christum esse illum vnum Deum. Cum enim possim ab illa significatione argumentari duobus modis, mediante scilicet nomine Iehoua, vel sine eo; quid prohibet, quominus pro meo arbitratu illo nunc vtar, isto dissimulato, aut in alium locum rejecto præsertim si ille, quàm iste, clarior aut facilior mihi videatur? Ex duabus viis eodem tendentibus facione inepte cum longiorem, si mihi tutior commodior facilior-que videatur, breuiori antepono? Adde quod reuera duo sunt media seu argumenta diuersa, illud quod à nomine Iehoua eiusque significatione ducitur, & illud quod ab illa significatione, non formaliter quatenus est significatio nominis Iehouæ, sed materialiter & per sese spectata peti potest. Quis enim non videt argumentationem qua vsi sumus, niti autoritate 70. interpretum, & præcipuè Apostolorum, Iehouam reddentium κύριον, non autem vi nominis citra relationem ad Hebræum Iehoua considerati? Hinc enim si liberet argumentari, duceretur argumentum à summo illo iure & dominio seu potestate, quam Christus habet in res omnes, certissimo diuinitatis eius indicio. Sed ea argumentandi ratio, vt non est huius loci, sic non est necessaria ad tuendum illud argumentum, quod hac disputatione tractamus.
units.tr: XVII. Socinus attacks this argument first with a dilemma and then tries to answer it, but in vain. The dilemma runs as follows. Either, he says, what is said of Christ, as signified by the name Jehovah, is of such a kind that it belongs to that one God alone; or it is not. If it is, what could be more absurd than to argue not straight from the thing said of Christ that he is that one God, but first to gather from it that the name which signifies it belongs to Christ, so that afterwards it may be concluded that Christ is that one God? If it is not, then Bellarmine reasons from the name, which he says belongs to Christ on account of the thing it signifies, and so concludes what he cannot conclude from the thing itself. Socinus is playing the sophist. For what does it matter where we begin our argument? Either the premises of our syllogism, which suffers from no fault of form, are both true, or both are false, or at least one of them is. If the first, why does he not grant the whole and give up? If the second, why does he not expose the falsehood directly by answering the argument? Why does he waste time in useless wrangling? Still, I reply to the dilemma. The signification of the name Jehovah is of such a kind that it belongs to that one God alone; yet we do not argue foolishly when, in this place, we do not conclude straight away, or immediately, that Christ is that one God from it. For since I can argue from that signification in two ways, namely either through the name Jehovah or without it, what prevents me from using now the one I choose, setting the other aside or leaving it for another place, especially if the one seems to me clearer or easier than the other? Would it be foolish to prefer the shorter of two roads leading to the same end, if the shorter seems to me safer, more convenient and easier? Add that there are in fact two different means or arguments: the one drawn from the name Jehovah and its signification, and the other drawn from that signification considered not formally, as the signification of the name Jehovah, but materially and in itself. For who does not see that the argument we have used rests on the authority of the Seventy, and above all of the Apostles, who render Jehovah by kyrion [κύριον], and not on the force of the name considered apart from its relation to the Hebrew Jehovah? For if one wished to argue from this, the argument would be drawn from that supreme right and dominion, or power, which Christ has over all things, a most certain sign of his divinity. But that mode of argument, though it does not belong to this place, is not needed to defend the argument we are treating in this disputation.

units.la: XVIII. Sic autem illud soluere conatus est Socinus. Respondeo, inquit, nec 70 interpretes, nec Hieronymum, eos imitatum, reddidisse nomen Iehouam κύριον seu Dominum, quia putarent, se hoc pacto nomen illud exprimere; sed quia nec 70 illis melius quidquam succurrit, quod gracis auribus inauditum non foret, nec Hieronymus hac in parte quidquam innouare voluit. Alioqui nomen Iehoua est nomen proprium, κύριος vero seu Dominus, appellatiuum & plurimis vulgò tributum: & idcirco, vel ob hoc solum valdè ineptum ad nomen Iehoua exprimendum. Ego verò non tam 70. interpretum & Hieronymi auctoritate nitor, quàm ipsorum Euangelistarum & Apostolorum, qui græcè scribentes, & loca Veteris Testamenti laudantes in quibus extat nomen Iehoua, illud constanter κύριον reddiderunt,non quod eis religio esset discedere à 70.interpretum versione, (eam enim non perpetuò sequuntur) sed quod nullum videretur græcum nomen hebræoIehouæ aptius refpondere. Quamuis enim nomen κυριος appellatiuum fit, & plurimis vulgò tributum, tamen positum absoluté, antonomasticè, κατ' ἐξοχὴν, Dei, cui seruire debent omnes creaturæ, proprium est, reciprocaturque in Scriptura cum nomine Iehoua. Quis porrò credat, aut nullum in lingua græca, qua nulla copiosior fuit, reperiri potuisse nomen non valdè ineptum ad nomen Iehoua exprimendum, aut si quod fuit, eo insuper habito maluisse ilto κυριε, ad eam rem, si credimus Socino, valdè inepto, tam sæpè tamque constanter vti, summo consensu, 70. Interpretes, Hieronymus, Euangelistæ & Apostoli? Haud satis enim religiosè & prudenter loca Scripturæ ex hebræo in græcum conuertere ille videtur, qui verbum pro verbo reddens id eligit, quod valdè ineptum est, præterito aptiore: idque eo minus in nomine Iehouæ interpretando faciendum fuit, quo, & frequentius extat in antiqua Scriptura, & nomen est magis memorabile, ac proprium Dei.
units.tr: XVIII. Socinus has tried to answer it in this way: I reply, he says, that neither the Seventy nor Jerome, who imitated them, rendered the name Jehovah by kyrios [κύριος] or Dominus because they thought they were thereby expressing that name; but because nothing better came to the Seventy, nothing that would not have been unheard of to Greek ears, and Jerome in this part wished to introduce nothing new. Otherwise, the name Jehovah is a proper name, whereas kyrios [κύριος] or Dominus is an appellative, commonly given to many; and therefore, for this reason alone, it is very unsuitable for expressing the name Jehovah. But I rest not so much on the authority of the Seventy and of Jerome as on that of the Evangelists and Apostles themselves, who, writing in Greek and quoting passages of the Old Testament in which the name Jehovah occurs, rendered it constantly by kyrion [κύριον]; not because they felt bound to depart from the version of the Seventy (for they do not always follow it), but because no Greek name seemed to correspond more fittingly to the Hebrew Jehovah. For although kyrios [κύριος] is an appellative, commonly given to many, yet when it is used absolutely, antonomastically, kat' exochēn [κατ' ἐξοχήν], it is proper to God, to whom all creatures ought to serve, and in Scripture it is interchangeable with the name Jehovah. Who would believe either that no name could be found in the Greek language, which was none richer, that was not very unsuitable for expressing the name Jehovah, or, if there was one, that they would have preferred to use so often and so constantly, with the greatest agreement of the Seventy, Jerome, the Evangelists and the Apostles, kyrie [κύριε], which, if we believe Socinus, is very unsuitable for that purpose, rather than it? For he seems not to have translated the passages of Scripture from Hebrew into Greek with sufficient piety and prudence, who, rendering word for word, chooses what is very unsuitable when a more fitting word was available; and this was all the less to be done in translating the name Jehovah, both because it occurs more frequently in ancient Scripture and because it is the more memorable and the proper name of God.

units.la: XIX. Pergit Socinus.
units.tr: XIX. Socinus goes on.

units.la: Conati tamen sunt 70 huic malo hac ratione mederi, vt scilicet nomen κυριος fere semper cum Iehoua loco ponitur, sit sine articulo; vt etiam alibi ante monuimus, quo commodius nomen proprium referre posset, neque enim solent appellativa nomina in græca lingua, cum subiecti locum tenent, efferri sine articulo. At Christus, cum κυριος subiectiuè (vt sic dixerim) appellatur, fere semper articulus præponitur nomini isti. Ex quo fit, vt Ego argumentum ab eodem nomine κυριος ductum in ipsum Bellarminum torqueam: & merito sic concludam, cum nomen κυριος, quando Iehouam significat, fere semper sine articulo efferatur, quando verò Christum, fere semper cum articulo; satis constare posse, Christum non esse Iehouam, &, quod κυριος nominetur, minimè propterea lehouam nominari. Si (quod fingit Socinus) illi scilicet malo mederi ea ratione 70 voluerunt, cur id non constanter obseruarunt, vt perpetuò κυριον pro Iehoua sine articulo ponerent? cur tot locis, vt non facilè eorum numerus iniri possit, articulum nomini κυριε præposuerunt? Hoc enim ab ijs factum est ita frequenter; præsertim in psalmis, quos fideles in delicijs habere debent, vt pro Iehoua positum cum articulo ὁ κυριος in omnibus fere psalmis occurrat, ac non raro in eodem psalmo bis ter quaterue, immò nonnunquam octies vt psalmo secundum editionem 70 trigesimo secundo, nouies vt pf. xcv. & cii. decies vt pf. xxxiii. &c. Fortè sic vsurpatum cum articulo pro nomine Iehouæ non occurrit in libris Mosis. Immò occurrit multis in locis, vt, exempli causa, Gen. 4. 3. & 8. 20. & 12. 8. & 13. 14. 18. & 18. 17. 33. Forte non legitur cum articulo in testimonijs Veteris Testamenti, quæ Apostoli conuerterunt & laudarunt in Nouo. Immò legitur, vt, exempli gratia, Act. 2. 25. Rom.15.11. 1. Cor. 10. 26. Heb. 8. 11. 1. Pet. 2. 3. Forte cauent Apostoli, ne nomen κύριος[?] sine articulo de Domino nostro Iesu Christo vsurpent. Immò tam crebrò de eo nomen illud sine articulo vsurpant, vt sic vsurpatum mihi percurrenti Nouum Testamentum plusquam septuaginta vicibus occurrerit. Cum igitur toties nomen κύριος[?], & pro Iehoua cum articulo, & de Christo sine articulo vsurpetur, apparet hanc Socini responsionem & retorsionem omninò vanam esse; Immò posse in ipsum Socinum retorqueri. Nam si nomen κύριος[?] absque articulo præfixo nomen est Dei Israëlis proprium passim loco Iehouæ vsurpatum; idque nomen itidem sine articulo passim Filio Dei tribuitur à sacris scriptoribus; quis non videt ea ratione sacros auctores innuere non obscurè, Filium Dei esse Deum Israëlis, esse Iehouam?
units.tr: The Seventy, however, have tried to remedy this evil by this method: that the word κύριος [kyrios] is almost always put in place of Iehovah without the article, as we also noted earlier, so that it could more conveniently refer to the proper name; for in Greek, appellative nouns used as the subject are not usually expressed without the article. But when Christ is called κύριος in the subjective sense (so to speak), the article almost always precedes that noun. From this it follows that I turn the argument drawn from the same word κύριος back against Bellarmine himself. I shall rightly conclude that, since the word κύριος, when it signifies Iehovah, is almost always expressed without the article, but when it signifies Christ, almost always with the article, it can be well established that Christ is not Iehovah, and that, because he is called κύριος, he is by no means for that reason named Iehovah. If (as Socinus imagines) the Seventy wished to remedy that evil by this method, why did they not observe it consistently, so that they always put κύριος without the article for Iehovah? Why, in so many places (their number is not easily counted), did they put the article before the noun κύριος? For they did this so often, especially in the Psalms, which the faithful ought to hold in delight, that ὁ κύριος [ho kyrios] with the article, standing for Iehovah, occurs in almost every Psalm, and often two, three or four times in the same Psalm, and sometimes even eight times, as in Psalm 32 according to the edition of the Seventy, nine times as in Psalms 95 and 102, and ten times as in Psalm 33, and so on. Perhaps it is not used with the article for the name of Iehovah in the books of Moses? Indeed it is, in many places, as for example Gen. 4. 3, 8. 20, 12. 8, 13. 14, 18, 18. 17, 33. Perhaps it is not found with the article in the testimonies of the Old Testament which the Apostles translated and quoted in the New? Indeed it is, as for example Acts 2. 25, Rom. 15. 11, 1 Cor. 10. 26, Heb. 8. 11, 1 Pet. 2. 3. Perhaps the Apostles were careful not to use the word κύριος without the article of our Lord Jesus Christ? Indeed they use that word without the article of him so often that, as I ran through the New Testament noting such uses, it occurred more than seventy times. Since, therefore, the word κύριος is used so often both for Iehovah with the article and for Christ without it, it appears that this answer and counter-argument of Socinus is wholly vain; indeed, it can be turned back upon Socinus himself. For if the word κύριος without a prefixed article is a proper name of the God of Israel, used everywhere in place of Iehovah, and if the same name without the article is likewise ascribed to the Son of God by the sacred writers, who does not see that by this means the sacred authors clearly indicate that the Son of God is the God of Israel, is Iehovah?

units.la: XX. Sic se habuit primum argumentum à nominis Iehouæ versione & interpretatione, quam ipsi Apostoli probarunt & confirmarunt, petitum. Alterum sequitur ductum ab ipsius vocis Iehouæ etymo & vi. Nulla autem mihi lis erit cum Aduersarijs ea de re. Sequar enim opinionem Crellij. Is nihil dubitat, veram istius vocabuli pronunciationem esse Ieheueh vel Iihueh, idque sua natura grammaticis verbum esse, quod significet erit: vsu autem nominis induisse naturam, qua ratione etiam prima huius verbi persona Ehjeh id est ero, aut integra oratio ero qui ero, quâ se appellavit Deus, in nomen quoddam migrauit. Hoc colligit ex Exod. 3. 13. quo loco, verba eius transscribam, Deus quærenti Mosi, quid responderé debeat Israëlitis interrogantibus, quodnam sit nomen Dei illius, à quo se missum assereret, ita, si ex Hebræo locum vertas, respondet: Ero qui Ero: quibus subjicit: Sic dices filijs Israël, Iehoua Deus Patrum vestrorum, Deus Abrahami, Deus Isaaci, & Deus Iacobi, misit me ad vos: hoc est nomen meum in seculum, & hoc memoriale meum in generationem & generationem, vbi vides, cùm primùm sese appellasset Deus, Ero qui Ero, deinde concisius; Ero; eundem postea verba, quibus Moses ad populares suos vti debeat, formantem, & sic in tertia persona de se loquentem, pro Ero ponere vocem Iehoua. Satis autem liquet, Deum in sequentibus verbis non aliud prorsus nomen pro eo, quod prius sibi indiderat, reponere, sed idem, pro persona loquentis ratione, diuersimodè formatum repetere. Cùm ergo in prima persona de se loquens, sese vocarit Ero qui Ero, vel vna voce Ero: certè nunc in tertia persona de se ipso per Mimesin loquens & simplici voce utens, Erit seipsum appellasse censendus est. Id autem Hebraïs est Ieheueh, vel Iihueh.
units.tr: XX. This was the first argument, drawn from the translation and interpretation of the name Iehovah, which the Apostles themselves approved and confirmed. The second follows, drawn from the etymology and force of the word Iehovah itself. I shall have no dispute with the opponents on this matter, for I shall follow the opinion of Crellius. He does not doubt that the true pronunciation of that word is Ieheueh or Iihueh, and that by its nature, as a grammarian would say, it is a verb meaning "he will be"; but by use the word has taken on the nature of a name, just as the first person of this verb, Ehjeh, that is "I shall be", or the whole phrase "I shall be who I shall be", by which God named himself, has passed into a certain name. He gathers this from Exod. 3. 13, and I shall transcribe his words from that passage: when Moses asked God what he should answer the Israelites who asked what was the name of that God by whom he claimed to have been sent, God replies (if you translate the passage from the Hebrew) thus: "I will be who I will be". To which he adds: "So shall you say to the sons of Israel, Iehovah, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you: this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial for generation and generation". Here you see that when God first named himself "I will be who I will be", and then more briefly "I will be"; and afterwards, when he is forming the words with which Moses ought to address his people, and speaks of himself in the third person, he puts the word Iehovah in place of "I will be". It is quite clear that God in the following words does not put forward an entirely different name in place of the one he had first given himself, but repeats the same name, formed in a different way according to the person speaking. Therefore, since in the first person, speaking of himself, he named himself "I will be who I will be", or by the single word "I will be", it must surely be judged that now, in the third person, speaking of himself by imitation and using a simple word, he named himself "He will be". Among the Hebrews this is Ieheueh or Iihueh.

units.la: XXI. Hoc vt fiat planius nonnihil adhuc addendum est, inquit, Cùm Deus seipsum appellavit Ero, Hebraicè dixit Ehieh. Huius tertia persona singularis, masculini generis, si & literas & puncta vocalia nostro more efferas, est Iihieh, idest, Erit. Verùm quia haec vox Hebraica in familiari vsu magis versatur; ideo, ne Dei ipsius nomen promiscuo vsu quodammodo profanaretur, sed à verbo illo vulgari facilius discerneretur: cognatum Ieheueh vel Iihueh eius loco fuit substitutum, quod & minus esset frequens, & eiusdem tamen cum illo significationis, ac vnâ tantum ab illo litera distaret. Nam loco i penultima litera est v, quae quidem litera apud Hebraeos nec figura multum distant, & inter se facile commutantur. Tantum autem videtur effecisse nominis diuini reuerentia, vt Ieheueh in vulgari etiam ac gennina significatione frequentari desierit. Hactenus Crellius, qui etiam obiuerat, non ita vocem illam, quae de agimus, nominis amulari ingenium, vt non suum etiam magna ex parte retineat. Nam nec variationem aliis nominibus vsitatam admittit, nec particulas sibi affigs patitur, quas idem illud verbum alias respueret. Addo simili modo tertias personas masculinas verborum יצחק & יעקב, quorum illud ridere, hoc supplantare significat, Patriarchis Isaaco & Iacobo nomina propria fuisse.
units.tr: XXI. So that this may be made somewhat clearer, he says, something more must still be added. When God named himself "I will be", he said in Hebrew Ehieh. The third person singular of this, masculine, if you pronounce both the letters and the vowel points in our manner, is Iihieh, that is, "he will be". But because this Hebrew word is more familiar in ordinary use, therefore, lest the very name of God should in some way be profaned by common use and be more easily distinguished from that ordinary verb, the cognate Ieheueh or Iihueh was substituted in its place, which was both less frequent and yet had the same meaning, and differed from the other by only one letter. For in place of the i, the penultimate letter is a v; and these letters among the Hebrews hardly differ in shape and are easily interchanged. Yet the reverence for the divine name seems to have brought it about that Ieheueh ceased to be used even in its ordinary and genuine sense. So far Crellius, who also observed that this word which we are discussing does not so much imitate the nature of a name as largely retain its own nature. For it admits no variation as other names commonly do, nor does it allow particles to be attached to it, which the same verb otherwise rejects. I add that in a similar way the third persons masculine of the verbs יצחק [yitschak] and יעקב [ya'aqov], of which the former means to laugh and the latter to supplant, were proper names for the patriarchs Isaac and Jacob.

units.la: XXII. Habemus nomen tetragrammaton (quod per puncta vocalia non sua, plerisque omnibus viris doctis & piis improbantibus, vulgò legitur Iehoua) proprie significare Erit, Graecè ὁ ἔσται, aut ad formam nominis propius, ὁ ἐσόμενος, ὁ ἐρχόμενος, qui futurus est, qui venturus est. Nunc qua mente, quoue sensu sibi hoc nomen Deus ipse imposuerit disquiciendum est: vel enim proprie significat eum, qui est fons essendi, & cum non habeat esse ab alio, dat rebus omnibus vt sint; vel, eum qui id sit praestiturus quod promisit; vel aliud quid. Primum affirmat Bellarminus, secundum Crellius, de tertio post videbimus. Non quaeritur hoc loco an primum illud aut secundum augustissimo illo nomine significetur per consequentias quasdam, aut spectata eius, cuius est nomen, natura ( id enim fortassis à nemine negabitur ) sed an significetur eo nomine recte proprie & formaliter? Socinus respondens Bellarmino mentem suam de nominis illius significa-tione aperire noluit, tantùm innuit primam illam significationem iure posse cum in dubium reuocari, tum in Bellarminum re-torqueri. Ne igitur aut ad eam confugiant Aduersarij, aut eam in nos torqueant, monemus lectorem nostrum, eam posse his ar-gumentis impugnari.
units.tr: XXII. We have the name Tetragrammaton (which, through vowel points that are not its own, most learned and pious men almost all disapprove, is commonly read Iehovah) properly meaning "he will be", in Greek ὁ ἔσται [ho estai], or, closer to the form of the name, ὁ ἐσόμενος [ho esomenos], ὁ ἐρχόμενος [ho erchomenos], "he who will be", "he who is to come". Now it must be inquired with what intention, or in what sense, God himself imposed this name on himself: for it either properly signifies him who is the fount of being, and since he has not his being from another, gives all things that they may be; or, him who will perform what he has promised; or something else. Bellarmine affirms the first, Crellius the second; the third we shall consider afterwards. The question here is not whether that first or second meaning is signified by that most august name through certain consequences, or with regard to the nature of him whose name it is (for this will perhaps be denied by no one), but whether it is rightly and formally signified by that name. Socinus, in answering Bellarmine, was unwilling to reveal his opinion about the meaning of that name; he only hinted that the first meaning could rightly be called into doubt, and turned back upon Bellarmine. Lest therefore our opponents either take refuge in it or turn it against us, we warn our reader that it can be assailed by the following arguments.

units.la: XXIII. Primum ab hoc ipso nomine ducitur, quod, cum sit tertia persona futuri verbi Haua, aut nomen ab ea formatum, proprie & per se futurum significat. Ponitur autem non raro in Scriptura futurum pro praeterito, sed tum futuri significationem deponit, quâ retentâ praeteritum aut praesens formaliter significare non potest; ac vt possit, tamen causa nulla est cur à propria futuri significatione discedamus: praesertim cum Deus ipse, quasi quid nominis sibi conueniret praetentans, non praeteritum aut participium praesentis, sed futurum Ehieh, bis de se vsurparit, innuens in imponendo sibi nomine se futuri rationem habere. Alterum ex eo peti potest, quod si nomen illud significaret formaliter eum, qui fons est essendi, & cum non habeat esse ab alio, dat rebus omnibus vt sint, consequens esset eo nomine aptius nullum fuisse ad historiam creationis, qua Deus dedit rebus omnibus vt sint, describendam; qui igitur factum est, vt toto primo capite geneseos, quo illa historia continetur, & Dei nomen plusquam trigesies repetitur, sacer auctor sibi ab hoc nomine vsurpando temperauerit? Cum enim ea historia, nisi ipso Deo reuelante, cognosci ab homine non potuerit, existimandum non est id casu nulloque consilio accidisse, vt toto illo primo capite nomen Elohim, id est, Deus vsurparetur solum; Deinde capite secundo, à verbis illis Ha sunt generationes coelorum & terrae &c ad finem vsque capitis, vsurparetur nomen Iehova, non tamen solum, sed sequente Elohim. Est igitur absque dubio illius rei ratio aliqua scitu digna, quae tamen reddi nulla omnino potest posità illa significatione nominis Iehoua.
units.tr: XXIII. The first argument comes from this very name. Since it is the third person of the future tense of the verb Haua, or a noun formed from it, it properly and in itself signifies "he will be." Scripture often uses the future for the past, but then the future sense is given up, and while that sense is retained the past or present cannot be formally signified. Even if it could, there is no reason to depart from the proper meaning of the future, especially since God himself, as if claiming what suited his name, twice used of himself not the past or the present participle but the future Ehieh, indicating that in giving himself this name he took account of the future. A second argument may be drawn from this. If the name formally signified him who is the fount of being, who has his being from no other and gives all things that they may be, then no name would have been more fitting for describing the history of creation, in which God gave all things that they might be. Why, then, did the sacred author, throughout the whole first chapter of Genesis, which contains that history, and where God's name is repeated more than thirty times, refrain from using this name? Since that history could not be known by man except by God's own revelation, it should not be supposed that it happened by chance and without design that the whole of that first chapter uses only the name Elohim, that is, God. Then in the second chapter, from the words "These are the generations of the heavens and the earth" to the end of the chapter, the name Jehovah is used, but not alone; it is followed by Elohim. There is therefore, without doubt, some reason for this that is worth knowing, yet it cannot be given at all if that meaning of the name Jehovah is posited.

units.la: XXIV. Tertium argumentum nobis suppeditant verba Dei Exod. 6. 2. quae sic habent ipso Crellio vertente, Ego sum Iehova: apparuique Abrahamo, Isaaco, & Iacobo in (nomine) De omnipotentis: at (in) nomine meo Iehova non sum cognitus illis &c.
units.tr: XXIV. The third argument is supplied by God's words in Exodus 6:2, which, in Crellius's own translation, read thus: "I am Jehovah. And I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in (the name) of Almighty God, but (in) my name Jehovah I was not known to them," etc.

units.la: (Agi autem in illis verbis de reuelatione non ipsius vocis, sed rei per eam significatæ ipso facto seu experimento cognoscendæ, inter omnes conuenit.) Quomodo enim dici potuit Deus apparuisse Patriarchis illis in nomine Dei omnipotentis seu sibi & aliis sufficientis, & tamen non apparuisse illis in nomine Iehova, si hoc nomen formaliter eum significat, qui fons est essendi & dat aliis vt sint? hoc enim est esse Deum omnipotentem, & si mihi ita loqui liceat, omnisufficientem. Annon etiam Deus illis Patriarchis cognitus fuit vt creator & conseruator & possessor cœli & terræ, quique pro suo arbitrio vterum claudit & aperit? Quomodo verò vt talis cognosci potuit, nec tamen cognosci vt fons essendi, dans aliis rebus vt sint?
units.tr: (That in those words the revelation concerns not the sound of the word itself but the thing signified by it, to be known by the fact itself or by experience, is agreed by all.) For how could it be said that God appeared to those patriarchs in the name of God Almighty, that is, sufficient in himself and for others, and yet did not appear to them in the name Jehovah, if this name formally signified him who is the fount of being and gives being to others? For this is what it is to be Almighty God, and, if I may so speak, all-sufficient. Was God not also known to those patriarchs as creator, preserver and possessor of heaven and earth, who at his own pleasure closes and opens the womb? But how could he be known as such, and yet not be known as the fount of being, giving other things that they may be?

units.la: XXV. His adde, capi animo non posse, si ea fuit nominis illius formalis & præcisa significatio, qui factum fuerit, vt non modo 70 interpretes, sed omnes Iudæi, omnes Euangelistæ & Apostoli, omnes Christiani aliquot seculis summo consensu nomen illud hebraicè Adonai, græcè κύριον, legerint & verterint? Succurrebant enim alia nomina ad eam significationem exprimendam magis accommodata, Hebræa & græca, verbi gratia, Iah, Hu, schaddai, El, Eloah &c, ὁ ὤν[?] quo nomine 70. reddiderunt Ehieh Exod. 6. & si qua sunt alia similia. Profectò tantus consensus à Deo approbatus non contigit sine instinctu quodam diuino, cuius ratio, admissâ illa significatione, nulla posse reddi videtur.
units.tr: XXV. Add to this that it cannot be understood, if that was the formal and precise meaning of that name, how it came about that not only the Seventy translators but all the Jews, all the evangelists and apostles, and all Christians for several centuries, with the greatest consensus, read and translated that name, in Hebrew Adonai, in Greek kyrios [κύριος]. For other names, Hebrew and Greek, better suited to express that meaning were at hand: for example Iah, Hu, Shaddai, El, Eloah, and ho ōn [ὁ ὤν], by which the Seventy rendered Ehieh in Exodus 6, and other similar names. Surely so great a consensus, approved by God, did not come about without some divine impulse, and the reason for it, if that meaning is admitted, seems impossible to give.

units.la: XXVI. Denique non sine singulari quadam prouidentia Dei accidit, vt tempore aduentus Christi ac reuelationis claræ Euangelij, nomen illud ab omnibus vbique locorum legi & pronunciari desierit, ac in eius locum suffectum fuerit maximo omnium consensu κύριος nomen, quod Christo non conuenit modò, sed etiam proprium est aliquomodo: tamen huius rei, si fontem essendi, vt Bellarminus dixit, formaliter significat, nulla concipi ratio potest. Debuit enim sub Euangelio maximè Deus vt fons essendi, eiusque omnibus rebus dator, & reuelari, & agnosci, & celebrari ab omnibus gentibus; nec causa vlla fuit, cur nomen quo id significetur splendore Euangelij obscuraretur & obsoles-ceret. Hæc argumenta examini & iudicio tuo, lector dilecte, li-bens subjicio, teque, vt ea apud te expendas, rogo & quæso.
units.tr: XXVI. Finally, it was not without a singular providence of God that at the time of Christ's coming and the clear revelation of the gospel that name ceased to be read and pronounced everywhere by all people, and in its place was substituted, by the greatest consensus of all, the name kyrios [κύριος], which not only belongs to Christ but is in some way proper to him. Yet if the name formally signifies the fount of being, as Bellarmine said, no reason for this change can be conceived. For under the gospel God above all ought to have been revealed, recognised and celebrated by all nations as the fount of being and giver of all things. Nor was there any cause why the name by which this is signified should be obscured and fall into disuse through the splendour of the gospel. I willingly submit these arguments to your examination and judgement, dear reader, and I ask and beg you to weigh them for yourself.

units.la: XXVII. Altera etiam expositio, Fidem nempe Dei ac constantiam in servandis promissis eo nomine potissimum, &, ut loquuntur, proprie & formaliter declarari, nec probari posse videtur, & potest similiter aliquot argumentis impugnari. Dico proprie & formaliter: quin enim per consequentiam ex eo nomine Dei fides & constantia elici possit, abest ut negem. Affirmat quidem Crellius ex verbis Dei Exod. 6. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. satis apparere, ideo Deum sese appellare Iehova, vel potius Ihueh, aut Ieheueh, id est, Erit, quia id praestiturus sit Israelitis, quod ipsorum patribus olim promiserat. Certe ex illis verbis satis apparet, Deum id praestiturum suisse Israelitis, quod ipsorum patribus olim promiserat; sed eum ideo sese Ieheueh vel Ihueh, id est, Erit, appellare, qua firma consequentia ex illis Dei verbis deduci possit, ego quidem non video. Immo cum tunc Deus in eo versaretur, ut reipsa id praestaret quod illis promiserat, ideo potius Est, quam Erit appellandus fuisse videri posset. Futurum enim Erit animos Israelitarum a tempore praesenti avocabat, & erigebat in expectationem futuri, & converti in praesens, aut praeteritum, aut tale quiddam oportebat simul ac Deus quod promiserat praestitisset. Quocirca hoc nomen vel significabat Deum praestiturum promissionem de liberanda posteritate Abrahami Isaaci & Iacobi ex Ægypto, eaque in terram Canaam introducenda; vel significabat spiritualem liberationem a peccato per Christum obventuram. Si prius, praestita & impleta illa promissione nomen illud non amplius futurum sed praeteritum significare debuit, ac proinde vel obsolescere vel mutari in aliud. Si posterius, Id jam non longe abest ab ea sententia quam sequendam duco, ac fatendum est, Deum non fuisse cognitum Israelitis in nomine illo suo Ieheueh vel Ihueh, nisi typicè, &, ut ita loquar umbratiliter: quod eo æquiore animo accipere eos decuit, quod ea. notitia ne patribus quidem ipsorum Abrahamo Isaaco & Iacobo indulta fuerat, & spes ipsis ostendebatur fore, ut tandem aliquando eam consequerentur.
units.tr: XXVII. The other explanation, that the name chiefly declares, and as they say properly and formally declares, God's faithfulness and constancy in keeping his promises, seems neither to be proved nor can it be easily refuted by a similar set of arguments. I say "properly and formally," for I by no means deny that faithfulness and constancy can be drawn from that name by consequence. Crellius indeed affirms that "from God's words in Exodus 6:2–7 it sufficiently appears that God called himself Jehovah, or rather Ihueh or Ieheueh, that is, 'He will be,' because he was going to do for the Israelites what he had promised their fathers long before." Certainly from those words it sufficiently appears that God was going to do for the Israelites what he had long before promised their fathers. But that he therefore called himself Ieheueh or Ihueh, that is, "He will be," I do not see by what firm consequence can be deduced from God's words. Indeed, since God was then engaged in actually doing what he had promised them, he might rather seem to have been called "He is" than "He will be." For the future "He will be" would draw the minds of the Israelites away from the present and raise them into expectation of the future; and it would have had to turn into the present, or the past, or something of the kind, as soon as God had accomplished what he had promised. Hence this name either signified that God would fulfil the promise to free the posterity of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob from Egypt and lead them into the land of Canaan, or it signified the spiritual deliverance from sin to come through Christ. If the former, then once that promise had been fulfilled the name ought no longer to signify the future but the past, and so either become obsolete or change into something else. If the latter, this is already not far from that opinion which I hold should be followed, and it must be confessed that God was not known to the Israelites by that name of his, Ieheueh or Ihueh, except typically and, as I may put it, in shadowy form. They ought to have accepted this with the more equanimity, since that knowledge had not been granted even to their fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and hope was shown to them that they would one day at last attain it.

units.la: XXVIII. At, inquit Crellius, illud Erit, vel Ero, quod plenius antea dixerat, Ero qui Ero, nihil significat aliud, quam reipsa ero, quem me futurum dixi; seu reipsa eum me praestabo, quem praestiturum promisi. Paulo enim aliter atque aliter vox Ero bis posita, in eadem oratione sumitur per antanaclasin: prius de facto ipso, posterius de iure, seu manus de obligatione. Atqui Deus se talem aut talem futurum non dixerat, sed se posteros Abrahae liberaturum tům ὁ κύριος Dominus significat, melius igitur responderet nomini Ichouæ ὁ πρὸς[?] quàm ὁ κύριος, cur igitur nemini venit in mentem vt id nomen verteret ἡ πρὸν[?], cum omnes summo consensu id reddiderint κύριον sine aut cum articulo præfixo? Adde quod quamuis opus sit potentia ad præstanda promissa, tamen nemo vnquam dominum dixit, vt constantem in promissis seruandis significaret. His accedit quod posita illa expositione nulla ratio reddi potest, cur sub Euangelio, quo præcipuè Dei fides & constantia in seruandis promissis reuelata & celebrata est, nomen Deo ad eam significandam impositum ac destinatum legi, pronunciari, atque adeò vsurpari desierit, inque eius locum id nomen suffectum sit, quod potentiam quidem significat, voluntatis verò constantiam non item.
units.tr: XXVIII. But, says Crellius, "that 'Ehyeh' or 'Ero', which he had said more fully before, 'I will be who I will be,' signifies nothing other than 'I will really be whom I said I would be,' or 'I will really show myself as the one I promised to show.' For the word 'Ero', used twice in the same speech, is taken somewhat differently each time, by antanaclasis: first of the fact itself, then of right, or of obligation." But God had not said that he would be this or that; he had said that he would free the posterity of Abraham. Then ho kyrios [ὁ κύριος] signifies "Dominus," and so the name Jehovah would answer better to ho ōn [ὁ ὤν]than to ho kyrios [ὁ κύριος]. Why, then, has it occurred to no one to render that name as to on [τὸ ὄν], since all have with the greatest consensus rendered it kyrios, with or without a prefixed article? Add that although power is needed to perform promises, no one has ever called someone "lord" to signify constancy in keeping promises. To this is added that on this explanation no reason can be given why under the gospel, in which God's faithfulness and constancy in keeping his promises was especially revealed and celebrated, the name given to God and destined to signify this ceased to be read, pronounced and so used, and in its place was substituted a name which indeed signifies power, but not constancy of will.

units.la: XXX. Quid ergo tandem formaliter significabit nomen hoc diuinum? Id quod dixit Crellius, Erit, quod græcè per participium melius effertur ὁ μέλλων vt Rom. 5. 14. ὁ ἐσόμενος futurus vt Apoc. 16. 5. ὁ ἐρχόμενος venturus vt Apoc. 1. 4. 8. & 4. 8. & 11. 17. Heb. 10. 37. Luc. 7. 19. &c. Mouet quæstionem Socinus, cur Iohannes in Apocalypsi non potius dixerit ὁ ἔσῃ, vel ὁ ἐσόμενος, quàm ὁ ἐρχόμενος? Et respondet, causam esse in promptu; nempe quia alia ista duo verba videntur omnino significare futuram existentiam eius rei quæ antea non esset; id quod in voce ἐρχόμενος non euenit, tunc etiam, cum pro futurus accipitur, optimè enim, immò multò magis proprie, significare potest essentiam futuram rei, quæ iam sit. Eam non fuisse mentem Iohannis, aut potius Spiritus sancti à quo ad scribendum agebatur, ex eo colligi potest, quod primò quominus ὁ ἔσῃ accipi posset de futura existentia rei quæ antea non esset, impediebant antecedentia ὁ ὢν ϰαὶ[?] ὁ ἦν qui est & qui erat, Secundò ὁ ἦν similiter videtur significare existentiam rei quæ amplius non est, & tamen nunquam dixit Iohannes ὁ ἤλθε qui venit, aut ὁ ἐληλύθει[?] qui venerat, sed constanter ὁ ἦν qui erat. Tertiò Deus, teste Crellio, passim se vocauit Iehueh seu Ihueh, quod propriè significat ὁ ἔσῃ, ὁ ἐσόμενος qui erit, qui futurus est, haud metuens ne significare videretur existentiam quæ antea non esset.
units.tr: XXX. What, then, will this divine name formally signify? What Crellius said: Erit ("he will be"), which in Greek is better rendered by a participle, "the one about to be" [ὁ μέλλων], as in Rom. 5. 14; "the one who will be" [ὁ ἐσόμενος], as in Apoc. 16. 5; "the one who is coming" [ὁ ἐρχόμενος], as in Apoc. 1. 4. 8, 4. 8 and 11. 17; Heb. 10. 37; Luc. 7. 19, and so on. Socinus raises the question why John in the Apocalypse did not rather write "the one who will be" [ὁ ἔσῃ] or [ὁ ἐσόμενος] instead of "the one who is coming" [ὁ ἐρχόμενος]. He answers that the reason is obvious: those other two words seem wholly to signify the future existence of a thing that did not previously exist, which does not happen with ἐρχόμενος, even when it is taken as futurus ("future"), since it can signify, very well and indeed much more properly, the future being of a thing that already exists, venturus ("coming"). That this was not John's meaning, or rather the meaning of the Holy Spirit by whom he was moved to write, may be gathered from the following. First, the preceding words "who is and who was" [ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν] prevented [ὁ ἔσῃ] from being taken of the future existence of a thing that previously did not exist. Secondly, [ὁ ἦν] similarly seems to signify the existence of a thing that no longer is, and yet John never wrote "who came" [ὁ ἤλθε] or "who had come" [ὁ ἐληλύθει], but constantly "who was" [ὁ ἦν]. Thirdly, God, as Crellius testifies, everywhere called himself Iehueh or Ihueh, which properly signifies "who will be" [ὁ ἔσῃ], "who is to be" [ὁ ἐσόμενος], not fearing lest it seem to signify an existence that previously was not.

units.la: Vera igitur causa meâ quidem sententia est, ne videatur Deus non aliter futurus in Ecclesia, quàm aut fuit olim aut nunc est, fuit enim olim quidem obtinente lege, & est nunc reuelato Euangelio, sed quasi absens ac procul à nobis habitans: in futuro verò seculo ita futurus est, ut nobis perpetuò praesens adsit, itaque dicitur venturus potius quàm futurus, quoniam ea vox accommodatior erat ad fideles solandos erigendos & ad officium faciendum incitandos, insinuato discrimine inter praesentem & futuram Dei in Ecclesia existentiam.
units.tr: The true cause, in my view, is this: God was not to seem to be going to be present in the Church otherwise than he was of old or is now. For he was indeed present in former times under the law, and is present now with the Gospel revealed, but as though absent and dwelling far from us. In the future age, however, he will be present in such a way that he is always with us. Therefore he is called "coming" rather than "future", since that word was better suited to console and raise up the faithful and to urge them to their duty, and it hints at the difference between God's present existence in the Church and his future existence.

units.la: XXXI. Cur igitur Deus in Veteri Testamento appellari voluit Iehueh seu Ihuch ὁ [illegible, ~6 letters] Ille futurus? quia nullum nomen illis temporibus aptius esse potuit ad populum Israëliticum ab idololatria abs-terrendum, & fidem, qua posset justificari, in eo excitandam & fovendam. Cum enim Deus Israëlis futuro Erit, tanquam nomine suo proprio, quo ab omnibus aliis dis distinguerétur, appellari voluit, nonne eo ipso significavit, alios omnes deos, quantumvis esse viderentur, & ab hominibus colerentur, tandem tamen nullos futuros, vanasque & irritas fore spes eorum, qui eis confisi fuerint: se vero, qui tunc temporis esse non videbatur, & aut à nulla gente, aut à sola Israëlitica agnoscebatur, tandem aliquando futurum esse, hoc est, patefacturum quàm revera sit?
units.tr: XXXI. Why, then, did God wish to be called Iehueh or Ihuch, "the one who will be" [ὁ ...] in the Old Testament? Because no name could have been more fitting in those times for keeping the Israelite people from idolatry and for stirring up and nourishing in them the faith by which they could be justified.
