For when God wished to be called by the Israelites futuro Erit, "He will be", as by his own proper name, by which he would be distinguished from all other gods, did he not by that very fact signify that all other gods, however much they seemed to exist and were worshipped by men, would at last not be, and that the hopes of those who trusted in them would be vain and void? And that he himself, who at that time did not seem to exist, and was acknowledged by no nation or only by the Israelite nation, would at some time be, that is, would show what he truly is?

units.la: XXXII. Quatenus igitur hoc nomen Dei Israëlis proprium fuit, ac comparatum ad eum ab omnibus aliis dis distinguendum & discernendum, ac proinde nulli alii deo convenire potuit, eatenus in eo continebatur adversus idola & idololatras comminatio, hoc est, praedictio non obscura destructionis eorum, juxta oraculum di, qui non fecerunt coelum & terram, tollentur de terra, & de sub coelis ipsis. Et, Dominus solus exalta-bitur in die illa. nam si de aliquo alio Deo dici potuisset vere illud Erit, id proprium non fuisset Dei Israëlis, nec accommodatum ad eum ab eiusmodi deo distinguendum. Quatenus vero futu-rum fuit aliquo modo praesenti & praeterito oppositum, eatenus in eo continebatur promissio seu praedictio futurae revelationis Dei Israëlis clarae & plenae, qua tandem aliquando omnibus palam fieret ipsum revera esse. id quod non potuit non esse maximo solatio piis qui Deum timebant & expectabant, & terrori impijs, quorum omnes cogitationes sunt non esse Deum. Atque haec causa videtur esse, cur tam saepè Deus mandatis & comminationibus suis illud subjungat & inculcet, se eum esse qui sic vocetur.
units.tr: XXXII. So far as this name was proper to the God of Israel, and was fitted to distinguish and separate him from all other gods, and therefore could belong to no other god, so far it contained a threat against idols and idolaters, that is, a plain prediction of their destruction, according to the oracle: the gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth, and from under these heavens. And: The Lord alone shall be exalted in that day. For if that Erit could truly have been said of some other god, it would not have been proper to the God of Israel, nor suited to distinguish him from such a god. But so far as the future was in some way opposed to the present and the past, so far it contained a promise or prediction of a clear and full future revelation of the God of Israel, by which at last it would become plain to all that he truly is. This could not but be a very great comfort to the pious who feared and waited for God, and a terror to the impious, whose all thoughts are that there is no God. And this seems to be the reason why God so often adds and impresses on his commands and threats that he is the one who is called by this name.

units.la: XXXIII. Hac nominis illius expositione posita, quae & voci, & rei convenit, & ipsa per se admodum momentosa est, & non potest ulla ratione refelli, & valet ad reddendam rationem eorum omnium quæ de nomine illo quæri possunt, sic argumentor. De quocunque verè & proprie dici potuit illud Iehueh, vel Iihueh, Erit, ille est Deus Israelis. De Christo verè & proprie dici potuit illud Iehueh, vel Iihueh Erit. Ergo Christus est Deus Israelis. Major vera est: Alioqui nomen illud Iehueh, vel Iihueh Erit, nec proprium fuisset Dei Israelis, nec aptum ad cum ab omni alio deo distinguendum. Minor quoque vera est: Nam non potuit Filius Dei annumerari diis illis, qui tandem aliquando destruendi erant, ac non futuri: erat enim futurus Deus benedictus in secula seculorum, juxta δοξολογίαν[?] omnis creaturæ Apoc. 5. 13. Sedenti in throno & Agno benedictio, & honor, & gloria, & potestas in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: XXXIII. With this explanation of the name set forth, which suits both the word and the thing, which is in itself of great weight, which cannot be refuted by any argument, and which serves to give the reason for everything that can be asked about that name, I argue thus. Of whomever "Iehueh" or "Ihueh", "Erit" ("he will be"), can truly and properly be said, that one is the God of Israel. Of Christ, "Iehueh" or "Ihueh", "Erit", can truly and properly be said. Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. The major premise is true: otherwise that name, Iehueh or Ihueh, "Erit", would be neither proper to the God of Israel nor apt to distinguish him from every other god. The minor premise is also true: for the Son of God could not be counted among those gods who were at last to be destroyed and were not to be, for he was to be the God blessed for ever and ever, according to the doxology of every creature, Apoc. 5. 13: To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: XXXIV. Dices, illud Erit etiam Angelis tribui potuisse. Hoc nego, vocantur quidem dii in Veteri Testamento, & erunt in æternum: At non erunt dii. Immò jam in Novo Testamento non amplius dii appellantur, sed apparent in ordinem servorum Filii, quem omnes adorare tenentur, redacti. Nimirum tenebris noctis obtinentibus, ac lucente duntaxat in domo Israelis Mosis ac Prophetarum lucerna, idque ob legis velum & umbras obscurius, mirum videri non debet, si Angeli aliquomodo dii visi & appellati fuerunt: sed sole iustitiæ exorto, & ipso eorum domino, ut loquuntur, in propria persona revelato, statim divinitas illa disparuit, nihilque nisi servi esse, & quidem illius, qui apparuit, Domini deinceps videri debuerunt. Dices, Christum tunc nondum fuisse, cum Deus Israelis hoc nomen sibi imposuit. Hoc falsum esse jam multis argumentis invictis demonstravi. Adde quod nomen istud Erit per se & formaliter tantum futurum significabat, & distinguebat Deum Israelis, habita ratione futuri, non modo à diis qui tunc colebantur, sed etiam ab iis, quos diaboli astutia & hominum stulta superstitio erat in posterum relatura in deorum numerum.
units.tr: XXXIV. You will say that Erit could also have been attributed to angels. This I deny. They are indeed called gods in the Old Testament, and they will be for ever, but they will not be gods. Indeed, in the New Testament they are no longer called gods, but are reduced to the rank of servants of the Son, whom all are bound to worship. While the darkness of night prevailed, and only the lamp of Moses and the Prophets shone in the house of Israel, and that more dimly because of the veil and shadows of the law, it ought not to seem strange if angels were in some way seen and called gods. But when the sun of righteousness had risen, and their Lord himself, as they say, had been revealed in his own person, that divinity at once vanished, and thereafter they ought to be seen as nothing but servants, and indeed servants of him who appeared. You will say that Christ was not yet when the God of Israel took this name to himself. I have already shown by many unanswerable arguments that this is false. Add that this name Erit signified in itself and formally only the future, and distinguished the God of Israel, with regard to the future, not only from the gods who were then worshipped, but also from those whom the cunning of the devil and the foolish superstition of men were afterwards to bring into the number of gods.

units.la: XXXV. Dices ultimo, illud Erit nomen esse proprium Dei Israelis, nisi acceptum κατ' ἐξοχὴν[?], &, ut ita dicam, antonomasticè: eoque sensu Christo non convenire. Respondeo id esse falsum. Nam primò nomen proprium non dicitur antonomasticè de eo cuius est nomen proprium. Deinde non significat hoc nomen Deum Israelis futurum magis aut excellentius quàm sint futuri alij dij: sed significat simpliciter alios deos non futuros; Deum verò Israelis solum futurum. Non enim eo distinguitur Deus Israelis à dijs gentium, quòd, cum utrique sint futuri, ille magis aut excellentiori ratione sit futurus quàm isti; sed quòd simpliciter ille sit futurus, hi verò tandem aliquando non sint futuri. Atque hæc fortasse causa est, cur paulò frequentius sine articulo ὢν[?] reddatur, quàm cum articulo ὁ ὢν[?], ut nempe significetur ὢν[?] tunc poni pro nomine, quod accipi debet non antonomasticè, sed, ut nomen proprium decet, propriè. Objicies, multas alias res futuras in æternum præter Deum Israelis. Fateor alias res futuras, sed nego alios deos futuros. Imposuit enim sibi Deus Israelis nomen proprium, quo discerneretur ab omnibus alijs dijs, non autem quo discerneretur ab omnibus alijs rebus, à quibus satis ipso Dei nomine distinguebatur. Adde quod sepositò originis discrimine, sine quo Filij à Patre nulla est distinctio, planè talis est Filius qualis Pater, tamque perfectè est Filius quàm Pater; nam si Pater habet vitam in seipso, Filius etiam habet vitam in seipso: si Pater vivificat quos vult, Filius etiam vivificat quos vult: si Pater habet omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra, Filius etiam habet omnem potestatem in cœlo & in terra. Uno verbo, quæcunque sunt Patris, eadem sunt etiam Filii, & vice versa quæcunque sunt Filij eadem etiam sunt Patris.
units.tr: XXXV. You will say last that Erit is the proper name of the God of Israel only if it is taken by pre-eminence [κατ' ἐξοχήν], as it were antonomastically, and that in this sense it does not belong to Christ. I answer that this is false. First, a proper name is not said antonomastically of the one whose proper name it is. Next, this name does not signify that the God of Israel will be future more, or more excellently, than the other gods will be; it simply signifies that the other gods will not be, and the God of Israel alone will be. For the God of Israel is not distinguished from the gods of the nations by being future in a greater or more excellent way than they, since both are future; he is distinguished by simply being future, while they at last will not be. And this is perhaps the reason why ὢν is more often rendered without the article than with ὁ ὢν, namely that it may be shown that ὢν is then used as a name, which must be taken not antonomastically but properly, as a proper name should be. You will object that many other things will be future for ever, besides the God of Israel. I grant that other things will be future, but I deny that other gods will be. For the God of Israel took to himself a proper name by which he would be distinguished from all other gods, not one by which he would be distinguished from all other things; from these he was sufficiently distinguished by the name of God itself. Add that, setting aside the distinction of origin, without which there is no distinction of the Son from the Father, the Son is altogether such as the Father, and is as perfectly Son as the Father is Father. For if the Father has life in himself, the Son also has life in himself; if the Father quickens whom he wills, the Son also quickens whom he wills; if the Father has all power in heaven and on earth, the Son also has all power in heaven and on earth. In a word, whatever belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son, and conversely whatever belongs to the Son belongs also to the Father.

units.la: XXXVI. Hoc argumentum eo confirmari potest, quod Christus is est qui sua, ut ita loquar, futuritione, suo adventu, atque excellentis suæ existentiæ renelatione deos gentium obscuravit, extinxit, immò abolevit jam aliqua ex parte, perfecturus istam abolitionem atque omnimodam, ut ita loquar, annihilationem illustri illo suo adventu quem expectamus. Ea enim est Christi persona, ut hoc ipso quod verè & uti par est, agnoscitur, desinant pro diis haberi aut coli omnia fictitia numina. Itaque merito illud Erit de eo usurpari potuit.
units.tr: XXXVI. This argument can be confirmed by the fact that Christ is he who, by his future coming, as I may put it, by his arrival and by the revelation of his surpassing existence, has obscured the gods of the nations, extinguished them, indeed has already in some measure abolished them, and will bring that abolition to completion, and total annihilation, as I may put it, at that glorious coming of his which we await. For such is the person of Christ that, by the very fact that he is acknowledged truly and as is fitting, all fictitious deities cease to be held as gods or to be worshipped. Therefore the word Erit ("He will be") could rightly be applied to him.

units.la: XXXVII. Huc accedit quod Deus Israelis sibi futurum Erit, vel plenius, ut Gen. 2.& passim alibi, Erit Deus, tanquam proprium nomen, quo ab omni alio discerneretur, imponendo significavit aperte, se Dominum mundi esse, & quidem solum. Quemadmodum enim cum amplæ alicuius possessionis dominus, vel mortuus sine hærede, vel nullus esse falsò putatur, eamque[?] alij tanquam vacuam occupant ac inter se partiuntur, si tandem aliquando Dominus illius legitimus reuera esse & viuere docetur ac demonstratur, eo ipso iure omni illi excidunt, qui bona eius occupauerant sibique ipsis asseruerant; sic cum Deus mundum quem creauerat, conseruaret, & regeret, ut Dei naturam prorsus inuisibilem & spiritualem decebat, inuisibili & spirituali modo, nec is uspiam in terris compareret, ac propterea nullus esse videretur, in mundi possessionem, quasi caducam & vacuam, dii multi inuolarunt, sibique multi homines deos pro arbitrio vel finxerunt vel elegerunt; ut nulla gens reperiri posset in toto mundo non occupata ab aliquo eiusmodi deo. Hâc tanta injuriâ sibi illatâ Dominus mundi dissimulatâ, eiusque ultione in certum quoddam tempus futurum mirabili eoque sapientissimo consilio dilatâ, interim gentem unam valdè exiguam manu forti, brachio extento, multis miraculis, multis prælijs & victoriis ab injusto dominio redemit, sibiq; vero & legitimo domino, veluti primitias generis humani, vendicauit; ac dum tempus illud expectaret, quo se aliis gentibus totiqueadeò mundo reuelaret quàm verè sit, eaque ratione omnes alios deos sua illa possessione quam usurparunt exueret, is sibi nomē proprium sumpsit, quo se totius mundi dominum esse insinuauit, nempe Erit Deus, vel concisiùs Erit: Eo enim significatum est, tandem aliquando tempus futurum, quo probatâ & demonstratâ Dei Israelis existentiâ, omnes alii dii omni iure, quod in mundum seu gentes habere videbantur, excidant priuenturque in perpetuum: quod est significare, Deum Israelis solum esse verum ac legitimum totius mundi Dominum.
units.tr: XXXVII. To this is added that the God of Israel signified, by imposing on himself the name Erit ("He will be"), or more fully, as in Gen. 2. and often elsewhere, Erit Deus ("God will be"), as a proper name by which he would be distinguished from every other, that he is openly the Lord of the world, and indeed the only one. For just as, when the lord of some large estate is falsely thought to have died without an heir, or to be non-existent, others seize that property as if it were vacant and divide it among themselves; yet if at last it is shown and demonstrated that its rightful lord really exists and lives, by that very right all those who had occupied his goods and claimed them for themselves lose everything. So too, when God preserved and governed the world which he had created, as befitted the wholly invisible and spiritual nature of God, he did so in an invisible and spiritual manner, and he did not appear anywhere on earth, so that he seemed to be no one at all. On that account many gods seized upon the possession of the world, as though it were ownerless and empty, and many men either made up gods for themselves at will or chose them; so that no nation could be found in the whole world that was not held by some such god. With this great wrong done to him, the Lord of the world overlooked it, and by a wondrous and most wise plan deferred his vengeance to a certain fixed time in the future. Meanwhile, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, through many miracles and many battles and victories, he redeemed one very small nation from unjust dominion, and claimed it for himself as the true and rightful lord, as the firstfruits of the human race. And while he awaited that time when he would reveal to the other nations, and indeed to the whole world, how truly he exists, and by that means strip all the other gods of the possession which they had usurped, he took to himself a proper name by which he gave notice that he is the Lord of the whole world, namely Erit Deus ("God will be"), or more briefly Erit. For by this it was signified that at last there would come a time when, the existence of the God of Israel having been proved and demonstrated, all the other gods would lose, and would be deprived for ever of, whatever right they seemed to have over the world or the nations: which is to say, that the God of Israel alone is the true and rightful Lord of the whole world.

units.la: XXXVIII. Hinc fortasse colligi potest ratio, cur nomini isti sæpenumero subjungatur nomen Elohim, id est, Deus, nonnunquam verò præmittatur Adonai, id est, Dominus. Nempe Elohim Deus, significat eum, qui potest vi sua operationes edere miraculosas, seu quæ naturæ vim superant: Et dicitur Deus eius vel populi vel hominis, quem in suam veluti fidem & clientelam recepit contracto cum eo fœdere. Id quod à nobis Deo dante probabitur alio loco. Hæc cum gentes omnes suis omnibus diis tribuerent, una potissimum inter fideles & idololatras versabatur controversia, quis esset Deus? Ieheueh, exempli gratia, an Bahal? quam controversiam isto suo nomine Deus significat tandem aliquando certo tempore futuro definitum iri, seque causam victurum: tunc enim se futurum Deum, præter se verò neminem. Adde quòd si Israelem cum aliis gentibus conferas, Deus quidem olim Israelis Deus erat, Gentium verò aliarum non item. Latebat igitur in eo nomine etiam vaticinium, fore, ut sancito novo foedere, cum ipsorum Iudaeorum nova quadam ratione, tum aliarum gentium euaderet Deus. Ex quo intelligere est cum verbo illo Erit, ut ita dicam, nominascente conuenientissimè nomen Elohim sic iunctum fuisse, ut illud praecederet, hoc sequeretur. Dispar verò ratio est nominis Adonai, quod Dominum significat: neque enim ea proprie fideles inter & idololatras erat quaestio, uter esset totius mundi dominus, verbi gratia, Iehoua, an aliquis alius? Dominum enim absolutè siue totius mundi, vel nullum agnoscebant Idololatrae, vel unum tantum putabant esse reliquorum deorum regem, ac propterea יהוה[?] Ieheueh seu Iihueh, Erit, non subjungitur Adonai Dominus vt praedicatum, sed praemittitur potius vt subjectum, de quo praedicetur futura existentia, vt sit sensus, cum, qui iure totius mundi est Dominus, tandem aliquando futurum esse, hoc est, quàm verè sit ostensurum, quod fieri non potuit, quin eo ipso iure & vsurpatione sua exciderent omnes alij dij, & malè esset idololatris ac rebellibus, benè fidelibus ac pijs.
units.tr: XXXVIII. From this perhaps the reason can be gathered why this name is often followed by the name Elohim, that is, God, and sometimes preceded by Adonai, that is, Lord. For Elohim, God, signifies him who can by his power perform miraculous works, or those which surpass the force of nature; and he is called the God of this or that people or person whom he has taken, as it were, under his faith and protection by a covenant made with him. This we shall prove in another place, God willing. Since all the nations attributed their gods to themselves, the controversy between the faithful and the idolaters was chiefly this: Who is God? Jehovah, for example, or Baal? This controversy the name Erit signifies will at some certain time in the future be settled, and that he will win the cause: for then he will be God, and no one besides him. Add to this that if you compare Israel with the other nations, God indeed was once the God of Israel, but not in the same way the God of the other nations. There was therefore hidden in that name also a prophecy, that when the new covenant was sanctioned he would become God in a new way both for the Jews themselves and for the other nations. From this it is to be understood that, with the word Erit, as I may say, the name Elohim was most suitably joined in such a way that the one went before and the other followed. The reasoning is different for the name Adonai, which means Lord: for the question between the faithful and the idolaters was not properly which of them was the lord of the whole world, for instance, Jehovah or someone else? For the idolaters either acknowledged no lord absolutely, that is, of the whole world, or thought there was only one king of the rest of the gods; and therefore Adonai Lord is not joined to יהוה, Jehovah, Erit, as a predicate, but rather placed before it as the subject, of which the future existence is predicated, so that the sense is: he who by right is Lord of the whole world will at last one day be, that is, will show how truly he is, which could not happen without all the other gods at once losing that right and their usurpation, and it going badly for the idolaters and rebels, and well for the faithful and pious.

units.la: XXXIX. Patet ex dictis cum Domino absolutè, seu totius mundi, reciprocari hoc nomen. Atqui negare non possunt Adversarii, quin Dominus noster Iesus Christus sit Dominus totius mundi. Vocatur, ipsis confitentibus, Dominus totius terra, & jubentur eum adorare omnes Angeli. Psal. 97. 5. 8. Heb. 1. 6. cui autem angelici parent exercitus, inquit ipse Crellius, quid non pareat? Habet omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra. Praeest toti mundo non tanquam alienae domui, sed tanquam suae, non tanquam vicarius Domini, sed tanquam Dominus, proprietarius, Patris Filius unigenitus, ac haeres ex asse.
units.tr: XXXIX. It is clear from what has been said that this name is reciprocal with Lord absolutely, or of the whole world. Yet our opponents cannot deny that our Lord Jesus Christ is Lord of the whole world. He is called, as they themselves confess, Lord of all the earth, and all the angels are commanded to worship him. Ps. 97. 5. 8. Heb. 1. 6. And to whom, says Crellius himself, do the angelic hosts not obey? He has all power in heaven and on earth. He rules over the whole world not as over a house that is another's, but as over his own; not as a deputy of the Lord, but as Lord, the owner, the only-begotten Son of the Father, and heir of the whole estate.

units.la: XL. Ad superiora hoc etiam accedit, quod, ut jam observauimus non sine singulari quadam providentia Dei factum est, ut Deo revelato in carne legi & pronunciari desierit hoc nomen ab omnibus tam Iudaeis quàm Christianis. Id enim superstitioni Iudaeorum ascribi non debere ex eo colligi potest, quod ea superstitio, ut aliae omnes Iudaicae, per Christum vel eius Apostolos sublata fuisset de Ecclesia. Quid enim obstare potuit, quominus Christus eiusque Apostoli id nomen aequè, ac Moses olim & Prophetæ, vsurparent? aut Christianis exponerent? aut etiam, vt alia multa nomina hebraea, Nouo Testamento inferrent? neque enim aut persecutionis aut scandali metu absterreri solebant, quominus liberè superstitiones Iudæorum, etiam eas quæ parui momenti videri possent, reprehenderent. Cur igitur nomen istud non vsurparunt? cur loca Veteris Testamenti laudantes in quibus extat, illud [illegible, ~5 letters] reddiderunt quasi eius loco, & legisset ipsi pro Iudæorum more, & legi vellent Adonai? Non enim decebat Ecclesiam Christianam hac in re deteriorem esse Iudaicâ antiquâ, quæ id Dei nomen legere & pronunciare sciuit, & frequenter vsurpauit. Huius profecto rei alia ratio reddi non potest quam ista, contineri in eo nomine vaticinium, quod Christi aduentu impletum fuit: Illud enim nomen proprie significare Erit: itaque Deum significare relatè ad certum quoddam tempus futurum, quo præsente aut præterito obsolescere debuit, & in aliud mutari tempori illi conuenientius. Quod tempus diuina prouidentia anticipari voluit à græca versione, quam in græcorum, ad Euangelium suo tempore recipiendum præparandorum, gratiam concinnari curauit. Cum igitur in eo nomine prædictio contineretur de Domini nostri Iesu Christi, vt ita loquar, futuritione, non sine admirabili quadam Dei prouidentia accidit, vt hoc nomen veluti antiquaretur, eiusque loco Euangelii tempore id nomen summo omnium consensu legeretur, quod Christo non convenit modò, sed singulari quadam ratione tanquam proprium vendicatur. Vt quemadmodum olim nomen illud fidelium animos erigebat in expectationem futuri, sic nomen, quod eius loco nunc legitur, confirmet, eum qui erat futurus venire ac esse illum qui singulari ratione Dominus appellatur. Eadem Dei prouidentia oblato vero sacrificio, quo peccata mundi expiata sunt, curauit templum Hierosolymitanum dirui, & cauit ne possent Iudæi sacrificia deinceps secundum legem offerre.
units.tr: XL. To the above is added this also: as we have already observed, not without a singular providence of God, it came about that this name, once God was revealed in the flesh, ceased to be read and pronounced by all, both Jews and Christians. That this should not be ascribed to the superstition of the Jews can be gathered from the fact that this superstition, like all the other Jewish ones, was not abolished from the Church by Christ or his Apostles. For what could have prevented Christ and his Apostles from using that name just as Moses and the Prophets once did, or from explaining it to Christians, or even from introducing it into the New Testament, as they did with many other Hebrew names? For they were not accustomed to be deterred by fear of persecution or of giving offence from freely rebuking the superstitions of the Jews, even those which might seem of little importance. Why then did they not use that name? Why, when quoting places of the Old Testament in which it stands, did they render it by something else, as if in its place, and wish it to be read and said as Adonai, after the manner of the Jews? For the Christian Church ought not in this matter to be worse than the ancient Jewish Church, which knew how to read and pronounce that name of God, and used it frequently. Assuredly no other reason can be given for this than that there was contained in that name a prophecy which was fulfilled at the coming of Christ: for that name properly signifies Erit, and so denotes God in relation to a certain future time, at which, once it was present or past, it ought to have become obsolete and been changed into something more fitting to that time. That time the divine providence willed to be anticipated by the Greek version, which it took care to prepare in the favour of the Greeks, to prepare them for receiving the Gospel in its own time. Since therefore in that name a prediction was contained concerning the future coming, as I may say, of our Lord Jesus Christ, it came about, not without a wonderful providence of God, that this name was as it were set aside, and in place of it, in the time of the Gospel, a name was read with the consent of all, which not only suits Christ but is claimed for him in a singular way as his own. So that, just as that name once lifted the hearts of the faithful in expectation of the future, so the name which is now read in its place may confirm that he who was to come has come, and is he who is called Lord in a singular manner. By the same providence of God, once the true sacrifice had been offered, by which the sins of the world were expiated, care was taken that the Temple of Jerusalem should be destroyed, and provision made that the Jews could no longer offer sacrifices according to the law.

units.la: XLI.
units.tr: XLI.

units.la: At, objiciet fortasse aliquis, nondum impletum fuit quicquid eo nomine prædicebatur. Nempe, referebatur nomen illud, Erit, ad vtrumque aduentum Christi: Eius enim impletionem[?] primo aduentu inchoari, secundo perfici oportuit. Porrò Dominus ratione primi aduentus futurus, ratione secundi venturus magis proprie dici potuit. Primo enim aduentu futurus erat id quod non erat, nimirum homo, necnon Deus omnium gentium pacto cum eis nouo foedere. Secundo verò aduentu nihil eius producetur. Itaque nunc potius ὁ ἐρχόμενος venturus, quàm ὁ ἐσόμενος futurus appellatur. Adde quod secundus aduentus est primi consequens ita necessarium, itaque clarè & distinctè passim in Nouo Testamento praedicitur & inculcatur, vt fieri non possit, quin credat secundum, quicunque credit primum: ac propterea nihil opus fuit eiusmodi nominis vsurpatione futurum illum aduentum obscurè innuere, sed satius multò fuit illius nominis, vt ita loquar, antiquatione Iudaeos gentesque admonere, mundi Dominum & Seruatorem iam venisse: id quod omni genere argumentorum Deo confirmare placuit: Eaque de causa etiam illos typos abrogare, quorum veritas maxima ex parte pendet ex secundo Christi aduentu. Nimirum, vt dixi, qui primum aduentum credit, is necessariò etiam credit secundum. Et nomen illud, Erit, erat consentaneum œconomiae Veteris Testamenti, quae tota in futurum tendebat, ac proinde cum illa abrogandum: congruebat etiam cum statu illius, qui nondum sese quis esset clarè & distinctè ostendisset mundo; haud verò æquè cum statu illius, qui se quis esset contemplandum cuilibet exposuisset.
units.tr: But someone will perhaps object that not everything foretold under that name has yet been fulfilled. The name Erit, he will say, refers to both comings of Christ, since its fulfilment had to begin at his first coming and be completed at his second. Moreover, the Lord could more properly be called futurus with respect to the first coming and venturus with respect to the second. At his first coming he was to be futurus, that is, to become what he was not: a man, and also God of all nations through a new covenant with them. At his second coming nothing of that kind will be produced, so he is now called rather ὁ ἐρχόμενος [ho erchomenos], venturus, than ὁ ἐσόμενος [ho esomenos], futurus. Add that the second coming follows so necessarily from the first, and is so clearly and distinctly foretold and pressed throughout the New Testament, that whoever believes in the first cannot fail to believe in the second. There was therefore no need to hint obscurely at that future coming by using such a name. It was much better, so to speak, to make the Jews and the nations aware by the abolition of that name that the Lord and Saviour of the world had already come, a truth God chose to confirm by every kind of argument. For the same reason he also abolished those types whose truth depends for the most part on the second coming of Christ. Indeed, as I have said, whoever believes in the first coming necessarily believes in the second. The name Erit was in keeping with the economy of the Old Testament, which all pointed toward the future, and so it had to be abolished along with that economy. It also suited the state of one who had not yet clearly and distinctly shown himself to the world, but would not suit the state of one who had set himself forth for anyone to contemplate.

units.la: XLII. Ergo, inquiet aliquis, nomen illud, Erit, proprium fuit Filij? Sanè, sed non ita, quin tribui potuerit, & tributum fuerit persæpè Patri. Pater enim est in Filio, & Filius in Patre: Pater & Filius vnum sunt: nec facilè potuit alter ab altero sub œconomia V. Test. internosci. Quanquam etiam in luce N. T. ita proprium est Patris nomen Dei, vt tamen tribuatur etiam Filio & Filij nomen Domini, vt tamen tribuatur etiam Patri. Nihil enim impediebat, quominus ab eo, quod peculiari quadam ratione proprium erat Filij, desumeretur nomen ad significandum Deum siue indistinctè vt Dominum, siue distinctè modò Patrem, modò Filium, modò etiam Spiritum sanctum pro locorum ratione & circunstantijs; praesertim cum id non ita proprium esset Filij, quin Patri etiam & Spiritui sancto tribui posset, licet minus proprie, & non sine aliquo ad Filium respectu. Atque haec dicta sunto de sacrosancto illo nomine.
units.tr: XLII. "Then," someone will say, "was the name Erit proper to the Son?" Certainly, but not so exclusively that it could not be, and was not very often, ascribed to the Father. For the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father; the Father and the Son are one, and under the economy of the Old Testament one could hardly distinguish one from the other. Yet even in the light of the New Testament, the name God is so proper to the Father that it is also ascribed to the Son, and the name Lord belongs to the Son while it is also ascribed to the Father. For nothing prevented a name derived from something peculiarly proper to the Son from being used to signify God, either indistinctly as Lord, or distinctly now as Father, now as Son, now also as the Holy Spirit, according to place and circumstance. This is especially so since the name was not so proper to the Son that it could not be ascribed to the Father and the Holy Spirit as well, though less properly, and not without some reference to the Son. Let these things be said about that most holy name.

units.la: XLIII. Ne autem haec sola disputatio sine certo Scripturae testimonio abeat, duo loca subnectam: alterum è veteri, alterum è Nouo Testamento. Prior extat Ose. 1. 7. Domus verò Iuda miserebor, & seruabo eos per Dominum Deum ipsorum, & non serua[illegible, ~1 letter] vabo eos per arcum, nec per gladium, nec per bellum, nec per equos aut equites. In quibus verbis distinguntur duæ personæ: una quæ miseretur & seruat; altera per quam illa seruat: utraque appellatur Dominus (vulgò Iehoua.) Si consulis Euangelium, illa est Pater, hæc Filius. Seruat enim nos Pater per Filium: nam non est in alio aliquo salus, nec enim aliud nomen est sub cælo datum hominibus, in quo oportet nos saluos fieri. Argumentum sic habet. Ille per quem Deus pater erat Ecclesiam seruaturus est Dominus Deus. Christus est ille per quem Deus pater erat Ecclesiam seruaturus. Ergo Christus est Dominus Deus.
units.tr: XLIII. So that this discussion does not proceed without a sure testimony of Scripture, I shall add two passages, one from the Old Testament and one from the New. The first is in Hosea 1:7: But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah, and will save them by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, nor by horses, nor by horsemen. In these words two persons are distinguished: one who has mercy and saves, and another through whom he saves. Both are called Lord (commonly Jehovah). If you consult the Gospel, the first is the Father and the second is the Son. For the Father saves us through the Son, since there is salvation in no other, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved. The argument runs thus: He through whom God the Father was to save the Church is the Lord God. Christ is he through whom God the Father was to save the Church. Therefore Christ is the Lord God.

units.la: XLIV. Quid potest responderi, nisi in loco illo Osæ, aut non agi de salute spirituali; aut per Dominum Deum Iudæorum illum ipsum intelligi qui seruaturus dicitur, ut sit sensus, Ego seruabo eos per me ipsum; aut denique per Dominum deum Iudæorum intelligi posse Spiritum sanctum? Atqui horum nullum responderi potest. Non primum: Argumentabor enim à minori ad majus. Nam si salutis temporalis Iudæorum, quæ præ spirituali & æterna nullius est momenti, non modo causa quæ seruare debuit esse Dominus Deus, sed etiam causa media per quam salus fieret, quanto magis existimandum est salutis spiritualis & æternæ causam non modo eam quæ seruat, sed etiam eam per quam salus fit, esse Dominum Deum? Hoc primum. Deinde quæ salus temporalis intelligeretur? Annon ea præcipuè, qua Iudæi liberati sunt à rege Assyriorum Angeli opera? vel igitur Angelus ille erat Dominus Deus Iudæorum, vel non erat. Si non erat, quomodo dixit Deus, se Iudæos seruaturum per Dominum Deum ipsorum? Intelligere enim eum causam mediam, &, ut ita dicam, instrumentalem verba quæ sequuntur docent, & non seruabo eos per arcum, nec per gladium &c. Si erat; non igitur erat natura angelus, seu angelus creatus: alioqui angelus creatus fuisset à Iudæis religiosè colendus & adorandus, & pro Domino Deoque suo habendus, duoque fuissent Domini (Iehouæ) diiqué Iudæorum totis essentiis diuersi, id quod quàm sit absurdum & pugnans cum Lege nemo, opinor, non videt. Præterea Deum loqui de salute spirituali, quæ in alio non est quàm in Christo, patet ex nominibus Iisreel, Lo-ruhama, Lo-ammi & Ν. 10. ac seqq. necnon ex alijs vaticinijs, Esai. 45.17. Israël seruabitur per Dominum salute æterna, Esai. 35.4. Deus ipse veniet, & seruabit vos. Tunc aperientur oculi cæcorum [?] &c.
units.tr: XLIV. What can be answered to this, except that either the passage in Hosea is not concerned with spiritual salvation; or that the Lord God of the Jews is understood to be the very one who is said to save, so that the sense is, "I will save them through myself"; or finally that the Lord God of the Jews can be understood to be the Holy Spirit? Yet none of these can be given as an answer. Not the first, for I shall argue from the lesser to the greater. If the temporal salvation of the Jews, which is of no account compared with spiritual and eternal salvation, required that the Lord God be not only the cause that was to save but also the intermediate cause through which the salvation was to come about, how much more must we think that the cause of spiritual and eternal salvation is the Lord God, not only as the one who saves but also as the one through whom salvation comes? That is the first point. Next, what temporal salvation would be meant? Is it not chiefly that by which the Jews were delivered from the king of the Assyrians by the work of an angel? Either that angel was the Lord God of the Jews, or he was not. If he was not, how did God say that he would save the Jews through their Lord God? The words that follow show that he understood this as the intermediate, so to speak instrumental, cause: and I will not save them by bow, nor by sword, and so on. If he was, then he was not a natural angel, or a created angel. Otherwise a created angel would have been religiously worshipped and adored by the Jews, and held as their Lord and God, and there would have been two Lords (Jehovahs), and gods of the Jews wholly different in essence, which I think no one fails to see is both absurd and contrary to the Law. Moreover, that God is speaking of spiritual salvation, which is found in no one other than Christ, is clear from the names Jezreel, Lo-ruhama, Lo-ammi, and from Hosea 1:10 and following, and also from other prophecies: Isaiah 45:17, Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation; Isaiah 35:4, God himself will come and save you. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened [?], and so on.

units.la: XLIV Non potest etiam responderi secundum: opponitur enim Dominus Deus hoc loco arcui, gladio, bello, equis, equitibus, Seruabo, inquit, eos per Dominum Deum ipsorum, & non seruabo eos per arcum, nec per gladium, nec per bellum, nec per equos & equites. Tenet igitur inter causas salutis eum locum Dominus Deus, quem tenerent equites, equi, bellum, immò gladius & arcus, si per eiusmodi instrumenta salus fieret. Tenet autem eum locum in salutis negotio, non ipse Deus pater, sed eius Filius. Pater non seruat immediatè per semetipsum, sed seruat mediatè per Filium. Filius igitur est ille Dominus Deus per quem Pater seruat. Dicitur enim seruaturus Iudæos per Dominum Deum ipsorum, ut excludat alias causas medias seu instrumentales, ut patet ex verbis sequentibus. Itaque significat Dominum Deum fore illud, ut vulgò loquuntur, medium, illud, ut ita dicam, instrumentum per quod seruandi erant.
units.tr: XLIV. Nor can the second answer be given either. For in this passage the Lord God is set over against the bow, the sword, battle, horses and horsemen: I will save them, he says, by the Lord their God, and will not save them by bow, nor by sword, nor by battle, nor by horses and horsemen. So the Lord God holds among the causes of salvation the place that horsemen, horses, battle, and even sword and bow would hold if salvation were brought about by such instruments. But in the business of salvation that place is held not by God the Father himself but by his Son. The Father does not save immediately through himself, but mediately through the Son. The Son, therefore, is that Lord God through whom the Father saves. For he is said to save the Jews by the Lord their God in order to exclude other intermediate or instrumental causes, as is clear from the words that follow. Thus it signifies that the Lord God would be that, as people commonly say, means, that instrument, so to speak, by which they were to be saved.

units.la: XLV. Tertium denique responderi non potest ab Aduersarijs: negant enim Spiritum sanctum Deum appellari in sacris literis. Deinde Spiritus sanctus distinguitur à Deo patre. Si igitur is est Dominus Deus Iudeorum, duæ erunt personæ distinctæ appellatæ Dominus Deus, Pater & Spiritus sanctus: (Est enim sine dubio Dominus Deus Iudæorum persona) & cum Filius soleat medius poni inter Patrem & Spiritum sanctum, & dicatur mittere Spiritum sanctum, & Spiritus sanctus esse Spiritus Filij dicatur, erit Filius medius inter Deum & Deum, & mittet Deum, & eius Spiritus erit Deus. quod quomodo esse possit, si Filius nihil est nisi homo seu creatura, haud sanè intelligo. Adde quod is qui proximè per Spiritum sanctum seruat est Filius, ut enim Pater misit Filium, sic Filius misit Spiritum sanctum, & per eum Ecclesiam illuminat, sanctificat, consolatur, regit.
units.tr: XLV. Finally, a third answer cannot be given by our opponents. For they deny that the Holy Spirit is called God in the sacred writings. Furthermore, the Holy Spirit is distinguished from God the Father. If then he is the Lord God of the Jews, there will be two distinct persons called Lord God, the Father and the Holy Spirit (for the Lord God of the Jews is without doubt a person). And since the Son is usually placed in the middle between the Father and the Holy Spirit, and is said to send the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is said to be the Spirit of the Son, the Son will be in the middle between God and God, and will send God, and his Spirit will be God. I certainly do not understand how this could be, if the Son is nothing but man or creature. Add that the one who saves most immediately through the Holy Spirit is the Son. For just as the Father sent the Son, so the Son sent the Holy Spirit, and through him enlightens, sanctifies, comforts and governs the Church.

units.la: XLVI. Alter locus habetur Rom. 10. 13. Quicunque invocaverit nomen Domini seruabitur, quod oraculum petitum est ex Ioele 2. 32. ubi est nomen tetragrammatum, quod Apostolus vertit κύριον, id est, Dominum. Si igitur probauero per Dominum eo loco Christum intelligi debere, probauero utique Christum esse, ut vulgò legunt, Iehouam. Id autem probo, quia idem sine dubio Dominus intelligitur ✠. 13. qui ✠. 12. proximo. Alioqui Apostolus paralogismum commisisset. Cum enim dixisset ✠. 12. { }eundem esse Dominum omnium, diuisitem in omnes à quibus innoca-tur. Id probauit Ꝟ[?] 13. testimonio Dei apud Ioëlem, cuius sunt hæc verba, quicunque innocauerit nomen Domini seruabitur. Si igitur alius Dominus Ꝟ[?] 12. alius Ꝟ[?] 13. intelligendus esset, hicque, ut volunt Aduersarij, absque illo inuocari posset, peccaret argumentatio Apostoli ignoratione Elenchi, in eaque essent quatuor termini. Iam autem Ꝟ[?] 12. per Dominum intelligendum esse Christum, manifestum est: nam & nomen Domini, & quæ de Domino eo versu dicuntur Christo conuenire in confesso est; & tractabat Apostolus de fide in Christum; & quicquid de Domino dixit Ꝟ[?] 12. id dixit ut confirmaret quod posuerat Ꝟ[?] 11. proximè antecedente, Quicunque credit in eum non pudefiet, per eum autem Christum intelligi patet cum ex verbis antecedentibus, tum ex illis ipsis verbis: petita enim sunt ex Esai. 28. 16. quo loco agi de Christo cuiuis perspicuum est.
units.tr: XLVI. Another passage is Romans 10:13, Whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved, which is taken from Joel 2:32, where the tetragrammaton stands and the Apostle renders it [κύριον], that is, Lord. If I therefore prove that Lord in that place must be understood as Christ, I shall certainly prove that Christ is, as they commonly read, Jehovah. I prove this because without doubt the same Lord is meant in verse 13 as in verse 12. Otherwise the Apostle would have committed a fallacy. For when he said in verse 12 that there is one and the same Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him, he proved this in verse 13 by the testimony of God in Joel, whose words are: whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved. If, then, a different Lord were to be understood in verse 12 and another in verse 13, and this one could be called upon without that one, as the adversaries wish, the Apostle's argument would commit the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi, and there would be four terms in it. Now that the Lord of verse 12 must be understood as Christ is plain: for it is admitted that both the name of the Lord and what is said of the Lord in that verse apply to Christ; the Apostle was treating of faith in Christ; and whatever he said of the Lord in verse 12 he said to confirm what he had laid down in verse 11 immediately before, whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. That by him Christ is meant is clear both from the preceding words and from those very words, for they are taken from Isaiah 28:16, a passage which is plainly about Christ to anyone.

units.la: XLVII. Addam velut cumulum tertium locum ex eodem Zacharia cap. x. Ꝟ[?] 12. Confortabo eos in Domino, & in nomine eius ambulabunt, dicit Dominus. Quis enim non videt eum Dominum, qui hoc dicit, distinguere se à Domino, in quo sit eos confortaturus, tanquam ab alia persona? Cum enim dicit, confortabo eos in Domino, siue per Dominum, distinguit personam quæ confortat ab ea per quam confortat, ut in superiore loco, seruabo eos in Domino Deo ipsorum, siue per Dominum Deum ipsorum, distinguit personam quæ seruat ab ea per quam seruat, & utramque Dominum vocat. Deinde cum addit, & in nomine eius ambulabunt, dicit Dominus, clarius adhuc distinctionem personarum reuelat: distinguit enim sese pronomine Eius is Dominus qui loquitur ab eo Domino de quo loquitur, tam certè, quàm apud eundem Zachariam cap. 2. 8. Dominus exercituum, cuius hæc sunt verba, Quoniam qui vos tangit, tangit pupillam oculi eius, eodem pronomine Eius sese aperte distinguit à Domino exercituum, à quo se profitetur missum fuisse. Constat autem nos & in Christo seu per Christum confortari, & in eius nomine ambulare.
units.tr: XLVII. I will add, as a third passage and by way of a climax, Zechariah 10:12: I will strengthen them in the Lord, and they shall walk in his name, says the Lord. For who does not see that the one who says this, the Lord, distinguishes himself from the Lord in whom he will strengthen them, as from another person? For when he says I will strengthen them in the Lord, or through the Lord, he distinguishes the person who strengthens from the person through whom he strengthens, just as in the earlier passage, I will save them in the Lord their God, or through the Lord their God, he distinguishes the person who saves from the person through whom he saves, and calls both of them Lord. Then, when he adds and they shall walk in his name, says the Lord, he reveals the distinction of persons even more clearly: by the pronoun his the Lord who speaks distinguishes himself from the Lord of whom he speaks, just as certainly as in the same Zechariah, chapter 2:8, the Lord of hosts, whose words are for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye, by the same pronoun his plainly distinguishes himself from the Lord of hosts, by whom he declares himself to have been sent. It is agreed, moreover, that we are strengthened in Christ, or through Christ, and walk in his name.

units.la: DISPUTATIO TRIGESIMA TERTIA
units.tr: Disputation Thirty-Third

units.la: De Arg. XXXIII. Ex Zach. 2. 8. &c. Quoniam sic dicit Dominus exercituum, post gloriam misit me ad gentes, quae spoliauerunt vos. &c.
units.tr: On Argument XXXIII, from Zech. 2. 8, etc.: Because thus says the Lord of hosts, after the glory he sent me to the nations which plundered you, etc.

units.la: I. LAVDABO adhuc quædam testimonia petita e[?] Zacharia. Primum habetur cap. 2. V. 8. Quia, sic dicit Dominus exercituum, Post gloriam misit me ad gentes, quæ spoliauerunt vos: propterea quod qui tangit vos, tangit pupillam oculi eius: propterea ecce ego agito manum meam super eos, & erunt præda seruis suis, & scietis quod Dominus exercituum misit me. In his verbis duæ personæ distinguuntur, vna quæ mittit, altera quæ mittitur, vtraque appellatur Dominus (Iehoua) exercituum. Quæ mittit est Deus Pater, nonne? Quæ mittitur si non est Filius Dei, quænam est?
units.tr: I. I shall still set out some further testimonies taken from Zechariah. The first is in chapter 2, verse 8: Because thus says the Lord of hosts: After the glory he sent me to the nations which plundered you; for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye; therefore, behold, I will lift my hand against them, and they shall be spoil for their servants, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me. In these words two persons are distinguished: one who sends and one who is sent, and each is called Lord (Jehovah) of hosts. The one who sends is God the Father, is he not? If the one who is sent is not the Son of God, who else is he?

units.la: II. Huic testimonio alterum addo ex eodem cap. 2. V. 10. & 11. Lauda & latare filia Sion, quoniam ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui, ait Dominus: & adiungentur gentes multae ad Dominum in die illa, & erunt mihi in populum, & habitabo in medio tui: & scies quod Dominus exercituum misit me ad te. Hic quoque Dominum (Iehouam) loqui manifestum est, & tamen is se missum profitetur à Domino exercituum.
units.tr: II. To this testimony I add another from the same chapter 2, verses 10 and 11: Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and will dwell in your midst, says the Lord; and many nations shall join themselves to the Lord in that day, and they shall be my people, and I will dwell in your midst; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. Here too it is plain that the Lord (Jehovah) is speaking, and yet he professes that he has been sent by the Lord of hosts.

units.la: III. His duobus testimonijs tertium adjungam ex cap. 4. V. 8. Et factum est verbum Domini ad me dicens, Manus Zorobabel fundauerunt domum istam, & manus eius perficient eam; & scies quod Dominus exercituum misit me ad vos. Potuitne clarius duarum personarum diuinarum distinctio proponi? Quænam autem persona diuina missa fuit vel ad hostes populi Dei subigendos, vel ad gentes ad Dominum conuertendas, & sibi in populum foedere inito comparandas, vel ad Domum Dei aedificandam, vel ad omnia illa agenda? Annon Filius?
units.tr: III. To these two testimonies I add a third, from chapter 4, verse 8: And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundations of this house, and his hands shall finish it; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. Could the distinction of the two divine persons be set forth more clearly? But which divine person was sent either to subdue the enemies of the people of God, or to convert the nations to the Lord and gain them for himself as a people by entering into a covenant, or to build the house of God, or to do all those things? Is it not the Son?

units.la: I V. Addi potest & quartum testimonium ex cap. 6. 13. Haec ait Dominus exercituum, dicens, Ecce vir, oriens nomen eius &c, & qui procul sunt venient & adificabunt in templo Domini, & scietis quia Dominus exercituum misit me ad vos. Erit autem hoc, si auditu audieritis vocem Domini Dei vestri. Negari enim non potest, quin verba, Et scietis quia Dominus exercituum misit me ad vos, eius sint cuius antecedentia: sunt autem antecedentia verba Domini exercituum, ut patet ex N[?]. 13. Profitetur ergo Dominus exercituum se missum fuisse à Domino exercituum, nempe Filium à Patre.
units.tr: IV. A fourth testimony may also be added, from chapter 6, verse 13: Thus says the Lord of hosts, saying: Behold the man whose name is the Branch, etc., and those who are far off shall come and build in the temple of the Lord, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. This will come to pass if you diligently hearken to the voice of the Lord your God. For it cannot be denied that the words And you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you belong to the one whose preceding words they are; and the preceding words are those of the Lord of hosts, as is clear from verse 13. The Lord of hosts therefore professes that he has been sent by the Lord of hosts, namely the Son by the Father.

units.la: V. Quid respondet Socinus? Breuiter, inquit, ex hoc argumento, si recte conclusum esset, nihil aliud posset colligi, nisi duos esse, quorum utrumque sit & vocetur Dominus siue Iehoua exercituum; sed quod alter eorum sit Christus, nullo modo. Hoc vero iam multum est. Nam si duo sunt, quorum utrumque sit & vocetur Dominus exercituum, falsa sunt Aduersariorum placita, solam Patris personam esse Dominum exercituum, nec esse nisi vnicam personam praeditam essentia diuina; concidunt que omnes illae rationes, quibus pluralitatem personarum diuinarum oppugnare soliti sunt.
units.tr: V. What does Socinus reply? Briefly, he says, if this argument were rightly concluded, nothing else could be inferred except that there are two, each of whom is and is called the Lord or Jehovah of hosts; but that one of them is Christ, by no means. But this already concedes a great deal. For if there are two, each of whom is and is called the Lord of hosts, then the opponents' positions are false: that only the person of the Father is the Lord of hosts, and that there is only one person endowed with the divine essence. All those arguments with which they have been accustomed to assail the plurality of divine persons collapse.

units.la: VI. Deinde longius progredior, & quæro, quis sit ille Dominus exercituum, qui se profitetur à Domino exercituum missum esse? Is sine dubio est aut Pater, aut Filius, aut Spiritus sanctus: merus enim angelus non est Dominus seu Iehoua exercituum. Num igitur est Pater? Nulla causa est, inquit Socinus, cur Pater ipse siue à Filio, siue à Spiritu sancto mitti non possit, si modo omnium & vniuscuiusque ipsorum eadem per omnia est dignitas, potentia, atque maiestas; ut ipsi trinitarij contendunt. Ponamus igitur Patrem missum dici hoc loco à Domino exercituum; siue ponatur missus à Filio, Filius erit Dominus exercituum, siue ponatur missus à Spiritu sancto, Spiritus sanctus erit Dominus exercituum; quod utrumque pugnat cum Aduersariorum dogmate. Sed quominus per Dominum exercituum missum à Domino exercituum Patrem intelligamus, obstant duo. Vnum, quod à Patre missus Filius, missus Spiritus sanctus saepe legitur, missus vero Pater à Filio aut à Spiritu sancto nunquam. Itaque qui diceret missum fuisse Patrem, is non consentanea Scripturæ diceret, & à forma seu exemplari saniorum sermonum discederet. Alterum quod inverteretur ordo naturæ, nec servaretur decorum, si mitteretur Pater vel à Filio quem genuit, vel à Spiritu sancto qui ab eo procedit. Naturæ enim seu essentiæ æqualitas personarum nec originem tollit, nec consentaneum origini ordinem.
units.tr: VI. Next I go further and ask who that Lord of hosts is who professes that he has been sent by the Lord of hosts. He is without doubt either the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, for a mere angel is not the Lord or Jehovah of hosts. Is he then the Father? There is no reason, says Socinus, why the Father himself could not be sent either by the Son or by the Holy Spirit, provided only that the dignity, power and majesty of all and of each of them are the same in every respect, as the Trinitarians contend. Let us suppose, then, that the Father is said in this place to be sent by the Lord of hosts. If he is supposed to be sent by the Son, the Son will be the Lord of hosts; if he is supposed to be sent by the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit will be the Lord of hosts. Both of these clash with the opponents' doctrine. But two things stand in the way of understanding by the Lord of hosts who is sent by the Lord of hosts the Father. One is that the Son sent by the Father, and the Holy Spirit sent, are often read of, but the Father sent by the Son or by the Holy Spirit never. Therefore whoever said that the Father was sent would be saying something not consonant with Scripture, and would depart from the pattern or model of sound speech. The other is that the order of nature would be overturned and propriety not preserved if the Father were sent either by the Son, whom he begat, or by the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him. For the equality of the persons in nature or essence removes neither their origin nor the order consonant with that origin.

units.la: VII. Estne igitur Spiritus sanctus? Is certè à Patre, immò à Filio missus est: Nec admodum refert eumne an Filium intelligas hoc loco. Nam si Spiritus sanctus est Dominus exercituum missus à Domino exercituum, Spiritus sanctus est persona, Spiritus sanctus est Deus; quod utrumque negant Aduersarij. Hactenus igitur causam vicimus. Deinde si Spiritus sanctus est Dominus exercituum, isque, vt Euangelium docet, & Socinus agnoscit, mittitur à Filio, necesse est vt Filius etiam ipse fit Dominus exercituum. Quid enim? mitteretur ne creator à creatura, Dominus à servo, Iehoua exercituum ab homine?
units.tr: VII. Is it then the Holy Spirit? He certainly is sent by the Father, and indeed by the Son. Nor does it matter much whether you understand the Spirit or the Son in this place. For if the Holy Spirit is the Lord of hosts sent by the Lord of hosts, the Holy Spirit is a person, the Holy Spirit is God; and the opponents deny both of these. So far, then, we have won the case. Next, if the Holy Spirit is the Lord of hosts, and he is, as the Gospel teaches and Socinus acknowledges, sent by the Son, it is necessary that the Son also himself be the Lord of hosts. For what follows? Would the Creator be sent by a creature, the Lord by a servant, the Lord (Jehovah) of hosts by a man?

units.la: VIII. Non contentus igitur prima illa responsione Socinus ad alteram confugit, & negat, istum, qui dicit, se esse missum à Domino exercituum, esse Dominum exercituum. Atque vt ad primum testimonii ex quatuor illis quæ laudauimus, respondeat, obseruat, eum qui apud Zachariam ista verba pronunciat, Hæc dicit Dominus exercituum, Post gloriam &c, esse angelum illum alterum, qui occurrit angelo loquenti cum Zacharia; quem etiam aloqui cœperat à v. 4. & pergit vsque ad finem cap: & in ipso sermonis initio facit mentionem Zachariæ, cui vult vt dicat ea, quæ sequuntur, inquiens, Loquere ad puerum istum, dicens, Absque muro, &c. Itaque apparet, quod præter illum, qui verba ista pronunciat, Hæc dicit Dominus &c, adsunt ibi, ipse sciente, cum quibus etiam loquitur, alij duo seu duæ aliæ personæ; nempe Zacharias, & angelus qui ab ipso prophetia initio cum ipso loquebatur. Hoc, quod apertissimum est, constituto, Dico, inquit, pronomen Me in verbis illis, misit me, non ad Dominum exercituum, sed ad alterum istum angelum, qui verba illa, Hæc dicit Dominus, profert, referendum esse, qui quamuis Dominum exercituum loquentem videatur inducere, tamen reipsa nihil agit aliud, nisi narrat, quid Dominus exercituum dicat; hoc nimirum pacto: Hæc (sive vt est in hebræo Sic) dicit Dominus exercituum, quòd post gloriam, &c. Nam particulã Quòd frequentissimè in sacris literis subaudiendam esse, nemo est qui ignoret. Hactenus Socinus, qui addit, Misit positum esse pro Mittet, praeteritum pro futuro. Hæc porrò eius interpretatio tribus aut quatuor argumentis refelli potest.
units.tr: VIII. Not content, therefore, with that first answer, Socinus takes refuge in another and denies that the one who says he is sent by the Lord of hosts is the Lord of hosts. And to answer the first of the four testimonies we have cited, he observes that the one who speaks those words in Zechariah, Thus says the Lord of hosts, After the glory, etc., is that other angel who met the angel speaking with Zechariah, whom he had begun to address from verse 4 and continues to the end of the chapter; and at the very beginning of the speech he mentions Zechariah, to whom he wishes him to say what follows, saying, Speak to that boy, saying, Without walls, etc. Thus it appears that besides the one who utters the words, Thus says the Lord, etc., there are present there, the speaker knowing it, two other persons or other persons with whom he also speaks: namely Zechariah, and the angel who from the beginning of the prophecy was speaking with him. Given this, which is most evident, I say, he continues, that the pronoun Me in those words, sent me, is not to be referred to the Lord of hosts, but to that other angel who utters the words, Thus says the Lord; who, although he seems to introduce the Lord of hosts as speaking, nevertheless in reality does nothing other than report what the Lord of hosts says; in this manner: Thus (or as it is in Hebrew, So) says the Lord of hosts, that after the glory, etc. For that the particle That is very frequently to be understood in the sacred letters, there is no one who does not know. So far Socinus, who adds that sent is put for will send, the past for the future. Now this interpretation of his can be refuted by three or four arguments.

units.la: IX. Primum ipse sibi Socinus objecit, & sic se habet. Quotiescunque apud Prophetas pronunciantur verba ista, Sic dicit Dominus, toties id quod postea subjungitur Dominum dicere, ex ipsius Domini persona dicitur, ipseque Dominus reuera loquens inducitur. Hoc autem loco apud Zachariam prophetam pronunciantur verba ista, Sic dicit Dominus. Ergo id quod subjungitur Dominum dicere, videlicet Post gloriam misit me ad gentes &c. id reuera ex ipsius Domini persona dicitur. Respondeo, inquit Socinus, istud, quamuis alibi fortasse perpetuò fiat, hic nullo pacto potuisse fieri. Propterea quia, vt docui, dua alia persona aderant, ipso sciente & cum eis loquente, qui verba ista, Sic dicit Dominus &c proferebat. Oportebat enim, si dominum ipsum loquentem inducere voluisset, ac dicentem quod se missurus esset, vt ad hunc modum dixisset, Sic dicit Dominus exercituum, Post gloriam mittam te ad gentes, & addidisset, non quidem, vt nunc legimus, quae spoliauerunt vos, sed quae spoliarunt populum meum, aut aliquid simile. Hoc posterius inefficacius fuisset, nec bene expressisset, istos spoliatos pertinere ad Zachariam, eumque ex illorum numero esse, vt exprimit pronomen vos. Prius autem illud incertum reddidisset, quis esset ille, quem missurus esset Dominus exercituum; an scilicet angelus ipse, qui eius verba referebat, an vero alter eorum qui praeter ipsum aderat, & vter ipsorum: sed praecipuè an alter ille angelus. Verum angelus qui Domini exercituum verba referebat, volebat (idque sanè velle, aut tacere debebat) istos duos qui aderant, certò scire se eum esse, quem Dominus exercituum missurus esset, & propterea coactus fuit seipsum expresse per pronomen Me nominare; quod facere non potuisset, si ipsum Dominum loquentem reuera induxisset, & non simpliciter, vt sine dubio fecit, quid diceret, retulisset. Subrisi cum vidi Socinum id probare aggredientem, quod probari non potest, & miratus sum hominis molimen aggestis tribus aut quatuor hypothesibus falsis aliam quandam falsitatem superillligantis.
units.tr: IX. First, Socinus himself raised an objection, and it runs as follows. Whenever these words, Thus says the Lord, are pronounced by the prophets, whatever is afterwards added as the Lord's saying is spoken in the person of the Lord himself, and the Lord himself is in fact introduced as speaking. Here, however, in the prophet Zechariah, the words Thus says the Lord are pronounced. Therefore what follows as the Lord's saying, namely After the glory he sent me to the nations, etc., is in fact spoken in the person of the Lord himself. I answer, says Socinus, that although this may perhaps always happen elsewhere, here it could not in any way have happened. For, as I have shown, two other persons were present, the speaker knowing it and speaking with them, the one who was uttering the words, Thus says the Lord, etc. For if he had wished to introduce the Lord himself as speaking, and saying that he was about to be sent, he ought to have spoken in this manner: Thus says the Lord of hosts, After the glory I will send you to the nations; and he would have added not, as we now read, which plundered you, but which plundered my people, or something similar. The latter would have been less effective, and would not have expressed well that those who were plundered pertain to Zechariah and that he is one of their number, as the pronoun you expresses. The former, moreover, would have left it uncertain who it was whom the Lord of hosts was about to send: whether the angel himself who was reporting his words, or the other one of those present besides him, and which of them; but above all, whether it was that other angel. But the angel who was reporting the words of the Lord of hosts wished (and he ought either to wish this clearly or to be silent) that those two who were present should know for certain that he was the one whom the Lord of hosts was about to send; and therefore he was compelled to name himself expressly by the pronoun Me; which he could not have done if he had in fact introduced the Lord himself as speaking, and had not simply reported, as he undoubtedly did, what he was to say. I smiled when I saw Socinus undertaking to prove what cannot be proved, and I marvelled at the man's labour, in piling up three or four false hypotheses and then overlaying them with yet another falsehood.

units.la: X. Prima eius hypothesis est, eum qui apud Zachariam verba[?] ista pronunciat, Quoniam sic dicit Dominus exercituum, non esse Dominum ( Iehouam ) quam hypothesium falsam esse patet ex verbis antecedentibus & conjunctione causali Quoniam. Quae enim antecedunt immediate sunt verba Domini, O ô, fugite de terra aquilonis, dicit Dominus, quia in quatuor ventos cœli dispersi vos, dicit Dominus. O Sion servare, quae habitas apud filiam Babylonis. Quoniam sic dicit Dominus exercituum &c. Quis enim non videt, verba ista, quoniam sic dicit Dominus &c, eiusdem verba esse, cuius sunt antecedentia, O Sion servare &c, & haec eiusdem esse cuius sunt superiora O ô fugite de terra aquilonis &c? Secunda eius hypothesis est pronomine vos in verbis post gloriam misit me ad gentes quae spoliaverunt vos, Prophetam compellari, id quod etiam falsum esse verba illa antecedentia & conjunctio quoniam docent: apparet enim esse Apostrophen ad Sionem, hoc est, Ecclesiam apud Babylonios degentem: erat autem Propheta tunc in Iudaea redux à captivitate.
units.tr: X. The first hypothesis of his is that the one who speaks the words in Zechariah, For thus says the LORD of hosts, is not the LORD (Jehovah). That this hypothesis is false is plain from the preceding words and from the causal conjunction for. For the words immediately before are the Lord's own: Ho, flee from the land of the north, says the LORD, for I have scattered you to the four winds of heaven, says the LORD. Ho, Zion, escape, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus says the LORD of hosts, etc. Who does not see that these words, for thus says the LORD, etc., belong to the same speaker as the words before them, Ho, Zion, escape, etc., and that these in turn belong to the same speaker as the earlier words, Ho, flee from the land of the north, etc.? The second hypothesis is that by the pronoun you in the words after glory he has sent me to the nations that plundered you, the prophet is addressed. The preceding words and the conjunction for show this to be false too. It appears to be an apostrophe to Zion, that is, to the Church living among the Babylonians, whereas the prophet was then back in Judea after the captivity.

units.la: XI.[?] Tertia hypothesis est, consilium eius, qui verba illa pronunciat, quoniam sic dicit Dominus, esse, exprimere istos spoliatos pertinere ad Zachariam, eumque ex illorum numero esse, idque exprimere pronomen vos. Hoc quoque falsum esse perspicuum est ex verbis proximè antecedentibus & causali quoniam. Manifestum enim est haec verba, quoniam sic dicit Dominus &c, rationem reddere, cur sit fugiendum Sion seu fidelibus ex Babylone, ipsque regionibus in quas dispersi fuerant. Intelligitur autem Babylon non tam proprie, quàm figuratè & spiritualiter sic dicta, ut patet, primò ex promissione antecedente V. 4. Absque muro habitabitur Ierusalem præ multitudine hominum & iumentorum in medio eius &c. Tam enim post captivitatem Babylonicam proprie dictam quàm antea terrena Ierusalem cincta muro fuit. Deinde ex promissione sequente V. 10. Lauda & lætare filia Sion: quia ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui, ait Dominus: & applicabuntur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illa &c. Hoc enim demum temporibus Novi Testamenti impleri coeptum est. Tum ex illis ipsis verbis, O ô, fugite de terra Aquilonis &c. O Sion fuge quae habitas apud filiam Babylonis. Reditus enim Iudaeorum è Babylone typica in Iudaam fuga proprie non fuit. Denique ex subiecta ratione, quia sic dicit Dominus exercituum, Post gloriam misit me ad gentes, quae spoliaverunt vos &c, hoc est, quia missus sum ad puniendas gentes quæ vos afflixerunt, itaque fugite è medio earum, ut plagas quibus afficientur effugiatis, id quod in Apocalypsi cap. 18. V. 4. exprimitur his verbis, Exite è Babylone populè mi, ne participes sitis peccatorum eius, & ne ex plagis eius accipiatis. Id quod non video quomodo de Babylone proprie dicta commodè accipi potuerit. Adde quod illa verba, Post gloriam, non sunt temerè adjecta, sed ad missionis tempus, &c, ut ita loquar, naturam innuendam. Est enim Domini missio duplex, una quæ gloriam eius antecessit, de qua passim in Evangelio, comparata duntaxat ad seruandum. Altera quæ glorificationem eius sequetur, de qua Act. 3. 20. comparata ad liberandos fideles adfl ctos, & affligendos eos à quibus afflgebantur, ut liquet ex 2. Thess. 1. 6. 7. qui locus egregius est huius commentarius. Videatur etiam Luc. 17. 28. 32. Falli etiam mihi videtur Socinus, cum putat per puerum siue Iuuenem V. 4. Zachariam prophetam esse intelligendum. Intelligitur enim potius vir ille, quem Propheta viderat cum funiculo mensorio euntem mensum Ierusalem. Hoc duo docent, Primò Mandatum curre: opus enim erat cursu, non ut Prophetam stantem, sed ut virum illum euntem, & jam aliquo memorabili interuallo distantem assequeretur. Deinde id quod iubetur angelus ei dicere: videtur enim pertinere ad eum à proposito dimouendum: monet enim futuram Ierusalem adeo amplam, ut sub certam mensuram cadere non possit.
units.tr: XI. The third hypothesis is that the purpose of the one who speaks the words for thus says the LORD is to show that these plundered people belong to Zechariah, that he is one of their number, and that the pronoun you expresses this. This too is plainly false, from the words immediately preceding and from the causal for. It is clear that the words for thus says the LORD, etc. give the reason why Zion, or the faithful, must flee from Babylon and from the regions into which they had been scattered. Now Babylon is to be understood not so much properly as figuratively and spiritually, as appears first from the promise just before, v. 4: Jerusalem will be inhabited without walls, because of the multitude of men and cattle in its midst, etc. For Jerusalem was walled both after the Babylonian captivity properly so called and before it. Next, from the promise that follows, v. 10: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and will dwell in your midst, says the LORD; and many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, etc. For this began to be fulfilled only in the times of the New Testament. Then from those very words, Ho, flee from the land of the north, etc. Ho, Zion, escape, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For the return of the Jews from Babylon to Judea was not properly a typical flight. Finally, from the reason added: for thus says the LORD of hosts, after glory he has sent me to the nations who plundered you, etc., that is, for I am sent to punish the nations that afflicted you, and so flee from their midst, that you may escape the plagues with which they will be struck. This is expressed in Revelation 18:4 in these words: Come out of her, my people, lest you share in her sins, and lest you receive of her plagues. I do not see how this could fitly be understood of Babylon properly so called. Add that the words after glory were not added carelessly, but to indicate, so to speak, the nature of the time of the sending. For the Lord's sending is twofold: one which preceded his glory, of which there is frequent mention in the Gospel, compared only with saving; and another which will follow his glorification, of which Acts 3:20 speaks, compared with delivering the afflicted faithful and with afflicting those by whom they were afflicted, as is clear from 2 Thessalonians 1:6, 7, a passage which is an excellent commentary on this. See also Luke 17:28-32. Socinus also seems to me to be mistaken when he thinks that in v. 4 the boy or young man is to be understood as the prophet Zechariah. For that man is rather to be understood whom the prophet had seen going with a measuring line to measure Jerusalem. Two things show this. First, the command run: there was need for running, not to overtake the prophet standing still, but that man going on and already at some memorable distance. Second, what the angel is commanded to say to him: it seems to pertain to removing him from his purpose, for it warns that the future Jerusalem will be so ample that it cannot be contained within a fixed measure.

units.la: XII. Quarta eius hypothesis est, verba, quoniam sic dicit Dominus, &c, non Domini, sed meri angeli verba esse, quæ prima est hypothesis jam conuicta falsitatis, sed ei aliam Socinus adjungit, nimirum, hunc angelum voluisse istos duos, qui aderant, certò scire se eum esse, quem Dominus exercituum missurus esset. Vnde quæso innotuit Socino angeli illius, si tamen angelus fuit, talem fuisse voluntatem? Id, inquit, velle aut tacere debebat. Itane, mi homo, tenes tam accuratè quod illius angeli officium fuerit? Vah, quàm sapiens es! Vt veritas illustrior fiat, demus (quamquam id falsum est) sed demus tamen Aduersarijs, illum qui dicebat, quoniam sic dicit Dominus, nihil nisi angelum fuisse; Demus eum qui missus vel mittendus dicitur, nihil etiam nisi angelum fuisse; Demus illum ipsum angelum, cuius sunt hæc verba, quoniam sic dicit Dominus, eum fuisse, quem Dominus missurus erat. Cum nihil angelus bonus faciat nisi admodum prudenter, nihilque à Prophetis scriptum fuerit nisi propter ædificationem Ecclesiæ; quæro cur iste angelus duos illos qui aderant , Prophetam scilicet, & Angelum qui cum eo loquebatur, voluisset certò scire, se eum esse, quem Dominus esset missurus ? grauem enim profectò causam subesse oportuit, cur mallet perpetuam & nunquam antea violatamScripturæ consuetudinem, non sine certo periculo conjiciendi Ecclesiam in errorem momentosum, violari, quàm non certò sciri à duobus illis, se eum esse, quem Dominus missurus esset. Quid tamen id faceret ad ædificationem aut consolationem Ecclesiæ, illum Angelum mitti potius quam eum, qui cum propheta colloquebatur, aut alium aliquem, vel assequi nequeo, vel id tanti non videtur, vt propterea violari tam periculosè mos Scripturæ tam constans debuerit.
units.tr: XII. The fourth hypothesis is that the words for thus says the LORD, etc. are not the words of the Lord but of a mere angel. This is the first hypothesis, already refuted as false, but Socinus adds to it another: namely, that this angel wished the two who were present to know for certain that he was the one whom the LORD of hosts would send. From where, I ask, did Socinus learn that such was the will of that angel, if indeed he was an angel? He ought, he says, either to will this or to keep silent. Is it so, my good man, that you hold so exactly what the office of that angel was? Ah, how wise you are! So that the truth may shine more clearly, let us grant to our opponents (although this is false) that he who said for thus says the LORD was nothing but an angel; let us grant that the one who is said to be sent or to be about to be sent was also nothing but an angel; let us grant that that very angel whose words these are, for thus says the LORD, was the one whom the Lord was about to send. Since a good angel does nothing except very prudently, and since nothing was written by the prophets except for the building up of the Church, I ask why this angel should have wished the two who were present, namely the prophet and the angel who was speaking with him, to know for certain that he was the one whom the Lord was to send. There must surely have been some grave cause why he preferred to violate a perpetual and never before broken custom of Scripture, with the certain danger of leading the Church into a serious error, rather than let those two not know for certain that he was the one whom the Lord would send. Yet how this would contribute to the building up or comfort of the Church, that that angel rather than the one speaking with the prophet, or some other, should be sent, I cannot grasp; nor does it seem of such weight that a custom so constant in Scripture should for its sake be violated so dangerously.

units.la: XIII. His falsis hypothesibus Socinus alias falsitates superstruxit, videlicet non potuisse angelum duo illa exprimere, & de numero spoliatorum illorum esse Prophetam, & se eum esse quem Deus esset missurus, si ipsum Dominum loquentem induxisset; ac propterea coactum fuisse seipsum expresse per pronomen Me nominare. Non potuisse enim Dominum ipsum loquentem inducere, nisi ad hunc modum, Sic dicit Dominus exercituum, Post gloriam mittam te ad gentes &c. Falsa omnia. Dato enim quod meri angeli verba illa fuerint, Sic dicit Dominus, Et quod voluerit utrumque illud exprimere, tamen potuit ipsum Dominum loquentem inducere & nihilominus utrumque illud exprimere, hoc modo, sic dixit ad me Dominus exercituum, post gloriam mittam te ad gentes, quæ spoliarunt populum meum; quoniam qui tangit vos, tangit pupillam oculi eius. Sed pergamus.
units.tr: XIII. Upon these false hypotheses Socinus has built other falsehoods, namely that the angel could not express those two things, that the prophet was one of those plundered, and that he himself was the one whom God would send, if he had introduced the Lord himself speaking; and therefore that he was forced to name himself expressly by the pronoun me. For he could not have introduced the Lord speaking except in this way: Thus says the LORD of hosts, after glory I will send you to the nations, etc. All of this is false. For granting that those words were a mere angel's, thus says the LORD, and granting that he wished to express both of those things, he could nevertheless have introduced the Lord himself speaking and expressed both things at once, in this way: thus the LORD of hosts said to me, after glory I will send you to the nations that plundered my people, for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye. But let us go on.

units.la: XIV. Subnectit Socinus aliam rationem. Quòd autem, inquit, nequaquam sit verisimile, nec merito quemquam posse suspicari, pronomen Me ad ipsum Dominum exercituum referendum esse, vel hinc pateat, quod alioqui non esset nominatus is, qui missurus esset, nec quis esset, liquidò constaret; id quod non modo ab vsu prophetiarum in Vetere testamento penitus abhorret, sed ipsum per se absurdissimum omnino censeri debet.
