Falsa falsis cumulat. Primò falsum est id abhorrere ab vsu prophetarum. Ezech. 2. 9. Et vidi, ecce manus missa est ad me, in qua erat involutus liber. Dan. x. 11. Sta in gradu tuo: nunc enim missus sum ad te, non nominatur is à quo manus illa missa fuit ad Ezechielem; nec is à quo angelus ille missus fuit ad Danielem. Sic huius ipsius prophetæ Zachariæ verba cap. 7. 2. multi ita vertunt, ut non sit nominatus qui misit, nominentur tantùm qui missi fuerunt. Deinde falsum est id esse absurdum: cum enim de missione Domini, aut angeli agitur, facilè Deus subauditur, cuius est ad populum suum vel liberatorem Deum, hoc est, Filium aut Spiritum suum, vel angelos, vel prophetas mittere, quique κατ' ἐξοχὴν הוא, ἐκεῖνος, Ille, nonnunquam appellatur. Præterea falsum est Dominum exercituum non nominare hoc loco eum à quo sit missus. Nominat enim eum versu sequente, & scietis, inquit, quod Dominus exercituum misit me. id quod etiam repetit XV. 11.
units.tr: XIV. Socinus adds another argument. That it is by no means probable, however, nor can anyone reasonably suspect, that the pronoun me refers to the LORD of hosts himself, is clear from this: otherwise the one who was to be sent would not have been named, nor would it be plain who he was; which is not only wholly alien to the practice of the prophecies in the Old Testament, but must be judged in itself altogether absurd. He piles falsehood upon falsehood. First, it is false that this is alien to the practice of the prophets. Ezekiel 2:9: And I saw, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which was a rolled book. Daniel 10:11: Stand in your place, for now I am sent to you. In these the one by whom that hand was sent to Ezekiel is not named, nor the one by whom that angel was sent to Daniel. So too in the words of this same prophet Zechariah, 7:2, many render them so that the one who sent is not named, only those who were sent are named. Next, it is false that this is absurd. For when there is talk of the sending of the Lord or of an angel, God is easily understood: it belongs to God to send, to his people, as their deliverer, his Son or his Spirit, or angels, or prophets; and he is sometimes called that one (in Hebrew הוא, in Greek ἐκεῖνος [hu], [ekeinos]) by way of eminence. Moreover, it is false that the LORD of hosts does not here name the one by whom he is sent. For he names him in the following verse: And you shall know, he says, that the LORD of hosts has sent me. He repeats this also in v. 11.

units.la: XV. Subjungit Socinus tertiam rationem, si tamen ratio appellari debet, cum simpliciter, id absurdissimum esse dicitur; non ostenditur, quod Aduersarius pro verissimo habet. Ut omittam, inquit, quod nihil absurdius, aut magis ridiculum excogitari potest (quamvis Aduersarij sibi in eo valdè placeant) quàm ita Scripturam interpretari, ut ita dicatur ipse Dominus exercituum ab aliquo mitti, & quidem ab ipso Domino exercituum. Itane nihil absurdius, nihil magis ridiculum? O blasphemum os, id absurdissimum maximèque ridiculum appellare ausum, quod ita diserte & clarè docetur in Scriptura, ut quod contradicat non habeat! Nouit scilicet melius quid Deo conueniat, quàm ipse Deus! Sed pergamus.
units.tr: XV. Socinus next adds a third reason, if it can be called a reason at all, since he simply declares the view to be most absurd, and he does not show what his opponent holds to be most true. "To pass over," he says, "that nothing more absurd or more ridiculous can be devised (though my opponents take great pleasure in it) than to interpret Scripture so that the Lord of hosts himself is said to be sent by someone, and indeed by the Lord of hosts himself." Is there really nothing more absurd, nothing more ridiculous? O blasphemous mouth, to dare to call absurd and most ridiculous what Scripture teaches so plainly and clearly that it contains no contrary statement! He evidently knows better what befits God than God himself! But let us go on.

units.la: XVI. Alterum argumentum, quo Socini interpretamentum refelli poterit, petitur ab aduerbio כה Sic: Nam si simpliciter scriptum esset, Dicit Dominus, post gloriam misit me ad gentes, posset fortasse, etsi non ex more Scripturæ, quod, subaudiri. Nunc verò cum sit scriptum, Sic dicit Dominus, post gloriam misit me, non potest quod subaudiri, nisi admodum ineptè. Habet enim hanc vim vocula illa Sic, ut qui verba illa pronunciat, Sic dicit Dominus, profiteatur se ipsa Domini verba referre, quæ tamen quominus recitet impedit illud Quòd, si subaudiatur. Ita enim qui verba illa pronunciat, Sic dicit Dominus, non ipsa Domini verba, sed mentem tantùm aliis verbis, hoc est, non ipsis Domini verbis, sed suis, referret. Pugnat igitur particula Sic, quominus altera ista Quòd subaudiri possit.
units.tr: XVI. A second argument by which Socinus's interpretation can be refuted is drawn from the adverb "thus" [כה]. For if it had simply been written, "The Lord says, after his glory he sent me to the nations," the word "that" might perhaps be understood, although that is not the manner of Scripture. But since it is written, "Thus says the Lord, after his glory he has sent me," the word "that" cannot be understood, except very awkwardly. For the little word "thus" has this force: the one who speaks the words "Thus says the Lord" professes that he is reporting the Lord's own words. The understood "that" would prevent this, since the speaker would then be reporting not the Lord's own words but only his meaning, in other words, not the Lord's words but his own. The particle "thus" therefore stands in the way of supplying the other word, "that."

units.la: XVII. Tertium argumentum ex eo ducitur, quod etiamsi Quod subaudiatur, nihilominus verba misit me ad gentes, erunt verba Domini, vt jam bis aut ter obseruaui. Cohærent enim verba, Sic dicit Dominus, cum antecedentibus vi coniunctionis ʒ[?] quo-niam ; ac propterea sunt verba eiusdem sermonem suum continuantis. Quae autem proximè antecedunt verba esse Domini, Dicit Dominus ter inculcatum dubitare non sinit. Cum igitur ille cuius hæc sunt verba, Quoniam sic dicit Dominus exercituum, sit Dominus (Iehoua,) quomodocunque accipiantur sequentia Post gloriam misit me ad gentes, necesse est vt sint verba Domini.
units.tr: XVII. A third argument is drawn from the fact that, even if "that" is understood, the words "he has sent me to the nations" will still be the words of the Lord, as I have now observed two or three times. For the words "Thus says the Lord" are joined to what precedes by the force of the conjunction "because," and so they are the words of one continuing his discourse. Moreover, the words immediately preceding, "The Lord says," repeated three times, do not allow us to doubt that they are the Lord's. Since, then, he whose words these are, "Because thus says the Lord of hosts," is the Lord (Jehovah), however the following words, "After his glory he has sent me to the nations," are taken, they must be the words of the Lord.

units.la: XVIII. Quartum argumentum nobis quæ sequuntur apud Prophetam suppeditant, Quia ecce ego agito manum meam super eas, & erunt prœda servis suis, & scietis quod Dominus exercituum misit me. Cuius enim quæso sunt hæc verba? Angeli,an Domini? Certè suntDomini rationem reddetis, cur hortetur fideles, seu Sionem, vt fugiant è Babylone, ijsque gentibus in quasdispersi[?] fuerat, ne participes fierent pœnarum, quas gentibus illis erat inflicturus. Adde quod verba, & scietis quod Dominus exercituum misit me, sine dubio eius verba sunt, cuius antecedentia, Ecce ego leuo (heb. agito) manum meam super eas, & erunt prœda his qui seruiunt ipsis. Hæc autem cuius quæso sunt? Angeli tantùm? Affirmat Socinus. Certum enim est, inquit, & posse & solere à Deo mitti Angelos, non vt simplices nuncios, sed tali potestate prœditos, vt ista, & maiora etiam de se affirmare possint. Esto: at non solent angeli prædicere, comminari, vel polliceri apud Prophetas quid ipsi facturi sint. Id Dei proprium est, cuius serui & ministri sunt. Deinde quos compellat, cum ait, & scietis, quod Dominus exercituum misit me? Prophetam, &, qui cum eo loquebatur, Angelum? non egebat, opinor, fides istius. Angeli eiusmodi confirmatione, nec fortasse Propheta, saltem solus, aut magis quàm dispersi per gentes alij fideles, quos è Babylone & aquilone, is qui hæc dicebat, sublata voce euocabat, & in spem certam erigebat, fore, vt ipsis quidem afflictis relaxatio, gentibus verò affligentibus afflictio per se vnum à Domino exercituum eo fine missum retribueretur. Illi igitur fideles sine dubio compellantur: quomodo autem vel sciuerunt, si iam impletum est illud vaticinium; vel scient, si nondum impletum est, illum angelum quem vult Socinus, non autem alium aliquem à Domino exercituum missum fuisse?
units.tr: XVIII. A fourth argument is supplied by what follows in the Prophet: "For behold, I will shake my hand over them, and they shall be spoil to their servants, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me." Whose words, I ask, are these? The angels', or the Lord's? Surely they are the Lord's, for he gives the reason why he exhorts the faithful, whether Zion or those scattered among those nations, to flee from Babylon, so that they may not share in the punishments which he was about to inflict on those nations. Add that the words "and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me" are without doubt the words of the one whose preceding words are, "Behold, I lift (Heb. shake) my hand over them, and they shall be spoil to those who serve them." But whose words, I ask, are these? The angel's alone? Socinus affirms so. "For it is certain," he says, "that God can and does send angels, not as mere messengers, but endowed with such power that they can affirm these and even greater things of themselves." Granted. But angels do not usually foretell, threaten, or promise in the Prophets what they themselves will do. That belongs to God, whose servants and ministers they are. Next, whom does he address when he says, "and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me"? The Prophet, and the angel who was speaking with him? I suppose the faith of such a person did not need that confirmation. Nor perhaps did the Prophet alone need it, or more than the other faithful scattered among the nations, whom the speaker called from Babylon and the north with a raised voice, and raised to a sure hope, that there would come to pass, for those who were afflicted, relief, and, for the nations that afflicted them, affliction by the one whom the Lord of hosts sent for this purpose. Those faithful are therefore without doubt the ones addressed. But how could they have known, if that prophecy has already been fulfilled, or how will they know, if it has not yet been fulfilled, that it was the angel whom Socinus wants, and not some other sent by the Lord of hosts?

units.la: XIX. Sed vis huius argumenti clarius cerni potest in ¥[?] f. 10.&
units.tr: XIX. But the force of this argument can be seen more clearly in the passage at Zech. 2, verses 10 and

units.la: 11. Lauda & laetare filia Sion, quoniam ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui, ait Dominus: & adiungentur gentes multae ad Dominum in die illa, & erunt mihi in populum, & habitabo in medio tui: & scies quod Dominus exercituum misit me ad te. Cuius enim sunt haec verba, & scies &c? Annon eiusdem, cuius proximè antecedentia, & habitabo in medio tui? Haec autem, confitente Socino, nonnisi à Iehova dici possunt. Quid ergo respondet Socinus? Iehova, inquit, verba durant usque ad illa, & scies &c. Vbi angelus ad suam ipsius personam redit. At quominus ista commata, & habitabo in medio tui, & scies quod Dominus exercituum misit me ad te, ita distrahantur, ut prius sit Domini, posterius Angeli, obstant coniunctiones copulatiuae, quibus inter se & cum antecedentibus, tanquam eiusdem sermonis continuatio, connectuntur: obstant verbum scies & pronomina tui, te, in textu hebraeo foeminini generis, quibus eadem Sion compellatur: obstat denique ipsa rerum seu euentuum connexio & series: sic enim ordine sese membra illa seu commata sequuntur, ut posterius pendeat à priori, sitque illius consequens. Cum igitur tot appareat continuati ab eodem sermonis indicia, reddere rationem oportet Aduersarios, cur tam coniuncta diuidant: tamen nullam reddunt; nec aliunde arcessere ullam queunt, quàm à suo dogmate, cui Scriptura ista congruere non potest, nisi sic discerpatur.
units.tr: 11: "Sing and rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord; and many nations shall join themselves to the Lord in that day, and they shall be my people, and I will dwell in your midst; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you." Whose words are these, "and you shall know, etc."? Are they not of the same speaker as the immediately preceding words, "and I will dwell in your midst"? Yet, as Socinus admits, these words "can be spoken only by Jehovah." What then does Socinus answer? "The words of Jehovah," he says, "continue as far as those, 'and you shall know, etc.' Where the angel returns to his own person." But the coordinating conjunctions, by which these clauses, "and I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you," are joined to one another and to what precedes, as a continuation of one discourse, stand in the way of dividing them so that the first belongs to the Lord and the second to the angel. The verb "you shall know," and the pronouns "your" and "you," which in the Hebrew text are feminine and address the same Zion, stand in the way. Finally, the very connection and sequence of the events stand in the way. For these members or clauses follow one another in such an order that the later depends on the earlier and is its consequence. Since, then, so many signs of one continuous discourse by the same speaker appear, the opponents ought to give a reason why they divide things so closely joined. Yet they give none, nor can they draw any from elsewhere except from their own dogma, with which this Scripture cannot agree unless it is torn apart in this way.

units.la: XX. Clamabunt enim, alioqui sequi absurdum, nimirum, Dominum exercituum profiteri se à Domino exercituum missum esse. Magnum scilicet absurdum, si se Filius profiteatur missum à Patre! At absurdum est Filium appellari Dominum exercituum. Cur? Estne hoc nomen praestantius, quàm ut ei conueniat, cui conuenit nomen quod est supra omne nomen, quíque est verè & proprie Deus, praeditus omni potestate in caelo & in terra, adorandus ab omnibus, non modò hominibus, sed etiam angelis? At Dominus exercituum nomen est proprium eius, qui est praeditus essentia diuina. Rectissimè; indè enim colligo, Filium Dei, cum vocetur Dominus exercituum, esse praeditum essentia diuina. Ergo, inquies, duae erunt personae vna eadèq; numero essentia diuina praeditae, quo nihil fingi potest absurdius. Id verò, modò tollatur vnitatis numericae imperfectio haud congruens essentiae Dei, adeò absurdum non est, ut sit prorsus necessarium. Qua de re Deo dante suo loco. Interim ut hanc Charybdin, quae nulla est, vites incidis in Scyllam, negans Filium eiusdem esse cum Patre suo naturæ: Quàm enim absurdum tibi videtur duas personas una numero essentia gaudere, tam debet absurdum videri, filium proprie dictum non esse eâdem genere, immò specie, natuâ præditum cum patre. Sed ea de re alias.
units.tr: XX. For they will cry out that otherwise it would follow that something absurd is said: namely, that the Lord of hosts declares himself to have been sent by the Lord of hosts. A great absurdity indeed, if the Son declares himself to have been sent by the Father! But it is absurd, they say, that the Son should be called the Lord of hosts. Why? Is this name too excellent to belong to him to whom belongs the name that is above every name, who is truly and properly God, endowed with all power in heaven and on earth, to be adored by all, not only by men but also by angels? But "Lord of hosts" is the proper name of him who is endowed with the divine essence. Quite right; for from this I conclude that the Son of God, since he is called Lord of hosts, is endowed with the divine essence. "Then," you will say, "there will be two persons, each endowed with one and the same numerical divine essence, which is the most absurd thing imaginable." But if the imperfection of numerical unity, which does not agree with the essence of God, is removed, this is not so absurd; indeed it is entirely necessary. Concerning this matter, God willing, in its own place. Meanwhile, while you avoid this Charybdis, which does not exist, you fall into Scylla, by denying that the Son is of the same nature as his Father. For as absurd as it seems to you that two persons should share one numerical essence, so absurd ought it to seem that the Son properly so called is not endowed with the same kind, indeed the same species of nature, as the Father. But of this matter, elsewhere.

units.la: XXI. Postremò dicit Socinus, Si quis Prophetarum verba velit ad exactas grammaticæ regulas revocare, præsertim linguæ latinæ, aut alterius cuiuspiam præter Hebraicam, eum in infinita absurda denaturum. Quem petat his verbis nescio. Nos enim quidem certè non sumus à grammaticæ latinæ, aut alterius cuiuspiam præter Hebraicam, regulis argumentati, sed à vi verborum hebræorum & perpetuo Scripturæ usu, & nunquam violata consuetudine. Qua in re quid possit reprehendi equidem non intelligo. Pergit, Oportet enim, inquit, in illis intelligendis iudicio ac prudentia potius quàm regulis grammaticalibus, uti: ac diligenter animadvertere, ad quem quodque referatur, non tam ex ipsorum verborum sono atque ordine, quàm ex verborum sententia: ac propterea sapius, vel verbum unum, aut plura subaudire, vel etiam verbis ipsis aliquam vim facere. Quid hoc est nisi tacita quædam confessio, se[?] verbis Prophetarum, ut ea ad hæresim suam inflectat, & addere aliquid, & vim facere? viderint igitur Adversarii quid responsuri sint ad verba Aguris, Prov. 30. 6. Ne addas quicquam verbis illius; & Samuelis 1. Sam. 15. 23. Quasi peccatum ariolandi est repugnare, & quasi scelus idolatriæ, nolle acquiescere.
units.tr: XXI. Finally, Socinus says: If anyone wishes to bring the words of the Prophets back to the exact rules of grammar, especially of the Latin language or of any language other than Hebrew, he will fall into endless absurdities. I do not know what he wants by these words. For our part we have argued not from the rules of Latin grammar, or of any language other than Hebrew, but from the force of the Hebrew words, the constant usage of Scripture, and a custom that has never been violated. I really do not see what can be blamed in this. He goes on: For in understanding those passages one must use judgment and prudence rather than grammatical rules, and carefully consider to what each thing refers, not so much from the sound and order of the words themselves as from the sense of the words; and therefore one must often supply one word or several, or even do some violence to the words themselves. What is this but a tacit admission that he himself bends the words of the Prophets to his heresy, adds something, and does violence to them? Let the Adversaries see, then, what they will answer to the words of Agur, Prov. 30.6: Do not add anything to his words; and to 1 Sam. 15.23: For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and stubbornness is as the wickedness of idolatry.

units.la: Iudicio quidem & prudentia utendum est, fateor, ad intelligenda verba Prophetarum, non tamen sic ut eorum aut significationem, aut constructionem secundum grammaticam hebræam, & consuetudinem loquendi Scripturæ sacræ, evertamus, aut illis, quod ad explendum sensum in alia lingua necessarium non sit, quicquam addamus, aut vim ullo modo faciamus: sed meminisse nos decet, Prophetas actos à Spiritu sancto scripsisse sapientissimè prudentissimeque: itaque eorum verba reverenter admodum tractanda esse; Eumque sensum esse veriorem, non qui magis congruit cum nostra opinione, sed qui magis congruit cum verbis, verborum constructione, stilo Scripturæ, antecedentibus, consequentibus, eventu ipso, &c.
units.tr: I admit that judgment and prudence must be used to understand the words of the Prophets, but not in such a way that we overturn their meaning or construction according to Hebrew grammar and the usage of holy Scripture, or add to them anything that is not needed to complete the sense in another language, or do violence to them in any way. We ought rather to remember that the Prophets, moved by the Holy Spirit, wrote most wisely and prudently; their words must therefore be handled with great reverence. That sense is the truer which agrees not with our opinion but with the words, the construction of the words, the style of Scripture, what comes before and after, the outcome itself, and so on.

units.la: XXII. Unum tantùm, subjungit Socinus, de tam multis exemplis afferam (quippe quod locus sit non absimilis huic nostro) Hierem. cap.27. in ipso initio; ubi sic legitur : In principio Regis Ioakim filij Iosiæ Regis Iuda factum est verbum istud ad Hieremiam à Domino, dicens, Hæc dicit Dominus ad me, Fac tibi vincula, &c.
units.tr: XXII. I will cite only one, Socinus adds, out of so many examples (since it is a place not unlike this one of ours), Jeremiah chapter 27 at the very beginning, where it is read thus: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord to me: Make yourself bonds, etc.

units.la: Quis erit, qui, ipsa verba, ut sonant accipere velit, non similiter, ut Aduersarij in isto loco Zachariæ faciunt, referat illud Me ad Dominum priore loco nominatum, ad quem Dominus nominatus posteriore loco ea dixerit, quæ sequuntur, Fac tibi vincula, &c ? Et tamen, ut ex istis ipsis, quæ sequuntur patet, necesse est, ut pronomen Me non quidem ad Dominum priore loco nominatum, qui idem prorsus est cum Domino posteriore loco nominato, sed ad Hieremiam referatur.
units.tr: Who will there be who wishes to take the words themselves as they sound, and does not likewise do what the Adversaries do in that passage of Zechariah, referring that Me to the Lord named in the earlier place, while the Lord named in the later place spoke those things which follow, Make yourself bonds, etc.? And yet, as is clear from those very things which follow, it is necessary that the pronoun Me be referred not to the Lord named in the earlier place, who is exactly the same as the Lord named in the later place, but to Jeremiah.

units.la: Vtinam plura exempla Socinus protulisset! Nam ad locum istum Hieremiæ quod attinet, is neque huic nostro Zachariæ similis est, &, ut extat in fonte hebræo, nihil habet difficultatis. Primùm enim non dicitur Dominus sic locutus esse ad Hieremiam, aut verbum Domini factum esse ad Hieremiam, sed factum esse verbum istud ad Hieremiam מאת יהוה à Domino: quæ locutio non flagitat, ut ipse Dominus inducatur tanquam ex sua ipsius persona loquens ea quæ sequuntur. Deinde in Hebræo est לאמר quod secundum regulas grammaticæ reddi potest, & debet eo loco, ad dicendum, vel ut diceret: cuius rei Socinum admonere potuit versus eiusdem cap. quartus, ubi Vulgata versio illud idem vocabulum reddidit, ut loquantur, consentientibus aliis versionibus. Atque ut sic vertatur quàm grammatica patitur, tam res exigit. Nam & verbum rectius dici quàm dicere scribitur, & iubetur Propheta hoc dicere in principio regni Iehojakim, mandare verò executioni aliquot post annis regnante Sedecia; atque adeò vaticinij, quod in illo mandato continetur, parte aliqua iam impleta, ex qua Iudæi intelligerent etiam alteram partem certissimè impletum iri.
units.tr: I wish Socinus had brought forward more examples! As far as that passage of Jeremiah goes, it is not like this one of Zechariah, and, as it stands in the Hebrew source, it presents no difficulty. First, it is not said that the Lord spoke thus to Jeremiah, or that the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, but that this word came to Jeremiah from the LORD [מאת יהוה]. This expression does not require that the Lord himself be introduced as speaking in his own person what follows. Next, in the Hebrew there is לאמר [leamor], which by the rules of grammar can and should be rendered in that place as to say, or that he should say. Socinus could have been reminded of this by the fourth verse of the same chapter, where the Vulgate rendered the same word as that they should speak, in agreement with other versions. And the matter requires that it be translated in this way as far as grammar allows. For the word is written as came rather than say, and the Prophet is ordered to say this at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, but to carry out the command some years later, under King Zedekiah; and so part of the prophecy contained in that command had already been fulfilled, from which the Jews would understand that the other part would certainly be fulfilled as well.

units.la: XXIII. Nunc hic locus totus accuratius explicandus est: fatet[?] enim argumentis. Ducam initium à vers. 4. Ierusalem habitabit פרזות[?] pagos absque muris, vel, pagarum[?] absque muris, propter multitudinem hominum & iumentorum in medio eius. Quibus verbis triplex discrimen innuitur inter Ierusalem, ut ita dicam, legalem, quam Apostolus ἡ[?] νῦν Ἱερουσαλὴμ appellat, & Ierusalem euangelicam, quam idem Apostolus ἡ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ vocat Gal. 4.25.26. Illa certi cuiusdam loci, haud sane magni, finibus comprehensa & circunscripta fuit. Hæc nullo certo loco definitur. Illa muro cincta fuit & propugnaculis munita, Hæc nihil habet eiusmodi. Illa in medio sui templum habuit magnificentissimum multaque regum[?] & magnatum palatia, quibus in rebus sita fuit eius gloria. Hæc verò ad modum pagorum se habet muris & propugnaculis destitutorum, quos homines pauperes & ignobiles & pecuariam exercentes potissimùm incolunt, ac proinde in quibus nihil est gloriosum, nihil magnificum.
units.tr: XXIII. Now this whole passage must be explained more carefully, for it supports our arguments. I shall begin at verse 4: Jerusalem shall dwell פרזות [perazot] as villages without walls, or, of villages without walls, because of the multitude of men and cattle in her midst. By these words a threefold distinction is indicated between the Jerusalem of the Law, as it were, which the Apostle calls ἡ νῦν Ἱερουσαλὴμ [the present Jerusalem], and the Gospel Jerusalem, which the same Apostle calls ἡ ἄνω Ἱερουσαλὴμ [the Jerusalem above], Gal. 4.25, 26. The former was enclosed and circumscribed within the bounds of a certain place, not especially large. The latter is defined by no fixed place. The former was surrounded by a wall and fortified with bulwarks; the latter has nothing of the kind. The former had in its midst a most magnificent temple and many palaces of kings and nobles, in which its glory lay. The latter, however, is like villages without walls and bulwarks, which are inhabited chiefly by poor and humble people who tend cattle, and therefore in which there is nothing glorious and nothing magnificent.

units.la: XXIV. Num ergo spiritualis ista siue euangelica Jerusalem omni muro, omni gloria priuabitur? Minimè. Ego ero ei, dicit Dominus, murus ignis in circuitu, & in gloriam in medio eius. Carebit mu-ro terreno quo se carnaliter tueatur, sed non carebit muro spirituali quo spiritualiter defendatur. Exposita erit perfecutionibus hominum secundum carnem, sed tamen omni ex parte Deo, tanquam muro igneo, ita circundabitur, ut ei nihil prorsus nocere possit. In medio eius non erit quidem Templum opera hominum magnificentissimè extructum, ac totum auro collucens, sed erit ipse Dominus gloriæ, templo & arca fœderis infinitis partibus præstantior. Ex quo intelligitur, multò amplic-rem[?], fortiorem, & magnificentiorem Jerusalem euangelicam, quàm legalem, futuram fuisse, sed in spiritu, non secundum carnem.
units.tr: XXIV. Will this spiritual or Gospel Jerusalem then be deprived of every wall and every glory? By no means. I will be to her, says the Lord, a wall of fire round about, and I will be the glory in her midst. She will lack an earthly wall by which she might defend herself in a carnal way, but she will not lack the spiritual wall by which she is defended spiritually. She will be exposed to the persecutions of men according to the flesh, yet on every side she will be surrounded by God, as by a wall of fire, so that nothing at all can harm her. In her midst there will indeed be no temple magnificently built by the hands of men and shining all over with gold, but the Lord of glory himself will be there, far more excellent than the temple and the ark of the covenant in infinite respects. From this it is understood that the Gospel Jerusalem was to be far larger, stronger, and more magnificent than the legal one, but in spirit, not according to the flesh.

units.la: XXV. Jam quis est ille, quo, tanquam muro igneo, Ecclesia Christiana cingitur in circuitu, hoc est, omni ex parte? Nonne ille per quem unum seruatur, in quo solo est salus, qui est omnia in omnibus fidelibus, qui dixit discipulis suis, Ecce ego sum vobiscum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem seculi, qui denique tenet in manu sua dextera omnes Ecclesiarum suarum pastores, immò omnes oues suas? Si igitur ille qui futurus erat Ecclesiæ Christianæ murus ignis in circuitu est Dominus (Iehoua) ut patet ex hoc vaticinio, Isque est Christus, ut liquet ex Euangelio, necesse est fateri Christum esse Dominum, seu, ut vulgò pronunciant, Jehovam. Certè urbem ingredienti murus primùm occurrit, & in muro porta, per quam qui ingreditur in-tra murum se recipit. Itaque per fidem & regenerationem intranti Ecclesiam Christus ut murus ignis suos illuminans ac tuens, ut porta seu ostium, quo necesse est ingredi, sese primum omnium offert: ac quoniam non modò totam collectiuè Ecclesiam cingit, sed unumquemque etiam fidelem seorsim, etiam dum iter facit, omni ex parte veluti circumpositus, & una mobilis tuetur ab omni injuria, etiam ab intrante in Ecclesiam indui per baptismum dicitur: quæ vestis nec noctu exui, nec visu atteri, nec vetustate consumi, nec à latronibus eripi potest, & cum novo homine, hoc ipso quod spiritualiter carne & sanguine Christi vescitur, crescit, decens ac splendida omni tempore.
units.tr: XXV. Now who is he by whom, as by a wall of fire, the Christian Church is surrounded on every side, that is, in every respect? Is it not he through whom alone she is saved, in whom alone is salvation, who is all in all to the faithful, who said to his disciples, Behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age, who finally holds in his right hand all the ministers of his churches, indeed all his sheep? If, then, he who was to be the wall of fire round about the Christian Church is the Lord (Jehovah), as is clear from this prophecy, and he is Christ, as is clear from the Gospel, it is necessary to confess that Christ is the Lord, or, as it is commonly pronounced, Jehovah. Certainly a wall is the first thing that meets one who enters a city, and in the wall there is a gate through which the one who enters is received within the wall. So Christ, to one entering the Church through faith and regeneration, as a wall of fire illuminating and guarding his own, presents himself first of all as the gate or door through which one must enter. And since he not only encompasses the whole Church collectively, but also surrounds each believer individually, on every side, and protects him as a moving wall from every injury even while he is on the way, it is said that whoever enters the Church is clothed with him through baptism. This garment cannot be taken off by night, nor worn away by sight, nor consumed by age, nor snatched away by robbers; and with the new man, precisely because he feeds spiritually on the flesh and blood of Christ, it grows, comely and splendid at all times.

units.la: XXVI. Tacco[?] murum esse vrbis partem, & Christum esse Ecclesiæ fundamentum, & se recipere intra Christum, vt sit in tuto, quicunque in eum credit; ac proinde Christum non modò Ecclesiæ suæ murum igneum esse in circuitu, sed hoc eius esse, si accuratissimè loqui uolumus, proprium. Sunt quidem angeli omnes circa Ecclesiam, sed veluti currus igneï[?], & equites, & milites Christi regis ac ducis nostri, iuxta murum urbis excubias pro nobis agentes; verùm ipsi non sunt pars urbis, nec nos tuentur à reatu peccati, à maledictione legis, ab ira Dei, à morte æterna: Hoc uni Christo Scriptura tribuit. Adde quod non potest unus idemque totam Ecclesiam per vniuersum orbem dispersam intra se colligere sub alas suas, ac omni ex parte velut murus cingere & tueri, quin fit omnipræsentia, omniscientia, & omnipotentia præditus, proprietatibus diuinis, atque adeo essentiâ diuinâ.
units.tr: XXVI. That the wall of the city is a part of it, and that Christ is the foundation of the Church, and that whoever believes in him takes refuge within Christ so as to be safe: and therefore Christ is not only a fiery wall round about his Church, but this is, if we wish to speak most accurately, his own property. Indeed all the angels are around the Church, but as fiery chariots and horsemen and soldiers of Christ our king and leader, keeping watch for us beside the wall of the city; yet they themselves are not part of the city, nor do they guard us from the guilt of sin, from the curse of the law, from the wrath of God, from eternal death: Scripture ascribes this to Christ alone. Add that one and the same being cannot gather the whole Church, scattered through the whole world, within himself under his wings, and surround and protect it on every side like a wall, unless he is endowed with omnipresence, omniscience and omnipotence, the divine properties, and so with the divine essence.

units.la: XXVII. Dicitur etiam hoc loco Dominus futurus in gloriam in medio Ierusalem Christianæ, hoc est, in templum & arcam fœderis, & , vt ipse loquitur apud Esaiam, cap. 8. V. 14. in sanctuarium: erat enim terrenum sanctuarium honor & gloria terrenæ Ierusalem in eius medio, vmbra & typus gloriæ Ierusalem Christianæ. Iam autem Christus est sanctuarij terreni & arcæ fœderis, potissimum propitiatorij, corpus & veritas, &, vt loquitur Simeon, gloria Israëlis. Nihil erat in medio Ierusalem terrenæ templo illustrius, sanctius, quodque ostenderetur ac visceretur dignius, & quo alijs omnibus totius mundi vrbibus præstaret magis. Idem de Christo respectu Ecclesiæ Christianæ assirmari potest & debet. Is[?] prædicatione Euangelij, & sacramentorum administratione & fidelium omnium confessione, immò vitâ ostenditur & monstratur, ad eum contemplandum omnes fideles ex omnibus regionibus confluunt, eum mirantur & adorant, in eo vno expiationem peccatorum, iustificationem, sanctificationem, benedictionem, Dei cultum & præsentiam salutarem reperiunt, denique de eo vno maximè gloriantur. Tota enim Ecclesiæ verè Christianæ excellentia & gloria, qua omnem aliam societatem religiosam longissimo superat interuallo, in uno Christo consistit. Itaque, cum non sit gloriandum nisi in Domino, in Christo gloriandum est potissimum, immò unicè.
units.tr: XXVII. Here it is also said that the Lord will be in the glory in the midst of Christian Jerusalem, that is, in the temple and the ark of the covenant, and, as he himself speaks to Isaiah, chap. 8, v. 14, in the sanctuary: for the earthly sanctuary was the honour and glory of earthly Jerusalem in its midst, a shadow and type of the glory of Christian Jerusalem. Now Christ is the body and truth of the earthly sanctuary and of the ark of the covenant, above all of the mercy seat, and, as Simeon says, the glory of Israel. Nothing in the midst of earthly Jerusalem was more illustrious or holier than the temple, nothing more worthy to be shown and looked upon, and in this it surpassed all the other cities of the whole world. The same can and must be affirmed of Christ with respect to the Christian Church. He is shown and displayed by the preaching of the Gospel, by the administration of the sacraments, by the confession of all the faithful, and indeed by their life; all the faithful flock from every region to contemplate him, they marvel at and adore him, in him alone they find the expiation of sins, justification, sanctification, blessing, the worship of God and his saving presence; finally, it is in him alone that they most of all glory. For the whole true excellence and glory of the Christian Church, by which it surpasses every other religious society by a very great distance, consists in Christ alone. Therefore, since one should glory only in the Lord, one should glory above all in Christ, indeed in him alone.

units.la: XXVIII. Poterat ex dictis Jerusalem Christiana videri nihil aliud futura, quàm multorum pagorum quasi concatenatio, plus loci quàm ulla alia mundi ciuitas occupans in terra Canaam. Cui carnali opinioni ut occuratur & clarius Jerusalem Christianæ status describatur, Dominus clamat, se eam in quatuor ventos coeli dispersisse. Itaque quasi eam in omnes gentes disseminatam è longinquo videret, sublata voce eam ex omnibus Mundi plagis euocat ad se. O, o fugite de terra aquilonis, dicit Dominus, quia in quatuor ventos coeli dispersi vos, dicit Dominus. Ex quo intelligitur, Christianam Jerusalem nihil aliud esse, quàm innumerabilem quandam multitudinem hominum, vbique terrarum disseminatorum, vnius Domini verbo euocatorum, ut inde fugiant non quidem corpore, sed corde, non locum mutando, sed animum, iuxta illud, Exite de medio eorum, & separamini, dicit Dominus &c. Ac quoniam futurum erat, ut potissimum habitaret inter illas gentes, quarum caput spiritualiter Babylon appellatur in Scriptura, idcirco Dominus vocationem suam repetit expressa mentione Babylonis, ac compellata Ecclesia sua vera nomine Sionis, & mutato verbo fugiendi in seruandi, prudentissimè, O Sion seruare, qua habitas apud filiam Babylonis.
units.tr: XXVIII. From what has been said, Christian Jerusalem might seem to be nothing other than a sort of chain of many villages, occupying more land in the land of Canaan than any other city of the world. To meet this carnal opinion, and so that the state of Christian Jerusalem may be described more clearly, the Lord cries out that he has scattered her to the four winds of heaven. Therefore, as if he saw her from afar, dispersed among all nations, he calls her to himself from every quarter of the world with raised voice: O, O flee from the land of the north, says the Lord, for I have scattered you to the four winds of heaven, says the Lord. From this it is understood that Christian Jerusalem is nothing other than an innumerable multitude of men, scattered throughout all lands, called by the word of the one Lord, so that they flee from there not indeed in body but in heart, changing not place but mind, according to that saying, Come out from among them, and be separate, says the Lord, etc. And since it was going to happen that she would dwell especially among those nations whose head is spiritually called Babylon in Scripture, the Lord therefore repeats his call with express mention of Babylon, and, addressing his true Church by the name of Zion, and changing the verb of fleeing into that of saving, very wisely says: O Zion, save yourself, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.

units.la: XXIX. Jam quis sic Ecclesiam euocat? Si consulis Prophetam, is est Dominus (Jehoua,) si Euangelium, & euentum, est Christus. Hic enim unus venit vocatum peccatores, & ut filios Dei, qui erant dispersi, congregaret in unum. Itaque eius vox ad omnem gentem peruenit.
units.tr: XXIX. Now who calls the Church thus? If you consult the Prophet, it is the Lord (Jehovah); if the Gospel and the event, it is Christ. For he alone came to call sinners, and to gather into one the children of God who were scattered. Therefore his voice has reached every nation.

units.la: XXX. Rationem cur fugere debeant è gentibus subiungit, Quoniam, inquit, Sic dicit Dominus exercituum, post gloriam misit me ad gentes, quae spoliarunt vos, &c. Quemadmodum qui vocat & fugere iubet non est angelus proprie dictus, sed Dominus; sic rationem subiicit petitam non à missione cuiusdam angeli, sed à missione Domini secuta eius gloriam. Congruit cum vaticinio euentus. Vocantur enim filii Dei dispersi è mundo, è gentibus, è Babylone, cuius voce seu Euangelio certè unius Domini Christi, non verò angeli; Isque organis ad vocem suam per omnes gentes deferendam vsus est Apostolis, non autem Angelis. Itaque freqūens vocantis, vocatorum, vocationis in Euangelio mentio: frequentia etiam mandata, Saluamini à generatione ista prava. Fugite à simulachrorum cultu. Exite de medio eorũ, &c. Exite è Babylone populę mi, &c. Horum autem mandatorum & similium ratio nunquam à missione alicuius angeli petitur, sed à missione Domini quæ glorificationem eius sequitur, vt gentibus quæ fideles afflixerunt afflictionem retribuat, vti à nobis iam fuit obseruatum § xi. Ab hac enim missione præmiorum & pœnarum distributio, bonorumque & malorum resurrectio dependet.
units.tr: XXX. He adds the reason why they ought to flee from the nations: Because, he says, thus says the Lord of hosts: after the glory he has sent me to the nations which have plundered you, etc. Just as the one who calls and bids them flee is not an angel properly so called, but the Lord, so he adds a reason drawn not from the sending of some angel but from the sending of the Lord which follows his glory. It agrees with the event of the prophecy. For the children of God are called out of the world, out of the nations, out of Babylon, by the voice or Gospel of the one Lord Christ, and not by an angel; and he used the Apostles, not Angels, as the instruments to carry his voice through all the nations. Thus there is frequent mention in the Gospel of the one who calls, of those called, and of the calling; there are also frequent commands: Save yourselves from this crooked generation. Flee from the worship of images. Come out from among them, etc. Come out of Babylon, my people, etc. But the reason for these commands and similar ones is never sought from the sending of some angel, but from the sending of the Lord which follows his glorification, so that he may repay affliction to the nations which afflicted the faithful, as we have already observed in § xi. For the distribution of rewards and punishments, and the resurrection of the good and the evil, depend on this sending.

units.la: XXXI.. Sequitur apud Prophetam Vs.[?] ix. Quia ecce ego agito manum meam super eos, & erunt præda his qui seruiebant sibi, & cognoscetis quia Dominus exercituum misit me. Primùm verbis illis, cognoscetis, &c compellantur ijdem qui antecedentibus, O, o fugite, &c, &, O Sion seruare,&c. ac propterea de tempore Noui Testamenti, vt superiora & sequentia, accipi debent. Deinde oportet hanc missionem dogma esse in Ecclesia Christiana maximi momenti, cuius prædictio tantò ante proposita est Ecclesiæ ab hoc Propheta, & iterata, atque inculcata aliquoties. Hunc enim missum esse, qui loquens inducitur hoc loco, vult Deus credi & cognosci, quasi ea cognitio ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem multùm conducat, sitque dogma, aut negatum, aut vocatum in dubium, aut non satis firmiter & accuratè creditum & cognitum ante illum euentum qui prædicitur. Iam autè mitti quidem a Deo in ministerium omnes angelos propter eos qui hereditatem accipient salutis, dogma est religionis Christianę; missum verò esse vnum aliquem certum angelum, qui scilicet hoc loco id prędixerit, nullum dogma est: Sed omnium dogmatum præcipuum, maximèque docendum, inculcandum, confirmandum istud est missum esse a Deo Patre Filium ejus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum: hinc enim pendet fides & salus Ecclesiæ. Id autem secunda Christi missione seu aduentu, quo retribuet afflictionem his qui nos afflixerint, ita fiet manifestum, vt reuocari amplius in dubium non possit.
units.tr: XXXI. In the Prophet there follows, verse 9: For behold, I will stretch out my hand over them, and they will be spoil to those who served them, and you will know that the Lord of hosts has sent me. First, the same persons are addressed by those words, you will know, etc., as by the preceding, O, O flee, etc., and O Zion, save yourself, etc.; and therefore they must be understood of the time of the New Testament, as are the preceding and following verses. Next, this sending must be a doctrine of the greatest importance in the Christian Church, whose prediction was set before the Church by this Prophet so long beforehand, and repeated and impressed several times. For God wishes that it be believed and known that he who is introduced speaking in this place has been sent, as if this knowledge greatly contributes to the edification of the Church, and as if it were a doctrine either denied, or called into doubt, or not believed and known firmly and accurately enough before that event which is foretold. Now that all the angels are indeed sent by God to minister for the sake of those who will receive the inheritance of salvation is a doctrine of the Christian religion; but that some one certain angel was sent, who, namely, foretold this in this place, is no doctrine at all. But the chief of all doctrines, and the one most to be taught, impressed and confirmed, is that God the Father sent his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: for on this depend the faith and salvation of the Church. This will become so manifest by the second mission or coming of Christ, in which he will repay affliction to those who have afflicted us, that it can no longer be called into doubt.

units.la: XXXII. Interim quoniam futuro illi suo iudicio nonnunquam, vt ita loquar, prolusit: atque aliquot illius veluti speciminibus missionem suam futuram & præteritam confirmauit, quæ verbis illis innuuntur, Ecce ego agito manum meam &c, ea quam vim habeant ad confirmandum & demonstrandum, missum fuisse a Deo patre, non jam certum quendam angelum, sed Dominum gloriæ paucis explicandum est.
units.tr: XXXII. Meanwhile, since he has sometimes, so to speak, given a foretaste of his future judgment, and has confirmed his future and past sending by some specimens of it, which are indicated by those words, Behold, I will stretch out my hand, etc., what force these have to confirm and demonstrate that he was sent by God the Father, not now some certain angel, but the Lord of glory, must be explained briefly.

units.la: XXXIII. Prima gens, quæ post glorificationem Christi populum eius afflixit, Iudaica fuit. Quapropter super eam Dominus manum suam ita agitauit, ut eius urbes destruxerit, templum funditus diruerit nunquam instaurandum, gentem totam sedibus suis revulsam in omnes gentes horribili iudicio disperserit[?]. Itaque a sexdecim fere seculis jacet gens illa misera, sine templo, sine rege, sine prophetis, sine sacerdotibus, sine urim & thummim, sine sacrificijs, sine patria, aliarum gentium ludibrijs exposita, necdum ulla ei affulget liberationis aurora. Cur? nisi quia horrendum quoddam scelus admisit, cuius eam nondum pœnituit? nempe Messiam promissum, Dei Filium, Dominum gloriæ Seruatorem suum non agnouit, sed reiecit, immò cruci per summum nefas suffixit, ac in sua illa contumacia & execranda nequitia ad hunc usque diem perseuerat. Aliud enim gentis illius peccatum a quo nondum resipuerit, tantum, ut propterea tam horrendum in modum tractanda a Deo fuerit, nullum apparet: ut nunc taceam utramque prædictam fuisse a Prophetis, & rejectionem Iudæorum, & reiectionis illius hanc causam, nimirum Messiæ seu Domini tam suauiter ad se eos vocantis rejectionem Dan. 9. 26. Esai. 6. 9. 11. & 8. 14. & 65. 12. & 66. 4. & Prou. 1. 24. &c. Quinetiam gens illa quæ Christianis dominata fuerat, eosque multis occisis spoliauerat, tandem redacta est in potestatem Christianorum. Cur, si Christum, si Apostolos Christi, si Christianos persequendo & occidendo rem fecit gratissimam Deo? Num ille sic zelum legis & suum, quo correpti Iudæi Euangelium rejecerunt, remuneratus fuisset, siquidem ipsi fuisset gratus & acceptus?
units.tr: XXXIII. The first nation which, after the glorification of Christ, afflicted his people was the Jewish. Therefore the Lord stretched out his hand over it in such a way that he destroyed its cities, utterly overthrew the temple never to be restored, and, with a dreadful judgment, scattered the whole nation, torn from its seats, among all nations. Thus for almost sixteen centuries that wretched people has lain without temple, without king, without prophets, without priests, without Urim and Thummim, without sacrifices, without a homeland, exposed to the mockery of the other nations, and no dawn of liberation has yet shone upon it. Why? Unless because it committed some dreadful crime, for which it has not yet repented? Namely, it did not acknowledge the promised Messiah, the Son of God, the Lord of glory, its Saviour, but rejected him, and indeed by the greatest wickedness fastened him to the cross, and it persists in that obstinacy and detestable wickedness up to this day. For no other sin of that nation, from which it has not yet repented, appears that could be the reason why it has been treated so dreadfully by God: not to mention now that both were foretold by the Prophets, the rejection of the Jews, and this cause of their rejection, namely the rejection of the Messiah, or Lord, who so sweetly calls them to himself: Dan. 9. 26; Isa. 6. 9, 11; 8. 14; 65. 12; 66. 4; and Prov. 1. 24, etc. Moreover, that nation which had dominated the Christians, and had despoiled them after killing many, was at last brought under the power of the Christians. Why, if it did a most pleasing deed to God by persecuting and killing Christ, the Apostles of Christ, and the Christians? Would he have so rewarded that zeal for the law, and its own, by which the Jews, seized by it, rejected the Gospel, if indeed it had been pleasing and acceptable to him?

units.la: XXXIV. Post Iudæos Ethnici Romani Christianos, hoc est, populum Dei multis modis vexarunt & persecuti sunt. Itaque etiam in eos manum suam Dominus, cuius unius est iudicare orbem, agitauit, eosque tandem Christianis quos oppresserant subjecit, magnum missionis Domini argumentum. Nam si is fuisset, ut blasphemant Iudæi, impostor, qui potuisset homo ex infima plebecula, Iudæus, habens pro discipulis paucos quosdam piscatores & publicanos, ab omnibus ordinibus gentis suæ damnatus, à præside romano actus in crucem, ignominiosum Romanis, execrabile Iudæis supplicium, post mortem, inuitis & obnixè repugnantibus Deo Iudæorum & Iudæis, dijs Romanorum & romanis ipsis, sibi tantum nomen comparare, quantum alius nemo ante aut post eum assequi unquam potuit, atque adeo pedibus suis potentissimos hostes tandem subjicere, non armis carnalibus, sed, ut loquitur Apostolus, demonstratione Spiritus & virtutis?
units.tr: XXXIV. After the Jews, the Roman heathen harassed and persecuted the Christians, that is, the people of God, in many ways. So the Lord, whose alone it is to judge the world, also stretched out his hand against them, and at last made them subject to the Christians whom they had oppressed, a great proof of the Lord's mission. For if he had been, as the Jews blaspheme, an impostor, how could a man from the lowest rabble, a Jew, with a few fishermen and tax-collectors for disciples, condemned by every order of his nation, led by a Roman governor to the cross, a punishment shameful to the Romans and accursed to the Jews, after his death, against the will and stubborn resistance of the God of the Jews and of the Jews, of the gods of the Romans and of the Romans themselves, have won for himself a name as great as no one else before or after him has ever achieved, and finally brought the most powerful enemies under his feet, not by carnal arms but, as the Apostle says, by demonstration of the Spirit and of power?

units.la: XXXV. Post Romanos ethnicos surrexit imperium quod prædicitur & describitur Apoc. 13. & 17. & 2. Thess. 2. &c. veræ Ecclesiæ infestissimum, cuius jam aliquam partem ijs quibus dominatum fuerat Christus subjecit, totum tandem aliquando subjecturus & aboliturus; unde facilè perspici potest, eum revera missum à Patre fuisse, qui quod per se & Apostolos suos tam diserte prædixerat, tam aperte implet, nec veritatem suam sinit opprimi. His iudicijs succedet tandem ultimum, quo omnes Christi & verè Christianorum hostes subjicientur pedibus eius, & punientur in æternum. Quæ omnia missionis Christi veritatem confirmant, non verò cuiusdam angeli.
units.tr: XXXV. After the heathen Romans there arose the empire which is foretold and described in Apoc. 13 and 17, and 2 Thess. 2, etc., most hostile to the true Church. Christ has already subjected some part of it to those over whom he had exercised dominion, and he will at last subject and abolish the whole of it. From this it can easily be seen that he truly was sent by the Father, since he fulfils so clearly what he so plainly foretold through himself and his Apostles, and does not allow his truth to be overwhelmed. After these judgements there will finally follow the last, by which all the enemies of Christ and of true Christians will be made subject to his feet and punished for ever. All these things confirm the truth of Christ's mission, and not that of some angel.

units.la: XXXVI. Sequuntur apud Prophetam hæc verba, Lauda & lætare filia Sion: quia ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui, ait Dominus. Et adiungentur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illa, & erunt mihi in populum, & habitabo in medio tui, & scies quia Dominus exercituum misit me ad te. Rursus eius qui loquitur missio proponitur Ecclesiæ credenda, quasi eam credi & cognosci ad gloriam Dei & fidelium salutem maximè interfit. Quibus autem argumentis eam probatum iri prædicit? Aggregatione gentium multarum ad Dominum, & habitatione Domini in medio filiæ zionis, hoc est, veræ Ecclesiæ. Hæc certè argumenta missum fuisse à Patre Filium probant, non verò missum fuisse certum quendam angelum. Aggregatio quidem gentium ad Dominum: Ea enim, cum toties prædicta fuerit in Vetere Testamento tanquam maximum bonum, sit autem per Christum data effecta Annon manifestum est, Christum, cum se dixit à Deo patre missum, haudquaquam mentitum fuisse? Quis enim credat, quod Moses, quod Prophetæ toties prædixerunt opus præclarissimum, & optimum, & maximum, id fuisse perficiendum, à pseudopropheta[?], ab impostore? Num potest in dubium revocari, quin ea ratione Dei Israëlis imperium, & gloria valdè amplificata fuerint, & diabolorum atque idolorum altaria & cultus & gloria in toto Imperio Romano aliisque regionibus destructa? Num hoc fieri potuit à seductore, Dei hoste, diaboli mancipio? Nonne ut id fieret, vinci oportuit oratorum eloquentiam, philosophorum subtilitates, tortorum sævitiam, pontificum rabiem, imperatorum potentiam, totius generis humani imperium, immò ipsorum diabolorum vim & astutiam? qui potuit id fieri ab impostore, plebeio, conspirantibus ad eius condemnationem Iudæis & Romanis ignominiosissime crucifixo, post mortem suam, absque vllis arribus[?], opibus, armis humanis? Nonne hic digitus Dei agnosci debet?
units.tr: XXXVI. In the Prophet there follow these words: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Sion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, saith the Lord. And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day, and they shall be my people, and I will dwell in the midst of you, and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you. Again, the mission of the one who speaks is set before the Church to be believed, as if it especially concerned the glory of God and the salvation of the faithful that it be believed and recognised. But by what arguments does he foretell that it will be proved? By the gathering of many nations to the Lord, and by the Lord's dwelling in the midst of the daughter of Zion, that is, of the true Church. These arguments certainly prove that the Son was sent by the Father, and not that some particular angel was sent. As for the gathering of the nations to the Lord: since this was so often foretold in the Old Testament as the greatest good, and has now been given and accomplished through Christ, is it not manifest that Christ, when he said that he had been sent by God the Father, did not lie at all? For who would believe that the most splendid, best and greatest work which Moses and the Prophets so often foretold was to be accomplished by a false prophet, by an impostor? Can it be called into doubt that by this means the empire of the God of Israel and his glory were greatly enlarged, and the altars, worship and glory of demons and idols were destroyed throughout the Roman Empire and other regions? Could this have been done by a seducer, an enemy of God, a slave of the devil? Was it not necessary, for this to happen, that the eloquence of orators, the subtleties of philosophers, the savagery of tyrants, the rage of priests, the power of emperors, the dominion of the whole human race, and even the force and cunning of the devils themselves should be overcome? How could this have been done by an impostor, a plebeian, crucified most shamefully by the Jews and Romans who conspired for his condemnation, after his death, without any human aid, resources or arms? Must not the finger of God be recognised here?

units.la: XXXVII. Habitatio quoque Domini in Ecclesia, in fidelibus hoc ipsum probat. Lauda, inquit, & latare filia Sion: quia Ecce ego venio, & habitabo in medio tui, dicit Dominus. Quis venit? Cuius adventus est materia lætitiæ & exultationis Ecclesiæ? Nonne is est Dominus, Christus? Et adiungentur gentes multæ ad Dominum in die illa. Cuius quæso adventus vocatio seu aggregatio gentium ad Dominum consequens, immò effectum fuit? Nonne Domini gloriæ, Servatoris mundi adventus id effecit? Nonne venit ut habitaret in medio Ecclesiæ? Certè. Nam corpore quidem reliquit mundum, & abijt ad Patrem; sed Spiritu venit ad suos. Est cum suis usque ad consummationem seculi. Ubicunque fuerint duo aut tres congregati in eius nomine, ibi est in medio eorum. Habitat in cordibus nostris per fidem. Ecce, inquit, sto ad ostium & pulso. Si quis audierit vocem meam, & aperuerit ianuam, introbo ad illum, & coenabo cum illo, & ipse mecum. Et alio loco, Si quis diligit me, Sermonem meum servabit, & Pater meus diliget eum, & ad eum veniemus, & mansionem apud eum faciemus. Quid? ista habitatio Domini, nonne certissimum eum in quo est reddit de veritate missionis Domini à Patre in mundum? sentitur nempe à fideli intus habitans Christus. Persentiscitur præsens numen in cordis penetralibus Spiritu promissionis sancto obsignati & arrhabone cœlestis hæreditatis donati. Quid? nonne sese ista Domini habitatio prodidit olim in Ecclesia plurimis & variis donis extraordinariis & miraculis illustrissimis, veritatis Euangelij atque adeo missionis Christi argumentis evidentissimis. Nonne ea se prodit, etiam ordinariè, in verè fidelibus, luce cognitionis Dei, sanctitate vitæ, charitate constante, patientia invicta, mansuetudine animi, &c? quæ certè, cum à mundo, à carne, à diabolo[?] proficisci nullo modo possint: (iis enim rebus per fidem & mundus vincitur, & diabolus fugatur, & caro mortificatur) Euangelij veritatem confirmant, donec Christus visibiliter iterum veniat, & habitet in Ecclesia, eaque ratione omnem dubitationem, si qua reliqua fuerit, ei prorsus eximat. Non modò igitur nobis fauet grammatica, sed etiam res ipsa, quæ nullo modo pati potest ut de missione cuiusdam angeli, aut alterius quàm Christi, verba ista intelligantur.
units.tr: XXXVII. The dwelling of the Lord in the Church, in the faithful, proves this very thing as well. Sing, he says, and rejoice, daughter of Sion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in the midst of you, says the Lord. Who comes? Whose coming is the matter of the Church's joy and exultation? Is it not the Lord, Christ? And many nations shall be joined to the Lord in that day. Whose coming, I ask, was the calling or gathering of the nations to the Lord that followed, or rather was brought about? Was it not the coming of the glorious Lord, the Saviour of the world, that brought this about? Did he not come to dwell in the midst of the Church? Certainly. For in body he left the world and departed to the Father, but in Spirit he came to his own. He is with his own even to the end of the age. Wherever two or three are gathered in his name, there he is in the midst of them. Christ dwells in our hearts through faith. Behold, he says, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him, and sup with him, and he with me. And in another place: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. What then? Does not this dwelling of the Lord make the truth of the Lord's mission from the Father into the world most certain, in the one in whom he dwells? Christ, dwelling within, is indeed felt by the faithful. The present divine power is perceived in the inmost recesses of the heart, by the Spirit of promise, the holy seal, and the pledge of the heavenly inheritance given. What then? Did not this dwelling of the Lord once reveal itself in the Church by very many and various extraordinary gifts and most illustrious miracles, as the most evident proofs of the truth of the Gospel and so of Christ's mission? Does it not also reveal itself, in the ordinary way, in those who are truly faithful, in the light of the knowledge of God, in holiness of life, in steadfast love, unconquered patience, gentleness of spirit, and so on? These things, since they can by no means proceed from the world, from the flesh or from the devil (for by such things the world is overcome through faith, the devil is put to flight, and the flesh is mortified), confirm the truth of the Gospel until Christ comes again visibly and dwells in the Church, and in this way wholly removes from it any doubt that may remain. Therefore grammar is not the only thing that favours us, but the thing itself as well, which by no means allows these words to be understood of the mission of some angel, or of anyone other than Christ.

units.la: DISPUTATIO TRIGESIMA QUARTA De Arg. XXXIV. Ex Zachar. cap.3. v.1. Et dixit Dominus ad Satan, Increpet Dominus te Satan, increpet te Dominus qui eligit Hierusalem.
units.tr: DISPUTATION THIRTY-FOUR On Argument XXXIV, from Zechariah chapter 3, verse 1: "And the Lord said to Satan, The Lord rebuke you, Satan; the Lord rebuke you, who chooses Jerusalem."

units.la: I. SUPERIORIBUS testimonijs addendum etiam est istud, quod habetur apud eundem Zachariam, cap.3. v.1. Ostendit mihi Dominus Iesum sacerdotem magnum, stantem coram Angelo Domini: & Satan stabat à dextris eius ut adversaretur ei. Et dixit Dominus ad Satan, Increpet te Dominus o Satan, increpet te Dominus qui eligit Ierusalem. Hic Dominus(Iehova) dicit ad Satan, increpet te Dominus(Iehova:) atque ita duae personae proponuntur, quarum utraque Dominus(Iehova) appellatur. Harum autem sine dubio altera est Pater, altera Filius. Filius igitur est Dominus, Iehova.
units.tr: I. To the earlier testimonies this must also be added, which is found in the same Zechariah, chapter 3, verse 1: "The Lord showed me Jesus the great priest, standing before the Angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan, The Lord rebuke you, O Satan; the Lord rebuke you, who chooses Jerusalem." Here the Lord (Jehovah) says to Satan, "The Lord (Jehovah) rebuke you," and so two persons are set before us, each of whom is called Lord (Jehovah). Of these two, one is without doubt the Father and the other the Son. The Son, therefore, is the Lord, Jehovah.

units.la: II. Respondeo, inquit Socinus, primùm, ut ad superius argumentum, Non posse ex loco isto ullo pacto concludi, alteram ex duabus istis personis, quarum utraque appellatur Iehova, esse Christum: sed tantùm duos esse, quorum uterque sit Iehova; si modo ex appellatione liceret semper ipsam essentiam colligere. Non repetam ea quae ad hanc Socini responsionem superiore Disputatione § v. vi. vii. diximus. Tantùm, ut ne hoc nostrum argumentum praecedenti nitatur, sed suum habeat proprium pondus, ita argumentabor. Aut duarum istarum personarum, quarum utraque appellatur Iehova, altera est Christus; aut neutra. Si prius, falsa est responsio. Si posterius, duae sunt personae divinae Christo, si quoad substantiam tantùm homo est vt volunt Aduersarij, multò digniores: id quod Euangelio aperte repugnat, Filium, vno Patre excepto, omnibus alijs personis anteponenti. Deinde quænam erunt duæ illæ personæ? vna sine dubio erit Pater. Quis erit altera? Spiritus sanctus? At hunc nolunt esse personam Aduersarij deinde est Spiritus Christi, ab eo mittitur, de eo quod est Christi accipit, Christum glorificat; Christus solet post Patrem ante Spiritum sanctum nominari, etiam in solemni baptismi formula, Christus dat Spiritum sanctum, quomodo ista vera esse possunt si Spiritus sanctus est Dominus (Iehoua) Christus verò non est Dominus (Iehoua) si Spiritus sanctus est persona prædita essentia diuina, Christus verò persona prædita tantùm essentia humana, si ille est creator, hic creatura? Quod si harum personarum altera neque Filius, neque Spiritus sanctus dicatur esse, erit persona diuina à Patre, à Filio, & Spiritu sancto distincta, Christi lumine non modo non reuelata, sed obscurata, immò extincta prorsus, quo nihil fingi potest magis absurdū. Nam in N. T. non cōparet.
units.tr: II. "I reply," says Socinus, "first, as to the earlier argument, that it cannot in any way be concluded from this place that one of these two persons, each of whom is called Jehovah, is Christ; there are only two, each of whom is Jehovah, if indeed one may always infer the essence itself from the name." I will not repeat what we said in the previous Disputation, sections 5, 6 and 7, in answer to this reply of Socinus. I will only argue so that this argument of ours does not rest on the preceding one but has its own proper weight. It goes like this. Either one of these two persons, each of whom is called Jehovah, is Christ, or neither is. If the former, Socinus's reply is false. If the latter, there are two divine persons besides Christ, who on the opponents' view is man only in his substance and far more worthy. That openly contradicts the Gospel, which places the Son above all other persons except the one Father. Next, who will these two persons be? One, without doubt, will be the Father. Who will the other be? The Holy Spirit? But our opponents do not want him to be a person. Further, he is the Spirit of Christ; he is sent by him, receives of what is Christ's, and glorifies Christ. Christ is customarily named after the Father and before the Holy Spirit, even in the solemn formula of baptism; Christ gives the Holy Spirit. How can these things be true if the Holy Spirit is Lord (Jehovah) and Christ is not Lord (Jehovah); if the Spirit is a person endowed with the divine essence, but Christ is a person endowed only with the human essence; if the one is the Creator and the other a creature? But if neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is said to be the other of these persons, then it will be a divine person distinct from the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, not merely left unrevealed by the light of Christ but obscured, indeed utterly extinguished. Nothing can be imagined more absurd than this. For it does not appear in the New Testament.

units.la: III. Adde quod Dominus qui sic loquitur, Increpet te Dominus ο satan, causam Ecclesiæ suscipit aduersus satanam, & contra eum pugnat, vt hominum mediatorem & intercessorem decébat, orando Patrem. Intercedit quidem etiam Spiritus sanctus pro fidelibus, sed vt Christi mediatoris nostri spiritum decet, efficiendo vt precemur. Idem etiam Dominus is est qui Zach. 3. 5. dicit Iesu siue Iehoscuæ, Ecce abstuli à te iniquitatem tuam, & indui te mutatorijs. Quis autem quæso auferet iniquitatem, & quidem à summo sacerdote, qualis erat Iehoscua? præter Deum Patrem & eius Filium Dominum nostrum nemo occurrit in Scriptura, cui hoc tribui possit. Necesse est igitur, vt duorum istorum, quorum vterque est Dominus, Iehoua, quàm vnus est Pater, tam alter sit Filius.
units.tr: III. Add that the Lord who speaks thus, "The Lord rebuke you, O Satan," takes up the cause of the Church against Satan and fights against him, as befits the mediator and intercessor of men, by praying to the Father. The Holy Spirit indeed also intercedes for the faithful, but as befits the Spirit of Christ our Mediator, by bringing it about that we pray. The same Lord is also he who says in Zech. 3. 5. to Jesus, or Jehoshua: "Behold, I have taken away your iniquity, and I have clothed you with garments of change." Now who, I ask, will take away iniquity, and that from the chief priest, such as Jehoshua was? Apart from God the Father and his Son our Lord, no one in Scripture presents himself to whom this can be attributed. It is necessary, therefore, that just as one of these two, each of whom is Lord, Jehovah, is the Father, so the other be the Son.

units.la: IV. Præterea isti Iesu súmo sacerdoti legali satan stans à dextris aduersatur. Cui cum resistere non posset obstante iniquitate sua, quam sacrificijs lege præscriptis auferre non potuerat, Dominus ei fert opem, primò intercessione sua apud Dominum qui elegit Ierusalem, qua repellit satanam; deinde auferendo à Iehosua iniquitatem, ne posset amplius accusari à satana: sic victoria de satana reportata est. Ex quo intelligitur, summum sacerdotem legá- lem, etiam pium, qualis erat Iehoschua, eguisse alio, qui iniquitatem eius aufferret, eumque sua intercessione tutum à satana præstaret: qui alius esse non potuit quàm Dominus noster Iesus Christus, solus hominum mediator apud Deum & seruator, verus summus sacerdos, id quod à Leuitico adumbrabatur quidem, sed præstari non poterat, peccata verè aufferens & satanam vincens.
units.tr: IV. Moreover, Satan standing at the right hand opposes Jesus the legal high priest. Since Jesus could not resist him, his iniquity standing in the way, which he had not been able to remove by the sacrifices prescribed by the law, the Lord brings him help: first by his intercession with the Lord who chooses Jerusalem, by which he drives back Satan; then by taking away the iniquity from Jehoshua, so that he could no longer be accused by Satan. Thus the victory over Satan was won. From this it is understood that the legal high priest, even a pious one such as Jehoshua was, needed another who would take away his iniquity and secure him against Satan by his intercession. This other could be no one but our Lord Jesus Christ, the only mediator and saviour of men before God, the true high priest, which the Levitical law indeed foreshadowed but could not accomplish, truly taking away sins and conquering Satan.

units.la: V. At, inquit Socinus, In ea visione Iesus sacerdos, si alioqui Christi typus erat, Christi personam representabat, nec videtur fieri posse, vt in ipsa eadem visione, eodem temporis momento, quis & in sua propria persona verè, & in altera representatiue seu adumbratè appareat, altera ab altera manifestè distincta, vt in hoc loco euenit. Primùm in ea visione Iesus sacerdos, Christi personam non repræsentabat: stabat enim coram Angelo Domini, non poterat per seipsum satanæ resistere, erat peccato inquinatus, egebat alio qui iniquitatem ipsius auferret, qui pro ipso intercederet, qui ipsum à satana defenderet; quibus eius imperfectionibus Christi persectiones prorsus dissimiles, imò oppositæ adumbrari non potuerunt. Deinde quid prohibet eodem temporis momento corpus & umbram, veritatem & typum apparere? Cur enim in visione videri non potuit, quod extra visionem reuera visum est? Nonne enim Christus eodem momento videbatur olim in templo & in sua propria persona verè, & in persona summi sacerdotis ab eo manifestò distincta repræsentatiuè seu adumbratè? Nonne in eadem cœna videbatur verè in sua propria persona, & typicè in agno paschali?
units.tr: V. "But," says Socinus, "in that vision, Jesus the priest, if he was otherwise a type of Christ, represented the person of Christ; nor does it seem possible that in the same vision, at the same moment of time, one should appear both truly in his own person and representatively or figuratively in another, the one clearly distinct from the other, as happens in this place." First, in that vision Jesus the priest did not represent the person of Christ. For he stood before the Angel of the Lord; he could not by himself resist Satan; he was defiled by sin; he needed another to take away his iniquity, to intercede for him and defend him from Satan. Christ's perfections, utterly unlike and indeed opposed to these imperfections of his, could not be shadowed forth by them. Next, what prevents the body and the shadow, the truth and the type, from appearing at the same moment of time? Why could that not be seen in the vision which was truly seen outside the vision? For did not Christ at one moment appear of old in the temple, truly in his own person, and representatively or figuratively in the person of the high priest, clearly distinct from him? Did he not appear in the same supper, truly in his own person, and typically in the paschal lamb?

units.la: VI. Refutata prima responsione Socini, veniamus ad secundam. Respondeo, inquit, secundo loco, appellari quidem hoc loco duos nomine Iehouae: sed tamen vnum tantum ex illis esse reuera Iehouam. Quandoquidem is, qui, Iehoua appellatus, allocutus est satanam, est vel angelus, qui ab initio cum Zacharia locutus est, vel angelus ille Iehoua, coram quo Iesus sacerdos stabat. Et paulò post addit, Angelum illum, qui ab initio cum Zacharia loquebatur, Iehoua nomine satis aperte appellari, idque sæpius, videlicet cap.1.N[?].7. & N.20. & cap.4.8. & 6.9.&c. Qua responsione magis confirmat argumentum nostrum quàm euertit. Nam si duorum, qui nomine Iehouæ hoc loco appellantur, alter etiam angelus Iehouæ nominatur, tantò clarius & certius persona eius ab altera illa, quæ Iehouæ etiam vocatur, distinguitur. Si is qui angelus Iehouæ dicitur, nomine Iehouæ appellatur, non semel atque iterum, sed sæpius, tantò apertius significatur, eum reuera Iehouam esse. Eundem enim Christum esse volumus, & Iehouam, & Iehouæ id est, Patris angelum: illud natura, hoc officio, quia Patris sui nuncius seu legatus est. Nuntium enim, vt iam aliquoties monui, nomen Angelus proprie significat, cum Iehoua nihil significet præter Deum Israelis. Nihil igitur quod argumento nostro officiat hæc responsio continet.
units.tr: VI. Having refuted Socinus's first reply, let us come to the second. "I reply," he says, "secondly, that indeed two are named here by the name of Jehovah, but only one of them is really Jehovah. For he who, called Jehovah, addressed Satan, is either the angel who from the beginning spoke with Zechariah, or that angel Jehovah before whom Jesus the priest stood." And a little later he adds that the angel who from the beginning spoke with Zechariah is quite clearly called by the name Jehovah, and that often, namely in chapter 1, verses 7 and 20, and chapter 4, verse 8, and chapter 6, verse 9, etc. By this reply he confirms our argument more than he overturns it. For if one of the two who are here named by the name of Jehovah is also named the angel of Jehovah, then his person is distinguished from that other, who is also called Jehovah, all the more clearly and certainly. If he who is called the angel of Jehovah is named by the name of Jehovah, not once or twice but often, it is signified all the more plainly that he is really Jehovah. For we hold that the same is Christ and Jehovah, and the angel of Jehovah, that is, of the Father: the first by nature, the second by office, because he is the messenger or envoy of his Father. For the name angel properly signifies a messenger, as I have several times already noted, whereas Jehovah signifies nothing except the God of Israel. Therefore this reply contains nothing that stands in the way of our argument.

units.la: VII. Quod si neget Aduersarius hunc angelum, qui Iehoua sæpius appellatur, verè Iehouam esse, malumus Deo id affirmanti, & quidem sæpius, credere, quàm Socino negauti. Potuit-ne dis‐fertius docere Scriptura, eum verè Iehouam esse, quàm cum Iehouæ nomine sæpius appellando? Quorsum enim pertinet huius appellationis repetitio & inculcatio frequens, nisi vt ne dubitemus, eum reuera Iehouam esse? rem enim quæ repetitur in Scriptura, & magni momenti, & certissimam esse repetitio confirmat. Mirum profecto est, nobis in Scriptura duos proponi, accuratèque inter se distingui, insignitos, idque sæpius, eodem nomine Iehouæ, proprio vnius Dei creatoris cœli & terræ. Cur enim id fit, si non sunt duæ personæ diuinæ, si nefas est existimare, duas esse personas diuinas, si vna tantùm persona verè est Iehoua? Equidem quorsum id pertineat non video, nisi ad præparandos hominum animos ad recipiendum dogma de diuinitate Filij Dei, deque diuinarum Trinitate personarum. Duo credimus, distinctionem personarum & vnitatem essentiæ. Nonne autem distinctio personarum satis aperte significatur, his verbis, Dixit Dominus ad Satan, increpet te Dominus ô Satan, & cum horum duorum, qui Domini nomine appellantur, vnus alterius angelus nominatur? Nonne rursus vnitas essentiæ, plusquam specifica, clarè docetur, cum vterq; eodem nomine proprio, absque vlla additione vel limitatione, absolutè, subiectiuè, atque adeò tanquam vtriusque proprio, designatur? Neminem enim latere potest, nomen Iehoua soli Deo Israelis impositum fuisse, eiusque proprium esse, eoque ab omnibus aliis distingui, itaque dogma fuisse præcipuum in Veteri Testamento, vnum tantùm Iehouam esse. Consistit ergo personarum diuinarum distinctio cum vnitate.
units.tr: VII. But if our opponent denies that this angel, who is so often called Jehovah, is truly Jehovah, we prefer to believe God, who affirms it, and that often, rather than Socinus, who denies it. Could Scripture have taught more plainly that he is truly Jehovah than by calling him by the name of Jehovah so often? For to what does the repetition and frequent insistence of this appellation tend, unless it is so that we may not doubt that he is really Jehovah? For repetition confirms that a thing repeated in Scripture is both of great moment and most certain. It is indeed remarkable that two are set before us in Scripture and carefully distinguished from each other, marked out, and that so often, by the same name Jehovah, which is the proper name of the one God, creator of heaven and earth. For why is this done, if there are not two divine persons, if it is wrong to think that there are two divine persons, if only one person is truly Jehovah? I for my part do not see to what else it would pertain, except to prepare men's minds to receive the doctrine of the deity of the Son of God and of the Trinity of the divine persons. We believe two things: the distinction of the persons and the unity of the essence. Is not the distinction of the persons sufficiently plainly signified by these words, "The Lord said to Satan, The Lord rebuke you, O Satan", and by the fact that one of these two, who are called by the name of Lord, is named the angel of the other? Is not the unity of essence, more than specific, also clearly taught, since each is designated by the same proper name, without any addition or limitation, absolutely, as subject, and thus as the proper name of both? For no one can be unaware that the name Jehovah was given to the God of Israel alone, that it is his proper name and distinguishes him from all others; and so it was the chief doctrine of the Old Testament that there is only one Jehovah. The distinction of the divine persons therefore stands together with the unity.
