units.la: VIII. Hîc, ne superiora repetam, neue ijs nitatur hæc disputatio, vno argumento nondum a me explicato probabo ipsum angelum, qui Iehouæ nomine appellatur, non esse de numero Angelorum. Nam si esset de numero Angelorum, non video qui potuerit auctor Epistolæ ad Hebræos concludere, Chri‐ tum esse praestantiorem Angelis, quia prestantiori nomine seu elogio ornatur in Scriptura veteris Testamenti. Quomodo enim excellentius pra illis sortitus est nomen, si eorum unus aliquis Iehouae nomine appellatur, & quidem saepe? isto enim nomine nullum est excellentius, immo ipsum excellentius est omni alio nomine. Affert autem primo loco is auctor, tanquam nomen excellentius, nomen Filij Iehouae. At tantum est, aut plus etiam, Iehouam dici quam Iehouae filium. Dignitas enim elogij huius non est a nomine filij, quod commune est multis, sed a nomine Iehouae, quo ab aliis, qui filij dici possunt, distinguitur.
units.tr: VIII. Here, lest I repeat what has gone before, and lest this disputation rest on arguments, I will prove, by one argument not yet explained by me, that the angel who is called by the name of Jehovah is not one of the number of the angels. For if he were one of the number of the angels, I do not see how the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews could conclude that Christ is superior to the angels because he has been given a more excellent name or title in the Scripture of the Old Testament. For how has he obtained a name "more excellent than theirs," if one of them is called by the name Jehovah, and indeed often? For no name is more excellent than this one; indeed it is more excellent than any other name. But that author first cites, as the more excellent name, the name Son of Jehovah. Yet to be called Jehovah is as much as, or even more than, to be called the son of Jehovah. For the dignity of this title does not come from the name of son, which is common to many, but from the name Jehovah, by which he is distinguished from others who can be called sons.

units.la: IX. Respondebunt fortasse Aduersarii, nomen Iehouae tribui Angelo, non quatenus consider abatur in propria sua persona, sed quatenus alienam, scilicet ipsius Dei, personam sustinebat: loqui autem Apostolum de nomine Christi in sua ipsius propria persona considerati. Itaque bonum esse ipsius argumentum. Verum quo argumento probabunt nomen Iehouae tributum fuisse Angelo illi ob alienam, quam sustineret, personam? Certe hoc loco ei nomen Iehouae non tribuitur, nisi cum orans Iehouam aduersus satanam inducitur: in qua actione orandi non sustinebat alienam Dei patris personam, ut cuius manifestum est. Deinde in testimonio psalmi secundi, quod Apostolus laudat, tribuitur Christo elogium Filij Dei attributiue, cum in hoc Zachariae loco, & alibi saepe, tribuatur nomen Iehova Angelo isti subiectiue: id quod quin plus sit, non differebuntur Aduersarij: pluris enim apud eos fit nomen Dei subiectiue quam attributiue de aliquo vsurpatum, ut suo loco videbitur. Tum Filius Iehouae raro dicitur in Veteri Testamento Christus, cum Angelus iste, ipso Socino confitente, Iehova appelletur saepius. Adde quod Iehova nomen est proprium Dei Israelis, quod in alium transferri non potest, quin in eum pariter transferatur honor & cultus Deo Israelis debitus. Id quod sine grandi piaculo fieri nequit.
units.tr: IX. The opponents will perhaps reply that the name Jehovah was given to the angel not insofar as he was considered in his own person, but insofar as he sustained another person, namely that of God himself; and that the Apostle speaks of the name of Christ considered in his own proper person; so that their argument is sound. But by what argument will they prove that the name Jehovah was given to that angel because of the other person which he sustained? Certainly in this place the name Jehovah is not given to him, except when he is introduced praying to Jehovah against Satan; and in that act of praying he was not sustaining the person of God the Father, as is clear. Next, in the testimony of the second Psalm, which the Apostle cites, the title Son of God is given to Christ attributively, whereas in this passage of Zechariah, and often elsewhere, the name Jehovah is given to that angel subjectively. And that this is more, the opponents will not deny: for among them the name of God used subjectively of someone is held in higher regard than that used attributively, as will be seen in its place. Moreover, Christ is rarely called the Son of Jehovah in the Old Testament, whereas that angel, as Socinus himself confesses, is called Jehovah more often. Add that Jehovah is the proper name of the God of Israel, which cannot be transferred to another without the honour and worship due to the God of Israel being transferred to him equally. This cannot be done without great sin.

units.la: X. Praeterea nunquam in Scriptura nomen vnius proprium alteri, quod illius personam sustineat, tribuitur. Quis igitur in ea credat, nomen Dei proprium tributum fuisse mero angelo, & quidem saepe, ac cum certo periculo Ecclesiam in errorem grauem conijciendi? Si quis etiam reponat Aduersarijs, etiam Christum ob regiam illam dignitatem, qua Patris personam singulari & eximia ratione sustinet, Filium Iehouae dici eo psalmo, non habebunt quò id refellant, & argumentum Apostoli defendant, siquidem suis hypothesibus stare volunt. Denique quo creatura magis Deum Israelis repræsentat, eo sine dubio præstantior est. Si igitur Angelus ita Deum Israelis repræsentauit, vt eodem cum eo nomine proprio maximéque alijs incommunicabili appellaretur & quidem sæpè, certè is Deum Israelis magis repræsentauit quàm ille qui nunquam eiusmodi nomine cohonestatus fuit. Ac proinde excellentior fuit Christo, qui, si fides Aduersarijs habetur, nunquam eo honore affectus fuit.
units.tr: X. Moreover, in Scripture the proper name of one is never given to another who sustains that one's person. Who then could believe in Scripture that the proper name of God was given to a mere angel, and indeed often, with the certain danger of leading the Church into grave error? If someone should reply to the opponents that Christ too, on account of that royal dignity by which he sustains the person of the Father in a singular and outstanding way, is called the Son of Jehovah in that Psalm, they will have no means of refuting this and defending the Apostle's argument, provided they wish to stand by their hypotheses. Finally, the more a creature represents the God of Israel, the without doubt more excellent it is. If therefore the angel represented the God of Israel in such a way that he was called by the same proper name, which is above all incommunicable to others, and indeed often, certainly he represented the God of Israel more than the one who was never honoured with a name of this kind. And accordingly he was more excellent than Christ, who, if the opponents' faith is to be held, was never honoured with that distinction.

units.la: XI. Cur ergo, inquiet forsitan Aduersarius, Auctor Epistolæ ad Hebræos non potius nomen Iehouæ, quàm elogium Filij Dei, adhibuit ad probandam Christi præ Angelis excellentiam? quia eadem opera & psalmum secundum illustrauit, & affirmando nomen Filij Dei excellentius nomen esse quàm sit vllum nomen alicui de numero Angelorum tributum in vetere Testamento, eo ipso non obscurè insinuauit, cum nomine Iehouæ appellatus occurrit Angelus, intelligendum non esse Angelum de numero Angelorum, sed Filium Dei potius, qui ob munus dicatur Angelus, ob naturam Iehoua. Cæterum præmissis aliquot testimoniis & elogijs tandem eò deuenit, vt etiam ipsum Iehouæ nomen & creatoris cœli & terræ tribuat Christo, laudato dequè eo exposito Testimonio è ps.[?] CII. quod testimonium vindicauimus ab Aduersariorum exceptionibus lib. I. Arg. XXXI. & hoc lib. Arg. XII.
units.tr: XI. Why then, the opponent will perhaps say, did the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews not rather use the name Jehovah than the title Son of God to prove the excellence of Christ above the angels? Because by the same stroke he both illuminated the second Psalm, and, by affirming that the name Son of God is more excellent than any name given to any one of the number of the angels in the Old Testament, he obscurely hinted that, when the angel appears called by the name Jehovah, one must understand not an angel of the number of the angels, but rather the Son of God, who is called an angel because of his office, and Jehovah because of his nature. Yet after citing several testimonies and titles, he at last arrives at the point of attributing to Christ the very name Jehovah and the title of creator of heaven and earth, having expounded the testimony of Psalm CII, which testimony we have defended against the objections of the opponents in Book I, Argument XXXI, and in this book, Argument XII.

units.la: DISPUTATIO TRIGESIMA QUINTA.
units.tr: DISPUTATION THIRTY-FIFTH.

units.la: De Arg. XXXV. Ex Psal. II. v.12. [?] Oscula- mini Filium, ne forte irascatur, & pereatis via: cum exarserit paululum ira eius. Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo.
units.tr: On Argument XXXV. From Psalm 2:12. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish in the way, when his anger is kindled but a little. Blessed are all who trust in him.

units.la: SUPERIORIBUS testimoniis unum tantum è Psalmis adiungemus, de quo nos præcedens admonuit. Id extat Psalmo 2. V.12. & 13. Osculamini Filium, ne forte irascatur, &c. Hinc geminum oritur argumentum. Prius ipse Socinus sic concepit.
units.tr: Besides the testimonies above, we will add one more from the Psalms, which our previous discussion has put in mind. It is found in Psalm 2:12 and 13: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, etc. From this a twofold argument arises. Socinus himself first framed it as follows.

units.la: Solus verus Deus habet imperium vitæ & mortis. Messias seu Christus habet imperium vitæ & mortis. Ergo Christus est verus Deus. Quid ergo Respondet?
units.tr: Only the true God has power over life and death. The Messiah, or Christ, has power over life and death. Therefore Christ is the true God. What does he reply?

units.la: Respondeo, inquit, hic nihil contra nos concludi; quippe qui fateamur, Christum esse verum Deum. Fatentur Christum esse verum Deum, & tamen negant eum esse natura seu essentia divina præditum, perinde ac si quis affirmaret metallum quoddam esse verum aurum, & tamen illud negaret præditum esse auri natura. Potestne apertior fieri contradictionis implicatio? Sed ne nunc de verbis disputemus, verus Deus à nobis is demum intelligitur, qui præditus est essentia divina, qui est ille unus Deus Israelis.
units.tr: I reply, he says, that nothing is concluded here against us, since we confess that Christ is the true God. They confess that Christ is the true God, and yet they deny that he is endowed with the divine essence or nature, just as if someone were to affirm that a certain metal is true gold, and yet deny that it has the nature of gold. Can a more obvious self-contradiction be devised? But let us not now quarrel over words. By the true God we understand only him who is endowed with the divine essence, that one God of Israel.

units.la: II. Itaque respondet Socinus, plus hîc assumi quàm ex psalmo secundo desumi possit. Ibi enim, inquit, habetur, perituros illos, quibus Messias irascitur, & beatos fore, qui in illo confidunt: Hîc verò, Messiam habere imperium vitæ & mortis; quod multò plus est, quàm illud. Quid? negatne Christum habere imperium vitæ & mortis? Non, inquit; modò id rectè intelligatur, neque extra fines regni ipsius Christi extendatur. Quorsum igitur tendit ista responsio? Modò enim assumptio vera sit, siue ea possit elici è psalmo secundo, sive non possit, solidum est argumentum. Ea autem plusquam sexcentis Scripturae locis firmari potest. Revera tamen etiam ex Psalmo 2. desumitur. Quid enim? Is qui gentium & finium terrae possessor est & Dominus, qui potest gentes, tanquam figulina vasa, sceptro ferreo confringere & comminuere, cui Reges & Principes subjicere se debent, & cavere ne ipsis irascatur, quoniam, si vel minimum eis irascatur, futurum sit ut pereant in via, hic non habeat imperium vitae & mortis? Si beati sunt qui ei confidunt, necesse est ut possit quoscunque velit servare, quomodo autem servare potest, si non habet vitae & mortis imperium?
units.tr: II. So Socinus replies that more is assumed here than can be drawn from the second Psalm. For there it is said, he says, that those against whom the Messiah is angry will perish, and that those who trust in him will be blessed; but here it is assumed that the Messiah has power over life and death, which is far more than that. What then? Does he deny that Christ has power over life and death? No, he says, provided this is rightly understood and not extended beyond the bounds of Christ's own kingdom. To what end, then, does this reply tend? For provided the assumption is true, whether or not it can be drawn from the second Psalm, the argument is sound. And it can be confirmed by more than six hundred passages of Scripture. Indeed, it is in fact drawn from Psalm 2 as well. For what is it? He who is the possessor and Lord of the nations and the ends of the earth, who can break and crush the nations like potters' vessels with an iron sceptre, to whom kings and princes ought to submit themselves and take care not to incur his anger, since if he is angered even a little they will perish in the way, does not have power over life and death? If those are blessed who trust in him, he must be able to save whomever he wishes; but how can he save, if he does not have power over life and death?

units.la: III. Sed quid sibi vult Socinus hac limitatione, modò id non extra fines regni ipsius Christi extendatur? Ostendant enim nobis quaeso Aduersarii, qui aut ubinam sint, in quos Christus non habeat imperium vitae & necis. Extra mundum sint necesse est: Is enim habet omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra, hoc est, in toto mundo; quomodo omnem, si non vitae & mortis? ubinam ergo sunt illi? In morte aut inferno? Etiam mortis & inferni ipse claves habet. Nec mirum; Iudex enim est viuorum & mortuorum absque ulla exceptione omnium, nec ab eo datur provocatio.
units.tr: III. But what does Socinus mean by this qualification, provided it is not extended beyond the bounds of Christ's own kingdom? Let our opponents show us, I beg, who or where they are over whom Christ does not have power of life and death. They must be outside the world, for he has all authority in heaven and on earth, that is, in the whole world. How can it be all authority if it is not power over life and death? Where then are they? In death or in hell? He himself also holds the keys of death and hell. Nor is this surprising; for he is the judge of the living and the dead, with no exception of anyone, and no appeal is allowed from him.

units.la: IV. Fallitur igitur Socinus, cum subjicit (quae tertia eius responsio videri possit) In eo differentiam apparere inter Christum & Deum in mortis & vitae imperio; cum Deus nullis omnino finibus circumscriptum istud imperium habeat, Christus autem sui regni & eorum, quae quovis modo ad illud pertinent, aut pertinere possunt, finibus habeat circumscriptum. Itane Christus habet imperium circumscriptum? ubi hoc legit Socinus? O miram hominis temeritatem & audaciam & ingratitudinem audentis non modò Filio Dei unigenito Seruatori suo naturam diuinam detrahere, sed etiam eius imperium certis limitibus circumscribere! Non repetam quae modo dixi, Filium Dei habere omnem potestatem in coelo & in terra: tenere claues mortis & inferni: Iudicem esse viuorum & mortuorum sine exceptione omnium. Non obseruabo, Christum esse tam absolute unum Dominum, quàm Pater est unus Deus: omnia quaecunque sunt Patris esse Filii: Christum esse haeredem omnium: aequalem Patri: ab omnibus Angelis, & Regibus adorandum. Tantum lectorem meum rogabo; ut verba illa Apostoli apud se perpendat. Eph. 1. 20. Eum sedere fecit ad dextram suam in caelestibus; supra omnem principatum, & potestatem, & virtutem, & dominium, & omne nomen quod nominatur non solum in hoc seculo, sed etiam in futuro. Et omnia subiecit sub pedibus eius. Heb. 2. 8. In hoc enim quod omnia ei subiecit, nihil omisit quod ei subiectum non sit. Itaque ei, qui est caput omnis principatus & potestatis, omnis omnino creatura ubicunque sit laudem & gloriam, perinde ac Patri tribuit Apoc. 5. 13. ut a nobis est observatum Disp. 12. § 4. & necesse est, ut in nomine Iesu curvetur omne genu caelestium, terrestrium, & infernorum, ac propterea fatendum est tam late patere imperium Filij quam Patris, neque esse aliquod imperium Patris, quod non sit etiam Filij.
units.tr: IV. Socinus is therefore mistaken when he adds (which might be taken as his third reply): There appears to be a difference between Christ and God in the power over life and death, since God holds this power bounded by no limits at all, while Christ holds it bounded by the limits of his kingdom and of those things which in any way pertain, or can pertain, to it. Does Christ then hold a limited power? Where does Socinus read this? O the remarkable rashness, boldness and ingratitude of the man, who dares not only to strip the only-begotten Son of God, his own Saviour, of the divine nature, but also to confine his power within fixed limits! I will not repeat what I have just said, that the Son of God has all power in heaven and on earth, holds the keys of death and hell, and is judge of the living and the dead without exception. I will not note that Christ is as absolutely the one Lord as the Father is the one God; that all things that are the Father's are the Son's; that Christ is heir of all things, equal to the Father, to be adored by all angels and kings. I will only ask my reader to weigh in his own mind those words of the Apostle. Eph. 1. 20. He made him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, and power, and virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the future. And he put all things under his feet. Heb. 2. 8. For in that he put all things under him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. Therefore to him, who is the head of every principality and power, every creature wherever it is gives praise and glory, just as it does to the Father, Apoc. 5. 13., as we observed in Disp. 12, § 4. And it is necessary that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Therefore we must confess that the Son's dominion extends as widely as the Father's, and that there is no dominion of the Father which is not also the Son's.

units.la: V. Addere videtur Socinus & quartam responsionem, cum subnectit haec verba, Praeter id, quod Deus a nemine imperium habet: Christus vero, ex ipsius dono & largitate. Quod ipsum, inquit, per se satis est ad argumentum Adversariorum convellendum; cum propositio illa, Solus unus Deus habet imperium vitae & mortis, si vera esse censenda est, non aliter intelligi debeat, quam illa, quae a Paulo Apostolo testimonium habet: videlicet, Solum unum Deum habere immortalitatem: cum tamen & Angeli habeant immortalitatem, & nos in resurrectione iustorum habituri simus; id est, ut de vita ac mortis imperio accipiatur, quod quis a nemine acceptum in seipso naturaliter & essentialiter habeat. Primum non potest ista limitatio ijs testimonijs adhiberi, quibus huiusce nostri argumenti maior nititur. Iacob. 4. 12. Unus est Legislator & Iudex, qui potest perdere & servare. Tu quis es qui iudicas alium? Limitatio illa, a semetipso, naturaliter aut essentialiter, ad scopum Iacobi nihil facit, sed obest potius. Sic enim Iacobus non negaret alios posse perdere & servare: tantum negaret alios posse perdere & servare a semetipsis; cum tamen eius consilium sit potestatem perdendi & servandi aliis omnibus detrahere, uni legislatori seu Iudici vendicare. Enimvero ille solus est legislator, reliqui omnes illius legibus parere debent: Ille solus Iudex est, reliqui omnes ab eo iudicandi sunt: solus legislator & Iudex perdere & servare potest, reliqui omnes eius lege & sententia perduntur, vel servantur. Itaque alius nemo sibi sumere debet legislatoris aut iudicis partes legem aut fratrem Iudicando.
units.tr: V. Socinus seems to add a fourth reply as well, when he subjoins these words: Besides the fact that God has power from no one, whereas Christ has it from God's gift and bounty. This alone, he says, is enough to overthrow the opponents' argument. For that proposition, The only one God has power over life and death, if it is to be held true, ought to be understood in no other way than that other which has the testimony of the Apostle Paul, namely, that only the one God has immortality; although angels too have immortality, and we shall have it at the resurrection of the just. That is, it must be taken as concerning power over life and death, that someone has of himself naturally and essentially what he has received from no one. First, this qualification cannot be applied to the testimonies on which the greater part of our present argument rests. James 4. 12. There is one Lawgiver and Judge, who is able to destroy and to save. Who are you that judge another? That qualification, of himself, naturally or essentially, does nothing for James's purpose; rather it harms it. For in that case James would not deny that others can destroy and save; he would only deny that they can destroy and save of themselves. Yet his purpose is to take away from all others the power of destroying and saving and to claim it for the one Lawgiver or Judge. Indeed he alone is the lawgiver, and all the rest must obey his laws. He alone is the Judge, and all the rest are to be judged by him. The sole lawgiver and judge can destroy and save; all the rest are destroyed or saved by his law and sentence. Therefore no one else ought to assume for himself the role of lawgiver or judge, by making laws or judging a brother.

units.la: VI. Porrò quis est iste legislator & Iudex? Deus pater præcisus a Filio? Non certè. Filius enim etiam legislator est. Esai. 42. 4. Legem eius insulæ expectabunt. 1. Cor. 9. 21. subiectus legi Christi. Gal. 6. 2. & ita completè legem Christi. Psal. 78. 1. Ausculta popule mi legem meam: inclinate aurem vestram verbis oris mei: Christi enim verba esse, qui ab Asapho loquens inducitur, patet ex sequentibus, Aperiam in parabolis os meum, eructabo abscondita ab initio, laudatis a Matthæo, & vendicatis Christo Matth. 13. 35. nec non ex illis ipsis verbis, Ausculta popule mi legem meam; sunt enim magnificentiora, quàm ut Asapho cantori, immò quàm ut mero homini convenire possint. Id quoniam ad propositum nostrum pertinet, probandum quidem est, sed breuiter.
units.tr: VI. Further, who is this lawgiver and judge? God the Father, apart from the Son? Certainly not. For the Son is also a lawgiver. Isa. 42. 4. The islands shall wait for his law. 1 Cor. 9. 21. under the law of Christ. Gal. 6. 2. and so fulfil the law of Christ. Ps. 78. 1. Give ear, O my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. That these are the words of Christ, who is introduced speaking through Asaph, is clear from what follows, I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter things hidden from the beginning, which Matthew cites and claims for Christ, Matt. 13. 35. and also from these very words, Give ear, O my people, to my law; for they are too majestic to suit Asaph the singer, or indeed any mere man. Since this bears on our purpose, it ought indeed to be proved, but briefly.

units.la: VII. Primùm compellatio illa, Popule mi, Deum potius quàm hominem decet. Sic enim solet Deus compellare Ecclesiam suam Ierem 51. 45. Exite de medio eius popule mi. Mich. 6. 3. Popule mi quid feci tibi. & 5. Popule mi recordare quæso &c. Homo verò, ò merus Ecclesiam vniuersam nunquàm sic compellat. Deinde qui sic Ecclesiam compellat, iubet eam attendere, Attende popule mi, quod etiam Dei proprium est Psal. 50. 8. & 81. 7. Audi popule mi. Esai. 51. 4. Attendite ad me popule mi. Dauid quidem ita affatus fuisse dicitur primores populi Israelitici cum filijs & seruis suis præcipuis, 1. Paral. 28. 2. Audite fratres mei & popule mi: sed primùm rex erat populi illius, cum huius psalmi scriptor fuerit Asaph vnus è leuitis cantoribus; deinde præmisit illud fratres mei; Tum non alloquebatur Ecclesiam vniuersam ad consummationem vsque mundi, vt sit[?] hic, sed eos tantùm qui aderant, quosque in locum vnum conuocauerat. Sed quod caput est qui sic Ecclesiam compellat ei legem suam commendat, Attende popule mi legem meam. Non dicit legem Dei, sed legem meam. Loquitur tanquam totius Ecclesiæ doctor & legislator cui auscultare & parere debeat. Nemo in Scriptura sic loquitur præter Deum, & Sapientiam primis libri Prouerbiorum capitibus, quam esse Filium Dei probauimus lib. i. Arg. XVIII. Cum enim Ecclesia sit Dei populus & domus, ea quatenus talis est, subesse debet legi vnius Dei, non verò legi alicuius meri homi-nis. Neque sit nobis verisimile vllum merum hominem de se modestè & humiliter, vti par est, sentientem ausurum fuisse Ecclesiam Dei ita coram Deo & Angelis affari, Attende populè mi legem meam. Non potest enim ipse Deus loqui maiestati suæ congruentius.
units.tr: VII. First, that address, My people, befits God rather than a man. God usually addresses his Church in this way: Get ye out from the midst of her, my people (Jer. 51:45); O my people, what have I done unto thee? (Mic. 6:3); and O my people, remember now (Mic. 6:5), and so on. A mere man never addresses the whole Church like this. Next, one who addresses the Church in this way bids it to attend: Hearken, O my people (Ps. 50:7–8; 81:8), which is also characteristic of God: Hearken unto me, my people (Isa. 51:4). It is true that David is said to have spoken thus to the chief men of Israel, with his sons and his chief servants: Hear me, my brethren, and my people (1 Chron. 28:2). But first, he was king of that people, whereas the author of this psalm was Asaph, one of the Levitical singers. Second, David prefaced it with my brethren. Moreover, he was not addressing the whole Church until the end of the world, as this passage does, but only those who were present and whom he had gathered into one place. But the main point is this: whoever addresses the Church in this way commends to it his law: Attend, O my people, to my law. He does not say the law of God, but my law. He speaks as the teacher and lawgiver of the whole Church, to whom it ought to listen and obey. No one in Scripture speaks in this way except God, and Wisdom in the first chapters of the book of Proverbs, which we have shown in book 1, argument 18, to be the Son of God. For since the Church is God's people and house, insofar as it is such it ought to be subject to the law of the one God, and not to the law of any mere man. Nor is it likely that any mere man, thinking of himself modestly and humbly as he ought, would have dared to address the Church of God in the presence of God and the angels with the words Attend, O my people, to my law. For God himself could not speak in a manner more fitting to his majesty.

units.la: VIII. Adde quod cum eius qui sic loquitur consilium sit audientiam sibi facere, & attentionem populi sui conciliare, ad eam rem multò aptius efficaciusque fuisset, legem Dei quàm suam appellare, siquidem Deus non esset. Obligat enim ad attentionem & obedientiam lex Dei, non quatenus est lex hominis, sed quatenus est lex Dei, ac propterea solent Prophetæ Deum ipsum loquentem inducere, aut saltem eius nomine & authoritate vaticinijs suis fidem conciliare. Cum igitur iste cuius sunt hæc verba, Audi populè mi legem meam , satis in se vno dignitatis & authoritatis esse arbitretur, nec alia vlla sibi opus esse ad commendandam doctrinam suam, & excitandam Ecclesiæ attentionem, annon hoc ipso se prodit Deum esse? loquitur enim cum authoritate, ac tanquam populo suo, hoc est, Ecclesiæ suæ quis sit notus esse debeat, & quæ sit eius authoritas perspecta, manifestumque sit, aut saltem esse debeat, legi suæ attentionem & obedientiam deberi propterea quod sua sit: eo enim vno nomine eam commendat, tanquam nullum esse deberet Ecclesiæ Dei notius, charius, sanctius, & ad impetrandam ab ea non vulgarem attentionem efficacius: significat etiam ea ratione legem suam non posse, quatenus sua est, contemni absque graui peccato, ac debere eo nomine fidelibus esse commendatissimam omni seculo.
units.tr: VIII. Add that since the purpose of one who speaks thus is to gain a hearing and win the attention of his people, it would have been far more apt and effective for that purpose to call the law "the law of God" rather than "my law", if he were not God. For the law of God binds to attention and obedience not insofar as it is a human law, but insofar as it is God's law. Therefore the prophets usually introduce God himself speaking, or at least win credence for their prophecies in his name and authority. Since, then, the one whose words these are, Hearken, O my people, to my law , thinks that he is in himself sufficient in dignity and authority, and that he needs no other means to commend his teaching and rouse the attention of the Church, does he not reveal by this very fact that he is God? For he speaks with authority, and as to his own people, that is, to his own Church, whose authority ought to be known and clearly perceived, and it is plain, or at least ought to be plain, that attention and obedience are owed to his law because it is his. For by this single name he commends it, as if nothing ought to be better known, dearer, or holier to the Church of God, and more effective for obtaining no ordinary attention from it. He also signifies by this that his law, insofar as it is his, cannot be despised without grave sin, and that for this reason it ought to be most strongly commended to the faithful in every age.

units.la: IX. Quoniam autem res est maximi momenti, & homines natura sunt increduli, non contentus compellatione illa, Attende legem meam populè mi, instat & vrget, eandemque attentionem aliis verbis exigit, Inclinate aurem vestram ad verba oris mei. Deinde ne putetur lex intelligi quæ lata fuerat olim è monte Sinai, significat se legem intelligere ferendam non latam, verba pronuncianda non verò jam pronunciata, duoque innuit inter legem olim latam & suam istam discrimina, quibus obseruatis sua agnosci possit, meritòque attentionem singularem requirat. Aperiam in parabolis os meum: eructabo abscondita ab initio. Magna est emphasis in verbis Aperiam os meum, necnon in verbo Eructabo, sed major in re ipsa: significat enim & quo modo & quid sit loquuturus.
units.tr: IX. But since the matter is of the greatest importance, and men are naturally unbelieving, he is not content with that address, Attend to my law, O my people, but presses and urges, and demands the same attention in other words: Incline your ear to the words of my mouth. Then, lest it be thought that the law meant is the one once delivered from Mount Sinai, he signifies that he is speaking of a law to be given, not one already given, of words to be uttered, not words already uttered. He also hints at two differences between the law once given and his own, by observing which one may recognise his law and rightly demand special attention: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the beginning. The emphasis in the words I will open my mouth is great, and also in the word utter, but greater still in the thing itself. For it signifies both the manner and the content of what he is about to say.

units.la: X. Modum scire vis? Aperiam, inquit, in parabolis os meum, innuens innuens se legem suam traditurum non vulgari nec consueto modo, sed extraordinario. Nihil enim causae erat cur hoc praeddiceret & promitteret, si eo modo aut semper, aut fere semper Deus, Moses, & Prophetae locuti essent. Talis enim praemonitio seu praedictio, nisi vehementer fallor, alibi non extat in Scriptura. Non dicit autem usitata phrasi sumam[?] aut assumā parabolā, quod in Scriptura, factum quidem fuisse a quibusdam narratur, facturum vero se nemo, quantum meminisse possum, praedicit: videri enim potuisset prolaturus γνώμας seu sententias, quales habentur in libro Proverbiorum: sed inusitata, Aperiam in parabola os meum, ut magis docendi modum, quam res docendas innueret, eumque non vulgarem. Ac propterea id accipi non potest de eo quod fit in reliquis huius psalmi versibus, in quibus ab usitato docendi modo nullo modo discessum est, nihilque occurrit singulare, quamobrem tali tamque insolita & magnifica praefatione commendari prae reliquis psalmis hic psalmus debuerit. Exponi igitur debet, ut ab Euangelista Matthaeo factum est, de Domino nostro Iesu Christo, qui aliter turbas docere non fuit solitus quam aperiendo in parabolis os suum, qui proprius eius docendi modus tam singularis & extraordinarius, ut cetera, praedici debuit in Vetere Testamento. Alibi tamen praedictus non est; nec potuit verbis magis propriis & disertis praedici, quam fit hoc loco. Praedictum est igitur sine dubio hoc loco.
units.tr: X. Do you want to know the manner? I will open, he says, my mouth in parables, hinting that he will deliver his law not in an ordinary and customary way, but in an extraordinary one. For there would have been no reason for him to foretell and promise this, if God, Moses and the prophets had always, or nearly always, spoken in that way. For such a forewarning or prediction, unless I am greatly mistaken, does not appear elsewhere in Scripture. He does not say, however, that he will take up a parable in the usual phrase, which, as is reported, some did in Scripture; no one, as far as I can remember, foretells that he will do so. For he might have seemed about to produce maxims [γνώμας] or sayings, of the kind found in the book of Proverbs. But he says something unusual, I will open my mouth in a parable, so as to indicate the manner of teaching rather than the things to be taught, and an uncommon manner at that. Therefore this cannot be understood of what occurs in the remaining verses of this psalm, in which there is by no means any departure from the customary manner of teaching, and nothing unusual occurs. Hence this psalm ought not to have been commended above the other psalms by such a rare and magnificent preface. It must therefore be explained, as the evangelist Matthew did, of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was accustomed to teach the crowds in no other way than by opening his mouth in parables. His own manner of teaching was so singular and extraordinary that it had to be foretold in the Old Testament, as other things were. Yet he is not foretold elsewhere; nor could he have been foretold in words more proper and clear than they are in this place. Therefore it is without doubt foretold in this place.

units.la: XI. Quid autem eo modo dicturus erat? Eructabo, inquit, ænigmata ab initio. Significat ex pectore suo tanquam ex fonte ebullitura ænigmata non recens excogitata, sed concepta ab initio, & veluti ad divinandum Ecclesiae proposita, nec dum intellecta. Ac proinde legem suam fore & novam & antiquam, positam in revelatione copiosa mentis divinae & mysteriorum occultorum ac ænigmatibus involutorum. Quod & erat ad conciliandam attentionem aptissimum, & neque in hoc psalmo, neque ab alio quam a Christo Mundi luce factum est.
units.tr: XI. But what was he about to say in this manner? I will utter, he says, riddles from the beginning. He signifies that he will pour forth from his breast, as from a fountain, riddles not newly devised but conceived from the beginning, and set before the Church as it were for guessing, not yet understood. And so his law will be both new and old, founded on the copious revelation of the divine mind and on mysteries hidden and wrapped in enigmas. This was most apt for winning attention, and it was done neither in this psalm nor by anyone other than Christ, the light of the world.

units.la: XII. Ne porro putaretur legem suam pronunciaturus terribili & miraculosa voce, quali lex vetus promulgata est e monte Sinaï, qui inductus est loquens ut Deus singulariter & magnifice versu primo, is versu tertio inducitur ut homo de semine Abrahami oriundus plurali numero loquens; ut significaret se hominem factum iri, & locuturum humano ore & voce, & sibi adjuncturum de eadem gente Israelitica alios quosdam qui conjunctim eadem docent, docent, inquam, Israelitarum posteros qui nascentur circa vltima tempora. Quoniam autem illi futuri erant paternarum traditionum admodum tenaces, & majorum suorum admiratores, eaq; de causa legem nouam contempturi, pollicetur se & suos traditiones verè diuinas non modò non reiecturos, sed inculcaturos diligenter, relatè nimirum ad earum legitimum vsum & finem, qui alius esse non potest, quàm vt discant posteri suam in vno Deo collocare fiduciam, non autem in humanis traditionibus, aut operibus suis. Alioqui cauendum esse diligenter ne majores suos imitentur qui fuerunt increduli & rebelles in deserto & in terra Canaam, nec vllis miraculis & beneficiis adduci potuerunt, vt sicut par est, fidem habèrent Deo; ac propterea castigati sunt à Deo saepè, rejectusque est ille locus in quo & primo & diu arca foederis mansit, nec-non ea tribus quæ prima & longo tempore honorem illum habuit, electusque est alius locus, qui dum arca erat in Scilo tenebatur à Iebusæis: qua vna in re latius explicanda reliquum psalmi consumitur, idque pluribus docetur, quod paucioribus dicitur psalmo 95. v. 8. Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra, sicut in exacerbatione, in die tentationis, in deserto, ubi tentauerunt me patres vestri &c. Ex his apparet Dominum nostrum eundem esse Deum & hominem, nostrumque legislatorem & iudicem, qui potest perdere & seruare.
units.tr: XII. Moreover, lest it be thought that he would proclaim his law with a terrible and miraculous voice, such as the old law was promulgated with from Mount Sinai, he who is introduced speaking as God in a singular and magnificent way in the first verse is introduced in the third verse as a man descended from the seed of Abraham, speaking in the plural number. This signifies that he will become a man and speak with a human mouth and voice, and that he will join to himself certain others of the same Israelite nation who teach the same things together. He teaches, I say, the posterity of Israel who will be born near the last times. Since those who were to come would be very tenacious of their fathers' traditions and admirers of their ancestors, and for this reason would despise the new law, he promises that he and his people will not only not reject the traditions that are truly divine, but will diligently inculcate them, of course in relation to their lawful use and end, which can be no other than that posterity should learn to place their trust in the one God, and not in human traditions or their own works. Otherwise they must be diligently warned not to imitate their ancestors, who were unbelieving and rebellious in the desert and in the land of Canaan, and who could not be brought by any miracles or benefits to have faith in God as they ought. Therefore they were often chastised by God, and that place was rejected in which the ark of the covenant had remained first and for a long time, and that tribe which had held that honour first and for a long time was rejected, and another place was chosen, which was held by the Jebusites while the ark was in Shiloh. In this one matter, which requires fuller explanation, the rest of the psalm is spent, and it is taught at greater length what is said more briefly in Psalm 95:8: Today if you will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, etc. From these things it is evident that our Lord is the same God and man, our lawgiver and judge, who is able to destroy and to save.

units.la: XIII. Alter locus, quo præcipuè major Argumenti nostri nititur, habetur Deut. 32. 39. videte nunc quod ego, ego sum, & non est Deus mecum. Ego occidam & viuificabo, vulnus infligam & ego sanabo, & non est qui de manu mea possit eruere. Non potest in his Dei verbis limitatio illa Sociniana subaudiri, Ego occidam & viuificabo, scilicet a meipso, essentialiter & naturaliter: non enim Deus occidit & viuificat essentialiter, sed pro liberrimo suo beneplacito; nec potest antecedentibus aut sequentibus verbis eiusmodi limitatio acco[?]mmodari. Non antecedentibus, & non est Deus mecum: Sic enim non excluderentur Dij gentium, quos nec esse quidem a seipsis sui cultores arbitrati sunt. Nec sequentibus, Et non est qui de manu mea possit eruere. Sunt enim sine vlla limitatione verissima, essetque ridiculus qui diceret, esse qui de manu Dei possit eruere, non quidem a seipso naturaliter aut essentialiter, sed tamen qui possit de manu Dei eruere. Vndecunque enim is talem habere potentiam, esset Deo potentior; Deusque non esset omnipotens, atque adeo non esset Deus. Manifestum etiam est Deum eo loco sese probare & demonstrare Deum esse, & quidem solum, hoc argumento, quod nunc videant eum pro suo arbitrio occidere & viuificare, nec esse alium Deum qui idem possit, aut qui possit eos de manu sua eruere: ac proinde necesse esse ut ad suam unius misericordiam confugiant, si velint seruari. Id quod ipsa quoque antecedentia Dei verba confirmant, Et dicet, vbi sunt dij eorum, petra in qua fiduciam suam collocabant? &c. Surgant, & opitulentur vobis, & sint vobis in latibulum. Videte nunc quod ego sum &c. significat enim præter se unum neminem posse eos seruare.
units.tr: XIII. The other passage, on which the main weight of our argument rests, is Deut. 32. 39: See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god with me: I kill, and I make alive; I wound, and I heal: neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand. The Socinian qualification, that the words I kill and I make alive are to be understood as meaning from himself, essentially and by nature, cannot be supplied into these words of God. God does not kill and make alive essentially, but by his most free good pleasure. Nor can such a qualification be applied to the words before or after. Not the words before, and there is no god with me: for in that case the gods of the nations would not be excluded, though their own worshippers did not even think they existed in themselves. Nor the words after, neither is there any that can deliver out of my hand: these are entirely true without any qualification. It would be ridiculous to say that there is someone who can deliver out of God's hand, not indeed naturally or essentially from himself, but still one who can deliver out of God's hand. For if anyone had such power, he would be more powerful than God, and God would not be omnipotent, and so would not be God. It is also clear that in that place God proves and shows that he alone is God, by this argument: that they now see him killing and making alive at his own will, and that there is no other god who can do the same or who can deliver them out of his hand; and therefore they must flee to his mercy alone, if they wish to be saved. The preceding words of God confirm this too: And he shall say, Where are their gods, the rock in which they trusted? … Let them rise up and help you, and be your refuge. See now that I am he, etc. For this signifies that, besides himself, no one can save them.

units.la: XIV. Deinde intelligi non potest, quomodo diuinum imperium diuino modo administrandum communicari potuerit non communicatâ diuinâ naturâ. Opus enim est ad rem tantam facultatibus intelligendi volendi & agendi plane diuinis, quæ a diuina natura separari non possunt. Nam, exempli causa, humanum imperium humano modo exercendum frustrà cum bruto animali communicaretur, nisi cum eo etiam humanæ facultates intelligendi volendi & loquendi communicarentur, quibus ei indultis non amplius brutum, sed rationale animal, id est, homo natura rationali seu humana præditus esset. Aut igitur Dominus noster præditus est intellectu voluntate & vi agendi diuinis, aut non. Si ijs præditus non est, quomodo potest imperium plane diuinum in cœlum & terram, in Angelos & homines, in viuentes & mortuos diuino modo tenere & exercere? Si præditus est, quomodo possunt in eo diuina mens, diuina voluntas, & diuina vis agendi absque diuina natura consistere? Sic igitur argumentor. Quicunque præditus est diuino intellectu, diuina voluntate, diuina vi agendi, is præditus est diuina naturâ seu essentia. Quicunque autem habet imperium diuinum seu absolutum vitæ & mortis in omnes creaturas, is est præditus diuino intellectu, diuina voluntate diuinaque agendi vi. Quicunque igitur habet imperium vitæ & mortis absolutum in omnes creaturas is est præditus essentia diuina.
units.tr: XIV. Further, it cannot be understood how the divine rule, to be administered in a divine manner, could be communicated without the divine nature being communicated. For for so great a matter there is need of faculties of understanding, willing and acting that are wholly divine, and these cannot be separated from the divine nature. For example, human dominion, to be exercised in a human manner, would be vainly communicated to a brute animal unless the human faculties of understanding, willing and speaking were communicated with it. By these being granted to it, it would no longer be a brute animal but a rational animal, that is, a man endowed with a rational or human nature. Either, then, our Lord is endowed with an understanding, will and power of acting that are divine, or he is not. If he is not endowed with these, how can he hold and exercise a rule that is wholly divine over heaven and earth, over angels and men, over the living and the dead, in a divine manner? If he is endowed with them, how can the divine mind, divine will and divine power of acting exist in him apart from the divine nature? I argue thus. Whoever is endowed with a divine understanding, a divine will and a divine power of acting, is endowed with the divine nature or essence. But whoever has a divine, that is, absolute, rule of life and death over all creatures, is endowed with a divine understanding, a divine will and a divine power of acting. Therefore whoever has an absolute rule of life and death over all creatures is endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: XV. Distinctio originis personarum quidem distinctionem inducit, qua fit ut alia Pater, alia Filius dici possit; sed non facit, ut specie aut genere differat natura Patris a Filij naturâ. Docent ergo nos Aduersarij, quomodo potuerit Pater imperium suum communicare cum Filio, nec tamen potuerit cum eo communicare facultates suas intelligendi volendi agendi ad tantum imperium administrandum necessarias. Aut si has potuit communicare cur non potuerit pariter naturam suam cum eo communicare? Filius enim habet a patre non minus naturam suam quàm imperium. Sicut enim Pater habet vitam in seipso, sic dedit & Filio habere vitam in seipso. Qualis igitur est vita Patris, talis est vita Filij: & ut illa pertinet ad naturam Patris, sic ista pertinet ad naturam Filij. Discrimen inter utriusque vitam nullum obseruari potest, nisi originis ad distinctionem personarum Patris & Filij prorsus necessarium: habet enim uterque vitam in seipso, qua non modo viuit, sed potest etiam quos vult viuificare, & a mortuis suscitare. Hinc ita argumentor. Personae quarum imperium non differt nisi origine, sunt ejusdem speciei. Patris & Filij imperium non differt nisi origine. Pater igitur & Filius sunt ejusdem speciei. Si sunt eiusdem speciei sunt praediti eâdem specie naturâ. Si igitur Patris natura est diuina, etiam Filij natura diuina est.
units.tr: XV. The distinction of origin does indeed introduce a distinction of persons, whereby one can be called Father and another Son. But it does not make the nature of the Father differ from the nature of the Son in species or kind. Our adversaries therefore teach us how the Father could communicate his rule with the Son, and yet could not communicate with him the faculties of understanding, willing and acting that are necessary for administering so great a rule. Or if he could communicate these, why could he not equally communicate his nature with him? For the Son has his nature from the Father no less than his rule. For as the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself. Therefore, as the life of the Father is, so is the life of the Son; and as the former pertains to the nature of the Father, so the latter pertains to the nature of the Son. No difference between the life of the one and the life of the other can be observed, except one that is wholly necessary for the distinction of persons, of Father and Son by origin. For each has life in himself, by which he not only lives but can also make alive whom he wills, and raise them from the dead. Hence I argue thus. Persons whose rule differs only by origin are of the same species. The rule of the Father and of the Son differs only by origin. Therefore the Father and the Son are of the same species. If they are of the same species, they are endowed with the same specific nature. If therefore the nature of the Father is divine, the nature of the Son is also divine.

units.la: XVI. Ergo, inquiet forte aliquis, alia est numero natura seu essentia Patris, alia Filij. Non sequitur. Non enim differt numero imperium Patris ab imperio Filij. Idem enim numero utriusque regnum est, idem thronus, iidem ministri & subditi, eadem gloria &c. Et tamen imperium habet Filius a Patre communicatum. Sed hac de re alio loco disputandum erit diligentius.
units.tr: XVI. "Therefore," someone may perhaps say, "the nature or essence of the Father is numerically other than that of the Son." It does not follow. For the rule of the Father does not differ numerically from the rule of the Son. For the kingdom of each is one and the same, the throne is the same, the ministers and subjects are the same, the glory is the same, and so on. And yet the Son has his rule communicated from the Father. But this matter will have to be discussed more carefully in another place.

units.la: XVII. Caeterum quod ait Socinus, Deum Patrem habere imperium essentialiter & naturaliter, id quomodo verum sit dispicere oportet. Est enim Dei imperium duplex, unum naturale, alterum acquisitum. Illud est in omnes creaturas, Hoc in Ecclesiam. Illud nititur Dei excellentia & creatione Mundi, Hoc redemptione. Eodem iure nititur Filii Dei imperium. Primùm enim quâ Filius haeres est Patris. Deinde Mundi Dominus est iure creationis, quia per eum factus est Mundus, per eum facta sunt secula, per eum sunt omnia, per eum creata sunt omnia. Tum Dominus est Ecclesiae, quia eam sanguine suo redemit sibique acquisiuit. Ut igitur naturam suam habet a Patre (alioqui Filius non esset) & tamen naturâ suam habet in se essentialiter & naturaliter; sic quod imperium habet a Patre, id non impedit, quominus dici possit illud habere naturaliter & essentialiter, hoc est, tanquâ naturae seu essentiae suae consequens quoddam necessarium. Ad illud autem quod Apostolus dixit, Solum Deum habere immortalitatem, iam responsum est. Arg. XX. §2. Arg. XXI. §2. & 3.
units.tr: XVII. Moreover, as to Socinus' claim that God the Father has rule essentially and by nature, we must examine how this is true. For the rule of God is twofold: one natural, the other acquired. The former extends over all creatures, the latter over the Church. The former rests on God's excellence and the creation of the world, the latter on redemption. The rule of the Son of God rests on the same right. First, because the Son is heir of the Father. Then he is Lord of the world by right of creation, because the world was made by him, the ages were made by him, all things are by him, all things were created by him. Then he is Lord of the Church, because he redeemed it with his own blood and acquired it for himself. Therefore, just as he has his nature from the Father (otherwise he would not be the Son), and yet has his nature in himself essentially and by nature, so the rule which he has from the Father does not prevent it from being said that he has it naturally and essentially, that is, as a certain necessary consequence of his nature or essence. As for what the Apostle said, that God alone has immortality, this has already been answered: see Arg. XX, §2; Arg. XXI, §§2 and 3.

units.la: XVIII. Posterius argumentum sic Socinus formauit. Soli vero Deo confidendum est. Sed Messia seu Christo confidendum est. Igitur Christus est nerus Deus. Propositionem Bellarminus & Vviekus firmauerant loco Hierem. 17. 5. 7. vbi Maledictus dicitur quicunque confidit in homine, & benedictus qui confidit in Deo: Assumptionem vero vltimis verbis psalmi secundi, Beati omnes qui confidunt in eo. Quid respondet Socinus? Negatne propositionem? Non. Propositio, inquit, si recte intelligatur, est Verissima. Negatne assumptionem? Minimè; libenter enim, inquit, nos quoque postrema psalmi verba ad Christum, seu Filium referimus. Quid ergo respondet? Primò negat propositionem ex Hierem. cap. 17. 5.7. probari posse. At siue ex eo loco probari possit, siue non possit, modo sit, vt fatetur Socinus, verissima, nobis sufficit.
units.tr: XVIII. Socinus formed the second argument thus: Only God is to be trusted. But the Messiah, or Christ, is to be trusted. Therefore Christ is a true God. Bellarmine and Wiek had confirmed the major premise from Jer. 17. 5, 7, where he who trusts in man is called cursed, and he who trusts in God is called blessed; and the minor premise from the last words of Psalm 2, Blessed are all who trust in him. What does Socinus reply? Does he deny the major premise? No. The premise, he says, if rightly understood, is most true. Does he deny the minor premise? By no means; for willingly, he says, we too refer the last words of the psalm to Christ, or the Son. What then does he reply? First, he denies that the major premise can be proved from Jer. 17. 5, 7. But whether it can be proved from that passage or not, provided it is, as Socinus admits, most true, it is enough for us.

units.la: XIX. Age tamen quid ad illum locum respondeat videamus. Propositio est, inquit, Soli vero Deo confidendum est, Productum vero testimonium habet, maledictum esse hominem, qui confidit in homine: & beatum esse qui in Deo confidit. Atqui reperitur, qui nec homo est, nec ille Deus, de quo hic agitur. Quare non sequitur ex testimonio isto, soli vero Deo confidendum esse. Non excludit, inquam, illud testimonium verbi gratia, angelos, quominus in illis quis confidere possit, nullus enim angelus est homo: etiamsi nullus eorum similiter sit ille Deus. Extra oleas fertur: non enim de angelo agitur in hac controuersia, sed tantùm de Deo & de homine: ac propterea modò particula exclusiua in propositione hominem excludat, ad propositum nostrum satis est.
units.tr: XIX. Let us see, however, how he answers that passage. The proposition is that trust must be placed in the true God alone. The quoted testimony says that the man who trusts in man is cursed, and that the one who trusts in God is blessed. But there is someone who is neither man nor that God of whom this passage speaks. Therefore it does not follow from this testimony that trust must be placed in the true God alone. I say that this testimony does not exclude, for example, angels, so that someone could trust in them, since no angel is a man, even though none of them is that God. But this is a digression: the controversy does not concern angels, only God and man. So, even if the exclusive particle in the proposition excludes only man, it is enough for our purpose.

units.la: XX. Quinimo possumus ex hoc Ieremiæ loco rectà argumentari, hoc modo. Qui confidit in homine est maledictus. Qui confidit in Christo non est maledictus. Ergo qui confidit in Christo non confidit in homine. Confidit tamen in homine, si Christus tantùm homo est. Est igitur Christus ita homo, vt sit etiam aliud quid quàm homo. Est igitur aut angelus, aut Deus. Non est autem angelus. Est igitur Deus. Sic ex verbis maledictus vir qui confidit in homine, conclusum est quod probare institueramus.
units.tr: XX. Indeed, we can argue directly from this passage of Jeremiah in the following way. The one who trusts in man is cursed. The one who trusts in Christ is not cursed. Therefore the one who trusts in Christ does not trust in man. Yet he would trust in man if Christ were only man. Christ is therefore man in such a way that he is also something more than man. He is therefore either an angel or God. But he is not an angel. Therefore he is God. Thus, from the words "cursed is the man who trusts in man," we have reached the conclusion we set out to prove.

units.la: XXI. Potest Etiam ex sequentibus verbis, benedictus qui con-fidit in Domino, aliquid argumenti colligi. Aut enim Domini nomine Christus comprehenditur, aut non. Si comprehenditur, est Dominus, seu, ut vulgò pronunciant, Iehova, Deus Israelis. Si non comprehenditur, benedictus est qui confidit in Domino, etiamsi non confidat in Christo. id quod falsum esse clamat Euangelium. Idē quoquesic potest cōcludi. Aut Dominus, qui hoc loco intelligitur, tota natura differt a Filio, aut non. Si non differt, cum Dominus sit prædicitus[?] natura diuina, eadem naturā prædicitum[?] esse oportet Filium. Si differt, potest aliquis in eo confidere, nec tamen confidere in Filio. Quid enim prohibeat, aliquem confidere in Domino & non confidere in eo qui non est Dominus, confidere in creatore & non confidere in mera creatura? Attamen implicat contradictionem aliquem confidere in Domino & non confidere in Filio. Simul enim esset benedictus est qui confidit in Domino teste ipso Domino Ierem. 17. 7. Et non benedictus sed maledictus, quia qui non credit in Filium iam damnatus est teste ipso Filio Ioh. 3. 18. & toto Euangelio. Qui autem non confidit in Filio hunc non credere in Filium manifestum est.
units.tr: XXI. Some argument can also be drawn from the following words, blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord. For either Christ is comprehended under the name of the Lord, or he is not. If he is comprehended, he is the Lord, or, as they commonly pronounce it, Jehovah, the God of Israel. If he is not comprehended, then blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord even if he does not trust in Christ, which the Gospel loudly declares to be false. The argument can also be concluded in this way. Either the Lord who is meant here differs from the Son in his whole nature, or he does not. If he does not differ, since the Lord is predicated of the divine nature, the Son must be predicated of the same nature. If he differs, someone could trust in him without trusting in the Son. For what would prevent someone from trusting in the Lord and not trusting in him who is not the Lord, from trusting in the Creator and not trusting in a mere creature? Yet it involves a contradiction to trust in the Lord and not to trust in the Son. For at the same time blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord, as the Lord himself says in Jeremiah 17:7, and he would not be blessed but cursed, because the one who does not believe in the Son is already condemned, as the Son himself says in John 3:18, and as the whole Gospel teaches. That the one who does not trust in the Son does not believe in the Son is plain.

units.la: XXII. Frustrà distinguent Aduersarii tempora Euangelii a temporibus quæ promulgatum Euangelium antecesserunt. Primùm enim mirum est non posse hoc tempore quenquam Deo Israelis fidere, qui Christo non fidat, si Deus Israelis & Christus totis essentiis differunt, nihilque iste est nisi creatura illius. Deinde, quid impedit quominus de utrisque temporibus idem iudicium fiat? An quia Filius tunc non erat? At fuisse tot argumentis probauimus, quot extant in hoc & superiore libro. An quia reuelatum non erat, confidendum esse Filio? At id reuelatum est apertissimé hoc, de quo agimus, loco Psal. 2. ¥[?]. 12. Tum posita illa distinctione pugnabit cum his oraculis Euangelium. Clamat Dominus apud Ieremiam maledictum esse qui confidit in homine, Euangelium contrà benedictum esse qui confidit in homine. Clamat Dominus apud Ieremiam benedictum esse qui confidit in Domino, Euangelium contrà maledictum esse qui confidit in Domino nisi simul confidat in homine: Salutem enim cum fide in hominem reciprocari Ioh. 3. 18. 36. &c. Conciliatio nobis facilis est, hominem illum nihil esse, nisi ipsum Dominum, qui sumpta hominis, immò serui, forma sese hominibus ostendit, vel ut verbis utar Apostoli Iohannis, Deum factum carnem, & Pauli Deum patefactum in carne: Itaque qui in eo confidit, non in homine, sed in Domino confidere. Adversariis vero, nisi vehementer fallimur, conciliatio difficilis, imo ó impossibilis est.
units.tr: XXII. The adversaries distinguish in vain the times of the Gospel from the times that preceded the proclamation of the Gospel. For, first, it is strange that in this time no one can trust in the God of Israel who does not trust in Christ, if the God of Israel and Christ differ in their whole essence, and Christ is nothing but a creature of him. Next, what prevents the same judgment from being made about both periods? Is it because the Son did not yet exist then? But we have proved this by as many arguments as are found in this book and the preceding one. Or is it because it had not yet been revealed that trust must be placed in the Son? But this has been revealed most plainly in the very passage we are discussing, Psalm 2:12. Then, with that distinction in place, the Gospel will clash with these oracles. The Lord cries out through Jeremiah that the one who trusts in man is cursed; the Gospel, on the contrary, declares that the one who trusts in man is blessed. The Lord cries out through Jeremiah that the one who trusts in the Lord is blessed; the Gospel, on the contrary, declares that the one who trusts in the Lord is cursed unless he also trusts in man, for salvation is bound up with faith in man (John 3:18, 36, etc.). The reconciliation is easy for us: that man is nothing but the Lord himself, who, taking on the form of a man, or rather of a servant, showed himself to men; or, to use the words of the Apostle John, God made flesh, and of Paul, God made manifest in the flesh. So whoever trusts in him trusts not in man but in the Lord. For the adversaries, unless I am greatly mistaken, the reconciliation is difficult, indeed impossible.

units.la: XXIII. Nunc pergat Socinus. Iam, inquit, quod ad Christum attinet, de quo est quaestio, is eiusmodi est, ut quamuis non sit ille Deus & sit homo, talis tamen sit homo, ut merito dici possit, eum non simpliciter esse hominem, sed diuinum hominem: praesertim post ipsius glorificationem; post quam reuera coepit habere locum id, quod psal. 2. de ei confidendo dictum est. Hoc non est respondere, sed diuinum oraculum eludere. Nam cum hominum alii nihil nisi communem naturam habere, alii supra aliorum sortem euecti[?] videantur, dicent huius seculi homines, illis qui nihil nisi homines sunt maledictum esse qui confidit, non vero istis qui non simpliciter sunt homines, sed diuini homines, quales ij sunt, qui Heroes & semidei, & ἰσόθεοι[?] a poetis vocantur, nec non supremi magistratus, qui etiam dij[?] appellantur in Scriptura, & si qui alij vel robore, vel prudentia, vel opibus, vel numeroso exercitu, vel sanctitate eminent inter homines. Certe posita illa distinctione nihil prohibuit, quominus fiducia reponeretur in Iohanne Baptista: Non-potest[?] enim negari, Iohannem Baptistam fuisse virum diuinum, inquit Smalcius Paraph. in Ioh. 1. 6. Si in Iohanne Baptista, multo magis in Apostolis, imo ó in quolibet cive regni coelorum: minimus enim in regno coelorum maior est Iohanne Baptista teste ipso Christo Matth. 11. 11. Caeterum confidendum fuisse Christo, etiam antequam glorificatus esset, ipse Christus docuit Ioh. 14. 1. Creditis in Deum, etiam in me credite. & Ioh. 3. 18. Qui credit in eum non condemnatur. Qui vero non credit iam condemnatus est, quia non credidit in nomen unigeniti Filij Dei, & passim alibi. Non intelligo autem quomodo credat in Filium Dei, qui ei non confidit.
units.tr: XXIII. Now let Socinus go on. Now, he says, as far as Christ is concerned, who is the subject of the question, he is of such a kind that, although he is not God and is man, he is nevertheless such a man that it can rightly be said that he is not simply a man but a divine man, especially after his glorification; after which what is said in Psalm 2 about trusting in him has in fact come into effect. This is not answering but mocking the divine oracle. For since some men seem to have nothing but common human nature, while others seem raised above the lot of others, the men of this age will say that it is the ones who are nothing but men who are cursed for trusting, and not those who are not simply men but divine men, such as those whom the poets call heroes and demigods and equal to gods [ἰσόθεοι], as well as the supreme magistrates, who are even called gods in Scripture, and any others who stand out among men by strength, prudence, wealth, a numerous army, or holiness. Certainly, with that distinction in place, nothing prevents trust being placed in John the Baptist: for it cannot be denied, says Smalcius in his Paraphrase on John 1:6, that John the Baptist was a divine man. If in John the Baptist, much more in the Apostles, indeed in any citizen of the kingdom of heaven, for the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than John the Baptist, as Christ himself testifies in Matthew 11:11. Moreover, that trust was to be placed in Christ even before he was glorified, Christ himself taught in John 14:1: You believe in God, believe also in me, and John 3:18: He who believes in him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God, and in many other places. But I do not understand how someone can believe in the Son of God who does not trust in him.

units.la: XXIV. His praemissis Socinus paulò diligentius testimonium ipsum expendit, & recitato versiculo 5. integro, Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, & ponit carnem brachium suum, & a Domino recedit cor eius, ait non simpliciter pronunciari hic maledictum hominem illum, qui in homine confidit, sed qui ita confidit, ut ponat carnem brachium suum, id est, in ipsis humanis viribus spem suam collocet, seu in homine ipso per se, citra spiritus ac virtutis divina opem. Accipit igitur verba, Et ponit carnem brachium suum &c tanquam limitationem seu restrictionem antecedentium, qui confidit in homine; cum tamen reuera nihil sint, nisi eorum expositio accommodata ad rationes insinuandas, cuius[?] sit maledictus qui confidit in homine. Ponere enim aliquem brachium suum & ei confidere phrases sunt æquipollentes. Caro autem hominem significat, & pro eo usurpatur passim, ut Gen. 6.
units.tr: XXIV. With these points premised, Socinus examines the testimony itself rather more carefully. After quoting verse 5 in full, Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord, he says that the man pronounced cursed here is not simply the one who trusts in man, but the one who so trusts that he makes flesh his arm, that is, who places his hope in human powers themselves, or in man himself by himself, apart from the help of the Spirit and divine power. He therefore takes the words and makes flesh his arm, etc. as a limitation or restriction of the preceding words, who trusts in man. Yet in reality they are nothing but an exposition of those words, adapted to suggest why the one who trusts in man is cursed. For to make someone one's arm and to trust in him are equivalent phrases. Moreover, flesh signifies man and is used for him everywhere, as in Gen. 6. 12. Deut. 5. 26. Psal. 56. 5 and 65. 3. Isa. 40. 5 and 49. 26. Jer. 25. 31 and 45. 5. Ezek. 21. 5, etc.

units.la: 12. Deut 5. 26. psal.[?] 56. 5. & 65. 3. Esa. 40. 5. & 49. 26. Hierem. 25. 31. & 45. 5. Ezech. 21. 5. &c. Ponere igitur carnem brachium suum & ponere hominem brachium suum seu homini confidere, idem sunt, nec differunt, nisi quod phrasis illa aptior est quam ista ad retegendam eiusmodi confidentiae inutilitatem & vanitatem. Uno verbo, cum homo caro sit, quicunque confidit homini confidit carni, nempe, inquit Aduersarius, si in ipsis humanis viribus spem suam collocet, seu in homine ipso perse, citra spiritus ac virtutis divinae opem. At inquam, si spem suam in spiritus ac virtutis divinae ope collocat, eam non iam in homine reponit, sed in Deo cuius est illa virtus, quique homini illi adest opemque præstat. Christus autem voluit in se credi, non tantum in Deum patrem. Creditis in Deum, inquit, etiam in me credite. Amen amen dico vobis, qui credit in me habet vitam aeternam. Quicunque contemplatur Filium & credit in eum habet vitam aeternam, & suscitabo eum ego ultimo die. venite ad me omnes qui laboratis &c.
units.tr: Therefore to make flesh one's arm and to make man one's arm, or to trust in man, are the same thing and differ only in that the former phrase is more apt than the latter for exposing the uselessness and vanity of such trust. In a word, since man is flesh, whoever trusts in man trusts in flesh; namely, says my opponent, if he places his hope in human powers themselves, or in man himself by himself, apart from the help of the Spirit and divine power. But I say: if he places his hope with the help of the Spirit and divine power, he does not then place it in man, but in God, to whom that power belongs, and who is present to that man and furnishes help. Christ, however, willed to be believed in himself, and not only in God the Father. You believe in God, he says, believe also in me. Verily, verily, I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life. Whoever beholds the Son and believes in him has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. Come to me, all you who labour, etc.

units.la: XXV. Responderi non potest, nec hominem ab illa virtute diuina nec virtutem diuinam ab homine seorsim spectari debere, sed coniunctim, ut sit obiectum fidei ac fiduciae homo ille diuina instructus virtute. Nam virtus illa diuina consideratur vel ut virtus aliena, Dei videlicet, qui homini illi fert opem; vel ut virtus hominis illius propria, in ipso residens & posita in potestate arbitrii ipsius. Si prius, recta in Deum fertur & recumbit fides, nec homini illi confidendum est, sed Deo, qui pro beneplacito suo liberrimo homini illi adest, eique virtute sua opitulatur. Si posterius, Quid sit illa virtus diuina consideranda est. Nam si est substantia, duae fuerunt hominis seu personae illius substantiae, una nobilior quae spiritus & virtus diuina appellatur, altera inferior quae caro, hoc est, natura humana imbecilla & caduca vocatur. Voluntne igitur Aduersarij Dominum nostrum praeditum fuisse duabus eiusmodi substantijs, quarum altera posset facere quicquid vellet, cæcorum oculos aperire, mortuos ad vitam reuocare &c; altera posset pati quicquid ei malorum infligere homines impij vellent? Hoc si concederent, confecta res esset. Facile enim euinceremus substantiam eiusmodi nonnisi diuinam esse naturam.
units.tr: XXV. It cannot be answered that the man should not be considered apart from that divine power, nor the divine power apart from the man, but that they must be considered together, so that the object of faith and trust is that man endowed with divine power. For that divine power is considered either as another's power, namely God's, who brings help to that man, or as that man's own power, residing in him and placed in the power of his own will. If the first, faith is directed toward God and rests in him, and it is not to that man that one must trust, but to God, who, by his most free good pleasure, stands by that man and aids him by his power. If the second, one must consider what that divine power is. For if it is a substance, there were two substances or persons in that man: one more noble, called the Spirit and divine power, and the other lower, called the flesh, that is, human nature, weak and frail. Do our opponents, then, wish our Lord to have been endowed with two such substances, one of which could do whatever it willed, open the eyes of the blind, call the dead back to life, and so on, and the other could suffer whatever evils wicked men chose to inflict on him? If they conceded this, the matter would be settled. For we could easily prove that a substance of this kind is nothing other than the divine nature.

units.la: Si vero dicatur esse accidens hominis Christi, quandoquidem Christus caro fuit, summa vis summaque imbecillitas, res admodum oppositæ, eidem carni, eidem, vt loquuntur, subiecto quo inhæserunt eodem tempore. Quod cum recta ratione conciliare Aduersarios non puto posse. Sequentur etiam alia absurda, quæ hic commemorare nihil opus est.
units.tr: But if it is said to be an accident of the man Christ, since Christ was flesh, then supreme power and supreme weakness, things entirely opposed, would inhere at the same time in the same flesh, in the same subject, as they say, in which. I do not think our opponents can reconcile this with sound reason. Other absurdities would also follow, which there is no need to recount here.

units.la: XXVI. Pergit Socinus. Additur, inquit, postremò expressè, & a Domino recedit cor eius. Vt scilicet intelligatur, Deum habituram aliquam rationem illorum, qui, licet homini cupiam plus æquo confidant, humanis viribus id tribuentes, quod ipsius Dei est proprium, tamen interea ab ipso Deo non deficiant, nec mentem ab ipso auersam aut alienam gerunt. Hic Socinus pugnantia dicit. Humanis enim viribus id tribuere quod ipsius Dei est proprium magna est iniustitia, & aduersus Deum ingratitudo, & iniuria sacro eius nomini illata, immò idololatria; ac propterea qui id facit ab ipso Deo, si non pro toto, vt loquuntur, saltem pro tanto, deficit, & mentem auersam gerit. Si quis potestatem ipsius Regis propriam alicui ex eius subditis tribueret, nonne eo ipso a Rege deficere putandus esset? Deus rivalem ferre non potest. Non colitur cum coluntur[?] vna cum eo dij alieni. Nemo potest, inquit ipse Dominus, duobus dominis seruire: aut enim vnum odio habebit, & alterum diliget, aut vni adhærebit, & alterum contemnet. Non potestis Deo seruire & Mammona. Nemo igitur potest Deo adhærere & homini, Deo confidere, & homini. Cui enim quis confidit huic adhæret & seruit. Itaque mihi Socinus ita loqui videtur vt mulier adultera, quæ id alij tribuendo quod mariti proprium esse debet, negaret se a marito suo deficere, aut mentem auersam vel alienam gerere.
units.tr: XXVI. Socinus goes on: "It is added, lastly and expressly, and his heart departs from the Lord. This is so that it may be understood that God will take some account of those who, although they trust in man more than is right, ascribing to human powers what is proper to God himself, nevertheless do not fall away from God himself, nor hold their minds turned away from him or estranged." Here Socinus says contradictory things. For to ascribe to human powers what is proper to God himself is a great injustice, an ingratitude toward God, and an insult offered to his holy name, indeed idolatry; and therefore whoever does this does fall away from God himself, if not wholly, as they say, at least in that respect, and holds his mind turned away. If someone were to ascribe to one of the king's subjects the power that belongs to the king himself, would he not be thought to have fallen away from the king by that very act? God cannot bear a rival. He is not worshipped when other gods are worshipped along with him. No one, says the Lord himself, can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and Mammon. No one therefore can cleave to God and to man, trust in God and in man. For whom a man trusts, to him he clings and serves. So Socinus seems to me to speak like an adulterous woman who, by ascribing to another what ought to belong to her husband alone, would deny that she had fallen away from her husband or held her mind turned away or estranged.

units.la: XXVII. Non sunt igitur in hoc oraculo, Maledictus homo qui confidit in homine, & ponit carnem brachium suum, & a Domino recedit cor eius, verba posteriora priorum restrictiones, sed, vt dixi, explanationes, quibus redduntur rationes, cur sit qui homini confidit homo maledictus, nempe primò nititur re caduca & imbecilla, quæque seruare non potest, carne videlicet: omnis enim homo est caro. Deinde quatenus confi-dit homini non confidit deo, sed ab eo recedit cor eius; ac proinde se necessario priuat fundamento & auxilio, Deique iram in se prouocat. Qui confidit in homine, is domum suam ædificat super arenam. Qui autem ædificat super arenam, is non ædificat super petram. Quapropter cadere eam tandem aliquando necesse est. Atqui, inquiunt, qui Christo confidit non nititur carne, nec deficit à Deo. Certè; nam Christus est Deus patefactus in carne. Itaque adhærere Christo est adhærere Deo, seruire Christo est seruire Deo, confidere Christo est confidere Deo.
units.tr: XXVII. Therefore the words that follow in this oracle, Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and his heart departs from the Lord, are not restrictions of the former words, but, as I have said, explanations, by which the reasons are given why the man who trusts in man is cursed. First, he rests on something frail and weak, which cannot save, namely flesh, for every man is flesh. Then, insofar as he trusts in man he does not trust in God, and his heart departs from him; and so he necessarily deprives himself of foundation and help, and provokes God's wrath against himself. He who trusts in man builds his house upon sand. But he who builds upon sand does not build upon the rock. Therefore it must at some time fall. But, they say, he who trusts in Christ does not rest on flesh, nor does he fall away from God. Certainly; for Christ is God made manifest in the flesh. Thus to cleave to Christ is to cleave to God, to serve Christ is to serve God, to trust in Christ is to trust in God.

units.la: XXVIII. Progreditur vlterius Socinus, & hoc idem oraculum in Bellarminum & Vvitkum retorquet. Dicant mihi, inquit, obsecro, ipsi, inquam, Pontifici, Annon virgo Maria Christi mater corpore & anima, vt ipsis placet, in cœlum assumpta est homo? An fortasse excellentior homo est quàm necesse sit Iesum ipsum Christum esse, si non est ille unus Deus? Non dicent opinor. Quomodo igitur, cum ipsa non sit ille unus Deus, eam tamen (vt cætera præteream, quibus demonstrant, se in illa confidere) spem suam vocant? Quid enim est in aliquo confidere, si hoc non est, eum spem suam esse statuere? Annon coguntur, si velint hoc suum factum tueri, ostendere non esse simpliciter vetitum in homine confidere? Hæc retorsio nullo modo nos tangit, qui virginem Mariam, Christi τὸ κατὰ σάρκα [?] matrem, beatam quidem prædicamus, præclaréque de ea sentimus & loquimur, ei tamen, cum Deus non sit, non confidimus. Ab ea autem quomodo se tueri possint Pontificij equidem nullus video.
units.tr: XXVIII. Socinus proceeds further, and turns this same oracle back against Bellarmine and Wittich. "Let them tell me, I beg," he says, "I say to the Pontiff himself: Was not the Virgin Mary, Christ's mother, taken up into heaven in body and soul, as they wish, a man? Or perhaps she is a more excellent man than it is necessary for Jesus Christ himself to be, if he is not that one God? They will not say so, I suppose. How then, since she is not that one God, do they nevertheless call her their hope (to pass over the other things by which they show that they trust in her)? For what is it to trust in someone, if it is not to set him up as one's hope?
