Are they not compelled, if they wish to defend this their practice, to show that it is not simply forbidden to trust in man?" This retort does not touch us in any way, who proclaim the Virgin Mary, mother of Christ according to the flesh [τὸ κατὰ σάρκα], indeed blessed, and think and speak highly of her, but we do not trust in her, since she is not God. From her, however, I truly see no way in which the Papists can defend themselves.

units.la: XXIX. Putat igitur Socinus, eos necessariò responsuros, Non omnem fiduciam in homine collocandam prohiberi: sed eam, qua, vt in nostra felicitatis auctore, (id est, vt mox exponit, sola & prima causa) collocetur. At quis est si Atheos & Epicureos seponas, qui vsque adeò insaniat, vt putet hominem solam & primam causam esse felicitatis hominis? Illi ipsi qui equis & armis & militibus confidunt, siue Christiani sint, siue Iudæi, siue Mahometani, siue Ethnici solent numinis opem implorare: Nec est quisquam ita amens qui non confiteatur, vires humanas, quibus nititur & confidit, a Deo esse: Eluditur igitur ea responsione hoc Dei testimonium, redditurque elumbe & inutile.
units.tr: XXIX. Socinus therefore thinks that they will necessarily reply: "It is not forbidden to place all trust in man, but only that trust by which one places it in him as the author of our happiness" (that is, as he explains shortly, the sole and first cause). But who, if you set aside the atheists and Epicureans, is so mad as to think that man is the sole and first cause of human happiness? Those very people who trust in horses and arms and soldiers, whether they are Christians, Jews, Mohammedans or heathens, are accustomed to implore the help of a divinity. Nor is there anyone so foolish as not to confess that the human strength on which he rests and trusts comes from God. This testimony of God is therefore mocked by such an answer, and rendered feeble and useless.

units.la: XXX. Eam autem responsionem Socinus pluribus persequitur, & ad Mariam virginem primùm ex Pontificiorum, vt ipse pūtat, sententia, deinde ad ipsum Christum accommodat, eaque dicit ex quibus, vt rem in pauciora contraham, talis colligitur solutio argumenti nostri. In solo Deo Confidendum est, scilicet, vt in nostra felicitatis auctore, id est, sola & prima causa. Atqui in Christo confidendum est, scilicet, non alia ratione, aliamue ob causam, quàm vt in secunda seu instrumentali efficiente felicitatis nostrae causa, & ob id, quòd ab illo vno Deo nobis absolutè felicitandis, hac conditione, vt illum pro tali habeamus, praefectus fuit. In qua responsione multa peccat. Primò discedit a forma tanorum[?] sermonū & stilo Scripturæ quæ constanter fiduciam nostrā ab hominibus alijsq; creaturis abstrahit, nulla eiusmodi distinctione vspiam insinuata. Deinde illis qui auro argento equis equitibus hominibus, alijsque id genus rebus, confidunt excusationem suppeditat peccati: dicent enim se illis non confidere, nisi vt causis secundis & instrumentalibus. Tum non attendit quanti sint momenti verba, Maledictus est homo qui confidit in homine. Cum enim in iis de summa rerum nostrarum agatur, cum nihil sit magis euitandum quàm maledictio, cum constet ipsius Dei verba esse, qui contrà affirmat, non esse maledictum hominem qui confidit in homine, hunc oportet propositionem suam auctoritate Scripturæ confirmare; aut si distinctionem vel limitationem verbis Dei adhibet, eam è Dei mente esse necessario aliquo argumento clarum facere, vt quàm constat, propositionem, Maledictus est qui confidit in homine, diuinam esse, tam etiam constet, diuinam esse propositionis illius distinctionem seu limitationem, qua fiat, vt propositio oppositā, Maledictus est qui confidit in homine, pro vera haberi debeat. Alioquin enim tutum non esse limitationes aut exceptiones pro ingenio comminisci, aut iis, qui eius quod Deus affirmant oppositum docent, fidem habere, testes sunt illustres historiae Saulis & viri Dei, quarum altera 1. Sam. cap. 15. altera 1. Reg. cap. 13. habetur.
units.tr: XXX. Socinus pursues that answer at greater length, and first applies it to the Virgin Mary, according to what he thinks is the view of the Papists, and then to Christ himself; and from these things he states, to reduce the matter to fewer words, that the following solution of our argument is drawn. One must trust in God alone, namely as the author of our happiness, that is, the sole and first cause. But one must trust in Christ, namely for no other reason or cause than that he is set over us as the secondary or instrumental efficient cause of our happiness, and because he was appointed by that one God to make us happy absolutely, on this condition, that we regard him as such. In this answer he errs in many ways. First, he departs from the manner of speaking and the style of Scripture, which consistently withdraws our trust from men and other creatures, no such distinction being hinted at anywhere. Then he supplies an excuse for sin to those who trust in gold, silver, horses, horsemen, men, and things of that kind: for they will say that they trust in these not as in the first causes but only as in secondary and instrumental causes. Next, he does not consider how weighty the words are, Cursed is the man who trusts in man. For since the highest matters of our lives are in question here, and since nothing is more to be avoided than a curse, and since it is certain that these are the words of God himself, who on the contrary affirms that the man who trusts in man is not cursed, he ought to confirm his proposition by the authority of Scripture; or, if he applies a distinction or limitation to God's words, he must make clear by some argument that it comes from God's mind, so that just as it is certain that the proposition "Cursed is he who trusts in man" is divine, so it is also certain that the distinction or limitation of that proposition is divine, by which the opposite proposition, "Cursed is he who trusts in man," ought to be held as true. Otherwise, that it is not safe to devise limitations or exceptions according to one's own wit, or to give credit to those who teach the opposite of what God affirms, is shown by the famous histories of Saul and the man of God, of which the first is found in 1 Sam. ch. 15 and the second in 1 Kings ch. 13.

units.la: XXXI.
units.tr: XXXI.

units.la: Præterea si potest homo confidere homini malè & benè; malè, si ei vt auctori seu primæ causæ, benè, si ei vt causæ secundæ & instrumentali felicitatis confidit, circuncidendum fuit fiduciæ in homine præputium, nosque à mala fiducia ad bonam reuocandi fuimus: quod tamen in Scriptura, quæ perfectissimam doctrinam perfectissimè continet, non sic vspiam. Dam-nat illa perpetuò fiduciam quæ collocatur in homine, nec ei perproprietatibus diuinæ naturæ, idololatra est ac iniuriam Deo maximam facit qui confidit in homine seu mera creatura; vt mirum videri non debeat, si clamat Scriptura, Maledictum esse hominem qui confidit in homine. Quare cum non prohibeamur confidere in Christo, sed iubeamur potius, immò id à nobis sub pœna damnationis exigatur, eo ipso profectò à nobis exigitur, vt eum pro omniscio, omnipotente, & omnipræsente, hoc est, Deo diuina essentia prædito habeamus.
units.tr: Moreover, if a man can trust in a man both wrongly and rightly (wrongly if he trusts in him as the author or first cause, rightly if he trusts in him as a secondary and instrumental cause of happiness), then trust in man ought to have been cut off like a foreskin, and we ought to have been called back from bad trust to good. Yet Scripture, which contains the most perfect doctrine in the most perfect way, nowhere does so. It condemns without exception any trust placed in man, and does not attribute to him the properties of the divine nature. He who trusts in a man, that is, in a mere creature, is an idolater and does the greatest wrong to God. So it should not seem strange that Scripture cries out, "Cursed is the man that trusteth in man." Therefore, since we are not forbidden to trust in Christ but are rather commanded to, and this is required of us on pain of damnation, it is certainly required of us that we hold him to be omniscient, omnipotent and omnipresent, that is, endowed with the divine essence.

units.la: XXXV. Quapropter falsum esse oportet quod affirmat Socinus, Dominum auctorem non esse, sed tantùm causam secundam seu instrumentalem efficientem felicitatis nostræ. Causam enim tantummodo instrumentalem si persona est, nihil nisi seruum esse necesse est. Dominus autem seruus quidem fuit, quatenus cum esset in forma Dei, nec rapinam duceret esse se æqualem Deo, semetipsum exinaniuit sumpta serui forma, reuera autem seruo opponitur vt Filius, vt Dominus, vti patet ex Heb. 3. 5. 6. & Socinus confitetur Disp. de Adoratione Christi cum Christiano Francken. Num. 60. Immò, inquit, Christus homo est Dominus omnium nostrum, adeòque angelorum omnium. Sic, vt nunc non modò conseruus noster simpliciter dici nequeat, quod nec vnquam potuit, sed ne Dei quidem ipsius seruus proprie dici posse videatur. Vnde verba illa Pauli 1. Cor. 15. Tunc & ipse filius subjectus erit ei, qui subjecit ipsi omnia, vt sit Deus omnia in omnibus. Hinc enim aperte constat, Paulum sensisse, non posse Christum hominem, cui Deus omnia subiecit, hoc tempore proprie Deo subiectum dici; quare neque etiam proprie eius seruum. Si igitur proprie non subjicitur Deo, nec est seruus Dei, quomodo proprie nihil est, nisi creatura, nisi instrumentum Dei? causa enim secunda & instrumentalis primæ & principali subjicitur & seruit.
units.tr: XXXV. It must therefore be false, what Socinus affirms, that the Lord is not the author but only the secondary or instrumental efficient cause of our happiness. For if a person is only an instrumental cause, he must be nothing but a servant. The Lord indeed was a servant, insofar as, though he was in the form of God and did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. But in truth the servant is set in opposition to the Son, as the Lord, as is clear from Heb. 3. 5. 6., and Socinus confesses this in his disputation on the Adoration of Christ with Christian Francken, n. 60. "Indeed," he says, "Christ as man is the Lord of all of us, and so of all the angels. So that now he cannot simply be called our fellow servant, which indeed he never could be, but he does not even seem to be properly called the servant of God himself. Hence those words of Paul, 1 Cor. 15: Then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all. For from this it is plainly evident that Paul thought that Christ as man, to whom God subjected all things, cannot at this time be properly said to be subject to God; therefore neither can he properly be called his servant." If then he is not properly subject to God, nor the servant of God, how is he properly nothing but a creature, nothing but an instrument of God? For a secondary and instrumental cause is subject to and serves the first and principal cause.

units.la: XXX VI. Si virtutes ad nos seruandos & beandos necessarias spectes, non pauciores nec minores quàm Pater, Filius exeruisse videtur, summum erga nos amorem, summam authoritatem, summam potentiam. Si laudem & gloriam quæ ex tanto opere consurgit, ea ad Filium non secus ac ad Patrem pertinet. Emit ipse nos si Patri, etiam sibi Apoc. 14. 4. Tit 2. 14. Si illis omnibus qui ipsi obediunt auctor est salutis æternæ vt Mediator, primus & summus est, immo vnicus Mediator: Si vt Sacerdos, in eo mune-re nemini subordinatur: Si vt Rex & Dominus, non modo non est Dominus secundus primi vicarius, sed quod magis est, solus est Dominus. Sed ne sim longior, si Filius non est nisi causa secunda & instrumentalis salutis nostrae, quomodo ipse Patre, Angelis, & tota Ecclesia audientibus clamat & inculcat, se esse Al-pha & omega, primum & ultimum, principium & finem? Haec enim sunt elogia causae primae & principalis, non vero illius, quae nihil nisi secunda sit & instrumentalis.
units.tr: XXXVI. If you look at the virtues necessary for saving and blessing us, the Son appears to have exerted no fewer or lesser ones than the Father: the highest love towards us, the highest authority, the highest power. If you look at the praise and glory that arise from so great a work, these pertain to the Son no less than to the Father. He himself bought us for the Father, and so also for himself (Rev. 14. 4.; Tit. 2. 14.). If he is the author of eternal salvation to all who obey him, as Mediator he is first and highest, indeed the only Mediator. If as Priest, in that office he is subordinate to no one. If as King and Lord, he is not merely a second Lord, the vicar of the first, but, what is more, he is the only Lord. But not to be too long: if the Son is only the secondary and instrumental cause of our salvation, how does he himself cry out and insist, in the hearing of the Father, the angels and the whole Church, that he is Alpha and Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end? For these are the titles of the first and principal cause, not of one who is nothing but secondary and instrumental.

units.la: XXXVII. His duobus argumentis, quibus frustra occurrere conatus est Socinus, tertium subnectam, quod sic habet. Soli Deo Israelis confidendum erat tempore Davidis. Filio confidendum erat tempore Davidis. Filius igitur est Deus Israelis. Negabunt Adversarij minorem. Ea probatur ex verbis istis psal. 2. beati qui confidunt in eo. Non enim dicit in futuro, qui confident, sed in praesenti qui confidunt; cur, si eo tempore nec poterant nec debebant in eo fideles confidere? cur etiam illorum seculorum hominibus miseriam suam sentientibus & beatitudinis sitientibus canebatur illud, & legendum identidem offerebatur, Beati qui confidunt in eo, nisi ut rationem cognoscerent, qua beati fieri possent? Quis enim credat hominibus beatitudinem appeten-tibus rationem beatitudinis consequendae divinitus propositam fuisse, quae ad eos nullo modo spectaret, & ad quam nullo modo aspirare possent? Quorsum enim id pertinuisset?
units.tr: XXXVII. To these two arguments, against which Socinus has tried in vain to make a stand, I add a third, which runs thus. The God of Israel alone was to be trusted in the time of David. The Son was to be trusted in the time of David. Therefore the Son is the God of Israel. Our opponents will deny the minor premise. It is proved from these words of Psalm 2: Blessed are all they that put their trust in him. For he does not say "who will trust" in the future, but "who trust" in the present. Why, if at that time the faithful neither could nor ought to trust in him? Why too was that saying sung to the people of those ages, who felt their misery and thirsted for blessedness, and repeatedly set before them to read, "Blessed are they that put their trust in him," unless that they might know the reason by which they could be made blessed? For who would believe that the reason for obtaining blessedness was divinely set before men who desired blessedness, a reason that in no way concerned them and to which they could in no way aspire? For to what purpose would that have been?

units.la: XXXVIII. Hoc idem confirmat collatio versus ultimi psalmi secundi cum versu primo psalmi primi. Sunt enim duae duntaxat consequendae iustificationis seu beatitudinis rationes: una ex merito, altera ex gratia; illa foedere legali, ista Evangelico; illa perfecta observatione legis, ista fide in Christum nititur. Tertia non datur, Ac, ut verbis Crellij comm. in Rom. cap. 1. &[?] 11. vtar, Nullus alius restat iustificationis modus. Nam vel operum meritis iustificatio quaerenda est, quem modum Lex prescribit: vel per fidem, quem modum & Evangelium proponit, & Veteris Testamenti scripta commendant & promittunt. Prior modus proponitur psalmo primo, Beatus vir qui non abijt in consilio im-piorum &c. Sed, quoniam nemo ita a malo abstinet & bonum facit, quin peccet interdum; omnis autem peccator Legis sententiâ maledictus est, ac propterea ex operibus Legis nulla caro iustificabitur in Dei conspectu, statim sequente psalmo alter iustificationis & beatitudinis obtinendae modus retegitur & declaratur, nempe fides in Filium Dei, cui, teste Petro, omnes Prophetæ te-stimonium perhibent, remissionem peccatorum accepturum per nomen eius omnem qui crediderit in eum. Per eum enim, ut verbis utar Pauli, quicunque credit ab omnibus iustificatur, à quibus per legem Mosis iustificari non potuit, cur igitur hominibus, qui priore modo iustificari, atque adeo beati fieri non poterant, statim secundus proponitur, nisi ut eum amplectantur, tanquam alteram post naufragium tabulam, aut potius nauem, qua tuto ad portum felicitatis appellantur? Ex quo, quamuis exiguum sit, specimine colligi potest, psalmos non esse temere in unum volumen conjectos, sed magno delectu, magnaque prudentia in optimum ordinem digestos ac dispositos.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The comparison of the last verse of the second Psalm with the first verse of the first Psalm confirms this same point. There are only two ways of obtaining justification or blessedness: one from merit, the other from grace; the former rests on the legal covenant, the latter on the Gospel; the former on the perfect observance of the law, the latter on faith in Christ. A third is not given. To use the words of Crellius in his commentary on Romans, chapters 1 and 11: There remains no other mode of justification. For either justification must be sought by the merits of works, which is the mode the Law prescribes; or by faith, which mode the Gospel also sets forth, and which the writings of the Old Testament commend and promise. The former mode is set forth in the first Psalm: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, etc. But since no one so abstains from evil and does good that he does not sometimes sin, and since every sinner is cursed by the sentence of the Law, and therefore by the works of the Law no flesh shall be justified in the sight of God, immediately in the following Psalm the other mode of obtaining justification and blessedness is revealed and declared, namely faith in the Son of God, to whom, as Peter bears witness, all the prophets bear witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins. For by him, to use Paul's words, everyone that believeth is justified from all things, from which they could not be justified by the law of Moses. Why then, if men could not be justified and so made blessed in the former way, is the second set before them immediately, unless that they might embrace it as a second plank after shipwreck, or rather as a ship by which they may safely reach the harbour of happiness? From this small specimen it can be gathered that the Psalms were not thrown together into one volume at random, but were arranged and ordered in the best order with great selection and great wisdom.

units.la: XXXIX. Denique rationem consequendæ iustificationis seu beatitudinis per fidem in Filium, quæ psalmo secundo revelatur, ad fideles, qui seculis illis vivebant, pertinuisse, ex eo liquet, quod illi sine dubio iustificati seu beati fuerunt: vel igitur per legem, vel per fidem in Filium Dei iustificati fuerunt. Non per Legem. Id enim Apostolus quinque primis Ep. ad Rom. capitibus, necnon Epist. ad Gal. abunde demonstravit. Ergo iustificati fuerunt per fidem in Filium Dei; Aut tertius iustificationis seu beatitudinis adipiscendæ modus excogitandus erit ab Adversarijs, fortiter reclamante Scriptura.
units.tr: XXXIX. Finally, that the way of obtaining justification or blessedness through faith in the Son, which is revealed in the second Psalm, pertained to the faithful who lived in those ages, is clear from this: those men were without doubt justified or blessed. Either, then, they were justified through the Law, or through faith in the Son of God. Not through the Law. The Apostle has amply shown this in the first five chapters of the Epistle to the Romans, as well as in the Epistle to the Galatians. Therefore they were justified through faith in the Son of God. Otherwise, the opponents will have to devise a third way of obtaining justification or blessedness, while Scripture strongly protests.

units.la: XL. Sunt alij Psalmorum loci quibus divina Domini nostri essentia probari possit. Cuiusmodi est, exempli causa, Psal. LXXXII. V. 8. Surge Deus, iudica terram: quoniam tu in hereditatem accipies omnes gentes. Quis enim surget, iudicabit terram, hæreditario iure gentes omnes possidebit, nisi Filius, qui est venturus ad iudicium, & cui datæ sunt gentes in hæreditatem? Sed mihi tempero [?], ac, quantum possum, brevitati consulo. est is quem Iudæi prouocarunt ad Zelotypiam. Christus est sponsus seu Maritus Ecclesiæ teste Iohanne Baptista Ioh. 3. Ergo Christus est is quem Iudæi prouocarunt ad Zelotypiam.
units.tr: XL. There are other passages of the Psalms by which the divine essence of our Lord can be proved. Of this kind is, for example, Psalm 82:8: Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations. For who will arise to judge the earth and possess all nations by hereditary right, except the Son, who is to come to judgment and to whom the nations are given for an inheritance? But I restrain myself and, as far as I can, I consult brevity. He is the one whom the Jews provoked to jealousy. Christ is the bridegroom or husband of the Church, as John the Baptist testifies, John 3. Therefore Christ is the one whom the Jews provoked to jealousy.

units.la: IV. Quartum argumentum ex eodem versu eruitur, Ipsi me pronocarunt[?] in eo qui non est Deus, & irritauerunt vanitatibus suis, Et ego pronocabo[?] eos in eo qui non est populus, & in gente stulta irritabo illos. Quemadmodum Iudæi Deum prouocarunt conuertendo se ad alium Deum, sic Deus Iudæos prouocauit conuertendo se ad alium populum, hoc est, ad gentes. Pœna est Talionis. Quia Iudæi Deum dereliquerunt, Deus eos dereliquit. Quia religiosè coluerunt eum qui non erat Deus, Deus complex-xus est eum qui non erat populus eius. Id factum est vocatione gentium, nec fieri potuit alia ratione. Hinc ita argumentor. Ille qui Iudæos prouocauit ad æmulationem seu Zelotypiam conuertendo se ad gentes, tanquam ad aliam vxorem, est Deus Israëlis. Is autem est Christus. Est igitur Christus Deus Israëlis. Majorem negari non patitur hic locus; nec minorem Euangelium. Cuius enim fuit Iudæos sic prouocare? Annon eius vnius, qui erat populi Iudaici Deus & maritus? Quis autem sic eos prouocauit? Certè Christus vnicus Ecclesiæ sponsus. Is enim Apostolum Paulum, aliosque seruos suos misit ad gentes sibi, tanquam sponsam sponso, conciliandas & adjungendas.
units.tr: IV. The fourth argument is drawn from the same verse: They have provoked me to jealousy with that which is not God; they have moved me to anger with their vanities. And I will provoke them to jealousy with those which are not a people; I will anger them with a foolish nation. Just as the Jews provoked God by turning to another god, so God provoked the Jews by turning to another people, that is, to the nations. This is a case of retaliation: because the Jews forsook God, God forsook them; because they worshipped with devotion one who was not God, God embraced one who was not his people. This came about through the calling of the nations, and it could not have happened in any other way. I argue as follows. He who provoked the Jews to jealousy, by turning to the nations as to another wife, is the God of Israel. But this is Christ. Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. This place does not allow the major premise to be denied, nor does the Gospel allow the minor. For whose right was it to provoke the Jews in this way, if not that of the one who was the God and husband of the Jewish people? And who provoked them in this way? Certainly Christ, the only bridegroom of the Church. For he sent the apostle Paul and his other servants to the nations, to win them and join them to himself as a bride to her bridegroom.

units.la: V. Quintum argumentum elicitur ex Ψ. 39. Videte nunc quod ego, Ego sum, Et non est Deus mecum. q.d. Noluistis antehac mi-hi seruisque meis nuntiantibus ac testantibus, quod ego sum, credere, ac propterea abscondi faciem meam à vobis, conuerti me ad alium populum, vos per-multa secula grauissimis calamitatibus affeci &c. Nunc vero videte, oculis vsurpate, (ita enim clarè reuelatum est, vt possit videri) quod ego, Ego, inquam, sum, & non est Deus præter me. Hanc enim esse verborum illorum sententiam, qui non prorsus oscitanter diuinum illud canticum perlegerit, facilè agnoscet. Sic igitur argumentor. Ille quem Iu-dæi noluerunt agnoscere & habere pro Deo, atque ob eam cau-sam reiecti sunt; & in eorum locum suffectæ gentes, est Deus Israëlis, vt patet ex hoc Ψ. 39. collato cum antecedentibus. Atqui Christus est ille quem Iudæi noluerunt agnoscere & habere pro Deo, atque ob eam causam reiecti sunt &c, vt patet ex Nouo Testamento. Christus igitur est Deus Israëlis. Dixerat Iudæis Christus, Ioh. 8. 24. Moriemini in peccatis vestris. Si enim non crediderit is quod ego sum, moriemini in peccatis vestris. Hoc illi non crediderunt. Itaque abscondit se ab eis, illudque praedixit, quod scriptum extat Matth. 23. 38. 39. & Luc 13. 35. divini huius carminis vaticinio consentaneum.
units.tr: V. The fifth argument is drawn from Ps. 39 (Ψ. 39.): See now that I, I am he, and there is no God with me. That is to say: you were unwilling before this to believe my servants when they announced and testified that I am; therefore I hid my face from you, turned myself to another people, and afflicted you for many ages with the most grievous calamities, and so on. But now see, use your eyes (for it has been revealed so clearly that it can be seen) that I, I say, am, and there is no God besides me. Anyone who has read this divine song not altogether carelessly will readily recognise that this is the meaning of those words. I argue thus. He whom the Jews were unwilling to acknowledge and to hold as God, and on account of which cause they were rejected, and the nations were raised up in their place, is the God of Israel, as is evident from this Ps. 39 compared with what goes before. But Christ is he whom the Jews were unwilling to acknowledge and to hold as God, and on account of which cause they were rejected, etc., as is evident from the New Testament. Therefore Christ is the God of Israel. Christ had said to the Jews, John 8:24: You will die in your sins. For if you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins. They did not believe this. And so he hid himself from them, and foretold what is written at Matt. 23:38, 39 and Luke 13:35, agreeing with the prophecy of this divine song.

units.la: VI. Sextum argumentum ex eodem versu oritur.
units.tr: VI. The sixth argument arises from the same verse.

units.la: Negari enim non potest, quin referri debeat ad tempus futurae conversionis populi Iudaici. Eam autem Christus efficiet tam clarè revelando & ostendendo populo illi quod ipse sit, ut populus ille eum videat & agnoscat. Ille igitur qui sic eos tum temporis alloquens inducitur, videte nunc quod ego, ego sum &c, alius esse non potest quam Christus. At, inquiet forte aliquis, negat alium Deum esse praeter se. Id cum fide nostra congruit, qui Patrem & Filium unum Deum esse credimus, haudquaquam vero cum errore adversariorum Patrem & Filium duos deos esse opinantium. Nam si sunt verba Filij, quomodo negat Filius ullum Deum esse praeter se, si praeter ipsum est alius Deus, nempe Pater? Si vero sunt verba Patris, quomodo negat Pater ullum Deum esse praeter se, si praeter ipsum est alius Deus, nempe Filius? Quomodo etiam Pater negaret ullum alium esse Deum praeter se, iuberetque ut id videant & agnoscant Iudaei, quo eos converteret ad Filium agnoscendum, (in qua agnitione sita erit Iudaeorum conversio) & pro Deo suo habendum? Nonne perinde faceret ac si quis eius quod probare instituisset negationem afferret pro argumento?
units.tr: For it cannot be denied that it must be referred to the time of the future conversion of the Jewish people. Christ will bring about that conversion by revealing and showing so clearly to that people that he himself is, so that the people will see him and acknowledge him. Therefore he who is introduced as speaking thus to them at that time, see now that I, I am he and so on, can be no other than Christ. But someone will perhaps object that he denies there is any other God besides himself. This agrees with our faith, since we believe that the Father and the Son are one God, but by no means with the error of our opponents, who think that the Father and the Son are two gods. For if these are the words of the Son, how does the Son deny that there is any God besides himself, if there is another God besides him, namely the Father? And if these are the words of the Father, how does the Father deny that there is any God besides himself, if there is another God besides him, namely the Son? Or how would the Father deny that there is any other God besides himself, and command the Jews to see and acknowledge this, so that he might turn them to acknowledging the Son (in which acknowledgement the conversion of the Jews will consist) and to holding him as their God? Would this not be just as if someone, wishing to prove something, offered the denial of it as his argument?

units.la: VII. Septimum denique argumentum ex eodem illo versu fluit.
units.tr: VII. Finally, the seventh argument flows from the same verse.

units.la: Videte nunc, quod ego, ego sum, & non est Deus praeter me. Ego occidam & vivificabo, vulnus infligam & ego sanabo, & non est qui eripiat de manu mea &c. Quis non videt verbis illis, Ego occidam & sequentibus argumentum contineri; quo qui loquitur docet, & probat, & quasi videndum proponit, se Deum esse, & praeter se alium neminem. Iam autem negari nequit, quin possit Christus eadem illa verba de semetipso usurpare. Negari igitur nequit, quin Christus sit Deus, & quidem eo sensu, quo is qui sic loquitur, videte nunc quod ego, ego sum &c, se Deum esse profitetur.
units.tr: See now that I, I am he, and there is no God besides me. I will kill and I will make alive; I will wound and I will heal; and there is none who can deliver out of my hand, and so on. Who does not see that in those words, I will kill, and the following ones, there is an argument, by which the speaker teaches and proves, and sets before us, as it were, to be seen, that he is God and that there is no other besides him? Now it cannot be denied that Christ could use these same words of himself. Therefore it cannot be denied that Christ is God, and indeed in that sense in which he who speaks thus, see now that I, I am he and so on, professes himself to be God.

units.la: DISPUTATIO TRIGESIMA SEPTIMA
units.tr: DISPUTATION THIRTY-SEVEN

units.la: De Arg. XXXVII. Ex Gen. cap. i. vf. 26. & iii. vf. 22. alijsque locis, Ex quibus plures esse personas diuinas colligi potest.
units.tr: On Argument XXXVII. From Genesis 1:26 and 3:22, and other passages, from which a plurality of divine persons can be gathered.

units.la: I. JAM prælo descripta erat præcedens disputatio, cum mihi aliud argumentum succurrit ductum à divinarum, ut ita loquar, pluralitate personarum. Id superioribus visum est, tanquam cumulum, addere. Sic autem habet.
units.tr: I. The preceding disputation was already sent to press when another argument occurred to me, drawn from what I may call the plurality of the divine persons. It seemed best to add it to the earlier ones as a kind of final addition. It runs as follows.

units.la: Si plures sunt personæ divinæ essentia præditæ, una ex illis est Filius. Prius autem est verum. Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If there are several divine persons endowed with the one essence, one of them is the Son. But the first is true. Therefore the second is true too.

units.la: Propositionem, opinor, non negabunt Aduersarij. Nam si Patris personam seponas, nulla occurrit in Scriptura dignior Filio, qui ad dexteram Patris sedens Patri æqualis regnat. Spiritus enim Sanctus nec persona esse ab Aduersarijs creditur, & à Filio mitti, Filijque Spiritus esse dicitur, ut si is divina persona sit, uti sine dubio est, etiam Filium divinam esse personam oporteat. Itaque omnis nostra opera in probando antecedente, seu Minore, collocanda est.
units.tr: The opponents, I suppose, will not deny the proposition. For if you set aside the person of the Father, no one in Scripture is more worthy than the Son, who sits at the right hand of the Father and reigns as his equal. The Holy Spirit, for the opponents do not even believe he is a person, is sent by the Son and is said to be the Spirit of the Son. So if he is a divine person, as he undoubtedly is, the Son must also be a divine person. Therefore all our effort should be directed to proving the antecedent, or minor premise.

units.la: II. Principiò mihi pluralitas aliqua videtur in natura divina insinuata nomine Elohim, quod esse numeri pluralis, terminatio, & singulare Eloah, & constructio cum adiectiuis & verbis pluralis numeri, & ad plures vel Angelos, vel iudices, vel falsos deos significandos usurpatio satis testantur. Hoc posito dico non temerè accidisse, quod in ea lingua, quæ Deum singulari ratione authorem habet, & in qua sunt multa Dei nomina singularis numeri, nomen plurale ad Deum significandum adhibitum fuerit, & quidem omnium frequentissimè. Multa enim lingua illa præ se fert sapientiæ autoris sui illustria argumenta. Sed malo eâ missâ Scripturæ, quæ verbum est Dei, autoritate niti. Multa apud eam occurrunt Dei nomina, sed nullum frequentius isto plurali. Cur magis delectatus est Deus plurali nomine quàm singulari, si vnica tantùm est maximéque singularis persona diuina? Nodum hunc arctius constringam. Historia creationis aliunde haberi non potuit quàm à revelatione diuina. Itaque omnium historiarum, quæ à Mose sunt scriptæ, diuinissima est, nihilque in ea temerè aut frustrà positum esse, spectatâ auctoris immensâ sapientiâ, firmiter credendum est. Atqui ad eam historiam primo Geneseos, atque adeò totius Scripturæ, capite prudentissimè describendam plurale istud nomen adhibitum est non modò primum, sed, quod plus est, solum. Putasne, pie lector, casu, temerè, sine ratione, nullo consilio ex omnibus Dei nominibus istud vnum plurale ad eam rem à Deo sapientissimo selectum esse, & omnibus nominibus diuinis numeri singularis prælatum? cur autem id factum sit, nisi vt pluralitas aliqua insinuetur?
units.tr: II. First, some plurality seems to me to be hinted at in the divine nature by the name Elohim. Its plural ending, the singular Eloah, its construction with adjectives and verbs of the plural number, and its use to signify several angels, judges, or false gods, sufficiently attest this. Given this, I say it was not by chance that, in that language, which has God as its author in a unique way and in which there are many divine names in the singular, a plural name was used to signify God, and indeed most frequently of all. For that language displays many illustrious proofs of the wisdom of its author. But I prefer to rest on the authority of Scripture, which is the word of God, setting that language aside. Many names of God occur in it, but none more often than this plural. Why has God taken more delight in a plural name than in a singular one, if the divine person is one and most singular? I will tighten this knot further. The history of creation could not have been known from any source other than divine revelation. Therefore, of all the histories written by Moses, it is the most divine, and, given the immense wisdom of the author, we must firmly believe that nothing in it was put there carelessly or in vain. Yet in describing that history, in the first chapter of Genesis and indeed of all Scripture, this plural name was used not only first but, what is more, alone. Do you think, pious reader, that this one plural name was chosen by the most wise God for this matter by chance, carelessly, without reason and without plan, from among all the names of God, and preferred to all the divine names in the singular? And why was this done, unless some plurality is being hinted at?

units.la: III. Vsitatum est in lingua Hebraea, vti in reliquis linguis, cum suo nominatiuo verbum numero congruere. Idque ipla[?] rerum natura exigere videtur. Toto tamen capite primo Genesis nomen istud plurale Elohim cum verbo singulari construitur constanter triginta duabus vicibus, deinde capite secundo vndecim continuis vicibus ei præfigitur nomen tetragrammatum numeri singularis. Huius rei causam aliquam esse oportet. Non enim id Deo imprudenti, & quidem tam saepè, excidere potuit. Nonne igitur ex eo quod de Deo verbum singularis numeri tam saepe vsurpatur, rectè colligitur, ei conuenire pluralitatem? cur igitur similiter ex eo quod de eo tam saepe vsurpatur nomen pluralis numeri, non colligitur ei conuenire pluralitatem? Cur etiam ex eo quod plurale istud nomen cum verbo singulari tam saepè construitur, non colligitur inter eiusmodi vnitatem & pluralitatem optimè conuenire, nec alteram alterà euerti, sed stabiliri potius? Quemadmodum enim si omnis vnitas aliena esset à Deo, verbum singularis numeri aut non omnino de Deo vsurparetur, aut non tàm saepe, sic, si omnis pluralitas aliena esset à Deo, nomen pluralis numeri, aut non omnino vsurparetur de Deo, aut non tam saepe. Quod si, cum de Deo non agitur, contingit aliquando plurale nomen cum singulari verbo vel adiectiuo construi, id & raro fit, & cur fiat ratio est penè obuia. Sic, exempli gratia, Priunum [?] Decalogi praeceptum, si verbum pro verbo reddas, conceptum est, Non erit tibi dij alieni coram me, vt omnis aliorum deorum singularitas & pluralitas prohiberi intelligatur, siue vnus colatur, siue plures, vt vt putentur subordinati aut consentientes vel est Ellipsis, Non erit tibi quisquam deorum alienorum coram me. Sic Gen. 9. 15. ad verbum, Non erit vltra aquae ad diluuium nempe diluuium multarum aquarum superiorum & inferiorum conspiratione & coalitione in vnam massam factum est. Itaque huiusmodi constructionibus perpetuò aliqua vnitas, aliaque pluralitas innuitur.
units.tr: III. In Hebrew, as in other languages, it is customary for a verb to agree in number with its nominative, and the nature of things seems to demand this. Yet throughout the whole first chapter of Genesis, this plural name Elohim is constantly construed with a singular verb, thirty-two times in all. Then in the second chapter it is preceded eleven times in succession by the singular Tetragrammaton. There must be some cause for this, for it cannot have slipped from God, who is not careless, and so often. Is it not rightly concluded, then, from the fact that a verb of the singular number is so often used of God, that unity belongs to him? Why, then, is it not likewise concluded from the fact that a plural name is so often used of him that plurality belongs to him? Again, from the fact that this plural name is so often construed with a singular verb, why is it not concluded that unity and plurality agree very well together, and that neither overturns the other, but rather each establishes the other? For just as, if all unity were foreign to God, a verb of the singular number would either not be used of God at all, or not so often, so, if all plurality were foreign to God, a plural name would either not be used of God at all, or not so often. But if, when God is not the subject, a plural name sometimes happens to be construed with a singular verb or adjective, this occurs rarely, and the reason for it is almost obvious. Thus, for example, the first precept of the Decalogue, if rendered word for word, reads: Non erit tibi dij alieni coram me ("There shall not be to you other gods before me"), so that the singularity and plurality of all other gods is understood to be forbidden, whether one is worshipped or several, or so that they may be thought subordinate or in agreement. Or there is an ellipsis: Non erit tibi ("there shall not be to you") quisquam ("anyone") deorum alienorum coram me ("of other gods before me"). So in Genesis 9:15, word for word: Non erit vltra aquae ad diluuium ("There shall no longer be waters for a flood"). The flood came about through the conspiracy and coalition of many waters, above and below, into one mass. Thus in such constructions a certain unity and a certain plurality are always hinted at.

units.la: IV. Non est autem plurale Elohim accommodatum ad plures eiusdem Dei vel potentias vel operationes, quarum nulla Deus appellatur aut appellari potest, innuendas: formaliter enim eius singulare Deum significat, non potentiam, aut operationem vel influxum Dei, & ipsum plurale adhibetur nonnunquam ad significandum plures Angelos, Iudices, idola. Nec fert, vt ego existimo, vllius linguae consuetudo, vt nomen personam significans numero multitudinis efferatur ad significandas vnius personae plures operationes vel potentias. Dixit quidem eleganter Sylla in vno Caesare plures esse Marios, sed nemo vnquam propter varietatem virtutum vel operationum Caesaris eum plurali numero homines, aut Caesares, aut Marios vocauit. Innuit ergo nomen Elohim personas, & quidem, cum non sit duale sed plurale, duabus plures, hoc est, ad minimum tres, non tamen inter se diuisas & separatas, quales sunt personae creatae finita natura praeditae, sed, vt infinitam essentiam decet, indiuisas, ἐν ἑνὶ [?] : atque ob eam causam fere semper cum verbo numeri singularis iungitur. Sicut autem nomen Schamaim, quamuis, quia duale est, plures esse coelos innuat, de vno tamen coelo non raro vsurpatur; sic nomen Elohim quamuis ad pluralitatem personarum diuinarum innuendam sit comparatum, de vna tamen persona diuina vsurpatur nonnunquam: quae siue Enallage numeri, siue synecdoche, eo magis consentanea videri debet, quod personarum diuinarum ea est vnitas, vt aliae in alijs sint, vnaque posita reliquae ponantur.
units.tr: IV. Moreover, the plural Elohim is not suited to indicate several powers or operations of the same God, none of which is, or can be, called God. For formally it signifies God in the singular, not a power, operation, or influence of God, and the plural itself is sometimes used to signify several angels, judges, or idols. Nor does the usage of any language, as I judge, allow a name signifying a person to be put in the plural to signify several operations or powers of one person. Sulla indeed elegantly said that there were many Mariuses in the one Caesar, but no one ever called Caesar, on account of the variety of his virtues or operations, by the plural, calling him Caesars or Mariuses. The name Elohim, therefore, hints at persons, and indeed, since it is not dual but plural, at more than two, that is, at least three. Yet these are not divided and separated from one another, as are created persons endowed with finite nature, but, as befits an infinite essence, undivided: ἐν ἑνὶ [in one]. For this reason it is almost always joined with a verb of the singular number. But just as the name Schamaim, although, because it is dual, it indicates that there are several heavens, is nevertheless not rarely used of one heaven, so the name Elohim, although it has been adapted to indicate the plurality of divine persons, is sometimes used of one divine person. Whether this is an enallage of number or a synecdoche, it ought to seem all the more consistent, since the unity of the divine persons is such that some are in others, and when one is posited the rest are posited with it.

units.la: V. Reponent sine dubio Aduersarij, Deum numero multitudinis Elohim appellari honoris causa. Hebraos enim ea nomina multitudinis numero efferre consueuisse, quae authoritatis ac dominatus continent significationem, quantumuis unico tantum cuipiam attributa, vt in vocibus Adon, & Baal videre est. Reuera duæ illæ voces de Deo pluraliter vsurpantur, & quidem prior sæpissimè id quod argumentum nostrum confirmat. Non enim id fieri honoris causa multa suadent. Primum, cur igitur similiter alia Dei nomina אל, שדי, &c de Deo plurali numero honoris causa non efferuntur? cur similiter alia nomina, quæ autoritatis & dominatus continent significationem, vt מלך Rex, שופט Iudex, אב Pater &c, numero multitudinis de Deo aut de vno homine nunquam dicuntur? cur cum inferior compellat superiorem, præsertim Regem, nunquam eum plurali nomine appellat, ne tum quidem cum eum maximè honorificè alloquitur? Quis etiam credat Deum de hero serui aut bouis pluralia vocum Adon & Baal vsurpare voluisse honoris causa Exod. 21. 4. 6. 8. 32. 29. &c. & non potius quia sæpissimè contingebat eiusdem serui, vel bouis, plures esse dominos? Nam vel proximus dominus erat alterius Domini seruus, vt Tsiba, cui erant viginti serui, seruus erat Mephiboseth, vel domini nomine comprehenduntur cum patrefamilias etiam eius vxor, & filij, præsertim primogenitus.
units.tr: V. Without doubt the opponents will reply that God is called Elohim in the plural out of respect, "for the Hebrews were accustomed to express by plural nouns those names which contain the meaning of authority and dominion, however much they are attributed to only one, as can be seen in the words Adon and Baal." Indeed both those words are used of God in the plural, and the former very often, which confirms our argument. For many considerations suggest that this is not done out of respect. First, why, then, are the other divine names, El [אל], Shaddai [שדי], and so on, not put in the plural of God out of respect? Why are the other names that contain the meaning of authority and dominion, such as melekh [מלך] king, shofet [שופט] judge, av [אב] father, and so on, never said in the plural of God or of one man? Why, when an inferior addresses a superior, especially a king, does he never call him by a plural name, not even when he addresses him with the greatest honour? Who would also believe that God wished to use the plurals of the words Adon and Baal of a servant's or an ox's master out of respect (Exod. 21. 4. 6. 8. 32. 29. etc.), and not rather because it very often happened that the same servant or ox had several masters? For either the nearer master was the servant of another master, as Ziba, who had twenty servants, was the servant of Mephibosheth, or the name of master comprehends, along with the head of the household, also his wife and sons, especially the firstborn.

units.la: VI. Præterea pluralia illa ad Deum significandum passim vsurpantur siue Deus hominem alloquatur siue homo Deum, siue Deus de se ipso aliquid narret siue homo de Deo. Id quod etiam ab earum linguarum vsu abhorret, in quibus vsuenit vt pluralis numerus vsurpetur de vno honoris gratia. Nunquam enim quisquam Regis aut Imperatoris historiam scribens, vt vt eum honorare voluerit, plurali nomine eum insigniuit, ne semel quidem, nedum sæpissimè. Adde quod in Nouo Testamento, quo Deus magis quàm vetere honoratur, nullum tamen nomen de Deo pluraliter vsurpatur. Nimirum reuelatis distinctè tribus personis diuinis, Patre Filio & Spiritu Sancto, nihil opus fuit obscura illa pluralitatis personarum diuinarum per numerum eiusmodi pluralem insinuatione. Nam si honoris causa Deus esset plurali nomine appellatus in Veteri Testamento, cur eiusmodi honore priuaretur in Nouo?
units.tr: VI. Moreover, those plural forms are used throughout to signify God, whether God addresses a human being or a human being addresses God, and whether God speaks of himself or a human speaks of God. This also runs against the usage of those languages in which a plural is sometimes used of one person out of respect. For no one who writes the history of a king or emperor, wishing to honour him, has ever given him a plural name, not even once, let alone very often. Add that in the New Testament, where God is honoured more than in the Old, no name of God is nevertheless used in the plural. Clearly, once the three divine persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, were revealed distinctly, there was no need to hint obscurely at the plurality of the divine persons by such a plural number. For if God had been called by a plural name in the Old Testament out of respect, why would he be deprived of that honour in the New?

units.la: VII. Hæc eadem personarum diuinarum pluralitas apertius innuitur eodem cap. 1. Genef. N[?]. 26. & dixit Deus, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram secundum similitudinem nostram &c. Cohortatio est ad alias personas creatrices. Vtitur enim & verbo & affixis seu pronominibus pluralis numeri. Non dicit faciam, sed faciamus; non imaginem meam, sed imaginem nostram; non similitudinem meam, sed similitudinem nostram, neque isto loquendi modo tam dissimili praecedentibus utitur temerè, sed certo consilio, ut nobis, in quorum gratiam scripta est illa historia innuat aliquid, quod meditando & ruminando attentè perpendamus. Ut enim in historia Melchisedeci quae Gen. cap. 14. habetur, sic in ista diuinissima historia, nihil est frustrà. Ne quod igitur relinquatur Aduersarijs effugium, sic diuidendo procedamus.
units.tr: VII. This same plurality of the divine persons is indicated more openly in the same first chapter of Genesis, verse 26: God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, etc. This is an exhortation addressed to the other persons who create. For it uses a plural verb and plural pronouns and suffixes. It does not say "I will make" but "let us make"; not "my image" but "our image"; not "my likeness" but "our likeness." Nor does it use this manner of speaking, so unlike what precedes, carelessly, but with a definite purpose, so that it may hint at something to us, for whose sake that history was written, which we should weigh carefully by meditating and pondering. For just as nothing is in vain in the history of Melchizedek in Genesis chapter 14, so in this most divine history nothing is in vain. So that the adversaries have no way of escape left, let us proceed by dividing the question in this way.

units.la: VIII. Aut Deus verbis illis personam aliquam alloquitur, aut nullam. Nullam nemo sanus dixerit. Agit enim rem maximé seriam. Non alloquitur nihil. Non alloquitur creaturas brutas, quae neque sermonis intelligentes, neque creationis Adami causae efficientes, neque exemplaria ad quorum imaginem homo crearetur fuerunt; sed alloquitur sine dubio & cohortatur ad opus absoluendū hominis creatione eas personas, quae creationis mundi causae fuerunt. Vel igitur suam ipsius unicam personam sic cohortatur, vel alias. Prius Aduersarijs maximè placuisse videtur. Eorum igitur responsiones audiamus.
units.tr: VIII. Either God addresses some person in those words, or none. No sane person would say none. For he is dealing with a most serious matter. He is not addressing nothing. He is not addressing brute creatures, which neither understood speech, nor were efficient causes in the creation of Adam, nor were the patterns according to whose image man was to be created; but he undoubtedly addresses and exhorts to the completion of the work of man's creation those persons who were the causes of the creation of the world. Either, then, he exhorts his own single person in this way, or others. The former seems to have pleased the adversaries most. Let us therefore hear their answers.

units.la: I X. Schlichtingius orditur ab objectione. Si verbum, inquit, singularis numeri de Deo vsurpatum, cuius rei innumera sunt exempla, unitatem personae diuinae non arguit; quid iuris habebit verbum plurale, ut plures personas in Deo designet? Mirum est si non vidit hoc quicquid est posse retorqueri. Si verbum plurale de Deo usurpatum pluralitatem personarum diuinarum non arguit, quid iuris habebit verbum singulare, ut unitatem personae diuinae designet? Si verbi singularitas personae unitatem significat, cur non similiter pluralitas designabit pluralitatem? Caeterum si verbum singularis numeri unitatem personae perpetuò significaret, prosectò Pater & Filius, una essent persona: verbum enim singularis numeri de iis duobus conjunctis interdum usurpatur, ut 1. Thess. 3. 11. Apoc. 11. 15. &c. Necnon ob eandem causam Mardochaeus & Esther Esth. 9. 29. 31. uxor & eius liberi Exod. 21. 4. Maria & Aaron Num. 12. 1.
units.tr: IX. Schlichting begins with an objection. If a verb of the singular number used of God, of which there are countless examples, does not prove the unity of the divine person, he says, what force will a plural verb have, to designate several persons in God? It is surprising that he did not see that this objection can be turned back on itself. If a plural verb used of God does not prove the plurality of the divine persons, what force will a singular verb have, to designate the unity of the divine person? If the singularity of the verb signifies the unity of the person, why will plurality not likewise signify plurality? Moreover, if a verb of the singular number always signified the unity of the person, then surely the Father and the Son would be one person; for a verb of the singular number is sometimes used of those two joined together, as in 1 Thess. 3:11 and Rev. 11:15, etc. And for the same reason Mordecai and Esther are used with a singular verb in Esth. 9:29, 31; a wife and her children in Exod. 21:4; Miriam and Aaron in Num. 12:1.

units.la: X. Respondet autem his verbis. Num vero, inquit, novum est & inusitatum, ut una persona pluralem de se numerum usurpet? Quod scimus, inquit Christus de seipso, loquimur, & quod vidimus testamur; & testimonium nostrum non accipitis. Ioh. 3. cui assimilabimus Regnum Dei? Mar. 4. 30. confer cum loco Luca 13. 18. Sic Paulus de seipso, Rom. 1. 5. Per quem accepimus Apostolatum in obedientiam fidei inter omnes gentes. Heb. 13. 18. Confidimus quod bonam conscientiam habeamus, in omnibus honestè volentes conversari. Plena sunt eiusmodi locutionum omnia: inprimis autem talis Enallage locum habet, quoties loquuntur, aut loquentes inducuntur personae, quae cum aliqua autoritate & dignitate constituta sunt, quaeque sunt cum imperio? Non est id quidem certè novum & inusitatum apud Graecos & Latinos, sed notum est & inusitatum apud Hebraeos, apud autores Veteris Testamenti, cuius nunc autoritate pugnamus. Nullus in eo homo, nulla persona in autoritate & dignitate constituta, nullus sacerdos, nullus Iudex, nullus Rex de se solo plurali numero loquitur.
units.tr: X. He replies to these words as follows. Is it then new and unusual, he says, for one person to use a plural number of himself? What we know, says Christ of himself, we speak, and what we have seen we testify; and you do not receive our testimony (John 3). To what shall we liken the kingdom of God? Mark 4:30; compare with the passage in Luke 13:18. So Paul of himself, Rom. 1:5: Through whom we have received apostleship to bring about obedience of faith among all nations. Heb. 13:18: We are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honourably in all things. All such expressions abound; and above all such an enallage has its place whenever persons who are set in some authority and dignity, and who have power, speak or are introduced as speaking. This is indeed not new and unusual among Greeks and Latins, but it is well known and unusual among the Hebrews, in the authors of the Old Testament, by whose authority we are now contending. No man in it, no person set in authority and dignity, no priest, no judge, no king speaks of himself alone in the plural number.

units.la: XI. Quorcirca mirari satis non possum breuem Hugonis Grotij ad hunc V. 26. Faciamus &c annotationem. Mos est, inquit, Hebraeis de Deo, ut de Rege loqui. Reges res magnas agunt de consilio primorum. 1. Reg. xii. 6. 11. Paral. x. 9, Sic & Deus 1. Reg. xxii. 20. Paucis enim istis verbis multa peccat. Primò Deus non inducitur sic loquens more Regum Hebraeorum. Nemo enim Regum, ut dixi, in libris Veteris Testamenti de se loquitur numero plurali. Deinde verbis, Faciamus hominem, non continetur deliberatio aut consultatio, sed cohortatio tantum. Tum loca 1. Reg. xii. 6. 11. Paral. x. 9. non sunt huic nostro similia. Illic Roboam petit consilium à senibus primùm, deinde à Juvenibus, hîc Deus omnino consilium non petit. Et quis ei à consilijs fuisset? cum quo iniisset consilium? Denique locus 1. Reg. xxii. 20. nec similis est loco 1. Reg. xii. 6. nec isti Gen. 1. 26. Non illi: Deus enim non dicit circumstantibus, ut Roboamus, date consilium quid sim dicturus aut facturus, sed duntaxat, quis decipiet Achab &c. Non exquirit consilium sed explorat voluntatem. Nec isti. Illic enim visio prophetica proponitur, hic narratur res gestae: illic omnis exercitus coelorum à dextris & à sinistris Dei stetisse dicitur, hic nihil tale memoratur: illic Deus Angelos bonos & malos alloquitur, hic vero nihil alloquitur praeter Deum creatorem hominis: illic tentat creaturarum voluntatem, praesertim malarum, hic non tentat, non explorat quemquam, sed cohortatur duntaxat, & quidem etiam semetipsum, Angelos vero neutiquam.
units.tr: XI. Therefore I cannot sufficiently wonder at Hugo Grotius's brief note on this verse 26, Let us make, etc. It is the custom, he says, for the Hebrews to speak of God as of a king. Kings do great things with the counsel of the chief men (1 Kings 12:6, 11; 1 Chron. 10:9). So also God (1 Kings 22:20). For in these few words he errs in many ways. First, God is not introduced speaking in the manner of the Hebrew kings. For no king, as I have said, in the books of the Old Testament speaks of himself in the plural number. Next, by the words Let us make man no deliberation or consultation is contained, but only an exhortation. Then the passages in 1 Kings 12:6, 11 and 2 Chron. 10:9 are not like this one of ours. There Rehoboam first seeks counsel from the elders, then from the young men; here God does not seek counsel at all. And who would have been his counsellor? With whom would he have taken counsel? Finally, the passage in 1 Kings 22:20 is not like 1 Kings 12:6, nor like that of Genesis 1:26. Not like the former: for God does not say to those standing by, as Rehoboam did, give counsel as to what I am to say or do, but only, who will deceive Ahab, etc. He does not seek counsel but tests the will. Nor is it like the latter. For there a prophetic vision is set forth, here a deed done is narrated; there the whole host of heaven is said to have stood at God's right hand and left, here nothing of the kind is recorded; there God addresses good and bad angels, here he addresses no one except God the Creator of man; there he tests the will of the creatures, especially the wicked ones, here he does not test or examine anyone, but only exhorts, and that indeed himself, but in no way the angels.

units.la: XII. Testimonia quae laudat Schlictingius ad rem nihil faciunt duabus de causis. Primò quia petita sunt è Nouo Testamento graecè & ad graecos scripto; ac propterea non possunt infirmare argumentum ductum ab visu linguae Hebraeae & stilo Veteris Testamenti. Secundò quia reuera in illis pluralis numerus de vna sola persona non vsurpatur. Nam quod attinet ad primum, quemadmodum verba, testimonium nostrum non accipitis, non de solo Nicodemo, sed de eo & sociis eius Pharisaeis vel doctoribus accipienda sunt, sic antecedentia, Quod scimus loquimur, & quod vidimus testamur, non de solo Christo, sed de eo & aliis eiusdem veritatis fidelibus testibus intelligi debet, quos sibi Christus plurali numero vtens adjungit, ne posset objici, nec vnius testimonium validum esse, nec mirum esse si nouum eius vnius inuentum doctor Israëlis Nicodemus nesciret. Marc. 4.30. cui assimilabimus Regnum Dei, Ego scilicet, & vos. Communicatio est rhetorica ad excitandos auditores, quos alloquitur, accommodata, quam figuram Marcus expressit, Lucas omisit. Rom. 1. 15. Per quem accepimus Apostolatum in obedientiam fidei inter omnes gentes. Accepimus ego scilicet & collegae: commune est plurium beneficium plurali numero cum vitandae arrogantiae causa, tum firmandae fidei gratia, insinuatâ testium pluralitate, significatum. Heb. 13. 18. Confidimus quod bonam conscientiam habeamus &c, scilicet ego & σωτῆρι [?]; Itaque vsus est verbo πεποίθαμεν [?] confidimus, haud satis, si de se solo loquutus fuisset, accommodato.
units.tr: XII. The testimonies which Schlichting cites do nothing to the point, for two reasons. First, because they are taken from the New Testament, written in Greek and for Greeks; and therefore they cannot weaken the argument drawn from the usage of the Hebrew language and the style of the Old Testament. Second, because in them the plural number is in fact not used of one person alone. For as regards the first point: just as the words you do not receive our testimony are to be understood not of Nicodemus alone, but of him and his fellow Pharisees or teachers, so the preceding words, we speak what we know, and testify what we have seen, should be understood not of Christ alone, but of him and the other faithful witnesses of the same truth, whom Christ joins to himself by using the plural number, so that it could not be objected either that one witness's testimony is not valid, or that it is no wonder that Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, did not know the novelty of this one man's discovery. Mark 4:30, To what shall we liken the kingdom of God? I, namely, and you. This is a rhetorical communication, suited to rousing the hearers whom he addresses, a figure which Mark expressed and Luke omitted. Rom. 1:15, Through whom we have received apostleship to bring about obedience of faith among all nations. We received it: I, namely, and my colleagues. A plural benefit is indicated in the plural number, both for the sake of avoiding arrogance and for the sake of confirming faith, by hinting at the plurality of witnesses. Heb. 13:18, We are confident that we have a good conscience, etc., namely I and my companions; and so he used the verb [πεποίθαμεν] we are confident, which would not have been quite suitable if he had spoken of himself alone.

units.la: XIII. Poterat Schlictingius similes locos ex antiquo Instrumento proferre. Gen. 29. 27. Exple hebdomadem huius; posteà dabimus tibi hanc, Ego scilicet vxor & fratres mei. Vt eximat omnem dubitationem Iacobo suam & aliorum, quorum intererat, voluntatem praestat. Alij singulari numero vertunt, 70. δώσω, vulg. dabo, vatab. locabitur, Munst. dabitur &c. 2. Sam. 16. 20. Dixit Abscalom ad Achitophel, inite consilium, nempe tu & alij consiliarij, quid agere debeamus ego & viri Israëlis qui sunt mecum. 1. Reg. 22. 3. Dixit Rex Israëlis ad servos suos, ignoratis quod nostra sit Ramoth Galead, & negligimus eam tollere de manu regis Syria. Nostrum & negligimus dixit modestè seruos suos le-cum[?] negligentiae blandè accusans, quod rem non suam vnius tantùm, sed totius gentis communem, vrbem nimirum Israëlis, vrbem perfugij sibi à Syris ereptam recuperare neglexissent. Iob. 18. 2. 3. Quando tandem imponetis finem sermonibus? Attendite & postea loquemur. Cur reputamur ut iumenta & immundi sumus in oculis vestris? loquitur Bildad Suhites & ad Iobum ac socios eius ut exprimit Elihu Iob. 35. 4. & de se & socijs suis. Dan. 2. 36. Hoc est somnium, interpretationem quoque dicemus coram Rege, Ego scilicet & socij mei Sidrach, Misach, & Abdenago, quorum precibus adjutus fuerat Ꝑ[?].17. 18. quosque Deo gratias agens jam sibi adjunxerat Ꝑ[?].23. Cantico cant. 1.4. Trahe me post te curremus & c Ego scilicet & puellae meae, vel de se pluraliter loquitur sponsa, id est, Ecclesia, quia non est una tantum persona, sed multarum collectio.
units.tr: XIII. Schlichting could have brought forward similar passages from the Old Testament. Gen. 29. 27. "Fulfil the week of this one; afterwards we will give you this one," meaning I, my wife and my brothers. To remove all doubt, he makes clear the will of Jacob and of the others whose concern it was. Others render it in the singular: the Seventy, I will give (δώσω); the Vulgate, I will give; Vatablus, it will be let; Münster, it will be given, and so on. 2 Sam. 16. 20. Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give counsel," that is, you and the other counsellors, "what we ought to do," I and the men of Israel who are with me. 1 Kings 22. 3. "The king of Israel said to his servants, Do you not know that Ramoth Gilead is ours, and we are negligent in taking it out of the hand of the king of Syria?" Here "ours" and "we are negligent" is modest speech by the king, who gently accuses his servants of negligence, because they had failed to recover a town that was not his alone but common to the whole nation: the city of Israel, a city of refuge snatched from the Syrians. Job 18. 2, 3. "How long will you put an end to words? Consider, and afterwards we will speak. Why are we reckoned as beasts, and are unclean in your eyes?" Bildad the Shuhite speaks to Job and his companions, as Elihu expresses at Job 35. 4, and speaks of himself and his companions. Dan. 2. 36. "This is the dream; we will also tell the interpretation before the king," meaning I and my companions Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, by whose prayers he had been helped (Dan. 2. 17, 18), and whom, giving thanks to God, he had already joined to himself (Dan. 2. 23). Song of Songs 1. 4. "Draw me after you, we will run," etc. I and my maidens; or the bride speaks in the plural of herself, that is, the Church, because she is not one person only but a gathering of many.

units.la: XIV. Uno verbo nullus occurrit locus in Scriptura, in quo una persona de se sola plurali numero loquatur. Abhorret Scriptura ab istiusmodi Enallage. Aut igitur hoc loco est Enallage numeri & ponitur pluralis pro singulari, aut non est Enallage, sed reuera pluralis numerus plures significat. Prius dici non potest obstante more perpetuo Scripturae. Posterius igitur verum est Reuera enim Deus sic pluraliter loquitur, ut se accommodet, aut ad usitatum apud homines loquendi morem, aut ad rem ipsam. Non prius. Homines enim nunquam sic de ipsis loquuntur in Scriptura. Non est eorum hic mos loquendi. Posterius igitur dicendum est. Atque hoc est primum argumentum, quo huiusmodi Enallagem ab his Dei verbis depellimus.
units.tr: XIV. In a word, no passage occurs in Scripture in which one person speaks of himself alone in the plural number. Scripture shrinks from such an enallage. Therefore either there is an enallage of number in this place, and the plural is put for the singular, or there is no enallage, and the plural in truth signifies several. The former cannot be said, since the constant manner of Scripture stands in the way. The latter is therefore true. For God speaks in the plural in such a way as to accommodate himself either to the customary manner of speaking among men or to the thing itself. Not the former: men never speak of themselves in this way in Scripture; it is not their manner of speaking. So the latter must be said. This is the first argument by which we drive this kind of enallage away from these words of God.

units.la: XV. Secundum argumentum ex eo peti potest, quod nunquam pluralis numerus de unico singulari usurpatur, nisi cum singulare illud habet commune cum alijs nomen, communemque naturam aut conditionem secundum quam spectatur. Hoc clarum faciam paucis exemplis. Matth. 2. 20. defuncti sunt enim qui quaerebant animam pueri. Illi enim plures fuerant, Herodes videlicet & satellites eius. Illo autem sublato, causa principali, hi eius instrumenta esse desierunt. Matth. 9. 8. Glorificauerunt Deum, qui dedit potestatem talem hominibus. plurale hominibus positum est pro singulari homini: plures enim sunt homines, & Christus spectabatur secundum naturam humanam illiusque conditionem pluribus communem, cuius ratione nihil ab alijs hominibus differre videbatur. Matth. 27. 44. Idipsum autem & latrones qui crucifixi erant cum eo exprobrabant ei. Non potuisset latrones pro latrone, nisi reuera & duo fuissent latrones crucifixi cum Christo & id vnus ex illis fecisset secundum communem sibi cum socio prauitatem & nequitiam, quam ab altero singulari priuilegio & misericordia Christus abstulit, alioqui similiter communicaturo. 1. Cor. 15. 19. Alioqui quid facient qui baptisantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non resurgunt? mihi videtur esse Enallage numeri, pro mortuis id est, pro mortuo. Nam si omnino mortui non resurgunt, Christus unus est ex mortuis, nihilque ab aliis mortuis differt, neque ab eo plus boni sperandum est quàm à quouis alio mortuo, ac propterea non minus & stulti & miseri sunt qui eius causa baptisantur, quàm si propter quemuis alium mortuum baptisarentur, quod ut insinuaret Apostolus plurali illo usus esse videtur. Non enim solet pluralis numerus pro singulari usurpari, nisi cum unus è pluribus significatur, & quidem indefinitè, aut saltem secundum communem quandam naturam vel conditionem. Id quod Gen. 1. 26. locum non habet. Nam si Deus unica est persona, & plures esse personas diuinas implicat contradictionem, nihil eo loco memoratur pluribus commune, nec spectatur Deus secundum naturam aut conditionem pluribus communem ullo modo. Nomen enim Deus, quo sensu hic accipitur, eius unius proprium est, sicuti etiam natura diuina, & ratio creatoris. Quare non est eo loco enallage numeri.
units.tr: XV. A second argument can be drawn from the fact that the plural number is never used of a single individual unless that singular shares with others a name and a common nature or condition under which it is viewed. I will make this clear with a few examples. Matt. 2. 20. "For they are dead who sought the life of the child." Those were several: Herod and his soldiers. But when the principal cause was removed, they ceased to be his instruments. Matt. 9. 8. "They glorified God, who gave such power to men." The plural "men" is put for the singular "man": there are many men, and Christ was viewed according to human nature and its condition, which is shared by many, and so in this respect he seemed to differ in nothing from other men. Matt. 27. 44. "And the robbers who were crucified with him likewise reproached him." The plural "robbers" could not stand for one robber unless two robbers had indeed been crucified with Christ, and one of them had done this out of the wickedness and malice he shared with his companion, from which Christ freed the other by a singular privilege and mercy, since the other would otherwise have shared it too. 1 Cor. 15. 19. "Otherwise what will they do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all?" It seems to me to be an enallage of number: "for the dead" that is, "for the dead man." For if the dead do not rise at all, Christ is one of the dead and differs in nothing from the other dead, nor is more good to be hoped from him than from any other dead person. Therefore those who are baptized for his sake are no less foolish and wretched than if they were baptized for any other dead man; and the Apostle, to suggest this, seems to have used the plural. For the plural is not usually put for the singular except when one of several is meant, and that indefinitely, or at least according to some common nature or condition. This does not apply to Gen. 1. 26. For if God is a single person, and several divine persons imply a contradiction, then nothing common to several is mentioned in that place, nor is God viewed in any way according to a nature or condition common to several. For the name God, in the sense in which it is taken here, belongs properly to that one, as does the divine nature and the character of Creator. Therefore there is no enallage of number in that place.

units.la: XVI. Tertium Argumentum mihi Dei sapientia suppeditat huius historiæ autoris, Is enim nihil temerè, nihil frustrà facit. Non igitur usus est inutili & periculosa Enallage numeri. Inutilem dico; quis enim eius est usus? quæ ratio afferri potest, cur satius fuerit eo loco pluralem numerum pro singulari, quàm singulare pro seipso ponere? Non enim propter Deum id scriptum est, sed propter nostram instructionem & ædificationem. Nulla autem ex eiusmodi Enallage seu permutatione numeri ad nos utilitas redire potest. Addo periculosam.: implicat enim lectorem, & peregrinitate sua remoratur, & ad credendam pluralitatem personarum diuinarum, ut experientia docet, inducit, multumque negotii Iudæis & Aduersariis nostris eam confiteri nolentibus facescit. Quis igitur credat Deum prudentissimum in tam excellenti historia, in loco tam illustri, figuram alias raram sine ratio-ne, sine ullo usu, (nam ne quidem ad ornatum sermonis quicquam confert) ac cum periculo seducendi lectorem, usurpare voluisse?
units.tr: XVI. The third argument is supplied to me by the wisdom of God, the author of this history, for he does nothing rashly and nothing in vain. Therefore he did not use a useless and dangerous enallage of number. I say useless: for what use is it? What reason can be given why it would have been better in that place to put the plural for the singular than the singular for itself? For this was not written for God's sake but for our instruction and edification, and no advantage can come back to us from this kind of enallage or change of number. I add dangerous: for it entangles the reader, delays him with its strangeness, and, as experience teaches, leads him to believe in a plurality of divine persons, and causes great trouble for the Jews and our opponents, who are unwilling to confess it. Who then would believe that God, the most prudent, wished to use in so excellent a history, in so illustrious a place, a figure otherwise rare, without reason, without any use (for it does not even contribute anything to the ornament of speech), and with the danger of leading the reader astray?

units.la: XVII. Dicent sine dubio Aduersarij, Deum de se solo plurali numero, quamuis vnica sit persona, loquutum esse; quia vt ita loqueretur poscebat linguae cuiusuis vsus, vel etiam necessitas. Nam (quae secunda est ad locum Gen. 1. 16. Schlichtingij responsio) vsitatissimum est, inquit, in omnibus linguis, vt is qui aliquid apud se ipsum decernit, & seipse ad aliquid faciendum cohortatur, licet vnus tantum sit, plurali numero subiunctiuo vtatur; cum singularis Imperatiui prima persona nullus detur. Itaque illius loco omnes vtuntur plurali subiunctiuo primae personae: nam singularis cum futuro conuenit. Exempla passim occurrunt. Sic Hannibal apud Liuium venenum hausturus; liberemus diuturna cura populum Romanum. Sic Patus Thrasea apud Tacitum, cum mori iussus sanguine humum respersisset; liberus, inquit, Ioui liberatori. Quomodo vsitatissimum est, si in sacra Scriptura, cuius vnius testimonijs & auctoritate nituntur vtrique, non est vsitatum? Quomodo exempla passim occurrunt, si ne vnum quidem proferre potuit e sacris literis Schlichtingius? Quomodo etiam id dicit esse vsitatissimum in omnibus linguis, cum sint linguae multae, Hebræa inprimis, quae ne subiunctiuum quidem habeant?
units.tr: XVII. Our opponents will doubtless say that God spoke of himself in the plural number, although he is one person, because the usage of any language, or even necessity, required him to speak thus. For (this is the second answer of Schlichting to the passage Gen. 1. 26): "It is most usual in all languages, he says, that one who decides something within himself and exhorts himself to do something, although he be only one, uses the plural subjunctive, since no first person of the singular imperative exists. Therefore in its place all use the plural subjunctive of the first person, for the singular agrees with the future. Examples occur everywhere." So Hannibal in Livy, about to drink the poison: "Let us free the Roman people by lasting care." So Paetus Thrasea in Tacitus, when ordered to die and having sprinkled the ground with blood: "Let us pour," he said, "to Jupiter the liberator." "How is it most usual, if it is not usual in Sacred Scripture, on whose testimony and authority both sides rest? How do examples occur everywhere, if Schlichting could not bring forward even one from the sacred letters? How also does he say that this is most usual in all languages, since there are many languages, Hebrew above all, which do not even have a subjunctive?"

units.la: XVIII. Multae aliae sunt inter Hebræam & Latinam linguam differentiae: Hæc comprimis, quod Latinè licet de se vno loqui plurali numero, Hebraicè non item. Itaque frustrà laborant Aduersarij, cum exempla petunt è lingua latina: Et tamen quae duo ex Tito Liuio & Cornelio Tacito colligere potuerunt, ea de pluribus exponi possunt. Liberemus diuturna cura Populum Romanum, Ego scilicet & vos, vos afferendo & præbendo mihi venenum, ego illud hauriendo, sunt enim verba Hannibalis poscentis venenum, seruosque suos aut amicos alloquentis, venenum, inquit Liuius, quod multò ante præparatum ad tales habebat casus, poposcit. Liberemus, inquit, diuturna cura Populum Romanum &c. Similiter Thrasea cum pronunciaret ista verba, Libemus Ioui liberatori, non se vnum alloquebatur, sed se simul & consulis quaestorem. Accepto, inquit Tacitus, Senatusconsulto Heluidium & Demetrium in cubiculum inducit, porrectisque vtriusque brachij venis, postquam cruorem effudit, humum super spargens, propius vocato quaestore, Libemus, inquit, Ioui liberatori: spectla Iuuenis &c. Libemus, Ego & tu. Alludit ad sacrificia Romanorum. Libabat enim non solus sacerdos, sed post cum etiam astantes. Ominatur quæstori similem casum, eumque exemplo suo confirmat.
units.tr: XVIII. There are many other differences between the Hebrew and the Latin language; this above all: in Latin one may speak of oneself alone in the plural number, but in Hebrew not so. Therefore the opponents labour in vain when they seek examples from the Latin language. Yet the two passages they could gather from Titus Livy and Cornelius Tacitus can be explained of several persons. "Let us free the Roman people by lasting care": I and you, you by offering and giving me the poison, I by drinking it. For these are the words of Hannibal asking for poison and addressing his servants or friends. "The poison," says Livy, "which he had long before prepared for such chances, he asked for. Let us free," he says, "the Roman people by lasting care," etc. Similarly, when Thrasea uttered those words, "Let us pour to Jupiter the liberator," he was not addressing himself alone but at the same time the quaestor. "Having received, says Tacitus, the decree of the Senate, he brings Helvidius and Demetrius into the chamber, and, their arm-veins having been opened, after he had poured out blood, sprinkling it over the ground, calling the quaestor nearer, 'Let us pour,' he says, 'to Jupiter the liberator; behold, young man,' etc." "Libemus": I and you. He alludes to Roman sacrifices, for not only the priest made the libation but afterwards also the bystanders. He foretells a similar fate for the quaestor and confirms it by his own example.

units.la: XIX. Sed fortasse fœlicius pugnat Schlich-tingius ratione quàm exemplis. Is enim responsioni suæ rationem quandam inseruit his verbis, cum singularis Imperativi prima persona nullus detur. Itaque illius loco omnes utuntur plurali subjunctivo prima persona: nam singularis cum futuro convenit. Qui omnes? Hebræi? de his enim solis quæstio nunc est. Atqui, ut iam dixi, ne subjunctivum quidem modum habent, pro eo utuntur ut plurimum futuro, uti etiam ab ipso Deo factum est hoc loco: נעשה[?] enim, quod per subjunctivum faciamus redditur, est prima pluralis futuri, qua utuntur Hebræi cum se & alios alloquuntur & hortantur. At cum persona una apud se aliquid decernit, aut se solam cohortatur, utitur prima singularis futuri, ut Exod. 3.3. Esai.5.1. Ier. 5.5. Hos.2.7. Cantic. 3.2. Ps. 39. 1. &c. Ipse etiam Deus eandem primam singularem eodem modo de seipso usurpat passim, ut Gen. 2. 17. & 6. 7. & 18. 21. Deut. 32. 20. Psal. 12. 6. &c. Aberrat igitur vehementer Schlichtingius & à veritate, cum asserit visitatissimum esse in lingua Hebræa, ut is qui aliquid apud se decernit &c plurali numero subjunctivi utatur, & à scopo cum exempla, aut rationem affert è lingua Latina.
