Singularis, inquit, Imperativi prima persona nullus datur. Quid tum? Ergo ei, qui aliquid faciendum apud se decernit, aut se ad aliquid faciendum hortatur, utendum est plurali numero subjunctivi? Non sequitur. Potest enim uti prima singulari subjunctivi, aut potius, si Hebraicè loquitur, Futuri. At prima singularis subjunctivi cum Futuro convenit. Ita quidem in tertia & quarta conjugatione verborum latinorum, Sed quid hoc impedit, quominus Hebræi æquè prima singulari ac prima plurali Futuri pro subjunctivo utantur?
units.tr: XIX. But perhaps Schlichtingius fights more successfully with argument than with examples. In his reply he inserts a certain argument in these words: "since no first person of the singular imperative is given, all therefore use the first person of the plural subjunctive in its place, for the singular agrees with the future." Who are "all"? The Hebrews? It is only of them that the question now concerns. But, as I have already said, they do not even have a subjunctive mood. In its place they mostly use the future, as God himself did in this passage: נעשה [naʻaseh], which is rendered "let us make" by the subjunctive, is the first person plural of the future, which the Hebrews use when they address and exhort themselves and others. But when one person decides something for himself, or exhorts only himself, he uses the first person singular of the future, as in Exod. 3.3; Isa. 5.1; Jer. 5.5; Hos. 2.7; Song 3.2; Ps. 39.1, etc. God himself also uses the same first person singular of himself in the same way throughout, as in Gen. 2.17; 6.7; 18.21; Deut. 32.20; Ps. 12.6, etc. Schlichtingius therefore greatly errs and strays from the truth when he asserts that it is most common in the Hebrew language that one who decides something for himself, etc., uses the plural number of the subjunctive; and he misses the mark when he brings examples or an argument from the Latin language. "The first person singular of the imperative," he says, "is not given." So what? Must one who decides within himself that something is to be done, or exhorts himself to do something, therefore use the plural of the subjunctive? It does not follow. He may use the first person singular of the subjunctive, or rather, if he is speaking Hebrew, of the future. And the first person singular of the subjunctive "agrees with the future." Indeed it does so in the third and fourth conjugations of Latin verbs. But what prevents the Hebrews from using the first person singular, just as much as the first person plural, of the future in place of the subjunctive?

units.la: XX. Si quis reponat, Deum de se solo sic plurali numero honoris causa locutum esse; Primùm id iam à me refutatum est. Deinde recurrit quæstio, quamobrem Deus sic de seipso honoris causa loqui voluisset hoc loco, potius quàm ijs locis, in quibus de se ipso loquitur honorificentissimè, ut cum exempli gratia, Legem promulgat, cum autoritatem sibi summam conciliat, cum magnificentissimè sese describit apud Prophetas? Tum, qui de se solo plurali numero loquitur, id modestiæ potius quàm honoris causa facere videtur. Est enim modestiæ sic de te loqui, quasi tibi ipsi soli nihil vendices, quasi quæ alij tibi fuerint præclaris de eo loqui quasi à pluribus productum esset, minuit magnitudinem opificis de eo loqui quasi ab aliis adjutus fuisset. Plus enim laudis meretur qui se solo maximum opus perficit, quàm qui pluribus adjuvantibus. Itaque exaggeratur virtus Dei & gloria amplificatur, cum dicitur solus extendere coelos Esai. 44. 19. solus facere mirabilia Psal. 72. 19. solus nosse corda hominum 1. Reg. 8. 31. solus esse Deus 2. Reg. 19. 15. Esai. 37. 15.
units.tr: XX. If someone should reply that God spoke of himself alone in the plural number out of honour, I have already refuted this first. Next the question recurs: why would God have wished to speak of himself in this way, out of honour, in this place rather than in those places where he speaks of himself most honourably, as when, for example, he promulgates the Law, when he claims for himself the highest authority, when he describes himself most magnificently before the Prophets? Moreover, one who speaks of himself alone in the plural seems to do so out of modesty rather than honour. For it is a mark of modesty to speak of yourself as though you claim nothing for yourself alone, as though what others have done well had been produced by many; it diminishes the greatness of a craftsman to speak of him as though he had been helped by others. For he who accomplishes a very great work alone deserves more praise than he who does so with many helping. Therefore the virtue of God is magnified and his glory enlarged when it is said that he alone stretches out the heavens (Isa. 44.19), alone does wonders (Ps. 72.19), alone knows the hearts of men (1 Kings 8.31), alone is God (2 Kings 19.15; Isa. 37.15).

units.la: XXIII. Adde quòd neque homines vti solent plurali numero pro singulari, cum rei de qua agitur gravitatem & magnitudinem exaggerare volunt, neque Deus item; qui cùm de rebus maximi momenti frequentissimè loquatur, ut cùm legem fert, cùm homini praescribit officium, cùm promittit, cùm comminatur, cùm se describit, cùm operum suorum magnitudinem exaggerat, cùm de redemptione nostra, quo nullum est praeclarius opus, verba facit &c singulari numero vtitur perpetuò, non solum in veteri, sed etiam in Novo Testamento, haud existimans de se pluraliter vel honorandi sui, vel exaggerandae rei causa sibi loquendum esse. Praeterea si rei de qua agebatur gravitas exaggeranda fuit, annon satis exaggeratur iis rebus quae de homine dicuntur, ut quod sit ad imaginem Dei conditus, & reliquorum animalium dominus constitutus &c? Quid igitur opus erat, ut ad eam exaggerandam Deus isto scilicet exaggerandi modo, tam incerto, tam obscuro, tam insolito, tam periculoso sine vlla necessitate vteretur ?
units.tr: XXIII. Add that neither do men customarily use the plural for the singular when they wish to heighten the weight and magnitude of the matter in question, nor does God either. Although he speaks very frequently about matters of the greatest moment, as when he gives the law, when he prescribes duty to man, when he promises, when he threatens, when he describes himself, when he magnifies the greatness of his works, when he speaks of our redemption, than which there is no more excellent work, he uses the singular number throughout, not only in the Old but also in the New Testament, never thinking that he must speak of himself in the plural either to honour himself or to heighten the matter. Moreover, if the weight of the matter under discussion was to be heightened, is it not heightened enough by the things said of man, such as that he was made in the image of God and appointed lord of the other animals, etc.? What need was there, then, for God to use to heighten it, that manner of heightening, so uncertain, so obscure, so unusual, so dangerous, without any necessity?

units.la: XXIV. Pergam igitur argumentari. Nemo, opinor, inficias ibit, quin pluralis numerus comparatus sit ad pluralem numerum, singularis ad singularem significandum; ac proinde non esse sine graui necessitate, aut singularem pro plurali, aut pluralem pro singulari accipiendum: sunt enim illi duo numeri & natura sua & hominum vsu inter se, non distincti modo, sed oppositi etiam. Ut igitur pluralem numerum pro plurali potius quàm pro singulari accipiamus, satis est causae, eam esse pluralis numeri propriam, vsitatam, naturalem significationem, à qua, nisi coactum, discedere interpretem haud decet. Ut verò pluralem pro singulari accipiamus, hoc est, oppositum pro opposito, causam esse oportet grauem, imò necessariam, & quae aliquo modo cogat. Quam igitur causam habent Aduersarij, cur nolint hoc loco pluralem numerum pluraliter exponi? Sunt enim verba Dei de re admodum graui loquentis, ac propterea summa cum religione & demissione animi tractanda, non vexanda, nec licenter interpretanda, praesertim cum de Deo dicantur, non aliunde quàm ex Dei verbis, salutariter noscendo. Aliam certè nullam habere possunt, quàm hanc vnam, quia nimirum plures esse personas diuinas impossibile sit. Quibus verò argumentis probant id esse impossibile? Testimonijs Scripturæ? nullo modo, sed rationibus philosophicis. Ita illis in hac de Deo controuersia Theologica summus iudex, hoc est, norma seu regula, non est Scriptura, sed philosophia. Afferunt enim è philosophia praejudicia quaedam, seu opiniones praeconceptas, ad quas ipsam Scripturam exigunt, & si minus congruit, vi quadam intorquent. Haud satis sani homines, qui Deum immensum pede & modulo creaturarum metiri volunt? qui cum ea ipsa, quæ oculis ipsorum quotidie obuersantur, perspecta non habeant (cui enim hominum id contigit?) tamen, quasi Deum haberent animo perceptum & comprehensum, malunt suo ipsorum ingenio, suis ratiocinijs philosophicis, quàm Dei sese reuelantis verbis (hæc enim ad illa exigunt, non contrà) fidere! Cæterum illorum rationes philosophicas suo lo-co Deo dante refutabimus. Interim nobis, qui nunc quidem in exquirenda Scripturæ sententia occupamur, satis sit, nostram sententiam cum Scripturæ verbis ad amussim congruere, à quibus sententia Aduersariorum ita discordat, vt cogantur plurale, repugnante eius propria & vsitata significatione, singulariter exponere.
units.tr: XXIV. I will therefore go on arguing. No one, I think, will deny that the plural number is used to signify the plural, and the singular to signify the singular; and consequently the singular is not to be taken for the plural, nor the plural for the singular, without a grave necessity. For those two numbers are distinct from one another, and opposed, both by their nature and by human usage. So, to take the plural number as plural rather than as singular, it is enough that this is its proper, customary, natural signification, from which an interpreter ought not to depart unless compelled. But to take the plural as singular, that is, the opposite for the opposite, there must be a grave and indeed necessary cause, one that in some way compels. What cause, then, do our opponents have for not wishing the plural number to be expounded as plural in this place? These are the words of God speaking about a very grave matter, and therefore they are to be handled with the utmost reverence and humility of mind, not mangled, nor interpreted at will, especially since they are said of God, and are to be known for salvation from nothing other than God's own words. They certainly can have no other cause than this one alone, namely that it is impossible for there to be several divine persons. But with what arguments do they prove that this is impossible? By testimonies of Scripture? By no means, but by philosophical reasons. Thus in this theological controversy about God, their supreme judge, that is, their norm or rule, is not Scripture but philosophy. For they bring from philosophy certain prejudices, or preconceived opinions, to which they force Scripture itself; and if it does not agree, they twist it by force. Are they not rather unsound men, who wish to measure the immense God by the foot and measure of creatures? They do not have a thorough knowledge of those very things which daily lie before their eyes (for who among men has ever achieved that?), and yet, as if they had God perceived and comprehended in their minds, they prefer to trust their own wit and their philosophical reasonings rather than the words of God revealing himself (for these are to be brought into line with those, not the reverse)! Moreover, we shall refute their philosophical arguments in their proper place, God willing. Meanwhile, for us, who are now occupied in seeking the sense of Scripture, it is enough that our opinion agrees exactly with the words of Scripture, from which the opinion of our opponents so differs that they are compelled to expound the plural in the singular, though its proper and customary signification opposes this.

units.la: XXV. Denique diligenter expendendum esse, quo numero Deus loquatur, plurali an singulari, docet nos Apostolus exemplo suo Gal. 3. 16. obseruat enim cum Abrahamo dictæ sunt promissiones, & Semini eius, Deum non dixisse, & feminibus, vt de multis, sed vt de vno, & semini tuo, qui est Christus. Quemadmodum igitur Deus, quoniam vnum quoddam singulare semen, non autem multa, intelligi voluit, constanter singulari numero vsus est, nunquam plurali; sic si voluisset vnicam tantum personam diuinam intelligi, nullo modo plures, singulari numero de se constanter loquutus fuisset, nunquam plurali. Cauisset enim pro sua summa prudentia & charitate, ne quam nobis errandi ansam præberet. Cum igitur videamus Deo tribui nomina, verba, pronomina, adjectiua singularis numeri, colligi-mus mus Deo conuenire vnitatem & singularitatem quandam. Rursus cum videamus ei tribui nomen pluralis numeri omnium primò & frequentissimè, necnon etiam interdum verba, pronomina, & adjectiua itidem pluralis numeri, colligimus similiter Deo convenire pluralitatem quandam. Pluralitas autem intelligi non potest attributorum aut effectuum, sed personarum. Nam & nomen personam significans, in plurali numero plures personas significat, non autem plura eiusdem personæ attributa vel effecta; & verba quoque & pronomina, & adjectiua, cum de persona vsurpantur, in plurali numero personas plures arguunt, non vnam tantùm.
units.tr: XXV. Finally, it must be carefully considered in which number God speaks, plural or singular. The Apostle teaches us this by his own example (Gal. 3.16): he observes that the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed, and that God did not say "and to seeds," as of many, but as of one, "and to your seed, who is Christ." Just as God, since he wished one single seed to be understood, and not many, used the singular number constantly and never the plural, so, if he had wished only one divine person to be understood, and not several, he would have spoken of himself constantly in the singular number and never in the plural. For in his great wisdom and love he would have taken care not to give us an occasion for error. Since, then, we see that the names, verbs, pronouns, and adjectives of the singular number are attributed to God, we gather that a unity and a certain singularity belong to God. Again, since we see that the name of the plural number is attributed to him first and most frequently, and sometimes also verbs, pronouns, and adjectives of the plural number, we likewise gather that a certain plurality belongs to God. But this plurality cannot be understood of attributes or effects, but of persons. For a name signifying a person, in the plural number, signifies several persons, not several attributes or effects of the same person; and verbs, pronouns, and adjectives too, when they are used of a person, in the plural number indicate several persons, not only one.

units.la: XXVI. His refutatis Aduersarij ad responsiones Iudæorum fortasse confugient, quorum alij Deum se & terram cohortari volunt, alij Angelos. Neutri recte. Non illi; cohortatur enim causas efficientes hominis, cuiusmodi causa terra non est vllo modo: ex ea quidem humani corporis materia sumpta est: sed materia patitur tantum, nihil efficit. Itaque ridiculus foret architectus, sutor, figulus, qui lapides, pannum, terram ad efficiendam domum, vestem, ollam cohortaretur. Deinde homo non est factus ad imaginem terræ, sed Dei, vt patet ex versu sequente; nec communis est vlla Dei & terræ imago ad quam homo sit factus, & eò pertinuit illa effectio, vt qui origine materiæ suæ terra erat, terræ perquam dissimilis fieret. Ac denique quominus terra intelligi possit obstat versus sequens, quo verborum illorum, Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram &c, executio describitur. Quos enim qui dixit faciamus hominem, hortatus est ad faciendum hominem, illi fecerunt hominem. Pluribus istam responsionem non refutabo: nimis enim mihi absurda videtur, quàm vt ab Aduersarijs probari possit. XXVII. Nec isti. Primum enim altum est in historia creationis de Angelis silentium. Cur, si ad eam intelligendam sunt necessarij? si fuerunt causæ efficientes hominis? si verbis illis faciamus hominem ad imaginē nostram, Deus eos compellauit? Cur etiam sacer autor non dixit, Et Deus dixit ad Angelos, Faciamus &c. siquidem ad Angelos hoc dixit, & dixisse ad eos intelligi voluit? Sic enim & quod res fuisset dixisset, & illis, qui pluralitatem personarum diuinarum agnoscere nolunt, non fixisset hoc in loco crucem. Deinde cur se & Angelos ad faciendum hominem ex- Vu citasset & hortatus esset, si Angeli hominem nullo modo secerunt? Eos enim hominem non fecisse ex eo intelligi potest, quod id nullo loco Scripturae affirmatur. Nunquam creatio vel mundi, vel hominis angelis tribuitur. Quod tam constans & perpetuum silentium maximi fieri debet, praesertim a nobis, quibus Scriptura merito suo regula est credendorum perfecta. Non modo autem illa Angelis non tribuitur, sed quod plus est soli Deo vendicatur, & quidem interdum plurali numero usurpato, ut Esai. 54. 4. Quoniam mariti tui, factores tui, Dominus exercituum nomen eius. Psal. 149. 2. Letetur Israel in factoribus suis; filij Sion exultent in Rege suo. Iob. 35. V. 10. vbi est Deus factores mei, dans cantica in nocte? &c.
units.tr: XXVI. Having refuted these views, the opponents will perhaps take refuge in the answers of the Jews, some of whom want God to be exhorting himself and the earth, others want it to be exhorting the angels. Neither is right. Not the first: the earth is not in any way an efficient cause of man, which is what an exhortation would require. It is true that the matter of the human body was taken from the earth, but matter only undergoes and contributes nothing to the making. So the builder, the cobbler or the potter would be ridiculous if he exhorted stones, cloth or clay to make a house, a garment or a pot. Further, man was not made in the image of the earth but of God, as the following verse makes plain, and there is no image common to God and the earth to which man could have been made, and that making could not have turned what was earth in its material origin into something utterly unlike earth. Finally, the following verse stands in the way of the earth being meant, since it describes the carrying out of the words Let us make man in our image, etc. For those whom he addressed in saying let us make man he exhorted to make man, and they made man. I shall not refute this answer at greater length, since it seems to me too absurd to be upheld by our opponents. XXVII. Nor is the second view right either. For first, there is a deep silence in the account of the creation about the angels. Why, if they were necessary for understanding it, if they were efficient causes of man, if God addressed them in the words let us make man in our image? Why did the sacred writer not say And God said to the angels, Let us make, etc., since if he said this to the angels, and wanted it to be understood that he spoke to them? For in that way he would both have said what was the case, and would not have fixed a cross in this place for those who refuse to acknowledge a plurality of divine persons. Next, why would he have summoned and exhorted the angels along with himself to make man, if the angels in no way made man? That the angels did not make man can be understood from the fact that this is nowhere affirmed in Scripture. Creation, whether of the world or of man, is never attributed to angels. Such a constant and perpetual silence ought to be given the greatest weight, especially by us, for whom Scripture, by its own merit, is the complete rule of what is to be believed. Yet not only is creation not attributed to the angels, but, what is more, it is claimed for God alone, and that sometimes with a plural noun used, as in Isaiah 54:5: For thy Makers are thy husband; the LORD of hosts is his name. Psalm 149:2: Let Israel rejoice in his Makers; let the children of Zion be joyful in their King. Job 35:10: But none saith, Where is God my Maker, who giveth songs in the night? etc.

units.la: XXVIII. Scripturae ratio succinit. Intelligi enim non potest quid ad creationem hominis conferre potuerint Angeli, vires creaturarum exsuperantem. Nec decet nos gloriam creationis generis humani absque expresso Dei testimonio vel mandato, creaturis tribuere. Meminisse enim nos convenit, Deum gloriam suam alteri non dare. Quod si Angeli nos una cum Deo creassent, essemus illorum opus, illisque eo nomine & gratias agere deberemus, & honorem exhibere. Quod tamen officium neque ullus Propheta vel Apostolus commendasse unquam legitur, nec sine manifesto idololatriae periculo fieri posset.
units.tr: XXVIII. The reasoning of Scripture agrees. For it cannot be understood what the angels could have contributed to the creation of man, a thing exceeding the powers of creatures. Nor is it fitting for us to attribute the glory of the creation of the human race to creatures without an express testimony or command of God. For we ought to remember that God does not give his glory to another. If the angels had made us together with God, we would be their work, and on that account we ought to give them thanks and render them honour. Yet no prophet or apostle is ever read to have commended this duty, nor could it be done without the manifest danger of idolatry.

units.la: XXI X. Sed nihil opus est argumentis aliunde conquisitis. Ipsa enim Dei verba hoc commentum respuunt. Faciamus, inquit, hominem ad imaginem nostram. Sumus ne igitur ad imaginem Dei & Angelorum facti? Dei; affirmat constanter utriusque testamenti Scriptura, Angelorum nunquam. Et sequitur continuo apud Mosem executio his verbis, Et Deus creavit hominem ad imaginem suam, verbo & pronomine singularis numeri cauens, ne angeli intelligantur, seu personae ab uno Deo diversae. Deinde aut eadem est Dei & Angelorum imago, aut diversae. Si diversae, dixisset Scriptura imagines, non perpetuo & constanter imaginem. Si eadem, esset eadem Dei & Angelorum natura. Quorum enim est eadem imago, eorum etiam est eadem natura.
units.tr: XXIX. But there is no need for arguments sought from elsewhere. For the words of God himself reject this invention. Let us, he says, make man in our image. Are we then made in the image of God and of the angels? Of God: the Scripture of both Testaments affirms this constantly; of the angels never. And immediately afterwards in Moses comes the carrying out, in these words: And God created man in his own image, using a verb and pronoun of the singular number to guard against the angels, or persons distinct from the one God, being understood. Next, either the image of God and of the angels is the same, or it is different. If different, Scripture would have said images, not constantly and always the image. If the same, the nature of God and of the angels would be the same. For those whose image is the same have also the same nature.

units.la: XXX. At Factus est homo similis Angelis; & brutis etiam animantibus prius creatis, ad quorum tamen imaginem factus dici non potest. Si ipsi etiam Angeli ad imaginem Dei creati fuerunt (quod tamen in Scriptura diversis[?] verbis non dicitur) mirum videri non debet, si, cum vtrique ad eiusdem Dei imaginem conditi fuerint, inter vtrosque similitudo intercedit non exigua. Sunt enim sine dubio inter se valdè similes ab eodem exemplari æquè immediatè expressæ imagines, quamuis propriè loquendo altera alterius nec exemplar, nec imago fit. Ita porrò ad imaginem Dei creati fuerunt Angeli & homines, vt tamen non eodem prorsus modo se habeat imago Dei in Angelis & in hominibus, sed satis diuersio.ld[?] quod explicare non est huius loci. Equidem hanc gloriam Deo creatori meo me debere arbitror, vt eum solum credam generis humani causam fuisse, vt finalem, sic efficientem, & exemplarem: Ex eo enim, & per eum, & in eum sunt omnia. Ei sit gloria in secula seculorum. Amen.
units.tr: XXX. But it is said, Man was made like the angels; and also like the living creatures created earlier, though he cannot be said to have been made in their image. If the angels themselves were also created in the image of God (which, however, is not said in Scripture in different words), it ought not to seem strange if, since both were made in the image of the same God, there is no small likeness between the two. For images equally immediately expressed from the same exemplar are without doubt very like one another, although, strictly speaking, neither becomes the exemplar or the image of the other. So then the angels and men were created in the image of God, but the image of God is not present in angels and in men in exactly the same way, but in a rather different manner, which it is not the place here to explain. For my part I think I owe this glory to God my creator, that I should believe him alone to have been the cause of the human race, as its final cause, and likewise its efficient and exemplary cause: For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: XXXI. Hic gradationem quandam deprehendere mihi videor. Primùm enim Deo tribuitur nomen pluralis numeri, quod, ne plures Deos significare putetur construitur cum verbis singularis numeri. Deinde Deus inducitur tanquam imperans alij personæ, quæ, ne putetur à Deo specie differre, etiam ipsa Deus vocatur. Tum Deus inducitur pluraliter loquens, ac se & alias personas creatrices ad hominem creandum excitans & cohortans; quæ, ne videantur aut Angeli esse, aut plures dij, statim nomine plurali Elohim junćto cum verbo & pronomine singularis numeri comprehenduntur. Denique, ne quis Enallagen numeri, aut tale quid, confingat, tam aperte pluralitas personarum significatur, vt omnis pertinacia expugnari possit, cum cap. 3. V.
units.tr: XXXI. Here I seem to detect a certain gradation. First, the name of the plural number is given to God, which, so that it should not be thought to mean several gods, is construed with verbs of the singular number. Next, God is introduced as commanding another person, who, so that he should not be thought to differ from God in kind, is himself also called God. Then God is introduced speaking in the plural, summoning and exhorting himself and the other creating persons to create man; and these, lest they seem to be angels or several gods, are at once comprehended by the plural name Elohim joined with a verb and pronoun of the singular number. Finally, lest anyone should invent an enallage of number or something of that kind, the plurality of persons is signified so openly that all obstinacy can be overcome, in chapter 3, verse

units.la: 22. Dominus Deus dicit; Ecce Adam quasi unus ex nobis factus est sciens bonum & malum. Negabuntne Aduersarij verbis, vnus ex nobis, pluralitatem personarum significari? Nonne jam vident Enallagem numeri, qua tanquam clypeo, aut potius ficulneis foliis se tegi sperabant, non esse de mente Dei?
units.tr: 22: The Lord God saith, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil. Will our opponents deny that the words as one of us signify a plurality of persons? Do they not already see that the enallage of number, behind which they hoped to shelter as behind a shield, or rather a fig-leaf, is not in the mind of God?

units.la: XXXII. Nondum tamen cedunt veritati. Intelligendum praeterea est, inquit VVolkelius, eadem verba ex Hebraico sic legi posse: Adam factus est tanquam vnus ex le[?] sciens bonum & malum: vt sensus sit, eum factum esse vnum eorum, qui ex seipsis sciunt bonum & malum. At, inquam, quominus sic legi aut verti possit, obstat primo vox אחד vnus. Dixisset enim simpliciter quasi ex se sciens, non vero quasi vnus ex se sciens. Quorsum enim illud vnus? Siccine vel Hebraei, vel Graeci, vel Latini loqui solent? Cum etiam Adami nomine ipsa quoque Heua comprehendatur, poscere videbatur non modo linguæ paritas, sed etiam res ipsa, vt vox vnus omitteretur? Deinde obstat vox sequens ממנו, quæ vel ablatiuus est pluralis pronominis primæ personæ אני, & significat ex nobis; vel ablatiuus singularis pronominis tertiæ הוא, & significat ex eo, nunquam ex se, ne apud Rabinos quidem: vtuntur illi potius vocibus מנפש & מעצמו. Deinde obstat constructio. Ita enim ממנו construeretur, non cum antecedente אחד, sed cum sequente לדעת, quod bis absurdum est. Nam, & ablatiuus, cui præfixa est præpositio מן, positus immediatè post nomen numerale אחד, cum eo construi debet, vt inductione probari potest; & idem si construi debuisset cum לדעת, ei fuisset postpositus. Si quid etiam intelligo, non dixisset Deus לדעת, sed sic potius concepisset illam sententiam כאחד מידעי מהם [?] quasi vnus ex scientibus à seipsis.
units.tr: XXXII. Yet they still do not yield to the truth. "It must further be understood," says Wolkelius, "that the same words can be read in Hebrew in this way: Adam became as one of them, knowing good and evil, so that the sense is that he became one of those who of themselves know good and evil." But I say that the following stands in the way of reading or translating it so: first the word אחד [echad, one]. For he would simply have said "as one knowing of himself", not "as one of those knowing of himself". For why that one? Do the Hebrews, the Greeks or the Latins usually speak so? And since the name Adam also includes Eve, did not the parity of the language, and the thing itself, seem to demand that the word one be omitted? Next, the following word ממנו [mimmenu] stands in the way: this is either the ablative of the plural of the first-person pronoun אני, and means from us; or the ablative of the singular of the third-person pronoun הוא, and means from him, never from himself, not even among the rabbis, who rather use the expressions מנפש [mi-nefesh] and מעצמו [me-atzmo]. Next, the construction stands in the way. For ממנו would then be construed not with the preceding אחד but with the following לדעת [le-da'at, to know], which is doubly absurd. For the ablative, with the preposition מן prefixed, placed immediately after the numeral אחד, must be construed with it, as induction can prove; and if it had had to be construed with לדעת, it would have been placed after it. If I understand anything, God would not have said לדעת, but would rather have conceived that sentence thus: כאחד מידעי מהם [ke-echad mi-yode'ei mehem, as one of those knowing from themselves], as one of those knowing from themselves.

units.la: XXXIII. Non modo autem eiusmodi versioni verba quibus Deus vsus est, & verborum constructio repugnant, sed res etiam ipsa. Affirmat enim VVolkelius, Deum, cum ad hunc modum loqueretur, ad illa serpentis verba respexisse: eritis sicut Dij scientes bonum & malum: in quibus nihil est quod respondeat verbis ex se. Non dicit serpens scientes ex vobis, sed simpliciter scientes. Immò pollicetur fore vt sciant bonum & malum non tam ex se ipsis, quam vi arboris scientiæ boni & mali. Ac propterea istud ex se à re qua de agebatur alienum censeri debet. Addi etiam potest, si accuratè loqui velimus, præter vnum Deum scire bonum & malum ex se neminem. Quid enim boni habent Angeli & homines quod non acceperint? Innueretur igitur illis verbis, Adamum factum esse quasi Deum summum. Id quod idem VVolkelius negat serpentem promisisse.
units.tr: XXXIII. Yet this kind of rendering conflicts not only with the words God used and the construction of those words, but also with the matter itself. For Volkelius maintains that God, in speaking this way, was looking back to the serpent's words, you will be like gods knowing good and evil, in which there is nothing that corresponds to the words of themselves. The serpent does not say knowing from yourselves, but simply knowing. Indeed he promises that they will know good and evil not so much of themselves as by the power of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore that of themselves ought to be judged foreign to the matter under discussion. It can also be added that, if we wish to speak accurately, apart from the one God no one knows good and evil of himself. For what good do angels and men have that they have not received? It would therefore be hinted by those words that Adam was made as if he were the highest God. Volkelius himself denies that the serpent promised this.

units.la: XXXIV. Missa igitur ista tam absona responsione, ad alteram venio. Hic quidem, inquit Schlichtingius, arguit plures personas, sed nequaquam in uno Deo. Nonne Deus sui & Angelorum respectu istud dicere iure potuit, Sicut vnus ex nobis, intellige Dijs, bonum & malum scientibus? quemadmodum etiam serpens promiserat fore: Aperientur oculi vestri, & eritis sicut dij scientes bonum & malum. Quæritur nunc quidem inter nos quas secum personas Deus verbis illis, vnus ex nobis, intelligat? Angelos affirmant Aduersarij, nos negamus. Sua cur affirment argumenta proserant prius. Nos cur negemus nostra subjiciemus. Vtra meliora sint tu, candide lector, judica. Deus, inquit Schlichtingius, sui & Angelorum respectu istud iure dicere potuit. Quid si dicam similiter, Deus, id est, Pater sui & Filij sui ac Spiritus sancti respectu istud iure dicere potuit? id enim Aduersarios aut confiteri oportet, aut refellere quaecunque isto & superiore libro disputaui nus. Non quaeritur quid potuerit Deus dicere, sed quid dixerit. Quid enim est quod Deus si velit non possit? Rationes cur istud non possit aut debeat de Deo & Angelis exponi, mox asseram: Nunc pergat Schlichtingius. Ille nos interrogationum aculeis pungere conatur. Num vero, inquit, Angeli Dij non sunt? Non certè, inquam. Vnus enim tantùm est Deus, reliqui omnes sunt eius creaturae & serui. Alioqui vicerint Ethnici contendentes, plures esse Deos, vnum summum, reliquos inferiores: Et Angeli, si sunt Dij, colendi erunt & adorandi religiosè. Quis est enim, qui quod Deum esse credit, adorandum non putet? At dij appellantur nonnunquam in Veteri Testamento. Fateor, sed improprie & figuratè: vti etiam supremi inter homines magistratus, quorum tamen si se Dei nomine aliquis, aut ipse appellaret, aut appellari ab alijs pateretur, grande piaculum esset, vti patuit in Herode Act. 12. 22. 23.
units.tr: XXXIV. Setting aside, then, that answer which is so absurd, I come to the other. Here indeed, says Schlichtingius, he argues for several persons, but by no means in the one God. Could not God, with respect to himself and the angels, rightly have said this, Like one of us, that is, of the gods, knowing good and evil? Just as the serpent had promised would happen: your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods knowing good and evil. The question between us now is which persons God means by those words, one of us. Our opponents affirm that he means the angels; we deny it. Let them first put forward their arguments for their view; we will set out our reasons for denying it. Let you, kind reader, judge which are the better. God, says Schlichtingius, could rightly have said this with respect to himself and the angels. But what if I say similarly that God, that is, the Father, could rightly have said this with respect to his Son and his Holy Spirit? For our opponents must either concede this or refute whatever I have argued in this and the previous book. The question is not what God could have said, but what he did say. For what is there that God could not do if he willed it? I shall presently set out the reasons why that cannot or should not be explained of God and the angels. Now let Schlichtingius continue. He tries to prick us with the barbs of questions. But surely, he says, the angels are not gods? Certainly not, I answer. For there is only one God; all the rest are his creatures and servants. Otherwise the heathen would have won, who contend that there are many gods, one supreme and the rest inferior; and the angels, if they were gods, would have to be worshipped and adored with religious devotion. For who, when he believes that something is God, does not think it ought to be adored? But they are sometimes called gods in the Old Testament. I grant it, but improperly and figuratively, just as the highest magistrates among men are also so called; yet if anyone were to call himself by the name of God, or allowed himself to be so called by others, it would be a great sacrilege, as was shown in Herod, Acts 12:22, 23.

units.la: XXXV. Num, addit, bonum & malum nesciunt? Nunc quidem scire malum arbitror: id enim in hominibus & diabolis videre potuerunt. Tunc vero sciuisse cum serpens Euam tentaret, mihi videtur temerarium affirmare. Equidem ad negandum suum propensior. Nam tunc primùm fortasse malum esse incipiebat: quod, si, antequam fieret, ab omnibus angelis probè cognitum fuisset, non intelligo qui potuissent angeli quidam malum bono anteponere: id enim magnam boni & mali ignorantiam arguit.
units.tr: XXXV. Surely, he adds, they do not know good and evil? Now I think they know evil, for they could see it in men and devils. But to affirm that they knew it when the serpent was tempting Eve seems to me rash. I am rather inclined to deny it. For then perhaps evil was only beginning to be; and if, before it came about, it had been thoroughly known to all the angels, I do not see how some angels could have preferred evil to good, for that would argue a great ignorance of good and evil.

units.la: XXXVI. Pergit Schlichtingius interrogare. Quid, inquit, non Angelis potius hac in parte quàm ipsis diuinis personis assimilandus homo fuerat? Neutris profectò. Mentiebatur enim serpens. Esus arboris scientiae boni & mali hominem fecit similem, non personis diuinis, nec bonis angelis, sed diabolis tantùm. Et quidem in peccato & miseria duntaxat. Ita enim factum est, vt experientiâ suâ quid sit malum culpae & poenae miser didicerit. Hanc eandem rationem, si tamen ratio est, V Volkelius his verbis proponit, Nimis etiam à rectâ rationis indicio alienum videtur, summum illum Deum, qui inexplicabili sapientia praditus, omnisque scientia primus autor est, hominem ex terra pulvéreque procreatum, boni malique scientiâ secum ipso nominatim aequare voluisse. Do[?] totum, addoque etiam absurdum[?] videri, Deum hominem boni malique scientiâ per peccatum & diabolum productâ cum bonis angelis aequare voluisse.
units.tr: XXXVI. Schlichtingius goes on asking questions. Why, he says, in this respect should man not rather have been made like the angels than like the divine persons? Certainly neither. For the serpent was lying. Eating of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil made man like, not the divine persons, nor the good angels, but the devils only. And indeed only in sin and misery. For it came about that the wretched man learned by his own experience what is the evil of guilt and punishment. Volkelius sets out this same reasoning, if it is reasoning, in these words: It seems too far removed from the sound judgment of reason that that supreme God, who is endowed with inexplicable wisdom and is the first author of all knowledge, should have wished to make man, created from earth and dust, equal to himself by name in the knowledge of good and evil. I grant the whole, and I add that it also seems absurd that God should have wished to make man equal to the good angels in the knowledge of good and evil, a knowledge brought into being through sin and the devil.

units.la: XXXVII. Atqui Deus, inquit, hoc in loco seriam orationem habet, nec per ironiam quandam Adamo veluti illudit.Seriam oratio-nem habere, nec illudere Adamo concedo, ironia non vti nego. Non potuit enim magis serio stulta ambitio Adami reprehendi, quàm factum est illa ironiâ. At, inquit, id duabus rationibus probari potest. Primò enim constat, arborem illam, scientiae boni & mali arborem có appellatam fuisse, quòd haud aliter illius fructu boni ac mali cognitio parabatur, quàm ex arboris vitae usu aetatis propagatio profluebat. Quomodo igitur Deum lusisse existimabimus, cum dixit, Ecce Adam factus est sicut[?] unus ex nobis, ad sciendum (ita enim sonant Hebraea) bonum & malum. h. e ita vt sciat bonum & malum? Hæc ratio primùm malè concludit: Deus enim cum id dixit non lusit, irati & punientis ironia lusus non est, sed grauis & aculeata reprehensio. Deinde nulla est. Non enim constat ex arboris vitae usu aetatis propagationem profluxisse. Potuit enim illa arbor nihil nisi vitae sacramentum fuisse, cuius utendi facultas ius viuendi, data indultu, denegata ademptum significaret. Quo posito, arbor scientiae boni & mali typus fuit seu symbolum peccati, rei quam unam Deus prohibet, quamque gustare homo non potest, quin tandem aliquando quod peccando amisit bonum, & contraxit malum vere sentiat & cognoscat. Fac tamen arborem vitae vi quadam physica praedicatam fuisse sanitatis & vitae prorogandae, non erit consequens, arborem scientiae boni & mali simili facultate scientiae boni & mali vel producendae vel augendae ornatam fuisse: illud enim agendo in corpus, istud nonnisi agendo in mentem fieri potuit. Agere autem in corpus quidem manducata arbor potuit, in mentem vero non item.
units.tr: XXXVII. But God, he says, in this place speaks in earnest and does not in some way mock Adam through irony. That he speaks in earnest and does not mock Adam I concede; that he does not use irony I deny. For foolish ambition in Adam could not have been rebuked more seriously than it was by that irony. But, he says, this can be proved on two grounds. For first, it is established that that tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because the knowledge of good and evil was obtained from its fruit in no other way than the propagation of life followed from the use of the tree of life. How then shall we suppose that God was mocking when he said, Behold Adam has become like one of us, to know (for so the Hebrew words sound) good and evil, that is, so that he may know good and evil? This argument, in the first place, concludes badly. For when God said this he was not mocking; the irony of an angry and punishing judge is not mockery, but a grave and cutting rebuke. Next, the argument has no force. For it is not established that the propagation of life flowed from the use of the tree of life. That tree may have been nothing more than a sacrament of life, whose power of use, granted by indulgence, signified the right to live, and whose denial signified its loss. Given this, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was a type or symbol of sin, of the one thing God forbids, and which man cannot taste without at last truly perceiving and knowing, through sinning, the good he has lost and the evil he has incurred. Yet grant that the tree of life was proclaimed to have some physical power of preserving and prolonging health and life; it does not follow that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was endowed with a like power to produce or increase the knowledge of good and evil. For the former could work upon the body, but the latter could only work upon the mind. Now the eaten tree could work upon the body, but not upon the mind.

units.la: XXXVIII. Deinde (quae altera est VVolkii[?] ratio) si Deus ex animo minimè locutus est, nequaquam quae subjiciuntur verba, rectè ex his, de quibus agimus, apta nexaque sunt. Sic enim ibidem statim subiungit: Nunc ergo, ne forte mittat manum suam, & sumat de ligno vitae, & viuat in aeternum, &c. Neque enim vl-lam aliam ob causam Deus illa verba praemisit: Ecce Adam factus est tanquam vnus ex nobis, ad sciendum bonum & malum, quàm vt rationem quodammodo redderet; quare à fruenda arbore vitæ Adamum prohiberet, nempe quia boni & mali scientiâ polleret, & ideo tum arboris ipsius vim, tum quantum in eâ ponendum esset, probè intelligeret; & porrò nequaquam vitæ suæ tam negligens esset suturus, quin fructum arboris decerperet, comederetque, & sic vitam viveret maximè diuturnam. Hæc est fallacia à non causa pro causa. Primum an verbis Ecce Adam factus est &c, rationem Deus reddat, quare à fruenda arbore vitæ Adamum prohibeat, in dubium vocari potest: quod enim vulgata Latina vertit Nunc ergo, in Heb. est ועתה, id est, Et nunc, vt etiam reddunt hoc loco 70. Interp. Et plerique omnes Latini. Deinde Adamum boni & mali scientia polluisse, unde habet Adversarius? qui potuit arbor corporea & materialis in mentem Adami immaterialem, vi sibi insita & inhærente, agere? qui potuit eam tanta scientia donare? qui potuit ei vim latentem in alia arbore revelare? Si eâ scientiâ vi comestæ illius arboris Adamus polluit, si quasi Deus factus est, vera fuit promissio serpentis, & Deus videri potuit summam illam perfectionem invidisse homini, quo nihil potest fingi absurdius. Quis credat Adamum lapsu suo ascendisse ad altiorem perfectionis & scientiæ gradum, sibique lucem non tenebras, acutiorem visum non cæcitatem comparasse? Quomodo ergo verba illa cohærent cum sequentibus? ridet Deus & redarguit Hominis stultitiam verbis illis, & quominus eam alterà cumulet prospiciendum docet verbis sequentibus. Quid opus est majore connexione?
units.tr: XXXVIII. Then (this is Volkelius's second argument) if God did not speak from his heart at all, the words that follow do not fit and connect properly with the matter we are discussing. For he goes on immediately after this: Now therefore, lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and live for ever, etc. For God put forward those words, Behold Adam has become as one of us to know good and evil, for no other reason than to give, as it were, a reason why he should keep Adam from enjoying the tree of life, namely because he was endowed with the knowledge of good and evil, and so understood well both the power of the tree itself and how much was to be put into it; and further he would by no means be so careless of his life as not to pluck and eat the fruit of the tree, and so live a life most long-lasting. This is the fallacy of taking a non-cause for a cause. First, whether God gives a reason, by the words Behold Adam has become etc., why he keeps Adam from enjoying the tree of life can be called in doubt; for what the Latin Vulgate renders Now therefore is in the Hebrew [ועתה], that is, And now, as the Seventy also render it in this place, and nearly all the Latin translators. Next, where does my opponent get the idea that Adam was endowed with the knowledge of good and evil? How could a corporeal and material tree act upon Adam's immaterial mind, by a power implanted and inherent in it? How could it bestow on him so great a knowledge? How could it reveal to him a power lying hidden in another tree? If Adam was endowed with that knowledge by the power of eating that tree, if he became as God, then the serpent's promise was true, and God could seem to have grudged man that supreme perfection, than which nothing can be imagined more absurd. Who would believe that by his fall Adam rose to a higher degree of perfection and knowledge, and that he acquired for himself light instead of darkness, and sharper sight instead of blindness? How then do those words cohere with what follows? God mocks and rebukes man's folly by those words, and by the words that follow he teaches that provision must be made lest he add to it another. What need is there of a closer connexion?

units.la: XXXIX. Demus tamen Adversariis non esse ironiam. Num hoc juvabit eorum causam? perimet potius. Cui enim factus est Adam similis? Diabolis? Hos, opinor, Deus non consociat secum pronomine Nobis. Angelis bonis? His dissimilis potius factus est, cognitione; lapsus enim est in errorem, sanctitate, factus enim est peccator, fœlicitate: factus enim est miser. Deo absolutè spectato? Huius imaginem, ad quam creatus fuerat, magna ex parte lapsu suo amisit. Itaque non dicit Deus, factus est sicut angeli, aut sicut Deus, aut sicut nos, sed sicut unus ex nobis. Nempe non est factus sicut Pater, nec sicut Spiritus sanctus, sed profectò factus est sicut Filius Dei. Negabis? Non potes. Duobus enim modis spectari potest Adamus, uno secundum rationem propriam, qua differebat ab Eva & reliquis hominibus: altero secundum rationem communem cum Eva & reliquis peccatoribus resipiscentibus. Utroque respectu factus est sicut Filius Dei.
units.tr: XXXIX. Let us nevertheless grant to our opponents that there is no irony. Will this help their cause? It will rather destroy it. To whom was Adam made similar? To the devils? These, I think, God does not associate with himself by the pronoun "Us." To the good angels? He was made rather unlike them in knowledge, for he fell into error; in holiness, for he became a sinner; in happiness, for he became wretched. To God considered absolutely? He lost, through his fall, to a great extent the image in which he had been created. Therefore God does not say, "He has become like the angels," or "like God," or "like us," but "like one of us." Surely he did not become like the Father, nor like the Holy Spirit, but truly he became like the Son of God. Will you deny it? You cannot. For Adam may be considered in two ways: in one, according to his own peculiar relation, by which he differed from Eve and the rest of mankind; in the other, according to the common relation he shared with Eve and the rest of sinners who repent. In either respect he was made like the Son of God.

units.la: XL. Et priore quidem: factus enim est umbra seu typus Christi, teste Apostolo Rom. 5. umbra autem similis est corpori suo, typus rei quam adumbrat. Posteriore vero: Nam Adamus agnouit nuditatem suam, & remedium quaesiuit: Deus egit seuerè cum serpente, clementer cum Adamo: maledixit serpenti, maledictionem ab Adamo transtulit in terram, Denunciauit serpenti exitium, homini liberationem per semen mulieris. Quam promissionem fide amplexus Adamus, ac sibi & uxori applicans, vocauit uxorem suam Evam, quod esset futura mater omnium viuentium, habita nimirum ratione seminis illius contriturî caput serpentis, in quo omnes viuificantur. Quam ob fidem Deus quasi placatus medicatus est ipsorum nuditati; vestesque pelliceas illis & fecit & induit. Quo perfecto jam ait, Adamum factum esse similem vni ex personis diuinis, hoc est, Filio Dei ad sciendum bonum & malum: Nam & solus Dei Filius ut nos seruaret mala nostra expertus est & didicit, nosque bona sua docuit & videre partim fecit, partim faciet, & quos Deus praenouit, hos etiam praedestinauit conformandos imagini filij sui: ut sit primogenitus inter multos fratres, qui ipsum induunt, unicum nuditatis nostrae spiritualis remedium. Ita, si cognitionem experimentalem spectes, non Pater, non Spiritus sanctus, non Angeli sciuerunt bonum & malum, sed solus Filius Dei Seruator, & homines qui per eum seruantur. Ille est exemplar cuius imagini hi fiunt conformes. Hinc intelligitur, cur mentio nominis Evae impositi sententiam diuinam statim sequatur, cur Deus tam misericorditer Adamum tractarit; cur hanc benevolentiae testificationem excipiant haec verba. Ecce Adam factus est &c; cur Deus dixerit unus ex nobis; cur Adamum solum nominauerit non Evam cum eo; cur denique sequantur illa, Nunc ergo ne forte mittat manum suam &c.
units.tr: XL. In the former respect, indeed: for he was made a shadow or type of Christ, as the Apostle witnesses in Rom. 5. A shadow, however, is similar to its body, a type to the thing it foreshadows. In the latter respect: for Adam recognised his nakedness and sought a remedy. God dealt severely with the serpent and mercifully with Adam: he cursed the serpent, transferred the curse from Adam to the earth, announced ruin to the serpent and deliverance to man through the seed of the woman. Adam, embracing this promise by faith and applying it to himself and his wife, called his wife "Eve," because she would be the mother of all living, having in mind, of course, that seed which would bruise the serpent's head, in whom all are made alive. On account of this faith God, as if appeased, showed mercy to their nakedness; he both made and clothed them in garments of skin. Having done this, he then said that Adam had become like one of the divine persons, that is, the Son of God, in knowing good and evil. For the Son of God alone, in order to save us, experienced and learned our evils, and taught us his good things, and partly has caused us to see them, and partly will cause it; and those whom God foreknew, these he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers, who put him on, the sole remedy for our spiritual nakedness. Thus, if you consider experiential knowledge, it was not the Father, not the Holy Spirit, not the angels who knew good and evil, but the Son of God alone, the Saviour, and the men who are saved through him. He is the pattern to whose image these are made conformed. Hence it is understood why mention of the name given to Eve immediately follows the divine sentence, why God treated Adam so mercifully, why these words follow this testimony of goodwill: "Behold, Adam has become," etc.; why God said "one of us"; why he named Adam alone and not Eve with him; and finally why there follow the words, "Now therefore, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand," etc.

units.la: XLI. Ultimum enim istud primum typi ratio flagitabat. Nam, ut Adam è paradiso terrestri emissus est ad colendam terram de qua sumptus fuerat, sic Filius Dei è paradiso coelesti missus est ad colendam Ecclesiam è qua secundum carnem sumptus est, &, ut collocati sunt Cherubim & lamina gladij flammea ad custodiencustodiendum iter arboris vitæ, ita ut non posset Adamus ad illam arborem aspirare nisi per mortem cruentam & initum cum illis cherubim prælium; sic ea quæ custodiebant viam ad arborem vitæ cœlestis seu gloriosam immortalitatem eiusmodi erant, ut ad eam nobis peccatoribus obtinendam necesse fuerit Filium Dei per mortem cruentam, per maledictionem legis Angelorum ministerio traditæ, per exercitus diabolorum victorem penetrare ad paradisum cœlestem. Deinde hoc ipsum exigebat conformitas servandorum cum Seruatore. Cum enim huius & paradisus & vita & fœlicitas terrena non sit sed cœlestis ac spiritualis, adimenda illis spes omnis fuit vitæ animalis prorogandæ in perpetuum, & reuertendi in paradisum terrestrem, necnon etiam typo adumbrandum, non nisi per varias tribulationes iter patere in paradisum cœlestem. Hæc obiter perstringimus hoc loco, accuratius explicanda in disputationibus de typis, si eas continuare clementissimus Dominus nobis dederit.
units.tr: XLI. For this last point the nature of the type itself required. For just as Adam was sent out of the terrestrial paradise to till the ground from which he had been taken, so the Son of God was sent out of the heavenly paradise to tend the Church from which he was taken according to the flesh; and just as the Cherubim and the flaming sword were placed to guard the way to the tree of life, so that Adam could not aspire to that tree except through a bloody death and a battle joined with those cherubim, so those things which guarded the way to the heavenly tree of life, or glorious immortality, were of such a kind that, for us sinners to obtain it, it was necessary for the Son of God to penetrate to the heavenly paradise through a bloody death, through the curse of the law delivered by the ministry of angels, and through the armies of devils, as their conqueror. Moreover, the very conformity of those to be saved with the Saviour demanded this. For since both the paradise and the life and happiness of these are not earthly but heavenly and spiritual, they had to be deprived of every hope of prolonging animal life forever and of returning to the earthly paradise, and also, to be foreshadowed by a type, the way into the heavenly paradise was open only through various tribulations. We touch on these matters in passing at this point; they are to be explained more precisely in the disputations on types, if the most merciful Lord grants us to continue them.

units.la: XLII. Conatur etiam alio argumento V. Volkelius probare, Deum verbis illis Angelos esse allocutum. Consentaneum enim est, inquit, Deum, cum ad hunc modum loqueretur; ad illa serpentis verba respexisse: Eritis sicut Dij, scientes bonum & malum. Quibus verbis cum serpens ille, ad vescendum fructu arboris boni ac mali, primos parentes nostros plane incendere studuerit, haud verisimile est, si summo illi Deo eos pares fore persuadere instituisset, simplici Deorum nomine eum usurum, & non multo luculentius altissimum illud numen expressurum fuisse, præsertim cum simplex Deorum commemoratio summum illum Deum necessario minime contineat.
units.tr: XLII. V. Volkelius also tries by another argument to prove that God, in those words, addressed the angels. "For it is consistent," he says, "that God, when speaking in this manner, had regard to those words of the serpent: 'You will be like gods, knowing good and evil.' Since with these words that serpent, to induce our first parents to eat the fruit of the tree of good and evil, eagerly sought to inflame them altogether, it is not probable that, if the supreme God had intended to persuade them that they would be equal to him, he would have used the simple name of gods, and would not have expressed that most high divinity much more plainly, especially since a simple mention of gods does not necessarily contain that supreme God."

units.la: Mira ratio! quasi vero nomen ullum aptius esset ad significandum Deum verum, seu, ut loqui amant, summum, quàm nomen istud Elohim, quod ad eum significandum, & omnium frequentissimè adhibetur in Scriptura, & solum usurpatum fuit à Mose in historia creationis describenda Gen. 1. immò à serpente ac Eua in hoc eorum colloquio!
units.tr: A remarkable argument! As if any name were more fitting for signifying the true God, or, as they like to say, the supreme God, than that name Elohim, which is used to signify him more frequently than any other in Scripture, and which was used alone by Moses in describing the history of creation, Gen. 1, indeed even by the serpent and Eve in this their conversation!

units.la: XLIII. Tria igitur peccata hoc loco committere mihi V. Volkelius videtur. Primò nomen Elohim in his serpentis verbis, Eritis sicut Elohim, aliter accipit quàm in superioribus scilicet Elohim &c, cum tamen causa nulla sit, cur aliter accipi debeat. Deinde ponit, Euam credidisse plures Deos, unum summum, multos subalternos, & hos etiam sciuisse bonum & malum: quæ tamen duo probari non possunt, neque autoritate Scripturæ, neque vlla ratione. Denique promissionem serpentis veram fuisse putat, illiqué assentitur. Concludit enim, tum Deum, tum serpentem, nihil aliud dicere voluisse, quàm Adamum, quod ad boni malique intelligentiam attinet, non amplius reliquis terrestribus animalibus, sed generatim loquendo cœlitibus, quorum malum à bono dignoscere proprium erat, similem esse, aut fore. Eua igitur, si VVolKelio [?] fides habetur, rectè fecit cum credidit serpenti; quippe scilicet vera dicebat, & pollicebatur: Et hoc ipso quod Adamus interdictum diuinum violauit grauissimeque peccauit, factus est multò quàm antè perfectior, ac dijs similior, sibique scientiam comparauit bonum dignoscendi à malo. Non pudet Aduersarios huius suæ tam absurdæ, ne dicam impiæ, opinionis? Mentiebatur profectò vt iam dixi, & seducebat serpens; neque ex huiusmodi seductione aliud per se oriri poterat, quàm error, ignorantia, cæcitas. Sed Deus serpenti iratus, & hominis misertus admirabili misericordia & sapientia hominem ita in Christo instauravit, vt contra mentem serpentis, ac nequicquam ringente & frendente diabolo, primùm scientia boni & mali, deinde sanctitate ac tandem felicitate & gloria Filio Dei similis factus fuerit. Id quod quia jam erat, non modò Dei consilio immutabili decretum, sed etiam in Adamo adumbratum, immò aliquomodo per eius fidem inchoatum, potuit causa fuisse, cur Deus sic loqueretur, Ecce Adam factus est sicut unus ex nobis, longè aliter quàm serpens: hic enim simpliciter dixerat sicut Elohim, hoc est, Deus, vel dij, non sicut unus ex Elohim.
units.tr: XLIII. Volkelius seems to me to commit three errors at this point. First, he takes the name Elohim in these words of the serpent, "You will be like Elohim," differently from its use above, namely "Elohim etc.," although there is no reason why it should be understood differently. Next, he holds that Eve believed there were several gods, one supreme and many subordinate, and that these also knew good and evil; yet these two things cannot be proved either by the authority of Scripture or by any reasoning. Finally, he thinks the serpent's promise was true, and assents to it. For he concludes that "both God and the serpent meant nothing else than that Adam, as far as the understanding of good and evil is concerned, had become, or would become, similar not to the remaining terrestrial animals but generally, speaking, to the heavenly beings, whose proper function was to distinguish evil from good." Eve, therefore, if credit is given to Volkelius, acted rightly when she believed the serpent; for of course he was saying true things and making promises. And by this very fact, that Adam violated the divine prohibition and sinned most gravely, he became far more perfect than before and more like the gods, and acquired for himself the knowledge of distinguishing good from evil. Are the opponents not ashamed of this opinion of theirs, so absurd, not to say impious? He was certainly lying, as I have already said, and the serpent was deceiving; and from such deception nothing else could arise by its own nature than error, ignorance, blindness. But God, angry with the serpent and merciful to man, with wonderful mercy and wisdom restored man in Christ, so that, contrary to the serpent's intention, and while the devil raged and gnashed his teeth in vain, he was made first like the Son of God in knowledge of good and evil, then in holiness, and at last in happiness and glory. This, since it already existed, was not only decreed by God's immutable counsel but also foreshadowed in Adam, and indeed in some way begun through his faith; and this could be the reason why God spoke thus, "Behold, Adam has become like one of us," in a manner quite different from the serpent. For the serpent had simply said "like Elohim," that is, God or gods, not "like one of the Elohim."

units.la: XLIV. Nihil aliud affert VVolKelius. Pergat igitur interrogare Schlichtingius. Quid, inquit, non Angelis potius hac in parte quàm ipsis diuinis personis assimilandus homo fuerat? Si vim hærentem in arbore scientiæ boni & mali, si inobedientiam Adami, si serpentis mentem spectes, neutris certè assimilandus fuerat. Mentiebatur enim & decipiebat, vt dixi, serpens. Sed si Dei gratiam spectes, assimilandus erat vni ex personis diuinis, nempe Filio, Angelis verò non ita proprie. Fuit enim Adamus typus, non Angelorum, sed Filij Dei; nec assimilandus per fidem angelis, sed Filio Dei; nec futuri sunt fideles Angelis similes, nisi quia futuri sunt similes Filio Dei, cui Angeli etiam similes sunt quibusdam in rebus.
units.tr: XLIV. Volkelius adds nothing else. Let Schlichting therefore go on asking: "Why, he says, ought man in this respect to have been likened rather to the angels than to the divine persons themselves?" If you look at the power clinging to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, at Adam's disobedience, or at the serpent's mind, he certainly ought to have been likened to neither. For the serpent, as I said, lied and deceived. But if you look at God's grace, he was to be likened to one of the divine persons, namely the Son, but not so properly to the angels. For Adam was a type not of the angels but of the Son of God. Nor is he to be likened through faith to the angels but to the Son of God. Nor will believers be like the angels, unless because they will be like the Son of God, to whom the angels too are similar in certain respects.

units.la: XLV. Addit rationem, Nam, inquit, Angelis Deum stipatum fuisse cum res ipsa eiusque suprema maiestas requirit, tum sequentia ostendunt. Si quis Auctori Epistolae ad Hebraeos Melchisedecum sic describenti, sine patre, sine matre, sine genealogia, neque initium dierum, neque vitae finem habens, obiceret, Melchisedecum sine patre, matre,initio dierum non fuisse rem ipsam ostendere, quid esset respondendum? Nonne hoc, Non debere considerari Melchisedecum ut fuit in seipso, sed ut describitur à Mose patrem eius, matrem, initium dierum &c destinato consilio occultante. Idem respondemus Schlichtingio, Deum non debere in hoc loco considerari nisi ut se ostendit in hac historia: sicut autem eum sese in hac historia ostendere & revelare, ut Angeli, sive ijs stipatus fuerit, sive non fuerit, prorsus non appareant; ac propterea eos eodem loco à nobis haberi debere in ista historia explicanda, ac si nulli fuissent. Fit quidem in ultimo capitis versu mentio cherubim & aciei gladij, sed illis Cherubim stipatum Deum fuisse nullo modo dicitur. Fuerit tamen Deus Angelis stipatus, quid inde sequitur? Deum Angelos fuisse alloquutum, aut designasse pronomine nobis? nullo modo. Id vidit Schlichtingius. Itaque subjungit, Neque hoc solum, sed etiam Deum ad Angelos sermonem suum convertisse docent. Itane hunc sermonem de quo est quaestio, Ecce Adam factus est sicut unus ex nobis? frustra laborat si alium intelligit. Audiamus igitur eius ratiocinationem. Postquam enim, inquit, dixisset; Ecce homo factus est sicut unus ex nobis ad sciendum bonum & malum; statim subjicit (prouisurus ne homo etiam de arbore vitae comedat: & sic in seculum vitam producat:) Et nunc, ne forte mittat manum suam, & sumat etiam de arbore vitae, & comedat & viuat in seculum. Quae verba cum adhuc imperfecto sensu pendeant, necesse est aliquid intelligamus additum. Quid autem aliud, quam Deum id iussisse quod statim Moses subjicit fuisse factum? Rem ipsam pro rei iussu ac decreto, brevitatis causa, statim referens. Quid vero factum sit, & qua ratione Deus illi rei, quam fieri nolebat, occurrit? Et emisit, inquit, Dominus Deus hominem de horto Heden &c. & collocavit ab oriente cherubim & aciem gladij, ad custodiendum viam arboris vitae. Duo fecit: hominem ex horto eiecit, & cherubinos viam arboris vitae custodire iussit. Quocirca post illa verba, quid aliud intelligendum est, quam dixisse Deum; vos o Angeli vel Cherubim; ne exactus redeat, custodite arboris vita viam. Quorsum ista? aut quid ad rem faciunt? Dixerit Deus post illa verba tale quid Cherubinis, an inde sequitur Deum superiora illa Ecce Adam &c dixisse Cherubinis, aut in superioribus illis verbis Cherubinos pronomine nobis esse significatos? miseret me tam inanis conatus Schlichtingij.
units.tr: XLV. He adds a reason: "For,' he says, 'that God was surrounded by angels is shown both by the thing itself and by its supreme majesty, and by what follows." Suppose someone objected to the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, who describes Melchizedek thus, "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life," that the thing itself shows Melchizedek was not without father, mother, or beginning of days. What would be the answer? Would it not be this: that Melchizedek should not be considered as he was in himself, but as Moses describes him, with his father, mother, and beginning of days, and so on, by a deliberate plan that conceals them? We give the same answer to Schlichting. God should not be considered in this passage except as he shows himself in this history. Just as he does not appear or reveal himself in this history as attended by angels, whether he was or was not, so we must hold the angels, in explaining this history, to be in the same place as if there were none. There is indeed mention of the cherubim and the flaming sword at the end of the chapter, but it is nowhere said that God was surrounded by those cherubim. Yet grant that God was surrounded by angels: what follows from that? That God addressed the angels, or designated them by the pronoun "us"? By no means. Schlichting saw this. So he adds: "And they teach not only this, but also that God turned his speech to the angels." Does he labour in vain if he understands this discourse under dispute, "Behold, Adam has become as one of us," to be another? Let us hear, then, his reasoning. "For after he had said: Behold, man has become as one of us, to know good and evil, he immediately adds (fearing that man might also eat from the tree of life and so live forever): And now, lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat and live forever." "Since these words hang with a still incomplete sense, we must understand something added. What else but that God commanded what Moses immediately adds was done? He briefly relates the thing itself right after the command and decree. But what was done, and by what reasoning did God meet that situation which he did not want to happen?" "And the Lord God sent him out of the garden of Eden, etc., and placed at the east the cherubim and a flaming sword, to guard the way of the tree of life." "He did two things: he cast man out of the garden, and he ordered the cherubim to guard the way of the tree of life. Therefore after those words, what else is to be understood than that God said: you, O angels or cherubim, guard the way of the tree of life, lest the expelled man return." Why these things? Or what do they contribute to the matter? Let God have said something of the kind to the cherubim after those words. Does it follow that God spoke those earlier words, "Behold, Adam," and so on, to the cherubim, or that in those earlier words the cherubim are signified by the pronoun "us"? I pity the empty effort of Schlichting.

units.la: XLVI. Ut igitur argumentari pergam, sic colligo. Deus verbis illis unus ex nobis, aut angelos intelligit, aut personas diuinas. Prius dici non potest, id quod probo his argumentis. Principio non negabunt Aduersarij, quin quas personas Deus alloquebatur cum diceret Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram, eadem alloquatur his verbis Ecce Adam factus est sicut unus ex nobis. Atqui illis verbis Faciamus hominem &c, non alloquebatur Angelos, uti a nobis probatum est §. 37.38.39. Ergo his quoque verbis Angelos non alloquitur.
units.tr: XLVI. So, to continue my argument, I conclude thus. By those words "one of us" God means either angels or the divine persons. The former cannot be said, and I prove this by the following arguments. First, the opponents will not deny that the persons whom God addressed when he said "Let us make man in our image" are the same persons whom he addresses with these words, "Behold, Adam has become as one of us." But in the words "Let us make man," etc., he did not address the angels, as we have shown in §§ 37, 38, 39. Therefore neither does he address the angels in these words.

units.la: XLVII. Deinde qui loquitur hoc loco appellatur Iehova Elohim, quod nomen maximè proprium est unius Dei creatoris cœli & terræ. Si igitur in Veteri Testamento duæ vel tres personæ occurrunt, quarum unaquæque non modo Elohim, sed etiam Iehova appellatur, consentaneum est rationi, ut illæ potius personæ intelligantur hoc loco, quàm aliæ, quibus Ichouæ nomen convenire non potest. Prius autem est verum, ut patuit ex disputationibus superioribus; Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: XLVII. Next, the one who speaks in this place is called Jehovah Elohim, a name most proper to the one God, creator of heaven and earth. If therefore two or three persons occur in the Old Testament, each of whom is called not only Elohim but also Jehovah, it accords with reason that those persons rather than others, to whom the name Jehovah cannot apply, be understood in this place. But the first is true, as appeared from the earlier disputations. Therefore the second is too.

units.la: XLVIII. Sed ne jam probatis nitamur, Si Deus verbis illis, Ecce Adam factus est sicut unus ex nobis, Angelos alloquutus est, secum sociauit, sociatosque a nobis intelligi voluit, cur diuinus autor id nullo modo innuit? Cur non scripsit aperte, Et Dominus Deus dixit ad Angelos; Aut cur saltem Deum non induxit[?] sic loquentem, Ecce Adam factus est sicut unus ex vobis? vel sicut unus ex Angelis? Quid enim erat causæ cur Angelos silentio tegeret? quis eiusmodi occultationis usus esse poterat? ostendit plures personas nomine Elohim, quod Deum significat, dignas, ac interim Angelos vero silentij operuit. Quorsum, nisi ut ne putemus Angelos intelligi? Cur Matth. 17. 8. obseruatum est, cum oraculum illud ederetur è nube, Hic est filius meus dilectus &c. Apostolos Petrum, Iacobum & Iohannem neminem vidisse nisi Iesum solum, nisi ut innotesceret, illud non de Mose, aut Elia, sed de Iesu solo dictum fuisse? Sic hoc loco cur Angeli latent, cur nihil præter Deum comparet, cum verba illa proferuntur sicut unus ex nobis, nisi ut ne personas intelligamus angelicas, aut Dei nomine & natura non comprehensas?
units.tr: XLVIII. But let us not labour over proofs already established. If God, in those words "Behold, Adam has become as one of us," addressed the angels, associated them with himself, and wished us to understand them as associated, why does the divine author in no way hint at this? Why did he not write plainly, "And the Lord God said to the angels"? Or why at least did he not have God speak thus: "Behold, Adam has become as one of you"? or "as one of the angels"? For what reason was there to hide the angels in silence? What use could such concealment have? He indicates several persons by the name Elohim, which signifies God, and meanwhile covers the angels with silence. To what end, unless so that we would not think the angels are meant? Why is it noted at Matth. 17. 8, when that oracle was delivered out of the cloud, "This is my beloved Son," etc., that the apostles Peter, James and John saw no one but Jesus alone? Was it not to make known that this was said not of Moses or Elijah but of Jesus alone? So in this place, why do the angels lie hidden, why does nothing appear beside God, when those words are uttered, "as one of us," unless so that we do not understand angelic persons, or persons not comprehended in the name and nature of God?

units.la: XLIX. Fit quidem non multò post mentio Cherubim, quo nomine Angelos significari volunt Aduersarij: Sed id causæ nostræ admodum fauet. Primùm enim eos diuinus autor non vocat Deos, nec Angelos, sed Cherubim, quod nomen nec quid significet satis liquet, nec relationem vllam habet vel ad promissionem serpentis eritis sicut Deus, vel ad verba Dei factus est sicut unus ex nobis, vel ad scientiam boni & mali. Deinde illis adjungit laminam seu aciem gladij. Collocauit, inquit, à plaga orientali Cherubim & laminam gladij versatilis, quam sine dubio verbis, sicut unus ex nobis, non intellexit. Tum ministerium illis attribuit planè seruile, quod nec Deos decere videtur, nec Dei consiliarios aut præcipuos ministros, dies scilicet & noctes in regione orientali horti ad viam arboris vitæ custodiendam & ab ea hominem arcendum consistere. Cauere nimirum omni ratione prudentissimus autor voluit, ne Deus alloqui Angelos videretur, & sibi, quasi Dij essent, sociare.
units.tr: XLIX. Mention is indeed made not long afterwards of the Cherubim, a name by which the opponents wish the angels to be signified. But this greatly favours our cause. For first, the divine author does not call them gods, nor angels, but Cherubim, a name whose meaning is not clear enough, and which has no relation either to the serpent's promise "you will be as God," or to God's words "has become as one of us," or to the knowledge of good and evil. Then he joins to them a blade, or flaming sword. "He placed," he says, "on the east side the Cherubim and a blade of a turning sword," which without doubt he did not understand by the words "as one of us." Then he assigns them a plainly servile ministry, which does not seem fitting for gods, nor for counsellors or chief ministers of God: namely, to stand day and night in the eastern region of the garden to guard the way of the tree of life and keep man away from it. The most prudent author, of course, wished by every means to prevent it from seeming that God addressed the angels and associated them with himself, as if they were gods.

units.la: L. Præterea, Si Deus verbis illis unus ex nobis secum consociat Angelos, is secundum id quod ipsi est aliquomodo eum Angelis commune, & sese ipse considerat, & vult à nobis considerari? qui factum est igitur, ut hoc loco non contentus nomine Dei, Elohim, quo solo passim appellatur, quodque rarissimè quidem, sed tamen nonnunquam ad significandos Angelos transfertur, voluerit ei adjungi & præmitti nomen Domini Iehova, quo (præsertim sequente Elohim) ab omnibus Angelis maximè distinguitur, & separatur? Neque enim duorum istorum nominum diuinorum facta est hoc loco temerè & sine ulla ratione consociatio: ut enim in mundo, sic in Scriptura, immensa Dei sapientia & providentia ad res omnes, etiam minutissimas, pertinet, eiusque vestigia, etiam in minimis, elucent & cerni possunt. Cur igitur Deus, cum verba ista pronunciat, Ecce Adam factus est sicut unus ex nobis, appellatur Iehova Elohim, quo no-mine maximo ab Angelis separatur naturæ & dignitatis interuallo, nisi ut intelligamus, verborum illorum hunc esse sensum, unus ex nobis? qui nimirum Iehova Elohim sumus; non verò unus ex nobis, qui Iehova Elohim & Angeli sumus?
units.tr: L. Moreover, if God by the words "one of us" associates the angels with himself, is he, in that which he is, somehow held in common with the angels, and does he consider himself, and wish to be considered by us, in that way? How then did it happen that in this place he was not content with the name God, Elohim, by which alone he is called everywhere, and which is very rarely, yet sometimes, transferred to signify angels, but chose to have the name of the Lord, Jehovah, joined and placed before it, by which (especially when Elohim follows) he is most of all distinguished and separated from all angels? For the association of these two divine names in this place is not made rashly and without reason. As in the world, so in Scripture, the immense wisdom and providence of God extends to all things, even the smallest, and its traces shine forth and can be discerned, even in the least things. Why then, when God utters these words, "Behold, Adam has become as one of us," is he called Jehovah Elohim, a name by which he is separated from the angels by the greatest interval of nature and dignity, unless we understand the sense of those words to be this: "one of us," namely we who are Jehovah Elohim; not "one of us" who are Jehovah Elohim and angels?

units.la: LI. Adhæc, quid significat illud vnus ex nobis ? quilibet ex nobis ? æquat igitur sibi personas quas alloquitur, quasi inter se & illas nihil, aut ferè nihil interesset. Non alloquitur igitur Angelos, sibi valdè & naturâ, & dignitate, & scientiâ dissimiles. Certus quidam vnus ex nobis ? si sic vnum quendam certum angelum designare voluisset, dixisset potius ex vobis, quàm ex nobis. Is enim qui hæc dicebat non erat angelus, nec de Angelorum numero.
units.tr: LI. Moreover, what does the phrase "one of us" (unus ex nobis) signify? Does it mean "any one of us"? Then it puts the persons addressed on a level with himself, as if there were little or hardly any difference between him and them. So he is not addressing angels, who are very unlike himself in nature, dignity and knowledge. Is it a certain particular "one of us"? If he had wished to designate some one particular angel, he would have said "one of you" rather than "one of us". For the one who was speaking was not an angel, nor of the number of angels.

units.la: LII. Denique Deus vel ironia vtitur, vel non. Si ironia vtitur, alludit ad verba serpentis eritis sicut Elohim. Quod nomen ego de Deo, Aduersarij de Angelis interpretantur. Vtra expositio melior ? Annon ea, quæ & vsitatam illius vocis significationem retinet, & nihil ponit, nisi quod constat reuera fuisse, jure suo anteponenda est ei, quæ, & ab vsitata nominis illius significatione discedit, & ponit quædam, quæ an fuerint sciri non possunt ?
