Talis est nostra. Solet enim ferè semper nomen illud Deum, vt loquuntur, summum significare, nec alio sensu à Mose, ab Eua, à serpente vsurpatum eousque fuerat, aut vsurpatur in sequentibus. Ponit etiam nostra interpretatio Euam cognouisse, Deum esse, scire bonum & malum, & appellari Elohim; quæ quin cognouerit nemini potest esse dubium. Aduersariorum verò interpretatio, vt jam obseruaui, & ab vsitata nominis Elohim significatione recedit, & ponit Euam tunc temporis sciuisse Angelos esse, scire bonum & malum, & vocari Elohim. Quod neque Scripturæ auctoritate, neque ratione probari potest. Si sine ironia loquutus est, considerandum est cui Adamus peccator similis factus fuerit. Si Scripturam consulamus, vnus nobis occurret Dei Filius, cuius typus factus est Adamus. Consentaneum est igitur, vt eum hoc loco intelligamus.
units.tr: LII. Finally, God either uses irony or he does not. If he uses irony, he alludes to the serpent's words, "you will be like Elohim". My opponents interpret that name of angels, I of God. Which explanation is better? Is it not the one that both keeps the usual meaning of that word and posits nothing except what is certain to have really happened, and so must rightly be preferred to the one that departs from the usual meaning of that name and posits things whose occurrence cannot be known? Such is ours. For that name almost always means God, as they say, the highest; and it was not used in any other sense by Moses, by Eve, or by the serpent up to that point, nor is it used in the following passages. Our interpretation also posits that Eve knew that God exists, knew good and evil, and was called Elohim; that she knew these things no one can doubt. But the interpretation of my opponents, as I have already observed, departs from the usual signification of the name Elohim, and posits that Eve at that time knew that angels exist, knew good and evil, and was called Elohim. This can be proved neither by the authority of Scripture nor by reason. If he spoke without irony, we must consider to whom the sinning Adam was made like. If we consult Scripture, one Son of God will present himself to us, of whom Adam was made a type. It is consistent, therefore, that we understand him in this place.

units.la: LIII. Sunt alia nonnulla Veteris Testamenti loca, quibus diuinarum pluralitas personarum non obscurè innuitur, vt Gen. xi. 6. 7. Et dixit Dominus &c, Agite descendamus & confundamus ibi linguam eorum. Gen. 20. 13. Et fuit cum errare me fecerunt dy à domo patris mei. Iof. 24. 19. Non poteritis servire Domi-no (Iehouah) quoniam dy sancti ipse est. 2. Sam. 7. 23. Et quæ est sicut populus tuus, sicut Israël, gens vna in terra, ad quam iuerint Dy redimendam sibi in populum &c. Sic enim, si verbum pro verbo reddere velis, verti debent illa loca. Sed illis & similibus vrgendis, studio breuitatis, supersedeo. Tantùm obseruo non posse elabi Aduersarios consociando Angelos cum Deo summo: istam enim consociationem apertissimè respuunt duo ista postremò à me laudata loca. Prius quidem: in eo enim ratio redditur, cur non possent Israelitæ seruire Iehouæ; eaque petitur ab eius summa sanctitate; Et sequuntur pronomina & elogia singularis numeri, ne videatur induci pluralitas, vt personarum diuinarum, sic etiam Deorum. Posterius verò: nam & illud præcessit versu proximè antecedente, Non est similis tui, Nec est Deus prater te; sequitur autem, ad redimendum sibi in populum, & comparandum sibi nomen &c, quæ de Angelis dici nequeunt. Adde quod eiusmodi consociatio pugnaret cum scopo Dei, cuius consilium fuit docere populum suum, se esse Deum, & prætér se neminem, juxta illud Deut. 4. 35. Tu per visiones edoctus es, quod Dominus (Iehouah) ipse est Deus (Elohim) nec est alius prater eum.
units.tr: LIII. There are some other places of the Old Testament in which the plurality of the divine persons is not obscurely hinted at, as Gen. 11:6-7: "And the Lord said, etc. Come, let us go down and confound their language there." Gen. 20:13: "And it was when they made me wander from the house of my father, dy." Josh. 24:19: "You will not be able to serve the Lord (Iehouah), for he is the holy dy." 2 Sam. 7:23: "And who is like your people, like Israel, one nation on the earth, whom the Dy went to redeem for themselves as a people, etc." For so, if you wish to render word for word, those places ought to be translated. But I pass over urging these and similar passages, for the sake of brevity. I only observe that my opponents cannot escape by joining the angels with the highest God; for those two last passages I have praised most clearly reject this association. The first indeed: for in it the reason is given why the Israelites could not serve Iehouah, and it is taken from his supreme holiness; and the pronouns and epithets of the singular number follow, lest a plurality be seemed to be introduced, as of divine persons, so also of gods. The second: for that also preceded in the immediately preceding verse, "There is none like you, nor is there any God besides you"; but there follows "to redeem for himself a people, and to make for himself a name, etc.", which cannot be said of angels. Add that such an association would conflict with the purpose of God, whose counsel was to teach his people that he himself is God, and besides him there is no one, according to that of Deut. 4:35: "You have been instructed by visions that the Lord (Iehouah) himself is God (Elohim), and there is no other besides him."

units.la: L I V. Plura testimonia Veteris Testamenti non laudabimus. Adeò enim nobis impares in hac causa sunt Aduersarij, vt ne vnum quidem è Vetere Testamento contra fidem nostram testimonium afferre possint, ita constanter nobis fauet tota illa Scriptura. Id quod magnum est argumentum veritatis sententiæ nostræ, cui cum multa sint in antiquo testamento quæ faueant aperté, nihil est prorsus quod, vel in speciem, repugnet: Et tamen Scripturam illam diuinissimam ipse Christus, eiusque Apostoli nobis admodum commendarunt, tanquam quæ nos possit ad salutem sapientes reddere per fidem, quæ est in Iesu Christo: eiusque testimonijs Religionis Christianæ dogmata cum ipsi confirmarunt oppositosque errores confutarunt, tum nobis vt idem, cum opus erit, faciamus exemplo suo autores fuerunt.
units.tr: LIV. We will not cite more testimonies of the Old Testament. For our opponents are so unequal to us in this cause that they cannot bring forward even one testimony from the Old Testament against our faith; so constantly does that whole Scripture favour us. This is a great argument for the truth of our opinion, since, while there are many things in the Old Testament that clearly favour it, there is absolutely nothing that, even in appearance, opposes it. And yet Christ himself and his Apostles have strongly commended that most divine Scripture to us, as one that can make us wise unto salvation through the faith which is in Jesus Christ; and when they confirmed the doctrines of the Christian religion by its testimonies and refuted the opposing errors, they set us an example to do the same when the need arises.

units.la: Hic igitur finis esto huius Sectionis, immò Libri. Quoniam enim hic liber superiorem numero argumentorum jam superat, & paginarum ferè æquat, visum est Testimonia Noui Testamenti conferre in librum sequentem. Deo Patri & Domino nostro Iesu Christo eius filio vnigenito Creatori & Seruatori nostro sit gloria in secula seculorum. AMEN.
units.tr: Let this, then, be the end of this Section, indeed of this Book. For since this book now exceeds the preceding one in number of arguments and nearly equals it in pages, it has seemed good to bring the Testimonies of the New Testament together into the following book. To God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Creator and Saviour, be glory for ever and ever. AMEN.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.

units.la: ADDENDA Ad Arg. XIX. Ex Esai. Cap. LIV. vs. 3. petitum.
units.tr: Addenda to Argument XIX, taken from Isaiah chapter 54, verse 3.

units.la: LIBRUM hunc penè absoluera m, cum mihi legendarum Socini ad amicos Epistolarum peropportunè copia facta est. Eas dum percurro, incidi in Epistolam ad Valentinum Smalcium octauam, in qua conatus est respondere ad Argumentum ex cap. LIV. Esaiæ petitum, quod nobis est in hoc libro decimum nonum. Quoniam autem eius responsiones, nec tum videre mihi contigerat, & simul ac legi falsæ visæ sunt, non absre erit eas hoc loco expendere & refellere.
units.tr: I had almost finished this book when a very timely opportunity came to me of reading Socinus's Letters to friends. While I was going through them, I came upon the eighth Letter, to Valentin Smalcius, in which he attempts to answer the argument taken from Isaiah chapter 54, which is the nineteenth argument in this book. Since I had not had the chance to see his replies before, and as soon as I read them they seemed false to me, it will not be out of place to weigh them here and refute them.

units.la: I. Argumentum nostrum sic ipse Socinus format & confirmat non incommodè. Quicunque est Ecclesiæ maritus is est unus ille Deus Israëlis. Sed Christus est Ecclesiæ Maritus. Christus igitur est ille unus Deus Israëlis. Maioris probatio propositionis, qua tota argumentatio nititur, petitur ex loco isto Esaiæ, iuncto eo quod inter omnes constare videtur, Ecclesiæ maritum non posse esse nisi unum quemadmodum fœminæ alicuius unus tantum vir esse potest. Ille siquidem unus Israëlis Deus isto in loco ait se esse, aut certè fore maritum illius sterilis quæ non pariebat. Nam hanc esse supernam Ierusalem, id est, Ecclesiam, interpretari videtur Paulus ad Gal. cap. 4. v. 26. & 27. De veritate minoris propositionis, constat ex iis quæ leguntur cap. 5. Epist. ad Ephes. v. 22. & deinceps. Unde etiam id confirmatur, quod ad maioris propositionis comprobationem diximus, unum tantùm esse posse maritum Ecclesiæ, ut mulieris alicuius unus tantum vir esse potest. Nam ex iis quæ ibi dicuntur, apparet Christi cum Ecclesia coniugium, in eoque coniugio summam, ut sic dixerim, unitionem adumbratam fuisse in maris fœminæque coniunctione, & porrò in viri & uxoris coniugio, quod Deus ipse ab initio instituit.
units.tr: I. Socinus himself states and confirms our argument fairly well: Whoever is the husband of the Church is that one God of Israel. But Christ is the husband of the Church. Therefore Christ is that one God of Israel. The proof of the major premise, on which the whole argument rests, is drawn from that passage of Isaiah, together with what is generally agreed, that the husband of the Church can be only one, just as a woman can have only one husband. For the one God of Israel says in that place that he is, or will certainly be, the husband of that barren woman who did not bear. Paul, in Galatians 4:26–27, seems to interpret this woman as the Jerusalem above, that is, the Church. The truth of the minor premise is clear from what is read in Ephesians 5:22 and following. From this too is confirmed what we said in proof of the major premise: the Church can have only one husband, just as a woman can have only one husband. For from what is said there it appears that the marriage of Christ with the Church, and in that marriage the highest union, so to speak, was foreshadowed in the joining of male and female, and further in the marriage of husband and wife, which God himself instituted from the beginning.

units.la: II. Ad hoc argumentum vt respondeat vertit se in omnes partes. Primum, inquit, negandum est, sterilem illam quae non pariebat esse Ecclesiam. Lege quaeso, Lector candide, totum illud caput Esaiae LIV. nec non cap. IV. Ep. ad Gal. à V. 22. ad finem usque, & miraberis hominis audaciam id quod sole meridiano clarius est negantis.
units.tr: II. To answer this argument, he turns himself in every direction. First, he says, it must be denied that that barren woman who did not bear is the Church. I ask you, kind reader, to read the whole of Isaiah 54 and also Galatians 4 from verse 22 to the end, and you will marvel at the audacity of a man who denies what is clearer than the noonday sun.

units.la: III. Negationem tamen istam suam fulcire conatur tribus rationibus, sed quae niterentur eodem falso fundamento, vt mox patebit. Quomodo enim, inquit, sterilis Ecclesia noui foederis tunc dici potuit, cum nondum esset? aut quando vnquam sterilis haec Ecclesia fuit, aut dici vllo modo potuit, nisi forte multis post Christum natum seculis? Atqui Esaiae verba ad ea tempora, quae statim post Christum exhibitum extiterunt omnino pertinere, & Pauli locus, antea pro argumento confirmando citatus, aperte docet, nec quisquam est qui neget, qui vaticinium illud ad noui foederis tempora spectare velit. Tunc quidem sterilis dici Ecclesia non potuit, cum nondum fuit. At non fuisse Ecclesiam antequam Christus veniret in carne salsissimum est. Vaticinium Esaiae ad tempus exhibiti Christi pertinet: est enim de mira foecunditate eius Ecclesiae quae mater est omnium fidelium. Ea autem demum aduentu Christi facta est foecunda, cum antea sterilis fuisset.
units.tr: III. Yet he tries to support this denial with three reasons, which rest on the same false foundation, as will soon be plain. For how, he says, could the Church of the new covenant be called barren at a time when it did not yet exist? Or when has this Church ever been barren, or how could it be called so in any way, unless perhaps many centuries after the birth of Christ? But Isaiah's words apply entirely to those times which came into being immediately after Christ was revealed, and the passage from Paul, cited earlier to confirm the argument, clearly teaches this; nor is there anyone who would deny that this prophecy looks to the times of the new covenant. Certainly the Church could not be called barren at a time when it did not yet exist. But it is most false that the Church did not exist before Christ came in the flesh. The prophecy of Isaiah refers to the time of Christ's appearing: it speaks of the wonderful fruitfulness of that Church which is the mother of all believers. And this Church was made fruitful only at the coming of Christ, having been barren before.

units.la: IV. Praeterea, addit Socinus, allegorica ista mulier desolata esse dicitur, id est, viro destituta, vt ex eo quod per antithesin statim subiungitur liquido constat. Id quod ad Ecclesiam siue sub veteri, siue sub nouo foedere, accommodari nequit. Veteri quidem accommodari non posse illi ipsi fatentur, qui volunt mulierem istam esse Ecclesiam. Idem enim volunt alteram coniugatam mulierem, cum qua illa conferetur esse veterem Ecclesiam. Nouae autem non posse accommodari id manifeste docet, quod simul atque ipsa extitit, suum virum habuit Christum, quo nunquam postea destituta fuit. Ante aduentum Christi quemadmodum duplex foedus fuit teste Apostolo Ep. ad Gal. cap. 3. V. 17. Vnum quod ratum factum est à Deo in Christum; ac propterea Euangelicum appellari potest. Alterum quod quadringentis & triginta post annis coepit, & vocari solet foedus legale; sic duplex fuit Ecclesia: vna antiquior nitens ad salutem priore illo foedere: Altera minor natu, quae nitebatur foedere posteriore. Illa cum suo foedere adumbrata fuit in Sara, ista in Agare. Illa, vt Sara, diu sterilis fuit expectans semen promissum, in quo benedicendæ erant omnes gentes. Ista dum expectabatur semen illud promissum, vt Agar, superaddita fuit. Sicut igitur conuerso Abrahamo ad Agarem mansit Sara desolata cubili vacuo, sine conjuge, sine liberis; sic conuerso Marito Ecclesiæ ad fœdus legale, eamque Ecclesiam, quæ illo nitebatur, fœcundabatur illud fœdus, illa Ecclesia, & pariebat in speciem quidem ad libertatem & spem hæreditatis, sed reuera ad seruitutem tantùm: ac interim fœdus illud prius cum ea spirituali Ecclesia quæ eo nitebatur, quasi neglectum & desertum jacebat, nec gignebat semen illud tantò ante promissum, tamque diu expectatum.
units.tr: IV. Furthermore, Socinus adds, this allegorical woman is said to be desolate, that is, deprived of a husband, as is plainly shown by what is immediately added by way of antithesis. This cannot be applied to the Church, whether under the old covenant or under the new. Those very people who want this woman to be the Church admit that it cannot be applied to the old, for they want the other, married woman, with whom she is compared, to be the old Church. But that it cannot be applied to the new is clearly shown by the fact that, as soon as it came into being, it had Christ as its husband, and it was never afterwards deprived of him. Before the coming of Christ there were, as the Apostle testifies in Galatians 3:17, two covenants. One was ratified by God in Christ and may therefore be called the Gospel covenant. The other began four hundred and thirty years later and is usually called the legal covenant. So there were two Churches: one older, resting for salvation on the former covenant, and another younger, resting on the later covenant. The first was foreshadowed in Sarah with her covenant, the second in Hagar. The first, like Sarah, was long barren, waiting for the promised seed in whom all nations were to be blessed. While that promised seed was awaited, the second, like Hagar, was added as a supplement. Therefore, just as when Abraham turned to Hagar, Sarah remained desolate, her bed empty, without husband and without children, so when the husband of the Church turned to the legal covenant, that covenant made fruitful the Church that rested on it, and that Church bore, in appearance indeed for liberty and the hope of inheritance, but in reality only for servitude. Meanwhile that earlier covenant, with that spiritual Church which rested on it, lay as if neglected and abandoned, and it did not bring forth that seed which had been promised so long before and so long awaited.

units.la: V. Addo, inquit Socinus, quod Deus fatetur, se mulierem istam ad breve tempus dereliquisse, qui tamen nunquam Ecclesiam dereliquit. Immò eam eo modo dereliquisse dici potest, quo modo Abraham dereliquit Saram, cum derelicto Sarae cubili venit ad Agarem, eamque, derelictâ Sarâ solâ, in sinum suum recepit, & conjugalem benevolentiam ad eam transtulit. Sic enim Deus Ecclesiam, quæ fide in promissionem ad justificationem suam nitebatur, dereliquisse dici potest, quatenus sese ad Legem ferendam, fovendam, vrgendam, inculcandam applicuit, eamque Ecclesiam, quæ legi addicta fuit, ornavit & fœcundavit, dedit quoque operam gignendis Legis filijs. Ita manserunt quidem simul in eadem domo Abrami, hoc est, Patris excelsi, nimirum Dei, Sara & Agar, Promissio & lex, fides & opera Legis, Ecclesia fide & promissione præcipuè nitens, & Ecclesia præcipuè nitens lege & operibus. Illa origine sua libera, hæc serva; Illa mansura perpetuò in domo patris excelsi, hæc ex illa tandem cum liberis suis ejicienda; Illa jure domina, hæc famula: Sed tamen ita ut dum expectatur tempus implendæ promissionis, pater excelsus sese à fide & promissione, quam olim summo cum affectu commendarat & inculcaverat, converterit ad Legem & Legis opera commendanda, vix aliqua Promissionis & fidei mentione injecta. Cum igitur in eo quod Ecclesia sterilis, desolata, derelicta dicitur, allusio fiat manifesta ad Saram, aliter exponi Epitheta illa non possunt, quàm quemadmodum à nobis exposita sunt.
units.tr: V. I add, says Socinus, that God confesses that he abandoned this woman for a short time, yet he never abandoned the Church. Rather, it can be said that he abandoned her in the way Abraham abandoned Sarah, when, leaving Sarah's bed, he went to Hagar and, Sarah having been left alone, took Hagar into his bosom and transferred his conjugal affection to her. For in this way God can be said to have abandoned the Church, which in faith rested on the promise for its justification, insofar as he applied himself to bringing in, fostering, urging and impressing the Law, and adorned and made fruitful the Church which was devoted to the Law, and also took pains to beget children of the Law. So indeed Sarah and Hagar, that is, Promise and Law, faith and the works of the Law, the Church resting chiefly on faith and promise and the Church resting chiefly on law and works, remained together in the one house of Abraham, that is, of the highest Father, namely God. The one was free by her origin, the other a slave; the one destined to remain forever in the house of the highest Father, the other finally to be cast out with her sons; the one lawfully mistress, the other a servant. Yet while the time for fulfilling the promise was awaited, the highest Father turned himself from faith and promise, which he had earlier commended and impressed with great affection, to the Law and the commending of the works of the Law, with scarcely any mention of promise and faith. Therefore, since the description of the Church as barren, desolate and abandoned clearly alludes to Sarah, those epithets cannot be explained in any other way than as we have explained them.

units.la: VI. Quænam est igitur ex Socini sententia sterilis ista, cuius se ipse Deus profitetur esse maritum, si Ecclesia non est ? Dicimus, inquit, illam, quatenus vaticinatio ista Esaiæ ad Christi tem{pora}pora, & sic ad argumentum ex ea formatum proprie pertinet, Gentes, sive incircumcisum populum esse, qui eo in loco Iudaico sen circumciso populo opponitur, & pro illo sterilis mulier, destituta viro, à Deoque derelicta meritissimo & Esaia tempore, & postea etiam usque ad Christi adventum atque Apostolorum praedicationem, immo etiam ante Esaiae seculum, per complura secula dici potuit. Nulli enim Deo filij ex incircumciso populo, iam inde ab Abrahamo, qui primus omnium circumcisus fuit, praesertim vero post legem circumciso populo datam, nascebantur; quippe quem Deus quodammodo reiecisset, sine quo, tanquam mulier sine viro, ipsi Deo filios parere non poterat. Haec vero expositio à mente Apostoli & Prophetae longe abit, aperte falsa & absurda. Nam ad Apostolum quod attinet, is vt probet iustificari & haeredem esse eum, non qui nititur operibus Legis, sed qui nititur fide & promissione, argumentum ducit plane inuictum à typo duarum mulierum Sarae & Agaris: quarum Ista typus fuit foederis Legalis è monte Arabiae Sina profecti & promulgati, necnon illius Ecclesiae quae eo foedere ad iustificationem suam nitebatur, qualis fuit terrena illa, quae tunc erat, Ierusalem, cum filijs suis persequentibus fideles è domo mariti ejicienda: Illa vero typus fuit foederis gratiae habentis promissiones, è monte Sion qui tangi non potest profecti & promulgati, necnon illius Ecclesiae, quae foedere illo & pro-missione fide firmiter apprehensa nititur, & vocatur ciuitas Dei viuentis, Ierusalem quae supernè est, in monte illo Sion aedificata, ac in aeternum mansura. Vt igitur Ierusalem seu Ecclesia lege nitens sine promissione foecunda fuit simul ac maritum habuit, vt Agar; sic Ierusalem quae supernè est, quamuis legitima esset atque vnica Patris excelsi sponsa, & promissiones haberet saepius repetitas seminis in quo benedicendae essent omnes gentes, tamen diu prae altera illa sterilis fuit, nec alios quàm alterius illius filios habere videbatur. Quae typi cum re adumbrata egregia analogia prorsus corrumpitur, si sterilis ista, cuius maritus esse dicitur Deus, verus pater excelsus, non est Ecclesia respondens Sarae, sed gentes incircumcisae & idololatrae, quibus semen benedictum non fuerat promissum.
units.tr: VI. What then, according to Socinus's view, is that barren woman, whose husband God himself declares himself to be, if she is not the Church? We say, he says, that she, insofar as this prophecy of Isaiah properly pertains to the times of Christ, and so to the argument formed from it, is the Gentiles, or the uncircumcised people, who in that place are set against the Jewish or circumcised people; and in their place a barren woman, deprived of a husband and deservedly forsaken by God, could be spoken of both in Isaiah's time and afterwards, until the coming of Christ and the preaching of the Apostles, and indeed even before Isaiah's age, for many centuries. For from the uncircumcised people no children were born to God, from Abraham onward, who was the first of all to be circumcised, and especially after the Law was given to the circumcised people; since God had, in a sense, rejected them, and without them, as a woman without a husband, could not bear sons to God himself. But this interpretation is far removed from the mind of the Apostle and the Prophet, and is plainly false and absurd. For as to the Apostle, in order to prove that he is justified and an heir not by one who relies on the works of the Law, but by one who relies on faith and promise, he draws a wholly unanswerable argument from the type of the two women, Sarah and Hagar. Of these, the one was the type of the legal covenant, proceeding and promulgated from Mount Sinai in Arabia, and also of that Church which, under that covenant, rested for its justification, such as that earthly Jerusalem which then existed, from which, with her sons who persecuted the faithful, she was to be cast out of the house of her husband. The other was the type of the covenant of grace, which has the promises, proceeding and promulgated from Mount Zion, which cannot be touched, and also of that Church which rests on that covenant and promise, firmly grasped by faith, and is called the city of the living God, the Jerusalem which is above, built on that Mount Zion, and destined to remain forever. Therefore, just as Jerusalem, or the Church resting on the Law without promise, was fruitful as soon as she had a husband, like Hagar, so the Jerusalem which is above, although she was the lawful and only bride of the highest Father, and had promises often repeated of a seed in whom all nations were to be blessed, nevertheless for a long time was barren compared with that other, and seemed to have no children except those of the other. These types are entirely corrupted, along with the excellent analogy between the figure and the thing foreshadowed, if that barren woman, whose husband God, the true highest Father, is said to be, is not the Church corresponding to Sarah, but the uncircumcised and idolatrous nations, to whom the blessed seed had not been promised.

units.la: VII. Id autem, vt nimirum Ecclesia, non vero populus gentium incircuncisus, intelligatur, flagitat non modo insignis huius typi analogia cum re significata quam Apostolus vrget, sed etiam connexio V.[?] 26. cum hoc 27. sic enim se habent duo illi versus apud Apostolum. Illa vero quæ sursum est Ierusalem, libera est, quæ est mater omnium nostrum. Scriptum est enim, Lætare sterilis quæ non paris. Erumpe & clama quæ non parturis, quoniam plures erunt liberi deserta, quàm eius quæ habet virum, τὸν ἄνδρα.
units.tr: VII. But that the Church, and not the uncircumcised Gentile people, is meant is required not only by the striking analogy of this type with the thing signified, which the Apostle presses, but also by the connection of verse 26 with this verse 27. For those two verses stand thus in the Apostle: But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all. For it is written, Rejoice, thou barren that bearest not; break forth and cry, thou that travailest not: for the desolate hath many more children than she which hath an husband. [τὸν ἄνδρα]

units.la: Quis, nisi præjudicio excæcatus fuerit, non videt, eandem ab Apostolo mulierem seu Ecclesiam intelligi, quæ ut Sara, perpetuò libera, diu sterilis, tandem mater facta est fœcundissima? Quænam iubetur lætari, erumpere, clamare, annon ea quæ dicitur mater omnium nostrum, hoc est, fidelium tam ex gentibus quàm ex Iudæis? Quænam alia quàm Ecclesia aut pro marito Deum habet, aut liberos parit Deo verè liberos ac hæredes? Num gentes incircuncisæ quæ non sunt Ecclesia Dei, pariunt Deo filios? num fideles quatenus sunt filij Dei eas pro suis habent matribus? Contrà est. Quominus enim fœdus gratiæ & Ecclesia illi fœderi respondens ex gentibus filios Deo pareret obstiterunt quantum potuerunt gentes; Et qui ex gentibus crediderunt, illi eo ipso desierunt gentes esse gentiumue filij, & facti sunt filij Ierusalem quæ superné est, oppositi gentium filiis. Quod si filij intelliguntur qui sunt filij Ecclesiæ, consentaneum est ut eorum mater esse Ecclesia intelligatur. Alioqui mira quædam erit æquivocatio, maleque cohærebit id quod pro ratione affertur ab Apostolo cum eo quod probare instituit.
units.tr: Who, unless he were blinded by prejudice, does not see that the Apostle means the same woman or Church, who, like Sarah, was always free, long barren, and at last made a most fruitful mother? Who is bidden to rejoice, break forth, and cry out, if not she who is called the mother of us all, that is, of believers both from the Gentiles and from the Jews? What other than the Church has God as her husband, or bears children who are truly free and heirs to God? Do the uncircumcised Gentiles, who are not the Church of God, bear sons to God? Do believers, insofar as they are sons of God, regard them as their mothers? The contrary is true. For the Gentiles have resisted as far as they could the bearing of sons to God from among the Gentiles by the covenant of grace and the Church corresponding to that covenant. And those from the Gentiles who believed ceased on that very account to be Gentiles or sons of Gentiles, and became sons of the Jerusalem which is above, set over against the sons of the Gentiles. But if the sons meant are those who are sons of the Church, it follows that the mother of them is understood to be the Church. Otherwise there will be a strange equivocation, and what the Apostle brings forward as the reason fits badly with what he undertook to prove.

units.la: VIII. Huic postremæ rationi obviam it Socinus. Paulini loci, inquit, sententia hæc est, supernam Ierusalem, quam facilè concedo Christi Ecclesiam significare, esse matrem omnium fidelium, & sic tunc temporis ad ipsam, tanquam filios eos etiam pertinuisse, qui ex gentibus crediderant; quandoquidem tam prædictum erat, ex gentibus multo plures fideles extituros, quàm ex Iudaico populo. Consilium igitur Apostoli, si Socino credimus, fuit prolato hoc Esaiæ vaticinio probare, plures ex gentibus quàm ex Iudæis credidisse aut credituroc fuisse; cuius tamen conclusionis probandæ neque vola neque vestigium apparet in verbis Apostoli: nec mirum; nihil enim facit ad scopum, ad quem collimat Apostolus in versibus antecedentibus & consequentibus. Apostoli autem, quâ sunt admirabili sapientia præditi, solent omnia, etiam illa quæ per parenthesin nonnunquam inserunt, ad scopum suum prudentissimè dirigere, nec ab eo vel latum, ut aiunt, unguem aberrare.
units.tr: VIII. Socinus meets this last argument. The sense of the Pauline passage, he says, is this: that the upper Jerusalem, which I readily grant signifies the Church of Christ, is the mother of all believers, and that thus at that time those also who had believed from among the Gentiles belonged to her as sons, since it had been foretold that far more believers would arise from the Gentiles than from the Jewish people. So, if we believe Socinus, the Apostle's purpose in citing this prophecy of Isaiah was to prove that more from the Gentiles than from the Jews believed, or were going to believe. Yet neither a sail nor a trace of this conclusion to be proved appears in the Apostle's words, and this is no wonder: for it has nothing to do with the aim at which the Apostle aims in the verses before and after. But the Apostles, who are endowed with admirable wisdom, are accustomed to direct everything, even those things which they sometimes insert in a parenthesis, most prudently to their own aim, and not to stray from it, as they say, even by the breadth of a nail.

units.la: IX. Ad superiora illud etiam accedit, quod quae compellatur, sterilis appellatur. Sterilis autem dici non potest quae virum non novit, quae non est vllo matrimonij foedere cum viro juncta, qualis erat populus gentium incircuncisus, idolorum quidem scortum admodum foecundum, Dei vero nullo modo conjunx: quippe, quod ad foedera promissionis attinet extraneus, spem non ha-bens, & absque Deo in mundo. At inquiet aliquis, deserta vocatur ista mulier & opponitur habenti virum. Nempe vocatur deserta scilicet a viro suo, & opponitur habenti τὸν ἄνδρα[?], scilicet virum desertae. Allusio est, ut dixi, ad Saram, cuius virum ad tempus Agar possedit, manente interim in eadem viri domo Sara quasi deserta, sed tamen neque repudiata, neque infideli. Itaque jubetur exultare, laetari, prae gaudio clamare, quoniam sic breui paritura, numerosaeque prolis mater futura. Quid enim laetius accidere potuisset sterili, cupiditates[?] & ut ita loquar, siti prolis prope enectae?
units.tr: IX. To the above is also added that the woman addressed is called barren. But she cannot be called barren who does not know a man, who is not joined to a man by any marriage covenant, such as the uncircumcised Gentile people were: indeed a most fruitful harlot of idols, but in no way the spouse of God; for they were strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. But someone will say that this woman is called desolate and is set over against her who has a husband. Indeed she is called desolate, namely by her husband, and is set over against her who has [τὸν ἄνδρα], namely the husband of the desolate woman. It is an allusion, as I said, to Sarah, whose husband Hagar possessed for a time, while meanwhile Sarah remained in the same husband's house as one as it were deserted, yet neither repudiated nor unfaithful. Therefore she is bidden to exult, rejoice, and cry out for joy, since she would soon bear and become the mother of a numerous offspring. For what could have happened more joyful to a barren woman, whose desires and, as I may say, thirst for offspring were almost extinguished?

units.la: X. Ad Prophetam quod spectat, clarius est apud eum Ecclesiam compellari toto illo cap. LIV. quam ut negari possit. Sic enim sterilem illam affatur Ѱ. 2.[?] dilata locum tentorii tui & pelles tabernaculorum tuorum extende &c, nimirum Ecclesia foecundata latius multo quam dum esset sterilis habitavit, eiusque limites valde dilatati sunt. Id quod de populo gentium incircunciso qui Ecclesia non est dici non potest. Sed ne sim longior in re manifesta probanda, quid clarius verbis illis Ѱ. 11. 12.[?] O afflicta, procellis agitata, consolatione destituta: Ecce ego collocaturus sum cum ornamento lapides tuos & fundaturus te saphiris, & disponam pyropos specularia tua, & portas tuas lapidibus carbunculi, denique totum terminum tuum lapidibus speciosissimis. Nonne haec descriptio est Ierusalem eius quae supernè est? Et quae sequuntur, Et omnes filij tui edocti erunt à Domino &c, verane sunt de omnibus filijs gentium quae non sunt Ecclesia? aut de solis fidelibus vocatis è gentibus, & non vel maximè de fidelibus Iudaeis, deque ipsis Apostolis, qui nullo modo filij fuerunt populi incircuncisi?
units.tr: X. As far as the Prophet is concerned, it is clearer in him that the Church is addressed throughout that whole fifty-fourth chapter than it can be denied. For he addresses that barren woman thus, verse 2: Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thy habitations, namely the Church, made fruitful, dwelt far more widely than when she was barren, and her boundaries were greatly enlarged. This cannot be said of the uncircumcised Gentile people, who are not the Church. But, not to be too long in proving a matter that is plain, what is clearer than those words, verses 11 and 12: O thou afflicted, tossed with tempests, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones. Is not this a description of Jerusalem, the one which is above? And what follows, And all thy children shall be taught of the Lord, etc., is it true of all the sons of the Gentiles who are not the Church? Or of believers called from the Gentiles alone, and not especially of believing Jews, and of the Apostles themselves, who were in no way sons of the uncircumcised people?

units.la: XI. Verum fingamus non intelligi Ecclesiam, sed, ut vult Socinus, gentes incircuncisas. Quid sequetur? Nonne hoc absurdum, Deum Patrem fuisse maritum gentium incircuncisarum quandiu fuerunt idololatrae, à foederibus divinis alienae, & absque Deo in mūdo; simul ac autem ab idolis conuersæ fuerunt ad Deum viuum, & diuinum fœdus viua fide amplexæ Deum Patrem desiisse earum maritum esse, easque Filio meræ, si audiuntur Aduersarij, creaturæ cessisse? Ita longè potiores erunt Filij quàm Patris, creaturæ quàm creatoris partes. Pater siquidem fuerit maritus populi Idololatrici, Christus Ecclesiæ, quæ multò est quàm populus idololatricus dignior, Ille adulteræ, hic castæ; Ille perituræ, hic futuræ in æternum beatæ. Hoccine Aduersarijs placet? Sic refutata est prima Socini responsio.
units.tr: XI. But let us suppose that the Church is not meant, but, as Socinus wishes, the uncircumcised Gentiles. What follows? Is it not absurd that God the Father was the husband of the uncircumcised Gentiles as long as they were idolaters, alien from the divine covenants and without God in the world; and that, as soon as they were converted from idols to the living God and embraced the divine covenant by living faith, God the Father ceased to be their husband, and, if the adversaries are heard, ceded them to the Son as mere creatures? Thus the parts of the sons would be far greater than those of the Father, and those of the creature greater than those of the Creator. For if the Father was the husband of the idolatrous people, Christ is the husband of the Church, which is far worthier than the idolatrous people: the former of an adulteress, the latter of a chaste one; the former of one destined to perish, the latter of one destined to be blessed forever. Does this please the adversaries? Thus the first response of Socinus is refuted.

units.la: XII. Alteram sic ipse concipit. Nihil, inquit, cogit, vt vox Hebraica Bahal quæ ibi legitur virum seu maritum significet, cum ea non minus Dominum significare queat; vt quidem tum Græca editio, tum vulgata Latina habet. Id quod alterius responsionis loco ad argumentum ipsum esse volumus. Quid? An cogi oportet Aduersarios ad proprias & vsitatas vocum Hebraicarum significationes admittendas? Ego verò contrà putabam ab ijs discedendum non esse, nisi quid cogat. Est autem propria & vsitata, inimò perpetua vocis Hebraicæ Bahal, quotiescunque de muliere agitur, significatio, vt virum seu maritum significet: Et verbum Bahal de matrimonio vsurpatur, immò de actu venereo Deut. 21. 13. & 24. 1. ac vtrumque & nomen & verbum de Sara & Abrahamo dicitur Gen. 20. 3. videturque בעל dici quasi בא על, quæ duæ voces ad significandum actum maritalem adhibentur Gen. 19. 31. & hoc ipso cap. Esai. 54. Ɣ. 1. בעולה vertente Apostolo est; ἢ ἔχουσα τὸν ἄνδρα[?],
units.tr: XII. He himself conceives the second thus: Nothing, he says, compels us to take the Hebrew word Bahal, which is read there, as meaning husband or spouse, since it can equally signify Lord, as indeed both the Greek edition and the Latin Vulgate have it. We wish this to stand as a response, in place of the other, to the argument itself. What? Ought the adversaries to be compelled to admit the proper and customary meanings of Hebrew words? I, on the contrary, thought that one should not depart from them unless something compelled it. But the proper and customary, indeed the constant, meaning of the Hebrew word Bahal, whenever a woman is spoken of, is to signify a husband or spouse. And the verb Bahal [בעל] is used of marriage, indeed of the sexual act, Deut. 21. 13 and 24. 1; and both the noun and the verb are said of Sarah and Abraham, Gen. 20. 3. And it seems that בעל is said as though it were [בא על], two words which are used to signify the marital act, Gen. 19. 31, and in this very chapter of Isaiah, 54. 1, where the Apostle renders [בעולה] as [ἢ ἔχουσα τὸν ἄνδρα].

units.la: XIII. Adde quod huius loci circumstantiæ aliam interpretationem ferre non possunt. Quæ enim compellatur, ea primùm sterilis fuisse, & ad aliquod tempus deserta à viro dicitur Ɣ. 1. Id quod maritam arguit. Deinde proles ei numerosa ac legitima promittitur Ɣ. 2. & 3. sine dubio ex legitimo viro. Tum, quoniam quæ diu steriles fuerunt cum conceperunt, verecundia quàdam timidæ esse solent, vt de Elizabetha matre Iohannis Baptistæ annotatum est à Luca cap. 1. Ɣ. 24. subjungitur Ɣ. 4. hæc hortatio, Ne timeto, quia non erubesces, & ne ignominia confusa esto, quia non pudebit te &c. Ratio affertur Ɣ. 5. quia, inquit, Maritus tuus est factor tuus: nomen eius est Dominus exercituum &c. Itaque causa non est cur te concepisse & peperisse pudeat, nec etiam cur sis de tam numerosa prole educanda & inter tot ho[?]sites conseruanda sollicita; nam & ex legitimo viro conceptisti, & is satis diues ac potens est, vt te coniugem filiosque tuos & suos alat, defendat, ac tandem honore & felicitate maxima beet.
units.tr: XIII. Add that the circumstances of this passage cannot bear any other interpretation. For she who is addressed is said first to have been barren, and for a certain time to have been deserted by her husband, verse 1. This points to a married woman. Then a numerous and lawful offspring is promised to her, verses 2 and 3, without doubt from her lawful husband. Then, since women who have been long barren are commonly somewhat timid when they conceive, as was noted by Luke of Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist, Luke 1:24, there follows in verse 4 this exhortation: Fear not, for thou shalt not be ashamed; neither be thou confounded, for thou shalt not be put to shame, etc. The reason is given in verse 5: for thy Maker is thy husband; the Lord of hosts is his name, etc. Therefore there is no cause why you should be ashamed that you have conceived and borne, nor why you should be anxious about rearing so numerous an offspring and preserving it among so many enemies; for you conceived by a lawful husband, and he is rich and powerful enough to feed, defend, and at last bless you, his wife and your sons and his own, with the greatest honour and happiness.

units.la: XIV. Præterea subnectit, se eam ad breue tempus, vt solebat vxorem vir iratus, dereliquisse, negat autem se illi in posterum iratum fore, aut eam derelicturum. Denique pollicetur se liberos illius, vt patrem decet, edocturum [?]V. 13. quæ omnia aperte significant, Deum sese hoc loco maritum eius quam compellat, hoc est, Ecclesiæ profiteri. Id quod alibi facit tam aperte, vt satis mirari non possim Socini obliuionem & incogitantiam. Fac enim isto loco vocem Bahal[?] maritum non significare, Nonne in alijs multis locis Deus Israëlis se disertis verbis testatur esse maritum Ecclesiæ, vt Esai. 50. 1. Hos. 2. Ierem. 3. Ezech. 16. & 23? Hoc autem ad argumentum nostrum satis est. Inde enim sequitur, aut eiusdem vxoris duos esse maritos, Patrem & filium, quo nihil fingi potest absurdius; aut Patrem fuisse maritum Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ, Filium Christianæ, quod ipsum quoque absurdum est; aut denique Filium esse illum Deum Israëlis qui se maritum esse Ecclesiæ testatur. Relegatur, si placet, Disputatio nostra decima nona. Sic etiam refutata est responsio secunda.
units.tr: XIV. Further, he adds that God abandoned her for a short time, as an angry husband was accustomed to abandon his wife, but he says that he will not be angry with her in future nor forsake her. Finally, he promises that he will teach her children, as a father ought [Esai. 54. vers. 13]. All these things plainly signify that God, in this place, addresses the Church as her husband, that is, declares himself to be her husband. He does this elsewhere so clearly that I cannot sufficiently wonder at Socinus' forgetfulness and thoughtlessness. For suppose that in this place the word Bahal [בעל] does not mean husband: do not many other places testify expressly that the God of Israel is the husband of the Church, as Isa. 50. 1, Hos. 2, Jer. 3, Ezek. 16 and 23? This, however, is enough for our argument. For it follows either that the same wife has two husbands, Father and Son, than which nothing can be imagined more absurd; or that the Father was husband of the Jewish Church and the Son of the Christian Church, which is itself absurd; or finally that the one who is the God of Israel, and who testifies that he is the husband of the Church, is the Son. Let our nineteenth disputation be reread, if you like. In this way the second answer was also refuted.

units.la: XV. Sed, inquit Socinus, tertio praterea loco responderi ad argumentum istud potest, non eandem esse rationem metaphoricarum appellationum & propriarum: nec si proprie Maritus appellatus unus tantum alicuius vera mulieris esse potest, similiter metaphoricè appellatum maritum unum tantum alicuius vicem mulieris explentis esse posse, concludendum vllo modo esse. Et paulò post, Nihil vetat, quominus Ecclesia plures maritos habere possit, cum necesse sit, quemadmodum ipsa est metaphorica mulier, sic etiam quisquis eius maritus sit, eum esse ipsius metaphoricum maritum. Sanus ne erat Socinus cum hæc scribebat? Non magis enim aduersus nos disputat, quàm aduersus ipsum Deum. Deus enim hoc idem in ista metaphorica Mariti & vxoris appellatione vrget, quod nos vrgemus. Itaque gentem Israëliticam adulterij accusat & damnat quod viro suo Deo non contenta ad alios se conuerterit. Cum igitur clamet & inculcet, non posse Ecclesiam alij adhærere quin eo ipso fiat adultera, cum se profiteatur Zelotypum esse, nec posse patirimonialem, cum ad exaggeranda peccata populi sui vtatur ista mulieris similitudine adulterio se polluentis, omnino docet istam metaphoricam appellatione mariti, nomininus [?] quàm si esset propria, pluralitatem maritorum excludere, legantur loca jam citata Ier. 3. Ezech. 16. & 23. Os. 2. &c. Nam si eo sensu quo Deus se maritum Ecclesiæ vocat, possent esse eiusdem mulieris vicem explentis mariti plures, posset illa sine crimine adulterij cum pluribus maritis consuescere, & potuisset autore Socino gens Iudaica Deo eam tanquam mulierem adulteram accusanti & grauter reprehendenti respondere, se quidem non posse absque crimine adulterij plures maritos habere proprie sic appellatos, sed maritos metaphoricè sic dictos, & quidem metaphora minus plena, quomodo Deus ipsius maritus appellatur, posse plures habere, nec propterea adulteram esse. Id enim teste Socino inter istam metaphoricam mariti & propriam appellationem discrimen intercedere, ut nullo modo concludi possit, adulteram esse quæ metaphorico illo sensu plures viros habeat. Non puto ita inuerecundos esse Adversarios, quin eos iam huius suæ tertiæ responsionis pudeat, ipsi Deo tam repugnantis.
units.tr: XV. But, says Socinus, a third answer can be given to this argument, namely that the reasoning about metaphorical appellations is not the same as that about proper ones: and even if one who is properly called husband can be the husband of only one true woman, it should in no way be concluded that a husband called metaphorically can be the husband of only one who takes the place of a wife. And a little later: Nothing prevents the Church from having several husbands, since, just as she herself is a metaphorical woman, so whoever is her husband must be her metaphorical husband. Was Socinus sane when he wrote this? For he disputes no less against God himself than against us. For God, in this very metaphorical appellation of husband and wife, presses the same point that we press. Therefore he accuses and condemns the Israelite nation of adultery, because, not content with her husband God, she turned to others. Since, then, he cries out and insists that the Church cannot cleave to another without thereby becoming an adulteress, since he declares himself to be a jealous God, and cannot be a polygamist, and since he uses this likeness of a woman polluting herself with adultery to magnify the sins of his people, he entirely teaches that this metaphorical appellation of husband excludes a plurality of husbands just as clearly as if it were proper. Let the passages already cited be read: Jer. 3, Ezek. 16 and 23, Hos. 2, etc. For if, in the sense in which God calls himself the husband of the Church, there could be several husbands of the same woman who takes the place of a wife, then she could live with several husbands without the crime of adultery; and, on Socinus' authority, the Jewish nation could have answered God, when he accused and sharply rebuked her as an adulterous woman, that indeed she could not have several husbands properly so called without the crime of adultery, but that she could have several husbands called so metaphorically, and indeed in the less full metaphor by which God is called her husband, and that therefore she is not an adulteress. For, on Socinus' testimony, there is such a difference between this metaphorical husband and a proper appellation that it cannot in any way be concluded that a woman who has several husbands in that metaphorical sense is an adulteress. I do not think the adversaries are so shameless that they are not ashamed of this third answer, which is so contrary to God himself.

units.la: XVI. Quoniam autem eam Socinus illustrare conatus est unico exemplo, quo aptius nullum reperire potuit, id quàm sit ineptum paucis ostendendum est. Exemplum sit, inquit, in patris appellatione, quæ quamvis uni tantùm proprie accepta conveniat, respectu unius: tamen metaphoricè accepta, pluribus, unius tantùm licet respectu, convenire invenietur. Id docet exemplo veritatis, quæ proprie sic dictum patrem nullum habet, cuius ait, vulgo patrem metaphoricè dici tempus; quod quidem intelligendum est, quatenus tantummodo illa apparet atque agnoscitur. Atqui secundum hanc ipsam rationem nemo negaverit, Deum quoque veritatis Patrem dici posse, idque multò pleniore metaphora: cum multò magis veritatis patefaciendæ auctor & causa Deus sit quàm tempus, cui nonnisi per accidens hoc idem tribui potest. Hoc exemplum duplici de causa ineptum est. Primò quia falsum est, patris appellationem uni tantùm proprie acceptam convenire respectu unius: possunt enim esse, immò sunt, eiusdem filij plures patres proprie dicti, unus proximus, plurimi remoti, patris nempe & matris patres, aui, proaui, abaui, ataui &c. Immò plures proximi, unus naturalis, alter adoptivus, tertius socer, quartus olim is defunctus cui ex vidua frater hæredem gignebat. Itaque nihil est absurdi si unus idemque filius plures homines patres suos appellet, immò id fit persæpe decenter. At si mulier aliqua plures viros appellaret maritos suos siue proprie, siue metaphoricè, illa eo ipso sese vel adulteram esse profiteretur vel adulteræ similem, maleque admodum id sonaret castis auribus: quia nimirum nihil tam castitati mulierum repugnat, quàm maritorum, aut eorum qui vices mariti expleant, pluralitas; hæc enim reciprocatur cum adulterio, proprie dicta quidem cum propriedicto, metaphoricè verò dicta cum dicto metaphoricè. Altera causa cur sit insulsum hoc exemplum est, quod Deus ipse, ut jam obseruaui, sibi istam mariti appellationem eo sensu tribuit, quo maritorum pluralitatem excludit. Alioqui accommodata non fuisset ad spiritualia Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ & Israëliticæ adulteria arguenda & exaggeranda, quem ad usum ab ipso Deo adhibetur locis laudatis.
units.tr: XVI. Since, however, Socinus has tried to illustrate it with a single example, for which he could find none more apt, it must be shown in a few words how inept it is. Let the example be, he says, the appellation of father, which, although it properly applies to only one person with respect to one child, yet when taken metaphorically will be found to apply to several, with respect to one child only. He teaches this by the example of truth, which has no proper father, of whom he says that time is commonly called father metaphorically; which indeed must be understood so far as it merely appears and is recognised. But according to this very reasoning, no one will deny that God can also be called the Father of truth, and that with a much fuller metaphor, since God is much more the author and cause of disclosing the truth than time is, to which this same thing can be attributed only accidentally. This example is inept for two reasons. First, because it is false that the appellation of father, properly taken, applies to only one person with respect to one child: for there can be, indeed there are, several proper fathers of the same son, one nearest and several remote, namely the father's and mother's fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, great-great-grandfathers and so on. Indeed, there are several nearest: one natural, another adoptive, a third father-in-law, and a fourth, long dead, by whose widow a brother begot an heir. So there is nothing absurd if one and the same son calls several men his fathers; indeed this is often done with propriety. But if some woman were to call several men her husbands, whether properly or metaphorically, she would thereby either profess herself an adulteress or make herself like one, and this would sound very bad to chaste ears: for nothing is so contrary to the chastity of women as a plurality of husbands, or of those who take the place of a husband. For this is reciprocal with adultery: properly taken with properly taken, and metaphorically taken with metaphorically taken. The second reason why this example is foolish is that God himself, as I have already observed, attributes to himself this appellation of husband in that sense in which he excludes a plurality of husbands. Otherwise it would not have been suited to exposing and magnifying the spiritual adulteries of the Jewish and Israelite Church, which God himself uses for this purpose in the places cited.

units.la: XVII. Videtur præterea Socinus nescio quid responsionis addere velle. Quid plura? inquit, Deus ante natum hominem Christum Iesum, seipsum non obscure maritum facit, tum Israelis, tum Iudae apud Ierem. cap. 3. Quanto igitur magis potuerit Deus, citra humanae Iesu Christi naturae considerationem, & Ecclesiam maritum se apud Esaiam vocare? Quod si ita est, quomodo quaeso ex isto Esaiae loco, etiamsi diserte ibi ille unus Deus Israelis se Ecclesiae maritum appellasset, concludi posset, Christum Iesum ob eam causam, quod Ecclesiae est maritus, esse unum illum Deum Israelis, cum sine ulla controversia Christus Iesus citra suae humanae naturae considerationem, non sit, nec esse possit ille Ecclesiae maritus seu sponsus, quem ipsum esse sacra testimonia docent? videtur potius his verbis contra argumentari quàm respondere.
units.tr: XVII. Socinus further seems to wish to add some sort of further answer. What more? he says. Before the man Christ Jesus was born, God openly made himself the husband both of Israel and of Judah, in Jer. chap. 3. How much more, then, could God, without considering the human nature of Jesus Christ, call himself the husband of the Church in Isaiah? But if this is so, I ask, how could it be concluded from that passage of Isaiah, even if the one God of Israel had there expressly called himself the husband of the Church, that Christ Jesus, because he is the husband of the Church, is that one God of Israel, since, without any controversy, Christ Jesus, apart from the consideration of his human nature, is not and cannot be that husband or bridegroom of the Church, which the sacred testimonies teach that he himself is? He seems rather to argue against us with these words than to answer.

units.la: Ut ut sit, quod affirmat, Deum an-te natum hominem Christum Iesum, seipsum non obscure maritum facere, cum Israelis, cum Iudae apud Ierem. cap. 3. verum est, & confirmat argumentum nostrum. Nam vel idem est Ecclesiae Christianae maritus qui fuit olim Ecclesiae Iudaicae; vel non. Si idem est, cum certum sit filium esse unicum maritum Ecclesiae Christianae, fatendum est eundem Filium fuisse olim maritum Ecclesiae Iudaicae. Hunc autem constat fuisse Deum. Fatendum est igitur Filium antequam homo fieret Deum fuisse. Si non est idem, dignior fuit Ecclesia Iudaica quàm Christiana, quippe dignioris vxor, videlicet Patris: & nunc, aut in resurrectione, cuius est aut erit vxor? durat enim post mortem & resurrectionem, immò maximè viget, spirituale Filij & Ecclesiæ conjugium. Eruntne tunc duæ sponsæ, duo sponsi, & non potius ex omnibus fidelibus qui vnquam fuerunt, vna constabit Ecclesia, vna sponsa, vna cœlestis Ierusalem vni viro Domino nostro æterno fœdere iuncta? Tunc dubitabile non erit, quin ipsius etiam Ecclesiæ Iudaicæ maritus sit Christus.
units.tr: However that may be, what he affirms, that before the man Christ Jesus was born, God openly made himself the husband both of Israel and of Judah in Jer. chap. 3, is true, and it confirms our argument. For either the husband of the Christian Church is the same as the husband of the Jewish Church once was, or he is not. If he is the same, then, since it is certain that the Son is the only husband of the Christian Church, it must be admitted that the same Son was once the husband of the Jewish Church. But it is established that this one was God. It must therefore be admitted that the Son was God before he became man. If he is not the same, then the Jewish Church was more worthy than the Christian, being the wife of a more worthy husband, namely the Father; and whose wife is she now, or will she be at the resurrection? For the spiritual marriage of the Son and the Church endures after death and resurrection, and indeed flourishes most of all. Will there then be two brides and two bridegrooms, or rather will one Church, one bride, one heavenly Jerusalem, joined by an eternal covenant to one husband, our Lord, be constituted out of all the faithful who have ever existed? Then there will be no doubt that Christ is also the husband of the Jewish Church itself.

units.la: XVIII. Quod inde deducit Socinus, Quanto igitur magis potuerit Deus, citra humanæ Iesu Christi naturæ considerationem, Ecclesiæ maritum se apud Esaiam vocare? ex eo nullo modo sequitur.
units.tr: XVIII. Socinus's inference, "How much more, then, could God, without considering the human nature of Jesus Christ, call himself the husband of the Church in Isaiah?", does not follow in any way from what has been said.

units.la: Deus enim appellatus non est maritus Ecclesiæ, nisi ratione fœderis cum ea initi. Nullum autem cum ea fœdus iniit citra considerationem naturæ humanæ Christi vel futuræ vel existentis. Nam & fœdus cum Abrahamo contractum ratum factum est, teste Apostolo, <bl>εἰς Χριστόν</bl>, & in promissionibus quæ datæ sunt Adamo & Patriarchis mentio facta est feminis contriturí caput serpentis, & in quo benedicendæ erant omnes gentes, nec est inchoatum spirituale istud matrimonium absque consensu & fide Ecclesiæ promissiones illas amplectentis, & ipsum fœdus legale pædagogus erat ad Christum, in eumque vt in suum finem tendebat. Taceo sine expiatione peccatorum nullam esse posse hominum reconciliationem cum Deo. Nullam autem esse realem & veram peccatorum expiationem præter eam quæ facta est Christi sacrificio. Ac proinde omnem hominum peccatorum cum Deo veram reconciliationem & consociationem fundatam fuisse in sacrificio Christi vel futuro, vel exhibito, quod sine humana Christi natura nec esse, nec intelligi potuit. Adde quod non fit vllo modo verisimile, Patrem contrahere matrimonium cum gente peccatrice absq; interuentu Mediatoris. Est autem Mediator vel typicus vel realis: ille Moses, hic Christus. Per mediatorem typicum non poterit contrahi matrimonium nisi typicum, cuiusmodi esse non potuit matrimonium Dei Patris cum Ecclesia, ita enim vt matrimonium illud fuisset typus matrimonij Christi & Ecclesiæ Christianæ, sic Deus Pater fuisset typus Christi, & Ecclesia Israëlitica typus Ecclesiæ Christianæ. Per realem autem Mediatorem, qui alius esse non potest quàm Christus, aliud nullum spirituale matrimonium contrahi potuit quàm ipsius Christi cum Ecclesia reale & perpetuum ac prorsus indissolubile, cuius Matrimonij typus ab ipso mundi exordio adumbrari cœpit in Adami & Euæ matrimonio. Deinde additis aliis typis multis & varijs paulatim expolitus est, & perfectus ita, vt nihil possit in matrimonio Christi & Ecclesiae obseruari, cuius non extet aliqua in Vetere Testamento adumbratio, fiatque ex omnibus eiusmodi typis inter se collatis tam perfecta repraesentatio, vt nihil vel desit vel superfluat. Ex quo perspicuum est æternum illud matrimonium, & ad illud perficiendum necessariam naturam humanam Christi Deum ab initio mundi quoties fœdus cum Ecclesia contraxit, ob oculos habuisse.
units.tr: God is not called the husband of the Church except by reason of the covenant made with her. But he made no covenant with her apart from consideration of the human nature of Christ, whether future or already existing. For the covenant with Abraham was ratified, as the Apostle witnesses, in Christ [εἰς Χριστόν]. In the promises given to Adam and the Patriarchs, mention was made of the seed who would crush the serpent's head, and in whom all nations were to be blessed. Nor could that spiritual marriage have been begun without the consent and faith of the Church, who embraced those promises. The legal covenant itself was a schoolmaster leading to Christ, and it tended toward him as its end. I say nothing of the fact that there can be no reconciliation of men with God without the expiation of sins. There is no real and true expiation of sins except that made by the sacrifice of Christ. Therefore every true reconciliation and fellowship of men with God was founded on the sacrifice of Christ, whether future or already offered, and this could neither exist nor be understood without the human nature of Christ. Add that it is in no way likely that the Father would contract marriage with a sinful people without the intervention of a Mediator. A Mediator is either typical or real: the former was Moses, the latter Christ. Through a typical mediator only a typical marriage could be contracted, and the marriage of God the Father with the Church could not have been of that kind. For then that marriage would have been a type of the marriage of Christ and the Christian Church, so that God the Father would have been a type of Christ, and the Israelite Church a type of the Christian Church. But through a real Mediator, who can be none other than Christ, no other spiritual marriage could be contracted than the real, perpetual and utterly indissoluble marriage of Christ himself with the Church. The type of this marriage began to be shadowed forth from the very beginning of the world, in the marriage of Adam and Eve. Then, with many other and varied types added gradually, it was refined and perfected, so that nothing can be observed in the marriage of Christ and the Church for which there is not some shadowing in the Old Testament. From all such types compared together there results so perfect a representation that nothing is either lacking or superfluous. From this it is plain that God, whenever he covenanted with the Church, had before his eyes that eternal marriage and the human nature of Christ necessary to bring it to completion, from the beginning of the world.

units.la: Responsio ad objectiones quasdam Socini.
units.tr: Response to certain objections of Socinus.

units.la: I. ABSOLVTO superiore additamento incidi in fragmenta duo Socini, quorum altero naturam Christi diuinam oppugnare, altero ad vltimum nostrum argumentum respondere conatus est. In priore legi hoc argumentum. Si Iesus Christus Dei filius seruator noster, esset ille Iehoua unicus Israelitarum & Christianorum Deus, manifeste, vt omnes fatentur, consequeretur, Deum hominem fuisse factum, quod, quum ab humana ratione penitus abhorreat, id quidem diserris [?] verbis, vt ita esse credamus, oporteret, & non in vno tantum, sed in quam plurimis sacrarum literarum locis scriptum extare, quod in omnibus, quae paululum modo ad credendum difficilia sunt, factum fuisse conspicimus. &c. At vero tantum abest, vt stupenda isthaec Dei metamorphosis à sacris auctoribus identidem nobis aperte praedicata fuerit, vt ne vno quidem loco obscure saltem significata deprehendatur. Quo fit, vt eius assertores, non claris diuinarum literarum testimoniis, imo ne testimoniis quidem vllis, sed potius meris quibusdam consecutionibus sententiam suam adstruere conentur &c. Quàm hoc verè ab eo affirmetur, iam, opinor, patet ex septuaginta istis testimoniis, quae hoc & superiore libro ab Aduersariorum exceptionibus & depravationibus Dei beneficio vindicauimus. Id etiam vti spero patebit ex ijs, quæ dante Deo laudabuntur à nobis in libro sequente, quibus omnibus cum responsum ab Aduersarijs fuerit solidè (quod nisi vehementissimè fallor, neque vnquam fiet, neque fieri potest) tum licebit eis de suo isto argumento gloriari. In quo sibi valdè placere videtur Socinus dilatando & perpoliendo, ac loca quædam Noui Testamenti percurrendo, non quæ à nostris citari solent (qualia sunt inter cæteros Ioh. 1. 14. & Phil 2. 6. 7. vbi disertis verbis mirabilis ista metamorphosis (si tamen eo nomine appellari potest) apertè traditur & celebratur: ex quibus locis argumenta duo duximus, quintum nimirum & sextum libri primi) sed alia quædam, in quibus pro sua sapientia, quæ sæpè à diuina longissimè abit, putat hoc mysterium debuisse ab Euangelistis & Apostolis, siquidem id credidissent, aperte doceri, vt cum Euangelistæ Matthæus & Lucas describunt natiuitatem Domini nostri, cum Petrus ad populum Hierosolymitanum, ad Seniores populi, ad Cornelium conciones habet, cum Paulus in Antiochensi Pisidiana synagoga Iudeos hortatur, Athenis in Areopago concionatur, & Cæsareæ coram Aggrippa rege & Festo præside aduersus Iudæos se defendit. Omisit callidè concionem Pauli quam Mileti ad Presbyteros seu episcopos Ecclesiæ Ephesinæ habuit, in qua disertis verbis dicit, Deum Ecclesiam acquisiuisse suo sanguine διὰ τῆ ἰδίᾳ αἵματ[?]
units.tr: I. Having finished the preceding addendum, I came upon two fragments of Socinus. In one he tries to attack the divine nature of Christ, and in the other he attempts to answer our last argument. In the first I read this argument: "If Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our Saviour, were that Jehovah, the sole God of the Israelites and Christians, it would manifestly follow, as everyone admits, that God had been made man. Since this is utterly abhorrent to human reason, it ought to be stated in clear words, so that we might believe it, and it should be found written not in one place only but in very many places of the sacred letters, as we see has been done in all matters that are somewhat hard to believe, etc." Yet so far is that stupendous metamorphosis of God from having been plainly and repeatedly proclaimed to us by the sacred authors, that it cannot be found indicated obscurely even in a single passage. "Whence it comes about that its asserters try to establish their view not by clear testimonies of the divine letters, nor indeed by any testimonies at all, but by mere inferences, etc." How truly this is asserted is now, I think, clear from those seventy testimonies which, in this and the preceding book, we have by God's blessing vindicated from the objections and distortions of our adversaries. I hope it will also be plain from those things which, God giving, we shall set out in the following book. When all these have been solidly answered by the adversaries (which, unless I am greatly mistaken, will never happen and cannot happen), then they may glory in this argument of theirs. In it Socinus seems to please himself greatly, by expanding and polishing, and by running through certain passages of the New Testament. These are not the ones our people are wont to cite (such as, among others, John 1:14 and Phil. 2:6, 7, where that wondrous metamorphosis, if indeed it can be called by that name, is openly taught and celebrated in plain words; from these passages we drew two arguments, namely the fifth and sixth of the first book). Instead he cites other passages, in which, according to his wisdom, which is very often far from divine, he thinks this mystery ought to have been openly taught by the Evangelists and Apostles, if they had believed it. Such are the passages where the Evangelists Matthew and Luke describe the birth of our Lord; where Peter addresses the Jerusalem people, the elders of the people, and Cornelius; where Paul in the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia exhorts the Jews, preaches at Athens in the Areopagus, and at Caesarea before King Agrippa and the governor Festus defends himself against the Jews. He craftily omitted the sermon Paul delivered at Miletus to the elders or bishops of the Ephesian Church, in which he says in plain words that God acquired the Church with his own blood [διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος].

units.la: II. Primùm autem meminisse Socinum oportebat, Euangelistas & Apostolos mysteria & dogmata religionis Christianæ non temerè & quolibet loco, & tempore, & quibusdam profundere sed prudenter admodum administrare, atque aliter apud Iudæos, aliter apud Græcos, aliter apud nondum conuersos, aliter apud iam conuersos, aliter apud Christianos infirmos & lactentes, aliter apud adultos & perfectos agere, exemplo ipsius Domini, qui ad tempus mortem suam futuram celauit Apostolos suos, eisque edixit, ne cui dicerent, ipsum esse Christum, & suam illam in monte metamorphosin patefieri aliis discipulis suis, antequam resurrexisset, noluit. Dabunt autem nobis, opinor, Aduersarij Euangelistas & Apostolos sapientiores Socino fuisse & melius eo sciuisse, quando, & quibus, & quomodo de Christi Deitate &, vt vulgò loquuntur, incarnatione sibi dicendum esset. Satis nobis est præstantissima ista dogmata passim in Euangelijs & reliquis Noui Testamenti libris micare, eumque fulgorem emittere, quem qui non agnoscit, sponte cæcutire mihi videtur. Nos certè illa, etiam in conceptionis Christi descriptione, & concionibus quibusdam Petri & Pauli, sed præcipuè in eorum Epistolis cernere nobis videmur.
units.tr: II. But first Socinus ought to have remembered that the Evangelists and Apostles did not pour out the mysteries and doctrines of the Christian religion rashly, at any place, time, or to anyone. They administered them with great prudence, and acted differently among Jews, differently among Greeks, differently among those not yet converted, differently among those already converted, differently among weak and infant Christians, and differently among adults and the perfect. The Lord himself set the example: for a time he concealed from his Apostles that his death was to come, and charged them to tell no one that he was Christ, and he did not wish his metamorphosis on the mountain to be revealed to his other disciples before he had risen. Our adversaries will, I think, grant us that the Evangelists and Apostles were wiser than Socinus and knew better when, to whom, and how they were to speak about the Deity of Christ and, as they commonly put it, the incarnation. It is enough for us that those most excellent doctrines gleam throughout the Gospels and the other books of the New Testament and send forth that brightness which whoever fails to recognise seems to me to be wilfully blind. We certainly seem to ourselves to discern them, even in the account of Christ's conception and in certain sermons of Peter and Paul, but chiefly in their Epistles.

units.la: III. Hoc vno argumento tot telis partim jam à nobis confosso, partim libro sequente confodiendo, contentus Socinus ad alia transit, & conatur probare, istam Dei αὐτοκράτων[?] nulla ratione fieri potuisse: agnoscit autem id demum à Deo fieri non posse, quod contradictionem implicat. Quomodo igitur demonstrat vnionem personalem naturæ humanæ cum divina persona contradictionem implicare? Primum, inquit, si illud verum est, quod Theologi omnes passim assi-mant, Deum videlicet esse immensum & substantia infinitum, certè, cum homo materialis & suis dimensionibus constet, & substantia finitus sit, rei autem finitæ ad infinitam, vt dicitur, nulla sit proportio, nemo non videt Deum cum materiali homine nullo pacto ita coniungi potuisse, vt ex utroque unum, vt vocant, suppositum factum fuerit. Verius dixisset nemo videt, quàm nemo non videt. Qui enim hoc videre se putant præ illis qui non vident pauci sunt, nec profectò vident quod videre se opinantur: quis enim quod non est id posset videre? Negamus personam infinitam vnire sibi personaliter non potuisse naturam humanam finitam. Proba si potes contrarium. Hoc enim ipsum est quod nunc inter nos quæritur, vtrum potuerit persona infinita[?] naturam finitam, videlicet humanam sibi hypostaticè vnire? Non potuisse contendis, & demonstraturum te polliceris. Quo igitur argumento vteris?
units.tr: III. Content with this one argument, already pierced in part by many of our weapons and to be pierced in part in the following book, Socinus passes to other matters and tries to prove that this [αὐτοκράτων] of God could in no way come about. He does admit, however, that God can do only what does not imply a contradiction. How then does he demonstrate that the personal union of the human nature with the divine person implies a contradiction? "First," he says, "if that is true which all theologians everywhere affirm, namely that God is immense and infinite in substance, then, since man is material, consists of his dimensions, and is finite in substance, and since there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite, as they say, no one fails to see that God could in no way be so joined with material man that one suppositum, as they call it, should be made of both." He would have spoken more truly had he said "no one sees" rather than "no one fails to see." For those who think they see this are few compared with those who do not see, and they certainly do not see what they suppose they see; for who could see what is not there? We deny that an infinite person could not personally unite to itself a finite human nature. Prove the contrary if you can. For this is the very thing now in question between us: whether an infinite person could hypostatically unite to itself a finite nature, namely human nature. You contend that it could not, and you promise to demonstrate it. What argument, then, do you use?

units.la: IV. Hoc fortasse. Oportet inter res vniendas esse proportionem. Atqui inter rem infinitâ & rem finitam nulla est proportio. Nullo igitur modo vniri possunt res finita & infinita. Nonne vides hoc eodem argumento probari posse, primò rem finitam non posse ab infinita produci: oportet enim proportionem esse inter causam & effectum. Atqui inter causam infinitam & effectum finitum nulla est proportio. Nullo igitur modo effectum finitum fieri potest à causa infinita. Secundò, Deum non posse à nobis cognosci: proportionem enim aliquam inter objectum & facultatem intercedere necesse est, quæ tamen inter objectum infinitum & facultatem finitam nulla est. Tertiò, nullam esse communionem fidelium cum Deo, quid dico fidelium? immò ipsius Christi: quî potest enim communio & amicitia inter eos locum habere, inter quos nulla est proportio? Quid ad hæc potest responderi, nisi hoc vnum, non esse quidem inter rem infinitam & rem finitam proportionem magnitudinis, sed hanc minimè vel ad vnionem, vel ad creationem, vel ad cognitionem, vel ad communionem esse necessariam. Id quod vel ex eo intelligi potest, quod cum Deus sit summum bonum creaturae rationalis, nihil magis expeti debet à creatura rationali, quàm vt vniatur cum Deo. Quod si Dei infinitas & hominis finitas, non impediunt, quominus aliqua intercedere possit inter Deum & hominem vnio, quo argumento demonstrare poterit Aduersarius, eas impedire, quominus natura humana diuinae personae hypostaticè vniri possit?
units.tr: IV. Perhaps you will say this: there must be a proportion between things to be united; but between an infinite thing and a finite thing there is no proportion; therefore a finite thing and an infinite thing cannot in any way be united. Do you not see that by this same argument one could prove, first, that a finite thing cannot be produced by an infinite one? For there must be a proportion between cause and effect; but between an infinite cause and a finite effect there is no proportion; therefore a finite effect can in no way come from an infinite cause. Second, that God cannot be known by us: for some proportion must lie between the object and the faculty; yet between an infinite object and a finite faculty there is none. Third, that there is no communion of believers with God, or I should say, of believers with Christ himself: for how can communion and friendship exist between those between whom there is no proportion? What can be replied to these things, except this one point: that between an infinite thing and a finite thing there is indeed no proportion of magnitude, but that this proportion is in no way necessary either for union, or for creation, or for knowledge, or for communion. This can be understood even from the fact that, since God is the highest good of a rational creature, nothing ought to be desired more by a rational creature than to be united with God. But if the infinity of God and the finitude of man do not prevent some union from existing between God and man, by what argument will the adversary be able to demonstrate that they prevent the human nature from being hypostatically united to a divine person?

units.la: V. Hoc fortasse demonstrat verbis sequentibus, oportet enim, inquit, vel materialem hominem immensum & substantia infinitum euasisse; vel Deum dimensionibus obnoxium & substantia finitum factum fuisse, quae nemo non videt, quàm non absurda modo, verum etiam impossibilia sint. Si intelligit hominem euadere infinitum mutata natura sua finita in infinitam, & Deum similiter euadere finitum, mutata natura sua infinita in naturam finitam, reuera id absurdum est & impossibile, sed tantum abest vt ad vnionem hypostaticam humanae naturae cum persona diuina sit necessarium, vt contrà cum ea consistere nullo modo possit: Id enim esset naturam humanam destruere & convertere in diuinam non verò vnire diuinae: Et similiter naturam diuinam destruere & convertere in humanam non verò vnire humanae. Hoc potest hominis exemplo illustrari, qui duabus naturis praeditus est, vna immateriali, spirituali, inuisibili, immortali; altera materiali, corporea, visibili, mortali. Vniuntur duae illae naturae personaliter in eodem homine, sed ita vt neque immaterialis mutetur in materialem, nec materialis in immaterialem. Retinet suas quaeque natura proprietates: alioqui vnio non esset spiritus & corporis, sed alterius in alterum conuersio.
units.tr: V. Perhaps he demonstrates this in the following words: "For it must be, he says, either that the material man has become immense and infinite in substance, or that God has been subjected to dimensions and made finite in substance; which everyone sees to be not only absurd but also impossible." If he means that man would become infinite, his finite nature being changed into an infinite one, and that God would likewise become finite, his infinite nature being changed into a finite one, then indeed this is absurd and impossible; but it is so far from being necessary for the hypostatic union of the human nature with the divine person that, on the contrary, it cannot in any way subsist together with it. For that would be to destroy the human nature and convert it into the divine, not to unite it to the divine; and similarly to destroy the divine nature and convert it into the human, not to unite it to the human. This can be illustrated by the example of man, who is endowed with two natures: one immaterial, spiritual, invisible, immortal; the other material, corporeal, visible, mortal.
