These two natures are united personally in the same man, but in such a way that neither is the immaterial changed into the material, nor the material into the immaterial. Each nature retains its own properties; otherwise the union would not be of spirit and body, but a conversion of one into the other.

units.la: VI. Addit Socinus, Substantiam autem infinitam, & substantiam finitam in vnum coaluisse, aut coalescere potuisse, quis sanae mentis vnquam dixerit, vtraque naturam & proprietatem suam retinente, quae innicem penitus dissident, neque vlla ratione conuenire possunt. Si in vnum coalescere nihil illi significat, nisi vniri, omnes aut prope omnes Christiani hoc dixerunt multis seculis constantissimè: nec tamen, opinor, nulli aut fere nulli Christiani sanae mentis fuere. Proprietates quidem naturae infinitae & proprietates naturae finitae valdè diuersae sunt, sed tamen inter se non pugnant: alioquin aut nullam naturam finitam infinita creasset, aut creatam jam pridem destruxisset. Cum igitur infinita finitam producat, conseruet, augeat, ornet, amet, & vice versa finita infinitam amet, colat, & placere ei unicè studeat, quomodo dici possunt inter se dissidere? Aut quamobrem non possunt ulla ratione convenire? Nam assertiones quidem video Socini nostræ sententiæ oppositas, & principij, ut loquuntur, petitiones, sed demonstrationes, quas pollicitus erat, nullas prorsus video.
units.tr: VI. Socinus adds: "That an infinite substance and a finite substance have coalesced, or could coalesce, into one, who of sound mind has ever said, while each retains its own nature and property, which are utterly at odds with one another and can in no way agree?" If to coalesce into one means nothing to him except to be united, then all or nearly all Christians have said this most steadfastly for many centuries; nor, I think, were there none, or almost none, of sound mind among the Christians. The properties of an infinite nature and the properties of a finite nature are indeed very different, but they do not fight with one another; otherwise either the infinite would never have created any finite nature, or, having created it, would long since have destroyed it. Since, therefore, the infinite produces, preserves, increases, adorns and loves the finite, and conversely the finite loves, worships and strives solely to please the infinite, how can they be said to be at odds with one another? Or why can they not agree in any way? For I see indeed Socinus's assertions opposed to our opinion, and what they call petitions of the principle, but I see no demonstrations at all, which he had promised.

units.la: VII. Cæterum non existimamus personam infinitam, & naturam finitam ita unitas fuisse ut coaluerint in unum quoddam tertium, quomodo anima rationalis & corpus coalescunt in unum tertium nempe hominem, qui neque est anima neque corpus, sed compositum quiddam ex utroque. Sed sine mutatione personæ infinitæ finita natura ei veluti innata atque unita est. Id potest illustrari exemplo personæ humanæ, cui jam existenti & completæ dens innascitur, qui profectò suppositum non est per se, sed unitur personæ illi hypostaticè, nec tamen persona illa propterea aut desinit persona esse, aut mutatur in aliam personam, aut coalescit cum illo dente in unum quoddam tertium, quod neq; sit illa persona, neque dens ille. Dices, persona illa non appellabitur dens aut contrà dens persona illa, cum tamen ob unionem hypostaticam Iesum Deum appelletis hominem, & hominem Deum. In promptu est responsio. Dens non est nomen concretum sed abstractum potius: rem enim significat, non habentem illam rem. Abstracta autem nomina quâ talia de suppositis non prædicantur in casu recto. Itaque homo non dicitur dens, sed dento vel dentatus, id est, habens dentem aut dentes. Deus verò & homo nomina sunt concreta: Deus significat eum qui habet deitatem seu qui præditus est diuina natura, & homo similiter significat eum qui habet humanitatem seu qui præditus est natura humana. Itaque mirum videri non debet si persona diuina, cui personaliter humana unita est natura, homo appellari possit & vice versa homo ille Deus.
units.tr: VII. Moreover, we do not hold that the infinite person and the finite nature were so united that they coalesced into a certain third thing, as a rational soul and a body coalesce into a third thing, namely man, which is neither soul nor body but a compound of both. Rather, without any change in the infinite person, the finite nature is, as it were, born in him and united to him. This can be illustrated by the example of a human person, to whom, already existing and complete, a tooth grows; this tooth is certainly not a subsistence in itself, but is united hypostatically to that person; yet that person does not on this account cease to be a person, nor is changed into another person, nor coalesces with that tooth into a third thing which is neither that person nor that tooth. You will say that that person is not called a tooth, nor the tooth a person, although on account of the hypostatic union you call Jesus God and man, and man God. The answer is ready. "Tooth" is not a concrete but rather an abstract name: it signifies a thing, not the thing that has it. Abstract names, as such, are not predicated of subjects in the nominative case. Thus a man is not called a tooth, but toothed or having teeth, that is, one who has a tooth or teeth. But "God" and "man" are concrete names: "God" signifies one who has deity, or who is endowed with the divine nature, and "man" similarly signifies one who has humanity, or who is endowed with human nature. Thus it ought not to seem strange if the divine person, to whom the human nature is united personally, can be called man, and conversely that man can be called God.

units.la: VIII. Objiciet fortè aliquis non posse eandem personam eodem tempore infinitam & finitam dici. Fateor secundum idem, nego secundum diuersas naturas. Quid enim prohibet eam dici infinitam secundum naturam diuinam & finitam secundum naturam humanam si utrâque naturâ prædita est? Succurrat nobis exemplum illius viri qui apparuit Abrahamo Gen. 18. & Iehoua septies appellatur. Num Abrahamus, si praejudiciis istis Socinianis altissime, vt solent Aduersarij nostri, imbutus fuisset, eum vt Deum supplex oraret? Dixisset potius, tu homo es materialis & finitus, Deus autem seu Iehova est infinitus. Tu igitur non es Deus. Impossibile est enim substantiam infinitam & substantiam finitam in vnum coalescere. Videntur certè Iudaei, degeneres Abrahami filij, id ipsum quod Socinus sensisse: aiebant enim Iesum blasphemare, quod Patrem suum dicendo Deum aequalem se faceret Deo; quodque homo cum esset, faceret seipsum Deum. Putabant enim impossibile esse, vt idem simul esset Deus & homo.
units.tr: VIII. Perhaps someone will object that the same person cannot at the same time be called infinite and finite. I admit it if it is meant in the same respect; I deny it with respect to the different natures. For what prevents him from being called infinite according to the divine nature and finite according to the human nature, if he is endowed with both natures? Let the example of that man who appeared to Abraham, Genesis 18, come to our aid, and who is called Jehovah seven times. Would Abraham, if he had been steeped in those Socinian prejudices most deeply, as our adversaries usually are, have prayed to him as God? Rather he would have said: "You are a material and finite man, but God, or Jehovah, is infinite. Therefore you are not God. For it is impossible that an infinite substance and a finite substance coalesce into one." Certainly the Jews, the degenerate sons of Abraham, seem to have thought the very same thing as Socinus: for they said that Jesus blasphemed, because by calling God his Father he made himself equal to God; and because, being a man, he made himself God. For they thought it impossible for the same one to be at once God and man.

units.la: IX. Age vero hoc argumentum Socini in Aduersarios nostros retorqueamus, & quidem ea ratione vt nulla arte ictus declinari possit. Si illud verum est quod Theologi omnes passim affirmant, Deum videlicet esse immensum & substantia infinitum, certè, cum homo materialis, & suis dimensionibus constet, & substantia finitus sit, rei autem finitae ad infinitam, vt dicitur, nulla sit proportio, nemo non videt Deo infinito hominem finitum nullo modo aequalem esse posse. Quomodo igitur volunt Aduersarij hominem Iesum, tantum hominem, Deo immenso secundum naturam humanam materialem & finitam, (aliam enim nullam eum habere patiuntur) aequalem esse? Distinguere enim non possunt proportionem magnitudinis quae inter rem infinitam & rem finitam nulla esse potest, à proportione necessaria ad vnionem. Cum enim aequalitas ratione magnitudinis dicatur, sublata omni proportione secundum magnitudinem omnis aequalitas tollitur, remanente ea proportione, si tamen proportio appellari debet, quae ad vnionem requiritur, nihil autem requiritur, cum Deus sit omnipotens, nisi non-repugnantia, seu non-implicatio contradictionis. Quanquam etiam inter personam diuinam & naturam humanam ea potest observari proportio, quae est inter causam & effectum, actum & potentiam: est enim natura humana respectu diuinae personae nihil nisi potentia. Quantum enim natura humana pati potest, tantum pati potest à persona diuina: & quantum habet entitatis tantum accepit à persona diuina. Quid est igitur cur personae diuinae, hoc est, principio, & causae suae vniri non possit? Dicant vero nobis Aduersarij, qui ratione sua etiam ipsum Deum metiri volunt, quomodo natura humana ma-terialis terialis & finita naturæ divinæ immensæ & infinitæ æqualis esse possit, cum finiti ad infinitum ne proportio quidem ulla sit? potestne æqualitas inter illas res esse, inter quas ne proportio quidem est?
units.tr: IX. Come now, let us turn this argument of Socinus back upon our adversaries, and in such a way that the blow can be avoided by no skill. If that is true which all theologians affirm everywhere, namely that God is immense and infinite in substance, then certainly, since man is material, consists of his dimensions, and is finite in substance, and since, as is said, there is no proportion of the finite to the infinite, everyone sees that a finite man can in no way be equal to the infinite God. How, then, do our adversaries want the man Jesus, only a man, to be equal to the immense God according to his material and finite human nature (for they allow him no other nature)? For they cannot distinguish the proportion of magnitude, which can be no proportion between an infinite thing and a finite thing, from the proportion necessary for union. For since equality is spoken of with respect to magnitude, once all proportion according to magnitude is removed, all equality is removed; but the proportion required for union remains, if indeed it ought to be called a proportion, and nothing is required for it, since God is omnipotent, except non-repugnance, or the non-implication of contradiction. Yet even between the divine person and the human nature there can be observed that proportion which exists between cause and effect, act and potency: for the human nature, with respect to the divine person, is nothing but potency. For as much as the human nature can undergo, so much can it undergo from the divine person; and as much as it has of being, so much it has received from the divine person. Why, then, should it be that the divine person, that is, its principle and its cause, cannot be united to it? But let our adversaries, who wish to measure even God himself by their reason, tell us how a material and finite human nature can be equal to the divine nature, which is immense and infinite, when there is not even any proportion between the finite and the infinite? Can there be equality between those things between which there is not even proportion?

units.la: X. Quo modo sese ex hoc argumento expedient Adversarij? Objicientne, ex Christi cum Deo æqualitate sequi euersionem sententiæ nostræ: Æquale enim semper aliam habere essentiam ab eo, cui æquale est. Alias idem sibi ipsi æquale esset: cum tamen æqualia relata, ac porrò opposita sint. Hoc enim nos Crellius argumento oppugnat. Non reponam tritum illud, contrà argumentari non esse respondere. Dicam tantùm, nunc quidem, nihil prohibere, quominus idem sibi ipsi æquale esse dicatur. Nihil malo, dicebat Cæsar in quadam Epistola ad Ciceronem, quàm & me mei similem esse, & illos sui. Et Socrates apud Platonem in Parmenide, Marsilio Ficino interprete, Si illi dissimilitudo ad alia competit, nonne ad seipsum similitudo convenit? Et paulò post, Ob hanc causam oportet uni similitudinem ad seipsum adesse. Oportet. Si potest idem sui simile dici, cur non & æquale? Ipsi, dicebat Apostolus, seipsos seipsis metiuntur, & semetipsos sibimetipsis comparant. Si potest idem sese ipso metiri, sese sibimetipsi comparare, quid est cur non possit dici sibi ipsi æqualis? Nonne similia æquè sunt relata & opposita ac æqualia? Nonne qui metitur, & quem metitur, & quo metitur itidem sunt relata & opposita? Sed quando jam philosophamur, audi rursus Socratem, quibus consideratis dicemus, ut arbitror, nihil unquam majus minusve fieri vel mole, vel numero, quandiu sibi ipsi æquale permanet, nonne ita? Thea. Ita prorsus. Potest igitur teste Platone aliquid sibi ipsi æquale dici: nec mirum, est enim ut verbis utar Iulij Scaligeri æqualitas in mathematicis, quasi quædam unitas magnitudinum. At unitas ab unitate non differt. Est enim quantitatum æqualitas idem quod identitas substantiarum. Quid igitur prohibet idem sibi ipsi dici æquale? Certè audientem affirmari, non esse idem sibi ipsi æquale, subit statim cogitatio, num igitur sibi ipsi est inæquale? num seipso majus, aut minus est? Nam si idem se ipso neque majus, neque minus est, videtur sibi ipsi esse æquale. At æqualia sunt relata ac porrò opposita. Argutiola nihil! quasi vero non possit idem ad seipsum aliquo modo referri! nonne patiens & agens, movens & mobile, sciens & scibile, amans & amatum sunt relata? Attamen nihil prohibet, eundem hominem eodem tempore, & quidem sui ipsius respectu, esse patientem & agentem, motorem & mobilem, scientem & scibilem, amantem & amatum. Potest enim idem agere in seipsum, & seipsum movere, & cognoscere, & amare. Ipse Dominus noster Iesus Christus nonne idem fuit Sacerdos & victima, is qui obtulit, & is qui oblatus est? Miror Adversarios in rebus tanti momenti solidius non disputare.
units.tr: X. How will the adversaries extricate themselves from this argument? Will they object that equality with God with Christ entails the overthrow of our position: What is equal always has a being other than that to which it is equal. Otherwise the same thing would be equal to itself, although equals are relatives and also opposites. Crellius attacks us with this argument. I shall not repeat the stale answer that arguing against a point is not answering it. I will say only that, for now, nothing prevents the same thing from being called equal to itself. I would prefer nothing, Caesar said in a certain letter to Cicero, than that I should be like myself and they like themselves. And Socrates in Plato's Parmenides, in the translation of Marsilio Ficino: If dissimilarity belongs to other things, does not similarity belong to itself? And a little later: For this reason it is necessary that similarity belong to the one itself. Necessary. If the same thing can be called like itself, why not equal? They, said the Apostle, measure themselves by themselves, and compare themselves with themselves. If the same thing can measure itself by itself and compare itself with itself, what reason is there why it cannot be called equal to itself? Are not like things relatives and opposites just as equal things are? Are not the one who measures, the one who is measured, and that by which he measures likewise relatives and opposites? But since we are now philosophising, hear Socrates again: Considering these things, we shall say, as I think, that nothing ever becomes greater or smaller in mass or number so long as it remains equal to itself. Is that not so? Theaet. Quite so. Therefore, by Plato's testimony, something can be called equal to itself; and this is no wonder, for, to use the words of Julius Scaliger, equality in mathematics is, as it were, a certain unity of magnitudes. But unity does not differ from unity. For equality of quantities is the same as identity of substances. Why then should the same thing not be called equal to itself? Certainly, on hearing it asserted that the same thing is not equal to itself, the thought immediately arises: is it then unequal to itself? Is it greater or less than itself? For if the same thing is neither greater nor less than itself, it seems to be equal to itself. But equals are relatives and also opposites. What trifling quibbling! As if the same thing could not in some way be referred to itself! Are not the one suffering and the one acting, the mover and the moved, the knower and the knowable, the lover and the beloved, relatives? Yet nothing prevents the same man, at the same time and indeed with respect to himself, from being both the one suffering and the one acting, the mover and the moved, the knower and the knowable, the lover and the beloved. For the same thing can act upon itself, move itself, know itself, and love itself. Was not our Lord Jesus Christ himself both the priest and the victim, the one who offered and the one who was offered? I wonder that the adversaries do not argue more solidly on matters of such importance.

units.la: XI. Quid ergo tandē respondebunt? Non negabunt Christum, etiam antequā glorificaretur, æqualem Deo fuisse. contradicerent enim & sibi ipsis id antehac saepe confessis, & Paulo testanti Christū non duxisse rapinam esse æqualem Deo, & ipsi Christo affirmanti, omnia quaecunq; Pater habet sua esse, & sic Patrem alloquenti, omnia mea tua sunt, & tua mea:qua æqualitate inter personas eiusdē speciei major nulla concipi solet, aut potest. Multò verò minus negabunt Filium post glorificationē suam Patri esse æqualem. Sepositâ enim originis consideratione, à qua Patris & Filij distinctio pendet, quæ potest nunc inter Patrem & Filium inæqualitas observari? Uterque vitam habet in seipso, uterque scrutatur corda & renes, uterque vivificat mortuos quoscunque vult, uterque habet omnem potestatem in cælo & in terra, utrumque adorare tenentur omnes creaturæ, etiam angelicæ, uterque regnat cum summa auctoritate. Si Pater est infinitus & Filius tantùm finitus, & finiti ad infinitum proportio nulla est, quomodo tanta est inter Patrem & Filium proportio immò æqualitas? Num mutata est natura Filij finita in infinitam? Non igitur amplius natura humana est sed merè divina, nec est Filius amplius homo sed Deus tantùm: quænam enim natura seu essentia infinita est aut esse potest præter divinam? Hoc igitur non dicent Adversarij, quod & cum suo dogmate pugnaret, & naturam humanam Christi destrueret, & naturæ infinitæ creationem & multiplicationem induceret, quod cum rectâ ratione pugnat, ut quod maximè. Quid ergo dicturi sunt? Si quid conjicio, Insuper habito Socini argumento eó deveniunt, ut negent Deum esse immensum & infinitum. id quod meâ sententiâ est Deum negare esse Deum. Si aliter, Lector, sentis, lege si placet duas nostras disputationes de Deo immenso, & vide an argumentis quibus Deum esse infinitum probamus, aut etiam demonstramus, respondere solidè possis.
units.tr: XI. What then will they answer at last? They will not deny that Christ, even before he was glorified, was equal to God. For they would contradict both themselves, who have often confessed this before, and Paul, who testifies that Christ did not regard being equal to God as a thing to be grasped, and Christ himself, who affirms that all things that the Father has are mine, and thus speaking to the Father, all my things are yours, and yours are mine; an equality than which none greater is commonly conceived, or can be conceived, between persons of the same kind. Much less will they deny that the Son after his glorification is equal to the Father. For, setting aside the consideration of origin, on which the distinction of Father and Son depends, what inequality can now be observed between the Father and the Son? Each has life in himself; each searches the hearts and reins; each quickens the dead whomever he wills; each has all power in heaven and on earth; all creatures, even the angelic, are bound to adore each; each reigns with supreme authority. If the Father is infinite and the Son only finite, and there is no proportion between the finite and the infinite, how is there so great a proportion, or rather equality, between the Father and the Son? Has the finite nature of the Son been changed into an infinite one? Therefore the human nature is no longer human but purely divine, and the Son is no longer man but God alone; for what infinite nature or essence is there, or can there be, apart from the divine? The adversaries, then, will not say this, since it would both clash with their own dogma and destroy Christ's human nature, and would introduce the creation and multiplication of an infinite nature, which fights with right reason as much as anything could. What then will they say? If I may conjecture, having disregarded Socinus' argument, they arrive at this: that they deny God to be immense and infinite; which in my view is to deny that God is God. If, reader, you think otherwise, read, if you please, our two disputations on the immense God, and see whether you can answer solidly the arguments by which we prove, or even demonstrate, that God is infinite.

units.la: XII. Pergit argumentari Socinus, Deinde, inquit, cum esse Deum, eamque ipsius substantiam, omnes & Philosophi & Theologi pro comperto habent, cui nihil unquam accidere possit, alioqui nec primus solus, & sempiternus motor, nec omnis prorsus alterationis (illorum voce utimur) & corruptionis expers suapte natura foret, denique summus omnium rerum princeps Deus non esset. At vero mortalem hominem ita vel induisse, vel assumpsisse, vt vnà cum eo in tertium aliquid euaserit, non solùm esset aliquid ei, eiusque substantiæ accidisse, sed maximi nomenti rem accidisse. nam & de eius substantia id nunc verè prædicari posset, quod antea nullo modo poterat, videlicet illi hominis substantiam inhærere, & ei homo, hoc est, res quæ sui natura à Deo quàm longissimè abest, indiuiduè coniunctus fuisset. Primùm laborat hoc argumentum ignoratione Elenchi. Quid enim eo concludi potest? nihil profectò nisi hoc vnum, Deum mortalem hominem ita vel induisse, vel assumpsisse, vt vnà cum eo in tertium aliquid euaserit, falsum esse. Quæ conclusio saluâ sententiâ nostrâ à nobis concedi potest. Nolumus enim Deum induisse vel assumpsisse hominem, sed humanam naturam. Nolumus Deum cum humana natura, quam sibi vniuit, in tertium aliquid euasisse: eiusmodi enim tertium proprie neque Deus neque homo esset. id quod à sententia nostra vehementissimè abhorret. At de eius substantia id nunc verè prædicari posset, quod antea nullo modo poterat. Quid tum? quis nescit multa de Deo nunc verè prædicari, quæ ante conditum mundum prædicari non poterant, actiones nimirum multas, &, quæ in actionibus fundantur, relationes?
units.tr: XII. Socinus continues to argue: Next, he says, since all philosophers and theologians hold as established that God exists, and that his substance is such that nothing can ever happen to it, otherwise he would not be the first and only and eternal mover, nor wholly free of all alteration (we use their word) and corruption by his own nature, and finally God would not be the supreme prince of all things. But that a mortal man should be so clothed or assumed by God that, together with him, he became something third, would not only mean that something had befallen him and his substance, but that something of the greatest moment had befallen him. For now there could truly be predicated of his substance what before could not be in any way predicated, namely that the substance of man inhered in him, and that man, that is, a thing which by its nature is as far as possible from God, had been indivisibly joined to him. First, this argument labours under the ignorance of refutation. For what can be concluded from it? Surely nothing except this one thing: that it is false that God so clothed or assumed a mortal man that together with him he became something third. This conclusion we can concede while our position stands. For we do not want God to have clothed or assumed a man, but human nature. We do not want God, together with the human nature which he united to himself, to have become something third: for such a third would properly be neither God nor man. This is what our position most vehemently abhors. But, Socinus says, there could now truly be predicated of his substance what could in no way be predicated before. What of it? Who does not know that many things can now truly be predicated of God which could not be predicated before the world was created, namely, certainly, many actions and, what are founded in actions, relations?

units.la: XII. Quid porrò de illius substantia, hoc est, persona nunc verè prædicari posset, quod antea non poterat? videlicet, inquit, illi hominis substantiam inhærere. Si inhærere intelligit, quo sensu accidens inhærere subjecto suo dicitur, negamus personæ diuinæ humanam inhærere substantiam: nam neque hæc accidens, neque illa subjectum inhæsionis esse potest. Si verò inhærere nihil illi significat hoc loco, nisi personæ diuinæ ita vnitam esse humanam substantiam seu naturam, vt hæc ab illa sustentetur, & vi illius subsistat, id confitemur, & negamus esse absurdum. Addit Socinus, & ei homo, (rectius dixisset humana natura) hoc est, res, quæ sui naturâ à Deo quàm longissimè abest, indiuidue coniunctus fuisset. Hoc rursus nego absurdum esse. Quid enim absurdi est, si dicatur natura humana Deo, hoc est, Dei Filio indiuiduè conjuncta? Est-ne in eo aliquid quod Dei sapientiæ, potentiæ, iustitiæ, bonitati repugnet, aut quod non sit ipsi illi naturæ humanæ, immò toti generi humano honorificentissimum? At illa à Deo quàm longissimè abest. Locone? Contrarium docet Apostolus Act. 17. 27. 28. & Dauid Ps. 139. voluntate? Illa cum Deo, ipsis Aduersarijs testibus, unum est voluntate. Similitudine? Nulla creatura Deo similior est, aut esse potest. quomodo igitur longissimè abest à Deo, cum, ipsis Aduersarijs fatentibus, Deo sit conjunctissima, tantùm negant illi conjunctam esse personaliter? Si longissimè abesse nihil significat Socino, nisi diuersitatem qua natura finita à persona infinita distinguitur, recurrit perpetuò quæstio, cur finita natura humana uniri non potuerit infinitæ personæ, hoc est, principio & fonti, unde ipsa manauit, & fini cui vehementissimo amore, qui est affectus seu appetitus unionis, agglutinatur?
units.tr: XII. What further could now truly be predicated of his substance, that is, of his person, which could not be predicated before? Namely, he says, that the substance of man inhered in him. If he means inhering in the sense in which an accident is said to inhere in its subject, we deny that human substance inheres in the divine person: for neither can the former be an accident nor the latter a subject of inherence. But if inhering signifies nothing to him in this place except that the human substance or nature is so united to the divine person that it is sustained by it and subsists by its power, we confess this, and deny that it is absurd. Socinus adds, and that man (he would have spoken more correctly if he had said human nature), that is, a thing which by its nature is as far as possible from God, had been indivisibly joined to him. Again I deny that this is absurd. For what is absurd if it is said that human nature is indivisibly joined to God, that is, to the Son of God? Is there in this anything that contradicts the wisdom, power, justice, or goodness of God, or anything that is not most honourable to that very human nature, and indeed to the whole human race? But it is as far as possible from God. Is it in place? The Apostle teaches the contrary, Acts 17. 27. 28., and David, Ps. 139. In will? It is, by the testimony of the adversaries themselves, one with God in will. In likeness? No creature is or can be more like God. How, then, is it as far as possible from God, when, as the adversaries themselves admit, it is most closely joined to God, and they only deny that it is joined to him personally? If for Socinus being as far as possible signifies nothing except the difference by which a finite nature is distinguished from an infinite person, the question keeps recurring why the finite human nature could not be united to the infinite person, that is, to the principle and source from which it flowed, and to the end to which it is bound by the most vehement love, which is the affection or appetite of union.

units.la: XIII. Fortasse illud nobis aliquis reponet, Deo nihil unquam accidere posse: Accidisse autem aliquid, si ei humana unita fuit natura. Respondeo, reuera nullum accidens proprièdictum naturæ diuinæ inhærere, aut ei de novo accidere posse: Deumque omnis prorsus alterationis, & corruptionis, expertem esse: Nihil etiam eius respectu accidere posse non ab ipso præuisum & prædecretum, multumque absumus ab opinione Aduersariorum Deum existimantium uno tempore aliquid determinatè nescire, alio scire, eiusque scientiam augeri quotidie, & quædam interdum ab eo non præscita euenire, quibus cognitis mutet quædam sua decreta. Sed si nihil unquam accidere posse Deo, usurpatur pro nullam naturam finitam ei unquam uniri potuisse, hæc objectio putida quædam petitio est, ut loquuntur, principii. Nam, & natura humana accidens aut qualitas non est, & non video cur illa Deo uniri non potuerit absque ulla naturæ diuinæ inmutatione, alteratione, aut corruptione: sese enim Deus ad illam unionem producendam actiuè tantùm habuit. Si magnes potest ferrum ad se trahere & sibi conjungere, non se, sed ferrum mouendo, quid est, cur Deus infinita sapientia & potentia præditus non potuerit naturam quandam humanam sibi iungere, non se, sed naturam illam producendo & afficiendo, atque adeo ei ab ipso ortu propensionem quandam naturalem ad se multò majorem & fortiorem, quàm ea sit quâ grauia feruntur in centrum, eique
units.tr: XIII. Perhaps someone will reply to us that nothing can ever happen to God, and that something would happen to him if a human nature were united to him. I answer that indeed no accident properly so called inheres in the divine nature, nor can one newly come to it, and that God is free from all alteration and corruption. Nor can anything happen with respect to him that was not foreseen and foreordained by him. We are far from the opinion of the Adversaries, who think that God at one time determinately does not know something and at another time knows it, that his knowledge grows daily, and that sometimes things happen which he did not foreknow, so that on learning them he changes some of his decrees. But if "nothing can ever happen to God" is taken to mean that no finite nature could ever be united to him, then this objection is a foolish petitio principii, as they say. For human nature is neither an accident nor a quality, and I do not see why it could not be united to God without any change, alteration or corruption of the divine nature. God was active only in producing that union. If a magnet can draw iron to itself and join it to itself, moving not itself but the iron, why could God, endowed with infinite wisdom and power, not join some human nature to himself, not by moving himself but by producing and affecting that nature? Why could he not implant in it from its very origin a natural inclination towards himself, much greater and stronger than that by which heavy bodies are carried to the centre, and make it adhere to him as closely as possible,

units.la: quàm possunt arctissimè adhærent, inserendo, sic vt natura illa omnem suam existentiam, vitam, motus, & actiones, à diuina illa persona eam intimè, tanquam organum sibi natum, omni ex parte penetrante, conseruante, mouente, regente, viuificante à principio existentiæ suæ in omnem æternitatem accipiat. factum est enim ea ratione, vt natura illa sit perpetuum symbolum præsentiæ personæ illius diuinæ, & organum naturaliter, immò essentialiter (loquor de propria naturæ illius, quatenus est talis, essentia)illi conjunctum & accommodatum, multò perfectiùs, quà membra corporis nostri sunt organa naturaliter animæ adjuncta & aptata. Itaque quicquid natura illa humana vel agit, vel patitur, id persona illa diuina merito agere & pati dicitur. Quid est quæso in hac nostra sententia, quod videri debeat impossibile, aut sese ipsum contradictione implicare, aut cum Dei immutabilitate pugnare?
units.tr: so that this nature receives from that divine person, from the beginning of its existence into all eternity, all its existence, life, motions and actions? He would penetrate it intimately, as an organ made for himself, on every side, preserving, moving, ruling and quickening it. The result of this arrangement is that this nature is a perpetual symbol of the presence of that divine person, and an organ naturally, indeed essentially (I speak of the essence of that nature as far as it is such) joined and fitted to him, far more perfectly than the members of our body are organs naturally joined and fitted to the soul. Therefore whatever that human nature either does or suffers, that divine person is rightly said to do or suffer. What, I ask, is there in our opinion that ought to seem impossible, or that entangles itself in contradiction, or fights against the immutability of God?

units.la: XIV. Subjungit Socinus aliud argumentum. Adde quod, inquit, isthæc conjunctio, vel inanis penitus & superuacanea fuit, id quod mox planum faciemus, vel illud effecit, quod etiam cogitare horremus, Deum scilicet verè & reipsa, non autem imaginarie, vt ita dicam, & per idiomatum communicationem passum fuisse, & humanas miserias mortemque ipsam expertum esse. Prius illud, istam conjunctionem esse penitus superuacaneam salsissimum est. Posterius verò, Deum scilicet verè & reipsa & non imaginariè passum fuisse, videlicet secundum naturam humanam sibi conjunctam, nos quidem certè firmiter credimus & cum summa diuinæ sapientiæ & misericordiæ admiratione confitemur. Cur enim ab ea locutione abhorreremus cum Socino, à qua Apostolus non abhorruit? Deus, inquit, Ecclesiam sibi suo sanguine acquisiuit, διὰ τῶ ἰδίω αἵματ[?]ος· per proprium sanguinem. Ne ipse Deus quidem ab ea abhorruit Zach. 12. 10. aspicient, inquit, ad me quem transfixerunt. ex quo loco ductum est Argumentum huius libri septimum. Verba etiam illa Apostoli 1. Cor. 2. 8. nunquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent, idem mihi sonare videntur ac si dixisset, nunquam Deum crucifixissent.
units.tr: XIV. Socinus adds another argument. Moreover, he says, this conjunction was either entirely empty and superfluous, as we shall soon make plain, or it brought about what we shudder even to think: namely, that God truly and in reality, and not merely in imagination, as I may say, suffered through the communication of properties, and experienced human miseries and death itself. The former claim, that this conjunction was entirely superfluous, is most false. As to the latter, that God truly and really suffered, and not in imagination, namely according to the human nature joined to him, we indeed firmly believe this and confess it with the greatest admiration of divine wisdom and mercy. For why should we shrink from that expression with Socinus, when the Apostle did not shrink from it? God, he says, acquired the Church for himself with his own blood, διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος [dia tou idiou haimatos]: through his own blood. God himself did not shrink from it either: Zach. 12. 10. They shall look on me whom they have pierced. From this passage the seventh argument of this book is drawn. The words of the Apostle also, 1 Cor. 2. 8. they would never have crucified the Lord of glory, seem to me to mean the same as if he had said, they would never have crucified God.

units.la: XV. Quod verò sequitur apud Socinum legens cohorrui. Quodsi, inquit, Christianorum Deus is est, cui hæc accidere possint, minimè mirandum videtur, si & Turcæ à Deo defecerunt, & Iudæi adhuc ei obstinatis animis reluctantur atque obedire recusant. Nos autem, qui ipsius Christi verbis indubitatam fidem adhibemus, illique nomen dedimus, omnium miserrimi sumus, quorum salus & vita, inter tot mala, totque mortis genera, quae subire coacti sumus, non aliunde, quàm ab eiusmodi Deo pendeat, qui verè non secus ac nos & afflictari & mori potuerit. Quid audio? Non credidit igitur Socinus Christum esse verè & proprie loquendo Deum? Non credidit à Christo salutem suam pendere? Ego verò beatos nos esse praedico, quorum salus & vita, inter tot mala, non aliunde quàm ab eiusmodi Deo, nempe Christo, pendet, qui verè, τὸ κατὰ σάρκα, non secus ac nos & afflictari & mori potuerit, atque adeo mortuus fuit pro nobis. tantùm enim abest ut propterea minus ad nos servandos Deus ille noster sit potens, ut salus nostra tota sit in eius morte fundata. tantùm abest ut mors eius nobis videatur justum argumentum scandali Judæis aut Turcis praebere, ut contrà nobis videatur veritatis Evangelij argumentum esse certissimum.
units.tr: XV. What I read next in Socinus makes me shudder. But if the God of the Christians is one to whom these things can happen, it is hardly surprising that the Turks have fallen away from God, and the Jews still resist him with obstinate minds and refuse to obey him. We, however, who give indubitable faith to the very words of Christ and have taken his name, are the most wretched of all men, since our salvation and life, amid so many evils and so many kinds of death which we are forced to undergo, depend on nothing else than on such a God, who could truly be afflicted and die no differently from us. What do I hear? Did Socinus therefore not believe that Christ is truly and properly God? Did he not believe that our salvation hangs on Christ? I, on the contrary, declare us blessed, whose salvation and life, amid so many evils, depend on nothing else than on such a God, namely Christ, who truly, τὸ κατὰ σάρκα [to kata sarka: according to the flesh], could be afflicted and die no differently from us, and indeed did die for us. So far is that God of ours from being any less able to save us for this reason, that our whole salvation is founded on his death. So far is his death from seeming to us to offer the Jews or the Turks a just occasion of offence, that on the contrary it seems to us a most certain argument for the truth of the Gospel.

units.la: XVI. His paucis argumentis, (si tamen argumenta dici merentur, quae nihil nisi principij petitiones fuerunt) contentus Socinus, quasi re feliciter confecta, triumphum agit. Satis, inquit, demonstratum esse videtur, (multa enim, quae ad idem comprobandum afferri possent, ne nimium philosophari videamur, con-sultò omittimus) quam Dei cum homine, sive substantia divina cum humana coniunctionem in Jesu Christo factam fuisse asserunt, inter ea recenseri debere, quae fieri omnino non possunt. Si validiora omi-sit, desidero in eo judicium. Si minus valida, cum tam debilia fuerint quae attulit, quid de omissis illis judicandum sit nemo non videt.
units.tr: XVI. Content with these few arguments (if indeed they deserve the name of arguments, since they are nothing but petitions of the principle), Socinus celebrates a triumph, as if the matter were happily settled. It seems sufficiently demonstrated, he says, (for we deliberately omit many things which could be brought forward to prove the same, lest we seem to philosophize too much) that the conjunction of God with man, or of the divine substance with the human, which they assert was made in Jesus Christ, must be counted among those things which absolutely cannot happen. If he has left out stronger arguments, I should like to hear his judgement on them. If they were weaker, then since the ones he brought forward are so feeble, no one fails to see what must be judged of those he omitted.

units.la: XVII. Interim tamen ita triumphat, ut præ suis istis, tam nullis, demonstrationibus verbi Dei testimonia nullo loco habeat. Sic enim ille ratiocinatur. Quemadmodū enim nec poenitere Deum, nec contristari sese, nec irasci, nec descendere, nec accedere, nec recedere ve-rè & proprie dicere audemus, licet horum omnium & satis frequentia, & apertissima extent sacra testimonia, nempe quod nihil eorum in Deum cadere posse persuasi rationibus & argumentis sumus, sed divina verba, in quibus haec vel iis similia clarissimè exprimi viden-tur, ita interpretamur, ut commodior sensus, quàm quem ipsa præ se ferunt, inde eliciatur, eàque propterea ab usitata, & magis propria significatione deflectere non veremur, sic etiam si aliqua in divi-nis monumentis loca reperiantur, ubi diserte scriptum extaret, Deum hominem factum fuisse, aut humanam carnem induisse, vel assump-fisse, quod tamen, ut diximus, nunquam in eis traditum reperies, non statim ita, ut sonant, verba accipienda essent, cum id divinae maiestati prorsus repugnet, sed ea ratione exponi deberent, ut per fi-guras a loquendi usu non penitus abhorrentes, & aptior sententia no-bis constaret, & ipsa natura funditus non everteretur.
units.tr: XVII. Meanwhile he triumphs in such a way that, in comparison with these demonstrations of his, which are so empty, he holds the testimonies of God's word in no regard at all. For he reasons thus: Just as we dare not say, truly and properly, that God repents, is grieved, is angry, descends, approaches or withdraws, although very frequent and most plain sacred testimonies exist for all of these, namely because we are persuaded by reasons and arguments that none of these can fall upon God, but we interpret the divine words, in which these or similar things seem to be expressed most clearly, so that a more suitable sense is drawn out than the one they present on their face, and therefore we do not hesitate to depart from the usual and more proper signification; so also, if any passages should be found in the divine records where it was plainly written that God was made man, or put on or assumed human flesh (which, as we have said, you will never find handed down in them), the words should not at once be taken as they sound, since that is wholly repugnant to the divine majesty, but they ought to be explained in such a way that by figures not wholly alien to the usage of speech a more apt sense may be established for us, and nature itself is not utterly overturned.

units.la: XVIII. Hoc argumentum æquè ac superiora leue est. Non enim eadem est ratio locorum quæ Deum pœnitere, irasci, descendere &c dicunt, & eorum quibus probamus eundem Christum esse Deum & hominem. Primùm enim, sunt argumenta necessaria, quibus probari potest, Deum proprie loquendo neque perturbationibus iræ, tristitiæ, pœnitentiæ &c esse obnoxium, neque loco moueri. Ego verò contendo nulla esse argumenta quæ probent, Deum non potuisse hominibus apparere in vera forma seu natura humana, quam in eum finem produxerit, & sibi accommodarit. vertant se in omnes partes Adversarii, id nunquam demonstrabunt esse impossibile. Deinde aliis locis Scriptura testatur disertis verbis, Deum non pœnitere, Deum non mutari ullo modo, Deum esse immensum & replere cœlum & terram. Itaque cum verbum Dei secum non pugnet, necesse est figuratè ea loca accipere, quæ eum pœnituisse, descendisse, ascendisse &c dicunt. At nulla prorsus extant loca Scripturæ, quæ vel disertis verbis, vel per consequentias docent, Deum non potuisse sumpta vera hominis forma hominibus ad eos docendos & servandos apparere. Sunt contrà quæ id docent valdè multa, & Deus ei rei ne putaretur aut impossibilis, aut minus majestatem suam decere, multis apparitionibus olim, ut ita dicam, præluserit. Præterea, quæ locis illis accommodari solet expositio eiusmodi est, quæ neque locorum illorum circunstantijs, neque aliis locis Scripturæ, neque rationi, neque fidei analogiæ ullo modo repugnet: cum expositiones locorum pro divinitate Domini nostri & eius incarnatione laudatorum, quas Adversarij commenti sunt, pugnent sæpenumero & cum illorum ipsorum locorum circunstantijs, & cum aliis locis Scripturæ, & cum recta ratione, & cum analogia fidei. Ego jam aliquoties affirmaui, & iterum affirmo, sententiam Adversariorum de Domino nostro Jesu Christo, si quis eam penitus introspiciat, non posse ullo modo cum recta ratione conciliari: cu-ius rei specimen quoddam in hac ipsa responsione ostendi.
units.tr: XVIII. This argument, like the earlier ones, is light. For the reason is not the same for the passages which say that God repented, was angry, descended, and so on, and for those by which we prove that the same Christ is God and man. First, there are necessary arguments by which it can be proved that God, properly speaking, is subject neither to the disturbances of anger, sorrow or repentance, nor to being moved from place. I, however, contend that there are no arguments which prove that God could not appear to men in the true form or nature of man, which he produced and adapted to himself for that purpose. Let the Adversaries turn themselves in every direction: they will never demonstrate this to be impossible. Next, in other places Scripture testifies in plain words that God does not repent, that God is not changed in any way, and that God is immense and fills heaven and earth. Therefore, since the word of God does not contradict itself, the passages which say that he repented, descended, ascended and so on must necessarily be taken figuratively. But there are absolutely no passages of Scripture which teach, either in plain words or by consequence, that God could not appear to men in the true form of man, to teach and save them. On the contrary, there are very many which teach that he could, and God, lest it be thought either impossible or less fitting to his majesty, has so to speak foreshadowed it in many earlier appearances. Moreover, the exposition usually applied to those passages is of such a kind that it contradicts neither their circumstances, nor other passages of Scripture, nor reason, nor the analogy of faith in any way. The explanations of the passages praised for the divinity of our Lord and his incarnation, which the Adversaries have devised, on the other hand, often conflict with the circumstances of those very passages, with other passages of Scripture, with right reason and with the analogy of faith. I have already affirmed this several times, and I affirm it again: the Adversaries' opinion about our Lord Jesus Christ, if one examines it thoroughly, cannot in any way be reconciled with right reason. I have shown a sample of this in this very reply.

units.la: XIX. His etiam illud accedit, quod cur verba poenitendi, irascendi, descendendi, ascendendi, &c vsurpentur de Deo, causa est in promptu, sunt enim hae locutiones sumptae de medio vsu vitae humanae. Deus alloquens homines simplices & rudes demittit se ad eorum captum, & quasi homo esset humanos afsectus & motus sibi accommodat, vt tanto magis eos afficiat, & illi effecta Dei illis plane similia, quae ab huiusmodi humanis perturbationibus & motibus proficisci solent, facilius percipiant animo. Sic soliti sunt qui puerulos alloquuntur sese ad eorum captum accommodare. Alioqui si Deus homines verbis diuinis, modo diuino, phrasibus ad suam naturam, non autem ad infirmitatem humanam accommodatis alloquutus fuisset, quis eum intellexisset? Profecto vix possibile est aliter homines de Deo loqui, quàm vsurpando de eo verba humana, quae Deo tributa ἀνθρωποπαθῶς[?], quantum pati potest humana infirmitas, intelligi debent θεοπρεπῶς[?]. Id quod & Christiani omnes, & ipsi etiam Iudaei confitentur.
units.tr: XIX. To this must be added that the reason why words of repenting, being angry, going down, going up, and so on are applied to God is obvious. These expressions are taken from common human usage. God, speaking to simple and rude people, lowers himself to their level and, as if he were a man, adapts to himself human affections and movements, so that he may move them all the more, and so that they may more easily grasp in their minds those effects of God which are quite like those that usually arise from such human passions and movements. Those who speak to little children are accustomed to adapt themselves in this way to the children's understanding. Otherwise, if God had spoken to men in divine words, in a divine manner, with phrases adapted to his own nature and not to human weakness, who would have understood him? Indeed, it is hardly possible for men to speak of God otherwise than by using human words of him, which must be understood as applied to God in a way fitting to God [θεοπρεπῶς], insofar as human weakness can bear them, and as anthropopathic [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς]. All Christians, and the Jews themselves, confess this.

units.la: Horum vero locorum, quae pro diuinitate aut incarnatione Christi citamus, longè alia est ratio. Non possunt exponi per ἀνθρωποπαθείαν[?]. Non exigebat humana infirmitas, vt sic loca illa conciperentur. Non sunt ab hominibus mutuatae illae locutiones quas vrgemus; quinetiam ab eorum vsu abhorrent nonnunquam. Nec intelligi potest quem vsum habeant, aut cur sint vsurpatae, si vera non est nostra de diuina Christi natura sententia. Denique omnium illorum locorum, in quibus Deo poenitentia, tristitia, ira, descensus, ascensus, &c tribuitur, eadem est expositio omnibus illis egregiè congruens. Locorum vero, quae nos citamus, expositiones excogitarunt pro ingenio suo Aduersarij admodum varias, & nonnunquam inter se pugnantes, easque saepe coactas, & vim verbis diuinis aperte inferentes. id quod est Scripturas, vt loquitur Apostolus Petrus, ad suam perniciem ἀπώλειαν[?]. Cauerat Deus eiusmodi locorum & multitudine & varietate, ne possent facile aliò detorqueri: Sed homines ingeniosi omne suum studium, omnem operam in illis inflectendis & contorquendis consumpserunt, nec tamen res illis successit ex voto.
units.tr: The case of those passages which we cite for the divinity or the incarnation of Christ is quite different. They cannot be explained by anthropopathy [ἀνθρωποπαθείαν]. Human weakness did not require that those passages be understood in this way. The expressions we press were not borrowed from men, and indeed they are sometimes out of keeping with human usage. Nor can one see what use they have, or why they were employed, if our view of the divine nature of Christ is not true. Finally, for all those passages in which repentance, sorrow, anger, descent, ascent, and so on are attributed to God, there is one and the same explanation, which agrees perfectly with all of them. But for the passages we cite, our opponents have devised explanations, each according to his own cleverness, which are quite varied and sometimes contradict one another, and these are often forced and openly do violence to the divine words. This is what Peter the Apostle means when he says that the Scriptures are wrested to their own destruction [ἀπώλειαν]. God had guarded against such passages, by their number and variety, from being easily twisted elsewhere. But clever men have spent all their zeal and effort on bending and twisting them, and yet their undertaking has not succeeded as they wished.

units.la: XX. Caeterum, vt loca iam laudata & vindicata raceram[?], conjun-ctas esse in Christo naturam diuinam & naturam humanam, Nouum Testamentum passim docet aperte. Vocatur enim Christus homo, & vocatur etiam Deus: appellatur saepe filius hominis, appellatur etiam, & quidem sæpius, filius Dei; tribuitur illi forma hominis & tribuitur forma Dei; tribuuntur illi proprietates humanæ, & proprietates etiam divinæ; actiones humanæ & actiones etiam divinæ; infirmitates humanæ, & virtutes divinæ; opera humana & opera planè divina; perpessiones humanæ, & gloria ac majestas prorsus divina; mors humana & vita divina vivificans mortuos; denique ignominia humana, & cultus verè divinus; ut quibus argumentis eum esse hominem mihi persuasum est, iisdem mihi persuadeatur, eum etiam esse Deum. Hæc nostra persuasio seu fides frustrà ridetur à Socino, & stultitia non sine blasphemia appellatur. Certè si stultitia est, ei stultitia est qui non capit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Si stultitia est, Dei stultitia est, quæ sapientior est quàm homines. Nos autem de tali stultitia gloriamur in Domino. Sed pergamus.
units.tr: XX. Furthermore, to return to the passages already cited and defended, the New Testament teaches plainly and everywhere that the divine and the human nature are joined in Christ. For Christ is called man, and he is also called God. He is often called the Son of Man, and he is also called, and indeed more often, the Son of God. To him is attributed the form of a man, and also the form of God; human properties are attributed to him, and divine properties too; human actions and also divine actions; human infirmities and divine powers; human works and plainly divine works; human sufferings, and glory and majesty altogether divine; human death, and divine life quickening the dead; in short, human disgrace and truly divine worship. So let him be persuaded that he is God by the same arguments by which he has been persuaded that he is man. This our persuasion or faith is vainly mocked by Socinus, and is called folly, not without blasphemy. Certainly, if it is folly, it is the folly of one who does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. If it is folly, it is the folly of God, which is wiser than men. We, however, glory in such folly in the Lord. But let us go on.

units.la: XXI. Conatur deinceps Socinus hanc admirabilem Dei incarnationem omnino supernaturaleam fuisse ostendere. Quo argumento? Certè, inquit, si velimus istam substantiam divinam cum humana coniunctionem frustra omnino factam non fuisse, fateri oportet, per eam aliquid effectum fuisse in alterutra, sive utraque earum substantiarum. Sed quia in humana nihil hac ratione effectum est, ut statim demonstrabitur, sequitur, ut in divina hoc contigisse dicamus. Primò negamus consequentiam. finis enim huius coniunctionis fuit non ipsa divina aut humana natura, ut aliquid in utraque vel alterutra produceretur, sed, ut Christus omnes Mediatoris functiones ad salutem & redemptionem nostram necessarias, vel utiles obire posset. Sic hominis functiones, quarum aliæ per animam, aliæ per corpus fieri debent, finis sunt coniunctionis animæ & corporis. Deinde poterit etiam negari minor. Nihil quidem prorsus in ipsa divina natura coniunctione illa productum est. tantùm eâ factum est, ut persona divina quæ antea sola natura divina prædita erat, prædita fuerit etiam natura humana, sibi ad opus redemptionis nostræ peragendum necessariâ. Sed pergat Socinus.
units.tr: XXI. Socinus next tries to show that this admirable incarnation of God was altogether supernatural. By what argument? Certainly, he says, if we want to hold that this union of the divine substance with the human was not made altogether in vain, we must confess that something was effected through it in one or the other of these substances, or in both. But since nothing was effected in the human nature by this means, as will be shown at once, it follows that we must say it happened in the divine. First, we deny the consequence. For the purpose of this union was not that something might be produced in the divine or the human nature, or in either of them, but that Christ might be able to discharge all the functions of Mediator necessary or useful for our salvation and redemption. So too the functions of a man, some of which must be performed through the soul and some through the body, are the purpose of the union of soul and body. Next, the minor premise can also be denied. Nothing at all was produced in the divine nature by that union; it only came about that the divine Person, who before was endowed with the divine nature alone, came to be endowed also with a human nature, which was necessary for him to carry out the work of our redemption. But let Socinus go on.

units.la: XXII. Illud verò, inquit, aliud esse non potest, quàm humanæ substantia sive natura qualitates eam suscepisse, adeò ut saltem aliqua ex parte vel alterari, vel corrumpi potuerit, quod quidem, uti supra diximus horribile planè est. Negamus naturam divinam humanæ qualitates suscepisse, aut potuisse alterari, vel corrumpi. id nullo modo ex unione naturæ humanæ cum persona divina con-sequitur, sed hoc tantùm, de persona illa divina prædicari naturam humanam, vt loquuntur, in concreto, &, secundum illam naturam humanam, omnes illius qualitates actiones & passiones. id quod negamus ullo modo absurdum esse. Itaque non potuit divina illa persona alterari ullo modo aut corrumpi secundum naturam suam divinam, potuit tamen alterari & mori secundum naturam suam humanam. suas utrique naturæ sine ulla confusione conservamus proprietates. Redeamus ad Socinum.
units.tr: XXII. Yet, he says, this cannot be other than that the human substance or nature took on qualities, so that it could be altered or corrupted at least in some part, which indeed, as we said above, is quite horrible. We deny that the divine nature took on human qualities, or could be altered or corrupted. This does not follow in any way from the union of the human nature with the divine Person, but only from this: that the human nature is predicated of that divine Person, as they say, in the concrete, and that, according to that human nature, all its qualities, actions and sufferings are predicated of him. We deny that this is absurd in any way. Therefore that divine Person could not be altered or corrupted in any way according to his divine nature, but he could be altered and could die according to his human nature. We preserve the properties of each nature without any confusion. Let us return to Socinus.

units.la: XXIII. In humana, inquit, substantia sive natura, nihil per coniunctionem istam cum divina effectum fuisse ex eo manifeste appareret, quod in homine illo Iesu Christo, nihil excellentissimum licet & divinissimum, & humanam naturam longe transgrediens, reperiri potest, quod ab ipsius patre, cuius personam minime ea ratione cum homine coniunctam fuisse, omnes fatentur, illi datum non legamus. Quid sibi vult istius verbis Socinus? Num sic colligit, Nihil habet Iesus Christus, quod non ei sit à Patre datum. Ergo nihil in natura eius humana per ipsius cum divina coniunctionem effectum est? Hoccine est eius argumentum? prorsus, si quid video. Nego igitur consequentiam. Quis enim ferat sic ratiocinanté, Ego nihil unquam boni habui, quod mihi datum à Deo non fuerit. Ergo nihil in corpore meo effectum est per eius cum anima mea conjunctionem. Ridiculus mihi ipse videar si sic colligam. Notum illud est tritum in scholis, subordinata non pugnant. Non loquitur Scriptura de Christo Deo & Christo homine tanquam de duabus personis, quarum ista ab illa præstantiam suam acceperit; sed tanquam de unica persona, quæ, quia Filius est Dei, Patri, vt Filium decebat, (præsertim eum, qui sumpta forma serui sese ultrò exinaniuisset, vt Patris legatum in terris ageret, & gloriam eius quæreret) omnia sua refert accepta. id quod non impediuit, quominus vim naturæ suæ divinæ in natura sua humana quatenus opus fuit, exereret. Adde quod quicquid facit Pater, id facit Filius similiter: & quicquid est Patris, est etiam Filij. itaque cum Filius accepit de eo quod est Patris, accepit de suo, vt ipse satis aperte docet Ioh. 16.15.
units.tr: XXIII. Now, he says, it is clear from this that nothing was effected in the human substance or nature by its union with the divine, because in that man Jesus Christ nothing can be found, however most excellent and most divine, and far surpassing human nature, which we do not read was given to him by his Father, whose person, as all confess, was in no way so joined to the man. What does Socinus mean by these words? Does he conclude in this way: Jesus Christ has nothing that has not been given him by the Father. Therefore nothing in his human nature was effected by the union of it with the divine? Is this really his argument? Certainly, so far as I can see. I therefore deny the consequence. For who would tolerate such reasoning: I never had anything good that was not given me by God. Therefore nothing in my body was effected by its union with my soul. I would look ridiculous if I drew such a conclusion. That familiar saying of the schools is well known: subordinate things do not conflict. Scripture does not speak of Christ the God and Christ the man as of two persons, of whom the one received his excellence from the other. It speaks of one person who, because he is the Son of God, rightly, as befits a Son (especially one who, having taken the form of a servant, had of his own accord emptied himself to act as the Father's envoy on earth and to seek his glory), refers all that he has to the Father as received from him. This did not prevent him from exercising the power of his divine nature in his human nature, insofar as there was need. Add that whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise, and whatever is the Father's is also the Son's. So when the Son receives from what is the Father's, he receives from what is his own, as he himself teaches quite plainly in John 16.15.

units.la: XXIV. At inquit Socinus, Nemo in se ipso aliquid efficere, vel sibi ipsi quicquam dare potest. Itane? Non potest aliquis in anima sua & actiones immanentes & habitus efficere? Non potest: sibi ipsi, si velit, mœrorem, laborem, dolorem, immò mortem dare, & corpori suo manus violentas inferre? Non potest, si peritus sit medicinæ, semetipsum sanare? Nihil accipit corpus ab anima, aut etiam animaà corpore? quid enim attinet cum Seneca disputare, an possit aliquis sibi ipsi beneficium dare, & gratiam referre? appella quocunque nomine volueris, satis mihi est multa ab anima in corpore, & à quolibet homine in semetipso efficiri posse.
units.tr: XXIV. But Socinus says: "No one can effect anything in himself, or give anything to himself." Really? Can no one effect anything within his own soul, such as immanent actions and habits? Can he not, if he wishes, give himself sorrow, toil, pain, even death, and lay violent hands on his own body? Can a man skilled in medicine not heal himself? Does the body receive nothing from the soul, or the soul nothing from the body? For what is the point of disputing with Seneca whether a man can confer a benefit on himself and return a favour to himself? Call it by whatever name you like; it is enough for me that many things can be effected by the soul in the body, and by any man in himself.

units.la: XXV. Utitur Socinus alia quadam ratione. Accedit eò, inquit, quòd frustrà id fieri, & superuacaneum esse rectè id dicitur, ex quo nihil efficitur, quod commodiore & magis compendiaria quadam via effici non potuerit. Hoc verum est. Pergat. Quare licet hominem illum Iesum Christum, seu potius eius humanam naturam atque substantiam, à diuina sibi incredibili illo modo copulata, omnia præstantiora quæ habet accipere potuisse, constaret, cum tamen ex sola diuina virtute ac potentia, sanctique spiritus operatione idem fieri potuisset (id quod vel ex eo, quod factum fuisse probauimus, satis cuilibet patere potest) quid opus fuerat, Deum ipsum ineffabili quadam ratione illi coniunctum esse, & suæ ipsius quodammodo maiestatis & gloriæ oblitum, seu potius prodigum & desertorem, humanam naturam despectam atque contemptam, infinitisque malis obnoxiam induere? Nego sola diuina virtute absque vnione naturæ humanæ cum persona diuina, quicquid effectum est effici potuisse, nedum vt commodiore & magis compendiaria quadam via effici potuerit. Verbi gratia absque illa vnione effici non potuit vt homo ille idem esset Deus, Filius Dei (quo sensu hoc ei nomen tribui solet) Seruator mundi, propria virtute mortuos viuificans, corda & renes scrutans, æqualis Deo Patri, summa cum potestate quicquid vult in cœlo & terra faciens &c. Ostendant Aduersarij absque ista admirabili conjunctione, loca Scripturæ quæcunque laudauimus, & quæcunque laudaturi sumus, commodum sensum habere posse, ac nostras omnes rationes solidè diluant, quibus probauimus, &, Deo benè fauente, probaturi sumus, Filium Dei esse reuera Deum præditum essentia diuina, actum certè probauerint absque illa vnione quicquid effectum est effici potuisse. Aliàs argutando operam perdent suam. Cæterum quod Dei Filius, cum esset in forma Dei, Deo æqualis, exinanivit seipsum formam serui accipiens, in similitudine hominum. factus, & figura inuentus vt homo humiliauit seipsum, factus obe-diens vsque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis, id. cu.n ab infinita quadam bonitate profectum, & Deo gloriosissimum, ac nobis summè necessarium & salutare fuerit, summis laudibus, vt gratos decet, celebrare debemus. Nam si suae majestatis & gloriae, vt loquitur irreuerenter Socinus, oblitus, prodigus, desertor fuit, in gratiam Patris & nostri id fecit, ea virtute, quam Angeli & homines satis admirari nequeunt, & quâ nulla major animo concipi potest.
units.tr: XXV. Socinus uses another argument. "Moreover," he says, "it is rightly said that a thing is done in vain and is superfluous if nothing is effected by it which could not have been effected by a more convenient and more direct way." That is true. Let him go on: "Therefore, although it was certain that this man Jesus Christ, or rather his human nature and substance, could receive all the more excellent things he has from the divine nature joined to him in that incredible manner, yet since the same could have been done by the divine power and might alone, and by the operation of the Holy Spirit (which can be clear enough to anyone from the fact that we have proved it was done), what need was there for God himself to be joined to him by some ineffable manner, and, forgetful of his own majesty and glory, or rather prodigal and deserter of it, to put on a human nature despised and contemptible and liable to infinite evils?" I deny that, without the union of the human nature with the divine person, whatever has been effected could have been effected by the divine power alone, let alone that it could have been effected by a more convenient and more direct way. For example, without that union it could not have been effected that this man was the same God, the Son of God (in which sense this name is commonly given to him), the Saviour of the world, quickening the dead by his own power, searching hearts and reins, equal to God the Father, with supreme power doing whatever he wills in heaven and earth, and so on. Let the adversaries show that, without this admirable conjunction, the passages of Scripture that we have cited and those we are about to cite can have a fitting sense, and that they solidly refute all our arguments by which we have proved, and, God favouring, shall prove, that the Son of God is truly God endowed with the divine essence. Otherwise they will be proving, by their reasoning, that whatever has been effected could have been effected without that union, and they will waste their labour. Moreover, that the Son of God, though he was in the form of God, equal to God, "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Phil. 2.). Since this proceeded from an infinite goodness, and was most glorious to God and most necessary and salutary to us, we ought, as is fitting for the grateful, to celebrate it with the highest praises. For if, as Socinus irreverently puts it, he forgot his majesty and glory, and was prodigal and deserter of it, he did so for the sake of the Father and of us, by that power which angels and men cannot sufficiently admire, and than which no greater can be conceived in the mind.

units.la: XXVI. Progreditur in ista sua ingratitudine & impietate longiùs Socinus, & ad rem ipsam, vt loquitur, propius accedens, conatur probare, nominatim ad salutem generis humani hypostaticam illam diuinae humanaeque substantiae coniunctionem non inanem tantummodo, verum etiam planè inutilem futuram. Quomodo id praestat? refutando argumentum, quo illius conjunctionis necessitas demonstratur, petitum à satisfactione, quam, & ad expiationem peccatorum necessariam fuisse, & absque hypostatica naturae diuinae & humanae conjunctione fieri non potuisse firmiter credimus. At multas etiam alias ob causas necessaria fuit illa conjunctio, quas Socinus alto silentio praeterit. Vin' tibi illarum specimen aliquod exhibeamus? Est Christus, ipsis Aduersarijs consitentibus, summus noster Propheta, & Sacerdos, & Rex. Ad Propheticum munus quod attinet. Is est doctor noster vnicus, adeoque perfectissimus. opus autem fuit natura humana vt homines doceret & verbo perquam familiariter ac suauiter & exemplo. Is enim demum perfectè docet qui docet vtroque illo modo. Opus etiam fuit vt doctor noster praeditus esset natura diuina, primùm in genere, vt esset omnium doctorum praestantissimus. quis enim doctor sicut Deus? Omnium autem praestantissima docendi ratio est, cum Deus sumptâ formâ humana homines dig-natur familiari colloquio, & cum eis prandendo, ambulando, &c se illis & audiendum & contemplandum praebet: quomodo olim docuisse legitur Patriarcham Abrahamum. nihil potuit accidere hominibus aut vtilius, aut honorificentius. Hanc igitur docendi rationem eum fuisse tum secutum credibile est, cum perfectiore modo, quàm vnquam antea, Ecclesiam suam docuit.
units.tr: XXVI. Socinus proceeds further in this ingratitude and impiety, and "coming closer, as he puts it, to the matter itself," tries to prove that "that hypostatic conjunction of the divine and human substance will be not only empty but also plainly useless, especially for the salvation of the human race." How does he accomplish this? By refuting the argument by which the necessity of that conjunction is demonstrated, drawn from satisfaction, which we firmly believe was necessary for the expiation of sins and could not be accomplished without the hypostatic conjunction of the divine and human nature. But that conjunction was necessary also for many other reasons, which Socinus passes over in deep silence. Do you want us to set out some sample of them? Christ is, as the adversaries themselves admit, our supreme Prophet, Priest and King. As for his prophetic office, he is our one teacher, and therefore most perfect. Now it was necessary for the human nature to teach men both by word, most familiarly and sweetly, and by example. For he teaches perfectly only if he teaches in both ways. It was also necessary that our teacher be endowed with the divine nature, first in general, so that he might be the most excellent of all teachers. For who is a teacher like God? Now the most excellent manner of teaching of all is when God, having taken on human form, condescends to men in familiar conversation, and shows himself to be both heard and beheld by them, eating with them, walking with them, and so on; in this way he is read to have taught the patriarch Abraham of old. Nothing could have happened to men that was either more useful or more honourable. It is therefore credible that he followed this method of teaching when he taught his Church in a more perfect way than ever before.

units.la: XXVII. Deinde in Christi munere prophetico consideranda sunt praecipuè haec quatuor, quid docuit, quomodo docuit, quibus argumentis confirmauit doctrinam suam, quomodo eam accepit à Patre. Prædicauit Christus, sed præcipuè semetipsum. reuelauit & ostendit Deum, sed reuelando & ostendendo semetipsum. vocauit homines, sed ad seipsum. Iussit credere, sed in seipsum. Pollicitus est vitam æternam, sed quam ipse daturus esset in seipsum credentibus. Salutem miseris peccatoribus annunciauit, sed in se vno repositam. Metum incussit iudicij futuri, sed quod ipse vnus exerceret. Remissionem peccatorum obtulit, sed credentibus in seipsum, & quam pro sua autoritate indulgeret. Promisit resurrectionem mortuorum, sed quam ipse vi sua effecturus esset; & regnum cœlorum, sed quod ijs ipse daturus esset qui ipsius rationè habuissent. Nonne eum vt sic docere[?] Deum esse oportuit? Nonne merus homo homines à se ad Deum amandasset, & cauisset diligenter, ne quam vel minimam diuinæ gloriæ particulam ad se transferret. Sic enim sese reliqui omnes & Prophetæ, & Apostoli, & fideles doctores gesserunt.
units.tr: XXVII. Next, in Christ's prophetic office four things are chiefly to be considered: what he taught, how he taught, by what arguments he confirmed his doctrine, and how he received it from the Father. Christ preached, but chiefly himself. He revealed and showed God, but by revealing and showing himself. He called men, but to himself. He commanded them to believe, but in himself. He promised eternal life, but that which he himself would give to those believing in himself. He announced salvation to wretched sinners, but laid up in himself alone. He instilled fear of future judgment, but that which he alone would exercise. He offered forgiveness of sins, but to those believing in himself, and which he would grant by his own authority. He promised the resurrection of the dead, but which he himself would effect by his own power; and the kingdom of heaven, but which he would give to those who had regard to him. Was it not necessary that he teach in this way if he was God? Would a mere man not have led men from himself to God, and taken care to ensure that he did not transfer to himself even the least particle of divine glory? For all the rest, both prophets, apostles and faithful teachers, have conducted themselves in exactly this way.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Hoc ipsum verò quomodo docuit? Cum duplex sit ratio docendi: vna humana, quæ fit ore humano, & voce extrinsecus aures pulsante, altera merè diuina, quæ fit mentem ipsam auditoris aperiendo & intus afficiendo. Vtramque Christus adhibuit. quàm autem ad illam necessaria fuit natura humana, tam ad istam necessaria fuit diuina. vt enim illa humano ore, humanis organis fieri debuit, sic ista alia vi fieri non potuit quàm merè diuina. Quàm autem organa humana absque natura humana esse non possunt, tam vis diuina absque diuina natura esse non potest. Hanc docendi facultatem agnouerunt Apostoli, Domine, inquiunt, adauge nobis fidem, quam orationem Dominus non improbauit, nec respondit vt olim Iacobus, qui petenti Racheli vt sibi daret liberos, ira excanduit, & respondit, Num pro Deo ego sum &c? Itaque Dominus postquam à mortuis resurrexit, aperuit illis mentem vt intelligerent Scripturas. Idem aperuit cor Eydia[?], vt attenderet his quæ dicebantur à Paulo: ac è summo cœlo die Pentecostes Spiritum sanctum in Apostolos suos insufflauit, eosque diuinissima ratione docuit; atque ita non è monte contrectabili Sina, sed è monte Sion, non è terra sed è cœlo, vt Deum decebat, in Apostolis suis loquens, & prædicationem eorum efficacia sua prosequens Ecclesiam suam vbique locorum docuit.
units.tr: But how did he teach this very thing? Teaching is of two kinds: one human, which is done by a human mouth and by a voice striking the ears from outside, and another purely divine, which is done by opening the hearer's own mind and acting on it from within. Christ used both. Just as human nature was necessary for the former, so divine nature was necessary for the latter. For just as the former had to be done by a human mouth and human organs, so the latter could not be done by any power other than purely divine power. And just as human organs cannot exist without human nature, so divine power cannot exist without the divine nature. The apostles recognised this power of teaching when they said, Lord, increase our faith (Luke 17), a prayer which the Lord did not disapprove, nor did he answer as Jacob once did, who, when Rachel asked him to give her children, was angry and replied, Am I in God's place? (Gen. 30). Thus, after he had risen from the dead, the Lord opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). Likewise he opened the heart of Lydia, so that she attended to what was said by Paul (Acts 16). And from the highest heaven on the day of Pentecost he breathed the Holy Spirit into his apostles and taught them by a most divine method. So, speaking in his apostles not from a touchable mountain, Sinai, but from Mount Zion, not from the earth but from heaven, as became God, and by his own efficacy following up their preaching, he taught his Church in every place.

units.la: XXIX. Ad doctrinam autem suam persuadendam vsus est miraculis & plurimis & maximis, quæ, non aliena virtute vt Prophetæ & Apostoli, sed duâ[?] ipsius edidit, id quod vt crederent ab hominibus exegit, creditis, inquiebat, me posse hoc facere? Dicant mihi Aduersarij, vis illa infinita qua hominum cogitationes videbat, omnis generis morbos puncto temporis sanabat, cæcorum oculos aperiebat, mortuos viuificabat, diabolos abigebat &c; quonam in subjecto hærebat? In eius corpore seu carne? Erat igitur & finita, & materialis saltem aliquo modo, & quo modo ex eadem carne non expellebat imbecillitatem & mortalitatem? quomodo etiam, carne Christi absente, & procul ab illa sese nonnunquam exercebat? In eius anima? vtrum igitur in intellectu, in voluntate, in phantasia, in appetitu sensitiuo, in facultate locomotrice, an immediatè in ipsa animæ rationalis essentia? vbicunque locetur, fuisset anima Christi admodum diuersa ab animabus aliorum hominum, & haud satis consentiens inter subjectum & suum accidens proportio, & quomodo egressum fuisset accidens illud ex anima Christi, vt procul ab ipsa in aliorum hominum corporibus sese exereret? quanquam cur accidens vocem nescio. quî potuit enim tanta facere merum accidens? Quod si fuit substantia, duæ fuerunt in Christo substantiæ, humana vna, & altera multò quàm humana, immò angelica, potentior; atque adeo planè diuina. Hæc tantùm obiter hoc loco attingo, alio loco, Deo dante, diligentius expendenda.
units.tr: XXIX. To persuade people of his teaching, he used very many and very great miracles, which he performed not by a power foreign to himself, as the prophets and apostles did, but by his own power. He demanded that people believe in this, saying, Do you believe that I can do this? Let my opponents tell me: that infinite power by which he saw men's thoughts, healed every kind of disease in an instant, opened the eyes of the blind, raised the dead to life, and drove out demons, etc.; in what subject did it inhere? In his body or flesh? Then it was finite, and at least in some way material. And how did it not drive weakness and mortality out of that same flesh? How also did it sometimes operate when Christ's flesh was absent and far away? In his soul? Then in which part: in the intellect, the will, the imagination, the sensitive appetite, the faculty of locomotion, or immediately in the very essence of the rational soul? Wherever it was located, the soul of Christ would have been very different from the souls of other men, and the proportion between the subject and its accident would hardly agree. And how would that accident have gone out from Christ's soul so as to show itself far from it, in the bodies of other men? Although I do not know why I call it an accident. For how could a mere accident do such great things? But if it was a substance, then there were two substances in Christ: one human, and the other far more than human, indeed angelic and more powerful, and therefore plainly divine. I touch on these matters only in passing here; they are to be weighed more carefully elsewhere, God willing.
