units.la: XXX. Dominus autem, quemadmodum decebat eum, qui sese voluntariè inaniuisset sumptâ serui formâ vt seruum & legatum Patris ageret, doctrinam suam Patri ascribit. Sed quomodo eam à Patre accepit? Legiturne aliquando, verbum Dei ad illum factum fuisse? aut Deum illi apparuisse? Notaturne ab aliquo Euangelistarum aut Apostolorum tempus, aut modus, aut sermo, quo Deus cum eo egerit? Nullo modo. Cur id factum non est, si Dominus nihil nisi creatura, nihil nisi homo fuit? Ipsa Dei consilia & decreta intima Dominus reuelauit, & quidem tanquam illorum perfectè conscius, & testis αὐτόπτης[?]. quomodo autem & quando fuerint ei à Patre reuelata non exprimitur: Cur quæso, si nihil nisi homo fuisset, id tacitum fuisset, quod ad fidem eius testimonio conciliandam plurimùm valuisset? Nam si nihil nisi homo fuit, Deus se illi patefecit certo quodam & tempore, & loco, & modo, & sermone. quæ omnia notari & literis mandari potuerunt. At si persona diuina fuit eâdem cum patre essentiâ prædita, ea Patris decreta & consilia perpetuò nota habuit & vidit immediatè, nec vlla eiusmodi inter eam & Patrem vel communicatio, vel communicationis circunstantia obseruari potuit. Eadem per humanas suas facultates & organa omnia illa, prout expediebat, cum discipulis suis communicauit, cuius communicationis circunstantias omnes, Euangelistæ, vti par erat,annotarunt satis diligenter.
units.tr: XXX. The Lord, however, as became one who had voluntarily emptied himself, taking the form of a servant so that he might act as the servant and envoy of the Father, ascribes his teaching to the Father. But how did he receive it from the Father? Is it ever read that the word of God came to him, or that God appeared to him? Does any of the evangelists or apostles note the time, the manner, or the speech by which God dealt with him? By no means. Why has this not been done, if the Lord was nothing but a creature, nothing but a man? The Lord revealed the very intimate counsels and decrees of God, and indeed as one perfectly acquainted with them, an ocular witness [αὐτόπτης]. But how and when they were revealed to him by the Father is not expressed. Why, I ask, if he had been nothing but a man, would this have been passed over in silence, when it would have greatly helped to win belief in his testimony? For if he was nothing but a man, God revealed himself to him at a certain time, and place, and manner, and by a certain speech. All these things could have been noted and committed to writing. But if he was a divine person endowed with the same essence as the Father, he always had and immediately saw those decrees and counsels of the Father, and no communication of this kind between him and the Father, nor any circumstance of such communication, could be observed. Through his human faculties and organs he communicated all those things to his disciples as was fitting, and the evangelists have, as was right, noted with sufficient care all the circumstances of this communication.

units.la: XXXI. Venio ad Sacerdotium Christi. Ei necessaria fuit natura humana ob eas causas, quas commemorat autor Ep. ad Heb. cap. 2. ℣. 14. & 17. necnon natura diuina, vt typo Melchisedeci responderet, qui absque initio dierum & fine vitæ fuisse dicitur Sacerdos æternus Heb. 7.3. typus æterni Filij Dei, facti Sacerdotis secundum potentiam vitæ indissolubilis ℣. 16. ac propterea hominibus infirmis oppositi ℣. 28. Et etiam ad sacrificium suum opus fuit, & corpore quod offerret semel, & spiritu æterno per quem offerret. Heb. 9. 14. Non fuisset victima si homo non fuisset sanctus & immaculatus, nec Sacerdos si Deus non fuisset, qui pro sua sapientia & potentia omnia quæcunque fuerunt ad ipsius immolationem necessaria administraret, & adhiberet, & regeret, instrumentis ad eam rem vtens prudenter. Est enim victimæ pati, Sacerdotis agere. Præterea si homo non fuisset, non habuisset sanguinem quem funderet, & fusum inferret in sanctum sanctorum coeleste. Et rursus si Deus non fuisset, non potuisset vi sua, vt Sacerdotem decebat, immolatâ victimâ in atrio tabernaculi (alibi enim nefas erat sacrificare) eius sanguinem in locum sanctissimum inferre, hoc est, in supremum coelum ascendere, omnibus alijs coelis trajectis. Quid enim absurdius, quàm cogitare Summum Sacerdotem, qui vi sua in tabernaculum suum ingredi non possit?
units.tr: XXXI. I come to the priesthood of Christ. He needed human nature for the reasons which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews mentions in chapter 2, verses 14 and 17. He also needed divine nature, so that he would correspond to the type Melchizedek, who is said to have been a priest forever, without beginning of days or end of life (Heb. 7:3), a type of the eternal Son of God, made a priest after the power of an indissoluble life (v. 16), and therefore set against weak men (v. 28). Also, for his sacrificial work he needed both a body, which he might offer once, and eternal spirit, through which he might offer it (Heb. 9:14). He would not have been the victim if he had not been a holy and spotless man, nor the priest if he had not been God, who by his wisdom and power arranged and applied and governed all things that were necessary for his immolation, using the instruments for that purpose prudently. For it belongs to the victim to suffer, and to the priest to act. Moreover, if he had not been a man, he would not have had blood to shed, and to carry the shed blood into the holy of holies in heaven. And again, if he had not been God, he could not, by his own power, as became a priest, carry his blood, once the victim had been slain in the court of the tabernacle (for it was unlawful to sacrifice elsewhere), into the most holy place, that is, to ascend into the highest heaven, having passed through all the other heavens. For what could be more absurd than to think of a high priest who by his own power could not enter his own tabernacle?

units.la: XXXII. Dicam aliquid amplius. Idem Christus qui est summus Sacerdos, est mediator noui foederis. Iam autem tabernaculum opus est Mediatoris. Vt enim se habuit Mediator typicus ad tabernaculum typicum, sic se habere debuit Mediator verus ad tabernaculum verum. Atqui Mediator typicus, hoc est, Moses, construxit tabernaculum typicum Exod. 26. 1.[?] illudque erexit Exod. 40. 16.[?] Mediator igitur verus suum tabernaculum facere & erigere debuit. Id quod Apostolus conferens Dominum cum Mose qui fecit tabernaculum Heb. 3.3. 4. & cum Aarone qui illud figebat Heb. 8. 2. aperte docet. Itaque non dubitauit idem autor affirmare, & per eum facta esse secula, & cœlos (sunt autem cœli tabernaculum noui fœderis) esse opera manuum eius. Et quomodo per eum non esset factum tabernaculum Noui Testamenti per quem facta sunt omnia, & per quem sunt omnia, & per quem quæcunque sunt in illo tabernaculo, facta & creata sunt? Mediatori igitur & summo sacerdoti nostro necessaria fuit natura diuina, ut ui sua non modo ingrederetur tabernaculum suum, sed etiam ut illud construeret, & figeret. Itaque ut prius fuit Mediator Moses & Sacerdos Aaron quàm esset tabernaculum ita prius etiam Filius fuit quàm tabernaculum cœleste; Et, ut Sacerdotes & Leuitæ tabernaculum cum opus erat, detrahebant, & eius aulæa circumuoluebant; Sic, cum opus erit, Sacerdos noster cœlos tabernaculi sui aulæa velut amictum, circumuoluet, teste eodem auctore Heb. 1. 12. ipso interim permanente, sicut permanebant Sacerdotes tabernaculo dissoluto.
units.tr: XXXII. I will say something more. The same Christ who is high priest is also the mediator of the new covenant. Now a tabernacle is the work of a mediator. For just as the typical mediator stood in relation to the typical tabernacle, so the true mediator ought to stand in relation to the true tabernacle. But the typical mediator, that is, Moses, built the typical tabernacle (Exod. 26:1) and set it up (Exod. 40:16). Therefore the true mediator ought to make and erect his own tabernacle. The apostle plainly teaches this when he compares the Lord with Moses, who built the tabernacle (Heb. 3:3-4), and with Aaron, who fixed it in place (Heb. 8:2). Thus the same author did not hesitate to affirm that through him the worlds were made, and the heavens (and the heavens are the tabernacle of the new covenant) are the works of his hands (Heb. 1:2, 10). And how could the tabernacle of the New Testament not have been made through him, through whom all things were made, and through whom all things are, and through whom whatever things are in that tabernacle were made and created? Therefore our mediator and high priest needed divine nature, so that by his power he might not only enter his own tabernacle, but also build and fix it. Thus, just as Moses the mediator and Aaron the priest existed before the tabernacle, so also the Son existed before the heavenly tabernacle. And just as the priests and Levites took down the tabernacle when there was need, and wrapped up its curtains, so, when there will be need, our priest will wrap up the heavens like a garment, like the curtains of his tabernacle, as the same author testifies (Heb. 1:12), while he himself remains, just as the priests remained when the tabernacle was taken down.

units.la: XXXIII. Sacerdotis est expiare peccata oblatione victimæ, quæ loco peccatoris mortem perpetiatur, & ita Dei iustitiæ pro peccatoribus satisfacere. id quod omnibus sacrificiis expiatorijs adumbratum est sub lege. Itaque Sacerdos est fœderis ἔγγυος[?], & tenetur portare iniquitatem populi. Hinc ducitur argumentum invictum, Oportuit Sacerdotem nostrum pro nobis apud Deum satisfacere, alioqui nequaquam feruandis. Non potuisset autem verè & reipsa pro peccatis nostris satisfacere, nisi simul Deus & homo fuisset. Oportuit igitur eum simul & Deum & hominem esse. Hoc unum argumentum Socinus delegit, quo soluendo ostenderet conjunctionem naturæ diuinæ & humanæ in Christo esse prorsus superuacaneam. Quid igitur Respondet? Negatne necessitatem satisfactionis? Negat quidem, sed quoniam res illa, ut in clarissimam lucem proferretur longiorem disputationem requireret &c, eam, inquit, illis in præsentia demus. Subjungit tamen statim, nos eam miserè[?] deceptos, diminutis oraculis licet undique reclamantibus, ipsaque ratione penitus abhorrente, confinxisse. quo certè nihil dici potuit salsius. Eam enim & Scriptura multis locis inculcat, & ratio agnoscit & probat, & nihil est in Scriptura, quod reclamet, aut in recta ratione quod ab ea abhorreat. Sed deceptus Socinus ratiociniis quibusdam falsis, vt opinationem suam tueretur, multis Scripturæ locis vim apertam intulit. Omittamus igitur, nunc quidem, quando ita visum est Socino hoc loco, prolixam illam disputationem, & accipiamus quod dat, quanquam id dat fide sublesta: statim enim auferre conatur quod dedit.
units.tr: XXXIII. It belongs to the priest to expiate sins by offering a victim, which suffers death in the place of the sinner, and so to make satisfaction to the justice of God on behalf of sinners. This was foreshadowed under the law by all the expiatory sacrifices. Therefore the priest is the surety [ἔγγυος] of the covenant, and is bound to bear the iniquity of the people. From this an unanswerable argument is drawn: our Priest had to make satisfaction to God for us, otherwise we could not be saved. But he could not have truly and really made satisfaction for our sins unless he were at the same time God and man. Therefore he had to be both God and man. Socinus chose this one argument, in order to show by its solution that the conjunction of the divine and human nature in Christ is wholly superfluous. What, then, does he reply? Does he deny the necessity of satisfaction? He does deny it, but since that matter, to be brought into the clearest light, would require a longer disputation, he says, "we will give it to them for the present." Yet he immediately adds that we, "miserably deceived, have invented it from diminished oracles, though they cry out against it on every side, and reason itself utterly abhors it." Nothing could be said more absurdly. For Scripture inculcates it in many places, reason recognises and proves it, and there is nothing in Scripture that cries out against it, nor anything in sound reason that abhors it. But Socinus, deceived by certain false reasonings, in order to defend his opinion has done open violence to many passages of Scripture. Let us therefore, for now, since Socinus has thought fit to do so at this point, set aside that lengthy disputation, and accept what he grants, although he grants it on a feeble footing: for he immediately tries to take back what he has given.

units.la: XXXIV. Oportuit igitur, vt ipsi aiunt, inquit, diuina iustitia de hominis sceleribus cumulatè satisfieri. Quid tum? An ipsemet Deus eas pœnas persoluere debuit? Non debuit certè quidem, sed tamen solus potuit. Itaque necesse fuit, vt aut ipsi periremus, aut ille earum persoluendarum onus in se susciperet, iuxta illud Dominus providebit. id quod aliundè quàm ab infinita misericordia proficisci non potuit. At inquit, Primùm id fieri nullo pacto potuit. Nullo igitur, inquam, pacto fieri potuit vt seruaremur. Hoc enim consequitur posità necessitate satisfactionis, quam nobis Socinus hoc loco dedit. Deus enim, addit, neque dolore assici, neque perpessiones aliquas experiri potest. nempe quâ Deus, seu secundum naturam diuinam. Atque hæc causa est cur oportuerit eum sibi vnire naturam humanam patibilem & mortalem. Id quod nos Auctor Ep. ad Heb. cap. 2. V. 14. docuit, Quoniam igitur, inquit, pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipse quoque consimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, vt per mortem destrueret eum qui habebat mortis imperium, id est, diabolum. Quomodo mori potuisset, si tantùm Deus fuisset? aut per mortem destruere diabolum qui mortis robur tenebat, si tantùm caro seu homo infirmus & mortalis fuisset? fortiorem enim eum esse oportuit diabolis omnibus.
units.tr: XXXIV. "It was therefore necessary, as they themselves say," he says, "that the divine justice be fully satisfied for the crimes of men. What then? Ought God himself to have paid those penalties?" He certainly ought not to have, yet he alone was able to. Therefore it was necessary that either we ourselves should perish, or that he should take upon himself the burden of paying them, according to the saying, "The Lord will provide." This could come from nowhere but infinite mercy. "But," he says, "first, this could not be done in any way." Then, I say, there was no way in which we could have been saved. For this follows, given the necessity of satisfaction, which Socinus here grants us. "For God," he adds, "can neither be affected by pain nor undergo any sufferings." Namely, insofar as he is God, or according to the divine nature. And this is the reason why it was necessary for him to unite to himself a human nature capable of suffering and mortal. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 2, verse 14, taught us this: "Since therefore the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he himself likewise took part in the same, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil." How could he have died if he had been God only? Or how could he destroy through death the devil, who held the strength of death, if he had been only flesh, or a weak and mortal man? For he had to be stronger than all the devils.

units.la: XXXV. Verum, inquit Socinus, eodem revolui videntur; nam neque adhæsio ista aliquid momenti allatura fuit, si humana tantùm natura verè pati poterat, cuius cruciatus omnes, utcunque eos consideres, finitos prorsus ac terminatos esse oporteret, quum infinitatis cuiusdam, vt ipsimet apertè profitentur, pœnas, quæ infinitæ diuinæ iustitiæ satisfaciendi causa persoluuntur, necesse sit esse participes. Distinguo. Pœnæ, quas Dominus secundùm naturam suam humanam perpessus est, quasque diuinæ iustitiæ satisfaciendi causa persoluit, duobus modis considerari possunt. Primò Physicè seu Metaphysicè, ratione entitatis quam habuerunt. Sic finitæ fuerunt, nec esse infinitæ potuerunt, aut debuerunt. Secundò forensi ratione seu æstimatione, quo modo esse infinitæ & debuerunt, & reuera fuerunt. Cum enim de satisfactione forensi dis-putemus, finitas vel infinitas poenarum intelligenda est secundum æstimationem forensem, quæ nullam habet rationem entitatis, vt patet in peccato, quod interdum nullam entitatem habet, neque formaliter, neque materialiter (cogor vti vocibus vsitatis in schola) vt, verbi gratia, omissio officij; & tamen in foro magni æstimatur, immò, cum de officio erga Deum infinitum agitur, aliquomodo infinitè. Quo enim major est eius qui offenditur dignitas, eo pluris æstimatur offensa: eo enim minus offendi debuerat, plusque adeò est in offensa indignitatis.
units.tr: XXXV. "But," says Socinus, "they seem to have turned back to the same point; for that union would bring no weight at all, if human nature alone could truly suffer, all whose torments, however you consider them, would have to be wholly finite and bounded, since, as they themselves openly profess, it is necessary that he share in the penalties of a certain infinity, which are paid for the sake of satisfying infinite divine justice." I distinguish. The penalties which the Lord suffered according to his human nature, and which he paid for the sake of satisfying divine justice, can be considered in two ways. First, physically or metaphysically, with respect to the entity they had. In this way they were finite, and could be neither infinite nor ought they to have been. Secondly, in a forensic sense or estimation, in which way they both ought to have been and actually were infinite. For since we are disputing about forensic satisfaction, the finiteness or infinitude of the penalties is to be understood according to forensic estimation, which has no relation to entity, as is clear in sin, which sometimes has no entity, neither formally nor materially (I am forced to use the usual terms of the schools), as, for example, the omission of a duty; and yet in court it is greatly esteemed, and indeed, when the duty concerns the infinite God, it is in some way infinite. For the greater the dignity of the one who is offended, the more the offence is esteemed; for the less he ought to have been offended, the more weight there is in the indignity of the offence.

units.la: XXXVI. Quamuis igitur poenæ, quas Dominus noster in natura sua humana perpessus est, si entitatem earum spectes, finitæ fuerint, tamen reuera infinitæ fuerunt æstimatione forensi propter vnionem illam personalem naturæ humanæ cum diuina persona. Quo enim major est eius qui punitur dignitas, eo pluris æstimatur poena quam perpetitur. eo enim minus puniri debuerat. plusque adeò est in poena indignitatis. Iam autem personæ diuinæ essentia præditæ dignitas est infinita. Si igitur in forma visibili seu natura assumpta puniatur, poena erit forensi æstimatione infinita. Entitas Estheræ, cum Assuero nupsit, aucta non est, sed aucta est tamen & multiplicata mirum in modum eius dignitas: & tamen eius cum Assuero conjunctio, nec personalis, nec ei naturalis, nec indissolubilis fuit. Quis igitur dubitare possit, quin naturæ humanæ dignitas aucta & multiplicata fuerit in immensum, cum est vnita Personæ dignitatis prorsus infinitæ, vnione, qua nulla cogitari potest major & perfectior, personali, & indissolubili, ac perpetua, & ipsi illi naturæ naturali ? possent igitur perpessiones Christi ob istam naturæ eius humanæ dignitatem tantam aliquo modo infinitæ æstimari, sed tamen in æstimandis perpessionibus seu poenis ferè tantùm dignitatis personæ quæ patitur aut punitur ratio haberi solet & debet, potius quàm naturæ aut partis secundum quam persona patitur aut punitur. Actiones enim & passiones, vt vulgò dicunt, sunt suppositorum, non autem naturarum.
units.tr: XXXVI. Therefore, although the penalties which our Lord suffered in his human nature, if you look at their entity, were finite, nevertheless they were in reality infinite by forensic estimation, on account of that personal union of the human nature with the divine person. For the greater the dignity of the one who is punished, the more the penalty he undergoes is esteemed; for the less he ought to have been punished, the more weight there is in the indignity of the penalty. Now the dignity of the divine person, endowed with an essence, is infinite. If therefore he is punished in a visible form, or in an assumed nature, the penalty will be infinite by forensic estimation. The entity of Esther did not increase when she married Ahasuerus, but nevertheless her dignity was increased and multiplied in a wonderful way; and yet her conjunction with Ahasuerus was neither personal, nor natural to her, nor indissoluble. Who then could doubt that the dignity of the human nature was increased and multiplied immensely, when it was united to a Person of wholly infinite dignity, by a union than which none greater or more perfect can be conceived, personal, indissoluble, perpetual, and natural to that very nature? Thus the sufferings of Christ could in some way be esteemed as of such great and infinite dignity on account of that human nature; yet in estimating sufferings or penalties, the consideration usually and rightly taken is chiefly that of the dignity of the person who suffers or is punished, rather than of the nature or part according to which the person suffers or is punished. For actions and passions, as is commonly said, belong to supposita, not to natures.

units.la: XXXVII. Quo autem pluris fieri debuerunt perpessiones, cruciatus, ignominia, mors denique maledicta quam Christus pro nobis passus est, eo pluris etiam fieri debuit charitas Patris, qui filio suo proprio & vnigenito pro nobis non pepercit, & Filij,qui posuit animam suam pro nobis & peccata nostra in corpore suo portauit. itaque ea nobis in Scriptura tanquam summa & infinita & omni notitia supereminentior vehementissimè commendatur. Eo etiam majoris fieri debuit exinanitio & obedientia Christi. Itaque eam Apostolus vt immensam, & infinitam, & summam describit Phil. 2. 6. institutâ inter illius, vt ita loquar, terminum à quo & terminum ad quem comparatione & oppositione. Quo enim major erat dignitas eius qui se demisit & obediuit, eo major fuit eius demissio & obedientia. Erat autem summa & infinita dignitas Christi. Nam quae potest forma dignior esse forma Dei? Atqui Christus erat in forma Dei, quae dignitas major dignitate Dei? Atqui Christus erat aequalis ἴσα τῷ Θεῷ [?] aequalitatis, prorsus aequalis Deo. Is autem sese vsque eò exinaniuit, vt opposita formam sumpserit, scilicet serui; nec eo gradu exinanitionis contentus infra eum sese ad eam obedientiam demisit, quam nemo exigat à seruo, luitque vltrò attrocissimum & ignominiosissimum & lege Dei maledictum supplicium crucis, vt Patri obediret & nos redimeret à maledictione legis. Itaque nihil ad infinitam poenae aestimationem desiderari iure potuit.
units.tr: XXXVII. But the more the sufferings, torments, ignominy, and finally the accursed death which Christ suffered for us ought to be esteemed, the more also ought the love of the Father to be esteemed, who did not spare his own and only-begotten Son for us, and the love of the Son, who laid down his soul for us and bore our sins in his body. Therefore Scripture most earnestly commends that love to us as supreme and infinite, and "surpassing all knowledge." The emptying and obedience of Christ also ought to be regarded as greater. Therefore the Apostle describes it as immense, infinite, and supreme, Phil. 2:6, by setting up a comparison and contrast between, so to speak, the terminus from which and the terminus to which he came. For the greater the dignity of the one who humbled himself and obeyed, the greater his humbling and obedience. But the dignity of Christ was supreme and infinite. For what form can be more worthy than the form of God? Yet Christ was in the form of God; what dignity is greater than the dignity of God? Yet Christ was equal [ἴσα τῷ Θεῷ] to God, of equal rank, wholly equal to God. He, however, emptied himself so far that he took the opposite form, namely that of a servant; and not content with that degree of emptying, he humbled himself further to that obedience which no one would require of a servant, and he willingly underwent the most atrocious and ignominious death of the cross, which is accursed by the law of God, so that he might obey the Father and redeem us from the curse of the law. Therefore nothing could rightly be wanting to the infinite estimation of the penalty.

units.la: XXXVIII. Pergit Socinus, neque, inquit, vt delictorum conscientia humanos animos amplius non excruciet, propter satisfactionem istam, in qua salutis suae spem positam habeant, Deum ipsum cui satisfaciendum erat, ad eam peragendam aut absoluendam propria personaulla ratione concurrisse dicendum est. necesse est enim omnino satisfacientis personam, ab eius, cui satisfit, distingui ac separari, alioqui veram satisfactionem factam fuisse, nemo sibi ipsi penitus persuadere poterit. Fallitur vehementer Socinus. Contrà enim prorsus res se habet. Sepositâ enim istâ satisfactione non videmus qui possit sedari aestus conscientiae. Obuersatur enim animo & recurrit cogitatio iustitiae Dei, qui cum sit Iudex mundi iustissimus, omnis iusti iudicis exemplar perfectissimum, intelligi non potest, qui id faciat, quod, & pugnat cum officio iusti iudicis, & Deo abominationi esse Spiritus Sanctus testatur, & ipse Deus seuerè prohibuit, hoc est, qui absoluat impios & iniustos & sceleratos absque vlla legi & iustitiae satisfactione, non quidem per ipsos (id enim illis erat prorsus impossibile) sed per aliquem vadem pro ipsis praestitâ. Hanc cogitationem altera acuit diuinae veritatis. Quoties enim peccator cogitat legis comminationes diuinas, vniuersales, absolutas, verissimas, fieri non potest quin trepidet, nisi succurrat alia cogitatio, illis esse pro nobis à sponsore seu vade nostro satisfactum plenissimè.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Socinus goes on: "Nor, so that the consciousness of sins no longer torments human minds, must it be said that God himself, to whom satisfaction was to be made, concurred in any way in person to carry out or complete that satisfaction, in which men have placed the hope of their salvation. For it is altogether necessary that the person of the one who makes satisfaction be distinguished and separated from the person of the one to whom satisfaction is made; otherwise no one will be able to persuade himself thoroughly that a true satisfaction has been made." Socinus is gravely mistaken. The matter stands entirely the other way. For without this satisfaction we do not see how the agitation of conscience could be calmed. The thought of the justice of God presents itself to the mind and recurs: since he is the most just judge of the world, the most perfect pattern of every just judge, it cannot be understood that he would do what both conflicts with the office of a just judge and what the Holy Spirit testifies is an abomination to God, and what God himself has strictly forbidden. That is, he would acquit the wicked, the unjust and the criminal without any satisfaction to the law and to justice, not indeed through themselves (for that was altogether impossible for them) but through some surety offered on their behalf. The thought of divine truth sharpens this one. For whenever the sinner considers the divine threats of the law, universal, absolute and most true, he cannot but tremble, unless another thought comes to his aid: that by our surety or guarantor full satisfaction has been made for us to those threats.

units.la: XXXIX. Quod enim aiunt, de suo quemque iure, quantum velit, cedere posse, id de eo iure, quod in officio positum est, verum non est. Non enim potest Iudex de eo iure, quod habet violatorem legis conuictum puniendi, aut legis obsequentem remunerandi, cedere pro arbitrio. Vt enim lex violatur, cum is, cuius est mandatum legis exequi, id non exequitur, aut facit oppositum; sic etiam lex violatur, cum is, cuius est legis comminationes & promissiones executioni mandare, id non facit, sed oppositum potius. Vt enim lex mandatis obligat ad obedientiam eos qui legi subjecti sunt, sic comminationibus & promissionibus obligat ad earum executionem Iudices. Inde enim tota pendet eius autoritas & majestas. Et quemadmodum eorum qui legi subjiciuntur iustitia posita est in actionum cum mandatis legis conformitate, sic iustitia Iudicis quatenus iudex est, consistit in conformitate actionum eius cum comminationibus & promissionibus legis, ad quas, tanquam ad normam, sententiam suam & sententiae executionem exigere tenetur. alioqui & legis & legislatoris veritatem & Majestatem, quae ipsi sacrosanctae esse debebant, violat, & abolet.
units.tr: XXXIX. What they say, that each may yield of his own right as much as he wishes, is not true of that right which is bound up with duty. A judge cannot at his discretion yield the right he has to punish a convicted violator of the law, or to reward one who obeys it. Just as the law is violated when he whose duty it is to carry out the law's commands does not carry them out, or does the opposite, so too the law is violated when he whose duty it is to execute the law's threats and promises fails to do so, or does the opposite. For just as the law by its commands binds those subject to it to obedience, so by its threats and promises it binds judges to carry them out. His whole authority and majesty depend on this. And just as the justice of those subject to the law lies in the conformity of their actions with the commands of the law, so the justice of the judge, insofar as he is judge, consists in the conformity of his actions with the threats and promises of the law, to which he is bound to conform his sentence and its execution as to a rule. Otherwise he violates and abolishes the truth and majesty of the law and of the lawgiver, which ought to be sacrosanct to him.

units.la: XL. At ex altera parte, inquiet forte aliquis, securas de sua iustificatione conscientias satis reddunt promissiones diuinae. Certè, sed quando inter comminationes maledictionis & promissiones benedictionis, inter iustitiam Dei & eius misericordiam, inter officium Iudicis mundi & eius clementiam tanta pugna apparet, vt nulla ratione conciliari posse videantur, fluctuare necesse est conscientiam, & inter saxum & sacrum, vt dicitur, stare. Cuius enim comminationes inanes esse videntur, eius promissiones minus firmae & ratae esse facilè creduntur. Omnis vero dubitatio tollitur & conscientiae eiusmodi aestus sedatur, cum intelligitur legis comminationi plenissimè satisfactum fuisse ab homine fidelium vade & capite, qui mortem maledictam, quam lex omnibus peccatoribus comminabatur, pro omnibus luit & vicit. Eo enim vno pro omnibus mortuo, omnes mortui sunt. Qui autem mortuus est, hoc est, qui poenam lege denunciatam in vade & capite suo luit, is iustificatus est à peccato, nec potest amplius lege damnari. Itaque nulla est condemnatio ijs qui sunt in Iesu Christo, eo per fidem induti, in eius mortem per baptismum consepulti; cuius rei argumentum certissimum est eorum à seruitute peccati per Christi resurrectionem virtute spiritus eius viuificantis liberatio.
units.tr: XL. But, someone may perhaps object on the other side, the divine promises are enough to make consciences secure about their justification. Certainly; but when between the threats of curse and the promises of blessing, between the justice of God and his mercy, between the office of the judge of the world and his clemency, so great a conflict appears that they seem impossible to reconcile by any means, the conscience must necessarily waver and, as the saying goes, stand between the rock and the hard place. For the promises of one whose threats seem empty are readily believed to be less firm and less binding. But every doubt is removed and such agitation of conscience is calmed when it is understood that the threat of the law has been fully satisfied by the man who is the surety and head of believers, who bore and overcame for all the cursed death which the law threatened to all sinners. For with one dead for all, all have died. Now he who has died, that is, who has borne in his surety and head the penalty denounced by the law, has been justified from sin, and can no longer be condemned by the law. Therefore there is no condemnation for those who are in Jesus Christ, who through faith are clothed in him and through baptism are buried with him in his death. The most certain proof of this is their deliverance from the slavery of sin through the resurrection of Christ, by the power of his life-giving Spirit.

units.la: XLI. At fortasse dubitationem & anxietatem aliquam affert haec cogitatio, ad istam satisfactionem peragendam personam diuinam aliquid contulisse. Contrà est. Nam si ab homine tantùm homine peracta diceretur, non haberet eam infinitatem aestimationis & valoris, quam ad satisfactionem pro tot hominibus & peccatis nemo non videt fuisse necessariam. Nunc verò, cum ad infirmitatem humanam ad patiendum necessariam infinitam personae diuinae dignitatem & potentiam accessisse videamus, quid est quamobrem de perfectione, & , ut ita loquar, sufficientia illius satisfactionis amplius dubitemus?
units.tr: XLI. But perhaps the thought that the divine person contributed something to carrying out this satisfaction brings some doubt and anxiety. The contrary is true. For if it were said to have been accomplished by a mere man, it would not have that infinite worth and value of satisfaction which everyone sees was necessary to make satisfaction for so many men and sins. But now, since we see that the infinite dignity and power of the divine person has been added to human weakness, which was necessary for suffering, why should we any longer doubt the perfection and, so to speak, the sufficiency of that satisfaction?

units.la: XLII. At, inquit Socinus, necesse est omnino satisfacientis personam, ab eius, cui satisfit, distingui ac separari, alioqui veram satisfactionem factam fuisse, nemo sibi ipsi penitus persuadere poterit. Equidem sum in sententia diuersa. Quo enim satisfacientis persona ei cui satisfit conjunctior est, eo mihi facilius persuadeo, sa-tisfactionem ab eo cui satisfit non repudiatum iri. At non erit vera satisfactio. Cur? quia oportet satisfacientis personam ab eius cui satisfit distingui & separari. Hoc quis dicit? Deus? ubi? Socinus? illi non credo. modò enim id fiat quod lex exigit ab eo qui sustinet peccatoris personam, siue is sit à iudice disiunctus & separatus siue non, satisfactum est legi, & quia legi, etiam iudici. id quod satis est. Non enim agitur de solutione pecuniae, aut reparatione damni, aut priuata satisfactione, sed de ea duntaxat, qua legis comminationi & Iudicis officio satisfit. Ni-hil enim prohibet, quominus transgressor legis impunè abeat, & peccatum ei condonetur, praeter legis comminationem, quam si-ne injustitia violare iudex non potest.
units.tr: XLII. But, says Socinus, "it is altogether necessary that the person of the one who makes satisfaction be distinguished and separated from the person of the one to whom satisfaction is made; otherwise no one will be able to persuade himself thoroughly that a true satisfaction has been made." I for my part am of a different opinion. The more closely the person making satisfaction is joined to the one to whom satisfaction is made, the more easily I am persuaded that the satisfaction will not be rejected by him. But will it not be a true satisfaction? Why? Because "the person of the one making satisfaction must be distinguished and separated from the one to whom satisfaction is made." Who says this? God? Where? Socinus? I do not believe him. Provided only that what the law requires is done by one who stands in the person of the sinner, whether he is distinct and separate from the judge or not, satisfaction has been made to the law, and because to the law, also to the judge; and that is enough. For it is not a matter of payment of money, or repair of damage, or private satisfaction, but only of that by which satisfaction is made to the threat of the law and to the office of the judge. For nothing prevents a transgressor of the law from going unpunished and having his sin forgiven, apart from the threat of the law, which a judge cannot violate without injustice.

units.la: XLIII. At, inquiet, forte aliquis, Iudex est Deus, autor & Dominus legis. Tanto, inquam, minus violabit legem à se latam. Vt enim creaturas obligauit ad exequenda mandata sua, sic. se iudicem obligauit ad exequendas promissiones & comina-tiones suas: non enim illae falsae & inanes fuerunt, & vana quae-dam terricula, seu μορμωλυκεῖα[?]. Annon apud Deum Iudicem sa-crosancta esse debet Dei legislatoris veritas, autoritas, majestas, Nonne Deus fuiipsius[?] summam rationem habere debet? At potest abrogare legem quam tulit: non, opinor, naturalem illam quae sine euersione ipsius naturae aboleri non potest, quandiu naturam vult conseruatam. Sic tamen ita: at quandiu lex viget fieri non potest, quin qui eam violat in poenam lege denunciatam incurrat. Itaque non potest Iudex, nisi aliqua ratione pro eo legi satisfiat, eum absoluere. Alioqui faceret injuriam Legislatori, cuius auctoritatem vel non agnosceret, vel contemneret.
units.tr: XLIII. But, someone will perhaps say, the judge is God, the author and Lord of the law. So much the less, I reply, will he violate the law he has enacted. For just as he has bound creatures to carry out his commands, so he has bound himself as judge to carry out his promises and threats. For these were not false and empty, nor vain bugbears [μορμωλυκεῖα]. Must not the truth, authority and majesty of God the lawgiver be sacrosanct to God the judge? Ought not God to have the highest regard for himself? But he can abrogate the law he has enacted: not, I suppose, that natural law which cannot be abolished without the overthrow of nature itself, for as long as he wills nature to be preserved. Yet even so, as long as the law is in force, it cannot happen that one who violates it does not incur the penalty denounced by the law. Therefore a judge cannot acquit him unless satisfaction is made to the law in some way. Otherwise he would do injury to the Lawgiver, whose authority he would either fail to acknowledge or would despise.

units.la: XLIV. Verum, inquit Socinus, Nemo potest sibi ipsi satisfacere. Primùm satisfecit pro nobis, non eadem persona sibi, sed Filius Patri, & quidem Filius non praecisè quâ Deus, sed potius quâ homo, humani generis membrum, & caput, & vas. Sed hic homo, quia idem Deus fuit infinita dignitate & virtute praeditus, tantum pondus atroci & maledictae morti, quam perpessus est, dignitate infinita personae suae conciliauit, vt plus fuerit eum ad breue tempus pati, quam si omnes homines in aeternum passi suissent. Quod enim ad dignitatem attinet, nulla inter eum ab omnibus hominibus & Angelis adorandum & homines peccatores est proportio. Idem etiam infinitâ sua virtute mortem, ad quam traditus fuerat, deuicit, partaque de morte & diabolo victoria, acceptis mortis & inferni clauibus, resurrexit & triumphauit.
units.tr: XLIV. But, says Socinus, no one can make satisfaction to himself. First, he made satisfaction for us, not the same person to himself, but the Son to the Father; and indeed the Son not precisely as God, but rather as man, a member, head and vessel of the human race. But this man, because he was the same God endowed with infinite dignity and power, gave such weight by the infinite dignity of his person to the atrocious and cursed death which he suffered, that his suffering for a short time was more than if all men had suffered for eternity. For as regards dignity, there is no proportion between him, who is to be adored by all men and angels, and sinful men. He also, by his infinite power, overcame the death to which he had been delivered, and, the victory over death and the devil having been won, he received the keys of death and hell, rose again and triumphed.

units.la: XLV. Cavillatur[?] Socinus nos sic respondendo, quaerere diverticula. Nonne, inquit, & filij persona iuxta illorum doctrinam satisfaciendum erat, in quam non minus quam in personam Patris homi-nes peccauerant? Non intellexit Socinus, de satisfactione à nobis agi, non qua satisfit personae offensae quâ persona offensa est, sed qua satisfit comminationi legis atque adeo Iudici quâ Iudex est, siue is sit pars offensa, siue non. Potest enim pars offensa, quâ talis cedere de iure suo & offensas condonare, sed iudex legis violationem remittere, reumve conuictum absoluere, sine injustitia non potest. Quandoquidem igitur Patris & Filij personae distinctae sunt, opus non fuit alia persona quàm Patris ad sustinendam Iudicis personam, nec aliâ quàm Filij facti hominis ad sustinendam hominum reorum personam.
units.tr: XLV. Socinus carps at our answer, saying that we are "seeking out evasions." "According to their doctrine," he says, "was not the person of the Son also required to make satisfaction, since men sinned against the person of the Father no less than against the Son?" Socinus did not understand that we are speaking of a satisfaction which is made not to the person offended, as the person offended, but to the threat of the law, and so to the Judge as Judge, whether or not he is the injured party. For the injured party, as such, can give up his right and remit offences; but a judge cannot remit a violation of the law or absolve a convicted offender without injustice. Since therefore the persons of the Father and the Son are distinct, there was no need for any other person than the Father to sustain the person of the Judge, nor for any other than the Son, made man, to sustain the person of sinful men.

units.la: {Rom.} XLVI. Deinde quid est, cur hoc genere satisfactionis non possit sibi ipsi aliquis satisfacere? Nonne potest aliquis sibi ipsi lex esse, se accusare, de se iudicare, in se peccare, se condemnare, immo seipsum punire, vt ille apud Terentium ἑαυτὸν τιμωρούμενος ? Cur igitur non potest sibi ipsi satisfacere? videtur certè posse, & quidem etiam cum de reparando damno agitur; ut, exempli gratia, si quis vel negligentiâ, vel infœlici alea damno aliquo se affecerit, potest sibi multam dicere, vel ieiunium, vel parciorem & viliorem cibum, vel laborem cum alioqui se quieti daturus suisset, vel laboris conduplicationem, donec damnum sit ea ratione resarcitum & reparatum. Potest etiam aliquis ut se à praua aliqua consuetudine abstrahat, verbi gratia, iurandi, se, quoties iurasse contigerit, aliqua pecunia multare, vel in pauperes erogandâ, vel in publicos vsus. Sic sibi, ut priuatus iudici, ipse satisfacit. Quid? nonne potest contingere, ut iudex ipse reus fiat legis violatæ? Fac igitur eum alioqui ita iustum esse, ut semetipsum damnet, tunc certè ipse sibi, tanquam reus iudici, reuera satisfaciet.
units.tr: {Rom.} XLVI. Next, why can someone not make satisfaction to himself in this kind of satisfaction? Can a person not be a law to himself, accuse himself, judge himself, sin against himself, condemn himself, and even punish himself, like the man in Terence who was ἑαυτὸν τιμωρούμενος? Why then can he not satisfy himself? Surely he can, and that even when a loss is to be repaired. For example, if someone has brought some loss on himself through carelessness or unlucky chance, he can impose on himself a fine, or fasting, or a plainer and cheaper diet, or labour in place of the rest he would otherwise have taken, or doubled labour, until the loss is made good and repaired in this way. A person can also, to break himself of some bad habit, such as swearing, fine himself some sum of money whenever he happens to swear, to be given to the poor or spent on public uses. So he satisfies himself, as a private judge. And what? Can it not happen that the judge himself becomes guilty of violating the law? Suppose, then, that he is otherwise so just that he condemns himself; then, as judge and as offender at once, he will truly satisfy himself.

units.la: Nemo, inquit Socinus, sibi ipsi aliquid soluit. Esto: non enim agitur hoc loco de pecunia soluenda, sed de poena luenda. Quid est autem cur non possit aliquis ut legis comminationi & iudicis officio satisfaciat, sibi ipsi poenam lege denunciatam vel per se vel per alios infligere, aut vltrò sese verberandum vel interficiendum hostibus tradere? Cum Attilius Regulus Carthaginem rediit, & ad exquisita supplicia vltrò profectus est, is fidei suæ, iurijurando suo, sibique adeo ipsi profecto satisfecit. Sed nimium forte immoror in refutanda ratione, aut potius affirmatione Socini, quam ille neque probauit, neque probare conatus est, ac propterea æquè simpliciter à nobis negari, ac ab illo affirmari, potuit.
units.tr: "No one," says Socinus, "pays anything to himself." Granted: for we are not speaking here of paying money but of bearing punishment. Why, however, should someone not be able to satisfy the threat of the law and the office of the judge by inflicting on himself, either personally or through others, the punishment the law has declared, or by voluntarily handing himself over to be beaten or killed by enemies? When Attilius Regulus returned to Carthage and of his own accord went to meet the exquisite tortures, he satisfied his faith, his oath, and indeed himself. But perhaps I dwell too long on refuting the argument, or rather the assertion, of Socinus, which he neither proved nor attempted to prove; and so it could be denied by us as simply as it was affirmed by him.

units.la: XLVII. Sed, inquit Socinus, dum Iesu Christi personam adeo sublimem atque excelsam effingere studeret, ut sui sanguinis fusione tantum ex alienum omnium nostrum nomine dissoluere potuerit, non animaduerterit, se illum, qui debitor potius quàm creditor esse potuisset (potest enim debitor, si soluendo sit, & pro se & pro aliis satisfacere) ipsummet creditorem facere, qui ex persona sua nonnisi gratuita condonatione debitores liberare potest, gratuitam inquam; quòd non solum ab ijsdemmet debitoribus nihil repetat, verum etiam quòd neminem pro illis quidquam sibi soluere velit. Nam si alium sibi solutionem facere vel postulet, vel patiatur, non quidem ex persona sua, sed ex aliena eos liberabit. Varia continentur in hac accusatione[?] seu reprehensione, quibus ordine respondendum est. Primum illud est, quod ait, nos Christum facere ipsummet creditorem. At si Christus teste auctore Ep. ad Heb. est mediator Noui Testamenti, Heb. 8. 6. & 9. 15. & 12. 24. & vas Heb. 7. 22. & testator Heb. 9. 16. Quid est cur non possit diuerso respectu & vas debitorum & creditor esse? Ipse certè non obscurè innuit se creditorem esse Luc. 7. V. 41.[?] & seqq. Matth. 25. 14. &c. Nec mirum: nam si eius sunt quaecunque sunt Patris, etiam quae Patri debentur, ei debentur. Adde quod qui soluit pro alio, is creditoris ius in debitorem sibi acquirit. Itaque Christus etiam dum ageret in terris pro sua auctoritate peccata remisit. id quod vnius Dei proprium esse cum Scribae & Pharisaei credebant, tum ipse Dominus non negauit, tantùm affirmauit & probauit se ea autoritate praeditum esse. Luc. 5 V. 20.[?] & seqq.
units.tr: XLVII. "But," says Socinus, "while he strove to portray the person of Jesus Christ as so sublime and exalted that by the shedding of his own blood he could pay the debt of all of us, he did not notice that he makes him the creditor himself, rather than the debtor, which he could have been (for a debtor, if he is able to pay, can make satisfaction both for himself and for others). For the one who acts from his own person can free debtors only by gratuitous remission, I say gratuitous, because he not only demands nothing from the very debtors themselves but also wishes that no one pay anything to him on their behalf. For if he either asks or allows another to make payment to him, he will free them not from his own person but from another's." Several points are contained in this accusation, or rebuke, and they must be answered in order. The first is what he says, that we make Christ the creditor himself. But if Christ, as the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews attests, is the mediator of the New Testament (Heb. 8. 6; 9. 15; 12. 24), and the surety (Heb. 7. 22), and the testator (Heb. 9. 16), why can he not be, in different respects, both the surety of debtors and the creditor? He himself clearly hints that he is a creditor (Luke 7. 41 ff.; Matt. 25. 14 etc.). Nor is this surprising: for if all that the Father has is his, then what is owed to the Father is owed to him too. Add that one who pays on behalf of another acquires for himself the right of a creditor against the debtor. Thus Christ, while on earth, also forgave sins by his own authority, which the scribes and Pharisees believed to belong to God alone, and the Lord himself did not deny it, but only affirmed and proved that he possessed that authority (Luke 5. 20 ff.).

units.la: XLVIII. Alterum est,quod Socinus pro confesso ponere videtur, inter peccata & debita nihil interesse, cum tamen plurimum interfit. Possunt enim peccata referri vel ad partem offensam praecisè consideratam, vel ad legis comminationem & iudicem. Respectu partis offensae praecisè consideratae eandem fere rationem habent quam debita respectu creditoris, sed ad istam veluti priuatam relationem accedit publica, quatenus sunt legis violationes, cuius veritas & majestas tam comminationes quam promissiones exequendo iudex tueri debet, etiamsi pars offensa, quatenus eius, quâ talis, interest, offensam condonauerit. Dispar est ratio debitorum propriè dictorum: cum enim violationes legis non sint, non prohibet legis comminatio, quominus remittantur debitoribus absque vlla satisfactione.
units.tr: XLVIII. The second point is that Socinus seems to take for granted that there is no difference between sins and debts, though there is a great difference. For sins can be regarded either in relation to the injured party considered strictly as such, or in relation to the threat of the law and the judge. In relation to the injured party considered strictly as such, they have almost the same character as debts in relation to a creditor; but to this private relation there is added a public one, insofar as they are violations of the law, whose truth and majesty the judge must uphold in executing both its threats and its promises, even if the injured party, insofar as it is his own interest, has remitted the offence. The case of debts properly so called is different: since they are not violations of the law, the threat of the law does not prevent their being forgiven to debtors without any satisfaction.

units.la: XLIX. Tertium quod Socinus affirmat est, creditorem, si alium sibi solutionem facere vel postulet, vel patiatur, non quidem ex persona sua, sed ex alienâ debitores liberaturum. Id quod verum est si duo ponas: vnum agi de creditore & debitis proprie dictis: alterum, alium istum qui solutionem facit totâ essentia disjunctum esse à creditore. Nos autem hoc loco de peccatis agimus, vt jam monui, non relatè ad partem offensam praecisè spectatam, quo respectu debitis similia sunt; sed relatè ad comminationem legis & officium Iudicis, quo respectu à debitis differunt. Deinde is qui satisfecit legis comminationi pro nobis & Dei filius est & Deus, idque fecit Patre mittente iubente & vehementissimè probante. Itaque quod nobis remittuntur peccata in nomine Filij 1. Cor. 6. 11. per nomen Filij Act. 10. 43. propter nomen Filij 1. Ioh. 2. 12. 2.12. charitati & gloriæ Patris nullo modo officit. Tantum autem abest vt hæc satisfactio misericordiam Dei obscuret, aut remissionem peccatorum efficiat minus gratuitam, vt immensum in modum eam commendet. Cum enim Deus duas veluti personas in hoc negotio sustineret, vnam partis offensæ, alteram Iudicis, is, quatenus pars est offensa, odium, iram, cupiditatem vindictæ omnino deposuit, versaque in misericordiam irâ, quoniam quominus peccatores resipiscentes iustificarentur impediebat legis comminatio & officium Iudicis, quod posita lege necessarium est, constituit hoc impedimentum tollere. quod, cum aliter fieri non posset quàm transferendo pœnam lege denunciatam in Filium suum vnigenitum, tanquam in hominum peccatorum vadem, id potius elegit quàm homines peccatores punire. Potuitne major animo concipi clementia & misericordia erga homines? Itaque in ea prædicanda & celebranda vix sibi satisfaciunt sacri auctores. Magnum est partem offensam non odisse eum à quo offensa sit grauissimè, Maius est illum amare, illius misereri, Maximum magnis beneficijs illum afficere, sed multo adhuc majus est, vt à morte maledicta redimatur, cum aliter legi satisfieri non possit, filium vnigenitum & dilectissimum, vel etiam semetipsum, ad mortem, & quidem talem, tradere. Hic summus est amoris & misericordiæ partis offensæ erga eos à quibus offensa est gradus, omnem humanum longè superans. Ita cum summa iudicis iustitia summa partis offensæ misericordia erga genus humanum conciliata est mirabiliter & facta est Dei iustitia misericors erga credentes & misericordia iusta. Nam alioqui misericordia, quæ legis comminationem & officium iudicis evertit, in vitio ponitur, & ab ipso Deo damnatur Deut. 13. 8. & 19. 13. 21. & 25. 12.
units.tr: XLIX. The third point which Socinus affirms is that a creditor, if he either asks or allows another to make payment to him, will free the debtors not from his own person but from another's. This is true if you assume two things: first, that we are speaking of a creditor and of debts properly so called; second, that this other person who makes the payment is wholly distinct in essence from the creditor. But we are not speaking here of debts, as I have already said, but of sins; and we consider them not in relation to the injured party strictly regarded, in which respect they are like debts, but in relation to the threat of the law and the office of the Judge, in respect of which they differ from debts. Furthermore, he who satisfied the threat of the law on our behalf is the Son of God and God, and he did so with the Father sending, commanding and most strongly approving. Therefore the fact that our sins are remitted in the name of the Son (1 Cor. 6. 11), through the name of the Son (Acts 10. 43), for the sake of the name of the Son (1 John 2. 12) in no way detracts from the charity and glory of the Father. Indeed, this satisfaction is so far from obscuring the mercy of God, or making the remission of sins less gratuitous, that it commends it immeasurably. For since God in this matter sustained, as it were, two persons, one of the injured party and one of the Judge, he, insofar as he is the injured party, laid aside altogether hatred, anger and the desire for vengeance, and, turning his anger into mercy, resolved to remove the obstacle which the threat of the law and the office of the Judge, which given the law is necessary, placed in the way of the justification of penitent sinners. Since this could not be done otherwise than by transferring the penalty declared by the law onto his only-begotten Son, as surety for sinful men, he chose this rather than punishing sinful men. Can a greater clemency and mercy toward men be conceived? Therefore in proclaiming and celebrating it the sacred authors can scarcely satisfy themselves. It is a great thing for the injured party not to hate the one by whom he has been most grievously offended; it is greater to love him and have compassion on him; greatest of all is to bestow great benefits upon him; but it is far greater still, when the law cannot otherwise be satisfied, that he should hand over, to death, and that a cursed death, his only-begotten and most beloved Son, or even himself, so that the offenders may be redeemed from the accursed death. This is the highest degree of the love and mercy of the injured party toward those by whom he was offended, far surpassing all human measure. Thus, with the highest justice of the Judge joined to the highest mercy of the injured party toward mankind, the justice of God has been wonderfully reconciled and has become a merciful justice toward believers, and a just mercy. For otherwise mercy, which overturns the threat of the law and the office of the judge, is counted a vice, and is condemned by God himself (Deut. 13. 8; 19. 13, 21; 25. 12).

units.la: L. Sic reprehensis nobis Socinus deinceps consulit. Itaque, inquit, præstabat à veritate non omnino discedentes, Iesum Christum non ipsummet vnicum Deum nostrum opinari, sed diuinissimum hominem agnoscere, tanta dignitate pollentem, vt tantum onus subire merito potuisset. neque enim vt ea, quæ humanæ naturæ deerant, supplerentur, si modo, quod ad propositum attinet, supplerí poterant, necesse erat Deum hominem fieri, sed satis fuisset, diuina potentia atque virtute, cui omnia sunt in manu, & cui nihil difficile est, eam penitus perpurgari, ac numeris omnibus absolutam reddi, eique infinitam vim, cuius participes omnes eius operationes forent, communicari. atque eo casu, quemadmodum si quis ab alio ita ditatus fuerit, ut ea, quorum illius benignitate plenam possessionem & dominium habet, summam illi à ceteris quibuscunque debitam, aestimatione vel aquent[?], vel etiam superent, possetis[?] profecto, si vellet, cunctorum debitorum nomine de suo eidem illi vere ac plenè satisfacere, sic etiam homo Christus Iesus, ipsimet Deo, à quo hanc facultatem dono accepisset, quicquid ei caeteri homines debent, persoluere potuisset, id quod nequaquam fieri potuit, si Deus facultatem hanc Christo homini plenè largitus non est, sed eam, vel eius saltem partem aliquam solus ita retinuit, ut ad solutionem perficiendam ipsius persona omnino opus fuisse dicamus, cum nullus creditor de pecunia sua, quam nemini donauit, sibi ipsi debitorum nomine satisfacere aliqua ratione queat.
units.tr: L. Having thus reproved us, Socinus next gives his advice. Accordingly, he says, it were better, without wholly departing from the truth, not to hold Jesus Christ to be the one God himself, but to acknowledge him as a most divine man, endowed with such great dignity that he could rightly undertake so great a burden. For it was not necessary, in order that those things which were lacking in human nature might be supplied (if indeed, as far as our purpose is concerned, they could be supplied), that God should become man; but it would have been enough that by the divine power and virtue, in whose hand are all things and to whom nothing is difficult, he should be thoroughly purified, made perfect in all respects, and furnished with infinite power, of which all his operations would partake. And in that case, just as if someone had been so enriched by another that he had full possession and lordship over those things by the other's kindness, and could, by their value, equal or even exceed the whole debt owed to someone else, you would surely, if he wished, be able to satisfy truly and fully, in the name of all debtors, from his own resources, that same person; so also the man Christ Jesus, having received this power as a gift from God himself, could have paid whatever other men owe. This could by no means have been done if God had not fully granted this power to Christ the man, but had himself retained it, or at least some part of it, in such a way that we must say the person himself was entirely needed to complete the payment, since no creditor can in any way satisfy a debt in his own name with money of his own which he has given to no one.

units.la: LI. Hoc consilium Socino dignum est, hoc est, eo qui non satis quid dicat attendit. Nam praeterquam quod ita perpetuò loquitur, ac si de reparatione damni & solutione pecuniae ageretur, (id quod est peccare ignorantiâ elenchi) quid per vim infinitam intelligit, cum vult natura humanae infinitam vim, cuius participes omnes eius operationes forent, communicari? Intelligitne illam ipsam vim infinitam eandem numero, quae in Deo est, an diuersam, creatam scilicet? Si prius eligitur, Primùm quomodo potest ipsa vis infinita Dei eadem numero communicari naturae humanae non communicatâ essentiâ diuinâ, à qua vis illa, si quid intelligo, nihil differt, & quidem ita communicari, vt illius plenam possessionem ac dominium habeat? Deinde qui potest ipsa Dei vis infinita, quae in ipso est & quam retinet, ad aliquid necessaria esse & concurrere, ad quod ipsa Dei persona necessaria non sit, nec concurrat? Hoc enim est vim naturae diuinae essentialem à natura diuina, potentiam naturalem personae à persona separare. id quod, nisi vehementer fallor, contradictionem implicat. Si posterius placet, Primùm ponetur vis infinita creata. id quod mihi videtur prorsus impossibile. Deinde cur non aequè multiplicari poterit natura infinita ac vis infinita? poterunt igitur esse plures naturae diuinae, plures dij; si duo, cur non tres, quatuor, quinque, & ita in infinitum. Tum, si potest creari & multiplicari vis infinita, ea vtique abstrahi potest ab existentia, & conuenit cum vi, quae Deo inest, specie, differt numero. Ex quo sequitur vim infinitam essentialiter siue à se ipsa non existere, nec implicari: contradictionem si Deus negetur esse. quo posito sequitur, Deum non esse.
units.tr: LI. This plan is worthy of Socinus, that is, of one who does not pay enough attention to what he is saying. For, apart from the fact that he speaks throughout as though the matter concerned making good a loss and paying money (which is to commit the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi), what does he mean by infinite power, when he wants infinite power of the human nature, of which all its operations would partake, to be communicated? Does he mean that same infinite power, numerically the same as that which is in God, or a different one, namely created? If the former is chosen: first, how can the very infinite power of God, numerically the same, be communicated to human nature without the communication of the divine essence, from which that power, so far as I understand, does not differ at all, and communicated in such a way that human nature has full possession and lordship over it? Next, how can the very infinite power of God, which is in him and which he retains, be necessary for, and concur in, something for which the person of God himself is not necessary and does not concur? For this is to separate the essential power of the divine nature from the divine nature, and the natural power of the person from the person; which, unless I am greatly mistaken, implies a contradiction. If the latter is preferred: first, there will be posited a created infinite power, which seems to me utterly impossible. Next, why could the infinite nature not be multiplied equally with infinite power? There could then be several divine natures, several gods; if two, why not three, four, five, and so on to infinity? Then, if infinite power can be created and multiplied, it can certainly be abstracted from existence, and while agreeing in species with the power which is in God, it differs in number. From this it follows that infinite power does not exist essentially or of itself, nor is it implied, which is a contradiction if God is denied to exist. Once this is granted, it follows that God does not exist.

units.la: LII. Praeterea est ne vis illa infinita substantia, an accidens? Si est substantia, duae erunt in Christo substantiae, una infinita, altera finita. id quod negant Aduersarij. porro substantia infinita necessario[?] est intelligens & completa, ac propterea persona. vis enim infinita non est, quae intelligere, quae velle, quae per se existere non potest. Si est accidens, primum non est infinita: potest enim vis infinita creare substantias finitas, & quidem in instanti. itaque neque ipsa, neque eius actio subjecto, cui inhaereat, indiget. Quod si ita imbecilla fit, ut ipsa per se existere seseque conseruare, & veluti sustentare non possit, quomodo vis infinita esse dicitur? vis infinita est ens infinitum, omnem entis per-fectionem in se formaliter vel eminenter continens, nullaque est actio sive substantialis, sive accidentalis, finita, quam producere non possit: alioqui vis infinita non est, sed finita & limitata. Adde intelligi non posse, quomodo vis infinita communicari possit & inhaerere subjecto finito, cum quo nullam habet proportionem. ut enim mare vniuersum contineri non potest in exiguo vasculo, sic vis infinitae capax non est subjectum finitum. Proportionem enim aliquam esse oportet inter capacitatem subjecti & id quod subjectum recipit, quodque illi inhaeret. Personam quidem infi-nitam vnire sibi potuisse humanam naturam finitam pro mea tenuitate vtcunq; intelligere mihi videor. vim vero infinitam com-municari potuisse naturae humanae finitae tanquam subjecto cui in-haereat, equidem intelligere non possum. Non capio etiam quomodo in eodem subjecto & parte subjecti simul esse potuerit vis finita & infinita, vis limitata & vis illimitata. Nos quidem fatemur, eandem personam, eodem tempore, vim habere infinitam & finitam, infinitam secundum naturam diuinam, finitam secundum naturam humanam. Sed eandem personam, eodem tempore, & secundum eandem naturam, immo naturae partem, vim habere finitam & infinitam, adeoque finitam & infinitam esse, id nobis apparet impossibile. Haec veluti obiter & cursim attingo, ut, vel ex hoc exiguo specimine, intelligant Aduersarij minus secum, quam putant, rectam concordare rationem.
units.tr: LII. Moreover, is that infinite power a substance or an accident? If it is a substance, there will be two substances in Christ, one infinite, the other finite; which the opponents deny. Further, an infinite substance is necessarily intelligent and complete, and therefore a person; for that which cannot understand, cannot will, and cannot exist of itself, is not infinite power. If it is an accident, then first it is not infinite: for infinite power can create finite substances, and indeed in an instant; and so it needs neither itself nor its action a subject in which to inhere. But if it is so feeble that it cannot exist of itself, preserve itself, and as it were sustain itself, how is it said to be infinite power? Infinite power is an infinite being, containing in itself formally or eminently every perfection of being, and there is no action, whether substantial or accidental, finite, which it cannot produce; otherwise it is not infinite power, but finite and limited. Add that it cannot be understood how infinite power can be communicated to, and inhere in, a finite subject, with which it has no proportion. For just as the whole sea cannot be contained in a tiny vessel, so a finite subject is not capable of infinite power. For there must be some proportion between the capacity of the subject and that which the subject receives and which inheres in it. Indeed, I seem to myself, in my slender way, to understand in some measure how an infinite person could unite to himself a finite human nature. But that infinite power could be communicated to a finite human nature as to a subject in which it inheres, I truly cannot understand. Nor do I grasp how finite and infinite power, limited power and unlimited power, could have been together at once in the same subject and the same part of the subject. We indeed confess that the same person, at the same time, has power both infinite and finite: infinite according to the divine nature, finite according to the human nature. But that the same person, at the same time, and according to the same nature, or indeed part of the nature, has finite and infinite power, and so is both finite and infinite, this appears to us impossible. I touch on these points as it were in passing and cursorily, so that, even from this small specimen, the opponents may understand that their reasoning agrees less well with right reason than they think.

units.la: LIII. Nam, vt aliquid etiam de munere Christi Regio dicam, quomodo, quaeso, id absque vi infinita exerceri potest? Primùm Judici & Regi nostro vincendi fuerunt omnes hostes nostri, mun-dus, peccatum, mors, diabolus; quam ad rem quanta vi opus fuerit nemo non videt. deinde opus ei fuit ut intelligendi plane infinita. Quid enim est in cœlo & in terra, quod eius oculis non pateat, qui scrutatur corda & renes? Tum opus etiam ei fuit vi agendi prorsus infinita, qua omnia sibi subjicere, omnes mortuos ad vitam revocare, miracula quaelibet patrare, fideles ubique terrarum regere, & protegere, ijs omni loco & tempore adesse, opem ferre &c, denique omnia quaecunque vult in cœlo & in terra facere possit. Quae enim est vis infinita, si haec non est? Quid potest Pater, quod Filius non possit? Quid facit Pater, quod Filius non faciat similiter? Est ne aliquod opus tantum, ut fieri à Filio non possit? Accedit ad haec auctoritas & majestas infinita, & cultus consentaneus. Oportuit igitur Regem nostrum esse infinitum. Quomodo autem infinitus est, si natura non est praeditus nisi finita? aut quomodo potuit natura eius finita fieri infinita, absque eius mutatione & conversione in aliam naturam? Est enim natura illa sine dubio infinita, quae praedita est infinita vi intelligendi, volendi, agendi. Natura autem infinita plusquàm genere differt à finita. Quod si ponatur ita infinita evasisse ut permansérit finita, illa eodem tempore, & secundum eandem partem, multo major erit Te ipsâ, immò ad semetipsam nullam habebit proportionem. quae si concoquunt Adversarij, cur reji-ciunt unionem personae infinitae cum natura humana finita, multò magis & Scripturae & rationi consentientem? Satis ex his, opinor, liquet, naturae divinae & humanae in Christo conjunctionem non esse supervacaneam. Nonnihil addit Socinus de Mediatore, quod reprehensionem quidem meretur, sed hoc loco minimè ne-cessariam.
units.tr: LIII. For, to say something also about Christ's kingly office, how, I ask, can it be exercised without infinite power? First, our Judge and King had to overcome all our enemies: the world, sin, death, the devil; and no one fails to see how much power was needed for this. Next, he needed a plainly infinite understanding. For what is there in heaven and on earth that is not open to the eyes of him who searches hearts and reins? Then he also needed a power of acting that was utterly infinite, by which he could subject all things to himself, call all the dead back to life, work any miracles, rule and protect the faithful throughout the earth, be present with them in every place and time, bring them help, and so forth; in short, be able to do whatever he wills in heaven and on earth. For what is infinite power, if this is not? What can the Father do that the Son cannot? What does the Father do that the Son does not likewise do? Is there any work so great that it cannot be done by the Son? To these is added infinite authority and majesty, and the worship that accords with them. It was therefore fitting that our King should be infinite. But how is he infinite if he is endowed with a finite nature only? Or how could his finite nature become infinite without its change and conversion into another nature? For that nature is without doubt infinite which is endowed with infinite power of understanding, willing and acting. An infinite nature, however, differs from a finite one by more than kind. But if it is supposed that he became so infinite that he remained finite, then at the same time and in the same part he would be far greater than himself, and would have no proportion to himself. If the opponents can digest this, why do they reject the union of an infinite person with a finite human nature, a thing far more in agreement both with Scripture and with reason? From these points, I think, it is sufficiently clear that the conjunction of the divine and human natures in Christ is not superfluous. Socinus adds something about the Mediator, which deserves reproof, but is by no means necessary at this point.

units.la: Ad Arg. XXXVII. Ex Gen. Cap. I. ῾vs. 26. & similibus locis petitum.
units.tr: On Argument XXXVII, taken from Genesis chapter 1, verse 26, and similar passages

units.la: I. [large woodcut initial]N posteriore Fragmento Socinus respondere conatur ad argumentum ex Gen. 1. 26. & 3. 22. & locis consimilibus petitum, quod est in hoc libro xxxvii. Orditur autem à responsione, quam, quia apud eum, aliosue eius sequaces nondum legere contigerat, non refutaui. Certè à Vvolkelio & Schlichtingio prætermissa est ob nimiam eius, vt ego arbitror, infirmitatem. Ea est, non minùs ex locis illis concludi posse, Dei personam vnam numero esse, essentias verò plures, quàm vnam numero essentiam, plures verò personas. Id quod mihi videtur ab eo dictum, vt alia multa, valdè inconsideratè. Nam si verba Scripturæ spectes, seu ducatur argumentum à nominibus pluralis numeri, quale est Elohim, nomina illa, cum sint, vt loquuntur scholastici, concreta, subjecta seu supposita significant, non præcisè naturas. Seu ducatur à verbis pluralis numeri, Faciamus, descendamus, inerunt dij &c, cum actiones non sint naturarum sed suppositorum seu personarum, pluralitas personarum ijs significatur, non verò naturarum. Significatur enim pluralitas eorum, quorum sunt illæ actiones. Seu ducatur à pronominibus pluralis numeri, in imagine nostra, secundum similitudinem nostram, quis nescit, pronomina personas significare, non autem præcisè naturas? loqui personas, non autem præcisè naturas? Seu denique ducatur ab illis verbis, Ecce Adam factus est sicut vnus ex nobis, mente captum esse oporteat, qui non intelligat vocibus vnus ex nobis plures personas significari. Vertant se in quascunque voluerint partes Aduersarij, non aliam pluralitatem ex verbis illis elicient, quàm personarum.
units.tr: [large woodcut initial]In the later fragment Socinus tries to answer the argument from Genesis 1:26, Genesis 3:22 and similar passages, which is set out in this book as argument XXXVII. He begins with a reply which I had not refuted, because it had not yet been my chance to read it in his work or in the works of his other followers. Volkelius and Schlichting certainly passed it over, I think because it is so weak. It runs: these passages allow us to conclude no less that the person of God is one in number, but the essences are more than one in number, than that the essence is one in number and the persons are more than one. This seems to me to be said very carelessly, as is much else. For if you look at the words of Scripture, whether the argument is drawn from nouns of the plural number, such as Elohim, those nouns, since they are, as the scholastics say, concrete terms, signify subjects or supposits, not nature strictly speaking. Or if it is drawn from plural verbs, let us make, let us go down, there will be gods, and so on, since these actions belong not to natures but to supposits or persons, the plurality they signify is a plurality of persons, not of natures. For they signify the plurality of those to whom the actions belong. Or if it is drawn from plural pronouns, in our image, according to our likeness, who does not know that pronouns signify persons, and not strictly natures, and speak of persons, not strictly of natures? Finally, if it is drawn from those words, Behold, Adam has become as one of us, a man would have to be out of his mind who did not understand that the words one of us signify several persons. Let the opponents turn themselves to whatever parts they like: they will extract from those words no plurality other than a plurality of persons.

units.la: I.I. Itaque inepta est ratio quam Socinus subjungit, Neque enim, inquit, minus absurdum est, vbi vna numero essentia est, pluresperfonas, quàm vbi vna numero est persona, plures essentias constituere. Nos enim argumentamur, non à reipsa in se spectata, sed à verbis Scripturæ, quæ si pluralitatem aliquam significant (significant autem certè) personarum vtique pluralitatem significant. Si igitur quod ad rem ipsam, aut ad rationem attinet, nihil interest, vtrum plures sint personæ vna essentia, an plures essentiæ vna persona, prius potius, cum sit verbis Scripturæ consentaneum, eligi debet, quàm posterius, quod ab illis abhorret.
units.tr: I.I. So the reasoning that Socinus adds is pointless: For, he says, it is no less absurd, where there is one essence in number, to posit more than one person, than where there is one person in number, to posit more than one essence. We do not argue from the thing itself considered in itself, but from the words of Scripture, which, if they signify any plurality (and they certainly do signify one), signify at least a plurality of persons. If therefore, so far as the thing itself or the reasoning is concerned, it makes no difference whether there are several persons in one essence or several essences in one person, the former ought to be chosen rather than the latter, since it agrees with the words of Scripture, while the latter is repugnant to them.

units.la: III. Cæterum absolutè loquendo neutrum putamus esse impossibile: nam & tres personas diuinas concicemur eadem essentia seu natura diuina prædiitas, & vnam personam duabus prædicatam naturis, diuina scilicet & humana; sed tamen facilius pluralitatem personarum diuinarum cum vnitate essentiæ diuinæ concilihamus, quàm pluralitatem naturarum diuinarum cum vnitate personæ diuinæ. Subjicit quidem Socinus, à se in superiore libro probatum fuisse, fieri non posse, vt in vna numero essentia plures distincta suis proprietatibus persona inueniantur. Sed h per superiorem librum superius fragmentum intelligit, quod cum isto in vnum volumen compingi solet, in eo probatio illa tota desideratur. Sin alium aliquem librum, is ad meas manus nondum peruenit. Id quidem probare conatus est Crellius lib. II. de vno Deo Patre, Sect. 1. corrasis vndecunq; potuit aliquot argumentis, Sed ea, cum nihil ferè nisi sophismata sint, nec difficile est soluere, & soluentur à nobis, Deo dante, in alio libro. Decet enim nos prius Deum in Scripturis loquentem consulere, quàm rationem humanam, quæ Deo subjici debet, non autem opponi, & , si credimus Aristoteli, se habetad ea quæ sunt natura omnium manifestissima, sicut oculi vespertilionum ad lumen diurnum.
units.tr: III. Moreover, speaking absolutely, we think that neither is impossible: for we may conceive of three divine persons endowed with the same essence or divine nature, and of one person endowed with two natures, divine and human. Yet we reconcile the plurality of divine persons with the unity of the divine essence more easily than the plurality of divine natures with the unity of the divine person. Socinus indeed adds that he had proved in his earlier book that it cannot be that in one essence, one in number, several persons distinct in their own properties are found. But by the earlier book he means the earlier fragment, which is usually bound into one volume with this one, and in it that proof is entirely lacking. If he means some other book, it has not yet come into my hands. Crellius did attempt to prove this, in book II of On the One God the Father, section 1, where he gathered together some arguments from wherever he could. But since these are almost nothing but sophisms, they are not hard to solve, and by God's help we will solve them in another book. For we ought first to consult God speaking in Scripture, rather than human reason, which ought to be subjected to God and not set against him; and, if we believe Aristotle, it stands in relation to those things which are most manifest in nature as the eyes of bats to the light of day.

units.la: IV. Necesse est vt credamus, aut vnam personam diuinam & plures naturas, aut vnam personam & vnam naturam, aut plures personas & plures naturas, aut plures personas & vnam naturam. Quominus primum credamus obstant Primò omnia illa argumenta, quibus plures esse personas diuinas euincimus.
