Deinde illa omnia, quibus pluralitas naturarum seu essentiarum diuinarum refelli potest. denique illa etiam omnia, quibus probari potest, Deum proprie loquendo non esse compositum, & plures essentias completas naturaliter constituere plures personas.
units.tr: IV. We must believe either one divine person and several natures, or one person and one nature, or several persons and several natures, or several persons and one nature. The first we cannot believe, because of the following: (1) all those arguments by which we prove that there are several divine persons; (2) all those by which the plurality of natures or divine essences can be refuted; (3) finally, all those by which it can be shown that God, properly speaking, is not composite, and that several complete essences naturally constituted yield several persons.

units.la: lib. II. metaph. cap. I.
units.tr: Metaphysics, book II, chapter 1.

units.la: V. Quominus secundum amplectamur impediunt omnia illa testimonia & argumenta, quæ pluralitatem seu trinitatem personarum diuinarum demonstrant. Possunt autem illa reuocari ad tres classes. Prima locos Scripturæ continet, in quibus de Deo, tanquam de pluribus personis, loquitur, tribuens ei nomina, pronomina, epitheta, verba, pluralis numeri. Secunda classis continet illa Scripturæ testimonia & argumenta, quibus probamus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum esse diuina natura præditum. Cum enim constet Patrem & Filium esse duas personas, & Patrem esse Deum, hoc ipso quod probamus Filium esse Deum diuina essentia præditum, probamus etiam duas esse personas diuinas. Huiusmodi autem testimoniis & argumentis scatet & micat tota Scriptura, vt partim ex hoc & superiore libro jam patet, partim ex sequenti aut sequentibus fiet manifestum. Tertia continet ea Scripturæ loca & argumenta, quibus probamus, Spiritum Sanctum esse personam à Patre & Filio distinctam, eundemque diuina præditum esse natura.
units.tr: V. As for the second, we embrace it, while all those testimonies and arguments hinder us which demonstrate the plurality, or trinity, of the divine persons. These can be reduced to three classes. The first contains passages of Scripture in which God is spoken of as of several persons, attributing to him nouns, pronouns, epithets and verbs of the plural number. The second class contains those testimonies and arguments of Scripture by which we prove that our Lord Jesus Christ is endowed with the divine nature. For since it is agreed that the Father and the Son are two persons, and that the Father is God, by the very fact that we prove the Son to be God endowed with the divine essence, we also prove that there are two divine persons. Now the whole of Scripture abounds and shines with testimonies and arguments of this kind, as is partly clear already from this book and the earlier one, and partly will become plain from the following book or books. The third contains those passages of Scripture and arguments by which we prove that the Holy Spirit is a person distinct from the Father and the Son, and that he too is endowed with the divine nature.

units.la: VI. Quominus tertium admittamus, obstant illa argumenta, quibus vnitas naturæ seu essentiæ diuinæ demonstrari potest. Petuntur autem illa partim è Scriptura, partim è Philosophia. Nam, & Scriptura vnitatem Dei multis locis inculcat, & Philosophia eam necessariis argumentis demonstrat, & nihil est, vel in Scriptura, vel in Philosophia, quod ei possit opponi, præter pluralitatem personarum diuinarum, quæ videtur cum vnitate essentiæ diuinæ consistere non posse. Sed cum, & constet inter nos, & multis ijsque necessariis argumentis demonstrari possit, Scripturam esse diuinitus inspiratam, eaque plurimis locis & pluralitatem personarum diuinarum & vnitatem diuinæ naturæ doceat & inculcet, omnino fatendum est, pluralitatem illam vnitatem istam nequaquam euertere. Non enim sibi Deus contradicit vnquam, nedum tam sæpè. Ex quo sequitur, omnia illa argumenta, quibus pluralitatem personarum diuinarum repugnare vnitati naturæ diuinæ probare student Aduersarij, falsa esse, nec nisi suâ ipsorum culpâ, illis vera videri posse.
units.tr: VI. As for the third, we admit it, while those arguments hinder us by which the unity of the divine nature or essence can be demonstrated. These are sought partly from Scripture, partly from philosophy. For Scripture inculcates the unity of God in many places, and philosophy demonstrates it by necessary arguments, and there is nothing, either in Scripture or in philosophy, that can be set against it except the plurality of divine persons, which seems unable to stand together with the unity of the divine essence. But since it is agreed among us, and can be demonstrated by many and necessary arguments, that Scripture is divinely inspired, and since Scripture in very many places both teaches and inculcates the plurality of divine persons and the unity of the divine nature, we must altogether confess that that plurality by no means overthrows that unity. For God never contradicts himself, much less so often. From this it follows that all those arguments by which the opponents strive to prove that the plurality of divine persons is incompatible with the unity of the divine nature are false, and that they can seem true only through their own fault.

units.la: VII. At vero, inquit Socinus, cum non persona essentiæ tantum ratione res aliqua una esse dici possit, si omnino statuere velimus pluralitatem personarum in Deo, quid prohibet, quominus, cum sacræ literæ Deum unum esse dicunt, id non ad essentiam, sed ad voluntatem pertinere existimemus, ita vt non vnam numero in Deo efsentiam, sed vnicam voluntatem, id est, in illis pluribus diuinis personis, summham indissolubilemque consensionem atque concordiam, esse agnoscamus? Absurdum quidem esse statuimus pluralitatem diuinarum essentiarum inducere, at impossibile plane est, vbi plures sint personæ, ibi vnam numero essentiam esse. Prohibent primò sacræ illæ literæ, quæ Deum vnum esse dicunt. Nam, vt cætera nunc omittam, quis mentis compos, cum legit illa verba, non est Deus nisi vnus, vel, Ego sum Deus & non est amplius, & similia, solam voluntatum plurium consensionem significari intelligit? Deinde prohibent ea omnia, quibus vnitas naturæ diuinæ demonstrari potest. Denique ipsa voluntatis vnitas essentiæ vnitatem vel arguit vel facit. Quomodo enim naturaliter & essentialiter erit vna voluntas, si vna natura seu essentia non est? Quod si non est essentialiter vna voluntas, non implicabitur contradictio, si non sic vna, hoc est, si ponantur esse plures naturæ diuinæ, plures dij discordes, ac inter se pugnantes contrariis voluntatibus. quo nihil potest fingi absurdius. Rursus, suntne personæ illæ diuinæ finitæ an infinitæ? si finitæ, quomodo sunt præditæ natura diuina? hæc enim certè infinita est. si sunt infinitæ, sese igitur aliæ alias penetrant: sese etiam aliæ alias & cognoscunt & amant perfectissimè, immò infinitè. est autem amor appetitus vnionis. vniuntur igitur quàm possunt perfectissimè. Præterea, vel vnus scit aliquid quod alius nescit, aut amat aliquid quod alius non amat, aut potest aliquid quod alius non potest, vel non. Si prius, quomodo sunt dij? Deus enim omnia scit, omnia potest. Si posterius, non modo eorum est vna voluntas, sed etiam vna mens, vna potentia, vna eademque scientia, vnus amor. Nunc cogita plures naturas eiusdem rationis sese mutuò penetrantes, ac summa quadam eâque æternâ propensione sese complectentes & vnientes, ita vt, & nulla ratione à se inuicem disiungi possint, & sit earum eadem cogitatio, voluntas, actio, nonne eo ipso intelliges, illas in vnam euasisse naturam, nec vllum amplius superesse discrimen, nisi forte positum in modis existendi, qui, quia, quatenus tales, se totis diuersi sunt, confundi non potuerunt? Vides nos vnitatem voluntatis ad vnitatem essentiæ deduxisse. id quod mirandum non est: non enim voluntas diuina res est ab eius natura seu essentia diuersa.
units.tr: VII. But indeed, says Socinus, since a thing cannot be called one in number by reason of essence alone, if we wish to posit altogether a plurality of persons in God, what prevents us from thinking that, when the holy letters say that God is one, this refers not to the essence but to the will, so that we acknowledge that in God there is not one essence in number but one will, that is, among those several divine persons, a supreme and indissoluble consent and concord? We state indeed that it is absurd to introduce a plurality of divine essences, but it is quite impossible that, where there are several persons, there should be one essence in number. First, those holy letters prohibit it, which say that God is one. For, to pass over the rest, who in his right mind, when he reads those words, there is no God but one, or I am God and there is none else, and similar ones, understands that only a consent of several wills is signified? Next, all those things prohibit it by which the unity of the divine nature can be demonstrated. Finally, the very unity of will either proves or produces the unity of essence. For how will there be one will naturally and essentially, if there is not one nature or essence? And if the will is not essentially one, no contradiction is involved if it is not thus one, that is, if several divine natures are posited, several gods at odds with one another and fighting with contrary wills, than which nothing more absurd can be imagined. Again, are those divine persons finite or infinite? If finite, how are they endowed with the divine nature? For that is certainly infinite. If they are infinite, then they penetrate one another; they also know and love one another most perfectly, indeed infinitely. Now love is the appetite for union. They therefore unite as perfectly as they can. Moreover, either one knows something that another does not know, or loves something that another does not love, or can do something that another cannot, or not. If the first, how are they gods? For God knows all things and can do all things. If the second, they have not only one will but also one mind, one power, one and the same knowledge, one love. Now consider several natures of the same kind penetrating one another, and embracing and uniting themselves with a certain supreme and eternal inclination, so that they cannot in any way be separated from one another, and their thought, will and action are the same: will you not by that very fact understand that they have passed into one nature, and that no distinction remains except perhaps one lying in the modes of existing, which, since as such they differ wholly from one another, could not be confused? You see that we have drawn the unity of will to the unity of essence. This is not to be wondered at: for the divine will is not a thing distinct from its nature or essence.

units.la: VIII. At, inquit, impossibile plane est; ubi plures sint personæ ibi unam numero essentiam esse. Ego vero multò magis impossibile esse duco, plures numero diuinas essentias esse. Inde enim sequerentur absurda multa, verbi gratia, plures Deos esse, plura infinita, plures omnipotentes, plures summos, plures causas primas, plures fines ultimos. quid dico plures? immò infinitos. Item, posse Deum Deo repugnare: cur enim necesse sit, quod eorum deorum quilibet profua libertate velit, id reliquos omnes velle? Item, Deum esse compositum Metaphysicis compositionibus ex genere & differentia, aut saltem ex specie & differentia indiuiduali, ex esse & essentia &c. Item, Deum non esse à se, non esse necessariò: non enim ulla esset necessaria connexio inter essentiam diuinam & hanc huius Dei differentiam indiuiduALEM & existentiam. hæc enim negatà non continuò negaretur essentia diuina, quippe quæ absque illa differentia & existentia in aliis indiuiduis seu dijs conseruaretur. Item sequeretur, Deum non esse omnipotentem: plus enim plures dij possent quam unus. Item Deum posse pati: quid enim prohiberet eiusmodi Deos naturis diversos in se invicem agere? mitto reliqua.
units.tr: VIII. "But," he says, "it is plainly impossible: where there are several persons, there the essence is one in number." Indeed I hold it far more impossible that there should be several divine essences in number. For from that would follow many absurdities: for example, that there are several Gods, several infinites, several omnipotents, several highest beings, several first causes, several ultimate ends. Why do I say several? Rather, infinitely many. Likewise, that God could be at odds with God: for why must it be that whatever one of those gods wills freely, all the others will it too? Likewise, that God is composed by metaphysical compositions of genus and difference, or at least of species and individual difference, of existence and essence, and so on. Likewise, that God is not from himself, not necessarily existing: for there would be no necessary connection between the divine essence and this individual difference and existence of this God. For if that were denied, the divine essence would not at once be denied, since it could be preserved without that difference and existence in other individuals or gods. Likewise it would follow that God is not omnipotent: for several gods could do more than one. Likewise that God can suffer: for what would prevent gods of such diverse natures from acting upon one another? I pass over the rest.

units.la: IX. Sit, inquiet forte aliquis, pluralitas naturarum diuinarum plane impossibilis. Eam Dei beneficio nemo nostrum credit. At quandiu illud fixum manet, itidem impossibile plane esse; ubi plures sint personæ, ibi unam numero essentiam esse, fieri non potest, quin hanc quoque pluralitatem personarum rejiciamus. At inquam, unde habes hoc esse plane impossibile? è Scriptura? Id ex ea nulla arte elici potest? è Philosophia, vel ratione? Quomodo ea potest certò iudicare de eo quod non capit? aut quomodo ita insanit, ut putet se cum sit finita infinitum, cum sit exigua immensum capere posse, & suo tam curto pede metiri? Innumera sunt in natura, quæ esse certò scimus, quomodo sint nescimus, quæ miramur magis quam capimus, quæ si attentius introspicere conamur & penetrare, retunditur acies mentis nostræ, quæ si explicare volumus, hæret nobis aqua, spinisque difficultatum omni ex parte constringimur. Vocabula personæ, essentiæ, unitatis numericæ, distinctionis realis, vix satis percipimus cum de hominibus dicuntur. Quomodo igitur illa perfectè caperemus, cum ab hominibus ad Deum, à rebus finitis ad infinitum translata & accommodata, modo, non amplius humano, sed diuino infinito que, ac propterea nobis ignoto accipi debeant ? Nos pueri sumus, immò lactentes τὸ λόγικον ἄδολον γάλα ἐπιποθῦντες[?], & de mysterijs istis tam sublimibus, quæ nunc per speculum in ænigmate cernimus, pro nostro puerili captu & modo loquimur. itaque mirum videri non debet, si in modo concipiendi & loquendi nostro aliquid sit imperfectionis, quod rationi nostræ facessit negotium.
units.tr: IX. Someone may perhaps say: let the plurality of divine natures be plainly impossible; none of us believes it by God's gift. But so long as that remains fixed, namely that "where there are several persons, there the essence is one in number" is plainly impossible, it cannot be that we do not also reject this plurality of persons. But I ask: where do you get the claim that this is plainly impossible? From Scripture? Can it not be drawn from it by any art? From philosophy, or from reason? How can reason judge with certainty about what it does not grasp? Or how can it be so mad as to think that, being finite, it can grasp the infinite, and, being tiny, can take in the immense, and measure it with its own so short foot? There are countless things in nature which we know with certainty to exist, yet we do not know how they are; we marvel at them more than we comprehend them. If we try to look into and penetrate them more closely, the edge of our mind is blunted; if we want to explain them, the water sticks to us, and we are hemmed in on every side by the thorns of difficulties. We scarcely understand the words person, essence, numerical unity, real distinction, even when they are said of human beings. How then could we grasp them perfectly, when they are transferred and adapted from men to God, from finite things to the infinite, and must be taken not in a human mode any longer but in a divine and infinite mode, and therefore unknown to us? We are children, indeed babes, longing for the guileless milk of the word, and about those mysteries so sublime, which we now see through a glass in a riddle, we speak according to our childish capacity and manner. So it ought not to seem strange if there is some imperfection in our manner of conceiving and speaking, which gives our reason trouble.

units.la: Quod non ideò à me dicitur, quòd aut minimè aut admodum difficulter solui posse videantur subtilitates illæ Aduersariorum, quibus sacrosanctam Trinitatem oppugnant: sunt enim illæ, vt jam aliquoties monui, vitro similes, quod leui ictu frangitur. Sed ideo à me dicitur, ne humanæ rationi, præsertim cum de Deo agitur, qui à nobis vti in se est cognosci nequit, nedum comprehendi, plus tribuamus quàm ipsi Deo in Scripturis loquenti, vt facere videntur Aduersarij qui falsis ratiocinijs fidentes audent contorquere verbum Dei.
units.tr: I do not say this because those subtleties of the adversaries, by which they assail the most holy Trinity, seem to be solved with no difficulty or only with great difficulty. For they are, as I have already warned several times, like glass, which breaks at a light blow. But I say it so that we do not attribute more to human reason, especially when the subject is God, who cannot be known by us as he is in himself, much less comprehended, than God speaking in the Scriptures does; as the adversaries seem to do, who, trusting in false reasonings, dare to twist the Word of God.

units.la: X. Præmissa hac responsione tanquam velite, Socinus sese ad alias conuertit, & ad argumentum ductum ex plurali numero nominis Elohim Respondet, apud Hebraeos vsitatum esse, in nominibus pluralem numerum pro singulari vsurpare, præsertim vero in iis, quæ imperium, dominationem, potentiam, gubernationemue aliquam declarant, vt patet in nominibus, Adon & Baal, quorum prius Dominum aut sustentatorem, alterum vero & dominum, & possessorem, & virum seu maritum significat. Quæ nomina licet plane appellatiua, & in sacris literis frequentius hominibus, quàm Deo tributa, numero tamen plurali, præsertim vero prius, sapissimè efferuntur, tunc etiam cum de vno homine est sermo. Primùm autem id non fit nisi in duobus istis nominibus Adon & Baal, Deinde id raro fit cum de hominibus agitur, & cum id fit, potest ferè semper cur id fiat ratio reddi.
units.tr: X. With this answer set down as a skirmishing screen, Socinus turns himself to other matters, and to the argument drawn from the plural number of the name Elohim he replies that "among the Hebrews it is customary to use the plural number for the singular in nouns, especially in those which express rule, lordship, power, government or any such thing, as is evident in the nouns Adon and Baal, of which the former signifies lord or sustainer, and the latter both lord, and owner, and husband or spouse. Although these nouns are plainly appellatives, and in the sacred letters are more often applied to men than to God, yet they are very often put in the plural, especially the former, even when the talk is of one man." But first, this happens only in those two nouns, Adon and Baal. Second, it happens rarely when men are in question, and when it does happen, a reason can almost always be given why it happens.

units.la: XI. Attulit Socinus pluralis Adonim in statu absoluto pro singulari positi exempla tria. 1. Reg. 22.N. 17. Lo Adonim Laelleh; Ad verbum, Non domini illis, id est inquit, Non habent dominum. At cur Deus eo loco pluralem numerum vsurparit causa erat grauis, quam quia non obseruarunt interpretes putarunt pluralem numerum positum fuisse pro singulari. Nimirum eo plurali significare voluit, nullum illis dominum esse vel fore qui exercitum in officio contineat & bellum inceptum persequatur: nam & statim extinctum iri regem, & nullum fore vel à rege constitutum, vel ab exercitu electum ducem, qui rege extincto exercitum regat, & obsidionem Ramoth Galaad continuet. Itaque futurum esse vt absque omni domino seu duce populus reuertatur, vt quisque poterit, in domum suam.
units.tr: XI. "Socinus has brought three examples of plural Adonim in the absolute state used for the singular." 1 Kings 22:17, Lo Adonim Laelleh; word for word, "Not lords to them," that is, he says, "They have no lord." But that God used the plural number in that place had a serious cause, which the interpreters did not observe; they thought the plural had been put for the singular. Surely by that plural he meant to signify that there was, or would be, no lord for them who would keep the army in its duty and pursue the war begun: for the king would be struck down at once, and there would be no leader appointed either by the king or chosen by the army to lead the army after the king's death and continue the siege of Ramoth Gilead. Thus it was to happen that the people would return, without any lord or leader, each as he could, to his own house.

units.la: XII. Esai19. 4. Et tradam Ægyptum in manum Adonim Kaschach[?], id est, dominorum duri, pro Domini, inquit Socinus, Dominorum dictum est. At cur sic Deus loquutus sit causa est in promptu. Voluit enim innuere se traditurum Ægyptum in varias factiones diuisam in manus plurium dominorum, qui ita numero plures erunt vt tamen duritie vnum sint. contingit enim nonnunquam vt regis ministri, & qui ab eo prouinciis & vrbibus præficiuntur sint duri cum ipse rex sit mollis & clemens, aut contrà vt rex durus sit, molles præfecti: sed cum & rex, & præfecti, & ministri regis omnes pariter duri sunt & intractabiles, tum extrema est populi seruitus & miseria, id autem est quod Deus Ægypto comminatur & prædicit eo loco Esaiæ.
units.tr: XII. Isaiah 19:4: And I will deliver Egypt into the hand of Adonim Kaschach, that is, of hard lords; for "lords," says Socinus, "is the sense." But why God spoke thus has a ready cause. For he meant to hint that he would deliver Egypt, divided into various factions, into the hands of several lords, who would be many in number and yet one in hardness. For it sometimes happens that the king's ministers, and those whom he sets over provinces and cities, are hard though the king himself is gentle and merciful, or conversely the king is hard and the prefects gentle. But when the king, the prefects and the king's ministers are all alike hard and intractable, then the people's servitude and misery is complete; and this is what God threatens and foretells to Egypt in that place of Isaiah.

units.la: XIII. Malach. 1. 6. Filius honorat Patrem, & seruus Adonau Dominos suos. Si ergo Pater ego sum, vbi honor meus? si etiam Adonim Domini ego sum, vbi est timor mei? In vno, inquit Socinus, & eodem versu, & cum affixo, & in statu absoluto habetur idem nomen in numero plurali pro singulari. Verùm quod Deus se plurali numero Dominos appellat, id argumentum nostrum confirmat. Quod autem seruum dixit honorare dominos suos potius quàm dominum suum, factum est ab eo prudenter, vt vim augeret argumenti sui. Erant enim sæpissimè, vt obseruatum est sup. p. 314. §. 5. eiusdem serui plures domini, paterfamilias, materfamilias, filius, & nonnunquam alius seruus. Omnes honorabat & timebat seruus. Si igitur, inquit Deus, seruus honorat & timet dominos suos herum, heri filium, heri vxorem, præfectum sibi ab hero seruum &c, nullo excepto, Ego autem sum Dominus, imò quicquid habetis dominorum, vbi est timor mei?
units.tr: XIII. Malachi 1:6: A son honours his father, and a servant his Adonai, his lords. If then I am a father, where is my honour? If also I am Adonim, the lords, where is my fear? "In one and the same verse," says Socinus, "and with a suffix, and in the absolute state, the same noun is found in the plural for the singular." But that God calls himself Lords in the plural number confirms our argument. As for his saying that the servant honours his lords rather than his lord, he did so prudently, to increase the force of his argument. For, as has been observed above, p. 314, §5, the same servant very often had several masters: the householder, the housewife, the son, and sometimes another servant. The servant honoured and feared them all. If then, says God, a servant honours and fears his masters, the master, the master's son, the master's wife, the servant set over him by the master, and so on, none excepted, and I am the Lord, indeed whatever masters you have, where is my fear?

units.la: XIV. Verùm quicquid sit de illis locis & similibus, (nolim enim ea de re cum quoquam acrius contendere) illud negari non potest quod jam notaui, idem in alijs nominibus vsu non venire. Deinde si nomen Adon plurali numero vicies in Scriptura de vno homine dicitur, id pluiquam[?] centies & vicies eodem numero vsurpatur de Deo. Immò plurale Adonai vnum est è nominibus Dei maximè proprijs. id quod mirabile est, si Deus nonnisi vnica est persona, cum sibi aptasse, tanquam propria, nomina pluralis numeri, eoque numero magis quàm singulari delectatum fuisse. Subesse certè ea in re mysterij aliquid oportet, idque memorabile, quod tam frequenti pluralium istorum nominum Elohim & Adonai repetitione tam sæpe Deus ob oculos lectoris reponit. {d}enim præ se fert aliquid veluti peregrinum, & à loquendi usu aliquomodo abhorrens. Nulla enim alia una, vel res, vel persona plurali nomine, tanquam proprio, gaudet. Mirum est prosectò singularia Eloah & Adon de Deo raro usurpari, cum de eo pluralia Elohim & Adonai frequentissimè usurpentur seu ipse de se, seu homines de eo, vel ad eum loquantur.
units.tr: XIV. Whatever may be the case with those passages and similar ones (for I would rather not argue sharply with anyone about this), it cannot be denied that what I have already noted does not happen with other names. Next, if the name Adon is used in the plural of one man some twenty times in Scripture, the same plural form is used of God more than a hundred and twenty times. Indeed the plural Adonai is among the most proper of God's names. This is remarkable. If God is only a single person, why would he have appropriated plural names as his own, and taken more delight in that number than in the singular? Surely some mystery must lie in this, and a notable one, since by such frequent repetition of the plurals Elohim and Adonai God so often sets them before the reader's eyes. For it presents something foreign, as it were, and somewhat at odds with ordinary usage. No other single thing or person takes pride in a plural name as though it were its own. It is truly remarkable that the singulars Eloah and Adon are rarely applied to God, while the plurals Elohim and Adonai are very often applied to him, whether he speaks of himself or men speak of him or to him.

units.la: XV. Sed, inquit Socinus, Eloah, quod est singulare nominis pluralis Elohim, quamvis κατ' ἐξοχὴν summi illius rerum omnium moderatoris potentissimi, quodammodo proprium factum sit, appellatinum tamen vere est nomen, non secus atque Θεὸς apud Græcos, & Deus apud Latinos, & iudicem sine gubernatorem, potentemque significat. Unde hoc habet? legitne alicubi in Scriptura singulare illud Eloah de iudice, gubernatore, aut potente homine usurpatum[?]? Quomodo igitur audet id affirmare, quod ne uno quidem exemplo firmari potest? Fortasse plurale Elohim de iudicibus seu gubernatoribus, potentibusque frequenter dicitur. Dicitur fortasse de illis, non quibuslibet, sed in terris supremis, quinquies aut sexies, cum plusquam vicies centies de Deo usurpetur. Verum igitur ex quinque aut sex locis propria illius nominis significatio æstimari potius debet, quàm ex duobus locorum millibus, aut etiam pluribus, in quibus aliud significat? Quis ex eo quod nonnunquam leo pro forti & generoso, vulpes pro astuto & callido ponitur, concludat, duorum illorum nominum alterum fortem & generosum, alterum astutum & callidum proprie significare?
units.tr: XV. But, says Socinus, Eloah, which is the singular of the plural Elohim, although by excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν] it has in some way become the proper name of that most powerful governor of all things, is nevertheless truly an appellative, no differently from θεός among the Greeks and Deus among the Latins, and it signifies a judge or governor or powerful man. Where does he get this? Does Scripture anywhere read that singular Eloah is used of a judge, governor, or powerful man? How then does he dare to affirm what cannot be confirmed by even a single example? Perhaps the plural Elohim is often said of judges or governors or powerful men. It is perhaps said of them, not of just anyone, but of the highest rulers on earth, five or six times, whereas it is used of God more than two thousand times. Should the proper meaning of that name be judged from five or six passages rather than from two thousand or more places in which it means something else? Who, because the lion is sometimes put for a brave and noble man, and the fox for a crafty and cunning one, would conclude that the first of those names properly means brave and noble, and the second crafty and cunning?

units.la: XVI. Quod si vel singulare Eloah, vel plurale Elohim, iudices, gubernatores, aut potentes proprie significaret, Num illud utrumque Deo Israelis, tanquam proprium, vendicaretur in Scriptura, negareturque diserte, & sæpe ulli alij conuenire? Cum Deus primo Decalogi mandato populum suum vetat alios habere Deos, vetatne alios habere iudices, gubernatores, potentes? Nonne si ea esset propria nominis illius significatio, proprie loquendo iudices, præcipuè autem reges, Elohim, hoc est, dij appellari possent? Nemo tamen iudicum aut Regum Israëlis vel Iu[?]de Deus appellatur in Scriptura, Nemo potest appellari sine scelere. Si Judices dicuntur dij in duobus aut tribus locis Scripturæ, id fit communiter non autem distributivè, attributivè, ut loquuntur, non subjectivè, figuratè non propriè, ob quandam potestatis & autoritatis similitudinem, vel etiam quia Deus censetur sedere in medio eorum, & illi tanquam eius assessores, aut potius organa, eius nomine & cum eo judicare; ut totus ille consessus, quia Elohim in medio sui habet, ab eo, quod est in eo præstantissimum, Elohim appelletur: qua cogitatione nulla est aptior ad judices, cum judicant metu Dei implendos, & ad justè judicandum absque ulla [?]ἀγωνοπλευσία animandos. Si nomina θεὸς apud Græcos & Deus apud Latinos appellativa sunt, id aliunde prosectum non est, quàm à Græcorum & Latinorum errore putantium plures esse Deos, quo errore sublato, tam propria euadunt quàm quæ maximè: quippe cum plures dii nec sint, nec esse possint.
units.tr: XVI. But if either the singular Eloah or the plural Elohim properly meant judges, governors, or powerful men, would not each of them be claimed in Scripture as proper to the God of Israel, and would it not be plainly denied, and often applied to no one else? When God, in the first commandment of the Decalogue, forbids his people to have other gods, does he forbid them to have other judges, governors, or powerful men? If that were the proper sense of the name, then judges, and especially kings, could properly be called Elohim, that is, gods. Yet no judge or king of Israel or Judah is called God in Scripture; no one can be so called without sin. If judges are called gods in two or three places of Scripture, this happens commonly, not distributively; attributively, as they say, not subjectively; figuratively, not properly; on account of a certain similarity of power and authority, or also because God is held to sit in the midst of them, and they judge as his assessors, or rather his instruments, in his name and with him. Thus that whole assembly, because it has Elohim in its midst, is called Elohim* from the most excellent thing in it, which is God. No thought is more fitting for judges, since when they judge they ought to be moved by the fear of God and encouraged to judge justly without any partiality [ἀγωνοπλευσία]. If the names θεός among the Greeks and Deus among the Latins are appellatives, this does not arise from anything else than from the error of the Greeks and Latins who thought there were many gods. Once that error is removed, they become as proper as any name can be, since there are not, and cannot be, many gods.

units.la: XVII. Hoc jacto fundamento tam debili Socinus aliam responsionem superstruit. Quod si, inquit, pluralitatem aliquam propter pluralem numerum omnino significari velimus, non personarum quidem, sed gubernationum, & potentiarum pluralitatem, quæ in Deo animadverti possunt, nomen Elohim significabit. & quamuis unus prorsus sit, tamen quasi essent plures potentes gubernatores, honoris gratia Deus eo nomine appellatus dicetur. At primùm aliud est gubernator aliud gubernatio. Ponitur quidem nonnunquam abstractum pro concreto, sed concretum pro abstracto usurpatum legere me non memini. Qui dicit plures gubernatores dicit plures personas, plures verò gubernationes non dicit, nisi quatenus pluralitas gubernationum consequens quoddam est pluraliratis personarum. Contingere autem potest ut sint plures gubernatores potentes, cum tamen non sit nisi una gubernatio, ut vi-dere est in regimine Aristocratico. Si igitur Deus pluralitatem gubernationum, & potentiarum præcisè, minimè verò gubernato-rum & potentium, seu personarum, nomine aliquo pluralis numeri significare voluisset, is usus fuisset nomine aliquo abstracto gubernationes & potentias, non autem concreto gubernatores & potentes, significante.
units.tr: XVII. Having laid this weak foundation, Socinus builds another answer upon it. But if, he says, we wish to signify some plurality because of the plural number, not of persons indeed, but of governments and powers, which can be observed in God, the name Elohim will signify that plurality; and although he is altogether one, nevertheless, as if there were several powerful governors, God will be said to be called by that name for the sake of honour. But first, a governor is one thing and a government another. It is true that the abstract is sometimes put for the concrete, but I do not recall reading the concrete used for the abstract. He who says several governors says several persons; but he does not say several governments, except insofar as a plurality of governments follows from a plurality of persons. It can happen that there are several powerful governors while there is only one government, as may be seen in an aristocratic regime. If therefore God had wished to signify, by some plural name, a plurality of governments and powers precisely, and not of governors and powers, that is, of persons, he would have used some abstract name signifying governments and powers, not a concrete name signifying governors and powers.

units.la: XVIII. Taceo istum hominem videri gubernationes & po-tentias pro eadem re ponere, cum tamen & nominibus & re valdè: inter se differant. Illa enim ad modum actionis, haec ad modum qualitatis concipitur, nec possunt ambae uno communi nomine comprehendi. Illud tacere non possum, cum potentia quae in Deo est sit ipsa essentia divina, aut saltem cum ea reciprocetur, intelligere me non posse, quomodo multiplicari possit potentia divina, non multiplicatâ naturâ divinâ. Si dixeris, potentiam Dei cum sit infinita, aequipollere multis potentijs, idem de eius essentia, deque eius persona dici pariter potest. sunt enim non minus infinitae quàm potentia.
units.tr: XVIII. I pass over the fact that this man seems to put governments and powers for the same thing, although in both name and reality they differ greatly. For the one is conceived in the manner of an action, the other in the manner of a quality, and both cannot be comprehended under one common name. But this I cannot pass over: since the power that is in God is the divine essence itself, or at least is interchangeable with it, I cannot understand how divine power can be multiplied without the divine nature being multiplied. If you say that God's power, since it is infinite, is equivalent to many powers, the same can equally be said of his essence and of his person, for these are no less infinite than his power.

units.la: Quod si potentiam propter pluralitatem effectuum ad modum plurium potentiarum concipias, haec pluralitas in mente tua erit, in Deo nullo modo, nihilque prohibebit quominus similiter Deum pro varietate eius actionum & relationum ad creaturas ad modum plurium personarum concipias, eiusque intellectum ad modum plurium intellectuum, voluntatem ad modum plurium voluntatum &c, & sic multae erunt pluralitates, sed, ut dixi, in mente tua non in Deo, nec causa est idonea, quamobrem Deus ob eiusmodi pluralitatem appellari se voluisset nominibus pluralis numeri.
units.tr: But if you conceive the power as plural, in the manner of several powers, because of the plurality of its effects, this plurality will be in your mind, not in God in any way. Nothing will prevent you from likewise conceiving God, on account of the variety of his actions and relations to creatures, in the manner of several persons, and his understanding in the manner of several understandings, his will in the manner of several wills, and so on. Thus there will be many pluralities, but, as I said, in your mind and not in God. Nor is there any suitable cause why God should have wished to be called by names of the plural number on account of such a plurality.

units.la: XIX. Hic Socinus obuiam ire conatur argumento, quod nos breuitatis studio vix attigimus. Nec vero est, inquit, quod quis adhuc urgeat, nomen numeri pluralis Elohim, de summo illo Deo simpliciter pro numeri singularis nomine usurpatum non fuisse, quia aut verbis, aut adiectiuis nominibus pluralis numeri nonnunquam iunctum reperiatur. Verbis, ut Gen. 20. 13. Hithu O hi Elohim, Ad verbum Errare me fecerunt dij &c. Nominibus adiectiuis, ut Iosue 24. 19. Non poteritis seruire Iehouæ, quoniam Elohim Kedoschim hu, id est, dij sancti ipse. Animaduertendum enim est in istis, & si qui similes sunt loci, habitam suisse rationem terminationis nominis Elohim, quae est numeri pluralis, & quamuis de uno tantum sit sermo, nomina quoque & verba illi adiuncta fuisse pluralis numeri amplioris adhuc honoris gratia, quem prater modum Deo tribui nunquam contingere potest. Primum, quis credat habitam esse rationem terminationis potius quàm significationis, literarum quàm vis nominis, soni quàm rei? Deinde, cum eadem sit nominis illius pluralis terminatio ubicunque usurpatum est, qui factum est, ut alibi nulla habita sit illius terminationis ratio? ubi enim eadem ratio fuit, cur nomini Elohim verba & adiectiua pluralis numeri adjungerentur, ibi quoque adjungenda illi fuerunt siquidem ratio illa & bona est, & sufficit. Cum certum sit, Deum tantâ sapientiâ Scripturam contexuisse, vt etiam Apostolus non dubitauerit argumentum ducere à constantia Dei in vsurpando numero singulari quoties de semine Abrahami in promissionibus suis loquitur, estne locus dubitandi, quin si voluisset, vt nomen illud Elohim crederemus sola terminatione plurale esse, significatione vero singulare, constans fuisset in adjungendis ei verbis & adjectiuis singularis numeri? Cur enim ab illa sua consuetudine in his locis, & similibus quibusdam discessit, nisi vt ne ab ea possemus argumentum ducere, quo probaremus, Elohim, cum de Deo vsurpatur, non esse pluraliter accipiendum? Confirmauit enim nominis illius pluralitatem adjunctis verbis & adjectiuis pluralis numeri, quae constat semper pluraliter in Scriptura accipi, quorumque cum terminatione significatio conspirat, quominusque singulariter accipiatur nomen Elohim conjunctim resistit.
units.tr: XIX. Here Socinus tries to meet an argument which, for the sake of brevity, we have barely touched upon. Nor is there, he says, anything that someone might still press, namely that the plural name Elohim was not used simply as a name of the singular number of that supreme God, because it is sometimes found joined with plural verbs or adjectives. With verbs, as in Gen. 20. 13, Hithu O hi Elohim, literally, the gods have caused me to err, etc. With adjectives, as in Joshua 24. 19, You will not be able to serve Jehovah, for he is Elohim Kedoschim hu, that is, he is holy gods. For it must be noted in these, and in any similar passages, that regard was had to the ending of the name Elohim, which is of the plural number, and although only one is spoken of, the names and verbs joined to it were also made plural, for the sake of a still greater honour, which can never properly be attributed to God. First, who would believe that regard was had to the ending rather than to the meaning, to the letters rather than to the word, to the sound rather than to the thing? Next, since that same plural ending of the name is used wherever it occurs, how is it that no regard to that ending was had elsewhere? For where the same reason existed why plural verbs and adjectives were joined to the name Elohim, there too they ought to have been joined to it, if that reason is sound and sufficient. Since it is certain that God wove Scripture with such wisdom that even the Apostle did not hesitate to draw an argument from God's constancy in using the singular number whenever he speaks of Abraham's seed in his promises, is there any room for doubt that, if he had wished us to believe that the name Elohim is plural only in its ending but singular in its meaning, he would have been consistent in joining to it verbs and adjectives of the singular number? For why did he depart from that custom in these and some similar passages, unless it was so that we could not draw from it an argument to prove that Elohim*, when used of God, is not to be taken in the plural? For by joining plural verbs and adjectives, which are always taken in the plural in Scripture, and whose meaning agrees with the ending, he confirmed the plurality of that name, and conjoined with it he resists any singular sense of the name Elohim.

units.la: XX. Praeterea merito quaeri poterit, cur Deus voluerit inter nominis sui terminationem & significationem intercedere repugnantiam? Nam si voluit nominis sui significationem esse singularem, cur non ei formam & terminationem dedit consentaneam? quis huius dissonantiae vsus esse potest? Nonne suppetebat nomen Eloah singularis numeri, quo vti potuisset, necnon El, Schaddai, & similia? Cur ista significationis & terminationis discordia ita delectatus fuisset, vt eâ totam fere Scripturam Veteris Testamenti respersam esse voluisset? Cur eam etiam auxisset appositis verbis & adjectiuis, in quibus eiusmodi pugna prorsus insolens esset, quaeque externa forma & terminatione aliud prae se ferrent, quàm quod revera significare deberent? Quis enim huius rei vsus esse potuisset, nisi ad decipiendos lectores, aut certè illos torquendos admiratione primùm, deinde inquisitione causae, quâ inventâ nullum esset operae pretium. nempe in plurali illo Elohim nihil reperirent praeter inanem terminationem pluralem vacuam significatione consentanea, in pluralibus verò verbis & adjectiuis adjunctis nihil, nisi habitam esse rationem inanis illius terminationis nominis Elohim. En scilicet egregium operae fructum! Dehonestant profectò isti homines ea ratione Scripturam Dei,mirabili sapientia ubique splendescentem.
units.tr: XX. Moreover, one may fairly ask why God wished there to be a discord between the termination of his name and its meaning. If he wished the meaning of his name to be singular, why did he not give it a form and termination to match? What purpose can this dissonance serve? Was the name Eloah in the singular not available, which he could have used, and likewise El, Shaddai, and similar names? Why would he have taken such delight in this clash between meaning and termination that he wished almost the whole of the Old Testament to be sprinkled with it? Why would he also have increased it by adding words and adjectives, where such a conflict is wholly out of place, and which by their outward form and termination would seem to signify something other than what they really ought to signify? For what purpose could this have served, except to deceive readers, or at least to vex them first with wonder and then with a search for the cause, which when found would prove to be not worth the effort? Indeed, in that plural Elohim they would find nothing but an empty plural termination with no corresponding meaning, and in the plural words and adjectives joined to it they would find nothing except that the termination of the name Elohim had been taken into account. Behold, the splendid fruit of their labour! Those men surely dishonour the Scripture of God in this way, which shines everywhere with wonderful wisdom.

units.la: XXI. Sed id fit, inquit Socinus, amplioris honoris gratia. Egregius scilicet honor, in sola plurali terminatione vocabulorum, prorsus inani, situs! Hunc scilicet honorem Deus expetit, positum in syllabis! Itaque, ne nimius videretur quàm vt posset conuenire Deo, Socinus addit, quem praeter modum Deo tribui nunquam contingere posset. Hic scilicet honoris est excessus quidam & summus gradus qui, si posset honos tribui Deo praeter modum, nimius esset. Non pudet eos qui profitentur religionem Christianam sic sentire de Dei honore? Si honorificum est Deo vnicam esse personam, nec posse plures esse, quo id apertius significatur siue nominibus, siue verbis, eo magis honoratur: quia id exprimitur in quo sita est eius gloria. minus vero honorari videtur, cum id quod ei gloriae opponitur, ei in speciem tribuitur nominibus & verbis numeri pluralis. Tum etiam ab hominibus afficitur honore, cum & de eo recte sentiunt, & fidei interiore[?] verba externa conueniunt, eamque apertius exprimunt. Si igitur piorum ea fides & fuit & debet esse, vnicam esse diuinam personam, non plures vllo modo, maiori honore afficitur Deus, cum nominibus & verbis singularis numeri fidem istam suam prositentur, & conuenienter exprimunt, quàm cum vtuntur nominibus & verbis suae isti fidei in speciem repugnantibus, pluralitatemque personarum in Diuinitate innuentibus.
units.tr: XXI. But, says Socinus, this is done for the sake of greater honour. An excellent honour, surely, that lies only in the plural termination of words, a termination entirely empty! God, it seems, desires this honour, placed in syllables! Therefore, lest it should seem excessive to the point that it could not suit God, Socinus adds which could never be attributed to God beyond measure. Here, it seems, is a certain excess of honour and its highest degree, which, if honour could be attributed to God beyond measure, would be too much. Are those who profess the Christian religion not ashamed to think this way about the honour of God? If it is honourable to God that he is one person, and that there cannot be several, then the more plainly this is signified, whether by names or by words, the more he is honoured, because that is what expresses the very thing in which his glory lies. He seems to be less honoured when what is opposed to that glory is attributed to him in appearance by names and words of the plural number. Moreover, he receives honour from men when they both think rightly about him and when their outward words agree with their inward faith and express it more clearly. If, then, it is and ought to be the faith of the godly that the divine person is one, and in no way more, God is honoured more when they profess that faith with names and words of the singular number, and express it fittingly, than when they use names and words that in appearance contradict that faith and suggest a plurality of persons in the Godhead.

units.la: XXII. Cum etiam controuersia esset maximi momenti illis temporibus inter fideles & idololatras, vtrum essent plures dij, necne? negarentq; fideles, affirmarent idololatrae, non est existimandum, Deum eo modo loquendi magis honoratum fuisse qui ad errorem idololatrarum magis accommodatus videri posset, quàm ad veram fidem. Non potuisset enim Abrahamus loqui magis ad errorem Gentium accommodatè, quàm fecit, cum dixit, cum dij errare me fecerunt à domo patris mei. Consilium igitur sacri autoris, cum sic se expressit, non fuit, vsurpare pluralem de Deo numerum amplioris honoris gratia, sed instinctu Spiritus sancti id fecit, vt notam quandam ibi poneret, vnde suo tempore agnosci posset Veteris Testamenti cum nouo in asserendo dogmate de Trinitate conspiratio.
units.tr: XXII. Since also the controversy between the faithful and the idolaters was of the greatest importance in those times, namely whether there were many gods or not, the faithful denying and the idolaters affirming it, we should not think that God was honoured more by a manner of speaking that could seem better suited to the error of the idolaters than to the true faith. For Abraham could not have spoken more accommodatingly to the error of the Gentiles than he did when he said, when the gods caused me to wander from my father's house. Therefore the purpose of the sacred author, in expressing himself thus, was not to use the plural number of God for the sake of greater honour, but he did it by the prompting of the Holy Spirit, so as to set down a certain mark there, by which in its own time the agreement of the Old Testament with the New in asserting the doctrine of the Trinity could be recognised.

units.la: XXIII. Obseruat Socinus non deesse, qui prius illud testimonium Gen. 20. 13. de Angelis interpretentur, quorum ministerio Deus, in alloquendo atque è paterna domo educendo Abrahamo, vsus fuisset. Cui simile est illud eodem libro cap. 35. &[?] 7. Nam ibi apparuerant ei dij &c. quem locum non pauci de angelis loqui affirmant.
units.tr: XXIII. Socinus observes that there are not lacking those who interpret that earlier testimony, Gen. 20:13, as referring to the angels, through whose ministry God made use in speaking to Abraham and leading him out of his father's house. Similar to this is that in the same book, chapter 35, verse 7: For there had appeared to him the gods etc., a passage which not a few affirm speaks of angels.

units.la: Quod autem ad prius illud testimonium attinet, quicunque illi sint qui ita sentiunt, falli mihi videntur. Primum enim causa nulla est, cur per Elohim eo loco Angelos intelligamus: vsurpantur enim alibi verba pluralis numeri de ipso Deo. Deinde cur Deum ipsum intelligamus causae sunt idoneae. Primò consensio horum Abrahami verborum cum eius ipsius historia, in qua qui ei apparuit, qui iussit è domo paterna egredi, quùm errare fecit in terra Canaam, & modo ad Aquilonem, modo ad meridem, modò ad ortum, modò ad occasum progredi, is perpetuò Dominus seu Iehoua appellatur, idemque est qui foedus cum eo ferit, & semen benedictum promittit. Deinde, cum certum sit ipsum Deum errare fecisse Abrahamum per terram Canaam, non fit verisimile, Abrahamum maluisse in[?], angelis quàm Deo ascribere, aut Deo adjunxisse Angelos, tanquam qui, & eiusdem speciei essent cum Deo, & cum eo eius è domo paterna errationis autores.
units.tr: As for that earlier testimony, whoever they are who think this way seem to me to be mistaken. For first, there is no reason why we should understand the Angels by Elohim in that place, since plural words are used elsewhere of God himself. Secondly, there are good grounds why we should understand God himself. First, the words of Abraham agree with his own history, in which the one who appeared to him, who bade him go out of his father's house, when he caused him to wander in the land of Canaan, and to advance now toward the north, now toward the south, now toward the east, now toward the west, is constantly called the Lord or Jehovah, and it is the same one who makes a covenant with him and promises a blessed seed. Secondly, since it is certain that God himself caused Abraham to wander through the land of Canaan, it is not likely that Abraham preferred to ascribe this to angels rather than to God, or that he joined angels to God as though they were of the same kind as God and were co-authors with him of that wandering from his father's house.

units.la: XXIV. Adde quod constat ex Gen. 22. 11. 13. reuera duas personas autores fuisse Abrahamo, vt sic per Canaam erraret, quarum vna appellatur simpliciter Iehoua, altera, vt ab illa distinguatur, Angelus Iehouae, sed tamen ita Angelus, vt idem fuisse Deus seu Iehoua non obscurè significetur. Ecce, inquit Moses, Angelus Domini de coelo clamauit ad eum dicens, Abraham, Abraham. Qui respondit, Adsum. & ille ait, ne mittas manum tuam in puerum, neque facias illi quicquam, quia iam cognoui quod times Deum, & non pepercisti filio tuo vnigenito propter me. dicendo propter me significat se illum fuisse qui hoc praeceperat Abrahamo, & cui voluit Abrahamus filium suum immolando obedire, & rem gratam facere. Is autem sine dubio est Deus. Non enim existimandum est, Abrahamum voluisse vnigenitum suum immolare in honorem meri angeli, aut vsque adeò amauisse certum quendam angelum creatum, vt propter eum non pepercerit filio dilecto suo, aut commendari hoc loco eius amorem erga angelum, & non potius erga Deum in quem crediderat, & quem sciebat posse mortuos suscitare.
units.tr: XXIV. Add that it is clear from Gen. 22:11, 13 that two persons were indeed the authors for Abraham of his wandering through Canaan in this way. One of them is called simply Jehovah, and the other, to be distinguished from him, is the Angel of Jehovah, yet so much an angel that it is not obscurely signified that he was also God or Jehovah. Behold, says Moses, the Angel of the Lord called to him from heaven, saying, Abraham, Abraham. And he answered, Here I am. And he said, Do not lay your hand upon the boy, nor do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, and you have not spared your only son for my sake. By saying for my sake he signifies that he was the one who had commanded this of Abraham, and the one whom Abraham wished to obey by sacrificing his son and to please. Now this is without doubt God. For it is not to be thought that Abraham wished to sacrifice his only son in honour of some mere angel, or loved some particular created angel so much that for his sake he did not spare his beloved son, or that his love toward an angel, rather than toward God in whom he had believed and whom he knew could raise the dead, is commended in this place.

units.la: XXV. Ad alterum verò locum Gen. 35. V. 7. quod spectat, Nam ibi apparuerant (vel potius revelati fuerant: est enim Heb. נגלו[?] ) eidy &c. per Elohim, deos, non esse intelligendos angelos multa suadent. Primò, quod Angeli quidem apparuerant ibi Iacobo, sed tantummodo ut nuntij Dei, non verò sub ea forma ob quam Elohim appellari possint. Sic enim revelatio illa narratur Gen. 28. 12. Et somniauit, & Ecce scala stans in terram, & summitas eius pertingebat ad cælum, & ecce angeli Dei ascendebant & descendebant per eam, & ecce Dominus stabat super eam, & dixit, Ego Dominus, Deus, ( heb. Elohe, dij ) Abrahami patris tui &c. Scala illa fuit Christus[?], eodem Christo teste Ioh. 1. 52. Ab hoc tempore videbitis cœlum apertum, & Angelos Dei ascendentes & descendentes super filium hominis. hoc est, vos re ipsa videbitis id ipsum quod Patriarcha Iacobus vidit per somnium. Ego sum illa scala quæ cœlum iungit terræ. Ego is[?] sum cuius beneficio communicatio est inter Deum & homines, & cuius vi Angeli seu nuntij Dei descendunt ad homines & ab his remeant ad Deum. Absque me foret, nulla esset inter cœlum & terram, Deum & homines pax, communio, commercium. Non enim vult significare Dominus à se nuntios seu angelos ad Deum mitti, & à Deo ad se: Intercedit enim inter Patrem & Filium immediata prorsus communicatio, neque opus habet Filius, ut veniant ad se à Deo nuntij: ita enim in terra erat, sicut ista scala quam Iacobus vidit, ut simul esset in cœlo, quemadmodum ipse testatur disertis verbis Ioh. 3. 13. Erat ipse in Patre & Pater in ipso, & quidem ita, ut alter absque altero videri non posset, essentque unum. Itaque scala illa non erat terminus à quo, vel ad quem ascensionis & descensionis Angelorum, sed medium & causa, & id quo omnis illa communicatio nitebatur, habebatque in una extremitate Iacobum dormientem, & in altera Deum loquentem ac promissione benevolentiam suam testificantem. nempe Christus quatenus eiusmodi est scala habet in una sui veluti extremitate se hominem verum Iacobum duodecim patriarcharum Ecclesiæ Christianæ parentem, somno mortis sepultum in terra, & in altera se verum Deum loquentem ac promittentem è cœlo hæreditatem cœlestis Canaam illis, qui per fidem in eius mortem cum eo consepulti sunt, & cum eo resurgunt, ut in novitate vitæ ambulent à domo paterna exulantes, & versus patriam cœlestem fugientes. ac propterea non considerantur hoc loco Angeli ut dij, sed simpliciter ut angeli, hoc est, nuntij, qui ascendunt ad cœlum & descendunt de cœlo beneficio scalæ, quâ nituntur, quæque eos sustinet, & sine qua ipsi, vt ita loquar, caderent propria infirmitate, nec angelorum seu nunciorum functiones obire possent inter cœlum & terram, seu Deum & homines.
units.tr: XXV. As for the other passage, Gen. 35:7, For there had appeared (or rather, had been revealed; for the Hebrew is [נגלו] ) to him etc. by Elohim, gods, many considerations suggest that angels are not to be understood. First, because angels indeed appeared to Jacob there, but only as messengers of God, and not under that form on account of which they could be called Elohim. For that revelation is narrated thus in Gen. 28:12: And he dreamed, and behold a ladder standing on the earth, and its top reached to heaven, and behold the angels of God were ascending and descending by it, and behold the Lord stood above it and said, I am the Lord, God (Hebrew Elohe, gods) of Abraham your father etc. That ladder was Christ, by the testimony of Christ himself in John 1:52: From now on you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man. That is, you will in very deed see the very thing that the patriarch Jacob saw in a dream. I am that ladder which joins heaven to earth. I am the one by whose benefit there is communication between God and men, and by whose power the angels, or messengers of God, descend to men and return from them to God. Without me there would be no peace, fellowship, or intercourse between heaven and earth, God and men. For the Lord does not mean to say that messengers or angels are sent from himself to God and from God to himself; for between the Father and the Son there is a wholly immediate communication, and the Son has no need for messengers to come to him from God. For he was on earth just as that ladder which Jacob saw was, so that he was at the same time in heaven, as he himself testifies in plain words in John 3:13: He himself was in the Father and the Father in him, and indeed in such a way that the one could not be seen without the other, and they are one. Therefore that ladder was not the terminus from which or to which the ascent and descent of the angels proceeded, but the middle and cause, the thing on which all that communication rested; and it had Jacob sleeping at one end and God speaking and attesting his goodwill by promise at the other. Christ, insofar as he is such a ladder, has at one end of himself, as it were, that he is the true man Jacob, the parent of the twelve patriarchs and of the Christian Church, buried in the sleep of death in the earth; and at the other end he is the true God speaking and promising from heaven the inheritance of the heavenly Canaan to those who through faith have been buried with him in his death and rise with him, so that they walk in newness of life, as exiles from their father's house, fleeing toward the heavenly homeland. Therefore the angels in this place are not considered as gods, but simply as angels, that is, messengers, who ascend to heaven and descend from heaven by the benefit of the ladder on which they rest, which sustains them, and without which they would, as I may say, fall by their own weakness, and could not perform the functions of angels or messengers between heaven and earth, or between God and men.

units.la: XXVI. Sed redeamus ad locum Gen. 35. 7. is sic habet, Et ædificauit ibi altare, & vocauit locum El Beth-El, quoniam ibi ei revelati fuerant dij, cum fugeret à facie fratris sui. Primùm igitur Iacobus extruxit altare: solent autem altaria extrui ad cultum, non Angelorum, sed Dei. Deinde nomen imposuit loco El BethEl, id est, Deus Domus Dei: potest autem domus vel nominatiui casus esse per appositionem, vel genitiui. Idem locus eodem capite ℣. 15. ab eodem Iacobo appellatur simpliciter Beth-El, id est, Domus Dei. Quomodo potuit locus ille Domus Dei esse & Deus, nisi typicè? Cuius autem rei fuit typus? Annon illius, quæ simul & templum seu domus Dei est, & Deus, in qua est scala terram cum cœlo iungens, & altare super quo Deus colitur? Ea autem alia esse non potest quàm Christus, qui idem est templum seu domus in qua corporaliter habitat omnis plenitudo Deitatis, & scala cœlum copulans cum terra, & altare absque quo frustrà colitur Deus, & Deus, verè, inquam, & proprie Deus, immò Deus domus Dei, hoc est, Ecclesiæ suæ, necnon cœli. Sic paulò ante Gen. 33. ℣. 20. idem Iacobus erexerat altare, illudque vocauerat El Elohe Israel, id est, Deus, Deus Israel, cuius typi veritas alibi quæri non debet quàm in Christo, qui solus est verum altare. id quod Deo patri convenire non potest. Non me fugit esse qui hunc postremum locum vertant aliter, nempe sic, & innocauit ibi Deum fortem Israelis, sed primùm לְ in verbis ויקרא לו non potest significare ibi: est enim sine dubio datiuus singularis pronominis tertiæ personæ הוא. Verbum autem קרא sequente datiuo non significat invocare, sed vocare, appellare. Deinde si seponas illud לְ, supererunt verba ויקרא אל אלהי ישראל quæ nihil poterunt significare, nisi vocauit Deum Deum Israelis. Qui sensus non est appositus.
units.tr: XXVI. But let us return to Gen. 35:7. It reads: And he built there an altar, and called the place El Beth-El, because there God had been revealed to him when he fled from the face of his brother. First, then, Jacob built an altar, but altars are normally built for the worship of God, not of angels. Next, he named the place El BethEl, that is, God, the House of God [אל בית אל]. The word "house" may be in apposition in the nominative, or it may be in the genitive. The same place is called, in verse 15 of the same chapter, simply Beth-El by the same Jacob, that is, House of God. How could that place be both the House of God and God, unless typically? And of what was it a type? Was it not a type of him who is at once the temple or house of God and God himself, in whom is the ladder joining heaven with earth, and the altar on which God is worshipped? That can be no one but Christ, who is the same temple or house in which all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, the ladder linking heaven with earth, and the altar without which God is worshipped in vain. He is God, truly and properly, I say, and indeed the God of the House of God, that is, of his Church, and of heaven. Thus shortly before, at Gen. 33:20, the same Jacob had erected an altar and called it El Elohe Israel, that is, God, the God of Israel [אל אלהי ישראל]. The truth of this type ought to be sought nowhere but in Christ, who alone is the true altar, which cannot be said of God the Father. I am not unaware that there are those who translate this last passage differently, namely: and he invoked there the strong God of Israel. But first, the לְ in the words ויקרא לו [vayiqra lo] cannot mean there; it is without doubt the dative of the singular pronoun of the third person, הוא. Moreover, the verb קרא, when followed by a dative, means not to invoke but to call or name. Next, if you set aside that לְ, the words ויקרא אל אלהי ישראל [vayiqra el elohe Yisra'el] remain, which can mean nothing except "he called God the God of Israel". That sense does not fit.

units.la: XXVII. Cur autem ibi Iacobus altare ædificauerit, & locum appellauerit El beth-el, id est, Deum, Domum Dei, ratio redditur verbis sequentibus, Nam ibi apparuerant ei dij, cum fugeret fratrem suum. Quæ ratio, si per Elohim qui illi apparuerant Deus intelligitur, optima est, vt quilibet videt; si vero intelliguntur Angeli, minus est apposita. Vocauit locum Domum Dei. Quid ita? Quia ibi Angeli Dei ipsi apparuerant. Ratio videtur minus firma: possunt enim Angeli in eo loco apparere, qui non sit domus Dei. At apparuerunt ascendentes & descendentes per scalam, id quod domum arguit, nec alius quàm Dei. Itaque cum enigilasset exclamauit Iacobus, Quàm terribilis est locus iste? Iste nihil est nisi Domus Dei, & ista est porta cœli. Fateor sic quidem recte colligi: sed hoc pacto considerabuntur Angeli Dei, non vt dij, aut vt domini domus, sed tantùm vt famuli. Quo respectu non videntur appellandi fuisse Elohim seu dij. Hoc primum. Deinde sic ratio nulla reddetur, cur locum appellauerit non modo Domum Dei, sed Deum Domus Dei, vel Domum Dei: Nam quæ hæc est ratio, locum appellauit Deum, Domum Dei: quia ibi ei apparuerant Angeli Dei? Ea vero optima est, vocauit locum Deum, Domum Dei, quia ibi personæ diuinæ ei reuelatæ fuerant; sic nimirum, vt earum vna esset simul & Deus, & Domus Dei, & scala cœlum cum terra iungens: quam rem non potuit Iacobus conuenientiore nomine notare, nec cur sic notata fuerit, conuenientiorem rationem Moses reddere.
units.tr: XXVII. The reason why Jacob built the altar there and called the place El Beth-El, that is, God, the House of God, is given in the following words: For there the gods had appeared to him when he fled from his brother. If the Elohim who appeared to him are understood as God, this reason is excellent, as anyone can see; but if angels are understood, it fits less well. He called the place the House of God. Why? Because the angels of God had appeared to him there. The reason seems weak, for angels may appear in a place which is not the house of God. But they appeared ascending and descending by the ladder, which points to a house, and to no other house than God's. So when he woke up, Jacob cried out: How awesome is this place! This is nothing other than the House of God, and this is the gate of heaven. I admit that this may rightly be inferred in this way; but in this way the angels of God will be regarded not as gods, nor as lords of the house, but only as servants. From this point of view they do not seem to have been rightly called Elohim or gods. This is the first point. Second, on this reading no reason is given why he called the place not only the House of God but God, the House of God. For what is the reason for saying "he called the place God, the House of God, because there the angels of God had appeared to him"? The best reason is this: he called the place God, the House of God, because there the divine persons had been revealed to him, so that one of them was at the same time both God and the House of God, and the ladder joining heaven with earth. Jacob could not have marked this with a more fitting name, nor could Moses have given a more fitting reason why it was so marked.

units.la: XXVIII. Huc accedit,quod necesse est per Deos qui apparuerant Iacobo, vel Deum Israelis, vel Angelos, vel simul Deum Israelis & Angelos eius intelligere. Primum si dicitur, id ipsum est quod nunc probatum volumus. Secundum dici non potest: primò quia ibi non solùm Angeli Dei, sed ipse etiam Deus Iacobo apparuerat: qui eò minùs prætermitti hoc loco debuit, quòd, & ei altare illud Iacobus extruxerat, & nomen El singulari numero de eo solo vsurpatur in Scriptura, & Deum quàm Angelos apparere multo majus est beneficium, & nomen Elohim de eo sine vlla comparatione frequentiùs dicitur, quàm de Angelis. Tertium pugnat cum versione, Nam ibi ei apparuerant Angeli. Deum enim Angelorum nomine, quasi de eorum numero esset, comprehendere non est rationi consentaneum. Sed neque etiam confundi Deus debet cum Angelis, ipsum eosque simul vno isto Deorum nomine, tanquam eodem sensu communi, intelligendo. Id enim est Angelos Deo aliquomodo æquare, & opinioni de pluribus Dijs non obscurè fauere. Non igitur verti debent ista verba, נגלו אליו האלהים apparuerant ei Angeli, sed, vt vertit ipse Vatablus, apparuerat ei Deus. Quæ versio cum eius annotatione ad marginem, apparuerant ei Angeli, ( siquidem interpretatio est, & non[?] potius additio, etiam Angelos ei apparuisse) pugnat aper-te.
units.tr: XXVIII. Moreover, by the gods who appeared to Jacob we must understand either the God of Israel, or angels, or the God of Israel together with his angels. The first is what we now want proved. The second cannot be said, first because there God himself, and not only the angels of God, had appeared to Jacob; this ought not to be passed over in this place, since Jacob built that altar for him, the name El in the singular is used of him alone in Scripture, appearing of God is a much greater benefit than appearing of angels, and the name Elohim is applied to him far more often than to the angels, beyond all comparison. The third conflicts with the rendering for there the angels had appeared to him. For it is not reasonable to include God under the name of the angels, as if he were one of their number. Nor ought God to be confused with the angels, understanding him and them together under this one name of gods, as if in a common sense. For that would be to make the angels in some way equal to God, and to favour, not obscurely, the opinion of many gods. Therefore these words, נגלו אליו האלהים [niglu elav ha-elohim], should not be rendered the angels had appeared to him, but, as Vatablus himself renders it, God had appeared to him. That version clearly conflicts with his marginal note, the angels had appeared to him (since it is an interpretation, and not rather an addition, that the angels also appeared to him).

units.la: XXIX. Objicit nobis Socinus, Elohim, quamuis de vno tantùm sermo esset, prolatum tamen fuisse numero multitudinis ab ijs, qui veri Dei cognitionem non habebant, quique pluralitatem aliquam personarum in vno Deo ne somniabant quidem. Nempe illi secuti sunt morem loquendi Hebræorum, qui nomen illud Elohim numero multitudinis de Deo Israelis, quem vnum esse profitebantur, vsurpare soliti erant, ipso Deo autore & comprobante. Quid hoc obest argumento nostro, quod non ducitur ab autoritate, aut cogitatione hominum nomen Elohim vsurpantium, sed Dei ipsius, qui non sine graui causa nomen pluralis numeri sibi ipse imposuit, eoque magis, quàm alijs nominibus dele-ctatus est?
units.tr: XXIX. Socinus objects to us that Elohim, although the discourse was about only one, was nevertheless uttered by those who had no knowledge of the true God, and who did not even dream of any plurality of persons in the one God, in the plural number. Namely, they followed the Hebrew manner of speaking, which customarily used that name Elohim in the plural of the God of Israel, whom they professed to be one, with God himself as author and approver. What harm is this to our argument, which is drawn not from the authority or thought of the men who use the name Elohim, but from God himself, who did not without serious cause impose on himself the name of the plural number, and was more pleased with it than with his other names?

units.la: XXX. Objicit etiam nobis Caluinum, qui in explicatione horum verborum, In principio creauit Deus, &c. parùm solidam sibi videri tantæ rei probationem, quæ ex nomine Elohim pluralis numeri duci solet, aperte significat. Quæ obiectio primùm aliena est ab hac controuersia, in qua Aduersarij nullam admittunt autoritatem præter diuinam sacrarum literarum, ac propterea etiam nos ab omni aliorum librorum laudatione abstinuimus. Magno quidem est in pretio apud nos Caluinus merito suo, sed tamen in eius verba non iurauimus. Vnicus est doctor noster Christus, qui per Apostolos suos doctrinam suam perscribi curauit, & per Spiritum suum, eam cui, & quando, & quantum vult reuelat. Deinde (quod fortasse prima fronte mirum lectori nostro videbitur) idem sentimus cum Caluino. Non enim ex eo quod nomen Elohim est pluralis numeri colligi posse arbitrantur, vbicunque vsurpatur de Deo, siue in primo capite Geneseos, siue alibi, id perpetuò tres personas notare. Fatemur enim vltrò, id modò Patrem, modò Filium, modò Spiritum sanctum, pro locorum circumstantijs, significare.
units.tr: XXX. Socinus also objects to us from Calvin, who, in explaining the words In the beginning God created, etc., said that the proof which is usually drawn from the plural name Elohim seemed to him not very solid, as it clearly signifies. This objection is first of all foreign to the present controversy, in which our opponents admit no authority except the divine authority of the holy letters; for this reason we too have abstained from all praise of other books. Calvin is indeed held in high esteem among us for his merit, but we have not sworn to his words. Our only teacher is Christ, who through his Apostles has taken care that his doctrine be written down, and through his Spirit reveals it to whom, when and how much he wills. Second, (which perhaps will seem surprising to our reader at first sight) we hold the same view as Calvin. For they do not think it can be inferred from the fact that the name Elohim is of the plural number that wherever it is used of God, whether in the first chapter of Genesis or elsewhere, it always signifies three persons. For we freely admit that it sometimes signifies the Father, sometimes the Son, sometimes the Holy Spirit, according to the circumstances of the passages.

units.la: XXXI. Quod ergo, inquiet aliquis, est tuum ex hoc nomine argumentum? Aut quomodo potes ex eo plurali personarum diuinarum pluralitatem colligere, quod de vnica persona vsurpari potuit, & reuera vsurpatur nonnunquam? Id quidem in-itio Disp. xxxvii. exposui, sed vereor ne breuis esse laborans obscurus fuesim[?]. Explicabo igitur quod tum dixi paulò clarius & vberius. Argumentum sic concipi potest. Si plurale nomen Elohim diuinitus impositum est Deo ob pluralitatem personarum diuinarum, necesse est esse plures personas diuinas. Non enim Deus illud nomen sibi ipse imposuit ob rationem falsam & absurdam. Atqui plurale nomen Elohim diuinitus impositum est Deo ob pluralitatem personarum diuinarum. Ergo necesse est esse plures personas diuinas. Negabunt sine dubio Aduersarij minorem. Ea igitur probanda nobis incumbit.
units.tr: XXXI. What, then, will someone say, is your argument from this name? Or how can you infer a plurality of divine persons from a plural which could be, and indeed sometimes is, applied to a single person? I set this out at the beginning of Disputation 37, but I fear that, labouring to be brief, I may have become obscure. I shall therefore explain what I said then a little more clearly and fully. The argument may be framed thus. If the plural name Elohim was imposed on God by divine appointment because of the plurality of divine persons, then there must be several divine persons. For God did not impose that name on himself for a false and absurd reason. But the plural name Elohim was imposed on God by divine appointment because of the plurality of divine persons. Therefore there must be several divine persons. Our opponents will doubtless deny the minor premise. It is therefore incumbent on us to prove it.

units.la: XXXII. Primùm autem non negabunt, plurale illud nomen impositum fuisse Deo significando. Id enim Deus in Scriptura sibi tribuit frequentissimè, immò priùs & frequentius, quàm vllum aliud ex suis nominibus, quorum nullum, præter plurale istud & eius singulare Eloah, (sine vlla comparatione minus vsitatum quàm plurale) Deum, quatenus talis est, si mihi ita loqui liceat, species Entis, significat: El enim interpretantur Fortem, Schaddai Omnipotentem, Adonai Dominum, Eljon supremum vel excelsum, Hu Ipsum, Ehjeh proprie est Ero, Iehouah Erit, Iah est Iehouah contractum, solum plurale istud Elohim & eius singulare Eloah proprie est Deus. Quod enim affirmauit Socinus hoc nomen significare potentes, gubernatores, iudices, id ab eo sine vlla prorsus ratione dictum est. Nullum certè nomen est quo melius exprimatur apud Græcos quàm θεὸς[?] & apud Latinos quàm Deus.
units.tr: XXXII. First, they will not deny that this plural name was given to God to signify him. For Scripture ascribes this name to God very frequently, indeed earlier and more often than any other of his names. None of his names, apart from this plural and its singular Eloah (which is far less in use than the plural, beyond all comparison), signifies God as such, if I may speak so, as a species of being. El means the Strong One, Shaddai the Almighty, Adonai the Lord, Elyon the Supreme or Most High, Hu Himself, Ehyeh properly "I will be," Yahweh "He will be," and Yah is Yahweh contracted. Only this plural Elohim and its singular Eloah properly mean God. As for Socinus's claim that this name signifies powerful ones, rulers, or judges, he asserted it without any reason at all. Certainly there is no name by which God is better expressed among the Greeks than [θεὸς, God], or among the Latins than Deus.

units.la: XXXIII. Non negabunt etiam, opinor, plurale istud nomen Deo impositum fuisse ab ipso Deo, non autem ab hominibus. Primùm enim lingua Hebræa omnium linguarum prima est, confessione omnium Iudæorum & Christianorum, id quod nomina imposita à Deo diei, noƈti, cœlis, terræ, mari, Adamo, &c, ab Adamo Euæ, ab Eua Caino & Setho, ab alijs Patriarchis filijs suis, abundè testantur. Ac propterea Deum habet singulari quadam ratione autorem. Quanquam etiamsi prima non fuisset, sed vna ex illis, quas Deus tunc creauit, cum hominum turrim Babel extruentium linguam confudit, tamen non posset alij, quàm Deo, autori ascribi. Itaque siue prima lingua sit, siue non sit, Deus huius suæ nominationis autor fuit. Deinde impositio nominum argumentum est autoritatis eius qui imponit in eas res quibus imponit. Qua propter Deus voluit Adamum nomina imponere cum Euæ vxori, tum alijs animalibus quorum dominum eum constituerat: præcipuis verò huius mundi partibus cœlo, terræ, mari, luci, tenebris, noluit Deus nomina imponi ab Adamo, sed ipse has partes sibi reservauit, ut intelligeret Adamus, non se, sed Deum mundi dominum esse. Quis igitur credat Deum voluisse sibi Adami & totius mundi domino nomen ab Adamo pro illius arbitrio imponi?
units.tr: XXXIII. I think they will also not deny that this plural name was given to God by God himself, and not by men. For first, the Hebrew language is the first of all languages, by the confession of all Jews and Christians, and the names imposed by God on day, night, heavens, earth, sea, on Adam, and so on, abundantly attest this: names given by Adam to Eve, by Eve to Cain and Seth, and by the other patriarchs to their sons. Therefore God has a unique claim to be its author. Yet even if it were not the first language, but one of those which God then created when he confused the language of the men building the tower of Babel, still it could not be ascribed to any author other than God. So whether it is the first language or not, God was the author of this naming of his. Next, the imposition of names is a proof of the authority of the one who imposes them on the things he names. For this reason God willed that Adam should impose names both on Eve his wife and on the other animals over which he had appointed him lord; but over the principal parts of this world, heaven, earth, sea, light, and darkness, God did not want names to be imposed by Adam, but reserved these parts for himself, so that Adam would understand that it is not he but God who is lord of the world.
