Who then could believe that God willed that his name should be imposed at Adam's discretion by Adam, the lord of Adam and of the whole world?

units.la: XXXIV. Fortasse, inquiet aliquis, Deus sibi nomen impofuit Eloah singulari numero, cuius plurale Elohim non tam divina impositione quàm hominum consuetudine, praesertim eorum qui plures Deos esse putabant, paulatim usurpari coeptum est de Deo. Quominus ita sentiamus obstat Moses, vel potius Deus, qui mundi creationem describens, & colloquium Evae cum serpente, necnon varios sermones primorum Patriarcharum referens plurali Elohim & primùm & frequentissimè utitur, singulari Eloah nunquam. Hoc enim singulare non comparet in quatuor primis libris Mosis, nec in quinto seu ultimo extat, nisi versus finem, ac bis tantummodo; Et, si Iobi librum excipias, in quo legitur quadragies, vix in tota Scriptura vicies occurrit. Ex quo intelligi potest, rarum fuisse apud Israelitas singularis illius usum, & iam ab initio mundi à primis parentibus usurpatum fuisse plurale Elohim Deo sine dubio autore, qui non tam sese & ipse nominavit, & ab hominibus nominari voluit singulari numero Eloah, quàm plurali Elohim. Non est autem quod quis reponat, Deum se nominasse potius Iehouam. Primùm enim id non obstat quominus ab initio sese & ipse appellarit, & ab hominibus appellari voluerit, & appellatus fuerit, Elohim. Deinde nomen Iehouah non significat Deum: alioqui quicunque Deus diceretur, diceretur etiam Ie-houah: sed est proprium nomen Dei Israelis, quo ab omnibus aliis diis distingui voluit; ac propterea, quamvis omnes dij gentium dij appellarentur, tamen eorum nemo Iehouah vocabatur. Cum enim Gentium dij propria nomina haberent, quibus à se invicem discernerentur, voluit etiam Deus sese à diis gentium proprio nomine discerni, quod nomen vulgò legunt Iehouam. Itaque Moses, cum Deus sese Elohim appellasset, intelligens nomen Elohim tanquam commune, Gentium diis tribui solere, proprium nomen scire voluit, quo Deus Israelis ab Ægyptiorum diis internosci posset, Exod. 3. 13. Ex dictis, ut ego arbitror, satis manifestum est, plurale istud Elohim divinitus Deo significando impositum fuisse.
units.tr: XXXIV. Perhaps, someone will say, God gave himself the singular name Eloah, and its plural Elohim came into use gradually for God, not so much by divine imposition as by human custom, especially among those who thought there were several gods. What stands in the way of our holding this view is Moses, or rather God, who, in describing the creation of the world and the conversation of Eve with the serpent, and in recording the various speeches of the first patriarchs, uses the plural Elohim both first and most frequently, and never the singular Eloah. For this singular does not appear in the first four books of Moses, and it occurs in the fifth or last book only near the end and only twice. And, if you except the book of Job, where it is read forty times, it hardly occurs twenty times in the whole of Scripture. From this it can be understood that the use of that singular was rare among the Israelites, and that from the beginning of the world the plural Elohim was used by the first parents, without doubt with God as its author, who named himself, and wished to be named by men, not so much with the singular Eloah as with the plural Elohim. Nor is there any reason for anyone to reply that God named himself rather Jehovah. For first, this does not prevent him from having named himself Elohim from the beginning, and wishing to be called by men, and being called, Elohim. Next, the name Jehovah does not mean God; otherwise whoever was called God would also be called Jehovah. It is the proper name of the God of Israel, by which he willed to be distinguished from all other gods; and therefore, although all the gods of the nations were called gods, none of them was called Jehovah. For since the gods of the nations had proper names by which they were distinguished from one another, God also willed to be distinguished from the gods of the nations by a proper name, which people commonly read as Jehovah. Thus Moses, when God had called himself Elohim, understanding that the name Elohim is common and usually given to the gods of the nations, wished to know a proper name by which the God of Israel could be distinguished from the gods of the Egyptians, Exod. 3:13. From what has been said, as I judge, it is sufficiently clear that this plural Elohim was given to God by divine appointment as a signifying name.

units.la: XXXV. Impositum est autem sine dubio non temerè & sine ratione, sed prudenter admodum, & ob rationem aliquam memorabilem. Id quod etiam ab Aduersarijs negatum iri non puto. Cum enim homines rei singulari nomen pluralis numeri imponere non soleant, præsertim cum res est vna per se & simplex, causam subesse oportet grauem, cur Deo qui natura sua maxime singularis est, & vnus, & simplex, nomen impositum fuerit pluralis numeri. Videbatur enim vnitati naturæ diuinæ conuenire magis numerus singularis quàm pluralis. Cur igitur in nominando Deo pluralis numerus antepositus sit singulari, & quidem ab ipso Deo, causam aliquam esse necesse est dignam nostra inquisitione. Non enim id potuit Deo excidisse imprudenti.
units.tr: XXXV. It was indeed imposed, without doubt, not rashly and without reason, but with great prudence and for some notable reason. I do not think our opponents will deny this either. For since men do not usually impose a plural name on a singular thing, especially when the thing is one in itself and simple, there must be some weighty cause why a plural name was given to God, who by his nature is most singular, and one, and simple. For the singular number seemed to fit the unity of the divine nature better than the plural. Therefore, why the plural number is placed before the singular in naming God, and indeed by God himself, there must be some cause worthy of our investigation. For this cannot have slipped from God by thoughtless inadvertence.

units.la: XXXVI. Accedat lector ad legendam Scripturam ut Dei cognitionem adipiscatur, qua nihil potest esse optabilius homini. Occurret ei statim in primo capite, in primo versu plurale istud Elohim. Putabit autem sine dubio hoc nomen sibi ante omnia expendendum esse. Non nihil enim ad rei nominatæ cognitionem conferre solet nominis prudenter impositi consideratio. Agnoscet igitur statim, & mirabitur, nomen esse pluralis numeri, huiusque rei causam inquiret. Animadvertet etiam nomen illud plurale construi cum verbo singulari, quam anomaliam mirabitur esse tam frequentem, plusquam enim tricies recurrit in primo capite Scripturæ. Vbi autem ad secundum accesserit, augebit admirationem huius nominis pluralis cum singulari Jehou[illegible, ~2 letters] frequens coniunctio. Ita enim duæ res quæ simul consistere non[?] posse videntur simul copulantur, unitas & multitudo, singularitas & pluralitas. Fit autem ad istam admirationem accessio aliqua ex rei huius insolentia. Quæ enim alia res, una perse cum sit, gaudet nomine plurali? Quæ alia res solet significari nomine plurali ferè perpetuò constructo cum verbo numeri pluralis? Quæ alia res solet duobus nominibus coniunctis appellari, quorum unum fit numeri singularis, alterum pluralis? Quis credat divino auctori ista excidisse temerè & sine ratione? Quis non agnoscat ea in re aliquid mysterij latere?
units.tr: XXXVI. Let the reader come to read Scripture so that he may attain the knowledge of God, than which nothing can be more desirable for man. At once, in the first chapter, in the first verse, he will meet this plural Elohim. He will doubtless think that this name must be considered before all else. For consideration of a name wisely given usually contributes something to knowledge of the thing named. He will therefore at once recognise, and be amazed, that the name is plural, and he will inquire into the cause of this. He will also notice that this plural name is construed with a singular verb, and he will wonder that this anomaly is so frequent, for it recurs more than thirty times in the first chapter of Scripture alone. But when he comes to the second chapter, the frequent conjunction of this plural name with the singular Jehovah will increase his amazement. Thus two things which seem unable to exist together are joined at once: unity and plurality, singularity and plurality. Moreover, some addition to this amazement arises from the strangeness of the thing. What other thing, since it is one in itself, enjoys a plural name? What other thing is usually signified by a plural name, almost always construed with a verb of the plural number? What other thing is usually called by two names joined together, one of the singular number and the other of the plural? Who would believe that these were let slip by the divine author rashly and without reason? Who would not acknowledge that some mystery lies hidden in this matter?

units.la: XXXVII. Noli mihi objicere pluralia, Adonim, & Baalim. Illa enim non sunt nomina uni alicui rei singulari impositæ. Illa significant formaliter relationes, quæ sunt in uno homine non ratò plures, quæque respectu eiusdem serui potuerunt esse, & divisæ inter plures dominos, & veluti collectæ & multiplicatæ in uno. Illa non solent ferè semper construi cum verbo singularis numeri. Illa non iunguntur cum nomine singularis numeri, ut duobus eius-modi nominibus, uno singulari altero plurali, tanquam nomine proprio, res aliqua singularis significetur. Illa non dicuntur de uno homine frequenter, & modò sine modò cum affixis; sed, & rarò, & non sine affixis; ac nisi plures essent domini, pluralia illa in rerum natura non extitissent. Illa denique pluralia nemo de seipso, aut de eo quem alloquitur usurpat in Scriptura, sed tantum de tertio.
units.tr: XXXVII. Do not object to me the plurals Adonim and Baalim. For these are not names imposed on some single singular thing. They formally signify relations, which are in one man, not rarely several, and which with respect to the same servant could be divided among several masters, and as it were gathered and multiplied in one. They do not usually, almost always, get construed with a verb of the singular number. They are not joined with a noun of the singular number, as with two such names, one singular and the other plural, as with a proper name, so that some singular thing is signified. They are not said of one man frequently, and sometimes with and sometimes without suffixes, but rarely, and not without suffixes; and unless there were several masters, these plurals would not have existed in the nature of things. Finally, no one in Scripture uses these plurals of himself, or of the one he addresses, but only of a third person.

units.la: XXXVIII. Cum igitur id factum non sit nisi ob grauem aliquam causam, in eam diligenter inquirendum est. Non enim Id frustrà Deus nobis ob oculos constituit, & quidem tam sæpè. Id factum fuisse dicunt Aduersarij honoris causa. Afferunt-ne probationem aliquam ? nullam prorsus. Judæos ea in re sequuntur male sentientes. Id jam à nobis, & quidem bis, refutatum est. Nec potest firmari exemplo modernarum linguarum, non modò quia ex illis æstimari non debet antiqua illa, & jam inde ab initio mundi usurpata lingua Hebræa, sed etiam quia nihil est simile. Agitur enim de nomine plurali Deo, & quidem ante omnia alia nomina impositio. Est-ne in ulla lingua mos uni rei singulari nomen plurale imponendi honoris causa ? tantum abest ut id fiat, ut ne quidem quisquam honoris gratia appellari soleat nomine plurali. Omnis iste honos in verbis & pronominibus poni solet, nunquam in nomine, quo compellatur, nisi forte cum utimur nomine abstracto. Hic autem contrà est. Verba & pronomina sunt ferè semper singularis numeri, nomen pluralis. Deinde utimur plurali numero aut de nobis ipsis, aut de eo quem compellamus, aut de tertio. De nobis numero multitudinis loquimur, non honoris, sed modestiæ causa. Etiam reges, (qui nunquam se nomine pluralis numeri appellant) cum verba de se & pronomina pluralia usurpant modestius loqui videntur, durius & majori cum ostentatione auctori-tatis cum usurpant singularia. Alios verò compellamus verbis & pronominibus numeri pluralis honorandi eos gratia: At cum de illis in tertia persona loquimur, nunquam utimur plurali. Hic verò fit aliter: nam quicunque loquuntur, seu Deus de semetipso, seu homines de Deo, vel ad Deum, illi in Scriptura plurali nomine Elohim uti solent constructo cum verbis & pronominibus singularis numeri. Id quod ab earum linguarum, quæ hodie obtinent, consuetudine valdè abhorret. Nomina etiam Adon & Baal, ut jam observavi, non usurpantur numero multitudinis de uno homine nisi in tertia persona. Nemo alium hominem nominibus illis compellat numero plurali. Solus Deus nomine plurali Adonai compellatur in Scriptura. Id eius proprium est. Adiunguntur autem illi plurali verba & pronomina singularis numeri.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Since this was done only for some weighty reason, we must inquire carefully into that reason. God would not have set this before our eyes so often without cause. Our opponents say it was done out of honour. Do they offer any proof? None at all. In this they follow the Jews, who think poorly of the matter. We have already refuted this, and twice. Nor can it be supported by the example of modern languages. Not only should that ancient Hebrew language, used from the beginning of the world, be judged by none of them, but there is also no real likeness. The matter concerns a plural noun imposed on God, and before all other names. Is there any language in which it is customary to give a single thing a plural name out of honour? Far from it: no one is ever addressed by a plural noun as a mark of respect. Such honour is usually expressed in verbs and pronouns, never in the noun by which someone is addressed, unless perhaps when we use an abstract noun. Here, however, the reverse holds. Verbs and pronouns are almost always singular, while the noun is plural. Moreover, we use the plural number either of ourselves, or of the person we address, or of a third person. We speak of ourselves in the plural of multitude, not out of honour but out of modesty. Even kings, who never call themselves by a plural noun, seem to speak more modestly when they use plural verbs and pronouns of themselves, and more harshly and with greater display of authority when they use singular ones. We address others with plural verbs and pronouns to honour them, but when we speak of them in the third person we never use the plural. Here, however, it is otherwise: whoever speaks, whether God of himself or men of God or to God, uses the plural noun Elohim in Scripture, joined with verbs and pronouns of the singular number. This is strongly contrary to the usage of the languages that prevail today. The names Adon and Baal, as I have already observed, are not used in the plural number of one man except in the third person. No one addresses another man with those names in the plural. Only God is addressed in Scripture with the plural name Adonai. This is peculiar to him. Yet with that plural they join verbs and pronouns of the singular number.

units.la: XXXIX. Denique in hodiernis linguis vernaculis, quos honoris causa compellamus, adhibitis, non iam nominibus, (id enim per absurdum haberetur.) Sed verbis & pronominibus pluralis numeri, eos perpetuò eodem modo compellamus. Si igitur honoris causa & nomina, & verba & adiectiva & pronomina usurparentur de Deo numero plurali, id semper fieret, aut saltem frequentissimè: semper enim honorandus est Deus, loquendumque & de eo, & ad eum admodum honorificè. Nam si eiusmodi pluralibus honore afficitur Deus, privatur is profectò debito honore, cum de eo, vel ad eum loquimur usurpato solo singulari numero, & mirum est eiusmodi honore eum fuisse in Novo Testamento à Christo, ab Apostolis & Evangelistis, à tota Ecclesia primis post promulgatum Evangelium seculis omnino privatum. Non est autem quod quis hoc argumentum existimet in nos ipsos posse retorqueri, hoc pacto. Si nomina, verba, pronomina & adiectiva, ob pluralitatem personarum divinarum plurali numero usurpantur de Deo, ea eodem illo numero usurpanda fuerunt de Deo aut semper, aut saepissimè ob eandem illam causam: quoniam semper pluralitas personarum convenit Deo. Non enim par est ratio. Nam honorandus est Deus semper. Nunquam de eo loquendum est aliter quàm honorificentissimè. Nunquam homines eum alloqui debent nisi cum summa reverentia, summo honore. At non fuit necesse dogma de Trinitate personarum divinarum ubique inculcari. Satis fuit illud certis locis modò apertiùs doceri, modò obscuriùs insinuari, prout visum fuit sapientiae divinae mysteria religionis Christianae in Veteris Testamenti variis locis varie revelare.
units.tr: XXXIX. Finally, in the vernacular languages of today, when we address those whom we honour, we do not use nouns (for that would be thought absurd), but verbs and pronouns of the plural number, and we always address them in this same way. If, then, nouns, verbs, adjectives and pronouns were used of God in the plural number out of honour, this would always happen, or at least very often, for God must always be honoured, and we must speak of him and to him in a very honourable manner. For if God were honoured in this way with plurals, he would certainly be deprived of due honour whenever we speak of or to him using only the singular number. And it is remarkable that in the New Testament he was entirely deprived of such honour by Christ, by the Apostles and Evangelists, and by the whole Church in the first centuries after the Gospel was published. Nor should anyone think that this argument can be turned back against us in the following way: if nouns, verbs, pronouns and adjectives are used in the plural of God on account of the plurality of the divine persons, then they ought to be used in that same plural of God always, or very often, for the same reason, since the plurality of persons always belongs to God. The reasoning is not the same. God must always be honoured. He must never be spoken of except in the most honourable terms, and men must never address him except with the greatest reverence and the highest honour. But it was not necessary that the doctrine of the Trinity of the divine persons be inculcated everywhere. It was enough that it be taught more openly in certain places, and hinted at more obscurely in others, as the wisdom of God chose to reveal the mysteries of the Christian religion in various ways in the various passages of the Old Testament.

units.la: XL. Jam igitur, opinor, constat, Deo nomen Elohim plurali potius quàm singulari numero tributum fuisse, non simpliciter honoris causa, sed ob aliam causam, quae alia esse non potest quàm pluralitas quaedam. Quid enim aliud significari possit numero plurali quàm pluralitas? Non enim differt à singulari nisi pluralitate. Dent nobis Adversarij si possunt aliam causam, ob quam plu[?]alis numerus potius quàm singularis tribuendus Deo fuerit. Nulla profectò alia animo concipi potest. Ob quam igitur pluralitatem Deus plurali numero appellari potuit & debuit Elohim? Profectò sic appellari non potuit ob aliam causam, quàm ob pluralitatem personarum.
units.tr: XL. Now, I think, it is established that the name Elohim was ascribed to God in the plural rather than the singular number, not simply out of honour but for another reason, which can be none other than a certain plurality. For what else can be signified by the plural number but plurality? It differs from the singular only by plurality. Let our opponents give us another reason, if they can, for which the plural number rather than the singular should have been ascribed to God. Certainly none other can be conceived in the mind. For what plurality, then, could Elohim have been called and ought to have been called God by the plural number? Surely it could not have been so called for any other reason than the plurality of persons.

units.la: XLI. Primùm enim alia nulla pluralitas idonea causa esse potuit huius appel-lationis. Non pluralitas relationum. Relationem enim nomen Elohim non significat. Alioqui Deus non fuisset ab æterno Elohim, id est, Deus. Antecedit etiam ista Dei appellatio in Scriptura omnem creaturæ ad quam Deus referri potuisset mentionem. vocatur quidem Deus Abrahami, Isaaci, & Jacobi, Deus Israëlis, Deus exercituum, sed quemadmodum nemo inde colliget, Abrahamum, Isaacum, Jacobum &c, proprie loquendo esse correlata, sic nemo colligere poterit, Elohim seu Deum esse relatum. Sic cum aliquis in Scriptura dicitur homo Dei, ineptus esset, qui inde confici posse putaret, hominem signi-ficare relationem. Addequod nemo unquam ob pluralitatem relationum plurali nomine appellatur. Erant Davidi plures filij filiæque, Salomoni plures uxores, Regi Persarum plura regna, num propterea vocati sunt plurali numero David patres, Salomon mariti, rex Persarum reges? Nimirum patres, mariti, reges, aliaque relationum nomina, ut loquuntur, concreta, pluralitatem significant non relationum, sed personarum in quibus relationes insunt.
units.tr: XLI. For, first, no other plurality could have been a suitable cause of this appellation. Not a plurality of relations. For the name Elohim does not signify a relation. Otherwise God would not have been Elohim, that is, God, from eternity. This appellation of God also precedes in Scripture any mention of a creature to which God might have been referred. God is indeed called the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God of Israel, the God of hosts; but just as no one infers from this that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob are, properly speaking, correlatives, so no one can infer that Elohim, or God, is related. So too, when someone in Scripture is called a man of God, it would be foolish to think that it follows from this that man signifies a relation. Moreover, no one is ever called by a plural name because of a plurality of relations. David had several sons and daughters, Solomon several wives, the King of Persia several kingdoms; were they therefore called fathers, husbands and kings in the plural, David fathers, Solomon husbands, the King of Persia kings? Clearly the nouns fathers, husbands, kings and other names of relations, as they are called, when concrete, signify a plurality not of relations but of the persons in whom the relations inhere.

units.la: XLII. Idem dicendum est de multitudine operationum. Nam neque nomen Elohim formaliter operatione significat, neq; multitudo operationum efficere potest, ut plurali nomine quisquam unus & singularis aut appelletur, aut appellari possit. Itaq; nemo ob multitudinem creationum Deum appellauerit creatores, aut ob multitudinem judiciorum judices, aut ob multitudinem actionum causas vel agentes. Nimirum nomina illa & similia non significant pluralitatem operationum, sed eorum, unde operationes proficiscuntur.
units.tr: XLII. The same must be said of a multitude of operations. For the name Elohim does not signify operation formally, nor can a multitude of operations bring it about that anyone who is one and single is, or can be, called by a plural name. Therefore no one has called God creators because of a multitude of creations, or judges because of a multitude of judgments, or causes or agents because of a multitude of actions. Clearly such names and similar ones do not signify a plurality of operations, but of those from which the operations proceed.

units.la: XLIII. Idem etiam existimandum est de multitudine potentiarum aut proprietatum. Non puto Elohim formaliter significare potentiam, sed deitatem: sic enim apud Græcos nomen Θεὸς [?] significat Θεότης [?], & apud Latinos nomen Deus significat deitatem. sed fac significare potentiam, ut loquuntur, in concreto, quemadmodum qui potentem dicit singulari numero, personam dicit præditam potentia; sic qui potentes dicit plurali numero, personas dicit præditas potentia. Perpetuò eiusmodi nomina, cum numero multitudinis efferuntur, multitudinem seu pluralitatem significant suppositorum seu personarum. Itaque Deus sibi potius abstractum nomen indidisset quàm concretum, si eius plurali pluralitatem potentiarum, aut actionum, aut relationum significare voluisset.
units.tr: XLIII. The same must also be thought of a multitude of powers or properties. I do not think Elohim signifies power formally, but deity: for among the Greeks the name theos [Θεὸς] signifies theotes [Θεότης], and among the Latins the name Deus signifies deity. But grant that it signifies power, as they say, in the concrete; just as one who says "powerful" in the singular speaks of a person endowed with power, so one who says "powerful" in the plural speaks of persons endowed with power. Such names, whenever they are put in the plural number, always signify a multitude or plurality of supposits or persons. Hence God would rather have given himself an abstract name than a concrete one, if by its plural he had wished to signify a plurality of powers, or of actions, or of relations.

units.la: XLIV. Deinde hoc ipsum sic potest confirmari. Quam rem nomen aliquod in singulari numero significat, eius rei pluralitatem idem nomen in plurali numero significare necesse est, siquidem retinet nomen plurale singularis sui significationem. Atqui nomen Eloah in singulari numero significat personam diuinam. Ergo idem nomen in plurali numero significare necesse est pluralitatem personarum diuinarum. retinet enim sui singularis significationem, nihilque ei addit præter pluralitatem. Eodem, inquiet aliquis, argumento probabo plurale Elohim significare pluralitatem Deorum. Nam si singulare significat Deum, certè plurale significat Deos. Prius autem est verum. Ergò & posterius. Quid autem, inquam, intelligis per Deum? Nonne personam diuinam? personam præditam natura diuina? Ergo per Deos intelligis personas diuinas, personas præditas natura diuina. Hactenus igitur objectio ab argumento nostro nihil differt. Iam autem personæ diuinæ seu diuina natura præditæ duobus modis concipi possunt: uno tanquam præditæ diuersis naturis: altero, tanquam præditæ eadem natura. Cum de diis gentium agitur, quoniam illi tanquam personæ diuersis naturis præditæ concipiebantur, significat singulare Eloah, Deum, hoc est, personam ab omni alia persona diuina diuersam natura, ac propterea plurale Elohim significat plures personas diuinas naturis diuersas, id est, plures Deos. At cum de personis verè diuinis agitur, quoniam illæ concipi debent tanquam præditæ eadem natura diuina, significat singulare Eloah Deum, hoc est, personam præditam diuina natura, non diuersâ ab ea, qua præditæ sunt aliæ personæ diuinæ, sed eâdem, ac propterea plurale Elohim significat plures personas eadem diuina natura præditas. id quod non est significare plures deos, sed plures personas quæ sint unus Deus. Illud igitur negari non potest, nomen Elohim plurali numero aliam pluralitatem significare non posse quàm personarum, siue personæ illæ naturis diuersis prædita sint, siue eâdem. Plures autem duabus personas illas esse necesse est: Elohim enim duale non est, sed plurale.
units.tr: XLIV. Further, this very point can be confirmed in the following way. Whatever thing a noun signifies in the singular number, the same noun in the plural must signify the plurality of that thing, since a plural noun retains the signification of its singular. But the name Eloah in the singular signifies a divine person. Therefore the same name in the plural must signify a plurality of divine persons, for it retains the signification of its singular and adds nothing to it except plurality. By the same argument, someone will say, I will prove that the plural Elohim signifies a plurality of gods. For if the singular signifies God, the plural certainly signifies gods. But the first is true; therefore the second is too. But what, I ask, do you understand by God? Surely a divine person, a person endowed with the divine nature? Then by gods you understand divine persons, persons endowed with the divine nature. So far, then, the objection differs in no way from our argument. Now divine persons, or those endowed with the divine nature, can be conceived in two ways: in one, as endowed with different natures; in the other, as endowed with the same nature. When we are dealing with the gods of the nations, since those were conceived as persons endowed with different natures, the singular Eloah signifies God, that is, a person differing in nature from every other divine person, and therefore the plural Elohim signifies several divine persons differing in nature, that is, several gods. But when we are dealing with persons who are truly divine, since they must be conceived as endowed with one and the same divine nature, the singular Eloah signifies God, that is, a person endowed with the divine nature, not a nature different from that which the other divine persons have, but the same; and therefore the plural Elohim signifies several persons endowed with the same divine nature. This is not to signify several gods, but several persons who are one God. It cannot therefore be denied that the plural name Elohim, in the plural number, cannot signify any plurality other than that of persons, whether those persons are endowed with different natures or with the same. But those persons must be more than two, for Elohim is not a dual but a plural.

units.la: XLV. Accedit ad superiora hoc quoque argumentum, quod cum hoc nomine res ipsa conspirat. Apparent enim in Scriptura plures personæ diuinæ, & quidem in ipso primo libro Mosis. Non reponam hoc loco ea loca & argumenta quæ jam laudaui. Gen. cap. 16. V. 10. Dixit ad eam Angelus Domini: multiplicando multiplicabo semen tuum, & non numerabitur pra multitudine. Hic duæ apparent personæ distinctæ. vna vocatur Dominus, vulgò Iehoua. altera Angelus Domini. Prior sine dubio est persona diuina. Posteriorem etiam personam diuinam esse probant; Primò eius verba, multiplicando multiplicabo semen tuum. quis enim ita loqui verè possit, præter vnum Deum naturæ & gratiæ authorem? Deinde verba Agaris XVI. 13. Et vocauit nomen Domini (Iehouæ) loquentis cum ea Tu Deus (Heb. El) vides me. Qui igitur cum ea loquebatur idem Angelus Domini erat & Dominus ac Deus. Sunt ergo plures personæ communi nomine Domini & Dei prædituæ.
units.tr: XLV. This argument also agrees with the previous ones, because the thing itself agrees with this name. Several divine persons appear in Scripture, and indeed in the very first book of Moses. I will not repeat here the passages and arguments I have already cited. Gen. 16. 10: The angel of the Lord said to her: I will multiply your seed exceedingly, and it shall not be numbered for multitude. Here two distinct persons appear. One is called the Lord, in the common version Iehoua; the other is the Angel of the Lord. The first is without doubt a divine person. That the second is also a divine person they prove, first from his words, I will multiply your seed exceedingly. For who could truly speak like this except the one God, the author of nature and of grace? Next, from the words of Hagar at 16. 13: And she called the name of the Lord (Iehoua) who spoke with her, You are God (Heb. El) who sees me. So the one who was speaking with her was both the Angel of the Lord and the Lord and God. There are therefore several persons, each bearing the common name of Lord and God.

units.la: XLVI. Confugient-ne iterum Aduersarij ad suam illam responsionem iam aliquoties à nobis refutatam, Angelum illum sustinuisse personam Dei, itaque & Deum & Dominum appellatum fuisse; necnon ita locutum, ac si reuera fuisset Deus. At quid erit tam disertum tamque perspicuum quod non possit ea ratione eludi? Aut quo argumento poterit persona aliqua probari diuina esse, si tam, vt loquuntur, formalia & expressa testimonia non sufficiunt? Ecquis non videt personas illas tam aperte distingui, vt confundi non debeant? Cum dicitur Angelus Domini dixit ad eam, multiplicando multiplicabo, &c, persona Angeli distinguitur aperte à persona Domini cuius fuit Angelus, quis ergo credat Angelum illum loqui non tanquam Angelum Domini, sed tanquam illam ipsam personam cuius dicitur Angelus? Quis credat eum deposita Angeli Domini persona, assumptaque Domini illius persona cuius angelus appellatur, id dixisse quod dixit? Quis credat cum vocatur Dominus & Deus, per Dominum & Deum eandem personam intelligi cuius dicitur Angelus? Quæ hæc esset personæ missæ & mittentis confusio? Quid? cum Angelus inducitur dicens, Ego sum Iehoua, Ego sum Deus Abrahami &c, vt fit nonnunquam, num sensus est, Ego sum illa persona cuius dicor An-gelus, Ego is sum à quo sum missus, & à quo venio nuntius? Ita Scriptura non sine aperta falsitatis & contradictionis specie personas relativè oppositas tribueret eidem eodem tempore. Cur Scriptura sic loquitur. Et dixit Angelus Domini ad eam: multiplicando multiplicabo semen tuum, nisi ut doceat verba illa, multiplicando multiplicabo &c, esse verba Angeli Domini? & cur docet esse verba Angeli Domini, nisi ut doceat Angelum Domini eum esse qui multiplicando multiplicaturus erat semen Agaris? Quod si hoc docere noluit Spiritus Sanctus, cur igitur non dixit simpliciter, Et dixit Dominus ad eam? Cur illius qui hoc dicit multiplicando multiplicabo &c personam describit, si is ex sua illa persona, quae describitur, hoc non dicit? Quorsum enim illa descriptio personae hoc dicentis ad Agarem pertinuisset, nisi ut videretur falsò sibi tribuere id quod sibi non convenibat? Nam si hoc non dicit ex persona Angeli Domini, sed ex persona illius ipsius Domini cuius appellatur Angelus, quis non videt inter descriptionem personae quae hoc dicit & eius verba pugnam quandam intercedere, minimeque servari decorum personae, quae loquens inducitur?
units.tr: XLVI. Will our opponents once again take refuge in their familiar answer, which we have already refuted many times, that the angel sustained the person of God, and so was called God and Lord, and spoke as if he were really God? But what is so clear and plain that it cannot be evaded in this way? Or by what argument can any person be shown to be divine, if such formal and express testimonies, as they call them, are not enough? Who does not see that these persons are so plainly distinguished that they must not be confused? When it is said, The Angel of the Lord said to her, I will multiply exceedingly, etc., the person of the Angel is clearly distinguished from the person of the Lord whose Angel he was. Who then could believe that the Angel spoke not as the Angel of the Lord, but as that very person whose Angel he is called? Who could believe that, laying aside the person of the Angel of the Lord and assuming the person of the Lord whose angel he is called, he said what he said? Who could believe that when he is called Lord and God, by Lord and God is meant the same person of whom he is called the Angel? What confusion of the sent and the sender would this be? Again, when the Angel is introduced saying, I am Iehoua, I am the God of Abraham, etc., as sometimes happens, does the sense become, I am that person whose Angel I am called, I am he by whom I am sent and from whom I come as messenger? In this way Scripture would ascribe opposed relative persons to the same being at the same time, with the appearance of plain falsehood and contradiction. Why does Scripture speak thus: And the Angel of the Lord said to her: I will multiply your seed exceedingly, unless to teach that those words, I will multiply exceedingly, are the words of the Angel of the Lord? And why does it teach that they are the words of the Angel of the Lord, unless to teach that the Angel of the Lord is the one who was to multiply the seed of Hagar? But if the Holy Spirit did not wish to teach this, why did he not simply say, And the Lord said to her? Why does he describe the person of the one who says I will multiply exceedingly, if he is not saying it out of that person which is described? For what would the description of the person who says this to Hagar have served, unless to make it appear that he falsely claimed for himself what did not belong to him? For if he does not speak in the person of the Angel of the Lord, but in the person of that very Lord whose Angel he is called, who does not see that there is a certain conflict between the description of the person who speaks and his words, and that the propriety of the person introduced as speaking is hardly preserved?

units.la: XLVII. Objiciet mihi forsitan aliquis exemplum Mosis, qui Deut. 11..14. 15. loquitur quasi esset Deus. Dabo, inquit, pluviam terrae vestrae in tempore suo &c. Dabo quoque herbam in agro tuo &c. versio Graeca & vulgata Latina habent in tertia persona Dabit, sed in textu hebraeo est נתתי [?] Et dabo. Si Moses eo loco assumpsit personam Dei, & loquutus est ut Deus, cur non potuit similiter Angelus Domini assumere personam Domini & loqui ut Dominus? Hanc objectionem in libris Adversariorum non legi, sed, ut alibi dixi, veritatis causâ scribo non victoriae. Non dicam subaudiri verba, dicit Dominus, calore dicendi, ut ita dicam, absumpta. Dicam hoc ipsum confirmare fidem nostram de divina Domini nostri natura. Eius enim Moses insignis typus fuit. Typo autem nonnunquam id tribuitur quod ei non convenit, sed rei tantùm significatae, ut patet ex 2. Sam. 7. 13. 14. Psal. 45. aliisque multis locis. Qualis igitur Moses fuit typicè talis esse debuit Christus reapse, qualis ille fuit umbratiliter talis hic fuit corporaliter. Concurrerunt quidem duo genera typorum ad eum mediatorem Dei & hominum adumbrandum Angeli & Homines, inprimis Moses. Illi eum adumbrarunt secundum eius naturam diuinam, hi secundum eius naturam humanam potissimùm. vt autem duarum illarum naturarum vnio personalis, quoad eius fieri potuit, etiam in Mose adumbraretur, Primùm iubetur sic dicere filijs Israëlis Exod. 3. 14. Ero[?] misit me ad vos, primam & tertiam personam simul copulans, vt innueret se illum qui futurus erat aliquomodo & esse & non esse: esse typicè & non esse reipsa: Illum autem, qui futurus erat, Deum Israëlis esse. Deinde Exod. 4. 16. Tu, dicit ei Deus, eris ei, nempe Aaroni, in Deum, & Exod. 7. 1. Ecce constitui te Deum Pharaoni, & Aaron frater tuus erit Propheta tuus. Denique hoc loco ipse Moses, quasi is esset quem adumbrabat, dabo, inquit, vobis pluuiam in tempore. sic in hoc Christi veri mediatoris typo nota quædam diuinitatis, sed, vt umbram decuit, obscura & umbratilis micuit.
units.tr: XLVII. Perhaps someone will object to me the example of Moses, who at Deut. 11. 14, 15 speaks as if he were God: I will give, he says, rain to your land in its season, etc. I will also give grass in your field, etc. The Greek version and the Latin Vulgate have the third person, he will give, but in the Hebrew text it is נתתי [I will give]. If Moses there assumed the person of God and spoke as God, why could the Angel of the Lord not similarly assume the person of the Lord and speak as the Lord? I have not read this objection in the books of our opponents, but, as I have said elsewhere, I write for the sake of truth and not for the sake of victory. I will not say that the words the Lord says are understood, and dropped through the heat of speaking, so to speak. I will say that this very thing confirms our faith concerning the divine nature of our Lord. For Moses was a notable type of him. Now to a type is sometimes ascribed what does not belong to it, but only to the thing signified, as is clear from 2 Sam. 7. 13, 14, Ps. 45, and many other places. Therefore what Moses was in type, Christ had to be in reality; what Moses was in shadow, Christ was in body. Indeed two kinds of types came together to foreshadow that mediator between God and men: angels and men, above all Moses. The angels foreshadowed him according to his divine nature, men chiefly according to his human nature. And so that the personal union of those two natures might, as far as possible, be foreshadowed even in Moses, first he is commanded to say to the sons of Israel, Exod. 3. 14: "I will be" has sent me to you, joining the first and third persons together, so as to signify that he who was to come would in some way both be and not be: be in type, and not be in reality; and that he who was to come was the God of Israel. Then Exod. 4. 16: You, God says to him, shall be to him, namely to Aaron, as God, and Exod. 7. 1: Behold, I have made you God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. Finally in this passage Moses himself, as if he were the one whom he foreshadowed, says, I will give you rain in its season. Thus in this type of Christ, the true mediator, a certain mark of divinity shines forth, but, as befits a shadow, dim and shadowy.

units.la: XLVIII. Vtar alio exemplo ex eadem Genesi petito cap. XIX. v. 24. Et Dominus pluit super Sodomam & Gomorrham ignem & sulphur à Domino è cælo. In his verbis persona quæ pluit distinguitur à persona à qua pluit, gaudetque vtraque communi Domini seu Iehouæ nomine. Si negas, doce igitur quare sit hoc additum, à Iehoua. Nonne enim verbis illis, Iehoua pluit, satis significatum fuerat, pluuiam illam profectam fuisse à Iehoua? Cur igitur non contentus dixisse Iehoua pluit, subjunxit à Iehoua? frustrà hoc additum est hoc loco quod alibi non legitur additum, quodque adeò cum sit rarissimum non potest non afficere lectorem? solent enim quæ sunt admodum rara diligentiùs considerari & majore in pretio haberi, quàm quæ minùs rara sunt.
units.tr: XLVIII. I will use another example taken from the same Genesis, chapter 19, verse 24: And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah fire and sulphur from the Lord out of heaven. In these words the person who rains is distinguished from the person from whom he rains, and both bear the common name of Lord or Iehoua. If you deny this, then explain why this was added, from Iehoua. For did the words Iehoua rained not sufficiently signify that the rain came from Iehoua? Why then, not content with saying Iehoua rained, did he add from Iehoua? This addition in this place is pointless, since it is not found added elsewhere; and because it is so very rare, it cannot fail to strike the reader. For things that are very rare are usually considered more carefully and held in higher regard than those that are less rare.

units.la: Significat, Inquies, Iehouam pluisse à seipso. scilicet verendum erat, ne putaretur Iehoua pluisse ab alio quàm à Iehoua! Sepositâ distinctione personarum diuinarum quorsum hæc observatio pertinere possit non intelligo. Dices eó pertinere, vt innuatur, Iehouam pluisse à seipso immediatè. Dixisset igitur, inquam, potius per Iehouam quàm à Iehoua. hæc enim locutio non est comparata ad excludendas causas instrumentales, nihilque prohibet, quominus Deus dicatur facere aliquid à seipso per angelos aut homines. Ioh. 10. 18. Pono, inquit Dominus, animam meam à me ipso. Hocne dicit vt excludat causas instrumentales, Iudæos & Romanos? 2. Chron.. xi. 4. à me facta est hæc res, quæ tamen facta fuerat per decem tribus Israëlis. Ac ne aliaexempla conquiramus, non est credibile sacrum historicum mi-nisterium eorum Angelorum excludere voluisse, qui se missos profitentur à Domino ad perdendam Sodomam hoc ipso cap. Gen. 19. V. 13. Omnino quoquo se vertant Aduersarij idoneam rationem afferre non poterunt, cur sit additum מאת יהוה πυρ̀ ωσεί, à Domino, Gallicè de la part du Seigneur. Fatendum est igitur duas personas diuinas innui, quarum vna pluit ignem & sulphur ab altera. Distinguuntur efficiendi modo & loco. Pluit enim vna ab altera, atque adeò haec per illam siue mediante illa. Pluit illa apparens in terra aut iuxta terram, haec verò sedens in coelo. Nam ex tribus illis viris qui Abrahamo apparuerant, ille qui, & Dominus appellatur, & loquitur tanquam iudex mundi, non legitur cum duobus alijs ingressus esse Sodomam & exceptus hospitio à Lotho, sed videtur Lotho è Sodoma educto apparuisse, atque eum fuisse quem Lothus precatur V. 19. & 20. quique, vt Dominum decebat, eum exaudit V. 21. Hoc autem totum sic prudentissimè scriptum est, vt extaret in ea historia typus vel specimen, vel, vt loquitur Iudas, ὑπόδειγμα, aut, vt ait Petrus, πρόδειγμα futuri impiorum iudicij. Descendet enim è coelo Filius, cui Pater omne iudicium dedit, isque à Patre suo destruet omnes impios igne aeterno ac sulphure. vt igitur hac quoque in parte typus & res adumbrata, aut si mauis specimen & id cuius est specimen sibi mutuò, vt par erat, responderent, duae personae inducendae fuerunt, quarum altera iudicium illud exerceret ab altera, Filius nempe à Patre.
units.tr: You will say that it means Iehoua rained from himself. Surely it had to be feared that someone might think Iehoua rained from something other than Iehoua! Setting aside the distinction of the divine persons, I do not understand what this remark could have to do with the matter. You will say it is there to indicate that Iehoua rained from himself immediately. Then, I reply, he would have said through Iehoua rather than from Iehoua. For this phrase is not framed to exclude instrumental causes, and nothing prevents God from being said to do something from himself through angels or men. John 10. 18: I lay down my life, says the Lord, from myself. Does he say this to exclude instrumental causes, the Jews and the Romans? 2 Chron. 11. 4: This thing is done from me, though it had in fact been done through the ten tribes of Israel. And, not to seek further examples, it is not credible that the sacred historian wished to exclude the ministry of those angels who profess to have been sent by the Lord to destroy Sodom in this very chapter, Gen. 19. 13. In any case, whichever way the opponents turn, they will not be able to give a suitable reason why the phrase מאת יהוה [from the Lord] and πυρ ὡσεί [fire, as it were] was added, from the Lord, in French, de la part du Seigneur. It must therefore be admitted that two divine persons are indicated, of whom one rains fire and sulphur from the other. They are distinguished by the mode and place of their action. For the one rains from the other, and so the latter rains through or by means of the former. The one raining appears on the earth or near the earth, while the other sits in heaven. For of the three men who had appeared to Abraham, that one who is also called the Lord and speaks as judge of the world is not read as having entered Sodom with the other two and been received as a guest by Lot. Rather, he seems to have appeared to Lot after he was led out of Sodom, and to be the one whom Lot entreats at verses 19 and 20, and who, as befits the Lord, grants his request at verse 21. Now all this is written with the greatest wisdom, so that there might be in that history a type or specimen, or, as Jude puts it, a hypodeigma [ὑπόδειγμα], or, as Peter says, a prodeigma [πρόδειγμα], of the future judgment of the wicked. For the Son, to whom the Father has given all judgment, will descend from heaven, and he will destroy all the wicked from his Father with eternal fire and sulphur. So in this part too, if the type and the thing foreshadowed, or if you prefer the specimen and that of which it is a specimen, were to correspond to each other as was fitting, two persons had to be introduced, of whom one would execute that judgment upon the other, namely the Son from the Father.

units.la: XLIX. Subiungam & tertium locum ex eodem libro Gen. XI. vbi Dominus, de quo vsurpata fuerant verba singularis numeri, Descendit, videret, dixit, verf.5. & 6. inducitur verf.7. sic se & alias personas diuinas cohortans, Agite, descendamus, & confundamus ibi labium eorum. Ad hunc locum respondet Socinus in hoc eodem fragmento his verbis, Obseruandum est hoc loco, paullò superiùs ab hominibus illis vrbem & turrim construere volentibus dictum fuisse, Venite faciamus lateres, &c. & iterum, venite faciamus nobis ciuitatem, & turrim. Vnde κατὰ μίμησιν quandam, ea verba à Deo, qui simul eos irridere, & eorum inceptum atque conatus irritos se facturum dicere volebat, prolata fuisse plane verisimile est, adeò vt etiamsi secum ipsum, & de seipso tantum loquentem Deum fuisse statuamus, nullam tamen pluralitatem in ipso per numerum il-lum. lum pluralem significari appareat. Primùm, Est-ne mimesis cum alio tempore, ad alias personas, alia verba serió pronunciantur, serióque executioni mandantur, sic, ut nihil sit simile praeter genius sermonis qui utrobique hortatorius est, & verborum numerum pluralem? Illi homines diu ante dixerant, venite faciamus lateres, &c. Venite & faciamus nobis civitatem & turrim, &c. Deus alio tempore ad alios dicit, Venite descendamus, & confundamus labium eorum. Quid est simile nisi illud venite heb. הבה interiectio hortantis Eia, Age, Agite? Fuitne in plurali numero, quo se alij alios, quia revera plures erant, cohortati fuerant, aliquid, aut falsi, aut inepti, quamobrem ficta[?] pluralis numeri imitatione, propterea quod usi essent numero plurali, deridendi essent? Erat-ne tanti apud Deum eiusmodi Mimesis, ut eam qualemcunque mallet, quàm personae suae & aedificationi Ecclesiae convenienter loqui? Loquantur sanè κατὰ μίμησιν aliter quàm oportet, illi, quorum consilium est aut fallere, aut delectare tantùm. Qui seriò aut historias scribunt, aut docent hos veritatis potius rationem habere decet quàm eiusmodi figurae sermonis, quae minùs, & veritati orationis conveniant, & gravitati loquentis.
units.tr: XLIX. I will add a third passage from the same book, Genesis 11, where the Lord, of whom singular verbs had been used, He descended, he saw, he said (vv. 5-6), is introduced in v. 7 exhorting himself and the other divine persons: Come, let us go down and confuse their language there. Socinus replies to this passage in the same fragment, in these words: It should be observed here that a little earlier those men, wishing to build a city and tower, had said, Come, let us make bricks, etc., and again, Come, let us make ourselves a city and a tower. Hence it is entirely probable that God uttered those words by a certain imitation [κατὰ μίμησιν], wishing both to mock them and to say that he would make their undertaking and efforts void, so that even if we suppose God was speaking with himself and only about himself, no plurality in him is shown to be signified by that plural. plural number. First, is there imitation when, at another time and to other persons, other words are seriously spoken and seriously carried out, so that there is nothing alike except the character of the speech, which in both cases is hortatory, and the plural number of the verbs? Those men had said long before, Come, let us make bricks, etc. Come, let us make ourselves a city and a tower, etc. At another time God says to others, Come, let us go down and confuse their language. What is alike here, except that come [הבה], the Hebrew interjection of one urging, Come, Go to, Let us go? Was there anything false or foolish in the plural number by which those men had urged one another, because they really were many, so that they deserved to be mocked for a pretended imitation of the plural, because they had used the plural? Was such an imitation so important to God that he would prefer it, whatever its character, to speaking in a way fitting to his own person and to the building up of the Church? Let those who deliberately aim only to deceive or to amuse speak by imitation otherwise than they ought. Those who write true histories or teach ought rather to take account of truth, and it is fitting that they do not use such figures of speech, which agree less with the truth of the discourse and the dignity of the speaker.

units.la: L. Adde quod iam Deus sese fuerat plurali numero cohortatus, faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram &c, nec tamen κατὰ μίμησιν. Iam se plures esse personas aperte & diserte docuerat dicendo, Ecce Adam factus est sicut unus ex nobis, nec tamen in eius illis verbis ulla fuerat Mimesis. Quod igitur pluralem de se numerum usurpat, id non est ascribendum studio homines illos imitandi, eorumque verba effingendi, deque sese uno sic loquendi quemadmodum illi de se pluribus loquuti fuerant. Quanquam etiamsi aliqua in verbis illis esset Mimesis, ea tamen figura impedire non deberet, quin quàm appositè de se pluralem numerum homines illi usurpauerant, tam etiam appositè & verè Deus de se pluralem usurparet numerum. An enim quia de pluribus pluraliter loquuti fuerant, ut eorum Deus imitaretur sermonem, ei fuit loquendum pluraliter de unica persona singulari? Num tanto studio eos homines imitandi flagrabat Deus, ut suae ipsius singularitatis obliuisceretur? Num ita tenebatur studio inanem quandam syllabarum similitudinem aucupandi, ut propterea sensum negligeret, pluraliterque efferret quod nollet accipi pluraliter? Num voluit lectores in eo plurali expendendo operam suam inutiliter collocare, ut post multam disquisitionem nihil invenirent, nisi pluralem illum esse inanem & vacuum sensu, studio imitandi pluralem illum numerum quo turris Babel extructores usi fuerant, à Deo (adeò impensè huiusmodi imitatione delectabatur) sine ullo alio usu effictum? Captatne Deus sine ullo fructu tales leviculas figuras, quibus delectari solent homines irrisores? Decetne nos ita versari licenter in verbis ipsius Dei interpretandis, ac si alicuius hominis essent? Quanquam nescio an eiusmodi Mimesis, qualis ista foret, cadere posset in auctorem prudentem & gravem.
units.tr: L. Add that God had already exhorted himself in the plural, Let us make man in our image, etc., and yet not by imitation [κατὰ μίμησιν]. He had already taught openly and plainly that there were several persons, saying, Behold, Adam has become as one of us, and yet there was no imitation in those words. Therefore, when he uses the plural of himself, this is not to be ascribed to a desire to imitate those men and to copy their words, and to speak of himself as one in the way they had spoken of themselves as many. Even if there were some imitation in those words, that figure ought not to prevent God from using the plural of himself just as appositely and truly as those men had used it of themselves. For is God to speak in the plural of a single singular person merely because they had spoken in the plural of many, so that he might imitate their speech? Did God burn with such zeal to imitate those men that he forgot his own singularity? Was he so bent on catching an empty likeness of syllables that he neglected the sense and uttered in the plural what he did not wish to be taken in the plural? Did he wish readers to waste their labour in weighing that plural, so that after long inquiry they would find nothing except that the plural was empty and void of meaning, formed by God without any other use, merely to imitate the plural number by which the builders of the tower of Babel had spoken (so greatly did he delight in such imitation)? Does God pursue such trivial figures without any profit, such as men who mock others are wont to enjoy? Is it fitting for us to handle the words of God himself so freely in interpreting them, as if they were the words of some man? Yet I do not know whether such an imitation, of the kind this would be, could fall upon a prudent and grave author.

units.la: LI. Præter superiorem responsionem huius loci propriam duas alias adhibet veluti subsidiarias Socinus, quas locis Gen. 1, 16. & 3. 22. jam aptaverat nosque à V Volkelio, & Schlichtingio propositas iam refutavimus. Earum responsionum prima est, Deum sese & Angelos suos compellare verbis illis, Venite descendamus, & confundamus linguam eorum. Id quod, inquit, hic tantò rectiùs dici potest, quantò in confundenda lingua eorum hominum verisimilius est, Deum angelorum opera usum fuisse, quàm in homine condendo, cum nulla hic prorsus suspicio sacrilegii futura sit, si eius operis, linguam scilicet hominum confundendi, angelos participes faciamus, per quos multò praestantiora opera Deum sæpius patrasse compertum est. Non repetam argumenta, quibus hoc commentum jam refutavi ad Arg. xxxvii. § 27.28.29.30.46.47.48. 49.50.51. Retorquebo illud ipsum quod Socinus hoc loco urget. Quid enim est hoc loco confundere linguam? Nonne in instanti maternnam linguam ex animo delere, & novam in illius loco creare? Tantumne igitur possunt in hominum mentes Angeli? Num Scriptura tale quiddam illis alicubi tribuit?
units.tr: LI. Besides the foregoing reply to this passage, Socinus brings forward two other replies as it were in support, which he had already applied to Genesis 1:26 and 3:22, and which we have already refuted when proposed by Volkelius and Schlichting. The first of these replies is that God addresses his angels with those words, Come, let us go down and confuse their language. He says: This can be said here all the more correctly, since it is more probable that God used the work of angels in confusing the language of those men than in making man, since there will be no suspicion of sacrilege here if we make the angels partakers in this work, that is, of confusing the language of men, through whom it is known God has very often accomplished far greater works. I shall not repeat the arguments by which I have already refuted this invention in the Argument xxxvii, §§ 27, 28, 29, 30, 46-51. I shall turn back upon Socinus the very point he presses here. For what does it mean to confuse a language here? Is it not to wipe out in an instant a mother tongue from the mind and create a new one in its place? Can angels then have such power over human minds? Does Scripture attribute any such thing to them anywhere?

units.la: LII. Certè hoc loco altum est de Angelis silentium. Qui loquitur, qui exequitur Dominus seu, ut vulgò pronunciant, Iehoua appellatur, quod nomen ei non est cum angelis commune. Quos autem secum cohortatur, eos, veluti socios & sibi naturâ æquales, compellat, ac tanquam secum eiusdem descen-sus par-ticipes, & confusionis linguarum autores, id quod est eos sibi æquare. Quorsum igitur id pertineret si angelos alloqueretur, nisi ut insinuaret, secum angelos divisum habere mundi imperium, esseque suos in genere humano creando & gubernando socios, sibi propterea in cultu ab hominibus exhibendo adiungene[?] dos? Fac ergo Deum angelorum opera ad confundendam linguam hominum & novas linguas in eorum animis creandas usum fuisse. usus ne est eorum opera tanquam seruorum suorum, an tanquam sociorum? tanquam seruorum, opinor. Cur igitur non dixit potius in imperativo, Agite, descendite, confundite linguam eorum? Cur se non tanquam Dominum, sed tanquam socium illis adjunxit? Cur haec linguae confusio, &, quae ea ratione facta est, hominum dispersio in sequentibus versibus soli Domino tribuitur, & quidem ter, adhibitis verbis singularis numeri, neque ei in eo opere adjunguntur angeli? Cur dixit Descendamus, quasi eodem sensu de suo & eorum quos secum alloquebatur descensu verbum illud usurparetur, cum certum sit longè alio sensu Deum, alio angelos dici descendere? Ille enim duntaxat figuratè, hi verò proprie descendere dicuntur. Cur denique dixit, & confundamus, quasi ipse per se immediatè una cum illis personis, quas alloquebatur, rem illam mandaturus esset executioni? Nam si usus est opera seu ministerio angelorum, partes eius fuerunt imperare, angelorum exequi.
units.tr: LII. Certainly Scripture is deeply silent about angels in this place. The one who speaks and carries out the work is called the Lord, or, as it is commonly pronounced, Jehovah, a name which is not common to him with the angels. But those whom he exhorts along with himself, he addresses as associates and as equal to himself by nature, and as partakers in the same descent and authors of the confusion of tongues. This is to make them equal to himself. What then would this have to do with it, if he were addressing angels, unless to suggest that he has the rule of the world divided with them, and that they are his partners in creating and governing the human race, and therefore to be joined with him in the worship to be offered by men? Suppose then God used the work of angels to confuse the language of men and to create new languages in their minds. Did he use their work as of his servants, or as of his associates? As of his servants, I suppose. Why then did he not rather say in the imperative, Go down, confuse their language? Why did he join himself to them not as Lord, but as an associate? Why is this confusion of language, and the scattering of men that followed from it, in the following verses attributed to the Lord alone, and indeed three times, with verbs of the singular number, and no angels joined with him in the work? Why did he say Let us go down, as if the verb were used in the same sense of his own descent and of the descent of those whom he addressed, when it is certain that God is said to descend in a quite different sense from angels? For he is said to descend only figuratively, but they are said to descend properly. Finally, why did he say and let us confuse, as if he himself were to carry out the matter immediately, together with those persons whom he addressed? For if he used the work or ministry of angels, their part would have been to be commanded, and to carry out.

units.la: LIII. Alteram responsionem Socinus his paucis verbis proponit. Quod verò, inquit, de numero plurali singularis loco usurpato diximus, hic plausibilius multò videri potest, cum Deus hoc loco manifestè, tanquam imperium & auctoritatem habens, loquatur. Hoc quoque ipsum retorqueo. Cum enim homines illi dicerent, quisque ad proximum suum, venite faciamus lateres &c, venite faciamus civitatem &c, num loquebantur tanquam imperium & auctoritatem habentes alij in alios? Contrà est potius. Loquebantur tanquàm socij ad socios. Cum igitur Deus dicit similiter, Venite descendamus, confundamus, non loquitur tanquam imperium & auctoritatem habens in eos quos secum alloquitur, sed contrà potius, tanquam qui unus sit de eorum numero, & qui velit cum illis manum operi illi admouere, immò quasi non minùs ab illis quàm ab ipso pendeat operis illius effectio, quasique non possit ab ipso fieri, nisi illis consentientibus ac concurrentibus. itaque non minus se, sibi sine dubio æqualem, quàm eos, verbis illis compellat & cohortatur, ac propterea nullam præ se ferunt verba illa auctoritatem, nullum imperium. Ex quo intelligitur, nec Angelos compellari, nec Deum de se ipso numerum pluralem usurpare honoris causa, aut auctoritatis ostendendae gratia.
units.tr: LIII. Socinus sets out the second reply in these few words: What we have said about the plural number used in place of the singular, may seem much more plausible here, since God here speaks manifestly as one having command and authority. I turn this very point back as well. For when those men said, each to his neighbour, Come, let us make bricks, etc., Come, let us make a city, etc., did they speak as having command and authority over one another? On the contrary, rather. They spoke as associates to associates. Therefore, when God similarly says, Come, let us go down, let us confuse, he does not speak as one having command and authority over those whom he addresses with himself. Rather, on the contrary, he speaks as one who is himself one of their number, and who wishes to put his hand to that work with them, and as if the completion of that work depended no less on them than on himself, as if it could not be done by him unless they consented and concurred. So he addresses and exhorts himself, no less than them, in those words, which without doubt are equal to himself; and therefore those words show no authority and no command. From this it is understood that neither are angels addressed, nor does God use the plural of himself for the sake of honour or to show authority.

units.la: LIV. Addam & quartum locum ex Pf. xcv. Vf.[?] 7. Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra, &c. Nonne hic duae apparent personae, vna quae loquitur, altera quae pronomine Eius significatur? Cur enim non dicit qui loquitur vocem meam, sed, vocem eius, nisi vt se ab eo cuius vocem commendat significet personam esse distinctam? Iam autem negari non potest, quin vtraque illa persona sit diuina, sit Deus. Illa quidem cuius vox commendatur: refertur enim pronomen Eius ad eum de quo agebatur, cuiusque nomen exprimitur in verbis antecedentibus. Is autem appellatur Dominus & Deus, & mare, & aridam, & homines fecisse affirmatur. Illa etiam quae loquens & Dei vocem commendans inducitur: Id enim ipsa testatur verbis sequentibus. Sicut in irritatione secundum diem tentationis in deserto, vbi tentauerunt me patres vestri: probauerunt & viderunt opera mea. Quadraginta annis offensus fui generatione illa, & dixi semper hi errant corde & isti non cognouerunt vias meas: & iurani in ira mea, Si introibunt in requiem meam. Sunt igitur saltem duae personae diuinae, quae in deserto suas partes egerunt. vna apparuit Mosi in monte Sinai, è cuius cacumine & Mosem & populum Israeliticum allocuta est certo tempore. Altera fuit cum Mose & populo Israelitico quandiu peregrinati sunt in deserto. Haec duae personae ita distinguntur, vt haec dicatur Angelus illius, sed Angelus in quo esset nomen Domini, quique esset praeditus summa auctoritate, vt patet ex cap. 23. Exod. Vf.[?] 20. 21. vt autem haec persona fuit Angelus Domini qui loquebatur è monte, sic Dominus qui è monte loquebatur erat Angelus Domini, vt patet ex Exod. 3.
units.tr: LIV. I will add a fourth passage, from Ps. xcv. (vers. 7): Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, etc. Do not two persons appear here, one who speaks and another signified by the pronoun his? For why does the speaker not say my voice but his voice, unless to show that he is a person distinct from the one whose voice he commends? Now it cannot be denied that each of these persons is divine, is God. The one whose voice is commended is certainly God: the pronoun his refers to him who was being discussed, whose name is expressed in the preceding words. He is called Lord and God, and is said to have made the sea, the dry land, and men. The other is the one introduced as speaking and commending God's voice, as he himself testifies in the following words: As in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the desert, where your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works. For forty years I was grieved with that generation, and said, They always err in heart, and they have not known my ways; so I swore in my anger, They shall not enter into my rest. There are therefore at least two divine persons who played their parts in the desert. One appeared to Moses on Mount Sinai, and from its summit addressed both Moses and the Israelite people at a set time. The other was with Moses and the Israelite people for as long as they wandered in the desert. These two persons are so distinguished that the one is called his Angel, yet an Angel in whom was the name of the Lord and who was endowed with supreme authority, as is plain from Exod. 23. 20, 21. And just as this person was the Angel of the Lord who spoke from the mountain, so the Lord who spoke from the mountain was the Angel of the Lord, as is plain from Exod. 3.

units.la: 2. Act. 7. 38. &c. Erant igitur tres personae. vna erat tantum Dominus ac mittens. Altera erat ita Dominus, vt tamen Angelus diceretur illius Domini. Tertia erat etiam ipsa & Dominus, & Angelus Domini illius qui loquebatur è Monte. Prima miserat secundam, secunda tertiam. Respondebant tres illae personae tribus personis diuinis in Euangelio reuelatis. Pater non mittitur sed mittit. Filius missus à Patre loquutus est certo tempore è cacumine montis Sion, foedusque Euangelicum promulgauit. Spiritus Sanctus missus à Filio, in medio fidelium est quandiu peregrinantur in hoc mundi deserto, eiusque partes sunt efficere, vt voci Filij auscultemus. itaque auctor Ep. ad Heb. obseruauit eum qui dicit, Hodie si vocem eius audieritis &c, esse Spiritum Sanctum.
units.tr: 2. Acts 7. 38, etc. There were therefore three persons. One was only the Lord and the sender. The second was the Lord in such a way that he was nevertheless called the Angel of that Lord. The third was himself both the Lord and the Angel of the Lord who spoke from the mountain. The first had sent the second, the second the third. These three persons correspond to the three divine persons revealed in the Gospel. The Father is not sent but sends. The Son, sent by the Father, spoke at a set time from the summit of Mount Sion and promulgated the gospel covenant. The Holy Spirit, sent by the Son, is in the midst of believers as long as they journey in this desert of the world, and his part is to bring it about that we listen to the voice of the Son. Thus the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews observed that the one who says, Today, if you hear his voice, etc., is the Holy Spirit.

units.la: LV. Hæ eædem tres personæ divinæ inducuntur loquentes Ps.
units.tr: LV. These same three divine persons are introduced as speaking in Ps.

units.la: 2. Pater ✠[?].6. Et ego vnxi regem meum super Sion montem sanctitatis meæ. Filius ✠[?]1.7. 8.9. Narrabo Decretum. Dominus dixit ad me, Filius meus es tu, hodie genui te. Spiritus Sanctus ✠[?]1.10.11.12. Nunc ergo Reges, &c. Horum trium testium divinis testimonijs & verbis, non autem armis carnalibus, patefactum est quàm stulti atque irriti fuerint hostium Domini nostri Iesu Christi, cum eum condemnarunt & morte affecerunt conatus, quàm vana consilia. Solo Patris, Filij, & Spiritus Sancti verbo, hostes Dei & Christi oppugnantur efficaciter, & debellantur. itaque nihil aliud eis eo psalmo opponitur.
units.tr: 2. The Father: Ps. 2.6. And I have set my king upon my holy hill of Sion. The Son: Ps. 2.7–9. I will declare the decree: the Lord has said to me, You are my son; this day have I begotten you. The Holy Spirit: Ps. 2.10–12. Now therefore, O kings, etc. By the divine testimonies and words of these three witnesses, not by carnal arms, it has been shown how foolish and futile were the enemies of our Lord Jesus Christ when they plotted to condemn him and put him to death, how vain their counsels were. By the word of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit alone the enemies of God and of Christ are effectively assailed and defeated. Therefore nothing else is set against them in that psalm.

units.la: LVI. Possem etiam addere hoc loco verba Domini apud Esai. 6. 8.: Quis ibit nobis, hoc est, mihi & Patri meo: sunt enim verba Filij, ut probatum est à nobis Disp. 1. necnon refellere ineptam Socini conjecturam, qui in hoc ipso fragmento affirmat, Deum in hoc loco sine dubio dixisse Mi jelech lanu pro Mi jelech lo mimmennu. Hoc est, Quis ibit nobis, pro quis ibit ex nobis. Aitque in ea re miram esse elegantiam, deque suo ilto[?] invento, tam scilicet egregio, modesta[?] quadam ratione gloriatur. Rationem huius suæ affirmationis & verborum illorum contortionis nullam affert. Putauit, opinor, sibi sine ratione, non minus quàm olim Pythagoræ, credi debere. Sed neque necesse est omnia ad examen revocare, & nolo istam additionem longiorem facere.
units.tr: LVI. I could also add here the words of the Lord in Isa. 6. 8: Who will go for us? that is, for me and my Father, for these are the words of the Son, as we have proved in our first Disputation. I could also refute the foolish conjecture of Socinus, who in this very passage asserts that God in this place undoubtedly said Mi jelech lanu [מִי יֵלֵךְ לָנוּ] for Mi jelech lo mimmennu [מִי יֵלֵךְ לוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ]; that is, Who will go for us, for who will go from among us. He says that in this matter there is a wonderful elegance, and with a certain modest air he boasts of his own discovery, so remarkable is it. He offers no reason for this assertion or for his twisting of those words. He thought, I suppose, that he ought to be believed without reason, no less than Pythagoras once was. But it is neither necessary to subject everything to examination, nor do I wish to make this addition longer.

units.la: LVII. Ut igitur ad plurale Elohim redeam, Si in utriusque Testamenti Scriptura plures personæ divinæ apparent, quid est quamobrem non existimemus, ob eam pluralitatem plurale illud nomen impositum Deo fuisse? Cur enim aliam fingamus pluralitatem, cum hæc sola sit & nominis illius numero, & significationi, & revelationi divinæ consentanea? Sic abundè confirmatum nobis videtur Argumentum nostrum ex numero plurali nominis illius petitum. Ne quis tamen scrupulus hæreat in animo lectoris, Distingui velim diligenter inter causam impositionis nominis & eius impositi usum. Quæ distinctio firmari potest multis exemplis. Nomina Hebræa membrorum, quæ sunt in corpore humano bina, loco pluralis numeri dualem habent. Cur,nisi quia in unoquoque homine non sunt eiusmodi membra plura duobus? Duæ tantum sunt aures, duo oculi, duæ manus, duo pedes &c. utuntur tamen istis dualibus nonnunquam Hebræi, tanquam pluralibus, ad plures oculos, manus, pedes &c. significandos. Ratio cur expanso seu cœlo nomen duale schamaÿm impositum fuit est cœlorum, vt ita loquar, dualitas: sunt enim duo cœli; vnum inferius supra quod sunt aquæ, alterum superius in quo sunt luminaria, tamen vsurpatur illud duale de vno cœlo, modo de hoc infimo in quo volant aues, qui propterea cœli volucres appellantur, modo de superiore in quo sunt sol & luna & stellæ, modo etiam de supremo illo quod Apostolus tertium vocat. Similiter dualis numeri est nomen hebræum Maÿm. cur? Nonne propter duas aquas, quarum aliæ sunt supra, aliæ infra expansum? Attamen id nomen sæpenumero de vnis aquis vsurpatur, modo de ijs solis quæ sunt supra expansum, modo de ijs solis quæ sunt infra expansum, vt ex Gen. 1.N. 6. & 7. & alijs plurimis locis liquere potest. Idem accidit nomini Elohim, quod plurali numero ob pluralem numerum personarum diuinarum, vt jam probauimus, impositum est Deo. Id enim interdum de vnica persona diuina, modo de Patre, modo de Filio, modo, sed rarius, de Spiritu sancto vsurpatur, manente interim vera ratione ob quam, cum plurale esset, ad Deum significandum destinatum, atque institutum, & selectum est. Reliqua quæ habentur in isto Socini fragmento, vel jam satis refutata videntur, vel etiam minus digna refutatione.
units.tr: LVII. To return, then, to the plural Elohim: if in the Scripture of both Testaments several divine persons appear, why should we not judge that this plural name was given to God on account of that plurality? For why should we invent some other plurality, when this alone agrees both with the number of that name, its meaning, and the divine revelation? Thus our argument drawn from the plural number of that name seems to us sufficiently confirmed. Yet lest any scruple stick in the reader's mind, I would have him carefully distinguish between the reason for imposing a name and the use of the name once imposed. This distinction can be confirmed by many examples. Hebrew names of the members of the human body that come in pairs have a dual form in place of the plural. Why? Surely because in each person there are not more than two such members. There are only two ears, two eyes, two hands, two feet, and so on. Yet the Hebrews sometimes use these duals as plurals, to signify more eyes, hands, feet, and so on. The reason why the dual name shamayim [שָׁמַיִם] was given to the expanse, or heaven, is the duality of the heavens, so to speak: for there are two heavens, one lower, above which are the waters, and the other higher, in which are the luminaries. Nevertheless that dual is used of one heaven: sometimes of the lowest, in which the birds fly, which for this reason are called the birds of heaven; sometimes of the higher, in which are the sun, moon, and stars; sometimes also of that highest heaven which the Apostle calls the third. Similarly the Hebrew name mayim [מַיִם] is dual. Why? Is it not on account of the two waters, some of which are above the expanse and some below? Yet that name is very often used of one kind of water: sometimes only of those above the expanse, sometimes only of those below it, as can be seen from Gen. 1. 6 and 7 and from very many other places. The same happens with the name Elohim, which was given to God in the plural number on account of the plural number of the divine persons, as we have already proved. For it is sometimes used of a single divine person: sometimes of the Father, sometimes of the Son, sometimes, though more rarely, of the Holy Spirit. Meanwhile the true reason remains for which, though it is plural, it was appointed, set apart, and chosen to signify God. The remaining points in this fragment of Socinus seem either already sufficiently refuted or hardly worth refuting.
